Its Ramsar link is as an International Organization Partner (IOP), alongside BirdLife International, IUCN, IWMI, WWF and Wetlands International itself.

Option (d), neither, is wrong because statement 2 correctly describes the work of Wetlands International. The organization develops and mobilizes knowledge, works at field level, and advocates for better policies on the basis of practical experience. Its thematic areas include coastal resilience, peatlands, water and sanitation, and waterbird conservation. It also works on the African-Eurasian Waterbird Agreement and the Asian Waterbird Census, which has run since 1987.
related: Ramsar Convention was signed in 1971 at Ramsar, Iran, and came into force in 1975.
World Wetlands Day is observed on 2 February each year.
Chilika Lake and Keoladeo National Park were India's first Ramsar sites, in 1981.
The Montreux Record lists Ramsar sites with adverse ecological change; Keoladeo and Loktak are the Indian entries.
Wetlands International was formed in 1995 and is headquartered in Wageningen, Netherlands.
The Ramsar Secretariat is in Gland, Switzerland, and is hosted by IUCN.
India's Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 replaced the 2010 rules.
Sundarbans, declared a Ramsar site in 2019, is India's largest Ramsar site.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Wetlands International is an independent non-profit NGO, not an intergovernmental organization formed by Ramsar signatories. It was created in 1995 by merging three wetland bodies: IWRB (founded 1954), the Asian Wetland Bureau and Wetlands for the Americas. Ramsar is a separate treaty adopted in 1971 and in force from 1975, and its Secretariat is in Gland, Switzerland. Wetlands International is a formal partner of Ramsar, which is a different relationship from having been founded by it. Its funding comes from governments, foundations and other donors, but its governance is that of an NGO.

2 — Correct: This matches the organization's stated mission. It works through a network of experts and offices on the ground, gathers and shares knowledge, and uses practical project experience to influence policy and practice. Its headquarters are in Wageningen, Netherlands. Its work includes the Asian Waterbird Census, Waterbird Population Estimates, peatland and mangrove restoration, and the Partners for Resilience programme. It operates in over 100 countries through offices and partners. Its slogan is to inspire and mobilise society to safeguard and restore wetlands for people and nature.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. Wetlands International is an independent, non-profit, non-governmental organization, not an intergovernmental body set up by Ramsar signatories. It works at field level, develops and mobilizes knowledge, and uses practical experience to advocate for better policies.
topic_notes: Wetlands are areas of marsh, fen, peatland or water, natural or artificial, permanent or temporary, with static or flowing water that is fresh, brackish or salt. They include marine water up to 6 m deep at low tide. The Ramsar Convention is the key treaty. It was adopted on 2 February 1971 at Ramsar, Iran, and came into force in 1975. World Wetlands Day is 2 February. India joined Ramsar in 1982. India now has over 80 Ramsar sites, including 75 declared by 2022 (Independence 75 target). The first Indian sites in 1981 were Chilika Lake (Odisha) and Keoladeo National Park (Rajasthan). Sundarbans was added in 2019 and is the largest Indian Ramsar site by area. The Montreux Record lists sites with adverse ecological change. Indian sites on it are Keoladeo and Loktak (Manipur). Loktak has the world's only floating national park, Keibul Lamjao. Chilika was removed from the Record in 2002. India regulates wetlands through the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017, which replaced the 2010 rules. The National Wetland Conservation Programme and the National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems (NPCA) are the main schemes. Wetlands International is an NGO that runs the Asian Waterbird Census and publishes Waterbird Population Estimates. Other organizations that UPSC may ask about are IUCN (founded 1948, Gland), which publishes the Red List, WWF, BirdLife International (the IBA programme) and the Bombay Natural History Society (the IBA partner in India). Other international instruments include CITES (1973), CMS or Bonn Convention (1979), CBD (1992, Rio) and the World Heritage Convention (1972).

ocr: With reference to a grouping of countries known as_ BRICS, consider the following statements : 1. The First Summit of BRICS was held in Rio de Janeiro in 2009. 2. South Africa was the last to join the BRICS grouping. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa) 1 only {b) 2 only fc} Both 1 and 2 fd) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Economy
detail: BRICS began as 'BRIC', a term coined by Jim O'Neill of Goldman Sachs in 2001. The four countries (Brazil, Russia, India, China) began meeting as a group in 2006 on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. The first formal leaders' summit was held at Yekaterinburg, Russia, on 16 June 2009. South Africa was invited in December 2010 and attended the Sanya (China) summit in April 2011, which turned BRIC into BRICS. Rio de Janeiro is a distractor: Brazil hosted the 2nd summit in Brasilia (2010) and the 6th in Fortaleza and Brasilia (2014), and Rio hosted the 2025 summit. Elimination logic: Statement 1 gives the wrong city and is false, so options (a) and (c) go. Statement 2 was true in 2014, because no country had joined after South Africa, so (d) goes and (b) remains. Later developments matter for current affairs: from 1 January 2024 Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE joined, and Indonesia joined in January 2025. Saudi Arabia's status remains ambiguous. So today Statement 2 would no longer hold.
explanations: (a) 1 only is wrong because Statement 1 names the wrong venue and year context. The first summit was in Yekaterinburg, Russia.
(b) 2 only is correct because Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 was true in 2014, since South Africa was the last to join.
(c) Both 1 and 2 is wrong because Statement 1 is false.
(d) Neither 1 nor 2 is wrong because Statement 2 was correct as South Africa was the last member admitted, in 2010.
keyfact: First BRIC summit: Yekaterinburg, Russia, 2009; South Africa joined in 2010 and was the last original member, making BRIC into BRICS.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: this would mean the first summit was in Rio de Janeiro in 2009. In fact the 2009 summit was in Yekaterinburg, Russia. Rio de Janeiro hosted the BRICS summit in July 2025, under Brazil's chairship. Brazil's earlier hosting was Brasilia (2010), Fortaleza and Brasilia (2014), and Brasilia (2019, virtual-era scheduling aside, held in person in November 2019). Do not confuse the host cities.

Option (b), 2 only: this is the official answer. South Africa's admission in December 2010 completed the original five-member BRICS. It was formalised at the Sanya summit of April 2011. South Africa has the smallest economy of the five but represents Africa. It hosted summits in Durban (2013), Johannesburg (2018) and Johannesburg (2023). The 2023 summit agreed to expand the group.

Option (c), Both 1 and 2: this would require both the Rio 2009 claim and the South Africa claim to be true. Since the first summit was in Yekaterinburg, this is false. Remember the sequence: Yekaterinburg 2009, Brasilia 2010, Sanya 2011 (South Africa's first), New Delhi 2012, Durban 2013. This sequence is a frequent exam item.

Option (d), Neither 1 nor 2: this would require South Africa not to be the last entrant. In 2014 it was the last, so this is wrong. It would become more plausible today because of the 2024 and 2025 expansion, which added Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the UAE and Indonesia. The question is dated, so use the 2014 facts.
related: The term BRIC was coined by Jim O'Neill of Goldman Sachs in 2001.
The first BRIC summit was at Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009.
South Africa joined in 2010 and first attended the Sanya summit in 2011.
The New Development Bank is headquartered in Shanghai and began in 2015.
The Contingent Reserve Arrangement has an initial size of US$100 billion.
Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE became BRICS members on 1 January 2024.
India hosted BRICS summits in 2012 (New Delhi), 2016 (Goa) and 2021 (virtual).
K.V. Kamath was the first president of the New Development Bank.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The first BRIC summit was held in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009, not in Rio de Janeiro. The group's first leaders' summit took place on 16 June 2009 with Brazil, Russia, India and China attending. Dmitry Medvedev hosted it. Earlier, foreign ministers had met in 2006 on the sidelines of the UNGA in New York. The summit discussed reform of the global financial architecture after the 2008 crisis, and the group sought a larger voice in the IMF and World Bank. Brazil's first hosted summit was in Brasilia in 2010. Rio de Janeiro hosted the 2025 summit, not the first.

2 — Correct (as of 2014): South Africa joined in December 2010 and was the last of the original five. China invited South Africa, and its first summit as a member was Sanya, China, in April 2011. The acronym changed from BRIC to BRICS with its entry. It is the only African founding member of the grouping. Later expansion added Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE in January 2024, and Indonesia in 2025. So the statement is correct only for the time of the 2014 paper.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. The First BRIC Summit was held in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in June 2009, not in Rio de Janeiro, so Statement 1 is wrong. South Africa joined in December 2010 and was the last of the original five members, so Statement 2 was correct for the time of the 2014 paper.
topic_notes: BRICS is an informal grouping of major emerging economies, with no charter or permanent secretariat. The term BRIC was coined in 2001 by Jim O'Neill of Goldman Sachs. Foreign ministers first met in 2006, and the first leaders' summit was held at Yekaterinburg in June 2009. South Africa joined in 2010, making it BRICS. Summit sequence: 2009 Yekaterinburg, 2010 Brasilia, 2011 Sanya, 2012 New Delhi (4th), 2013 Durban (5th), 2014 Fortaleza (6th), 2015 Ufa, 2016 Goa (8th), 2017 Xiamen, 2018 Johannesburg, 2019 Brasilia, 2020 Russia (virtual), 2021 India (virtual), 2022 China (virtual), 2023 Johannesburg (15th), 2024 Kazan, 2025 Rio de Janeiro. Institutions: the New Development Bank (NDB), agreed at Durban 2013 and signed at Fortaleza 2014, is headquartered in Shanghai and began operating in 2015. Its first president was K.V. Kamath of India. The Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA) is a US$100 billion pool to help members facing balance-of-payments pressure. Expansion: at the 2023 Johannesburg summit, Argentina, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE were invited. Argentina declined. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE joined on 1 January 2024. Indonesia joined in January 2025. Saudi Arabia has not formally confirmed. Several other countries have partner status. BRICS accounts for roughly 40 percent of world population and a large share of global GDP. India's chairship was in 2016 and 2021, with the 2016 theme of 'Building Responsive, Inclusive and Collective Solutions'. Other angles UPSC may ask include NDB membership, CRA, the group's stance on reform of the UNSC, IMF and WTO, and de-dollarisation debates.

ocr: Consider the following diseases : 1. Diphtheria 2, Chickenpox 3. Smallpox Which of the above diseases has/have been eradicated in India? fa) 1 and 2 only {b) 3 only fc) 1, 2 and 3 (a) None
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Eradication means permanent reduction of a disease's worldwide incidence to zero through deliberate efforts, so that interventions are no longer needed. Only two diseases have been eradicated globally: smallpox (human disease, declared by the WHO in May 1980 after the World Health Assembly's certification in December 1979) and rinderpest (cattle disease, declared in 2011). India's last natural smallpox case was in May 1975 (Assam, Bibi Jan Bibi, Variola major). India was declared smallpox-free in April 1977 after two years without cases. The last natural case worldwide was Ali Maow Maalin in Somalia in 1977 (Variola minor). Smallpox was suited to eradication because it has no animal reservoir, no carrier state, a visible rash, and a stable, effective vaccine (Edward Jenner, 1796). The strategy was surveillance and ring vaccination. Diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae) is a bacterial disease, covered by the DPT/pentavalent vaccine under the Universal Immunization Programme, and cases still occur in India. Chickenpox (varicella-zoster virus) remains common, and its vaccine is not in the national schedule. Elimination logic: only one disease is eradicated, so (b) is correct. (a), (c) and (d) are wrong.
explanations: Wrong: it includes diphtheria and chickenpox, neither of which is eradicated, and it leaves out smallpox, which is.
Correct: only smallpox has been eradicated in India (1977), as part of global eradication certified in 1980.
Wrong: diphtheria and chickenpox continue to occur in India, so not all three are eradicated.
Wrong: smallpox has been eradicated, so 'None' cannot be right.
keyfact: Smallpox is the only human disease eradicated (India 1977, world 1980); polio is eliminated in India (2014), not eradicated.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only: Diphtheria and chickenpox are both still present in India. Diphtheria is a bacterial throat disease, controlled with the DPT/pentavalent vaccine. Chickenpox is a viral disease (varicella-zoster) that is common, especially in children, and has a vaccine that is not in the national schedule. Neither is classed as eradicated or even eliminated in India, so this option is wrong.

3 only: Smallpox alone has been eradicated. It was caused by the Variola virus and eradicated through a WHO campaign (1967-80) using surveillance and ring vaccination. India was declared free in 1977 and the world in 1980. Rinderpest, a cattle disease, was declared eradicated in 2011 as the second disease ever eradicated. Polio-free certification for India (South-East Asia Region) came in 2014, but polio is eliminated regionally, not eradicated globally.

1, 2 and 3: This would require all three diseases to be gone from India. Only smallpox is. Diphtheria and chickenpox are vaccine-preventable diseases that still cause cases. The option is therefore wrong, even though smallpox is correctly included in it.

None: This would mean that no disease among the three has been eradicated. That is wrong because smallpox was eradicated in India in 1977 and worldwide in 1980. Eradication differs from elimination (zero cases in a region, as with India's polio-free status in 2014 and maternal and neonatal tetanus elimination in 2015) and from control.
related: Smallpox is the first human disease to be eradicated (WHO, 1980).
Rinderpest, a cattle disease, is the second disease eradicated (2011).
India's last smallpox case was in 1975; the country was declared free in 1977.
India was certified polio-free by WHO in March 2014, which is regional elimination, not global eradication.
India's last wild polio case was in West Bengal in January 2011.
Edward Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine in 1796 using cowpox.
Maternal and neonatal tetanus was eliminated in India in 2015.
Smallpox is caused by the Variola virus; chickenpox by the varicella-zoster virus.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Diphtheria has not been eradicated in India; cases and outbreaks still occur. Diphtheria is a bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, which produces a toxin that forms a grey pseudomembrane in the throat and can cause airway obstruction and myocarditis. It spreads by respiratory droplets. Prevention is by the DPT vaccine, now part of the pentavalent vaccine, with boosters (DPT and Td) under the Universal Immunization Programme. Treatment is with diphtheria antitoxin and antibiotics. India has among the highest numbers of reported cases worldwide, and outbreaks continue in under-immunised pockets.

2 — Incorrect: Chickenpox is still prevalent in India and has not been eradicated. It is caused by the varicella-zoster virus (a herpesvirus), which spreads through the air and by contact, producing itchy vesicular rashes. After recovery the virus stays latent and can reactivate later as shingles (herpes zoster). A live attenuated vaccine (the Oka strain) exists. It is not part of India's universal schedule but is recommended by the Indian Academy of Pediatrics. Chickenpox is often mistaken for smallpox, but smallpox is caused by Variola virus, an orthopoxvirus, and was far deadlier.

3 — Correct: Smallpox was eradicated in India (declared 1977) and globally (WHO, 1980). It was caused by the Variola virus (Variola major and minor) and was highly fatal, with about 30% mortality in Variola major. Edward Jenner developed the vaccine in 1796 using cowpox. The WHO Intensified Smallpox Eradication Programme began in 1967, led by D.A. Henderson. India's last case was in 1975, and the last natural case worldwide was in Somalia in 1977. Stocks of the virus remain only in two WHO-approved labs, in the US (CDC) and Russia (VECTOR).
summary: The answer is (b) 3 only. Smallpox is the only one of the three diseases eradicated; India was declared smallpox-free in 1977 and the WHO certified global eradication in 1980. Diphtheria and chickenpox still circulate in India and are controlled only by vaccination.
topic_notes: Disease control terms: control means reducing incidence; elimination means zero cases in a defined region (for example, polio-free South-East Asia in 2014, and maternal and neonatal tetanus elimination in India in 2015); eradication means permanent global zero (smallpox 1980, rinderpest 2011). Smallpox: caused by the Variola virus; Jenner's vaccine in 1796; WHO's Intensified Eradication Programme from 1967; the last Indian case was in 1975 (Assam); India was certified free in 1977; the last natural case worldwide was in Somalia in 1977; the last cases ever were a lab-linked outbreak in Birmingham in 1978. The WHO declared global eradication in 1980. India's polio campaign: the Pulse Polio Programme began in 1995; the last wild poliovirus case was in January 2011 in West Bengal; WHO certified India polio-free in March 2014. Wild poliovirus types 2 and 3 are eradicated globally; type 1 persists in Afghanistan and Pakistan. Guinea worm (dracunculiasis) is close to eradication. Yaws was eliminated from India in 2016. Targets: measles and rubella elimination by 2026 in India; leprosy eliminated as a public health problem in 2005 (below 1 per 10,000); kala-azar elimination target below 1 per 10,000 at block level; malaria elimination targeted by 2030. The Universal Immunization Programme (1985) covers vaccines against diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, polio, measles, hepatitis B, TB (BCG), rotavirus, pneumococcal (PCV), Hib and others. Mission Indradhanush (2014) aims to raise immunisation coverage. Chickenpox, HIV and dengue have no eradication status. Diphtheria's causative agent is a bacterium, while smallpox and chickenpox are viral diseases.

ocr: Which of the following phenomena might have influenced the evolution of organisms? 1. Continental drift 2. Glacial cycles Select the correct answer using the code given below. , fa) 1 only (b) 2 only (c}) Both 1 and 2 (a) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Environment
detail: Evolution responds to changes in the physical environment, and both phenomena listed are large-scale drivers of such change. Continental drift, explained by Alfred Wegener's 1912 hypothesis and later by plate tectonics, describes the movement of crustal plates. Pangaea began breaking up about 200 million years ago into Laurasia and Gondwana. Separation isolated populations and caused allopatric speciation. Marsupials of Australia and South America, ratites (ostrich, emu, rhea, kiwi) and the camelid distribution all reflect this. Collision of landmasses, such as the formation of the Panama land bridge about 3 million years ago, caused the Great American Biotic Interchange. Glacial cycles (Pleistocene ice ages, from about 2.6 million years ago) lowered sea levels and exposed land bridges like Beringia. They also pushed species into refugia, fragmented ranges, caused megafaunal extinctions such as the mammoth, and shaped human evolution and dispersal. Elimination logic: since both are well-established influences on evolution, options (a), (b) and (d) are wrong, and only (c) is correct.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out glacial cycles, which also influenced evolution through climate and habitat change.
Wrong: it leaves out continental drift, which influenced evolution by isolating or joining populations and biotas.
Correct: both continental drift and glacial cycles are recognised influences on the evolution of organisms.
Wrong: both phenomena influenced evolution, so 'neither' is false.
keyfact: Continental drift (isolation of landmasses) and glacial cycles (climate and sea-level change) both influenced the evolution of organisms, so the answer is (c).
option_notes: Option (a) names continental drift alone. Continental drift is the slow movement of continents over geological time, proposed by Alfred Wegener in 1912 and explained by plate tectonics. It accounts for the breakup of Pangaea about 200 million years ago and for the distribution of related fossils and species across continents. It is a valid influence on evolution but not the only one listed.

Option (b) names glacial cycles alone. Glacial cycles are alternating ice ages and warmer interglacials, driven by Milankovitch cycles. The Pleistocene glaciations began about 2.6 million years ago and the last glacial maximum was about 20,000 years ago. They changed sea level by around 120 m, created land bridges and refugia, and caused extinctions. They are a valid influence on evolution but not the only one listed.

Option (c) says both 1 and 2, and it is the official answer. Both processes act on evolution. Continental drift works over hundreds of millions of years, through isolation and the joining of biotas. Glacial cycles work over thousands to millions of years, through climate swings, sea-level change and habitat shifts. Together they explain much of modern biogeography and the patterns of speciation and extinction.

Option (d) says neither. This is false, since both continental drift and glacial cycles are well-documented drivers of evolutionary change. Other environmental drivers include volcanism, meteorite impacts such as the one at the end of the Cretaceous about 66 million years ago, ocean chemistry changes and mass extinctions. Such 'neither' options are usually traps in UPSC questions.
related: Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912 and the supercontinent Pangaea.
Harry Hess proposed sea-floor spreading in the 1960s, which supplied the mechanism for drift.
India collided with Asia about 50 million years ago, raising the Himalaya.
Milankovitch cycles (eccentricity, tilt, precession) drive glacial-interglacial cycles.
Beringia was the land bridge that allowed human and animal migration into the Americas.
The Permian extinction about 252 million years ago was the largest mass extinction.
Darwin's finches in the Galapagos are the classic example of adaptive radiation.
Wallace's Line marks the boundary between Asian and Australasian fauna.
statements: 1 — Correct: Continental drift moved landmasses, isolating or joining biotas and so shaping speciation, extinction and biogeography. Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912, and his book 'The Origin of Continents and Oceans' appeared in 1915. He proposed the supercontinent Pangaea, surrounded by the Panthalassa ocean. Evidence includes the jigsaw fit of the Atlantic coasts, matching fossils such as Glossopteris and Mesosaurus across southern continents, and matching rock formations. His hypothesis was rejected at first because he offered no mechanism. Sea-floor spreading (Harry Hess, 1960s) and plate tectonics later confirmed it. Pangaea broke up about 200 million years ago into Laurasia and Gondwana.

2 — Correct: Glacial cycles changed climate, sea level and habitats, driving migration, extinction, adaptation and human dispersal. Glacial cycles are alternating cold glacial and warm interglacial periods. They are driven by Milankovitch cycles (variations in Earth's eccentricity, axial tilt and precession). The Quaternary Ice Age began about 2.6 million years ago, and the last glacial maximum was about 20,000 years ago. Sea levels fell by around 120 m, exposing land bridges such as Beringia, which enabled movement of animals and humans into the Americas. Species retreated into refugia, populations fragmented, and megafauna such as woolly mammoths went extinct. The present Holocene interglacial began about 11,700 years ago.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. Continental drift changed the positions of landmasses and isolated or joined populations, which drove speciation and extinction. Glacial cycles repeatedly changed climate, sea level and habitats, which forced migration, extinction and adaptation.
topic_notes: Evolution is shaped by both biotic and abiotic factors. The main abiotic drivers are plate tectonics, climate change, glaciations, sea-level change, volcanism and extraterrestrial impacts. Plate tectonics: Wegener (1912) proposed continental drift, Harry Hess (1960s) proposed sea-floor spreading, and the theory of plate tectonics emerged in the late 1960s. Pangaea began to break up about 200 million years ago. Gondwana included South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica. India separated from Gondwana, drifted north and collided with Asia about 50 million years ago, raising the Himalaya. Biogeographic evidence includes marsupials in Australia and South America, ratite birds, lungfish, and Glossopteris fossils across southern continents. Madagascar's lemurs reflect long isolation. Wallace's Line separates Asian and Australasian fauna. The Panama land bridge (about 3 million years ago) led to the Great American Biotic Interchange. Glaciations: the Quaternary Ice Age began about 2.6 million years ago and Milankovitch cycles explain the glacial-interglacial pattern. Beringia allowed human and animal migration. Glacial refugia preserved biodiversity, and the Himalaya and the Western Ghats served as refugia. Mass extinctions: the Big Five are the Ordovician, Late Devonian, Permian (about 252 million years ago, the largest), Triassic and Cretaceous (about 66 million years ago, dinosaurs, linked to the Chicxulub impact). The Anthropocene is sometimes described as the sixth mass extinction. Other evolution concepts UPSC may ask: Darwin's natural selection, Lamarck's inheritance of acquired characters, Hugo de Vries's mutation theory, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, adaptive radiation (Darwin's finches), convergent and divergent evolution, and homologous and analogous organs.

question:
Other than poaching, what are the possible reasons for the decline in the population of Ganges River Dolphins?
1. Construction of dams and barrages on rivers
2. Increase in the population of crocodiles in rivers
3. Getting trapped in fishing nets accidentally
4. Use of synthetic fertilizers and other agricultural chemicals in crop-fields in the vicinity of rivers Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Geography
detail: The Ganges River Dolphin (Platanista gangetica) is an obligate freshwater, almost blind mammal that uses echolocation. It is India's National Aquatic Animal (declared 2009) and is listed as Endangered by the IUCN. It is in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Appendix I of CITES and Appendix II of CMS. Its main threats are: (i) dams, barrages and water abstraction that fragment populations, block movement and reduce dry-season flow and depth; (ii) bycatch in gillnets and other fishing gear; (iii) pollution from industrial effluents, sewage, pesticides and fertilizer run-off, which affects water quality and prey; (iv) deliberate killing for oil used as fish bait; and (v) river traffic and noise, and sand mining. Statement 2 is wrong because crocodiles (gharial, mugger) are themselves threatened, with small and recovering populations, and they are not a significant predator of dolphins. Elimination: since 2 is wrong, options (a), (b) and (d) all fail, leaving (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 2, which is not a recognised cause of the dolphin's decline, and leaves out the valid statements 3 and 4.
Wrong: it includes statement 2 and omits statements 1 and 4, which are valid threats.
Correct: dams and barrages, accidental entanglement in nets, and agrochemical pollution are all established threats, while crocodile increase is not.
Wrong: it wrongly includes statement 2, as crocodiles are not a significant predator and are themselves endangered.
keyfact: Ganges River Dolphin (National Aquatic Animal, Endangered) declines due to dams and barrages, fishing-net bycatch, and pollution, not crocodiles.
option_notes: Options (a) 1 and 2 only: pairs dams with crocodile increase. Dams are a real threat, but crocodiles are not. Related fact: the gharial is Critically Endangered, found mainly in the Chambal, and the mugger is Vulnerable. Crocodilians are protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife Act, and the National Chambal Sanctuary covers Rajasthan, MP and UP. Neither is known to cause dolphin decline, so the combination is false.

Options (b) 2 and 3 only: pairs crocodile increase with net entanglement. Bycatch is genuine, but crocodile increase is not. Dolphins are Endangered in the IUCN Red List, and entanglement in gillnets is a major cause of mortality. Nets are a problem for gharials as well. The option omits dams and pollution, which are also major threats, so it is wrong.

Options (c) 1, 3 and 4 only: the correct set. It lists habitat fragmentation by dams and barrages, bycatch in fishing nets, and agrochemical and industrial pollution. These match the IUCN and Indian government assessments for Platanista gangetica. The species lives in the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna and Karnaphuli-Sangu systems across India, Bangladesh and Nepal. Total numbers are estimated at about 3,000-4,000 individuals, with a 2024 survey estimate of about 6,327.

Options (d) 1, 2, 3 and 4: this treats every statement as a threat. It is wrong only because of statement 2. UPSC often adds one plausible but false item to make an all-of-the-above option tempting. Always check each statement against known conservation facts, such as what the Project Dolphin mission (announced 2020) lists as threats.
related: Ganges River Dolphin is India's National Aquatic Animal, declared in 2009.
Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary in Bhagalpur, Bihar, is the only dolphin sanctuary in India.
Project Dolphin was announced on 15 August 2020 for conservation of river and marine dolphins.
The IUCN lists the Ganges River Dolphin as Endangered.
The Ganges River Dolphin is in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972.
The Indus River Dolphin (Platanista minor) is found in the Beas river in Punjab.
The Irrawaddy dolphin is found in Chilika Lake, Odisha.
National Dolphin Day is celebrated on 5 October.
statements: 1 — Correct: Dams and barrages fragment dolphin habitat and reduce flow. Facts: Farakka, Bhimgoda (Haridwar), Narora and Gandak barrages have isolated sub-populations. Dolphins prefer deep pools near confluences and need adequate flow. Barrages restrict movement between upstream and downstream stretches, reduce gene flow and strand animals in irrigation canals. Dry-season water diversion shrinks usable habitat. The Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary (Bhagalpur, Bihar, declared 1991) is the only dedicated dolphin sanctuary in India.

2 — Incorrect: Crocodile numbers are not rising to a level that threatens dolphins. Facts: the gharial (Gavialis gangeticus) is Critically Endangered, and the mugger is Vulnerable. Both are themselves threatened by habitat loss, sand mining and fishing nets. The National Chambal Sanctuary protects gharials, and the same stretch also holds Ganges dolphins. Gharials eat fish, and neither crocodilian is identified as a major predator of the dolphin. Real threats are human-caused, not predation.

3 — Correct: Accidental bycatch in fishing nets is a leading cause of death. Facts: dolphins surface to breathe every 30-120 seconds and get entangled in gillnets and monofilament nets, then drown. Bycatch is considered the biggest direct human threat after habitat alteration. Dolphin oil is also used illegally as fish attractant, mainly for catfish. Mitigation involves community awareness, fisher participation, and alternative bait such as fish-oil substitutes, as promoted under Project Dolphin.

4 — Correct: Agrochemicals and other pollution harm dolphins and their prey. Facts: pesticides, synthetic fertilizers and industrial effluents run off into the Ganga, Brahmaputra and tributaries. As top predators, dolphins bioaccumulate toxins such as organochlorines and heavy metals. Nutrient loading reduces oxygen and fish stocks. Pollution control under Namami Gange and the National Mission for Clean Ganga supports habitat recovery. The species also faces threats from noise from vessels and from sand mining.
summary: The answer is (c) 1, 3 and 4 only. Ganges River Dolphin numbers fall because dams and barrages fragment habitat, accidental entanglement in fishing nets kills animals, and agrochemical and other pollution degrades water quality and prey. An increase in crocodile numbers is not a recognised threat.
topic_notes: Ganges River Dolphin (Platanista gangetica gangetica), locally called susu or Shushuk, is a freshwater cetacean found in the Ganga, Brahmaputra, Meghna and Karnaphuli-Sangu river systems of India, Nepal and Bangladesh. It is effectively blind because its eye lacks a lens, and it navigates by echolocation. It often swims on its side. Females are larger than males, and calves are born chocolate-brown. It was declared India's National Aquatic Animal in 2009 by the National Ganga River Basin Authority. It is listed as Endangered by the IUCN, in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, in CITES Appendix I and in CMS Appendix II. The Indus River Dolphin (Platanista minor) is a separate species found in the Beas in Punjab and in Pakistan's Indus. Both were once treated as one species and are now recognised as two. The Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary lies in the Ganga in Bhagalpur, Bihar, and is the only dolphin sanctuary in India. Project Dolphin was announced on 15 August 2020, and its framework is similar to Project Tiger. National Dolphin Day is observed on 5 October. In 2012 the Ganga stretch between Bijnor and Narora was also notified as a protected area for dolphins. Other freshwater or coastal cetaceans include the Irrawaddy dolphin in Chilika lake and the finless porpoise. The Chilika Irrawaddy dolphin is a brackish-water species. A comprehensive survey in 2021-23 reported about 6,327 Ganges dolphins, with Uttar Pradesh having the largest number. Threats are dams and barrages, bycatch, pollution, oil poaching, sand mining and vessel traffic. Inland waterway development under National Waterway-1 (Ganga) may increase noise. UPSC may ask about the dolphin's status, legal protection, location of sanctuaries, and threats.

ocr: The Radcliffe Committee was appointed to (a) solve the problem of minorities in India (b}) give effect to the Independence Bill {c) delimit the boundaries between India and Pakistan (ad) enquire into the riots in East Bengal
subject: Polity
detail: After the Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947 accepted Partition, the Indian Independence Act 1947 provided for two dominions, India and Pakistan, from 15 August 1947. Two Boundary Commissions were set up, one for Punjab and one for Bengal (with Assam's Sylhet handled separately), each with an impartial chairman, Sir Cyril Radcliffe, and four judges nominated by the Congress and the Muslim League. The members could not agree, so Radcliffe gave the final award. It used 'contiguous majority areas' of Muslims and non-Muslims as the main criterion, along with 'other factors'. The award was finalised by about 12-13 August but was published on 17 August 1947. This caused great uncertainty, large-scale communal violence and mass migration. The line is the basis of today's India-Pakistan border in the west and the India-Bangladesh border in the east. Elimination: (a) minorities were handled by the Minorities Advisory Committee of the Constituent Assembly, headed by Sardar Patel. (b) The Independence Bill was drafted by the British government and Mountbatten's staff, and was passed by the British Parliament as the Indian Independence Act. (d) The riots in East Bengal (Noakhali, 1946) were not Radcliffe's remit. Hence (c).
explanations: Incorrect: minority rights were examined by the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal Areas of the Constituent Assembly under Patel, not by Radcliffe.
Incorrect: the Independence Bill was prepared by the British government and Parliament, with Mountbatten and V.P. Menon contributing to the plan. It was not Radcliffe's task.
Correct: Radcliffe chaired the Punjab and Bengal Boundary Commissions that demarcated the India-Pakistan boundary, known as the Radcliffe Line.
Incorrect: the 1946 Noakhali riots in East Bengal were dealt with through relief and peace efforts, with Gandhi visiting in person. No Radcliffe inquiry was involved.
keyfact: Radcliffe chaired the 1947 Boundary Commissions that drew the India-Pakistan border (Radcliffe Line, announced 17 August 1947).
option_notes: Minorities in the Constituent Assembly: the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas was chaired by Sardar Patel and set up in January 1947. It had sub-committees on fundamental rights (J.B. Kripalani), minorities (H.C. Mukherjee), and tribal and excluded areas (Gopinath Bardoloi). It recommended safeguards for minorities, and in 1949 the Assembly ended separate electorates and reservation of seats for religious minorities, other than for SC/ST.

The Independence Bill was introduced in the British House of Commons in July 1947 on the basis of the Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947. It became the Indian Independence Act 1947, receiving Royal Assent on 18 July 1947. It created two dominions, ended British paramountcy over princely states, allowed the Constituent Assemblies to frame constitutions, and made the Governor-General a constitutional head. The Act came into force on 15 August 1947.

The Radcliffe Line is the boundary drawn by Sir Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer who had never been to India before. He worked in about five weeks. The award was signed on 12-13 August and publicly released on 17 August 1947. It divided Punjab and Bengal on the basis of contiguous Muslim and non-Muslim majority areas. Disputes arose over Gurdaspur, Chittagong Hill Tracts, Murshidabad and Khulna, and the line triggered mass migration and violence. The Radcliffe Line is today the border with Pakistan and with Bangladesh.

The Noakhali riots broke out in October 1946 in East Bengal (present-day Bangladesh), after the Direct Action Day violence in Calcutta in August 1946. Hindus were targeted in Noakhali and Tippera. Gandhi visited Noakhali from November 1946 to early 1947, walking through villages to restore peace. The riots were followed by reprisal violence in Bihar and fed into the acceptance of Partition. They were not part of any Radcliffe Committee work.
related: Sir Cyril Radcliffe chaired both the Punjab and the Bengal Boundary Commissions in 1947.
The Radcliffe Award was published on 17 August 1947, two days after independence.
The 3 June 1947 Mountbatten Plan accepted Partition and gave a choice to the princely states.
Sylhet was decided by referendum in July 1947 and joined East Pakistan.
The Indian Independence Act 1947 received Royal Assent on 18 July 1947.
The 100th Constitutional Amendment (2015) implemented the India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement.
The Durand Line separates Pakistan and Afghanistan; the McMahon Line is the India-China boundary in the east.
The Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities was chaired by Sardar Patel.
summary: The answer is (c). The Radcliffe Committee, more precisely the Boundary Commissions chaired by Sir Cyril Radcliffe, was appointed in 1947 to delimit the boundaries between India and Pakistan in Punjab and Bengal. The Radcliffe Line was announced on 17 August 1947, just after independence.
topic_notes: Partition process: The Cabinet Mission Plan of May 1946 failed after the Muslim League withdrew its acceptance. Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) led to the Calcutta killings. Attlee's statement of 20 February 1947 fixed June 1948 as the deadline for transfer of power. Mountbatten became Viceroy in March 1947 and presented the Plan of 3 June 1947 (also called the Dickie Bird Plan). The date of transfer was advanced to 15 August 1947. The Indian Independence Act 1947 provided for two dominions and ended the Viceroy's office. A Partition Council was set up for dividing assets. Two Boundary Commissions were created, each with a chairman (Radcliffe) and four members, two nominated by the Congress and two by the League. Sylhet in Assam was decided by a referendum in July 1947 and joined East Pakistan. The North-West Frontier Province also voted by referendum and joined Pakistan. Punjab and Bengal legislatures voted on partition of their provinces. Princely states were integrated under Sardar Patel and V.P. Menon through the Instrument of Accession and the Standstill Agreement. Related boundary issues: the Durand Line (1893) with Afghanistan, McMahon Line (1914) with China, Radcliffe Line (1947), and Sir Creek and Kashmir disputes with Pakistan. The Radcliffe Line later led to enclave issues with Bangladesh, resolved through the Land Boundary Agreement (1974, ratified 2015 via the 100th Constitutional Amendment). Possible UPSC angles: the role of Mountbatten, the 3 June Plan, the 1947 Act, Boundary Commission composition, Radcliffe's criteria, and the accession of Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir.

question:
Brominated flame retardants are used in many household products like mattresses and upholstery. Why is there some concern about their use?
1. They are highly resistant to degradation in the environment.
2. They are able to accumulate in humans and animals. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Environment
detail: Brominated flame retardants are organobromine compounds added to plastics, foams, textiles, mattresses, upholstery, electronics casings and circuit boards to slow ignition and fire spread. The concern arises from their chemistry. The carbon-bromine bond is stable, so many BFRs resist chemical, biological and photolytic breakdown, making them persistent. They are lipophilic (fat-loving), so they accumulate in fatty tissue of organisms, build up through the food chain (biomagnification), and have been found in human breast milk, blood, fish, birds and marine mammals. They also travel long distances through air and water, reaching the Arctic. Health concerns include endocrine and thyroid disruption, neurodevelopmental effects and possible carcinogenicity. Some, such as PBDEs (polybrominated diphenyl ethers: commercial penta-BDE, octa-BDE) and HBCD, have been listed under the Stockholm Convention on POPs. Elimination logic: statement 1 describes persistence, statement 2 describes bioaccumulation, and both are textbook properties of POPs. Since both are true, options (a), (b) and (d) fail, leaving (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it ignores statement 2: BFRs also bioaccumulate in humans and animals, so statement 1 alone is incomplete.
(b) is wrong because it ignores statement 1: BFRs are also highly persistent and resist environmental degradation.
(c) is correct because both persistence and bioaccumulation are established properties of BFRs and the reason for concern.
(d) is wrong because both statements are true, so neither can be rejected.
keyfact: BFRs (PBDEs, HBCD, TBBPA) are persistent and bioaccumulative, so they are treated as POPs under the Stockholm Convention; answer (c).
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only, would mean BFRs are persistent but do not accumulate in organisms. In reality persistence usually goes with bioaccumulation for lipophilic halogenated compounds like PBDEs. Persistence means a long half-life in soil, water, sediment or air, and it is one of the four POP criteria under the Stockholm Convention (2001, in force 2004). Persistent chemicals can travel long distances, so they reach remote regions like the Arctic far from where they were used.

Option (b), 2 only, would mean BFRs accumulate but are not persistent. Bioaccumulation is the build-up of a chemical in an organism faster than it is excreted, typically in fat for lipophilic substances. Biomagnification is the increase in concentration up trophic levels. BFRs show both, which is why predators, fish-eating birds and breastfed infants carry high loads. Accumulation depends in part on the chemical's persistence, so the two properties are linked.

Option (c), both 1 and 2, is the official answer. It reflects that BFRs are persistent, bioaccumulative and toxic, qualifying many of them as POPs. Key examples are PBDEs, HBCD and TBBPA. Regulation includes the Stockholm Convention listings, the EU RoHS Directive restricting PBDEs and PBB in electronics, and national bans on some PBDEs in furniture foam. Safer alternatives include phosphorus-based and mineral flame retardants.

Option (d), neither, would mean BFRs are neither persistent nor bioaccumulative, which is false. If it were true there would be little environmental concern about them. The actual concern led to global restrictions: penta-BDE and octa-BDE were phased out in the EU in 2004 and in the US around 2004 by voluntary industry action, and were listed under the Stockholm Convention in 2009.
related: POPs are defined by persistence, bioaccumulation, long-range transport and toxicity.
The Stockholm Convention was adopted in 2001 and came into force in 2004; India ratified it in 2006.
PBDEs were listed under the Stockholm Convention in 2009; HBCD in 2013.
Biomagnification is the increasing concentration of a toxin at higher trophic levels.
The Basel Convention regulates transboundary movement of hazardous wastes, including e-waste.
The Rotterdam Convention deals with prior informed consent for hazardous chemicals; the Minamata Convention deals with mercury.
India's E-Waste (Management) Rules 2016 restrict hazardous substances, including PBB and PBDE, in electronics.
TBBPA is the most widely used BFR, often chemically bound in circuit boards.
statements: 1 — Correct: BFRs are chemically stable and resist degradation, so they persist in soil, sediment, water and air for long periods. Persistence is one of the four defining POP criteria (persistence, bioaccumulation, long-range transport, toxicity). PBDEs such as penta-BDE and octa-BDE were listed under the Stockholm Convention in 2009. HBCD was listed in 2013 (Annex A), and decaBDE later. They leach out of products into household dust, from which people are exposed, and they are also released during e-waste recycling and burning. Common BFRs include PBDEs, TBBPA and HBCD.

2 — Correct: BFRs are lipophilic and accumulate in the fatty tissue of animals and humans, and they biomagnify up the food chain. They have been detected in human blood, breast milk and adipose tissue, and in fish, seabirds, seals, polar bears and whales. Documented health concerns include thyroid hormone disruption, neurodevelopmental and learning effects in children, reproductive effects and possible cancer links. Bioaccumulation is why top predators and breastfed infants show high body burdens. The effects are often studied through household dust and diet exposure routes.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. Brominated flame retardants (BFRs) are persistent in the environment and bioaccumulate in humans and animals, which is why they are a concern as persistent organic pollutants.
topic_notes: Flame retardants are chemicals added to combustible materials to delay ignition and slow fire spread. Main classes are halogenated (brominated and chlorinated), organophosphorus, nitrogen-based and inorganic (aluminium hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide). Brominated flame retardants (BFRs) are the largest group by market. Major types are PBDEs (penta-, octa-, deca-BDE), TBBPA (tetrabromobisphenol A, the most used, often chemically bound in circuit boards so less likely to leach), HBCD (used in polystyrene insulation foam) and PBBs. Additive BFRs are mixed into the material rather than chemically bonded, so they escape easily into dust and air. Exposure routes include household dust, food (fatty fish, meat, dairy), breast milk and e-waste handling. Health concerns: endocrine and thyroid disruption, impaired neurodevelopment, reproductive toxicity and possible carcinogenicity. Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) are governed by the Stockholm Convention (adopted 2001, in force 2004), which began with the 'dirty dozen' (aldrin, chlordane, dieldrin, endrin, heptachlor, mirex, toxaphene, HCB, PCBs, DDT, dioxins, furans). Later additions include lindane, chlordecone, PBDEs, PFOS, HBCD and endosulfan. India ratified the convention in 2006. The Basel Convention covers hazardous waste movement, and the Rotterdam Convention covers prior informed consent for hazardous chemicals and pesticides. The Minamata Convention covers mercury. UPSC often links these with bioaccumulation, biomagnification, e-waste rules and microplastics. Related ideas to revise: bioaccumulation vs biomagnification, Arctic contamination via the 'grasshopper effect', India's E-Waste (Management) Rules 2016 and the RoHS-style restrictions in them.

ocr: Consider the following : 1. Bats 2. Bears 3. Rodents The phenomenon of hibernation can be observed in which of the above kinds of animals? (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 only () 1, 2 and 3 (ad) Hibernation cannot be observed in any of the above
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Hibernation is a physiological state of inactivity and greatly reduced metabolism that some animals enter during winter, when food is scarce and temperatures are low. Body temperature, heart rate and breathing rate drop, and the animal survives on stored fat. It is seen in many mammals, including bats (insectivorous temperate species such as the little brown bat), rodents (ground squirrels, marmots, dormice, hamsters, chipmunks) and bears (black, brown and grizzly bears). Bear hibernation is shallower: body temperature falls only by about 4-6 degrees Celsius, so some call it winter lethargy or torpor. Even so, it is accepted as hibernation in standard texts, and UPSC's answer treats it that way. Related phenomena are aestivation (summer dormancy, seen in lungfish, snails and some amphibians), diapause (arrested insect development) and daily torpor (hummingbirds). Hibernation is different from migration, which is seasonal movement to avoid harsh conditions. Elimination logic: bats and rodents are classic hibernators, so (b) 'bears only' fails. Bears are widely cited too, so (a) fails because it omits rodents. Option (d) is clearly wrong because hibernation is common among mammals. That leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong: this leaves out rodents, which are well-known hibernators, so the list is incomplete.
Wrong: bears do hibernate, but so do bats and rodents, so 'bears only' is too narrow.
Correct: bats, bears and rodents all show hibernation or winter torpor, matching the official answer.
Wrong: hibernation is a well-documented phenomenon in all three groups, so this denial is false.
keyfact: Bats, bears and rodents all hibernate (bears in a shallow form), so the answer is (c).
option_notes: Option (a), 1 and 2 only, covers bats and bears. Both groups do hibernate, but the option wrongly excludes rodents. Bats show deep torpor and bears show shallow winter dormancy. This is a partly true but incomplete option, which is a common UPSC trap.

Option (b), 2 only, picks bears alone. Bears (family Ursidae) such as black, brown and grizzly bears den in winter for months without eating. Their body temperature falls only a few degrees, so it is called light hibernation. Polar bears generally do not hibernate, though pregnant females den.

Option (c), 1, 2 and 3, is correct. Hibernation is a seasonal state of reduced metabolism and body temperature that lets animals survive winter scarcity. It is found in bats, bears, rodents, some primates such as the fat-tailed dwarf lemur, hedgehogs and some marsupials. It relies on stored body fat and may include periodic arousals.

Option (d) says hibernation cannot be observed in any of these. This is false. Hibernation is common in mammals of cold climates. Related terms include aestivation (summer dormancy), diapause in insects, brumation in reptiles and daily torpor in small birds and mammals.
related: Aestivation is summer dormancy, seen in lungfish and snails.
Brumation is the reptile version of hibernation.
Bears are shallow hibernators with only a slight drop in body temperature.
Bats belong to order Chiroptera and are the only flying mammals.
Diapause is arrested development in insects.
Polar bears do not usually hibernate; only pregnant females den.
White-nose syndrome is a fungal disease killing hibernating bats.
Himalayan marmots hibernate for many months in Ladakh and Spiti.
statements: 1 — Correct: Many temperate-zone bats hibernate in caves, mines and buildings. Hibernation is true deep torpor in these bats. Facts: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight, belonging to order Chiroptera. Insect-eating species face winter food scarcity and so hibernate, with body temperature close to the surroundings and a heart rate falling from hundreds to a few beats per minute. Fat reserves are used. Disturbance during hibernation can be fatal, and white-nose syndrome, a fungal disease, has killed millions of North American bats. Some tropical bats do not hibernate. Fruit bats (flying foxes) are generally non-hibernating.

2 — Correct: Bears undergo winter dormancy, which UPSC treats as hibernation. Facts: Black bears, brown bears and grizzlies den for several months, living on stored fat without eating, drinking, urinating or defecating. Their body temperature drops only slightly and they can wake easily, so they are called light or shallow hibernators. Females give birth to cubs during dormancy. Polar bears mostly do not hibernate, except pregnant females, who den. In India, the sloth bear and Himalayan brown bear occur; the Himalayan brown bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus) is a winter dormant species of high altitudes and is listed in the IUCN Red List and Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.

3 — Correct: Many rodents are true deep hibernators. Facts: Ground squirrels, marmots, dormice, hamsters, chipmunks and jumping mice drop body temperature to near freezing, with heart rate and breathing falling sharply. They wake periodically, rewarm and sleep again. Arctic ground squirrels can supercool below 0 degrees Celsius. Rodents form the largest mammalian order, Rodentia, with about 40 percent of mammal species. They have continuously growing incisors. Not all rodents hibernate, since rats and mice generally do not. Himalayan marmots in Ladakh and Spiti hibernate for roughly six months or more.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1, 2 and 3. Hibernation, a state of prolonged torpor in winter, is seen in bats, bears and many rodents. All three groups reduce metabolism and body temperature, or in bears' case enter a winter dormancy, to survive cold and food scarcity.
topic_notes: Hibernation is a seasonal strategy to survive cold and food scarcity. The animal enters torpor, lowering its metabolic rate, heart rate, breathing and body temperature, and lives on fat stored earlier (and brown adipose tissue helps rewarming). True deep hibernators include ground squirrels, marmots, dormice, hedgehogs and many bats. Bears are shallow hibernators: their temperature falls only slightly, they can be roused quickly, and females give birth in the den. Hibernation is triggered by shortening day length, falling temperature and food shortage, and is controlled by hormones and the nervous system. Related dormancy forms: aestivation is dormancy in hot, dry periods, as in lungfish, snails, some frogs and desert tortoises. Brumation is the reptile equivalent of hibernation. Diapause is a pause in insect development. Daily torpor occurs in hummingbirds and some bats. Migration is a different strategy, as in Siberian cranes, which reach Bharatpur in winter, and the Arctic tern, which makes the longest migration. Hibernating mammals are endotherms, whereas reptiles and amphibians are ectotherms. Other angles for UPSC: adaptation types (behavioural, physiological, structural), endothermy vs ectothermy, hibernating species of the Himalayas (Himalayan brown bear, marmots), threats such as white-nose syndrome in bats, and conservation status in IUCN and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Research on human induced torpor for space travel and medicine is also an emerging topic.

question: Which one of the following is the largest Committee of the Parliament? ;
subject: Polity
detail: The Committee on Estimates is a standing committee of 30 members, all elected by the Lok Sabha from among its own members by proportional representation through the single transferable vote. Rajya Sabha has no representation on it. It originated from a standing financial committee set up in 1921, and it became a statutory-style parliamentary committee in 1950 on the recommendation of John Mathai, then Finance Minister. It examines the estimates in the budget, suggests economies and alternative policies for efficiency, and checks whether money is well laid out within the policy implied by the estimates. It is called the 'continuous economy committee' because it works throughout the year. The Public Accounts Committee has 22 members (15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha) and scrutinises CAG audit reports. The Committee on Public Undertakings also has 22 members (15 Lok Sabha and 7 Rajya Sabha). The Committee on Petitions in Lok Sabha has 15 members. Elimination: recall 30 versus 22, 22 and 15, and (b) is the only one at the top. Remember that the Estimates Committee is the only one with only Lok Sabha members among the three financial committees, and that a minister cannot be a member of any of them.
explanations: Incorrect: the Public Accounts Committee has 22 members (15 Lok Sabha, 7 Rajya Sabha), fewer than the Estimates Committee's 30.
Correct: the Committee on Estimates has 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha, making it the largest parliamentary committee.
Incorrect: the Committee on Public Undertakings has 22 members (15 Lok Sabha, 7 Rajya Sabha), so it is smaller than the Estimates Committee.
Incorrect: the Committee on Petitions is much smaller, with 15 members in the Lok Sabha, and it deals with petitions on bills and public grievances.
keyfact: Estimates Committee: 30 members, all from Lok Sabha, the largest committee; PAC and COPU have 22 each.
option_notes: The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) examines the appropriation accounts and the CAG's audit reports to check that money was spent as Parliament authorised. It has 22 members: 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha. It was first set up in 1921 under the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms. Its chairman has been from the Opposition by convention since 1967. Ministers cannot be members, and the CAG is described as its friend, philosopher and guide.

The Committee on Estimates has 30 members, all from Lok Sabha, elected annually by proportional representation with the single transferable vote. It was recommended by John Mathai in 1950, and it scrutinises the budget estimates and suggests economies and administrative reforms. It is known as the continuous economy committee. The chairman is appointed by the Speaker from among its members, and ministers cannot serve on it.

The Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU) was created in 1964 on the recommendation of the Krishna Menon Committee. It has 22 members: 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha. It examines the reports and accounts of public sector undertakings and the CAG reports on them. It checks whether PSUs are run efficiently and on sound business principles. Ministers cannot be members.

The Committee on Petitions is a Lok Sabha committee with 15 members, and Rajya Sabha has a similar committee. It examines petitions on bills pending before the House and on matters of general public interest that are not on the list of subjects of any other committee. It can suggest remedies, and its reports are presented to the House. It is a standing committee.
related: Estimates Committee: 30 members, all from Lok Sabha.
PAC: 22 members (15 Lok Sabha plus 7 Rajya Sabha); the chairman is from the Opposition by convention.
COPU: formed in 1964 on the Krishna Menon Committee's recommendation; 22 members.
The Estimates Committee originated from John Mathai's recommendation in 1950.
DRSCs: created in 1993; 24 committees of 31 members each (21 plus 10).
Ministers cannot be members of the PAC, the Estimates Committee or the COPU.
The Estimates Committee is called the continuous economy committee.
The Committee on Petitions in Lok Sabha has 15 members.
summary: The answer is (b) The Committee on Estimates. It has 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha, which makes it the largest parliamentary committee. The Public Accounts Committee has 22 members and the Committee on Public Undertakings has 22.
topic_notes: Parliamentary committees are of two broad kinds: standing committees, which are permanent and constituted every year or periodically, and ad hoc committees, which are temporary and are dissolved once their task is finished. The three financial committees are the Public Accounts Committee, the Estimates Committee and the Committee on Public Undertakings. Their sizes are: Estimates, 30 members (all Lok Sabha); PAC, 22 members (15 Lok Sabha plus 7 Rajya Sabha); COPU, 22 members (15 Lok Sabha plus 7 Rajya Sabha). The term of each is one year. Members are elected by proportional representation through the single transferable vote. Ministers cannot be members of any of them. The PAC is a post-audit body that works with the CAG, while the Estimates Committee examines the budget estimates. The COPU was created in 1964 on the recommendation of the Krishna Menon Committee. Departmentally related standing committees (DRSCs) were created in 1993 and now number 24, each with 31 members (21 from Lok Sabha and 10 from Rajya Sabha). Other committees to know: the Committee on Government Assurances, the Committee on Subordinate Legislation (15 members), the Committee on Papers Laid on the Table (15), the Committee on Privileges (15 in Lok Sabha), the Business Advisory Committee (15 in Lok Sabha) and the Rules Committee. Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPCs) are ad hoc committees drawing on both Houses, and the Speaker or Chairman appoints their chairpersons. Committee reports are presented to the House or the Speaker, and the decisions of committees are recommendatory in nature rather than binding. Parliament delegates much detailed scrutiny to these bodies because it has too little time for it on the floor of the House.

question:
Which of the following adds/add carbon dioxide to the carbon cycle on the planet Earth?
1. Voleanic action
2. Respiration
3. Photosynthesis
4. Decay of organic matter Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Environment
detail: The carbon cycle is the movement of carbon among the atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and pedosphere. Processes are either sources, which add CO2 to the atmosphere, or sinks, which remove it. Sources include volcanic eruptions and degassing (releasing carbon from the mantle and from carbonate rocks), respiration by plants, animals and microbes (oxidising glucose to CO2 and water), decomposition of dead organic matter by bacteria and fungi, combustion of biomass and fossil fuels, and weathering or calcination of limestone as in cement making. Sinks include photosynthesis (6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2), dissolution in oceans, formation of carbonate shells and limestone, and burial as coal, oil and peat. Elimination logic: photosynthesis (statement 3) takes CO2 in, so any option containing 3, namely (a) and (d), is wrong. Option (b) is wrong because it ignores volcanic action and decay. Only (c) lists all three emitting processes. The atmosphere holds roughly 420 ppm CO2 today, up from about 280 ppm before the Industrial Revolution.
explanations: Wrong: it includes photosynthesis, which removes CO2, and leaves out respiration and decay, which add it.
Wrong: respiration does add CO2, but volcanic action and decay of organic matter also add it, so 'only 2' is incomplete.
Right: volcanic action, respiration and decay of organic matter all release CO2, while photosynthesis does not.
Wrong: photosynthesis consumes CO2 rather than adding it, so including statement 3 makes this option incorrect.
keyfact: CO2 sources: respiration, decay, volcanoes, combustion; CO2 sink: photosynthesis (also oceans and carbonate formation).
option_notes: Volcanic action plus photosynthesis: volcanoes are a geological CO2 source, emitting from mantle degassing and carbonate decomposition. Photosynthesis is the biological process converting CO2 and water into glucose and oxygen using light, mainly in chloroplasts. Together they illustrate a source and a sink. Volcanic emissions are about 0.3 to 0.4 Gt CO2 per year, which is much less than human emissions of about 37 Gt CO2 per year from fossil fuels.

Respiration alone: the biochemical process by which cells oxidise glucose to release ATP, CO2 and water. It occurs in plants, animals and microbes, and may be aerobic or anaerobic. Anaerobic forms such as fermentation yield less energy and produce ethanol or lactic acid. Respiration is a major biological CO2 source and together with photosynthesis drives the fast carbon cycle. Soil respiration is a large terrestrial flux.

Volcanic action, respiration and decay: the correct combination of CO2 sources. They represent geological (volcanic) and biological (respiration, decomposition) emissions. Other sources include fossil fuel combustion, deforestation, forest fires and cement manufacture. The carbon cycle is balanced when sources and sinks are equal, but human activity has raised atmospheric CO2 above 420 ppm, from about 280 ppm in pre-industrial times.

All four processes: this would treat photosynthesis as an addition of CO2, which is wrong. Photosynthesis is the main biological sink, fixing about 120 Gt of carbon per year as gross primary production on land. Remember that the carbon cycle comprises sources (respiration, decay, volcanoes, combustion) and sinks (photosynthesis, ocean uptake, carbonate formation, burial).
related: Photosynthesis is the main natural sink of atmospheric CO2.
Phosphorus cycle is a sedimentary cycle with no significant gaseous phase.
Oceans are the largest active carbon sink; their uptake causes acidification.
Methane has a global warming potential about 28 times that of CO2 over 100 years.
Paris Agreement (2015) aims to limit warming to well below 2 degrees C, pursuing 1.5 degrees C.
Blue carbon refers to carbon stored in mangroves, seagrass and salt marshes.
India's net-zero target is 2070, announced at COP26 (Glasgow, 2021).
Anaerobic decomposition in wetlands and paddy fields produces methane rather than CO2.
statements: 1 — Correct: Volcanoes emit CO2 into the atmosphere. Volcanic eruptions and degassing release CO2 from the mantle and from heated carbonate rocks. This is a natural, geological-timescale source, though it is far smaller than human emissions, which are roughly 100 times greater annually. Over millions of years volcanic CO2 balances the CO2 removed by silicate weathering, which keeps climate stable. Massive volcanism, such as the Deccan Traps about 66 million years ago and the Siberian Traps about 252 million years ago, has been linked to climate change and mass extinctions.

2 — Correct: Respiration releases CO2. All aerobic organisms oxidise organic food, mainly glucose, to release energy, CO2 and water. Plants also respire, day and night, but in daytime photosynthesis usually exceeds it. Soil respiration by roots and microbes is a major land-based flux. Net primary productivity is gross primary productivity minus respiration losses. The overall reaction is C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy. Respiration and photosynthesis are roughly balanced in the fast biological carbon cycle.

3 — Incorrect: Photosynthesis removes CO2 from the atmosphere and fixes it into carbohydrates, releasing oxygen. It is carried out by green plants, algae and cyanobacteria using chlorophyll and sunlight. It is the main natural carbon sink and the entry point of carbon into food chains. The reaction is 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. Forests, grasslands and phytoplankton are major sinks. Oceans' phytoplankton account for roughly half of global photosynthesis. Afforestation and REDD+ aim to enhance this sink.

4 — Correct: Decay of organic matter releases CO2. Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead plants and animals, returning carbon to the atmosphere as CO2 under aerobic conditions and as methane under anaerobic conditions, such as in wetlands and paddy fields. Decomposition also recycles nutrients into the soil as humus. Its rate rises with temperature and moisture, so warming can speed up soil carbon loss. If decay is prevented, as in waterlogged or anoxic conditions, organic carbon is buried and can become peat, coal or oil.
summary: The answer is (c) 1, 2 and 4 only. Volcanic action, respiration and decay of organic matter release CO2 into the atmosphere, while photosynthesis removes CO2 and so does not add it.
topic_notes:
The carbon cycle describes carbon's circulation through the atmosphere, biosphere, oceans, soils and rocks. It is a gaseous, biogeochemical cycle with a sedimentary component. The main reservoirs are sedimentary rocks (the largest, mostly limestone and kerogen), oceans (about 38,000 Gt C, mainly as dissolved inorganic carbon), fossil fuels, soils, the atmosphere (about 850 Gt C) and living biomass.

Fast cycle: photosynthesis and respiration, decomposition, and air-sea exchange operate over days to centuries. Slow cycle: weathering of rocks, ocean sediment formation, subduction and volcanic outgassing operate over millions of years.

Sources of CO2: respiration, decomposition, volcanism, forest fires, fossil fuel burning, deforestation, cement production and ocean outgassing. Sinks: photosynthesis, oceans (physical solubility pump and biological pump), carbonate precipitation by corals and molluscs, peat and coal burial, and soils.

Human impact: burning fossil fuels and changing land use have raised atmospheric CO2 from about 280 ppm to over 420 ppm. CO2 is the main anthropogenic greenhouse gas. Ocean uptake causes ocean acidification, lowering pH and harming corals and shell-forming organisms.

Related policy: UNFCCC (1992), Kyoto Protocol (1997), Paris Agreement (2015, aims to hold warming well below 2 degrees C and pursue 1.5 degrees C), India's net-zero target of 2070, carbon credits, the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, REDD+, blue carbon (mangroves, seagrass, salt marshes), carbon capture and storage, and the Green India Mission.

Other UPSC angles: nitrogen, phosphorus and sulphur cycles (phosphorus is purely sedimentary), the role of methane (about 28 times CO2's warming potential over 100 years), carbon sequestration in forests and soils, and carbon sinks in the Himalaya and Western Ghats.

ocr: If you walk through countryside, you are likely to see some birds stalking alongside the cattle to seize the insects disturbed by their movement through grasses. Which of the following is/are such bird/birds? 1. Painted Stork 2. Common Myna 3. Black-necked Crane Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1 and 2 (b) 2 only (c) 2 and 3 {d@) 3 only
subject: Environment
detail: The question tests the idea of commensal or foraging associations, in which one animal benefits from another's movement without harming it. Grazing cattle disturb insects such as grasshoppers and crickets. Birds that exploit this are called 'followers' or 'attendants'. The Common Myna (Acridotheres tristis) is a classic example, and the Cattle Egret (Bubulcus ibis) is the other well-known one. Both are open-country, ground-foraging birds that live close to humans and livestock. The Painted Stork (Mycteria leucocephala) is a large wading bird. It feeds mostly on fish by wading in shallow water and sweeping its partly open bill, and it does not follow cattle. The Black-necked Crane (Grus nigricollis) is a high-altitude wetland species of the Tibetan plateau. In India it is found in Ladakh and in Arunachal Pradesh, where it winters at Sangti and Zemithang valleys. It eats roots, tubers, insects, and small animals in marshes and meadows, but it is not a typical cattle follower. Elimination logic: once Common Myna (2) is confirmed, options (a) and (c) are dropped if either 1 or 3 is rejected. Only (b) is consistent with rejecting both 1 and 3.
explanations: (a) 1 and 2 is wrong. The Common Myna is right, but the Painted Stork is a fish-eating wader and does not follow cattle.
(b) 2 only is correct. Only the Common Myna routinely stalks alongside cattle to seize insects stirred up by their movement.
(c) 2 and 3 is wrong. The Common Myna is right, but the Black-necked Crane is a high-altitude marsh crane and does not feed in association with cattle.
(d) 3 only is wrong. It leaves out the Common Myna, the one bird that does show this behaviour, and includes the Black-necked Crane, which does not.
keyfact: Common Myna (and Cattle Egret) follow cattle to catch flushed insects; Painted Stork is a fish-eating wader and Black-necked Crane is a high-altitude marsh crane.
related: Cattle Egret (Bubulcus ibis) is the classic cattle-following bird.
Commensalism: one species benefits, the other is unaffected.
Painted Stork is rated Near Threatened by the IUCN.
Black-necked Crane is the state bird of Ladakh and winters at Sangti and Zemithang in Arunachal Pradesh.
Common Myna is listed among the world's 100 worst invasive species by the IUCN.
Great Indian Bustard is Critically Endangered, with its main population in Rajasthan.
Sarus Crane is the tallest flying bird in the world.
Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 gives the highest protection.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Painted Stork is a wetland wader that catches fish, frogs and crustaceans. It does not follow cattle for insects. Mycteria leucocephala is a large wading bird of South and Southeast Asia, with white plumage, a pink tertial feather tinge, a black breast band and a yellow bill that curves down at the tip. It forages by wading in shallow water and sweeping its partly open bill, and it often feeds in groups. It nests colonially in trees, often with other waterbirds. It is listed as Near Threatened by the IUCN. Well-known Indian heronries and nesting sites include Keoladeo National Park (Bharatpur), Kokkare Bellur in Karnataka and Ranganathittu Bird Sanctuary.

2 — Correct: The Common Myna walks alongside grazing cattle and catches the insects they flush from the grass. Acridotheres tristis belongs to the starling family (Sturnidae). It is brown with a black head, and has yellow bill, legs and eye patch. It is omnivorous, eating insects, grains, fruits and scraps. It is found throughout the Indian subcontinent, usually near human habitation, and has been introduced to Australia, South Africa, Hawaii and elsewhere. It is among the world's most invasive birds and is on the IUCN list of '100 worst invasive species'. Its IUCN status is Least Concern. It is an excellent mimic and is often seen foraging behind cattle, buffaloes and ploughs.

3 — Incorrect: The Black-necked Crane is a high-altitude wetland crane, not a cattle follower. Grus nigricollis breeds on the Tibetan plateau and in Ladakh (Chushul, Tso Kar), and winters in Bhutan, Arunachal Pradesh (Sangti and Zemithang valleys of Tawang and West Kameng) and Yunnan and Guizhou in China. It has a black head and neck, a red crown patch and a grey-white body. It eats tubers, roots, grain, insects, fish and amphibians. It is the only alpine crane species. The IUCN lists it as Near Threatened. It is the state bird of Ladakh (UT) and is revered in Buddhist culture. It is under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. The Common Myna is the bird that habitually walks alongside grazing cattle and seizes the insects they flush out of the grass. The Painted Stork and Black-necked Crane are not cattle-associated insect gleaners in this way.
topic_notes: This question is about animal interactions and bird ecology. The key idea is commensalism, in which one species benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed. Cattle flush insects, and birds eat them. The Cattle Egret (Bubulcus ibis) is the best-known follower and is often seen on the backs of cattle and buffalo. The Common Myna, the Black Drongo and the Indian Pond Heron are also often seen near grazing animals. Other associations UPSC may ask about: mutualism, as with oxpeckers and large African mammals, and the clownfish and sea anemone. Also: the plover and crocodile, which is often described as mutualism, though evidence is weak. Bird identification questions are common in UPSC. Painted Storks are waders and nest colonially in trees. Black-necked Cranes are the only high-altitude crane and are found in Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh. The Sarus Crane is the tallest flying bird in the world and is found in the Gangetic plains. The Great Indian Bustard is Critically Endangered and is found in Rajasthan (Desert National Park). The Siberian Crane is a winter migrant that has become very rare in India. Related legal and conservation points include the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, whose Schedule I gives the highest protection, the IUCN Red List categories, the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) and Ramsar sites. Birds are also often asked about in terms of habitat (wetland, grassland, forest, alpine) and diet (insectivore, piscivore, frugivore, omnivore).

ocr: In medieval India, the designations ‘Mahattara’ and ‘Pattakila’ were used for (a) military officers (b) village headmen (c) specialists in Vedic rituals (dj chiefs of craft guilds
subject: Ancient History
detail: The question tests knowledge of medieval (early medieval, c. 8th-13th century) rural administration. 'Mahattara' (also Mahtara, later Mehta/Mahto) meant the elder or chief of a village and was a respected local authority, often consulted in land grants. 'Pattakila' (Pattakilla, later Patel/Patil) was the village headman responsible for the village's revenue and records, and the term is associated with the Gujarat and Rajasthan regions. Both appear in inscriptions and copper-plate land grants of the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas and other dynasties, where the king orders the local officials, including the Mahattaras and Pattakilas, to respect the grant. Modern surnames such as Patel, Patil, Mehta and Mahto trace back to these offices.
