Major REDD+ vehicles include the World Bank's Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF, 2008), with a Readiness Fund and a Carbon Fund; the BioCarbon Fund ISFL (2013), which is landscape-level and covers agriculture as well as forests; and UN-REDD (2008), a joint programme of FAO, UNDP and UNEP. Other related bodies: the Forest Investment Program under the Climate Investment Funds, the Green Climate Fund (set up at COP16 in Cancun, with its secretariat in Songdo, South Korea), the Global Environment Facility (established in 1991 and serving as financial mechanism for several conventions), and the Adaptation Fund under the Kyoto Protocol. Norway has been a major REDD+ donor, with deals such as those with Brazil's Amazon Fund and Indonesia. India's relevant policies include the National Afforestation Programme, the Green India Mission under NAPCC, CAMPA, and India's NDC pledge of an additional carbon sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes CO2 equivalent by 2030 through forest and tree cover. UPSC often asks which international body manages which fund or report, so link each institution to its outputs: for example, the World Bank to carbon funds, UNEP to the Emissions Gap Report, the IMF to the World Economic Outlook, and the FAO to the Global Forest Resources Assessment and the State of the World's Forests.

ocr: India is a member of which among the following? 1. Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation 2. Association of South-East Asian Nations 3. East Asia Summit Select the correct answer using the code given below. {a} 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only fc) 1, 2 and 3 (d) India is a member of none of them
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The question tests the difference between membership and partnership in Asia-Pacific groupings. APEC, founded in 1989 in Canberra, has 21 member economies; India has applied since the 1990s but remains outside, partly because of a moratorium on new members (1997 onward, long extended) and because India is not on the Pacific rim. ASEAN, founded by the Bangkok Declaration of 1967, has 10 members (Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam); India became a Sectoral Dialogue Partner in 1992, a Full Dialogue Partner in 1996, and a Summit-level Partner in 2002, and the partnership was upgraded to a Strategic Partnership in 2012. The East Asia Summit, first held in Kuala Lumpur in December 2005, began with 16 members (ASEAN-10 plus India, China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand); the USA and Russia joined in 2011, making 18. Elimination logic: once you know India is not in APEC, options (a) and (c) fall; once you know India is in the EAS, option (d) falls, leaving (b).
explanations: Wrong: it claims membership of APEC and ASEAN. India is in neither; APEC excludes it and ASEAN only has it as a dialogue partner.
Correct: India is a member of the East Asia Summit only, and not of APEC or ASEAN.
Wrong: it would require India to be in APEC and ASEAN too, which it is not.
Wrong: India is a member of the East Asia Summit, so it is not true that it belongs to none of them.
keyfact: India is a member of the East Asia Summit (2005), but only a dialogue partner of ASEAN and not a member of APEC.
option_notes: Not applicable for numbered-combination option; see statements.
Not applicable for numbered-combination option; see statements.
Not applicable for numbered-combination option; see statements.
Not applicable for numbered-combination option; see statements.
related: India joined the East Asia Summit as a founding member in 2005 (Kuala Lumpur).
EAS membership rose to 18 in 2011 with the entry of the USA and Russia.
ASEAN was formed on 8 August 1967 through the Bangkok Declaration; secretariat in Jakarta.
India became an ASEAN Summit-level partner in 2002 and Strategic Partner in 2012.
APEC was founded in 1989 and India is not a member.
India withdrew from RCEP negotiations in November 2019.
India's Act East Policy was announced in 2014, replacing the 1991 Look East Policy.
BIMSTEC (1997) includes India but not Indonesia or Malaysia.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: India is not a member of APEC. APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) was founded in 1989 in Canberra on Australia's initiative and now has 21 member economies, including the USA, China, Japan, Russia, Australia, Indonesia and others. It operates by non-binding consensus and calls its members 'economies', which is why Taiwan (as Chinese Taipei) and Hong Kong participate. A moratorium on new members began in 1997 and India has not been admitted. Its secretariat is in Singapore. Its goal is trade and investment liberalisation, exemplified by the Bogor Goals of 1994.

2 — Incorrect: India is not a member of ASEAN; it is only a dialogue partner. ASEAN was founded on 8 August 1967 by the Bangkok Declaration, with five founders: Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand. Brunei, Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and Cambodia joined later, giving 10 members. Its secretariat is in Jakarta. India's partnership has run from Sectoral (1992) to Full Dialogue (1996) to Summit level (2002) to Strategic (2012). The ASEAN–India FTA in goods came into force in 2010. Timor-Leste was admitted as the 11th member in 2025. India's Act East Policy rests on ASEAN centrality.

3 — Correct: India is a member of the East Asia Summit. The EAS is a leaders-led forum for strategic, political and economic issues in the Indo-Pacific. Its first summit was in Kuala Lumpur in 2005 and India has been a founding member. Members: ASEAN-10 plus Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, plus Russia and the USA since 2011, making 18 in total. ASEAN is the driving force, and the summit is held annually alongside the ASEAN Summit. It has no permanent secretariat; the ASEAN Secretariat provides support. Priority areas include energy, education, finance, health, disaster management and maritime cooperation.
summary: The answer is (b) 3 only. India is a member of the East Asia Summit (EAS) since its inception in 2005, but it is not a member of APEC (which has repeatedly excluded India) and it is only a Sectoral/Summit-level Dialogue Partner of ASEAN, not a member.
topic_notes: Regional groupings in Asia-Pacific are a recurring UPSC theme. ASEAN (1967, Bangkok Declaration; Jakarta secretariat; 10 members, with Timor-Leste admitted as the 11th in 2025) is the hub of several forums. ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF, 1994) is a security dialogue in which India has participated since 1996 and which has 27 members. ASEAN+3 comprises China, Japan and South Korea. The East Asia Summit (2005) has 18 members, with the USA and Russia added in 2011. RCEP was signed in 2020 by ASEAN plus China, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand; India withdrew from negotiations in November 2019 over trade deficit and market access concerns. APEC (1989) has 21 economies and India is not among them; the USA, China, Japan, Russia, Australia, Indonesia, Mexico, Chile, Peru and others are. India's Look East policy was launched in 1991-92 under Narasimha Rao and was upgraded to the Act East Policy in 2014. BIMSTEC (1997) links India with Bangladesh, Bhutan, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand; it is distinct from ASEAN. Mekong-Ganga Cooperation (2000) involves India with Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam. India is also a member of SCO (since 2017), BRICS, the Quad (informal), IORA and the Commonwealth. Other angles: ADMM-Plus, the ASEAN-India FTA (2010), the India-Myanmar-Thailand trilateral highway, the Kaladan project, and the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative. Always check whether a body has 'members' or 'partners' and the year of joining.

question: In India, the steel production industry requires the import of
subject: Economy
detail: Integrated steel plants using the blast furnace-basic oxygen furnace route need metallurgical (coking) coal to make coke. Coke acts as both the fuel and the reducing agent that converts iron ore into pig iron. Indian coking coal, found mainly in Jharia (Jharkhand) and Raniganj (West Bengal), is generally high in ash (often 17-20% or more) and low in quality. Steelmakers therefore import low-ash coking coal, chiefly from Australia (Queensland), and also from the USA, Russia, Canada and Mozambique. India imports roughly 50-55 million tonnes a year, and the National Steel Policy 2017 targeted lower import dependence. Saltpetre (potassium nitrate) is used in fertilisers, gunpowder, explosives and fireworks. Rock phosphate is the raw material for phosphatic fertilisers such as DAP and SSP, and India imports it from Morocco, Jordan and others. Neither is a steel input. Elimination: (a) and (b) are wrong because they serve other industries, so (d) falls too, leaving (c).
explanations: Wrong: saltpetre (potassium nitrate) is used in explosives, fertilisers and fireworks, not in steel production.
Wrong: rock phosphate is imported for the phosphatic fertiliser industry, not for steel.
Correct: coking coal is essential for making coke for blast furnaces, and India's domestic supply is insufficient and of poor quality (high ash), so it is imported.
Wrong: 'All of the above' fails because only coking coal is a steel input.
keyfact: India's steel industry imports coking coal (mainly from Australia) because domestic coking coal is scarce and high in ash; saltpetre and rock phosphate are not steel inputs.
option_notes: Saltpetre is potassium nitrate (KNO3), also called niter. It is used in gunpowder, fertilisers, food preservation, fireworks and glass making. Natural deposits are found in parts of India, notably Bihar, and historically it was exported and traded by European companies. It is a nitrogen and potassium source but plays no role in the reduction of iron ore.

Rock phosphate is a sedimentary rock rich in apatite minerals. It is the main raw material for phosphatic fertilisers such as DAP and SSP, and for phosphoric acid. India has limited reserves, in Rajasthan (Udaipur, Jhabua belt in MP) and Uttar Pradesh, and imports from Morocco, Jordan, Togo and Senegal. Its demand is tied to agriculture, not steel.

Coking coal (metallurgical coal) is bituminous coal with low ash, low sulphur and low phosphorus content that becomes coke when heated without air. It is used in blast furnaces for the reduction of iron ore. Indian reserves are at Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro, and are mostly high ash, so washing is needed. Major import sources are Australia, USA, Russia and Mozambique.

This option combines all three items. It is incorrect because only coking coal is needed for steelmaking. Saltpetre belongs to the explosives and fertiliser industries, and rock phosphate to the fertiliser industry. UPSC uses 'All of the above' as a trap when one item is clearly valid and the others belong to different industries.
related: Coking coal is mainly imported from Australia, with smaller volumes from the USA, Russia and Mozambique.
Jharia in Jharkhand is India's main coking coal field.
Bituminous coal is the best for coke making; anthracite has the highest carbon content.
India is the world's largest producer of sponge iron (DRI).
SAIL plants: Bhilai, Bokaro, Durgapur, Rourkela and Burnpur.
Rock phosphate is imported for phosphatic fertilisers such as DAP.
Mission Coking Coal aims to raise domestic coking coal output and reduce imports.
Neyveli in Tamil Nadu is the major lignite centre.
summary: The answer is (c) coking coal. India has limited reserves of good-quality low-ash coking coal, so its blast furnace steel industry imports a large share of it, mainly from Australia, with smaller volumes from the USA, Russia and Mozambique. Saltpetre and rock phosphate are not inputs for steelmaking.
topic_notes: Steelmaking inputs: iron ore, coking coal, limestone, dolomite and manganese. Blast furnace route: iron ore, coke and limestone yield pig iron, then steel in a basic oxygen furnace. Alternative routes are the electric arc furnace (scrap) and DRI or sponge iron, where India is the world's largest producer and which uses non-coking coal or natural gas. India is the world's second-largest crude steel producer after China, with output of about 140 million tonnes and a National Steel Policy 2017 target of 300 MT capacity by 2030-31. Major plants are SAIL's Bhilai, Bokaro, Durgapur, Rourkela and Burnpur, along with Tata Steel (Jamshedpur), JSW, Vizag Steel (RINL) and Essar. Iron ore comes from Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Goa. India has large coal reserves, but coking coal is only a small share, around 5 percent, and mostly of inferior quality. Coal types by carbon content: anthracite (highest), bituminous, sub-bituminous, lignite and peat. Gondwana coalfields hold most coking coal. Lignite is found at Neyveli in Tamil Nadu. India also imports other items: crude oil, gold, fertilisers (rock phosphate, potash), and thermal coal for coastal power plants. Policy steps include coal washeries, the Mission Coking Coal announced in 2021 to raise domestic output, and long-term agreements with Australia under the India-Australia ECTA, signed in 2022. Possible UPSC angles: locations of steel plants, raw material orientation of industries, minerals by state, and import dependence of fertiliser, energy and metals.

question: The provisions in Fifth Schedule and Sixth Schedule in the Constitution of India are made in order to
options: protect the interests of Scheduled Tribes
determine the powers, authority and responsibilities of Panchayats
protect the interests of all the border States B-AQN-O-JUA/63A
subject: Polity
detail: Article 244 of the Constitution provides for special administration of tribal areas. Under Article 244(1), the Fifth Schedule governs the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in all states except Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Under Article 244(2), the Sixth Schedule governs tribal areas in these four northeastern states. Under the Fifth Schedule, the Governor can direct that a central or state law does not apply to a Scheduled Area, or applies with modifications. The Governor can also regulate the transfer of tribal land and the business of moneylending. A Tribes Advisory Council advises on tribal welfare. The Sixth Schedule creates Autonomous District Councils and Regional Councils with legislative, judicial, executive and financial powers. Elimination: boundaries between States are dealt with under Articles 3 and 4 and the First Schedule, so (b) is wrong. Panchayats are covered by Part IX (Articles 243 to 243O) and the Eleventh Schedule, so (c) is wrong. The Schedules do not cover all border States, and (d) ignores their tribal focus, so it is wrong. Only (a) fits.
explanations: Correct. Both Schedules, under Article 244, exist to protect the interests, land rights, culture and self-governance of Scheduled Tribes.
Wrong. State boundaries are altered under Articles 3 and 4, and the territories of the States are listed in the First Schedule.
Wrong. Panchayats fall under Part IX (Articles 243 to 243O), and the Eleventh Schedule lists their 29 subjects.
Wrong. The Schedules are not linked to border States as such. They apply to tribal areas, and some of those areas happen to lie in border States.
keyfact: Fifth Schedule: Scheduled Areas in ten States; Sixth Schedule: tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; both aim to protect Scheduled Tribes under Article 244.
option_notes: Protecting Scheduled Tribes is the aim of Article 244, Articles 342 and 275(1), the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, the PESA Act 1996 and the Forest Rights Act 2006. Article 342 lets the President notify Scheduled Tribes. Article 46 directs the State to promote the educational and economic interests of weaker sections, and Article 338A set up the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes, created by the 89th Amendment in 2003.

Boundaries between States are governed by Article 3, under which Parliament may form new States or alter areas, boundaries or names, and by Article 4. The First Schedule lists the States and Union Territories. The States Reorganisation Act 1956 followed the Fazl Ali Commission (1953) and reorganised States on a linguistic basis. Inter-state boundary disputes include Assam-Meghalaya and Belagavi (Belgaum), and Parliament can resolve them by law.

Panchayats were given constitutional status by the 73rd Amendment Act 1992, which inserted Part IX (Articles 243 to 243O) and the Eleventh Schedule. It came into force on 24 April 1993, now observed as National Panchayati Raj Day. It provides a three-tier structure, Gram Sabha, reservation for SC, ST and women (not less than one-third), five-year terms, State Election Commissions and State Finance Commissions.

This is a distractor. There is no Schedule specifically for border States. Special provisions for some States appear in Article 371 to 371J, for example Nagaland (371A), Assam (371B), Manipur (371C), Sikkim (371F), Mizoram (371G) and Arunachal Pradesh (371H). Border area development is handled by the Border Area Development Programme, run by the Ministry of Home Affairs.
related: Article 244(1) refers to the Fifth Schedule and Article 244(2) to the Sixth Schedule.
The Sixth Schedule applies to Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
The President declares Scheduled Areas under the Fifth Schedule; the Governor administers them.
PESA Act 1996 extends Panchayat provisions to Scheduled Areas.
Article 342 deals with notification of Scheduled Tribes; Article 341 with Scheduled Castes.
Eleventh Schedule lists 29 Panchayat subjects; Twelfth Schedule lists 18 municipal subjects.
The Bordoloi Committee shaped the Sixth Schedule.
Article 371 to 371J give special provisions to certain States.
summary: The answer is (a). The Fifth and Sixth Schedules contain special provisions for the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and tribal areas, and their purpose is to protect the land, culture, autonomy and interests of Scheduled Tribes.
topic_notes:
Article 244 is the source of special administration for tribal regions. The Fifth Schedule covers Scheduled Areas outside the four northeastern States, and as of now ten States have such areas: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha and Rajasthan. The President declares Scheduled Areas, and can alter them in consultation with the Governor. The Governor submits an annual report on administration, and the Union can give directions. The Tribes Advisory Council has up to 20 members, three-fourths of them tribal MLAs. The Governor may make regulations on land transfer, allotment and moneylending, and can modify or bar Acts of Parliament or the Legislature.

The Sixth Schedule covers Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Each has Autonomous Districts, and Autonomous Regions where different tribes live. A District Council has up to 30 members, of whom 4 are nominated by the Governor and the rest elected for five years. Councils make laws on land, forests, shifting cultivation, village administration, inheritance and marriage, and subject to Governor's assent they can collect taxes and set up courts. Examples include the Bodoland Territorial Council, the Karbi Anglong, Dima Hasao, Garo Hills, Khasi Hills, Jaintia Hills, Chakma, Lai and Mara Councils, and the Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council. The Sixth Schedule came from the Bordoloi Committee (1947). Ladakh has been demanding Sixth Schedule inclusion.

Related laws: PESA 1996 extends Panchayats to Scheduled Areas and gives powers to Gram Sabhas, and the Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises forest dwellers' rights. Other topics: the Dhebar Commission (1960) on Scheduled Areas and Tribes, the Bhuria Committee (1991), and the Lokur Committee on lists of Scheduled Tribes.

question: With reference to the Union Government, consider the following statements : 1 The Department of Revenue is responsible for the preparation of Union Budget that is presented to the Parliament. No amount can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India without the authorization from the Parliament of India. All the disbursements made from Public Account also need the authorization from the Parliament of India. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: The Union finances sit in three funds. The Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 266(1)) holds all revenues received, loans raised and loan recoveries. Money can be withdrawn from it only through an appropriation law, as Art. 266(3) and Art. 114(3) require. Charged expenditure (Art. 112(3)) is not voted but still comes from this fund. The Contingency Fund of India (Art. 267) is an imprest at the President's disposal for urgent unforeseen expenditure, and Parliament later approves and replenishes it. The Public Account (Art. 266(2)) holds money the government receives as a banker or trustee, such as provident funds, small savings, deposits and reserve funds. The executive operates it like a bank account, so withdrawals do not need parliamentary authorisation, although the CAG audits them. The Budget Division of the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance, prepares the Budget. The Department of Revenue deals with taxation. Elimination logic: statement 3 is wrong, which rules out (b) and (d). Statement 1 is wrong, which rules out (a). That leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is incorrect because the Department of Economic Affairs prepares the Budget, not the Department of Revenue.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is incorrect because Public Account payments do not need parliamentary authorisation.
Correct: only statement 2 holds. Consolidated Fund withdrawals need an appropriation law.
Wrong: statements 1 and 3 are both incorrect.
keyfact: Only Consolidated Fund withdrawals need parliamentary appropriation. The Public Account does not, and the Budget is prepared by the Department of Economic Affairs.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only: this combination fails because statement 1 is wrong. The Budget Division of the Department of Economic Affairs prepares the Budget. The Department of Revenue, with the CBDT and CBIC, manages tax policy and collection and advises on tax proposals, but it does not compile the Budget. The Finance Bill carries the tax proposals.

2 and 3 only: this combination fails because statement 3 is wrong. The Public Account under Art. 266(2) holds funds received as banker or trustee, such as provident funds and deposits. The executive withdraws from it without a parliamentary vote, though the CAG audits the account. Statement 2 in this option is correct.

2 only: the correct option. Art. 266(3) and Art. 114(3) require parliamentary authorisation, through an Appropriation Act, for any withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund. The Budget is prepared by the Department of Economic Affairs, and Public Account payments need no parliamentary approval. The Contingency Fund under Art. 267 is the third fund.

1, 2 and 3: this fails because statements 1 and 3 are both wrong. It would imply that the Department of Revenue prepares the Budget and that Parliament authorises Public Account payments. Neither is true. Only the Consolidated Fund requires parliamentary appropriation.
related: Art. 112 requires the annual financial statement (Budget) to be laid before Parliament.
Art. 266 creates the Consolidated Fund and Public Account. Art. 267 creates the Contingency Fund.
Charged expenditure is not voted by Parliament but is drawn from the Consolidated Fund.
The Budget Division of the Department of Economic Affairs prepares the Union Budget.
The Contingency Fund corpus is Rs 30,000 crore, held on behalf of the President by the Finance Secretary.
Only the Lok Sabha votes on demands for grants.
Art. 116 provides for a vote on account for interim spending.
The Public Accounts Committee examines CAG audit reports.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Budget is prepared by the Budget Division of the Department of Economic Affairs, not the Department of Revenue. The Union Budget (the annual financial statement under Art. 112) is presented by the Finance Minister. The Budget Division works under the Economic Affairs Secretary and runs the whole exercise, from issuing circulars to ministries to collecting estimates and compiling the documents. The Department of Revenue handles direct and indirect taxes through the CBDT and CBIC. Since 2017 the Budget has been presented on 1 February and the Railway Budget was merged into it. Parliament passes it through the Appropriation Bill and the Finance Bill.

2 — Correct: Art. 266(3) and Art. 114(3) bar any withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund without a law of appropriation. The Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 266(1)) receives all revenues, loans raised by the government and loan repayments. Voted expenditure needs Lok Sabha approval through demands for grants. Charged expenditure, such as the President's emoluments, judges' salaries, the CAG's salary and debt charges, is not voted but is still drawn from this fund. Parliament passes the Appropriation Act to authorise the withdrawals. A vote on account allows interim spending.

3 — Incorrect: The Public Account (Art. 266(2)) holds money received by the government as a banker or trustee, so it is not government revenue. Examples are provident funds, small savings, deposits, and the reserve funds of departments. Because the money belongs to others and must be repaid, the executive can withdraw it without a parliamentary appropriation, much like a bank customer. Parliament does not vote on it, but the CAG audits it. Its main sections are Small Savings, Provident Funds, Reserve Funds, Deposits and Advances, and Remittances.
summary: The answer is (c) 2 only. Withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund of India need parliamentary authorisation under Article 266(3) and Article 114(3). Statement 1 is wrong because the Department of Economic Affairs prepares the Budget, and statement 3 is wrong because Public Account disbursements need no parliamentary authorisation.
topic_notes: India has three funds. The Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 266(1)) receives all revenues, loans and loan recoveries. Withdrawals need an appropriation law (Art. 266(3), 114(3)). Expenditure on it is either charged (not voted, though it can be discussed) or voted by the Lok Sabha. The Public Account (Art. 266(2)) holds money received as banker or trustee, such as PF, small savings and deposits. The executive operates it without a parliamentary vote, and the CAG audits it. The Contingency Fund (Art. 267) is an imprest of Rs 500 crore, raised to Rs 30,000 crore in 2005. The President has it at his disposal for urgent unforeseen expenditure, and it is held by the Finance Secretary on his behalf. Parliament later approves and replenishes the amount. Budget process: the annual financial statement under Art. 112 is laid before Parliament. The Budget Division of the Department of Economic Affairs prepares it, and the Finance Minister presents it. Since 2017 it has been presented on 1 February and merged with the Railway Budget. Stages: presentation, general discussion, scrutiny by departmental committees, voting on demands for grants (only in the Lok Sabha), the Appropriation Bill, the Finance Bill, and then assent. The Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes to money bills. Related tools: vote on account (Art. 116), vote on credit, exceptional grant, supplementary grants, cut motions (policy, economy, token), and the guillotine. A Money Bill is defined in Art. 110, and the Speaker certifies it. The Public Accounts Committee examines CAG audit reports. The Finance Commission under Art. 280 recommends tax devolution. FRBM Act 2003 governs fiscal deficit targets. Article 113 covers procedure in Parliament for estimates.

question: Who/Which of the following is the custodian of the Constitution of India?
subject: Polity
detail: The Supreme Court of India (established 28 January 1950 under Part V, Chapter IV, Articles 124-147) is regarded as the custodian or guardian of the Constitution. It interprets the Constitution authoritatively (Article 141 makes its law binding on all courts in India), enforces Fundamental Rights through writs under Article 32 (called the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution by Dr B R Ambedkar), and exercises judicial review over legislative and executive acts (Articles 13, 32, 131-136, 226 for High Courts). In Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973) it laid down the Basic Structure doctrine, limiting Parliament's amending power under Article 368. The President only takes an oath to 'preserve, protect and defend the Constitution' (Article 60), but is a constitutional head, not its custodian. The Prime Minister heads the executive and is answerable to Parliament. The Lok Sabha Secretariat is a administrative body serving the House under the Speaker. Elimination logic: the custodian must be an independent body that checks all organs, and only the judiciary fits.
explanations: Wrong: the President takes an oath to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution (Article 60), but acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74) and cannot invalidate laws.
Wrong: the Prime Minister is head of the government, accountable to the Lok Sabha, and is part of the organ that the Constitution restrains, so cannot be its custodian.

Wrong: the Lok Sabha Secretariat is only an administrative support body functioning under the Speaker (Article 98 deals with the secretariat of Parliament), with no power over constitutional interpretation.
Correct: the Supreme Court is the guardian and final interpreter of the Constitution, using judicial review, writ jurisdiction (Article 32) and the Basic Structure doctrine.
keyfact: The Supreme Court of India is the guardian and final interpreter of the Constitution, through judicial review and Article 32.
option_notes: The President of India is the constitutional head of state (Article 52), elected indirectly by an Electoral College (Article 54) for a five-year term (Article 56). Executive power is vested in the President (Article 53), exercised through ministers. Can be removed by impeachment (Article 61). Takes oath before the Chief Justice of India (Article 60). Has ordinance power (Article 123), pardoning power (Article 72) and can return a bill, but by the 42nd and 44th Amendments must follow ministerial advice.

The Prime Minister is appointed by the President (Article 75) and heads the Council of Ministers, which aid and advise the President (Article 74). The PM is the real executive head in the parliamentary system, usually leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha, and the link between the President and the Cabinet (Article 78). Collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha applies under Article 75(3). The PM is 'first among equals' in the Cabinet.

The Lok Sabha Secretariat is the administrative arm of the lower House, functioning under the overall guidance of the Speaker. It is headed by the Secretary-General, a post of high rank appointed by the Speaker. Its role includes assisting in legislative business, committees, records and parliamentary research. Article 98 provides each House of Parliament a separate secretariat staff. It has no constitutional role in interpretation or protection.

The Supreme Court of India is the apex court and highest judicial authority, inaugurated on 28 January 1950 and housed in Delhi. Consists of the CJI and up to 33 other judges (34 total, by the 2019 amendment of the Act). It has original (Art 131), appellate (Arts 132-136), advisory (Art 143) and writ (Art 32) jurisdiction. It is a court of record (Art 129) and exercises judicial review, enforcing Fundamental Rights and the Constitution's supremacy.
related: Article 32 is the right to constitutional remedies, called the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution by Ambedkar.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) gave the Basic Structure doctrine.
Article 13 declares laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void, giving the basis for judicial review.
Article 141: the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India.
Article 143 gives the President advisory jurisdiction over the Supreme Court.
Article 124 establishes the Supreme Court; Article 226 gives High Courts writ power.
The Supreme Court has the CJI plus 33 other judges (sanctioned strength 34).
The NJAC (99th Amendment) was struck down in 2015 and the Collegium system continues.
summary: The answer is (d) The Supreme Court of India. The Supreme Court is the guardian and final interpreter of the Constitution, with the power of judicial review to strike down laws and executive actions that violate it.
topic_notes: The Indian Constitution gives the judiciary a unique role as guardian of the Constitution and protector of Fundamental Rights. Key powers include judicial review, derived from Articles 13, 32, 131, 136, 226 and 227, and the Court's ability to declare any law or executive action void if it conflicts with the Constitution. Landmark cases: Golaknath (1967) held Fundamental Rights cannot be amended; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the Basic Structure doctrine with a 7:6 verdict by a 13-judge bench; Minerva Mills (1980) struck down parts of the 42nd Amendment; Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Article 21; S R Bommai (1994) restricted misuse of Article 356; Indira Sawhney (1992) on reservations; Puttaswamy (2017) recognised privacy as a fundamental right. Independence of the judiciary is secured by security of tenure (judges removed only by impeachment-like process, Article 124(4)), fixed salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund, separation from the executive (Article 50) and the Collegium system for appointments (Second Judges case 1993; NJAC struck down in 2015 via the 99th Amendment case). Retirement age is 65 for SC judges and 62 for High Court judges. Article 142 allows 'complete justice' orders. Article 143 gives advisory jurisdiction. Public interest litigation expanded access to the Court. Other guardians: the Comptroller and Auditor General is the guardian of public purse; the Election Commission safeguards free elections (Art 324); Parliament is the supreme law-making body but subject to the Constitution. Dr Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.

ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. The Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme was launched during 1996-97 to provide loan assistance to poor farmers. The Command Area Development Programme was launched in 1974-75 for the development of water-use efficiency. , Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only fb) 2 only {c) Both 1 and 2 {d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The question tests India's irrigation-sector programmes. AIBP was launched in 1996-97 by the Ministry of Water Resources. It gave central loan assistance to states so that they could complete large irrigation projects that were ongoing and in an advanced stage of completion, which would create irrigation potential quickly. Its beneficiaries are projects and states, not individual poor farmers. It was later modified to give grants (a central grant component) for special-category states and drought-prone areas, and in 2015-16 it was folded into the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY). The Command Area Development (CAD) Programme began in 1974-75 as a centrally sponsored scheme. It aimed to bridge the gap between irrigation potential created and potential utilised, and to improve water-use efficiency through on-farm development works, the construction of field channels, land levelling, and the warabandi (rotational water distribution) system. It was later restructured as CADWM (Command Area Development and Water Management) in 2004 and also merged into PMKSY. Elimination logic: statement 1 describes AIBP as help for poor farmers, which is wrong because it is a state-level project-financing scheme. Statement 2 matches the standard facts. So only 2 is correct, which is option (b). Options (a), (c) and (d) all fail the test of statement 1 being wrong and statement 2 being right.
explanations: Wrong: (a) says only statement 1 is correct, but statement 1 misdescribes AIBP as loans to poor farmers, and statement 2 is actually correct.
Correct: statement 1 is false because AIBP assisted states with irrigation projects, while statement 2 is true because CAD was launched in 1974-75 for water-use efficiency.
Wrong: (c) would need statement 1 to be correct as well, but AIBP did not provide loan assistance to poor farmers.
Wrong: (d) says neither is correct, but statement 2 about CAD is factually right.
keyfact: AIBP (1996-97) = central assistance to states for completing irrigation projects; CAD (1974-75) = better water-use efficiency; both are now under PMKSY.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only, refers to AIBP. The Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme started in 1996-97 to give central assistance to states for completing ongoing major and medium irrigation projects in an advanced stage. It first took the form of loans, then grants for special-category states, drought-prone, tribal and flood-prone regions. It was administered by the Ministry of Water Resources, and in 2015-16 it was included in PMKSY. Its aim is to expand irrigation potential quickly, and it is not a farm-loan scheme for poor farmers.

Option (b), statement 2 only, refers to the CAD Programme. It was launched in 1974-75 as a centrally sponsored scheme to bridge the gap between irrigation potential created and utilised. It covers on-farm development works, field channels, land levelling, warabandi and the consolidation of holdings. Command Area Development Authorities carry out the work. It was renamed CADWM in 2004 and merged with PMKSY in 2015-16. This is the official correct answer.

Option (c), both 1 and 2, would require AIBP to be a loan scheme for poor farmers. In fact, AIBP is for project completion by states and CAD is for efficiency of water use. Both programmes are part of India's irrigation and water-management efforts, and both now fall under PMKSY, whose components include AIBP, Har Khet Ko Pani, Watershed Development and Per Drop More Crop. Combining the two statements gives a wrong result because statement 1 is flawed.

Option (d), neither 1 nor 2, would mean both programmes are described wrongly. That does not hold, because the CAD statement matches the facts, including the 1974-75 launch and the water-use efficiency objective. PMKSY, launched in 2015 with the slogan 'Har Khet Ko Pani', integrates AIBP, CADWM, watershed development and micro-irrigation efforts. Irrigation questions in UPSC often test scheme objectives and launch years.
related: AIBP was launched in 1996-97 for completing ongoing major and medium irrigation projects.
The CAD Programme began in 1974-75 and was restructured as CADWM in 2004.
PMKSY was launched in 2015 with the slogan 'Har Khet Ko Pani'.
PMKSY has four components: AIBP, Har Khet Ko Pani, Per Drop More Crop and Watershed Development.
Warabandi is a rotational system of water distribution in a canal command area.
A major irrigation project has a CCA above 10,000 ha; a minor one has under 2,000 ha.
Groundwater (tube wells and wells) is India's largest source of irrigation.
The Ministry of Jal Shakti was created in 2019 by merging the Water Resources and Drinking Water ministries.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: AIBP gave central loan assistance to states for completing irrigation projects, not loans to poor farmers. AIBP was launched in 1996-97 under the Ministry of Water Resources to accelerate incomplete major and medium irrigation projects, those in an advanced stage of completion, so that irrigation potential could be created fast. Initially it gave loans to states; later grants were added, especially for special-category states, drought-prone areas and the tribal regions. Minor irrigation projects in some regions were also included. Funding was routed through the states, and the programme was later subsumed within PMKSY (2015-16) as a component of its 'Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme' (AIBP) stream. Its purpose was to expand irrigation coverage and bring areas under assured irrigation, not to give individual credit.

2 — Correct: CAD Programme was launched in 1974-75 to improve irrigation utilisation and water-use efficiency. It was a centrally sponsored scheme begun in the Fifth Five-Year Plan period. Its main objectives were to bridge the gap between irrigation potential created and utilised, and to improve agricultural productivity through efficient water management. Activities covered the construction of field channels and drains, land levelling and shaping, the warabandi system of rotational water supply, and consolidation of holdings. Command Area Development Authorities were set up for projects. In 2004 it was restructured as the Command Area Development and Water Management (CADWM) programme, and from 2015-16 it was merged with PMKSY's 'Har Khet Ko Pani' component.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP) was launched in 1996-97 to give central loan assistance to states to complete incomplete major and medium irrigation projects, not to provide loans to poor farmers. The Command Area Development Programme was launched in 1974-75 to improve water-use efficiency.
topic_notes: Irrigation in India is largely a state subject (Entry 17, State List), but the Centre supports it through schemes and the Ministry of Jal Shakti, formed in 2019 by merging the Ministry of Water Resources with Drinking Water and Sanitation. Major irrigation projects have a culturable command area (CCA) above 10,000 ha, medium projects between 2,000 and 10,000 ha, and minor projects below 2,000 ha. The Fifth Plan period began the CAD programme in 1974-75 because of the large gap between irrigation potential created and utilised. Its tools include warabandi, the construction of field channels and drains, land levelling, and participatory irrigation management. AIBP, launched in 1996-97, aimed to speed up projects close to completion. After 2005 it carried a grant component for special-category states, the KBK districts of Odisha and drought-prone areas. In 2015 the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY) was launched to unify efforts under the slogan 'Har Khet Ko Pani', with four components: AIBP, Har Khet Ko Pani (source creation, distribution and ground water development), Per Drop More Crop (micro-irrigation) and Watershed Development. CADWM merged into the AIBP stream. Other related topics are the Command Area Development Authorities, Participatory Irrigation Management, water user associations, the National Water Policy (1987, 2002, 2012), the Central Water Commission (1945), the Central Ground Water Board, and micro-irrigation methods such as drip and sprinkler systems. The largest share of India's irrigation comes from groundwater, with tube wells the main source, followed by canals and tanks. The Indo-Gangetic plains, Punjab and Haryana have very high irrigation intensity. Future UPSC questions may ask about the sources of irrigation, the scheme objectives, the Ministry in charge, or the types of projects covered by each programme.

question: The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee is constituted under the
options: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999
subject: Science & Tech
detail: GEAC is the apex statutory body that appraises activities involving large-scale use of hazardous microorganisms and recombinants in research and industrial production from the environmental angle. It also appraises proposals for the release of genetically engineered (GE) organisms and products, including GM crops, into the environment, including experimental field trials. It functions under the 'Rules for the Manufacture, Use, Import, Export and Storage of Hazardous Micro-organisms, Genetically Engineered Organisms or Cells, 1989', notified under Sections 6, 8 and 25 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. It is chaired by the Special Secretary/Additional Secretary of MoEFCC, with a co-chair from the Department of Biotechnology (DBT). Other bodies under the same Rules include the Recombinant DNA Advisory Committee (RDAC), the Institutional Biosafety Committee (IBSC), the Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation (RCGM, under DBT), the State Biotechnology Coordination Committee (SBCC) and the District Level Committee (DLC). Elimination: the Food Safety Act, 2006 created FSSAI, the GI Act, 1999 deals with registration of GIs, and the Wildlife Act, 1972 deals with species and protected areas. None of these concerns GM organisms. GEAC's approval is needed for commercial release, as in the Bt cotton approval of 2002.
explanations: Incorrect: the FSS Act, 2006 set up FSSAI for food standards. GM food is regulated under it, but GEAC is not constituted under this Act.
Incorrect: the GI Act, 1999 governs registration and protection of geographical indications through the GI Registry in Chennai. It has nothing to do with GEAC.
Correct: GEAC is constituted under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, through the 1989 Rules notified by MoEFCC.
Incorrect: the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 protects wild animals and plants and provides for sanctuaries, national parks and the NBWL. It has no role in appraising GM organisms.
keyfact: GEAC (MoEFCC) is the apex body for GM organism approvals, set up under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 via the 1989 Rules.
option_notes: The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 consolidated earlier food laws, including the PFA Act 1954, and established the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), headquartered in Delhi. It sets science-based food standards and regulates manufacture, storage, distribution, sale and import of food. It is administered by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. FSSAI's chairperson is appointed by the Centre. GM food regulation falls under it, with the GEAC giving environmental clearance.

The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 came into force in 2003 and complies with the TRIPS Agreement. The GI Registry is in Chennai. A GI tag lasts 10 years and is renewable. Darjeeling Tea was the first Indian product registered, in 2004-05. The Act is administered by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 was enacted after the Bhopal gas tragedy (1984), under Article 253 to implement the 1972 Stockholm Conference decisions. It is an umbrella Act empowering the Centre to take measures to protect and improve the environment. Rules under it cover hazardous waste, EIA, noise pollution and GM organisms. Penalty for violation is up to 5 years' imprisonment or a fine up to Rs 1 lakh, or both.

The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 provides for protection of wild animals, birds and plants and for the management of their habitats. It created Schedules I-VI, with Schedule I giving the highest protection, and it provides for Sanctuaries, National Parks, Conservation and Community Reserves. It established the National Board for Wildlife and the Central Zoo Authority. The 2002 amendment created the NTCA, and the 2022 amendment reduced the Schedules to four.
related: GEAC functions under MoEFCC; its co-chair is from DBT.
The 1989 Rules were notified under Sections 6, 8 and 25 of the EPA, 1986.
Bt cotton, approved in 2002, is the only GM crop commercially grown in India.
Bt brinjal was put under a moratorium in 2010.
GM mustard (DMH-11) was cleared by GEAC in 2022; the Supreme Court delivered a split verdict in 2024.
Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000) regulates transboundary movement of living modified organisms.
RCGM, under DBT, monitors GM research; IBSC works at the institution level.
FSSAI regulates GM food under the FSS Act, 2006.
summary: The answer is (c) Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) is constituted under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) through the 1989 Rules framed under the EPA, 1986.
topic_notes: GEAC is the apex regulator for GM organisms in India. It sits in MoEFCC and is chaired by the Special Secretary/Additional Secretary of MoEFCC, with the DBT representative as co-chair. Its legal basis is the 1989 Rules under the EPA, 1986. The Rules also created other bodies. The IBSC works at the institutional level. The RCGM in DBT oversees research and monitoring. The SBCC and the DLC work at the state and district levels. The RDAC in DBT is advisory and reviews biotechnology developments. The GEAC approves commercial release of GM crops and large-scale use of hazardous microbes. It can also take punitive action under the EPA, 1986. Bt cotton, approved in 2002, is the only GM crop commercially cultivated in India. In 2022 GEAC cleared the environmental release of GM mustard (DMH-11), which was challenged in the Supreme Court. The Court delivered a split verdict in July 2024 and referred the matter to a larger bench, and it directed the Centre to frame a National Policy on GM crops. Bt brinjal was recommended by GEAC in 2009, but then Environment Minister Jairam Ramesh imposed a moratorium in 2010. Import of GM food needs GEAC approval and FSSAI regulation, and FSSAI's 2022 GM food regulations apply. India is a party to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000), under the Convention on Biological Diversity. It regulates transboundary movement of living modified organisms. India hosted COP-11 of the CBD and the MOP-6 of the Cartagena Protocol at Hyderabad in 2012. The Nagoya-Kuala Lumpur Supplementary Protocol covers liability and redress. The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 is another related law, with NBA at Chennai.

ocr: In the Mekong-Ganga Cooperation, an initiative of six countries, which of the following is/are not a participant/ participants? 1. Bangladesh 2. Cambodia 3. China 4. Myanmar 5. Thailand 22 B-AQN-O-JUA/63A Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 only (b) 2, 3 and 4 (o} i and 3 (d) 1,2 and 5
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Mekong-Ganga Cooperation (MGC) was launched on 10 November 2000 at Vientiane, Laos. Its six members are India, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam. It focuses on four areas of cooperation: tourism, culture, education, and transport and communication. It is named after the Ganga and the Mekong, both rivers of civilisational importance. The MGC is separate from the Mekong River Commission (MRC), whose members are Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam. China and Myanmar are only dialogue partners in the MRC. China is a Mekong riparian state, which causes confusion, but it is not an MGC member; it runs its own Lancang-Mekong Cooperation (LMC, 2016). Bangladesh is a Ganga riparian and a BIMSTEC member, but it is not in the MGC. The question asks which are NOT participants. Cambodia, Myanmar and Thailand are members, so options (b) and (d) fail because they include members. Option (a) fails because it omits China. Only Bangladesh and China are outside the group, so (c) is correct. The MGC also has a Quick Impact Projects (QIPs) component run by India for the Mekong states.
explanations: Wrong: it names only Bangladesh, but China is also a non-participant, so the list is incomplete.
Wrong: Cambodia, Myanmar and China are listed, but Cambodia and Myanmar are MGC members.
Correct: Bangladesh and China are the only two of the five countries that are not MGC members.
Wrong: Cambodia and Thailand are MGC members, so including them as non-participants is incorrect.
keyfact: MGC = India + Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam (2000); China and Bangladesh are not members.
option_notes: Option (a) 'Bangladesh only' would be right only if China were a member. Bangladesh sits in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta and belongs to BIMSTEC, SAARC, BBIN and IORA. It is not in the MGC. Its capital is Dhaka. It shares a land border with India of about 4,096 km, the longest India has with any neighbour. Its Padma River is the main distributary of the Ganga. It was created in 1971 after the Liberation War.

Option (b) '2, 3 and 4' lists Cambodia, China and Myanmar. Cambodia and Myanmar are MGC members, and China is not. Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam are the five Mekong members, often grouped as CLMVT. China is the upstream Mekong state and operates the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation (2016). The Mekong is about 4,350 km long and flows through six countries to the South China Sea.

Option (c) '1 and 3' is Bangladesh and China, the two non-members. The MGC has six members: India, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam. It was launched in Vientiane in November 2000, and its areas are tourism, culture, education and transport and communication. It complements India's Look East and Act East Policy and ASEAN engagement. India offers Quick Impact Projects to the Mekong countries under it.

Option (d) '1, 2 and 5' contains Bangladesh, which is not a member, plus Cambodia and Thailand, which are. It is therefore wrong. Thailand and Cambodia are both in ASEAN, and Thailand is also in BIMSTEC. The Mekong River Commission (1995) includes Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam as members. Its secretariat is in Vientiane and Phnom Penh. The MRC works on water-resource management of the lower Mekong basin.
related: MGC was launched in November 2000 at Vientiane, Laos.
MGC covers tourism, culture, education and transport and communication.
MGC members: India, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam.
The Mekong River Commission has four members: Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, Vietnam.
China's Lancang-Mekong Cooperation was launched in 2016.
BIMSTEC includes Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Nepal, Bhutan.
The Mekong rises in the Tibetan Plateau and drains into the South China Sea.
The India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway links Moreh to Mae Sot.
statements: 1 — Correct (as a non-participant): Bangladesh is not an MGC member. Bangladesh is a Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta country and belongs to BIMSTEC, SAARC, BBIN and IORA. It is not among the six MGC countries, which pair India with the five Mekong states. Its Bay of Bengal location often leads students to assume it is in the MGC. Its main groupings are BIMSTEC (1997, with Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Bhutan, Nepal and Myanmar), SAARC (1985, Dhaka summit) and BBIN (the motor vehicles agreement of 2015). Dhaka is the BIMSTEC secretariat location (permanent secretariat).

2 — Incorrect (it is a participant): Cambodia is a founding MGC member. Cambodia is a Mekong riparian state and a member of ASEAN (joined 1999), the Mekong River Commission and the CLMV group. Its capital is Phnom Penh. The Angkor Wat temple complex, a UNESCO site, reflects strong Indian cultural links. The Archaeological Survey of India has restored Ta Prohm and parts of Angkor Wat. Cambodia is also part of the Greater Mekong Subregion (GMS) programme backed by the ADB and a participant in the India-ASEAN Mekong-related Quick Impact Projects.

3 — Correct (as a non-participant): China is not an MGC member even though the Mekong (Lancang) rises in the Tibetan Plateau and flows through Yunnan. China instead leads the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation (LMC), launched in 2016 with the six countries China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam. China is a dialogue partner in the Mekong River Commission. It is also a member of the GMS programme. The upstream dams on the Lancang are a major source of concern for the downstream states.

4 — Incorrect (it is a participant): Myanmar is an MGC member. It is the land bridge between India and Southeast Asia. Myanmar is also a member of BIMSTEC and ASEAN (1997), and a GMS participant. The Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project (Kolkata-Sittwe-Paletwa-Mizoram) and the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway are key connectivity projects. Myanmar is only a dialogue partner of the MRC, not a full member.

5 — Incorrect (it is a participant): Thailand is an MGC member. It is also a founding ASEAN member (1967), a BIMSTEC member and a full MRC member. The India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway (about 1,400 km, Moreh to Mae Sot) aims to link India with Thailand by road. Thailand is a treaty ally of the US and a key partner in India's Act East Policy. Its capital is Bangkok.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3. The Mekong-Ganga Cooperation (MGC) has six members: India and the five Mekong countries Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam. Bangladesh and China are not members, so statements 1 and 3 are the ones that are 'not' participants.
topic_notes: The Mekong-Ganga Cooperation (MGC) was launched on 10 November 2000 at Vientiane, Laos. Its six members are India, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam. It focuses on tourism, culture, education and transport and communication. The Vientiane Declaration set up the initiative, and an MGC Plan of Action covers 2016-2018 and later years. India funds Quick Impact Projects (QIPs) in the Mekong states. The MGC is a way of connecting two civilisational rivers and strengthening India's Look East (now Act East) Policy. The Mekong is about 4,350 km long, rises in the Tibetan Plateau (where it is called Lancang), and flows through China, Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam before reaching the South China Sea. Key groupings to compare: (1) Mekong River Commission (1995), whose members are Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam, with China and Myanmar as dialogue partners; (2) the Greater Mekong Subregion (GMS) programme (1992, ADB-backed), which includes China (Yunnan and Guangxi), Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam; (3) the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation (2016, China-led); (4) BIMSTEC (1997), which links South Asia and Southeast Asia, with Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Nepal and Bhutan as members; (5) ASEAN (1967), with ten members; (6) the Mekong-Japan and Mekong-US/Korea partnerships. CLMV refers to Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and Vietnam. Connectivity projects UPSC may ask about: the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway, the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project, and the proposed extension to Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam. Possible angles are river origins, riparian countries, dam disputes, and which grouping a country belongs to.

question: Basel II] Accord’ or simply ‘Basel IH’, often seen in the news, seeks to
options: develop national strategies for the conservation and sustainable use of biological diversity
improve banking sector’s ability to deal with financial and economic stress and improve risk management
reduce the greenhouse gas emissions but places a heavier burden on developed countries
transfer technology from developed countries to poor countries to enable them to replace the use of chiorofluorocarbons in refrigeration with harmless chemicals
subject: Environment
detail: Basel norms are global banking standards issued by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, which was set up in 1974 under the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), headquartered in Basel, Switzerland. Basel I (1988) introduced minimum capital against credit risk. Basel II (2004) rested on three pillars: minimum capital, supervisory review and market discipline. Basel III was agreed in 2010-11 after the 2008 crisis. It raises the quality and quantity of capital (Common Equity Tier 1), adds a capital conservation buffer and a countercyclical buffer, introduces a leverage ratio, and adds liquidity standards (Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio). It also tightens rules on systemically important banks. The RBI has been implementing it in India in phases. Elimination: option (a) describes the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), whose Article 6 covers national strategies. Option (c) describes the Kyoto Protocol, with its common but differentiated responsibilities. Option (d) describes the Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting substances. Only (b) concerns banking.
explanations: Wrong. National strategies for conserving and sustainably using biodiversity come from the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992), not from Basel norms.
Correct. Basel III strengthens bank capital, liquidity and leverage so that banks can withstand financial and economic stress, and it improves risk management and governance.
Wrong. Cutting greenhouse gas emissions with heavier burdens on developed countries describes the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the UNFCCC principle of common but differentiated responsibilities.
Wrong. Technology transfer to help poorer countries replace CFCs is a feature of the Montreal Protocol (1987), which has a Multilateral Fund for this purpose.
keyfact: Basel III (BCBS, post-2008) strengthens bank capital, liquidity and leverage to withstand financial stress and improve risk management.
option_notes: The Convention on Biological Diversity was opened at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and came into force in 1993. Its three goals are conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair sharing of benefits from genetic resources. Article 6 requires national biodiversity strategies and action plans (NBSAPs). The Cartagena Protocol covers biosafety and the Nagoya Protocol covers access and benefit sharing. The Aichi Targets were followed by the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022). India's Biological Diversity Act is from 2002.

This is the correct option. Basel III is a set of BCBS reforms from 2010-11 that followed the 2008 crisis. It sets a minimum CET1 ratio of 4.5 percent, a total capital ratio of 8 percent, a 2.5 percent capital conservation buffer, a countercyclical buffer of up to 2.5 percent, a leverage ratio, LCR and NSFR. It also adds extra requirements for global systemically important banks (G-SIBs). The RBI adopted it for Indian banks in phases from 2013.

The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in 1997 and came into force in 2005. It set binding emission reduction targets for developed (Annex I) countries, based on common but differentiated responsibilities. It introduced flexibility mechanisms: emissions trading, the Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation. Its first commitment period ran 2008-12 and the Doha Amendment covered 2013-20. The Paris Agreement (2015) later replaced its approach with nationally determined contributions.

The Montreal Protocol (1987) phases out ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs, halons and HCFCs. It was adopted under the Vienna Convention (1985) and has achieved universal ratification. Developing countries get a longer phase-out schedule and financial and technical help through the Multilateral Fund. The Kigali Amendment (2016) added the phase-down of HFCs, which are potent greenhouse gases but not ozone-depleting.
related: BCBS was established in 1974 and sits under the Bank for International Settlements in Basel, Switzerland.
Basel III was a response to the 2008 global financial crisis.
Basel III liquidity measures are the LCR and the NSFR.
India's D-SIBs are SBI, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank.
Basel II rested on three pillars: minimum capital, supervisory review and market discipline.
The Financial Stability Board was created by the G20 in 2009 and is based in Basel.
Basel norms are not legally binding; national regulators such as the RBI implement them.
summary: The answer is (b). Basel III is a global regulatory framework from the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) that makes banks stronger against financial and economic stress and improves risk management. It was drawn up after the 2008 global financial crisis.
topic_notes:
Basel norms are international banking regulations from the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), formed in 1974 by G10 central bank governors and hosted by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) in Basel. The standards are not legally binding, and each country implements them through its own regulator, which in India is the RBI.

Basel I (1988) set a minimum capital of 8 percent of risk-weighted assets, mainly against credit risk. Basel II (2004) added operational and market risk and the three-pillar structure. Basel III (2010-11) responded to the 2008 crisis with these main elements:
- Higher and better-quality capital, centred on Common Equity Tier 1.
- A capital conservation buffer of 2.5 percent and a countercyclical buffer.
- A non-risk-based leverage ratio.
- Liquidity standards: the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (30-day stress) and the Net Stable Funding Ratio (one-year horizon).
- Extra loss-absorbency for G-SIBs and D-SIBs.

In India, the RBI began phasing in Basel III in 2013. Indian banks must keep a minimum total capital ratio of 9 percent, higher than the Basel minimum of 8 percent, plus a capital conservation buffer of 2.5 percent. The RBI also identifies domestic systemically important banks (D-SIBs): SBI, HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank. The final reforms, often called Basel IV or the Basel III endgame, revise the standardised approaches to credit risk and operational risk and add an output floor.

Other angles for UPSC: the Financial Stability Board (FSB), the BIS as the central banks' bank, Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital, risk-weighted assets, the Prompt Corrective Action framework, and the global bodies that govern finance (IMF, World Bank, FATF).

ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. The winds which blow between 30° N and 60° § latitudes through- out the year are known as westerlies, 2. The moist air masses that cause winter rains in North-Western region of India are part of westerlies. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa) 1 only (b) 2 only (co) Both 1 and 2 (da) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Geography
detail: Westerlies are the prevailing winds that blow from the subtropical high-pressure belts (about 30°-35°) toward the sub-polar low-pressure belts (about 60°-65°) in both hemispheres. They blow from the south-west in the Northern Hemisphere and from the north-west in the Southern Hemisphere, because of the Coriolis effect. The statement's range of '30° N to 60° S' is geographically meaningless, since it would take in the whole tropics and the equator and mix two hemispheres. It is also wrong to say they blow in that range 'throughout the year', because the belts shift with the sun and the pattern is described per hemisphere. Westerlies are strongest in the Southern Hemisphere, where there is little land, giving the Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties and Shrieking Sixties. In winter the subtropical jet stream shifts south of the Himalaya. It steers extratropical cyclones from the Mediterranean region, called western disturbances, across Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan into north-west India. They bring winter rain and snow to Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh, which is vital for the rabi wheat crop. Elimination: once statement 1 is rejected for its faulty latitude range, only (b) remains.
explanations: Wrong: it accepts statement 1, which is incorrect because of the faulty latitude range of 30° N to 60° S, and it rejects statement 2, which is correct.
Correct: statement 1 is wrong because of its geographic error, and statement 2 is right because western disturbances, which are part of the westerlies, bring winter rain to north-west India.
Wrong: this needs statement 1 to be true, but the westerlies do not blow between 30° N and 60° S as a single belt.
Wrong: statement 2 is correct, so 'neither' cannot be the answer.
keyfact: Westerlies blow from subtropical highs to sub-polar lows (about 30°-60° in each hemisphere), and western disturbances carried by them give north-west India its winter rain.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would mean the westerlies blow between 30° N and 60° S, which is not correct. The westerlies are two separate belts, one in each hemisphere, between about 30° and 60° latitude. They blow from the subtropical high-pressure belts toward the sub-polar lows. The Southern Hemisphere belt is stronger because of the vast oceans and the lack of land barriers, and it gives the Roaring Forties. In the Northern Hemisphere the belt is more irregular because of land masses and mountains. They are the prevailing winds of the mid-latitudes.

Option (b), '2 only', is the official answer. It reflects the fact that western disturbances, which are part of the westerly circulation, cause winter rain in north-west India. They originate over the Mediterranean region and move east on the subtropical westerly jet stream. They bring rain and snow, mainly between December and March, to Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, western Uttar Pradesh and the Himalayan states. The rain helps rabi crops, especially wheat. This winter precipitation is distinct from the monsoon rain of the summer season.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', would need the latitude description in statement 1 to be right, which it is not. Properly, the westerlies are located between 30°-60° in each hemisphere. The idea of a single belt from 30° N to 60° S would include the equatorial region, the trade-wind belts and the doldrums, where the winds are very different. Statement 2 is right, but that alone does not make both correct. It is therefore wrong.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', would mean western disturbances are not part of the westerlies, which is wrong. Western disturbances are extratropical storms carried by the westerlies and the subtropical jet stream into the Indian subcontinent. In the Indian winter, the jet stream splits around the Tibetan Plateau, and its northern branch runs along the Himalaya while the southern branch passes south of it, steering these disturbances. Statement 2 is therefore correct, which makes this option wrong.
related: Westerlies blow between about 30°-60° latitude in both hemispheres, not as one belt.
Western disturbances come from the Mediterranean region and bring winter rain to north-west India.
Trade winds blow toward the equator from about 30° latitude; Northern Hemisphere ones are north-easterly.
Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties and Shrieking Sixties are strong Southern Hemisphere westerlies.
The subtropical westerly jet shifts north of the Himalaya in June, marking the monsoon's onset.
Western disturbances help rabi crops, especially wheat, in north India.
Winter rain in Tamil Nadu comes from the north-east (retreating) monsoon, not western disturbances.
The Ferrel cell lies between 30° and 60° and contains the westerlies.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Westerlies blow between about 30° and 60° latitude in each hemisphere (N and S separately), not between 30° N and 60° S, and they are not a single belt spanning the equator. Facts: they flow from the subtropical highs (horse latitudes) to the sub-polar lows. They are south-westerly in the Northern Hemisphere and north-westerly in the Southern Hemisphere. They are stronger and steadier over the oceans of the Southern Hemisphere, where they are called the Roaring Forties (40°S), Furious Fifties (50°S) and Shrieking Sixties (60°S). They bring cyclonic weather and moderate, rainy climates to the west coasts of continents, such as north-west Europe, British Columbia, Chile and Tasmania/New Zealand. Sailors used them for the eastward passage across oceans.

2 — Correct: The moist air masses behind India's winter rain in the north-west are part of the westerlies, carried as western disturbances. Facts: western disturbances are extratropical cyclonic storms that originate over the Mediterranean, Caspian and Black Sea region. They travel east on the subtropical westerly jet and reach India from about December to March. They bring rain in the plains and snow in the Himalaya, and they are very important for rabi crops such as wheat, barley and mustard. Heavy western disturbances can cause floods, cold waves and cloudy weather. They are different from the tropical cyclones of the monsoon and post-monsoon seasons, and also from the Northeast (retreating) monsoon that gives winter rain to Tamil Nadu.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. Statement 2 is correct because the moist air masses that bring winter rain to north-western India are part of the westerlies, which reach India as western disturbances. Statement 1 is wrong because the westerlies blow between roughly 30° and 60° latitude in each hemisphere, not between 30° N and 60° S.
topic_notes: Planetary winds are the permanent winds that blow over large parts of the globe, caused by the pressure belts and the Earth's rotation (Coriolis force). The three main systems are the trade winds, the westerlies and the polar easterlies. Trade winds blow from the subtropical highs (about 30°) toward the equatorial low (the ITCZ), as north-easterlies in the Northern Hemisphere and south-easterlies in the Southern Hemisphere. Westerlies blow from the subtropical highs toward the sub-polar lows (about 60°), as south-westerlies in the north and north-westerlies in the south. Polar easterlies flow from the polar highs toward the sub-polar lows. Ferrel's law says that winds are deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. The three-cell model has the Hadley cell (0°-30°), the Ferrel cell (30°-60°) and the Polar cell (60°-90°). The westerlies lie in the Ferrel cell. Southern Hemisphere westerlies are called the Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties and Shrieking Sixties. Western disturbances are important for India. They are extratropical storms from the Mediterranean region that bring winter rain to north-west India, helping rabi crops, especially wheat. They are steered by the subtropical westerly jet stream. The jet stream moves north of the Himalaya in summer, around June, which marks the onset of the monsoon in India. Other related ideas include the tropical easterly jet in summer, the Somali jet, the polar front, mid-latitude cyclones and the climate types on the west coasts of continents (Mediterranean and west-coast marine). Local winds such as the loo, mango showers, the nor'westers (Kalbaisakhi) and the Chinook, Foehn and Mistral are also frequently asked. UPSC often asks about the direction and latitude ranges of winds, the effects on climate, and the Indian examples.

ocr: With reference to Indian Ocean Rim Association for Regional Cooperation (IOR-ARC)’, consider the following statements : 1. It was established very recently in response to incidents of piracy and accidents of oil spills. 2. It is an alliance meant for maritime security only. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa) 1 only (6) 2 only (c} Both 1 and 2 (@) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Geography
detail: The Indian Ocean Rim Association for Regional Cooperation was launched in March 1997 at Mauritius, following an initiative by Mauritius and South Africa after the 1995 Port Louis meeting and Nelson Mandela's 1995 visit to India. It is an inter-governmental organisation aiming at sustainable growth and balanced development of the region and its member states, so its core is economic, trade and investment cooperation. It was not created in response to piracy or oil spills, so statement 1 fails on both the timing and the cause. It is also not an alliance, since it is a cooperation forum without any military or collective-defence function. Statement 2 fails because the mandate is wide. The priority areas are maritime safety and security; trade and investment facilitation; fisheries management; disaster risk management; academic, science and technology cooperation; and tourism and cultural exchanges. The Blue Economy and Women's Economic Empowerment are cross-cutting priorities. The Secretariat is at Ebene, Mauritius. Elimination logic: both statements contain absolutes or wrong origins (very recently, only), and UPSC commonly uses such words as traps. Rejecting either statement leads to (d), because each is independently wrong.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Statement 1 is incorrect because the body dates to 1997 and was created for economic cooperation, not as a response to piracy or oil spills.
(b) Wrong: Statement 2 is incorrect because IORA covers six priority areas and is not an alliance or a maritime-security-only body.
(c) Wrong: Neither statement is correct, so they cannot both be right.
(d) Correct: Both statements fail, since the body is old (1997), is economic in orientation, and covers many areas beyond security.
keyfact: IORA (ex-IOR-ARC) was founded in 1997 at Mauritius as an economic cooperation forum; maritime security is only one of six priorities, so the answer is (d).
option_notes: Option (a) 'Statement 1 only' would imply IORA was a recent response to piracy and oil spills. In fact IORA was formed in 1997 as IOR-ARC, with Mauritius, India, South Africa, Australia, Kenya, Oman, Singapore, Sri Lanka, Tanzania, Yemen, Madagascar, Indonesia, Malaysia and Mozambique among the early members. It was renamed in 2013. Its purpose is trade, investment and sustainable development, so piracy and oil spills were never its founding reason.

Option (b) 'Statement 2 only' would imply IORA is a maritime-security alliance. In reality it is a cooperation forum with no military function. Maritime safety and security is just one of six priority areas, alongside trade, fisheries, disaster risk management, academic and S&T cooperation, and tourism and culture. Its Blue Economy focus was highlighted at the 2014 Perth meeting and the 2017 Jakarta Concord, which also stressed maritime safety.

Option (c) 'Both 1 and 2' is wrong because neither statement holds. Decision-making in IORA is by consensus, and the Charter excludes bilateral and contentious issues. The Council of Ministers meets annually, the Committee of Senior Officials meets regularly, and the Chair rotates every two years. India chaired 2011-13 and again 2023-25 as Vice-Chair/Chair rotation proceeds. The Secretariat is in Mauritius.

Option (d) 'Neither 1 nor 2' is correct. IORA, founded 1997 and renamed in 2013, is a 23-member inter-governmental organisation with 11 dialogue partners. It promotes trade, investment, blue economy, fisheries, disaster management, tourism and academic cooperation, plus maritime safety. Its Secretariat is at Ebene, Mauritius, and it was a key platform for the Indian Ocean Conference debates and Indonesia's 2017 Jakarta Concord.
related: IORA was founded in 1997 in Mauritius as IOR-ARC; renamed IORA in 2013.
IORA Secretariat is at Ebene, Mauritius.
IORA has six priority areas, with Blue Economy as a cross-cutting theme.
IONS (2008) is a naval forum, distinct from IORA.
Jakarta Concord 2017 was adopted at the first IORA Leaders' Summit.
SAGAR was announced by PM Modi in 2015 at Mauritius.
IORA decisions are by consensus; bilateral issues are excluded.
Djibouti Code of Conduct deals with piracy in the western Indian Ocean.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: IOR-ARC was formed in 1997, not very recently, and its purpose was regional economic cooperation, not a reaction to piracy or oil spills. Facts: The idea arose from Nelson Mandela's 1995 visit to India and the Mauritius initiative. It was formally launched in Mauritius in March 1997 with 14 founding members. It was renamed IORA in 2013. Piracy off Somalia became a major concern only after 2005, and IORA treats it under maritime safety and security. Membership has grown to 23 states, with 11 dialogue partners.

2 — Incorrect: It is not an alliance and is not for maritime security only. Facts: IORA is a multilateral, consensus-based forum for economic and technical cooperation. Its six priority areas are maritime safety and security, trade and investment facilitation, fisheries management, disaster risk management, academic and science and technology cooperation, and tourism and cultural exchanges.
