Tropical deciduous forests are the most widespread. The moist deciduous belt is dominated by teak and sal, with sal in the wetter east and teak in the drier peninsular regions. Dry deciduous forests have teak, sal, peepal, neem and tendu, and merge toward thorn scrub in the west. Teak is Tectona grandis; the largest teak forests are in Madhya Pradesh (Bastar and Satpura), Maharashtra, Karnataka and Kerala (Nilambur has a famous teak plantation and the world's oldest teak plantation, Conolly's Plot). Mangroves such as Sundari (Heritiera fomes) dominate the Sundarbans delta forests. The India State of Forest Report (ISFR), published by the Forest Survey of India (Dehradun) every two years, gives forest cover; the National Forest Policy 1988 targets 33% of land area under forest and tree cover, and 66% in hill regions. Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest area; Mizoram has the highest percentage of forest cover. Also remember social forestry, Joint Forest Management, the Forest Rights Act 2006 and CAMPA.

question: Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action’, often seen in the news, is
options: a strategy to tackle the regional terrorism, an outcome of a meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization
a plan of action for sustainable economic growth in the Asia-Pacific Region, an outcome of the deliberations of the Asia-Pacific Economic Forum
an agenda for women’s empowerment, an outcome of a World Conference convened by the United Nations
a strategy to combat wildlife trafficking, a declaration of the East Asia Summit
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (BPfA) was adopted unanimously by 189 governments at the Fourth World Conference on Women, Beijing, 4-15 September 1995. It is regarded as the most comprehensive global policy framework on gender equality. It identifies 12 critical areas of concern: women and poverty; education and training; health; violence against women; armed conflict; economy; power and decision-making; institutional mechanisms; human rights; media; environment; and the girl child. The Commission on the Status of Women (CSW), a functional commission of ECOSOC, monitors its implementation, with review events at 5-year intervals (Beijing+5, +10, +15, +20 in 2015, +25 in 2020). Earlier world conferences on women were Mexico City 1975, Copenhagen 1980 and Nairobi 1985. The 1995 conference is also famous for Hillary Clinton's line 'women's rights are human rights'. Elimination logic: the SCO deals with regional security and terrorism through RATS (Tashkent), APEC deals with trade and investment, and the East Asia Summit is a strategic forum; none issued a document with this name. The word 'Beijing' is merely the venue, so do not link it to Chinese-led groupings.
explanations: Incorrect: The SCO's counter-terrorism work is done through the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS), not the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action.
Incorrect: APEC's growth documents are the Bogor Goals (1994) and the Putrajaya Vision 2040; the BPfA is not an APEC outcome.
Correct: The BPfA is the women's empowerment agenda adopted at the UN Fourth World Conference on Women in Beijing in 1995.
Incorrect: Wildlife trafficking is not the subject of this declaration; the East Asia Summit did not adopt it, and the East Asia Summit did adopt a separate statement on wildlife trafficking in 2015.
keyfact: Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action = UN Fourth World Conference on Women (1995), the global agenda for gender equality with 12 critical areas.
option_notes: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation was founded in 2001 as a successor to the Shanghai Five (1996). Its members include China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, India and Pakistan (both joined in 2017) and Iran (2023). Its secretariat is in Beijing and RATS is in Tashkent. It focuses on the 'three evils': terrorism, separatism and extremism.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation was founded in 1989 in Canberra. It is a forum for trade and investment liberalisation, not a treaty body, with 21 member economies. India is not a member. Its secretariat is in Singapore. The Bogor Goals (1994) set free trade targets for developed members by 2010 and developing members by 2020.

The Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action is the 1995 UN agenda for gender equality, adopted by 189 countries. It has 12 critical areas of concern. The follow-up is by the CSW under ECOSOC, and UN Women (formed 2010) leads the follow-up and review work. India took part and endorsed it.

The East Asia Summit was launched in 2005 in Kuala Lumpur. It has 18 members, including the 10 ASEAN states, India, China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand, Russia and the US. It is a leaders-led forum for strategic, political and economic dialogue, with ASEAN at its centre. It is not a wildlife body; wildlife trade is covered by CITES (1973).
related: The Beijing conference was the UN Fourth World Conference on Women, 1995.
The BPfA has 12 critical areas of concern.
The CSW monitors the BPfA and operates under ECOSOC.
CEDAW was adopted in 1979 and came into force in 1981.
UN Women was created in 2010 by merging four UN entities.
The first World Conference on Women was held in Mexico City in 1975.
SDG 5 is gender equality.
The Women's Reservation Act 2023 is the 106th Constitutional Amendment.
summary: The correct answer is (c). The Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action is the agenda for women's empowerment and gender equality adopted at the UN Fourth World Conference on Women, held in Beijing in September 1995.
topic_notes: The Beijing conference of 1995 was the largest UN gathering on women to that date, with a parallel NGO Forum at Huairou. The BPfA built on CEDAW (adopted 1979, in force 1981), often called the international bill of rights for women. India ratified CEDAW in 1993 with some declarations. The BPfA introduced gender mainstreaming as the main strategy and called for national action plans and gender-sensitive budgeting. Key UN bodies: the Commission on the Status of Women (set up 1946, 45 members); UN Women (created 2010 by merging UNIFEM, INSTRAW, OSAGI and DAW), headquartered in New York; and the Gender Inequality Index in the UNDP's Human Development Report. The Sustainable Development Goals include Goal 5 on gender equality. Other UN conferences to remember: Rio Earth Summit 1992, Cairo ICPD 1994 (population and development), Copenhagen Social Summit 1995, and Habitat conferences. Indian context: the National Policy for Empowerment of Women 2001, the 73rd and 74th Amendments with one-third reservation for women in local bodies, Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (2015), and the Women's Reservation Act 2023 (106th Amendment) reserving one-third of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats. Global indices: the WEF Global Gender Gap Report and the Gender Development Index. UPSC often asks to match declarations to bodies or conferences.

ocr: “Each day is more or less the same, the morning is clear and bright with a sea breeze; as the Sun climbs high in the sky, heat mounts up, dark clouds form, then rain comes with thunder and lightning. But rain is soon over.” Which of the following regions is described in the above passage? (a) Savannah {b) Equatorial (} Monsoon (dj Mediterranean
subject: Geography
detail: The equatorial climate (Af in Koeppen's scheme) lies roughly within 5°-10° N and S of the equator, as in the Amazon basin, the Congo basin and the East Indies. Its main feature is uniformity: every day is much like the last. Temperatures stay high all year (mean about 27°C), with a very small annual range (about 2-3°C) and a larger diurnal range. Intense insolation heats the ground in the morning, and moist air rises. Convection then builds cumulonimbus clouds by afternoon, giving heavy convectional rain with thunder and lightning, usually in the late afternoon and soon over. Annual rainfall exceeds 250 cm and is spread through the year. Humidity is high and the air is sultry. Elimination: the Savannah has distinct wet and dry seasons. The Monsoon region has seasonal wind reversal and a rainy season that lasts for months. The Mediterranean has hot dry summers and mild wet winters, with winter rain from westerlies. Only the equatorial region has daily repeated convectional rain with no seasonal change.
explanations: Wrong. The Savannah (Aw) has a distinct dry season and a wet summer season. The passage describes the same weather every day, with no seasons.
Correct. Sea breeze, a bright morning, rising heat, afternoon convectional clouds, and a short thunderstorm every day describe equatorial weather, which is uniform all year.
Wrong. The Monsoon climate is defined by seasonal reversal of winds and a marked rainy season. Rain is not a short daily event, and the year divides into hot, wet and cool seasons.
Wrong. The Mediterranean climate has dry, sunny summers and rain in winter from the westerlies. It has no daily thunderstorms, and its rain comes from frontal or cyclonic systems.
keyfact: Equatorial climate: the same weather every day, with a hot morning, afternoon convectional thunderstorm, rain above 250 cm, and an annual range of only 2-3°C.
option_notes: Savannah (tropical wet and dry, Aw) lies between about 5° and 20° latitude on either side of the equator, in the Sudan region of Africa, the Llanos, the Campos and northern Australia. It has tall grass with scattered trees, a dry winter and a wet summer, and rainfall of 75-150 cm. It is known for wildlife and is called the 'Big Game Country'. Its climate is the transition between the equatorial and desert zones.

Equatorial (Af) climate lies within about 10° N and S of the equator, in the Amazon, the Congo basin and Malaysia and Indonesia. Temperatures are about 27°C all year with a very small annual range, and rainfall exceeds 250 cm and falls daily as convectional rain in the afternoon. The vegetation is dense evergreen rainforest with multiple layers and high biodiversity. Its soils are leached lateritic soils.

Monsoon (Am) climate is found in India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Southeast Asia and northern Australia. Its key feature is the seasonal reversal of winds: the southwest monsoon brings summer rain and the northeast monsoon brings winter wind. The year has hot, wet and cool dry seasons. Rainfall depends on relief, and the vegetation is tropical deciduous. Agriculture depends heavily on the monsoon, which gives rise to the saying that the Indian budget is a gamble on it.

Mediterranean climate (Cs) occurs on the western sides of continents between 30° and 45° latitude: around the Mediterranean Sea, California, central Chile, the Cape region of South Africa and southwest Australia. Summers are hot and dry under subtropical high pressure, and winters are mild and rainy from the westerlies. Vegetation is evergreen, drought-resistant scrub, and the region is famous for citrus fruit and grapes (viticulture) and is called the 'orchard of the world'.
related: Equatorial regions have convectional rain every afternoon with thunder, and the annual temperature range is only about 2-3°C.
The Amazon basin holds the largest tropical rainforest in the world; the Congo basin is second.
The Doldrums are the calm equatorial belt of low pressure and weak winds, formed by the ITCZ.
Koeppen's Af is tropical rainforest, Am is monsoon and Aw is savannah.
The Mediterranean climate has dry summers and wet winters, and is found on the western margins of continents at 30°-45°.
Savannah is called the 'Big Game Country' because of its wildlife.
Equatorial vegetation is evergreen, multi-layered rainforest, with mahogany, ebony and rosewood as typical trees.
Tropical monsoon climate shows a seasonal reversal of winds, in contrast to the equatorial climate's uniform weather.
summary: The answer is (b) Equatorial. The passage describes a daily cycle that barely changes: a clear, bright morning with a sea breeze, rising heat, afternoon convectional clouds, then a short thunderstorm. This is the classic weather of the equatorial (tropical rainforest) region, which has no real seasons.
topic_notes: Climatic regions are usually classified by the Koeppen scheme, which uses temperature and precipitation and letters for groups: A (tropical humid), B (dry), C (warm temperate), D (cold snow-forest), E (cold polar) and H (highland). Group A has Af (equatorial rainforest), Am (monsoon) and Aw (savannah). Equatorial climate: located around 0°-10° N and S; temperatures about 27°C, annual range 2-3°C; rainfall above 250 cm, convectional, mostly in the afternoon; very high humidity; no winter, so there is no real seasonal change. Vegetation: tropical evergreen rainforest with a dense canopy, lianas and epiphytes, and trees such as mahogany, ebony and rosewood. The Amazon is the largest rainforest, and the Congo basin is second. Soils are acidic and leached, and nutrients are held in the vegetation. People of the region include the Pygmies of the Congo and the Orang Asli of Malaysia. Related climates: Tropical monsoon, Savannah, Hot deserts (BWh), Steppe (BSk), Mediterranean (Cs), China type (Cfa), British type or marine west coast (Cfb), Siberian or taiga (Dfc), Tundra (ET) and Polar ice cap (EF). Other angles UPSC could use: the ITCZ (the equatorial low-pressure belt called the doldrums), the Doldrums and calms, differences between convectional, orographic and cyclonic rainfall, characteristic wind systems, regions with the same latitude but different climates, and the conditions of rainforests as biodiversity hotspots and carbon sinks.

ocr: With reference to Indian economy, consider the following statements : 1. The rate of growth of Real Gross Domestic Product has steadily increased in the last decade. The Gross Domestic Product at market prices (in rupees) has steadily increased in the last decade. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (aj i only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Economy
detail: The question tests the difference between nominal and real GDP and between a level and a growth rate. GDP at market prices in rupees is a nominal (current-price) measure. It includes inflation, so with positive inflation and a growing economy it rises almost every year. The only notable exception in recent history is a real contraction, and even then nominal GDP in FY2020-21 was affected. Taken over the decade the question refers to (2005-06 to 2014-15, the paper being 2015), nominal GDP rose steadily. Real GDP is measured at constant prices (base year 2004-05 then, 2011-12 now), so it strips out price changes. The rate of growth of real GDP is a rate of change and does not rise monotonically. India grew about 9.5% in 2005-06, 9.6% in 2006-07 and 9.3% in 2007-08, fell to about 6.7% in 2008-09 after the global financial crisis, rebounded to about 8.6% and 8.9% in 2009-10 and 2010-11, then slowed to about 6.7%, 4.5% and 4.7% in 2011-12 to 2013-14 (old series). Statement 1 says 'steadily increased', which is false. Statement 2 is true. Elimination: once Statement 1 is rejected, only (b) or (d) remain, and Statement 2 is plainly true, so (b) is the answer.
explanations: (a) 1 only is wrong because Statement 1 is false (the real GDP growth rate fluctuated) and Statement 2 is true, so the pairing is reversed.
(b) 2 only is correct because nominal GDP at market prices rose steadily, while the real GDP growth rate rose and fell over the decade.
(c) Both 1 and 2 is wrong because Statement 1 wrongly claims a steady rise in the real growth rate, which is contradicted by the post-2008 slowdown and the 2011-14 slump.
(d) Neither 1 nor 2 is wrong because Statement 2 is correct: nominal GDP in rupees increases year after year, driven by growth plus inflation.
keyfact: Nominal GDP (current prices) rises steadily with inflation, but the real GDP growth rate fluctuates, so only Statement 2 is correct.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only would mean only the claim about steadily rising real GDP growth rate is right. That claim is false. Real GDP growth in India has moved in cycles, peaking at about 9%+ in 2005-08, dipping in 2008-09 and falling again in 2012-14. It is not a steady upward trend, so this option is wrong.

Option (b) 2 only is the official answer. It treats nominal GDP at market prices as steadily increasing. This is a current-price measure that contains inflation, so it rises almost every year even when real growth slows. Real GDP growth, by contrast, is a rate that fluctuates with business cycles, shocks and policy.

Option (c) Both 1 and 2 would require the real GDP growth rate to rise steadily as well as nominal GDP. This fails on Statement 1. Events like the 2008 global financial crisis, the 2011-13 slowdown with high inflation and current account deficit, and later COVID-19 all show that growth did not rise steadily.

Option (d) Neither 1 nor 2 would mean even nominal GDP did not rise steadily. This is wrong because nominal GDP is inflated by the general price rise and is a level that grows nearly every year. A fall in nominal GDP is rare, and it would need real contraction combined with deflation or very low inflation.
related: Real GDP is measured at constant base-year prices; nominal GDP at current prices.
GDP deflator equals nominal GDP divided by real GDP times 100.
GDP at market prices equals GDP at factor cost plus indirect taxes minus subsidies.
India's GDP base year was revised from 2004-05 to 2011-12 in January 2015.
From 2015 the CSO began headlining GVA at basic prices and GDP at market prices.
NSO under MoSPI releases GDP estimates, with CSO and NSSO merged in 2019.
India's FY2020-21 real GDP contracted by about 5.8-6% due to COVID-19.
GNP equals GDP plus net factor income from abroad.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The growth rate of real GDP fell and rose in cycles during the decade rather than increasing steadily. Real GDP is GDP at constant (base-year) prices, so it excludes the effect of price changes. Its growth rate is the percentage change over the previous year. India's growth peaked at about 9-9.6% in 2005-08, dipped to about 6.7% in 2008-09 after the global financial crisis, recovered to about 8.5-9% in 2009-11, then slowed to under 5% in 2012-14 (old series). Base year was 2004-05, revised to 2011-12 in January 2015 and moved by the CSO to a market-price-based GDP headline. Later shocks include COVID-19, when FY2020-21 real GDP contracted about 5.8-6%. The Central Statistics Office (now under NSO, MoSPI) releases these estimates.

2 — Correct: GDP at market prices in rupees is nominal GDP, which rises with both output growth and inflation, so it has risen every year in the period. GDP at market prices equals GDP at factor cost plus indirect taxes minus subsidies. Since the January 2015 revision, India headlines GDP at market prices and Gross Value Added (GVA) at basic prices, replacing GDP at factor cost. Nominal GDP is measured at current prices. The GDP deflator is the ratio of nominal to real GDP and captures the price effect. Nominal GDP rose from roughly Rs 32 lakh crore in 2005-06 to over Rs 100 lakh crore by 2013-14 (old series). Nominal GDP is used for ratios such as fiscal deficit to GDP and debt to GDP.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. Nominal GDP at market prices (in rupees) has risen every year over the last decade, but the growth rate of Real GDP has fluctuated rather than increasing steadily.
topic_notes: GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year. Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP uses constant base-year prices. The GDP deflator is nominal GDP divided by real GDP times 100 and measures economy-wide inflation. GDP at market prices equals GDP at factor cost plus indirect taxes minus subsidies. In January 2015 the CSO moved the base year from 2004-05 to 2011-12, adopted GVA at basic prices as the main measure of output, and began headlining GDP at market prices. GNP equals GDP plus net factor income from abroad. NNP at factor cost is national income. Per capita income equals national income divided by population. The Central Statistics Office was merged with the NSSO into the National Statistical Office (NSO) under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) in 2019. The statistical body releases Advance Estimates, then Provisional, then Revised estimates. Growth trend: roughly 9% for 2005-08, a fall in 2008-09, recovery in 2009-11, slowdown in 2012-14, strong post-2014 growth in the new series, FY2020-21 contraction of about 5.8-6% due to COVID-19, then a sharp recovery. Related ideas UPSC may ask are real versus nominal variables, the base year, the GDP deflator versus CPI and WPI, difference between GVA and GDP, factor cost versus market price, the output, income and expenditure methods of national income, and the Green GDP concept. Also remember that India's first national income estimate was by Dadabhai Naoroji, and that V.K.R.V. Rao made early scientific estimates. The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015.

ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. The Legislative Council of a State in India can be larger in size than half of the Legislative Assembly of that particular State. The Governor of a State nominates the Chairman of Legislative Council of that particular State. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 only Both 1 and 2 (dq) Neither 1 nor 2 30 B-AQN-O-JUA/63A
subject: Polity
detail: Articles 168 to 212 of Part VI of the Constitution deal with State Legislatures. Article 169 lets Parliament create or abolish a Legislative Council by ordinary law, provided the State Assembly first passes a resolution by a special majority (a majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting). Article 171 fixes the composition: the Council's strength cannot exceed one-third of the Assembly's strength, and it cannot be below 40 (J&K, with 36 under its earlier special provision, was an exception). Of the members, 1/3 are elected by local bodies, 1/12 by graduates, 1/12 by teachers, 1/3 by MLAs, and about 1/6 are nominated by the Governor from persons with special knowledge in literature, science, art, the cooperative movement and social service. Article 182 provides that the Council chooses its own Chairman and Deputy Chairman from among its members. The Council is a permanent house, with one-third of its members retiring every two years. Elimination: Statement 1 contradicts the one-third ceiling, and Statement 2 contradicts Article 182. Both are wrong, so (d) follows.
explanations: (a) is wrong. Statement 1 is incorrect, because the Council can have at most one-third of the Assembly's strength, so it can never exceed half.
(b) is wrong. Statement 2 is incorrect, because the Chairman is elected by the Council's members and is not nominated by the Governor.
(c) is wrong. Neither statement is correct, so they cannot both hold.
(d) is correct. Statement 1 breaches the one-third ceiling of Article 171, and Statement 2 breaches Article 182, under which the Council elects its Chairman.
keyfact: The Council has at most one-third of the Assembly's strength (minimum 40), and its Chairman is elected by its own members, not nominated by the Governor.
option_notes: Option (a) says only Statement 1 is correct. It would hold only if Councils could exceed half the Assembly's size, but the Constitution caps them at one-third, with a floor of 40 members. UP's Council is the largest, with 100 members against an Assembly of 403. As of recent years, only about six States have Councils: UP, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. Councils in Punjab, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal were abolished at different times, and Jammu and Kashmir's Council ended with the 2019 reorganisation.

Option (b) says only Statement 2 is correct. It rests on the false idea that the Governor appoints the Council's presiding officer. In fact the Council elects its Chairman and Deputy Chairman (Article 182). The Governor's real role is to nominate about one-sixth of the members from fields such as literature, science, art, the cooperative movement and social service (Article 171(3)(e)). The Governor also summons, prorogues and addresses the House, and can dissolve the Assembly, but cannot dissolve the Council because it is a permanent house.

Option (c) says both statements are correct. This would need a Council larger than half the Assembly and a Governor-nominated Chairman, and both ideas are false. It is a typical UPSC trap that mixes up the Council's size with the share of nominated members. Remember that the Council is capped at one-third of the Assembly and that the Governor nominates about one-sixth of the Council's members. The Council presides under its own elected Chairman, and the Governor plays no part in choosing him.

Option (d) is the correct answer, and it says neither statement is right. Size: at most one-third of the Assembly (Article 171), with at least 40 members. Chairman: elected by the Council from among its members (Article 182). The Council is a permanent, indirectly elected upper house with limited powers. Its members are chosen by local authorities, graduates, teachers, MLAs and Governor nomination. A Council is created or abolished by Parliament under Article 169, after the Assembly passes a special-majority resolution.
related: Article 169 allows creation or abolition of a Legislative Council by Parliament through an ordinary law, not a constitutional amendment.
Uttar Pradesh has the largest Legislative Council, with 100 members.
Article 171 limits the Council to one-third of the Assembly's strength, with a minimum of 40 members.
The Governor nominates about one-sixth of the Council's members from literature, science, art, the cooperative movement and social service.
The Council's Chairman is elected by its own members under Article 182.
The Council is a permanent house, and one-third of its members retire every two years.
A Council can delay a Money Bill for only 14 days.
The minimum age for membership of the Legislative Council is 30 years.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Council's size is capped at one-third of the Assembly's strength (Article 171(1)) and it must have at least 40 members, so it can never exceed half the Assembly. Facts: Uttar Pradesh has the largest Council with 100 members, against 403 in its Assembly. Bihar has 75, Maharashtra 78, Karnataka 75, Telangana 40 and Andhra Pradesh 58. The Council is a permanent house, with a member's term being 6 years and one-third retiring every 2 years. Its powers are weaker than the Assembly's. It can delay a Money Bill for only 14 days and an ordinary bill for 3 months at most, and it cannot vote on the Budget demands for grants. Parliament may create or abolish a Council under Article 169.

2 — Incorrect: The Chairman of the Legislative Council is elected by the Council's own members (Article 182), not nominated by the Governor. Facts: the Governor nominates only about one-sixth of the members (Article 171(3)(e)), from literature, science, art, the cooperative movement and social service. The Chairman can be removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council, with 14 days' notice (Article 183). The Chairman resigns by writing to the Deputy Chairman. The Chairman presides over the Council and does not vote except to break a tie. In the Assembly, the Speaker and Deputy Speaker are likewise elected by its members (Article 178). The Rajya Sabha has a parallel arrangement: the Vice-President is its ex officio Chairman.
summary: The answer is (d) Neither 1 nor 2. Under Article 171, a Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) can have at most one-third of the strength of the Legislative Assembly, and never fewer than 40 members. Its Chairman is elected by the Council from among its own members, not nominated by the Governor.
topic_notes:
Bicameralism in the States is optional. Article 168 says a State legislature consists of the Governor and one House (the Assembly) or two Houses (the Assembly and the Council). Article 169 lets Parliament create or abolish a Council by ordinary law, after the Assembly passes a resolution by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting. Such a law is not an amendment under Article 368. Councils now exist in six States: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh.

Composition under Article 171: the strength is at most one-third of the Assembly and at least 40. Election pattern: 1/3 elected by local bodies (municipalities, district boards), 1/12 by graduates of at least three years' standing, 1/12 by teachers of at least three years' standing in secondary schools or higher, 1/3 by MLAs from outside the Assembly, and the remainder nominated by the Governor. Election is by proportional representation with the single transferable vote. A member must be at least 30 years old. The term is 6 years, with one-third retiring every 2 years.

Presiding officers: the Chairman and Deputy Chairman are elected by the Council (Article 182) and removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members (Article 183).

Powers: the Council is weaker than the Assembly. A Money Bill can be delayed for only 14 days. For an ordinary bill, the Council can delay it by 3 months the first time, and on the second passage by the Assembly by 1 month, and the Assembly's will finally prevails. The Council cannot vote on demands for grants. It has no part in the election of the President, and its members do not take part in the impeachment of the President. It cannot pass a no-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers, and a Chief Minister may be a Council member.

Other facts: Article 171(5) sets out the nomination criteria. Article 172 gives the term. Article 190 deals with vacation of seats. Parliament abolished the Councils of Punjab, West Bengal and Tamil Nadu at different times.

ocr: “To uphold and protect the Sovereignty, Unity and Integrity of India” is a provision made in the (a) Preamble of the Constitution (b) Directive Principles of State Policy (c} Fundamental Rights (2) Fundamental Duties
subject: Polity
detail: Part IV-A of the Constitution, containing only Article 51A, lists the Fundamental Duties. They were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee (1976), and were inspired by the USSR Constitution. Originally there were 10 duties. The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 added the eleventh, clause (k): a parent or guardian must provide opportunities for education to a child aged 6-14 years. Article 51A(c) is the duty to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India. Duties are non-justiciable and carry no direct legal sanction, but courts use them to interpret laws. They apply to citizens only, unlike some Fundamental Rights that also cover foreigners. Elimination logic: the Preamble speaks of 'unity and integrity of the Nation' as a goal, and the word 'sovereign' appears there, but it does not use the phrase 'uphold and protect'. Fundamental Rights are claims against the State, and DPSPs are directives to the State, whereas this wording is addressed to the citizen as a duty. The verb 'uphold and protect' signals a duty. The Preamble also says 'integrity', not 'Sovereignty, Unity and Integrity of India' as a duty.
explanations: Incorrect: the Preamble resolves to secure justice, liberty, equality and fraternity 'assuring the unity and integrity of the Nation'. It does not use the phrase 'uphold and protect the Sovereignty, Unity and Integrity of India'.
Incorrect: DPSPs (Part IV, Articles 36-51) direct the State on social and economic welfare, and Article 51 deals with international peace. None imposes this duty on citizens.

Incorrect: Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12-35) are enforceable claims of individuals against the State. They are not duties, though Article 19(2) allows restrictions in the interest of sovereignty and integrity.
Correct: Article 51A(c) in Part IV-A states exactly this duty for every citizen.
keyfact: Article 51A(c), a Fundamental Duty in Part IV-A, requires every citizen to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.
option_notes: The Preamble is the introductory statement of the Constitution. It declares India a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic. 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added, and 'unity of the Nation' was changed to 'unity and integrity of the Nation', by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. It is based on the Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru in 1946. In the Berubari case (1960) the Supreme Court held it is not a part of the Constitution, but in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) it was held to be a part. It can be amended without altering its basic structure.

DPSPs are in Part IV (Articles 36-51) and were borrowed from the Irish Constitution. They are non-justiciable (Article 37) but fundamental in governance. They are divided into socialistic, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual principles. Examples: Article 40 (village panchayats), Article 44 (Uniform Civil Code), Article 48 (cow protection, modern agriculture) and Article 50 (separation of the judiciary from the executive). The 42nd and 44th Amendments added Articles 39A, 43A, 43B and 48A.

Fundamental Rights are in Part III (Articles 12-35) and are justiciable, enforced through Article 32. There are six: equality (14-18), freedom (19-22), against exploitation (23-24), religion (25-28), cultural and educational rights (29-30) and constitutional remedies (32). The right to property was removed from this list by the 44th Amendment in 1978 and is now Article 300A. Dr Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. They can be suspended during Emergency, except Articles 20 and 21.

Fundamental Duties are in Part IV-A, Article 51A, added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976 on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation. They were originally ten, and the 86th Amendment (2002) added the eleventh, on education for children aged 6-14. They include respect for the Constitution, the national flag and the national anthem, protecting the environment and public property, developing scientific temper, and safeguarding public property. They are non-justiciable and apply only to citizens.
related: Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation.
Part IV-A contains only Article 51A.
Originally there were 10 Fundamental Duties; the 86th Amendment (2002) added an 11th.
Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable and apply only to citizens.
The idea of Fundamental Duties was borrowed from the USSR Constitution.
Article 51A(k) relates to a parent's duty to educate a child aged 6-14 years, and links to Article 21A.
The Preamble was amended once, by the 42nd Amendment, which added 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity'.
The Verma Committee (1999) examined the operationalisation of Fundamental Duties.
summary: The answer is (d) Fundamental Duties. Article 51A(c) says it is the duty of every citizen of India 'to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India'. The Preamble, DPSP and Fundamental Rights do not contain this as a citizen's duty.
topic_notes: Fundamental Duties are in Part IV-A, which has a single article, Article 51A. They were introduced by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 (the 'mini-Constitution') during the Emergency, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, which proposed eight duties; ten were incorporated. The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 added the eleventh, clause (k), on parental duty regarding education of children aged 6-14, in connection with Article 21A. The idea was borrowed from the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR. The eleven duties are: (a) abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals, institutions, the National Flag and National Anthem; (b) cherish the noble ideals of the freedom struggle; (c) uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; (d) defend the country and render national service when called upon; (e) promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood and renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women; (f) value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture; (g) protect and improve the natural environment; (h) develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform; (i) safeguard public property and abjure violence; (j) strive towards excellence in individual and collective activity; (k) provide opportunities for education to a child between 6 and 14 years. Features: they are non-justiciable, are addressed to citizens only, and have no legal sanction. The Verma Committee (1999) identified existing legal provisions for enforcing some duties, such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971. In AIIMS Students Union v. AIIMS (2001), the Supreme Court held that Fundamental Duties are equally important as Fundamental Rights. In Ramlila Maidan Incident case (2012), courts also reiterated their relevance. UPSC can ask about the number of duties, the amendment responsible, the committee, and the relation to Fundamental Rights and DPSPs.

question: Which one of the following is the best description of the term ‘ecosystem’?
options: A community of organisms interacting with one another
That part of the Earth which is inhabited by living organisms
) A community of organisms together with the environment in which they live
The flora and fauna of a geographical area
subject: Environment
detail: An ecosystem is a structural and functional unit of nature in which biotic components (producers, consumers, decomposers) interact with each other and with abiotic components (sunlight, air, water, soil, temperature, nutrients). The term was coined by British ecologist Arthur G. Tansley in 1935. Its two defining functions are one-way energy flow (sun to producers to consumers to decomposers, with roughly 10% transfer between trophic levels per Lindeman's law) and cyclic movement of nutrients (biogeochemical cycles). Ecosystems can be natural (forest, grassland, desert, wetland, ocean) or artificial (cropland, aquarium, reservoir), and have no fixed size. Elimination logic: (a) describes only a biotic community and leaves out the abiotic environment. (b) describes the biosphere, the global sum of all ecosystems. (d) describes flora and fauna only, which is biodiversity or biota and again ignores the physical environment. Only (c) joins the living community with its environment, which is the essence of the concept. Remember the hierarchy: organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome, biosphere.
explanations: Wrong: this describes a biotic community alone. It omits the abiotic environment and the energy and nutrient exchange that define an ecosystem.
Wrong: this is the definition of the biosphere (ecosphere), the zone of Earth where life exists, which is the largest ecological unit and not a single ecosystem.
Correct: it captures both biotic community and the physical environment as an interacting system, matching Tansley's concept.
Wrong: flora and fauna of an area is the biota (or biodiversity inventory); it leaves out the non-living components and interactions.
keyfact: Ecosystem = biotic community + abiotic environment functioning together (Tansley, 1935); biosphere = sum of all ecosystems.
option_notes: A biotic community is an assemblage of populations of different species living and interacting in a defined area, for example a forest community of trees, insects, birds and microbes. It includes only living organisms. Community ecology studies species richness, dominance, stratification, competition, predation and succession. It is a component of an ecosystem, not the whole. Ecotone and edge effect arise where two communities meet.

The biosphere is the part of Earth (lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere) where life exists, extending from the deep ocean trenches to a few kilometres into the atmosphere. The term was popularised by Eduard Suess and developed by Vladimir Vernadsky. It is the sum of all ecosystems and the global ecological system. Biosphere Reserves under UNESCO's MAB programme (1971) are protected areas named after it.

An ecosystem is a community of organisms plus the abiotic environment functioning together via energy flow and nutrient cycling. Tansley coined the term in 1935. Components are producers, consumers, decomposers and abiotic factors. Types include terrestrial, aquatic, natural and artificial ecosystems. Key functions are productivity, decomposition, energy flow, nutrient cycling and homeostasis. Examples are a pond (Lindeman studied Cedar Bog Lake), forest, grassland and coral reef.

Flora and fauna together make up the biota of a region, the plant and animal life, studied in biodiversity inventories and floristic or faunal surveys. India has about 8% of recorded global species and four biodiversity hotspots: Himalaya, Western Ghats, Indo-Burma and Sundaland (Nicobar). Biota excludes abiotic factors, so it is only one component of an ecosystem.
related: The term 'ecosystem' was coined by A.G. Tansley in 1935.
The term 'ecology' was coined by Ernst Haeckel in 1866.
Lindeman's 10% law governs energy transfer between trophic levels.
The biosphere is the sum of all ecosystems on Earth.
An ecotone is a transition zone between two ecosystems or communities.
The energy pyramid is always upright, whereas number and biomass pyramids may be inverted.
The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005) classified services as provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting.
Producers (autotrophs) form the first trophic level of every ecosystem.
summary: The answer is (c): an ecosystem is a community of organisms together with the physical environment in which they live. The term, coined by A.G. Tansley in 1935, stresses that living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) components interact as one functional unit through energy flow and nutrient cycling.
topic_notes: Ecology is the study of interactions between organisms and their environment; the term was coined by Ernst Haeckel (1866). The hierarchy runs: organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome, biosphere. Tansley coined 'ecosystem' in 1935; Raymond Lindeman (1942) formulated the trophic-dynamic concept and the 10% law. Components: abiotic (climate, soil, water, light) and biotic (autotrophs or producers, heterotrophs or consumers, saprotrophs or decomposers). Functions: productivity (gross primary productivity minus respiration equals net primary productivity), decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling. Energy flow is unidirectional, while nutrients cycle. Food chains are grazing (starting with plants) or detritus type; food webs are interlinked chains. Ecological pyramids of number, biomass and energy: the energy pyramid is always upright, while the number and biomass pyramids can be inverted (for example, a pond's biomass pyramid or a tree's number pyramid). Ecological succession: primary (bare rock, pioneer species such as lichens) and secondary; ends in a climax community. Ecotone is the transition zone between two ecosystems and shows the edge effect. Keystone species, indicator species, and flagship species are frequently asked. Ecosystem services (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment 2005) are provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting. Major biomes: tundra, taiga, temperate forest, tropical rainforest, savanna, grassland and desert. India's Ramsar sites, biosphere reserves (18) and the Biological Diversity Act 2002 are linked topics. Limiting factors, Shelford's law of tolerance and Liebig's law of the minimum are other conceptual angles.

ocr: The fundamental object of Panchayati Raj system is to ensure which among the following? 1. People’s participation in development 2, Political accountability 3. Democratic decentralization 4, Financial mobilization Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1, 2 and 3 only (b) 2 and 4 only (ec) 1 and 3 only (a) 1, 2,3 and 4
subject: Polity
detail: Panchayati Raj was introduced after the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended a three-tier structure of 'democratic decentralization' to secure people's participation in community development programmes, which were failing because they were bureaucratically driven. Rajasthan (Nagaur, 2 October 1959) was the first state to adopt it, followed by Andhra Pradesh. The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 (in force 24 April 1993) gave constitutional status through Part IX (Articles 243 to 243-O) and the Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects, Article 243-G). Article 40 (DPSP) directs the State to organise village panchayats as units of self-government. The core purpose is to transfer power, functions and resources to the local level so that people take part in planning and implementing development. Elimination logic: Statements 1 and 3 capture this purpose directly. Statement 2 (political accountability) and statement 4 (financial mobilization) are desirable outcomes or instruments; panchayats have weak own-revenue sources and depend on grants from Union and State Finance Commissions. Hence any option containing 2 or 4 (a, b, d) is rejected, leaving (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 2 (political accountability), which is an outcome of the system rather than its fundamental object.
Wrong: it excludes both correct statements 1 and 3 and includes 2 and 4, which are secondary.
Correct: people's participation in development (1) and democratic decentralization (3) are the fundamental object of Panchayati Raj.
Wrong: it adds statements 2 and 4, which are instruments or outcomes, not the fundamental object.
keyfact: Fundamental object of Panchayati Raj = democratic decentralization and people's participation in development (Balwant Rai Mehta, 1957; 73rd Amendment, 1992); accountability and finance are only means or outcomes.
related: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj and the term 'democratic decentralization'.
Panchayati Raj was first launched at Nagaur, Rajasthan on 2 October 1959 by Jawaharlal Nehru.
73rd Constitutional Amendment Act 1992 added Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects); effective 24 April 1993.
Article 243-I provides for the State Finance Commission, constituted every five years.
Article 243-K provides for the State Election Commission to conduct panchayat elections.
Article 40 (DPSP) directs the State to organise village panchayats.
PESA Act 1996 extended Panchayati Raj to Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas.
The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) recommended a two-tier system.
statements: 1 — Correct: People's participation in development is the central aim of Panchayati Raj, as stated by the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee. Community Development Programme (1952) and National Extension Service (1953) failed to evoke local participation, so the committee (appointed January 1957, reported November 1957) recommended a three-tier system: Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti and Zila Parishad. Gram Sabha, defined in Article 243(b), is the body of all registered voters in the village and is the main forum for participation, social audit and beneficiary selection. The 73rd Amendment also mandates one-third reservation for women, and reservation for SCs and STs.

2 — Incorrect: Political accountability is a result of regular elections and Gram Sabha oversight, not the fundamental object. Article 243-E fixes a five-year term; Article 243-K creates State Election Commissions to conduct elections; if dissolved, elections must be held within six months. Article 243-J provides audit of accounts. Social audit under MGNREGA (2005) improves accountability. Panchayats are accountable to the Gram Sabha, but this is a feature of the system, not its foundational purpose, so the statement is not accepted as the fundamental object.

3 — Correct: Democratic decentralization is the very idea behind Panchayati Raj, a term used by the Mehta Committee. It means devolving power, authority and responsibilities from the Union and State to local self-government. The 73rd Amendment (1992, effective 24 April 1993) gave constitutional status, introduced a uniform three-tier structure for states with population over 20 lakh, direct elections, reservations, State Finance Commissions (Article 243-I) and District Planning Committees (Article 243-ZD). Panchayat Day is 24 April. Subjects are in the Eleventh Schedule, but devolution is left to state legislatures.

4 — Incorrect: Financial mobilization is a means to enable functioning, not the fundamental object. Panchayats can levy taxes under Article 243-H, but mostly depend on devolved funds and grants from Central and State Finance Commissions. Article 243-I requires a State Finance Commission every five years; Article 280(3)(bb) lets the Union Finance Commission recommend measures to augment state Consolidated Funds for panchayat resources. The 14th Finance Commission increased direct grants to Gram Panchayats. Weak own-source revenue is a persistent problem, showing that finance is a challenge, not the aim.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. The fundamental object of the Panchayati Raj system is democratic decentralization, which ensures people's participation in development and planning at the grassroots level. Political accountability and financial mobilization are by-products or means, not the fundamental object.
topic_notes: Evolution: Community Development Programme (1952) and National Extension Service (1953) led to the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957), which recommended a three-tier system with the block as the unit. Rajasthan (Nagaur, 2 Oct 1959) was first, then Andhra Pradesh. Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) recommended a two-tier system (Zila Parishad and Mandal Panchayat) and political party involvement. G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985) and L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) recommended constitutional recognition; Singhvi suggested more financial resources for village panchayats. The 64th Amendment Bill (1989) failed in the Rajya Sabha. The 73rd Amendment Act 1992 (effective 24 April 1993) added Part IX (Articles 243 to 243-O) and the Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects). Key provisions: Gram Sabha; three tiers (intermediate tier optional if population is under 20 lakh); direct elections to all seats; five-year term; one-third reservation for women (many states now give 50%); reservation for SC/ST in proportion to population; State Election Commission (Article 243-K); State Finance Commission (243-I). Compulsory provisions versus voluntary provisions are a common question. Exempt areas: Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas, Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, hill areas of Manipur, and Darjeeling district in West Bengal. PESA Act 1996 extended panchayats to Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas. Related: Article 40 (DPSP), 74th Amendment for urban local bodies (Twelfth Schedule, 18 subjects), Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan, Gram Panchayat Development Plan, SVAMITVA, e-Gram Swaraj. Panchayati Raj is a State subject (Seventh Schedule, List II, Entry 5), and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj was created in 2004.

ocr: With reference to Indian economy, consider the following : 1. Bank rate 2. Open market operations 3. Public debt 4. Public revenue Which of the above is/are component/ components of Monetary Policy? (a) 1 only (b) 2,3 and 4 () land 2 (a) 1,3 and 4
subject: Economy
detail: Monetary policy is the regulation of money supply, liquidity and the cost and availability of credit by the central bank, the RBI, to achieve price stability, growth and financial stability. Its legal basis is the RBI Act, 1934, as amended in 2016 to create a statutory Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) and a flexible inflation targeting framework. The inflation target is 4% CPI with a tolerance band of +/-2% (2% to 6%), reviewed every five years. The MPC has 6 members: 3 from the RBI (including the Governor, who has a casting vote) and 3 external members appointed by the Centre. Quantitative tools are CRR, SLR, repo and reverse repo, MSF, Bank Rate and OMOs. Qualitative tools are margin requirements, moral suasion and selective credit control. Fiscal policy is the Government's use of taxation, expenditure, borrowing and public debt, presented in the Union Budget under Article 112. Elimination logic: public revenue (taxes, non-tax receipts) and public debt (government borrowing) are Finance Ministry instruments, so any option containing 3 or 4 is wrong. This eliminates (b) and (d). Option (a) is incomplete because OMOs are a standard RBI tool. Only (c) remains.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Bank rate is a monetary instrument, but this option leaves out open market operations, which are also a monetary policy tool.
(b) Wrong: It omits Bank rate and includes public debt and public revenue, which are fiscal and not monetary instruments.
(c) Correct: Bank rate and OMOs are both RBI instruments used to control liquidity and credit, which is why this matches the official answer.
(d) Wrong: Public debt and public revenue are fiscal policy components, so adding 3 and 4 makes the option incorrect.
keyfact: Monetary policy (RBI): Bank rate, OMOs, repo, CRR and SLR; fiscal policy (Government): taxes, public debt, public expenditure.
option_notes: Bank rate alone: the rate at which the RBI lends long-term funds to banks without collateral. Since 2012 it equals the MSF rate (Repo + 0.25%). It is a penal rate and is used as a benchmark for penalties on CRR/SLR defaults. Historically it was the main policy rate before the LAF was introduced in 2000. Repo is the effective operating policy rate today. Changes in the Bank rate are signalling devices rather than the main tool of liquidity management.

2, 3 and 4: this combination mixes one monetary tool (OMOs) with two fiscal items (public debt and public revenue). OMOs are the RBI's buying and selling of government securities to manage liquidity. Public debt is government borrowing under Articles 292 and 293. Public revenue is the tax and non-tax receipts of the Government. Fiscal policy is carried out through the Union Budget by the Finance Ministry under Article 112.

1 and 2: Bank rate and open market operations. This is the correct combination. Both are RBI tools of quantitative credit control. Bank rate is the long-term lending rate to banks (MSF-aligned). OMOs involve buying and selling government securities to inject or absorb liquidity. The other quantitative tools are CRR, SLR, repo, reverse repo, MSF and MSS. The MPC under the RBI Act 1934 (amended 2016) decides the policy rate to meet the 4% (+/-2%) inflation target.

1, 3 and 4: this option combines Bank rate (monetary) with public debt and public revenue (both fiscal). Public debt means government borrowing from the market, from banks, small savings and abroad. Public revenue means taxes plus non-tax income. Both are used in the Budget, and are governed by the FRBM Act 2003 targets for deficit and debt. The option is wrong because these two are not tools of the RBI.
related: Monetary policy is formulated by the RBI's MPC, while fiscal policy is framed by the Union Government.
The MPC has six members and the RBI Governor has a casting vote in the event of a tie.
The flexible inflation target is 4% CPI with a tolerance band of +/-2%.
Bank rate equals the MSF rate, which is Repo + 0.25%.
The LAF was introduced in 2000 following the Narasimham Committee recommendation, and it consists of repo and reverse repo operations.
Article 112 provides for the Annual Financial Statement (the Budget), and Articles 292 and 293 deal with Union and State borrowing.
The Market Stabilisation Scheme (2004) is used to absorb excess liquidity caused by capital inflows.
The FRBM Act was enacted in 2003 to institutionalise fiscal discipline.
statements: 1 — Correct: Bank rate is a monetary policy instrument set by the RBI. Bank rate is the rate at which the RBI lends long-term funds to commercial banks without any collateral or repurchase agreement. Since 2012 it has been aligned with the MSF rate, which is Repo + 0.25 percentage points (25 basis points). It is a penal rate and a signal of the RBI's policy stance. It is also used to compute CRR/SLR shortfall penalties. The repo rate is now the main operating policy rate, and the Bank Rate is largely a reference rate.

2 — Correct: Open market operations are a monetary policy tool. OMOs are the RBI's outright purchase or sale of government securities in the market. Buying securities injects liquidity into the system, and selling them absorbs it. They are used to manage liquidity and to influence interest rates and yields. Related tools include the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS, introduced 2004) for absorbing excess liquidity, and the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF, introduced 2000), which works through repo and reverse repo. Twist operations and G-SAP are recent OMO-type innovations.

3 — Incorrect: Public debt is a fiscal policy instrument, not a monetary one. It is the borrowing by the Government, both internal and external, to finance the fiscal deficit. In India it is governed by Article 292 (Union borrowing) and Article 293 (State borrowing). The RBI manages the government's debt as its debt manager, but the decision to borrow is a fiscal matter. The FRBM Act, 2003 sets debt and deficit targets. Debt consists of market borrowings, T-bills, small savings and external loans.

4 — Incorrect: Public revenue is a fiscal policy instrument. It covers tax revenue (direct and indirect taxes such as income tax, corporation tax and GST) and non-tax revenue (dividends, interest receipts, fees and spectrum charges). It is presented in the Annual Financial Statement under Article 112, and the Consolidated Fund is dealt with under Article 266. Taxes can only be levied by authority of law under Article 265. Tax policy adjusts the aggregate demand, and the Finance Ministry, not the RBI, determines it.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 2. Bank rate and open market operations are instruments of monetary policy, which the RBI uses to control money supply and credit. Public debt and public revenue are instruments of fiscal policy, which the Government uses through its budget.
topic_notes: Monetary policy is the RBI's management of money supply, interest rates and credit to achieve macroeconomic objectives such as price stability, growth and financial stability. The RBI was established in 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934 and nationalised in 1949. The 2016 amendment created the six-member MPC, with the Governor as chair and a casting vote. The inflation target is 4% CPI, with a band of 2% to 6%, set by the Government in consultation with the RBI and reviewed every five years. If inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must report to the Government. Quantitative instruments: CRR (the share of NDTL held with the RBI as cash, with no interest), SLR (the share of NDTL held in liquid assets such as gold, cash and government securities), repo rate (the rate at which the RBI lends short-term to banks against securities), reverse repo (the rate at which the RBI borrows from banks), the standing deposit facility (SDF, 2022, which has become the floor of the LAF corridor), MSF (an emergency overnight facility at Repo + 0.25%), Bank rate, and OMOs. Qualitative instruments: moral suasion, selective credit control, margin requirements and direct action. Fiscal policy, by contrast, is conducted by the Union Government through taxation, public expenditure, public debt and subsidies. It is presented in the Budget under Article 112, and the FRBM Act, 2003 governs the fiscal deficit and debt targets. Policy mix: expansionary monetary policy lowers rates, while expansionary fiscal policy raises spending or cuts taxes. Possible angles for future questions are the LAF corridor, the effects of rate changes on inflation and growth, the MPC's composition, the difference between CRR and SLR, and the use of OMOs for liquidity.

ocr: With reference to inflation in India, which of the following statements is correct? (a) Controlling the inflation in India is the responsibility of the Government of India only (b) The Reserve Bank of India has no role in controlling the inflation (c} Decreased money circulation helps in controlling the inflation (ad) Increased money circulation helps in controlling the inflation
subject: Economy
detail: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. Demand-pull inflation arises when aggregate demand and money supply outrun output; cost-push inflation arises from higher input costs. Monetary tools reduce money in circulation: raising the repo rate, reverse repo/SDF rate, CRR and SLR, and conducting open market operations (selling G-secs) and MSF changes. Since the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement (Feb 2015) and the RBI Act amendment of 2016, the RBI follows flexible inflation targeting with a Monetary Policy Committee (six members: three RBI, three government-appointed). The target is CPI inflation of 4% with a tolerance band of +/-2% (2%-6%), reviewed every five years. The Government contributes through fiscal policy (lower deficits, taxes, subsidies), supply management (buffer stocks, imports, export curbs, MSP management) and the Essential Commodities Act. Elimination: (a) is wrong because the RBI is also responsible; (b) is wrong because the RBI is the monetary authority with the key role; (d) is wrong because more money in circulation fuels inflation, it does not control it. Hence only (c) is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: control of inflation is not the Government's sole job. The RBI controls it through monetary policy, and the Government through fiscal and supply-side measures, so 'only' makes it wrong.
Incorrect: the RBI has a central role. It sets the policy repo rate through the MPC, manages liquidity via CRR, SLR and OMOs, and is mandated to meet the inflation target.

Correct: reducing money supply and liquidity reduces aggregate demand and eases price pressure. This is the basis of contractionary monetary policy, such as raising rates or CRR and selling securities.
Incorrect: increasing money circulation raises demand relative to supply and so adds to inflation. It is an expansionary measure used to counter recession or deflation.
keyfact: Less money in circulation (tight monetary policy) lowers inflation; the RBI's MPC targets CPI inflation of 4% (+/-2%), while the Government also helps through fiscal and supply measures.
option_notes: Government of India's role in inflation control: it uses fiscal policy (taxation, public expenditure, fiscal deficit management) and supply-side tools such as buffer stocks through FCI, imports or duty cuts, export bans, stock limits, and the Essential Commodities Act 1955. The Department of Consumer Affairs monitors prices. However, it works alongside the RBI. Since 2016, the Government sets the inflation target in consultation with the RBI, and it appoints the three external MPC members.

The RBI, founded 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act 1934 and nationalised in 1949, is India's central bank and monetary authority. It issues currency, acts as banker to the Government and to banks, and regulates the financial system. Its main tool against inflation is the policy rate (repo rate), along with CRR, SLR, OMOs, MSF and the Standing Deposit Facility. Under the 2016 amendment, it has a statutory inflation-targeting mandate, implemented via the MPC.

Decreased money circulation means contractionary monetary policy, also called tight or dear money policy. It is carried out by raising the repo rate, CRR or SLR, selling government securities in OMOs, and absorbing liquidity via the reverse repo or SDF. It reduces credit growth, spending and demand, thereby lowering inflation, but may slow growth. Quantity theory of money (MV=PT) links less money to lower price levels.

Increased money circulation is expansionary or 'cheap money' policy: cutting repo rate, CRR, SLR, buying securities via OMOs, or injecting liquidity through LAF and TLTROs. It raises credit and demand, supporting growth and employment in recession, as with the RBI's 2020 COVID-era repo cut to 4%. If supply does not keep up, it causes demand-pull inflation, so it is not an inflation-control measure.
related: Inflation target in India: 4% CPI, with a tolerance band of 2%-6%.
MPC has six members: three from the RBI and three appointed by the Central Government; the Governor has a casting vote.
Raising repo rate or CRR lowers liquidity and inflation; cutting them does the opposite.
Headline inflation in India is measured by CPI-Combined (base 2012); WPI base year is 2011-12.
Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommended CPI as the nominal anchor and inflation targeting.
Core inflation excludes food and fuel items.
Disinflation is a fall in the rate of inflation, while deflation is a fall in the price level itself.
Marginal Standing Facility rate equals repo rate plus 0.25%.
summary: The correct answer is (c): decreased money circulation helps in controlling inflation. Inflation is 'too much money chasing too few goods', so reducing money supply and liquidity lowers demand-side pressure on prices. Control of inflation in India is shared between the RBI (monetary policy) and the Government (fiscal and supply-side measures).
topic_notes: Inflation measurement: In India, CPI (Combined) from NSO under MoSPI is the headline index for the inflation target, with base year 2012. WPI is published by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, with base year 2011-12. The RBI shifted to CPI as the nominal anchor after the Urjit Patel Committee (2014). Flexible Inflation Targeting: introduced via the RBI Act amendment (Finance Act 2016); target 4% with a +/-2% band, reviewed every five years (last in 2021 for 2021-26). If inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must report to the Government with reasons and remedial action. MPC: six members, the RBI Governor is chair with a casting vote; meets at least four times a year; decisions by majority. Monetary tools: quantitative tools include repo, reverse repo, CRR (on NDTL, no interest paid), SLR (in liquid assets), OMO, MSF (repo plus 25 bps), Bank Rate, and the Standing Deposit Facility (introduced 2022); qualitative tools include margin requirements, moral suasion and selective credit control. Types of inflation: demand-pull, cost-push, structural, core (excluding food and fuel), headline, stagflation, reflation, disinflation (fall in rate of inflation) and deflation (falling prices). Effects: it hurts fixed-income earners and creditors, and benefits debtors. Fiscal measures include lower deficits, indirect tax cuts, release of buffer stock, and import liberalisation. Related: Phillips curve, Fisher effect, FRBM Act 2003 for fiscal discipline. Future angles: differences between CPI and WPI, who sets the target, the composition of the MPC, how CRR and repo changes affect liquidity, and the effect of hikes on borrowers.

ocr: Consider the following countries : 1. China 2. France 3. India 4. Israel 5. Pakistan Which among the above are Nuclear Weapons States as recognized by the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, commonly known as Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT)? fa} 1 and 2 only (b) 1, 3, 4 and 5 only (c) 2, 4 and 5 only (a 1, 2,3, 4 and 5 B-AQN-O-JUA/63A 32
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Article IX(3) of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons says a nuclear-weapon State is one that manufactured and exploded a nuclear weapon or other nuclear explosive device before 1 January 1967. Five states fit: the USA (1945), the USSR (1949, now Russia), the UK (1952), France (1960) and China (1964). These are also the five permanent members of the UN Security Council. The treaty was opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force on 5 March 1970. It was extended indefinitely in 1995. It rests on three pillars: non-proliferation, disarmament (Article VI) and the peaceful use of nuclear energy (Article IV). India, Pakistan and Israel never joined the NPT as non-nuclear-weapon states. India tested in 1974 (Pokhran-I) and 1998 (Pokhran-II), and Pakistan tested in 1998, so both came after the 1967 cut-off date. Israel has a policy of opacity and has never confirmed or denied having nuclear weapons. North Korea joined the NPT and withdrew in 2003. Elimination: any option containing 3, 4 or 5 is wrong, because those states are not recognised as NWS under the treaty. That leaves option (a).
explanations: Correct: China and France are the only two listed states that tested before 1 January 1967, so they are the only NWS under the NPT here.
Wrong: India (3), Israel (4) and Pakistan (5) are not NPT parties and are not recognised NWS. Including 1 is right, but the rest of the option is wrong.
Wrong: it omits China, which is an NWS, and includes Israel and Pakistan, which are not.
Wrong: it includes India, Israel and Pakistan, none of which are recognised as NWS under the NPT.
keyfact: NPT recognises as nuclear weapon states only those that tested before 1 Jan 1967: USA, Russia, UK, France, China; India, Pakistan and Israel are outside it.
option_notes: Option (a) is China and France, two of the five recognised NWS. China tested in 1964 and acceded in 1992. France tested in 1960 and acceded in 1992. Both are permanent UNSC members with veto power. Both are also members of the Nuclear Suppliers Group. France has an independent nuclear deterrent, and China follows a No First Use policy.

Option (b) is India, Israel, Pakistan and China. India, Israel and Pakistan are the three nuclear-armed states outside the NPT. China is an NWS. Together India, Pakistan and Israel are called de facto nuclear states, and they have never joined the treaty as non-nuclear-weapon states. India tested in 1974 and 1998, Pakistan in 1998, and Israel has never openly tested.

Option (c) is France, Israel and Pakistan. France is a recognised NWS. Israel and Pakistan are outside the NPT. Israel keeps its arsenal ambiguous and Pakistan tested in 1998. Neither can be recognised as an NWS because both fall after the 1967 cut-off and never joined the treaty.

Option (d) lists all five countries. It mixes the 2 NPT-recognised NWS (China and France) with the 3 states outside the NPT (India, Israel, Pakistan). The complete P5 recognised list also includes the USA, Russia and the UK, which are not given here. North Korea is another nuclear-armed state that withdrew from the NPT in 2003.
related: NPT cut-off for NWS status: nuclear test before 1 January 1967.
NPT entered into force on 5 March 1970 and was extended indefinitely in 1995.
The five NWS under the NPT are the P5 of the UNSC: USA, Russia, UK, France and China.
India, Pakistan and Israel never signed the NPT; North Korea withdrew in 2003.
India's first nuclear test, Pokhran-I, was in 1974 and Pokhran-II in May 1998.
The NSG was formed in 1974 after India's test; India got a waiver in 2008 but is not a member.
The CTBT (1996) has not entered into force; India has not signed it.
The TPNW (2017) entered into force in January 2021; India and nuclear-armed states did not join.
statements: 1 — Correct: China exploded its first nuclear device in 1964 (Lop Nur), before the 1967 cut-off, and acceded to the NPT in 1992. China is a P5 member of the UN Security Council. It has declared a No First Use policy. It is a recognised NWS under the NPT.

2 — Correct: France tested its first nuclear weapon in 1960 (Gerboise Bleue, Algeria), before the cut-off. It acceded to the NPT in 1992. It is a permanent UNSC member and the only EU state with nuclear weapons after Brexit. It has an independent deterrent called the force de frappe.

3 — Incorrect: India did not sign the NPT, calling it discriminatory. It conducted Pokhran-I (1974, a 'peaceful nuclear explosion') and Pokhran-II (May 1998). India declared a voluntary moratorium on testing and follows a No First Use doctrine (2003). It received an NSG waiver in 2008 after the Indo-US nuclear deal, but it is not recognised as an NWS under the NPT.

4 — Incorrect: Israel has never signed the NPT. It follows a policy of deliberate ambiguity (amimut) and is widely believed to have a nuclear arsenal, with Dimona as its main facility. It has never publicly declared that it has nuclear weapons, so it has no NWS status under the treaty.

5 — Incorrect: Pakistan is not an NPT party. It tested at Chagai Hills in May 1998 in response to India. It has an NCA (National Command Authority). It has not adopted a No First Use policy. It is not an NWS under the NPT, and the Pakistan nuclear programme is associated with A.Q. Khan's proliferation network.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 and 2 only. The NPT (1968, in force 1970) defines a Nuclear Weapons State (NWS) as one that manufactured and exploded a nuclear device before 1 January 1967. Only the US, USSR/Russia, UK, France and China meet this test, so among the listed countries only China and France qualify.
topic_notes: The NPT is the cornerstone of the global nuclear order. It was opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force on 5 March 1970. It was extended indefinitely in 1995, and it has about 191 parties. It has three pillars: non-proliferation (Articles I and II), disarmament (Article VI) and the peaceful use of nuclear energy (Article IV). The five recognised NWS are the USA, Russia, UK, France and China, and they are also the P5 of the UNSC. Review conferences are held every five years. The IAEA (Vienna, 1957) verifies safeguards. States outside the treaty: India, Pakistan and Israel. North Korea withdrew in 2003 and has since tested six times (2006-2017). South Africa gave up its weapons and joined as a non-nuclear state in 1991. Belarus, Kazakhstan and Ukraine gave up Soviet-era weapons and joined as non-nuclear states. Related treaties: the CTBT (1996, not in force; India has not signed it), the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW, adopted 2017, in force 2021), the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963), the New START treaty (US-Russia), and the INF treaty (collapsed 2019). Export-control groups include the Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG, formed 1974 after India's test), the Missile Technology Control Regime (India joined in 2016), the Wassenaar Arrangement (India joined in 2017) and the Australia Group (India joined in 2018). India says the NPT is discriminatory because it divides states into haves and have-nots. India's Nuclear Doctrine (2003) includes No First Use and credible minimum deterrence. India has not been admitted to the NSG, mainly because of China's objection.

ocr: The ideal of ‘Welfare State’ in the Indian Constitution is enshrined in its (a) Preamble (6) Directive Principles of State Policy fc) Fundamental Rights (dq) Seventh Schedule
subject: Polity
detail: The Indian Constitution does not use the phrase 'Welfare State', but its substance lies in the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), Part IV, Articles 36-51, borrowed from the Irish Constitution. Article 38 directs the State to promote the welfare of the people by securing a social order informed by justice (social, economic and political) and to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities. Article 39 covers adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work, and the distribution of material resources to subserve the common good. Article 41 covers the right to work, education and public assistance; Article 42 covers just and humane work conditions and maternity relief; Article 43 covers a living wage; Article 47 covers nutrition and public health. DPSPs are non-justiciable (Article 37) but fundamental in governance. Elimination: the Preamble states broad ideals (Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity) and the Fundamental Rights (Part III) are justiciable civil and political guarantees, whereas the Seventh Schedule only divides legislative powers among the Union, States and Concurrent lists. So (b) is the best answer, since the DPSPs embody the welfare-state ideal in operational form.
explanations: Incorrect as the best answer: the Preamble mentions justice, liberty, equality and fraternity and describes India as a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic, but it states general ideals rather than the specific welfare-state obligations of the State. These are elaborated in Part IV.

Correct: Part IV (Arts. 36-51) lays down the socio-economic goals and welfare duties of the State, such as minimising inequality (Art. 38), the right to adequate livelihood and equal pay (Art. 39), the right to work and public assistance (Art. 41), a living wage (Art. 43) and public health (Art. 47). This is the constitutional embodiment of the welfare-state ideal.

Incorrect: Fundamental Rights (Part III, Arts. 12-35) are justiciable individual rights against the State, mainly civil and political liberties. They restrain State action rather than set out its positive welfare goals.
Incorrect: the Seventh Schedule contains the Union, State and Concurrent Lists, which allocate legislative subjects between the Centre and the States. It has no bearing on welfare ideals.
keyfact: Welfare State ideal = Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV, Arts. 36-51), non-justiciable but fundamental in governance.
option_notes: The Preamble is the introductory statement of the Constitution, based on Nehru's Objectives Resolution (1946). It declares India a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic and secures justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the Supreme Court held it to be part of the Constitution, and in the Berubari case (1960) it had held that it is not a part. It is non-justiciable.

Part IV, Articles 36-51, comprises the Directive Principles, inspired by the Irish Constitution, which in turn drew on the Spanish. They are non-justiciable (Art. 37) but fundamental to governance. They fall into socialistic, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual categories. Added by amendments: Art. 39A (free legal aid), 43A (workers' participation in management), 48A (environment), and 43B (cooperatives, 97th Amendment). The Minerva Mills (1980) case held that Fundamental Rights and DPSPs must be harmonised.

Part III, Articles 12-35, contains the Fundamental Rights, which are justiciable and enforceable through Articles 32 and 226. The six categories are equality (14-18), freedom (19-22), against exploitation (23-24), religion (25-28), cultural and educational (29-30) and constitutional remedies (32). The right to property was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978) and is now Article 300A. Art. 21A (education) was added by the 86th Amendment (2002). Borrowed from the US Bill of Rights.

The Seventh Schedule, under Article 246, distributes legislative powers through the Union List (originally 97 subjects, now 98), the State List (66, originally 66 and now 59 after changes) and the Concurrent List (47, originally 47). The 42nd Amendment (1976) moved education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and the administration of justice to the Concurrent List. The Government of India Act 1935 was the source of the three-list scheme. Residuary powers rest with the Union.
related: DPSPs are in Part IV, Articles 36-51, and are non-justiciable under Article 37.
The DPSPs were borrowed from the Irish Constitution.
Article 44 provides for a Uniform Civil Code; Article 40 for village panchayats.
Article 39A (free legal aid) was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
Article 45 was changed by the 86th Amendment (2002) to cover early childhood care for children under six.
Minerva Mills (1980) held that harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs is a basic feature.
