Claims for localised risks and post-harvest losses are assessed at the individual farm level, and farmers must intimate loss within 72 hours through the insurance company, bank, agriculture department or the Crop Insurance App/helpline 14447.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 2 only. Under PMFBY, farmers pay a uniform premium of 2% only for Kharif food crops and oilseeds, 1.5% for Rabi food crops and oilseeds, and 5% for annual commercial/horticultural crops, so statement 1 is wrong. The scheme does cover post-harvest losses from specified perils (cyclone, cyclonic rain, unseasonal rain) for up to 14 days after harvest on crops left to dry in the field, so statement 2 is correct.
topic_notes: PMFBY was approved by the Union Cabinet on 13 January 2016 and started from Kharif 2016, under the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. It replaced the National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS, 1999) and the Modified NAIS. Objectives: provide insurance coverage and financial support to farmers suffering crop loss from unforeseen events, stabilise farm income, encourage innovative practices and ensure credit flow. Premium: farmers pay a maximum of 2% (Kharif food grains and oilseeds), 1.5% (Rabi food grains and oilseeds) and 5% (annual commercial and horticultural crops). The balance of the actuarial premium is shared by Centre and States equally, with no cap on government subsidy. Coverage: all food crops (cereals, millets, pulses), oilseeds, and annual commercial/horticultural crops for which past yield data is available. Risks covered: prevented sowing, standing crop losses (drought, dry spell, flood, pests and disease, natural fire, lightning, hailstorm, landslide, cyclone, storm), post-harvest losses (14 days), and localised calamities. Methodology: area approach using Crop Cutting Experiments, with technology such as remote sensing, drones, satellite imagery and smartphones (CROPIC) to improve estimates. Enrolment became voluntary for all farmers from Kharif 2020 (earlier compulsory for loanee farmers). A Restructured Weather Based Crop Insurance Scheme (RWBCIS) runs alongside, using weather parameters such as rainfall and temperature as index triggers. Related items: Kisan Credit Card, Soil Health Card, e-NAM, PM-KISAN (2019, Rs 6,000 per year in three instalments), Minimum Support Price and the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund. Farmers must report localised losses within 72 hours. A National Crop Insurance Portal and the Crop Insurance App support enrolment, premium calculation and claims. Likely UPSC angles: premium rates, the replaced schemes, coverage stages, the difference between area-based and weather-based indices, and the role of the Centre and States in subsidy.

ocr: In which of the following regions of India ° ~are you"most likely-to’'come across the ‘Great Indian Hornbill’ in its natural habitat? fa) Sand deserts of northwest India (bj) Higher Himalayas of Jammu and Kashmir (c) Salt marshes of western Gujarat (d) Western Ghats
subject: Geography
detail: The Great Indian Hornbill (Buceros bicornis), also called the Great Pied Hornbill, is the largest hornbill in India and is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. It is in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and in Appendix I of CITES. It is a canopy-dwelling frugivore that needs large, tall, old-growth trees for nesting in natural cavities. The female seals herself inside the cavity with a wall of mud and droppings and leaves only a slit for the male to pass food. Because of this it is called a 'farmer of the forest' for dispersing the seeds of figs and other trees. In India it is found in the Western Ghats (Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra), the Himalayan foothills (Uttarakhand to Arunachal Pradesh) and the northeast. Its main threats are habitat loss, logging and hunting for its casque and feathers. The Arunachal Pradesh Hornbill Nest Adoption Programme, the Nagaland Hornbill Festival and the state bird status in Kerala and Arunachal Pradesh are the usual current-affairs hooks. Elimination logic: hot sandy deserts (a), the high alpine Himalayas (b) and saline marshes (c) have no tall evergreen forest, so a forest hornbill cannot live there. This leaves the Western Ghats.
explanations: Incorrect: the Thar and other northwest sand deserts have thorny scrub and no tall, dense fruiting trees. A forest hornbill that nests in giant tree cavities cannot live there. Desert birds include the Great Indian Bustard.

Incorrect: the higher Himalayas of Jammu and Kashmir are cold, alpine and treeless or coniferous at high altitude. The hornbill occurs only in the lower, moist foothill forests further east, not in J&K highlands.
Incorrect: the salt marshes of western Gujarat (Rann of Kachchh, Little Rann) are saline, treeless flats. They are known for flamingos, the Indian wild ass and the Kachchh bustard, not hornbills.

Correct: the Western Ghats have the evergreen and moist deciduous forests with tall fig and other fruiting trees that the Great Indian Hornbill needs for food and nesting. It is a signature species there, and this matches the official answer.
keyfact: Great Indian Hornbill: Vulnerable, Schedule I, forest-canopy fruit-eater of the Western Ghats, Himalayan foothills and northeast; state bird of Kerala and Arunachal Pradesh.
option_notes: The sand deserts of northwest India include the Thar Desert in Rajasthan and parts of Gujarat, Punjab and Haryana. They have arid scrub, sand dunes and sparse vegetation. The Desert National Park near Jaisalmer is the key protected area. It is home to the Great Indian Bustard (Critically Endangered), the chinkara, the desert fox and the spiny-tailed lizard. The Thar is the most densely populated desert in the world.

The higher Himalayas of Jammu and Kashmir are an alpine and cold-desert zone, with Ladakh as part of it. Notable species are the snow leopard, Tibetan antelope (chiru), Himalayan ibex, Kashmir stag (hangul) and black-necked crane. Protected areas include Dachigam National Park (hangul), Hemis National Park (snow leopard) and the Changthang Cold Desert Sanctuary. Hornbills do not live at this altitude.

The salt marshes of western Gujarat are the Rann of Kachchh, a seasonally flooded salt desert, and the Little Rann of Kachchh. The Little Rann holds the Indian Wild Ass Sanctuary, the only home of the Indian wild ass (khur). The Rann also hosts greater and lesser flamingos at their breeding sites. The Rann of Kachchh is a Ramsar-linked wetland area, and Dholavira, a Harappan site in the Rann, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The Western Ghats are a mountain chain along India's west coast, running through Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu. They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012) and one of the world's biodiversity hotspots. They have high endemism, including the lion-tailed macaque, Nilgiri tahr and Malabar giant squirrel. The Great Indian Hornbill and the Malabar grey hornbill live here. Agasthyamalai, Nilgiri and Silent Valley are important areas.
related: The Great Indian Hornbill is the state bird of Kerala and Arunachal Pradesh.
The Narcondam hornbill is endemic to Narcondam Island in the Andaman Sea.
The Hornbill Festival is held every December at Kisama, Nagaland.
The Great Indian Hornbill is Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List and in Schedule I of the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972.
The female hornbill seals herself in a tree cavity during nesting.
The Western Ghats became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.
The Great Indian Bustard is Critically Endangered and found mainly in the Thar region.
The Pakke Tiger Reserve runs a hornbill nest adoption programme.
summary: The correct answer is (d) Western Ghats. The Great Indian Hornbill (Buceros bicornis) is a large forest hornbill that lives in the evergreen and moist deciduous forests of the Western Ghats, the Himalayan foothills and the northeast. It is not found in deserts, high alpine zones or salt marshes.
topic_notes: Hornbills (family Bucerotidae) are large birds with a big curved bill topped with a casque. India has nine species: Great Indian, Malabar Pied, Indian Grey, Malabar Grey, Oriental Pied, Rufous-necked, Wreathed, Brown (Austen's Brown) and Narcondam hornbills. The Great Indian Hornbill (Buceros bicornis) is the largest, Vulnerable on IUCN, in CITES Appendix I and Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. It is the state bird of Kerala and Arunachal Pradesh. Its habitat is the evergreen and moist deciduous forests of the Western Ghats, the Himalayan foothills and the northeast. Its nesting habit is distinctive. The female seals herself in a tree cavity with mud, droppings and fruit pulp, and the male feeds her through a slit until the chick is ready. Hornbills are fruit-eaters (figs), and are called 'farmers of the forest' or 'forest engineers' for seed dispersal. The Narcondam hornbill (Rhyticeros narcondami) is endemic to Narcondam Island in the Andamans and is Vulnerable. The Nagaland Hornbill Festival (Kisama, December) is named for the bird. The Nest Adoption Programme in Pakke Tiger Reserve, Arunachal Pradesh, involves the Nyishi tribe, who once hunted hornbills for their casques. Threats include logging of nest trees, hunting and the pet trade. Other forest-bird facts UPSC may ask: the Great Indian Bustard (Critically Endangered, Thar, Schedule I), Sarus crane (tallest flying bird), Forest Owlet and Siberian crane. Also revise the biodiversity hotspots (Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats–Sri Lanka, Sundaland) and which species belong to which biome.

ocr: Which of the following are the key features of ‘National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA)’? 1. River basin is the unit of planning and management. 2. It spearheads the river conser- vation efforts at the national level. 3. One of the Chief Ministers of the States through which the Ganga flows becomes the Chairman of NGRBA on rotation basis. Select the correct answer using the code given below, fa) 1 and 2 only {b) 2 and 3 only {ce} 1 and 3 only {d) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Geography
detail: The National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA) was constituted in February 2009 under Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. It was a planning, financing, monitoring and coordinating authority for the Ganga. Its central idea was a departure from the older approach of town-by-town pollution abatement under the Ganga Action Plan (1985) and the National River Conservation Plan: the entire river basin was to be the unit of planning and management, which is statement 1. The Authority was meant to spearhead river conservation at the national level, which is statement 2. It was chaired by the Prime Minister, and its members included the Union Ministers concerned and the Chief Ministers of the Ganga basin states (Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal). There was no rotating chairmanship by a Chief Minister, so statement 3 is incorrect. Ganga was declared the National River in November 2008. In 2016 NGRBA was dissolved and replaced by the National Council for Rejuvenation, Protection and Management of River Ganga (National Ganga Council), with the Namami Gange programme as the implementing mission. Elimination logic: once statement 3 is rejected, options (b), (c) and (d) all fall, leaving (a).
explanations: Correct. Statements 1 and 2 describe NGRBA accurately, and statement 3 is false because the Prime Minister chaired the body.
Wrong. It includes statement 3, which is false: there was no rotating Chief Minister as Chairman.
Wrong. It includes statement 3 and leaves out statement 2, which is true.
Wrong. Statement 3 is false, so 'all three' cannot be correct.
keyfact: NGRBA (2009) used the river basin as the planning unit and was chaired by the Prime Minister, not a rotating Chief Minister; it was replaced by the National Ganga Council in 2016.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only: this is the combination of the two true statements and is the official answer. NGRBA (2009) used the river basin as the planning unit and led national-level conservation of the Ganga. It was chaired by the Prime Minister and was replaced by the National Ganga Council in 2016. The Ganga was declared the National River in 2008, and the Namami Gange programme is run by NMCG.

2 and 3 only: this pairs one true statement with the false claim of a rotating Chief Minister as Chairman. NGRBA was always chaired by the Prime Minister. Chief Ministers of Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand and West Bengal were members. The 2016 National Ganga Council also has the Prime Minister at its head, and there is no rotational chairmanship.

1 and 3 only: this combines the true basin-approach statement with the false rotating-chair statement. The basin approach was a core NGRBA principle, but the chair was the Prime Minister. The Ganga Action Plan (1985) by contrast was a town-based pollution abatement scheme, and it was followed by the National River Conservation Plan.

1, 2 and 3: this would be correct only if all three statements were true, but statement 3 is false. NGRBA was established in 2009 under Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, and its Chairman was the Prime Minister. It was dissolved in 2016 in favour of the National Ganga Council.
related: The Ganga was declared the National River of India in November 2008.
NGRBA was constituted in 2009 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, and was chaired by the Prime Minister.
NGRBA was dissolved in 2016 and replaced by the National Ganga Council.
The Ganga Action Plan was launched in 1985 and was the first river action plan in India.
Namami Gange was launched in 2014-15 and is implemented by the National Mission for Clean Ganga.
The Bhagirathi and Alaknanda meet at Devprayag to form the Ganga.
The Gangetic river dolphin is the National Aquatic Animal, declared in 2009.
The National River Conservation Plan (1995) extended river cleaning to other rivers.
statements: 1 — Correct: NGRBA adopted the river basin as the unit of planning and management, in place of piecemeal, city-based pollution control. This basin approach is the main feature separating it from the earlier Ganga Action Plan. NGRBA was created in 2009 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, with World Bank support for the National Ganga River Basin Project. The basin approach means integrated planning across states, covering pollution, flows, sewage treatment and industrial effluents. The Ganga basin spans 11 states, and the mainstem flows through five: Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand and West Bengal. The Ganga was declared the National River in 2008.

2 — Correct: NGRBA was the national-level authority that spearheaded and coordinated conservation of the Ganga. It was a planning, financing, monitoring and coordinating body, and it was meant to ensure a minimum ecological flow in the river. It was formed in 2009 and was chaired by the Prime Minister. Its work was supported by the Ministry of Environment and Forests, and later by the Ministry of Water Resources. It was dissolved in 2016 when the National Ganga Council took over. Implementation now runs through the National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG), a registered society, under the Namami Gange programme launched in 2014-15.

3 — Incorrect: the Chairman of NGRBA was the Prime Minister of India, not a Chief Minister serving on rotation. Chief Ministers of the Ganga basin states were only members. The authority's structure was: Prime Minister as Chairman, the Union Minister of Environment and Forests as Vice-Chairman, and members including Union Ministers and the Chief Ministers of the concerned states. Under the 2016 order, the National Ganga Council is also headed by the Prime Minister. A rotating chairmanship by Chief Ministers is a feature of no Ganga body, so this statement is a plausible-sounding distractor.
summary: The correct answer is (a) 1 and 2 only. NGRBA, set up in 2009 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, adopted the river basin as the unit of planning and management and led national-level efforts to conserve the Ganga. Its Chairman was the Prime Minister, not a rotating Chief Minister, so statement 3 is wrong.
topic_notes: Ganga conservation has moved through several phases. The Ganga Action Plan (GAP-I) began in 1985 under Rajiv Gandhi, with the aim of intercepting and treating sewage, and it was fully centrally funded. GAP-II (1993) was merged into the National River Conservation Plan (NRCP) in 1995, which extended the work to other rivers. In November 2008 the Ganga was declared the National River. In 2009 the National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA) was set up under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, chaired by the Prime Minister, with the river basin as the planning unit and with World Bank assistance. The National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG) was registered as a society in 2011. In 2014-15 the Namami Gange programme was launched as a flagship programme with an initial outlay of about Rs 20,000 crore. In 2016 NGRBA was dissolved and the National Council for Rejuvenation, Protection and Management of River Ganga (National Ganga Council) was formed, with NMCG as its implementing arm. Namami Gange has several components: sewage treatment infrastructure, river-front development, river surface cleaning, biodiversity conservation, afforestation, industrial effluent monitoring, public awareness and the Ganga Gram scheme. The Hybrid Annuity Model and One City One Operator are used for sewage projects. The Ganga rises as the Bhagirathi at Gaumukh (Gangotri glacier) and becomes the Ganga at Devprayag, where it meets the Alaknanda. Its main tributaries include the Yamuna, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi, Son and Ramganga. The Gangetic river dolphin is the National Aquatic Animal. Possible future questions include the Ganga Action Plan, the Namami Gange components, tributaries, the Ganga basin states, the river dolphin and Ramsar sites on the river.

question: Why does the Government of India promote the use of ‘Neem-coated Urea’ in agriculture?
options: Release of Neem oil in the soil increases nitrogen fixation by the soil microorganisms
) Neem coating slows down the rate of dissolution of urea in the soil
Nitrous oxide, which is a greenhouse gas, is not at all released into atmosphere by crop ; fields
It is a combination of a weedicide and a fertilizer for particular crops
subject: Geography
detail: Neem-coated urea (NCU) is ordinary urea coated with neem oil (about 0.5 kg/tonne in practice). Neem contains triterpenoids such as nimbin and azadirachtin that act as nitrification inhibitors. They slow the conversion of ammonium to nitrite and nitrate by Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter, so nitrogen stays available to crops for longer. This reduces leaching of nitrate into groundwater and lowers volatilisation and N2O emissions. Because plants take up more of the applied nitrogen, farmers need less urea per hectare, and the saving is estimated at roughly 5-10%. Since 2015 the Government has made all domestic urea production neem-coated. Neem-coated urea is also unsuitable for industrial use, such as making plastics, resins and synthetic milk, which curbs diversion of subsidised agricultural urea. Elimination: (a) is wrong because neem does not fix nitrogen; fixation is done by Rhizobium, Azotobacter and similar organisms, and neem coating actually inhibits nitrifiers. (c) is wrong because of the words 'not at all'; N2O emissions are reduced, not eliminated. (d) is wrong because neem oil is not a weedicide, and the product is not a combined weedicide-fertilizer. Absolute words like 'not at all' are a common sign of a wrong option in UPSC.
explanations: Incorrect: neem oil does not increase nitrogen fixation. It inhibits nitrification and slows nitrogen conversion, and fixation is carried out by other microbes.
Correct: neem coating slows urea dissolution and nitrification, giving slow, steady nitrogen release, better uptake and less loss.
Incorrect: N2O emissions are reduced but not eliminated, so 'not at all released' is false.
Incorrect: neem-coated urea is a fertilizer with a nitrification-inhibiting coating, not a weedicide-fertilizer combination.
keyfact: Neem-coated urea slows nitrification and urea dissolution, giving gradual nitrogen release and higher efficiency; it also curbs industrial diversion.
option_notes: Biological nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric N2 into ammonia. It is done by symbiotic Rhizobium in legume root nodules, by free-living Azotobacter and Clostridium, and by Azospirillum, Anabaena and Azolla (with cyanobacteria) in rice fields. Neem oil does not drive this process. Legumes enrich soil nitrogen, which is why crop rotation and biofertilisers are promoted.

Slower dissolution of urea is the real benefit of neem coating. Neem oil, with nimbin and azadirachtin, acts as a nitrification inhibitor and slows urea hydrolysis. Nitrogen is released over a longer period, nitrate leaching and ammonia volatilisation fall, and use efficiency rises. The Government made neem coating mandatory for all domestic urea from 2015 and it is also used to curb diversion.

Nitrous oxide (N2O) is a greenhouse gas with a global warming potential of about 265-298 times CO2 over 100 years. It also depletes stratospheric ozone. Agriculture, mainly nitrogen fertilisers, is the largest anthropogenic source. It forms through nitrification and denitrification in soils. Neem coating reduces but does not eliminate these emissions.

Weedicides (herbicides) such as 2,4-D, glyphosate and atrazine kill weeds. Fertilisers supply nutrients. Neem-coated urea is simply urea (46% N) with neem oil, so it is not a combination product. Neem is better known as a biopesticide with azadirachtin as the active ingredient, and it is also used in organic farming.
related: Urea contains 46% nitrogen, the highest among solid nitrogenous fertilisers.
Neem coating became mandatory for all domestic urea from 2015.
Neem-coated urea cannot be easily used for industrial purposes, which curbs diversion.
Active neem compounds: azadirachtin, nimbin and salannin.
Nano urea was developed by IFFCO and launched in 2021.
Soil Health Card scheme was launched in February 2015 at Suratgarh, Rajasthan.
Nitrous oxide has a global warming potential about 265-298 times CO2.
Sikkim became India's first fully organic state in 2016.
summary: The answer is (b). Neem coating slows the dissolution and nitrification of urea in the soil, so nitrogen is released gradually, which improves nitrogen use efficiency and reduces losses and wasteful or illegal diversion.
topic_notes: Urea is India's most used fertiliser. It contains 46% nitrogen, is subsidised and sold at a controlled maximum retail price (MRP), about Rs 242 per 45 kg bag. India is among the world's largest consumers and imports a share of its requirement. Nitrogen use efficiency in Indian agriculture is low (roughly 30-35% for urea), so much of the nitrogen is lost as nitrate leaching, ammonia volatilisation and N2O. Policy measures: the New Urea Policy 2015 made neem coating mandatory for all domestic producers and aimed to improve efficiency, curb diversion to industry and raise domestic production. The Soil Health Card scheme (2015) promotes balanced fertiliser use. Direct Benefit Transfer in fertiliser subsidy is routed via PoS machines with Aadhaar-linked sales. Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) applies to P and K fertilisers, while urea remains outside it. Other related ideas include nano urea (IFFCO, liquid, launched 2021), Urea Gold (sulphur-coated urea), the fertiliser-subsidy burden on the budget, and the Haber-Bosch process for ammonia. Fertiliser grades: DAP is 18-46-0, and MOP is 60% K2O. Nitrification inhibitors include neem, DCD and nitrapyrin. Environmental angles are eutrophication, blue-baby syndrome (nitrate in water), N2O as a greenhouse gas, and the Kigali, Montreal and Kyoto protocols. UPSC may also ask on biofertilisers (Rhizobium, Azolla, blue-green algae, mycorrhiza), organic farming (PKVY, Sikkim as the first fully organic state) and zero budget natural farming.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Chief Secretary in a State is appointed by the Governor of that State.
2. The Chief Secretary in a State has a fixed tenure. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: The Chief Secretary (CS) is the head of the state civil service and the administrative head of the state secretariat. The Constitution does not mention the post; it exists by convention and by the Rules of Business of each state. The CS is selected by the Chief Minister from among the senior-most IAS officers of the state cadre, and the appointment is formally issued by the state government. The Governor does not appoint the CS, so statement 1 fails. Unlike the Cabinet Secretary at the Centre, who has had a fixed two-year tenure since 2005 (extendable up to four years), no such rule applies to state Chief Secretaries. Tenure depends on the officer's superannuation at 60 and the CM's confidence. Extensions are granted by the Centre on the state's request. Hence statement 2 also fails. Elimination: once either statement is shown false, options (a), (b) and (c) fall, leaving (d). The Supreme Court in Prakash Singh (2006) fixed tenures for DGPs, not for Chief Secretaries.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is false: the Chief Minister selects the CS, and the Governor does not appoint.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 is false: the state CS has no fixed tenure.
(c) is wrong because neither statement is correct.
(d) is right because both statements are incorrect: appointment is by the state government on the CM's choice, and there is no fixed tenure.
keyfact: The state Chief Secretary is chosen by the Chief Minister, not the Governor, and has no fixed tenure, unlike the Cabinet Secretary with a two-year tenure.
option_notes: Option (a) says only statement 1 is correct. This would hold only if the Governor appointed the CS, which is not the case. The Governor does appoint the Advocate General, the State Election Commissioner and the State Public Service Commission members, and these are the likely sources of confusion. The CS is chosen by the CM from senior IAS officers of the state cadre. The Governor's role in executive matters is formal, exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers under Article 163, except for discretionary matters.

Option (b) says only statement 2 is correct. This would hold if the CS had a fixed tenure, but no law or rule prescribes one. Fixed tenures exist for the Cabinet Secretary (two years since 2005, extendable to four), the Chief Election Commissioner (six years or age 65), the Comptroller and Auditor General (six years or age 65), and the DGP (minimum two years after Prakash Singh, 2006). The CS serves until retirement at 60, or until replaced, with extensions only by Centre approval.

Option (c) says both statements are correct. It is wrong because both are false. It reflects a common mix-up between state and Union positions: the Cabinet Secretary is appointed by the Prime Minister (formally by the President) and has a fixed tenure, but the state CS equivalent has neither a Governor appointment nor a fixed term. The CS is a convention-based post and is not constitutionally defined, unlike the Governor, Advocate General, and the Public Service Commission.

Option (d) says neither statement is correct, which is the official answer. The Chief Secretary is chosen by the Chief Minister and appointed by the state government, and there is no fixed tenure. The CS heads the state secretariat, the civil services, and is Secretary to the Cabinet. The CS is an IAS officer of the state cadre, and the post is the equivalent of the Cabinet Secretary at the Centre in function, but not in tenure or in the method of appointment.
related: The Cabinet Secretary has a fixed tenure of two years since 2005, extendable up to four years.
The Chief Secretary is not a constitutional post; it exists through the Rules of Business and convention.
The Governor appoints the Advocate General of a state under Article 165.
The State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Governor under Article 243K.
Article 312 empowers Parliament to create All India Services, including the IAS and IPS.
The Prakash Singh case (2006) directed a minimum two-year tenure for DGPs.
The CS is the Secretary to the state Cabinet and head of the state secretariat.
The Second ARC (2005) was chaired by M. Veerappa Moily.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Governor does not appoint the Chief Secretary; the Chief Minister chooses the officer and the state government issues the order. Details: The CS is the senior-most civil servant of a state, usually from the IAS. Although the Governor acts as the formal head, the real executive power lies with the Council of Ministers headed by the CM, who selects the CS in practice. The CS is Secretary to the Cabinet, ex-officio head of the Civil Services Board, and chief adviser to the CM. The post is not mentioned in the Constitution and is governed by the state's Rules of Business. The Centre's consent is not formally needed, but the officer must belong to the state cadre.

2 — Incorrect: There is no fixed tenure for a state Chief Secretary. Details: The CS serves until superannuation (age 60) or until the government replaces them, and so serves effectively at the pleasure of the government. Extensions of service beyond retirement require Centre approval under the All India Services rules. This contrasts with the Cabinet Secretary, whose tenure was fixed at two years in 2005 and may extend up to four years. The Supreme Court in Prakash Singh (2006) laid down minimum two-year tenures for DGPs, not CSs. Frequent transfers of CSs are often cited as politicisation of the bureaucracy, and the Second ARC discussed related reforms.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. The Chief Secretary is appointed by the Chief Minister (the state government, with the CM's choice from senior IAS officers), not by the Governor, and has no fixed tenure; the post is held at the pleasure of the government.
topic_notes: The Chief Secretary is the highest-ranking civil servant of a state and the head of its administrative machinery. The post is not mentioned in the Constitution, and is created by the state's Rules of Business and by convention. The CS is selected by the Chief Minister from the senior-most IAS officers in the cadre, and the appointment is formalised by the state government. Roles include: Secretary to the state Cabinet, ex-officio head of the Civil Services Board, head of the secretariat, principal adviser to the CM on policy, chief coordinator among departments, and chair of many committees. The CS also represents the state in dealings with the Centre, and is the state's chief of crisis management, for example in disasters and law and order. At the Union level, the equivalent is the Cabinet Secretary, who is appointed by the PM, is the head of the Civil Services Board, and has had a fixed two-year tenure since 2005, extendable up to four years. The Cabinet Secretary also heads the Indian Administrative Service as its cadre controlling authority. Other posts with fixed tenures include the CEC and CAG (six years or age 65/65), UPSC members (six years or age 65), and SPSC members (six years or age 62). The Governor appoints the Advocate General, SPSC members and the State Election Commissioner. Related ideas: All India Services Act 1951, the Administrative Reforms Commissions (First 1966, Second 2005), the Prakash Singh case on police reforms, and Article 312 on All India Services. Future questions could test the differences between the Cabinet Secretary and the Chief Secretary, and the constitutional versus convention-based posts.

ocr: With reference to ‘Stand Up India Scheme’, which of the following statements is/are correct? l. its purpose is to promote entrepreneurship among SC/ST and women entrepreneurs. 2. It provides for refinance through SIDBI. Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1 only (bj 2 only {c) Both 1 and 2 {d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Geography
detail: Stand-Up India was announced in the Budget 2015-16 speech (Finance Minister Arun Jaitley) and launched by PM Narendra Modi on 5 April 2016. It facilitates bank loans between Rs 10 lakh and Rs 1 crore to at least one SC or ST borrower and at least one woman borrower per bank branch, for setting up a greenfield enterprise in manufacturing, services, the trading sector (added later) or agri-allied activities. For non-individual enterprises, at least 51% of the shareholding and controlling stake must be held by an SC/ST or woman entrepreneur. The scheme is run by the Department of Financial Services, with SIDBI as the lead implementing agency; SIDBI provides refinance window of Rs 10,000 crore initially. A credit guarantee is offered through the Credit Guarantee Fund for Stand-Up India (CGFSIL), managed by NCGTC. Support also comes through the Stand-Up Connect Centres and the portal standupmitra.in. Elimination logic: Statement 1 states the purpose correctly, so (b) and (d) go. Statement 2 is also correct since SIDBI refinance is a core feature, so (a) goes. Hence (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 2 is also correct; SIDBI refinance is a feature of the scheme.
(b) is wrong because statement 1 is also correct; the scheme targets SC/ST and women entrepreneurs.
(c) is correct because both statements accurately describe the scheme's purpose and its refinance support through SIDBI.
(d) is wrong because both statements are correct, so at least one is valid.
keyfact: Stand-Up India (5 April 2016): Rs 10 lakh–1 crore bank loans for SC/ST and women greenfield enterprises, with SIDBI refinance and lead agency role.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: it would hold if SIDBI refinance were not part of the scheme. In fact SIDBI is the lead agency with a Rs 10,000 crore refinance window. Remember that the scheme loan range is Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore, covers greenfield enterprises, and requires at least one SC/ST and one woman borrower per bank branch. The Stand-Up Mitra portal gives handholding, and the scheme was announced in Budget 2015-16 and launched on 5 April 2016.

Option (b), 2 only: it would hold if the purpose in statement 1 were incorrect. SIDBI, set up in 1990 and headquartered in Lucknow, is the main financial institution for MSME financing and provides refinance, direct credit and development support. It also manages funds like the Fund of Funds for Startups (FFS) and acts as the lead agency in the Stand-Up India and Start-up India initiatives.

Option (c), both 1 and 2: the official correct answer. Stand-Up India aims to promote entrepreneurship among SC/ST and women through bank loans of Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore for greenfield ventures. SIDBI provides refinance (Rs 10,000 crore window), and NCGTC manages the credit guarantee fund. The scheme is overseen by the Department of Financial Services in the Ministry of Finance and has been extended up to 2025.

Option (d), neither: it would hold only if both statements were false. Common confusions here are Start-up India (launched 16 January 2015 with an Action Plan, DPIIT-recognised startups, tax benefits, Fund of Funds) and Stand-Up India (focused on SC/ST and women bank credit). Neither statement is false, so this option is wrong.
related: Stand-Up India launched on 5 April 2016; announced in Budget 2015-16.
Loan range under Stand-Up India: Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore.
SIDBI was established in 1990 and is headquartered in Lucknow.
Start-up India was launched on 16 January 2015 with a 19-point Action Plan.
Mudra loans: Shishu (up to Rs 50,000), Kishor (Rs 50,000 to 5 lakh), Tarun (Rs 5 lakh to 10 lakh).
Credit guarantee for Stand-Up India is handled by NCGTC.
Stand-Up India requires at least one SC/ST and one woman borrower per bank branch.
Stand-Up Mitra portal (standupmitra.in) provides handholding support to borrowers.
statements: 1 — Correct: The scheme's purpose is to promote entrepreneurship among SC/ST and women entrepreneurs. Stand-Up India was launched on 5 April 2016 at Noida by PM Modi. It targets credit gaps faced by underserved groups, giving composite loans of Rs 10 lakh to Rs 1 crore from scheduled commercial banks for greenfield projects in manufacturing, services, trading and agri-allied activities. Each bank branch must lend to at least one SC/ST borrower and one woman borrower. The scheme was initially to run till 2025 and has been extended to 2025-26. Borrowers can access handholding support through the Stand-Up Mitra portal.

2 — Correct: The scheme provides refinance through SIDBI. A refinance window of Rs 10,000 crore was set up through SIDBI, with initial contribution from the Government. SIDBI (Small Industries Development Bank of India) was established in 1990 under an Act of Parliament as a subsidiary of IDBI and later became independent. It is the principal financial institution for promoting, financing and developing MSMEs, and is also the lead bank for Stand-Up India. The Credit Guarantee Fund for Stand-Up India is managed by NCGTC, which provides the guarantee cover.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. Stand-Up India (launched 5 April 2016) aims to promote entrepreneurship among SC/ST and women by facilitating bank loans, and it provides refinance support through SIDBI.
topic_notes: Stand-Up India Scheme was announced in the Union Budget 2015-16 and launched on 5 April 2016 (Babu Jagjivan Ram's birth anniversary) by PM Modi. Objective: facilitate bank loans between Rs 10 lakh and Rs 1 crore to at least one SC or ST borrower and at least one woman borrower per bank branch for setting up a greenfield enterprise in manufacturing, services, trading or agri-allied activities. For non-individual enterprises, 51% of the shareholding and controlling stake must be held by an SC/ST or woman entrepreneur. Borrowers must be above 18 years and not in default to any bank or financial institution. Loans are composite (term loan plus working capital), with repayment up to 7 years and a maximum moratorium of 18 months. The implementing agency is SIDBI, which provides refinance (initial Rs 10,000 crore window) and runs the Stand-Up Mitra portal (standupmitra.in). Credit guarantee is provided through the Credit Guarantee Fund for Stand-Up India (CGFSIL), managed by NCGTC. Ministry: Department of Financial Services, Ministry of Finance. Related programs: Start-up India (16 Jan 2015 action plan, DPIIT recognition, 3-year tax holiday under Section 80-IAC, Fund of Funds with Rs 10,000 crore managed by SIDBI), Pradhan Mantri Mudra Yojana (April 2015, Shishu up to Rs 50,000, Kishor up to Rs 5 lakh, Tarun up to Rs 10 lakh, later Tarun Plus up to Rs 20 lakh), Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE), PM Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP, KVIC), and MSME Champions. SIDBI facts: established 1990, HQ Lucknow, apex financial institution for MSMEs. UPSC may ask about institution roles, scheme target groups, loan limits, and distinctions between Start-up India, Stand-Up India and Mudra.

ocr: The FAO accords the status of ‘Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System {GIAHS)’ to traditional agricultural systems. What is the overall goal of this initiative? 1. To provide modern technology, training in modern farming methods and financial support to local communities of identified GIAHS so as to greatly enhance their agricultural productivity 2: “To identify and safeguard eco-friendly traditional farm practices and their associated landscapes, agricultural biodiversity and knowledge systems of the local communities 3. To provide Geographical Indication status to all the varieties
subject: Economy
detail: GIAHS was launched by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) in 2002, at the World Summit on Sustainable Development in Johannesburg. It recognises outstanding land-use systems and landscapes that are rich in globally significant biodiversity and that evolved from the co-adaptation of a community with its environment. The aim is dynamic conservation: it protects the agro-ecological practices, agrobiodiversity, traditional knowledge, culture and resilient landscapes that sustain local livelihoods and food security. The status is a recognition, not a funding or technology scheme, and it does not confer a legal IP right. Elimination logic: Statement 1 reverses the philosophy, because GIAHS conserves traditional methods and does not replace them with modern technology to maximise productivity. Statement 3 confuses GIAHS with Geographical Indications, which are a legal IP regime under the WTO TRIPS Agreement and, in India, the GI of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999. GIAHS gives no GI status to produce. Only statement 2 matches the stated goal, so (b) is correct. In India, Koraput (Odisha), Kuttanad (Kerala) and the Kashmir saffron heritage were recognised as GIAHS sites.
explanations: Wrong. It includes statement 1 (modern technology and productivity push), which contradicts GIAHS's conservation philosophy, and statement 3 (GI status), which is a different regime.
Correct. Only statement 2 describes the goal of GIAHS: identifying and safeguarding traditional eco-friendly farming systems, landscapes, biodiversity and knowledge.
Wrong. Statement 3 is incorrect because GIAHS does not give GI status, and this option leaves out the correct statement 2.
Wrong. Statements 1 and 3 are both incorrect, so 'all three' cannot be right.
keyfact: GIAHS (FAO, 2002) conserves traditional eco-friendly farming systems, landscapes and knowledge; it is not a technology-transfer scheme and gives no GI tag.
option_notes: Not applicable: this option is a combination of statement numbers (1 and 3 only).
Not applicable: this option is a combination of statement numbers (2 only).
Not applicable: this option is a combination of statement numbers (2 and 3 only).
Not applicable: this option is a combination of statement numbers (1, 2 and 3).
related: GIAHS was launched by FAO in 2002 at the World Summit on Sustainable Development in Johannesburg.
India's first GIAHS site was Koraput in Odisha (2012); Kuttanad in Kerala followed in 2013.
Pampore saffron heritage of Kashmir was recognised as a GIAHS site in 2023.
GI protection in India is under the GI of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, administered by the GI Registry in Chennai.
Darjeeling tea was India's first GI-tagged product (2004).
Biodiversity Heritage Sites are notified under Section 37 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.
FAO is headquartered in Rome and was founded in 1945.
GIAHS recognition carries no legal IP protection and gives no direct funding.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: GIAHS does not aim to supply modern technology, training or finance to maximise productivity; it aims to conserve traditional systems. FAO's approach is dynamic conservation, meaning these systems are safeguarded while they adapt. Recognition draws attention, supports sustainable development, and can help communities access national or international support. It does not transform the systems with modern inputs. Examples include rice-fish culture in China (the first site, Qingtian, 2005), Andean agriculture and Ifugao rice terraces. The programme is run by FAO with partners such as the GEF and national governments.

2 — Correct: GIAHS identifies and safeguards eco-friendly traditional farming practices and the associated landscapes, agrobiodiversity and knowledge systems. It was launched in 2002, and the first sites were designated in 2005 (China, Chile, Peru, Algeria, Tunisia, Philippines). Selection criteria are food and livelihood security, agrobiodiversity, local and traditional knowledge, cultures and value systems, and landscape features. India's sites are Koraput traditional agriculture (Odisha, 2012), Kuttanad below-sea-level farming (Kerala, 2013) and Kashmir saffron heritage (Pampore, 2023). The FAO Secretariat for the programme is in Rome.

3 — Incorrect: GIAHS does not grant Geographical Indication status to produce. GI is a separate intellectual property right covering goods whose qualities are linked to their geographical origin. It is protected internationally under TRIPS (Articles 22-24) and in India under the GI Act, 1999, which came into force in 2003 and is administered by the GI Registry in Chennai. Darjeeling tea was India's first GI-tagged product (2004). GIAHS is a recognition by FAO and carries no legal IP protection.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 2 only. FAO's GIAHS programme aims to identify and safeguard traditional, eco-friendly farming systems, along with their landscapes, agricultural biodiversity and knowledge systems. It is a conservation and recognition initiative, not a programme of modern technology transfer or GI tagging.
topic_notes: GIAHS is an FAO programme launched in 2002 to recognise and conserve agricultural heritage systems. These are living, evolving systems of land use shaped by the co-adaptation of communities with their environment. They provide food and livelihood security, maintain agrobiodiversity, and carry traditional knowledge and cultural value. Selection criteria are food and livelihood security, agrobiodiversity, local and traditional knowledge systems, cultures, value systems and social organisation, and landscape or seascape features. The first sites were designated in 2005. China has the largest number of sites, and Japan, India, Korea and Iran also have several. The programme is supported by the GEF and other partners and coordinated from FAO headquarters in Rome. Designation is a recognition. It is not a legal protection like a GI, and it does not involve direct funding. It is meant to draw attention, encourage sustainable management and help local communities with market access, ecotourism and policy support. In India, the recognised sites are Koraput (Odisha, 2012), Kuttanad (Kerala, 2013) and Pampore saffron heritage (Kashmir, 2023). Related concepts that UPSC may test: Geographical Indications (the TRIPS Agreement, the GI Act 1999, the GI Registry in Chennai), UNESCO World Heritage Sites (cultural and natural), Ramsar sites, the Biological Diversity Act 2002, the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act 2001, the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources (ITPGRFA), the National Biodiversity Authority, and Biodiversity Heritage Sites under Section 37 of the BD Act. Possible angles: which body gives the status (FAO), the year of launch (2002), the objectives, India's sites, and how GIAHS differs from GI or UNESCO status.

ocr: Which of the following is/are tributary/ tributaries of Brahmaputra? 1. Dibang 2, Kameng 3. Lohit Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa} 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (da) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Brahmaputra (Tsangpo in Tibet, Siang/Dihang in Arunachal Pradesh, Jamuna in Bangladesh) rises near the Chemayungdung glacier in the Kailash range, southeast of Mansarovar. It flows east through Tibet, takes a U-turn at Namcha Barwa around the Great Bend, and enters India as the Siang. At Kobo near Sadiya, the Dibang and Lohit meet it and from there it is called the Brahmaputra. In Assam its north-bank tributaries include the Subansiri, Jia Bhareli (Kameng), Dhansiri (N), Puthimari, Pagladiya, Manas and Sankosh. Its south-bank tributaries include the Burhi Dihing, Disang, Dhansiri (S) and Kopili. Because the three listed names are all Arunachal Pradesh rivers draining the eastern Himalaya into the Brahmaputra, none can be eliminated. A student who knows even one wrong-looking name, such as the Kameng being a tributary, can rule out (a) and (c) and reach (d) logically. The river is braided, flood-prone and has Majuli, one of the largest river islands in the world.
explanations: (a) Incorrect: it says only Dibang is a tributary, but the Kameng and Lohit are tributaries too.
(b) Incorrect: it leaves out Dibang, which is a major tributary of the Brahmaputra.
(c) Incorrect: it leaves out Kameng (Jia Bhareli), which joins the Brahmaputra from the north bank in Assam.
(d) Correct: Dibang, Kameng and Lohit are all tributaries, so statements 1, 2 and 3 are all correct.
keyfact: Dibang, Kameng (Jia Bhareli) and Lohit are all Brahmaputra tributaries, so the answer is (d).
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would mean that Dibang alone is a tributary. The Dibang rises in the Mishmi Hills in Arunachal Pradesh, flows through the Dibang Valley, and joins the Brahmaputra near Sadiya with the Lohit and Siang. The Dibang Multipurpose Project is India's tallest dam under construction. The option is wrong because it ignores two other tributaries, the Kameng and Lohit. UPSC often tests partial-selection traps of this kind.

Option (b), '2 and 3 only', would include Kameng and Lohit but exclude Dibang. The Kameng (Jia Bhareli) joins from the north bank near Tezpur, and the Lohit joins from the east near Kobo. It is wrong because the Dibang also meets the Brahmaputra near Sadiya. The Dibang has the Mishmi Hills catchment and the Dibang Wildlife Sanctuary, and the 2,880 MW Dibang hydroelectric project is located on it.

Option (c), '1 and 3 only', would include Dibang and Lohit but exclude Kameng. The Dibang and Lohit are eastern tributaries that join in Upper Assam around Sadiya and Kobo. The option is wrong because the Kameng, known as the Jia Bhareli in Assam, is also a north-bank tributary. The Kameng flows through Nameri National Park and the Pakke Tiger Reserve before reaching the Brahmaputra.

Option (d), '1, 2 and 3', is the official answer. It covers the Dibang, Kameng and Lohit, three Arunachal Pradesh rivers draining the eastern Himalaya into the Brahmaputra. The Lohit and Dibang join near Kobo and Sadiya to form the Brahmaputra with the Siang, and the Kameng joins as the Jia Bhareli on the north bank. The Brahmaputra's drainage includes more than 20 tributaries in India.
related: Brahmaputra is called Tsangpo in Tibet, Siang or Dihang in Arunachal Pradesh, and Jamuna in Bangladesh.
The Great Bend of the Tsangpo is at Namcha Barwa, and it is among the deepest gorges in the world.
Subansiri is the largest tributary of the Brahmaputra and rises in Tibet.
Majuli in Assam is the world's largest river island in a river.
The Lohit, Dibang and Siang meet near Kobo and Sadiya to form the Brahmaputra.
The Kameng is called Jia Bhareli in Assam and flows by Nameri National Park.
The Teesta is a Sikkim river and joins the Brahmaputra (Jamuna) in Bangladesh.
The Bogibeel bridge near Dibrugarh is India's longest rail-cum-road bridge.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Dibang is a major left-bank tributary of the Brahmaputra. The Dibang rises in the Mishmi Hills near the Tibet border in Arunachal Pradesh. It flows through the Dibang Valley and the Lower Dibang Valley districts, and it meets the Lohit and Siang in the plains of Assam near Sadiya. The Dibang Multipurpose Project, about 2,880 MW, is India's highest dam under construction at about 278 m. The Dibang Wildlife Sanctuary and the Mishmi tribes (Idu Mishmi) are located here. The valley has high rainfall and rich biodiversity.

2 — Correct: The Kameng, called the Jia Bhareli in Assam, is a north-bank tributary of the Brahmaputra. The Kameng rises from the Gori Chen glacier region in Arunachal Pradesh near the Tibet border. It flows through West and East Kameng and Tawang's neighbouring areas, then enters Assam near Tezpur as the Jia Bhareli. The Kameng is known for Nameri National Park and the Pakke Tiger Reserve, which lie along its course. Bichom and Dikrong rivers are related regional rivers. The Kameng hydroelectric project, 600 MW, is in West Kameng.

3 — Correct: The Lohit is a major eastern tributary of the Brahmaputra. The Lohit rises in eastern Tibet, where it is called the Zayul Chu, and flows through Arunachal Pradesh, in the Lohit district. It passes the Parshuram Kund pilgrimage site and Namdapha National Park is nearby. It meets the Dibang and Dihang (Siang) near Kobo, from where the combined stream is called the Brahmaputra. The Lohit flows through the Mishmi Hills and the Kamlang Wildlife Sanctuary lies in its basin. The Lohit is also the district name of the Tezu region.
summary: The correct answer is (d): Dibang, Kameng and Lohit are all tributaries of the Brahmaputra. Dibang and Lohit join it from the east in Arunachal Pradesh and Assam, and the Kameng (Jia Bhareli) joins it from the north bank in Assam.
topic_notes:
The Brahmaputra is about 2,900 km long, of which about 916 km are in India. It is called the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet, Siang or Dihang in Arunachal Pradesh, Brahmaputra in Assam and Jamuna in Bangladesh, where it joins the Ganga (Padma) and then the Meghna before reaching the Bay of Bengal. It rises near the Chemayungdung glacier in the Kailash range, close to Mansarovar. The Tsangpo flows east for nearly 1,200 km in Tibet, and the Great Bend around Namcha Barwa takes it through the Tsangpo gorge, one of the deepest canyons in the world. It enters India near Gelling in Arunachal Pradesh.

Major north-bank tributaries: Subansiri (largest, rises in Tibet), Kameng (Jia Bhareli), Manas, Dhansiri (N), Puthimari, Pagladiya, Sankosh, Raidak and Tista in the lower part. Major south-bank tributaries: Lohit, Dibang, Burhi Dihing, Disang, Dhansiri (S), Kopili and Dhaleswari. Sadiya is the point where the river is formally called the Brahmaputra.

Features: it is a braided river, flood-prone, with high silt load, carries a large volume of water, and has changing channels. Majuli is the world's largest river island in a river. Kaziranga and Manas are in its floodplain. Dibrugarh and Guwahati are important towns, and Bogibeel is a rail-cum-road bridge near Dibrugarh. Inland waterway NW-2 runs from Sadiya to Dhubri.

Geopolitics: the Indus Waters Treaty applies to the western rivers, but India and China have an expert-level mechanism and share flood data on the Brahmaputra. China is building the Zangmu dam in Tibet. India's Siang Upper Multipurpose Project is planned in Arunachal Pradesh.

ocr: The term ‘Core Banking Solutions’ is sometimes seen in the news, Which of the following statements best describes/ describe this term? 1, It is a networking of a bank's branches which enables customers to operate their accounts from any branch of the bank on its network regardless of where they open their accounts. 2. It is an effort to increase RBI’s control over commercial banks through computerization. 3. It is a detailed procedure by which a bank with huge non-performing assets is taken over by another bank. Select the correct answer using the cod given below. - SSS fa) 1 only (b) 2 and 3
subject: Economy
detail: Core Banking Solutions (CBS) is a centralised, real-time banking software and networking platform. 'Core' originally stood for Centralised Online Real-time Exchange. All branch data sits on a central server or data centre, so a customer becomes a customer of the bank rather than of one branch. This enables anywhere banking: deposits, withdrawals, transfers, loan repayments and balance enquiries at any networked branch, along with ATMs, internet and mobile banking, and a platform for NEFT, RTGS and UPI. In India, CBS rollout began in the early 2000s, led by private banks like ICICI and HDFC. RBI pushed public sector banks to complete CBS, and by about 2012-13 nearly all PSBs, and then Regional Rural Banks and cooperative banks, were on CBS. Popular software includes Finacle (Infosys) and BaNCS (TCS). Elimination logic: statement 2 is wrong because CBS is a bank-level operational tool, not an RBI supervisory mechanism. Statement 3 describes a merger, amalgamation or resolution of a stressed bank, a separate process governed by the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and RBI schemes. Only statement 1 is correct, so (a).
explanations: Correct. Only statement 1 describes CBS accurately. Statements 2 and 3 are unrelated to what CBS is, so '1 only' is right.
Incorrect. Both 2 and 3 are wrong. CBS is not about RBI control or takeovers of banks with large NPAs.
Incorrect. Statement 1 is correct, but statement 3 is wrong because it describes a merger or resolution procedure, not CBS.
Incorrect. Statements 2 and 3 are wrong, so 'all three' cannot be right.
keyfact: CBS = networked branches on a central server enabling anywhere banking; it is not RBI control or bank takeover. Answer: (a).
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only. It is the correct answer. CBS networks branches on a central server, enabling anywhere banking. It started with private banks around the late 1990s and 2000s. Public sector banks, RRBs and cooperative banks were later brought onto it under RBI's push. Platforms include Finacle and TCS BaNCS. It underpins ATMs, internet and mobile banking, NEFT, RTGS and UPI connectivity, and gives real-time account updates.

Option (b), statements 2 and 3. This is wrong. Statement 2 confuses CBS with RBI supervision. Statement 3 describes bank mergers or resolution of stressed banks. Related facts: RBI's tools include CRR, SLR, repo rate, inspections and PCA. Mergers are done under Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. In 2019-20 several PSBs were consolidated, reducing public sector banks from 27 in 2017 to 12 by 2020.

Option (c), statements 1 and 3. This is wrong because statement 3 is not CBS. Bank takeovers involve a scheme of amalgamation approved by RBI and the Government, with share-swap ratios, protection of depositors and employees, and sometimes moratoriums. Examples are the 2020 Yes Bank reconstruction by RBI with SBI-led investment, and the Lakshmi Vilas Bank merger with DBS India in 2020.

Option (d), all three statements. This is wrong because 2 and 3 are false. CBS is only a networking and centralised software solution. RBI regulates banks through law and policy, not through CBS. Takeovers of weak banks are separate regulatory events. UPSC often offers 'all of the above' as a distractor when one statement is clearly correct.
related: CBS stands for Core Banking Solutions, from Centralised Online Real-time Exchange.
IDRBT in Hyderabad was set up by RBI in 1996 for banking technology.
NPCI was established in 2008 and operates UPI, RuPay and IMPS.
Finacle (Infosys) and BaNCS (TCS) are common CBS software platforms.
Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 allows RBI-led amalgamation of troubled banks.
PCA (Prompt Corrective Action) is used by RBI to restrict weak banks.
PMJDY launched in August 2014 for universal access to bank accounts.
PSBs were consolidated from 27 (2017) to 12 (2020).
statements: 1 — Correct: This is the standard description of CBS, which networks branches so customers can operate accounts from any branch regardless of where they opened them. Facts: CBS runs on a central server and data centre with real-time updating of transactions. It makes the customer 'the bank's customer', not a particular branch's customer. Services include anywhere banking, ATMs, internet and mobile banking, and payment-system integration. Private banks adopted it first in the late 1990s and early 2000s. PSBs largely completed it by about 2012-13, followed by RRBs and cooperative banks. Common platforms are Finacle (Infosys) and TCS BaNCS. Benefits are speed, accuracy, lower paperwork, and easier MIS and compliance reporting.

2 — Incorrect: CBS is a technology platform used by individual banks to run operations. It is not a means for RBI to increase control over commercial banks. RBI already controls banks through the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, CRR and SLR, repo-rate policy, prudential norms, inspections and licensing. Facts: RBI was set up in 1935 and nationalised in 1949. RBI supervision uses tools like CAMELS, Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) and risk-based supervision. Computerisation helps with reporting, for example through XBRL returns, but that is a side benefit and not the purpose of CBS.

3 — Incorrect: A takeover of a bank with huge NPAs is a merger, amalgamation or resolution, not CBS. Facts: Under Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act, RBI can propose a moratorium and amalgamation of a troubled bank. Examples include the Global Trust Bank merger with Oriental Bank of Commerce (2004), the merger of SBI's associate banks with SBI (2017), and the 2019-20 PSB consolidation of Bank of Baroda with Vijaya and Dena, and others. Stressed assets are also handled under the SARFAESI Act 2002, the IBC 2016 and PCA norms. Banks with high NPAs may be placed under PCA restrictions.
summary: The correct answer is (a) 1 only. Core Banking Solutions (CBS) is the networking of a bank's branches on a centralised platform, so a customer can operate an account from any branch on the network. It is not a tool for RBI control, and it has nothing to do with the takeover of banks that hold large NPAs.
topic_notes: Core Banking Solutions (CBS) refers to the centralised software and network that lets a bank's branches share one real-time database. Customers can then bank at any branch, and also through ATMs, internet and mobile banking. Features include real-time transaction processing, a single customer view, centralised MIS, easier regulatory reporting and integration with payment systems like NEFT, RTGS, IMPS and UPI. RBI pushed banks toward computerisation after the Rangarajan Committee reports on computerisation (1980s). It later set technology guidelines through the Vasudevan Committee (1998-99) on technology upgradation in banking. Private and foreign banks were quicker to adopt CBS, and public sector banks followed, with nearly all branches on CBS by about 2012-13. The Indian Financial Technology and Allied Services (IFTAS) and the Institute for Development and Research in Banking Technology (IDRBT, Hyderabad, set up by RBI in 1996) support banking technology. INFINET is the banking network, and the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI, 2008) runs retail payment systems like UPI, RuPay, IMPS and NACH. Other angles UPSC may ask: differences between CBS and mobile banking, Financial Inclusion schemes like PMJDY (2014), Payments Banks and Small Finance Banks, bank mergers and consolidation, NPAs and the IBC, PCA framework, SARFAESI Act, RBI's role and instruments, and cybersecurity in banking. Also know that CBS adoption supports financial inclusion by enabling Business Correspondents to use handheld devices linked to core systems. Risks include cyber fraud, system outages and data breaches, which prompted RBI's cyber security framework for banks (2016).

ocr: Consider the following pairs : Terms sometimes Their origin seen in the news Annex-I Countries : Cartagena Protocol 2. Certified Emissions Reductions : Nagoya Protocol 3. Clean Development Mechanism : Kyoto Protocol Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched? fa) 1 and 2 only (b}) 2 and 3 only (c) 3 only (da) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Environment
detail: The question tests whether you can separate the climate-change treaties (UNFCCC, Kyoto Protocol, Paris Agreement) from the biodiversity treaties (CBD, Cartagena Protocol, Nagoya Protocol). The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in December 1997 at COP-3 and entered into force on 16 February 2005. It set binding emission-reduction targets for developed (Annex-I) countries and created three flexibility mechanisms: Emissions Trading (Article 17), Joint Implementation (Article 6) and the Clean Development Mechanism (Article 12). The CDM lets an Annex-I country finance an emission-reduction project in a developing country and earn Certified Emission Reduction (CER) credits, each equal to one tonne of CO2 equivalent. The Cartagena Protocol (adopted 2000, in force 2003) is a CBD protocol on the safe handling and transboundary movement of living modified organisms (LMOs/GMOs), governed by the Advance Informed Agreement procedure. The Nagoya Protocol (adopted 2010, in force 2014) deals with Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) of genetic resources. Elimination: pairs 1 and 2 attach climate terms to biodiversity protocols, so they are wrong. Only pair 3 is right, so (c) is the answer.
explanations: Wrong: it counts pairs 1 and 2 as correct, but Annex-I countries are not from the Cartagena Protocol and CERs are not from the Nagoya Protocol.
Wrong: it includes pair 2, which is incorrect because CERs come from the Kyoto Protocol's CDM, not the Nagoya Protocol.
Correct: only pair 3 is right, since the CDM is a Kyoto Protocol mechanism under Article 12.
Wrong: it needs all three pairs correct, but pairs 1 and 2 are mismatched.
keyfact: CDM and CERs belong to the Kyoto Protocol (climate); Cartagena is biosafety and Nagoya is access and benefit sharing (biodiversity).
option_notes: Not applicable to the pairs given: this option combines pairs 1 and 2, both mismatched.
Not applicable to the pairs given: this option combines pairs 2 and 3, and pair 2 is mismatched.
Not applicable to the pairs given: this option is the official answer, pair 3 alone.
Not applicable to the pairs given: this option claims all three pairs are correct, which is false.
related: Kyoto Protocol: adopted 1997 at COP-3, in force 2005.
CDM is under Article 12 of the Kyoto Protocol; one CER = 1 tonne CO2e.
Cartagena Protocol (2000) concerns biosafety and living modified organisms.
Nagoya Protocol (2010) concerns access and benefit sharing of genetic resources.
Paris Agreement (2015) uses NDCs and targets 1.5-2°C.
Kigali Amendment (2016) phases down HFCs under the Montreal Protocol.
Doha Amendment (2012) set Kyoto's second commitment period (2013-2020).
The Paris Agreement's Article 6.4 mechanism succeeds the CDM.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Annex-I countries originate from the UNFCCC (1992) and are used in the Kyoto Protocol, not from the Cartagena Protocol. Annex-I lists the industrialised countries and economies in transition that were OECD members in 1992 or in transition to a market economy. These countries took the lead in cutting greenhouse gas emissions. Annex-II is a subset of OECD members that must give financial and technology support to developing countries. Non-Annex-I parties are mostly developing countries, including India and China. Kyoto Annex B lists the countries with binding targets. The Cartagena Protocol deals only with biosafety.

2 — Incorrect: Certified Emission Reductions (CERs) are carbon credits created under the Kyoto Protocol's CDM, not the Nagoya Protocol. One CER equals one tonne of CO2 equivalent and is issued by the CDM Executive Board after a project has been verified. CERs can be traded and used by Annex-I countries to meet their Kyoto targets. CER prices collapsed after about 2012 because supply exceeded demand. The Nagoya Protocol concerns Access and Benefit Sharing of genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge, and has no connection with carbon credits.

3 — Correct: The Clean Development Mechanism is defined in Article 12 of the Kyoto Protocol. It allows Annex-I countries to implement emission-reduction projects in developing countries and earn CERs. Its aims are sustainable development in the host country and cost-effective compliance for industrialised countries. Typical projects include renewable energy, afforestation and methane capture. It is supervised by the CDM Executive Board under the UNFCCC. India has been among the largest CDM host countries, along with China and Brazil. Under the Paris Agreement, the CDM is succeeded by the Article 6.4 Sustainable Development Mechanism.
summary: The correct answer is (c): only pair 3 is correctly matched. The Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) is a flexible market mechanism under Article 12 of the Kyoto Protocol, while Annex-I countries and Certified Emissions Reductions (CERs) both come from the Kyoto Protocol/UNFCCC framework, not from the Cartagena or Nagoya Protocols.
topic_notes: Climate treaties: The UNFCCC was adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and came into force in 1994. Its principle is Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC). The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in 1997 and came into force in 2005. Its first commitment period ran 2008-2012 and aimed at about a 5% cut below 1990 levels. The second commitment period, under the Doha Amendment (2012), ran 2013-2020. The USA never ratified Kyoto, and Canada withdrew in 2011. Its six greenhouse gases are CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs and SF6, and NF3 was added by the Doha Amendment. Its three flexibility mechanisms are Joint Implementation (Article 6, producing Emission Reduction Units), the CDM (Article 12, producing CERs) and Emissions Trading (Article 17, using Assigned Amount Units). The Paris Agreement was adopted in 2015 and came into force in 2016. It aims to hold warming well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C, and it works through Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). The Kigali Amendment (2016) to the Montreal Protocol phases down HFCs. Biodiversity treaties: The CBD was adopted in 1992 and came into force in 1993. Its three objectives are conservation, sustainable use and equitable benefit sharing. The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety covers LMOs. The Nagoya-Kuala Lumpur Supplementary Protocol covers liability and redress. The Nagoya Protocol covers ABS, and the Aichi Targets (2010) were replaced by the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022), which includes the 30x30 target. Other related items are CITES, Ramsar, CMS and the Minamata Convention on mercury. UPSC often tests which treaty belongs to which theme.

question: In the context of the developments in Bioinformatics, the term ‘transcriptome’, sometimes seen in the news, refers to
options: arange of enzymes used in genome editing
the full range of mRNA molecules expressed by an organism
the description of the mechanism of gene expression
a mechanism of genetic mutations taking place in cells !
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The transcriptome is the total set of RNA molecules transcribed from the genome, including mRNA, rRNA, tRNA and non-coding RNAs such as miRNA and lncRNA. In UPSC's framing it is the full range of mRNA molecules expressed by an organism. Unlike the genome, which is nearly constant in an individual, the transcriptome varies with cell type, developmental stage, environment and disease. The central dogma runs DNA to RNA (transcription) to protein (translation), so the transcriptome sits between the genome and the proteome. It is studied with microarrays and, now mainly, RNA-Seq (next-generation sequencing); single-cell RNA-seq is a newer refinement. Applications include finding differentially expressed genes, cancer biomarkers, drug-target discovery and understanding stress responses in crops. Elimination logic: (a) describes genome-editing tools such as CRISPR-Cas9, ZFNs and TALENs, which are enzymes and not a transcriptome. (c) describes gene expression as a process or mechanism, whereas the transcriptome is the product, a set of molecules. (d) describes mutation mechanisms, which concern changes in DNA sequence. Only (b) fits.
explanations: Incorrect: enzymes used in genome editing (Cas9, nucleases, etc.) are tools, not the transcriptome.
Correct: the transcriptome is the complete set of RNA transcripts, mainly mRNA, expressed by a genome in a cell or organism.
Incorrect: the mechanism of gene expression is transcription plus translation, a process; the transcriptome is the set of its RNA products.
Incorrect: mutation mechanisms concern changes in DNA (substitution, deletion, insertion, radiation or chemical damage), unrelated to the transcriptome.
keyfact: Transcriptome = the complete set of RNA (mainly mRNA) transcripts expressed by a genome in a cell or organism at a given time.
option_notes: Genome-editing enzymes are programmable nucleases that cut DNA at chosen sites. They include Zinc Finger Nucleases, TALENs and CRISPR-Cas9, which uses a guide RNA to direct Cas9. CRISPR was adapted from bacterial immune defence, and Doudna and Charpentier won the 2020 Chemistry Nobel for it. India has used it in research, and gene-edited rice varieties were released in 2025. These enzymes are tools and are not the transcriptome.

The transcriptome is the full set of RNA transcripts, chiefly mRNA, made by a cell, tissue or organism at a particular time. It reflects active genes and varies with tissue, stage and conditions. It is measured by microarray or RNA-Seq. It links the genome to the proteome and is used in disease biomarker work, cancer research and crop stress studies. This is the correct option.

Gene expression is the process by which information in a gene is used to make a functional product, usually a protein. It involves transcription (DNA to mRNA in the nucleus), RNA processing (splicing, capping, polyadenylation) and translation at ribosomes. It is regulated by promoters, enhancers, transcription factors and epigenetic marks. This describes a process, whereas the transcriptome is the set of RNAs the process yields.

A mutation is a heritable change in the DNA sequence. Types include point mutations (substitution), insertions, deletions, frameshifts and chromosomal rearrangements. Causes include replication errors, UV and ionising radiation, and chemical mutagens. Mutations can be silent, missense or nonsense, and are the raw material of evolution and of diseases such as sickle-cell anaemia and cancer. They are not what the transcriptome means.
related: Proteome is the entire set of proteins expressed by a genome; the metabolome is all metabolites.
RNA-Seq (next-generation sequencing) is the main modern method to measure the transcriptome.
The Human Genome Project was completed in 2003 and found about 20,000-25,000 genes.
CRISPR-Cas9 won the 2020 Chemistry Nobel for Doudna and Charpentier.
GenomeIndia project sequenced 10,000 Indian genomes; data is held at the IBDC, Faridabad.
Metagenomics studies the collective genomes of microbial communities in an environment sample.
mRNA vaccines (Pfizer, Moderna) deliver mRNA coding for the spike protein.
Pharmacogenomics studies how genes affect individual drug response.
summary: The answer is (b). The transcriptome is the complete set of RNA transcripts, chiefly mRNA, produced by the genome of a cell, tissue or organism at a given time under given conditions. It shows which genes are actively expressed.
topic_notes: Omics is the large-scale study of biological molecules, and bioinformatics supplies the computing tools to analyse the data. The levels run: genome (the complete DNA), transcriptome (all RNA transcripts), proteome (all proteins), metabolome (all small-molecule metabolites) and epigenome (heritable chemical marks on DNA and histones). The central dogma, DNA to RNA to protein, links the first three. The genome is essentially fixed, while the transcriptome and proteome are dynamic, changing with tissue, time and environment. Main technologies: DNA microarrays, RNA-Seq with next-generation sequencing, single-cell RNA-seq, and mass spectrometry for proteomics. The Human Genome Project (1990-2003) sequenced about 3 billion base pairs and about 20,000-25,000 genes. India has the GenomeIndia project, which sequenced 10,000 genomes, and the Indian Biological Data Centre (IBDC) at Faridabad. India also sequenced the genomes of rice, jute, tea and the Indian Lion-tailed macaque in various projects. Genome editing tools (CRISPR-Cas9) are often confused with these terms. Transcriptomics is used in cancer subtyping, finding drug targets, understanding plant stress tolerance and tracking viral responses, as in COVID-19 studies. Other areas UPSC can ask next: DNA barcoding, metagenomics, pharmacogenomics, DNA fingerprinting, gene therapy, mRNA vaccines and RNA interference.

ocr: ‘Mission Indradhanush’ launched by the Government of India pertains to (a) immunization of children _and_ e pregnant women (b) construction of smart cities across the country t (c) India’s own search for the 4 Earth-like planets in outer space ' (a) New Educational Policy 33; ‘Which of the following best describes/ describe the aim of ‘Green India Mission’ of the Government of India? . . ‘ 1. Incorporating environmental! benefits and costs into the Union and State Budgets thereby implementing the ‘green accounting’ 2. Launching the second” green revolution to enhance agricultural output so as
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Mission Indradhanush (MI) was launched by the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare on 25 December 2014. It targets children under 2 years and pregnant women who are unvaccinated or only partially vaccinated. Its original aim was to raise full immunization coverage from about 65% (then) to at least 90%. It covers vaccines against seven diseases under the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP): diphtheria, whooping cough (pertussis), tetanus, polio, tuberculosis, measles and hepatitis B. Later phases added vaccines for other diseases, including Japanese encephalitis and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). The programme began in 201 low-performing districts. Intensified Mission Indradhanush (IMI) followed in 2017, and IMI 2.0 in 2019-20. The name 'Indradhanush' means rainbow, which stands for the seven vaccine-preventable diseases. Elimination logic: smart cities are the Smart Cities Mission (2015), under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. The search for Earth-like planets has no link to a mission with this name. The New Educational Policy is a policy document from the education ministry, so none of these are health programmes. Only (a) fits a health mission with a rainbow-themed name.
explanations: Correct. Mission Indradhanush is the immunization drive for children up to 2 years and pregnant women, launched in December 2014 by the Health Ministry.
Wrong. Smart cities fall under the Smart Cities Mission, launched in June 2015 by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, with 100 cities selected.
Wrong. India's space research is run by ISRO and the Department of Space. Mission Indradhanush has nothing to do with exoplanet search.
Wrong. Education policy is the domain of the Ministry of Education. The National Education Policy 2020 replaced the 1986 policy (modified in 1992); Indradhanush is not an education policy.
keyfact: Mission Indradhanush (25 Dec 2014) = full immunization of children under 2 and pregnant women against vaccine-preventable diseases.
option_notes: Immunization of children and pregnant women: this is the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP), begun in 1985, and Mission Indradhanush strengthens it. It targets children under 2 and pregnant women who are unvaccinated or partially vaccinated. It was launched on 25 December 2014 and first covered 201 high-focus districts. It covers 7 diseases at launch, with more added later. Intensified Mission Indradhanush followed in 2017, and IMI 2.0 in 2019-20. Vaccination is tracked through the U-WIN portal and the earlier eVIN system, which monitors cold-chain stock.

Smart cities: the Smart Cities Mission was launched on 25 June 2015 by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. It aimed to develop 100 smart cities over five years, using area-based development and pan-city solutions, with each city run by a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV). It was launched together with AMRUT (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation) and the PMAY-Urban housing scheme. The original timeline was extended to 2025.

Search for Earth-like planets: this is an astronomy and space science topic, not a government mission by this name. ISRO runs India's space programme. Its major missions include Chandrayaan (Moon), Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission, 2013-14) and AstroSat (2015, the first Indian multi-wavelength space observatory).
