Members are the heads of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA and the Finance Ministry's department secretaries. The Chief Economic Adviser is also a member. The FMC was a member until it merged with SEBI in 2015. Functions are financial stability, inter-regulatory coordination, financial sector development, financial literacy, financial inclusion, macroprudential supervision and the monitoring of large financial conglomerates. Its secretariat sits in the Department of Economic Affairs. The Financial Stability Report is published by RBI twice a year, in June and December. Related bodies and ideas include the Financial Stability Board (FSB, G20, Basel, set up in 2009), the Joint Forum, the Financial Action Task Force, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India, and the Banking Regulation Act. Other angles UPSC could ask are the distinction between micro- and macroprudential regulation, systemically important banks (D-SIBs: SBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank), and the difference between statutory, non-statutory and constitutional bodies. Also note that NITI Aayog (2015) is a non-statutory think-tank and not a financial regulator.

ocr: With reference to ‘Agenda 21’, sometimes seen in the news, consider the following statements : 1. It is a global action plan for sustainable development. 2. It originated in the World Summit on Sustainable Development held in Johannesburg in 2002. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa} 1 only ‘(bj 2 only {c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Agenda 21 is a comprehensive, voluntary, non-binding programme of action for sustainable development, adopted by more than 178 governments at the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED), the Earth Summit, held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in June 1992. The '21' refers to the 21st century. It has 40 chapters in four sections: social and economic dimensions, conservation and management of resources, strengthening the role of major groups, and means of implementation. Its signature idea is 'Local Agenda 21', which asks local authorities to prepare community-level sustainability plans ('think globally, act locally'). The 2002 World Summit on Sustainable Development (Rio+10) in Johannesburg did not create Agenda 21. It reviewed progress and produced the Johannesburg Declaration and a Plan of Implementation. Rio+20 (2012) produced 'The Future We Want', and the Sustainable Development Goals followed in the 2030 Agenda (2015). Elimination logic: statement 1 is a standard textbook definition and is true. Statement 2 gives the wrong venue and year, so it is false. That leaves only option (a).
explanations: Correct. Statement 1 is true because Agenda 21 is a global sustainable development action plan, and statement 2 is false because its origin is Rio 1992.
Wrong. Statement 2 is false: the Johannesburg 2002 summit reviewed Agenda 21 but did not originate it.
Wrong. Both cannot be correct because statement 2 misattributes the origin of Agenda 21.
Wrong. Statement 1 is correct, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: Agenda 21 = non-binding global sustainable development plan from the 1992 Rio Earth Summit; Johannesburg 2002 (Rio+10) only reviewed it.
option_notes: Statement 1 only is the official answer. It reflects that Agenda 21 is a global, voluntary action plan from the 1992 Rio Earth Summit. Related: UNFCCC, CBD and UNCCD were also opened for signature at or around Rio 1992, and the Rio Declaration (27 principles) and the Forest Principles were adopted there. The Rio Declaration includes the precautionary principle and the polluter-pays principle.

Statement 2 only is wrong. The World Summit on Sustainable Development (WSSD), Johannesburg, 2002, is known as Rio+10. It was held to review 10 years of progress since Rio. Outcomes were the Johannesburg Declaration on Sustainable Development and the Plan of Implementation, with goals on halving the proportion of people without sanitation by 2015, and on restoring fish stocks. It did not originate Agenda 21.

Both 1 and 2 is wrong because only statement 1 is true. To be correct, the origin would need to be Johannesburg 2002 as well, which it is not. Agenda 21 came ten years earlier, at Rio in 1992. Johannesburg is the follow-up and review summit. The later Rio+20 (2012) conference reaffirmed commitments and launched the process that led to the SDGs.

Neither 1 nor 2 is wrong because statement 1 is accurate. Agenda 21 is a plan of action for sustainable development. Candidates sometimes confuse it with the Agenda 2030 for Sustainable Development (adopted 2015 at the UN General Assembly), which has 17 SDGs and 169 targets, but that is a separate document. Agenda 21 was the 1992 predecessor and it influenced the later SDG framework.
related: Agenda 21 was adopted at the Rio Earth Summit (UNCED), June 1992.
Agenda 21 is non-binding and has 40 chapters.
Local Agenda 21 involves local authorities in sustainability planning.
The Johannesburg WSSD of 2002 is called Rio+10.
Rio+20 (2012) produced 'The Future We Want' and launched the SDG process.
The 2030 Agenda has 17 SDGs and 169 targets (adopted 2015).
The Brundtland Report (1987) defined sustainable development.
The Stockholm Conference of 1972 led to the creation of UNEP.
statements: 1 — Correct: Agenda 21 is a global action plan for sustainable development, adopted at Rio in 1992. It is a non-binding, voluntary blueprint covering poverty, consumption patterns, health, human settlements, atmosphere, oceans, freshwater, forests, biodiversity, waste, and the roles of women, youth, indigenous people, NGOs, business and local authorities. It has 40 chapters. Implementation is meant to occur at national, regional and local levels through Local Agenda 21. The UN Commission on Sustainable Development (CSD) was created in 1992 to monitor it. The CSD was later replaced by the High-level Political Forum (2013).

2 — Incorrect: Agenda 21 originated at the UN Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED), the Earth Summit, in Rio de Janeiro in June 1992, not at Johannesburg in 2002. The Johannesburg World Summit on Sustainable Development (26 Aug–4 Sep 2002), also called Rio+10 or Earth Summit 2002, reviewed Agenda 21's progress. It adopted the Johannesburg Declaration and the Plan of Implementation, with targets on water, sanitation, energy and fisheries, and encouraged public-private partnerships ('Type II outcomes').
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 1 is correct. Agenda 21 is a global, non-binding action plan for sustainable development, but it originated at the 1992 Earth Summit (UNCED) in Rio de Janeiro, not at the 2002 Johannesburg World Summit.
topic_notes: Agenda 21 was the key outcome of the UN Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED), the Earth Summit, held at Rio de Janeiro on 3–14 June 1992. It is a voluntary, non-binding plan with 40 chapters in four sections. Local Agenda 21 encourages local authorities to prepare community sustainability plans. The Commission on Sustainable Development (CSD) was set up in 1992 to follow up on it. Other Rio 1992 outcomes: the Rio Declaration with 27 principles (including the precautionary principle, polluter pays, and common but differentiated responsibilities), the Statement of Forest Principles, the UNFCCC and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). The UNCCD followed in 1994. Milestones in the sustainable development timeline: Stockholm Conference 1972 (first major UN conference on the human environment; led to UNEP; World Environment Day on 5 June); Brundtland Report 'Our Common Future' 1987 (defined sustainable development); Rio 1992; Kyoto Protocol 1997; Johannesburg WSSD 2002 (Rio+10); Rio+20 in 2012 ('The Future We Want', which decided on SDGs and replaced the CSD with the High-level Political Forum); the Millennium Development Goals (2000–2015) replaced by the 2030 Agenda and 17 SDGs (adopted September 2015); the Paris Agreement (COP21, 2015). The Earth Summit also popularised the concept of sustainable development and the role of Major Groups (women, children and youth, indigenous peoples, NGOs, local authorities, workers and trade unions, business and industry, scientific and technological community, farmers). UPSC may ask about the Rio Declaration, Rio+20, the Green Economy, the SDGs, the Brundtland Commission, and the differences between Agenda 21 and Agenda 2030.

question: Satya Shodhak Samaj organized
options: a movement for upliftment of tribals in Bihar
subject: Economy
detail: Satya Shodhak Samaj (Society of Truth Seekers) was founded on 24 September 1873 at Pune by Jyotirao (Jyotiba) Govindrao Phule, a Mali by caste, with Savitribai Phule as a close collaborator. Its aims were to liberate Shudras, Atishudras (Dalits) and women from Brahmin priestly domination, to reject the authority of the Vedas and the Puranas as instruments of oppression, and to promote rationalism, education and equality. It encouraged marriages without Brahmin priests and opposed idol worship and the caste hierarchy. Phule's key works are Gulamgiri (1873), Shetkaryacha Asud (Cultivator's Whipcord, 1881) and Sarvajanik Satyadharma. He also opened the first girls' school in Pune in 1848 and a home for widows' children. After Phule's death in 1890 the movement was carried on by Satyashodhak leaders such as Krishnarao Bhalekar and later Bhaskarrao Jadhav, and it influenced the non-Brahmin movement of Maharashtra and Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur. Elimination: Bihar tribal upliftment suggests Birsa Munda or Tana Bhagats, Gujarat temple entry is unrelated to Phule, and the Punjab peasant movement suggests the Pagri Sambhal Jatta or Kisan Sabha movements. The Samaj was based in Maharashtra and was anti-caste, so (c) is correct.
explanations: Wrong: the tribal upliftment movements in Bihar and Jharkhand were linked to Birsa Munda (Ulgulan) and the Tana Bhagat movement, not to Satya Shodhak Samaj.
Wrong: Satya Shodhak Samaj was not a temple-entry movement and did not operate in Gujarat. Temple-entry struggles were Vaikom (Kerala), Guruvayur, Nashik's Kalaram Temple (Ambedkar, 1930) and others.
Correct: it was founded by Jyotiba Phule in Pune in 1873 and fought caste hierarchy and Brahminical dominance in Maharashtra.
Wrong: peasant movements in Punjab include the Pagri Sambhal Jatta agitation (1907) and the Kisan Sabha activities, with no connection to Phule's organisation.
keyfact: Satya Shodhak Samaj = Jyotiba Phule, Pune, 1873, anti-caste and anti-Brahminical movement in Maharashtra.
option_notes: Tribal upliftment in Bihar: the major tribal movements were Birsa Munda's Ulgulan (1899-1900) in the Chotanagpur region, the Santhal Hul (1855-56) led by Sido and Kanhu, and the Tana Bhagat movement (1914) led by Jatra Bhagat. Birsa Munda founded the Birsaite faith and opposed dikus (outsiders), landlords and missionaries. Birsa was arrested in 1900 and died in Ranchi jail. Jharkhand state was formed in 2000, and 15 November (Birsa's birth anniversary) is celebrated as Janjatiya Gaurav Divas.

Temple-entry movement in Gujarat: Gujarat is not the setting of the best-known temple-entry movements. The prominent ones were the Vaikom Satyagraha (1924-25, Kerala, T.K. Madhavan, Periyar), the Guruvayur Satyagraha (1931-32, K. Kelappan), the Kalaram Temple Satyagraha at Nashik (1930, B.R. Ambedkar) and the Travancore Temple Entry Proclamation (1936). Gandhi's Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932) and the Harijan tours also promoted temple entry.

Anti-caste movement in Maharashtra: this is the correct option. Satya Shodhak Samaj was founded at Pune in 1873 by Jyotiba Phule, who is also known for Gulamgiri, schools for girls and untouchables, and the Shetkaryacha Asud. It stressed equality, rationalism, and removal of Brahmin priests from rituals. It influenced later non-Brahmin movements, Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur (who introduced 50 percent reservation in 1902) and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, who regarded Phule as one of his gurus.

Peasant movement in Punjab: key examples include the Pagri Sambhal Jatta movement (1907) against the Punjab Colonization Bill, led by Ajit Singh and Banke Dayal, and the Kisan Sabha movement in the 1930s. The Punjab Land Alienation Act (1900) and the Canal Colonies were major grievances. The Kuka (Namdhari) movement led by Baba Ram Singh in the 1870s was a religious and political movement in Punjab, and the Akali movement was Sikh gurdwara reform.
related: Satya Shodhak Samaj was founded in 1873 at Pune by Jyotiba Phule.
Gulamgiri (1873) was written by Phule and compared caste oppression with slavery.
Shetkaryacha Asud (1881) by Phule dealt with the plight of peasants.
Phule and Savitribai opened the first girls' school in Pune in 1848.
Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur introduced 50 percent reservation for backward classes in 1902.
Self-Respect Movement (1925) was started by Periyar E.V. Ramasamy in Tamil Nadu.
Ambedkar's Mahad Satyagraha (1927) asserted Dalits' right to use the Chavdar Tank water.
Prarthana Samaj was founded in 1867 in Bombay with Atmaram Pandurang and M.G. Ranade associated.
summary: The answer is (c): Satya Shodhak Samaj organized an anti-caste movement in Maharashtra. It was founded by Jyotiba Phule in Pune in 1873 to challenge Brahminical dominance and secure social justice for the lower castes, Shudras, Atishudras and women.
topic_notes: Social reform movements in 19th-century India were a response to colonial modernity, Western education and Orientalist critiques of Indian society. Reformers split broadly into upper-caste Hindu reform and non-Brahmin or Dalit-led anti-caste movements. Jyotiba Phule (1827-1890) was the pioneer of the second kind. He started the first girls' school at Bhidewada, Pune, in 1848, set up the Balhatya Pratibandhak Griha (infanticide prevention home), supported widow remarriage and wrote Gulamgiri (1873), which compared the caste system with American slavery and dedicated the work to the African-American abolitionists. Satya Shodhak Samaj, founded 1873, rejected Brahmin intermediaries, promoted Satyashodhak marriages and held that the Aryan invaders had subjugated the original inhabitants, an idea which influenced Dravidian thought. Its journal Deenbandhu was launched by Krishnarao Bhalekar in 1877. Savitribai Phule is regarded as India's first woman teacher. Other key reform bodies: Brahmo Samaj (1828, Raja Ram Mohan Roy), Prarthana Samaj (1867, Atmaram Pandurang), Arya Samaj (1875, Dayananda Saraswati), Ramakrishna Mission (1897, Vivekananda), Deccan Education Society (1884), SNDP Yogam (1903, Sree Narayana Guru), the Self-Respect Movement (1925, Periyar E.V. Ramasamy), Justice Party (1916), Depressed Classes Mission (1906, V.R. Shinde), Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924, Ambedkar), Mahad Satyagraha (1927), and Poona Pact (1932). Later non-Brahmin leaders in Maharashtra were Shahu Maharaj, Bhaskarrao Jadhav and Keshavrao Jedhe. Phule is also called Mahatma, a title given in 1888 by Vithalrao Krishnaji Vandekar.

question: Which of the following statements is/are correct? Viruses can infect 1. bacteria 2. fungi 3. plants ~*~" "Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Viruses are acellular, obligate intracellular parasites. They have a nucleic acid genome (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat (capsid), sometimes with a lipid envelope, and they replicate only inside living host cells. Host range is determined by receptor and cellular machinery compatibility, and viruses exist for every cellular life form: animals, plants, fungi, protists, bacteria and archaea. Bacteriophages (such as T4, lambda and M13) infect bacteria; Félix d'Hérelle and Frederick Twort are credited with their discovery (1915-1917). Mycoviruses (fungal viruses) infect fungi such as Saccharomyces, Penicillium and Cryphonectria parasitica, and are often latent. Plant viruses, such as Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV), the first virus discovered (Ivanovsky 1892, Beijerinck 1898, Stanley crystallised it in 1935), infect plants, usually through insect vectors or mechanical injury. Elimination logic: since all three statements are true, any option that leaves out one of them (a, b, c) is wrong, and only (d) includes all three. A student who knows just one fact, for example that phages infect bacteria, can still eliminate (b), and then recall of mycoviruses or plant viruses settles the choice.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out plants. Plant viruses such as TMV are well established.
Wrong: it leaves out bacteria and fungi. Bacteriophages and mycoviruses are real, so viruses are not restricted to plants.
Wrong: it leaves out fungi. Mycoviruses infect fungi, so statement 2 is also correct.
Correct: bacteria (bacteriophages), fungi (mycoviruses) and plants (plant viruses such as TMV) can all be infected by viruses.
keyfact: Viruses infect all life forms: bacteria (bacteriophages), fungi (mycoviruses), plants (e.g. TMV), animals, protists and archaea.
option_notes: Option (a), bacteria and fungi only, is a partial answer. It covers bacteriophages and mycoviruses, which are real, but excludes plant viruses. Bacteriophages are viruses with a head and tail structure, as in T4 phage. Mycoviruses are mostly dsRNA viruses of fungi, often symptomless. The option is wrong because plants are also hosts of numerous viruses such as TMV and the Cauliflower Mosaic Virus.

Option (b), plants only, reflects the common notion that viruses are agents of plant and animal disease. Plant viruses such as TMV, Potato Virus Y, Tomato Leaf Curl Virus and Banana Bunchy Top Virus cause major crop losses, and many are spread by aphids and whiteflies. The option is wrong because bacteria and fungi also have their own viruses.

Option (c), bacteria and plants only, is also partial. Bacteriophages and plant viruses are the better-known groups, and this is the trap for students unaware of fungal viruses. Mycoviruses, mostly dsRNA, were discovered in mushrooms in the 1960s and infect yeasts and filamentous fungi. Excluding fungi makes the option wrong.

Option (d), 1, 2 and 3, is correct. It reflects that viruses are obligate intracellular parasites with host-specific forms across all cellular life: bacteriophages for bacteria, mycoviruses for fungi, plant viruses for plants, and others for animals, protists and archaea. Giant viruses such as Mimivirus infect amoebae. Some archaeal viruses withstand extreme heat and acidity.
related: Bacteriophages infect bacteria; discovered by Twort (1915) and d'Hérelle (1917).
TMV was the first virus discovered and the first crystallised (Stanley, 1935).
Mycoviruses infect fungi and are mostly dsRNA viruses.
Viroids are naked infectious RNA molecules found in plants (T.O. Diener, 1971).
Prions are infectious proteins causing BSE and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
Retroviruses such as HIV use reverse transcriptase to make DNA from RNA.
Antibiotics do not work against viruses; vaccines and antivirals are used.
Smallpox was declared eradicated by WHO in 1980.
statements: 1 — Correct: Viruses that infect bacteria are called bacteriophages. Phages were discovered by Frederick Twort (1915) and Félix d'Hérelle (1917), who coined the name. They have lytic and lysogenic cycles; T4 is a classic lytic phage and lambda a temperate one. Transduction, the transfer of bacterial genes by phages, is a method of horizontal gene transfer. Phage therapy is being revived against antibiotic-resistant bacteria, and phages were used in the Hershey-Chase experiment (1952), which showed DNA is the genetic material.

2 — Correct: Fungal viruses are called mycoviruses. They were first noticed in the 1960s in cultivated mushrooms (Agaricus bisporus), where a disease called La France disease was linked to them. Most have dsRNA genomes and spread through spores or hyphal fusion, not through extracellular transmission. Many cause no visible symptoms. Some cause hypovirulence, as in Cryphonectria parasitica (chestnut blight), which makes them potential biocontrol agents. The yeast killer toxin system in Saccharomyces is also encoded by dsRNA viruses.

3 — Correct: Plant viruses cause diseases such as mosaics, leaf curl and yellowing. Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV) was the first virus discovered: Dmitri Ivanovsky (1892) and Martinus Beijerinck (1898) studied it, and Wendell Stanley crystallised it (1935). Most plant viruses have ssRNA genomes. They enter through wounds and are spread by vectors such as aphids and whiteflies, and also by nematodes and fungi. Other examples are Cauliflower Mosaic Virus (a DNA virus), Potato Virus X, Banana Bunchy Top Virus, and Tomato Leaf Curl Virus. Viroids are even smaller infectious RNAs that infect plants.
summary: The answer is (d): viruses can infect bacteria, fungi and plants. Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites, and there are specific viruses (bacteriophages, mycoviruses, plant viruses) for each of these host groups.
topic_notes: Viruses are non-cellular entities on the border of living and non-living. They have either DNA or RNA (never both) as genetic material, a protein capsid made of capsomeres, and sometimes an envelope. They lack ribosomes and metabolism, so they cannot reproduce outside a host. Replication proceeds by attachment, entry, synthesis of components, assembly and release. Bacteriophages follow lytic cycles (host cell bursts) or lysogenic cycles (the genome integrates as a prophage). Classification is by host (animal, plant, bacterial, fungal), genome type (Baltimore classification) and shape (helical, icosahedral, complex). History: Ivanovsky (1892) showed that the TMV agent passed through bacterial filters; Beijerinck (1898) called it contagium vivum fluidum; Stanley crystallised TMV (1935, Nobel 1946); Twort and d'Hérelle discovered phages. Examples of human diseases: HIV (retrovirus, RNA), influenza, SARS-CoV-2, dengue, Zika, hepatitis, polio, rabies, measles, smallpox (eradicated 1980) and HPV. Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase (Temin and Baltimore, 1970). Viroids (Diener, 1971) are naked RNA that infect plants, and prions are infectious proteins that cause diseases such as mad cow disease (BSE) and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Antibiotics do not act on viruses; antivirals (acyclovir, oseltamivir) and vaccines are used instead. Interferons are proteins produced by host cells in response to viral infection. Applications: phages as biocontrol and therapy, viral vectors in gene therapy and vaccines, and baculoviruses as biopesticides.

ocr: The term ‘Base Erosion and Profit Shifting’ is sometimes seen in the news in the context of (a) mining operation by multinational companies in resource-rich but backward areas (b) curbing of the tax evasion by multinational companies {c} exploitation of genetic resources of a country by multinational companies (ad) lack of consideration of environmental costs in the planning and implementation of developmental projects
subject: Economy
detail: BEPS describes strategies used mainly by multinational enterprises (MNEs) to exploit gaps, mismatches and loopholes between national tax systems so that profits are shifted to low-tax or no-tax locations where little real economic activity occurs. The tax base of the countries where the value is actually created is thereby eroded. The OECD estimated global revenue losses at about 4-10% of global corporate income tax revenue, roughly USD 100-240 billion a year. The G20 mandated the OECD to act, and the OECD/G20 BEPS Action Plan with 15 Actions was delivered in October 2015 and endorsed by the G20 at Antalya (Turkey) in November 2015. Four minimum standards were set: harmful tax practices (Action 5), treaty shopping/abuse (Action 6), country-by-country reporting (Action 13), and dispute resolution (Action 14). The Inclusive Framework on BEPS now has over 140 member jurisdictions, including India. Later, a two-pillar solution was agreed: Pillar One reallocates taxing rights, and Pillar Two sets a 15% global minimum tax. Elimination: (a) mining, (c) biopiracy and (d) environmental impact assessment are unrelated to taxation, so (b) is the only fit.
explanations: Wrong: mining by MNCs in resource-rich backward areas is a resource-extraction and displacement issue, not about tax base erosion or profit shifting.
Correct: BEPS is about MNCs shifting profits to low-tax jurisdictions to avoid tax, and the OECD/G20 BEPS project aims to curb this avoidance and evasion.
Wrong: exploitation of a country's genetic resources by MNCs is biopiracy, dealt with under the Convention on Biological Diversity and the Nagoya Protocol (access and benefit sharing).
Wrong: neglect of environmental costs in development projects relates to Environmental Impact Assessment and sustainable development, not taxation.
keyfact: BEPS = MNCs shifting profits to low-tax havens to erode the tax base; the OECD/G20 15-Action plan (2015) is the response to curb tax avoidance.
option_notes: Mining by MNCs in resource-rich but backward areas: a recurring issue in India's tribal and mineral-rich belts (Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh). It is tied to the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, PESA 1996, the Forest Rights Act 2006, the Samata judgment (1997), the Niyamgiri/Vedanta case (2013) and District Mineral Foundations under the MMDR Amendment Act 2015.

Curbing tax evasion/avoidance by MNCs: this is the BEPS agenda. The OECD/G20 project has 15 Actions (2015) and the Inclusive Framework (2016). Key tools are country-by-country reporting, the Multilateral Instrument (MLI) to amend tax treaties, and the Pillar Two 15% global minimum tax. India introduced the equalisation levy in 2016 on digital advertising and GAAR from 2017.

Exploitation of genetic resources by MNCs: this is biopiracy, for example the neem, turmeric and basmati patent disputes. The Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) and the Nagoya Protocol (2010) govern access and benefit sharing. India's Biological Diversity Act 2002 created the National Biodiversity Authority in Chennai, and the TKDL database guards against wrongful patents.

Lack of consideration of environmental costs in development projects: this concerns Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), which in India rests on the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 and the EIA Notification 2006. Related ideas are green GDP, natural capital accounting, the polluter-pays principle, and the National Green Tribunal (2010) as the forum for disputes.
related: BEPS project was initiated by the OECD at the request of the G20; the final package came in October 2015.
The BEPS Action Plan has 15 Actions; Action 13 mandates country-by-country reporting.
The Multilateral Instrument (MLI) modifies bilateral tax treaties without renegotiating each one; India ratified it in 2019.
Pillar Two sets a 15% global minimum corporate tax rate.
India's GAAR came into force on 1 April 2017.
The Equalisation Levy was introduced in India in 2016 on digital advertising, following BEPS Action 1.
The OECD is headquartered in Paris; India is not a member but a key partner and a member of the Inclusive Framework.
The Common Reporting Standard (CRS) enables automatic exchange of financial account information among tax authorities.
summary: The answer is (b) curbing of tax evasion by multinational companies. Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) refers to tax-planning strategies that exploit gaps and mismatches in tax rules to shift profits artificially to low- or no-tax jurisdictions, and the OECD/G20 BEPS project was launched to curb this.
topic_notes: BEPS refers to tax-avoidance strategies by which MNEs use mismatches between national tax rules to move profits to low-tax jurisdictions (tax havens) and thereby erode the tax base of countries where real activity takes place. Common techniques include transfer pricing manipulation, treaty shopping, hybrid mismatch arrangements, excessive interest deductions and holding IP in low-tax entities (the 'Double Irish with a Dutch Sandwich'). The OECD, backed by the G20, published the 15-point BEPS Action Plan in 2013 and the final package in October 2015. Key actions: Action 1 taxing the digital economy; Action 2 hybrid mismatches; Action 4 interest deductions; Action 5 harmful tax practices; Action 6 treaty abuse; Actions 8-10 transfer pricing aligned with value creation; Action 13 transfer pricing documentation and country-by-country reporting (CbCR); Action 14 dispute resolution; Action 15 the Multilateral Instrument (MLI), signed in Paris in June 2017 and in force from July 2018. The Inclusive Framework (2016) has 140+ members, including India. In October 2021 over 130 jurisdictions agreed on a Two-Pillar solution: Pillar One reallocates part of profits of the largest MNEs to market jurisdictions, and Pillar Two sets a 15% global minimum corporate tax. India's measures include the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR, effective April 2017), the Place of Effective Management test, the 6% equalisation levy on online advertising (2016, later extended and then abolished in 2024), Advance Pricing Agreements, the Black Money Act 2015, and renegotiated tax treaties with Mauritius, Singapore and Cyprus. Other related terms: tax haven, Panama Papers (2016), Paradise Papers (2017), Common Reporting Standard (CRS) for automatic exchange of information, FATCA (US), and the OECD Global Forum on Transparency.

ocr: Recently, India’s first ‘National Investment and Manufacturing Zone’ was proposed to be set up in fa) Andhra Pradesh {b) Gujarat (c) Maharashtra {d) Uttar Pradesh
subject: Economy
detail: National Investment and Manufacturing Zones (NIMZs) were introduced by the National Manufacturing Policy (NMP), announced in November 2011 by the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion (DIPP), Ministry of Commerce and Industry. The policy aimed to raise manufacturing's share in GDP from about 16% to 25% within a decade and to create 100 million additional jobs. An NIMZ is a large greenfield industrial township with a minimum area of 5,000 hectares, with land, power, water, logistics, environmental and skill-development infrastructure planned in an integrated way. The State government identifies and develops the land, while the Centre helps with exemptions and support for master planning and external infrastructure. NIMZs differ from SEZs: they are not export-focused, they have no mandatory net-foreign-exchange condition, and they have a more liberal exit policy and labour regime. In the 2016 context, the first NIMZ was proposed at Prakasam district, Andhra Pradesh, with others proposed in Chittoor, Maharashtra (Dighi Port, Aurangabad and Nagpur-Wardha), Gujarat (Dholera and Pipavav) and elsewhere. Elimination logic: Andhra Pradesh was cited as the first, so the other three, though they also have NIMZs, are not first.
explanations: Correct. The first NIMZ was proposed in Prakasam district, Andhra Pradesh, and UPSC's official key accepts this.
Incorrect for 'first'. Gujarat has NIMZ projects, such as Dholera, but it is better known for the Dholera SIR and DMIC, and it was not named first.
Incorrect for 'first'. Maharashtra has NIMZ projects such as Dighi and Nagpur-Wardha, but these were not the first ones proposed.
Incorrect. Uttar Pradesh has no NIMZ that was named first in this context.
keyfact: First NIMZ (National Manufacturing Policy 2011) was proposed at Prakasam, Andhra Pradesh; minimum area 5,000 ha.
option_notes: Andhra Pradesh: a southern State with its capital then at Hyderabad and later Amaravati. It has a long coastline and ports. Prakasam and Chittoor have NIMZ sites. It is also on the Chennai-Vizag industrial corridor, and Sri City is a well-known industrial hub. Its Special Category Status demand was prominent after the 2014 bifurcation from Telangana.

Gujarat: a western State with the longest coastline in India (about 1,600 km). It hosts the Dholera Special Investment Region on the Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor, the GIFT City financial hub, Mundra port, and the Vibrant Gujarat summits. It also has several SEZs and NIMZ-type proposals such as Pipavav.

Maharashtra: India's most industrialised State and its financial capital, Mumbai. It is a major part of the Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor, with proposed NIMZs at Dighi Port, Aurangabad and Nagpur-Wardha. It has JNPT, the largest container port, and large auto, pharma and IT sectors.

Uttar Pradesh: India's most populous State. It is part of the Delhi-Mumbai and Amritsar-Kolkata industrial corridors, and Greater Noida and Noida are manufacturing and electronics hubs. It has a defence industrial corridor with nodes at Lucknow, Kanpur and Jhansi, but it was not the site of the first NIMZ.
related: National Manufacturing Policy was announced in 2011 by DIPP.
The NMP aimed for a 25% manufacturing share in GDP and 100 million jobs.
An NIMZ needs a minimum of 5,000 hectares of land.
NIMZs are not export-oriented, unlike SEZs, which are governed by the SEZ Act 2005.
Make in India was launched in September 2014 with 25 focus sectors.
Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor is implemented via NICDC.
Dholera in Gujarat is a Special Investment Region on the DMIC.
PLI schemes for manufacturing were introduced in 2020.
summary: The answer is (a) Andhra Pradesh. India's first National Investment and Manufacturing Zone (NIMZ) under the National Manufacturing Policy 2011 was proposed at Prakasam district in Andhra Pradesh. NIMZs are large integrated industrial townships meant to raise manufacturing's share of GDP to 25% and create 100 million jobs.
topic_notes: National Manufacturing Policy 2011: announced by the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion (DIPP, now DPIIT) under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. Its goals were to increase manufacturing's share of GDP to 25% by 2022, to create 100 million jobs, to increase domestic value addition, and to improve global competitiveness. Its main instrument was the NIMZ, with a minimum area of 5,000 hectares. The policy also included rationalised and simplified business regulation, a simpler exit policy, technology development measures, skill development, and incentives for green technology. NIMZ vs SEZ: SEZs were established under the SEZ Act 2005, are export-oriented and require positive net foreign exchange, while NIMZs are not export-bound and are governed by the NMP rather than a dedicated Act. NIMZ proposals included Prakasam (AP), Chittoor (AP), Medak (Telangana), Kalinganagar (Odisha), Nagpur and Dighi (Maharashtra), Dholera and Pipavav (Gujarat), Ponneri-Gummidipoondi (Tamil Nadu), Kolar (Karnataka), Nagaur (Rajasthan), Jhansi (UP), and Kanpur-related areas. Related initiatives include Make in India (September 2014), Smart Cities, the National Industrial Corridor Development Programme with the Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC), Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes from 2020, the National Industrial Corridor Development Corporation (NICDC), and the PM GatiShakti plan. UPSC could also ask about Special Investment Regions (SIRs), the Industrial Corridor list, and the manufacturing share of GDP, which has remained around 15–17%.

ocr: What is/are the purpose/purposes of ‘District Mineral Foundations’ in India? 1. Promoting mineral exploration activities in mineral-rich districts 2. Protecting the interests of the persons affected by mining operations 3. Authorizing State ‘Governments to issue licences for mineral exploration “Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1 and 2 only {b) 2 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d@) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Geography
detail: The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2015 inserted Section 9B, which requires the State Government to establish a District Mineral Foundation in every district affected by mining. A DMF is a non-profit body, a trust, whose objective is to work for the interest and benefit of persons and areas affected by mining. Mining leaseholders contribute to it: 10% of royalty for leases granted on or after 12 January 2015, and 30% of royalty for leases granted before that date. The Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana (PMKKKY), launched in 2015, uses DMF funds. It prioritises 'high priority' areas such as drinking water, health, education, women and child welfare, and the environment, and sets aside a portion for infrastructure and other items. Exploration is financed separately by the National Mineral Exploration Trust (NMET), funded by 2% of royalty, so statement 1 is wrong. Licences and leases are granted by State Governments under the MMDR Act and Mineral Concession Rules, but this is a statutory power of the State and not a DMF function, so statement 3 is wrong. Since only statement 2 is correct, option (b) is the answer.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement 1; exploration promotion is NMET's role, not the DMF's, even though statement 2 is right.
(b) is right because only statement 2 is correct: DMFs protect and benefit persons and areas affected by mining. Statements 1 and 3 describe different bodies and powers.
(c) is wrong because both statements 1 and 3 are incorrect: exploration is funded by NMET, and State Governments, not DMFs, issue licences. It also omits the correct statement 2.
(d) is wrong because it accepts all three statements, but 1 and 3 are not DMF functions.
keyfact: DMF (Section 9B, MMDR Act, 2015) is a non-profit trust that works for the benefit of persons and areas affected by mining; exploration belongs to NMET, licences to States.
related: DMFs are established under Section 9B of the MMDR Act, 1957, inserted by the 2015 Amendment.
DMF contribution: 10% of royalty for leases after 12 January 2015, 30% for earlier leases.
PMKKKY, launched in 2015, uses DMF funds for mining-affected areas.
NMET (Section 9C) is funded by 2% of royalty and finances mineral exploration.
The Samatha judgment (1997) restricted transfer of tribal land to non-tribals for mining in Scheduled Areas.
Mineral regulation is in Entry 54 of the Union List and Entry 23 of the State List.
The Indian Bureau of Mines, under the Ministry of Mines, regulates mineral conservation.
The 2015 Amendment made auction the method for granting mining leases for major minerals.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Promoting exploration is the job of the National Mineral Exploration Trust (NMET), not DMFs. DMFs are about welfare of mining-affected people. Facts: NMET was created under Section 9C of the MMDR Act by the 2015 Amendment. It is funded by holders of mining leases paying 2% of royalty. It finances regional and detailed exploration of minerals, and the Ministry of Mines administers it. The Geological Survey of India and other agencies carry out exploration projects funded through NMET. The aim is to increase the mineral resource base and reduce dependence on imports.

2 — Correct: DMFs exist to work for the interest and benefit of persons and areas affected by mining-related operations. Facts: Section 9B of the MMDR Act, inserted in 2015, mandates DMFs as non-profit trusts in mining districts. Contributions are 10% of royalty for new leases and 30% for old ones, and 10% for leases granted from 2015 onwards. The composition and functions are set by State Governments, and the District Collector often heads the governing council. The DMF was recommended following concerns over displacement and tribal rights, particularly in Fifth Schedule areas. PMKKKY, launched in 2015, directs how DMF money is used and prioritises drinking water, health, education, women and child welfare, sanitation, and the environment.

3 — Incorrect: Licences and leases for minerals are granted by State Governments under the MMDR Act, 1957, and Mineral Concession Rules. DMFs have no authorising role. Facts: Minerals are in the Union List (Entry 54) to the extent the Union takes control through law, and in the State List (Entry 23) subject to that. Since the 2015 Amendment, mining leases for major minerals are granted by auction, which improves transparency. Minor minerals fall under State rules. Authorisation power rests with the State, and DMFs are only trusts that receive contributions and spend funds on welfare.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 2 only. District Mineral Foundations (DMFs) are non-profit trusts set up under Section 9B of the MMDR Act, 1957 (inserted by the 2015 Amendment) in districts affected by mining. Their purpose is to work for the interest and benefit of persons and areas affected by mining-related operations, not to promote exploration or to authorise licences.
topic_notes: District Mineral Foundations come from the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2015, which inserted Section 9B. A DMF is a non-profit trust set up by State Governments in districts affected by mining. Its goal is to work for the interest and benefit of people and areas affected by mining operations. Mining leaseholders pay into it: 30% of royalty for leases granted before 12 January 2015 and 10% for leases granted on or after that date. Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana (PMKKKY), launched in 2015 by the Ministry of Mines, guides the use of DMF funds. It sets 'high priority' items such as drinking water, health care, education, welfare of women and children, aged and disabled people, skill development, and sanitation, and 'other priority' items such as physical infrastructure, irrigation, energy and watershed development, and environment measures. At least 60% of the funds go to high-priority areas and 40% to other items. Directly and indirectly affected areas are defined, with 60% of funds to be used in directly affected areas. The 2015 Amendment also introduced auctions as the mode of granting mineral concessions, and created the National Mineral Exploration Trust (Section 9C) funded by 2% of royalty. The Samatha judgment (1997) of the Supreme Court on tribal land and mining in Scheduled Areas is a related background. Other angles: Fifth and Sixth Schedule protections, Forest Rights Act 2006, PESA 1996, and the 2021 amendment to the MMDR Act that removed the distinction between captive and merchant mines. Mining royalty is on the Second Schedule of the MMDR Act. The Ministry of Mines runs the Mining Surveillance System and the Star Rating of Mines. The Indian Bureau of Mines regulates conservation and scientific mining.

question: SWAYAM’, an_ initiative of the Government of India, aims at
options: promoting the Self Help Groups in rural areas
providing financial and technical assistance to young start-up entrepreneurs
promoting the education and health of adolescent girls
) providing affordable and quality education to the citizens for free
subject: Economy
detail: SWAYAM stands for Study Webs of Active-Learning for Young Aspiring Minds. It was launched by the Government of India (Ministry of Education, formerly MHRD) in 2017 (the 2016 UPSC question refers to the initiative announced earlier), and is built on the principles of the national education policy: access, equity and quality. It hosts courses from Class 9 through postgraduate level, delivered by top institutions and teachers, and all courses are interactive and free to access; only those who want a certificate pay a modest fee for a proctored exam. Courses are produced by national coordinators such as NPTEL (IITs, engineering), UGC, CEC, NCERT, NIOS, IGNOU, IIMB and the Consortium for Educational Communication. SWAYAM also supports credit transfer, with up to 20 to 40 percent of credits in a programme possible through SWAYAM courses under UGC rules. Elimination: (a) describes the National Rural Livelihood Mission or SHG-Bank Linkage; (b) matches Start-up India, Stand-Up India or MUDRA; (c) matches schemes such as Kishori Shakti Yojana, SABLA or Beti Bachao Beti Padhao. Only (d) concerns education access.
explanations: Wrong: promoting Self Help Groups in rural areas is the work of DAY-NRLM (Aajeevika) and the NABARD SHG-Bank Linkage Programme, not SWAYAM.
Wrong: financial and technical help to young start-up entrepreneurs belongs to Start-up India, Stand-Up India, Atal Innovation Mission and MUDRA, not an online education platform.

Wrong: education and health of adolescent girls is targeted by schemes like SABLA (Rajiv Gandhi Scheme for Empowerment of Adolescent Girls), Kishori Shakti Yojana and Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, not SWAYAM.
Correct: SWAYAM is a national MOOCs platform providing high-quality, affordable (free to access) education to all citizens, including those outside the formal system.
keyfact: SWAYAM = India's free national MOOCs platform (Ministry of Education) giving quality courses from Class 9 to postgraduate level.
option_notes: Self Help Groups (SHGs) are small voluntary groups, usually of 10-20 poor women, who save and lend among themselves. The NABARD SHG-Bank Linkage Programme began in 1992. The Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana-National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM, launched 2011 as Aajeevika) is the main Government of India programme for mobilising rural poor households into SHGs, with credit access and livelihood support. It is run by the Ministry of Rural Development.

Support for young entrepreneurs includes Start-up India (launched January 2016, with a tax holiday and recognition by DPIIT), Stand-Up India (April 2016, bank loans of Rs 10 lakh to 1 crore for SC/ST and women entrepreneurs), MUDRA Yojana (April 2015, loans up to Rs 10 lakh under Shishu, Kishore, Tarun categories) and the Atal Innovation Mission run by NITI Aayog.

Adolescent girls' education and health is addressed by SABLA (Rajiv Gandhi Scheme for Empowerment of Adolescent Girls, 2010-11, for girls aged 11-18, now merged into the Scheme for Adolescent Girls under Mission Poshan 2.0), Kishori Shakti Yojana under ICDS, and Beti Bachao Beti Padhao (January 2015, from Panipat, Haryana) to address the declining child sex ratio and promote girls' education.

SWAYAM (Study Webs of Active-Learning for Young Aspiring Minds) is India's national MOOCs platform, developed by the Ministry of Education with Microsoft's help and launched in 2017. Courses from Class 9 to postgraduate level are offered free, with an optional paid certificate exam. Courses are run by national coordinators including NPTEL, UGC, CEC, NCERT, NIOS, IGNOU and IIMB, and are accessible online at swayam.gov.in. Credit transfer is allowed.
related: SWAYAM expands to Study Webs of Active-Learning for Young Aspiring Minds.
SWAYAM Prabha is a set of DTH educational TV channels broadcast via GSAT-15.
NPTEL is run by the IITs and IISc and is a national coordinator for SWAYAM engineering courses.
National Digital Library of India is hosted by IIT Kharagpur.
DIKSHA is the national digital platform for school education.
PM eVidya (2020) integrates digital, online and on-air education.
Stand-Up India supports SC/ST and women entrepreneurs with loans of Rs 10 lakh to 1 crore.
DAY-NRLM (Aajeevika) is the national scheme for rural SHGs.
summary: The answer is (d). SWAYAM is the Government of India's national MOOCs (Massive Open Online Courses) platform that offers quality higher-education and school-level courses online, free of cost to learners, so that the digital and educational divide is reduced.
topic_notes: SWAYAM is the flagship Indian MOOCs platform and a pillar of digital education policy. Its three guiding principles are access, equity and quality. Each course has four quadrants: video lectures, specially prepared reading material, self-assessment tests and quizzes, and an online discussion forum to clear doubts. Courses are free to take; learners wanting certification register for proctored exams at a nominal fee, held at designated centres. UGC regulations permit universities to transfer credits for SWAYAM courses (up to 40 percent of a programme). National coordinators who produce content include AICTE (self-paced and international courses), NPTEL (engineering and sciences, run by the IITs), UGC (non-technical postgraduate courses), CEC (undergraduate), NCERT (school), NIOS (school), IGNOU (out-of-school), and IIMB (management programmes). Related digital initiatives: SWAYAM Prabha, a group of DTH channels (originally 32) broadcasting educational content 24x7 through GSAT-15; National Digital Library of India (IIT Kharagpur); National Academic Depository (NAD) and DigiLocker for academic records; e-PG Pathshala for postgraduate content; Virtual Labs; DIKSHA for school teachers and students; PM eVidya (2020) which unified digital education efforts; and the Spoken Tutorial project of IIT Bombay. The National Education Policy 2020 encourages online and blended learning, and the National Educational Technology Forum (NETF). Other angles UPSC could ask: the ministry in charge, the expansion of the name, difference between MOOCs and open universities, and which scheme targets which group (SHGs, start-ups, girls).

ocr: The Montague-Chelmsford Proposals were related to fa) social reforms {b) educational reforms (c) reforms in police administration {d) constitutional reforms . What is/are common to the two historical places known as Ajanta’ and Mahabalipuram? 1. Both were built in the same period. 2. Both belong to the same religious denomination. 3. Both have rock-cut monuments. Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c} 1 and 3 only {d) None of the statements given above is correct
subject: Polity
detail: The Montagu-Chelmsford Report was published in July 1918, authored by Edwin Montagu (Secretary of State for India) and Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy, 1916-21). It followed Montagu's August 1917 Declaration, which promised 'gradual development of self-governing institutions' and 'progressive realisation of responsible government' in India as an integral part of the British Empire. The proposals were enacted as the Government of India Act 1919, in force from 1921. Key features: dyarchy in the provinces, with subjects split into Reserved (law and order, finance, land revenue, irrigation, administered by the Governor and his executive council) and Transferred (education, health, local self-government, agriculture, administered by Indian ministers responsible to the legislature); a bicameral central legislature (Council of State and Legislative Assembly); separate electorates extended to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans; a limited franchise; a High Commissioner for India in London; and a provision for a statutory commission after 10 years (which became the Simon Commission, 1927). Since the proposals were about the structure of government and the distribution of power, they are constitutional reforms. Social, educational and police reforms were not their subject, although education was a transferred subject. Option (d) is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: social reforms such as the abolition of sati or widow remarriage were handled by separate laws and not by these proposals.

Incorrect: education was merely one subject transferred to Indian ministers under dyarchy, but the proposals were not about educational reform. Educational policy was dealt with by bodies such as the Sadler Commission (1917-19) and the Hunter Commission (1882).

Incorrect: police reforms came from the Police Commission 1902-03 (Andrew Fraser) and the Police Act 1861. Police was a reserved subject under 1919, but the proposals did not concern police administration as such.

Correct: the proposals restructured governance by introducing dyarchy, a bicameral central legislature and an expanded franchise, which were constitutional changes enacted in the Government of India Act 1919.
keyfact: Montagu-Chelmsford Proposals (1918) → Government of India Act 1919 → dyarchy in provinces: a constitutional reform.
option_notes: Social reforms in colonial India included the abolition of sati (1829, Bentinck), the Widow Remarriage Act 1856, the Age of Consent Act 1891 and the Sarda Act 1929 (Child Marriage Restraint). Reformers included Raja Ram Mohan Roy, Vidyasagar, Jyotiba Phule and Ranade. These measures came through separate legislation and movements, not the Montagu-Chelmsford Proposals.

Educational reforms include Macaulay's Minute (1835), Wood's Despatch (1854, the 'Magna Carta' of English education in India), the Hunter Commission (1882), the Indian Universities Act 1904 (Curzon), the Calcutta University Commission or Sadler Commission (1917-19) and the Hartog Committee (1929). Wood's Despatch led to universities in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras in 1857.

Police reforms: the Police Act 1861 created the modern police structure based on the Irish Constabulary model. The Fraser Commission (1902-03) recommended the creation of the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) and the appointment of provincial police services. Under the 1919 Act, law and order and police were reserved subjects held by the Governor. Post-independence there were the Prakash Singh case (2006) directions.

Constitutional reforms in British India include the Regulating Act 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784, Charter Act 1833, Indian Councils Acts 1861, 1892 and 1909 (Morley-Minto), Government of India Act 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford), the Government of India Act 1935 (provincial autonomy, federation proposed) and the Indian Independence Act 1947. The Montagu-Chelmsford Proposals belong here.
related: Montagu's August 1917 Declaration promised responsible government as the goal of British policy in India.
Dyarchy, devised by Lionel Curtis, was introduced in the provinces by the 1919 Act.
Transferred subjects were under Indian ministers; Reserved subjects under the Governor.
The 1919 Act created a bicameral central legislature: Council of State and Legislative Assembly.
The Government of India Act 1935 abolished dyarchy in provinces and introduced provincial autonomy.
The Morley-Minto Reforms 1909 introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
The Simon Commission (1927) was appointed to review the working of the 1919 Act.
Sadler Commission (1917-19) reviewed Calcutta University and education.
summary: The answer is (d) constitutional reforms. The Montagu-Chelmsford Proposals (1918) led to the Government of India Act 1919, which introduced dyarchy in the provinces and was a constitutional reform measure.
topic_notes: The Montagu-Chelmsford reforms came during the First World War, when India contributed troops and resources and Home Rule agitation (Tilak and Annie Besant, 1916) and the Lucknow Pact (1916) raised political pressure. Montagu's Declaration of 20 August 1917 for the first time spoke of responsible government as the goal. Montagu toured India in winter 1917-18 and wrote the report with Chelmsford, published in July 1918. The Government of India Act 1919 followed. Features: dyarchy in provinces (introduced in eight provinces, later Assam, Central Provinces and others), the Governor's powers to certify legislation, the Central Legislature with a Council of State (60 members, 34 elected) and a Legislative Assembly (145 members, 104 elected), the Viceroy's Executive Council with three Indian members, the Public Service Commission (established 1926), the separation of provincial and central budgets (Railway budget separated in 1924 following the Acworth Committee), and the bar on the franchise for most (about 10% of adult males). Indian reaction: the Congress, in the Special Session at Bombay (Aug 1918, under Hasan Imam), declared the reforms 'disappointing and unsatisfactory'; Moderates led by Surendranath Banerjee welcomed them and left to form the Indian National Liberal Federation. Rowlatt Act (1919), Jallianwala Bagh (April 1919) and the Khilafat issue followed, leading to Non-Cooperation (1920). Dyarchy was abolished by the Government of India Act 1935, which brought in provincial autonomy. Related UPSC angles: the Morley-Minto reforms 1909 (separate electorates), the Simon Commission 1927, the Nehru Report 1928, Jinnah's Fourteen Points, the Communal Award 1932, and the Cripps Mission 1942.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q65.
ocr: The Montague-Chelmsford Proposals were related to fa) social reforms {b) educational reforms (c) reforms in police administration {d) constitutional reforms . What is/are common to the two historical places known as Ajanta’ and Mahabalipuram? 1. Both were built in the same period. 2. Both belong to the same religious denomination. 3. Both have rock-cut monuments. Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c} 1 and 3 only {d) None of the statements given above is correct
subject: Polity
detail: Ajanta and Mahabalipuram are both famous for rock-cut architecture, which is the only thing they share. Ajanta, near Aurangabad in Maharashtra, has about 30 Buddhist caves cut into a horseshoe-shaped gorge of the Waghora river. They were built in two phases: the Satavahana-era Hinayana phase (c. 2nd century BCE to 1st century CE) and the Vakataka-era Mahayana phase (c. 5th-6th century CE, patronised by Harishena). The caves are known for chaityas, viharas and murals depicting the Jataka tales. Mahabalipuram (Mamallapuram), in Tamil Nadu, was a Pallava port city. Its monuments date to the 7th-8th centuries CE under Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla) and Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha). They include monolithic rathas (the Pancha Rathas), mandapas, the Descent of the Ganga (Arjuna's Penance) relief and the structural Shore Temple. These are mainly Hindu (Shaiva and Vaishnava). Elimination: Statement 1 fails because the periods differ by centuries. Statement 2 fails because Ajanta is Buddhist and Mahabalipuram is Hindu. Statement 3 is true, so only (b) works. Both are UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Ajanta was inscribed in 1983 and Mahabalipuram in 1984.
explanations: Wrong: this includes statements 1 and 2, both of which are false because the sites differ in period and religion.
Correct: only statement 3 holds. Both sites have rock-cut monuments, while their periods and religions differ.
Wrong: statement 1 is false, since Ajanta predates Mahabalipuram by centuries, even though statement 3 is true.
Wrong: statement 3 is correct, so this option, which says none of the statements is correct, cannot be right.
keyfact: Ajanta (Buddhist, c. 2nd century BCE-6th century CE) and Mahabalipuram (Hindu, Pallava, 7th-8th century CE) share only one thing: rock-cut monuments.
related: Ajanta caves: Buddhist, Waghora river gorge, Maharashtra, UNESCO site 1983.
Mahabalipuram: Pallava, 7th-8th century CE, UNESCO site 1984.
Pancha Rathas of Mahabalipuram are monolithic and are linked to Narasimhavarman I Mamalla.
Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram is a structural temple built under Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha.
Ellora's Kailasa temple (Cave 16) was built under Rashtrakuta king Krishna I.
Barabar caves (Bihar) are the earliest rock-cut caves, from the Mauryan period.
Ajanta's Vakataka phase patron was Harishena, and its murals depict Jataka stories.
Arjuna's Penance (Descent of the Ganga) is a giant bas-relief at Mahabalipuram.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Ajanta's caves span c. 2nd century BCE to 6th century CE, while Mahabalipuram's monuments are Pallava work of the 7th-8th century CE, so they were not built in the same period. Ajanta was built in two phases. The first, Hinayana, phase falls under the Satavahanas, and the second, Mahayana, phase under the Vakatakas, notably Harishena. Mahabalipuram flourished under Narasimhavarman I Mamalla and Narasimhavarman II Rajasimha. The Shore Temple dates to Rajasimha's reign. Chinese traveller Xuanzang mentioned the Pallava region, and Ajanta was rediscovered by British officers in 1819.

2 — Incorrect: Ajanta is Buddhist, while Mahabalipuram is predominantly Hindu (Shaiva and Vaishnava), so they do not share a religious denomination. Ajanta has chaityas (prayer halls) and viharas (monasteries) with Buddha and Bodhisattva imagery, including the famous Padmapani and Vajrapani paintings. Mahabalipuram has the Pancha Rathas (named after the Pandavas and Draupadi, though not actually dedicated to them), the Varaha cave, Mahishasuramardini cave and the Shore Temple, which houses Shiva and Vishnu shrines. The Pallava style is Dravidian in origin. Both sites are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

3 — Correct: Both sites have rock-cut monuments. Ajanta's caves are excavated into a basalt cliff, and Mahabalipuram has rock-cut cave temples (mandapas) and monolithic rathas carved from single rock outcrops. Rock-cut architecture in India began with the Barabar caves of the Mauryan period (Ashoka and Dasaratha, in Bihar), and flourished at Karle, Bhaja, Ellora, Elephanta and Udayagiri. Mahabalipuram's Arjuna's Penance (Descent of the Ganga) is a giant open-air bas-relief about 30 m long. The Shore Temple, by contrast, is a structural temple built of cut granite blocks, and is not rock-cut.
summary: The answer is (b) 3 only. Ajanta (Buddhist rock-cut caves, c. 2nd century BCE to c. 5th-6th century CE) and Mahabalipuram (Pallava monuments, 7th-8th century CE) are both rock-cut sites, but they differ in period and religious affiliation.
topic_notes: Rock-cut architecture in India evolved from the Mauryan Barabar and Nagarjuni caves (3rd century BCE, Ajivika sect, with the polished Mauryan finish) to the Buddhist chaitya and vihara caves of the Western Ghats: Bhaja, Karle, Kanheri, Nasik and Ajanta. Chaityas are prayer halls with a stupa, and viharas are monastic residences. Ajanta (30 caves) is famous for murals, mostly Jataka scenes, with the Vakataka-period work being the finest. Caves 9, 10, 19 and 26 are chaityas. Ellora (Maharashtra, Rashtrakuta period) has 34 caves: Buddhist (1-12), Hindu (13-29) and Jain (30-34). The Kailasa temple (Cave 16) was built under Krishna I and is a monolithic structure carved top-down from a single rock. Elephanta (Mumbai) is a Shaiva cave site with the Trimurti image. The Pallavas developed South Indian rock-cut and then structural temples in stages: the Mahendravarman I style (cave temples), the Mamalla style (monolithic rathas, Mahabalipuram), the Rajasimha style (structural temples such as the Shore Temple and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram) and the Nandivarman style. Mahabalipuram has been a UNESCO site since 1984, and Ajanta and Ellora since 1983. Other UNESCO sites in the same group include the Elephanta Caves (not a UNESCO site, though protected by the ASI) and the Great Living Chola Temples. Mahabalipuram was a port of the Pallavas, with trade links to Southeast Asia. The Ajanta caves lie in the Waghora river valley and were rediscovered in 1819 by John Smith, a British army officer. UPSC often asks about the periods, dynasties and religions linked to each cave complex.

question:
With reference to Bitcoins’, sometimes seen in the news, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. Bitcoins are tracked by the Central Banks of the countries.
2. Anyone with a Bitcoin address can send and receive Bitcoins from anyone else with a Bitcoin address.
3. Online payments can be sent without either side knowing the identity of the other. 24 B—APM-P-CKB/65A4 Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Economy
detail: Bitcoin was proposed in 2008 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto, and the network went live in January 2009. It is a decentralised digital currency that runs on a peer-to-peer network. Transactions are verified by nodes (miners) through cryptography and recorded on a public distributed ledger called the blockchain, with no central authority such as a central bank or government. Each user holds a public address, which acts like an account number, and a private key used to sign transactions. Anyone with an address can send or receive bitcoins to or from any other address. Identities are not tied to addresses, so the system is pseudonymous: the transactions are public, but real-world identity is not directly recorded. This is why statement 3 is accepted as correct. Statement 1 fails because central banks neither issue, regulate nor track Bitcoin. The RBI has cautioned the public about virtual currencies since 2013, and in 2018 it barred regulated entities from servicing them, a ban the Supreme Court struck down in March 2020. Elimination logic: statement 1 is wrong, which removes (a) and (d). Statement 3 is correct, which leaves (b) and (c). Statement 2 is also correct, so only (b) remains.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is false: central banks do not track Bitcoin, which has no central authority. It is also incomplete, since it leaves out statement 3.
(b) is correct because statements 2 and 3 are both true: the network is peer-to-peer and transactions are pseudonymous.
(c) is wrong because it leaves out statement 2, which is correct: any Bitcoin address can transact with any other.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement 1, which is false since Bitcoin is not tracked by central banks.
keyfact: Bitcoin is decentralised, peer-to-peer and pseudonymous: any address can pay any other, and no central bank tracks or issues it.
option_notes: Option (a), statements 1 and 2 only. It is wrong because statement 1 attributes tracking to central banks. Bitcoin works on a decentralised blockchain with no controlling authority. Central banks such as the RBI have at most issued cautions and regulatory restrictions. India does not recognise Bitcoin as legal tender. The rupee is the only legal tender under the RBI Act, 1934, and the RBI's own digital currency is the e-rupee (CBDC), piloted from December 2022.

Option (b), statements 2 and 3 only. This is the official correct answer. It captures the two defining features of Bitcoin: peer-to-peer transfer between any addresses, and pseudonymity, meaning no identity is needed to transact. Bitcoin was launched in 2009 by Satoshi Nakamoto, uses blockchain and proof-of-work mining, and has a capped supply of 21 million coins. It operates without any bank or intermediary.

Option (c), statement 3 only. It is wrong because it denies statement 2. Bitcoin's open peer-to-peer design lets any holder of an address send to or receive from any other address, with no permission needed. Wallets hold the private keys. The network validates transactions through miners and records them on a public ledger that anyone can inspect.

Option (d), all three statements. It is wrong because statement 1 is false. Bitcoin is not issued, tracked or backed by any central bank or government. Regulators approach it through anti-money-laundering, taxation and consumer-protection rules, not by controlling the network. In India, VDAs are taxed at 30% on gains under Section 115BBH, with 1% TDS under Section 194S.
related: Bitcoin was created by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto, and the network began in 2009.
Bitcoin supply is capped at 21 million coins.
Blockchain is a distributed, tamper-resistant public ledger.
Mining uses proof-of-work, whereas Ethereum moved to proof-of-stake in 2022.
The Supreme Court struck down the RBI's 2018 crypto banking ban in March 2020.
India taxes virtual digital assets at 30% (Section 115BBH) with 1% TDS (Section 194S).
The RBI's e-rupee (CBDC) pilot started in December 2022.
El Salvador became the first country to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender, in 2021.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Bitcoin is decentralised and no central bank tracks or controls it. Bitcoin has no issuer. New coins are created by mining, in which miners earn block rewards for validating transactions. The supply is capped at 21 million coins, and the reward halves about every four years. Central banks, including the RBI, have only issued warnings and regulatory advisories. The RBI cautioned users in 2013, 2014 and 2017. The 2018 RBI circular banning banks from dealing in virtual currency was set aside by the Supreme Court in Internet and Mobile Association of India v. RBI (2020). India's Budget 2022 introduced a 30% tax on gains from virtual digital assets.

2 — Correct: Bitcoin is peer-to-peer, so any address-holder can send to or receive from any other. A Bitcoin address is a string of alphanumeric characters derived from a public key. Wallets, which may be software, hardware or paper, store the private keys that authorise spending. Transfers need no intermediary such as a bank or payment gateway. Transactions are broadcast to the network, confirmed by miners using proof-of-work, and added to blocks on the blockchain. Transactions are irreversible once confirmed, and the unit of account is the satoshi, one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin.

3 — Correct: payments can be made without the two sides knowing each other's identity. Bitcoin is pseudonymous rather than fully anonymous. The ledger is public and shows addresses and amounts, but it does not record names. Identity may be linked when coins are bought or sold on regulated exchanges that follow KYC (know-your-customer) rules. This feature attracts concern about money laundering and terror financing, and about illicit markets such as Silk Road. India's PMLA was extended to virtual digital asset service providers in March 2023. Privacy coins such as Monero offer stronger anonymity.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 2 and 3 are correct, statement 1 is wrong. Bitcoin is a decentralised peer-to-peer cryptocurrency that no central bank issues or tracks. Anyone holding a Bitcoin address can transact with any other address-holder, and users are pseudonymous, so payments can be made without either party knowing the other's real identity.
topic_notes: Bitcoin is the first and best-known cryptocurrency. It was described in the 2008 white paper 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System' by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto, and the network started in January 2009. It runs on blockchain, a distributed ledger replicated across many nodes, with transactions grouped into blocks and secured by cryptographic hashing. Miners compete to solve proof-of-work puzzles, and the winner adds the block and earns a reward plus fees. Supply is capped at 21 million coins, and the reward halves roughly every four years (halvings in 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024). Users hold a public key (address) and a private key. The system is pseudonymous, not fully anonymous. Related ideas include altcoins such as Ethereum (smart contracts, proof-of-stake since 2022), stablecoins, and CBDCs, which are issued and backed by central banks, unlike Bitcoin. Indian regulatory context: the RBI issued cautions in 2013, 2014 and 2017, and a circular in April 2018 barred banks from serving crypto businesses. The Supreme Court quashed it in March 2020. The Banking Regulation Act and PMLA have been invoked, and the Cryptocurrency and Regulation of Official Digital Currency Bill has been discussed but not enacted. Budget 2022 defined virtual digital assets, imposing a 30% tax and 1% TDS. The e-rupee pilot began in late 2022. El Salvador made Bitcoin legal tender in 2021, and China banned crypto trading and mining. Likely future angles are blockchain applications, mining, CBDCs, the difference between cryptocurrency and fiat money, and international regulators such as the FATF and FSB.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. New Development Bank has been set up by APEC.
2. The headquarters of New Development Bank is in Shanghai. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: The New Development Bank, initially called the BRICS Development Bank, was agreed at the 6th BRICS Summit in Fortaleza, Brazil (July 2014). The Agreement on the NDB was signed then and came into force in 2015. The bank formally opened in July 2015 with its headquarters in Shanghai. Its first president was K. V. Kamath of India, followed by Marcos Troyjo of Brazil and then Dilma Rousseff, who was elected in 2023. The initial subscribed capital was US$50 billion and the authorised capital US$100 billion, with equal shares among the five founding members (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa). The NDB funds infrastructure and sustainable development projects in BRICS and other emerging economies. It is separate from the Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA), a US$100 billion currency reserve pool set up alongside it. APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) is a regional economic forum for trade and investment facilitation. It has no lending bank of this kind. Elimination logic: statement 1 is wrong because the founder was BRICS, not APEC. This removes (a) and (c). Statement 2 is right, so (d) is also out, leaving (b).
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because the NDB was created by BRICS, not APEC, so 'statement 1 only' cannot be right.
Correct: statement 2 is true, since the NDB's headquarters is in Shanghai, and statement 1 is false.
Wrong: this requires statement 1 to be true, but APEC did not set up the NDB.
Wrong: statement 2 is correct, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: NDB = BRICS bank, headquartered in Shanghai; it was not set up by APEC.
option_notes: Statement 1 only is the option that treats APEC as founder. APEC, founded in 1989, is a forum of 21 Pacific Rim economies promoting free trade and economic cooperation. Its secretariat is in Singapore. It is a non-binding forum, not a lender, and it did not create the NDB. India is not a member, though it has sought membership. Its decisions are made by consensus.

Statement 2 only is the correct option. The NDB is a multilateral development bank run by BRICS members, headquartered in Shanghai. It began operating in 2015 and finances infrastructure and sustainable development projects, including renewable energy, transport and water. It issues green bonds, including panda bonds in China. Each founding member holds an equal 20% voting share.

Both 1 and 2 would be right only if APEC had founded the NDB. In reality APEC has no such bank. The institution actually linked to Asia-Pacific development financing is the Asian Development Bank (ADB), headquartered in Manila, Philippines, established in 1966. The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a separate Chinese-led bank headquartered in Beijing, which began operating in 2016.

Neither 1 nor 2 is wrong because the Shanghai headquarters is correct. Do not confuse the NDB with the AIIB, which is in Beijing, or the World Bank, which is in Washington DC. The IMF is also headquartered in Washington DC. The BIS is in Basel, Switzerland.
related: NDB headquarters: Shanghai, China.
NDB was agreed at the 6th BRICS Summit in Fortaleza (2014) and began operating in 2015.
First NDB president: K. V. Kamath of India.
NDB authorised capital is US$100 billion, and initial subscribed capital is US$50 billion.
The BRICS Contingent Reserve Arrangement is a US$100 billion reserve pool.
AIIB headquarters is in Beijing, and it began operating in 2016.
ADB headquarters is in Manila, and it was founded in 1966.
APEC secretariat is in Singapore, and India is not a member.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The NDB was established by the BRICS nations, not by APEC. APEC is a forum with no development bank. The NDB was agreed at the Fortaleza Summit in July 2014 and the Agreement entered into force on 3 July 2015. It was created to mobilise resources for infrastructure and sustainable development projects in emerging markets and developing countries, as a complement to existing multilateral and regional financial institutions such as the World Bank and IMF. Its founding members are Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. Later members include Bangladesh, UAE, Egypt and Algeria, and Uruguay is a prospective member.

2 — Correct: The NDB's headquarters is in Shanghai, China. Its first regional office, the Africa Regional Centre, is in Johannesburg, South Africa. A regional office has also been opened in Russia. The bank was launched in July 2015, and its first president was K. V. Kamath of India. The presidency rotates among the founding members. Brazil's Marcos Troyjo followed, and Dilma Rousseff was appointed in 2023. The initial authorised capital is US$100 billion, with subscribed capital of US$50 billion. Voting power is held equally by the founding members, and no member has a veto.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. The New Development Bank (NDB) was set up by the BRICS countries, not APEC, and its headquarters is in Shanghai, China.
topic_notes: The NDB is a BRICS multilateral development bank. The idea was proposed by India at the 2012 New Delhi BRICS Summit. The 2013 Durban Summit agreed on its establishment, and the Fortaleza Summit in 2014 signed the founding agreement. It opened in 2015 in Shanghai. Authorised capital is US$100 billion and initial subscribed capital is US$50 billion, shared equally among the five founders. Its purpose is to mobilise resources for infrastructure and sustainable development in BRICS and other emerging and developing economies. The presidency rotates: K. V. Kamath (India) was first, then Marcos Troyjo (Brazil), then Dilma Rousseff (Brazil) from 2023. The Africa Regional Centre is in Johannesburg. New members include Bangladesh, UAE, Egypt and Algeria. The Contingent Reserve Arrangement is a US$100 billion pool to help members facing short-term balance of payments pressure. BRICS itself grew from the 'BRIC' term coined by Jim O'Neill in 2001. South Africa joined in 2010, and in 2024 Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE joined, with Indonesia joining in 2025. Other institutions to compare: the AIIB (Beijing, 2016), ADB (Manila, 1966), World Bank (Washington DC), IMF (Washington DC), and the BIS (Basel). Common UPSC angles are headquarters, founding year, the capital subscriptions, the currency reserve pool, and the leaders' names.

ocr: ‘Gadgil Committee Report’ and ‘Kasturirangan Committee Report’, sometimes scen in the news, are related to fa) constitutional reforms (b) Ganga Action Plan (c) linking of rivers (a) protection of Western Ghats
subject: Economy
detail: Both committees dealt with the same subject, the ecological protection of the Western Ghats, a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012) and one of the world's eight 'hottest' biodiversity hotspots. The Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel (WGEEP), chaired by ecologist Madhav Gadgil, submitted its report in August 2011. It proposed that the entire Western Ghats be treated as an Ecologically Sensitive Area (ESA) and divided into three zones, ESZ-1, ESZ-2 and ESZ-3, with graded restrictions on mining, quarrying, thermal power, large dams and polluting industries. It also favoured a bottom-up, decentralised approach to governance. Because states objected, the government formed a High Level Working Group under K. Kasturirangan in 2012. It reported in April 2013 and recommended that only about 37% of the Western Ghats (roughly 60,000 sq km) be designated ESA, with a ban on mining, quarrying and sand mining, no new thermal power plants, a prohibition on building and township projects over 20,000 sq m, and a 'red' category of industries to be barred. The Ghats cover six states: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Elimination: constitutional reforms are handled by bodies such as the Sarkaria or Venkatachaliah commissions, the Ganga Action Plan by the environment ministry, and river linking by the National Water Development Agency (NWDA) and the Task Force of Suresh Prabhu.
explanations: Incorrect: constitutional reform commissions include Sarkaria (Centre-state relations), Punchhi and Venkatachaliah (NCRWC). Neither Gadgil nor Kasturirangan dealt with this.
Incorrect: the Ganga Action Plan (1985) was a pollution abatement programme, followed by the National Mission for Clean Ganga. It is unrelated to these committees.
Incorrect: river linking is handled by the NWDA and the National Perspective Plan (1980). It has no connection to the Gadgil or Kasturirangan reports.
Correct: both committees were appointed by the MoEF to recommend measures for conserving the Western Ghats and defining Ecologically Sensitive Areas.
