keyfact: Gadgil (2011) and Kasturirangan (2013) reports are both about protecting the Western Ghats, with Gadgil proposing the whole range as ESA and Kasturirangan only about 37%.
option_notes: Constitutional reforms: India's reform bodies include the Sarkaria Commission (1983) on Centre-state relations, the Punchhi Commission (2007), the Venkatachaliah NCRWC (2000) that reviewed the Constitution, and the Administrative Reforms Commissions (1966 and 2005). Amendments are made under Article 368. None of these is linked to the Gadgil or Kasturirangan names.

Ganga Action Plan: launched in 1985 by Rajiv Gandhi to reduce pollution in the Ganga through sewage interception and treatment. It was fully centrally funded at first. The National Ganga River Basin Authority was set up in 2009 and the Ganga was declared the National River in 2008. Namami Gange, launched in 2014-15, is run by the National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG).

Linking of rivers: the National Perspective Plan (1980) has Himalayan and Peninsular components. The NWDA was set up in 1982. The Ken-Betwa link is the first project under the National River Linking Project, with a 2021 agreement between Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh. The Supreme Court in 2012 directed that a special committee be set up. The Gadgil and Kasturirangan committees had nothing to do with it.

Western Ghats: this is a mountain range of about 1,600 km running parallel to the western coast from the Tapi valley to Kanyakumari. It is older than the Himalayas. Anamudi (2,695 m) is its highest peak. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012, 39 sites) and a biodiversity hotspot. It is the source of the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri rivers. The Palghat Gap divides it, and it has rich endemic flora and fauna.
related: Gadgil Committee (WGEEP) was chaired by Madhav Gadgil and reported in 2011.
Kasturirangan High Level Working Group on Western Ghats reported in 2013 and proposed 37% as ESA.
Western Ghats became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.
Western Ghats cover Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Anamudi (2,695 m) is the highest peak of the Western Ghats and of peninsular India.
India has four biodiversity hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (Nicobar).
Ecologically Sensitive Areas are notified under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
K. Kasturirangan also headed the committee that drafted the National Education Policy 2020.
summary: The answer is (d) protection of Western Ghats. The Gadgil Committee (Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel, 2010-11) and the Kasturirangan Committee (High Level Working Group, 2013) were both set up by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change to recommend how to conserve and regulate development in the ecologically fragile Western Ghats.
topic_notes: The Western Ghats (Sahyadri) are a chain of hills along India's west coast, about 30-50 km inland, covering roughly 1.6 lakh sq km across six states. They are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012, 39 serial sites) and one of the world's eight hottest biodiversity hotspots. They intercept the southwest monsoon and cause heavy rainfall on the windward side, with a rain shadow to the east. The main passes are Thal Ghat, Bhor Ghat and Palghat Gap. Anamudi in the Anamalai range of Kerala is the highest peak in peninsular India. The Nilgiris, Cardamom Hills and Agasthyamalai are important sub-ranges. Endemic species include the Nilgiri tahr, lion-tailed macaque and Malabar civet. There are many protected areas, such as Silent Valley, Periyar, Bandipur, Nagarhole and the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (India's first, 1986). Conservation debate: the Gadgil report (WGEEP, 2011) proposed that the whole Ghats be ESA with three graded zones and community participation. The Kasturirangan report (2013) limited ESA to about 37% (about 60,000 sq km), distinguishing 'cultural landscape' from 'natural landscape', which covers about 90% of the area outside the ESA. The MoEF issued draft ESA notifications in 2014 and later, and states, especially Kerala, resisted the proposals. The Kerala floods of 2018 and landslides revived the debate. Related committees: the Kasturirangan report on the National Education Policy 2020 draft is a different report by the same person, and the Madhav Gadgil name is also tied to the Biodiversity Act's people's biodiversity registers. Other angles UPSC could ask on are ESAs under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, the Eco-Sensitive Zones around protected areas, and biodiversity hotspots such as the Eastern Himalayas, Indo-Burma and Sundaland.

ocr: Consider the following : 1. Calcutta Unitarian Committee 2. ‘Tabernacle of New Dispensation 3. Indian Reform Association Keshab Chandra Sen is associated with the establishment of which of ‘the above? fa) 1 and 3 only (b}) 2 and 3 only (c) 3 only (d) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Keshab Chandra Sen (1838-84) joined the Brahmo Samaj in 1857 and was made Acharya by Debendranath Tagore. His radical stance on caste, the sacred thread and inter-caste marriage led to the 1866 split: Sen's Brahmo Samaj of India, and Debendranath's Adi Brahmo Samaj. In 1870 he founded the Indian Reform Association, which had five sections: cheap literature, education, women's improvement, temperance, and charity. It also led to the Indian Mirror and to Sulabh Samachar, a penny newspaper. He campaigned for the Native Marriage Act (Civil Marriage Act) of 1872, which set the minimum marriage age at 18 for boys and 14 for girls. After his daughter's marriage to the Maharaja of Cooch Behar in 1878 broke his own principles, his followers split again and formed the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj. In 1881 Sen announced the Church of the New Dispensation (Nava Vidhan), at the Tabernacle, with a syncretic message. Elimination: statement 1 belongs to Rammohan Roy's era (1821), so any option with 1 is wrong. Options (a) and (d) are eliminated, and (c) is incomplete, which leaves (b).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, and the Calcutta Unitarian Committee is not Sen's creation. It was set up by Rammohan Roy and William Adam in 1821.
Correct: Sen founded the Tabernacle of New Dispensation (1881) and the Indian Reform Association (1870), and had no role in the Unitarian Committee.
Wrong: it is incomplete, because it leaves out the Tabernacle of New Dispensation, which Sen definitely founded in 1881.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is not associated with Sen but with Rammohan Roy and Adam.
keyfact: Keshab Chandra Sen: Indian Reform Association (1870) + Tabernacle of New Dispensation (1881); the Unitarian Committee (1821) was Rammohan Roy's.
option_notes: Options (a)-(d) here are combinations of numbered statements, so the notes follow the statements.

The combination 2 and 3 corresponds to the Nava Vidhan Tabernacle (1881) and the Indian Reform Association (1870), both Sen's creations. The Indian Reform Association worked for women's improvement, education, cheap literature, temperance and charity. The Nava Vidhan was a church of religious synthesis. Sen also set up the Brahmo Samaj of India (1866) and the Bharat Ashram (1872).

The combination 3 only would correctly include the Indian Reform Association (1870) and ignore the Tabernacle. The Indian Reform Association had five sections and led to the Native Marriage Act, 1872.
The combination 1, 2 and 3 is wrong because the Calcutta Unitarian Committee (1821) was formed by Rammohan Roy and William Adam long before Sen's activity.
related: Keshab Chandra Sen founded the Indian Reform Association in 1870.
Nava Vidhan (Church of New Dispensation) was proclaimed by Sen in 1881.
The Native Marriage Act 1872 was passed after Sen's campaign.
The Calcutta Unitarian Committee (1821) was founded by Rammohan Roy and William Adam.
Sadharan Brahmo Samaj was formed in 1878 after Sen's daughter's marriage with the Cooch Behar prince.
Prarthana Samaj (1867) in Bombay was inspired by Keshab Chandra Sen.
Sen's weekly Sulabh Samachar sold for one paisa.
Debendranath Tagore founded the Tattvabodhini Sabha in 1839.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Calcutta Unitarian Committee was formed in 1821 by Rammohan Roy with William Adam, not by Keshab Chandra Sen. Adam, a Baptist missionary, converted to Unitarianism and was called 'the second fallen Adam'. The Committee promoted Unitarian Christianity and pure monotheism. It was a precursor to the Brahmo Sabha of 1828, which became the Brahmo Samaj. Roy had also written 'The Precepts of Jesus' (1820), a book that stressed Christ's ethics over his miracles. Sen was born in 1838, so he could not have founded the Committee. It operated in Calcutta and was linked to the Unitarian Christians of Britain and America.

2 — Correct: The Tabernacle of New Dispensation (Nava Vidhan) was established by Keshab Chandra Sen in 1881, after the Brahmo split of 1878 over his daughter's underage marriage to the Maharaja of Cooch Behar. It was a church for a synthesis of religions: Hinduism, Christianity, Islam, Buddhism and others. Sen was influenced by Ramakrishna Paramahamsa, whom he met in 1875. The Nava Vidhan used a set of rituals, including homa and the 'pilgrimage to saints' idea. Sen held that he was working for a harmony of faiths. He died in 1884.

3 — Correct: The Indian Reform Association was founded by Keshab Chandra Sen in 1870 after his visit to England in 1870. It had five sections: Female Improvement, Education, Cheap Literature, Temperance, and Charity. It led to the Native Marriage Act, 1872, which legalised marriage in the Brahmo form and set the minimum marriage age at 18 for boys and 14 for girls. The weekly Sulabh Samachar sold at one paisa, and the Indian Mirror was another Sen publication. The Bamabodhini Patrika was a women's journal of the time.
summary: The answer is (b): Keshab Chandra Sen is associated with the Tabernacle of New Dispensation (Nava Vidhan, 1881) and the Indian Reform Association (1870). The Calcutta Unitarian Committee is linked to Raja Rammohan Roy and William Adam (1821), not to Sen.
topic_notes: Brahmo Samaj history. 1828: Rammohan Roy founded the Brahmo Sabha, renamed the Brahmo Samaj in 1830 on the opening of its Chitpur building. Roy campaigned against sati, which was banned in 1829 under Bentinck, and published Sambad Kaumudi and Mirat-ul-Akhbar. He received the title 'Raja' from the Mughal emperor Akbar II. He founded the Vedanta College in 1825 and the Atmiya Sabha in 1815. Debendranath Tagore founded the Tattvabodhini Sabha in 1839, with its journal Tattvabodhini Patrika (edited by Akshay Kumar Datta), and he revived the Brahmo Samaj in 1843. Keshab Chandra Sen joined in 1857. In 1866 the split came, with Sen's Brahmo Samaj of India. In 1878 came the second split, when the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj was formed by Ananda Mohan Bose, Sivanath Sastri and others. Sen's Nava Vidhan came in 1881. Other points: Prarthana Samaj (1867, Bombay) by Atmaram Pandurang, inspired by Sen, with M.G. Ranade and R.G. Bhandarkar as notable members. The Brahmo Marriage Act (Native Marriage Act) of 1872. Sen visited England in 1870 and met Queen Victoria and Max Muller. Related movements to compare include the Arya Samaj (1875, Dayananda Saraswati), Ramakrishna Mission (1897, Vivekananda), Theosophical Society (1875 New York, 1882 Adyar), the Satya Shodhak Samaj (1873, Jyotiba Phule), and the Servants of India Society (1905, Gokhale). Expect questions on who founded which body, on the dates of the Brahmo splits, and on the social legislation connected with these reformers.

ocr: Which of the following is not a member of ‘Gulf Cooperation Council’? (a) Iran (b) Saudi Arabia (c) Oman (ad) Kuwait
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the Gulf, commonly called the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), was founded on 25 May 1981 at an Abu Dhabi summit. It is a regional political, economic and security grouping with its secretariat in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The six founding members are Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain and Oman, and no other state has joined since. The GCC was formed against the backdrop of the Iranian Revolution (1979) and the Iran-Iraq War (1980-88), which made Arab Gulf monarchies seek collective security. Membership rests on Arab identity, monarchical systems and shared Gulf geography, so Iran, a Persian, non-Arab and republican state, is excluded. Its main aims are coordination in economic, financial, trade, customs and security matters, a customs union (2003), a common market (2008) and a proposed monetary union. The Peninsula Shield Force is its joint military arm. Elimination logic: Saudi Arabia, Oman and Kuwait are all founding members, so by elimination Iran is the odd one out. A diplomatic rift in 2017 saw Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain and Egypt cut ties with Qatar, resolved by the Al-Ula Declaration in January 2021.
explanations: Correct answer. Iran lies across the Persian Gulf but is not an Arab monarchy and has never been a GCC member.
Wrong choice for a 'not a member' question. Saudi Arabia is a founding member and hosts the GCC secretariat in Riyadh.
Wrong choice. Oman is a founding member of the GCC (1981), so it cannot be the answer.
Wrong choice. Kuwait is a founding member of the GCC, so it is not the exception.
keyfact: GCC (1981) = Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman; Iran is not a member.
option_notes: Iran is an Islamic Republic with a Persian, mostly Shia population, on the Gulf's northern coast. It became a republic after the 1979 revolution, controls the Strait of Hormuz's northern shore and is a member of OPEC, SCO (since 2023) and BRICS (since 2024). Chabahar port, developed with India, lies in its Sistan-Baluchestan province. It is not a GCC member and has often been the GCC's strategic rival. The 2015 JCPOA nuclear deal was signed with it, and the US withdrew in 2018.

Saudi Arabia is an absolute monarchy and the largest GCC economy, with capital Riyadh. It hosts the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. It is a founding member of the GCC, OPEC, OIC and the Arab League, and a G20 member. Its Vision 2030 programme seeks to diversify away from oil. It is the largest oil exporter among GCC states and the Aramco company is its energy giant.

Oman is a sultanate on the southeastern Arabian Peninsula with capital Muscat. It lies along the Strait of Hormuz, Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea. Sultan Haitham bin Tariq has ruled since 2020, after Qaboos bin Said. It is a founding GCC member, known for a neutral foreign policy and for mediating between Iran and the West. It has Duqm port, where India has access for naval use.

Kuwait is an emirate at the northern head of the Persian Gulf with capital Kuwait City. Iraq invaded it in August 1990, leading to the Gulf War and its liberation by a US-led coalition in 1991. It is a founding GCC member and an OPEC member. It has the most active elected parliament (National Assembly) among GCC states. Its currency, the Kuwaiti dinar, is among the highest valued in the world.
related: GCC founded 25 May 1981 in Abu Dhabi; headquarters in Riyadh.
GCC has six members: Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman.
Iran, Iraq and Yemen are Gulf-region states but not GCC members.
Peninsula Shield Force is the GCC's joint military force (1984).
GCC customs union came in 2003 and common market in 2008.
Qatar was under a Saudi-led blockade from 2017 until the Al-Ula Declaration of January 2021.
Chabahar port in Iran is being developed by India as a gateway to Afghanistan and Central Asia.
The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea.
summary: The answer is (a) Iran. The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) has six members: Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, UAE, Qatar, Bahrain and Oman. Iran is a Persian Gulf littoral state but has never been a GCC member.
topic_notes: The GCC was created on 25 May 1981 in Abu Dhabi, with its Charter signed by six states: Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, UAE, Qatar, Bahrain and Oman. Headquarters: Riyadh. The Supreme Council of heads of state is the highest authority, with a Ministerial Council and a Secretariat-General. Aims include coordination, integration and inter-connection in economic, social, cultural and security affairs. Key milestones: unified economic agreement (1981), Peninsula Shield Force (1984), customs union (2003), common market (2008), monetary union agreed in 2009 (not yet implemented; Oman and UAE opted out at different points). GCC states hold a large share of world oil and gas reserves, and Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait and Qatar are major producers. India-GCC relations are significant: the GCC is India's largest regional trading bloc, and nearly 9 million Indians live in the Gulf, sending large remittances. India and the GCC have been negotiating a free trade agreement, and India signed a CEPA with the UAE in 2022. Other regional bodies to differentiate: the Arab League (1945, Cairo), OPEC (1960, Vienna), OIC (1969, Jeddah), and OPEC+. Possible future questions: Strait of Hormuz, Gulf geography, GCC members versus OPEC members, Qatar blockade (2017-2021), Al-Ula Declaration, Yemen conflict and the Saudi-led coalition, Abraham Accords (UAE and Bahrain, 2020), I2U2 and the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC, announced in 2023).

ocr: What is/are the purpose/purposes of Government’s ‘Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme’ and ‘Gold Monetization Scheme’? 1. To bring the idle gold lying with Indian households into the economy 2. To promote FDI in the gold and jewellery sector 3. To reduce India’s dependence on gold imports Select the correct answer using the code given below. fa) 1 only {b) 2 and 3 only {c) 1 and 3 only (a) 1,2 and 3
subject: Economy
detail: India is one of the world's largest consumers of gold and imports almost all of it. Gold imports widen the current account deficit (CAD) and put pressure on the rupee. Households and temples hold an estimated 20,000+ tonnes of gold that sits idle and unproductive. In November 2015 the government launched the Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme and the revamped Gold Monetization Scheme (replacing the 1999 Gold Deposit Scheme) to channel this savings into financial form. SGBs are issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India. They are denominated in grams of gold, carry a fixed interest of 2.5% a year (later 2.5% on the issue price) and have an 8-year tenure with an exit option after year 5. The GMS lets people deposit gold with designated banks for short, medium and long term deposits. The banks and the government can then use or auction the gold, which cuts fresh imports. Elimination: statement 2 (promoting FDI) is wrong because these schemes are about domestic mobilisation of gold, not foreign investment. Since statement 2 is incorrect, options (b) and (d) are eliminated, and since statements 1 and 3 are both correct, (a) is eliminated, leaving (c).
explanations: (a) 1 only is wrong because statement 3 is also correct: the schemes are meant to reduce reliance on imported gold.
(b) 2 and 3 only is wrong because statement 2 is incorrect: the schemes do not promote FDI in the gold and jewellery sector, and it also omits statement 1.
(c) 1 and 3 only is correct: the schemes mobilise idle household gold and reduce gold imports, and statement 2 is wrong.
(d) 1, 2 and 3 is wrong because it includes statement 2, which is incorrect.
keyfact: SGB and GMS (Nov 2015) mobilise idle household gold and cut gold imports; they are not for promoting FDI.
related: SGBs are issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India.
SGB tenure is 8 years with an exit option after the 5th year.
SGB interest rate is 2.5% a year, paid half-yearly.
The GMS 2015 replaced the Gold Deposit Scheme 1999.
Maximum SGB subscription is 4 kg per individual per financial year.
India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX) is located at GIFT City, Gujarat.
BIS runs the mandatory hallmarking of gold jewellery in India.
Capital gains on SGB redemption at maturity are exempt from tax.
statements: 1 — Correct: Both schemes aim to bring household and institutional idle gold into the formal financial system. Facts: India's households and temples hold roughly 20,000+ tonnes of gold. The GMS 2015 lets residents deposit gold (raw gold, bars, coins, jewellery excluding stones) with designated banks in short-term (1-3 years), medium-term (5-7 years) and long-term (12-15 years) deposits, with assaying at Collection and Purity Testing Centres (CPTCs). The medium and long-term deposits are government deposits, and the short-term deposits are bank deposits. The GMS replaced the Gold Deposit Scheme 1999 and the Gold Metal Loan Scheme. Interest is exempt from income tax and capital gains tax.

2 — Incorrect: Neither scheme is intended to promote FDI in the gold or jewellery sector. Facts: FDI in gold and jewellery is a separate policy matter, and 100% FDI is allowed under the automatic route in the sector. The SGB and GMS are domestic savings mobilisation instruments aimed at residents, not at foreign investors. SGBs can be held only by resident individuals, HUFs, trusts, universities and charitable institutions, and not by non-residents. The schemes address household savings and import dependence, not capital inflows from abroad.

3 — Correct: By converting physical demand into paper gold (SGB) and recycling deposited gold (GMS), the schemes aim to cut gold imports and reduce the current account deficit. Facts: SGBs are issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India and are denominated in units of 1 gram of gold and multiples of it. Tenure is 8 years with an exit option after the 5th year. Interest is 2.5% a year, paid half-yearly, on the initial investment. Redemption is at the average closing price of 999-purity gold of the previous three business days. The maximum limit is 4 kg per individual per financial year, 4 kg for HUFs and 20 kg for trusts. Capital gains tax is exempt on redemption at maturity.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. The Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme (SGB) and the Gold Monetization Scheme (GMS), both launched in November 2015, aim to mobilise the idle gold held by Indian households and to reduce physical gold imports, and so ease pressure on the current account deficit. Neither scheme is meant to promote FDI in the gold and jewellery sector.
topic_notes: Gold and the economy: India is the second-largest consumer of gold after China and imports about 800-900 tonnes a year, mainly from Switzerland, UAE and South Africa. Gold imports are a major contributor to the trade deficit and CAD. The government has tried several tools, including import duty changes (the duty was cut to 6% in July 2024), the 80:20 rule (2013, later withdrawn), and hallmarking. Sovereign Gold Bond Scheme (Nov 2015): issued by the RBI on behalf of the GoI, in tranches. Eligible investors are resident individuals, HUFs, trusts, universities and charitable institutions. Minimum 1 gram, maximum 4 kg per individual per financial year, 20 kg for trusts. Tenure 8 years, with premature redemption allowed from the 5th year on interest payment dates. Interest 2.5% fixed (taxable), paid half-yearly. They can be traded on stock exchanges, used as collateral for loans, and are held in demat or paper form. Capital gains on redemption at maturity are tax-exempt. Bonds are sold through banks, SHCIL, post offices, and recognised stock exchanges. Gold Monetization Scheme (Nov 2015): a revamp of the 1999 Gold Deposit Scheme. Minimum deposit 10 grams of raw gold, with no upper limit. The gold is tested at BIS-certified CPTCs. Short-term bank deposits (1-3 years), medium (5-7 years) and long (12-15 years) deposits. Interest is paid in rupees, and redemption is in rupees or gold. Interest and capital gains are exempt. The government also launched the Indian Gold Coin (with Ashoka Chakra) in 2015. In 2024, the government announced the discontinuation of the medium and long-term deposit components of the GMS (March 2025). Related institutions: RBI, BIS (hallmarking), World Gold Council, and the India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX) at GIFT City, launched in 2022. Other angles UPSC may ask: effect of gold imports on CAD and the rupee, gold ETFs, and digital gold regulated by SEBI.

ocr: ‘Belt and Road Initiative’ is sometimes mentioned in the news in the context of the affairs of - - . —-- (a) African Union (b) Brazil ; {c) European Union (dj China B-APM-P-CKB/65A
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), earlier called One Belt One Road (OBOR), was announced by Xi Jinping in 2013, with the Silk Road Economic Belt unveiled in Astana, Kazakhstan (September 2013) and the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road in Indonesia (October 2013). It aims to build land corridors and sea lanes linking China with Central Asia, South Asia, West Asia, Africa and Europe through ports, railways, roads, pipelines and industrial parks. It is financed largely through Chinese policy banks, the Silk Road Fund (2014) and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB, HQ Beijing, operational 2016). The six main corridors include the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) and the BCIM Economic Corridor. India has refused to join, objecting that CPEC passes through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and violates its sovereignty; it also raises debt-trap concerns, as with Sri Lanka's Hambantota port leased to China for 99 years in 2017. Elimination: the African Union, Brazil and the European Union are not the originators of BRI; they are at most participants or partners. The initiative is a Chinese foreign-policy and economic programme, so (d) is right.
explanations: Incorrect: The African Union is a continental body of 55 member states. Many African countries take part in BRI projects, but the initiative is not part of the AU's own affairs.
Incorrect: Brazil is a BRICS member and a major trade partner of China, but it is not the originator of BRI and has not formally joined it in the sense relevant to this question.
Incorrect: The European Union is a partner and sometimes a critic. It has its own Global Gateway strategy (2021) as a counter-offer, so BRI is not an EU matter.
Correct: BRI was proposed by Xi Jinping in 2013 and is driven, financed and branded by China, so news about it concerns China's affairs.
keyfact: Belt and Road Initiative = China's 2013 Xi Jinping-led global connectivity project; India opposes it because CPEC crosses PoK.
option_notes: The African Union (AU) replaced the Organisation of African Unity in 2002 and is headquartered in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. It has 55 member states. Its development blueprint is Agenda 2063. The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) came into force in 2019. In 2023 India championed the AU's permanent membership of the G20, which was granted at the New Delhi Summit.

Brazil is the largest country in South America, with its capital at Brasília. It is a founding member of BRICS (2009 with Russia, India and China; South Africa joined in 2010) and of Mercosur (1991). It hosts the Amazon rainforest. China is its largest trading partner. Brazil hosted the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio and COP30 in Belém in 2025.

The European Union is a political and economic union of 27 member states (after Brexit in 2020). It originated with the Treaty of Rome (1957) and was formally created by the Maastricht Treaty (1992/93). Its institutions include the European Commission, the European Parliament and the Council. The euro is used by 20 members. It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2012. HQ is Brussels.

China is the world's second-largest economy, with its capital at Beijing, ruled by the Communist Party under Xi Jinping. It is a permanent UN Security Council member. It launched BRI in 2013, founded the AIIB (2016) and the New Development Bank with BRICS partners. It shares a disputed border with India (LAC) and is involved in the South China Sea disputes.
related: BRI was announced by Xi Jinping in 2013, in Kazakhstan and Indonesia.
CPEC connects Kashgar (Xinjiang) to Gwadar (Pakistan).
India has opposed BRI because CPEC passes through PoK.
The AIIB is headquartered in Beijing and began operating in 2016.
Sri Lanka leased Hambantota port to China for 99 years in 2017.
IMEC was announced at the G20 summit in New Delhi in 2023.
BCIM corridor links Kunming with Kolkata.
The Silk Road Fund was set up in 2014 to finance BRI projects.
summary: The correct answer is (d) China. The Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) is China's flagship global infrastructure and connectivity programme, launched by President Xi Jinping in 2013, so it appears in the news in the context of China's affairs.
topic_notes: The Belt and Road Initiative is China's largest foreign-policy and infrastructure project, announced by Xi Jinping in 2013. It has two parts: the overland Silk Road Economic Belt and the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road. It draws on the historic Silk Road of the Han dynasty era. Over 140 countries have signed cooperation documents. Funding comes from the China Development Bank, Exim Bank of China, the Silk Road Fund (US$40 billion, 2014) and the AIIB. The six economic corridors are: China-Mongolia-Russia; New Eurasian Land Bridge; China-Central Asia-West Asia; China-Indochina Peninsula; China-Pakistan (CPEC); and Bangladesh-China-India-Myanmar (BCIM). CPEC links Kashgar in Xinjiang with Gwadar port in Balochistan and runs through Gilgit-Baltistan, which India claims as part of Jammu and Kashmir. India boycotted the Belt and Road Forums of 2017 and 2019 on sovereignty grounds. Critics point to debt-trap diplomacy, as with Hambantota (Sri Lanka), Kenya's railway, and Laos. Italy joined in 2019 but left in 2023. India's own counter-initiatives include Project Mausam, the Asia-Africa Growth Corridor with Japan, the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) via Chabahar, and the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), announced at the G20 in 2023. The G7 launched the Partnership for Global Infrastructure and Investment (PGII) in 2022 as an alternative. Related institutions: SCO, BRICS, the New Development Bank (Shanghai, 2015) and the AIIB (Beijing).

question: Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana is aimed at bringing the small entrepreneurs
options: into forma] financial system providing loans to poor farmers for
cultivating particular crops providing pensions to old and
destitute persons funding the voluntary organizations
involved in the promotion of skill development and employment generation
subject: Economy
detail: PMMY was launched on 8 April 2015 by PM Narendra Modi. It works through the Micro Units Development and Refinance Agency (MUDRA) Ltd, a non-banking financial company and subsidiary of SIDBI, set up to refinance banks, NBFCs and microfinance institutions (MFIs) that lend to micro enterprises. It does not lend directly to borrowers; loans come from banks, RRBs, small finance banks, MFIs and NBFCs. Loans are collateral-free, with no subsidy by default, and are for non-farm income-generating activities in manufacturing, trading and services, plus allied agricultural activities such as poultry, dairy and beekeeping, but not crop cultivation itself. Three categories were set by loan size: Shishu (up to Rs 50,000), Kishore (Rs 50,001 to 5 lakh) and Tarun (Rs 5 lakh to 10 lakh). In 2024 a fourth category, Tarun Plus (up to Rs 20 lakh), was added. Elimination: (b) is wrong because crop loans are covered by the Kisan Credit Card; (c) is wrong because pensions are covered by the NSAP and the Atal Pension Yojana; (d) is wrong because funding voluntary organisations is not the scheme's purpose, and skill development is handled by PMKVY.
explanations: Correct. PMMY gives small and micro entrepreneurs collateral-free institutional credit up to Rs 10 lakh, bringing them into the formal financial system.
Incorrect. Loans to farmers for particular crops come under the Kisan Credit Card and NABARD-refinanced crop loans. PMMY covers non-farm micro enterprises and allied activities, not crop cultivation.
Incorrect. Pensions for the old and destitute come under the National Social Assistance Programme (Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme) and the Atal Pension Yojana, not MUDRA.
Incorrect. PMMY lends to individual micro enterprises and does not fund voluntary organisations. Skill development is the domain of PMKVY and the NSDC.
keyfact: PMMY (8 April 2015) gives collateral-free loans up to Rs 10 lakh to micro enterprises via MUDRA Ltd (a SIDBI subsidiary) to promote formal financial inclusion.
option_notes: Financial inclusion of small entrepreneurs means bringing unregistered micro and small units into formal credit channels. PMMY, launched 8 April 2015, offers loans up to Rs 10 lakh without collateral through banks, NBFCs and MFIs. It is refinanced by MUDRA Ltd, a SIDBI subsidiary. Loan categories are Shishu, Kishore and Tarun, with Tarun Plus added in 2024. Borrowers receive a MUDRA card, a debit card for working capital.

Crop loans to farmers are given mainly through the Kisan Credit Card (KCC), introduced in 1998 on the recommendation of the R.K. Hegde committee. Interest subvention is available, with prompt repayment incentives. NABARD refinances cooperative banks and RRBs for agriculture. KCC was extended to fisheries and animal husbandry in 2018-19. PM-KISAN gives Rs 6,000 a year in income support, which is separate from credit.

Pensions for the elderly and destitute are delivered through the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP), launched 1995 under Article 41 (Directive Principles). It includes the Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme for those aged 60 and above in BPL households. The Atal Pension Yojana (2015) is a contributory pension for unorganised-sector workers aged 18 to 40, with a guaranteed pension of Rs 1,000 to 5,000 a month from age 60.

Skill development and employment generation efforts include the Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (2015), run by the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC) under the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, created in 2014. Other efforts are Skill India Mission (2015), the PMEGP for self-employment, and MGNREGA, which guarantees 100 days of wage employment. These are not delivered through MUDRA.
related: PMMY was launched on 8 April 2015.
MUDRA Ltd is a subsidiary of SIDBI.
PMMY loan categories: Shishu, Kishore, Tarun, plus Tarun Plus from 2024.
MUDRA loans are collateral-free and cover non-farm activities.
Stand-Up India (2016) targets SC/ST and women entrepreneurs with loans of Rs 10 lakh to 1 crore.
Kisan Credit Card provides crop loans to farmers.
PM SVANidhi (2020) offers working-capital loans to street vendors.
CGTMSE provides credit guarantees for collateral-free loans to MSMEs.
summary: The answer is (a). Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana (PMMY) aims to bring small and micro entrepreneurs, especially the unfunded and unregistered ones, into the formal financial system by giving them collateral-free institutional credit up to Rs 10 lakh.
topic_notes: MUDRA stands for Micro Units Development and Refinance Agency. It was announced in the Union Budget 2015-16 with a corpus of Rs 20,000 crore and a credit guarantee corpus of Rs 3,000 crore. It was set up as a subsidiary of SIDBI, and its regulatory ties lie with the RBI. The PMMY was launched on 8 April 2015. The target group is non-corporate, non-farm small and micro enterprises, which are mostly proprietorships, partnerships, small manufacturers, shopkeepers, vendors, artisans and food-service units. Loan sizes: Shishu up to Rs 50,000, Kishore Rs 50,000 to 5 lakh, Tarun Rs 5 to 10 lakh, and Tarun Plus up to Rs 20 lakh for those who repaid earlier Tarun loans. No collateral is required and the loan can be a term loan or working capital. Under the MUDRA card, working capital is drawn through a RuPay debit card. Lending institutions include commercial banks, RRBs, cooperative banks, small finance banks, MFIs and NBFCs. Most borrowers have been Shishu category borrowers, and women and SC/ST/OBC borrowers make up a large share. The scheme has faced concern over NPAs, mainly in the Kishore and Tarun segments. Related schemes UPSC may ask about: Stand-Up India (2016) gives loans between Rs 10 lakh and 1 crore to SC/ST and women entrepreneurs for greenfield enterprises; Start-up India (2016); PM SVANidhi for street vendors (2020); the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE); and PMEGP, which provides a credit-linked subsidy through KVIC. Know also the definitions of MSMEs, revised in 2020 on investment and turnover criteria.

ocr: In which of the following regions of India are shale gas resources found? Cambay Basin T; Cauvery Basin ai 3. Krishna-Godavari Basin Select the correct answer using the code given below. 1 and 2 only (a) 3 only (b) 2 and 3 only {c) 1, 2 and 3 (d)
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Shale gas is natural gas trapped within fine-grained, organic-rich sedimentary rock (shale), and it is extracted using horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing (fracking). India's shale potential has been assessed by the USGS/EIA, the Directorate General of Hydrocarbons (DGH), ONGC and the Oil and Gas Industry. ONGC drilled India's first shale gas well in 2011 at Durgapur in West Bengal (Damodar Valley basin). The Government announced a Shale Gas and Oil Policy in October 2013 that allowed National Oil Companies (ONGC, OIL) to explore shale gas in their nominated blocks, and the policy did not extend to private bidders in that phase. The main shale-bearing basins are Cambay (Gujarat), Krishna-Godavari (Andhra Pradesh, coastal), Cauvery (Tamil Nadu), Damodar Valley (Jharkhand-West Bengal), Assam-Arakan, Vindhyan, Pranhita-Godavari and the Rajasthan basins. The elimination logic is simple: since all three of the listed basins are recognised shale-bearing basins, any option that excludes one is wrong. Knowing even two of the three correctly leads you to (d), because the only option that includes both Cambay and Cauvery along with KG basin is (d). Remember that potential resource does not equal commercial production, and India has no significant commercial shale gas output so far.
explanations: (a) 1 and 2 only is wrong because it omits statement 3; the Krishna-Godavari Basin also holds shale gas resources.
(b) 3 only is wrong because it excludes the Cambay and Cauvery basins, both of which have identified shale gas potential.
(c) 2 and 3 only is wrong because it omits statement 1; the Cambay Basin has recognised shale gas resources.
(d) 1, 2 and 3 is correct because Cambay, Cauvery and Krishna-Godavari basins all have shale gas resources, as confirmed by the official UPSC key.
keyfact: Cambay, Cauvery and Krishna-Godavari basins all have shale gas resources, so the answer is (d).
related: India's first shale gas well was drilled by ONGC at Durgapur (West Bengal) in 2011.
Shale Gas and Oil Policy was announced in 2013 for National Oil Companies.
HELP (2016) introduced OALP and a uniform licence for all hydrocarbons.
Shale gas is extracted by hydraulic fracturing (fracking).
Gas hydrates have been found in the Krishna-Godavari basin offshore.
Coal bed methane is found in Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro and Sohagpur coalfields.
DGH is the technical advisory body under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
The USA led the global shale gas revolution.
statements: 1 — Correct: Cambay Basin has shale gas potential. Located in Gujarat, it is a rift-graben basin filled with Tertiary sediments, and its Cambay Shale is a key source rock. It is one of India's oldest producing petroleum basins (Ankleshwar, Kalol, Gandhar fields). ONGC has identified shale formations here, and DGH has assessed it among the prospective shale basins. Mehsana, Ahmedabad, Cambay and Broach are the major sub-blocks.

2 — Correct: Cauvery Basin has shale gas potential. Spread over Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, onshore and offshore, it is a pericratonic rift basin with Mesozoic-Tertiary sediments. Source rocks include the Andimadam and Sattapadi shales. Existing production includes oil and gas from fields such as Narimanam and Kovilkalappal, and ONGC has drilled exploratory shale wells there. It is among the basins listed by the DGH and EIA for shale potential.

3 — Correct: Krishna-Godavari (KG) Basin has shale gas potential. This east-coast basin spans Andhra Pradesh, both onshore and deep-water offshore, and is famous for the Reliance D6 gas field and ONGC finds. Permian-Triassic and Cretaceous shales such as the Kommugudem shale are source rocks. The EIA and DGH list KG among the most promising shale gas basins in India, and ONGC has tested shale wells there.
summary: The correct answer is (d) 1, 2 and 3. Shale gas resources in India have been identified in the Cambay, Cauvery and Krishna-Godavari basins, along with others such as Damodar Valley and Assam-Arakan. All three listed basins therefore qualify.
topic_notes: Shale gas is unconventional natural gas held in low-permeability, organic-rich shale. It is extracted through horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing, which pumps water, sand and chemicals at high pressure. Concerns include heavy water use, groundwater contamination, induced seismicity and methane leakage. Major producers are the USA (the shale revolution), Canada, China and Argentina. India's potential: the EIA and USGS have estimated sizeable technically recoverable resources, and the Indian assessments (DGH, ONGC) identify basins such as Cambay, KG, Cauvery, Damodar Valley, Assam-Arakan, Vindhyan and Pranhita-Godavari. ONGC drilled the first shale gas well at Durgapur, West Bengal, in 2011 (RB-1). The Government's Shale Gas and Oil Policy of 2013 permitted National Oil Companies to explore in their nominated blocks under existing PSC and nomination licences. Later, the Hydrocarbon Exploration and Licensing Policy (HELP, 2016) introduced a uniform licence, the Open Acreage Licensing Policy (OALP) and a revenue-sharing model, covering all hydrocarbons including shale gas, coal bed methane and gas hydrates. Related unconventional resources: coal bed methane (Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro, Sohagpur), tight gas, and gas hydrates (found in the KG basin offshore, Mahanadi and Andaman). Regulatory bodies: the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, the DGH (technical arm) and PNGRB for downstream. The key limiting factors for India are water scarcity, high population density, land acquisition and lack of technology and rigs.

question: Global Financial Stability. Report’ is prepared by the European, Central Bank
options: Reconstruction and Development Organization for Economic
subject: Economy
detail: The GFSR is prepared by the IMF's Monetary and Capital Markets Department and published twice a year, in April and October, alongside the World Economic Outlook (WEO) and the Fiscal Monitor. It began in 2002 and succeeded the earlier International Capital Markets reports. It covers market risks, the stability of banks and non-bank financial institutions, sovereign debt, capital flows, asset valuations and emerging-market vulnerabilities. It also gives policy advice for safeguarding stability. The IMF was conceived at Bretton Woods in 1944, began operating in 1945, has its headquarters in Washington DC and has about 190 members. Its surveillance function (Article IV consultations, WEO, GFSR) is the basis for this report. For elimination, match each body to its own flagship output. The European Central Bank (ECB) publishes a Financial Stability Review for the euro area, not a global report. The World Bank's IBRD publishes the World Development Report and Global Economic Prospects. The OECD publishes the Economic Outlook, PISA and the Better Life Index. 'Global' plus 'financial stability' points to the IMF, which monitors the international monetary system.
explanations: Incorrect for this question: the ECB is the euro-area central bank in Frankfurt. It publishes a regional Financial Stability Review, not the Global Financial Stability Report.
Correct: the IMF, through its Monetary and Capital Markets Department, prepares and publishes the GFSR twice a year, in April and October.
Incorrect: the IBRD, part of the World Bank Group, focuses on development lending and publishes the World Development Report and Global Economic Prospects, not the GFSR.
Incorrect: the OECD is a Paris-based policy forum of mostly developed economies. It publishes the Economic Outlook and PISA results, not the GFSR.
keyfact: Global Financial Stability Report = IMF (April and October), alongside the World Economic Outlook and Fiscal Monitor.
option_notes: The European Central Bank was established in 1998 and is headquartered in Frankfurt. It is the central bank for the 20 euro-area countries (as of 2023) and sets monetary policy for the euro. Its main goal is price stability, with inflation targeted at 2 percent over the medium term. It supervises large banks through the Single Supervisory Mechanism and publishes the Financial Stability Review twice a year. It is not a global body.

The International Monetary Fund was created at the Bretton Woods Conference in 1944 and began operations in 1945. It is headquartered in Washington DC and has about 190 members. Its functions are surveillance, lending to countries with balance-of-payments problems and capacity development. It issues Special Drawing Rights (SDRs). It publishes the WEO, GFSR and Fiscal Monitor. Its Managing Director since 2019 is Kristalina Georgieva. Voting power is based on quotas.

The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development was set up in 1944 at Bretton Woods and is the original institution of the World Bank Group. It lends to middle-income and creditworthy low-income governments for development and poverty reduction. It is headquartered in Washington DC. The group also includes IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID. It publishes the World Development Report and Global Economic Prospects. The Doing Business report was discontinued in 2021.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development was formed in 1961, succeeding the OEEC of the Marshall Plan era. It is headquartered in Paris and has 38 members. India is not a member but is a key partner. It is a policy-research and standard-setting forum. Its outputs include the Economic Outlook, PISA (education), the Better Life Index and work on base erosion and profit shifting (BEPS) and tax cooperation.
related: GFSR is published by the IMF twice a year, in April and October.
The World Economic Outlook and Fiscal Monitor are also IMF flagship reports.
The RBI's Financial Stability Report comes out in June and December.
The World Bank publishes the World Development Report and Global Economic Prospects.
The OECD publishes PISA and the Economic Outlook; its headquarters are in Paris.
The Financial Stability Board is based in Basel and was formed by the G20 in 2009.
The IMF's SDR basket includes the dollar, euro, yuan, yen and pound.
UNCTAD publishes the World Investment Report; UNDP publishes the Human Development Report.
summary: The answer is (b), the International Monetary Fund. The Global Financial Stability Report (GFSR) is an IMF flagship publication that assesses risks to the global financial system and capital markets.
topic_notes: The IMF, set up at Bretton Woods in July 1944 and operational from 1945, promotes monetary cooperation, exchange-rate stability and balanced trade growth. Its core activities are surveillance, financial assistance and technical assistance. Surveillance includes annual Article IV consultations with member countries, the Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP, with the World Bank) and regular flagship reports. The main flagships are the World Economic Outlook (April and October, with updates in January and July), the Global Financial Stability Report (April and October) and the Fiscal Monitor. The External Sector Report is a further regular publication. The GFSR focuses on systemic risk, market liquidity, leverage, sovereign-bank links, shadow banking and capital-flow volatility. Quotas decide each member's subscription, voting power and access to financing. India's quota share is about 2.75 percent. The IMF's reserve asset is the SDR, whose basket has five currencies: the US dollar, euro, Chinese yuan, Japanese yen and British pound. Yuan inclusion took effect in October 2016. The Managing Director has traditionally been European, and the World Bank president American. Other bodies and their reports are commonly confused with the GFSR. The Financial Stability Board, set up by the G20 in 2009 and based in Basel, coordinates regulatory reform. The BIS in Basel hosts the Basel Committee and publishes an Annual Economic Report. The RBI publishes its own Financial Stability Report twice a year, in June and December. The World Bank publishes the World Development Report and Global Economic Prospects. UNCTAD publishes the World Investment Report. The WEF publishes the Global Competitiveness Report, Global Risks Report and Global Gender Gap Report. UNDP publishes the Human Development Report.

ocr: Regarding ‘Atal Pension Yojana’, which of the following statements is/are correct? l. It is a minimum guaranteed pension scheme mainly targeted at unorganized sector workers. 2. Only one member of a family can join the scheme. 3. Same amount of pension is guaranteed for the spouse for life after subscriber’s death. Select the correct answer using the code given below, fa) 1 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c} 1 and 3 only (da) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Atal Pension Yojana was announced in the Union Budget 2015-16 and launched on 9 May 2015 at Kolkata, replacing the earlier Swavalamban Scheme. It is administered by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) through the National Pension System (NPS) architecture. It targets workers in the unorganised sector, who typically lack formal pension coverage. Subscribers aged 18-40 can join through a bank account, and contributions continue until age 60. The scheme guarantees a fixed minimum monthly pension of Rs 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, 4,000 or 5,000 from age 60, depending on the contribution, which in turn depends on the joining age. If the subscriber dies, the spouse receives the same pension for life. After both die, the accumulated corpus at age 60 is returned to the nominee. The government originally co-contributed 50% of the subscriber's contribution or Rs 1,000 a year, whichever was lower, for five years for those who joined by 31 March 2016 and were not income-tax payers or members of statutory social security schemes. Elimination logic: statement 1 is correct, and statement 3 is correct. Statement 2 is incorrect because the scheme is individual-based, so each eligible person, including a husband and wife, can hold a separate APY account. That leaves option (c).
explanations: Wrong: 1 is correct, but it omits statement 3, which is also correct, so this option is incomplete.
Wrong: this option includes statement 2, which is false. It also leaves out statement 1, which is true.
Correct: statements 1 and 3 are true, and statement 2 is false because the scheme is not limited to one member per family.
Wrong: statement 2 is false, since several family members, including both spouses, can join the scheme separately.
keyfact: APY: PFRDA-run, launched 9 May 2015, ages 18-40, guaranteed Rs 1,000-5,000 a month from age 60, same pension to spouse for life, corpus to nominee, and not one-per-family.
option_notes: Option (a) covers only statement 1. The statement itself is true: APY offers a government-guaranteed minimum pension of Rs 1,000-5,000 a month from age 60. It is run by PFRDA and aimed at unorganised sector workers aged 18-40. The option is wrong only because it leaves out statement 3. In UPSC's format, a correct statement can still sit inside an incomplete option, so always check every statement.

Option (b) says '2 and 3 only'. Statement 2 is wrong because APY is an individual scheme: each eligible person can open an account, including both spouses of a family. Statement 3 is correct, since the spouse gets the same pension for life, and the nominee receives the corpus after both die. It is wrong because it includes statement 2 and omits statement 1.

Option (c) says '1 and 3 only', the official answer. APY is a pension scheme guaranteeing a minimum monthly pension, aimed at the unorganised sector, and the same pension continues to the spouse for life after the subscriber's death. It was launched on 9 May 2015 and is administered by PFRDA through NPS. Entry age is 18-40, and the pension starts at 60. The corpus goes to the nominee after both die.

Option (d) says '1, 2 and 3'. It would be right only if all three statements were true, but statement 2 is false. APY permits any eligible individual aged 18-40 with a bank account to join, so a husband and wife can each hold their own account and receive their own pension. Always test every statement before choosing 'all of the above'.
related: APY was launched on 9 May 2015 and is regulated by PFRDA.
Entry age for APY is 18-40 years; the pension starts at age 60.
APY guaranteed pension slabs are Rs 1,000 to Rs 5,000 a month.
APY replaced the Swavalamban Scheme.
The spouse receives the same pension after the subscriber's death; the nominee receives the corpus after both die.
NPS began in 2004 for government employees and opened to all citizens in 2009.
PM-SYM (2019) offers Rs 3,000 a month after age 60 for unorganised workers.
PMJJBY, PMSBY and APY were launched together in May 2015.
statements: 1 — Correct: APY guarantees a minimum monthly pension and is aimed mainly at unorganised sector workers. APY was launched on 9 May 2015 and is run by PFRDA under NPS. Eligible subscribers are aged 18-40 and hold a savings bank or post office account. The guaranteed monthly pension is Rs 1,000-5,000 from age 60. Contributions are monthly, quarterly or half-yearly, and auto-debited from the bank account. The central government guarantees the minimum pension, so if returns fall short, the government funds the gap. It replaced Swavalamban. Since 2022, income-tax payers are not eligible to join.

2 — Incorrect: Nothing in the scheme limits membership to one member per family. It is an individual-account scheme, and every eligible citizen aged 18-40 with a bank account can enrol. Husband and wife can both subscribe separately, each getting their own pension entitlement and spousal benefit. The pension amount is chosen at enrolment, and the contribution varies with the joining age: a later joining age means a higher contribution for the same pension. Aadhaar is the preferred identity document for enrolment but is not mandatory. Subscribers may exit early only in limited cases, such as death or terminal illness.

3 — Correct: After the subscriber dies, the spouse is entitled to the same guaranteed pension for life. When both the subscriber and the spouse die, the nominee receives the pension corpus accumulated up to age 60. If the subscriber dies before 60, the spouse can continue the account for the remaining period or exit and withdraw the corpus. The pension amount is fixed at joining, and the return of corpus to the nominee is the scheme's third tier of protection. The pension is paid monthly and is not linked to inflation, so its real value declines over time.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. Atal Pension Yojana (APY) is a government-backed pension scheme with a guaranteed minimum monthly pension, aimed mainly at unorganised sector workers. After the subscriber dies, the spouse gets the same pension for life. Statement 2 is wrong because both spouses can each join separately.
topic_notes: Atal Pension Yojana (APY) is a social security scheme for the unorganised sector, announced in Budget 2015-16 and launched on 9 May 2015. It is run by PFRDA under the NPS framework. It replaced the Swavalamban Scheme, which was a co-contributory NPS-based scheme for the unorganised sector. Eligibility is age 18-40, with a savings bank or post office account and a mobile number. Contributions are made until age 60, and the guaranteed pension of Rs 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, 4,000 or 5,000 a month starts at 60. The contribution depends on the chosen pension and the joining age; joining younger costs less per month. Contributions are auto-debited monthly, quarterly or half-yearly. The government originally co-contributed 50% of the subscriber's contribution or Rs 1,000 a year, whichever was lower, for five years for eligible new subscribers who joined by 31 March 2016. From 1 October 2022, income-tax payers are not eligible to join. If the subscriber dies, the spouse gets the same pension, and after both die the nominee gets the corpus accumulated by age 60. Related schemes: Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (life insurance), Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (accident insurance), and Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (financial inclusion); these were launched together in 2015. Also remember the National Pension System (NPS), which began in 2004 for government employees and opened to all citizens in 2009, and the Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maan-dhan (PM-SYM) scheme of 2019 for unorganised workers, which gives Rs 3,000 a month after age 60. Likely angles: the regulator, entry age, pension slabs, the minimum guarantee, the spouse and nominee rules, and comparisons with NPS and PM-SYM.

ocr: The term ‘Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership’ often appears in the news in the context of the affairs of a group of countries known as {a} G20 (b) ASEAN fc) SCO (dq) SAARC
subject: Current Affairs
detail: RCEP was launched at the ASEAN Summit in Phnom Penh in November 2012, with negotiations beginning in 2013. It brings together the 10 ASEAN members (Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam) and ASEAN's six FTA partners: China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand and India. The idea was to merge the existing ASEAN+1 FTAs into one agreement that covers trade in goods and services, investment, economic and technical cooperation, intellectual property, competition and dispute settlement. ASEAN centrality is the guiding principle. India withdrew in November 2019 (Bangkok summit) over concerns about the trade deficit with China, inadequate protection against import surges, and market access. The other 15 countries signed the agreement in November 2020 (Vietnam, virtual), and it came into force on 1 January 2022. It covers about 30% of global GDP and population. Elimination logic: G20 is a forum of major economies, SCO is a Eurasian political-security grouping, and SAARC is South Asian and has no trade-deal link to RCEP. Only ASEAN fits the context.
explanations: Incorrect: G20 is a forum for global economic governance among major economies. RCEP is not its initiative, and several G20 members are not in RCEP.
Correct: RCEP is an ASEAN-led initiative, launched in 2012 by ASEAN and its six FTA partners, and ASEAN is at the centre of its structure.
Incorrect: SCO is a Eurasian political, economic and security grouping. RCEP is not negotiated through it, and Central Asian states and Russia are not part of RCEP.
Incorrect: SAARC is a South Asian regional body. Only India (until it withdrew) among its members was in the RCEP negotiations, and SAARC has its own SAFTA.
keyfact: RCEP is an ASEAN-led mega trade deal (launched 2012, in force 2022) and India withdrew in 2019.
option_notes: G20 (Group of Twenty) is a forum of 19 countries plus the EU (the African Union joined as a permanent member in 2023). It began in 1999 as a finance ministers' forum after the Asian financial crisis, and its leaders' summits started in 2008. It has no permanent secretariat; the presidency rotates. India held the presidency in 2023 and hosted the New Delhi summit. Its members account for about 85% of world GDP.

ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, was founded on 8 August 1967 by the Bangkok Declaration, with five founders: Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore and Thailand. It has 10 members, and Timor-Leste was admitted as the 11th in 2025. Its secretariat is in Jakarta. The ASEAN Charter has been in force since 2008. Its principles include consensus and non-interference. It has three pillars: political-security, economic and socio-cultural. It leads RCEP, the East Asia Summit and the ASEAN Regional Forum.

SCO, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, was established in 2001 and grew out of the Shanghai Five of 1996. Its founding members were China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. India and Pakistan joined in 2017, Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024. Its secretariat is in Beijing and its Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS) is in Tashkent. It focuses on security, counter-terrorism and regional cooperation.

SAARC, the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, was founded in Dhaka in 1985 and its secretariat is in Kathmandu. It has eight members: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. The SAARC summit has been stalled since 2014, and the 2016 Islamabad summit was not held. SAFTA came into effect in 2006. India now emphasises BIMSTEC as an alternative.
related: RCEP was launched in 2012 at the ASEAN Summit in Phnom Penh.
India withdrew from RCEP negotiations in November 2019 at the Bangkok summit.
RCEP was signed on 15 November 2020 and came into force on 1 January 2022.
The ASEAN secretariat is in Jakarta, Indonesia.
RCEP's six ASEAN FTA partners are China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand and India.
India's Act East Policy was launched in 2014, replacing the Look East Policy of 1992.
Timor-Leste became the 11th ASEAN member in 2025.
CPTPP is a separate trade bloc and India is not a member.
summary: The answer is (b) ASEAN. The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) is a proposed mega free trade agreement that ASEAN launched and leads, and it involves ASEAN's 10 members and their six FTA partners.
topic_notes: RCEP is a mega-regional trade agreement among 15 Asia-Pacific economies. It was proposed in 2011 and launched in 2012 at the ASEAN Summit in Phnom Penh, with negotiations starting in 2013. The 16 original negotiators were the 10 ASEAN members plus China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand and India. India left the negotiations in November 2019, citing the large trade deficit with China, risk of import surges, weak protection for farmers and MSMEs, and inadequate safeguards on rules of origin. The agreement was signed on 15 November 2020 and came into force on 1 January 2022. It is the world's largest trading bloc by GDP and population, covering about 30% of both. It cuts tariffs, sets common rules of origin, and covers e-commerce, IPR, competition and SMEs. India still has the option to rejoin, and the other members have kept the door open. Related ASEAN-led and Asia-Pacific groupings: ASEAN+3 (China, Japan, South Korea), the East Asia Summit (18 members, including the US and Russia since 2011), and the ASEAN Regional Forum. CPTPP (the successor to TPP after the US withdrawal in 2017) is a different trade bloc, and the UK joined it in 2024. APEC has 21 economies, and India is not a member. IPEF is a US-led framework launched in 2022, which India joined, except for the trade pillar. India's ASEAN ties: the Look East Policy (1992) became the Act East Policy (2014), and the India-ASEAN FTA in goods took effect in 2010. The ASEAN-India trade in goods agreement (AITIGA) is under review. Possible future questions include the members, the headquarters of ASEAN and its secretariat, and the reasons India stayed out.

ocr: On which of the following can you find - the Bureau of Energy Efficiency Star Label? 1. Ceiling fans 2. Electric geysers 3. Tubular fluorescent lamps B-APM-P-CKB/65A 28 Select the correct answer using the code given below, {a) 1 and 2 only (b) 3 only (c}) 2 and 3 only fd) 1, 2 and 3
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) is a statutory body under the Ministry of Power, set up on 1 March 2002 under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001. Its Standards & Labelling (S&L) programme, launched in 2006, rates appliances on a 1-to-5 star scale, where 5 stars means the most energy-efficient. The label helps consumers compare the energy consumption of similar products. The programme began with frost-free refrigerators, tubular fluorescent lamps, room air conditioners and distribution transformers. Coverage later grew to ceiling fans, electric geysers (storage water heaters), colour TVs, washing machines, LED lamps, induction motors, pump sets and others. Labelling became mandatory (notified under the Act) for items such as tubular fluorescent lamps, room ACs, frost-free refrigerators, distribution transformers, and later ceiling fans, geysers, colour TVs and LED lamps. Other items remain voluntary. Elimination logic: all three items in the question have been on the BEE list, so any option that leaves one out is wrong. Options (a), (b) and (c) each omit one item, so only (d) is correct.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it leaves out tubular fluorescent lamps, which do carry the BEE Star Label.
(b) is wrong because it names only tubular fluorescent lamps and omits ceiling fans and geysers, which are also labelled.
(c) is wrong because it omits ceiling fans, which also carry the BEE Star Label.
(d) is correct because ceiling fans, electric geysers and tubular fluorescent lamps all fall under the BEE Standards & Labelling programme.
keyfact: BEE's Standards & Labelling programme (star ratings from 1 to 5) covers ceiling fans, electric geysers and tubular fluorescent lamps, so the answer is (d).
related: BEE was set up in March 2002 under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001 and works under the Ministry of Power.
The BEE star label rates appliances from 1 to 5 stars, and 5 stars means the most energy-efficient.
The PAT scheme falls under the National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (NMEEE), part of the NAPCC.
The Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC) was launched in 2007 for commercial buildings.
EESL implements the UJALA LED bulb scheme, launched in January 2015.
The S&L programme began in 2006 with refrigerators, tubular fluorescent lamps, room ACs and distribution transformers.
The Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022 introduced carbon credit trading and mandated renewable energy use for large consumers.
statements: 1 — Correct: Ceiling fans carry the BEE Star Label. Ceiling fans were brought under the S&L programme (voluntary from 2009, mandatory from 2010 and later). The label shows star ratings based on service value, i.e. air delivery per watt (m³/min per watt). Fans are a major household load in India, so efficiency gains matter. BLDC (brushless DC) fans can reach 5 stars and use roughly half the power of ordinary fans.

2 — Correct: Electric geysers (storage water heaters) carry the BEE Star Label. They were covered under the S&L programme from about 2009, with mandatory labelling later. Ratings depend on standing-loss (heat loss while the water is kept hot) and on the capacity of the storage tank. Star ratings help consumers choose models with better insulation and lower electricity use. Water heating is a significant share of household electricity use in cold regions and in winter.

3 — Correct: Tubular fluorescent lamps (TFL) were among the first four appliances labelled by BEE in 2006 and were made mandatory in 2009. Ratings are based on luminous efficacy (lumens per watt). Fluorescent tubes are more efficient than incandescent bulbs, though LEDs have since largely replaced them. Under the UJALA scheme (2015), LED bulbs were distributed and also carry BEE ratings.
summary: The correct answer is (d): ceiling fans, electric geysers and tubular fluorescent lamps all carry the BEE Star Label. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency's Standards & Labelling (S&L) programme covers all three, and the label is mandatory for some appliances and voluntary for others.
topic_notes: The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) was set up on 1 March 2002 under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001. It is a statutory body under the Ministry of Power and is headquartered in New Delhi. Its job is to reduce the energy intensity of the Indian economy through market-based approaches and regulation. The Act was amended in 2010 and 2022. The 2022 amendment introduced carbon markets and mandated renewable energy use by designated consumers. Main programmes: (1) Standards & Labelling (S&L), launched in 2006, with star ratings from 1 to 5. Labels are mandatory for some products and voluntary for others, and cover more than 25 appliances, including ACs, refrigerators, TVs, geysers, fans, LED lamps, washing machines, transformers, pump sets and motors. (2) Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT), launched in 2012 under the National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (NMEEE), one of the eight missions of the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC). PAT sets energy-saving targets for energy-intensive industries called Designated Consumers and issues tradable Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts). (3) Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC), launched in 2007 for commercial buildings, with ECBC 2017 and the residential code Eco Niwas Samhita. (4) UJALA (Unnat Jyoti by Affordable LEDs for All), launched in January 2015 and run by EESL, an energy-services company under the Ministry of Power, along with the Street Lighting National Programme (SLNP). (5) Demand-side management and agricultural pumping programmes. (6) The Energy Efficiency Financing Platform and the Partial Risk Guarantee Fund. Related UPSC angles include the star label colours, the ECBC and EESL, and India's NDC targets under the Paris Agreement.

question: India is an important member of the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor’. If this experiment succeeds, what is the immediate advantage for India?
options: It can use thorium in place of uranium for power generation
It can attain a global role in satellite navigation
It can drastically improve the efficiency of its fission reactors in power generation
It can build fusion reactors for power generation
subject: Science & Tech
detail: ITER (International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor) is a collaborative project to demonstrate that nuclear fusion can produce energy on a commercial scale. It is being built at Cadarache in southern France. It uses a tokamak, a doughnut-shaped magnetic confinement device, to hold deuterium-tritium plasma at about 150 million degrees Celsius. The aim is Q greater than or equal to 10, meaning fusion output of about 500 MW from about 50 MW of input heating power. The ITER Agreement was signed in 2006 and entered into force in 2007. The members are the EU (host), India, China, Japan, South Korea, Russia and the USA. India formally joined in 2005 and contributes mostly in kind, including the cryostat, in-wall shielding, cooling water systems and power supplies, with the Institute for Plasma Research (IPR), Gandhinagar, as the lead agency. Elimination: (a) thorium use relates to India's three-stage nuclear programme, which is fission-based, and has nothing to do with ITER. (b) Satellite navigation relates to ISRO's NavIC. (c) Fusion is a different process from fission and does not improve fission reactors. So only (d) follows directly from ITER's success.
explanations: Wrong. Using thorium in place of uranium is the aim of India's three-stage fission programme (the AHWR and fast breeder reactors). ITER is about fusion and does not enable this.
Wrong. Satellite navigation is ISRO's domain (IRNSS/NavIC) and has no connection with a fusion experiment.
Wrong. ITER does not improve fission reactors. Fusion joins light nuclei, while fission splits heavy nuclei, so they are separate technologies.

Correct. ITER's success would demonstrate the feasibility of fusion power. As a member sharing the technology and intellectual property, India could then build its own fusion reactors for power generation.
keyfact: ITER is a fusion (not fission) tokamak project at Cadarache, France, and its success would let India build fusion reactors for power.
option_notes: Thorium is a fertile material, and Th-232 converts to fissile U-233 in a reactor. India has about a quarter of the world's thorium reserves, mostly in monazite sands in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Odisha. Homi Bhabha's three-stage programme runs from PHWRs to fast breeder reactors to thorium-based reactors. The Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) is designed for thorium, and the PFBR at Kalpakkam is the second-stage reactor.

NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation), formerly IRNSS, is India's regional satellite navigation system run by ISRO. It has a constellation of seven satellites, in geostationary and inclined geosynchronous orbits. It covers India and about 1,500 km beyond its borders, and provides the Standard Positioning Service and a restricted service. Global systems include GPS (USA), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (EU) and BeiDou (China).

Fission reactors split heavy nuclei such as U-235 or Pu-239 and release heat, which is used to make steam. India's fleet includes PHWRs, BWRs at Tarapur, and VVER units at Kudankulam. Efficiency depends on fuel, moderator and coolant design. Fusion research does not feed into these designs. The Indo-US civil nuclear deal of 2008 and the NSG waiver gave India access to fuel and reactors.

Fusion combines light nuclei such as deuterium and tritium into helium and releases neutrons and energy. It is the process that powers the Sun. Its advantages are abundant fuel, no chain reaction, little long-lived waste and no carbon emissions. ITER is a tokamak experiment. A follow-on demonstration reactor, DEMO, would be the step towards commercial power.
related: ITER is located at Cadarache, southern France.
ITER uses a tokamak, which confines plasma with magnetic fields.
ITER members: EU, India, China, Japan, South Korea, Russia and the USA.
India's lead agency for ITER is the Institute for Plasma Research, Gandhinagar.
Fusion fuel is deuterium and tritium, and tritium is bred from lithium.
India's SST-1 is a steady-state superconducting tokamak.
Stage 3 of India's nuclear programme uses thorium and U-233.
PFBR at Kalpakkam is India's prototype fast breeder reactor.
summary: The answer is (d). ITER is an experimental nuclear fusion project, so if it succeeds, India, as a member, gains access to fusion technology and can build fusion reactors for power generation. It has no direct link to thorium use, satellite navigation or fission reactor efficiency.
topic_notes:
ITER is the world's largest fusion experiment, being built at Saint-Paul-lez-Durance (Cadarache), France. Its members are the EU (host, with the largest share), the USA, Russia, Japan, China, South Korea and India, covering over half the world's population. The ITER Agreement was signed in November 2006 and ITER Organization was established in 2007. India joined in 2005. India's contribution is mainly in kind, through the Institute for Plasma Research (IPR) in Gandhinagar under the Department of Atomic Energy; the cryostat was made by L&T. The design is a tokamak, a magnetic confinement device with superconducting magnets, and the fuel is a deuterium-tritium plasma. Tritium is bred from lithium. The target is Q of 10 (500 MW from 50 MW input) and first plasma has been delayed, with research operations now planned for the 2030s.

Fusion versus fission: fusion joins light nuclei, needs extremely high temperatures, has no runaway chain reaction and produces little long-lived waste. Fission splits heavy nuclei. Indian fusion work includes the SST-1 tokamak at IPR and the earlier Aditya tokamak. India's nuclear energy base is the three-stage programme conceived by Homi Bhabha, using natural uranium PHWRs in stage 1, plutonium fast breeder reactors in stage 2 (PFBR at Kalpakkam) and thorium-U233 reactors in stage 3. Other ideas that UPSC may ask about: the Atomic Energy Act 1962, the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act 2010 and the NSG membership issue. Related facility: the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, in which India is an associate member.

ocr: In the context of the history of India, - consider the following pairs : Term Description. 1. Eripatti : Land, revenue from which was set apart for the main- tenance of the village tank 2. Taniyurs ; Villages donated to a single Brahmin or a group of Brahmins 3. Ghatikas : Colleges generally attached to the temples Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched? : fa} 1 and 2 (b} 3 only (c) 2 and 3 (d) 1 and 3
subject: Art & Culture
detail: This question tests the vocabulary of South Indian (Pallava-Chola) agrarian and local administration, which UPSC often asks about. Irrigation was central to the agrarian economy of Tamil country. Eripatti was land assigned, or its revenue earmarked, for maintaining the eri (village tank). Villages were classified by the dominant group or tenure. Ur was a non-Brahmin peasant settlement, Sabha or Mahasabha was the assembly of a Brahmadeya or Agrahara village, and Nagaram was a merchant settlement. Brahmadeya or Agrahara villages were donated to Brahmins, either a single Brahmin or a group. Taniyur was a big village or group of villages that stood alone as a separate administrative unit, often with a dominant community, and it is not the same as a Brahmadeya. Ghatikas were centres of higher learning attached to temples in early medieval South India. The Kanchi Ghatika under the Pallavas is the best-known example. Elimination logic: if you know that Ghatikas are temple colleges, pair 3 is correct, which leaves (b), (c) or (d). Knowing that Eripatti is correct gives (a) or (d). Together these point to (d).
explanations: Wrong: pair 1 is correct, but this option adds pair 2, which is incorrect because Taniyurs were not villages donated to Brahmins.
Wrong: pair 3 is correct, but pair 1 is also correct, so '3 only' is incomplete.
Wrong: pair 2 is incorrect (Taniyurs were not Brahmin donated villages), so including it makes the option wrong.
Correct: Eripatti (land for tank maintenance) and Ghatikas (temple colleges) are rightly matched. Pair 2 is the only incorrect one.
keyfact: Eripatti = land for tank upkeep; Ghatikas = temple colleges; Taniyur = a separate large village, not a Brahmin gift (that is Brahmadeya), so the answer is 1 and 3.
option_notes: Pairs 1 and 2: this combination pairs Eripatti with Taniyurs as Brahmin-donated villages. Eripatti was land assigned for tank maintenance in Chola-era Tamil Nadu, while Brahmin-donated villages were called Brahmadeya or Agrahara, and were run by a Sabha. Taniyur was a separate large village or group of villages treated as an independent unit.

3 only: Ghatikas were temple-attached colleges in early medieval South India. The Kanchi Ghatika under the Pallavas was the best known. They taught Vedic learning, grammar and philosophy with royal grants. Other terms to know are Salai (a Chola-period school) and Matha (a monastic centre). The option is incomplete because pair 1 is also correct.

Pairs 2 and 3: this combines the incorrect pair 2 (Taniyurs) with the correct pair 3 (Ghatikas). A Brahmadeya was a gift village for Brahmins, managed by a Sabha, with Uttaramerur as the best-known example. Taniyurs were independent large villages. Ghatikas were temple colleges, as at Kanchi.

Pairs 1 and 3: this is the correct option. Eripatti was land or revenue assigned for tank maintenance, important for Chola irrigation. Ghatikas were temple colleges, with Kanchi the famous example. Both belong to the Pallava-Chola south Indian system of agrarian and educational institutions.
related: Eripatti: land or its revenue assigned for maintaining the village tank (eri) in Tamil country.
