Pigeonpea was the first food legume with a draft genome sequenced, in 2011 by an ICRISAT-led consortium.
Improved Samba Mahsuri is a bacterial blight-resistant rice developed using marker-assisted selection.
CRISPR-Cas9 is a genome-editing tool; India exempted SDN-1 and SDN-2 edited plants from GM rules in 2022.
The National Gene Bank is at NBPGR, New Delhi.
GenomeIndia project aims to sequence 10,000 Indian human genomes.
The International Rice Genome Sequencing Project completed the rice genome in 2005.
statements: 1 — Correct: sequencing allows identification of genes, QTLs and SNP markers linked to traits like disease resistance and drought tolerance. Breeders use these for selection. Examples include the Sub1 submergence-tolerance gene in rice (Swarna-Sub1), the Xa21 bacterial blight resistance gene, and the drought-tolerance QTL work in chickpea and pigeonpea at ICRISAT. India's National Agricultural Science Fund and NIPGR, Delhi, support such crop genomics, and the pigeonpea genome was completed in 2011.

2 — Correct: markers let breeders select the right plants at seedling stage without waiting for field phenotyping. This cuts breeding time from roughly a decade to perhaps half that. Related techniques are marker-assisted backcrossing, genomic selection, speed breeding and doubled haploids. Improved Samba Mahsuri, a bacterial blight-resistant rice variety developed by CCMB, ICAR-IIRR and others, is an Indian example of MAS being used to develop a variety.

3 — Correct: sequencing host and pathogen genomes shows how pathogens infect and how plants defend themselves. It identifies effector proteins, R genes and the evolution of virulence. Examples include rice blast, wheat rust, potato late blight (Phytophthora infestans) and banana Fusarium wilt. Transcriptomics and metagenomics are combined with it. The knowledge helps in designing durable resistance, gene pyramiding, surveillance of new strains and targeted biocontrol or CRISPR-based editing.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. Genome sequencing finds genetic markers for traits such as disease resistance and drought tolerance, speeds up breeding through marker-assisted selection, and helps decode how crops and pathogens interact.
topic_notes: Genome sequencing reads the complete nucleotide sequence of an organism's DNA. The Human Genome Project (1990-2003) was the landmark effort, and the first plant genome, Arabidopsis thaliana, was completed in 2000. Rice followed in 2002-2005 through the International Rice Genome Sequencing Project. In India, key sequenced crops include pigeonpea (2011, ICRISAT with ICAR), chickpea (2013), tomato, mango, jute, sesame and wheat varieties. Sequencing supports several applications. Marker-assisted selection uses DNA markers such as SSRs and SNPs linked to traits. QTL mapping locates regions controlling quantitative traits such as yield and drought tolerance. Genomic selection predicts breeding value from genome-wide markers. Gene pyramiding combines several resistance genes in one variety. Sequencing also helps with germplasm characterisation, authentication of varieties, and tracking pathogen strains. Related technologies are transgenics (Bt cotton is the only GM crop approved for cultivation in India, 2002), genome editing with CRISPR-Cas9, and speed breeding. India's institutions include ICAR, NBPGR, NIPGR, NRCPB, ICRISAT and CCMB. India released two genome-edited rice varieties in 2025, and SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome-edited plants were exempted from certain GM regulations in 2022. GM crop regulation is by the GEAC under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. Other angles UPSC may ask include the Indian Genome Variation Consortium, the GenomeIndia project (10,000 human genomes) and the Earth BioGenome Project. Also covered are DNA barcoding, biofortified varieties and gene banks (the National Gene Bank at NBPGR, Delhi, and Svalbard Global Seed Vault).

question: The main advantage of the parliamentary form of government is that
options: the executive and legislature work independently
it provides continuity of policy and is more efficient
the executive remains responsible to the legislature
the head of the government cannot be changed without election
subject: Polity
detail: In a parliamentary system, as adopted in India under Articles 74-75 and 163-164, the real executive is the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister, drawn from the legislature. Article 75(3) states that the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. This is the central feature and chief advantage: the government survives only while it commands majority support, and it is held to account through question hour, motions, debates, committees, adjournment motions, and the no-confidence motion. There is no rigid separation of powers; the executive and legislature work in close coordination, which is why (a) describes the presidential system (USA). Option (b) is a claimed benefit of presidential systems with fixed terms, and parliamentary governments can fall mid-term, causing instability (e.g., 1979, 1990, 1997-99). Option (d) is wrong because the PM can be changed without election through loss of majority, resignation, or party decision. Elimination: (a) and (d) are factually wrong, (b) is doubtful, and (c) is the textbook answer. Bagehot and Ivor Jennings described this responsibility as its essence.
explanations: Wrong: independent working of executive and legislature is the hallmark of the presidential system with separation of powers, as in the USA. Parliamentary government is built on fusion and coordination.

Wrong: continuity of policy and efficiency are generally claimed for presidential systems with fixed tenure. Parliamentary governments can fall on losing a majority, so stability is not guaranteed and it is not the main advantage.

Correct: Article 75(3) makes the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. This accountability to the legislature is the defining and principal advantage of the parliamentary system.

Wrong: the head of government can be changed without a general election, by a no-confidence vote, loss of majority, resignation, or the ruling party replacing its leader (e.g., Britain, where PMs changed mid-term).
keyfact: The parliamentary system's key advantage is responsibility of the executive to the legislature (Article 75(3)).
option_notes: Independence of executive and legislature: this is the separation-of-powers feature of the presidential system, found in the USA, where the President and Congress are elected separately and the President cannot be removed by a no-confidence vote. India has partial separation only, with the executive drawn from and answerable to Parliament, while the judiciary is independent.

Continuity of policy and efficiency: usually attributed to presidential systems with fixed terms (the US President serves four years). In parliamentary systems, governments can fall, as did the VP Singh, Chandra Shekhar, Deve Gowda and Gujral governments and the 1999 Vajpayee government, leading to instability. Parliamentary systems may still provide continuity under stable majorities.

Executive responsibility to the legislature: the core of the Westminster model, adopted in India. Collective responsibility under Article 75(3) means the whole ministry sinks or swims together. Individual responsibility operates at the President's pleasure. Tools include the no-confidence motion (Rule 198, Lok Sabha), censure motion, cut motions, and the defeat of money bills, which is treated as a loss of confidence.

Head of government not changeable without election: this describes the fixed-tenure presidential model, where the President is removed only by impeachment or at the end of the term. In India the PM holds office as long as the Lok Sabha majority supports them and can change by resignation, defeat, or death, as with Lal Bahadur Shastri's succession in 1966, without a general election.
related: Article 75(3): Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
Article 74 provides for a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President.
91st Amendment (2003) limits ministers to 15% of the House strength.
The Westminster model of parliamentary government comes from Britain.
The USA has a presidential system with strict separation of powers.
Ambedkar preferred responsibility over stability in choosing the parliamentary system.
A no-confidence motion can be moved only in the Lok Sabha, not in the Rajya Sabha.
The 44th Amendment allows the President to return ministerial advice once for reconsideration.
summary: The answer is (c). The defining advantage of the parliamentary system is that the executive (Council of Ministers) stays collectively responsible to the legislature, specifically the Lok Sabha, and must resign if it loses the House's confidence. This makes the government accountable and answerable on a continuous basis.
topic_notes: Parliamentary government originated in Britain (the Westminster model) and India adopted it in the Constitution for both Centre (Articles 74-75) and States (Articles 163-164). Its features: nominal head of state (President or Governor) and real executive (Council of Ministers); collective responsibility to the lower house; the majority party forms the government; the PM is the leader; ministers are members of the legislature; dissolution of the lower house is possible; secrecy of proceedings; a double membership. Advantages: harmony between executive and legislature, responsible government, a prevention of authoritarianism, wide representation, and flexibility, as a leader can be changed in a crisis (Britain in 1940). Disadvantages: instability, no fixed tenure, a possible tendency toward cabinet dictatorship, and weak separation of powers. Presidential system: the USA, with a fixed tenure, separation of powers, checks and balances, and the executive not responsible to the legislature. Comparison with India: the Indian President is a nominal head, elected indirectly (Article 54), and the 42nd Amendment (1976) made ministerial advice binding, which the 44th Amendment (1978) modified to allow the President to ask the Council to reconsider once. Collective responsibility is in Article 75(3), and the 91st Amendment (2003) capped the Council of Ministers at 15% of the House's strength. Related: the Ambedkar view in the Constituent Assembly, that responsibility is preferred to stability, and the Dr. Ambedkar argument for daily assessment versus periodic assessment. Others: Semi-presidential systems (France), and Switzerland's collegiate executive.

question: In the context of India, which one of the following is the correct relationship between Rights and Duties ?
options: Rights are personal and _ hence independent of society and Duties
Rights, not Duties, are important for the advancement of the personality of the citizen
Duties, not Rights, are important for the stability of the State
subject: Economy
detail: The question tests political theory as reflected in the Indian Constitution. Rights and duties are two sides of one coin: my right to life or speech is someone else's duty not to violate it, and my enjoyment of rights depends on performing my duties to society. The original Constitution (1950) listed Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12-35) and Directive Principles (Part IV) but no Fundamental Duties. On the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee (1976), the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 added Part IVA with Article 51A, which originally listed 10 duties. The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 added the 11th duty (parents/guardians to provide education to children aged 6-14). Duties are non-justiciable, but courts use them to interpret laws and uphold their constitutionality. Elimination: (b) is wrong because rights exist within society and are limited by reasonable restrictions. (c) and (d) are wrong because each is one-sided; both rights and duties are needed for personal development and for the stability of the State. Only (a) captures the balanced, interdependent relationship.
explanations: Correct. Rights and duties are correlative: one person's right entails duties on others and the State, and citizens must perform duties (Article 51A) to enjoy rights in an orderly society.

Incorrect. Rights are not independent of society; they arise in society and are subject to reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order, morality, health, sovereignty and integrity of India. They also imply duties of respecting others' rights.
Incorrect. Personality development needs both rights (freedoms, opportunities) and duties (discipline, responsibility toward others). Treating rights alone as important ignores the correlation.

Incorrect. State stability depends on both a guarantee of rights and the observance of duties by citizens. Emphasising duties alone would justify authoritarianism and is not the constitutional position.
keyfact: Rights and duties are correlative; Article 51A (Part IVA, 42nd Amendment, 1976) lists 11 non-justiciable Fundamental Duties for citizens.
option_notes: Correlative rights and duties: a concept from political theory (Laski, Green) that every right carries a corresponding obligation. In India, Part III gives Fundamental Rights and Part IVA (Article 51A) gives Fundamental Duties, added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation. Duties are non-justiciable but morally and interpretatively significant. Duties are also drawn from the USSR Constitution's influence. They apply to citizens only.

The view that rights are purely personal and independent of society is the extreme natural-rights or individualist position. Indian Fundamental Rights are not absolute; Articles 19(2)-(6) allow reasonable restrictions, and Article 21 can be limited by procedure established by law. Rights such as Article 17 (untouchability) and Article 23 also bind private persons, showing a social dimension.

This is a one-sided, rights-only view. Rights do help develop personality (Article 21 includes dignity; Article 19 freedoms; Articles 29-30 culture and education), but Article 51A duties such as developing scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry also shape citizens. Hence the claim that duties are unimportant is false.

This is a duties-only, authoritarian view. A stable State, in India's constitutional democracy, rests on rule of law, justice, liberty, equality and fraternity (Preamble) as well as on civic duties. Emergency-era (1976) emphasis on duties was criticised for this reason. Rights and duties must be balanced.
related: Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA, Article 51A.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Fundamental Duties on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation.
The 86th Amendment (2002) added the 11th duty on education for children aged 6-14.
Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable and apply only to citizens.
The Fundamental Duties were inspired by the USSR Constitution.
The right to property was removed from Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment (1978); it is now Article 300A.
Article 32 is the right to constitutional remedies, called the heart and soul of the Constitution by Ambedkar.
Originally there were 10 Fundamental Duties; there are now 11.
summary: The correct answer is (a): Rights are correlative with Duties. In the Indian constitutional scheme a right enjoyed by one person implies a duty on others (and the State) to respect it, and citizens also owe duties to the nation, so the two go together.
topic_notes: Rights and duties in India. Fundamental Rights: Part III, Articles 12-35; originally seven, now six after the 44th Amendment (1978) removed the right to property (Article 31) from the list and made it a legal right under Article 300A. The six are Equality (14-18), Freedom (19-22), Exploitation (23-24), Religion (25-28), Cultural and Educational (29-30), and Constitutional Remedies (32). Dr Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. Fundamental Duties: Part IVA, Article 51A, added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 (the 'mini-Constitution') on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation; the Committee proposed 8 duties, 10 were added, and the 86th Amendment (2002) added the 11th. Duties include respecting the Constitution, the National Flag and Anthem, cherishing the ideals of the freedom struggle, upholding sovereignty and integrity, defending the country, promoting harmony and brotherhood, renouncing practices derogatory to women, preserving composite culture, protecting the natural environment, developing scientific temper, safeguarding public property, striving for excellence, and providing education to a child aged 6-14. Duties apply to citizens only, are non-justiciable, and carry no legal sanction, though laws such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 give effect to some. The Verma Committee (1999) identified enforcement methods. In Ranganath Mishra and AIIMS Students Union cases the Supreme Court discussed duties alongside rights. Directive Principles (Part IV, Articles 36-51) are non-justiciable guidelines for the State. Other angles: Gandhi's view that the right to live is earned by performing duties; the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948); the Japan, USSR and other constitutions with duties; Article 13 on laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights; and the Kesavananda Bharati (1973) basic structure doctrine.

question: The mind of the makers of the Constitution of India is reflected in which of the following ?
options: The Directive Principles of State Policy
subject: Polity
detail: The Preamble to the Constitution of India is based on the Objectives Resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 January 1947. The Preamble was adopted along with the Constitution on 26 November 1949. It declares India a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic, and secures Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), Equality (status, opportunity) and Fraternity (dignity of the individual, unity and integrity of the nation). The words Socialist, Secular and Integrity were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976. In Berubari Union case (1960) the Supreme Court held the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution; in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) it overruled this and held it is a part, though neither a source of power nor a limitation on power. Ernest Barker called it the 'key-note' of the Constitution. Elimination: Fundamental Rights, DPSPs and Fundamental Duties are specific operative parts dealing with individual rights, state policy and citizen obligations; each reflects only a portion of the framers' vision, while the Preamble sums up the whole.
explanations: Correct: the Preamble encapsulates the philosophy, ideals and aims of the framers, drawn from the Objectives Resolution, and is regarded as the expression of their mind.
Wrong: Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12-35) are justiciable guarantees to individuals against the State; they reflect one aspect, not the overall vision.
Wrong: DPSPs (Part IV, Articles 36-51) are non-justiciable guidelines for governance, reflecting the social and economic goals only in part.
Wrong: Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Article 51A) were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976 on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation, so they cannot reflect the original framers' mind.
keyfact: The Preamble, rooted in Nehru's Objectives Resolution, reflects the mind and ideals of the Constitution's makers.
option_notes: The Preamble is the introductory text of the Constitution, derived from Nehru's Objectives Resolution (1946). It states the source of authority ('We, the people of India'), nature of the State (Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic) and objectives (Justice, Liberty, Equality, Fraternity). Adopted on 26 November 1949, amended only once, in 1976 by the 42nd Amendment. It is part of the basic structure per Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and the LIC case (1995).

Fundamental Rights are in Part III (Articles 12-35), borrowed in idea from the US Bill of Rights. They include equality (14-18), freedom (19-22), against exploitation (23-24), religion (25-28), cultural and educational rights (29-30) and constitutional remedies (32). Right to property was removed by the 44th Amendment in 1978 and made Article 300A. Dr Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.

Directive Principles are in Part IV (Articles 36-51), inspired by the Irish Constitution. They are non-justiciable (Article 37) but fundamental in governance. They cover a welfare state, uniform civil code (44), village panchayats (40), and separation of judiciary from executive (50). Granville Austin called FRs and DPSPs the 'conscience of the Constitution'. Minerva Mills (1980) stressed their harmony with FRs.

Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA, Article 51A, added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation, with 10 duties originally. The 86th Amendment (2002) added the 11th duty, on education of children aged 6-14. The idea is borrowed from the USSR Constitution. They are non-justiciable and apply to citizens only.
related: Preamble is based on Nehru's Objectives Resolution of 1946.
Berubari case (1960): Preamble not part of Constitution; overruled in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
42nd Amendment (1976) added Socialist, Secular and Integrity to the Preamble.
Preamble has been amended only once so far.
Preamble is non-justiciable and is neither a source of power nor a limitation.
K. M. Munshi called the Preamble the 'horoscope' of the Constitution.
The Preamble idea was borrowed from the USA; justice ideal from the Russian Revolution.
Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment on Swaran Singh Committee advice.
summary: The answer is (a) The Preamble. It is the introductory statement that embodies the philosophy, objectives and ideals of the framers, so it is said to reflect their mind and the 'key to open the mind of the makers'.
topic_notes: The Preamble is the Constitution's introduction and the most direct statement of the framers' intent. Its text originates in the Objectives Resolution of Nehru (moved 13 Dec 1946, adopted 22 Jan 1947). The Drafting Committee, chaired by B. R. Ambedkar, finalised the text, and the Constituent Assembly (President Rajendra Prasad) adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949; it came into force on 26 January 1950. Key components: source of authority is the people of India; nature is a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic; objectives are justice, liberty, equality and fraternity; the date of adoption is 26 Nov 1949. Judicial journey: In re Berubari Union (1960) held it is not part of the Constitution; Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) held it is a part and can be amended without altering the basic structure; LIC of India v. Consumer Education and Research Centre (1995) reaffirmed it is an integral part. S. R. Bommai (1994) linked secularism to the basic structure. The Preamble is neither enforceable in court nor a source of legislative power, nor does it limit powers, but it helps interpret ambiguous provisions. Amendment: 42nd Amendment Act 1976 added 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity'. K. M. Munshi called it the 'horoscope' of the Constitution; Ernest Barker called it the 'key-note'; N. A. Palkhivala called it the 'identity card' of the Constitution. The American Constitution was the first to begin with a Preamble; India's Preamble follows its style, while ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity come from the French Revolution, and justice from the Russian Revolution.

question: If you travel by road from Kohima to Kottayam, what is the minimum number of States within India through which you can travel, including the origin and_ the destination ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a map-based question that tests how well a student knows the road geography of India. Kohima is the capital of Nagaland, and Kottayam is in central Kerala. From Kohima one goes down to Dimapur and enters Assam. The route then crosses the narrow Siliguri corridor in West Bengal, which links the North-East to the rest of India. Bihar is not needed, because the road runs south-west through West Bengal along the NH 16 (Golden Quadrilateral east coast stretch, formerly NH 5/NH 6 in part) towards Kolkata and Kharagpur. The route then continues through Odisha (Balasore, Bhubaneswar) and along the coast of Andhra Pradesh (Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada). It enters Tamil Nadu near Chennai and goes on to Coimbatore or Madurai, and from there into Kerala. The States are Nagaland, Assam, West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Kerala, so the count is 7. Options (a) 6 is too few, because no route skips any of these States. Options (c) 8 and (d) 9 count extra States (such as Bihar, Jharkhand, Karnataka or Telangana) that a shorter route avoids. The word 'minimum' is the key to the elimination logic.
explanations: Incorrect: 6 States is not possible, because the road must cross seven States, from Nagaland to Kerala, and none of them can be bypassed.
Correct: the minimum route is Nagaland, Assam, West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Kerala, which is 7 States.
Incorrect: 8 would be the count if an extra State such as Bihar or Karnataka were included, but the question asks for the minimum.
Incorrect: 9 States would be a longer, roundabout route and not the minimum.
keyfact: Kohima to Kottayam by road: Nagaland, Assam, West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Kerala = 7 States.
option_notes: 6 States: this is a distractor that is too low. The seven States on the route are Nagaland, Assam, West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Kerala. Leaving out any one of them would break the connection between the North-East and the south, so six is not achievable by road.

7 States: this is the correct count. The route goes from Kohima through Dimapur to Assam, then across the Siliguri corridor in West Bengal, down the east coast through Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, then Tamil Nadu and finally Kerala. The Siliguri (Chicken's Neck) corridor is only about 20-22 km wide at its narrowest.

8 States: this would apply to a longer route that adds a State such as Bihar or Karnataka. For example, a route through Bihar or Jharkhand instead of going directly through West Bengal and Odisha adds States. Since the question asks for the minimum, this option is wrong.
9 States: this would apply to a much longer, roundabout route, such as one through Bihar, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Telangana and Karnataka. It is not the minimum, so it is wrong.
related: Siliguri corridor (Chicken's Neck) is about 20-22 km wide at its narrowest.
The Tropic of Cancer passes through 8 Indian States.
Kohima is the capital of Nagaland; Dimapur is its main railhead.
NH 16 is the east coast highway linking Kolkata and Chennai, part of the Golden Quadrilateral.
The North-South corridor of NHDP links Srinagar to Kanyakumari.
The East-West corridor links Silchar (Assam) to Porbandar (Gujarat).
Kottayam in Kerala is a major rubber-growing and trading centre.
summary: The answer is (b) 7. The shortest road route from Kohima (Nagaland) to Kottayam (Kerala) passes through Nagaland, Assam, West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Kerala, which makes 7 States including the origin and destination.
topic_notes: This question belongs to the 'Indian geography: location and connectivity' theme, which UPSC tests with map-based questions. The key idea is to picture the map and find the shortest continuous land route. The North-East is connected to the rest of India only through the Siliguri corridor (Chicken's Neck) in West Bengal, which is bordered by Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh. Every road journey from the North-East to the mainland therefore passes through Assam and West Bengal. The east coast highway (NH 16, part of the Golden Quadrilateral) runs from Kolkata through Odisha and Andhra Pradesh to Chennai. The Golden Quadrilateral connects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata and was built under NHDP. The North-South-East-West Corridor connects Srinagar to Kanyakumari and Silchar to Porbandar. Kohima is the capital of Nagaland, near Dimapur, the State's railhead and airport. Kottayam is in Kerala and is known for rubber, backwaters and 100% literacy as a district. Similar UPSC-style questions ask about the number of States touched by a river, a highway or a latitude. For example, the Tropic of Cancer passes through 8 States: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram. Other angles include States sharing borders with the most neighbours (Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra border 8 each, counting differently) and States bordering international countries. Always draw a rough map and list States in order.

question:
The Parliament of India exercises control over the functions of the Council of Ministers through qi Adjournment motion
2. Question hour
3. Supplementary questions Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Polity
detail: India has a parliamentary system in which the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)). Parliament enforces this through many devices: questions (starred, unstarred, short notice, and supplementaries), Zero Hour, half-an-hour discussion, calling attention notice, adjournment motion, no-confidence motion (Rule 198), censure motion, cut motions, discussion on the Budget, and the Committees such as PAC, Estimates and Committee on Public Undertakings. Question Hour is the first hour of a sitting, and it is the main tool for day-to-day scrutiny. A supplementary question follows an oral (starred) answer, and the Speaker permits it so that members can probe the minister's reply further. It is a spontaneous check on ministers. An adjournment motion interrupts the normal business of the House to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance. It needs the support of 50 members, and it implies censure of the government. It is available only in the Lok Sabha. Since all three are recognised control devices, the elimination is simple: (a), (b) and (c) each omit one valid device, so only (d) is correct.
explanations: (a) is wrong because the adjournment motion is valid, but Question Hour and supplementary questions are also control devices, so '1 only' is incomplete.
(b) is wrong because Question Hour and supplementaries are valid but it omits the adjournment motion, which also censures the government on an urgent matter.
(c) is wrong because it leaves out Question Hour, which is the principal daily device for scrutinising the executive.
(d) is correct because adjournment motion, Question Hour and supplementary questions all hold the Council of Ministers accountable to Parliament.
keyfact: Adjournment motion, Question Hour and supplementary questions are all devices of parliamentary control over the executive under Article 75(3); the adjournment motion is Lok Sabha-only and needs 50 members.
option_notes: Option (a) '1 only' refers to the adjournment motion alone. The adjournment motion is a Lok Sabha-only device to discuss an urgent matter of public importance. It needs 50 members' support and the Speaker's consent, and it involves an element of censure. It must be a specific matter, it cannot be about a matter that is sub judice, and it interrupts the House's normal business. It is rarely admitted, but it is a significant control device.

Option (b) '2 and 3 only' refers to Question Hour and supplementary questions. Question Hour is the first hour of a sitting, in which members ask ministers questions. Supplementaries follow oral replies to starred questions, with the Speaker's permission. Together they are the daily means of scrutinising administration. They are governed by the Rules of Procedure and are not mentioned in the Constitution. They provide spontaneous accountability, and the questions are put to individual ministers.

Option (c) '1 and 3 only' pairs the adjournment motion with supplementary questions. The adjournment motion is an urgent-matter device of the Lok Sabha, needing 50 members' support. Supplementary questions follow starred (oral) questions and are allowed by the Speaker. Starred questions are answered orally, while unstarred questions get written answers. It omits Question Hour, the hour at which these questions are taken, which is why it is incomplete.

Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' is the correct answer: adjournment motion, Question Hour and supplementary questions. These are all legislative devices to keep the Council of Ministers accountable under Article 75(3). Parliament also uses no-confidence motions, censure motions, cut motions, calling attention notices, Zero Hour, half-an-hour discussions and committees like the PAC. Together they ensure collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha.
related: Article 75(3): the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
Adjournment motion is available only in the Lok Sabha, and needs 50 members' support.
No-confidence motion is moved under Rule 198 of the Lok Sabha rules, and needs 50 members' support.
Zero Hour is an Indian innovation, from 1962, with no basis in the Rules of Procedure.
The Public Accounts Committee has 22 members: 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha.
The Estimates Committee has 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha.
Department-related standing committees were set up in 1993.
Starred questions are answered orally and allow supplementaries; unstarred questions get written replies.
statements: 1 — Correct: The adjournment motion is a device for censuring the government on an urgent matter. Introduced in the Lok Sabha, it needs the support of 50 members. It sets aside the regular business of the House to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance, and it is not available in the Rajya Sabha. The matter must be specific, factual and urgent, and it cannot be a privilege issue or a matter that is sub judice. The discussion lasts at least 2 hours 30 minutes. The Speaker admits it, and it is an extraordinary device. It rarely succeeds, but it draws attention to government lapses.

2 — Correct: Question Hour is the first hour of every sitting, usually 11 am to 12 noon. It is a parliamentary procedure for asking ministers questions on administration. Questions are starred (oral answer, supplementaries allowed), unstarred (written answer), short notice (10 days' notice not required) and for the Rajya Sabha also to private members. The Presiding Officer decides admissibility. It is mentioned in the Rules of Procedure, not the Constitution. Ministers are held accountable through it, and it is a key means of executive accountability. It can be suspended, as it was in 2020 during COVID-19.

3 — Correct: A supplementary question is asked by a member after the original starred question has been answered orally. Only starred questions, which need an oral answer, allow supplementaries, and the Speaker has discretion to allow them. They let members probe the minister's reply and expose weaknesses in policy. A starred question is marked with an asterisk and a minister answers it orally; unstarred questions get written replies and no supplementaries. A member can give notice of a question at least 15 clear days in advance. Supplementaries are spontaneous, which is why they are an effective check on ministers.
summary: The answer is (d): all three devices, the adjournment motion, Question Hour and supplementary questions, are tools by which Parliament controls the Council of Ministers. They enforce the executive's accountability to the Lok Sabha under Article 75(3) (collective responsibility).
topic_notes: Parliamentary control over the executive is the essence of the Westminster model that India adopted. Article 75(3) states that the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. Ministers hold office during the President's pleasure but in practice as long as they have Lok Sabha confidence. Control works before, during and after policy action. Devices include: (1) Questions: starred (oral, with supplementaries), unstarred (written), short notice (less than 10 days' notice), and questions to private members. Notice period is normally 15 clear days. (2) Zero Hour: an Indian innovation, from 1962, without a basis in the Rules; it starts around noon. (3) Half-an-hour discussion: on a matter of sufficient public importance that was answered in a question, held usually on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays. (4) Short duration discussion (Rule 193). (5) Calling attention motion: borrowed from Indian procedure, introduced in 1954; draws a minister's attention to an urgent matter. (6) Adjournment motion: Lok Sabha only, 50 members. (7) No-confidence motion: Lok Sabha only, 50 members' support under Rule 198; no ground need be stated. (8) Censure motion: must state the reasons, and can be against an individual minister or the whole council. (9) Motion of thanks on the President's address. (10) Budget discussions and cut motions: policy cut, economy cut, token cut. (11) Financial committees: the PAC (22 members; 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha) examines CAG reports, the Estimates Committee (30 members, all from Lok Sabha), and the COPU. (12) Department-related standing committees, set up in 1993. The Rajya Sabha cannot remove the government but can scrutinise it through questions and discussions. A government that loses a vote on a money bill or a confidence motion must resign.

question: Which one of the following was a very 54. important seaport in the Kakatiya kingdom ?
subject: Economy
detail: The Kakatiyas of Warangal (c. 1000-1323 CE) controlled the Telugu country and, under Ganapatideva (r. 1199-1262), extended their rule to the coast of the Krishna-Godavari delta. This gave them access to ports, of which Motupalli (Mottupalli, in present Prakasam/Bapatla district) was the most important. Marco Polo, who visited around 1289-93 during Rudramadevi's reign, described 'Mutfili' as a kingdom/port, noting the diamond trade of the region and the queen's good governance. The Motupalli inscription of 1244/1245 CE records the abhaya sasanam of Ganapatideva, assuring foreign merchants protection from plunder and reduced duties on exports and imports. Exports included fine cotton textiles, diamonds, spices, and imports included horses and luxury goods. Elimination: Kakinada and Machilipatnam rose to importance later; Machilipatnam especially under the Qutb Shahis and European companies (Dutch, English, French) in the 17th century. Nelluru (Nellore) was an important Telugu Chola/Chola-Kakatiya-era town but not the key Kakatiya seaport. Hence (b).
explanations: Kakinada developed as a port mainly in the colonial period (Coringa and Kakinada under the British and the Dutch/French), not as a key Kakatiya port, so it is wrong.
Motupalli was the major Kakatiya seaport, known from Ganapatideva's 1244 abhaya sasanam and Marco Polo's account, so it is correct.
Machilipatnam became a major port under the Qutb Shahis and European trading companies in the 16th-17th centuries, later than the Kakatiyas, so it is wrong.
Nelluru (Nellore) was an important political centre of the Telugu Chodas and a regional town, not the Kakatiyas' principal port, so it is wrong.
keyfact: Motupalli was the Kakatiya seaport, linked to Ganapatideva's 1244 abhaya sasanam and Marco Polo's visit.
option_notes: Kakinada lies in the Godavari delta, East Godavari district, Andhra Pradesh. It was historically linked with Coringa and was used by the Dutch, French and British. Today it is a deep-water port and a hub for fertiliser and rice exports and offshore oil and gas activity in the KG basin. It is not associated with Kakatiya maritime trade.

Motupalli is a coastal village in Prakasam/Bapatla district, Andhra Pradesh, on the Bay of Bengal. It was the chief port of the Kakatiyas, famous for the 1244 CE abhaya sasanam of Ganapatideva safeguarding merchants. Marco Polo visited it around 1290 and described its diamonds and cotton cloth. It traded with Southeast Asia and Sri Lanka and declined later as other ports rose.

Machilipatnam (Masulipatnam) in Krishna district was a famous port of the Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda. The Dutch (1605) and English (1611) set up factories here. It was famed for painted and printed cotton textiles (Kalamkari) and was a major Coromandel trade centre. It was also contested by the French and British in the 18th century.

Nelluru (Nellore) lies on the Penna river in southern Andhra Pradesh. It was a seat of the Telugu Chodas, later under Kakatiya, Vijayanagara and Nawabs of Arcot. Tikkana, the Telugu poet who translated the Mahabharata, was from the Nellore court of Manumasiddhi. It was a regional capital and agricultural area, not the Kakatiyas' principal seaport.
related: Motupalli abhaya sasanam of Ganapatideva dates to 1244/45 CE.
Marco Polo visited the Kakatiya kingdom during Rudramadevi's reign (c. 1289-93).
Rudramadevi was among the few female rulers in medieval India.
Ramappa temple (Palampet) became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.
Prataparudra II was defeated by the Delhi Sultanate in 1323.
Kakatiya capital: Orugallu (Warangal); earlier Hanamkonda.
Nayankara system: Kakatiya military-land grant system adopted later by Vijayanagara.
Machilipatnam was a leading Qutb Shahi and European trading port.
summary: The answer is (b) Motupalli. It was the premier seaport of the Kakatiya kingdom on the Andhra coast (Guntur/Bapatla region), through which overseas trade of the Deccan flowed, and was made famous by Ganapatideva's abhaya sasanam (c. 1244 CE) guaranteeing safety to traders.
topic_notes: The Kakatiyas ruled from Orugallu (Warangal), first as feudatories of the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani, becoming independent under Prola II and Rudra. Key rulers: Prola II, Rudradeva (built Warangal fort and Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamkonda, 1163), Ganapatideva (1199-1262, the greatest, who brought the coastal Andhra under his rule and promoted trade and ports like Motupalli), and Rudramadevi (1262-1289, a female ruler, praised by Marco Polo). Prataparudra II (1289-1323) was defeated by Ulugh Khan (Muhammad bin Tughlaq) in 1323, ending the dynasty. Administration used the nayankara system, granting land to military chiefs (nayakas), which later influenced Vijayanagara. Irrigation was a hallmark: tank building such as Ramappa, Pakhal, Laknavaram and Ghanpur lakes. Architecture: the Ramappa (Rudreshwara) temple at Palampet, built by Recherla Rudra under Ganapatideva, was inscribed a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021; its floating bricks and sandbox foundation technology are noted. Thousand Pillar Temple, Warangal Fort with kirti toranas. Literature: Tikkana, Palkuriki Somanatha, Jayapa Senani's Nritta Ratnavali (on dance), and Gona Budda Reddy. Koh-i-Noor diamond is traditionally linked to Kollur mines in the Kakatiya domain, and later came to Delhi sultans. Other Deccan ports: Masulipatnam (Qutb Shahi), Pulicat, Nizampatnam, Kakinada, Vishakhapatnam. Contemporary dynasties: Yadavas of Devagiri, Hoysalas of Dwarasamudra, Pandyas of Madurai.

question:
With reference to ‘Global Climate Change Alliance’, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. Itis an initiative of the European Union.
2. It provides technical and _ financial 55. support to targeted developing countries - to integrate climate change into their development policies and budgets.
3. It is coordinated by World Resources Institute (WRI) and World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD). Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Environment
detail: The Global Climate Change Alliance was launched by the European Commission in 2007 to strengthen dialogue and cooperation with developing countries most exposed to climate change, mainly Least Developed Countries (LDCs) and Small Island Developing States (SIDS). It works as a financing and technical-assistance vehicle. It supports countries in mainstreaming climate change into poverty reduction and development strategies, national budgets and planning, and in adaptation, disaster risk reduction, REDD+ (forest-based mitigation) and preparation for UNFCCC negotiations. Its successor is the GCCA+ (GCCA Plus), a flagship initiative under the EU's development cooperation. It is implemented through EU delegations and partner governments, with funding from the EU and some member states. The WRI and WBCSD are different bodies: they jointly developed the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, the corporate carbon-accounting standard. They have no role in coordinating GCCA. Elimination logic: once you know the GCCA is an EU initiative, statements 1 and 2 hold, so options (b), (c) and (d), which all include statement 3, can be discarded. Only (a) remains.
explanations: Correct. Statements 1 and 2 are both true, and statement 3 is false, so '1 and 2 only' is right.
Incorrect. Statement 3 is false, because WRI and WBCSD do not coordinate GCCA. Statements 1 and 2 are true, so '3 only' is also wrong.
Incorrect. It includes statement 3, which is false, and it leaves out statement 1, which is true.
Incorrect. It includes the false statement 3, so not all three statements are correct.
keyfact: GCCA = EU initiative (2007) giving technical and financial support to LDCs and SIDS to mainstream climate change into development policies and budgets; WRI and WBCSD are linked to the GHG Protocol, not to GCCA.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 and 2 only: this is the correct combination. It recognises GCCA as an EU initiative (2007) that gives technical and financial support to vulnerable developing countries, especially LDCs and SIDS, to mainstream climate change into policies and budgets. It rejects the claim about WRI and WBCSD coordination, which has nothing to do with GCCA.

Option (b), 3 only: this would make the WRI/WBCSD claim the only true one. WRI is a global research NGO founded in 1982 and WBCSD is a CEO-led business body formed in 1995. They are best known for the Greenhouse Gas Protocol. They do not coordinate GCCA, so this option is wrong.

Option (c), 2 and 3 only: this accepts the support-for-mainstreaming description but also the false WRI/WBCSD claim, while rejecting the EU origin. GCCA clearly belongs to the EU, so the option fails on both counts. The WRI and WBCSD link is a distractor drawn from the Greenhouse Gas Protocol.

Option (d), 1, 2 and 3: this is the all-statements option and would be right only if WRI and WBCSD coordinated GCCA. They do not. UPSC often adds one plausible-sounding but false institutional link to a set of true statements, and this option is built on that trap.
related: GCCA was launched by the European Union in 2007 and its successor is GCCA+.
GCCA targets mainly Least Developed Countries and Small Island Developing States.
WRI and WBCSD developed the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, the corporate emissions accounting standard.
Green Climate Fund: set up in 2010 at COP16 Cancun, headquartered in Songdo, South Korea.
International Solar Alliance: launched by India and France in 2015 at COP21, headquarters in Gurugram.
Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) was launched by India in 2019.
Adaptation Fund was established under the Kyoto Protocol.
REDD+ means reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation, plus conservation and sustainable management of forests.
statements: 1 — Correct: GCCA was launched by the European Union (European Commission) in 2007. It was created to deepen climate dialogue and practical cooperation with developing countries, particularly LDCs and SIDS, which are most vulnerable but have contributed least to emissions. It has funded hundreds of projects across Africa, the Caribbean, the Pacific and Asia. In later years it became GCCA+, a flagship EU initiative with a broader scope that includes adaptation, mitigation and climate-related migration. It is managed by the EU's international partnerships directorate.

2 — Correct: GCCA gives both technical help and finance to targeted developing countries, mainly LDCs and SIDS, to integrate climate change into their development policies, strategies and budgets. Typical areas are adaptation, disaster risk reduction, sustainable land and forest management including REDD+, coastal protection, and capacity building for UNFCCC negotiations. Support is delivered through budget support, project grants and regional programmes. The idea of mainstreaming climate considerations into national planning is the key feature of the alliance.

3 — Incorrect: WRI (World Resources Institute) and WBCSD (World Business Council for Sustainable Development) do not coordinate GCCA. They are known for jointly creating the Greenhouse Gas Protocol (1998 onwards), the widely used standard for corporate greenhouse gas accounting. WRI is a US-based global research NGO founded in 1982, and WBCSD is a CEO-led business association based in Geneva, formed in 1995. GCCA is run by the European Commission with partner governments.
summary: The answer is (a): statements 1 and 2 are correct and statement 3 is wrong. The Global Climate Change Alliance (GCCA) is an European Union initiative that gives technical and financial support to vulnerable developing countries to integrate climate change into their development policies and budgets. It is not coordinated by WRI or WBCSD.
topic_notes: The Global Climate Change Alliance was set up by the European Commission in 2007 as a political and financial platform for climate cooperation with the developing countries most affected by climate change, namely LDCs and SIDS. Its purposes are to exchange views and experience, and to provide technical and financial support for adaptation and mitigation. It also supports integration of climate change into poverty reduction and development strategies and budgets, disaster risk reduction, and REDD+ activities. The successor programme, GCCA+, extends the scope and is a flagship initiative within the EU's international cooperation. The same paper also tested other climate-related bodies and mechanisms, so keep the following in mind. The Greenhouse Gas Protocol, developed by WRI and WBCSD, is the most widely used accounting standard for corporate and national emissions. subject: Ancient History
detail: Q58 tests physical geography of India, specifically how many States each major feature spans. The Himalayas stretch about 2,400 km from Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh in the west to Arunachal Pradesh in the east. They cover Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh and parts of West Bengal (Darjeeling), Assam hills and the north-eastern hill States (Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura, Meghalaya), so there are far more than five. The Western Ghats (Sahyadri) run for about 1,600 km along the west coast through six States: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Their six-State spread is a UNESCO World Heritage Site fact and is often asked. Pulicat Lake is the second largest brackish water lagoon in India after Chilika. It straddles Andhra Pradesh (Nellore/Tirupati district) and Tamil Nadu (Tiruvallur district) and is separated from the Bay of Bengal by the Sriharikota barrier island, which hosts the ISRO launch centre. Elimination logic: once you know the Himalayas exceed five States, options (a) and (d) are eliminated. Knowing the Western Ghats cover six States eliminates (c). Only (b) remains.
explanations: Wrong: it accepts statement 1, but the Himalayas cover far more than five States, and it excludes statement 3, which is correct.
Correct: only statement 3 is right. Pulicat Lake is shared by Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, while the Himalayas and Western Ghats span more than five States.
Wrong: statement 2 is incorrect because the Western Ghats cover six States, and it also leaves out the correct statement 3.
Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because the Himalayas are not limited to five States, though statement 3 is correct.
keyfact: Pulicat Lake is shared by Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu (2 States), the Western Ghats span six States, and the Himalayas span far more than five.
related: Chilika Lake (Odisha) is Asia's largest brackish water lagoon and a Ramsar site.
Western Ghats UNESCO World Heritage listing came in 2012 with 39 sites across four States.
Anai Mudi (2,695 m, Kerala) is the highest peak in peninsular India.
Vembanad is the longest lake in India and a Ramsar site in Kerala.
Loktak Lake in Manipur is the largest freshwater lake in the Northeast.
Kanchenjunga is the highest peak entirely in India.
Sriharikota separates Pulicat Lake from the Bay of Bengal.
Palghat Gap links Kerala and Tamil Nadu between the Nilgiris and Anamalai.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Himalayas are spread over many more than five States and Union Territories. They run through Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh and the hill areas of West Bengal and the north-eastern States. The Indian Himalayan Region, as defined by the IHR framework, covers 11 full States/UTs and two hill districts of Assam and West Bengal. The range is about 2,400 km long, includes the Greater Himalaya (Himadri), Lesser Himalaya (Himachal) and Shiwaliks, and the Purvanchal hills in the east.

2 — Incorrect: The Western Ghats are spread over six States, not five: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu. They are about 1,600 km long, begin near the Tapi river, and end near Kanyakumari. Anai Mudi (2,695 m) is the highest peak. Palghat Gap separates the Nilgiris from the Anamalai range. They are a biodiversity hotspot and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2012 (39 sites). The Gadgil and Kasturirangan committees dealt with their ecological protection.

3 — Correct: Pulicat Lake lies on the border of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, so it is spread over two States. It is India's second largest brackish water lagoon after Chilika and is separated from the Bay of Bengal by the Sriharikota island. The Pulicat Lake Bird Sanctuary protects it. It is known for flamingos and migratory birds. The Buckingham Canal and the Arani and Kalangi rivers feed it. Dutch Fort Geldria was located at Pulicat town.
summary: The answer is (b) 3 only. Pulicat Lake, a brackish lagoon, lies on the Andhra Pradesh–Tamil Nadu border, so it is spread over two States. Statements 1 and 2 understate the number of States.
topic_notes: Indian physiography and State-wise spread of features is a favourite UPSC area. The Himalayas are young fold mountains with three parallel ranges: Greater Himalaya (Himadri), Lesser Himalaya (Himachal) and Outer Himalaya (Shiwalik), plus the trans-Himalaya (Karakoram, Ladakh, Zaskar) to the north. Key peaks are Kanchenjunga (the highest in India), Nanda Devi, K2 (Godwin Austen, in PoK) and Namcha Barwa as the eastern anchor. The Himalayas also include the Purvanchal hills (Patkai, Naga, Manipur, Mizo). The Western Ghats are a block mountain-like escarpment and the source of the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. Their sections are the Sahyadri (north), Nilgiris, Anamalai, Cardamom and Palani hills. The Eastern Ghats are discontinuous and run through Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, with Mahendragiri as a notable peak. They meet the Western Ghats at the Nilgiris. Lagoons and wetlands: Chilika (Odisha, largest brackish lagoon in India and a Ramsar site), Pulicat (AP and TN), Vembanad (Kerala, the longest lake in India and a Ramsar site), Kolleru (AP, freshwater), Loktak (Manipur, the largest freshwater lake in the Northeast, with Keibul Lamjao floating national park), Sambhar (Rajasthan, the largest inland saline lake) and Wular (J&K). Other points of State sharing: the Sundarbans are shared by India and Bangladesh. The Thar desert spans Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab and Haryana. The Deccan Plateau covers many States. UPSC often asks which State has the most of something, such as coastline (Gujarat), borders (Uttar Pradesh with the most neighbouring States), or Ramsar sites (Tamil Nadu).

question: Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) is a standard criterion for
options: Computing oxygen levels. in forest ecosystems
Assessing oxygen levels in high altitude regions
subject: Environment
detail: Biological Oxygen Demand (also called Biochemical Oxygen Demand) is the amount of dissolved oxygen needed by aerobic microbes to break down organic matter in water over a set time, conventionally 5 days at 20°C (BOD5). The more biodegradable organic waste (sewage, food-processing effluent, paper-mill waste) present, the more oxygen microbes consume, and the higher the BOD. High BOD means low dissolved oxygen is left for fish and other aquatic life, leading to stress, fish kills and eutrophic or anoxic conditions. Clean rivers usually have BOD below about 2 mg/L, and the CPCB's 'Class A' drinking-water source (without conventional treatment but after disinfection) requires BOD of 2 mg/L or less; water with BOD above 5 mg/L is considered polluted, and raw sewage is often 150-300 mg/L. It is therefore a standard test for water pollution, used for sewage treatment plant performance and effluent standards. Elimination: (a) blood oxygen is measured by pulse oximetry or blood gas analysis; (b) forest ecosystems are not assessed by BOD; (d) altitude oxygen is a matter of partial pressure and atmospheric measurement. Only (c) fits, since BOD is a water-quality indicator.
explanations: Wrong: blood oxygen is measured by pulse oximetry (SpO2) or arterial blood gas tests, not BOD, which concerns water samples and microbial oxygen consumption.
Wrong: BOD is not used to compute oxygen levels in forests. Forest ecosystems are studied through productivity, biomass and carbon flux, while BOD applies to water.
Correct: BOD is a standard measure of organic pollution in water bodies and effluents, because it reflects the oxygen microbes need to decompose organic waste.
Wrong: oxygen at high altitude is a matter of lower atmospheric partial pressure, measured by atmospheric methods and unrelated to BOD.
keyfact: BOD = oxygen needed by aerobic microbes to decompose organic matter in water (5 days, 20°C); higher BOD means more polluted water.
option_notes: Blood oxygen levels are measured through pulse oximetry, which gives oxygen saturation (SpO2, normally 95-100%), and arterial blood gas analysis, which gives PaO2. Haemoglobin carries most oxygen as oxyhaemoglobin. Hypoxaemia is low blood oxygen. These are clinical measures of human physiology and have nothing to do with BOD, which is an environmental water-quality parameter.

Oxygen in forest ecosystems is linked to photosynthesis, respiration and net primary productivity. Forests are often called carbon sinks, and the claim that the Amazon is the 'lungs of the Earth' is a popular oversimplification. Forest health is assessed by biomass, canopy cover (such as in the India State of Forest Report), and carbon stock, not by BOD, a test applied to water.

Pollution assay in aquatic ecosystems is the correct use. BOD, along with Dissolved Oxygen (DO) and Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD), is a key water-quality indicator. BOD5 is measured over 5 days at 20°C. CPCB uses it for river classification and effluent standards. High BOD signals heavy organic load and oxygen depletion. Biological indicators such as algal blooms and coliform counts supplement it.

Oxygen at high altitude has the same percentage (about 21%) as at sea level, but the partial pressure falls with height, causing hypoxia and altitude sickness. Acclimatisation raises red blood cell count. Measurement involves barometric pressure and partial pressure of oxygen. BOD is irrelevant here, as it measures microbial oxygen demand in water.
related: BOD is measured conventionally over 5 days at 20°C (BOD5).
Higher BOD means more organic pollution and less dissolved oxygen.
COD is generally greater than or equal to BOD and is measured with a chemical oxidant such as potassium dichromate.
Eutrophication (nutrient enrichment) leads to algal blooms and raised BOD.
The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was passed in 1974; the CPCB was set up under it.
Coliform counts indicate faecal contamination of water.
Namami Gange was launched in 2014-15 to clean the Ganga.
summary: The answer is (c) Pollution assay in aquatic ecosystems. BOD measures the amount of dissolved oxygen that aerobic microorganisms consume to decompose organic matter in a water sample, so it indicates how much biodegradable organic pollution the water carries.
topic_notes: Water-quality indicators are a frequent UPSC theme. Dissolved Oxygen (DO) is the oxygen dissolved in water; healthy aquatic life generally needs more than about 4-5 mg/L, and DO falls as temperature and organic pollution rise. BOD is the oxygen consumed by aerobic microbes decomposing biodegradable organic matter, standardly at 20°C for 5 days. It rises with sewage and organic waste, so high BOD means low DO and poor water quality. COD (Chemical Oxygen Demand) is the oxygen equivalent of all chemically oxidisable matter, biodegradable or not, found using a strong chemical oxidant such as potassium dichromate; COD is always equal to or greater than BOD and its test takes only a few hours. Treated sewage is expected to have low BOD; CPCB general standards set the effluent limit for discharge into inland surface waters at about 30 mg/L BOD, and a lower value of 20 mg/L is required for some sewage treatment plants in sensitive areas. Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment (nitrates, phosphates) causing algal blooms, then decay, then high BOD and oxygen depletion, and fish kills. Biological indicators include coliform bacteria (faecal pollution), and certain species like stoneflies (clean water) versus tubifex worms and chironomid larvae (polluted water). Related institutions and programmes: Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB, under the Water Act 1974), National Mission for Clean Ganga (Namami Gange, 2014-15), National Water Quality Monitoring Programme, and the Ramsar Convention for wetlands. Possible future angles: ranking of pollutants by BOD, the meaning of zero DO (anoxic), 'dead zones', and the difference between BOD and COD.

subject: Current Affairs
detail: UN-Habitat (United Nations Human Settlements Programme) is the UN agency for sustainable urbanisation and human settlements, headquartered in Nairobi, Kenya. It grew out of the 1976 Habitat I conference in Vancouver. The UN Commission on Human Settlements and the Habitat Centre were set up in 1978. The General Assembly upgraded the body to a programme in 2001 (Resolution 56/206), and its mandate comes from the Habitat Agenda (Istanbul, 1996) and the Istanbul Declaration. Its focus is socially and environmentally sustainable towns and cities and adequate shelter for all. It is the focal point for SDG 11 (sustainable cities and communities) and for the New Urban Agenda, adopted at Habitat III in Quito in 2016. Its work also supports the UN-wide goals of poverty reduction, safe drinking water and basic sanitation. Its Habitat Agenda partners include governments, local authorities, NGOs, civil society, the private sector, academia, foundations and professional bodies. Elimination logic: the word 'only' in statement 2 makes it too restrictive, so (a) and (c) fall. Statement 3 is correct, so (d) falls, leaving (b).
explanations: Wrong: statement 2 is incorrect because UN-Habitat's partners go well beyond governments and local authorities, so 1, 2 and 3 cannot all be correct.
Correct: statements 1 and 3 are correct, and statement 2 is wrong because it limits partners to governments and local authorities 'only'.
Wrong: this option includes statement 2, which is incorrect, and leaves out statement 1, which is correct.
Wrong: statement 1 is correct, but statement 3 is also correct, so 'only 1' is incomplete.
keyfact: UN-Habitat (Nairobi, mandated by UNGA, 2001) promotes sustainable cities and shelter for all, and works with many partners, not just governments.
option_notes: Option (a) claims 1, 2 and 3 are all correct. It is wrong because of statement 2. UN-Habitat works with a wide partner base: governments, local authorities, NGOs, civil society, the private sector, academia and foundations. Its partnership approach comes from the Habitat Agenda (Istanbul, 1996). It convenes the World Urban Forum, a biennial conference on urbanisation. Its Executive Board and the UN-Habitat Assembly, a universal-membership body of 193 states created in 2019, govern it.

Option (b) is the official answer: statements 1 and 3 are correct. UN-Habitat is the UN agency for human settlements, based in Nairobi. It promotes sustainable urbanisation, adequate shelter, slum upgrading, and access to water and sanitation. Its mandate was strengthened by General Assembly Resolution 56/206 in 2001. It leads follow-up on the New Urban Agenda (Quito, 2016) and is the focal point for SDG 11. It also publishes the World Cities Report.

Option (c) claims 2 and 3 only are correct. It is wrong because it accepts statement 2 and rejects statement 1. Statement 1 is accurate, since the General Assembly mandates UN-Habitat to promote socially and environmentally sustainable towns and cities and adequate shelter for all. The 1976 Vancouver Habitat I conference, the 1996 Istanbul Habitat II conference and the 2016 Quito Habitat III conference mark its major milestones.

Option (d) claims only statement 1 is correct. It is wrong because it rejects statement 3. UN-Habitat does contribute to poverty reduction and to access to safe drinking water and basic sanitation, through its Water, Sanitation and Hygiene work and urban basic services programmes. These support MDG Target 7.C and 7.D and now SDG 6 and SDG 11. Its Water for Asian Cities programme is one example.
related: UN-Habitat is headquartered in Nairobi, Kenya.
Habitat I was in Vancouver in 1976, Habitat II in Istanbul in 1996, and Habitat III in Quito in 2016.
The New Urban Agenda was adopted at Quito in 2016.
SDG 11 covers sustainable cities and communities.
World Habitat Day falls on the first Monday of October; World Cities Day is 31 October.
The General Assembly made UN-Habitat a full programme in 2001 (Resolution 56/206).
The World Urban Forum is convened by UN-Habitat.
Its flagship publication is the World Cities Report.
statements: 1 — Correct: The UN General Assembly mandates UN-Habitat to promote socially and environmentally sustainable towns and cities and adequate shelter for all. UN-Habitat began as the UN Centre for Human Settlements (Habitat) in 1978, after the 1976 Vancouver conference. The General Assembly turned it into a full programme in 2001 through Resolution 56/206. It is headquartered in Nairobi. Its mandate rests on the Habitat Agenda (1996) and the New Urban Agenda (2016), and it is the focal agency for SDG 11.

2 — Incorrect: UN-Habitat's partners are not only governments or local urban authorities. They also include NGOs, civil society and community organisations, the private sector, foundations, academic and research institutions, professional groups, and other UN bodies. The Habitat Agenda explicitly promotes a partnership approach, and the World Urban Forum, convened by UN-Habitat, brings all of these together. The word 'only' makes the statement wrong. UN-Habitat is also funded by voluntary contributions and by the regular UN budget.

3 — Correct: UN-Habitat contributes to the UN system's overall objectives of reducing poverty and promoting access to safe drinking water and basic sanitation. This work is carried out through its Water and Sanitation programmes, slum upgrading, and urban basic services. It supports the Millennium Development Goals (Target 7.D on slum dwellers) and now the SDGs, mainly SDG 11, with links to SDG 6 and SDG 1. Its flagship reports are the World Cities Report and the Global Report on Human Settlements.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 1 and 3 are correct, and statement 2 is wrong. UN-Habitat is mandated by the UN General Assembly to promote sustainable towns and cities with adequate shelter for all, and it contributes to poverty reduction and access to safe drinking water and basic sanitation. Its partners are not limited to governments and local authorities.
topic_notes: UN-Habitat is the UN programme for human settlements and sustainable urban development. It is headquartered in Nairobi, Kenya, and is one of the few major UN bodies based in the Global South. Its origin is the 1976 UN Conference on Human Settlements (Habitat I) in Vancouver. The UN Commission on Human Settlements and the UN Centre for Human Settlements (Habitat) were created in 1978. In 2001 the General Assembly (Resolution 56/206) transformed the Centre into the UN Human Settlements Programme, UN-Habitat. Habitat II was held in Istanbul in 1996 and produced the Habitat Agenda and the Istanbul Declaration, with the goals of adequate shelter for all and sustainable human settlements. Habitat III was held in Quito in October 2016 and adopted the New Urban Agenda, a 20-year framework. The UN-Habitat Assembly, with all 193 member states, has met since 2019, and an Executive Board oversees its work. Its core areas include urban legislation, land and governance, urban planning and design, urban economy and municipal finance, basic services (water, sanitation, mobility, energy), slum upgrading and housing, risk reduction and rehabilitation, and research and capacity development. It is the focal point for SDG 11 (sustainable cities and communities) and monitors Target 11.1 on adequate, safe and affordable housing. Its periodic flagship publications are the World Cities Report and the Global Report on Human Settlements. It convenes the World Urban Forum, and World Habitat Day is observed on the first Monday of October, while World Cities Day is on 31 October. Related Indian initiatives UPSC may link to this topic include the Smart Cities Mission, AMRUT, Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban), PMAY-Urban and HRIDAY. Related global frameworks include the Sendai Framework, the Paris Agreement and the 2030 Agenda.

ocr: With reference to ‘National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF)’, which of the statements given below is/are correct ? 1. Under NSQF, a learner can acquire the certification for competency only through formal learning. 2. An outcome expected from the implementation of NSQF is the mobility between vocational and _ general education. Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) 1 only (b) 2only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 65. 62. In the context of Indian history, the principle of ‘Dyarchy (diarchy)’ refers to (a) Division of the central legislature into two houses. (b) I
subject: Polity
detail: The National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF) is a competency-based framework that organises all qualifications according to a series of levels of knowledge, skills and aptitude. The levels run from 1 to 10 and are graded by learning outcomes, which the learner must achieve whether the learning happens in a formal, non-formal or informal setting. It was notified by the Government of India on 27 December 2013, and the National Skill Development Agency (NSDA) was associated with its implementation. In 2018 it was made more comprehensive, with the National Skill Qualification Committee (NSQC) as the approving body. Its objectives include: (i) providing standards for the quality and quantity of learning outcomes; (ii) enabling multiple entry and exit points between vocational education, skill training and general education, including higher education; (iii) recognising prior learning (RPL); (iv) promoting vertical and horizontal mobility; and (v) improving international acceptance of Indian qualifications. Elimination logic: statement 1 uses the restrictive word 'only', and such absolute wording is usually a trap. Since NSQF explicitly recognises informal learning through RPL, statement 1 is false. That removes (a) and (c). Statement 2 is true, so (d) is also out, leaving (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is false. NSQF recognises non-formal and informal learning as well as formal learning.
(b) is right because statement 2 is true: mobility between vocational and general education is an expected outcome, while statement 1 is false.
(c) is wrong because it would require statement 1 to be true, and it is not.
(d) is wrong because statement 2 is true, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: NSQF (notified Dec 2013, 10 levels) certifies competency from formal, non-formal and informal learning and enables mobility between vocational and general education.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would mean certification is available only through formal learning. That is not how NSQF works. NSQF is built to give recognition to competencies however they were acquired, including on-the-job experience, apprenticeships and prior learning. Formal education is only one route. The NSQF levels range from 1 to 10, and each is defined by learning outcomes, not by the type of institution attended. This is why Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) was made a central feature of the Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana.

Option (b), '2 only', is the correct choice. It captures the key point that NSQF allows learners to move between skill-based vocational pathways and general academic education. This works through multiple entry and exit points, credit accumulation and transfer, and alignment of levels across systems. NSQF was notified in December 2013 and covers school, vocational, technical and higher education. It also aims to raise the status of vocational learning, which has often been seen as a lesser option than general academic study.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', is wrong because the 'only' in statement 1 makes it false. This kind of option is often attractive when a statement looks partly right, because formal learning is indeed one valid route to NSQF certification. But UPSC regularly uses restrictive words such as 'only', 'all' and 'never' to turn a half-true statement into a false one. Remember that NSQF recognises formal, non-formal and informal learning alike.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', is wrong because statement 2 correctly states an outcome of NSQF. NSQF aims to remove the divide between vocational and academic education so that learners can progress both vertically and horizontally. The framework also supports lifelong learning and is linked to the National Credit Framework. Anyone who thought the framework had nothing to do with general education would pick this option, but integration with general education is a stated aim.
related: NSQF was notified on 27 December 2013 and has 10 levels, numbered 1 to 10.
Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) assesses and certifies skills learned informally.
NSDC was set up in 2008 as a public-private partnership under the Companies Act.
Skill India Mission was launched on 15 July 2015, the same date as World Youth Skills Day.
NCVET, formed in 2018, is the regulator for vocational education and training.
Sector Skill Councils are industry-led bodies that develop National Occupational Standards.
NEP 2020 proposes integrating vocational education into mainstream schooling from Class 6.
MSDE was created as a separate ministry in November 2014.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: NSQF certifies competency regardless of whether it was acquired through formal, non-formal or informal learning, so 'only through formal learning' is wrong. Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) is a core feature, allowing workers who learned on the job, such as artisans, masons and electricians, to be assessed and certified against NSQF levels. The framework has levels 1 to 10, each defined by process, professional knowledge, professional skill, core skill and responsibility. Qualifications are developed by Sector Skill Councils and approved by the NSQC, and they are aligned with National Occupational Standards (NOS). Certificates are linked to the national credit system.

2 — Correct: A key outcome of NSQF is mobility between vocational and general education, giving learners multiple entry and exit points and credit transfer. A student can move from skill training into diploma or degree education, and back again, without losing recognition of past learning. NSQF was notified on 27 December 2013 by the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, which replaced the earlier National Vocational Education Qualification Framework (NVEQF) of the Ministry of Education. It also aims to align Indian qualifications with international frameworks, so that they gain global recognition and workers can move across borders.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. NSQF is a competency-based framework that allows learners to earn certification through formal, non-formal or informal learning, so statement 1 is wrong. One of its core aims is mobility between vocational and general education, so statement 2 is right.
topic_notes: NSQF is a competency-based quality assurance framework that organises qualifications by levels of knowledge, skills and aptitude. Notified on 27 December 2013, it has 10 levels, and each level is described by five descriptors: process, professional knowledge, professional skill, core skill and responsibility. It is run by the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE), with the National Skill Development Agency (NSDA) and later the National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET) playing key roles. NCVET was formed in 2018 and takes over regulatory functions from the earlier National Council for Vocational Training and the NSDA. Its objectives include creating multiple entry and exit points, recognising prior learning, promoting mobility between vocational and general education, encouraging lifelong learning, and aligning Indian qualifications with global standards. Related institutions include Sector Skill Councils (SSCs), industry-led bodies set up under the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC), which was created in 2008 as a public-private partnership. SSCs develop National Occupational Standards (NOS) and Qualification Packs (QPs). Skill India Mission was launched on 15 July 2015, the date also marked as World Youth Skills Day. The Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) offers short-term training and RPL aligned to NSQF. Other schemes include the Skill Acquisition and Knowledge Awareness for Livelihood Promotion (SANKALP) programme, Skills Strengthening for Industrial Value Enhancement (STRIVE), Jan Shikshan Sansthan, and the National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme. The National Education Policy 2020 supports integrating vocational education with general education from Class 6 onwards, and it proposes a National Higher Education Qualifications Framework (NHEQF) and a National Credit Framework (NCrF). Potential future questions may cover who notified NSQF, how many levels it has, what RPL means, what Sector Skill Councils do, and which agency regulates vocational qualifications.

ocr: With reference to ‘National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF)’, which of the statements given below is/are correct ? 1. Under NSQF, a learner can acquire the certification for competency only through formal learning. 2. An outcome expected from the implementation of NSQF is the mobility between vocational and _ general education. Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) 1 only (b) 2only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 65. 62. In the context of Indian history, the principle of ‘Dyarchy (diarchy)’ refers to (a) Division of the central legislature into two houses. (b) I
subject: Polity
