In India, cosmetics fall under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and BIS standards. Lead has been phased out of petrol and paints in most countries. It remains a concern in water, batteries and some imported toys.

Option (b), pairs 2 and 3 only: BVO and MSG are both valid pairs. BVO is an emulsifier once used in citrus soft drinks and banned in the EU, Japan and (since 2024) the USA. MSG is the sodium salt of glutamic acid, a flavour enhancer first isolated by Kikunae Ikeda in 1908 and sold as Ajinomoto. It is widely used in Chinese-style food, soups and instant noodles. FSSAI regulates it and requires a label warning for infants.

Option (c), pairs 1 and 3 only: lead in lipstick and MSG in Chinese fast food are both valid. Lead is a heavy metal toxin found in some cosmetics, and MSG is a flavour enhancer (umami). Both were in the news during the 2015 Maggi controversy, when FSSAI tested noodles for lead and MSG. The option is wrong only because it excludes pair 2, since BVO is indeed linked to soft drinks. Recall that the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 created FSSAI.

Option (d), all three pairs: this is the official answer. Lipstick can contain lead, soft drinks have used brominated vegetable oils as emulsifiers, and Chinese fast food often uses MSG as a flavour enhancer. These are the 'unwanted or controversial' chemicals in the question. FSSAI, set up under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, regulates additives in food, while cosmetics fall under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.
related: FSSAI was established under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and is under the Union Health Ministry.
BVO is a vegetable oil bonded with bromine used as an emulsifier; the US FDA revoked it in 2024.
MSG is the sodium salt of glutamic acid, first isolated by Kikunae Ikeda in 1908 and sold as Ajinomoto.
Maggi noodles were banned in 2015 over excess lead and undeclared MSG claims, and the ban was later lifted.
FSSAI banned potassium bromate in 2016 after CSE findings.
Lead is a neurotoxin, especially harmful to children, and India phased out leaded petrol in 2000.
Minamata disease is caused by mercury; Itai-itai disease by cadmium.
CSE reports on pesticide residue in soft drinks came out in 2003 and 2006.
statements: 1 — Correct: Lipstick is a recognised source of lead exposure. Lead is a heavy metal that occurs as a trace contaminant in pigments and mineral colourants. Facts: Lead is a neurotoxin and is especially harmful to children and pregnant women, and no safe exposure level is established. Studies by the US FDA (2010 and later) and Indian groups such as Toxics Link found lead in many lipsticks. India's Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) sets limits for heavy metals in cosmetics (IS 4707), and the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 governs cosmetics in India. Lead can also be found in old paints, petrol (now phased out) and water pipes.

2 — Correct: Brominated vegetable oil (BVO) was used in some citrus-flavoured soft drinks. Facts: BVO is vegetable oil bound with bromine and acts as an emulsifier and clouding agent, preventing flavour oils from separating. Concerns include bromine build-up in tissues and effects on the thyroid and nervous system. It was banned in the EU and Japan, and in 2024 the US FDA revoked its authorisation for use in food. Companies like Coca-Cola and PepsiCo had earlier removed it from their products. In India, the CSE raised concerns about soft drink additives and pesticide residues in 2003 and 2006.

3 — Correct: Monosodium glutamate (MSG) is commonly found in Chinese fast food. Facts: MSG is the sodium salt of glutamic acid, an amino acid, and gives the savoury 'umami' taste. It was first isolated by the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda in 1908 and is marketed as Ajinomoto. It is used in soups, sauces, instant noodles and snacks. The US FDA classifies it as 'generally recognised as safe', but it remains controversial because of reports of headache and flushing ('Chinese restaurant syndrome'). In India, FSSAI requires a label warning that it is not recommended for infants under 12 months, and the 2015 Maggi controversy involved MSG and lead.
summary: The answer is (d): all three pairs are correctly matched. Lipstick can contain lead, brominated vegetable oils (BVO) have been used in some soft drinks, and Chinese fast food often contains monosodium glutamate (MSG) as a flavour enhancer.
topic_notes: The topic is controversial chemicals and additives in everyday consumer goods, and the regulatory framework around them. Food in India is regulated by FSSAI, a statutory body under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, established under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, with its headquarters in Delhi. Cosmetics and drugs are regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 through the CDSCO, and BIS sets standards. Key chemicals: lead (neurotoxic heavy metal, found in old paints, some cosmetics, contaminated water and leaded petrol, which India phased out in 2000); BVO (emulsifier in citrus soft drinks, banned in the EU, Japan, and the US from 2024); MSG (flavour enhancer, umami, Kikunae Ikeda 1908, Ajinomoto); potassium bromate (a flour improver banned by FSSAI in 2016 after CSE findings, and a possible carcinogen); Sudan dyes (illegal industrial dyes in chilli powder); calcium carbide (illegal fruit ripener, acetylene gas); and formalin in fish. Other angles: CSE reports on pesticides in soft drinks (2003, 2006) and in honey (2020), and on antibiotics in honey; Toxics Link studies on cosmetics; trans fats, with FSSAI capping industrial trans fat at 2 per cent by 2022; the Eat Right India movement; fortification of staples; and the labelling rules for HFSS foods. Related international bodies: Codex Alimentarius Commission (FAO and WHO), the Stockholm Convention on POPs, the Minamata Convention on mercury, and the Basel Convention. Heavy metals and their effects: lead (neurotoxicity), mercury (Minamata disease), cadmium (Itai-itai disease), arsenic (blackfoot disease), and chromium.

question:
Organic Light Emitting Diodes (OLEDs) are 76, used to create digital display in many devices. What are the advantages of OLED displays over Liquid Crystal displays ?
1. OLED displays can be fabricated on flexible plastic substrates.
2. Roll-up displays embedded in clothing can be made using OLEDs. 3; Transparent displays are possible using OLEDs. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
options: None of the above statements is correct
subject: Science & Tech
detail: An Organic Light Emitting Diode (OLED) uses thin films of organic compounds, placed between two electrodes, that emit light when current passes through them (electroluminescence). Because each pixel produces its own light, an OLED needs no backlight, colour filter-heavy stack or rigid glass layers of the kind an LCD requires. An LCD works differently: liquid crystals only modulate light from an LED or CCFL backlight, which needs a rigid, thick assembly with polarisers. This difference gives OLEDs their advantages: thinner and lighter panels, true blacks, high contrast, wide viewing angles and fast response. Because the organic layers are thin and can be deposited at low temperature, plastic (for example polyimide) substrates can be used, so flexible, foldable and rollable displays are possible. Such displays can be woven or embedded into fabrics and clothing (wearables). If the electrodes are made transparent (for example ITO), the panel itself becomes see-through, which allows transparent displays. Elimination logic: statements 1, 2 and 3 are all recognised OLED applications, so options (a), (b) and (d) are wrong. Drawbacks of OLEDs include shorter lifetime of blue emitters, burn-in, moisture sensitivity and higher cost.
explanations: Incorrect: this option omits statement 2, which is also correct, since roll-up displays embedded in clothing are possible with OLEDs.
Incorrect: it accepts only statement 2, but statements 1 and 3 are also valid OLED advantages.
Correct: flexible substrates, roll-up and wearable displays and transparent displays are all advantages of OLEDs over LCDs.
Incorrect: the statements are correct, so this option cannot be true.
keyfact: OLEDs are self-emissive organic films with no backlight, enabling flexible, rollable, wearable and transparent displays that LCDs cannot easily match.
option_notes: Options (a) 1 and 3 only: a partial answer. Flexible and transparent OLEDs are both real technologies. Flexible OLEDs are built on plastic such as polyimide and are used in curved and foldable phones. Transparent OLEDs use transparent electrodes and are used in windows, signage and automotive displays. This combination wrongly leaves out the roll-up and clothing-embedded displays, which are also possible.

Option (b) 2 only: it picks out roll-up displays embedded in clothing. Rollable OLEDs exist, for example the LG rollable OLED TV, and wearable OLED textiles are under research. Rollability depends on the same thin, flexible, backlight-free structure that makes statements 1 and 3 true, so accepting only 2 is illogical.

Option (c) 1, 2 and 3: the official answer. OLED displays are self-emissive, so they need no backlight. This allows thin, flexible, rollable, wearable and transparent displays. Further advantages include better contrast, wider viewing angle, faster response and lower power use for dark content. Disadvantages are organic degradation, burn-in and cost.

Option (d) None of the above: this would hold only if OLEDs had none of these abilities. In fact flexible, rollable and transparent OLEDs are commercial or demonstrated products, such as foldable phones, rollable TVs and transparent signage, so this option is factually wrong.
related: OLED stands for Organic Light Emitting Diode and works by electroluminescence.
An OLED needs no backlight, but an LCD does.
AMOLED uses an active-matrix thin-film transistor backplane.
Kodak's Tang and Van Slyke demonstrated an efficient OLED in 1987.
The 2000 Chemistry Nobel recognised conducting polymers.
QLED is quantum dots over an LCD backlight, not self-emissive OLED.
OLED weaknesses: burn-in and blue-emitter degradation.
Quantum dots are nanoscale semiconductor crystals, and the 2023 Chemistry Nobel recognised their discovery.
statements: 1 — Correct: OLED layers are thin and can be deposited on plastic substrates, so flexible panels are possible. Flexible OLEDs use polyimide or similar plastic instead of glass, and the absence of a backlight lets the panel bend. Samsung's Galaxy Round and Edge phones, LG's rollable TV and foldable phones all use flexible OLED (POLED/AMOLED). LCDs need rigid backlight units and a fixed liquid-crystal cell gap, which limits bending.

2 — Correct: Roll-up and wearable displays embedded in clothing and fabrics are an established OLED application. Since the panel is ultra-thin, light and bendable, it can be rolled or integrated into textiles, smart garments and wearable devices. Research on OLED fibres and textiles is ongoing, and LG has shown a rollable OLED TV (Signature OLED R, 2019-20). Rolling an LCD is impractical because of the backlight and rigid glass layers.

3 — Correct: Transparent OLED (TOLED) displays are possible because the panel needs no backlight and its electrodes can be made transparent, such as ITO or thin metal. They are used in shop windows, vehicle head-up displays, smart windows and signage. Samsung and LG have shown transparent OLED panels, and the display shows images while letting the background be seen. LCDs generally need a backlight, so they are normally opaque.
summary: The answer is (c): all three statements are correct. OLEDs are self-emissive organic thin films that need no backlight and can be deposited on flexible or transparent substrates, which LCDs cannot easily match.
topic_notes: OLED technology: an OLED has organic emissive layers (emissive layer, conductive layer, hole and electron transport layers) between a cathode and an anode on a substrate. Applying voltage injects electrons and holes that recombine in the emissive layer and release photons, a process called electroluminescence. Types include PMOLED (passive matrix), AMOLED (active matrix with a thin-film transistor backplane, used in phones and TVs), TOLED (transparent), FOLED (flexible), WOLED (white OLED, used by LG with colour filters) and QD-OLED (Samsung, combining quantum dots with OLED). Origin: Ching Tang and Steven Van Slyke at Eastman Kodak demonstrated an efficient organic EL device in 1987. The 2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (Heeger, MacDiarmid, Shirakawa) was for conductive polymers, the basis of polymer OLEDs. Advantages over LCD: no backlight, thinner and lighter, perfect blacks, high contrast, wide viewing angles, fast response time, flexibility and transparency, and lower power use in dark scenes. Limitations: blue emitters degrade faster, so lifespan is shorter, with burn-in, sensitivity to moisture and oxygen, lower peak brightness than some LED/mini-LED panels, and higher cost. LCD works by liquid crystals modulating polarised light from an LED backlight. Related display technologies: LED (inorganic semiconductors), QLED (quantum dot film over an LCD backlight), micro-LED (self-emissive inorganic) and e-paper (electrophoretic, used in e-readers). Applications: smartphones, TVs, smartwatches, VR headsets, automotive displays and lighting panels. UPSC often tests the working principle, the full form, the advantages over LCD and the related quantum dot topics.

question:
Which of the following is/are famous for Sun temples ? ir. Arasavalli 2, Amarakantak
3. Omkareshwar Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Art & Culture
detail: Sun worship (Surya Upasana) has a long history in India, with major Sun temples at Konark (Odisha, 13th century, Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, a UNESCO site), Modhera (Gujarat, 1026-27 CE, Solanki king Bhimdev I), Martand (Kashmir, Karkota dynasty, 8th century, attributed to Lalitaditya Muktapida), Suryanarayana temple at Arasavalli (Andhra Pradesh, 7th century, attributed to the Eastern Ganga/Kalinga rulers), Dakshinarka at Gaya, Bihar, and Unao and Deo in Bihar. Arasavalli is distinctive because the idol is worshipped as Surya Narayana, and on certain days of the year the rays of the rising sun fall on the deity's feet. Amarkantak, in Madhya Pradesh, is the source of the Narmada and is a Shaiva and Narmada pilgrimage site with the Narmada Udgam temple. Omkareshwar, on Mandhata island in the Narmada, is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas of Shiva. Elimination: since 2 and 3 are Narmada and Shaiva sites, any option containing them is wrong, leaving (a).
explanations: Correct: only Arasavalli among the three is famous for a Sun temple, and the official answer is 1 only.
Wrong: it includes Amarkantak, which is the origin of the Narmada, and Omkareshwar, a Jyotirlinga site, neither of which is known for a Sun temple.
Wrong: Omkareshwar is a Shiva Jyotirlinga site, so adding it to Arasavalli makes the option incorrect.
Wrong: it includes both Amarkantak and Omkareshwar, which are not Sun temple sites.
keyfact: Arasavalli (Srikakulam, Andhra Pradesh) has a Sun temple; Amarkantak is the Narmada source and Omkareshwar is a Jyotirlinga.
option_notes: 1 only: Arasavalli, in Srikakulam district, Andhra Pradesh, has the Surya Narayana temple, believed to be from the 7th century. The idol is of black granite, with Usha and Chhaya as consorts. The sun's rays touch the deity's feet during an annual phenomenon in March and October. It is a rare surviving ancient Sun temple still in worship, and a popular pilgrimage site in coastal Andhra.

2 and 3 only: this combines Amarkantak and Omkareshwar, both on or near the Narmada in Madhya Pradesh. Amarkantak is the source of the Narmada, in Anuppur district, and has Kalachuri temples. Omkareshwar is a Jyotirlinga island in Khandwa district. Both are Shaiva and river pilgrimage centres, not Sun temple centres, so the combination is wrong.

1 and 3 only: this adds Omkareshwar to Arasavalli. Omkareshwar is a Jyotirlinga of Shiva on Mandhata island in the Narmada, Madhya Pradesh. It is one of 12 Jyotirlingas, together with Mahakaleshwar in Ujjain, which is also in Madhya Pradesh. It is not a Sun temple site, so this option is incorrect.

1, 2 and 3: this claims all three have Sun temples. Only Arasavalli does. Amarkantak is the Narmada source, and Omkareshwar is a Jyotirlinga. Such all-inclusive options are often wrong when even one item fails, as here.
related: Konark Sun Temple: Odisha, 13th century, Narasimhadeva I, UNESCO site since 1984.
Modhera Sun Temple: Gujarat, 1026-27 CE, Solanki king Bhimdev I.
Martand Sun Temple: Kashmir, built by Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota dynasty.
Arasavalli Sun Temple: Srikakulam, Andhra Pradesh.
Katarmal Sun Temple: Almora, Uttarakhand, Katyuri period.
Narmada originates at Amarkantak, Anuppur district, Madhya Pradesh.
Omkareshwar: one of 12 Jyotirlingas, on the Narmada in Madhya Pradesh.
Deo Sun Temple in Bihar is famous for Chhath Puja.
statements: 1 — Correct: Arasavalli is famous for its Sun temple. It lies near Srikakulam in Andhra Pradesh. The temple is dedicated to Surya Narayana Swamy and is believed to date to the 7th century, built by a Kalinga ruler (the Eastern Ganga or Kalinga dynasty). The black granite idol stands with his consorts Usha and Chhaya. Twice a year, in March and October, the first rays of the sun fall on the feet of the deity. It is one of very few ancient Sun temples where worship continues to this day.

2 — Incorrect: Amarkantak, on the Maikal range in Anuppur district, Madhya Pradesh, is famous as the source of the Narmada, also of the Son and Johilla. It is known for the Narmada Udgam temple, the Kalachuri-era Karna temples (11th century), and the Amarkantak Biosphere Reserve (Achanakmar-Amarkantak). It is a Hindu pilgrimage site, not noted for any Sun temple.

3 — Incorrect: Omkareshwar is on the island of Mandhata (Shivapuri) in the Narmada, Khandwa district, Madhya Pradesh. Its Omkareshwar-Mamleshwar temple is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas of Shiva. The island is shaped like the Om symbol. The Omkareshwar dam and a large hydroelectric and solar project are located nearby. It is a Shaiva site, not a Sun temple site.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. Arasavalli in Srikakulam district, Andhra Pradesh, is famous for its ancient Surya (Sun) temple. Amarkantak and Omkareshwar are known for other religious associations, not Sun temples.
topic_notes: Sun temples of India are a recurring theme in UPSC art and culture. Konark Sun Temple, Odisha, was built in the 13th century by Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty in Kalinga style, designed as a chariot with 24 wheels and seven horses, and was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984. Modhera Sun Temple, Gujarat, on the Pushpavati river, was built in 1026-27 CE under Bhimdev I of the Solanki (Chaulukya) dynasty, and has a stepped tank (Surya Kund). Martand Sun Temple, near Anantnag in Kashmir, is attributed to Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota dynasty (8th century). Arasavalli, in Andhra Pradesh, is a 7th-century temple. Others include Suryanar Kovil in Tamil Nadu (a Navagraha temple), Dakshinaarka in Gaya, Deo Sun Temple in Aurangabad (Bihar), famous for Chhath, Sun temple at Unao (Madhya Pradesh), Katarmal in Almora, Uttarakhand (Katyuri dynasty), and Surya Pahar in Assam. Related angles: Surya as one of the Adityas in the Vedas, the Surya cult and Shaka (Magi) influence, Samba Purana, and Chhath Puja. UPSC also asks about Jyotirlingas (Omkareshwar, Mahakaleshwar, Somnath, Kedarnath), the Narmada's origin at Amarkantak, and the temple styles of Nagara, Dravida and Vesara.

question: Consider the following statements : In the election for Lok Sabha or State Ls Assembly, the winning candidate must get at least 50 percent of the votes polled, to be declared elected. According to the provisions laid down in the Constitution of India, in Lok Sabha, the Speaker’s post goes to the majority party and the Deputy Speaker’s to the Opposition. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: Statement 1 confuses plurality with majority. In Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections held in single-member constituencies, the candidate who secures the highest number of votes is declared elected, even if that is well below 50 percent. This is the first-past-the-post (simple plurality) system, under the Representation of the People Act, 1951. An absolute majority is required only in some indirect elections, which use the single transferable vote, such as those of the President and Vice-President (a quota applies). Statement 2 fails because Articles 93 and 178 only say that the House shall choose its Speaker and Deputy Speaker as soon as may be. Nothing is said about party affiliation. Convention, not constitutional provision, has given the Deputy Speaker's post to the Opposition at times (this was common from the 10th to the 16th Lok Sabha, though the 17th Lok Sabha had no Deputy Speaker elected). Since the question asks about constitutional provisions, a convention cannot make the statement correct. Elimination: both statements are false, so (a), (b) and (c) fail.
explanations: (a) is wrong because Statement 1 is false; India uses first-past-the-post, so a plurality is enough and 50 percent is not needed.
(b) is wrong because Statement 2 is false; the Constitution does not assign the Speaker or Deputy Speaker posts by party, and the Deputy Speaker going to the Opposition is only a convention.
(c) is wrong because neither statement is correct, so they cannot both be right.
(d) is correct because both statements are incorrect: elections are decided by plurality, and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker allocation is not constitutionally prescribed.
keyfact: India elects MPs and MLAs by plurality (first-past-the-post), and the Constitution does not tie the Speaker or Deputy Speaker posts to the ruling party or the Opposition.
option_notes: Statement 1 only: this would be right only for a system requiring an absolute majority. India's direct elections to the Lok Sabha and Assemblies do not use such a system. They use first-past-the-post in single-member constituencies. A candidate may win with, for example, 30 to 40 percent of votes if the opposition vote is split. Absolute majority systems such as runoff voting are used in countries such as France for presidential elections, but not in India.

Statement 2 only: this would be right if the Constitution fixed party roles for the presiding officers. It does not. Articles 93 and 178 only require the House to elect them. The Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha, decides on disqualification under the Tenth Schedule, certifies Money Bills and has a casting vote. The Deputy Speaker acts when the post of Speaker is vacant. Opposition allotment of the Deputy Speaker post is a parliamentary convention that has not always been followed.

Both 1 and 2: this would mean the election needs 50 percent of votes and that the Constitution fixes the party of the presiding officers. Both claims are false. The option is a typical trap built on common misconceptions about majority rule and about parliamentary convention being treated as law. In UPSC, always separate constitutional provisions from statutes, conventions and practice.

Neither 1 nor 2: this is the official answer. Elections to the Lok Sabha and Assemblies are decided by simple plurality (first-past-the-post). The Speaker and Deputy Speaker are elected by members of the House, and the Constitution does not link these posts to the majority party or the Opposition. Any Opposition role for the Deputy Speaker rests on convention only, which is why the statement fails.
related: First-past-the-post elects the candidate with the most votes, not necessarily a majority.
Articles 93 and 178 deal with the election of Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha and Assemblies.
Article 94 governs the vacation, resignation and removal of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
The Speaker has only a casting vote, used in the event of a tie.
The Speaker certifies Money Bills under Article 110.
The President and Vice-President are elected by proportional representation through a single transferable vote.
A candidate loses the security deposit if they get less than one-sixth of valid votes polled.
The Deputy Speaker post going to the Opposition is a convention, not a constitutional rule.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Election is by plurality, not by 50 percent of votes polled. First-past-the-post means the candidate with the most votes wins in a single-member constituency. Many MPs and MLAs win with under 50 percent. The system is provided for by the Representation of the People Act, 1951, under the Article 324 framework of the Election Commission. Its advantages are simplicity and stable outcomes, while its criticism is that seats and vote shares can diverge widely. Alternatives such as proportional representation with the single transferable vote are used for the Rajya Sabha, the President and the Vice-President. A majority of valid votes polled is not needed for Lok Sabha seats.

2 — Incorrect: The Constitution does not allocate the Speaker's post to the majority party or the Deputy Speaker's post to the Opposition. Articles 93 (Lok Sabha) and 178 (Assemblies) simply require the House to choose its Speaker and Deputy as soon as possible. The Speaker is elected by a simple majority of members present and voting. Practice varies: Speakers usually come from the ruling party or alliance, and the Deputy Speaker's post going to the Opposition is only a convention, not binding. The first Deputy Speaker, M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar, was from the ruling Congress. Article 94 deals with vacation, resignation and removal of these officers.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. Indian elections use the first-past-the-post system where a plurality suffices, and the Constitution says nothing about the Speaker going to the majority party or the Deputy Speaker to the Opposition.
topic_notes: Electoral system: India follows first-past-the-post for the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and Legislative Council seats elected by local bodies in some cases are by STV. The Election Commission is established under Article 324. Elections are governed by the Representation of the People Act 1950 (electoral rolls, seat allocation) and 1951 (conduct, disqualifications, disputes). Candidates must forfeit their security deposit if they secure less than one-sixth of valid votes. Indirect elections for the President and Vice-President use proportional representation by single transferable vote; the Rajya Sabha also uses STV by State Legislative Assembly members. Presiding officers: Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha are elected from among its members under Article 93; Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is the Vice-President (Article 89), with a Deputy Chairman elected from the members. The Speaker may be removed by a resolution passed by an effective majority (majority of all then members) with 14 days' notice (Article 94, 96). While such a resolution is under consideration, the Speaker may attend and speak but cannot vote at first, though he can vote in a tie on other matters. The Speaker does not vacate office on dissolution of the House; he continues until the new House meets. The Speaker pro tem administers oaths to new members. G.V. Mavalankar was the first Speaker, and Ananthasayanam Ayyangar the first Deputy Speaker. The Tenth Schedule (anti-defection, 52nd Amendment 1985) gives the Speaker authority on disqualification, as reviewed in Kihoto Hollohan (1992). Future questions may ask about the Speaker's casting vote, Money Bill certification, joint sittings, and the role of the pro tem Speaker.

ocr: Which of the following has/have occurred in India after its liberalization of economic policies in 1991 ? Share of agriculture in GDP increased I. enormously. Share of India’s exports in world trade increased. FDI inflows increased. India’s foreign exchange reserves increased enormously. , Select the correct answer using the codes given below : 1 and 4 only (a) 2, 3 and 4 only (b) 2 and 3 only (ce) 1, 2,3 and 4 (d) What is the application of Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer Technology ? Production of biolarvicides (a) Manufacture of biodegradable plastics (b) Reproductive cloning of animals (c) P
subject: Economy
detail: The 1991 reforms (LPG: liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation) were launched by the Narasimha Rao government, with Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister. They followed a balance-of-payments crisis in which reserves fell to about $1.1-1.2 billion, roughly two to three weeks of imports. India pledged gold with the Bank of England and the Union Bank of Switzerland, took IMF support, and devalued the rupee by about 18-19% in two steps in July 1991. The New Industrial Policy of 24 July 1991 abolished industrial licensing for most sectors, cut the public-sector reservation list, relaxed MRTP limits and allowed automatic FDI approval in priority industries. Tariffs were cut and FERA was later replaced by the softer FEMA in 1999. Outcomes: FDI rose from about $0.1 billion in 1991-92 to about $60 billion by 2016-17. Reserves rose from about $1 billion to over $370 billion by 2017. India's share in world merchandise exports rose from about 0.5% to about 1.6%. Agriculture's GDP share fell from about 29% to about 15-17%, because industry and especially services grew faster. Elimination: statement 1 is false, which removes (a) and (d). Statements 2, 3 and 4 are true, so (b) is correct, and (c) omits statement 4.
explanations: (a) 1 and 4 only is wrong because statement 1 is false: agriculture's share in GDP fell sharply after 1991, even though statement 4 is true.
(b) 2, 3 and 4 only is correct. Exports' world share, FDI inflows and forex reserves all increased greatly, while agriculture's GDP share declined.
(c) 2 and 3 only is wrong because it leaves out statement 4. Forex reserves rose enormously, from about $1 billion to hundreds of billions of dollars.
(d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 is wrong because it includes statement 1, and agriculture's GDP share did not increase.
keyfact: After 1991: agriculture's GDP share fell, while exports' world share, FDI inflows and forex reserves rose, so the answer is 2, 3 and 4 only.
related: The New Industrial Policy was announced on 24 July 1991 by PM Narasimha Rao's government.
Manmohan Singh was Finance Minister during the 1991 reforms.
FERA (1973) was replaced by FEMA (1999).
India's gold was pledged with the Bank of England and Union Bank of Switzerland in 1991.
India accepted current account convertibility under IMF Article VIII in August 1994.
The FIPB was abolished in 2017; FDI proposals now go through the concerned ministries and DPIIT.
Services contribute over 50% of India's GVA, while agriculture contributes about 15-18%.
India's forex reserves peaked at about $642 billion in September 2021.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: agriculture's share in GDP declined, not increased. It fell from about 29% (1990-91) to about 15-17% (2016-17), while services rose to over 50%. This is structural transformation: agriculture still employs about 42-45% of the workforce, so productivity and income gaps persist. Related terms are the Lewis model, premature tertiarisation and disguised unemployment. Farm reforms and agri-GDP growth of about 3-4% a year lagged behind the rest of the economy.

2 — Correct: India's share in world merchandise exports roughly tripled, from about 0.5-0.6% in 1991 to about 1.6-1.7% by 2016-17. India's share of world commercial services exports is higher, at about 3.3-3.5%, led by IT and BPO. Export growth was supported by lower tariffs, a market-determined exchange rate regime (LERMS 1992, full current account convertibility in 1994), SEZs (policy 2000, Act 2005) and the WTO (India a founding member in 1995). The Foreign Trade Policy is announced by the Commerce Ministry through the DGFT.

3 — Correct: FDI inflows rose from about $129 million in 1991-92 to about $60 billion in 2016-17, and to a record of about $82 billion in 2020-21. Automatic route approval was introduced in 1991 and FIPB handled other cases until it was abolished in 2017. Top source countries are Mauritius, Singapore and the USA, and services, computer software and telecom attract the most. FDI policy is framed by DPIIT, and FEMA 1999 governs foreign investment.

4 — Correct: forex reserves rose from about $1.2 billion in mid-1991 to about $370 billion in 2017 and a peak of about $642 billion in September 2021. They consist of foreign currency assets (the largest part), gold, SDRs and the reserve tranche position at the IMF. The RBI manages them. Large reserves buffer against external shocks, but they are partly driven by volatile capital inflows, and the 2013 taper tantrum showed their limits.
summary: The answer is (b), 2, 3 and 4 only. After the 1991 reforms India's exports, FDI inflows and foreign exchange reserves all rose sharply. The share of agriculture in GDP fell, so statement 1 is wrong.
topic_notes: The 1991 crisis came from fiscal deficits of about 8% of GDP, a current account deficit of about 3% of GDP, the Gulf War oil price shock, loss of remittances and the political instability of 1990-91. Reserves fell to a level that covered about three weeks of imports. The response was stabilisation, meaning devaluation, the IMF stand-by arrangement and fiscal correction, together with structural reforms. Key reforms: (1) industrial licensing abolished except for a few strategic or hazardous industries; (2) the public sector's reserved list cut from 17 industries to a handful; (3) MRTP restrictions on large firms relaxed; (4) trade liberalisation, with peak customs duty cut from over 300% to about 150% and then lower, and quantitative restrictions removed; (5) financial sector reform under the Narasimham Committee (1991 and 1998), including lower SLR and CRR, interest rate deregulation and private banks; (6) SEBI given statutory powers in 1992, and NSE started in 1994; (7) tax reform under the Chelliah Committee; (8) rupee made convertible on the current account in 1994. Later milestones: WTO membership in 1995, FRBM Act 2003, GST in 2017, the end of the Planning Commission in 2015 (replaced by NITI Aayog), and the PLI schemes. Outcomes: GDP growth averaged about 6-7% from the 1990s, services became the largest sector, poverty fell, and inequality and jobless growth became concerns. Another angle UPSC could ask: critics' views that reforms favoured services over agriculture and manufacturing, regional disparities, and the balance-of-payments crises of 1966, 1981 and 1991 as a comparison.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q78.
ocr: Which of the following has/have occurred in India after its liberalization of economic policies in 1991 ? Share of agriculture in GDP increased I. enormously. Share of India’s exports in world trade increased. FDI inflows increased. India’s foreign exchange reserves increased enormously. , Select the correct answer using the codes given below : 1 and 4 only (a) 2, 3 and 4 only (b) 2 and 3 only (ce) 1, 2,3 and 4 (d) What is the application of Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer Technology ? Production of biolarvicides (a) Manufacture of biodegradable plastics (b) Reproductive cloning of animals (c) P
subject: Economy
detail: In SCNT the nucleus of a somatic (non-reproductive, diploid) cell is removed from a donor and inserted into an oocyte whose own nucleus has been removed. A mild electric pulse or chemical stimulus then triggers the egg to divide as if it had been fertilised. The embryo carries nearly the same nuclear DNA as the donor. If the embryo is implanted in a surrogate mother and carried to term, the result is reproductive cloning, a genetically near-identical animal. If the embryo is instead used to derive embryonic stem cells, this is therapeutic cloning. The landmark case is Dolly the sheep, born 5 July 1996 at the Roslin Institute, Scotland (Ian Wilmut and colleagues). She was the first mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell, taken from the mammary gland, and she died in 2003. Elimination logic: biolarvicides are microbial products such as Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis. Biodegradable plastics come from microbial fermentation, giving PHA/PHB and PLA. Disease-free plants come from meristem or tissue culture. None of these involves nuclear transfer, so only (c) fits.
explanations: (a) Wrong. Biolarvicides are microbial agents such as Bt israelensis and Bacillus sphaericus used against mosquito larvae. They do not involve nuclear transfer.
(b) Wrong. Biodegradable plastics such as PHA, PHB and PLA are made by microbial fermentation or from plant starch. SCNT is not involved.
(c) Correct. SCNT is the technique behind reproductive cloning of animals, for example Dolly the sheep, Noori the pashmina goat and Garima the buffalo.

(d) Wrong. Disease-free organisms, especially plants, are produced by meristem culture and micropropagation, which is tissue culture. SCNT does not remove disease and instead copies the donor's genome.
keyfact: SCNT = somatic cell nucleus put into an enucleated egg; it is used for reproductive cloning of animals (Dolly, 1996).
option_notes: Biolarvicides are biological agents that kill mosquito and other insect larvae. Examples are Bacillus thuringiensis var. israelensis (Bti) and Bacillus sphaericus, and the fungus Beauveria bassiana is used as a biopesticide. They are used in vector control for malaria, dengue and filariasis. They are eco-friendly alternatives to chemical larvicides such as temephos. Gambusia and Guppy fish are also used as biological control agents of larvae.

Biodegradable plastics are polymers that microbes can break down. Examples are PHA and PHB (polyhydroxyalkanoates, made by bacteria such as Ralstonia eutropha or Alcaligenes), PLA (polylactic acid, from fermented corn starch) and starch blends. They reduce plastic pollution, but they need suitable composting conditions. They are made by industrial biotechnology and fermentation, not by cloning. India has Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, with later amendments.

Reproductive cloning creates a genetically near-identical copy of an animal. SCNT is used, and the embryo is implanted in a surrogate. Dolly the sheep (1996) was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. India's examples: Garima, a buffalo calf cloned at NDRI Karnal in 2009, and Noori, a pashmina goat cloned at SKUAST Srinagar in 2012. Others: Snuppy the dog (2005) and the macaques Zhong Zhong and Hua Hua (2018). Mitochondrial DNA comes from the egg, so the clone is not perfectly identical.

Producing organisms free of disease is done mainly in plants by meristem culture. The apical meristem is usually virus-free, so it can be grown in vitro to give healthy plantlets by micropropagation. This is used for banana, sugarcane, potato and orchids. It is based on plant totipotency, a concept associated with Haberlandt, and on tissue culture methods developed by Skoog and Miller. It is not an application of SCNT.
related: Dolly the sheep was born on 5 July 1996 at the Roslin Institute and was cloned by SCNT.
Garima, the first cloned buffalo calf in India, was born at NDRI Karnal in 2009.
Noori, a cloned pashmina goat, was born at SKUAST Srinagar in 2012.
Therapeutic cloning derives embryonic stem cells and does not involve implantation.
iPSCs were discovered by Shinya Yamanaka in 2006, and the 2012 Nobel Prize was shared with John Gurdon.
Bt israelensis is a microbial larvicide against mosquito larvae.
Meristem culture produces virus-free plants.
The GEAC under MoEFCC regulates GM organisms in India.
summary: The answer is (c). Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer (SCNT) puts the nucleus of a body (somatic) cell into an enucleated egg cell. This can produce a cloned embryo, which is the basis of reproductive cloning of animals, as with Dolly the sheep.
topic_notes: Cloning is the production of genetically identical copies of cells, tissues or organisms. Natural clones include identical twins and asexual reproduction. In SCNT, a somatic cell nucleus is injected into an enucleated oocyte and activated to form an embryo. There are two uses. In reproductive cloning the embryo is implanted in a surrogate uterus, giving a living clone. In therapeutic cloning the blastocyst is used to derive embryonic stem cells that are genetically matched to the patient, for regenerative medicine, and no pregnancy is established. Dolly (Roslin Institute and PPL Therapeutics, 1996) was cloned from a mammary gland cell of a Finn Dorset ewe, using a Scottish Blackface surrogate. She died in 2003 of a lung disease, after developing arthritis. Other cloned animals include the mouse Cumulina (1997), Snuppy the Afghan hound (2005, Seoul National University), the camel Injaz (Dubai, 2009), Garima (NDRI Karnal, 2009), Noori (SKUAST-Kashmir, 2012) and the macaques Zhong Zhong and Hua Hua (2018, China). Shinya Yamanaka's iPSCs (2006) and John Gurdon's nuclear transfer in frogs earned the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Human reproductive cloning is banned in most countries. In India, ICMR's National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research prohibit human reproductive cloning. Other angles for UPSC include stem cell types (totipotent, pluripotent, multipotent), CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, transgenic animals, gene therapy, DNA fingerprinting, tissue culture, and the Biological Diversity Act and the GEAC for GM organisms.

ocr: Consider the following statements : 82. 1. National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). helps in promoting the financial inclusion in the country. 2. NPCI has launched RuPay, a card payment scheme. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) lonly (b) 2only (ec) Both 1and2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 83.
subject: Economy
detail: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) was set up in 2008 as an initiative of the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. It is a not-for-profit company incorporated under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013). Its job is to run retail payment and settlement systems in India. Its products include RuPay (domestic card network, launched 2012), IMPS (2010), NACH, AePS, the National Financial Switch (NFS, taken over from IDRBT in 2009), UPI (2016), BHIM app, Bharat BillPay, NETC (FASTag) and the CTS cheque clearing system. Many of these products serve unbanked and rural users at low cost, so NPCI directly advances financial inclusion. RuPay was designed as an Indian alternative to Visa and MasterCard, and the name combines 'Rupee' and 'Payment'. It underpins PMJDY debit cards. Elimination logic: once you know that RuPay is an NPCI product, statement 2 is certainly correct, which removes (a) and (d). Statement 1 is also correct given NPCI's inclusion-focused products such as AePS, UPI and RuPay, which removes (b). Only (c) is left.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 2 is also correct. NPCI launched RuPay, so '1 only' leaves out a true statement.
(b) is wrong because statement 1 is also correct. NPCI's products promote financial inclusion, so '2 only' leaves out a true statement.
(c) is correct because both statements are true: NPCI promotes financial inclusion and launched the RuPay card scheme. This matches the official UPSC answer.
(d) is wrong because at least one statement, and in fact both, are correct, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: NPCI (2008, RBI + IBA, Section 8 company) runs RuPay (2012), IMPS, UPI, NACH and AePS, and supports financial inclusion.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would mean NPCI promotes financial inclusion but did not launch RuPay. That is false. RuPay, launched in 2012, is NPCI's flagship domestic card scheme. NPCI is an umbrella body for retail payments, set up in 2008 by the RBI and IBA, which is why RuPay and several other payment systems all sit under it.

Option (b), '2 only', would mean NPCI launched RuPay but plays no role in financial inclusion. That is false. NPCI's AePS, UPI, IMPS, NACH and the RuPay cards issued under PMJDY all aim at wider inclusion. Financial inclusion means affordable access to banking, credit, insurance and payments for all, especially weaker sections and rural areas, and NPCI's low-cost interoperable systems serve this goal.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', is the correct answer. It reflects that NPCI is the RBI- and IBA-promoted umbrella body for retail payments, formed in 2008 as a Section 25 (now Section 8) not-for-profit company. It operates RuPay (2012), IMPS, UPI (2016), NACH, AePS, NFS, Bharat BillPay and FASTag. Its subsidiary NIPL handles international expansion of UPI and RuPay.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', would deny both facts and is wrong. Both statements are factually true. This option is a typical distractor that tests whether the student knows NPCI's role in the payments ecosystem. NPCI works under RBI oversight and regulation as a Payment System Operator authorised under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.
related: NPCI was set up in 2008 by the RBI and IBA under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.
RuPay was launched in 2012 as India's domestic alternative to Visa and MasterCard.
UPI was launched in April 2016 and is built on IMPS.
IMPS provides 24x7 instant interbank mobile payments, launched in 2010.
RTGS and NEFT are operated by the RBI, not NPCI.
AePS uses Aadhaar authentication for banking through business correspondents.
NIPL is NPCI's international arm, set up in 2020 to expand UPI and RuPay abroad.
NPCI is a Section 8 (earlier Section 25) not-for-profit company headquartered in Mumbai.
statements: 1 — Correct: NPCI promotes financial inclusion through low-cost, interoperable products such as UPI, IMPS, AePS, RuPay and NACH. NPCI was incorporated in December 2008 and received RBI authorisation in 2009 as a payment system operator. Its promoter banks initially included SBI, PNB, Canara Bank, Bank of Baroda, BoI, Union Bank, ICICI, HDFC and Citibank, and the shareholder base was later widened. Headquartered in Mumbai, it is a not-for-profit Section 8 company. It also runs NFS, which connects ATMs across banks, and AePS, which allows Aadhaar-based banking through micro-ATMs and business correspondents. These tools extend banking to rural and unbanked citizens, supporting schemes such as PMJDY and DBT.

2 — Correct: RuPay is India's indigenous card payment network, launched by NPCI in 2012 (first transaction in March 2012, formal launch 26 March 2012) as a rival to Visa and MasterCard. Its name blends 'Rupee' and 'Payment'. RuPay cards are issued by banks as debit, credit and prepaid cards, and over 20 crore PMJDY accounts were given RuPay debit cards with built-in accident insurance. It reduces the cost of processing domestic transactions and keeps data within India. RuPay has also gone global through tie-ups with Discover/Diners Club, JCB and networks in Singapore, UAE, Bhutan, Nepal and others. It also supports contactless payments, NCMC (the National Common Mobility Card) and RuPay Select/Platinum variants.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. NPCI is the umbrella organisation for retail payments in India and promotes financial inclusion through products like UPI, IMPS, AePS and NACH, and it launched the RuPay domestic card payment scheme in 2012.
topic_notes: NPCI was formed in 2008 by the RBI, with the IBA as partner, under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. It is a Section 8 not-for-profit company headquartered in Mumbai. Its purpose is to create a robust, low-cost, interoperable retail payments and settlement infrastructure. Core products: (1) RuPay, the domestic card network launched in 2012; (2) IMPS, the 24x7 instant interbank mobile payment service launched in 2010; (3) NFS, the ATM switch network; (4) NACH, for bulk and recurring payments such as salaries, subsidies and EMIs; (5) AePS, Aadhaar-enabled payments through business correspondents; (6) UPI, launched in April 2016, which allows instant real-time payments through virtual payment addresses and has become the world's largest real-time payment system by volume; (7) BHIM, the app launched in December 2016; (8) Bharat BillPay (BBPS); (9) NETC/FASTag for tolls; (10) CTS, the Cheque Truncation System; (11) NCMC, the common mobility card; (12) e-RUPI, a prepaid voucher. NPCI International Payments Limited (NIPL), set up in 2020, takes UPI and RuPay abroad, with links to Singapore (PayNow), Bhutan, Nepal, UAE, France and others. Related bodies and concepts: the RBI is the regulator; the Payments Council of India; the Payments Regulatory Board; the Payment Systems Vision documents; RTGS and NEFT are run by the RBI, not NPCI. PMJDY (2014) gave RuPay debit cards to account holders. UPSC may ask who regulates payment systems, which system is run by whom, the full forms (UPI, IMPS, AePS, NACH), and the features of UPI such as its Virtual Payment Address and its 2-factor authentication with a UPI PIN.

question: The term ‘M-STrIPES’ is sometimes seen in the news in the context of
subject: Environment
detail: M-STrIPES is a mobile and GIS-based monitoring system developed by the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) with the Wildlife Institute of India, Dehradun, and launched in 2010 in Corbett Tiger Reserve. Forest guards carry GPS-enabled devices on patrols and record tiger sightings, signs such as pugmarks and scat, prey, human disturbance, poaching evidence and fire incidents. The data is uploaded to a central system, where it is mapped and analysed to plan patrol routes and management action. It supports the all-India tiger estimation exercise, which is conducted every four years, and is used in reserves under Project Tiger (launched 1973). The NTCA is a statutory body created under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 through the 2006 amendment. Elimination: captive breeding is linked to zoos and the Central Zoo Authority; the indigenous satellite navigation system is NavIC/IRNSS run by ISRO; national highway security is the concern of NHAI and the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. The 'Tr' and 'Tigers' in the expansion point directly to tiger conservation.
explanations: Incorrect: captive breeding of wild fauna is the domain of zoos, the Central Zoo Authority and ex-situ programmes. M-STrIPES monitors tigers in the wild.
Correct: M-STrIPES is the NTCA's monitoring system for protecting tigers and managing habitat in tiger reserves.
Incorrect: India's indigenous satellite navigation system is NavIC (IRNSS) from ISRO, not M-STrIPES.
Incorrect: National highway security is not related to this system. It has no link with NHAI or road security.
keyfact: M-STrIPES = NTCA's GPS-based Monitoring System for Tigers: Intensive Protection and Ecological Status, launched in 2010 for tiger reserves.
option_notes: Captive breeding means breeding wild animals under human care, in zoos or breeding centres, as ex-situ conservation. In India the Central Zoo Authority (set up in 1992 under the Wildlife Protection Act) regulates zoos and coordinates breeding programmes for species such as the Asiatic lion, the pygmy hog (Assam) and the gharial. Programmes often aim at reintroduction. It contrasts with in-situ conservation in national parks and reserves.

Tiger reserves are protected areas managed under Project Tiger (launched 1973) and governed by the NTCA, with a core or critical tiger habitat and a buffer zone. India had 53 tiger reserves by 2023 and holds about 70 percent of the world's wild tigers. The 2022 census estimated about 3,167 tigers. Maintenance covers anti-poaching patrols, habitat management, relocation of villages and monitoring through M-STrIPES and camera traps.

NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation), earlier called IRNSS, is India's regional navigation satellite system built by ISRO. It has seven satellites, with the first, IRNSS-1A, launched in 2013. It covers India and a region extending about 1,500 km beyond its borders. It provides a Standard Positioning Service and a restricted service for strategic users. It is India's counterpart to the American GPS, Russian GLONASS and European Galileo.

The security and management of national highways falls to the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), formed in 1988 and operating under the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. It handles construction, tolling (FASTag), and the Highway Patrol and Incident Management systems. Programmes include Bharatmala and the National Highways Development Project. None of these use the M-STrIPES name, which belongs to wildlife protection.
related: Project Tiger was launched in 1973; the first reserve was Corbett.
NTCA became a statutory body in 2006 through an amendment to the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
M-STrIPES was launched in 2010 and is developed with the Wildlife Institute of India.
The 2022 tiger estimate was about 3,167; Madhya Pradesh has the highest count.
Tiger estimation is held every four years.
International Big Cat Alliance was launched in 2023 at Mysuru.
NavIC is India's indigenous regional satellite navigation system by ISRO.
Global Tiger Day is observed on 29 July.
summary: The answer is (b) Maintenance of Tiger Reserves. M-STrIPES (Monitoring System for Tigers: Intensive Protection and Ecological Status) is a software-based monitoring system launched by the NTCA in 2010 to strengthen tiger protection and track patrolling and ecological data in tiger reserves.
topic_notes: Project Tiger was launched on 1 April 1973 with nine reserves, with Corbett National Park, Uttarakhand, as the first. It is a centrally sponsored scheme under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. The NTCA became statutory in 2006 through an amendment to the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and it is chaired by the Union Environment Minister. Tiger reserves have a core or critical tiger habitat, which is inviolate, and a buffer zone allowing regulated use. The Tiger Task Force of 2005 was formed after the Sariska tiger losses. The M-STrIPES software supports field monitoring, using GPS patrol tracking. The all-India tiger estimation is held every four years, using camera traps and capture-recapture methods. It is carried out by the NTCA, the Wildlife Institute of India and state forest departments. The estimates were 1,411 (2006), 1,706 (2010), 2,226 (2014), 2,967 (2018) and at least 3,167 (2022). Madhya Pradesh has the most tigers (785 in 2022), followed by Karnataka and Uttarakhand. Related international frameworks include the Global Tiger Forum, the St Petersburg Declaration of 2010 (Tx2, doubling tigers by 2022) and the TX2 goal, which India met early in 2018. The Global Tiger Day is 29 July. International Big Cat Alliance was launched in April 2023 at Mysuru, on the 50th anniversary of Project Tiger. The Tiger Conservation Foundation exists for each reserve. Other monitoring tools are camera traps, the Tigernet portal, and the CAT (Conservation Assured Tiger Standards) accreditation, which sets management standards for reserves. Other species programmes include Project Elephant (1992), Project Snow Leopard (2009) and Project Cheetah (2022).

ocr: What is/are the most likely advantages of implementing ‘Goods and Services Tax (GSTY? 1. It will replace multiple taxes collected by multiple authorities and will thus create a single market in India. 2. It will drastically reduce the ‘Current | 84- Account Deficit’ of India and will enable it to increase its foreign exchange reserves. 8. It will enormously increase the growth and size of economy of India and will enable it to overtake China in the near future. Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) lonly (b) 2and 3 only (c) land3 only (d) 1,2and3 ‘Broad-based Trade and Inv
subject: Economy
detail: GST was introduced from 1 July 2017 through the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, which inserted Article 246A (concurrent power of Centre and states to tax goods and services), Article 269A (IGST on inter-state supplies) and Article 279A (GST Council), and omitted Article 268A. It is a destination-based, multi-stage tax with input tax credit, levied as CGST, SGST/UTGST and IGST. It subsumed central excise duty, service tax, additional customs duty (CVD/SAD), VAT, entry tax, octroi, luxury tax and others. Its chief advantages are removal of cascading (tax on tax), a uniform tax structure, fewer check-posts and smoother inter-state movement of goods, and better compliance through the GSTN, all of which create a single common market. Statement 2 is wrong because the Current Account Deficit depends on trade balance, oil prices, remittances and capital flows, so GST cannot 'drastically' reduce it. Statement 3 is wrong because the 'overtake China' claim is speculative and exaggerated. In UPSC questions, extreme words like 'drastically', 'enormously' and 'overtake China' signal incorrect statements. Only statement 1 survives, so the answer is (a).
explanations: Correct: only statement 1 states a direct, accepted advantage of GST, namely subsuming many taxes and creating a single market.
Incorrect: it includes statement 2 and 3, both of which are exaggerated or unrelated to the direct effects of GST.
Incorrect: it includes statement 3, a speculative claim about overtaking China, and omits the correct statement 1.
Incorrect: statements 2 and 3 are overstated, so 1, 2 and 3 together cannot be correct.
keyfact: GST (101st Amendment, effective 1 July 2017, Arts. 246A/269A/279A) creates one national market by subsuming many indirect taxes; it is not a cure for the CAD or a route to overtaking China.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only: this is the official answer, since statement 1 describes GST's core benefit of one common national market. Statements 2 and 3 use extreme wording ('drastically', 'enormously', 'overtake China'). GST came through the 101st Amendment, with Articles 246A, 269A and 279A added, and operates through the GST Council and GSTN.

Option (b) 2 and 3 only: this would make both overstated claims correct and exclude the true statement. The CAD is a balance of payments concept affected by oil, gold and capital flows, not tax design. Growth depends on investment, productivity and demand; GST gives only a moderate gain, estimated at 1 to 2 percent of GDP.

Option (c) 1 and 3 only: this includes the true statement 1 but wrongly adds the claim of overtaking China. India's GDP is far below China's, and no single tax reform can guarantee overtaking it. China has had a VAT since 1994, and its economy is roughly five times India's in nominal terms.

Option (d) 1, 2 and 3: this accepts all statements, which ignores the exaggerated wording of 2 and 3. UPSC often uses absolute terms to mark wrong statements. GST helps efficiency and compliance, and may help exports via input tax credit refunds, but it does not by itself fix the CAD or ensure overtaking China.
related: GST was launched on 1 July 2017 following the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016.
Article 279A provides for the GST Council; Article 246A gives concurrent taxing power on GST.
Article 269A governs IGST on inter-state trade, levied and collected by the Centre.
Petrol, diesel, crude, natural gas and ATF remain outside GST; alcohol for human consumption is also outside.
GST Council decisions need three-fourths majority of weighted votes; the Centre holds one-third weight.
GST is destination-based, unlike the earlier origin-based Central Sales Tax.
BTIA (the other question on the page) refers to negotiations between India and the European Union.
The GST compensation cess funded state compensation for five years, up to June 2022.
statements: 1 — Correct: GST replaces many indirect taxes levied by the Centre and states and so builds a unified national market. GST is a destination-based, value-added tax on supply of goods and services, with input tax credit across the chain. Launched 1 July 2017 at midnight in Central Hall of Parliament. Dual structure: CGST and SGST on intra-state supply, IGST on inter-state supply. Petroleum crude, diesel, petrol, natural gas, ATF and (initially) alcohol for human consumption are outside GST. The GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister, decides rates and rules. Standard slabs were 0, 5, 12, 18 and 28 percent, with compensation cess on demerit goods.

2 — Incorrect: GST cannot be expected to drastically cut the Current Account Deficit or raise forex reserves. The CAD is the excess of imports of goods, services and transfers over exports, measured against GDP. It is driven by crude oil prices, gold imports, export competitiveness, remittances and services exports. Forex reserves are affected by capital inflows (FDI, FPI), the trade balance and RBI operations. GST may indirectly help exports through refund of input taxes and zero-rating of exports, but the effect is modest and indirect. India's CAD peaked at about 4.8 percent of GDP in 2012-13 during the taper tantrum period.

3 — Incorrect: The claim that GST will enormously increase growth and let India overtake China soon is speculative and exaggerated. Studies had estimated a gain of roughly 1 to 2 percent of GDP from GST over time, which is moderate. China is much larger in nominal GDP, about five times India's, and has a VAT-based system since 1994. India became the fifth-largest economy by nominal GDP around 2022 and is among the fastest-growing major economies, but overtaking China depends on many factors including investment, manufacturing, productivity and demographics, not on one tax reform.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. GST subsumes many central and state indirect taxes into one destination-based tax, creating a unified national market. Claims that it will drastically cut the Current Account Deficit or help India overtake China are speculative and not its direct advantages.
topic_notes: GST is India's biggest indirect tax reform. Constitutional basis: the 122nd Amendment Bill became the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, which received assent on 8 September 2016. It inserted Article 246A, Article 269A (IGST, collected by the Centre and apportioned), Article 279A (GST Council) and Article 366(12A) and 366(26A) definitions, and omitted Article 268A. Launch date was 1 July 2017. The GST Council is a constitutional body chaired by the Union Finance Minister, with the Union MoS Finance and state finance ministers as members. Decisions need three-fourths of the weighted votes, where the Centre has one-third weight and states together two-thirds. Four laws: CGST Act, IGST Act, UTGST Act and the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017, plus state SGST Acts. States were promised compensation for revenue loss for five years, up to June 2022, at 14 percent annual growth over the 2015-16 base, funded by the compensation cess. GSTN is a non-profit company that runs the IT backbone. Taxes subsumed: central excise, service tax, CVD, SAD, central surcharges and cesses, state VAT, entry tax, octroi, luxury tax, purchase tax and taxes on lottery and betting. Exclusions: alcohol for human consumption, and petroleum products (crude, petrol, diesel, ATF, natural gas) pending Council decision; electricity and stamp duty are also outside. Features include input tax credit, the composition scheme for small taxpayers, the e-way bill, anti-profiteering authority and the reverse charge mechanism. Kelkar Task Force and the Asim Dasgupta committee were early drivers. Other angles: GST in other countries, such as the French first adoption in 1954, Canada's dual GST/HST model, and Australia and New Zealand's single-rate systems. India's dual model resembles Canada's.

ocr: Consider the following statements : a India has ratified the Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) of WTO. 2. TFA is a part of WTO’s Bali Ministerial Package of 2013. 3. TFA came into force in January 2016. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) land 2 only (b) 1and3 only (ec) 2and3 only (d) .1,2and3 What is the importance of developing Chabahar Port by India ? (a) India’s trade with African countries will enormously increase. (b) India’s relations with oil-producing Arab countries will be strengthened. (¢). India will not depend on Pakistan for access to Afghanistan and Central
subject: Economy
detail: The Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) aims to speed up the movement, release and clearance of goods, including goods in transit, and to improve customs cooperation. It cuts red tape and makes procedures transparent. It was negotiated and concluded at the 9th WTO Ministerial Conference in Bali, Indonesia (3-7 December 2013) as part of the Bali Package. The package also covered agriculture (public stockholding for food security, the 'peace clause', general services), cotton and LDC issues. Because the TFA needed an amendment to the WTO rules, the Protocol of Amendment was adopted by the General Council in November 2014 and then opened for acceptance. The TFA could enter into force only after two-thirds of members (110 at the time) ratified it. India deposited its instrument of acceptance in April 2016, and the threshold was reached on 22 February 2017. It was the first multilateral trade agreement concluded since the WTO was created in 1995. Elimination logic: statement 1 is true and statement 2 is true, so any option that excludes either is wrong. Statement 3 is false because the date is February 2017. That removes (b), (c) and (d), leaving (a).
explanations: Correct. Statements 1 and 2 are true, and statement 3 is false because the TFA came into force in February 2017.
Incorrect. It treats statement 3 as true, but the TFA did not come into force in January 2016, so this option wrongly includes it.
Incorrect. It wrongly excludes statement 1, although India did ratify the TFA in April 2016, and it wrongly includes statement 3.
Incorrect. It says all three statements are true, but statement 3 has the wrong date (the TFA took effect on 22 February 2017).
keyfact: TFA: concluded at Bali (Dec 2013), India ratified April 2016, in force 22 Feb 2017, the WTO's first multilateral agreement since 1995.
related: The TFA was concluded at the WTO's 9th Ministerial Conference in Bali in December 2013.
The TFA entered into force on 22 February 2017 after two-thirds of members ratified it.
India ratified the TFA in April 2016.
The TFA was the first multilateral trade agreement since the WTO was founded in 1995.
India's National Committee on Trade Facilitation (NCTF) is chaired by the Cabinet Secretary.
TFA implementation commitments are classified into Categories A, B and C.
The Nairobi Ministerial (MC10, 2015) agreed to abolish agricultural export subsidies.
The WTO Fisheries Subsidies Agreement was adopted at MC12 in Geneva in June 2022.
statements: 1 — Correct: India ratified the TFA in April 2016 (it was around the 76th member to do so). The TFA is the WTO's first multilateral agreement since 1995 and covers customs and border procedures. India set up a National Committee on Trade Facilitation (NCTF), headed by the Cabinet Secretary, to implement it. It notified its commitments under Categories A (immediate implementation), B (after a transition period) and C (after a transition period plus capacity-building support). Measures include advance rulings, a Single Window, risk management, pre-arrival processing, and faster release of perishables. The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) leads on implementation.

2 — Correct: The TFA is part of the Bali Package adopted at the 9th WTO Ministerial Conference (MC9) in Bali, Indonesia, 3-7 December 2013. The package had three main strands: trade facilitation, agriculture (food-security stockholding with a 'peace clause' protecting developing-country programmes, plus general services and tariff-quota administration) and LDC issues (including cotton and duty-free access). India linked its TFA support to a permanent solution on public stockholding. In November 2014 India and the US reached an understanding that unblocked the TFA protocol. MC10 was held in Nairobi (2015) and MC11 in Buenos Aires (2017).

3 — Incorrect: The TFA entered into force on 22 February 2017, not in January 2016. Entry into force required acceptance by two-thirds of WTO members (110 of 164). The Protocol of Amendment inserting the TFA into Annex 1A of the WTO Agreement was adopted in November 2014. Rwanda, Hong Kong, Singapore, Mauritius and the US were among the early ratifiers, and India ratified in April 2016. After entry into force, a WTO Committee on Trade Facilitation was established. The Trade Facilitation Agreement Facility (TFAF) helps developing countries and LDCs with implementation.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 and 2 only. India ratified the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement in April 2016, and the TFA is part of the Bali Package of December 2013. It did not come into force in January 2016. It entered into force on 22 February 2017, once two-thirds of WTO members had ratified it.
topic_notes: The WTO, set up on 1 January 1995 and headquartered in Geneva, replaced GATT. Its highest body is the Ministerial Conference, which meets at least every two years. Ministerial conferences: Singapore 1996, Geneva 1998, Seattle 1999 (failed), Doha 2001 (launch of the Doha Development Agenda), Cancun 2003, Hong Kong 2005, Geneva 2009, Geneva 2011, Bali 2013 (MC9), Nairobi 2015 (MC10), Buenos Aires 2017 (MC11), Geneva 2022 (MC12), Abu Dhabi 2024 (MC13). The Bali Package (2013) was the first significant multilateral outcome since the WTO was created. Its TFA part streamlines customs procedures. The agreement has two sections. Section I contains the technical provisions, such as publication and availability of information, advance rulings, appeal procedures, fees and charges, release and clearance of goods, border agency cooperation, transit and customs cooperation. Section II contains special and differential treatment, through Categories A, B and C. The 2013 agriculture decision on public stockholding (PSH) was important for India's food security programmes. It offered an interim 'peace clause' that protects developing countries from legal challenge if they exceed the subsidy limits. India wanted a permanent solution, and this remains unresolved. At Nairobi in 2015 members agreed to abolish agricultural export subsidies. At MC12 (2022) members concluded an agreement on fisheries subsidies, and it needs two-thirds acceptance to enter into force. The Dispute Settlement Body's Appellate Body has been non-functional since December 2019 because the US has blocked appointments. India's domestic measures on trade facilitation include the Single Window Interface for Facilitating Trade (SWIFT), the National Trade Facilitation Action Plan, the Customs Faceless Assessment initiative and the Indian Customs Electronic Gateway (ICEGATE). Other angles UPSC could ask: India's tariff policy, Trade Policy Review, GATT versus WTO, the Agreement on Agriculture, TRIPS, and the 'Green Box' and 'Amber Box' subsidy categories.

TFA came into force in January 2016. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) land 2 only (b) 1and3 only (ec) 2and3 only (d) .1,2and3 What is the importance of developing Chabahar Port by India ? (a) India’s trade with African countries will enormously increase. (b) India’s relations with oil-producing Arab countries will be strengthened. (¢). India will not depend on Pakistan for access to Afghanistan and Central
subject: Economy
detail: The TFA aims to speed up the movement, release and clearance of goods across borders, cut red tape and improve transparency. It was concluded at the 9th WTO Ministerial Conference in Bali in December 2013. Because it was a new agreement, it needed a Protocol of Amendment to insert it into Annex 1A of the WTO Agreement. The General Council adopted that Protocol in November 2014. Under Article X:3 of the Marrakesh Agreement, the amendment takes effect only after two-thirds of members (110 of 164) accept it. That threshold was reached on 22 February 2017, which is when the TFA came into force. India deposited its instrument of acceptance on 22 April 2016, becoming the 76th member to do so. Elimination logic: statement 3 gives January 2016, which is before the two-thirds ratification was even close, so it is wrong. Any option containing 3 (b, c, d) is therefore out, leaving (a). Statements 1 and 2 are both verifiably true. The TFA was the first multilateral trade agreement concluded since the WTO was created in 1995.
explanations: Correct. Statements 1 and 2 are true and statement 3 is false, so '1 and 2 only' is right. This matches the official answer.
Incorrect. It includes statement 3, which gives the wrong date. The TFA came into force on 22 February 2017.
Incorrect. It leaves out statement 1 (India ratified in April 2016) and includes the false statement 3.
Incorrect. Statement 3 is false, so 'all three' cannot be right.
keyfact: TFA: agreed at Bali (Dec 2013), India ratified April 2016, in force 22 Feb 2017 (the first multilateral WTO-era agreement).
related: TFA was concluded at the WTO's 9th Ministerial Conference, Bali, December 2013.
TFA entered into force on 22 February 2017 after ratification by two-thirds of WTO members.
India ratified the TFA in April 2016 and set up a National Committee on Trade Facilitation.
TFA categories: A (immediate), B (after a transition period), C (after a transition period with capacity-building support).
The Bali Package's agriculture pillar included the 'peace clause' on public stockholding for food security.
Nairobi Ministerial (MC10, 2015) agreed to abolish agricultural export subsidies.
The WTO was established on 1 January 1995 and is headquartered in Geneva.
Amendments to WTO agreements need two-thirds acceptance under Article X of the Marrakesh Agreement.
statements: 1 — Correct: India ratified the TFA on 22 April 2016. India formally notified its acceptance of the Protocol of Amendment, becoming the 76th WTO member to do so. It had earlier pushed to link trade facilitation with food security (public stockholding) before agreeing in November 2014. Domestically, a National Committee on Trade Facilitation (NCTF) under the Cabinet Secretary was set up to implement the agreement. India notified its Category A commitments and has since implemented measures such as the Single Window Interface for Facilitating Trade (SWIFT), faster customs clearance and advance rulings.

2 — Correct: The TFA is a core part of the Bali Ministerial Package, adopted at the 9th WTO Ministerial Conference (MC9) in Bali, Indonesia, in December 2013. The package had three main pillars: trade facilitation, agriculture (including the public stockholding issue and the 'peace clause' for developing countries' food security programmes), and development/LDC issues (including cotton and preferential access). The TFA was the only legally binding outcome. The conference was chaired by Indonesia's trade minister Gita Wirjawan, and Director-General Roberto Azevêdo was prominent in brokering the deal.

3 — Incorrect: The TFA did not enter into force in January 2016. It entered into force on 22 February 2017, when Rwanda, Oman, Chad and Jordan deposited their acceptances and the two-thirds threshold of 110 members was reached. The Protocol of Amendment was adopted in November 2014. Hong Kong, China was the first member to ratify, in December 2014. The Agreement has Sections I and II. Section II contains special and differential treatment, with Category A (immediate implementation), B (after a transition period) and C (after a transition period with capacity-building support). The Trade Facilitation Agreement Facility (TFAF) helps developing countries implement it.
summary: The answer is (a): statements 1 and 2 are correct and statement 3 is wrong. India ratified the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) in April 2016, and the TFA is part of the Bali Ministerial Package of December 2013. It entered into force on 22 February 2017, not in January 2016.
topic_notes: The Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) is a WTO agreement on simplifying and harmonising customs and border procedures. It was concluded at the Bali Ministerial (MC9), 3–7 December 2013, and adopted via a Protocol of Amendment by the General Council in November 2014. It entered into force on 22 February 2017 after two-thirds of members (110) had ratified it. It was the first multilateral agreement of the WTO era (since 1995). Key provisions: publication and availability of information, advance rulings, appeal procedures, fees and charges disciplines, release and clearance of goods, pre-arrival processing, risk management, authorised operators, border agency cooperation, freedom of transit, and a national committee on trade facilitation. Special and differential treatment: developing and least-developed members classify provisions into Categories A, B and C, and the agreement links implementation to capacity-building support. The Trade Facilitation Agreement Facility (TFAF), launched in 2014, supports this. The WTO estimates full implementation could cut trade costs by around 14% on average and raise global trade substantially. India's interest was to link the TFA with a permanent solution on public stockholding for food security. Agreement was reached in November 2014 through a US–India understanding, and the 'peace clause' protects such programmes until a permanent solution is found. India's institutional steps include the National Committee on Trade Facilitation, the Single Window Interface for Facilitating Trade (SWIFT), the National Trade Facilitation Action Plan, and the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) reforms. Related ministerials: MC10 in Nairobi (2015) abolished agricultural export subsidies, and MC11 in Buenos Aires (2017) produced little. Other angles for the exam include the WTO's structure, dispute settlement, the Information Technology Agreement, the Doha Development Agenda, the Green Box and AMS, and TRIPS.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q84.
ocr: Consider the following statements : a India has ratified the Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) of WTO. 2. TFA is a part of WTO’s Bali Ministerial Package of 2013. 3. TFA came into force in January 2016. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) land 2 only (b) 1and3 only (ec) 2and3 only (d) .1,2and3 What is the importance of developing Chabahar Port by India ? (a) India’s trade with African countries will enormously increase. (b) India’s relations with oil-producing Arab countries will be strengthened. (¢). India will not depend on Pakistan for access to Afghanistan and Central
subject: Economy
detail: Chabahar port is in Sistan-Baluchestan province, Iran, on the Gulf of Oman, outside the Strait of Hormuz. India's interest is strategic connectivity. Pakistan does not allow India land transit to Afghanistan, so Indian goods cannot go through Wagah-Attari to Kabul. Chabahar, linked to Afghanistan by the Zaranj-Delaram highway that India built in 2009, gives an alternative route. It also links to the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) running to Russia and Europe via the Caspian. In May 2016 India, Iran and Afghanistan signed a trilateral transit agreement during PM Modi's Tehran visit. India Ports Global Ltd (IPGL) operates the Shahid Beheshti terminal, and a 10-year contract was signed in May 2024. The port is also seen as a counter to Chinese-run Gwadar in Pakistan, about 170 km away. Elimination: (a) African trade is served by west-coast Indian ports and does not depend on Chabahar.
