(b) Relations with Arab oil producers are not the main purpose, and Iran is not an Arab country. (d) Pakistan has no role in Chabahar and has never agreed to protect an Iraq-India pipeline, which does not exist. Only (c) states the core rationale.
explanations: Incorrect: Chabahar is mainly a gateway to Afghanistan and Central Asia. India's trade with Africa goes by sea from its west-coast ports, and Chabahar adds no 'enormous' increase.
Incorrect: Iran is Persian, not Arab, and India's ties with Gulf Arab oil producers rest on energy, diaspora and trade, not on Chabahar. This is at most a side effect, not the importance of the port.

Correct: Pakistan denies India overland transit to Afghanistan. Chabahar plus the Zaranj-Delaram road gives India a route to Afghanistan and Central Asia that avoids Pakistan. This is the official answer.
Incorrect: Pakistan is not a party to Chabahar. No Iraq-India gas pipeline is planned, and the proposed pipelines are Iran-Pakistan-India (IPI) and TAPI. The option is fictitious.
keyfact: Chabahar (Iran) lets India reach Afghanistan and Central Asia bypassing Pakistan, via the INSTC and the Zaranj-Delaram road.
option_notes: Trade with Africa: India trades with Africa mostly by sea from Mundra, Kandla, Mumbai (JNPT) and others. Africa's main trade partners for India are Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt and Angola. India-Africa Forum Summits (since 2008) guide the relationship, and India has pushed the Asia-Africa Growth Corridor with Japan. Chabahar is not a major route for African trade.

Relations with Arab oil producers: India imports crude mainly from Iraq, Saudi Arabia, UAE and Kuwait, and about 8-9 million Indians live in the Gulf Cooperation Council countries. The GCC has six members: Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain and Oman. Iran is not Arab and not in the GCC. India's 'Link West' policy covers Gulf ties, and Chabahar is not central to them.

Access to Afghanistan and Central Asia: Afghanistan is landlocked and Pakistan denies India transit. India built the 218 km Zaranj-Delaram highway (2009, by BRO), and Chabahar links to it. India sent wheat to Afghanistan via Chabahar in 2017. Central Asia is reached via INSTC. The trilateral India-Iran-Afghanistan agreement of May 2016 provided for about $500 million of Indian investment. This is the correct rationale.

Gas pipeline Iraq-India via Pakistan: no such project exists. The real proposals are the Iran-Pakistan-India (IPI) 'peace pipeline', which India left around 2009 over price and security concerns, and the Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan-India (TAPI) pipeline, about 1,814 km, whose construction began in Turkmenistan in 2015. India has also considered an undersea Oman-India pipeline.
related: Chabahar is in Sistan-Baluchestan, Iran, on the Gulf of Oman.
India-Iran-Afghanistan trilateral transit agreement was signed in May 2016 in Tehran.
India built the 218 km Zaranj-Delaram highway in Afghanistan.
INSTC links India, Iran and Russia, with Mumbai-Bandar Abbas-Caspian-Moscow as the core route.
Gwadar port in Pakistan is China-developed under CPEC.
India joined the Ashgabat Agreement on transit corridors in 2018.
The Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA) of the WTO came into force on 22 February 2017, and India ratified it in April 2016.
TAPI pipeline runs from Turkmenistan through Afghanistan and Pakistan to India.
summary: The answer is (c). Chabahar, on Iran's Makran coast, gives India a sea-plus-land route to Afghanistan and Central Asia that bypasses Pakistan, which has denied India overland transit. The other options are exaggerated or factually baseless.
topic_notes: Chabahar is Iran's only ocean port, on the Makran coast of Sistan-Baluchestan, with two terminals, Shahid Kalantari and Shahid Beheshti. India first proposed development in 2003 under the Vajpayee-Khatami agreement, but progress stalled because of sanctions on Iran. After the 2015 Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA), the May 2016 trilateral agreement was signed by India, Iran and Afghanistan, with India committing about $500 million. India Ports Global Ltd, a joint venture of the Deendayal Port Trust and Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust, began operating Shahid Beheshti in December 2018, and a 10-year contract was signed in May 2024. The US granted a sanctions exemption for Chabahar in 2018 because of its role in Afghan reconstruction, though later US policy shifts have created uncertainty. Linked projects: Zaranj-Delaram highway (218 km, India-built, inaugurated 2009), the Chabahar-Zahedan railway (IRCON), and the INSTC, a 7,200 km multimodal route among India, Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Central Asia and Europe that was launched in 2000 and reduces transit time and cost compared with the Suez route. Rival: Gwadar port in Pakistan, built by China under CPEC, about 170 km east. Geography: Chabahar is outside the Strait of Hormuz, so it is not a chokepoint risk. Other angles UPSC may ask: Iran's neighbours, Gulf of Oman and Strait of Hormuz, Afghanistan's land-locked status, India's Afghanistan projects (Salma Dam, now Afghan-India Friendship Dam, and the Parliament building in Kabul), Ashgabat Agreement (India joined 2018), Eurasian connectivity projects, and China's BRI.

question:
In India, it is legally mandatory for which of 88. the following to report on cyber security incidents ? Ls Service providers
2. Data centres
3. Body corporate Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Economy
detail: India's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) is the national agency for cyber security incidents. It was designated under Section 70B of the Information Technology Act, 2000, through the 2008 amendment, which came into force on 27 October 2009. Section 70B(6) empowers CERT-In to call for information from service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporate and any other person. Section 70B(7) penalises failure to provide information or comply with directions, with imprisonment up to one year, a fine up to Rs 1 lakh, or both. The Information Technology (The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team and Manner of Performing Functions and Duties) Rules, 2013 require these entities to report incidents 'as early as possible'. The Directions of 28 April 2022 tightened this to within 6 hours of noticing an incident. They also require logs to be kept for 180 days within India, and VPN providers, cloud providers and virtual asset service providers to maintain records. Because the statute names all three categories, none can be left out. That rules out (a), (b) and (c). Elimination logic: the moment you recall that 'service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporate' appear together in Section 70B(6), (d) is the only option that includes all three.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out data centres and body corporate, both of which are expressly named in Section 70B(6) of the IT Act.
Wrong: it omits body corporate, which is also covered by the reporting obligation under the IT Act and the CERT-In Rules.
Wrong: body corporate are covered, but so are service providers and data centres, so this option is incomplete.
Correct: service providers, data centres and body corporate are all legally obliged to report cyber security incidents to CERT-In.
keyfact: Section 70B(6) of the IT Act: service providers, intermediaries, data centres and body corporate must report cyber incidents to CERT-In, now within 6 hours.
option_notes: Option (a), service providers, means telecom operators, ISPs and other intermediaries as defined in Section 2(1)(w) of the IT Act. They are covered under Section 70B(6) and the CERT-In Rules, 2013. They must report cyber incidents, keep logs for 180 days under the 2022 Directions, and designate a point of contact. Intermediaries also get safe-harbour protection under Section 79 only if they observe due diligence. This option is incomplete because it covers only one category.

Option (b), service providers and data centres, lists two of the three categories. Data centres are facilities hosting servers, storage and networking equipment, including cloud infrastructure. Both categories are named in Section 70B(6), and the 2022 CERT-In Directions apply to them. The option is wrong only because it omits body corporate. Related policy: the National Data Centre Policy, and the MeitY data centre incentive framework, aim to expand India's data centre capacity.

Option (c), body corporate, means companies, firms, sole proprietorships and associations engaged in commercial or professional activity, as defined in Section 43A. They are liable to compensate for failure to protect sensitive personal data. They must also report incidents to CERT-In under Section 70B(6) and the 2013 Rules. The option is incomplete, since service providers and data centres are covered too.

Option (d), all three, is the official answer. Section 70B(6) lets CERT-In seek information from service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporate and any other person. Non-compliance is punishable under Section 70B(7) with up to one year's imprisonment, a fine up to Rs 1 lakh, or both. The 2022 Directions fixed a 6-hour reporting window. CERT-In functions under MeitY, and its Director General is the head.
related: CERT-In was designated under Section 70B of the IT Act, 2000.
The 2022 CERT-In Directions require incident reporting within 6 hours.
Logs must be maintained for 180 days within Indian jurisdiction.
NCIIPC was created under Section 70A and works under NTRO.
Section 66A of the IT Act was struck down in Shreya Singhal (2015).
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 sets up the Data Protection Board of India.
I4C (Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre) functions under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
India is not a signatory to the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime.
statements: 1 — Correct: Service providers are named in Section 70B(6) and in the CERT-In Rules, 2013 as entities obliged to report incidents. Service providers include telecom and internet service providers and other intermediaries as defined in Section 2(1)(w) of the IT Act. The 2022 Directions require them to report within 6 hours, synchronise system clocks to NIC or NPL time servers, and keep ICT logs for 180 days. They must also designate a point of contact for CERT-In. Failure to comply attracts penal consequences under Section 70B(7), and also under Section 44(b) for non-furnishing of information.

2 — Correct: Data centres are expressly listed in Section 70B(6) along with service providers, intermediaries and body corporate. A data centre is a facility housing computing and storage systems, including those of cloud providers. The 2022 Directions apply to data centres and cloud service providers, who must report incidents such as unauthorised access, data breaches, data leaks and attacks on servers. Data centres must also maintain logs in India for 180 days. CERT-In can seek information from them and issue binding directions during incident response.

3 — Correct: Body corporate is defined in Section 43A of the IT Act as any company, including a firm, sole proprietorship or other association of individuals engaged in commercial or professional activities. Section 70B(6) lets CERT-In call for information from body corporate. The 2013 Rules, and the 2022 Directions, require them to report incidents such as targeted scanning, compromise of critical systems, data breaches, identity theft, spoofing, phishing and attacks on IoT devices, applications, cloud systems and AI/ML systems. Section 43A also makes body corporate liable to pay compensation for negligence in protecting sensitive personal data.
summary: The answer is (d) 1, 2 and 3. Under Section 70B of the IT Act, 2000 and the CERT-In Rules, 2013, service providers, intermediaries, data centres and body corporates must report cyber security incidents to CERT-In. The 28 April 2022 Directions made the six-hour reporting window explicit.
topic_notes: CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team) is the nodal national agency for cyber security. It was set up in 2004 and operates under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY). It was given statutory backing by the IT (Amendment) Act, 2008, which inserted Section 70B and came into force on 27 October 2009. Its functions include collecting, analysing and disseminating information on cyber incidents, issuing alerts and advisories, emergency response, and coordinating incident response. The CERT-In Rules, 2013 detail how it performs these duties. The 28 April 2022 Directions under Section 70B(6) came into effect after 60 days, with a later extension for MSMEs. They require reporting within 6 hours, 180-day log retention in India, and KYC records for VPN and virtual asset service providers. Related bodies: the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC), set up in 2014 under Section 70A and housed in the NTRO, protects critical information infrastructure. The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) is under the MHA. The National Cyber Security Policy was issued in 2013. The National Cyber Security Coordinator sits in the National Security Council Secretariat. CSIRT-Fin handles the financial sector. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires data fiduciaries to notify the Data Protection Board and affected persons of breaches. Other IT Act provisions: Section 66 (computer-related offences), 66C (identity theft), 66D (cheating by personation), 66F (cyber terrorism), 67 (obscene material), 69 (interception and decryption powers), 69A (blocking), and Section 66A (struck down in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, 2015). The Budapest Convention is the international treaty on cybercrime, and India is not a signatory. Cyber Surakshit Bharat is a MeitY initiative.

question: Right to vote and to be elected in India is a
subject: Polity
detail: Rights are classified as natural, moral, fundamental, constitutional, legal (statutory) and human rights. A constitutional right is one conferred or recognised by the Constitution but not necessarily listed in Part III as a Fundamental Right. Article 326 provides that elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies shall be on the basis of adult suffrage, so every citizen aged 18 or above (lowered from 21 by the 61st Amendment, 1988, effective 1989) who is not disqualified is entitled to be registered as a voter. Article 324 vests superintendence of elections in the Election Commission. Article 327 empowers Parliament to legislate on elections, which is why the detailed rules on candidacy (qualifications, disqualifications, age 25 for Lok Sabha) sit in the RP Act, 1951. The Supreme Court in Jyoti Basu v. Debi Ghosal (1982), N.P. Ponnuswami (1952) and Kuldip Nayar (2006) held that the right to vote and to contest is a statutory or constitutional right, not a fundamental or common-law right. Elimination: (a) is garbled; (b) natural rights are inherent and not created by law; (d) legal is narrower, and the voting right is rooted in the Constitution itself. Hence (c).
explanations: (a) The option is garbled by OCR; it matches no recognised category of right and cannot be correct, and the official answer is (c).
(b) Incorrect. Natural rights are inherent to human beings, independent of the State or law. Voting is created and regulated by the Constitution and statutes.
(c) Correct. Article 326 guarantees adult suffrage, and Articles 324 and 327 set up the electoral machinery, so voting is a constitutional right (candidacy is regulated by statute).

(d) Incorrect as the best answer. Legal or statutory rights come purely from ordinary laws such as the RP Acts. The right to vote has its source in the Constitution, so 'constitutional' is the more precise choice.
keyfact: Right to vote: constitutional right under Article 326 (adult suffrage, age 18); right to contest is statutory under RP Act 1951; neither is a Fundamental Right.
option_notes: Option (a) is unreadable after OCR, so it is not a valid category. It was likely 'Fundamental Right' (Part III, Articles 12-35), which are justiciable rights enforceable under Article 32 and Article 226. Voting is not listed there; the Supreme Court has repeatedly said it is not a fundamental right.

Natural rights are those a person has by virtue of being human: life, liberty and property in John Locke's theory. They exist prior to the State and are not granted by it. Natural law ideas influenced the American Declaration of Independence (1776) and the French Declaration of the Rights of Man (1789). The Indian Constitution gives these rights legal form, for instance in Articles 14-21.

Constitutional rights are those given by the Constitution, including both Fundamental Rights and other provisions outside Part III such as Article 300A (property), Article 265 (no tax without law), Article 326 (adult suffrage) and Article 301 (freedom of trade). Their protection may differ: Article 32 applies only to Fundamental Rights. Amending them requires the Article 368 procedure.

Legal or statutory rights are created by ordinary legislation passed by Parliament or the State Legislatures and can be changed by a simple majority. Examples are the Right to Information (RTI Act 2005), the Right to Education (RTE Act 2009, though Article 21A is constitutional), the right to food (NFSA 2013) and election-related rights under the RP Acts 1950 and 1951.
related: Article 326: elections to Lok Sabha and Assemblies are on the basis of adult suffrage.
61st Amendment 1988 reduced the voting age from 21 to 18.
Article 324: Election Commission superintends, directs and controls elections.
Right to vote is a constitutional/statutory right, not a Fundamental Right (N.P. Ponnuswami, Kuldip Nayar).
Minimum age to contest: 25 years for Lok Sabha and Assembly, 30 years for Rajya Sabha.
Article 329 bars courts from interfering in electoral matters.
NOTA was introduced after the PUCL case (2013).
RP Act 1951 governs disqualifications, corrupt practices and election disputes.
summary: The answer is (c) Constitutional Right. The right to vote is granted by Article 326 of the Constitution (adult suffrage), though the right to be elected is statutory, under the Representation of the People Acts, 1950 and 1951. UPSC treats the answer as (c) because the right to vote has a direct constitutional basis and the electoral system is established by the Constitution.
topic_notes: Suffrage and elections form a key polity topic. Article 324 gives the Election Commission superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President. Article 325 prohibits exclusion from electoral rolls on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex. Article 326 provides adult suffrage; the voting age fell from 21 to 18 through the 61st Amendment (1988). Article 327 gives Parliament power over elections to legislatures, and Article 328 gives States similar power. Article 329 bars courts from interfering in electoral matters and provides that election disputes go through election petitions. The RP Act 1950 deals with delimitation, allocation of seats and preparation of electoral rolls; the RP Act 1951 covers conduct of elections, qualifications, disqualifications, corrupt practices and disputes. Qualifications for candidacy: age 25 for Lok Sabha and Assemblies, 30 for Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils. Section 8 of the 1951 Act disqualifies those convicted with a sentence of two years or more; Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013) struck down the protection for sitting members. In PUCL v. Union of India (2003), the Court held that the right to information about candidates is part of Article 19(1)(a), and in 2013 it introduced NOTA. In Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India (2006), the Court upheld removal of the domicile requirement for Rajya Sabha and an open ballot, stating that the right to vote is a statutory right. Anoop Baranwal (2023) set up a collegium for appointing Election Commissioners. The Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge. Other angles: EVMs and VVPAT, the Model Code of Conduct, delimitation commissions, and Tenth Schedule anti-defection law.

question: What is the purpose of ‘evolved Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (eLISA)’ project ?
options: To detect the effectiveness of missile defence system
To study the effect of solar flares on our communication systems
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime produced by accelerating massive objects such as merging black holes or neutron stars. Albert Einstein predicted them in 1916 in General Relativity. LIGO (USA) made the first direct detection on 14 September 2015 (announced 11 February 2016, from a binary black hole merger), and the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne. Ground detectors such as LIGO, Virgo (Italy), GEO600 (Germany) and KAGRA (Japan) are limited to high-frequency waves. LIGO-India is planned at Hingoli, Maharashtra. eLISA was the ESA-led concept of three spacecraft in a triangular formation with arms of about 1 million km, in a heliocentric orbit trailing Earth, to detect low-frequency waves from supermassive black holes. The mission is now called LISA, adopted by ESA in 2024 for a launch in the mid-2030s. LISA Pathfinder (launched December 2015) tested the technology. Elimination: neutrinos are detected by underground or ice detectors such as Super-Kamiokande and IceCube. Missile defence uses radars and interceptors. Solar flares are studied by solar observatories such as SOHO and Aditya-L1. The word 'Interferometer' points to gravitational waves.
explanations: Wrong. Neutrinos are detected by large underground, underwater or ice detectors (Super-Kamiokande, IceCube, India-based Neutrino Observatory proposal), not by a laser interferometer in space.
Correct. eLISA was designed to detect gravitational waves in the low-frequency band using laser interferometry between spacecraft.
Wrong. Missile defence effectiveness is tested with radars, interceptors and test ranges and has nothing to do with eLISA.
Wrong. Solar flare effects on communications are studied by solar and space-weather missions such as SOHO, SDO and Aditya-L1, not eLISA.
keyfact: eLISA (now LISA, ESA) is a space-based laser interferometer to detect low-frequency gravitational waves.
option_notes: Neutrinos are nearly massless, electrically neutral subatomic particles that rarely interact with matter. They are produced in the Sun, supernovae and nuclear reactions. Detectors include Super-Kamiokande (Japan), IceCube (Antarctica) and SNO (Canada). The India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) was proposed in the Theni district of Tamil Nadu. Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald won the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physics for neutrino oscillations, which show that neutrinos have mass.

Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime from accelerating massive bodies, predicted by Einstein in 1916. LIGO first detected them on 14 September 2015 (event GW150914, a binary black hole merger about 1.3 billion light-years away). Detectors include LIGO, Virgo, GEO600 and KAGRA. LIGO-India is planned at Hingoli, Maharashtra. The 2017 Nobel Prize went to Weiss, Barish and Thorne. eLISA/LISA is the space-based version, led by ESA.

Missile defence systems detect, track and intercept incoming ballistic missiles. Examples are the US THAAD and Patriot, Israel's Iron Dome and Arrow, Russia's S-400 (which India has bought) and India's Ballistic Missile Defence programme run by DRDO, with Prithvi Air Defence (PAD) and Advanced Air Defence (AAD) interceptors. India tested BMD phase-I in the 2010s. None of this involves eLISA.

Solar flares are sudden bursts of radiation from the Sun's atmosphere linked to sunspots. Along with coronal mass ejections, they can disrupt radio communication, GPS, satellites and power grids by causing geomagnetic storms. They are studied by SOHO, SDO, Parker Solar Probe and India's Aditya-L1 (launched 2 September 2023, placed at the Sun-Earth L1 point in January 2024). This work is separate from gravitational wave astronomy.
related: Einstein predicted gravitational waves in 1916 through General Relativity.
LIGO made the first direct detection on 14 September 2015 (announced 11 February 2016).
The 2017 Physics Nobel went to Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne for LIGO.
LIGO-India is planned at Hingoli, Maharashtra.
LISA Pathfinder (ESA, Dec 2015) tested technology for space-based gravitational wave detection.
GW170817 was the first neutron star merger seen in both gravitational waves and light.
The Event Horizon Telescope imaged the black hole in M87 in 2019.
The India-based Neutrino Observatory is a separate proposed project for neutrino detection.
summary: The answer is (b): eLISA was a proposed European Space Agency space-based observatory meant to detect gravitational waves. It would use laser interferometry between spacecraft millions of kilometres apart to sense tiny ripples in spacetime.
topic_notes: Gravitational waves are disturbances in the fabric of spacetime generated by accelerating masses, especially violent cosmic events such as black hole or neutron star mergers. Einstein predicted them in 1916. Indirect evidence came from the Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar (Nobel 1993). The first direct detection was by the two LIGO detectors at Hanford and Livingston on 14 September 2015 (GW150914), announced in February 2016. The 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Weiss, Barish and Thorne. In August 2017 the Virgo and LIGO detectors detected a neutron star merger (GW170817) that was also observed in light, opening multi-messenger astronomy. Detectors use laser interferometry, in which laser beams travel along long perpendicular arms and a passing wave changes the arm lengths by a tiny fraction of a proton's width. Ground detectors include LIGO (4 km arms), Virgo (3 km), GEO600 and KAGRA (underground in Japan). LIGO-India was approved by the Indian Cabinet in 2023 for Aundha, Hingoli district, Maharashtra, with DAE and DST involved. Space-based detection requires very long arms. eLISA, later called LISA, will be a trio of satellites about 2.5 million km apart (the earlier eLISA design used 1 million km) and will detect low-frequency waves from supermassive black hole mergers. LISA Pathfinder (ESA, December 2015) validated the technology. Pulsar timing arrays (NANOGrav, with India's GMRT in the Indian PTA) reported evidence of a nanohertz gravitational wave background in 2023. Related UPSC topics include black holes, the Event Horizon Telescope image (2019), neutron stars, ISRO's Astrosat, and other space observatories.

question:
What is the purpose of ‘Vidyanjali Yojana’ ? L To enable the famous . foreign educational institutions to open their campuses in India.
2. To increase the quality of education provided in government schools by taking help from the private sector and the community.
3. To encourage voluntary monetary contributions from private individuals and organizations so as to improve the infrastructure facilities for primary and secondary schools. Select the correct answer using the code. given below :
subject: Economy
detail: Vidyanjali was launched by the Ministry of Education (then MHRD) on 25 July 2016 as a school volunteer programme, a one-stop platform for volunteers to engage with government and government-aided elementary schools. Its aim is to improve school quality by bringing community and private-sector involvement into schools. Volunteers contribute services such as teaching, mentoring, and help with sports, arts and activities. They can also give assets or materials, but the scheme does not collect cash, and the Vidyanjali portal records the contribution rather than receiving it. This is the key point for eliminating statement 3, which speaks of monetary contributions for infrastructure. Statement 1 is about foreign university campuses in India, which falls under UGC regulations and the 2023 UGC rules on foreign higher education institutions, and has no link to Vidyanjali. Statement 2 therefore matches the scheme and statements 1 and 3 do not. Only (a) includes statement 2 alone. The 'volunteer, not money' feature is the usual trap in this question. Vidyanjali 2.0 was later launched in 2018 with a wider scope.
explanations: Correct: statement 2 alone describes Vidyanjali, a volunteer programme to improve government schools with community and private-sector help.
Wrong: a combination with statement 1 is wrong because foreign campuses are unrelated to the scheme, and this option also includes a statement that does not fit.
Wrong: this option wrongly includes statement 1 (foreign campuses) and does not match the scheme's actual purpose.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, but Vidyanjali does not accept cash; it involves volunteers giving services, assets or materials.
keyfact: Vidyanjali (2016) is a school volunteer programme that brings community and private-sector help to government schools, not a cash-donation or foreign-campus scheme.
related: Vidyanjali was launched on 25 July 2016 by the MHRD.
Vidyanjali is a school volunteer programme for government and aided elementary schools.
Volunteers give time, skills or materials, not cash, through the portal.
Samagra Shiksha (2018) merged SSA, RMSA and teacher education.
Article 21A gives the right to education for ages 6 to 14, inserted by the 86th Amendment 2002.
The RTE Act 2009 reserves 25 percent seats in private schools for disadvantaged groups.
PM POSHAN is the renamed Mid-Day Meal scheme (2021).
NEP 2020 proposes a 5+3+3+4 school structure.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Vidyanjali has nothing to do with foreign campuses. Foreign institutions entering India is a higher-education issue. The Foreign Educational Institutions Bill was proposed in 2010 but lapsed. The UGC (Setting up and Operation of Campuses of Foreign Higher Educational Institutions in India) Regulations were notified in 2023 under NEP 2020. Universities such as Southampton, and others, have since received approval. Vidyanjali targets government elementary schools, not higher education.

2 — Correct: Vidyanjali aims to strengthen government schools through volunteers from the community, corporates, NGOs, retired professionals and alumni. It was launched on 25 July 2016 by the MHRD and has a web portal. Volunteers offer time, skills and material support, and schools list their needs. It was initially piloted in 2015 in a few states and later extended nationwide. Vidyanjali 2.0 followed in 2018, and the programme falls under the Department of School Education and Literacy.

3 — Incorrect: The scheme does not collect monetary donations. Volunteers give services, and may give assets, materials or equipment, but not cash through the portal. Cash-based approaches elsewhere include the Swachh Vidyalaya initiative and the Swachh Bharat Kosh, and CSR funds under Section 135 of the Companies Act 2013 also go to schools. The statement is wrong because it presents money as the scheme's central purpose.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 2 is correct. Vidyanjali, launched in 2016, is a school volunteer programme that brings in the community and the private sector to improve the quality of education in government schools, mainly through services such as time and skills, not money.
topic_notes: Vidyanjali was launched on 25 July 2016 by the Ministry of Human Resource Development, now the Ministry of Education. It is a school volunteer programme in which volunteers, including professionals, retired persons, corporate employees, alumni and students, support government and government-aided elementary schools. Contributions are in the form of services, such as teaching, mentoring, and help with activities, and may also include assets, materials or equipment. The aim is to bridge gaps in school quality and to build community ownership of schools. A web portal lets schools register their needs and volunteers sign up, and Vidyanjali 2.0 followed in 2018. A related set of school-sector schemes is worth revising. Samagra Shiksha (2018) merged Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan and teacher education. Mid-Day Meal became PM POSHAN in 2021. Right to Education Act 2009 (Article 21A, 86th Amendment 2002) guarantees free and compulsory education for ages 6 to 14 and has a 25 percent reservation in private schools for disadvantaged groups. Other initiatives include Swachh Vidyalaya (2014), Padhe Bharat Badhe Bharat, Rashtriya Avishkar Abhiyan, DIKSHA, SWAYAM, PM e-Vidya, NIPUN Bharat (2021, foundational literacy and numeracy), PM SHRI schools (2022), and the Unnat Bharat Abhiyan (higher education institutions adopting villages). NEP 2020 proposes a 5+3+3+4 structure, 6 percent of GDP for education, and foreign campuses in India. Expect questions on scheme purposes, launching ministries and years, and statement-based comparisons.

question: What is the aim of the programme ‘Unnat Bharat Abhiyan’ ?
options: Achieving 100% literacy by promoting collaboration between voluntary organizations and government’s education system and local communities
Connecting institutions of higher education with local communities to address development challenges through appropriate technologies
Strengthening India’s scientific research institutions in order to make India a scientific and technological power
Developing human capital by allocating special funds for health care and education of rural and urban poor, and organizing skill development programmes and vocational training for ; them
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Unnat Bharat Abhiyan was launched by the Ministry of Education (then MHRD) in 2014 and is inspired by the vision of Mahatma Gandhi on self-reliant villages. It is mentored by IIT Delhi, which acts as the National Coordinating Institute, and the programme is run through participating HEIs such as IITs, NITs, IISERs, central and state universities and colleges. UBA 2.0 was launched in 2018 to widen the scope and include more institutions. Each participating institution adopts at least 5 villages (clusters), identifies problems in areas such as water, sanitation, energy, livelihood, agriculture and rural technology, and applies low-cost, appropriate technology solutions. It also helps the villages prepare development plans and link up with government schemes. The aim is to make HEIs a catalyst of rural development and to make their curriculum relevant to society. Elimination logic: (a) describes literacy missions like Saakshar Bharat; (c) describes science and technology promotion initiatives such as the Department of Science and Technology (DST) programmes or the INSPIRE scheme; (d) describes human capital and skilling schemes such as Skill India or the National Rural Livelihood Mission (NRLM). Only (b) names the link between institutions of higher education and communities.
explanations: Incorrect: 100% literacy through voluntary organisations is the theme of adult education programmes like Saakshar Bharat, not UBA, which is about higher education institutions.
Correct: UBA connects higher education institutions with local communities (adopted villages) to tackle development challenges using appropriate technologies.
Incorrect: Strengthening scientific research institutions to make India a science and technology power is not UBA's aim; UBA is outreach-oriented and community-focused.
Incorrect: Special funds for health and education of the poor and skilling are features of other schemes (Skill India, NRLM, DDU-GKY), not UBA.
keyfact: Unnat Bharat Abhiyan (2014, IIT Delhi as NCI) links higher education institutions with villages to solve local development problems using appropriate technology.
option_notes: Achieving 100% literacy: this is the idea behind the National Literacy Mission (1988) and Saakshar Bharat (2009), which focused on adult literacy, especially among women, with a target of 80% literacy. These programmes involved panchayats, NGOs and state literacy missions. Saakshar Bharat was subsumed under the Padhna Likhna Abhiyan and later the New India Literacy Programme (2022-27). It has no link with UBA.

Connecting higher education institutions with local communities: this is exactly UBA, launched in 2014 by the Ministry of Education. IIT Delhi is the National Coordinating Institute. Each participating institution adopts at least 5 villages. UBA 2.0 started in 2018. Focus areas include appropriate technology, livelihood, water, sanitation and energy, with the aim of making HEIs a catalyst of rural development.

Strengthening scientific research institutions: this refers to science policy aims such as those of DST, CSIR, the Science and Technology policies (2003, 2013) and schemes like INSPIRE, KVPY, and the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (2023). Their goal is to raise research quality and R&D spending, not to run community outreach in villages. This is a different domain from UBA.

Developing human capital through health, education funds and skilling: this describes broad human development and skilling efforts such as Skill India (2015), Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana, DDU-GKY, NRLM and the National Health Mission. They provide training, vocational education and welfare outlays to the poor. UBA does not allocate special funds in this way and instead uses institutional expertise.
related: Unnat Bharat Abhiyan was launched in 2014 by the Ministry of Education (then MHRD).
IIT Delhi is the National Coordinating Institute of UBA.
UBA 2.0 was launched in 2018 to expand the scheme to more institutions.
Saansad Adarsh Gram Yojana (2014) requires each MP to adopt villages as model villages.
Shyama Prasad Mukherji Rurban Mission was launched in 2016 to develop rural clusters.
Saakshar Bharat (2009) targeted adult literacy, especially women.
PURA (Providing Urban Amenities in Rural Areas) was proposed by Dr APJ Abdul Kalam.
Skill India Mission was launched in 2015.
summary: The answer is (b). Unnat Bharat Abhiyan (UBA) links higher education institutions (HEIs) with local communities, mainly villages, so that the institutions can help address development challenges using appropriate technologies and their own knowledge base.
topic_notes: Unnat Bharat Abhiyan (UBA) is a flagship outreach programme of the Ministry of Education, launched in 2014 following a vision of Gandhian self-reliant villages. Its objective is to engage the knowledge institutions of the country in the process of rural development and build the architecture of an inclusive India. IIT Delhi is the National Coordinating Institute (NCI), with a National Advisory Committee and Regional Coordinating Institutes (RCIs) such as other IITs and NITs supporting it at the regional level. Participating HEIs adopt villages (initially 5, later clusters), survey needs, prepare village development plans, and offer solutions in areas like water management, sanitation, renewable energy, organic farming, rural technology, skill training and digital literacy. Faculty and students are involved through community work, which also sensitises them to rural realities and makes research and teaching more relevant. UBA 2.0 (2018) expanded the number of institutions and included a larger variety of HEIs, with funding support from the Ministry for the activities of the institutions. Related schemes to remember: Saansad Adarsh Gram Yojana (2014; MPs adopt villages), Rurban Mission (Shyama Prasad Mukherji Rurban Mission, 2016), PURA concept (by Dr APJ Abdul Kalam), Swachh Bharat, and the Digital India programme. UPSC tends to test the objectives of schemes, the ministry in charge and the year of launch, so students should compare similar-sounding initiatives such as UBA, SAGY and the Rurban Mission and distinguish those that involve MPs, those involving institutions and those based on cluster infrastructure. Other aspects likely to be asked: the role of appropriate technology, Gandhian ideals, and the National Education Policy 2020, which emphasises community engagement by HEIs.

question:
Consider the following statements : 92. it, The Election Commission of India is a five-member body.
2. Union Ministry of Home Affairs decides the election schedule for the conduct of both general elections and bye-elections.
3. Election Commission resolves the’ disputes relating to splits/mergers of recognised political parties. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: The Election Commission of India is a constitutional body under Article 324, which vests superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, the President and the Vice-President in the Commission. It was a single-member body until 15 October 1989, when two Election Commissioners were added. Since 1 October 1993 it has been a multi-member body of the Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners, so it is a three-member body, not five. Statement 1 is therefore wrong. The ECI alone announces the schedule for general elections and bye-elections, after consulting the government on logistics such as security forces, but the Home Ministry has no power to decide it. Statement 2 is therefore wrong. Paragraph 15 of the Symbols Order, 1968 empowers the ECI to decide disputes between rival groups or sections of a recognised party, each claiming to be that party. The Supreme Court upheld this in Sadiq Ali v. ECI (1971). Hence only statement 3 is correct, and elimination leaves (d). Disputes over mergers are likewise handled by the ECI under its symbol and recognition powers.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false because the ECI has three members, and statement 2, which is also false because the ECI fixes the schedule.
Wrong: statement 2 is false because the Home Ministry does not decide the election schedule. The ECI does.
Wrong: it includes statement 2, which is false, even though statement 3 is true.
Correct: only statement 3 is true. The ECI settles disputes over splits and mergers of recognised parties under Paragraph 15 of the Symbols Order, 1968.
keyfact: The ECI is a three-member body that sets election schedules itself and settles party split disputes under Paragraph 15 of the Symbols Order, 1968.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only: This would make the ECI a five-member body whose schedule is fixed by the Home Ministry. Both claims are false. The ECI is a three-member body under Article 324 and the 1991 Act, and it has full authority over election scheduling. The Home Ministry only provides security forces and advice on law and order.

2 only: This would give the Union Home Ministry the power to fix election dates. In reality the ECI has this power. The Ministry assists by deploying Central Armed Police Forces, and the ECI consults it, but the final decision is the Commission's. This independence reflects Article 324's mandate and protects free and fair elections.

2 and 3 only: This pairs the false claim about the Home Ministry with the true claim about party disputes. The party-dispute power comes from Paragraph 15 of the Symbols Order, 1968, and was upheld in Sadiq Ali (1971). The scheduling claim is false, so this option fails.

3 only: This is the correct option. The ECI adjudicates disputes among rival factions of recognised parties over name and symbol under Paragraph 15 of the Symbols Order, 1968. Examples include the Shiv Sena and NCP disputes. It is a quasi-judicial power of the Commission. Its decisions can be challenged in the High Courts and the Supreme Court.
related: Article 324 vests the control of elections in the ECI.
The ECI became a three-member body in 1993.
The Symbols Order, 1968 governs recognition of parties and allotment of symbols.
Panchayat and municipal elections are conducted by State Election Commissions under Articles 243K and 243ZA.
The CEC can be removed in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge.
The Speaker or Chairman decides defection disqualification cases under the Tenth Schedule, not the ECI.
The Model Code of Conduct comes into force when the schedule is announced.
National Voters' Day is 25 January.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: the ECI has three members (the CEC and two ECs), not five. The Commission was single-member from 1950 to 1989. On 16 October 1989 two Election Commissioners were appointed, though that arrangement was short-lived. The multi-member model was made permanent by the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Conditions of Service) Act, 1991, and the 1993 amendment confirmed the three-member body. Decisions are taken by majority, and the CEC can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge. The tenure is six years or until age 65, whichever is earlier. Appointments are now governed by the 2023 Act, with a selection committee of the PM, the Leader of Opposition and a Union Cabinet Minister.

2 — Incorrect: the ECI announces election schedules independently under Article 324 and Section 30 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. It consults the government and security agencies on feasibility, but the Home Ministry cannot fix dates. The ECI also decides bye-election timing, which must happen within six months of a vacancy under Section 151A of the RP Act, 1951. Notifications are issued by the President or Governor, but the dates are set by the ECI. The Model Code of Conduct comes into force as soon as the schedule is announced. This independence is a key feature of the Commission's constitutional autonomy.

3 — Correct: Paragraph 15 of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 gives the ECI power to decide disputes among rival groups of a recognised party over the party name and symbol. The Supreme Court upheld this in Sadiq Ali v. ECI (1971). Well-known cases include the Congress split of 1969, the AIADMK split after MGR's death, the Shiv Sena dispute in 2022-23 and the NCP dispute in 2023-24. The Commission applies tests such as the test of aims and objects, the test of party constitution and the test of legislative and organisational majority. Appeals against its decision go to the High Court or the Supreme Court.
summary: The answer is (d) 3 only. Only statement 3 is correct: under Paragraph 15 of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, the Election Commission decides disputes over splits and mergers of recognised parties. The Commission is not a five-member body, and the election schedule is decided by the ECI, not the Ministry of Home Affairs.
topic_notes: The Election Commission of India is a permanent, independent constitutional body under Article 324, established on 25 January 1950 (celebrated as National Voters' Day). Articles 324-329 in Part XV deal with elections. Article 324 gives it superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, the offices of President and Vice-President. It does not cover elections to Panchayats and Municipalities, which are conducted by State Election Commissions under Articles 243K and 243ZA. Composition: the CEC and such number of other ECs as the President may fix. The Commission has had three members since 1993. The CEC and ECs have equal powers and receive salary and allowances equal to a Supreme Court judge. Tenure is six years or until age 65, whichever is earlier. The CEC can be removed only in the manner and on the grounds of a Supreme Court judge, while ECs can be removed by the President on the CEC's recommendation. The 2023 Act changed the appointment process to a committee of the PM, the Leader of Opposition and a Union Cabinet Minister, replacing the 2023 Anoop Baranwal interim arrangement of the Supreme Court. Functions: delimitation (with the Delimitation Commission), preparation of electoral rolls, recognition of parties and allotment of symbols, advising on disqualification of MPs and MLAs under Article 103 and 192, and enforcing the Model Code of Conduct. The ECI can also countermand polls and deregister parties. Its quasi-judicial functions include settling disputes about symbols and recognition. Key cases: Mohinder Singh Gill (1978) on the wide scope of Article 324, and Sadiq Ali (1971) on the Symbols Order. Related topics include the Representation of the People Acts of 1950 and 1951, EVMs and VVPAT, NOTA (2013, PUCL case), and the Anti-Defection Law under the Tenth Schedule, where the Speaker or Chairman decides, not the ECI.

question: In India, if a species of tortoise is declared protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife 94. (Protection) Act, 1972, what does it imply ?
options: It enjoys the same level of protection as the tiger
It no longer exists in the wild, a few "individuals are under captive protection; and now it is impossible to prevent its extinction
It is endemic to a particular region of |. India
Both (b) and (c) stated above are correct in this context
subject: Environment
detail: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 classifies species into schedules that decide the degree of protection and the penalty. Schedule I (with Part II of Schedule II) carries the highest protection and the severest punishment. Hunting is prohibited except under Section 11 (dangerous to human life) and Section 12 (scientific research or management, with permission). The tiger, Asiatic lion, elephant, snow leopard, Gangetic dolphin and many tortoises and turtles are listed here. A first offence attracts imprisonment of 3 to 7 years and a fine of at least Rs 10,000 (raised by the 2022 Amendment to Rs 25,000 in some cases). Schedule II covers species with high but slightly lower protection. Schedule III and IV cover protected species with lesser penalties. Schedule V lists vermin, which may be hunted. Schedule VI covers specified plants, whose cultivation and trade are regulated. The 2022 Amendment reduced the schedules from six to four. Elimination: (b) describes the IUCN category 'Extinct in the Wild', which is a different classification. (c) endemism is a biogeographic fact, unrelated to the schedule, and many Schedule I tortoises such as the Indian star tortoise are not endemic to one region. (d) combines two wrong claims. So only (a) holds.
explanations: Correct. Schedule I species get the highest legal protection, the same as the tiger, with the same strict penalties.

Wrong. Being 'Extinct in the Wild' is an IUCN Red List category and has nothing to do with a Schedule I listing. Schedule I species can be endangered but still living in the wild, and extinction is not declared inevitable.
Wrong. Endemism is not a criterion for Schedule I. Many listed species have wide ranges across India and beyond.
Wrong. Both (b) and (c) are incorrect, so the combination is incorrect.
keyfact: Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 means the highest legal protection, the same tier as the tiger, and says nothing about extinction in the wild or endemism.
option_notes: Tiger-level protection: the tiger (Panthera tigris) is in Schedule I. Hunting is banned, and offences carry imprisonment of at least 3 years, extendable to 7, with a fine. Tiger reserves are notified under Section 38V. Project Tiger began in 1973, and the NTCA became statutory in 2006. Many other species, including several tortoises, share this top legal tier.

Extinct in the Wild (EW) is an IUCN Red List category for species surviving only in captivity or as naturalised populations outside their range. Examples include the Hawaiian crow and Socorro dove. Such a category does not follow from a Schedule I listing, and the claim of impossible prevention of extinction is unfounded.

Endemic species occur naturally only in a particular region. Examples are the Nilgiri tahr, lion-tailed macaque and Malabar civet in the Western Ghats. Endemism is a biogeographical fact and not a basis for Schedule I listing. Many Schedule I species, like the Indian star tortoise, are not endemic.

Option (d) combines the claims that the species is extinct in the wild and that it is endemic. Both are unrelated to schedule status, so the combination is invalid. Schedule listing reflects the legal protection level required, not the ecological or biogeographic status.
related: Schedule I animals get the highest protection under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, with the severest penalties.
The 2022 Amendment reduced the schedules from six to four.
IUCN Red List categories include Extinct, Extinct in the Wild, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened and Least Concern.
CITES Appendix I bans commercial international trade in listed species.
Project Tiger was launched in 1973 and the NTCA became a statutory body in 2006.
The Indian star tortoise (Geochelone elegans) is a heavily trafficked species listed in Schedule I.
Hunting of Schedule I species is allowed only under Sections 11 and 12 of the Act.
summary: The answer is (a). Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 gives species the highest level of legal protection, the same as the tiger, with the strictest penalties for hunting or trade. The schedule says nothing about whether a species is extinct in the wild or endemic.
topic_notes: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 was enacted for protecting wild animals, birds and plants and regulating trade in wildlife products. It created the Wildlife Advisory Board, the Central Zoo Authority, the National Board for Wildlife and the National Tiger Conservation Authority (via the 2006 amendment), and provides for the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau. It allows creation of protected areas: national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, conservation reserves and community reserves. Before the 2022 Amendment there were six schedules: I and II (highest protection for animals), III and IV (lesser protection, lower penalties), V (vermin) and VI (plants). The 2022 Amendment reduced them to four: Schedule I for species with highest protection, Schedule II for species with lesser protection, Schedule III for plants, and Schedule IV for CITES Appendix species. It also implemented CITES obligations, and Schedule I species such as tortoises and turtles face strict penalties for trade. Indian tortoises and freshwater turtles are heavily trafficked for the pet trade, so many were moved to Schedule I. Examples include the Indian star tortoise, Indian flapshell turtle and Indian softshell turtle. Related topics UPSC may ask: IUCN Red List categories (EX, EW, CR, EN, VU, NT, LC, DD, NE), CITES appendices I to III, the Biological Diversity Act 2002, the Forest Rights Act, the Convention on Migratory Species, and Ramsar sites. Also remember the difference between legal protection under Indian law and the IUCN's global assessment.

question: In India, Judicial Review implies the power of the Judiciary to pronounce
options: upon the constitutionality of laws and executive orders. the power of the Judiciary to question
the wisdom of the laws enacted by the Legislatures. the power of the Judiciary to review all
the legislative enactments before they are assented to by the President. the power of the Judiciary to review its
own judgements given éarlier in similar or different cases
subject: Polity
detail: Judicial Review is the power of courts to test the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive actions and declare them null and void if they violate the Constitution. It is a basic feature of the Constitution (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997; Minerva Mills, 1980). Textual basis: Art. 13 (laws inconsistent with or in derogation of Fundamental Rights are void), Art. 32 and 226 (writ jurisdiction), Art. 131-136 (SC jurisdiction), Art. 143 (advisory), Art. 246 and the Seventh Schedule (federal distribution of powers), and Art. 251/254. Marbury v. Madison (1803) in the USA established the doctrine; India follows a narrower model than the US, because Art. 21 speaks of 'procedure established by law' (A.K. Gopalan, later widened by Maneka Gandhi, 1978). Key cases: Golak Nath, Kesavananda Bharati (1973, basic structure), Minerva Mills. Elimination: (b) is wrong because courts review legality, not the wisdom or policy merits, of laws. (c) is wrong because review is post-enactment, not pre-assent (advisory opinion under Art. 143 is an exception, not review). (d) describes the curative or review jurisdiction (Art. 137), which is a different power. Hence (a).
explanations: Correct: Judicial Review means the courts pronounce on the constitutionality of legislation and executive orders and can invalidate them if they violate the Constitution.
Incorrect: Courts do not question the wisdom or policy of a law; they only test its constitutional validity and legislative competence.
Incorrect: Courts review laws after enactment, not before the President's assent. Bills are not generally subject to pre-enactment judicial scrutiny.
Incorrect: Reviewing its own judgments is the review power under Art. 137 (and curative petitions), which is separate from Judicial Review of laws.
keyfact: Judicial Review = power of courts to test the constitutionality of laws and executive actions (Art. 13, 32, 226); it concerns legality, not wisdom, and is part of the basic structure.
option_notes: Judicial Review of laws and executive orders: the power of the SC and HCs to examine constitutionality and strike down unconstitutional laws or actions. Rooted in Arts. 13, 32, 226, 131-136, 246. Considered part of the basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati; L. Chandra Kumar, 1997). It flows from the Constitution's supremacy and the federal division of powers between the Union and the States.

Questioning the wisdom of laws: this concerns policy merits and is outside judicial review in India. Courts follow restraint, leaving policy choices to the legislature and executive, and intervene only for violation of the Constitution, lack of legislative competence, arbitrariness (Art. 14), or violation of fundamental rights. This is the line between judicial review and judicial activism or overreach.

Review of bills before assent: India has no general pre-enactment judicial review. The President may seek the SC's advisory opinion under Art. 143, which is non-binding, and the SC has declined to answer some references (for example the Ayodhya reference, 1993). Pre-enactment review exists in some countries, such as France's Constitutional Council.

Review of its own judgments: the SC can review its judgments under Art. 137, subject to rules (Order XLVII). Curative petitions were created in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002). Art. 141 makes SC law binding on all courts, and the SC can overrule its earlier decisions, as it did in Golak Nath, which Kesavananda Bharati overruled.
related: Art. 13 declares laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void.
Judicial review is part of the basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati 1973; L. Chandra Kumar 1997).
Art. 32 is the right to constitutional remedies; Art. 226 gives HCs wider writ power.
I.R. Coelho (2007): Ninth Schedule laws are reviewable if they violate the basic structure.
Art. 137 gives the SC power to review its own judgments; curative petitions came from Rupa Ashok Hurra (2002).
Marbury v. Madison (1803) established judicial review in the USA.
NJAC and the 99th Amendment were struck down in 2015 (Fourth Judges Case).
S.R. Bommai (1994) made President's Rule under Art. 356 justiciable.
summary: The answer is (a). In India, Judicial Review is the power of the higher judiciary (Supreme Court under Art. 32 and 131-136, and High Courts under Art. 226) to examine whether laws and executive orders conform to the Constitution, and to strike down those that do not.
topic_notes: Judicial Review is the cornerstone of constitutional supremacy. The Constitution has no explicit phrase 'judicial review', but it is implied in Art. 13 (laws violating Part III are void), Art. 32 (SC writs; Dr Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul'), Art. 226 (HC writs, wider as it covers 'any other purpose'), Art. 131 (Centre-State disputes), Art. 136 (SLP), Art. 143, and Arts. 124-147. The 24th, 25th, 42nd and 43rd Amendments tried to curb or restore review. The 42nd Amendment (1976) restricted it; the 43rd Amendment restored it. Key cases: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) upheld Parliament's amending power; Golak Nath (1967) held that amendments are 'law' under Art. 13; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) laid down the basic structure doctrine; Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975); Minerva Mills (1980); S.R. Bommai (1994) allowed review of President's Rule; I.R. Coelho (2007) allowed review of laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973; L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that tribunals are subject to HC review. In 2015 the NJAC Act and the 99th Amendment were struck down. Related ideas: Judicial activism, PIL (S.P. Gupta, 1981), judicial restraint, doctrine of severability, eclipse, and pith and substance. In the USA review derives from Marbury v. Madison (1803); the UK has parliamentary sovereignty; India is a mix of the two.

question:
With reference to Indian freedom struggle, consider the following events : Mutiny in Royal Indian Navy dL.
2. Quit India Movement launched
3. Second Round Table Conference What is the correct chronological sequence of the above events ?
subject: Modern History
detail: This question tests the sequence of major events from the Civil Disobedience phase through the endgame of British rule. The Second Round Table Conference (September-December 1931, London) followed the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931). Gandhi attended as the sole Congress representative and the conference ended without agreement, mainly over separate electorates for minorities. Civil Disobedience was resumed in January 1932. The Quit India Movement was launched on 8 August 1942 after the Congress Bombay session passed the resolution at Gowalia Tank, with Gandhi giving the call 'Do or Die'. It followed the failure of the Cripps Mission (March 1942). The Royal Indian Navy (RIN) Mutiny began on 18 February 1946 on HMIS Talwar in Bombay, triggered by racial discrimination, poor food and the trials of INA officers. It spread to many ships and shore establishments. It ended after Sardar Patel and Jinnah intervened, and the ratings surrendered on 23 February. Elimination: the RIN Mutiny is the latest of the three events (1946), so options (a), (b) and (d), which all place it before another event, are wrong. Only (c) puts it last.
explanations: (a) 1-2-3 is wrong because it places the 1946 Navy Mutiny first and the 1931 conference last, which is the exact reverse of the real order.
(b) 2-1-3 is wrong because the Second Round Table Conference (1931) came before both Quit India (1942) and the Navy Mutiny (1946).
(c) 3-2-1 is correct: Second Round Table Conference (1931), then Quit India (1942), then RIN Mutiny (1946).
(d) 3-1-2 is wrong because it places the 1946 Navy Mutiny before the 1942 Quit India Movement, although it happened after it.
keyfact: Second RTC (1931) → Quit India (Aug 1942) → RIN Mutiny (Feb 1946).
option_notes: Sequence 1-2-3 would run RIN Mutiny, Quit India, Second Round Table Conference. It is a reverse-chronological trap. The true order of these events runs from 1931 to 1946, so it is wrong. Keep in mind the key dates: Second RTC (1931), Quit India (1942), RIN Mutiny (1946). The Cabinet Mission (March 1946) and the Interim Government (September 1946) followed, and independence came on 15 August 1947 after the Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947.

Sequence 2-1-3 would run Quit India, RIN Mutiny, Second Round Table Conference. It is wrong because the 1931 conference preceded both of the other events. Quit India (1942) was the last mass movement led by Gandhi, and it was brutally suppressed, with over 100,000 arrests and many deaths. The Round Table Conferences (1930-32) were held to discuss the Simon Commission's proposals and constitutional reform. They led to the Government of India Act 1935.

Sequence 3-2-1 is the correct chronological order: the Second Round Table Conference in 1931, the Quit India Movement in 1942 and the RIN Mutiny in 1946. It shows the movement from negotiation, to a mass struggle, to the final uprisings in the armed forces that convinced the British that the loyalty of the Indian armed forces could no longer be relied on. Other events of 1945-46 include the INA trials at the Red Fort and the Cabinet Mission.

Sequence 3-1-2 would run the Second Round Table Conference, RIN Mutiny, Quit India. It gets the first event right but wrongly puts the Mutiny (1946) before Quit India (1942). A common error is to forget the date of the RIN Mutiny, which is after the Second World War ended in 1945. Quit India took place during the war, when Japan was advancing in Burma and the Cripps Mission had failed in March 1942.
related: First Round Table Conference: November 1930 to January 1931, chaired by Ramsay MacDonald; Congress did not attend.
Gandhi-Irwin Pact: signed 5 March 1931, also called the Delhi Pact.
Quit India resolution: passed at Gowalia Tank, Bombay, on 8 August 1942.
Cripps Mission: March 1942, preceded Quit India and was rejected by Congress.
RIN Mutiny: began 18 February 1946 on HMIS Talwar, Bombay.
Cabinet Mission: March 1946, with Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander.
Poona Pact: 24 September 1932 between Gandhi and Ambedkar.
Communal Award: announced August 1932 by Ramsay MacDonald.
statements: 1 — Correct in the sequence as the last event: the Royal Indian Navy Mutiny occurred in February 1946, after the other two events. It began on 18 February 1946 on HMIS Talwar, when ratings protested against racial discrimination, bad food and the treatment of INA prisoners. It spread to about 78 ships and 20 shore establishments, involving about 20,000 ratings. The Naval Central Strike Committee was led by M.S. Khan. The Congress and the Muslim League did not support it, though the Communist Party did. Patel and Jinnah persuaded the ratings to surrender. It hastened the British decision to leave and the Cabinet Mission followed.

2 — Correct in the sequence as the middle event: the Quit India Movement was launched on 8 August 1942, in the middle of the three. The Congress Working Committee passed the resolution at Wardha in July 1942, and the AICC ratified it at Bombay on 8 August. Gandhi gave the 'Do or Die' slogan. Congress leaders were arrested on 9 August, and Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank. Parallel governments emerged at Ballia, Tamluk and Satara. Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia and Usha Mehta (Congress Radio) were prominent. The Muslim League, Communists and Hindu Mahasabha stayed away.

3 — Correct in the sequence as the first event: the Second Round Table Conference was held in London from September to December 1931. Gandhi attended as the Congress representative after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March 1931, sailing on SS Rajputana. Sarojini Naidu and Madan Mohan Malaviya were also present. The main stumbling block was the communal question and separate electorates, which Gandhi opposed, and the conference failed. Ramsay MacDonald announced the Communal Award in August 1932. The Poona Pact followed in September 1932. The First conference was in 1930 and the Third in 1932, and Congress did not attend either.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 3-2-1. The Second Round Table Conference was held in 1931, the Quit India Movement was launched in August 1942, and the Royal Indian Navy Mutiny took place in February 1946.
topic_notes: This question covers the final three decades of the national movement, so students should learn it as a timeline. 1930: Dandi March (12 March) and the start of Civil Disobedience; First Round Table Conference (Nov 1930-Jan 1931), boycotted by Congress. 1931: Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March); Karachi session under Sardar Patel; Second RTC (Sept-Dec). 1932: Communal Award (August), Poona Pact (24 September, Gandhi and Ambedkar), Third RTC. 1935: Government of India Act. 1937: provincial elections and Congress ministries. 1939: outbreak of war, resignation of Congress ministries. 1940: August Offer and Individual Satyagraha; Lahore Resolution of the League (March). 1942: Cripps Mission (March), Quit India (8 August). 1944: C. Rajagopalachari formula and Gandhi-Jinnah talks. 1945: Wavell Plan and the Simla Conference; INA trials begin. 1946: RIN Mutiny (Feb), Cabinet Mission (March-May), Direct Action Day (16 August), Interim Government (2 September). 1947: Attlee's announcement (20 February), Mountbatten Plan (3 June), Indian Independence Act (18 July), Independence on 15 August. Subhas Chandra Bose formed the Azad Hind Fauj and the Provisional Government of Free India in 1943. Other mutinies in 1946 included those in the Royal Indian Air Force and the Jabalpur Signal Corps. Attlee's Labour government came to power in July 1945. UPSC often asks for chronological ordering, for the people behind each event and for the constitutional documents that followed.

ocr: Consider the following statements : Tax revenue as a percent of GDP of ly India has steadily increased in the last decade. Fiscal deficit as a percent of GDP of India has steadily increased in the last decade. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) lonly (b) 2only (c) Both 1 and 2 Neither 1 nor 2 (d)
subject: Economy
detail: The question tests whether you know the broad trends in India's public finances rather than exact figures. The word 'steadily' makes both statements wrong, because neither series moved in one direction. The Centre's gross tax revenue was about 10-11% of GDP in 2012-13 to 2016-17 (the paper's 'last decade' window). It rose to about 11.7% by 2018-19, then fell to about 10.2% in 2019-20 and 2020-21 before recovering later. The general government (Centre plus States) tax-to-GDP ratio is roughly 16-18%, so it has been broadly stagnant. The fiscal deficit of the Centre fell from about 5.9% of GDP in 2011-12 to 3.5% in 2016-17 under the FRBM glide path, rose to about 4.6% in 2019-20 and 9.2% in 2020-21 (Covid), and has since been consolidated toward 4.5% by 2025-26. Elimination: if statement 1 is judged false, options (a) and (c) go. If statement 2 is judged false, option (b) goes. Only (d) remains. In UPSC, absolute words like 'steadily' usually signal a false statement.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Statement 1 is incorrect because the tax-to-GDP ratio has not increased steadily; it dipped in 2019-21.
(b) Wrong: Statement 2 is incorrect because the fiscal deficit ratio fell during 2012-18 and was consolidated again after the Covid spike, so it did not rise steadily.
(c) Wrong: Both statements fail the test of a steady increase, so 'both' cannot be right.
(d) Correct: Neither the tax-to-GDP ratio nor the fiscal deficit-to-GDP ratio rose steadily over the decade, so neither statement holds.
keyfact: India's tax-to-GDP ratio and fiscal deficit-to-GDP ratio have both fluctuated, not risen steadily, so the answer is (d).
option_notes: Option (a) '1 only' would mean tax-to-GDP has risen steadily while the fiscal deficit has not. In reality the Centre's gross tax-to-GDP ratio stayed around 10-12% and only edged up to about 11.7% in 2018-19 before falling. The general government ratio is about 17-18%. Tax-to-GDP is a key indicator of fiscal capacity, and India's ratio is lower than the OECD average of about 34%.

Option (b) '2 only' would mean the fiscal deficit has risen steadily. It has not. The deficit is the gap between total expenditure and total receipts excluding borrowings, and it measures the government's borrowing need. It was about 5.9% in 2011-12, 3.5% in 2016-17 and 9.2% in 2020-21, and the government now targets below 4.5% by 2025-26. The FRBM Act 2003 sets the legal framework.

Option (c) 'Both 1 and 2' would mean both ratios rose steadily. Neither did. This option is the kind of trap UPSC sets by using absolute words like 'steadily'. Both ratios were affected by GST rollout in 2017, the 2019 corporate tax cut (from 30% to 22% for existing companies) and the Covid shock in 2020-21, so neither follows a smooth path.

Option (d) 'Neither 1 nor 2' is the official answer. It reflects that both ratios moved up and down over the decade. Tax revenue was hit by the corporate tax cut of September 2019 and the pandemic, then recovered with GST buoyancy and higher direct tax collections. The fiscal deficit was consolidated until 2018-19, spiked in 2020-21 and has been reduced since. Neither shows a steady rise.
related: Fiscal deficit = total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings.
FRBM Act was enacted in 2003; the N.K. Singh Committee reported in 2017.
The Centre's fiscal deficit hit about 9.2% of GDP in 2020-21 because of Covid.
GST came into effect on 1 July 2017 under the 101st Constitutional Amendment.
Article 279A provides for the GST Council.
The 15th Finance Commission recommended 41% devolution to States.
India's general government tax-to-GDP ratio is about 17-18%, lower than the OECD average.
Corporate tax rate was cut to 22% for existing companies in September 2019.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The tax-to-GDP ratio has fluctuated and has not risen steadily. The Centre's gross tax revenue was about 10-11% of GDP in the mid-2010s, peaked around 11.7% in 2018-19, fell to about 10.2% in 2019-20 and 2020-21, and recovered only later. Tax-to-GDP is total tax revenue as a share of national output and measures the state's capacity to mobilise resources. India's general government ratio is about 17-18%, below the OECD average of about 34% and below many emerging peers. The Centre's gross tax revenue includes direct taxes (income tax, corporation tax) and indirect taxes (GST, customs, excise). GST was introduced on 1 July 2017 (101st Amendment Act, 2016). Buoyancy is the responsiveness of tax revenue to GDP growth. The Kelkar Committee and Tax Administration Reform Commission discussed improving the ratio.

2 — Incorrect: The fiscal deficit-to-GDP ratio has not risen steadily. It fell from about 5.9% in 2011-12 to 3.5% in 2016-17, and stayed near 3.4-3.5% until 2018-19. It then rose to 4.6% in 2019-20 and spiked to about 9.2% in 2020-21 because of Covid, before declining again to about 6.7% in 2022-23, 5.6% in 2023-24 and 4.8% in 2024-25. Fiscal deficit is total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings. The FRBM Act 2003 set targets for the deficit, and the N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended a 3% target and a debt-to-GDP anchor of 60% for general government. The government has committed to bringing the deficit below 4.5% by 2025-26.
summary: The answer is (d) Neither 1 nor 2. India's tax-to-GDP ratio has not risen steadily over the decade (it rose, stagnated and dipped, with a sharp fall in 2020-21). The fiscal deficit-to-GDP ratio has fallen over most of the period, with a spike in 2020-21, so it has not increased steadily either.
topic_notes: Fiscal indicators are a recurring UPSC theme. The fiscal deficit equals total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings. Gross primary deficit equals fiscal deficit minus interest payments. Revenue deficit equals revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. Effective revenue deficit equals revenue deficit minus grants for creation of capital assets. The FRBM Act 2003 aimed at eliminating the revenue deficit and bringing the fiscal deficit to 3% of GDP. It was suspended or relaxed in 2008-09 (global financial crisis) and 2020-21 (Covid). The N.K. Singh FRBM Review Committee (2017) recommended a debt-to-GDP target of 60% for general government (40% for Centre, 20% for States), a 3% fiscal deficit anchor, and a Fiscal Council. The government instead used the FRBM amendment of 2018 to set a Centre debt target of 40% by 2024-25. Tax revenue comprises direct taxes (personal income tax, corporation tax) and indirect taxes (GST, customs, Union excise on petroleum and tobacco). India's gross tax-to-GDP ratio for the Centre is about 11-12%, while the general government ratio is about 17-18%. Tax buoyancy is the ratio of tax revenue growth to GDP growth. GST was launched on 1 July 2017, with the GST Council under Article 279A. Compensation to States for revenue loss ran for five years until June 2022. Non-tax revenue includes dividends from the RBI and PSUs, interest receipts and spectrum fees. Capital receipts include borrowings, recovery of loans and disinvestment. The Union Budget is presented under Article 112 as the Annual Financial Statement. Article 266 covers the Consolidated Fund of India. Article 267 covers the Contingency Fund. The Finance Commission under Article 280 recommends devolution; the 15th FC (N.K. Singh) set States' share of divisible pool at 41%, and the 16th FC is chaired by Arvind Panagariya.

question: Recently there was a proposal to translocate some of the lions from their natural habitat in Gujarat to which one of the following sites ?
subject: Environment
detail: The Asiatic lion (Panthera leo persica) survives in the wild only in Gujarat's Gir landscape (Gir National Park and Sanctuary, Pania, Mitiyala, Girnar and surrounding areas). Because one population is exposed to epidemics (such as the 2018 canine distemper outbreak that killed many lions), fire, flood or cyclone, the Wildlife Institute of India recommended a second site in the 1990s. Kuno Palpur in Sheopur and Morena districts of Madhya Pradesh was chosen after surveys for its suitable habitat, prey base and the relocation of villages. The Supreme Court in April 2013 directed that lions be translocated to Kuno within six months, but Gujarat resisted and the move did not happen. Kuno later received African cheetahs (Namibia, September 2022; South Africa, 2023) under Project Cheetah. Elimination logic: Corbett (Uttarakhand) is a tiger and elephant reserve; Mudumalai (Tamil Nadu) is in the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve with tigers and elephants; Sariska (Rajasthan) is a tiger reserve that saw tiger reintroduction in 2008. None was proposed for lions.
explanations: Incorrect: Corbett National Park in Uttarakhand is a tiger habitat, and no lion translocation was proposed there.
Correct: Kuno Palpur Wildlife Sanctuary in Madhya Pradesh was the site identified for the second Asiatic lion population, and the Supreme Court backed this in 2013.
Incorrect: Mudumalai Wildlife Sanctuary in Tamil Nadu is a tiger and elephant area and was never proposed for lions.
Incorrect: Sariska National Park in Rajasthan is known for tiger reintroduction from Ranthambore starting in 2008, not for lions.
keyfact: Asiatic lions from Gir were proposed for translocation to Kuno Palpur (Madhya Pradesh) as a second home, backed by the Supreme Court in 2013.
option_notes: Corbett National Park, Uttarakhand, is India's oldest national park, established in 1936 as Hailey National Park. It lies in Nainital and Pauri Garhwal districts on the Ramganga river. It was the first reserve under Project Tiger in 1973 and holds a high tiger density along with elephants.

Kuno Palpur Wildlife Sanctuary is in Sheopur and Morena districts of Madhya Pradesh, on the Kuno river, a tributary of the Chambal. It was notified as a sanctuary in 1981 and upgraded to a national park in 2018. It was prepared as the Asiatic lion reintroduction site and became the site of Project Cheetah in 2022.

Mudumalai Wildlife Sanctuary is in the Nilgiri district of Tamil Nadu, at the junction of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Kerala. It is part of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve and was declared a tiger reserve in 2007. It has tigers, elephants, gaur and leopards, with the Moyar river flowing through it.

Sariska National Park is in Alwar district, Rajasthan, in the Aravalli hills. It became a tiger reserve in 1978 under Project Tiger. All its tigers were lost to poaching by 2004-05, and tigers were reintroduced from Ranthambore from 2008, the first such tiger translocation in the world.
related: Asiatic lions in the wild exist only in Gujarat's Gir landscape.
