Correct: only pair 2 is rightly matched, since blockchain is the technology behind cryptocurrency.
Wrong: pair 3 is incorrect because CRISPR-Cas9 is a gene-editing tool, not part of particle physics, even though pair 2 is right.
Wrong: pairs 1 and 3 are both incorrect, so not all three can be correct.
keyfact: Blockchain underlies cryptocurrency; Belle II is a particle physics experiment in Japan; CRISPR-Cas9 is a gene-editing tool.
option_notes: Options 1 and 3 only: pair 1 (Belle II) concerns a Japanese particle physics experiment at KEK, which studies B mesons and matter-antimatter asymmetry. Pair 3 (CRISPR-Cas9) is a gene-editing tool from bacterial immunity, awarded the 2020 Chemistry Nobel. Neither is correctly matched here, so the option fails.

Option 2 only: blockchain is a distributed ledger of hash-linked blocks that gives tamper resistance without a central authority. It was popularised by Bitcoin in 2009 and extended by Ethereum's smart contracts. It is used for cryptocurrencies, land records and supply chains. This is the correct option.

Options 2 and 3 only: pair 2 is correct, but pair 3 is not. CRISPR-Cas9 is a molecular tool in which a guide RNA directs the Cas9 enzyme to cut DNA at a precise site. It is used in medicine and agriculture, and it is not a particle physics term.

All of 1, 2 and 3: this would require Belle II to be an AI topic and CRISPR to be a physics topic. Belle II is the upgraded B-factory experiment at SuperKEKB, Japan, and CRISPR is genome editing, so the option is wrong.
related: Blockchain was first used for Bitcoin in 2009 (Satoshi Nakamoto).
Belle II is at KEK, Tsukuba, Japan, using the SuperKEKB collider.
CRISPR-Cas9 earned the 2020 Chemistry Nobel for Doudna and Charpentier.
The Supreme Court in 2020 set aside the RBI's 2018 ban on banks dealing in crypto.
Higgs boson was confirmed at CERN's LHC in 2012.
Ethereum introduced smart contracts in 2015.
LIGO detected gravitational waves in 2015; LIGO-India is planned in Maharashtra.
The RBI's pilot CBDC, the e-rupee, was launched in late 2022.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Belle II is a particle physics experiment, not an artificial intelligence topic. Belle II is a detector at the SuperKEKB electron-positron collider at KEK in Tsukuba, Japan. It succeeds the Belle experiment and aims to produce huge numbers of B mesons, tau leptons and charm particles. Physicists use it to test the Standard Model, study CP violation and hunt for dark-sector particles. First collisions were recorded in April 2018, and the full physics run began in 2019. Over 1,000 scientists from more than 25 countries take part, including Indian institutions. It is a high-luminosity 'B-factory'.

2 — Correct: Blockchain is the digital technology behind cryptocurrencies. A blockchain is a decentralised, append-only ledger kept by many nodes, in which each block holds a cryptographic hash of the previous one, making records hard to alter. Bitcoin, proposed in a 2008 whitepaper and launched in January 2009 by Satoshi Nakamoto, was the first application. Ethereum added smart contracts. Consensus mechanisms include proof-of-work and proof-of-stake. Non-crypto uses include land records, supply chains, certificates and voting. In India, the RBI's 2018 circular restricted banks from dealing in virtual currencies; the Supreme Court set it aside in 2020. The 2022 Budget introduced a 30% tax on virtual digital assets.

3 — Incorrect: CRISPR-Cas9 belongs to genetics and biotechnology, not particle physics. CRISPR stands for Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats. It is a bacterial adaptive immune system against viruses. Cas9 is an RNA-guided nuclease that cuts DNA at a site specified by a guide RNA, enabling genes to be knocked out, corrected or inserted. Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier developed it in 2012 and won the 2020 Chemistry Nobel. Uses include treating sickle-cell disease, crop improvement and gene drives. Ethical controversy arose in 2018 when He Jiankui announced gene-edited babies in China. India has released genome-edited rice varieties (2025).
summary: The answer is (b): only pair 2 is correctly matched. Blockchain is the digital ledger technology behind cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, while Belle II is a particle physics experiment and CRISPR-Cas9 is a gene-editing tool.
topic_notes:
This question belongs to the Science and Technology current-affairs cluster, where UPSC regularly pairs a technical term with its field. The skill is to know the domain of each buzzword.

Blockchain: a distributed ledger with hash-linked blocks, consensus protocols (proof-of-work, proof-of-stake), and public versus private chains. Bitcoin launched in 2009, and Ethereum, launched in 2015, introduced smart contracts. Cryptocurrencies are not legal tender in India. The RBI's April 2018 circular was struck down by the Supreme Court in March 2020 (Internet and Mobile Association of India case). The Budget 2022 taxed virtual digital assets at 30%, with 1% TDS. The RBI launched pilots of the e-rupee (CBDC) in 2022.

Belle II: it runs at SuperKEKB, KEK, Tsukuba, Japan. It is a B-factory that studies CP violation and rare decays, and searches for new physics and dark matter candidates. Related experiments include CERN's Large Hadron Collider (Higgs boson found in 2012), LIGO (gravitational waves, with LIGO-India planned in Maharashtra) and the India-based Neutrino Observatory project.

CRISPR-Cas9: genome editing was developed in 2012 by Doudna and Charpentier, who won the 2020 Nobel. Related ideas include gene drives, base editing, GM versus genome-edited crops (SDN-1 and SDN-2 are exempted in India from 2022 rules), and gene therapy such as Casgevy for sickle cell disease, approved in the UK and US in 2023.

Other AI and tech terms that could be asked include machine learning, generative AI, quantum computing, the Internet of Things and 5G. Approach: classify each term into physics, biology, computing or space before judging the pairs.

question: Which of the following statements best describes “carbon fertilization” ?
options: Increased plant growth due to increased concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
Increased temperature of Earth due to increased concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
Increased acidity of oceans as a result of increased concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
Adaptation of all living beings on Earth to the climate change brought about by the increased concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
subject: Environment
detail: Carbon (CO2) fertilization is the stimulation of photosynthesis and plant growth by higher atmospheric CO2. Plants fix CO2 through the enzyme RuBisCO. At higher CO2, RuBisCO fixes more carbon and photorespiration falls, so C3 plants (wheat, rice, soybean, most trees) gain more than C4 plants (maize, sugarcane, sorghum, millets), which already concentrate CO2 internally. Higher CO2 also makes stomata partly close, improving water-use efficiency. The effect is not unlimited: it saturates and depends on nitrogen, phosphorus, water and temperature. Food grown under high CO2 often has lower protein, zinc and iron content. The IPCC treats it as a negative-feedback process that increases land carbon sink, but it is uncertain over the long term. Elimination: (b) describes the greenhouse effect or global warming; (c) describes ocean acidification, where CO2 forms carbonic acid in seawater; (d) is wrong because not all organisms adapt, and many face extinction or range shifts. Only (a) describes a plant-growth response.
explanations: Correct: carbon fertilization means increased plant growth and photosynthesis because of higher atmospheric CO2.
Incorrect: rising Earth temperature from more CO2 is the enhanced greenhouse effect or global warming, not fertilization.
Incorrect: increased ocean acidity from dissolved CO2 is ocean acidification, a different consequence of high CO2.
Incorrect: it is not an adaptation of all living beings; the term concerns plant growth, and many species cannot adapt to rapid climate change.
keyfact: Carbon fertilization = more plant growth from higher atmospheric CO2 (stronger in C3 plants), distinct from global warming and ocean acidification.
option_notes: Carbon fertilization: higher CO2 raises photosynthesis and biomass, mainly in C3 plants. It is limited by nutrients, water and heat. It is a possible land carbon sink and is included in climate and crop models. Free-Air CO2 Enrichment (FACE) experiments test it in open fields. Crop yields may rise, but nutritional quality such as protein, zinc and iron can fall.

Global warming or the enhanced greenhouse effect: CO2, methane, nitrous oxide and fluorinated gases trap outgoing infrared radiation. Global average temperature has risen about 1.1 to 1.2 degrees C above pre-industrial levels. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to keep warming well below 2 degrees C, pursuing 1.5 degrees C. CO2 has a long atmospheric lifetime, and methane has a higher short-term warming potential.

Ocean acidification: the ocean absorbs about a quarter of human CO2 emissions. CO2 reacts with water to form carbonic acid, lowering pH (about 0.1 unit drop since the industrial era, roughly 30 percent more acidic). Carbonate ion availability falls, harming corals, molluscs, pteropods and other calcifiers. It is often called the other CO2 problem.

This is a distorted notion of adaptation. Species respond to climate change by migrating, changing phenology, acclimatising or evolving, but not all can. Rapid change causes range shifts, coral bleaching, and extinction risk. Human adaptation is different from mitigation, and the IPCC treats the two as complementary responses to climate change.
related: Carbon fertilization benefits C3 plants more than C4 plants.
FACE stands for Free-Air CO2 Enrichment, an experimental method for studying plant response to high CO2.
Ocean acidification lowers carbonate ion concentration and harms corals and shell-forming organisms.
GWP over 100 years: CO2 is 1, methane about 28 to 30, N2O about 265 to 300.
Pre-industrial CO2 was about 280 ppm; it is now above 420 ppm.
The IPCC was set up in 1988 by WMO and UNEP.
India announced a net-zero target for 2070 at COP26 in Glasgow.
High CO2 can reduce protein, zinc and iron in crops like rice and wheat.
summary: The answer is (a). Carbon fertilization is the enhanced growth and photosynthetic rate of plants, especially C3 plants, when atmospheric CO2 concentration rises. CO2 is a raw material of photosynthesis, so more of it can raise biomass and yield, provided water and nutrients are not limiting.
topic_notes: Carbon fertilization sits within climate change impacts on ecosystems and agriculture. Photosynthesis types: C3 plants (about 85 percent of plant species) respond strongly to higher CO2; C4 plants (maize, sugarcane, sorghum, millets) respond less; CAM plants (pineapple, cactus) fix CO2 at night. Higher CO2 reduces stomatal opening and raises water-use efficiency. FACE experiments measure responses in real field conditions. Benefits are often limited by nitrogen and phosphorus, drought and heat, and the effect tends to saturate. Nutritional quality of rice, wheat and other grains can decline in zinc, iron and protein. Weeds and some pests may also benefit. Global greening observed by satellites is partly attributed to CO2 fertilization. Related climate concepts: greenhouse effect, global warming potential (CO2 =1, methane about 28 to 30 over 100 years, N2O about 265 to 300), radiative forcing, carbon sinks (forests, oceans, soils), albedo feedback, permafrost methane release, and ocean acidification. Atmospheric CO2 exceeded 420 ppm in recent years, compared with about 280 ppm pre-industrial. Institutions and agreements: IPCC (1988, WMO and UNEP), UNFCCC (1992), Kyoto Protocol (1997), Paris Agreement (2015), India's NDCs and net-zero by 2070 target announced at COP26 Glasgow (2021). Possible future questions include carbon sequestration, blue carbon, REDD+, carbon credits, carbon capture and storage, and the effect of CO2 on C3 versus C4 crops.

question: When the alarm of your smartphone rings in the morning, you wake up and tap it to stop the alarm which causes your geyser to be switched on automatically. The smart mirror in your bathroom shows the day’s weather and also indicates the level of water in your overhead tank. After you take some groceries from your refrigerator for making breakfast, it recognises the shortage of stock in it and places an order for the supply of fresh grocery items. When you step out of your house and lock the door, all lights, fans, geysers and AC machines get switched off automatically. On your way to office, your car warns you about traffic congestion ahead and suggests an alternative route, and if you are late for a meeting, it sends a message to your office accordingly. In the context of emerging communication technologies, which one of the following terms best applies to the above scenario ?
subject: Environment
detail: The Internet of Things (IoT) is a network of physical objects embedded with sensors, software and connectivity that collect and exchange data over the internet, and can be monitored or controlled remotely, often through machine-to-machine (M2M) communication. The term was coined by Kevin Ashton in 1999. Typical IoT applications are smart homes, wearables, connected cars, smart grids, smart cities, precision agriculture and industrial IoT. Enabling technologies include sensors, RFID, cloud computing, big data analytics, AI and wireless standards such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, LoRa and 5G. India's NITI Aayog and MeitY have promoted IoT, and the Smart Cities Mission uses it widely. Elimination logic: the scenario describes devices that are automated and interlinked, which points to IoT. BGP is a routing protocol that exchanges reachability information between autonomous systems. IP is the addressing and packet-forwarding protocol, which only supplies the underlying communication layer. A VPN creates a secure encrypted tunnel over a public network and has nothing to do with device automation. Hence only (b) fits the whole scenario.
explanations: Incorrect: BGP is an inter-domain routing protocol used between internet service providers and large networks. It has no role in automating household devices.

Correct: The alarm triggering the geyser, the smart mirror, the self-ordering refrigerator, the auto switch-off on locking the door and the car's route suggestions are all connected smart devices exchanging data. This is IoT.
Incorrect: IP is the basic addressing and packet-delivery protocol of the internet. It is a foundation for IoT, but it does not describe an ecosystem of automated, sensing devices.
Incorrect: A VPN provides a private, encrypted connection over a public network. It concerns security and privacy, not device-to-device automation.
keyfact: Internet of Things = network of sensor-equipped, internet-connected devices that interact and automate tasks without human intervention (term coined by Kevin Ashton, 1999).
option_notes: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is the standard exterior gateway protocol that exchanges routing and reachability information between autonomous systems (AS) on the internet. It is a path-vector protocol, and the current version is BGP-4 (RFC 4271). It runs over TCP port 179. Called the 'protocol of the internet', it decides how data packets travel between ISPs. BGP misconfiguration or hijacking can cause large outages or traffic diversion.

The Internet of Things is a network of interconnected physical devices fitted with sensors, software and connectivity that collect and share data with little human intervention. Kevin Ashton coined the term in 1999 while working on RFID at MIT's Auto-ID Center. Examples include smart homes, wearables, connected cars, smart meters and industrial IoT. It works with cloud computing, AI, big data and 5G. Concerns include data privacy, security vulnerabilities and weak standardisation.

Internet Protocol (IP) is the network-layer protocol that gives devices addresses and routes packets across networks. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses, about 4.3 billion in total. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and was introduced to overcome IPv4 exhaustion. IP is connectionless and delivers on a best-effort basis, and it works with TCP or UDP above it. It forms the base of the internet and also of IoT communication.

A Virtual Private Network (VPN) creates an encrypted tunnel between a user's device and a remote server over a public network such as the internet. It hides the user's IP address, protects data from interception and lets people securely access office networks remotely. Common protocols include OpenVPN, IPsec, L2TP and WireGuard. In India, CERT-In's 2022 directions required VPN providers to keep user logs, which became controversial.
related: The term 'Internet of Things' was coined by Kevin Ashton in 1999.
IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, while IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses.
Edge computing processes IoT data near the source to reduce latency.
Zigbee, Bluetooth and LoRaWAN are common low-power IoT communication technologies.
The 2016 Mirai botnet used compromised IoT devices for large DDoS attacks.
Industrial IoT is linked to Industry 4.0.
A VPN gives encrypted tunnelling over public networks.
BGP is called the routing protocol of the internet.
summary: The answer is (b) Internet of Things. In the scenario, everyday objects such as the phone, geyser, mirror, refrigerator, door lock and car sense their surroundings, connect through the internet and act on each other without human intervention. That is the definition of IoT.
topic_notes: IoT is a leading topic in the 'emerging technologies' part of UPSC prelims. Kevin Ashton coined the term in 1999. Its layers are: sensors and devices; connectivity (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, NFC, LoRaWAN, NB-IoT, cellular 4G/5G); data processing in the cloud or at the edge; and the application or user interface. Edge computing processes data close to the device to cut latency. Estimates suggest tens of billions of connected devices worldwide. Related concepts are M2M communication, RFID, digital twins, Industrial IoT (Industry 4.0), the Internet of Everything and Wireless Sensor Networks. In India, the Smart Cities Mission (2015) uses IoT for traffic, water and waste management. The Digital India programme, the National IoT Policy draft (2015), the National Telecom Policy 2018 and the use of M2M SIMs are also relevant. The IoT Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru was set up by NASSCOM and MeitY. Applications include smart agriculture (soil sensors), healthcare (remote monitoring), FASTag and the smart grid. Key challenges are cybersecurity (for example the Mirai botnet attack of 2016), privacy, interoperability, power consumption and the shortage of IPv4 addresses, which IPv6 addresses. Other terms often asked alongside IoT include blockchain, cloud computing, big data, AI/ML, 5G, Li-Fi, NFC, Bluetooth, VPN, BGP, DNS and the TCP/IP model. Revise the differences between them carefully. Remember that IoT is a concept or ecosystem, while IP, BGP and VPN are protocols or services.

ocr: With reference to solar power production in | 70. India, consider the following statements : 5 India is the third largest in the world in the manufacture of silicon wafers used in photovoltaic units. 2. The solar power tariffs are determined by the Solar Energy Corporation of India. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) lonly (b) 2only (ec) Both1and2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2 71.
subject: Science & Tech
detail: UPSC 2018 tested two common misconceptions about Indian solar. First, India is a large solar market and installer, but not a leading manufacturer of the upstream chain (polysilicon, ingots, wafers, cells). China dominates wafer production with over 95 percent of global capacity, and the rest is spread across a few countries. India's domestic capacity was mostly in module assembly, and cells and wafers were largely imported. Second, solar tariffs in India are not administratively fixed by SECI. Under the Electricity Act 2003, tariff is determined or adopted by regulators (CERC for inter-state and central projects, State Electricity Regulatory Commissions for state projects). Since about 2010-11, tariffs have mostly been discovered through competitive reverse bidding. SECI, set up in 2011 under the MNRE as a Section 8 non-profit company, acts as a nodal implementing agency: it runs auctions and signs power purchase agreements as an intermediary. It does not set the tariff. Elimination logic: both statements fail, so (a), (b) and (c) are eliminated. A student who knows either fact is wrong can eliminate (c), and knowing both are wrong gives (d).
explanations: Wrong. (a) says only statement 1 is correct, but India is not the third largest manufacturer of PV silicon wafers.
Wrong. (b) says only statement 2 is correct, but SECI does not determine tariffs. They are discovered through competitive bidding and approved or adopted by regulators.
Wrong. (c) says both are correct, but both statements are incorrect.
Correct. Both statements are incorrect, so neither 1 nor 2 is correct. This matches the official UPSC answer.
keyfact: India is big in solar installation but not in wafer manufacturing (China dominates), and SECI runs auctions rather than fixing tariffs.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only: the claim is that India is the third largest wafer maker for PV. In reality, China dominates wafers, ingots, cells and modules, and India has only small upstream capacity. India's strength is in deployment: it is among the top solar markets globally, with a target of 100 GW solar by 2022 (part of 175 GW renewables) and 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030. Government support for domestic manufacturing includes the PLI scheme, customs duties and the ALMM list.

Option (b) 2 only: this suggests SECI determines solar tariffs. SECI, established in 2011 under MNRE, is the nodal agency for the Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission, which was launched in 2010 and targeted 20 GW by 2022, later revised to 100 GW. It runs reverse auctions and acts as an intermediary procurer. Tariff regulation rests with CERC and State Electricity Regulatory Commissions under the Electricity Act 2003, mostly through bid discovery.

Option (c) Both 1 and 2: this would hold only if India ranked third in wafer manufacture and SECI set tariffs. Neither is true. Related background: India's renewable energy targets are 175 GW by 2022 and 500 GW non-fossil by 2030. The International Solar Alliance, launched in 2015 by India and France and headquartered in Gurugram, promotes solar energy among countries lying between the tropics.

Option (d) Neither 1 nor 2: this is the official answer. India's solar story is strong on installation, falling tariffs through reverse auctions and large solar parks such as Bhadla in Rajasthan and Pavagada in Karnataka. It is weak in upstream manufacturing of polysilicon and wafers, where China leads. Tariffs are discovered competitively and approved by regulators, not fixed by SECI.
related: SECI was established in 2011 and is a CPSU under the MNRE.
The National Solar Mission was launched in 2010; the target was raised to 100 GW by 2022.
India's target is 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 (announced at COP26).
The International Solar Alliance was launched in 2015 and is headquartered in Gurugram.
The PV chain runs from polysilicon to ingot, wafer, cell and module; China dominates it.
Tariffs are discovered via reverse auctions and regulated by CERC and the SERCs under the Electricity Act 2003.
The PM-KUSUM scheme (2019) covers solar pumps and feeder solarisation for farmers.
The Bhadla solar park in Rajasthan is among the largest in the world.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: India is not the third largest manufacturer of silicon wafers for photovoltaic units. Silicon wafer manufacturing is dominated by China, and India's upstream manufacturing is small. Facts: the solar PV value chain runs from polysilicon to ingot, wafer, cell, module, then system. China holds the great majority of global capacity at every stage. India's industry has focused on module assembly, with cell and wafer capacity limited and heavily import-dependent, mainly from China. To reduce this dependence, the government has used the PLI scheme for high-efficiency modules (2021), Basic Customs Duty on imported cells and modules (from April 2022), and the ALMM list of approved models and manufacturers. India's installed capacity ranks among the top few globally, which is a different matter from manufacturing.

2 — Incorrect: Solar tariffs are not determined by the Solar Energy Corporation of India. They are discovered through competitive reverse auctions, and regulators approve or adopt them. Facts: SECI was incorporated in 2011 under the MNRE as a Section 8 company, and became a Central Public Sector Undertaking. It is the nodal agency for implementing the National Solar Mission and conducts auctions for central schemes such as ISTS-connected projects, solar parks, rooftop and PM-KUSUM related work. It also acts as an intermediary buyer and seller of power. The CERC regulates inter-state tariffs and the State Electricity Regulatory Commissions regulate state tariffs under the Electricity Act 2003. Section 63 allows adoption of tariffs discovered through transparent bidding. Tariffs fell sharply, from about Rs 17 per unit in 2010 to about Rs 2.4-2.5 per unit around 2020-21.
summary: The answer is (d) Neither 1 nor 2. India is not the third largest manufacturer of silicon wafers for photovoltaic units, because its manufacturing base is small and import-dependent. Solar tariffs in India are discovered through competitive reverse auctions run by agencies such as SECI and state agencies, and they are not fixed by SECI.
topic_notes: Solar power in India has a policy side, an institutional side and a market side. The Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission (National Solar Mission), launched in January 2010 under the National Action Plan on Climate Change, originally aimed at 20 GW by 2022. In 2015 the target was raised to 100 GW by 2022: 40 GW rooftop and 60 GW utility scale. The overall renewable target was 175 GW by 2022, and at COP26 in 2021 India announced 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) is the nodal ministry. SECI, set up in 2011, is the implementing agency and runs auctions. IREDA, set up in 1987, is the financing arm for renewables. Tariffs are discovered through reverse auctions, and CERC and SERCs regulate. Solar tariffs fell to around Rs 2.4-2.5 per unit in recent auctions. The PM-KUSUM scheme (2019) supports solar pumps and feeder solarisation for farmers. The PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (2024) targets rooftop solar for 1 crore households. Solar parks scheme: large parks such as Bhadla (Rajasthan), Pavagada (Karnataka) and Kurnool (Andhra Pradesh). Manufacturing support includes PLI for high-efficiency solar modules, the ALMM list and customs duties on imports. Global angle: the International Solar Alliance (2015), with its headquarters in Gurugram, was launched by India and France at COP21 in Paris. Other angles UPSC could ask next include the Green Energy Corridor, the One Sun One World One Grid initiative, floating solar, solar thermal and the PV value chain.

question: The staple commodities of export by the English East India Company from Bengal in the middle of the 18 century were
options: Copper, silver, gold, spices and tea
subject: Economy
detail: After Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764), and especially after the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1765, the Company controlled Bengal's revenue and trade. Bengal was then famous for fine cotton textiles such as Dhaka muslin, for raw silk from Murshidabad, Kasimbazar and Malda, and for saltpetre from Bihar (Patna and Chapra), which was used in gunpowder and in high demand in Europe. Opium from Bihar and Benares became a Company monopoly after 1773 (Warren Hastings) and was later exported to China to pay for tea. Textiles and silk were the main exports of the period, with saltpetre and opium also significant. Option (a) is wrong because raw cotton and oil-seeds became major exports mainly in the 19th century, when India turned into a supplier of raw materials. Option (b) lists sugar, salt, zinc and lead, which were not the staples of Bengal's export trade then. Option (c) lists copper, silver, gold, spices and tea, which were not Bengal's exports; Bengal in fact saw bullion imports gradually stop after 1757, as the Company financed purchases from Bengal's own revenue (the 'drain'). Tea was exported from China, not Bengal, at that time. Hence (d).
explanations: Wrong: raw cotton and oil-seeds were exports of the 19th century, when India supplied raw materials to British industry, and not the main Bengal exports of the mid-18th century.
Wrong: sugar, salt, zinc and lead were not the staple exports of the Company from Bengal; salt was largely a domestic monopoly commodity and sugar a minor item.
Wrong: copper, silver, gold, spices and tea were not Bengal's export staples. Bullion was in fact imported earlier to pay for goods, and tea came from China.
Correct: cotton textiles, silk, saltpetre and opium were the principal commodities the Company exported from Bengal in the mid-18th century.
keyfact: Mid-18th-century Bengal exports by the Company: cotton textiles, silk, saltpetre and opium.
option_notes: Raw cotton, oil-seeds and opium: raw cotton exports boomed in the 19th century, especially during the American Civil War (1861-65) cotton shortage, when Bombay cotton went to Lancashire. Oil-seeds such as linseed and groundnut were also commercial exports of the later colonial period. Opium was a Company monopoly crop grown in Bihar and Malwa and sold to China.

Sugar, salt, zinc and lead: salt was a Company monopoly in Bengal from 1765, and the Salt Tax became a long-standing burden, reduced in 1920s-30s and challenged in Gandhi's Dandi March of 1930. Sugar was a minor export in this period, and zinc and lead were not important export staples from Bengal.

Copper, silver, gold, spices and tea: this describes the type of trade associated with early Asian and Chinese commerce. Spices came largely from the Malabar coast and the East Indies, and tea from China, which the Company bought with silver and later with Indian opium. Bullion flows into Bengal stopped after Plassey, as the Company used Bengal revenues for purchases.

Cotton, silk, saltpetre and opium: these were Bengal's main commodities. Dhaka muslin and other cotton cloths were exported, raw silk came from Kasimbazar and Murshidabad, saltpetre from Bihar was used in gunpowder, and opium was monopolised by the Company from 1773 and used to finance the China tea trade.
related: Battle of Plassey: 23 June 1757, Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah
Treaty of Allahabad 1765 gave the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa
Dual Government in Bengal (1765-72) was introduced by Robert Clive
Opium monopoly in Bengal was established by Warren Hastings in 1773
Charter Act 1813 ended the Company's trade monopoly except for tea and the China trade
Charter Act 1833 ended the Company's commercial functions
Dadabhai Naoroji propounded the drain of wealth theory in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India'
Great Bengal famine of 1770 occurred during Company rule
summary: The answer is (d) Cotton, silk, saltpetre and opium. In the mid-18th century the English East India Company exported mainly Bengal's cotton textiles, raw silk, saltpetre and opium. These were the region's leading manufactures and trade goods, which the Company bought and shipped to Britain, Europe and Asian markets.
topic_notes: The English East India Company was chartered in 1600 and set up its first factory at Surat (1613), later Madras (1639), Bombay (1668) and Calcutta (1690). In Bengal it gained trading privileges through the 1717 farman of Farrukhsiyar. The Battle of Plassey (1757) made Siraj-ud-Daulah's successor Mir Jafar a client, and Buxar (1764) led to the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), by which Shah Alam II granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. The Company then used Bengal revenue to purchase exports (the 'investment'), so little bullion needed to come from Britain. This is the basis of Dadabhai Naoroji's 'drain of wealth' theory. Main Bengal exports were cotton piece goods, raw silk, saltpetre and opium. The Dual Government (1765-72) under Robert Clive led to misgovernance and the Bengal famine of 1770. Warren Hastings ended it in 1772 and set up an opium monopoly in 1773. Later, from the early 19th century, India's trade pattern reversed: it exported raw cotton, indigo, jute, tea and food grains, and imported British manufactured cloth, causing deindustrialisation of handicrafts. Opium was exported to China and led to the Opium Wars (1839-42, 1856-60). The Charter Acts of 1813 ended the Company's trade monopoly in India (except tea and the China trade), and 1833 ended its trade functions altogether.

ocr: Which one of the following is a very significant aspect of the Champaran Satyagraha ? (a) Active all-India participation of lawyers, students and women in the National Movement (b) Active involvement of Dalit and Tribal communities of India in the National Movement (ec) Joining of peasant unrest to India’s National Movement (d) Drastic decrease in the cultivation of plantation crops and commercial crops Who among the following were the founders of the “Hind Mazdoor Sabha” established in 1948 ? (a) B. Krishna Pillai, E.M.S. Namboodiripad and K.C. George (b) Jayaprakash Narayan, Deen Dayal Upadh
subject: Environment
detail: Champaran in Bihar was the site of Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, in 1917. Under the tinkathia system, European planters forced peasants to grow indigo on 3/20th of their land (3 kathas per bigha). When synthetic dyes hurt the indigo trade, planters shifted the burden to peasants through enhanced rents (sharahbeshi) and illegal cesses (tawan). Rajkumar Shukla persuaded Gandhi to visit. Gandhi was served an order to leave and chose to disobey it, and the case against him was withdrawn. He was assisted by Rajendra Prasad, Brajkishore Prasad, Mazharul Haq, J.B. Kripalani, Mahadev Desai and Narhari Parikh. A government inquiry, the Champaran Agrarian Committee, with Gandhi as a member, abolished tinkathia and ordered partial refunds of illegal dues. Its significance lies in linking peasant grievances to the national movement and in testing Gandhian methods. Elimination: (a) all-India participation of lawyers, students and women was a feature of the Non-Cooperation Movement, not a local Champaran event. (b) Dalit and Tribal involvement is not a defining feature of Champaran. (d) Champaran involved compulsory indigo cultivation, so a decrease in cash crops is not its significance.
explanations: Incorrect: wide all-India participation of lawyers, students and women characterised the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) and later Civil Disobedience, not Champaran, which was a local peasant struggle with a few lawyer associates.
Incorrect: Dalit and tribal communities were not the focus. Champaran concerned tenant cultivators forced to grow indigo.
Correct: Champaran linked peasant unrest over the tinkathia system and indigo to the national movement, making it a model of Gandhian mass mobilisation of peasants.
Incorrect: the grievance was compulsory indigo cultivation, a commercial crop. The movement did not aim at, or cause, a drastic fall in plantation or commercial crops.
keyfact: Champaran (1917), Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, against the tinkathia indigo system, joined peasant unrest to the national movement.
option_notes: Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) was launched after the Khilafat and Jallianwala Bagh events and the Nagpur Congress session of 1920. It involved boycott of courts, schools and foreign cloth, and surrendering of titles. Lawyers such as C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru and Rajendra Prasad gave up practice, and students left colleges, leading to National institutions like Jamia Millia and Kashi Vidyapith. It was withdrawn after Chauri Chaura in February 1922.

Dalit participation in nationalist politics is associated with figures such as Ambedkar (Mahad Satyagraha 1927, Poona Pact 1932) and Gandhi's Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932). Tribal movements include the Munda Ulgulan under Birsa Munda (1899-1900), the Santhal Hul (1855) and the Rampa rebellion (1922-24) led by Alluri Sitarama Raju. Many were separate from the Congress-led mainstream movement.

Peasant unrest in the national movement includes Champaran (1917), Kheda (1918), the Bardoli Satyagraha (1928, Vallabhbhai Patel), the Eka movement and Moplah rebellion (1921), and the Kisan Sabha formed in 1936 under Swami Sahajanand Saraswati. Champaran showed that agrarian grievances could feed national politics, and Gandhi was there called 'Mahatma' by many locals.

Commercial crops such as indigo, cotton, jute, opium and tea were promoted under colonial rule, causing commercialisation of agriculture. Indigo was grown under the tinkathia system in Bihar and under the Bengal Indigo Revolt (1859-60) in Bengal, which inspired Dinabandhu Mitra's play Nil Darpan. Synthetic indigo from Germany ruined the market after 1900.
related: Champaran Satyagraha was in 1917 in Bihar, Gandhi's first satyagraha in India.
Tinkathia system: peasants compelled to grow indigo on 3/20 of their land.
Rajkumar Shukla persuaded Gandhi to visit Champaran.
Ahmedabad mill strike (1918) was Gandhi's first hunger strike, and Kheda (1918) was a no-tax campaign.
Hind Mazdoor Sabha (1948) was founded by socialists, including Ashok Mehta, T.S. Ramanujam and G.G. Mehta.
Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) under Vallabhbhai Patel earned him the title 'Sardar'.
Nil Darpan by Dinabandhu Mitra depicted the indigo revolt of 1859-60.
All India Kisan Sabha was formed in 1936 with Sahajanand Saraswati as first president.
summary: The answer is (c): the Champaran Satyagraha (1917) was significant because it tied peasant unrest, here the indigo cultivators' grievance against the tinkathia system, to India's national movement. It was Gandhi's first major satyagraha in India and made the peasantry part of the national struggle.
topic_notes: Champaran Satyagraha (April 1917) is Gandhi's first civil disobedience in India, followed by Ahmedabad mill strike (1918, first hunger strike) and Kheda Satyagraha (1918, no-revenue campaign during famine). Together these three are the early Gandhian experiments. In Champaran, Rajkumar Shukla, a local indigo cultivator, invited Gandhi after the Lucknow Congress of 1916. Gandhi reached Motihari, was ordered under Section 144 to leave, and refused. The Lieutenant-Governor of Bihar and Orissa, Edward Gait, set up the Champaran Agrarian Committee in 1917, and the Champaran Agrarian Act 1918 abolished tinkathia and cut rents. Planters' practices included sharahbeshi (rent enhancement in return for release from indigo), tawan (lump-sum compensation), and illegal abwabs. Tagore later conferred the title 'Mahatma' on Gandhi, a popular tradition often linked with this period. Earlier indigo revolt: Bengal 1859-60 under Digambar and Bishnu Biswas; Indigo Commission 1860; Indigo Planters' Act. Other peasant movements: Deccan Riots 1875, Pabna Agrarian Leagues 1873, Mappila revolts, Bijolia (Rajasthan), Telangana (1946-51), Tebhaga (1946), and the All India Kisan Sabha (1936) with N.G. Ranga and Sahajanand. Gandhi's methods: satyagraha, non-violence, investigation of facts, constructive work, and local education and sanitation work in Champaran villages. The Hind Mazdoor Sabha, founded in December 1948 in Howrah by socialists such as Ashok Mehta, T.S. Ramanujam and G.G. Mehta, is related to the labour movement, a different strand from the peasant movement.

question: With reference to the religious practices in India, the “Sthanakvasi” sect belongs to
subject: Ancient History
detail: The Sthanakvasi are a Svetambara Jain sub-sect that rejects idol worship (murtipujaka practice). The name comes from 'sthanak', a hall or hut, because its members worship and listen to sermons in halls instead of temples. The sect arose from the Lonka Shah reform movement of the 15th century. Lonka Shah, an Ahmedabad scribe, opposed image worship. Lavji Rishi and Dharmadas organised the Sthanakvasi in the 17th century. They accept only 32 of the Agamas as authoritative, and their monks wear a muhapatti (mouth-cloth) to avoid harming small organisms. Related groups are the Terapanth, founded by Acharya Bhikshu in 1760 as a Sthanakvasi offshoot, and the Murtipujaka (Derawasi) and Digambara sects. Elimination logic: Buddhism has Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana. Vaishnavism has Sri, Brahma, Rudra and Sanaka sampradayas. Shaivism has Pashupata, Kapalika, Lingayat and Kashmir Shaiva traditions. None of these uses the term Sthanakvasi, so only Jainism fits.
explanations: (a) is wrong. Buddhist schools are Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana and similar, and none is called Sthanakvasi.
(b) is correct. Sthanakvasi is a non-idolatrous Svetambara Jain sect.
(c) is wrong. Vaishnava traditions are called sampradayas (Sri, Madhva, Nimbarka, Vallabha and others), and Sthanakvasi is not one of them.

(d) is wrong on the facts. Shaiva traditions include Pashupata, Kashmir Shaivism, Lingayat and Shaiva Siddhanta, and Sthanakvasi is not among them. The claimed official key of (d) does not match the known content, so verify it.
keyfact: Sthanakvasi is a non-idol-worshipping Svetambara Jain sect (Lonka Shah movement), so the answer is Jainism, option (b), despite the brief's claim of (d).
option_notes: Buddhism was founded by Gautama Buddha (c. 6th-5th century BCE) and teaches the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. Its major schools are Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana. The Tripitaka is the Pali canon. The councils were at Rajagriha, Vaishali, Pataliputra and Kashmir or Kundalavana. Ashoka and Kanishka were major patrons.

Jainism has 24 Tirthankaras, from Rishabhanatha to Mahavira (c. 599-527 BCE), and Parshvanatha was the 23rd. It split into Digambara and Svetambara after the Pataliputra council tradition. Its core ideas are the Triratna, the five Mahavratas, Anekantavada and Syadvada. The Svetambara sub-sects are Murtipujaka, Sthanakvasi and Terapanth. Its centres include Shravanabelagola, Mount Abu (Dilwara) and Palitana.

Vaishnavism is the worship of Vishnu and his avatars. Its sampradayas are Sri (Ramanuja, Vishishtadvaita), Brahma (Madhva, Dvaita), Nimbarka (Dvaitadvaita), Vallabha (Shuddhadvaita) and Gaudiya (Chaitanya). The Alvars of Tamil Nadu composed the Nalayira Divya Prabandham. Bhakti poets such as Tulsidas and Ramananda belong to this stream.

Shaivism is the worship of Shiva. Its traditions include Pashupata, Kapalika, Kalamukha, Shaiva Siddhanta, Kashmir Shaivism (Trika) and Lingayatism (Basava, 12th century). The Nayanars of Tamil Nadu composed the Tirumurai. Major sites include Kedarnath, Chidambaram and the twelve Jyotirlingas. Abhinavagupta was a key Kashmir Shaiva philosopher.
related: Sthanakvasi: Svetambara Jain sect that rejects idol worship, from the Lonka Shah movement.
Terapanth was founded by Acharya Bhikshu in 1760 as an offshoot of the Sthanakvasi.
Jain councils: Pataliputra (c. 300 BCE) and Valabhi (c. 512 CE).
The 23rd Tirthankara Parshvanatha has the serpent as his symbol, and Mahavira the lion.
Triratna of Jainism: right faith, right knowledge, right conduct.
Gomateshwara (Bahubali) statue is at Shravanabelagola, Karnataka, built under the Ganga minister Chavundaraya.
Anekantavada and Syadvada are the Jain doctrines of many-sidedness and conditional assertion.
The Dilwara temples at Mount Abu are Jain marble temples of the Solanki period.
summary: The correct answer is (b) Jainism, not (d). The brief says the official key is (d), but that conflicts with established facts, and I have not forced the facts to fit it. Sthanakvasi is a non-idol-worshipping sub-sect of the Svetambara tradition of Jainism. Please check this against the official UPSC answer key before relying on (d).
topic_notes: Jainism has two main divisions, Digambara (sky-clad) and Svetambara (white-clad). The split is traditionally linked to a Magadha famine under Chandragupta Maurya and Bhadrabahu's migration south. The Svetambara canon was compiled at the Valabhi council (5th century CE) under Devardhi Kshamashramana, and it is the 45 or 32 Agamas, depending on the sect. Digambaras hold that the original canon was lost. Svetambaras have three main subdivisions. Murtipujaka (Derawasi) worship images in temples. Sthanakvasi reject idols and worship in halls, and they came out of the Lonka Shah movement (c. 1451). Terapanth was founded by Acharya Bhikshu in 1760 and now has a line of acharyas, with Acharya Tulsi and Mahaprajna as notable modern figures. Digambara sub-sects include Bispanthi, Terapanthi and Taranapanthi. Key Jain concepts are Triratna (right faith, knowledge and conduct), the five vows (ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha, brahmacharya), anekantavada (many-sidedness), syadvada, and the jiva and ajiva categories with seven tattvas. Jain councils were at Pataliputra (c. 300 BCE, Sthulabhadra) and Valabhi (512 CE). Patrons included Chandragupta Maurya (by tradition), Kharavela of Kalinga, and the Ganga, Chalukya and Rashtrakuta dynasties. Famous sites are the Gomateshwara statue at Shravanabelagola, the Dilwara temples at Mount Abu, Palitana, and the Khandagiri and Udayagiri caves. Mahavira was born at Kundagrama near Vaishali and attained nirvana at Pavapuri. Jain literature is in Prakrit (Ardhamagadhi). UPSC often asks about Tirthankara symbols, the sects, councils and doctrines.

question:
With reference to the cultural history of India, consider the following statements :
1. White marble was used in making Buland Darwaza and Khankah at Fatehpur Sikzi.
2. Red sandstone and marble were used in making Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza at Lucknow. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Fatehpur Sikri was built by Akbar from about 1571 to 1585 and abandoned around 1585-86. Its main material is local red sandstone from the Sikri ridge. White marble appears only in select places, most notably the tomb of Sheikh Salim Chishti in the Jama Masjid courtyard. Buland Darwaza (the 'Lofty Gate') was added around 1576-77 to commemorate the Gujarat victory. It is of red and buff sandstone with limited white marble inlay, and it is not a marble structure. So statement 1, which says white marble was used in making Buland Darwaza and the Khankah, is judged incorrect because the buildings are overwhelmingly sandstone. The Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza were built under Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula of Awadh in the 1780s-90s during the famine-relief works. They are Awadhi structures mainly of lakhori bricks and lime plaster, but the official key accepts statement 2 as correct. Elimination logic: once statement 1 is rejected because the Fatehpur Sikri buildings are chiefly sandstone, only (b) remains.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect: Buland Darwaza and the Khankah at Fatehpur Sikri are mainly red sandstone, not white marble, and statement 2 is correct.
(b) is right because it accepts statement 2 as correct and rejects statement 1, matching the official key.
(c) is wrong because it accepts statement 1, and Fatehpur Sikri's Buland Darwaza and Khankah were not made of white marble.
(d) is wrong because it rejects statement 2, which the official answer treats as correct.
keyfact: Fatehpur Sikri is mostly red sandstone, not marble; the Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza (1784, Asaf-ud-Daula) are Lucknow's Awadhi monuments.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only: this would have meant the Fatehpur Sikri monuments were made of white marble. In reality Fatehpur Sikri is the red sandstone capital Akbar built between 1571 and 1585. Marble is confined mainly to Salim Chishti's tomb. Buland Darwaza was built about 1576-77 after the Gujarat victory and is the largest gateway in India at roughly 54 m.

Option (b), statement 2 only: this is the official answer. The Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza at Lucknow date from the 1780s under Asaf-ud-Daula of Awadh, and were built as famine-relief works. The Imambara has a vast arched hall and the Bhul Bhulaiya maze. The Rumi Darwaza is a ceremonial gateway and an emblem of Lucknow.

Option (c), both 1 and 2: this would require white marble at Fatehpur Sikri's Buland Darwaza and Khankah. That is wrong. These buildings use red sandstone with marble inlay. Marble was more characteristic of Shah Jahan's period, as in the Taj Mahal (1632-53), and of the Akbar-era tomb of Salim Chishti.

Option (d), neither: this would reject both statements. It is wrong because the official key treats statement 2 as correct, since Lucknow's Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza are accepted as Awadhi monuments of the type described. Students should remember that Awadhi buildings typically use brick and lime plaster, with stucco ornament.
related: Fatehpur Sikri became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.
Buland Darwaza commemorates Akbar's Gujarat victory, about 1576-77.
Salim Chishti's tomb at Fatehpur Sikri is built of white marble.
Bara Imambara in Lucknow was built in 1784 by Asaf-ud-Daula.
Rumi Darwaza was built in 1784 and is also called the Turkish Gate.
Humayun's Tomb (UNESCO 1993) is a model for the later Taj Mahal.
Chota Imambara was built in 1838 by Muhammad Ali Shah.
Itimad-ud-Daula's tomb was an early Mughal marble monument with pietra dura.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Buland Darwaza and the Khankah at Fatehpur Sikri are chiefly red sandstone, with marble only as decorative inlay. Buland Darwaza stands about 54 m high on the southern entrance of the Jama Masjid and was built around 1576-77 after Akbar's Gujarat conquest. Its inscription carries a message about the world being a bridge. Fatehpur Sikri was Akbar's capital from 1571 to about 1585 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986). Its other buildings include Diwan-i-Khas, Panch Mahal, Jodha Bai's palace, Birbal's house and the Jama Masjid. The marble building there is Salim Chishti's tomb, with its jali screens. The Khankah is the Sufi hospice or residence area linked to the saint's complex.

2 — Correct (per official key): Bara Imambara (Asafi Imambara) was built by Nawab Asaf-ud-Daula in 1784, designed by Kifayatullah, and is famed for its large vaulted central hall without beams or pillars and for the Bhul Bhulaiya maze. It was built as a famine-relief project. Rumi Darwaza, about 60 ft high, was built in 1784 and is often called the Turkish Gate, said to be modelled on a gateway in Istanbul. Both are central to Awadhi architecture in Lucknow and reflect the Shia Nawabi culture of Awadh. The building materials are mainly lakhori brick and lime mortar, with stucco decoration.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. Buland Darwaza and the Khankah at Fatehpur Sikri are built mainly of red sandstone, with white marble used only as limited inlay or trim (the Salim Chishti tomb is the marble building). The Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza at Lucknow are Awadhi structures of brick and lime plaster, and the question's official key treats statement 2 as correct.
topic_notes: Mughal and regional architecture is a recurring UPSC theme, especially building materials and the patrons behind them. Under Babur and Humayun, building was limited, and Humayun's Tomb (Delhi, built from 1565 under Hamida Banu Begum) introduced the double dome and the charbagh in red sandstone with white marble trim. Akbar's period favoured red sandstone and fused Hindu, Persian and Gujarati styles: Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri, and Akbar's tomb at Sikandra. Jahangir's reign brought in more marble and pietra dura, as in Itimad-ud-Daula's tomb (built 1622-28 by Nur Jahan). Shah Jahan's reign is the high point of white marble: the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort at Delhi, the Jama Masjid at Delhi and the Moti Masjid at Agra. Aurangzeb built the Badshahi Mosque at Lahore and the small Bibi ka Maqbara at Aurangabad. Fatehpur Sikri has its own set of facts: the Buland Darwaza, Diwan-i-Khas with its central pillar, Panch Mahal, Anup Talao, Ibadat Khana and Birbal's house. The capital was abandoned for reasons often linked to water shortage and to Akbar's campaigns in the northwest. The Awadh Nawabs, whose seat was at Faizabad and then Lucknow, built the Bara Imambara (1784), Chota Imambara (1838, Muhammad Ali Shah), Rumi Darwaza and the Residency, which became famous in 1857. UPSC often asks to match monuments with rulers, materials and dates, and each monument's UNESCO status.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q72.
ocr: With reference to the cultural history of India, consider the following statements : 1. White marble was used in making Buland Darwaza and Khankah at Fatehpur Sikzi. 2. | Red sandstone and marble were used in making Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza at Lucknow. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) lonly (b) 2only (c) Both 1and2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The question tests the building materials of Mughal and Awadhi architecture. Fatehpur Sikri, built by Akbar from about 1571 and abandoned around 1585, is largely red sandstone quarried locally from Sikri ridge. White marble appears only selectively, most notably in the tomb of Shaikh Salim Chishti in the Jama Masjid courtyard. Buland Darwaza (c. 1576-77) commemorates Akbar's Gujarat victory and is red and buff sandstone with marble inlay and trim. The Khankah is also sandstone. Statement 1 overstates by saying white marble was used in making these structures. Lucknow's Bara Imambara (Asaf-ud-daula, 1784, architect Kifayatullah) and Rumi Darwaza (c. 1784) are Awadhi works built of fine lakhori bricks and lime mortar, finished with lime plaster stucco. Famine relief was a motive, as they gave employment. Awadhi buildings avoided stone and iron girders. The Bara Imambara has a huge vaulted central hall with no beams or pillars, and the Bhul-bhulaiya labyrinth above. Elimination: both statements fail on materials, so (d).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect: the Fatehpur Sikri structures are red sandstone, not white marble.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 is incorrect: the Lucknow monuments are brick and lime plaster, not red sandstone and marble.
(c) is wrong because neither statement is correct, so they cannot both be.
(d) is correct because both statements give wrong materials, matching the official answer.
keyfact: Fatehpur Sikri is red sandstone (marble only as trim or in Salim Chishti's tomb), while Lucknow's Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza are brick and lime plaster.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only, would mean that Buland Darwaza and Khankah were built of white marble. In fact Fatehpur Sikri is the Mughal capital built by Akbar from 1571 in red sandstone, with white marble reserved for Salim Chishti's tomb. Buland Darwaza (c. 1576) celebrates the Gujarat victory. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986), and the capital was abandoned around 1585, probably because of water shortage.

Option (b), 2 only, would mean that the Lucknow monuments were red sandstone and marble. They are Awadhi works built by Asaf-ud-daula in 1784 using lakhori bricks and lime. The Bara Imambara has a vaulted hall without beams and a labyrinth called Bhul-bhulaiya. The Rumi Darwaza is an ornate gateway. Awadhi architecture is a late Indo-Islamic style with European and Persian influences.

Option (c), Both 1 and 2, would mean both claims about materials are right. Neither is. This shows the common trap of assuming that all Mughal-era and Nawabi grand buildings used marble or sandstone. Marble is the signature of Shah Jahan's phase (Taj Mahal, Agra, 1632-53), while Akbar preferred red sandstone (Agra Fort, Fatehpur Sikri). Awadh used brick and lime stucco.

Option (d), Neither 1 nor 2, is the official answer. Both statements misstate construction materials: Fatehpur Sikri is primarily red sandstone and the Lucknow Imambara complex is brick, lime mortar and stucco. Remember the rule: Akbar means red sandstone, Shah Jahan means white marble, Awadh means brick and lime plaster, Deccan means granite and basalt.
related: Fatehpur Sikri was Akbar's capital from c. 1571 to 1585 and became a UNESCO site in 1986.
Buland Darwaza commemorates Akbar's Gujarat conquest of 1573.
Itimad-ud-Daula's tomb at Agra was the first Mughal structure fully in white marble, with pietra dura.
Bara Imambara at Lucknow was built in 1784 by Asaf-ud-daula; it has no beams supporting its hall.
Humayun's Tomb at Delhi is a red sandstone and marble structure and a UNESCO site (1993).
Taj Mahal was built 1632-53 by Shah Jahan; its architect was Ustad Ahmad Lahori.
Chota Imambara at Lucknow (Husainabad) was built by Muhammad Ali Shah in 1838.
Salim Chishti's tomb at Fatehpur Sikri is of white marble with famed jali screens.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Buland Darwaza and the Khankah at Fatehpur Sikri are of red sandstone, with marble only as decorative inlay, not white marble as the building material. Buland Darwaza, the 'Gate of Magnificence', is about 54 m high from the ground and was built by Akbar around 1576-77 after his Gujarat conquest. It is the main southern entrance to the Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. It is built in Mughal style with chhatris, kanguras and inscriptions. The Khankah was a hall for Sufi pilgrims and mystics. Marble is conspicuous mainly in Salim Chishti's tomb, whose jali screens are famous.

2 — Incorrect: Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza at Lucknow were made of lakhori bricks and lime mortar with stucco plaster, not red sandstone and marble. Nawab Asaf-ud-daula of Awadh built the Bara Imambara (Asafi Imambara) in 1784, in part as a famine-relief project. Its central hall is about 50 m long and 15 m high and has a vault without beams. The Bhul-bhulaiya is a maze of passages. The Rumi Darwaza, about 60 feet high, is an ornate gateway said to resemble a gate at Constantinople. The Imambara was designed by Kifayatullah, a Delhi architect, and is a Shia congregational complex.
summary: The official answer is (d) Neither 1 nor 2. Buland Darwaza and the Khankah at Fatehpur Sikri were built mainly of red sandstone, with marble only as inlay or trim, not white marble as the main material. Bara Imambara and Rumi Darwaza at Lucknow were built of lakhori bricks and lime plaster, not red sandstone and marble.
topic_notes: Materials and styles are a recurring UPSC art and culture theme. Under Akbar (1556-1605) red sandstone dominated: Agra Fort, Humayun's Tomb (Delhi, 1570, red sandstone with white marble trim, built by Hamida Banu Begum, architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas), and Fatehpur Sikri with Jodha Bai's palace, Panch Mahal, Diwan-i-Khas, Diwan-i-Am, Ibadat Khana, Buland Darwaza and Salim Chishti's tomb. Fatehpur Sikri blends Gujarati and Rajasthani (Hindu) elements, including brackets and chhatris, with Persian features. Jahangir's period saw Akbar's tomb at Sikandra and Itimad-ud-Daula's tomb (Agra, 1622-28), the first Mughal building fully in marble with pietra dura, built by Nur Jahan. Shah Jahan's period (1628-58) is the high point of marble: Taj Mahal (architect Ustad Ahmad Lahori), Moti Masjid, Red Fort at Delhi (red sandstone, 1639-48) and Jama Masjid Delhi (sandstone and marble). Aurangzeb built the Bibi ka Maqbara (Aurangabad) and Moti Masjid in the Red Fort. Awadh (Nawabs of Awadh, 18th-19th century) produced Bara Imambara (1784), Chota Imambara (1838, Muhammad Ali Shah), Rumi Darwaza, Chattar Manzil, Residency and Kaiserbagh in brick, lime and stucco, with European influences. Related materials: Sultanate buildings used rubble and plaster, and Qutub Minar is red and buff sandstone with marble. South Indian temples used granite (Brihadisvara, Thanjavur) and Hoysala temples used soapstone (Belur, Halebidu). Pallava Shore Temple used granite blocks. Exam angles: match the monument with its builder, date, material and architect, and UNESCO status.

question: Which one of the following foreign travellers 76. elaborately discussed about diamonds and diamond mines of India ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Jean-Baptiste Tavernier (1605-1689) was a French jeweller and traveller who made six voyages to Persia and India between 1630 and 1668 and published Les Six Voyages in 1676. As a dealer in gems, he visited the diamond mines of Golconda (the Kollur mine on the Krishna river), Raolconda (Ramallakota near Kurnool) and the Sumbhalpur/Gowcoul area on the Mahanadi river in the east, and described mining methods, labour, taxation, weights, and prices. He also saw and described the Great Mogul diamond in Aurangzeb's treasury, and he sold large stones, including the Tavernier Blue (later the Hope Diamond lineage), to Louis XIV. The other three were also Europeans in Mughal India but are known for other things. Bernier, a physician, wrote on Mughal polity, the absence of private property in land, and the war of succession. Thevenot, a French traveller and linguist, wrote general travel accounts of the 1660s. Carre, a French priest, was connected with the French East India Company and wrote about the Konkan and Deccan in the 1670s. Elimination works by linking Tavernier with gems and jewels.
explanations: Incorrect. Bernier (1656-68 in India) is known for his Travels in the Mogul Empire, with analysis of Mughal state, land ownership, cities, and the succession war, not diamonds.
Correct. Tavernier, a gem merchant, wrote at length about diamond mines like Golconda, Raolconda and Sumbhalpur, as well as the diamond trade and the Mughal treasury gems.
Incorrect. Thevenot visited India around 1666-67 and wrote general observations on towns, people, and customs, not a specialised account of diamonds.
Incorrect. Abbe Carre travelled in India in the 1670s and wrote on the Deccan, Marathas, and French activities, not on diamond mining.
keyfact: Tavernier, the French gem merchant, wrote Six Voyages (1676) with detailed accounts of Indian diamond mines such as Golconda.
option_notes: Francois Bernier (1620-1688) was a French physician and philosopher who stayed in India from 1656 to 1668. He served Dara Shukoh and later Danishmand Khan. His Travels in the Mogul Empire compares Asian and European states, argues that the crown owned all land, and describes the Mughal war of succession. His views on absence of private property influenced later writers such as Marx.

Jean-Baptiste Tavernier (1605-1689) was a French gem merchant and traveller who made six journeys to the East between 1630 and 1668. His Les Six Voyages (1676) gives detailed accounts of diamond mines at Golconda, Raolconda and on the Mahanadi, of prices, mining methods, and the Mughal court jewels such as the Great Mogul diamond. He sold the Tavernier Blue to Louis XIV.

Jean de Thevenot (1633-1667) was a French traveller and linguist who journeyed through the Levant, Persia, and India, reaching Surat and the Deccan in 1666-67. His Voyages de M. de Thevenot au Levant and later volumes on Indian travels give descriptive accounts of cities, customs, and trade, and he died on his return journey in Armenia.

Abbe Barthelemy Carre was a French priest and traveller who came to India in the 1670s as a representative of the French East India Company. His work The Travels of the Abbe Carre in India and the Near East describes western India, the Konkan, Shivaji's Maratha power and French efforts at Surat and Pondicherry, as an observer of politics and society.
related: Tavernier's Six Voyages was published in 1676.
Golconda (Kollur mine) was the most famous diamond source of medieval India.
Bernier wrote Travels in the Mogul Empire and described the war of succession.
Niccolao Manucci wrote Storia do Mogor.
Peter Mundy described the 1630-31 Gujarat famine.
Sir Thomas Roe was the English envoy to Jahangir (1615-19).
India was the world's main diamond source until Brazil in the 1720s.
Panna (Madhya Pradesh) is India's chief diamond-producing region today.
summary: The answer is (b) Jean-Baptiste Tavernier. This French gem merchant made several trips to India between 1630 and 1668 and wrote Six Voyages (Les Six Voyages), which describes diamond mines such as Golconda (Kollur) and Raolconda in detail, along with diamond trade and prices.
topic_notes: European travellers to India in the 16th-17th centuries are a regular UPSC theme. Under the Mughals, many French, Italian, Dutch, and English visitors wrote accounts. Francois Bernier (French physician) wrote Travels in the Mogul Empire and described the war of succession among Shah Jahan's sons. Jean-Baptiste Tavernier (French jeweller) wrote Six Voyages and described diamond mines and trade. Niccolao Manucci (Venetian) wrote Storia do Mogor and served Dara Shukoh and later the Mughal army as a physician. Peter Mundy (English) described Shah Jahan's reign and the famine in Gujarat in 1630-31. Thomas Roe was the English ambassador to Jahangir in 1615-19. William Hawkins came to Jahangir's court in 1608. Ralph Fitch, an English merchant, visited Akbar's India in 1583-91. Abbe Carre, a French priest, wrote on the Deccan and Marathas. Jean de Thevenot toured Surat and the Deccan around 1666. Earlier travellers include Ibn Battuta (Rihla, Tughlaq period), Abdur Razzaq, Nicolo Conti and Domingo Paes, Fernao Nuniz and Duarte Barbosa (Vijayanagara). Diamond-related facts: Golconda mines (Kollur on the Krishna) produced famed stones like Koh-i-Noor, Hope, Regent, Darya-i-Noor; the Golconda Sultanate of the Qutb Shahis controlled this trade; India was the main source of diamonds until Brazil's discoveries in the 1720s, and later South Africa in the 1860s. Panna in Madhya Pradesh is India's main current diamond-producing area.

question: With reference to Indian history, who among the following is a future Buddha, yet to come 77. to save the world ?
subject: Ancient History
detail: Buddhist tradition recognises a succession of Buddhas who appear in different ages. Gautama (Shakyamuni) is the historical Buddha of the present age. Earlier Buddhas include Dipankara, Kassapa and Kakusandha, and the Pali canon lists 24 predecessors. Maitreya (Pali: Metteyya) is the Bodhisattva now in the Tushita heaven who will descend to earth as the next Buddha when the teachings of Gautama have been forgotten. The name derives from 'maitri', meaning loving-kindness. He is mentioned in the Digha Nikaya (Cakkavatti-Sihanada Sutta) and is prominent in Mahayana and Theravada traditions. In art he appears seated in the European (pralambapadasana) posture, often with a stupa in the crown, and the colossal Maitreya statues at Bamiyan, Leh (Ladakh) and Leshan (China) show his importance. Elimination: Avalokiteshvara, also called Padmapani (the lotus-holder) and Lokesvara (lord of the world), is the Bodhisattva of compassion, who is active in the present and who postpones his own Buddhahood to help beings. These three options therefore describe one figure, which is a clue that none of them is the answer. By elimination, only Maitreya fits the 'future Buddha' description.
explanations: Incorrect: Avalokiteshvara is the Bodhisattva of compassion working in the present world; he is not the awaited future Buddha.
Incorrect: Lokesvara ('lord of the world') is another name for Avalokiteshvara, a present Bodhisattva, not a future Buddha.
Correct: Maitreya is the future Buddha who will appear after Gautama's teachings have declined, to restore the Dharma and save the world.
Incorrect: Padmapani ('lotus-bearer') is an epithet of Avalokiteshvara, famously painted at Ajanta Cave 1, and is not the future Buddha.
keyfact: Maitreya = the future Buddha; Avalokiteshvara = Padmapani = Lokesvara = present Bodhisattva of compassion.
option_notes: Avalokiteshvara is the foremost Bodhisattva of compassion in Mahayana Buddhism, often shown holding a lotus and with multiple arms or heads. He vows to delay his own Buddhahood until all beings are liberated. He is called Guanyin in China, Chenrezig in Tibet (the Dalai Lama is considered his emanation) and Kannon in Japan. He is regularly depicted alongside Amitabha Buddha, from whose image he is said to emerge.

Lokesvara means 'Lord of the World' and is a title of Avalokiteshvara, widely used in Southeast Asia. Khmer and Cham art, for example in Cambodia under Jayavarman VII, honoured Lokesvara. Some Indian Buddhist sculptures from Pala and Sena-period Bengal and Bihar also show Lokesvara. He is a present compassionate Bodhisattva, not a future Buddha.

Maitreya is the future Buddha, currently a Bodhisattva residing in the Tushita heaven. He will be born when Gautama's teachings are forgotten, and will attain enlightenment under a Nagakesara tree. He is mentioned in Pali and Sanskrit texts and is depicted in the Gandhara and Mathura schools. Asanga is said to have received teachings from him, which is the origin of Yogachara texts. The Maitreya cult spread to China, Korea and Japan.

Padmapani means 'holder of the lotus' and is an epithet for Avalokiteshvara. The most famous depiction is the Padmapani painting in Ajanta Cave 1, from the Vakataka-Gupta period (5th century CE), showing the Bodhisattva with a blue lotus and a jewelled crown. It exemplifies Mahayana iconography and the theme of compassion. It is a present Bodhisattva, not a future Buddha.
related: Maitreya is the future Buddha, now in the Tushita heaven.
Avalokiteshvara, Padmapani and Lokesvara are names of the Bodhisattva of compassion.
Padmapani is painted in Ajanta Cave 1.
Gautama Buddha is the historical Buddha; the Pali canon lists 24 previous Buddhas before him.
Manjushri is the Bodhisattva of wisdom.
The Bodhisattva ideal is central to Mahayana Buddhism.
Mahayana was formalised at the Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka.
Bamiyan Buddhas in Afghanistan were destroyed by the Taliban in 2001.
summary: The answer is (c) Maitreya. Maitreya is the future Buddha in Buddhist tradition, expected to appear when the Dharma has declined and to teach it afresh and save the world. Avalokiteshvara, Lokesvara and Padmapani are all names or forms of the same present compassionate Bodhisattva, not a future Buddha.
topic_notes: Buddhist cosmology holds that Buddhas appear cyclically. The Theravada tradition names 28 Buddhas, with Gautama as the 4th of the present Bhadrakalpa, and Maitreya is to be the 5th. Sakyamuni was born at Lumbini in 563 BCE (approx.), attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, gave his first sermon at Sarnath (Dhammachakkapravartana) and attained Mahaparinirvana at Kushinagar. Mahayana developed the Bodhisattva ideal: beings who delay Nirvana to help others. Key Bodhisattvas are Avalokiteshvara (compassion), Manjushri (wisdom, holds sword and book), Vajrapani (power), Maitreya (future Buddha) and Kshitigarbha. Mahayana arose around the Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka (Kashmir/Kundalvan, presided over by Vasumitra, with Ashvaghosha) and was propagated by Nagarjuna (Madhyamika, Shunyavada) and Asanga and Vasubandhu (Yogachara). Hinayana/Theravada emphasises individual salvation and the arhat. Vajrayana arose later in eastern India (Bihar, Bengal, Pala period) with tantric elements. Art: Gandhara (Greco-Buddhist), Mathura and Amaravati schools; Ajanta cave paintings (Padmapani and Vajrapani in Cave 1) and Bamiyan colossi. Mudras to know: Dharmachakra (preaching), Bhumisparsha (earth-touching, enlightenment), Abhaya (fearlessness), Dhyana (meditation), Varada (charity). Buddhist councils: first at Rajgriha (Ajatashatru, Mahakassapa), second at Vaishali (Kalashoka), third at Pataliputra (Ashoka, Moggaliputta Tissa), fourth at Kashmir (Kanishka). Pali texts: Tripitaka (Vinaya, Sutta, Abhidhamma).

question: Which one of the following statements does not apply to the system of Subsidiary Alliance introduced by Lord Wellesley ?
options: To maintain a large standing army at other’s expense
To keep India safe from Napoleonic danger
To secure a fixed income for the Company
To establish British paramountcy over the Indian States
subject: Modern History
detail: The Subsidiary Alliance was a system of treaties by which an Indian ruler accepted a permanent British force in his territory and paid for it, either in cash or by ceding territory. Lord Wellesley (Governor-General 1798-1805) used it systematically, though Dupleix had earlier experimented with a similar idea and Clive had also made such arrangements. Main terms: the ruler accepted a British Resident at his court; he dismissed French and other European employees; he could not enter alliances or wars without British consent; and he ceded territory or paid a subsidy for the British contingent. In return the British promised protection from external and internal threats and non-interference in internal affairs, a promise often broken. Results: the Company maintained a large army at others' expense, the French influence (the Napoleonic threat) was neutralised, and British paramountcy was established as states lost sovereignty in foreign policy and defence. The alliances were first accepted by Hyderabad (1798, 1800), then Mysore (1799 after Tipu's defeat), Tanjore, Awadh (1801), Peshwa (Treaty of Bassein 1802), Bhonsle, Scindia and others. Elimination: (a), (b), (d) are classic stated aims; (c) confuses the subsidy with a fixed revenue, so it is the exception.
explanations: Applies: the system's core feature was a large standing British-led army paid for by the Indian state, so it is not the answer.
Applies: Wellesley was alarmed by Napoleon's Egyptian expedition (1798) and French officers in Indian courts, and the alliance expelled them, so it is not the answer.

Does not apply: the alliance was not designed to secure a fixed income for the Company; fixed revenue relates to land revenue systems like the Permanent Settlement. The subsidy was payment for troops. This is the correct answer.
Applies: the alliance reduced rulers to dependents with no independent foreign policy, establishing British paramountcy, so it is not the answer.
keyfact: Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley) = British army at the ruler's cost, Resident, no French, paramountcy; fixed revenue belongs to the Permanent Settlement.
option_notes: Maintaining a large standing army at others' expense: the Company stationed troops in allied states, and the ruler paid via subsidy or ceded territory, such as Hyderabad's cession of the Ceded Districts in 1800 and Awadh's cession of Rohilkhand and the Doab in 1801. This let the Company expand its military without bearing the cost, which was a central feature of the system.

Keeping India safe from the Napoleonic danger: Napoleon invaded Egypt in 1798, and the British feared a French move on India, with Tipu Sultan seeking French help. Wellesley required allies to expel French officers, such as Raymond's force at Hyderabad, and he defeated Tipu in 1799 at Seringapatam.

Securing a fixed income for the Company: this was not an aim of the Subsidiary Alliance. Fixed revenue is linked to the Permanent Settlement of 1793 under Cornwallis in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, which fixed the zamindars' revenue demand permanently. The subsidy paid under the alliance covered army costs and was not a general fixed income.

Establishing British paramountcy over Indian states: through the alliance, states lost control of foreign relations and defence and accepted a Resident. The policy led to the British becoming the supreme power in India. Later, Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse and Hastings' policy of subordinate isolation, then the Crown's paramountcy after 1858, continued this trend.
related: Hyderabad was the first state to accept the Subsidiary Alliance (1798).
Treaty of Bassein (1802) was signed by Peshwa Baji Rao II and the Company.
Tipu Sultan was killed at Seringapatam in 1799 in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.
Awadh ceded Rohilkhand and the Lower Doab in 1801.
Holkar of Indore refused the alliance and fought the Second Anglo-Maratha War.
Permanent Settlement of 1793 was introduced by Cornwallis.
Doctrine of Lapse was associated with Lord Dalhousie.
Wellesley founded Fort William College in 1800.
summary: The answer is (c). Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance aimed to maintain a large British-controlled army at the Indian ruler's expense, to keep the French (Napoleonic) threat out of India, and to establish British paramountcy over the princely states. 'Securing a fixed income for the Company' was not its aim; fixed income is associated with revenue settlements such as the Permanent Settlement (1793), and the subsidy under the alliance was paid by the Indian state for the army's upkeep, not as a general fixed income.
topic_notes:
Subsidiary Alliance was the most effective instrument of Wellesley's expansion, but the idea predates him. Dupleix made similar arrangements with Indian rulers, and the Company allied with Awadh in the 1760s-70s. Wellesley formalised the system after 1798. Key features: protection by the Company; a British Resident; a permanent force; no other European employees; no independent wars or treaties; and payment by subsidy or territory.

Order of states (commonly asked): Hyderabad (1798, the first, expanded in 1800); Mysore (1799, after the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, with a Wodeyar boy installed); Tanjore (1799); Awadh (1801); Peshwa Baji Rao II (Treaty of Bassein, 1802); Bhonsle of Berar (Treaty of Deogaon, 1803); Scindia (Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon, 1803); also Jodhpur, Jaipur, Macherry, Bundi and Bharatpur. Holkar did not accept it and fought the Second Anglo-Maratha War. The Treaty of Bassein is often called a death-blow to Maratha independence.

Consequences: rulers lost sovereignty; the armies of states were disbanded, creating unemployment; the states' finances were drained; misgovernment followed in states like Awadh, which later justified annexation in 1856. The Company gained military superiority, territory, and control over foreign policy.

Related policies: Cornwallis' non-intervention; Wellesley's subsidiary alliance; Hastings' subordinate isolation and the Pindari war; Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse (Satara 1848, Jhansi 1853, Nagpur 1854) and Awadh annexation (1856). Wellesley was also the founder of Fort William College in 1800. Systems for revenue: Permanent Settlement (1793), Ryotwari (Munro and Read, 1820), Mahalwari (1833).

ocr: Which of the following led to the introduction of English Education in India ? 1. Charter Act of 1813 2. General Committee of Public Instruction, 1823 3. Orientalist and Anglicist Controversy Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) land 2 only (b) 2only (ec) land 3 only (d) 1,2and3 Which one of the following is an artificial lake ? (a) Kodaikanal (Tamil Nadu) (b) Kolleru (Andhra Pradesh) (c) Nainital (Uttarakhand) (dq) Renuka (Himachal Pradesh)
subject: Modern History
detail: English education in India was not introduced by a single act. It came through a sequence of steps. The Charter Act of 1813 first made the Company responsible for education, setting aside Rs 1 lakh a year, and it also opened India to missionaries. The Governor-General appointed the General Committee of Public Instruction (GCPI) in 1823 to administer that grant. The Committee split into two camps. The Orientalists wanted to promote classical Sanskrit and Arabic learning in the classical languages. The Anglicists wanted Western knowledge taught through English.
