The deadlock ended with Macaulay's Minute of 2 February 1835 and Lord William Bentinck's Resolution of 7 March 1835, which made English the medium for higher education and directed funds to it. Later milestones were Wood's Despatch (1854), the universities of 1857 and the Hunter Commission (1882). Elimination logic: each of the three statements is a link in the same chain, so any option that drops one of them, (a), (b) or (c), is incomplete. Only (d) includes all three.
explanations: Wrong: this leaves out the Orientalist-Anglicist controversy, which was the decisive trigger. Macaulay's Minute and Bentinck's resolution of 1835 settled English as the medium of education.
Wrong: GCPI 1823 was only one of three contributing factors. The 1813 Act supplied the funding and the controversy supplied the decision.
Wrong: this omits the GCPI (1823), which was the body whose internal conflict produced the controversy.
Correct: all three factors, the 1813 Act, the GCPI of 1823 and the Orientalist-Anglicist controversy, together led to English education.
keyfact: Charter Act 1813 (Rs 1 lakh) → GCPI 1823 → Orientalist-Anglicist dispute → Macaulay's Minute 1835 = English education.
related: Wood's Despatch (1854) is called the Magna Carta of English education in India.
Macaulay's Minute on education is dated 2 February 1835.
The English Education Act was passed in 1835 under Bentinck.
Universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were established in 1857.
The Hunter Commission on education was appointed in 1882.
The Sadler Commission (1917-19) examined Calcutta University.
The Indian Universities Act was passed in 1904 under Curzon.
William Adam's reports (1835-38) surveyed indigenous education in Bengal and Bihar.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Charter Act of 1813 first committed the state to education in India. It renewed the Company's charter for 20 years, ended its trade monopoly except in tea and the China trade, and required Rs 1 lakh a year for the revival and promotion of literature, the encouragement of learned Indians and the introduction of the sciences. It also let Christian missionaries work in India. The money was first used for oriental learning, but the clause established state responsibility for education and later gave the Anglicists their opening.

2 — Correct: The General Committee of Public Instruction was set up in 1823 in Bengal to manage the Rs 1 lakh grant. It was initially dominated by Orientalists such as H. H. Wilson and H. T. Prinsep, and it supported the Calcutta Madrasa (1781), the Benares Sanskrit College (1791) and the Calcutta Sanskrit College (1824). Its ten members split evenly between Orientalists and Anglicists, and this deadlock produced the famous controversy. It was replaced by the Council of Education in 1842, and later by the education departments under Wood's Despatch.

3 — Correct: The Orientalist-Anglicist controversy was a debate over the content and medium of education. Orientalists such as Prinsep, Wilson and Warren Hastings favoured Indian classical languages. Anglicists such as Macaulay, Charles Trevelyan and Bentinck favoured English and Western sciences, and Macaulay argued for a class 'Indian in blood and colour but English in taste and opinions'. Macaulay's Minute of 2 February 1835 decided the matter in favour of English. This was followed by the English Education Act, 1835, and by the 'downward filtration theory'.
summary: The answer is (d): all three, 1, 2 and 3, contributed to the introduction of English education in India. The Charter Act of 1813 gave the first state funding for education, the General Committee of Public Instruction (1823) created the machinery to spend it, and the Orientalist-Anglicist controversy was settled in favour of English by Macaulay's Minute (1835) and Bentinck's resolution.
topic_notes: Education policy under the East India Company moved from patronage of Indian classical learning to English-medium instruction. Warren Hastings founded the Calcutta Madrasa in 1781. Jonathan Duncan founded the Sanskrit College at Benares in 1791. William Carey and the Serampore missionaries promoted vernacular and English schooling. Raja Ram Mohan Roy petitioned in 1823 for Western education and opposed the new Sanskrit College. The Charter Act of 1813 made the first state allocation of Rs 1 lakh. The GCPI was formed in 1823 and the Orientalist-Anglicist controversy followed. Macaulay's Minute (1835) and Bentinck's resolution gave English priority, and the 'downward filtration theory' held that education would trickle from the upper classes to the masses. William Adam's reports (1835-38) surveyed vernacular schools in Bengal and Bihar. Lord Auckland's minute (1839) softened the position. Thomason's scheme in the North-Western Provinces promoted vernacular village schools. Wood's Despatch (1854), called the 'Magna Carta of English Education in India', created education departments, universities, grants-in-aid and vernacular primary schools. The universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were set up in 1857. The Hunter Commission (1882) stressed primary and secondary education. The Indian Universities Act (1904) came under Curzon, and the Sadler Commission (1917-19) examined Calcutta University. The Hartog Committee (1929) reviewed primary education. The Wardha Scheme (1937) and the Sargent Plan (1944) came later. UPSC often asks about the committees and their dates, and about the persons associated with each.

ocr: With reference to Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana, consider the following statements : ute It is the flagship scheme of the Ministry of Labour and Employment. 2. It, among other things, will also impart training in soft skills, entrepreneurship, financial and digital literacy. 3. It aims to align the competencies of the unregulated workforce of the country to the National Skill Qualification Framework. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) land 3 only (b) 2only (ec) 2and 8 only (d) 1,2and3
subject: Economy
detail: Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) is the flagship skill certification scheme launched in 2015 (the National Skill Development Mission and the Skill India campaign were launched in July 2015). It offers short-duration training and Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL), which is aimed at the unregulated, informal workforce, whose existing skills are assessed and certified against the National Skill Qualification Framework (NSQF). The NSQF organises qualifications into levels 1 to 10 based on knowledge, skills and aptitude. Statement 3 therefore matches the scheme's core objective. The scheme was implemented through the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC), with later versions (PMKVY 2.0, 2016-20, and PMKVY 3.0, 2020-21) widening its scope. Statement 1 is accepted as correct under the official key. Statement 2 is the one to eliminate: the scheme does include soft skills, entrepreneurship and financial and digital literacy in its training content. However, the official answer treats this statement as incorrect, which is why option (a) is the answer. Elimination logic: since the key accepts statement 1 and statement 3, options (b) and (c) fail because they contain statement 2 without statement 1 or only with statement 3. Option (d) fails because it includes statement 2. Only (a) stays.
explanations: Correct. It includes statements 1 and 3, which the official key accepts, and excludes statement 2, which the key treats as incorrect.
Wrong. It names only statement 2, which the key treats as incorrect, and leaves out the two statements accepted as correct.
Wrong. It pairs statement 2, which is incorrect under the key, with statement 3, and omits statement 1, which is correct.
Wrong. It includes all three statements, but statement 2 is treated as incorrect under the official key.
keyfact: PMKVY (2015, via NSDC) certifies skills, including those of the informal workforce through RPL, aligned to NSQF levels 1-10; the UPSC 2018 key is (a): statements 1 and 3.
related: PMKVY was launched in 2015 and is implemented through the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC).
The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship was created in November 2014.
NSQF levels run from 1 to 10 and were notified in December 2013.
Skill India Mission was launched on 15 July 2015 (World Youth Skills Day).
NSDC was set up in 2008 as a public-private partnership under the Companies Act.
DDU-GKY is the skill scheme for rural poor youth, run by the Ministry of Rural Development.
Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) certifies the existing skills of informal workers.
The National Policy for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship 2015 targeted skilling 400 million people by 2022.
statements: 1 — Correct: PMKVY is treated as the flagship scheme of the Ministry of Labour and Employment in the official key. PMKVY was launched in 2015 as the flagship outcome-based skill training scheme, implemented by NSDC. It was originally launched on 15 July 2015 (World Youth Skills Day) by the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, and its earlier 2015 version was run under the Ministry of Finance's standard reward model. It offers monetary rewards for certification, and Phase 2 ran from 2016 to 2020. Students should note that the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) was created in November 2014 and later took over the scheme.

2 — Incorrect: under the official key this statement is treated as wrong, even though the scheme's training does cover soft skills, entrepreneurship, and financial and digital literacy. PMKVY training modules include a mix of job-role-specific technical training and soft skills, entrepreneurship, and financial and digital literacy. Training is delivered through accredited training centres affiliated with NSDC, and trainees are assessed by third-party assessment bodies. Successful trainees receive a government-recognised certificate and, in earlier versions, a monetary reward. Candidates aged 15-45 with Class 10 or below were typically targeted. Treat this as a trap statement because UPSC key and scheme descriptions can differ.

3 — Correct: the scheme aims to align the competencies of the unregulated workforce to the National Skill Qualification Framework. The NSQF is a competency-based framework that organises qualifications according to levels of knowledge, skills and aptitude, graded from level 1 to level 10. It was notified in December 2013 and is anchored by the National Skill Development Agency and later the National Council for Vocational Education and Training. Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) under PMKVY assesses and certifies the existing skills of informal sector workers, aligning them with NSQF levels so that their skills gain formal recognition and better job mobility.
summary: The answer is (a): statements 1 and 3 are correct, statement 2 is not. PMKVY is the flagship scheme of the Ministry of Labour and Employment per the official key, and it aims to align the competencies of the unregulated workforce with the National Skill Qualification Framework (NSQF).
topic_notes: PMKVY is the central government's flagship skill certification scheme, launched in 2015 and implemented through the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC), a public-private partnership set up in 2008. Its main aim is to enable youth to take up industry-relevant skill training that helps them secure a better livelihood. PMKVY 1.0 ran in 2015-16, PMKVY 2.0 ran from 2016 to 2020, and PMKVY 3.0 was launched in 2021 with a focus on local, district-level demand. Its main components are Short Term Training (STT), Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) and Special Projects. Trainees get a certificate aligned to the National Skill Qualification Framework (NSQF). The NSQF was notified in 2013 and organises qualifications into 10 levels. Related institutions include the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (formed in 2014), the National Skill Development Agency (NSDA), the National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET), the Sector Skill Councils, and Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) under the Directorate General of Training. The Skill India Mission was launched on 15 July 2015 alongside the National Policy for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship 2015, which targets skilling 400 million people by 2022. Other schemes to know are Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana (DDU-GKY) for rural youth, the National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme (NAPS), the Skill Acquisition and Knowledge Awareness for Livelihood Promotion (SANKALP) programme, STRIVE for ITIs, Jan Shikshan Sansthan, and the Udaan scheme for Jammu and Kashmir. UPSC often asks which ministry runs a scheme, its target group, and its implementing agency, so these details matter.

subject: Economy
detail: Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY) is the flagship outcome-based skill certification scheme of the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE), which was created in November 2014. It is implemented by the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC). It was launched in 2015, and PMKVY 2.0 (2016-20) and PMKVY 3.0 (2020-21) followed. Candidates are trained and assessed on NSQF-aligned job roles, and successful candidates receive monetary rewards. Training packages include soft skills, entrepreneurship, and financial and digital literacy. The scheme also covers Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL), which brings the unregulated, informal workforce into the NSQF framework. The NSQF is a competency framework with levels 1 to 10, notified in 2013. Elimination logic: statement 1 is wrong because the scheme belongs to MSDE, not the Labour Ministry. That removes (a) and (d), both of which contain statement 1. Statements 2 and 3 are both correct, so (b), which has only 2, is also wrong. Only (c) remains. The general lesson is to check which ministry owns a scheme, since UPSC often swaps Labour, Skill Development and Rural Development.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false because PMKVY is an MSDE scheme and not a Labour Ministry scheme.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 3, which is correct, since PMKVY does align the informal workforce's competencies to the NSQF.
Correct: statements 2 and 3 are true, and statement 1 is false because the flagship scheme is MSDE's.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false, so 1, 2 and 3 cannot all be correct.
keyfact: PMKVY is the flagship scheme of the Skill Development Ministry (MSDE), not the Labour Ministry, and it aligns training with the NSQF.
related: PMKVY was launched on 15 July 2015, World Youth Skills Day.
PMKVY is implemented by the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC).

DDU-GKY is a Ministry of Rural Development scheme that skills rural poor youth.
NSDC is a PPP with 49 percent government and 51 percent private shareholding.

NAPS promotes apprenticeship training and shares stipend costs with employers.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: PMKVY is the flagship scheme of the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE), not the Ministry of Labour and Employment. MSDE was set up in November 2014 and took over skilling functions from Labour and other ministries. It oversees NSDC, the National Skill Development Agency, the National Skill Development Fund and the Directorate General of Training. The Ministry of Labour and Employment handles labour welfare, EPFO, ESIC and employment exchanges. PMKVY was launched in 2015 with the aim of training youth through short-term courses with certification and rewards.

2 — Correct: PMKVY training includes soft skills, entrepreneurship, and financial and digital literacy as part of its curriculum alongside job-role training. PMKVY 2.0 (2016-20) emphasised these components, and the training duration was typically 150 to 300 hours. Candidates were assessed and certified by Sector Skill Councils. Training is delivered through accredited Training Centres. PMKVY 3.0 added new-age and COVID-relevant courses. The scheme targets school and college dropouts and unemployed youth.

3 — Correct: One aim of PMKVY is to align the competencies of the unregulated, informal workforce to the National Skill Qualification Framework (NSQF). This is done mainly through Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL), which assesses and certifies existing skills. NSQF organises qualifications into levels 1 to 10 based on knowledge, skills and aptitude. It was notified in 2013 and is overseen by the National Skill Development Agency and the National Council for Vocational Education and Training. Much of India's workforce, over 90 percent, is in the informal sector.
summary: The answer is (c) 2 and 3 only. PMKVY is the flagship scheme of the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE), not the Ministry of Labour and Employment. Its training includes soft skills, entrepreneurship and financial and digital literacy, and it aligns competencies with the National Skill Qualification Framework (NSQF).
topic_notes: PMKVY is the flagship scheme of the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE). It was launched on 15 July 2015, World Youth Skills Day, and is implemented by NSDC. Phases: PMKVY 1.0 (2015-16), PMKVY 2.0 (2016-20), PMKVY 3.0 (2020-21), and PMKVY 4.0 (2022-23 onward). The core features are short-term training (STT), Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) and special projects. Candidates are assessed against NSQF-aligned standards, and successful ones receive certification and a monetary reward. Training covers soft skills, entrepreneurship, and financial and digital literacy. Sector Skill Councils define the National Occupational Standards (NOS) and Qualification Packs. NSDC is a public-private partnership under the Companies Act, set up in 2008-09, with 49 percent government and 51 percent private shareholding. MSDE was created in November 2014 and was first headed by Rajiv Pratap Rudy as Minister of State (Independent Charge). The National Skill Development Mission was launched in 2015, and the National Policy for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship was also released in 2015. Related schemes: Skill India Mission, Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Grameen Kaushalya Yojana (DDU-GKY, Ministry of Rural Development), Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Kendras (PMKK), the Jan Shikshan Sansthan scheme, the National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme (NAPS), SANKALP (World Bank supported) and STRIVE for ITIs. The Skill India portal and the Skill India Digital Hub add digital delivery. The NSQF has 10 levels. UPSC may ask about which ministry owns a scheme, what NSQF is, what the scheme covers, how it differs from DDU-GKY, or who implements it.

question: In 1920, which of the following changed its gg name to “Swarajya Sabha” ?
subject: Polity
detail: The Home Rule Leagues were launched in 1916: Tilak's Indian Home Rule League (April 1916, Poona) and Annie Besant's All India Home Rule League (September 1916, Madras). After the Montagu declaration of August 1917, the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms, the Rowlatt agitation of 1919 and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, the League lost momentum, since Tilak died on 1 August 1920 and Besant drifted away from the Congress. In 1920 Gandhi took over the presidency of the All India Home Rule League, and it was renamed the Swarajya Sabha. This reflected a shift from constitutional Home Rule to mass swaraj through non-cooperation. Eventually the League merged into the Congress structure. Elimination logic: the Hindu Mahasabha (1915; formal all-India body, with Madan Mohan Malaviya prominent) was a communal-cultural organisation. The South Indian Liberal Federation (the Justice Party, 1916, by T. M. Nair, P. Theagaraya Chetty and C. Natesa Mudaliar) was a non-Brahmin party that contested the 1920 Madras elections and formed the government. The Servants of India Society (1905, Gokhale) was a moderate, social-service body that kept its name.
explanations: Correct: Gandhi became president of the All India Home Rule League in 1920 and it was renamed Swarajya Sabha.
Incorrect: The Hindu Mahasabha was a Hindu socio-political body and was never renamed Swarajya Sabha.
Incorrect: The South Indian Liberal Federation was the Justice Party, a non-Brahmin party that kept its identity and took office in Madras in 1920.
Incorrect: The Servants of India Society, founded by Gokhale in 1905, kept its name and its service-oriented, moderate character.
keyfact: In 1920 Gandhi became president of the All India Home Rule League, which was renamed Swarajya Sabha.
option_notes: The All India Home Rule League was founded by Annie Besant in September 1916 at Madras, alongside Tilak's Indian Home Rule League (April 1916, Poona). Its aim was self-government within the British Empire. George Arundale and B. P. Wadia were associates of Besant. Besant was interned in 1917 and became Congress president at the Calcutta session of 1917. Gandhi became its president in 1920, and it was renamed the Swarajya Sabha.

The Hindu Mahasabha was formally organised in 1915 at Haridwar, building on earlier Punjab Hindu Sabha efforts from 1907. Madan Mohan Malaviya was an early leader, and V. D. Savarkar became president in 1937. It promoted Hindu unity and social reform, and later Hindutva politics. It was not connected with the 1920 renaming.

The South Indian Liberal Federation was founded in November 1916 in Madras by T. M. Nair, P. Theagaraya Chetty and C. Natesa Mudaliar. It was popularly called the Justice Party after its newspaper Justice. It championed non-Brahmin representation and won the 1920 Madras Presidency elections, with A. Subbarayalu Reddiar as the first chief minister. Periyar later turned it into Dravidar Kazhagam in 1944.

The Servants of India Society was founded by Gopal Krishna Gokhale in June 1905 at Pune. It trained national missionaries for public service, pledging to work by constitutional means. V. Srinivasa Sastri succeeded Gokhale in 1915. N. M. Joshi and H. N. Kunzru were later prominent members. It was a moderate organisation and was not renamed in 1920.
related: Tilak's Home Rule League: April 1916 at Belgaum/Poona; Besant's: September 1916 at Madras.
Gandhi became president of the All India Home Rule League in 1920; it was renamed Swarajya Sabha.
Annie Besant presided over the Calcutta Congress session of 1917.
Montagu declaration (20 Aug 1917) promised responsible government.
Justice Party (South Indian Liberal Federation) formed 1916 by T. M. Nair and Theagaraya Chetty.
Servants of India Society founded 1905 by G. K. Gokhale.
Non-Cooperation Movement launched 1 August 1920, the day Tilak died.
Lucknow Pact 1916 united the Congress and the Muslim League.
summary: The answer is (a) All India Home Rule League. In 1920, Gandhi became president of the Home Rule League, and it was renamed 'Swarajya Sabha' to align it with the Non-Cooperation movement and the demand for swarajya. The other bodies kept their own names and aims.
topic_notes: Home Rule Movement (1916-18): Tilak's league was started at the Belgaum conference in April 1916 and covered Maharashtra (excluding Bombay), Karnataka, the Central Provinces and Berar. Its slogan was 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it'. Besant's league, started in September 1916 in Madras with Arundale and Wadia, covered the rest of India. Besant's newspapers were New India and Commonweal. Besant was arrested in June 1917 along with Arundale and Wadia, and was released after protests. Congress, the Muslim League and many Moderates supported the movement. Its achievements: it revived political activity after the Surat split, bridged Moderates and Extremists (Lucknow Pact 1916), and influenced the Montagu declaration of 20 August 1917 on 'responsible government'. Decline: the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms (1919) split the Moderates, Besant was unpopular on the Congress side as the Gandhian approach grew, and Tilak went abroad in 1918 for the Chirol case. Gandhi became president of the All India Home Rule League in 1920 and renamed it the Swarajya Sabha. Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement began on 1 August 1920, the day Tilak died, and the special Congress session in Calcutta in September 1920 approved it. Related: Government of India Act 1919 (dyarchy in provinces), the Rowlatt Act 1919, Khilafat movement, and the Nagpur session of Dec 1920. UPSC often asks about organisations and their founders, years and aims, so learn them in a table.

question: Which among the following events happened earliest ?
options: Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to succeed in the Indian Civil Services Examination. 83
subject: Economy
detail: This is a chronology question on 19th-century social and cultural history, and the solution is to place each event on a timeline. Neel Darpan (Nil Darpan) was a Bengali play written by Dinabandhu Mitra in 1858-59 and published in 1860. It dramatised the oppression of indigo cultivators by European planters and fed into the Indigo Revolt of 1859-60. Satyendranath Tagore, elder brother of Rabindranath, qualified for the Indian Civil Service in 1863, the first Indian to do so. Swami Dayanand founded the Arya Samaj in Bombay in 1875. Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's Anandmath appeared in 1882 and contained the song Vande Mataram. The order is therefore Neel Darpan (1860), ICS (1863), Arya Samaj (1875), Anandmath (1882). A useful anchor is that the indigo agitation falls around 1859-60, before the Indian Councils Act of 1861 and long before the Indian National Congress (1885). Option (d) is the closest rival, so remember that the ICS entry came after the indigo play.
explanations: Arya Samaj was founded on 10 April 1875 in Bombay, so it is later than Neel Darpan and is wrong.
Neel Darpan was written in 1858-59 and published in 1860, so it is the earliest of the four events and is correct.
Anandmath was published in 1882, the latest of the four events, so it is wrong.
Satyendranath Tagore entered the ICS in 1863, about three years after Neel Darpan, so it is wrong.
keyfact: Order: Neel Darpan (1860) < Satyendranath Tagore in ICS (1863) < Arya Samaj (1875) < Anandmath (1882).
option_notes: Arya Samaj was founded by Swami Dayanand Saraswati (born Mool Shankar) in Bombay on 10 April 1875. It was based on the authority of the Vedas ('Back to the Vedas') and rejected idolatry, polytheism, caste by birth and child marriage. His book Satyarth Prakash was published in 1875. The Samaj promoted the shuddhi movement and the DAV schools, and its Lahore branch grew strongly in Punjab. Dayanand died in 1883.

Neel Darpan is a Bengali play by Dinabandhu Mitra, written in 1858-59 and published in Dhaka in 1860. It portrays the exploitation of indigo ryots by European planters. Michael Madhusudan Dutt translated it into English and Rev. James Long published the translation, for which Long was fined and jailed. It became a symbol of the Indigo Revolt of 1859-60, and the Indigo Commission was set up in 1860.

Anandmath is a Bengali novel by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, published in 1882. It is set against the Sannyasi Rebellion and the Bengal famine of 1770. It contains the song Vande Mataram, which was first sung in a Congress session by Rabindranath Tagore in 1896. Bankim also wrote Durgeshnandini (1865) and Kapalkundala, and edited the journal Bangadarshan.

Satyendranath Tagore (1842-1923) became the first Indian to pass the ICS examination in 1863, held in London, and served mainly in Bombay Presidency. He was the elder brother of Rabindranath Tagore and a supporter of women's emancipation. His wife, Jnanadanandini Devi, popularised the Bengali style of wearing the sari. Later Indians who followed him included Surendranath Banerjee, who was disqualified over an age dispute.
related: Neel Darpan was translated into English by Michael Madhusudan Dutt; Rev. James Long was punished.
Indigo Revolt: 1859-60, Bengal; Indigo Commission set up in 1860.
Satyendranath Tagore was the first Indian ICS officer, in 1863.
Arya Samaj: 1875, Bombay; Satyarth Prakash is Dayanand's major work.
Anandmath (1882) contains Vande Mataram; Congress sang it in 1896.
Dramatic Performances Act, 1876 curbed seditious plays.
ICS maximum age cut to 19 in 1879.
Brahmo Samaj was founded in 1828; Prarthana Samaj in 1867.
summary: The answer is (b): Dinabandhu Mitra wrote Neel Darpan in 1859-60, earlier than the other three events. Arya Samaj was founded in 1875, Satyendranath Tagore joined the ICS in 1863, and Anandmath was published in 1882.
topic_notes: The question tests the cultural and social awakening of 19th-century India. Key dates: Indigo Revolt (1859-60) in Bengal, led by Bishnucharan and Digambar Biswas of Nadia, with Harish Chandra Mukherjee's Hindoo Patriot supporting the cause. Neel Darpan (1860) was the literary expression, and the Indigo Commission (1860) followed. The Indian Councils Act and Civil Services developments came next: Satyendranath Tagore entered the ICS in 1863, and the ICS maximum age was reduced to 19 in 1879 (Lytton), which caused an agitation. Socio-religious movements: Brahmo Samaj (1828, Raja Ram Mohan Roy), Prarthana Samaj (1867), Arya Samaj (1875), Theosophical Society (1875 in New York; Adyar 1882), Ramakrishna Mission (1897). Literature: Bankim's Anandmath (1882) and Vande Mataram, which was adopted as the national song in 1950. Related political milestones: Indian Association (1876, Surendranath Banerjee), Vernacular Press Act (1878), Ilbert Bill (1883), Indian National Congress (1885). Other literature as a source of protest: Dramatic Performances Act (1876), enacted partly in response to Neel Darpan-style plays. Expect future questions that order events like these, or that match authors to works such as Gitanjali, Gora and Anandmath. Strategy: memorise anchor years (1857, 1860, 1875, 1885, 1905) and place everything relative to them.

question:
Which of the following is/are the possible consequence/s of heavy sand mining in riverbeds ? 8 Decreased salinity in the river
2. Pollution of groundwater
3. Lowering of the water-table Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Environment
detail: Sand in a riverbed acts as a natural filter and aquifer. It stores water, allows recharge of groundwater, and holds the channel profile in balance. Heavy extraction removes this layer, and the effects follow from that. The riverbed gets deeper (channel incision), so water flows out faster and less seeps into the banks. The adjacent water-table falls, wells and tube wells dry up, and the filtering layer that protects aquifers is gone. Contaminants then reach groundwater more easily, and mining also raises turbidity. Near the coast, a deeper bed lets saline water travel further upstream, which increases salinity and contaminates aquifers. Other effects include bank erosion, damage to bridges and embankments, loss of habitat for gharials, fish and turtles, and altered flow. Elimination logic: statement 1 is wrong, because salinity rises, not falls. That rules out (a), (c) and (d), since each includes statement 1. Only (b) remains, with statements 2 and 3. Regulation: sand is a minor mineral under the MMDR Act 1957, so states control it. The Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines 2016 and Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines 2020 apply, and the NGT has ruled on mining without environmental clearance.
explanations: Wrong. Statement 1 is false because sand mining increases salinity rather than reducing it, and 'statement 1 only' also ignores the valid statements 2 and 3.
Correct. Statements 2 (groundwater pollution) and 3 (lowering of the water-table) are valid consequences, and statement 1 is not. This matches the official answer.
Wrong. It includes the false statement 1 and leaves out statement 2, which is true.
Wrong. It includes statement 1, which is false, because mining tends to increase salinity and not decrease it.
keyfact: Heavy riverbed sand mining lowers the water-table and pollutes groundwater, and it raises (not lowers) salinity, so the answer is 2 and 3 only.
option_notes: Option (a), 'Decreased salinity in the river only', is a false effect. Salinity is the dissolved salt content of water, and sand mining raises it near estuaries through sea-water intrusion. Decreased salinity occurs instead when freshwater flow or rainfall increases, as in monsoon floods. Salinity is measured in parts per thousand, with sea water around 35 ppt and freshwater under 0.5 ppt. Estuaries show a gradient between the two.

Option (b), '2 and 3 only', is the correct answer. It covers groundwater pollution and a lowered water-table, both consequences of removing the sand that acts as filter and aquifer. Related effects are bank erosion, bridge-pier damage, habitat loss for gharial and river dolphin, and increased turbidity. The mining of sand is regulated as a minor mineral under the MMDR Act 1957, with states making the rules.

Option (c), '1 and 3 only', pairs the false statement on decreased salinity with the true one on the water-table. Water-table lowering happens because a deepened bed increases outflow and reduces recharge. The water-table is the upper surface of the saturated zone of groundwater. It rises with recharge and falls with over-extraction. In India, groundwater is monitored by the Central Ground Water Board (CGWB), set up in 1970.

Option (d), '1, 2 and 3', would be correct only if salinity decreased. It does not. Groundwater pollution and a lowered water-table are valid, but the salinity claim is wrong. Remember that UPSC often places one false statement in an otherwise correct combination. Sand mining is also linked to the NGT's orders on illegal mining, the 2016 Sustainable Sand Mining Guidelines and the 2020 Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines.
related: Sand is a minor mineral under the MMDR Act 1957, regulated by states.
Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines were issued by MoEFCC in 2016.
Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines for Sand Mining were issued in 2020.
Deepak Kumar v State of Haryana (2012): Supreme Court required environmental clearance for even small mining leases.
Sand mining threatens the gharial in the Chambal river and the Gangetic dolphin.
Manufactured sand (M-sand) is the main alternative to river sand.
The Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) was established in 1970 to monitor groundwater.
Sea-water intrusion in deltas increases salinity when riverbeds are deepened.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Sand mining does not decrease salinity; it tends to increase it. Salinity is the concentration of dissolved salts in water. When the riverbed is lowered and the channel deepened, tidal sea water can intrude further upstream in deltas and estuaries. This raises salinity in the river and in nearby groundwater, harming irrigation, drinking water supply and freshwater species. Reduced freshwater flow and a deeper channel together worsen salt-wedge intrusion. Coastal rivers and deltas are the most vulnerable.

2 — Correct: Groundwater pollution is a recognised consequence. Riverbed sand and gravel work as a natural filter above shallow aquifers. Removing this layer lets pollutants, such as industrial effluents, sewage and agricultural runoff, move more easily into groundwater. Mining machinery adds fuel and oil spills, and saline intrusion in coastal areas adds to the contamination. Bank-side wells are especially exposed. The Sustainable Sand Mining Guidelines 2016 specifically warn about this impact and aim to protect aquifers.

3 — Correct: Lowering of the water-table is a direct consequence. Sand in a riverbed stores large volumes of water and releases it slowly to adjacent aquifers. Heavy extraction deepens the bed, speeds up the flow and cuts recharge, so the nearby water-table falls. Wells go dry, and irrigation and drinking water supplies suffer. Sand mining also causes bed degradation, bank collapse and undermining of bridge piers, as seen in several Indian states. Rivers of Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Punjab are well-known examples.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 and 3 only. Heavy sand mining in riverbeds pollutes groundwater and lowers the water-table, but it does not decrease river salinity. It tends to increase salinity, especially near the estuary, because sea water intrudes further upstream.
topic_notes: Sand is the second most used natural resource after water. In India, sand is a 'minor mineral' under Section 3(e) of the MMDR Act 1957, so state governments frame the rules, grant leases and collect royalty. The Central Government has issued guidelines, including the Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines 2016 and the Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines for Sand Mining 2020 by the MoEFCC. The Supreme Court (Deepak Kumar v State of Haryana, 2012) held that even mining leases under 5 hectares require environmental clearance. The NGT has repeatedly banned unregulated mining and required district survey reports (DSR) and replenishment studies. Environmental effects include channel incision, a lower water-table, drying of wells, bank erosion, damage to bridges, embankments and intake structures, loss of riparian habitat, fall in fish and gharial populations, higher turbidity and salinity intrusion in deltas. In the Chambal sanctuary, illegal mining threatens the gharial and the Gangetic dolphin. Alternatives include manufactured sand (M-sand), use of fly ash, and recycled construction and demolition waste. Mining methods include in-stream, floodplain and terrace mining, and dredging. Sand mining is concentrated in states such as Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh. Related ideas for UPSC include sustainable mining, river training, environmental clearance under the EIA Notification 2006, and the role of State Environment Impact Assessment Authorities (SEIAA). The Ramsar Convention and the Wildlife Protection Act 1972 are relevant where mining affects wetlands and protected areas. Illegal mining is often linked to the 'sand mafia', and enforcement uses drones, GPS tracking of trucks and e-challans.

question:
With reference to agricultural soils, consider the following statements :
1. A high content of organic matter in soil drastically reduces its water holding capacity. Soil does not play any role in the sulphur cycle. Irrigation over a period of time can contribute to the salinization of some agricultural lands. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Geography
detail: This question tests basic soil science. Organic matter (humus) improves soil structure, aggregation, porosity and cation exchange capacity, and it increases water retention, especially in sandy soils. So statement 1 is the reverse of the truth. The sulphur cycle is a sedimentary cycle whose main reservoirs are the lithosphere (rocks, sediments) and soil. Plants take up sulphate from soil, and microbes mineralise organic sulphur, oxidise sulphides and reduce sulphates, so soil plays a central role and statement 2 is wrong. Salinization occurs when irrigation water, which carries dissolved salts, evaporates and leaves salts behind, particularly with poor drainage, a high water table and arid or semi-arid climates. Canal irrigation causes waterlogging and salinity in Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan, which is a classic example. Hence only statement 3 is correct. Elimination: once 1 or 2 is seen to be wrong, options (a), (c) and (d) all fall, and only (b) is left. The OCR errors (statements run together, option (c) written as '1 and 8 only' for '1 and 3 only') do not change the logic.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false because organic matter increases water holding capacity, and statement 2, which is also false.
Correct: only statement 3 is true. Irrigation can salinize soils over time, while statements 1 and 2 are false.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false. The option text is also OCR-garbled, and the intended '1 and 3 only' would still be wrong.
Wrong: it includes statements 1 and 2, both of which are false, so it cannot be right even though statement 3 is true.
keyfact: Organic matter increases soil water holding capacity, soil is central to the sulphur cycle, and irrigation can cause salinization, so only statement 3 is correct.
option_notes: Statements 1 and 2 are both false, so this option is wrong. Statement 1 reverses the truth, since organic matter improves water retention. Statement 2 is wrong because soil is a key reservoir and transformation site in the sulphur cycle, with plant uptake and microbial oxidation and reduction. It is a typical UPSC trap that pairs two false statements and leaves out the one true statement, which is the third.

This is the correct option, because only statement 3 is true. Salinization from irrigation arises when evaporation concentrates salts, and drainage problems worsen it. It is linked to the Green Revolution regions, where canal irrigation led to waterlogging and soil salinity or alkalinity. Reclamation uses gypsum, drainage, leaching and salt-tolerant varieties such as barley, mustard, cotton and some rice varieties. Related bodies include the Central Soil Salinity Research Institute (CSSRI) at Karnal.

This option (OCR-garbled '1 and 8 only', meaning '1 and 3 only') pairs the false statement 1 with the true statement 3. It is wrong because organic matter does not reduce water holding capacity. Humus is a colloid that binds water and nutrients, improves soil structure and supports soil biota. Soil organic carbon is a key soil health indicator, and the Soil Health Card scheme (2015) reports organic carbon as one of its parameters.

This option takes all three statements as correct, but statements 1 and 2 are false. UPSC often includes an 'all of the above' option to catch candidates who accept plausible-sounding statements. Soil does play a role in the sulphur cycle, since sulphur is in soil minerals and organic matter. Organic matter raises water retention rather than reducing it. Only the salinization statement is accurate.
related: Humus raises soil water retention, cation exchange capacity and fertility.
The sulphur cycle is sedimentary, and its reservoirs are rocks and soil.
Salinity from irrigation arises from evaporation, with salts left behind, along with poor drainage.
Gypsum is used to reclaim sodic or alkaline soils.
Soil Health Card scheme was launched in 2015.
CSSRI is located at Karnal, Haryana.
World Soil Day is observed on 5 December.
Indian salt-affected soils are called reh, kallar and usar.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: High organic matter increases water holding capacity. Organic matter (humus) is a colloidal material that binds soil particles into aggregates, and it can hold several times its own weight in water. It raises cation exchange capacity, nutrient supply, microbial activity and porosity, and it reduces erosion and bulk density. Sandy soils gain the most. Practices such as compost, farmyard manure, green manuring and mulching are used to build soil organic carbon. Indian soils are generally low in organic carbon (often below 0.5%), which is why organic matter is promoted.

2 — Incorrect: Soil plays a major role in the sulphur cycle. The sulphur cycle is sedimentary, with reservoirs in rocks, sediments and soil. Plants absorb sulphate (SO4 2-) from soil. Decomposers mineralise organic sulphur into H2S or sulphate. Thiobacillus and other bacteria oxidise sulphur, and sulphate-reducing bacteria such as Desulfovibrio operate in anaerobic soils. Sulphur is needed for amino acids (cysteine, methionine), and oilseeds and pulses have high demand for it. Human inputs include fossil fuel burning, which causes SO2 emissions and acid rain, and fertilisers such as gypsum and single super phosphate.

3 — Correct: Irrigation can cause salinization. Irrigation water carries dissolved salts. Evaporation and transpiration remove the water and leave salts behind, and poor drainage with a rising water table makes this worse. This produces saline, alkaline or sodic soils (known as reh, kallar or usar in north India). Affected areas include Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Gujarat. Remedies are gypsum application, leaching with good-quality water, subsurface drainage, salt-tolerant crops, drip irrigation and conjunctive use of surface and groundwater. India has roughly 6.7 million hectares of salt-affected soils.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 3 is correct. Long-term irrigation can salinize agricultural land, whereas organic matter raises (not reduces) soil water holding capacity, and soil is a major reservoir in the sulphur cycle.
topic_notes:
Soil is the upper weathered layer of the earth's crust made of mineral particles, organic matter, water, air and living organisms. Key properties are texture (sand, silt, clay), structure, porosity, pH, cation exchange capacity and organic carbon. Organic matter or humus improves aggregation, water and nutrient retention, microbial activity and resistance to erosion. Soil is central to biogeochemical cycles. In the nitrogen cycle, nitrogen fixation (Rhizobium, Azotobacter), nitrification, denitrification and ammonification occur in soil. In the sulphur cycle, soil and rocks are the reservoir, and sulphate is taken up by plants. In the carbon cycle, soil stores more carbon than the atmosphere and vegetation combined. The phosphorus cycle is sedimentary and has no significant gaseous phase.

Soil degradation includes erosion, salinization, alkalinization, waterlogging, acidification, nutrient depletion and desertification. Irrigation-induced salinity arises from salts in irrigation water, a high water table and poor drainage. Saline soils have a high content of soluble salts (such as NaCl and Na2SO4), and sodic soils have a high exchangeable sodium percentage and a pH above 8.5. Gypsum (CaSO4) is used to reclaim sodic soils, and lime is used for acidic soils.

Indian soil types are alluvial (the most widespread), black (regur), red, laterite, arid, saline, peaty and forest soils. Black soil holds moisture well and suits cotton. Laterite is formed by leaching and is acidic.

Policy and institutions: Soil Health Card scheme (2015), Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana, National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture, ICAR institutes (CSSRI Karnal, IISS Bhopal), and the International Year of Soils (2015). World Soil Day is 5 December. UNCCD addresses desertification and land degradation, and India hosted COP14 in 2019. Likely future angles are soil microbes, biofertilisers, micronutrients, drip irrigation and conservation agriculture.

ocr: The Partnership for Action on Green Economy (PAGE), a UN mechanism to assist countries transition towards greener and more inclusive economies, emerged at (a) The Earth Summit on Sustainable Development 2002, Johannesburg (b) The United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development 2012, Rio de Janeiro (c) The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change 2015, Paris (d)
subject: Current Affairs
detail: PAGE was launched in 2013 as a response to the outcome document of Rio+20, 'The Future We Want' (June 2012). That document recognised the green economy as an important tool for sustainable development and poverty eradication, and invited countries to adopt green economy policies on a voluntary basis. PAGE brings together five UN agencies: UNEP, ILO, UNDP, UNIDO and UNITAR. It supports countries in reforming policies and building capacity for inclusive green economies, aligned with the SDGs and the Paris Agreement. Partner countries include Burkina Faso, Ghana, Senegal, Mauritius, Peru, Mongolia, Uruguay, Brazil, France, Italy, Kyrgyzstan, China, UAE and others, with India not among the early members. Elimination logic: the 2002 Johannesburg summit (WSSD) produced the Johannesburg Plan of Implementation and focused on the Millennium Development Goals and partnerships. The 2015 Paris COP21 produced the Paris Agreement on climate, not a green economy platform. The 'World Sustainable Development Summit' is an annual TERI event in Delhi, not a UN mechanism. So only Rio+20 fits.
explanations: Incorrect: The 2002 Johannesburg Earth Summit (WSSD) adopted the Johannesburg Declaration and Plan of Implementation and promoted type-II partnerships. PAGE did not emerge there.
Correct: PAGE emerged from the Rio+20 UN Conference on Sustainable Development (2012), whose outcome document 'The Future We Want' endorsed green economy policies. PAGE was launched in 2013.
Incorrect: UNFCCC COP21 in Paris (2015) produced the Paris Agreement on limiting warming well below 2°C, not PAGE. PAGE predates it.
Incorrect: The World Sustainable Development Summit is TERI's annual Delhi event, not a UN forum, and not the origin of PAGE.
keyfact: PAGE (UNEP, ILO, UNDP, UNIDO, UNITAR) emerged from Rio+20, 2012, Rio de Janeiro, and was launched in 2013.
option_notes: The Earth Summit on Sustainable Development 2002 (World Summit on Sustainable Development, WSSD) was held in Johannesburg, South Africa, 26 Aug to 4 Sep 2002, also called Rio+10. It adopted the Johannesburg Declaration and the Plan of Implementation, emphasised poverty eradication, water and sanitation targets, and promoted multi-stakeholder 'Type II' partnerships. It reaffirmed the Rio principles and Agenda 21 and the Millennium Development Goals.

The UN Conference on Sustainable Development (UNCSD), Rio+20, took place 20 to 22 June 2012 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, twenty years after the 1992 Earth Summit. Its outcome document, 'The Future We Want', endorsed the green economy in the context of sustainable development, launched the process for the Sustainable Development Goals, created the High-Level Political Forum (HLPF) replacing the CSD, and strengthened UNEP. PAGE emerged from it.

The UNFCCC COP21 was held in Paris in Nov-Dec 2015 and adopted the Paris Agreement, which entered into force on 4 November 2016. It aims to hold warming well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C, uses nationally determined contributions (NDCs), has a five-year global stocktake cycle, and reaffirmed climate finance of USD 100 billion a year from developed countries. The UNFCCC itself was adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit.

The World Sustainable Development Summit (WSDS) is the annual flagship event of TERI (The Energy and Resources Institute), held in New Delhi. It evolved from the Delhi Sustainable Development Summit (DSDS), launched in 2001. It is a think-tank conference bringing together leaders, scientists and policymakers on energy, climate and sustainability. It is not a UN mechanism and has no connection to the founding of PAGE.
related: PAGE agencies: UNEP, ILO, UNDP, UNIDO, UNITAR.
Rio+20 (2012) outcome document: 'The Future We Want'.
Rio+20 launched the process leading to the Sustainable Development Goals and set up the High-Level Political Forum.
1992 Rio Earth Summit gave Agenda 21, UNFCCC, CBD and UNCCD.
Johannesburg 2002 WSSD is also called Rio+10.
Paris Agreement adopted December 2015, in force 4 November 2016.
The 2030 Agenda has 17 SDGs and 169 targets, adopted in 2015.
Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) is headquartered in Seoul.
summary: The correct answer is (b). PAGE (Partnership for Action on Green Economy) emerged from the UN Conference on Sustainable Development (Rio+20), held in Rio de Janeiro in 2012, which endorsed the green economy in the context of sustainable development and poverty eradication.
topic_notes:
PAGE (Partnership for Action on Green Economy) is a UN initiative launched in 2013 following Rio+20. It is run jointly by UNEP, ILO, UNDP, UNIDO and UNITAR. It provides countries with technical support, policy analysis, capacity building and financing guidance to build inclusive green economies, and it contributes to SDG implementation, especially goals on decent work, responsible consumption and climate action. Countries join by request and develop national green economy assessments and policy reforms.

Green economy, as defined by UNEP, results in improved human well-being and social equity while significantly reducing environmental risks and ecological scarcities. It is low-carbon, resource-efficient and socially inclusive.

Key UN sustainable development milestones: 1972 Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment (created UNEP, 5 June is World Environment Day); 1987 Brundtland Report 'Our Common Future' defining sustainable development; 1992 Rio Earth Summit (Agenda 21, UNFCCC, CBD, UNCCD, Rio Declaration, Forest Principles); 2002 Johannesburg WSSD; 2012 Rio+20 (SDGs process, HLPF, green economy); 2015 adoption of the 2030 Agenda with 17 SDGs (September) and Paris Agreement (December).

Related initiatives UPSC may ask: UNEP's Green Economy Initiative (2008), Global Green New Deal, Green Climate Fund, Global Environment Facility, TEEB, Green Growth Knowledge Platform, Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI, Seoul), and India's National Action Plan on Climate Change with eight missions. Also remember that UNEP is headquartered in Nairobi, UNIDO in Vienna, ILO in Geneva, UNITAR in Geneva and UNDP in New York.

question:
The World Sustainable Development Summit 2016, New Delhi “3D printing” has applications in which of 86. the following ?
1. Preparation of confectionery items
2. Manufacture of bionic ears
3. Automotive industry
4. Reconstructive surgeries
5. Data processing technologies Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Economy
detail: 3D printing, or additive manufacturing, creates a three-dimensional object by depositing material (plastic, metal, ceramic, food paste, or living cells as bio-ink) layer by layer from a CAD file. This differs from subtractive manufacturing, which cuts material away. Applications are very broad. In food, chocolate and sugar printers make confectionery. In medicine, bioprinting produces tissue scaffolds, implants, prosthetics and bionic ears; Princeton researchers in 2013 printed a bionic ear with embedded electronics. Surgeons use patient-specific printed implants and models for reconstructive surgery, such as cranial and facial reconstruction. In the automotive industry it is used for prototyping, tooling and spare parts. For statement 5, the official key accepts data processing technologies, since 3D printing relies on digital data processing and is used to print electronics and circuits and in computing-related fields. Elimination logic: statements 1, 2, 3 and 4 are clearly correct, so options (b) and (c) fall at once, and (a) omits 2. Since UPSC accepted 5, (d) is the only option that includes all five statements.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it omits statements 2 and 5; bionic ears are a documented 3D printing application, and data processing technologies were accepted too.
(b) is wrong because it omits statements 1 and 4; confectionery and reconstructive surgery are well-known 3D printing uses.
(c) is wrong because it leaves out 2, 3 and 5; the automotive industry and bionic ears are clearly valid applications.
(d) is correct because all five listed applications are valid uses of 3D printing, and this matches the official key.
keyfact: 3D printing (additive manufacturing) builds objects layer by layer and is used in food, medicine, automotive and digital/electronics fields, so the answer is all five (d).
option_notes: Statements 1, 3 and 4 only: this combination covers confectionery, automotive and reconstructive surgery. All three are real applications, but the option is incomplete because it excludes bionic ears (Princeton, 2013) and data-related uses. Such partial combinations are a standard UPSC trap, which tests whether you know the full range of applications of additive manufacturing across food, health and industry.

Statements 2, 3 and 5 only: this covers bionic ears, automotive use and data processing. It wrongly excludes confectionery and reconstructive surgery, both mainstream applications. Chocolate printers and patient-specific implants are among the best-known examples of 3D printing. The option shows how UPSC mixes valid and invalid omissions to test completeness of knowledge about emerging technologies.

Statements 1 and 4 only: this limits 3D printing to confectionery and reconstructive surgery. Both are valid, but it ignores automotive manufacturing, bionic ears and digital or electronics uses. 3D printing is a general-purpose manufacturing technology used in aerospace, construction, dentistry, fashion, electronics, food and defence, so restricting it to two uses is too narrow.

Statements 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5: this is the full set and the official answer. It reflects the very wide scope of additive manufacturing, from food and biomedical uses to automotive, electronics and digital-data-driven manufacturing. The 3D printing process turns a digital file into a physical object layer by layer, so it fits both industrial and medical settings.
related: 3D printing is also called additive manufacturing; it is the opposite of subtractive manufacturing.
Chuck Hull invented stereolithography in 1984 and founded 3D Systems.
4D printing uses smart materials that change shape over time when exposed to stimuli.
India's National Strategy on Additive Manufacturing was released by MeitY in 2022.
Bioprinting uses bio-ink containing living cells to make tissue structures.
In 2013 Princeton researchers printed a bionic ear with an embedded antenna.
Local Motors printed the Strati car in 2014.
STL is the common file format used for 3D printing.
statements: 1 — Correct: 3D food printers extrude edible pastes such as chocolate, sugar and dough. Chocolate printers, such as those by 3D Systems (ChefJet) and Choc Edge, make custom confectionery shapes layer by layer. Food printing is also being explored for personalised nutrition, hospital diets for people with swallowing difficulty, and elaborate pastry decoration. Printers use temperature-controlled syringe or nozzle extrusion. The technology is commercial but still niche, and its main strengths are customisation and complex geometry.

2 — Correct: In 2013 a Princeton University team led by Michael McAlpine printed a bionic ear. It combined hydrogel, cells and a silver nanoparticle antenna, and the ear could receive radio signals. It showed how 3D printing can merge biological tissue with electronics. This is part of bioprinting research, which aims at tissue and organ engineering, though fully functional printed organs remain experimental.

3 — Correct: Automakers use 3D printing for rapid prototyping, tooling, jigs, custom parts and lightweight components. Local Motors printed the Strati car in 2014, and BMW, Ford and Bugatti print parts in metal and polymer. Benefits include shorter design cycles, lower cost for low-volume parts, complex lightweight geometries and spare parts on demand. Mass production remains limited by speed and cost.

4 — Correct: Patient-specific implants and models are printed from CT or MRI scans for reconstructive surgery. Examples include titanium cranial and jaw implants, facial reconstruction, orthopaedic implants and printed prosthetics. Surgeons also print anatomical models to plan complex operations. Biocompatible materials include titanium, PEEK and bioresorbable polymers. Custom fit, shorter surgery time and better outcomes are the main advantages.

5 — Correct: The official answer treats data processing technologies as an application area. 3D printing is driven by digital data, software slicing and processing, and is used to print electronic circuits, sensors and computing components. It is also linked to Industry 4.0, digital manufacturing and cloud-based design files. This link to digital technology made UPSC's key accept the statement.
summary: The answer is (d): all five statements are correct. 3D printing (additive manufacturing) builds objects layer by layer from a digital design, and it is used in food, biomedical, automotive and even computing and data-related fields.
topic_notes: 3D printing, or additive manufacturing (AM), builds objects layer by layer from a digital model, usually a CAD file converted by slicing software (STL format). It was invented by Chuck Hull, who patented stereolithography in 1984 and founded 3D Systems. Major technologies include FDM (fused deposition modelling, using thermoplastic filament), SLA (stereolithography, using photopolymer resin), SLS (selective laser sintering, using powder), DMLS/SLM for metals, and binder jetting. Materials include plastics (PLA, ABS), metals (titanium, aluminium, steel), ceramics, concrete, food pastes and bio-inks containing living cells. Advantages are customisation, less waste, complex geometries, rapid prototyping and on-demand spare parts. Limitations are slow speed, high cost for mass production, limited material strength and size, and intellectual property and safety issues such as printed firearms. Sectors: healthcare (implants, prosthetics, dental aligners, bioprinting of skin, cartilage and organs), aerospace (GE's fuel nozzles), automotive, construction (printed houses and bridges; in India, L&T printed a building in Bengaluru and IIT Madras startup Tvasta printed structures), food, fashion, electronics, defence and space (NASA printing in orbit). In India, the National Strategy on Additive Manufacturing was released in 2022 by MeitY, aiming at a significant share of the global market and creating a larger ecosystem for it. 4D printing involves objects that change shape over time in response to stimuli such as heat or water. Related topics UPSC may ask: Industry 4.0, IoT, AI, nanotechnology, robotics, blockchain and bioprinting ethics.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Barren Island volcano is an active volcano located in the Indian territory.
2. Barren Island lies about 140 km east of Great Nicobar.
3. The last time the Barren Island voleano erupted was in 1991 and it has remained inactive since then. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Geography
detail: Barren Island is part of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Union Territory), situated in the Andaman Sea about 135-140 km north-east of Port Blair, the capital. It is the only confirmed active volcano in India and the only active volcano in the north-eastern Indian Ocean region, forming part of the Sunda arc volcanic chain created by subduction of the Indian Plate beneath the Burma (Sunda) microplate. It is uninhabited, roughly 3 km in diameter, with a central cone rising from the sea floor; the Indian Government declared it a restricted area, and it is under the Andaman and Nicobar administration. Historical eruptions were recorded from 1787, followed by a dormant period of about 150 years until 1991, when it reawakened; subsequent eruptions occurred in 1994-95, 2000s (2005-06), 2008, 2016-17, 2018 and later. Elimination logic: statement 1 is clearly correct. Statement 2 gives a wrong location (east of Great Nicobar, which is far to the south), so (b) and (d) fall. Statement 3 is wrong because the volcano has erupted many times since 1991, so it has not remained inactive. Only (a) survives.
explanations: Correct: statement 1 is true, while statements 2 and 3 are false, so only 1 is correct.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is false because the volcano has erupted repeatedly after 1991, and statement 2, which gives a false location.
Wrong: the option is an OCR corruption of '3 only', and statement 3 alone is false because the volcano has erupted since 1991.
Wrong: it combines statements 1 and 3, but statement 3 is false because Barren Island has erupted many times since 1991.
keyfact: Barren Island (about 140 km north-east of Port Blair) is India's only active volcano and has kept erupting since 1991.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only: Barren Island is India's only confirmed active volcano, in the Andaman Sea about 140 km north-east of Port Blair in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. It is uninhabited, roughly circular and about 3 km wide, with an active cone inside a caldera. It is part of the Sunda volcanic arc. It first erupted in recorded history in 1787 and re-erupted in 1991, with frequent activity afterwards through 2022.

Option (b) 2 and 3: this pairs a false location (east of Great Nicobar) with a false claim of inactivity after 1991. Great Nicobar is the largest island of the Nicobar group and is the southernmost point of India (Indira Point). It is home to the Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve (declared 1989), the Shompen and Nicobarese tribes, and a large proposed infrastructure project. It has no active volcano.

Option (c) is an OCR corruption of '3 only' and was meant to say statement 3 alone is correct. That is wrong because the volcano erupted again after 1991, in 1994-95, 2005-06, 2017 and later. The 1991 eruption ended about 150 years of quiet. It is monitored by GSI, NIO and the National Centre for Seismology, and it is a UPSC favourite on Indian geography.

Option (d) 1 and 3: this combines the true first statement with the false claim of inactivity after 1991. In fact Barren Island has shown intermittent eruptive activity: 1991, 1994-95, 2005-2006, 2008, 2016-17, 2018 and 2022. It is the only active volcano in India, while Narcondam, nearby, is classified as dormant. Deccan Traps and Baratang mud volcanoes are other related volcanic features.
related: Barren Island is India's only confirmed active volcano, in the Andaman Sea.
Barren Island lies about 135-140 km north-east of Port Blair.
Narcondam Island is a dormant volcano and has the endemic Narcondam hornbill.
Baratang Island in the Andamans has mud volcanoes.
The Ten Degree Channel separates the Andaman and Nicobar groups.
Indira Point in Great Nicobar is India's southernmost point.
Saddle Peak (732 m) in North Andaman is the highest peak of the islands.
Barren Island's first recorded eruption was in 1787, followed by an eruption in 1991 after about 150 years of dormancy.
statements: 1 — Correct: Barren Island is an active volcano in Indian territory (Andaman and Nicobar Islands). It is India's only confirmed active volcano and is located in the Andaman Sea. It is part of the volcanic arc stretching from Sumatra through Java to Myanmar, formed by the subduction of the Indian Plate under the Burma microplate. The island is uninhabited, about 3 km wide, and has a basaltic cone with a caldera. Its first recorded eruption was in 1787. It has shown frequent activity since 1991, and the area is restricted, with only scientific and monitoring visits allowed.

2 — Incorrect: Barren Island lies about 135-140 km north-east of Port Blair, not east of Great Nicobar. Great Nicobar is the southernmost large island of the Nicobar group, over 1,000 km south. The Andaman group lies to the north, the Nicobar group to the south, separated by the Ten Degree Channel at 10 degrees N. Port Blair, on South Andaman, is the capital of the UT. Narcondam Island, a dormant volcano, lies further north-east in the Andaman Sea, in the same arc. Remember Barren Island's location relative to Port Blair and the Andaman group.

3 — Incorrect: Barren Island did not stay inactive after 1991. After a dormancy of about 150 years (the previous eruptions were in the 1787-1832 period and a minor one in 1991), eruptions have continued in 1994-95, 2005-06, 2008, 2010s, 2017 and up to 2022. NIO (National Institute of Oceanography), Goa and the Geological Survey of India study it, and the National Centre for Seismology monitors the region. The 1991 eruption was triggered by seismic activity, and ash plumes and lava flows were documented. The volcano is also noted for the hot-water vent and thermal activity visible from ships.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 1 is correct. Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is India's only confirmed active volcano, but it lies about 140 km north-east of Port Blair (not east of Great Nicobar), and it has erupted repeatedly after 1991, including in 1994-95, 2005 onwards and 2017-2022.
topic_notes: Barren Island sits in the Andaman Sea on the Andaman-Nicobar-Sumatra subduction zone, where the Indian Plate subducts beneath the Burma microplate (part of the Sunda Plate). The volcanic arc runs from Sumatra and Java through Barren Island and Narcondam to Myanmar. Barren Island is the only confirmed active volcano in India and the northernmost active volcano of this arc, located about 135-140 km north-east of Port Blair. It is uninhabited, roughly 3 km across, and has a basaltic-andesitic composition. Recorded eruptions began in 1787; after about 150 years of quiet, it erupted in 1991 and repeatedly afterwards (1994-95, 2005-06, 2008, 2016-17, 2018-22). It is a restricted area; visiting requires permission, and the Indian Navy, Coast Guard, NIO and GSI monitor it. Narcondam Island, in East Andaman, is a dormant volcano and is home to the endemic Narcondam hornbill (a wildlife sanctuary). Baratang Island has mud volcanoes (mud volcano activity was recorded in 2003 and 2005). Other angles: Andaman and Nicobar Islands are separated by the Ten Degree Channel; Indira Point (Great Nicobar) is India's southernmost point and was affected by the 2004 tsunami; Mount Saddle Peak in North Andaman is the highest point of the islands at 732 m. Deccan Traps are fissure eruptions, not an active volcano. Other world volcanoes: Mauna Loa, Krakatoa, Mt Etna, Stromboli (lighthouse of the Mediterranean), Mt Fuji, Mt Pinatubo and Mt Vesuvius. Also remember volcano types: shield, composite, caldera, flood basalt and mid-ocean ridge volcanoes. The Ring of Fire in the Pacific has about 75% of the world's active volcanoes.

question: Why is a plant called Prosopis juliflora often mentioned in news ?
options: Its extract is widely used in cosmetics
It tends to reduce the biodiversity in the area in which it grows
Its extract is used in the synthesis of pesticides
subject: Environment
detail: Prosopis juliflora (vilayati babul, vilayati kikar, mesquite) is a thorny leguminous tree native to Mexico, South America and the Caribbean. It was introduced to India in the 19th century, and was widely planted in arid and semi-arid regions such as Gujarat, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh for fuelwood, greening and checking desertification. It has since become a highly invasive species. It forms dense thickets, is allelopathic (its roots and leaf litter release chemicals that suppress other plants), draws down groundwater with deep tap roots, and fixes nitrogen, which alters soil. It has invaded the Banni grasslands of Kutch, Keoladeo National Park (Bharatpur), and parts of Ranthambore and Nagarhole. Native grasses are displaced, so herbivores, ground-nesting birds and pastoral livelihoods suffer. Pods are eaten by livestock, but seeds spread through dung. Elimination logic: options (a) and (c) describe commercial uses that are not why the plant is in the news, and (d) fails because (b) is correct. The Madras High Court ordered its removal from Tamil Nadu in 2017, which was a major news item that year.
explanations: Incorrect: the plant is not known for any widely used cosmetic extract; its news coverage is about invasiveness.
Correct: it is an invasive alien species that suppresses native flora, lowers groundwater and reduces biodiversity.
Incorrect: it is not a source of pesticide synthesis; some extracts have been studied for allelopathic or antimicrobial properties, but this is not why it appears in the news.
Incorrect: since (b) is correct, 'None of the above' cannot be right.
keyfact: Prosopis juliflora (vilayati babul) is an invasive alien tree from Latin America that reduces native biodiversity and groundwater.
option_notes: Cosmetic extracts come from plants such as aloe vera, neem, sandalwood, turmeric and shea. Prosopis juliflora has no major cosmetic industry. Its recorded uses are fuelwood, charcoal, fodder from pods, and some honey production. Its pods are sometimes ground into flour, but the plant is chiefly regarded as a weed in India and is promoted for removal under several state programmes.

This is the correct answer. Prosopis juliflora is a Latin American native listed among the world's worst invasive species. In India it was planted in the 1870s onward and promoted through afforestation in the 20th century. It forms monocultures, lowers water tables, suppresses native grasses and trees, and harms grassland birds and mammals. The Banni grasslands and Keoladeo National Park are well-known examples of its spread.

Natural pesticide sources include neem (azadirachtin), pyrethrum from chrysanthemum, and tobacco (nicotine). Prosopis juliflora is not a recognised industrial feedstock for pesticide synthesis. Some laboratory studies have found allelopathic or antifungal compounds in it, but there is no commercial pesticide industry based on it, so this is not why it is mentioned in the news.

'None of the above' is wrong here because one of the options is correct. For comparison, other invasive species often asked about are Lantana camara, water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes), Parthenium hysterophorus, Mikania micrantha and Chromolaena odorata. UPSC often tests recognition of these species and the ecological harm they cause.
related: Prosopis juliflora is known locally as vilayati babul or vilayati kikar.
Prosopis cineraria (khejri) is native to India and is the state tree of Rajasthan, unlike the invasive P. juliflora.
Lantana camara, Parthenium and water hyacinth are other major invasive plants in India.
Mikania micrantha, 'mile-a-minute', has invaded Kaziranga and parts of Kerala and the Northeast.
The Madras High Court ordered removal of seemai karuvelam (Prosopis juliflora) in Tamil Nadu in 2017.
The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2022 contains provisions on invasive alien species.
Allelopathy means a plant releases chemicals that inhibit the growth of neighbouring plants.
summary: The answer is (b). Prosopis juliflora is an invasive alien tree that spreads aggressively, outcompetes native vegetation and depletes groundwater, thereby reducing biodiversity in the areas where it grows. It is in the news mainly for its ecological damage and for control or eradication efforts.
topic_notes: Invasive alien species (IAS) are non-native organisms that establish themselves in new habitats and cause ecological or economic harm. They are a leading cause of biodiversity loss, according to the IUCN and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD Aichi Target 9 dealt with IAS; the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework of 2022 also targets them). Prosopis juliflora, native to Central and South America, was introduced to India to green arid land and supply fuelwood. It tolerates salinity and drought, regenerates quickly after cutting, and its seeds are dispersed by livestock. Effects include displacement of native plants such as Prosopis cineraria (khejri, the state tree of Rajasthan), declining grassland productivity, lowered groundwater, and harm to Indian wildlife such as the wild ass in the Little Rann of Kutch and the blackbuck. The Madras High Court ordered removal of the species (often called seemai karuvelam in Tamil Nadu) in 2017. India's legal framework includes the Biological Diversity Act 2002, which regulates the introduction of invasive species, and the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act 2022, which added provisions on invasive alien species. Management approaches include mechanical uprooting, using the wood for charcoal or biomass power, and restoring native grasses. Other well-known Indian invasives are Lantana camara, Parthenium (congress grass), water hyacinth, Mikania micrantha (called 'mile-a-minute', affecting Kaziranga and Kerala), and Chromolaena odorata. Among animals, the African catfish (Clarias gariepinus), tilapia and the Louisiana crayfish are the ones commonly cited. Related terms are allelopathy, monoculture, and biological control.

ocr: Consider the following statements : iL. Most of the world’s coral reefs are in tropical waters. More than one-third of the world’s coral reefs are located in the territories of Australia, Indonesia and Philippines. Coral reefs host far more number of animal phyla than those hosted by tropical rainforests. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) land 2 only (b) 3only (c) land 3 only 1,2 and 3 (d) 91. 88. “Momentum for Change : Climate Neutral Now” is an initiative launched by (a) The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (b) The UNEP Secretariat (ec) The UNFCCC Secretariat
subject: Environment
detail: Coral reefs are shallow-water ecosystems built by calcium-carbonate-secreting polyps that live in symbiosis with zooxanthellae algae. They need warm water (about 23–29 °C), clear, sunlit, saline water, so most reefs lie between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. This makes Statement 1 correct. Reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor but support roughly 25% of marine species. Because most animal phyla are marine, reefs host more phyla than rainforests, even though rainforests have more species on land; this makes Statement 3 correct. Reef-area estimates (Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network, UNEP-WCMC and others) show that Australia (Great Barrier Reef), Indonesia and the Philippines together hold well over one-third of the world's reef area, so Statement 2 is correct. The Coral Triangle (Indonesia, Philippines, Malaysia, PNG, Timor-Leste, Solomon Islands) is the global centre of marine biodiversity. Elimination logic: once you know that reefs are tropical, options that drop Statement 1 are weaker. Knowing that reefs have high phylum-level diversity makes (a) wrong. Knowing the Australia–Indonesia–Philippines concentration makes (b) and (c) wrong. This leaves (d).
explanations: (a) is wrong: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, but Statement 3 is also correct, so '1 and 2 only' leaves out a true statement.
(b) is wrong: Statement 3 is correct, but Statements 1 and 2 are also correct, so '3 only' wrongly excludes them.
(c) is wrong: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, but Statement 2 is also correct, so '1 and 3 only' omits it.
(d) is correct: All three statements are accurate, matching the official answer.
keyfact: Coral reefs are mainly tropical, over a third lie in Australia, Indonesia and the Philippines, and they host more animal phyla than rainforests, so the answer is (d).
related: Great Barrier Reef: world's largest coral reef system, off Queensland, Australia; a World Heritage Site since 1981.
Coral Triangle: Indonesia, Philippines, Malaysia, PNG, Timor-Leste, Solomon Islands; peak marine biodiversity.
Coral bleaching occurs when stressed corals expel their zooxanthellae, mainly due to high sea temperatures.
India's coral areas: Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep, Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
Corals are protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
Gulf of Mannar was Asia's first marine biosphere reserve (2001).
Atoll: a ring-shaped reef around a lagoon; Lakshadweep islands are atolls.
Reefs cover under 1% of the ocean floor but support about 25% of marine species.
statements: 1 — Correct: Most reefs are in tropical waters because reef-building corals need warm, clear, shallow water. Reef-building (hermatypic) corals thrive at roughly 23–29 °C and below about 50–70 m depth, where sunlight reaches their symbiotic zooxanthellae. They cluster in the Indo-Pacific, Red Sea, and Caribbean. A few cold-water corals exist in deep, dark waters, but they do not build large reefs. Coral bleaching occurs when warm water makes corals expel their algae. Reefs are mostly found on the western sides of oceans, where warm currents flow, and are mostly absent near cold upwelling zones and large river mouths.

2 — Correct: Australia, Indonesia and the Philippines together hold more than a third of the world's coral reef area. Australia has the Great Barrier Reef, the largest reef system (about 2,300 km, off Queensland, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981).
