Wrong. Statement 3 is false because asset return is a hallmark of UNCAC, not UNTOC. Statements 2 and 4 are true, but 3 cannot be included.
Correct. Statements 2 and 4 are true, and statements 1 and 3 are false because each assigns a feature to the wrong convention.
Wrong. Statements 1 and 3 are false, so 'all four' cannot be right.
keyfact: UNCAC (2003) = first binding global anti-corruption treaty with an asset-recovery chapter; the Migrants Smuggling Protocol belongs to UNTOC; UNODC serves both.
related: UNCAC came into force on 14 December 2005; International Anti-Corruption Day is 9 December.
UNCAC is the only legally binding universal anti-corruption instrument.
UNTOC is also called the Palermo Convention and was adopted in 2000.
UNTOC has three protocols: trafficking in persons, smuggling of migrants, and firearms.
UNODC is headquartered in Vienna and is the guardian of UNCAC and UNTOC.
India ratified UNCAC in 2011 and UNTOC in 2002.
The StAR Initiative is a joint World Bank and UNODC programme for asset recovery.
Chapter V of UNCAC covers asset recovery.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Protocol against the Smuggling of Migrants by Land, Sea and Air supplements UNTOC, not UNCAC. UNTOC (Palermo Convention) was adopted in November 2000 and entered into force on 29 September 2003. It has three protocols: Trafficking in Persons (especially women and children), Smuggling of Migrants, and Firearms. The Migrants protocol entered into force in January 2004. India ratified UNTOC in 2002 and acceded to the protocols on trafficking and smuggling later.

2 — Correct: UNCAC is the first and only legally binding universal anti-corruption instrument. It was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 31 October 2003 and signed at Merida, Mexico, in December 2003. It came into force on 14 December 2005, which is observed as International Anti-Corruption Day on 9 December. It covers prevention, criminalisation, international cooperation and asset recovery. India ratified it in May 2011. Implementation is reviewed through a peer review mechanism.

3 — Incorrect: The asset-return chapter is the highlight of UNCAC (Chapter V on asset recovery), not UNTOC. Asset return is called a fundamental principle of UNCAC. It is a major issue for developing countries whose wealth has been looted and hidden abroad. UNTOC focuses on criminalising organised criminal groups, money laundering, confiscation, extradition, mutual legal assistance and joint investigations. UNCAC's Stolen Asset Recovery (StAR) Initiative is run by the World Bank and UNODC.

4 — Correct: UNODC, set up in 1997 and headquartered in Vienna, is mandated by member states to help implement both UNCAC and UNTOC. It serves as the secretariat of their Conferences of the Parties. It also provides technical assistance, legal advice, research and capacity-building. It publishes the World Drug Report each year, and its work also covers drugs, terrorism prevention and crime prevention. It is funded mainly by voluntary contributions.
summary: The answer is (c) 2 and 4 only. UNCAC (2003) is the first legally binding global anti-corruption instrument, and UNODC is mandated to help states implement both UNCAC and UNTOC. The Migrants Smuggling Protocol belongs to UNTOC, and the asset-return chapter is a highlight of UNCAC.
topic_notes:
UNCAC: Adopted by the UNGA on 31 October 2003, opened for signature at Merida in December 2003, and in force from 14 December 2005. It has 8 chapters and about 71 articles. Its main areas are prevention, criminalisation, international cooperation, asset recovery and technical assistance. Its review is carried out through the Implementation Review Mechanism. Bribery of foreign public officials is a non-mandatory provision. India ratified it in 2011.

UNTOC (Palermo Convention): Adopted in 2000, in force from 2003. It defines an organised criminal group as three or more persons acting together to commit a serious crime for material benefit. The three protocols cover trafficking in persons (the Palermo Protocol), smuggling of migrants, and firearms. India ratified UNTOC in 2002.

UNODC: Created in 1997 by merging the UN Drug Control Programme and the Centre for International Crime Prevention. Headquartered in Vienna. Publishes the World Drug Report and the Global Report on Trafficking in Persons. It is the guardian of the UN drug conventions of 1961, 1971 and 1988.

Other related instruments: the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention of 1997, the African Union Convention on Preventing and Combating Corruption, the Inter-American Convention against Corruption of 1996 (the first of its kind), FATF for money laundering, and the Transparency International Corruption Perceptions Index. In India, the relevant laws are the Prevention of Corruption Act 1988 (amended 2018), the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013, the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018 and the PMLA 2002.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. As per recent amendment to the Indian Forest Act, 1927, forest dwellers have the right to feil the bamboos grown on forest areas.
2. As per the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, bamboo is a minor forest produce.
3. The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 allows ownership of minor forest produce to forest dwellers. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA) recognises individual and community forest rights. Section 2(i) defines 'minor forest produce' as all non-timber forest produce of plant origin, including bamboo, brushwood, stumps, cane, tussar, cocoons, honey, wax, lac, tendu or kendu leaves, medicinal plants and herbs, roots and tubers. Section 3(1)(c) recognises the right of ownership, access to collect, use and dispose of minor forest produce that has been traditionally collected within or outside village boundaries. The Indian Forest (Amendment) Ordinance, 2017 amended section 2(7) of the 1927 Act so that bamboo grown on non-forest land is not a 'tree'. This exempted it from felling and transit permits. The change was meant to promote bamboo cultivation by farmers and was later enacted by Parliament. It did not touch bamboo in forest areas, which remains governed by forest law, and the FRA gives gram sabhas rights over it. Elimination: statement 1 is wrong because the amendment concerns non-forest land, which rules out (a) and (d). Statement 3 is correct, so (c) is incomplete. Only (b) remains.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement 1, which is incorrect: the 2017 amendment relates to bamboo on non-forest land and not to forest dwellers' right to fell bamboo in forests.

(b) is correct because statement 2 (bamboo is minor forest produce under the FRA) and statement 3 (the FRA gives ownership of minor forest produce to forest dwellers) are both correct. Statement 1 is incorrect.
(c) is wrong because it omits statement 2, which is correct: the FRA's definition of minor forest produce includes bamboo.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement 1, which is incorrect, so not all three statements are correct.
keyfact: Under the FRA 2006, bamboo is minor forest produce owned by forest dwellers; the 2017 Forest Act amendment only freed bamboo on non-forest land from 'tree' rules.
option_notes: Option (a) pairs statements 1 and 2. Statement 2 is accurate, but statement 1 wrongly describes the 2017 amendment of the Indian Forest Act, 1927. That amendment removed bamboo grown on non-forest land from the definition of 'tree' so that farmers need no felling or transit permit. It gave no felling right to forest dwellers in forest areas. This option is therefore wrong.

Option (b) is the correct combination. The FRA 2006 includes bamboo in minor forest produce under section 2(i). It also recognises ownership, collection, use and disposal of minor forest produce under section 3(1)(c). The Act is administered by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, and gram sabhas initiate recognition of rights. Statement 1 is left out because the 2017 amendment concerns non-forest land.

Option (c) says only statement 3 is correct. Statement 3 is true: section 3(1)(c) of the FRA gives forest dwellers ownership of minor forest produce. But it ignores that bamboo is expressly classed as minor forest produce under section 2(i), which makes statement 2 correct as well. The option is incomplete and therefore wrong.

Option (d) claims all three statements are correct. Statements 2 and 3 are right, but statement 1 is not. The Indian Forest (Amendment) Act, 2017 freed bamboo grown on non-forest land from permit requirements. It did not create a felling right for forest dwellers in forest areas. Hence the option fails.
related: FRA 2006 section 2(i) defines minor forest produce and includes bamboo.
FRA section 3(1)(c) gives ownership of minor forest produce; section 3(1)(i) gives community forest resource rights.
Individual forest rights under the FRA are capped at 4 hectares.
Indian Forest (Amendment) Act, 2017 removed bamboo on non-forest land from the definition of 'tree'.
PESA Act 1996 gives gram sabhas ownership of minor forest produce in Scheduled Areas.
Cut-off date for FRA eligibility is 13 December 2005, with 75 years' residence for other traditional forest dwellers.
Ministry of Tribal Affairs is the nodal ministry for the FRA.
In the Niyamgiri case (2013) the Supreme Court gave gram sabhas the decisive role on mining.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The 2017 amendment exempted bamboo grown on non-forest land from the definition of 'tree'. It did not give forest dwellers a right to fell bamboo in forest areas. The Indian Forest (Amendment) Ordinance was promulgated in November 2017, and a bill was introduced to replace it. It amended section 2(7) of the Indian Forest Act, 1927, so that felled bamboo on private land needs no felling or transit permit. The aim was to boost farmer income, bamboo cultivation and the bamboo industry, in line with the National Bamboo Mission. Bamboo inside forests continues to be regulated under forest law, though the FRA gives community rights over it.

2 — Correct: Section 2(i) of the FRA expressly includes bamboo in minor forest produce. Minor forest produce means all non-timber forest produce of plant origin. The list includes bamboo, brushwood, stumps, cane, tussar, cocoons, honey, wax, lac, tendu or kendu leaves, medicinal plants and herbs, roots and tubers. Bamboo had earlier been treated as timber, so it was a state monopoly and was controlled through permits. The FRA reclassified it as minor forest produce, and the Ministry of Tribal Affairs later clarified in 2011 that bamboo is minor forest produce, which allows gram sabhas to manage, harvest and sell it.

3 — Correct: Section 3(1)(c) of the FRA recognises the right of ownership, access to collect, use and dispose of minor forest produce traditionally collected within or outside village boundaries. The FRA was enacted in 2006 and its rules came in 2008. It was amended in 2012. It recognises individual forest rights (up to 4 hectares), community rights and community forest resource rights under section 3(1)(i). Gram sabhas are the authority that initiates the process of determining rights. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs is the nodal ministry, and the Act is also known as the Forest Rights Act or Tribal Rights Act.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 2 and 3 are correct and statement 1 is not. The Forest Rights Act, 2006 defines bamboo as minor forest produce and gives forest dwellers ownership of it. The 2017 amendment to the Indian Forest Act, 1927 only removed bamboo grown on non-forest (private) land from the definition of 'tree', so it does not give forest dwellers a right to fell bamboo in forest areas.
topic_notes: Forest Rights Act, 2006: it came into force on 1 January 2008, with rules notified in 2008 and amended in 2012. It aims to undo the 'historical injustice' done to forest dwellers by recognising their rights. Nodal ministry: Ministry of Tribal Affairs. Eligible groups are Scheduled Tribes residing in forests and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers, who must have lived there for 75 years (three generations) before 13 December 2005. Rights recognised under section 3 include: individual title to cultivated land up to 4 hectares; community rights such as nistar; ownership, collection and disposal of minor forest produce; grazing and fishing rights; habitat rights for Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs); and the right to protect, regenerate and manage the community forest resource (section 3(1)(i)). Procedure: the gram sabha passes resolutions and forms Forest Rights Committees. The claim then goes to the Sub-Divisional Level Committee, then the District Level Committee, which makes the final decision. Section 4(2) allows rights in critical tiger habitats and the creation of inviolate areas only under strict conditions. The Niyamgiri case (2013) upheld the gram sabha's role in decisions on bauxite mining. The Indian Forest Act, 1927 classifies forests as reserved, protected and village forests. Under the 2017 amendment, bamboo grown on non-forest land is exempted from felling and transit permits. Related: the National Bamboo Mission (restructured in 2018), minimum support price for minor forest produce through the Van Dhan scheme, and the PESA Act, 1996, which gives gram sabhas ownership of minor forest produce in Scheduled Areas. The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 and the Forest Conservation Act, 1980 also interact with the FRA. Forest Conservation Rules, 2022 have been criticised for diluting the gram sabha's consent requirement.

question: Which Article of the Constitution of India safeguards one’s right to marry the person of one’s choice?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 21 states that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. Since Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the article has been read expansively, and the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable. The Court has since brought dignity, privacy and autonomy of choice within it. In Lata Singh v. State of UP (2006), the Court protected adult inter-caste marriages. In Shakti Vahini v. Union of India (2018), it condemned honour killings and khap interference and held that the choice of a partner is a facet of Article 21. In Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M. (Hadiya case, 2018), it held that choosing a faith and a life partner lies at the core of personal liberty. In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), privacy was declared a fundamental right under Article 21, and it covers decisions about marriage. Elimination: Article 19 covers the six freedoms (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession). Article 25 covers freedom of religion. Article 29 protects the interests of minorities, including their language, script and culture. None of these deals with the choice of a spouse, so (b) is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: Article 19 gives freedoms such as speech, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession. It does not specifically guarantee the choice of a spouse, which the Court has located in Article 21.
Correct: Article 21, the right to life and personal liberty, has been interpreted to include the right to marry a person of one's choice, as in Lata Singh, Shakti Vahini and the Hadiya case.

Incorrect: Article 25 protects freedom of conscience and the free profession, practice and propagation of religion. It is not the source of the right to marry, though the Hadiya case touched on faith as well.

Incorrect: Article 29 protects the language, script and culture of minorities and bars denial of admission to educational institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste or language. It has nothing to do with marriage choice.
keyfact: Right to marry a person of one's choice is part of Article 21 (life and personal liberty), per Lata Singh, Shakti Vahini and Hadiya.
option_notes: Article 19(1) originally guaranteed seven freedoms. Property was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978), leaving six: speech and expression, peaceful assembly, association, movement, residence and profession. Article 19(2) to 19(6) allow reasonable restrictions. Article 19 is available only to citizens, not to foreigners. Freedom of speech includes press freedom and the right to information.

Article 21 says no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. It is available to citizens and non-citizens alike. Its scope was widened after Maneka Gandhi (1978). It now covers privacy, dignity, livelihood, education (Article 21A, added by the 86th Amendment in 2002), a clean environment and speedy trial. Marriage choice is part of it.

Article 25 guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion to all persons, subject to public order, morality and health. It permits the State to regulate secular activity and to provide social reform, such as opening Hindu temples to all classes. The Sikh kirpan is explained as included in the profession of religion.

Article 29 protects the interests of minorities. Clause (1) gives any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture the right to conserve it. Clause (2) bars denial of admission to State-run or State-aided institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste or language. It covers minorities and also the majority. Article 30 gives minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions.
related: Article 21A: free and compulsory education for ages 6 to 14 (86th Amendment, 2002).
Puttaswamy (2017): nine-judge bench held privacy a fundamental right under Article 21.
Maneka Gandhi (1978) made 'procedure established by law' require fairness and reasonableness.
Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended during a National Emergency (44th Amendment, 1978).
Shakti Vahini (2018): the Court issued guidelines against honour killings.
Navtej Singh Johar (2018): Section 377 IPC read down for consensual adult same-sex acts.
Article 21 applies to both citizens and foreigners.
Special Marriage Act 1954 governs civil inter-faith marriages.
summary: The answer is (b) Article 21. The Supreme Court has held that the right to marry a person of one's choice is part of the right to life and personal liberty, which includes dignity, autonomy and privacy.
topic_notes: Article 21 is the most expansively interpreted fundamental right. Originally, in A.K. Gopalan (1950), the Court read 'procedure established by law' narrowly. Maneka Gandhi (1978) linked Articles 14, 19 and 21 and required that the procedure be fair, just and reasonable, which gave the article substantive content. Rights read into Article 21 include privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017), dignity, livelihood (Olga Tellis), a clean environment, a speedy trial, legal aid, the right to die with dignity through passive euthanasia (Common Cause, 2018), freedom from custodial torture, and the right to health. Article 21A (education for ages 6 to 14) was added by the 86th Amendment in 2002. Article 20 gives protection in respect of conviction for offences. Article 22 gives protection against arbitrary arrest and detention. Under Article 359, Article 21 can no longer be suspended during an Emergency (44th Amendment), nor can Article 20. Marriage-related cases: Lata Singh (2006) on inter-caste marriage, Shakti Vahini (2018) on honour crimes, Shafin Jahan (2018) on adult choice of partner, and Navtej Singh Johar (2018), which decriminalised consensual same-sex relations by reading down Section 377 IPC. Supriyo (2023) declined to recognise same-sex marriage as a fundamental right, leaving it to Parliament. The Special Marriage Act 1954 allows inter-faith civil marriage.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. According to the Indian Patents Act, a biological process to create a seed can be patented in India.
2. In India, there is no Intellectual Property Appellate Board.
3. Plant varieties are not eligible to be patented in India. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: Section 3 of the Patents Act, 1970 lists what are not inventions. Section 3(j) excludes plants and animals in whole or any part thereof, including seeds, varieties and species, and essentially biological processes for the production or propagation of plants and animals. Microorganisms are patentable (the Diamond v. Chakrabarty principle, and TRIPS Art. 27.3(b) allows exclusion of plants and animals but requires protection of plant varieties by patents or an effective sui generis system). India chose the sui generis route: the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights (PPV&FR) Act, 2001, administered by the PPV&FR Authority in New Delhi. The IPAB was set up in 2003 (Chennai HQ) under the Trade Marks Act, 1999 to hear appeals against the Registrar's and Controller's decisions on trademarks, geographical indications and patents. The Tribunals Reforms Ordinance/Act 2021 abolished it and transferred its functions to High Courts and commercial courts. Elimination: statement 1 is wrong, so (a) and (d) go. Statement 2 was wrong in 2019, so (b) goes. That leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong: it takes statement 1 as correct, but essentially biological processes for producing seeds and plants are excluded under Section 3(j).
Wrong: it takes statement 2 as correct, but the IPAB existed in 2019 (it was abolished only in 2021).
Correct: only statement 3 holds, since plant varieties are not patentable in India and are protected under the PPV&FR Act, 2001.
Wrong: statements 1 and 2 are both incorrect, so the full set cannot be right.
keyfact: Plants, seeds, varieties and essentially biological processes are not patentable in India (Sec 3(j)); plant varieties are protected under the PPV&FR Act, 2001; IPAB existed until 2021.
option_notes: 1 and 3 only: pairs the wrong statement 1 with the right statement 3. Statement 1 fails because Section 3(j) of the Patents Act, 1970 excludes essentially biological processes for plants and seeds. Only microorganisms and non-biological, technical processes can qualify for patents in India. Patent term is 20 years from filing. This option is a trap for students who know only that biotech can be patented.

2 and 3 only: pairs the right statement 3 with statement 2, which was wrong in 2019. The IPAB was created in 2003 with its seat in Chennai to hear appeals on trademarks, GIs and patents. It was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, and appeals now go to High Courts. A student who knows only the 2021 abolition would be caught by this option.

3 only: the correct option. Plant varieties are excluded from patents by Section 3(j), and protection comes through the PPV&FR Act, 2001, which is a sui generis system recognised under TRIPS Art. 27.3(b). It combines breeders' rights with farmers' rights. The PPV&FR Authority is headquartered in New Delhi. Registration covers new, extant and farmers' varieties and essentially derived varieties.

1, 2 and 3: accepts all three statements as correct. It is wrong because statements 1 and 2 are incorrect. It is the all-inclusive option that tempts students unsure of the Patents Act exclusions and the IPAB's existence. Always test each statement independently in such questions.
related: Section 3(j) of the Patents Act excludes plants, animals and essentially biological processes.
Microorganisms are patentable in India if they meet the criteria.
PPV&FR Act, 2001 is India's sui generis plant variety law; the Authority is in New Delhi.
Section 3(d) was upheld in Novartis v. Union of India (2013), the Glivec case.
IPAB (est. 2003, Chennai) was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021.
Patent term in India is 20 years from the date of filing.
TRIPS Art. 27.3(b) allows members to exclude plants and animals but requires protection of plant varieties.
National IPR Policy 2016 is nodally handled by DPIIT.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Section 3(j) bars patents on essentially biological processes for producing plants, animals and seeds. Section 3(j) of the Patents Act, 1970 declares plants and animals in whole or part (including seeds, varieties and species) and essentially biological processes for their production or propagation to be non-inventions. A process that depends on natural crossing, selection or breeding is 'essentially biological'. A non-biological, technical process such as a microbiological or genetic-engineering process involving real human intervention may be considered. Microorganisms, being non-plant, non-animal, can be patented if they satisfy novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability. The 2002 amendment aligned the Act with TRIPS. Patent term is 20 years from filing.

2 — Incorrect (as of 2019): the IPAB existed. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board was constituted in September 2003 under the Trade Marks Act, 1999, with its headquarters in Chennai and benches in Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and Ahmedabad. It heard appeals against decisions of the Registrar of Trade Marks, the Controller of Patents and the Registrar of GIs, and from 2007 also patent matters. The Tribunals Reforms Ordinance, 2021 and the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 abolished it in April 2021. Its work passed to High Courts, with commercial divisions or IP Divisions (Delhi HC has an IP Division since 2021) handling appeals. So the statement would be false for the 2019 paper.

3 — Correct: plant varieties cannot be patented in India. Plant varieties are excluded under Section 3(j) of the Patents Act. India protects them under the PPV&FR Act, 2001, a sui generis system under TRIPS Art. 27.3(b) and consistent with UPOV-style breeders' rights but with farmers' rights added. The PPV&FR Authority (Delhi) registers new, distinct, uniform and stable (DUS) varieties and extant and farmers' varieties. Breeders get protection of 15 years for most crops (18 for trees and vines). Farmers can save, use, sow, exchange and sell farm-saved seed, except branded seed. The 2005 PepsiCo potato (FL-2027) dispute is a well-known case.
summary: The answer is (c): only statement 3 is correct. Section 3(j) of the Indian Patents Act, 1970 excludes plants, animals and essentially biological processes for their production from patenting, so statements 1 is wrong. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB) existed in 2019 (it was abolished only in April 2021), so statement 2 was wrong at the time of the exam.
topic_notes: Patentability in India is governed by the Patents Act, 1970, amended in 1999, 2002 and 2005 (the 2005 amendment introduced product patents in all fields, including drugs, to comply with TRIPS). An invention needs novelty, an inventive step and industrial applicability. Section 3 lists non-inventions: 3(d) bars new forms of known substances without enhanced efficacy (the Novartis v. Union of India Glivec case, 2013); 3(j) bars plants, animals and essentially biological processes; 3(k) bars mathematical or business methods, computer programs per se and algorithms; 3(b) bars inventions against public order or morality; 3(p) bars traditional knowledge. Section 4 covers inventions relating to atomic energy. Patent term is 20 years. The Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM) is headquartered in Mumbai, and patent offices are at Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata and Chennai. Plant protection: PPV&FR Act, 2001 (the PPV&FR Authority, plus the Gene Fund and Plant Varieties Registry). Biodiversity: the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (National Biodiversity Authority in Chennai) regulates access and benefit-sharing. International: TRIPS (WTO, 1995), UPOV (India is not a member), the Budapest Treaty on deposit of microorganisms (India acceded in 2001), the Nagoya Protocol and the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources (ITPGRFA). The National IPR Policy, 2016 has the DPIIT as the nodal department and the slogan 'Creative India; Innovative India'. Geographical Indications are covered by the GI Act, 1999 (Darjeeling tea was the first, 2004-05). The IPAB was set up in 2003 and abolished in 2021. Other areas of focus are the Copyright Act, 1957, the Trade Marks Act, 1999 and the Designs Act, 2000.

ocr: Consider the following statements : The Environment Protection Act, 1986 empowers the Government of India to 1. state the requirement of public participation in the process of environmental protection, and the procedure and manner in which it is sought 2. lay down the standards for emission or discharge of environmental pollutants from various sources Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Economy
detail: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (EPA) is an umbrella legislation enacted under Article 253 to implement the decisions of the 1972 Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment. It was passed in the aftermath of the Bhopal Gas Tragedy (December 1984). It came into force on 19 November 1986 and extends to the whole of India. Section 3 empowers the Central Government to take all measures necessary to protect and improve environmental quality, including coordinating actions, planning nationwide programmes, laying down standards for environmental quality and for emission or discharge of pollutants from various sources, restricting industrial locations, and laying down procedures and safeguards for handling hazardous substances. Section 6 allows rules to regulate environmental pollution. Section 5 allows directions, including closure of industries or stopping of power and water supply. Section 15 prescribes penalties of up to five years' imprisonment or a fine of up to Rs 1 lakh. The Act does not itself lay down a procedure for public participation. The public hearing requirement arises from the EIA Notification of 2006, which is delegated legislation under Sections 3 and 6 of the EPA. Elimination logic: statement 2 is textbook EPA language, so (a) and (d) go. Statement 1 sounds plausible but describes the EIA rules, not the Act's own text, so (c) goes. That leaves (b).
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is not an authority conferred by the Act itself. Public participation arises from the EIA Notification, 2006, so 'statement 1 only' is incorrect.
Correct: the Act's Section 3 explicitly empowers the Centre to lay down standards for emission or discharge of pollutants, while statement 1 does not fit the Act. Hence 2 only.
Wrong: this would require statement 1 to be correct as well, but public participation procedure is not in the Act's text.
Wrong: statement 2 is correct, as the Act clearly gives the power to set emission and discharge standards, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: EPA 1986 lets the Centre set emission/discharge standards (Sec 3, 6); public hearing comes from the EIA Notification 2006, not the Act itself.
option_notes: Option (a) 'Statement 1 only' would make public participation the Act's power. In reality public participation is in the EIA Notification, 2006, under which the State Pollution Control Board conducts a public hearing for Category A and B1 projects. The hearing needs a 30-day notice period, and the report goes to the regulatory authority. Public hearing was first made mandatory in 1994 and later reformed in 2006. Some projects are exempt, such as modernisation of irrigation, expansion of roads and highways in specified cases, and defence projects.

Option (b) 'Statement 2 only' is the official answer. It reflects Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, under which the Centre sets standards for emissions and discharges. The Act was passed after Bhopal under Article 253 and implements the Stockholm Conference 1972 decisions. The Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986 give schedule-wise standards. The Act also gives powers of entry, inspection, sampling and direction, such as closure of industry under Section 5.

Option (c) 'Both 1 and 2' wrongly treats the Act as directly laying down public participation procedure. The EPA is an umbrella enabling Act, and the EIA process sits under delegated legislation. The EIA Notification of 2006 has four stages: screening, scoping, public consultation and appraisal. The Environment Impact Assessment was made statutory in 1994 and the draft EIA Notification 2020 triggered much public debate. Public consultation is one element, not a power listed in the Act.

Option (d) 'Neither 1 nor 2' is wrong because the Act clearly includes emission and discharge standards. Section 3(2)(iv) and the Rules of 1986 contain these. Pollution standards also exist under the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 and Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, but EPA fills gaps and provides the umbrella. Penalty under Section 15 is up to five years' imprisonment or a fine up to Rs 1 lakh, or both, and the 2022 amendment decriminalised some provisions.
related: EPA 1986 was enacted under Article 253 after the Stockholm Conference 1972.
The Act was a response to the Bhopal Gas Tragedy of December 1984.
EIA Notification 2006 made public consultation a stage of the EIA process, under the EPA.
Section 5 of the EPA empowers the Centre to direct closure of an industry or stop its electricity and water supply.
The NGT was established in 2010 and sits as a specialised body for environmental disputes.
Article 48A (DPSP) and Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty) deal with environment protection.
Water Act 1974 was the first major pollution law, followed by the Air Act 1981.
The Central Pollution Control Board was set up in 1974 under the Water Act.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Act contains no provision that states the requirement of public participation or the procedure for seeking it. Public hearings are mandated by the EIA Notification, 2006, a subordinate rule. Public consultation under EIA has two parts: a public hearing near the project site, conducted by the State Pollution Control Board, and written responses invited from stakeholders. The 1994 EIA Notification first made public hearing mandatory. The 2006 notification classified projects into Category A (appraised by the Expert Appraisal Committee at the Centre) and Category B (appraised by the State level committee, SEIAA). Some projects, such as defence and strategic ones, are exempted from public hearing. The Act itself only gives the general enabling power.

2 — Correct: Section 3(2)(iv) of the Act empowers the Central Government to lay down standards for emission or discharge of environmental pollutants from various sources, and Section 3(2)(iii) covers standards for the quality of the environment. The Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986 contain the detailed standards in schedules, covering effluents, air emissions and noise. Rule 3 and the schedules set limits for industries. Later notifications have set standards for industries such as thermal power plants, sugar, cement and distilleries. The Central Pollution Control Board and State Pollution Control Boards help in implementation. The Noise Pollution Rules, 2000 and the Bharat Stage emission norms also derive from the Act.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 empowers the Central Government to lay down standards for emission or discharge of pollutants (Section 3 and Section 6), but it does not prescribe public participation in environmental protection. Public participation and hearings come from the EIA Notification, 2006 (and earlier 1994), issued under the Act.
topic_notes: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is India's umbrella environmental law. It was enacted under Article 253 (legislation for giving effect to international agreements) to implement the Stockholm Conference 1972 decisions, and was triggered by the Bhopal Gas Tragedy of 1984. It came into force on 19 November 1986, which is observed as National Environment Day in some contexts. It defines 'environment' to include water, air, land and their interrelationships with humans, other living creatures, plants, microorganisms and property. Key sections: Section 3 (general powers of the Centre), Section 5 (power to give directions, including closure and stopping of utilities), Section 6 (rule-making on standards, hazardous substances and industrial locations), Section 15 (penalties, up to five years' imprisonment or fine up to Rs 1 lakh), Section 19 (cognizance of offences, a complaint after 60 days' notice can be made by any person). The Act is administered by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC). Rules made under it include the Hazardous Waste Rules, Solid Waste Management Rules 2016, Plastic Waste Management Rules, E-Waste Rules, Noise Pollution Rules 2000, Coastal Regulation Zone Notifications and the Environment Impact Assessment Notification 2006. Related laws: Water Act 1974, Air Act 1981, Wildlife Protection Act 1972, Forest Conservation Act 1980, Biological Diversity Act 2002, National Green Tribunal Act 2010 (NGT, set up on 18 October 2010) and the Public Liability Insurance Act 1991. The Constitution has Article 48A (DPSP) and Article 51A(g) (fundamental duty) on environment, and the 42nd Amendment 1976 added these. Courts have read the right to a healthy environment into Article 21. Principles upheld by the Supreme Court include the polluter pays principle, the precautionary principle and public trust doctrine. Possible future angles are the EIA stages, categories of projects, CRZ zones, NGT powers and the Jan Vishwas amendments of 2023.

question: As per the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 in India, which one of the following statements is correct? Waste generator has to segregate
options: waste into five categories. The Rules are applicable to notified
urban local bodies, notified towns and all industrial townships only. The Rules provide for exact and
elaborate criteria for the identification of sites for landfills and waste processing facilities. It is mandatory on the part of waste
generator that the waste generated in one district cannot be moved to another district
subject: Environment
detail: The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 (notified by MoEFCC in April 2016, replacing the Municipal Solid Wastes (Management and Handling) Rules, 2000) widened the scope well beyond municipal areas. They apply to urban local bodies, outgrowths in urban agglomerations, census towns, notified areas, notified industrial townships, areas under Indian Railways, airports, airbases, ports and harbours, defence establishments, special economic zones, State and Central government organisations, places of pilgrimage, religious and historical importance, and to every domestic, institutional, commercial and other non-residential solid waste generator. Waste generators must segregate waste at source into three streams: biodegradable (wet), non-biodegradable (dry) and domestic hazardous waste (sanitary waste, diapers, etc.), and hand it over to authorised collectors. Schedule I gives detailed criteria for site selection of landfills and processing facilities, such as distance from water bodies, airports, habitation, floodplains and critical habitats. Elimination logic: (a) is wrong because there are three categories, not five. (b) is wrong because the applicability is far wider. (d) is wrong because no such blanket ban exists, and regional or common facilities across local bodies are in fact encouraged.
explanations: Incorrect: the Rules require segregation into three streams (wet/biodegradable, dry/non-biodegradable, domestic hazardous), not five categories.

Incorrect: the Rules apply far beyond urban local bodies, notified towns and industrial townships. They also cover census towns, urban agglomerations, railways, airports, ports, defence establishments, SEZs, pilgrimage places and bulk generators.
Correct: Schedule I of the Rules specifies detailed criteria for selecting sites for landfills and waste processing facilities, as the official answer confirms.

Incorrect: the Rules contain no mandatory bar on moving waste between districts. They encourage regional sanitary landfills shared by several local bodies, and waste-to-energy plants often draw waste from multiple areas.
keyfact: SWM Rules 2016: three-way source segregation (wet, dry, domestic hazardous), very wide applicability, and Schedule I gives detailed landfill and processing site criteria.
option_notes: Five-category segregation is not part of the 2016 Rules. The Rules prescribe three streams: biodegradable, non-biodegradable (dry, including recyclables) and domestic hazardous waste such as sanitary pads, diapers, used batteries, bulbs and chemical containers. Bulk generators must also segregate at source, and the 2000 Rules had much looser requirements. Fines for non-segregation are decided by local bodies as 'spot fines' under the byelaws. Separate rules exist for plastic, e-waste, bio-medical, construction and demolition and hazardous waste.

Applicability of the 2016 Rules is much wider than urban local bodies. They extend to urban agglomerations, census towns, notified areas, industrial townships, railways, airports, ports, defence and government establishments, SEZs, pilgrimage and heritage sites, and all waste generators. This broader coverage is a key difference from the Municipal Solid Wastes Rules, 2000, which were limited to municipal areas. Rural areas are mostly handled under the Swachh Bharat Mission (Gramin) framework.

Schedule I of the 2016 Rules provides criteria for site selection of landfills and processing facilities. Landfills should be away from water bodies, floodplains, airports (generally 20 km from major airports), habitation and protected areas, and have liners and leachate collection. Landfill use is limited to non-usable, non-recyclable, non-biodegradable, non-combustible and non-reactive inert waste. Local bodies must set up facilities, and the CPCB, SPCBs and Pollution Control Committees monitor compliance. Standards for compost, leachate, and emissions from waste-to-energy plants are also specified.

There is no rule that waste generated in a district cannot be moved to another. The Rules in fact encourage regional or common landfills and processing facilities shared by neighbouring local bodies, with State Urban Development Departments and the district magistrate coordinating. Cluster approaches reduce costs. Transport of waste must be in covered vehicles. Hazardous waste, in contrast, is governed by the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016, which regulate movement through manifests.
related: SWM Rules 2016 replaced the Municipal Solid Wastes (Management and Handling) Rules, 2000.
Waste must be segregated at source into three streams: wet, dry and domestic hazardous.
Schedule I of the SWM Rules 2016 deals with site criteria for landfills and processing facilities.
Non-recyclable waste with calorific value of 1500 kcal/kg or more is to go to waste-to-energy rather than landfill.
Bulk waste generators are required to process wet waste at their own premises.
Rules were issued under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016 introduced Extended Producer Responsibility.
Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) 2.0 was launched in 2021 with the aim of garbage-free cities.
summary: The correct answer is (c). The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 lay down detailed and elaborate criteria for identifying sites for landfills and waste processing facilities (Schedule I). The other options misstate the number of segregation categories, the Rules' applicability, and inter-district movement of waste.
topic_notes: Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 were notified under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, replacing the MSW Rules, 2000. Key features: (1) Wide applicability beyond municipal limits. (2) Source segregation into wet, dry and domestic hazardous waste. (3) Duties of waste generators: segregate, hand over to authorised collectors, pay user fees and spot fines, and not litter or burn waste. (4) Bulk waste generators (generally those with floor area over 20,000 sq m, water consumption over 100 kLD or waste over 100 kg/day) must process wet waste on site. (5) Gated communities and institutions must compost biodegradable waste. (6) Local bodies must arrange door-to-door collection, set up material recovery facilities, promote composting and biomethanation, and frame byelaws. (7) Manufacturers of sanitary products must provide a pouch for disposal. (8) Waste-to-energy: non-recyclable waste with calorific value of 1500 kcal/kg or more must not be landfilled and should go to energy recovery. (9) Landfill and processing site criteria in Schedule I, with standards in Schedule II. (10) Central Monitoring Committee under the MoEFCC supervises implementation, and the CPCB prepares guidelines and standards. (11) Rules mandate setting up a State-level Advisory Body. (12) Fixed timelines apply for setting up facilities. Related framework: Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 (amended 2018, 2021 with a single-use plastic ban from July 2022), E-Waste Rules 2016 (replaced 2022), Bio-Medical Waste Rules 2016, Construction and Demolition Waste Rules 2016, Hazardous Waste Rules 2016. Programmes: Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) 2.0 aims at garbage-free cities, and the National Green Tribunal enforces compliance. Principles: polluter pays, extended producer responsibility, and the waste hierarchy.

ocr: Consider the following statements : per the Industrial. Employment As (Standing Orders) Central (Amendment) Rules, 2018 if rules for fixed-term employment 1. are implemented, it becomes easier for the firms/companies to lay off workers no notice of termination of employment shall be necessary in the case of temporary workman Which of the statements given above is/are correct? 1 only 2 only (b) Both 1 and 2 (c) Neither 1 nor 2 (a) [ P.7.0.
subject: Economy
detail: The Ministry of Labour and Employment notified the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central (Amendment) Rules, 2018 on 16 March 2018. They amend the Central Rules of 1946 made under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. The Act requires establishments with 100 or more workers (the threshold applies to industrial establishments) to define and publish conditions of service through Model Standing Orders. Fixed Term Employment (FTE) was first brought in for the apparel manufacturing sector in 2016 and was then extended to all sectors in 2018. An FTE worker is hired on a written contract for a fixed period and gets the same wages, hours, allowances and statutory benefits as a permanent worker, along with benefits such as gratuity pro rata, even if the service is shorter than the usual qualifying period. The contract ends at the end of its term without notice or retrenchment compensation, so employers find it easier to scale workforce up or down, which is why critics (trade unions) say it makes 'hire and fire' easier. The Model Standing Orders also provide that the services of a temporary workman may be terminated without notice. Both statements follow, so (c) is right and (a), (b), (d) fail.
explanations: Wrong: it ignores that statement 2 is also correct, since the rules provide no notice is needed to terminate a temporary workman.
Wrong: it ignores that statement 1 is also correct, since fixed-term employment makes it easier for firms to part with workers.
Right: both statements correctly reflect the 2018 amendment rules, fixed-term employment and no notice for temporary workmen.
Wrong: at least one statement is correct, in fact both are.
keyfact: 2018 Standing Orders amendment (16 March 2018): fixed term employment extended to all sectors, and no termination notice for temporary workmen.
option_notes: 1 only: this would be right only if statement 2 were wrong. It is a partial-correct option, not the official answer. Statement 1 concerns fixed-term employment, which the 2018 amendment extended to all sectors after apparel in 2016. The option is a trap for students who recall FTE but not the temporary workman provision in the Model Standing Orders.

2 only: this would hold only if statement 1 were wrong. Statement 2 is correct, as the Model Standing Orders say no notice of termination is needed for a temporary workman. But the option wrongly excludes statement 1, since FTE does ease exit for employers. A trap for those who consider FTE benign and ignore the unions' criticism.

Both 1 and 2: the official answer. The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central (Amendment) Rules, 2018, notified 16 March 2018 by the Ministry of Labour and Employment, introduced fixed term employment across sectors and carried the temporary workman termination provision. They amend the Central Rules, 1946 under the Standing Orders Act, 1946.

Neither 1 nor 2: this is wrong since both statements match the rules. It would suit a student who believes FTE gives equal protection and so does not ease lay-offs, or who thinks notice is always required. In truth, FTE workers are paid the same as permanent ones, but the contract simply lapses with no retrenchment compensation.
related: Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 originally applied to industrial establishments with 100 or more workers.
Fixed term employment was introduced first for apparel manufacturing in 2016, extended to all sectors on 16 March 2018.
FTE workers get the same wages and benefits as permanent workers, with pro rata benefits such as gratuity.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 subsumed the Standing Orders Act, the Industrial Disputes Act and the Trade Unions Act.
The IR Code raised the threshold for government permission on lay-off and retrenchment from 100 to 300 workers.
Four labour codes: Wages, Industrial Relations, Social Security, and OSH and Working Conditions.
Labour is a Concurrent List subject in the Seventh Schedule.
Chapter V-B of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 dealt with lay-off, retrenchment and closure permission.
statements: 1 — Correct: Fixed-term employment lets firms hire for a defined period and let the contract lapse without retrenchment procedure, so unions say it eases lay-offs. Facts: FTE was notified for apparel in Oct 2016 and extended to all sectors on 16 March 2018. FTE workers get parity in wages and benefits with permanent staff, and gratuity eligibility is pro rata even without five years of service. The contract is in writing, and non-renewal is not treated as retrenchment. The government argued that it formalises contract labour and reduces unfair contractualisation, while trade unions opposed it as eroding job security. It has since been carried into the Industrial Relations Code, 2020.

2 — Correct: Under the amended Model Standing Orders, no notice of termination is necessary in the case of a temporary workman. Facts: the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 applies to establishments with 100 or more workers (many states have raised the threshold). Standing Orders define classes of workmen such as permanent, probationer, badli, casual, temporary and apprentice. A temporary workman is employed for work of an essentially temporary nature, likely to finish within a limited period. Permanent workers by contrast need notice or pay in lieu. The 1946 Act's provisions are now subsumed into the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, which has been passed but whose implementation is still pending.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Central (Amendment) Rules, 2018 introduced 'fixed term employment' for all sectors, which gives firms flexibility to hire and exit workers without retrenchment procedures. The rules also say no notice of termination is needed for a temporary workman.
topic_notes: The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 requires employers of industrial establishments with 100 or more workers (originally) to define conditions of employment, such as classification of workers, shifts, attendance, leave, holidays, termination, disciplinary action and grievance redress, in Standing Orders certified by a certifying officer. Model Standing Orders are provided in the Central Rules, 1946. Amendments: in 2016 the Government notified fixed term employment for the apparel manufacturing sector, in 2018 it was extended to all sectors (notification 16 March 2018). Features of FTE: a worker is hired directly on a written contract for a fixed period; hours, wages, allowances and other benefits are not less than those of a permanent worker in the same work; statutory benefits are available proportionately, with gratuity even if service is below five years; no notice or retrenchment compensation is needed when the term ends; renewal is possible. Government's argument: it promotes formal employment, ease of doing business and employment generation, replaces indirect contract labour, and gives workers direct contracts. Critics: it undermines job security and the Industrial Disputes Act's protections (Chapter V-B requires government permission for lay-off or retrenchment in establishments with 100 or more workers; this threshold was raised to 300 in the Industrial Relations Code, 2020). Labour codes: the four codes are the Code on Wages 2019, Industrial Relations Code 2020, Code on Social Security 2020, and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020. The IR Code subsumed the Trade Unions Act 1926, the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946 and the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, and it formally recognises fixed term employment. Labour is in the Concurrent List (Entries 22, 23, 24 of List III). Related themes: contract labour, ease of doing business, the Shops and Establishments Acts, and the 2019 and 2020 labour reforms.

question: The Service Area Approach was implemented under the purview of
options: Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Lead Bank Scheme (LBS) was introduced by the RBI in December 1969 on the recommendation of the Gadgil Study Group and the F.K.F. Nariman Committee (1969), under which each district was allotted to one bank (public or private) that would lead credit coordination there. The Service Area Approach was introduced in April 1989 as a refinement of the LBS. Under it, each rural and semi-urban bank branch was allotted about 15-25 villages as its service area, so that it planned and delivered credit for those villages. This improved accountability, avoided overlapping of branches, and ensured proper credit planning through the Service Area Credit Plan and the District Credit Plan. The SLBC (State Level Bankers' Committee) and DCC (District Consultative Committee) are the forums for coordination. The approach was reviewed and relaxed from 1996-97 for better flexibility, with borrowers free to approach any bank, and the 2000s saw further liberalisation. Elimination: IRDP (1978-80) was an asset-based poverty alleviation scheme, MGNREGS (2005) is a wage employment guarantee, and the National Skill Development Mission (2015) is about skilling. None of these is a banking credit-allocation framework.
explanations: Incorrect: IRDP (launched 1978-79, expanded nationwide 1980) gave subsidised bank credit and assets to poor families. It used banks but did not create the service area allocation of villages to branches.
Correct: SAA (1989) was implemented under the Lead Bank Scheme, allotting villages to bank branches for credit planning and delivery.
Incorrect: MGNREGS (2005, MGNREGA Act) guarantees 100 days of unskilled wage employment per rural household; it has nothing to do with bank branch village allocation.
Incorrect: The National Skill Development Mission (2015) coordinates skilling efforts across sectors and states; it is unrelated to bank credit planning.
keyfact: Service Area Approach (1989) was part of the RBI's Lead Bank Scheme (1969): each rural bank branch was allotted about 15-25 villages.
option_notes: The Integrated Rural Development Programme was launched in 1978-79 in selected blocks and extended to all blocks from 2 October 1980. It provided subsidy-linked bank loans to rural poor for self-employment assets such as livestock and small trades. It was merged with TRYSEM, DWCRA and others into the Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) in 1999, later restructured as the NRLM (Aajeevika) in 2011.

The Lead Bank Scheme was launched by the RBI in 1969 following the Gadgil Study Group and Nariman Committee recommendations. Each district is assigned to a lead bank that coordinates credit planning through the DCC and SLBC. It aims at area-based banking development and financial inclusion. The Service Area Approach (1989) was introduced under it, and the scheme remains operational today with the Lead District Manager at the helm.

MGNREGS was enacted as the NREGA in 2005 and renamed MGNREGA in 2009. It guarantees 100 days of wage employment per year to rural households whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work. It is demand-driven, administered by the Ministry of Rural Development, funded mostly by the Centre, with Gram Panchayats as principal implementing bodies and social audit mandatory.

The National Skill Development Mission was launched on 15 July 2015 (World Youth Skills Day) to converge skilling activities across the Centre and states. It sits under the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, formed in 2014. Related efforts include the National Skill Development Corporation (2008), Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (2015), and the National Policy for Skill Development and Entrepreneurship 2015.
related: Lead Bank Scheme was launched by RBI in 1969 on the basis of the Gadgil Study Group and the Nariman Committee.
Service Area Approach was introduced in 1989 and relaxed in 1996-97.
NABARD was set up in 1982 on the Shivaraman Committee recommendation.
Regional Rural Banks were established in 1975 under the RRB Act 1976.
SLBC and DCC are the coordination forums of the Lead Bank Scheme.
Kisan Credit Card scheme was launched in 1998.
The SHG-Bank Linkage Programme began in 1992 under NABARD.
Priority sector lending target for domestic commercial banks is 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit.
summary: The answer is (b) Lead Bank Scheme. The Service Area Approach (SAA), introduced by the RBI in 1989, assigned specific villages to specific bank branches for rural credit planning, and it operated within the Lead Bank Scheme framework.
topic_notes: Rural credit architecture in India has evolved in stages. After the All India Rural Credit Survey (1954) and the nationalisation of 14 banks in 1969 (6 more in 1980), the RBI launched the Lead Bank Scheme in December 1969 on the basis of the Gadgil Study Group and Nariman Committee. Under it each district is assigned to one lead bank, which acts as a consortium leader for development of banking and credit in that district. Coordination forums are the State Level Bankers' Committee (SLBC), District Consultative Committee (DCC) and the District Level Review Committee (DLRC). The Lead District Manager (LDM) is the lead bank's officer in charge of the district. The Service Area Approach was introduced in 1989 following the recommendations of the Committee on Agricultural Credit and the Kelkar/Gadgil style reviews, assigning villages to specific rural and semi-urban branches (roughly 15-25 villages each) for credit planning. Relaxations came in 1996-97, and after 2000 borrowers could borrow from any bank. Related institutions: Regional Rural Banks (1975, Narasimham Committee on RRBs, RRB Act 1976), NABARD (1982, on the recommendation of the Shivaraman Committee), Priority Sector Lending (introduced 1972, formal targets from 1980: 40% for domestic banks), Kisan Credit Card (1998), Self Help Group-Bank Linkage Programme (1992), and the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (2014) for financial inclusion. The Financial Inclusion Fund and Financial Inclusion Technology Fund were created in 2007-08. Other angles UPSC asks: Differential Rate of Interest scheme (1972, at 4%), IRDP, SGSY, NRLM, and the role of the Lead Bank in the district credit plan and the Annual Credit Plan.

ocr: With reference to the management of minor minerals in India, consider the following statements : 1. Sand is a ‘minor mineral’ according to the prevailing law in the country. 2. State Governments have the power to grant mining leases of minor minerals, but the powers regarding the formation of rules related to the grant of minor minerals lie with the Central Government. 3. State Governments have the power to frame rules to prevent illegal mining of minor minerals. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 and 3 only (6) 2 and 3 only (co) 3 only (d@) 1,2 and 3 qd
subject: Geography
detail: Under the MMDR Act, 1957, minerals are divided into major minerals and minor minerals. Section 3(e) defines minor minerals as building stones, gravel, ordinary clay, ordinary sand (other than sand used for prescribed purposes such as atomic energy or industrial use), and any other mineral the Central Government notifies as minor. Hence the Centre decides what counts as 'minor' by notification, but the administration of minor minerals is delegated to the States. Section 15 empowers State Governments to make rules for the grant of quarry leases, mining leases and other mineral concessions for minor minerals, and also to make rules to prevent illegal mining, transport and storage. Major minerals, by contrast, are governed by Section 13 and the Mineral Concession Rules, with the Centre holding the rule-making power and the State granting leases with Central approval in certain cases. The 2015 amendment introduced auctions for major minerals. The 2016 Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines and the 2020 Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines for Sand Mining supplement the framework. Elimination logic: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so options (b), (c) and (d) fall away once statement 2 is recognised as wrong, which leaves (a).
explanations: Correct. Statements 1 and 3 are both correct, and statement 2 is incorrect, so '1 and 3 only' matches the official answer.
Wrong. This option includes statement 2, which wrongly says the Central Government holds the rule-making power for minor minerals. It also omits statement 1, which is correct.
Wrong. Statement 1 is correct, so '3 only' leaves out a valid statement. Sand is a notified minor mineral under Section 3(e).
Wrong. This option accepts statement 2, which is incorrect because the States hold the rule-making power for minor minerals under Section 15.
keyfact: Sand is a minor mineral (Sec 3(e) MMDR Act, 1957); States make rules for minor minerals (Sec 15) and against illegal mining (Sec 23C), while the Centre only notifies which minerals are minor.
related: Section 3(e) of the MMDR Act, 1957 defines minor minerals.
Section 15 of the MMDR Act lets States make rules for minor mineral concessions.
Section 23C, added in 2015, lets States make rules against illegal mining, transport and storage.
The District Mineral Foundation is created under Section 9B of the MMDR Act (2015 amendment).
Entry 54 of the Union List and Entry 23 of the State List together govern the mining subject.
The Samatha judgment (1997) restricted transfer of tribal land to non-tribals for mining in Scheduled Areas.
The Indian Bureau of Mines functions under the Ministry of Mines.
The Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Act, 2002 governs mining in India's offshore areas.
statements: 1 — Correct: Ordinary sand is expressly listed as a minor mineral in Section 3(e) of the MMDR Act, 1957. Minor minerals include building stone, gravel, ordinary clay, ordinary sand used for filling or building, road metal, earth used for filling and brick-making, and boulders, plus any mineral the Centre declares minor by notification in the Official Gazette. Sand used for atomic energy or for industrial purposes is excluded from the 'ordinary sand' category. Sand mining is regulated by States under their own Minor Mineral Concession Rules, and it is a major source of illegal mining disputes. The Supreme Court in Deepak Kumar v. State of Haryana (2012) required environmental clearance even for mining leases under 5 hectares, and the NGT has also actively supervised sand mining.

2 — Incorrect: The power to make rules for the grant of minor mineral concessions lies with State Governments under Section 15 of the MMDR Act, not with the Centre. The Centre's role is limited mainly to defining or notifying what counts as a minor mineral under Section 3(e). For major minerals, Section 13 gives the Centre the rule-making power, and the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 and the Mineral (Auction) Rules, 2015 apply. The State Minor Mineral Concession Rules, such as the Tamil Nadu Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1959, govern quarrying leases, royalty and permits. Royalty on major minerals is set by the Centre in the Second Schedule, while minor mineral royalty is set by States.

3 — Correct: Section 23C of the MMDR Act (inserted by the 2015 amendment) explicitly empowers State Governments to make rules to prevent illegal mining, transportation and storage of minerals and for related matters. Illegal mining of minor minerals such as sand, stone and gravel is a recurring problem, and States respond with measures such as GPS tracking of vehicles, transit passes, e-permits, drone surveillance and special enforcement squads. The Act also provides for penalties, including imprisonment up to 2 years and a fine up to Rs 5 lakh per hectare for unauthorised mining under Section 21. The 2015 amendment also permitted States to set up special courts to try offences.
summary: The official answer is (a) 1 and 3 only. Sand is a 'minor mineral' under Section 3(e) of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act), and State Governments have the power to frame rules under Section 15 to prevent illegal mining, transport and storage of minor minerals. Statement 2 is wrong because the rule-making power for minor minerals lies with the States, not the Centre.
topic_notes: The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 is the central law governing mining in India. It rests on Entry 54 of the Union List, which allows Parliament to regulate mines and mineral development when it declares this expedient in the public interest, and on Entry 23 of the State List, which gives States power over mines and minerals subject to Union control. Minerals are grouped into fuel minerals (coal, lignite, petroleum), atomic minerals, metallic minerals and non-metallic minerals. Legally, they are classed as major or minor. Section 3(e) defines minor minerals as building stones, gravel, ordinary clay, ordinary sand, and others the Centre notifies. Section 15 gives States the power to make rules on minor minerals. Section 13 empowers the Centre to make rules for major minerals. Section 23C empowers States to make rules to curb illegal mining. Major amendments came in 2015, which introduced auctions for mineral concessions and created the District Mineral Foundation (DMF) under Section 9B, funded by contributions from miners to benefit mining-affected communities, and the National Mineral Exploration Trust (NMET). In 2021 further amendments removed the distinction between captive and merchant mines and allowed captive mines to sell up to 50 percent of annual production after meeting their end-use needs. Environmental regulation applies too. The 2006 EIA notification and the Supreme Court's Deepak Kumar (2012) judgment required environmental clearance for all mining leases. The Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines (2016) and the Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines (2020) address sand mining. The Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM), under the Ministry of Mines, regulates mineral conservation and development. The Mineral Conservation and Development Rules apply to major minerals. The Geological Survey of India carries out exploration. Possible future angles include the DMF, the Samatha judgment (1997) on tribal land and mining in Fifth Schedule areas, the Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana, and offshore minerals under the Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Act, 2002.

ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. Most of India’s external debt is owed by governmental entities. 2. All of India’s external debt is denominated in US dollars. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (ad) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Geography
detail: India's external debt is the outstanding liability owed to non-residents, repayable in foreign currency or goods and services. It is published by the Ministry of Finance (Department of Economic Affairs) in its 'India's External Debt: A Status Report' and quarterly by RBI data. At end-March 2019, the total was about US$543 billion, and at end-March 2024 about US$663 billion. The key compositional fact is that sovereign (government) external debt is only about 20-23% of the total, while non-government debt (commercial borrowings, NRI deposits, short-term trade credit) is nearly 77-80%. So Statement 1 fails. On currency, the US dollar is the largest share, about 53-54%, followed by the Indian rupee (about 31%, mainly NRI deposits and masala bonds), the SDR, Japanese yen, euro and others. So 'all in US dollars' in Statement 2 is plainly false. Elimination: once either statement is seen as false, (c) goes. 'All' in Statement 2 is an absolute, a typical UPSC trap, and Statement 1 is also false, which leaves (d). Trap: confusing 'government' debt with total external debt.
explanations: (a) 1 only is wrong: Statement 1 is false because government debt is only about one-fifth of the total.
(b) 2 only is wrong: Statement 2 is false because the debt is in many currencies, with USD about half.
(c) Both 1 and 2 is wrong: neither statement is correct.
(d) Neither 1 nor 2 is correct, matching the official answer: non-government borrowers dominate and the currency mix is diversified.
keyfact: India's external debt is mostly non-government (about 77-80%) and multi-currency (USD about 53%), so both statements are wrong: answer (d).
option_notes: 1 only: This would claim that India's external debt is mostly sovereign. In fact, sovereign external debt (borrowings from multilaterals such as the World Bank and ADB, bilateral lenders such as Japan, and the IMF, plus government securities held by foreigners) is about 20-23% of total external debt. Non-government debt is far larger. Sovereign debt is generally on concessional terms with long maturities.

2 only: This would claim that all external debt is in US dollars. The USD is the largest component, at roughly 53%, but not the whole. The rupee, SDR, yen and euro also feature. A currency-wise breakdown is published by the Ministry of Finance in its status report, and the dollar share indicates the exposure to rupee depreciation.

Both 1 and 2: This would mean the debt is mainly governmental and entirely in dollars. Both are factually wrong. India's external debt is mostly private, with commercial borrowings and NRI deposits leading, and it is multi-currency. Such 'both' options are common in UPSC statement questions as plausible-looking distractors.

Neither 1 nor 2: This is the correct, official answer. India's external debt was about US$663 billion at end-March 2024, about 18.7% of GDP. Foreign exchange reserves cover about 90+% of the debt. Non-government debt dominates (about 77-80%), and the currency mix includes USD, INR, SDR, yen and euro. India's debt position is considered sustainable.
related: Non-government borrowers hold roughly 77-80% of India's external debt.
The US dollar is the largest currency in India's external debt, at about 53-54%.
Commercial borrowings are the largest component of external debt, followed by NRI deposits.
Masala bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued abroad; the first was issued by IFC in 2014.
ECBs are regulated by RBI under FEMA 1999.
India's external debt was about US$663 billion at end-March 2024, about 18.7% of GDP.
The 1991 BoP crisis led to pledging gold and to economic reforms.
The SDR is the IMF's reserve asset, with a basket of USD, euro, yuan, yen and pound.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Government (sovereign) debt is only about one-fifth of India's external debt; the bulk is non-government. Facts: India's external debt includes multilateral, bilateral, IMF, trade credit, commercial borrowings, NRI deposits, rupee debt and short-term debt. The sovereign share has been about 20-23% in recent years. Commercial borrowings are the largest component (about a third), followed by NRI deposits. Multilateral lenders include the World Bank and ADB. Long-term debt is about 80% of the total, short-term about 19-20%. The ratio of external debt to GDP is about 19% (2023-24), so India is not at high risk.

2 — Incorrect: Only about 53% of the debt is in US dollars; the rest is in rupees, SDRs, yen, euros and other currencies. Facts: The USD is the largest currency, followed by the Indian rupee (about 31%, including NRI deposits and masala bonds), then the yen, SDR and euro. Rupee-denominated debt shifts exchange-rate risk to the lender. Masala bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued overseas, first issued by IFC in 2014; the RBI regulates them under ECB rules. The SDR is the IMF's reserve asset, with a basket of USD, euro, yuan, yen and pound.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. Most of India's external debt is owed by non-government borrowers (commercial borrowings, NRI deposits, trade credit), not by the government, and India's external debt is spread across several currencies, not just US dollars.
topic_notes: External debt is the part of a country's total debt owed to creditors outside the country, repayable in foreign currency, goods or services. India's definition covers outstanding disbursed, non-contingent liabilities owed to non-residents. Data comes from the Ministry of Finance (Department of Economic Affairs), which publishes the status report, with RBI and the World Bank's International Debt Statistics. Main components: multilateral, bilateral, IMF, trade credit (buyers' and suppliers' credit), external commercial borrowings (ECBs), NRI deposits, rupee debt, long-term and short-term debt. Recent figures: about US$543 billion in March 2019, US$663 billion in March 2024. Debt to GDP is about 19%, forex reserves cover about 95% of debt at times, and short-term debt (original maturity) is about 18-20% of total. Sovereign debt is about 20-23%, and non-government debt is about 77-80%. Commercial borrowings are the largest component (about 33-37%), then NRI deposits (about 23%), then short-term trade credit (about 17%). Currency: USD about 53-54%, INR about 31%, SDR, yen and euro the remainder. ECBs are commercial loans raised by Indian resident entities from non-resident lenders, regulated by RBI under FEMA. Masala bonds are rupee-denominated overseas bonds, with the first issue by IFC in 2014; the first Indian corporate issue was HDFC in 2015. Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) FCNR(B) deposits are in foreign currency; NRE deposits are in rupees; NRO deposits are also in rupees. Likely angles: debt-service ratio, the debt-to-GDP ratio, the difference between external and public debt, the 1991 balance of payments crisis, the IMF's SDR, and the difference between external debt and the net international investment position.

question: Which of the following is not included in the assets of a commercial bank in India?
options: Money at call and short notice
subject: Economy
detail: A commercial bank's balance sheet has two sides. Liabilities show the sources of funds: capital, reserves and surplus, deposits (demand, savings, term), and borrowings. Assets show how those funds are used: cash in hand, balances with the RBI (CRR), balances with other banks, money at call and short notice, investments (mainly SLR securities such as government securities), loans and advances (cash credit, overdrafts, term loans, bills purchased and discounted), fixed assets and other assets. A deposit is money the bank must repay to the depositor, which is why it is a liability. Money at call and short notice is a very short-term interbank loan (overnight to 14 days) that the bank has lent out, so it counts as a liquid asset. Investments and advances earn the bank income. Elimination logic: any item that earns the bank income or can be quickly converted to cash is an asset, while anything the bank owes to others is a liability. Only deposits fall in the second group. Note that a deposit is an asset for the depositor, not for the bank.
explanations: (a) is wrong as an answer: advances (loans, cash credit, overdraft, bills discounted) are the bank's main income-earning asset, since borrowers owe this money to the bank.
(b) is correct: deposits are money owed by the bank to the public, so they are a liability, not an asset. This is why (b) is the item that is not included in assets.
(c) is wrong as an answer: investments, mainly in government and other approved securities held for SLR, are assets of the bank.
(d) is wrong as an answer: money at call and short notice is a short-term interbank loan that the bank has lent out and can recall, so it is a liquid asset.
keyfact: Deposits are a bank's liability; advances, investments, cash and call money are its assets.
option_notes: Advances are loans given by banks to customers, such as cash credit, overdrafts, term loans and bills purchased or discounted. They are the largest income-earning asset and generate interest income. Non-performing advances (NPAs) are advances where interest or principal is overdue for more than 90 days. The credit-deposit (CD) ratio measures advances against deposits.

Deposits are funds placed with a bank by the public and are the bank's main source of funds. Types are current (demand), savings, fixed or term, and recurring deposits. They are liabilities because the bank must repay them. Demand deposits carry no or low interest, and term deposits carry higher interest. Deposits up to Rs 5 lakh per depositor per bank are insured by DICGC.

Investments are the bank's holdings of securities. Most are government securities (G-secs) and treasury bills held to meet the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR), plus bonds, debentures and shares. They are classified as held to maturity (HTM), available for sale (AFS) and held for trading (HFT). They are an asset that earns interest and provides liquidity.

Money at call and short notice is lending in the interbank call money market. Call money is for one day, notice money is for 2 to 14 days. It is a highly liquid asset for the lending bank and sits in the balance sheet under 'balances with banks and money at call and short notice'. The rate is the call rate, which is closely linked to the RBI's policy rate corridor.
related: Deposits, borrowings and capital are bank liabilities; loans, investments and cash are assets.
CRR is held as cash with the RBI and earns no interest; SLR is held with the bank itself in cash, gold or G-secs.
Call money covers 1 day, notice money 2 to 14 days.
An NPA is a loan overdue for more than 90 days.
DICGC insures deposits up to Rs 5 lakh per depositor per bank.
The MSF rate equals the repo rate plus 25 basis points.
The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 governs the format of bank balance sheets.
Basel III minimum capital requirement in India is 9 percent CRAR.
