LTE was standardised by 3GPP in Release 8 (2008) and first commercially launched in Oslo and Stockholm in December 2009 by TeliaSonera. The ITU originally defined true 4G as IMT-Advanced, with LTE-Advanced and WiMAX 2 qualifying. LTE was later allowed to be marketed as 4G, hence the labels '3.9G' and '4G LTE'. VoLTE is simply the voice service delivered over LTE using IMS and does not belong to the 3G family. 3G technologies include UMTS/WCDMA and HSPA, which are different from LTE.

2 — Incorrect: LTE is not data-only, and VoLTE is not voice-only. LTE is an all-IP network that carries any traffic as packets, including voice (as VoLTE), video and internet data. VoLTE runs on the same LTE network, so users can make calls while using mobile data at full 4G speed, unlike CSFB where data drops to 3G or 2G during a call. VoLTE uses IMS, SIP signalling, and the AMR-WB (HD Voice) codec. Jio launched the first VoLTE-only network in India in 2016, and Airtel and Vi (Vodafone Idea) followed later. VoLTE can also support video calling (ViLTE).
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. LTE is marketed as 4G (not 3G) and VoLTE is voice carried over the LTE network as packet data (not 'advanced 3G'); LTE is not data-only, and VoLTE is not voice-only.
topic_notes: Generations of mobile technology: 1G (analog voice, 1980s, AMPS); 2G (digital voice and SMS, GSM and CDMA, 1990s; GPRS and EDGE are 2.5G); 3G (UMTS/WCDMA, HSPA, CDMA2000, around 2001, with mobile internet and video calling); 4G (LTE and LTE-Advanced, all-IP, from about 2009–2010); 5G (NR, with eMBB, URLLC and mMTC use cases, speeds up to about 10–20 Gbps in theory, low latency of about 1 ms). 3GPP (3rd Generation Partnership Project) sets the GSM/UMTS/LTE/5G standards, and the ITU sets IMT requirements (IMT-2000 for 3G, IMT-Advanced for 4G, IMT-2020 for 5G). LTE uses OFDMA in the downlink and SC-FDMA in the uplink, along with MIMO antennas. LTE offers FDD and TDD modes, and in India TDD-LTE was used by Bharti Airtel and Jio in the 2300 MHz band, while Jio holds 850/1800 MHz as well. VoLTE needs IMS, HD voice codecs, and a VoLTE-capable handset. CSFB means a call drops the phone back to 2G/3G. India: 5G services launched on 1 October 2022 (India Mobile Congress), with Jio's standalone (SA) 5G and Airtel's non-standalone (NSA) 5G. The 2022 spectrum auction was the largest ever. Other possible angles: Bharat 6G Vision, Telecommunications Act 2023, TRAI, DoT, BharatNet, Wi-Fi 6, Li-Fi, NB-IoT, and VoWiFi.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017?
1. Pregnant women are entitled for three months pre-delivery and three months post-delivery paid leave. 2.. Enterprises with créches must allow the mother minimum six créche visits daily.
3. Women with two children get reduced entitlements. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Polity
detail: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 was amended in 2017 (in force from 1 April 2017). Paid maternity leave rose from 12 to 26 weeks for the first two children. Of the 26 weeks, no more than 8 weeks may be taken before the expected delivery date. This is not the 'three months before and three months after' split in statement 1. For a woman who already has two or more surviving children, leave stays at 12 weeks, of which no more than 6 weeks may be pre-delivery. So statement 3 is correct. A commissioning mother (using a surrogate) and an adopting mother (child under three months) get 12 weeks. Every establishment with 50 or more employees must provide a créche facility. The mother is allowed four visits a day, including her rest interval, not six, so statement 2 is wrong. Employers may permit work from home after the leave ends, if the nature of the work allows. Employers must inform women of these benefits in writing or electronically at the time of appointment. Elimination logic: statements 1 and 2 are both wrong, so only (c) can be right.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statements 1 and 2, and both are factually incorrect. Statement 1 gets the leave split wrong and statement 2 gets the number of visits wrong.
Wrong: statement 2 is incorrect because the Act provides four créche visits a day, not six, so '2 only' cannot be right.
Correct: statement 3 is the only correct one. Women with two or more surviving children get 12 weeks instead of 26 weeks.
Wrong: statements 1 and 2 are incorrect, so 'all three' fails.
keyfact: Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017: 26 weeks of paid leave for the first two children (at most 8 before delivery), 12 weeks for the third child, and four créche visits a day.
option_notes: Option (a) pairs statements 1 and 2. Statement 1 claims three months before and three months after delivery, but the Act gives 26 weeks with at most 8 weeks before delivery. Statement 2 claims six créche visits, but the Act allows four. The paid leave increase from 12 to 26 weeks came into force on 1 April 2017. Establishments with 50 or more employees must provide a créche. Both claims are wrong, so this option fails.

Option (b) picks statement 2 alone. It says enterprises with créches must allow six visits a day. The real figure is four visits a day, including the rest interval. The créche is mandatory for establishments with 50 or more employees. This facility was strengthened by the 2017 amendment. Because the number is wrong, this option is incorrect.

Option (c) picks statement 3 alone and is the official answer. A woman with two or more surviving children gets 12 weeks of paid leave, with at most 6 weeks before delivery. The first two children get 26 weeks. The amendment came into force on 1 April 2017. It covers establishments with 10 or more employees. Adopting and commissioning mothers get 12 weeks.

Option (d) claims all three statements are correct. Only statement 3 holds. Statements 1 and 2 fail on facts: the leave is 26 weeks with at most 8 before delivery, and créche visits are four a day. The Act applies to women in the organised sector, in establishments with 10 or more employees. Work from home may be allowed after the leave.
related: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 was amended in 2017 and the changes took effect on 1 April 2017.
Paid maternity leave is 26 weeks for the first two children; pre-delivery leave is at most 8 weeks.
For a third child, leave is 12 weeks (6 weeks before delivery).
Adopting a child under 3 months, or being a commissioning mother, gives 12 weeks of leave.
Créche is compulsory in establishments with 50 or more employees, with four visits a day.
Article 42 of the Constitution directs the State to provide maternity relief.
Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana gives ₹5,000 for the first living child.
ILO Maternity Protection Convention, 2000 (No. 183) sets a minimum of 14 weeks of leave.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The entitlement is 26 weeks in total, with at most 8 weeks before delivery, not 3 months before and 3 months after. The 1961 Act originally gave 12 weeks, with up to 6 weeks before delivery. The 2017 amendment raised this to 26 weeks for the first two children. India thereby became one of the more generous countries on paid maternity leave, ahead of many developed economies. The benefit applies to establishments with 10 or more employees: factories, mines, plantations, shops and others. The wage paid is the average daily wage over the preceding three months. A woman must have worked at least 80 days in the 12 months before the expected delivery to qualify. The Act also prohibits dismissing a woman during maternity leave.

2 — Incorrect: The Act allows four créche visits a day, not six. The créche is mandatory for establishments with 50 or more employees. The four visits include the woman's normal rest interval. Earlier, the 1961 Act required only a créche facility for establishments with 50 or more employees, without a visit limit. The 2017 amendment made it a statutory right and allowed the woman to visit the créche four times a day. Employers must also tell women about this facility at the time of appointment. This provision is an important part of the amendment because it supports childcare near the workplace. The créche may be within the establishment or shared in the vicinity.

3 — Correct: A woman who already has two or more surviving children gets only 12 weeks of paid leave, of which no more than 6 weeks can be before the expected delivery date. The 26-week entitlement applies only to the first two children. This differential treatment is a notable feature of the amendment, and critics have raised it as a concern. A woman adopting a child below three months old, or a commissioning mother, gets 12 weeks from the date the child is handed over. The Act also lets an employer permit work from home after the leave ends, by mutual agreement, where the nature of the work allows. Medical bonus of ₹3,500 applies if the employer provides no pre-natal or post-natal care.
summary: The official answer is (c) 3 only. Only statement 3 is correct: under the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017, a woman with two or more surviving children gets 12 weeks of paid leave, not the 26 weeks given for the first two children. Statement 1 is wrong on the leave split, and statement 2 is wrong on the number of créche visits.
topic_notes: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 regulates the employment of women in certain establishments for a fixed period before and after childbirth and provides maternity benefit. It covers factories, mines, plantations, shops and establishments employing 10 or more people. The Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017 was passed by Parliament in March 2017 and came into force on 1 April 2017. Key changes: (1) Paid leave raised from 12 to 26 weeks for the first two children, with at most 8 weeks before delivery. (2) For a woman with two or more surviving children, leave remains 12 weeks (6 before delivery). (3) Adopting mothers (child under 3 months) and commissioning mothers get 12 weeks. (4) Créche facility is mandatory in establishments with 50 or more employees, with four visits a day allowed. (5) Employers may permit work from home after the leave, if the nature of work allows. (6) Employers must inform women of benefits at the time of appointment, in writing and electronically. Eligibility needs at least 80 days of work in the 12 months before the expected delivery. Payment is at the average daily wage. A medical bonus of ₹3,500 is payable if the employer provides no pre-natal or post-natal care. Dismissal during maternity leave is prohibited. Related: the Code on Social Security, 2020 subsumes this Act. Under the Employees' State Insurance Act, 1948, maternity benefit is provided to insured women. The Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (2017) gives ₹5,000 in instalments for the first living child. The Janani Suraksha Yojana promotes institutional delivery. Constitutional links: Article 42 (just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief) is a Directive Principle. Possible future angles: the 2017 changes, the India vs ILO standard of 14 weeks, and the Code on Social Security.

question: Which one of the following is not a sub-index of the World Bank’s Ease of Doing Business Index’?
options: Dealing with construction permits India, ‘extended producer
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Doing Business report was published annually by the World Bank Group from 2003. It ranked 190 economies on how easy it was for a domestic small or medium-sized firm to operate under local regulation. The ranking was based on the average of 10 topic scores: Starting a Business, Dealing with Construction Permits, Getting Electricity, Registering Property, Getting Credit, Protecting Minority Investors, Paying Taxes, Trading across Borders, Enforcing Contracts and Resolving Insolvency. Each indicator measured the procedures, time, cost and, where relevant, quality of regulation, using standardised case studies in the largest business city (and in the second largest for economies with more than 100 million people, such as India with Delhi and Mumbai). Broad governance matters such as law and order, security, corruption levels, macroeconomic stability and the quality of infrastructure were explicitly outside its scope. Elimination logic: (b), (c) and (d) are literal indicator names, so by elimination (a) is the odd one out. India rose from 142nd in 2014 to 77th in 2018 and 63rd in 2019 (2020 report). In September 2021 the World Bank discontinued the series after data irregularities in the 2018 and 2020 editions involving China, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Azerbaijan.
explanations: Correct answer. Maintenance of law and order is not one of the 10 indicators in the EoDB index, so it is the option that is not a sub-index.
Wrong as an answer. Paying taxes is an official sub-index, measuring the number of tax payments, time and total tax and contribution rate for a firm.
Wrong as an answer. Registering property is an official sub-index, measuring the procedures, time and cost to transfer property, plus land administration quality.
Wrong as an answer. Dealing with construction permits is an official sub-index, covering the procedures, time and cost to build a warehouse, plus building quality control.
keyfact: Ease of Doing Business had 10 ranked indicators (starting a business to resolving insolvency); law and order was never one of them.
option_notes: Maintenance of law and order is a state function under the Seventh Schedule (Police and Public Order are State List subjects in India). It is a governance matter that the Doing Business report did not score. It is relevant to other measures such as the Global Peace Index, the Worldwide Governance Indicators (Political Stability and Absence of Violence, Rule of Law) and the Rule of Law Index of the World Justice Project.

Paying taxes measures the number of tax payments a year, the time to prepare, file and pay, the total tax and contribution rate as a share of profit, and post-filing processes. It is one of the 10 EoDB indicators. India's reforms here include GST, introduced on 1 July 2017, and online filing of returns.

Registering property measures the number of procedures, time and cost to transfer property between two local companies, and also the quality of land administration (reliability, transparency, coverage, dispute resolution). It is one of the 10 EoDB indicators. India's related efforts include digitisation of land records under DILRMP.

Dealing with construction permits records the procedures, time and cost to build a standard warehouse, including inspections and utility connections, plus a building quality control index. It is one of the 10 EoDB indicators. India improved sharply here in 2018 through online single-window systems in Delhi and Mumbai.
related: Doing Business report began in 2003 and was discontinued by the World Bank in September 2021.
India ranked 63rd of 190 economies in Doing Business 2020, up from 77th in 2019.
The ranking used 10 indicators, with Employing Workers and Contracting with the Government excluded from it.
For India, data were collected for two cities: Delhi and Mumbai.
The replacement for Doing Business is the B-READY (Business Ready) project.
DPIIT coordinates the Business Reform Action Plan (BRAP) for states.
The Logistics Performance Index is published by the World Bank, and the Global Competitiveness Index by the WEF.
Police and Public Order are State List subjects in the Seventh Schedule.
summary: The answer is (a) Maintenance of law and order. The World Bank's Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) index ranked economies on 10 specific regulatory indicators of a firm's life cycle, and 'law and order' was never one of them. Paying taxes, registering property and dealing with construction permits were all official sub-indices.
topic_notes: The World Bank's Doing Business report was launched in 2003 and ranked economies by the distance to frontier (DTF) score, from 0 to 100. The 10 indicators in the ranking were Starting a Business, Dealing with Construction Permits, Getting Electricity, Registering Property, Getting Credit, Protecting Minority Investors, Paying Taxes, Trading across Borders, Enforcing Contracts and Resolving Insolvency. Two further areas, Employing Workers and Contracting with the Government, were tracked but not included in the ranking. Data came from local experts such as lawyers, accountants and engineers, and covered the largest business city only (two cities for India: Delhi and Mumbai). The report did not capture security, corruption, labour skills, macroeconomic stability or the informal sector, which were frequent criticisms. India's rank was 142 (2014), 130 (2016), 100 (2018) and 77 (2019), then 63 (2020, out of 190). New Zealand and Singapore were typically at the top. In 2020 India was among the top 10 improvers for the third consecutive year. The DPIIT, under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, coordinated reforms, and the Business Reform Action Plan (BRAP) ranks states. The World Bank discontinued the report in September 2021 after data irregularities and announced a replacement, the Business Ready (B-READY) project, first report in 2024. Related indices UPSC may ask about: the Global Competitiveness Index (WEF), the Logistics Performance Index (World Bank), the Global Innovation Index (WIPO), the Human Capital Index (World Bank) and the Global Peace Index (IEP).

ocr: In responsibility’ was introduced as an important feature in which of the following? The Bio-medical Waste (a) (Management and Handling) Rules, 1998 The Recycled | Plastic (b) (Manufacturing and Usage) Rules, 1999 The e-Waste (Management and () Handling) Rules, 2011 The Food Safety. and Standard (a) Regulations, 2011
subject: Environment
detail: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) is a policy principle, part of the 'polluter pays' approach, under which a producer remains responsible for a product through its post-consumer stage, including take-back, recycling and safe disposal. In India it was first introduced in the E-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011, notified under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and in force from 1 May 2012. They applied to producers, consumers, collection centres, dismantlers and recyclers of electrical and electronic equipment. They were replaced by the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2016, which added targets, the Producer Responsibility Organisation (PRO) and Deposit Refund Scheme, and later by the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 with EPR certificates. EPR was then extended to plastics (Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016, amended 2022), batteries (Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022) and others. Elimination: the 1998 bio-medical rules focused on segregation, treatment and the 'duty of care' of the occupier. The 1999 recycled plastics rules regulated the thickness and colour of carry bags, and the FSS Regulations 2011 concern food standards and have nothing to do with producer take-back. So (c) is the only fit.
explanations: Incorrect: the 1998 Bio-medical Waste Rules placed responsibility on the occupier or operator of a facility and introduced segregation, colour coding and treatment, not producer take-back.

Incorrect: the 1999 Recycled Plastics Rules regulated manufacture and use of carry bags (minimum thickness, colour pigments for recycled plastic), and had no EPR clause. EPR came to plastics only in 2016.

Correct: the E-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011 first introduced EPR in India, making producers responsible for collecting and environmentally sound disposal of end-of-life electronic products.
Incorrect: the Food Safety and Standards Regulations, 2011 deal with licensing, hygiene and standards for food businesses under the FSS Act, 2006, not producer responsibility for waste.
keyfact: EPR in India began with the E-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011, effective 1 May 2012.
option_notes: The Bio-medical Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 1998 were notified under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and applied to those generating, collecting, treating or disposing of bio-medical waste. They introduced segregation, colour-coded containers, and treatment methods such as incineration, autoclaving and deep burial. They were replaced by the 2016 Rules, which extended coverage to vaccination camps and blood donation camps, and tightened the standards for incinerators.

The Recycled Plastics (Manufacture and Usage) Rules, 1999 were notified under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. They prescribed standards for carry bags and containers made from recycled plastic, including minimum thickness, colour pigments and a ban on recycled plastic for storing food items. They were amended in 2003 and superseded by the Plastic Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011 and later the 2016 Rules.

The E-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011 came into force on 1 May 2012 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. They covered IT and telecom equipment and consumer electronics, introduced EPR, and restricted hazardous substances such as lead, mercury, cadmium and hexavalent chromium under the RoHS approach. They were replaced by the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2016, and then the 2022 Rules.

The Food Safety and Standards Regulations, 2011 were framed by the FSSAI under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. They cover licensing and registration of food businesses, packaging and labelling, food additives, contaminants and laboratory sampling. FSSAI, headquartered in Delhi, is under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. These regulations have no link to EPR.
related: EPR in India first appeared in the E-Waste Rules, 2011, effective 1 May 2012.
E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2016 added PRO and the Deposit Refund Scheme.
E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 took effect 1 April 2023 and introduced EPR certificates.
Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016 extended EPR to plastic packaging; single-use plastic items were banned from 1 July 2022.
Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 apply EPR to all batteries.
Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 replaced the Municipal Solid Wastes Rules, 2000.
The Basel Convention regulates transboundary movement of hazardous wastes.
Waste rules are notified under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
summary: The answer is (c) The e-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011. These rules first brought Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) into Indian law for electronic waste, making producers responsible for collecting and channelling end-of-life products.
topic_notes: Extended Producer Responsibility is a policy approach, based on the 'polluter pays' principle, that makes manufacturers, importers and brand owners responsible for the whole life cycle of their products, especially take-back, recycling and final disposal. India's waste law is framed mainly under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. EPR first appeared in the E-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2011 (effective 1 May 2012). The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2016 set collection targets, brought in the Producer Responsibility Organisation (PRO), the Deposit Refund Scheme and Extended Producer Responsibility Authorisation, and covered compact fluorescent lamps and other mercury-containing lamps. The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 (effective 1 April 2023) introduced EPR certificates, a centralised online portal, a role for the CPCB, and covered 106 types of equipment. Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016 introduced EPR for producers, importers and brand owners; the 2022 amendment made EPR guidelines on plastic packaging mandatory, with categories 1 to 4 and a ban on identified single-use plastics from 1 July 2022. The Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 apply EPR to all types of batteries, including electric vehicle batteries. The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 replaced the Municipal Solid Wastes Rules, 2000, and require segregation at source and make waste generators pay user fees. The Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules, 2016 govern hazardous waste, and the Construction and Demolition Waste Rules, 2016 govern C&D waste. The Central Pollution Control Board monitors compliance, and the Basel Convention governs transboundary movement of hazardous wastes. Future questions may ask about the 3Rs, the polluter pays principle (recognised by the Supreme Court in Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India), the National Green Tribunal and the Swachh Bharat Mission.

ocr: The economic cost of food grains to the Food Corporation of India is Minimum Support Price and bonus {if any) paid to the farmers plus transportation cost only (a) interest cost only (b) procurement incidentals and (e) distribution cost procurement incidentals and (a) charges for godowns
subject: Economy
detail: The FCI was set up in 1965 under the Food Corporations Act, 1964. It procures foodgrains (mainly wheat and rice) at MSP, stores them, moves them across the country, and distributes them to State agencies for the Public Distribution System (PDS) and other welfare schemes. The economic cost has three layers. First is the acquisition cost: the MSP plus any state bonus paid to farmers. Second is procurement incidentals: mandi charges, labour, gunny bags, mandi taxes, commission to arhtiyas, and similar costs. Third is distribution cost: freight, handling, storage and godown charges, interest on working capital, transit losses, and administrative overheads. Economic cost = acquisition cost + procurement incidentals + distribution cost. The Central Issue Price (CIP) is what the Centre charges States for PDS grain under the National Food Security Act, 2013 (Rs 3/2/1 per kg for rice/wheat/coarse grains, later made free under PMGKAY). The gap between economic cost and CIP is the food subsidy. Elimination: (a) and (b) name only single components, so they are incomplete. (d) leaves out the whole distribution side, and godown charges are only one part of the cost. Only (c) captures both procurement incidentals and distribution cost, and is the official answer.
explanations: Wrong: transportation (freight) is only one part of distribution cost. The economic cost also includes procurement incidentals, storage, interest, and overheads, so 'only' makes this option incomplete.
Wrong: interest cost on working capital is one element of the carrying cost. Calling it the only addition ignores incidentals, freight, handling and storage.

Correct: economic cost = MSP + bonus + procurement incidentals (mandi fees, labour, bags, commission) + distribution cost (freight, handling, storage, interest, overheads). This matches the official answer.
Wrong: it includes procurement incidentals and godown charges but omits the distribution cost (transport, handling, interest, overheads). The inclusion of only godown charges makes it incomplete.
keyfact: Economic cost of grain to FCI = MSP + bonus + procurement incidentals + distribution cost.
option_notes: Transportation cost is the freight FCI pays to move grain by rail, road, and water from surplus States (Punjab, Haryana, MP, Chhattisgarh) to deficit regions (the South, the North-East, hill States). It is a major part of distribution cost. Rail movement is by 'rake' loads. It is one component, not the whole of the economic cost.

Interest cost is the financing cost of the money FCI borrows to hold grain stocks. Funding comes through cash credit limits from banks, and since 2020-21 largely through loans from the National Small Savings Fund (NSSF) to cut the interest burden. It is a component of carrying cost but not the only add-on.

Procurement incidentals are the expenses of purchasing grain: mandi fees, arhtiya commission, labour, packaging (jute bags), cess, and purchase tax charged by States such as Punjab and Haryana. Distribution cost covers freight, handling, storage, interest, shrinkage, and overheads up to the point of issue. Together with MSP and bonus, they make up the economic cost.

Godown charges are the cost of storing grain in FCI-owned, State-agency, or hired warehouses (Central Warehousing Corporation, State Warehousing Corporations, private guarantee schemes). Storage is part of distribution cost. Treating it alone, together with incidentals, leaves out freight, handling, and interest.
related: FCI was established in 1965 under the Food Corporations Act, 1964.
MSP is recommended by CACP and approved by the CCEA.
Economic cost = MSP + bonus + procurement incidentals + distribution cost.
Food subsidy = economic cost minus Central Issue Price recoveries.
NFSA 2013 covers up to 75% of rural and 50% of urban population.
AAY families get 35 kg of grain per month.
Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) recommended restructuring the FCI.
The Open Market Sale Scheme (OMSS) sells FCI surplus grain to stabilise prices.
summary: The correct answer is (c). The economic cost of foodgrains to the Food Corporation of India (FCI) is the Minimum Support Price (MSP) plus bonus (if any) paid to farmers, plus procurement incidentals and distribution cost. It is the full cost of acquiring, storing, and delivering grain, not just one component.
topic_notes: The Food Corporation of India was established on 14 January 1965 at Thanjavur under the Food Corporations Act, 1964, and is headquartered in New Delhi. Its main functions are procuring grain at MSP, maintaining buffer stocks for food security, distributing grain through the PDS, and stabilising market prices. MSP is recommended by the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP, set up in 1965) and approved by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA). MSP covers 22 mandated crops plus FRP for sugarcane. Effective procurement is concentrated in wheat and rice, mainly in Punjab, Haryana, and Madhya Pradesh, with growing procurement in Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Telangana, and Andhra Pradesh. Under decentralised procurement (DCP), States such as Chhattisgarh, MP, and Odisha procure and distribute themselves, and the Centre reimburses economic cost. Key terms: Central Issue Price (CIP) is the subsidised price for PDS under the NFSA, 2013, which covers up to 75% of rural and 50% of urban population (about 81 crore people) at 5 kg per person per month. Priority households pay Rs 3, 2, and 1 per kg for rice, wheat, and coarse grains, and AAY households receive 35 kg per family per month. Since January 2023, PMGKAY provides free grain. Food subsidy equals economic cost minus CIP-based recoveries. Buffer norms are laid down quarterly for 1 April, 1 July, 1 October, and 1 January. The Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) recommended restructuring FCI, reducing coverage to 40% of the population, and shifting to cash transfers. Open Market Sale Scheme (OMSS) offloads surplus grain to curb prices. Other angles include the Open-ended procurement policy, the CAP (Cover and Plinth) storage problem, the Silo programme, and the Essential Commodities Act.

question: In the context of any country, which one of the following would be considered as part of its social capital? The proportion of literates in the
options: population The stock of its buildings, other
infrastructure and machines : The size of population in the
working age group The level of mutual trust ‘and
subject: Economy
detail: Social capital is the set of networks, shared norms, values and mutual trust that allow people to cooperate for common goals. The idea is associated with Pierre Bourdieu, James Coleman and especially Robert Putnam (Bowling Alone; Making Democracy Work), and it is used by the World Bank and OECD. It is distinct from other forms of capital. Physical capital means buildings, machines and infrastructure. Human capital means the skills, knowledge, health and literacy embodied in people (Schultz, Becker). Demographic features, such as the size of the working-age population, relate to the demographic dividend, not social capital. Natural capital means resources such as land, forests and minerals. Social capital is intangible and relational. It lowers transaction costs, supports institutions and collective action, and helps governance and development, as seen in self-help groups and cooperatives. Elimination: (a) literacy is human capital; (b) buildings and machines are physical capital; (c) working-age population is a demographic factor and part of the labour force; (d) trust and harmony are the core of social capital. So (d) is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: the proportion of literates is a measure of human capital (education), not social capital.
Incorrect: buildings, other infrastructure and machines are physical or produced capital.
Incorrect: the size of the working-age population is a demographic variable that feeds the demographic dividend, not a social relationship.
Correct: mutual trust and harmony in society are the essence of social capital, as they enable cooperation, networks and collective action.
keyfact: Social capital = trust, norms and networks (mutual trust and harmony); literacy is human capital, and buildings and machines are physical capital.
option_notes: Literacy proportion: the literacy rate is the share of the population able to read and write with understanding. India's Census 2011 figure was 74.04%, and NSO surveys have since put it higher. It is an indicator of human capital and appears in the Human Development Index's education component, along with mean and expected years of schooling.

Stock of buildings, infrastructure and machines: this is physical (man-made) capital, the produced assets used in production. It is measured through gross fixed capital formation. Roads, ports, power plants and factory machinery all count. Physical capital is a classical factor of production, along with land, labour and entrepreneurship.

Size of the working-age population: the working-age group is generally 15-64 years. A large share of it relative to dependents gives the demographic dividend. India's working-age share is rising, and the dividend window is expected to last until roughly the 2040s. It is a demographic, not social, asset.

Mutual trust and harmony: this is the core of social capital, meaning networks, norms and trust enabling cooperation. Putnam linked it to civic engagement and good governance. The World Bank treats it as a form of capital alongside natural, physical and human capital. High-trust societies show lower transaction costs and stronger institutions.
related: Human capital means education, skills and health embodied in people.
Robert Putnam wrote Bowling Alone and popularised social capital.
Bonding, bridging and linking are the three types of social capital.
Working-age population is 15-64 years, and a high share of it yields the demographic dividend.
The HDI is published by UNDP and covers health, education and income.
Physical capital is measured via gross fixed capital formation.
The World Bank launched the Human Capital Project in 2018.
Self-help groups are an Indian example of social capital.
summary: The answer is (d): the level of mutual trust and harmony in society. Social capital refers to networks, shared norms, trust and cooperation that enable collective action, rather than physical assets, education levels or demographic size.
topic_notes: Types of capital: natural capital (land, water, forests, minerals), physical capital (machines, buildings, infrastructure), human capital (education, skills, health) and social capital (trust, norms, networks). Financial capital is money and financial assets. Intellectual capital covers knowledge and patents. Social capital thinkers: Pierre Bourdieu (social networks and resources), James Coleman (social structure facilitating action), Robert Putnam (civic associations, trust, reciprocity). Putnam distinguishes bonding capital (within homogeneous groups), bridging capital (across diverse groups) and linking capital (across power hierarchies). Examples in India: self-help groups, cooperatives such as Amul, village panchayats, community forest management and caste or community networks. Benefits: lower transaction costs, better public service delivery, easier credit access, resilience in disasters and stronger democracy. Downsides: exclusion, nepotism and cartel-like closed networks. Related concepts: Human Development Index (UNDP: health, education, income), Human Capital Index (World Bank), the Human Capital Project (2018), the demographic dividend and the Economic Survey's emphasis on human capital. Theodore Schultz and Gary Becker developed human capital theory. The World Bank's 'Where is the Wealth of Nations' framework counts produced, natural and human or institutional capital. UPSC often tests such definitions through classification: decide whether an item is physical, human, natural, social or financial capital.

ocr: With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements : 1. No High Court shall have the jurisdiction to declare any central law to be constitutionally invalid. 2. An amendment to the Constitution of India cannot be called into question by the Supreme Court of India. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? fa) 1 only (b) 2 only (c} Both 1 and 2 (a) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Polity
detail: Judicial review is the power of courts to test the validity of legislative and executive action against the Constitution, and it is itself part of the Basic Structure. Both the Supreme Court (Articles 32 and 131-136) and the High Courts (Article 226) exercise it. A High Court can strike down a central or state law as unconstitutional, although its ruling binds only courts within its territorial jurisdiction, and the Supreme Court is the final arbiter on appeal. Article 226 is wider than Article 32 because it can be used for any other purpose besides enforcing fundamental rights. The 42nd Amendment (1976) tried to curb High Court review by inserting Article 226A and Article 228A, but the 43rd Amendment (1977) repealed them. Constitutional amendments under Article 368 are also reviewable. Golaknath (1967) held that Parliament could not amend fundamental rights. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that Parliament can amend any provision but cannot alter the Basic Structure. Minerva Mills (1980) struck down the clauses of Article 368 that barred judicial review. Elimination logic: Statement 1 is false because High Courts do review central laws. Statement 2 is false because amendments are subject to Basic Structure review. So only (d) fits.
explanations: Wrong: (a) accepts Statement 1, but High Courts can strike down central laws under Article 226.
Wrong: (b) accepts Statement 2, but amendments can be challenged under the Basic Structure doctrine.
Wrong: (c) would require both statements to be true, but both are false.
Correct: (d) is right because High Courts have review powers over central laws and the Supreme Court can review constitutional amendments for Basic Structure violations.
keyfact: High Courts (Art. 226) can strike down central laws, and the Supreme Court can strike down constitutional amendments that violate the Basic Structure, so both statements are wrong.
option_notes: Option (a) 'Statement 1 only' would mean that High Courts cannot invalidate central laws. That was the intent of Article 226A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) during the Emergency, which would have reserved the power to the Supreme Court. It was repealed by the 43rd Amendment (1977) under the Janata government. High Courts therefore retain full judicial review, and the power is a Basic Structure feature (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997).

Option (b) 'Statement 2 only' would mean amendments are immune from Supreme Court review. This was the aim of Article 368(4) and (5), added by the 42nd Amendment, which declared that amendments could not be questioned in any court. Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) struck these clauses down. Parliament's amending power is limited, and the Supreme Court can strike down amendments that violate the Basic Structure.

Option (c) 'Both 1 and 2' would mean both High Courts and the Supreme Court are barred from reviewing, respectively, central laws and constitutional amendments. This describes a regime of parliamentary supremacy, as in the UK. India instead has a written Constitution with constitutional supremacy, where judicial review is a Basic Structure feature (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973; Minerva Mills, 1980). Neither claim holds.

Option (d) 'Neither 1 nor 2' is the correct answer. India follows constitutional supremacy with an independent judiciary that can review ordinary laws and constitutional amendments. High Courts act under Articles 226 and 227, and the Supreme Court under Articles 32 and 136. Judicial review itself is part of the Basic Structure, so it cannot be removed even by a constitutional amendment.
related: Basic Structure doctrine was established in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973).
Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for enforcing fundamental rights and for any other purpose.
Article 32 is itself a fundamental right, called by Ambedkar the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.
Article 226A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and repealed by the 43rd Amendment (1977).
Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Article 368(4) and (5) and held that limited amending power is itself a Basic Structure feature.
L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that High Court and Supreme Court judicial review is part of the Basic Structure.
I.R. Coelho (2007) held that Ninth Schedule laws are open to Basic Structure review.
Judicial review of laws originates from Marbury v. Madison (1803) in the USA, though Indian law is based on Article 13.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: High Courts can declare central laws unconstitutional under Article 226 (and review under 227). Their power of judicial review is part of the Basic Structure, as held in L. Chandra Kumar (1997). The 42nd Amendment inserted Article 226A, which barred High Courts from deciding the validity of central laws, but the 43rd Amendment (1977) removed it. A High Court's declaration has effect within its territory, though in practice the law is treated as invalid unless the Supreme Court or another High Court disagrees. The Supreme Court has the final say on appeal under Articles 132-136. The Supreme Court in L. Chandra Kumar also held that the tribunals' jurisdiction cannot exclude High Court review under Articles 226/227.

2 — Incorrect: Constitutional amendments can be reviewed by the Supreme Court. Article 368(4) and (5), inserted by the 42nd Amendment, declared amendments immune from judicial challenge, but Minerva Mills (1980) struck them down as violating the Basic Structure. Earlier, Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) held that Article 13 did not cover amendments, but Golaknath (1967) reversed this. Kesavananda Bharati (1973, 7:6 majority, 13-judge bench) established the Basic Structure doctrine. Waman Rao (1981) fixed 24 April 1973 as the cut-off date for the doctrine's application to the Ninth Schedule. I.R. Coelho (2007) held that Ninth Schedule laws enacted after 24 April 1973 can be challenged for Basic Structure violations. The 99th Amendment (NJAC) was struck down in 2015.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. High Courts have the power of judicial review under Articles 226 and 227 and can declare central laws unconstitutional, and constitutional amendments can be reviewed by the Supreme Court under the Basic Structure doctrine.
topic_notes: Judicial review in India is based on Articles 13, 32, 131-136, 143, 226, 227 and 246. Article 13 declares that laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are void, and Article 13(2) bars the State from making such laws. India follows a hybrid model that mixes parliamentary sovereignty and judicial supremacy, but ultimately constitutional supremacy. Key amendment cases: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) held that Parliament could amend fundamental rights. Golaknath (1967) reversed this (11 judges) and applied the doctrine of prospective overruling. Parliament responded with the 24th Amendment (1971), which stated that Article 13 does not apply to Article 368 amendments. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) upheld the 24th Amendment but limited Parliament's power through the Basic Structure doctrine. The 42nd Amendment (1976) tried to reverse it by giving Parliament unlimited amending power and curbing High Court jurisdiction. The Supreme Court struck down parts of it in Minerva Mills (1980). Other Basic Structure cases: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), S.R. Bommai (1994, federalism and secularism), and L. Chandra Kumar (1997, High Court review under Articles 226/227 and Supreme Court review under 32 are Basic Structure). The Ninth Schedule was added by the 1st Amendment (1951) to protect land reform laws, and I.R. Coelho (2007) made it open to review. Elements of the Basic Structure recognised by courts include the supremacy of the Constitution, the rule of law, separation of powers, federalism, secularism, free and fair elections, judicial independence, and judicial review. Article 226 is broader than Article 32 because High Courts can issue writs for other purposes as well. Article 32 is itself a fundamental right, while Article 226 is not. The Supreme Court's advisory jurisdiction is under Article 143. The NJAC (99th Amendment) was struck down in the Fourth Judges case (2015).

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) exchange rates are calculated by comparing the prices of the same basket of goods and services in different countries.
2. In terms of PPP dollars, India is the sixth largest economy in the world. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: Purchasing Power Parity rests on the 'law of one price': an identical basket of goods and services should cost the same in different countries once converted at the right exchange rate. The PPP conversion factor is therefore the number of local currency units needed to buy what one US dollar buys in the US. The World Bank's International Comparison Program (ICP) collects the price data, and the IMF and World Bank publish PPP-adjusted GDP. PPP corrects for differences in price levels, so it gives a better comparison of living standards and real output than market (nominal) exchange rates. Statement 1 is therefore correct. Statement 2 is wrong on rank. In nominal GDP, India was about 5th-7th in 2018-19, which is the likely source of the 'sixth' trap. In PPP terms India has been third since about 2011 (World Bank ICP 2011 and 2017 rounds, IMF WEO), behind China and the USA. Elimination: once statement 1 is known to be correct, options (b) and (d) go out. Knowing India is third in PPP rules out (c), leaving (a).
explanations: Correct: statement 1 correctly describes PPP, and statement 2 is false because India is third largest in PPP terms, not sixth.
Wrong: statement 2 cannot be correct, since India ranks third in PPP-adjusted GDP, not sixth.
Wrong: statement 1 is correct, but statement 2 is not, so 'both' fails.
Wrong: statement 1 is a standard, correct description of PPP, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: PPP compares prices of the same basket across countries; India is the world's 3rd largest economy in PPP terms (after China and the USA).
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: this reflects the true position. PPP exchange rates come from comparing the price of the same basket across countries. The basket idea underlies the World Bank's ICP, and PPP is used for real income comparisons. The option is correct here because the statement on India's rank is false.

Option (b), 2 only: this would mean India is sixth in PPP terms and PPP is not based on a common basket. Both claims are false. India is third in PPP (after China and the USA). Sixth-ish ranks are closer to India's nominal GDP position around 2018-19, which makes this a typical trap option.

Option (c), both 1 and 2: this would need India to be sixth in PPP. India is third in PPP-adjusted GDP according to the IMF and World Bank. In nominal GDP it was close to fifth to seventh around 2018-19, and it reached fifth in 2022. So the option fails on statement 2.

Option (d), neither: this would deny the basic definition of PPP. PPP is a comparison of the cost of an identical basket of goods and services across countries. It is the theoretical exchange rate that equalises purchasing power. The definition is standard in economics textbooks and in World Bank ICP methodology.
related: India is the third largest economy in PPP terms, after China and the USA.
The World Bank's International Comparison Program (ICP) produces PPP estimates.
The Big Mac Index was created by The Economist in 1986 as an informal PPP guide.
The HDI uses GNI per capita in PPP dollars.
The World Bank international poverty line was $1.90 (2011 PPP), then $2.15 (2017 PPP), then $3.00 (2021 PPP).
India became the fifth largest economy in nominal GDP in 2022, overtaking the UK.
REER is the weighted average of a currency against a basket of currencies, adjusted for inflation differences.
statements: 1 — Correct: PPP rates are computed by comparing prices of the same basket of goods and services across countries. PPP is based on the law of one price (Gustav Cassel popularised the term in the 1910s-20s). The World Bank-led International Comparison Program (started 1968, with rounds in 2005, 2011, 2017 and 2021) collects the price data. The PPP conversion factor is the local currency units per international dollar. The Big Mac Index from The Economist is an informal, light-hearted PPP measure. PPP is used to compare real output and living standards, and the IMF uses it to compute country weights in global growth estimates.

2 — Incorrect: India is the third largest economy in PPP terms, not sixth. China is first (since about 2014 on IMF data), the USA is second, and India is third, ahead of Japan and Germany. India overtook Japan around 2011 on PPP. In nominal GDP, India was roughly 5th-7th around 2018-19 (it overtook the UK and France at different points) and became 5th in 2022, then moved towards 4th. So 'sixth' mixes up rank in nominal terms with rank in PPP terms. Per-capita PPP income is still low, and India ranks well below 100th in nominal GDP per capita.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 1 is correct. PPP exchange rates are derived by comparing the prices of an identical basket of goods and services across countries, but in PPP terms India ranked third largest (after China and the USA) around 2019, not sixth.
topic_notes: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) is a theory and measure for comparing currencies and economies by the purchasing power of money rather than market exchange rates. Absolute PPP says the exchange rate equals the ratio of price levels of the same basket in two countries. Relative PPP links changes in the exchange rate to differences in inflation. The World Bank's International Comparison Program (ICP), run with national statistical offices, the OECD and Eurostat, publishes PPPs; major rounds were in 2005, 2011, 2017 and 2021. The 'international dollar' is a hypothetical currency with the same purchasing power as the US dollar in the US. PPP-adjusted GDP is larger than nominal GDP for lower-price economies such as India and China, because non-traded services are cheaper there. India's PPP rank: third, after China and the USA, with Japan, Germany and Russia next. In nominal GDP India moved from sixth (2018, behind the USA, China, Japan, Germany, UK/France) to fifth in 2022 after overtaking the UK, and is projected to move up further. Uses of PPP: comparing living standards, setting international poverty lines (the World Bank's $1.90 a day was based on 2011 PPP, raised to $2.15 on 2017 PPP and $3.00 on 2021 PPP), the Human Development Index (GNI per capita in PPP), IMF quota and weight calculations, and cross-country productivity studies. Limitations: baskets differ across countries, non-tradable goods, quality differences, and data collection gaps. Related ideas: Big Mac Index, Balassa-Samuelson effect, real effective exchange rate (REER) and nominal effective exchange rate (NEER). The Reserve Bank of India publishes REER and NEER indices (36-currency and 6-currency baskets).

ocr: With reference to the cultivation of Kharif crops in India in the last five years, consider the following statements : 1. Area under rice cultivation is the highest. , 2. Area under the cultivation of jowar is more than that of oilseeds. 3. Area of cotton cultivgtion is more than that of sugarcane. ~ 4. Area under sugarcane cultivation has steadily decreased. Which of the statements given above are correct? fa) 1 and 3 only (b) 2, 3 and 4 only vs (c) 2 and 4 only (d) 1,2, 3 and 4
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Kharif crops are sown with the onset of the south-west monsoon (June-July) and harvested in September-October. Major Kharif crops are rice, jowar, bajra, maize, ragi, cotton, jute, sugarcane, groundnut, soybean, tur (arhar), moong and urad. Rice is the single largest Kharif crop, at roughly 43-44 million ha, so statement 1 is correct. Cotton occupies roughly 12-13 million ha, while sugarcane occupies about 4.5-5.5 million ha, so statement 3 is correct. Kharif oilseeds (soybean, groundnut, sunflower, sesamum, castor, niger) together cover roughly 17-19 million ha, with soybean alone at about 11-12 million ha. Jowar (Kharif) covers only about 2-3 million ha, so statement 2 is incorrect. Sugarcane area has moved between roughly 4.4 and 5.7 million ha, rising in recent years, so 'steadily decreased' in statement 4 is incorrect. Elimination: spotting that statement 2 or 4 is false removes (b), (c) and (d), leaving (a). Knowing that rice is highest and cotton is larger than sugarcane is enough to answer the question.
explanations: Correct: statements 1 and 3 are true, and statements 2 and 4 are false.
Wrong: it includes statement 2 and statement 4. Jowar area is smaller than oilseeds, and sugarcane area has not steadily decreased.
Wrong: it leaves out the true statements 1 and 3 and consists entirely of false statements.
Wrong: it includes the false statements 2 and 4, even though 1 and 3 are true.
keyfact: Among Kharif crops, rice has the largest area, cotton area is more than twice that of sugarcane, and jowar area is far below that of oilseeds.
related: Kharif season runs roughly June to October and depends on the south-west monsoon.
Rice is the largest Kharif crop and wheat is the largest Rabi crop by area.
Soybean is India's largest oilseed crop by area, with Madhya Pradesh as the leading state.
Bt cotton is the only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation in India.
PMFBY premium for Kharif food crops and oilseeds is 2 percent of the sum insured.
Sugarcane price is set as FRP and the sugar season runs October-September.
Jowar, bajra and ragi are classified as nutri-cereals or millets (Shree Anna).
Jute is a Kharif fibre crop mainly grown in West Bengal.
statements: 1 — Correct: Rice is the largest Kharif crop by area. Rice is the staple cereal of India, grown mainly in West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Odisha, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh and Assam. India is the second-largest producer after China and the largest exporter. It needs high temperature (above 25 C), high humidity and rainfall above 100 cm. The main varieties are Aus, Aman and Boro. The MSP is announced by the CCEA on CACP recommendation. The IRRI is in the Philippines, and the Indian rice research institute (NRRI) is at Cuttack.

2 — Incorrect: Jowar (sorghum) is a coarse cereal or nutri-cereal with a small Kharif area, around 2-3 million ha, which is far below the combined area of oilseeds such as soybean and groundnut. Jowar is grown mainly in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. It is a rain-fed crop that tolerates drought and is used for food and fodder. Millets were promoted during the International Year of Millets 2023, and jowar has a Geographical Indication-related focus in Maharashtra (Maldandi). Its area has been declining for decades.

3 — Correct: Cotton, a Kharif fibre crop, has an area of about 12-13 million ha, which is more than twice that of sugarcane. India has the largest cotton area in the world, and is among the top producers with China. It grows on black (regur) soil in the Deccan, with major states being Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana, Karnataka and Rajasthan. It needs 21-30 C temperature, at least 210 frost-free days and 50-100 cm rainfall. Bt cotton is the only GM crop permitted in India (since 2002). The Cotton Corporation of India handles MSP operations.

4 — Incorrect: Sugarcane area has not fallen steadily, as it has risen and fallen from year to year, for example about 4.4 million ha in 2014-15 and about 5.5 million ha in recent years. India is the second-largest sugarcane producer after Brazil, with Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka leading. The crop is a 10-18 month crop and is priced by the Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) under the Sugarcane (Control) Order 1966. Ethanol blending has supported demand. The Sugarcane Breeding Institute is at Coimbatore.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 and 3 only. Rice has the largest area among Kharif crops in India, and cotton area (about 12-13 million ha) exceeds sugarcane (about 5 million ha). Jowar covers less area than oilseeds, and sugarcane area has fluctuated rather than steadily fallen.
topic_notes: Cropping seasons: Kharif (June-October, monsoon-sown), Rabi (October-March, winter-sown, harvested April-June, e.g. wheat, barley, gram, mustard, peas) and Zaid (March-June, between Rabi and Kharif, e.g. watermelon, cucumber, fodder, moong). Kharif crop area is roughly 100-110 million ha in total. Rice leads at about 40-44 million ha, followed by oilseeds (soybean, groundnut), pulses (tur, moong, urad), coarse cereals (maize, bajra, jowar, ragi), cotton and sugarcane. Maize, bajra and jowar are the main Kharif coarse cereals. Cotton is the main fibre crop and jute is a second one grown in West Bengal, Bihar and Assam. Minimum Support Prices are announced for 22 mandated crops (plus FRP for sugarcane) by the CCEA based on CACP recommendations, and MSP for Kharif crops is usually announced around May-June. Related schemes include PM-KISAN, PMFBY (crop insurance, with a premium of 2 percent for Kharif crops, 1.5 percent for Rabi and 5 percent for commercial and horticultural crops), the National Food Security Mission, and Soil Health Card. Rice leading area, wheat leading Rabi, and cotton and sugarcane as cash crops are repeatedly tested. UPSC often asks about crop-state pairings, climatic requirements, soil types and Bt cotton. Land use data comes from the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, with advance estimates released each season.

question: Among the agricultural commodities imported by India, which one of the following accounts for the highest imports in terms of value in the last five years?
subject: Economy
detail: India's domestic oilseed output (groundnut, mustard, soybean, sunflower, sesame etc.) falls well short of demand driven by rising population, incomes and per capita consumption. As a result India imports about 14-16 million tonnes of edible oils a year, costing roughly US$10-19 billion depending on prices (2021-22 was a record at around US$19 billion). Palm oil comes mainly from Indonesia and Malaysia, soybean oil from Argentina and Brazil, and sunflower oil from Ukraine and Russia. Vegetable oils usually account for over half or more of India's agricultural import bill. Other major agricultural imports are pulses (tur, urad from Myanmar, Africa; lentils from Canada and Australia; yellow peas), fresh fruits (apples, dates, almonds and other nuts, mainly dry fruits) and cashew (raw). Spices are net exports; India is the largest producer, consumer and exporter of spices. Elimination logic: spices are mostly exported, so (a) fails; fresh fruits imports are modest in value; pulses, though large in volume in some years (about US$2-4 billion), are still far below oils. Hence (d). Policy responses include the National Mission on Edible Oils - Oil Palm (NMEO-OP, 2021) and import duty adjustments.
explanations: Incorrect: Spices are a net export category. India is the world's largest producer, consumer and exporter, and its spice imports (pepper, cinnamon, etc.) are small in value.
Incorrect: Fresh fruit imports (apples, kiwi, citrus, dates, etc.) are a modest share of agri-imports, far below edible oils in value.
Incorrect: Pulses are an important import, with a few billion US dollars in some years, but they remain well below vegetable oils in value.
Correct: Vegetable oils (palm, soybean, sunflower) top India's agricultural import bill, often over half of it, because of the large gap between demand and domestic supply.
keyfact: Vegetable (edible) oils are India's biggest agricultural import by value, with about 55-60% of demand met by imports, mainly palm, soybean and sunflower oil.
option_notes: Spices: India is the 'Land of Spices'. It produces about 75 of the 109 spices listed by ISO. Main exports are chilli, cumin, turmeric, pepper and cardamom. The Spices Board (Kochi, under the Ministry of Commerce) regulates and promotes spice exports. Kerala, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh are key producers. Imports are limited to items like pepper, cinnamon and nutmeg.

Fresh fruits: India is the second-largest fruit producer, after China, and a leading producer of mango, banana and papaya. Imports include apples (Washington, New Zealand, Turkey, Iran), kiwi, pears, citrus and dates, plus dry fruits like almonds from the USA. Value is modest relative to oils. Import duties on apples (50%) and minimum import price rules have been used to protect Himachal and J&K growers.

Pulses: India is the world's largest producer and consumer of pulses (about 25% of global output). Imports include tur from Mozambique, Tanzania and Myanmar, urad from Myanmar, lentils from Canada and Australia, and chickpea and yellow peas from Russia and Canada. Pulse prices are managed through MSP, buffer stocks, import quotas and the National Food Security Mission - Pulses. The 2016 International Year of Pulses was declared by the UN.

Vegetable oils: India imports about 55-60% of its edible oil needs. Palm oil (Indonesia, Malaysia), soybean oil (Argentina, Brazil) and sunflower oil (Ukraine, Russia) dominate. Import duties are changed often to balance farmer and consumer interests. The National Mission on Edible Oils - Oil Palm (NMEO-OP), launched in 2021 with an outlay of about Rs 11,040 crore, targets domestic palm cultivation, especially in the Northeast and Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
related: The Yellow Revolution refers to the increase in oilseed production, especially mustard.
NMEO-Oil Palm was launched in 2021 with an outlay of about Rs 11,040 crore.
India is the world's largest importer of vegetable oils and the largest producer and consumer of pulses.
Palm oil mainly comes from Indonesia and Malaysia; sunflower oil from Ukraine and Russia.
The Spices Board of India is headquartered in Kochi.
The Technology Mission on Oilseeds was launched in 1986.
APEDA was established in 1985 under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
PM-AASHA (2018) covers price support and procurement for pulses, oilseeds and copra.
summary: The answer is (d) Vegetable oils. India is the world's largest importer of edible oils, bringing in roughly 55-60% of its requirement (palm, soybean and sunflower oil), so by value vegetable oils far exceed any other agricultural import.
topic_notes: India's agricultural trade is generally in surplus, with exports such as rice (including basmati), marine products, sugar, spices, buffalo meat, cotton and coffee outweighing imports. Key export markets are the USA, UAE, Bangladesh, China and Vietnam. APEDA (Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority, 1985) promotes exports of fruits, vegetables and rice; MPEDA handles marine products, the Spices Board covers spices, and the Tea, Coffee and Rubber Boards cover their commodities. Major agricultural imports by value are vegetable oils first, then pulses, fresh and dry fruits (including nuts), cashew, sugar in some years, cotton in some years, and spices in small amounts. India has long been the biggest edible oil importer worldwide, followed by China and the EU. Reasons for dependence: low oilseed yields, rainfed cultivation, price volatility, low productivity compared with palm. Government interventions: the Technology Mission on Oilseeds (1986), the National Mission on Oilseeds and Oil Palm (NMOOP), NMEO-Oilseeds (2024-25 to 2030-31), MSP for oilseeds, and variable import tariffs. Pulses: National Food Security Mission, buffer stock of 3 million tonnes, and Pradhan Mantri Annadata Aay SanraksHan Abhiyan (PM-AASHA, 2018) for procurement. The Yellow Revolution relates to oilseeds, especially mustard. Palm oil import sources shift with Indonesian export bans (such as April 2022). Trade is governed by the DGFT under the Foreign Trade Policy, and the WTO Agreement on Agriculture limits subsidies.

question: In the context of polity, which one of the following would you accept as the most appropriate definition of liberty?
options: Protection against the tyranny of political rulers
Opportunity to do whatever one likes
Opportunity to develop oneself fully [ P.T.O
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Political theory distinguishes negative liberty (absence of external restraint, associated with Hobbes, Bentham, J.S. Mill and Isaiah Berlin's 'Two Concepts of Liberty', 1958) from positive liberty (the capacity for self-realisation, associated with T.H. Green, Rousseau and Harold Laski). The question asks for the most appropriate and complete definition, which is the positive, developmental one: liberty is the opportunity to develop one's personality and capacities to the fullest. Laski described liberty as the eager maintenance of that atmosphere in which men have the opportunity to be their best selves. Liberty is never absolute; it coexists with reasonable restrictions so that one person's freedom does not destroy another's. The Indian Constitution reflects this: the Preamble secures 'Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship' to all citizens, and Article 19 (freedoms) is subject to reasonable restrictions, while Article 21 protects life and personal liberty. Elimination: (a) is only one safeguard and is too narrow; (b) is only the negative conception and would permit anarchy; (c) is licence, not liberty, as it ignores others' rights. Only (d) captures the complete, positive meaning.
explanations: Wrong: protection against tyranny of rulers is one aspect of political liberty (civil liberties against the state), but it is too narrow and does not define liberty as a whole.
Wrong: absence of restraint is the negative conception only; in society some restraints are needed, and the definition ignores the enabling conditions for growth.
Wrong: doing whatever one likes is licence, which would violate others' liberty and lead to anarchy; liberty is always subject to reasonable limits.
Correct: the opportunity to develop oneself fully is the positive, comprehensive definition of liberty accepted in political theory (Laski, T.H. Green) and consistent with the Constitution's aims.
keyfact: Liberty in political theory = opportunity for full self-development (positive liberty), not mere absence of restraint or licence.
option_notes: Protection against tyranny of rulers: this reflects the liberal tradition of limiting state power through rights, constitutionalism, separation of powers and judicial review. Fundamental Rights (Part III) in India act as limits on the State under Article 12. It is a means of securing liberty, not a full definition of it.

Absence of restraint: the 'negative liberty' of Hobbes, Bentham and Isaiah Berlin, meaning freedom from interference by others or the State. It is a classical laissez-faire notion. Its limitation is that it ignores social and economic conditions that enable people to use freedom meaningfully.

Opportunity to do whatever one likes: this is licence, not liberty. J.S. Mill's harm principle (On Liberty, 1859) holds that individual freedom can be limited only to prevent harm to others. Unrestrained freedom for all would produce conflict, so liberty needs rules and equal rights.

Opportunity to develop oneself fully: the positive concept of liberty, linked to T.H. Green, Rousseau's self-mastery and Harold Laski. It requires rights, education, economic security and democratic participation. It underlies the Preamble's liberty and the Directive Principles seeking conditions for all-round development.
related: Preamble words: Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.
Preamble's ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity were inspired by the French Revolution.
Isaiah Berlin wrote 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958), distinguishing negative and positive liberty.
J.S. Mill's 'On Liberty' (1859) propounded the harm principle.
Article 19 freedoms are subject to reasonable restrictions; Article 19(1)(f) property was dropped by the 44th Amendment (1978).
Maneka Gandhi case (1978) broadened Article 21 to require a just, fair and reasonable procedure.
K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) declared the right to privacy a fundamental right under Article 21.
Harold Laski defined liberty as the absence of restraint on the existence of social conditions necessary for development of personality.
summary: The answer is (d) Opportunity to develop oneself fully. In political theory, liberty is not mere freedom from restraint but the creation of social conditions in which individuals can develop their personality and potential, subject to reasonable restrictions that protect others' equal liberty.
topic_notes: Liberty is a core concept in political theory, alongside equality, justice and rights. Two main conceptions: negative liberty (freedom from interference; Hobbes, Locke, Bentham, Mill, Berlin) and positive liberty (freedom to realise one's potential; Rousseau, Hegel, Green, Laski). Berlin's 1958 lecture 'Two Concepts of Liberty' made this distinction famous. Mill's On Liberty (1859) set out the harm principle and defended freedom of thought and expression. Liberty and equality are seen as complementary: Lord Acton and de Tocqueville worried about conflicts, while Rousseau and Tawney stressed that without equality liberty is hollow. In India, the Preamble secures liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; the idea was drawn from the French Revolution's triad (liberty, equality, fraternity), with the Russian Revolution's influence on justice. Fundamental Rights: Articles 19-22 (Right to Freedom), Article 19(1)(a)-(g) six freedoms (property was removed by the 44th Amendment, 1978), Article 21 life and personal liberty (expanded in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, 1978), Article 21A education, Article 22 protection against arrest and detention. Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2)-(6) include sovereignty and integrity, security of the State, public order, decency and morality, contempt of court and defamation. Puttaswamy (2017) recognised privacy as a fundamental right. Related ideas: civil, political and economic liberty; Laski's categories of private, political and economic liberty; Gandhi's swaraj as self-rule and self-discipline.

question: Which ene.of the following is not the most likely measure the Government/ RBI takes to stop the slide of Indian rupee?
options: Curbing imports of ‘non-essential goods and promoting exports
Encouraging Indian borrowers to issue rupee denominated Masala Bonds a
Easing conditions: relating to external commercial borrowing
subject: Economy
detail: The rupee's exchange rate is determined by the demand for and supply of foreign currency (mainly the US dollar) under a managed-float regime in which the RBI intervenes to curb volatility. To stop depreciation, the authorities must either raise dollar inflows or reduce dollar demand. Curbing non-essential imports (for example through higher customs duties, as in 2013 on gold) lowers dollar demand, and promoting exports raises supply. Masala Bonds, introduced in 2014-15 and first issued by IFC in November 2014, are rupee-denominated bonds issued overseas, so the exchange-rate risk lies with the investor, not the borrower; they bring in foreign capital without currency risk for the issuer. Easing External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) norms under FEMA, such as wider eligibility, relaxed end-use rules and a lower minimum maturity, attracts dollar inflows. By contrast, expansionary monetary policy (repo rate cuts, lower CRR, open market purchases) lowers domestic yields, makes rupee assets less attractive to foreign investors, raises money supply and inflation, and weakens the rupee further. The RBI's usual tools are tight monetary policy, selling dollars from forex reserves, and measures to attract NRI deposits. The question asks for the measure that is NOT likely, so (d) is the answer.
explanations: Wrong as the answer: curbing non-essential imports and promoting exports reduces dollar demand and raises dollar supply, which supports the rupee. It is a likely measure.
Wrong as the answer: Masala Bonds attract foreign capital in rupee terms, increasing dollar inflows without exchange-rate risk for the issuer. It is a likely measure.
Wrong as the answer: easing ECB conditions encourages Indian firms to borrow abroad, bringing in foreign currency and supporting the rupee. It is a likely measure.

Correct answer: expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates and raises liquidity and inflation, which prompts capital outflow and depreciation. It is the opposite of what is needed, so it is the measure NOT likely to be taken.
keyfact: Expansionary monetary policy (lower rates, more liquidity) weakens the rupee; stopping its slide needs tighter policy, more dollar inflows (Masala Bonds, ECB easing) and import curbs.
option_notes: Import curbs and export promotion are trade-policy tools for narrowing the current account deficit (CAD). Examples include higher customs duty on gold and electronics, and export incentives such as the MEIS and later the RoDTEP scheme. In 2013 and 2018 India raised duties on non-essential imports to ease pressure on the rupee. A lower CAD means less dollar demand and a more stable currency.

Masala Bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued by Indian entities in overseas markets. The name was coined by the IFC, which issued the first one in November 2014 and later listed a green Masala Bond in London. The currency risk is borne by the investor. India's first corporate Masala Bond was issued by HDFC in 2015. The RBI framework allows issuance under the ECB regime, with a minimum maturity of 3 years (originally 5), and has since been relaxed.

External Commercial Borrowings are loans raised by Indian residents from non-resident lenders in foreign currency or rupees, governed by FEMA and RBI guidelines. They include bank loans, floating or fixed rate bonds, buyers' and suppliers' credit, and FCCBs. The RBI regulates eligible borrowers, recognised lenders, end use, maturity and all-in-cost ceilings. In 2018-19 these norms were liberalised to attract more foreign currency. ECBs add to forex inflows but also raise external debt.

Expansionary monetary policy aims to boost growth by lowering the repo rate, CRR and SLR, or by injecting liquidity through open market operations. It reduces the interest-rate differential with other economies, discourages foreign portfolio inflows, stimulates demand for imports and raises inflation. All of these weaken the currency. It is therefore used for growth revival, not for currency defence, which calls for tightening.
related: Masala Bonds: rupee-denominated overseas bonds, first issued by IFC in November 2014; the investor bears the currency risk.
India follows a managed floating exchange rate; the RBI intervenes to reduce volatility, not to fix a level.
FEMA, 1999 replaced FERA, 1973 and governs foreign exchange transactions.
The rupee is fully convertible on the current account but only partly on the capital account.
Tarapore Committees (1997 and 2006) dealt with capital account convertibility.
In 2013 the RBI opened an FCNR(B) swap window to attract NRI dollar deposits and stabilise the rupee.
A higher repo rate attracts foreign debt inflows and supports the rupee.
A fall in REER means the rupee has become more competitive.
summary: The answer is (d). An expansionary monetary policy (lower interest rates, more liquidity) reduces returns on rupee assets, encourages capital outflow and fuels inflation, so it would deepen the rupee's slide rather than stop it. Options (a), (b) and (c) all raise foreign-currency supply or cut its demand.
topic_notes: Exchange rate regime: India follows a market-determined, managed floating rate since the 1993 unification of the dual rate, after the 1991 devaluation and the LERMS (1992) dual-rate system. The RBI does not target a specific level but intervenes to curb volatility. Rupee depreciation arises from a high current account deficit, capital outflows (FPI selling), crude oil price rises, a strong US dollar, US Fed rate hikes and domestic inflation. Policy responses are of three kinds. First, monetary: raise the repo rate, tighten liquidity, sell dollars from forex reserves, or conduct USD-INR swaps. Second, capital-account measures: attract NRI deposits (FCNR(B) swap window in 2013 raised about $34 billion), ease ECB norms, allow Masala Bonds, raise FPI limits in debt, and relax FDI. Third, trade-related: curb non-essential imports through duties, and promote exports. Related concepts include the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER), the Balance of Payments, the J-curve effect, devaluation versus depreciation, and Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, which replaced FERA 1973. India's forex reserves exceeded $600 billion in 2021. Convertibility: the rupee is fully convertible on the current account (since 1994, with Article VIII of the IMF accepted) but only partially on the capital account (Tarapore Committee 1997 and 2006). Appreciation brings the opposite effects, hurting exporters and helping importers. Masala Bonds and the ECB route are part of debt-creating capital flows. Also note the 2015 Masala Bond tax concession and the RBI's 2019 move to treat these inflows more liberally.

ocr: Consider the following statements : The Reserve Bank of India’s. recent directives. relating to ‘Storage of Payinent System Data’, popularly known as data. diktat, command the payment system providers that 1. they shall ensure that entire data relating to payment systems operated by them are stored in a system only in India 2. they shall ensure that the systems are owned and operated by public sector enterprises 3. - they shall submit the consolidated system audit report to the Comptroller and Auditor General of India by the end of ‘the calendar year : ‘ Which of the statements given above is/
subject: Economy
detail: The RBI issued the circular 'Storage of Payment System Data' on 6 April 2018 under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, which gives the RBI the power to regulate and supervise payment systems. Providers had to comply within six months, by 15 October 2018. The core requirement is data localisation. The entire data relating to payment systems operated by a provider (full end-to-end transaction details, and information collected, carried or processed as part of the payment message) must be stored only in India. If processing takes place abroad, the data must be deleted from foreign systems and brought back to India within one business day or 24 hours, whichever is earlier, and then stored only in India.
