The aim was unfettered supervisory access and better protection of financial data. Foreign firms such as Visa, Mastercard, Google Pay, Amazon Pay and WhatsApp were affected. The RBI also required a System Audit Report (SAR) from a CERT-In empanelled auditor. That report goes to the RBI, not to the CAG. The directive is neutral about ownership, so private and foreign operators may continue, provided they localise data. Elimination: statement 2 is wrong (no public-sector ownership requirement), and statement 3 is wrong (the audit report goes to the RBI, not the CAG). Only 1 survives, so (a).
explanations: Correct. Only statement 1 matches the RBI directive on data localisation. Statements 2 and 3 are false.
Wrong. Statement 2 is incorrect because the directive does not require public sector ownership or operation, so '1 and 2 only' fails.
Wrong. Statement 3 is incorrect because the audit report goes to the RBI, not the CAG. Statement 1 is also correct, so '3 only' fails.
Wrong. Statements 2 and 3 are both incorrect, so '1, 2 and 3' fails.
keyfact: RBI's April 2018 'data diktat': payment data must be stored only in India; audit report goes to RBI, with no public-sector ownership rule.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', is the official answer. It corresponds to the data localisation rule in the RBI circular of 6 April 2018. The rule requires payment data to be stored only in India, with a compliance deadline of 15 October 2018. It was issued under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. Foreign payment firms had to build or use Indian data storage. Later RBI actions, such as restrictions on new card onboarding for some firms, were linked to compliance.

Option (b), '1 and 2 only', is wrong because statement 2 is false. India does not require payment systems to be public sector owned. Operators include private banks, fintech companies and foreign networks. The NPCI is an RBI and IBA promoted not-for-profit company that runs UPI, RuPay, IMPS, NACH and BHIM. Public ownership of payment systems is not a legal requirement.

Option (c), '3 only', is wrong because it relies on the false statement 3 and leaves out the true statement 1. The CAG is a constitutional authority under Article 148, appointed by the President and removable like a Supreme Court judge. The CAG audits the Union and state governments and bodies substantially funded by them. It does not audit private payment operators. Payment system audit reports go to the RBI.

Option (d), '1, 2 and 3', is wrong because two of the three statements are false. It would only be right if the RBI had imposed public sector ownership and CAG audit, and it did neither. The RBI's real compliance tools are data localisation, a CERT-In empanelled auditor's system audit report, and supervisory powers under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.
related: RBI circular on storage of payment system data: 6 April 2018; compliance deadline 15 October 2018
Legal basis: Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007
System Audit Report must be from a CERT-In empanelled auditor and goes to the RBI
Justice B. N. Srikrishna Committee (2017) drafted India's data protection framework
Puttaswamy judgment (2017): right to privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 replaced the withdrawn 2019 Bill
EU GDPR: adopted April 2016, in force from 25 May 2018
NPCI runs UPI, RuPay and IMPS; CAG is a constitutional body under Article 148
statements: 1 — Correct: The RBI circular of 6 April 2018 requires payment system providers to store the entire payment data only in India. Details: The circular was issued under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, and the deadline for compliance was 15 October 2018. It covers full end-to-end transaction details and information collected, carried or processed with each payment message. Where processing happens abroad, the data must be deleted abroad and brought back to India within 24 hours or one business day, whichever is earlier. A copy may be kept abroad only for the foreign leg of a transaction. The RBI's reasons were supervisory access and data security. The move is popularly called the 'data diktat' and was opposed by some global firms but supported by Indian fintech firms.

2 — Incorrect: The directive does not require systems to be owned or operated by public sector enterprises. Details: Payment system operators in India include private firms, banks, foreign companies and the quasi-public NPCI, which runs UPI, RuPay and IMPS. Authorisation under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 is open to any eligible entity. The RBI is the designated regulator, and its Board for Regulation and Supervision of Payment and Settlement Systems (BPSS) oversees the sector. Entities such as Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm, Visa and Mastercard operate here. The requirement is about where data is located, not who owns the system.

3 — Incorrect: The system audit report is submitted to the RBI, not to the CAG. Details: Providers must submit a System Audit Report (SAR) conducted by a CERT-In empanelled auditor. The report had to be filed within a stipulated period (originally by 31 December 2018) and the board of the entity had to approve it. It covers compliance with the data storage rules. The CAG is a constitutional authority under Article 148 that audits government accounts and public bodies, and it has no role in auditing private payment systems. CERT-In is the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team under MeitY.
summary: The correct answer is (a): only statement 1 is correct. The RBI's April 2018 directive on 'Storage of Payment System Data' requires all payment system providers to store the entire payment data only in systems located in India. It does not require public sector ownership, and it does not require audit reports to be submitted to the CAG.
topic_notes: Data localisation means requiring data about a country's users or transactions to be stored or processed within that country. India's push came through several channels. The RBI circular of 6 April 2018 on 'Storage of Payment System Data' applied to all authorised payment system operators, including card networks, wallets and UPI apps. Providers had six months to comply, and a System Audit Report from a CERT-In empanelled auditor was required. The RBI later issued FAQs clarifying that foreign processing is allowed if the data is deleted abroad and brought back to India within 24 hours or one business day. The RBI has since used supervisory action, such as barring some firms from onboarding new customers, to enforce compliance. The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 is the legal basis, and the RBI's Board for Regulation and Supervision of Payment and Settlement Systems (BPSS) is the oversight body. The Justice B. N. Srikrishna Committee (2017-18) drafted a data protection bill with localisation features. The Personal Data Protection Bill, 2019 was withdrawn in 2022, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 now governs personal data, with a Data Protection Board of India. The Supreme Court's 2017 Puttaswamy judgment held privacy to be a fundamental right under Article 21. Internationally, the EU's General Data Protection Regulation was adopted in April 2016 and has applied since 25 May 2018. The NPCI runs UPI, RuPay and IMPS. Other angles UPSC could ask: CERT-In and its role, the IT Act 2000 including Section 43A and Section 69, and the cross-border data transfer provisions of the DPDP Act 2023.

ocr: Consider the following statements : The Reserve Bank of India’s. recent directives. relating to ‘Storage of Payinent System Data’, popularly known as data. diktat, command the payment system providers that 1. they shall ensure that entire data relating to payment systems operated by them are stored in a system only in India 2. they shall ensure that the systems are owned and operated by public sector enterprises 3. - they shall submit the consolidated system audit report to the Comptroller and Auditor General of India by the end of ‘the calendar year : ‘ Which of the statements given above is/
subject: Economy
detail: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is the EU's comprehensive data protection and privacy law. It was adopted by the European Parliament and Council on 27 April 2016, entered into force in May 2016, and applied from 25 May 2018 after a two-year transition. It replaced the Data Protection Directive 95/46/EC. Being a Regulation (not a Directive), it is directly binding in all member states without national transposition. It has extraterritorial reach: it applies to any organisation processing personal data of persons in the EU, wherever the organisation is located. Key features: consent requirements, right of access, right to erasure (right to be forgotten), data portability, breach notification within 72 hours, Data Protection Officers, privacy by design, and fines up to 20 million euros or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher. Elimination logic: Australia has the Privacy Act 1988; Canada has PIPEDA (2000); the USA has no single federal data law and relies on sectoral laws and state laws such as the California Consumer Privacy Act. The terms 'Regulation', 'April 2016' and 'May 2018' point to the EU, a bloc that legislates through Regulations and Directives.
explanations: Incorrect: Australia's framework is the Privacy Act 1988 with Australian Privacy Principles; it did not adopt the GDPR.
Incorrect: Canada relies on PIPEDA (2000) and the Privacy Act (1983); it has not adopted the GDPR.
Correct: The European Union adopted the GDPR in April 2016 and began enforcement on 25 May 2018.
Incorrect: The USA has no comprehensive federal data protection law; it uses sectoral laws (HIPAA, COPPA) and state laws such as the CCPA (2018).
keyfact: GDPR: adopted by the European Union in April 2016, enforced from 25 May 2018, with fines up to 4% of global turnover.
option_notes: Australia: its main privacy law is the Privacy Act 1988, containing 13 Australian Privacy Principles, administered by the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC). The Notifiable Data Breaches scheme began in February 2018. It is a Commonwealth country and member of the Five Eyes alliance, AUKUS and Quad. Its approach differs from the GDPR, though it has been reviewing reforms to align more closely.

Canada: the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA), 2000, governs private-sector data handling, while the Privacy Act 1983 covers federal public bodies. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner oversees enforcement. Quebec passed Law 25 (2021) with GDPR-like provisions. The EU has given Canada partial adequacy status for commercial organisations under PIPEDA.

The European Union: a political and economic union of 27 member states (after Brexit in 2020), headquartered institutionally in Brussels, Strasbourg and Luxembourg. Its main bodies are the European Commission, Parliament, Council and Court of Justice. It enacted the GDPR, applicable from 25 May 2018, and later the Digital Services Act, Digital Markets Act and AI Act. The European Data Protection Board coordinates enforcement.

The United States of America: it has no single comprehensive federal privacy law. It uses sectoral laws such as HIPAA (health), COPPA (children), GLBA (finance) and the Privacy Act 1974, plus state laws such as the California Consumer Privacy Act (2018, effective 2020). The EU-US Data Privacy Framework (2023) replaced the invalidated Privacy Shield, which the CJEU struck down in the Schrems II case (2020).
related: GDPR applied from 25 May 2018; adopted on 27 April 2016.
GDPR fines can reach 20 million euros or 4% of global turnover.
Puttaswamy case (2017): privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21.
Srikrishna Committee (2017) drafted India's data protection framework.
India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act was enacted in 2023.
RBI's 2018 directive required payment data to be stored only in India.
GDPR replaced the 1995 EU Data Protection Directive.
The 'right to be forgotten' is a GDPR right under Article 17.
summary: The answer is (c) The European Union. The GDPR was adopted by the EU in April 2016 (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) and became enforceable from 25 May 2018, replacing the 1995 Data Protection Directive.
topic_notes: The GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) is the global benchmark for data protection. Adopted 27 April 2016, it applied from 25 May 2018. It protects personal data of natural persons and has extraterritorial scope. Core principles: lawfulness, fairness and transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality, and accountability. Data subject rights: access, rectification, erasure (right to be forgotten), restriction, portability, objection, and rights regarding automated decision-making. Obligations: breach notification to the authority within 72 hours, Data Protection Impact Assessments, appointment of Data Protection Officers, and cross-border transfer rules (adequacy decisions, Standard Contractual Clauses). Penalties: up to 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide turnover. India context: the Supreme Court in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) declared privacy a fundamental right under Article 21. The Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee (2017-18) drafted a data protection bill. The Personal Data Protection Bill 2019 was withdrawn in 2022, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 was enacted, creating the Data Protection Board of India, concepts of Data Fiduciary and Data Principal, and consent-based processing. The RBI's 2018 circular on storage of payment system data required data localisation in India, which was the subject of Q87 in the same paper. The IT Act 2000 (Section 43A, 72A) earlier governed data protection. Other angles: the CJEU's Schrems cases, the Cambridge Analytica scandal (2018), the California CCPA, China's PIPL (2021), and the Council of Europe's Convention 108.

question: Recently, India signed a deal known as ‘Action Plan for Prioritization and Impleméntation of Cooperation Areas in the Nuclear Field’ with which of the following countries?
subject: Geography
detail: The Action Plan was signed in 2017 between Rosatom (Russia's state atomic energy corporation) and India's Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), after the annual summit discussions between PM Modi and President Putin. It prioritised cooperation areas such as building Russian-designed VVER reactors at Kudankulam (Tamil Nadu), Units 3 to 6 under the 2014 Strategic Vision for strengthening cooperation in peaceful uses of nuclear energy, and Russian-designed reactors at a second site in India. It also covers localisation of manufacturing in India, nuclear fuel supply, and cooperation in third countries (for example Bangladesh's Rooppur plant). Russia is India's longest-standing civil nuclear partner: the first Kudankulam agreement dates to 1988 (Gorbachev-Rajiv Gandhi) and the 1998 intergovernmental agreement. Elimination logic: Japan signed a civil nuclear agreement with India in 2016 (in force 2017), the US has the 123 Agreement (2008) with Westinghouse plans at Kovvada, and the UK signed a civil nuclear deal in 2015. None of these used the phrase 'Action Plan for Prioritization and Implementation'. The Kudankulam link to Russia points to (b).
explanations: Incorrect: India-Japan civil nuclear cooperation rests on the 2016 agreement, not this Action Plan.
Correct: The Action Plan for prioritising nuclear cooperation areas was signed with Russia (Rosatom and India's DAE), centred on Kudankulam and new sites.
Incorrect: The UK-India civil nuclear agreement was announced in 2015 and concerns uranium supply and cooperation, not this Action Plan.
Incorrect: India-US nuclear cooperation is under the 123 Agreement (2008) and related commercial talks with Westinghouse, not this document.
keyfact: The 2019 UPSC 'Action Plan for Prioritization and Implementation of Cooperation Areas in the Nuclear Field' was with Russia (Rosatom), centred on Kudankulam.
option_notes: Japan: The India-Japan Agreement for Cooperation in the Peaceful Uses of Nuclear Energy was signed in November 2016 and entered into force in July 2018. Japan is a non-NPT state's partner only after India gave assurances on testing moratorium. It allows export of nuclear technology and equipment, important as Japanese firms supply key components to US and French reactor builders. Japan is the only nuclear-bombed country to sign such a deal with India.

Russia: Russia is India's oldest civil nuclear partner. Rosatom builds VVER-1000 reactors at Kudankulam in Tamil Nadu, where Units 1 and 2 are operational and Units 3 to 6 are under construction. The 1988 agreement, the 2008 inter-governmental accord and the 2014 Strategic Vision document support this. Russia also backs India's NSG membership and cooperates in Bangladesh's Rooppur plant with India as a third-country partner.

United Kingdom: India and the UK signed a civil nuclear cooperation agreement during PM Modi's November 2015 visit to London, following a 2010 declaration. It enables cooperation in nuclear research, safety and supply of nuclear fuel including uranium. The UK is a Nuclear Weapon State under the NPT and a member of the NSG, and it supported India's NSG membership bid in principle.

United States: The India-US civil nuclear deal, the 123 Agreement, was signed in October 2008 after the 2005 Joint Statement and the 2006 Hyde Act. It followed the IAEA safeguards agreement and the NSG waiver of 2008. It ended India's nuclear isolation after the 1974 and 1998 tests. Westinghouse planned six AP1000 reactors at Kovvada in Andhra Pradesh, though liability concerns under the 2010 CLND Act slowed progress.
related: Kudankulam units 1 and 2 are operational; Units 3 to 6 are under construction with Russian help.
Kudankulam uses Russian VVER-1000 pressurised water reactors.
India-US 123 Agreement was signed in 2008.
India is not an NPT or NSG member; China opposes its NSG entry.
Rosatom is Russia's state atomic energy corporation.
CLND Act 2010 provides for supplier recourse and has deterred foreign suppliers.
Jaitapur in Maharashtra is the proposed site for French EPR reactors.
India's three-stage nuclear programme was designed by Homi Bhabha.
summary: The answer is (b) Russia. In June 2019 India and Russia signed the 'Action Plan for Prioritization and Implementation of Cooperation Areas in the Nuclear Field' to deepen civil nuclear cooperation, mainly the Kudankulam project and new sites.
topic_notes: India's civil nuclear diplomacy follows its three-stage nuclear programme (Homi Bhabha): stage 1 uses PHWRs with natural uranium, stage 2 uses fast breeder reactors with plutonium, and stage 3 uses thorium-based reactors. Because India lacks uranium but has large thorium reserves, imports and international partnerships matter. After the 1974 Pokhran-I test India faced isolation; the NSG was created in 1974 in response. The 2008 NSG waiver allowed trade, and India has since signed civil nuclear agreements with the US, Russia, France, UK, Canada, Australia (2014 uranium supply), Japan, Kazakhstan, Mongolia, Argentina, Namibia and others. The Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act 2010 holds operators liable with right of recourse against suppliers, which has deterred foreign suppliers. India separated its civil and military nuclear facilities in 2006 and signed an IAEA safeguards agreement and the Additional Protocol (2014). Major plants include Kudankulam (Russia, 1000 MW units), Tarapur, Rawatbhata, Kakrapar, Kalpakkam (PFBR, BHAVINI), Jaitapur (planned with France's EDF, 6 EPR units in Maharashtra) and Kovvada (US). India fleet-mode PHWR plan in 2017 approved 10 indigenous 700 MW reactors. India is not an NPT signatory and is not an NSG member; China blocks its entry, citing NPT non-signing. India follows a No First Use policy and has a credible minimum deterrence doctrine. Agencies: DAE, NPCIL, AERB (regulator), BARC, IGCAR.

question: The. money multiplier in an economy ‘ increases with which one of the following?
options: Increase in the cash reserve ratio
Increase in the banking habit of the population
Increase in the. statutory liquidity ratio ;
Increase in the population of the country wee oo PRTO
subject: Economy
detail: The money multiplier links the money supply (M3 or M1) to high-powered money (reserve money, M0). In its simple form, m = (1 + c) / (c + r), where c is the currency-deposit ratio (the public's preference for cash over deposits) and r is the reserve-deposit ratio (CRR plus excess reserves). A greater banking habit means people keep more of their money as bank deposits and less as cash. That lowers c, reduces the leakage of cash out of the banking system, and raises the multiplier. A higher CRR means banks must park more deposits with the RBI, which raises r, shrinks lendable funds, and lowers the multiplier. A higher SLR requires banks to hold more of their deposits in liquid assets such as G-secs, gold and cash, which reduces credit creation and lowers the multiplier. Population size has no direct link to the multiplier. What matters is how people hold money and how banks behave, not how many people there are. Elimination: (a) and (c) lower the multiplier, (d) is irrelevant, so (b) is the only choice that works. The RBI controls the multiplier mainly through CRR, repo rate and open market operations.
explanations: Wrong. A higher CRR raises the reserve ratio, leaves banks less to lend, and lowers the money multiplier.
Correct. A greater banking habit lowers the currency-deposit ratio, so more money stays in the banking system and is re-lent. This raises the multiplier.
Wrong. A higher SLR forces banks to hold more liquid assets, which reduces lendable resources and lowers the multiplier.
Wrong. Population size has no direct bearing on the multiplier. It depends on c and r, not on headcount.
keyfact: The money multiplier = (1+c)/(c+r): it rises with more banking habit (lower c) and falls when CRR or SLR rise.
option_notes: Cash Reserve Ratio is the share of a bank's net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) that scheduled banks must keep as cash with the RBI. It is set by the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934 (Section 42), within a statutory range, and no interest is paid on it. It is a quantitative tool of monetary policy. The CRR has been 4% since 2022 (it was cut to 3% in 2020 and restored in stages). Raising it drains liquidity and lowers the multiplier.

Banking habit is the tendency of the public to hold money as bank deposits rather than as cash. It is raised by financial inclusion drives such as PM Jan Dhan Yojana (2014), by branch expansion, and by digital payments. It reduces the currency-deposit ratio and strengthens credit creation. Greater banking habit means more deposits, a higher multiplier, and more effective monetary transmission.

Statutory Liquidity Ratio is the share of NDTL that banks must hold in liquid assets: cash, gold, and unencumbered approved securities (G-secs, T-bills, SDLs). It is set by the RBI under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The floor is 0 and the ceiling is 40% under the law. It has been 18% since 2020. A higher SLR reduces banks' lending capacity and so lowers the multiplier. It also ensures bank solvency and helps finance the government's borrowing.

Population is the number of people in the country, and India is now the most populous country. It affects aggregate demand and the demand for money, but it does not change the money multiplier mechanically. The multiplier depends on the public's cash-holding behaviour and on banks' reserve requirements, not on the size of the population.
related: Money multiplier = M3 / reserve money (M0).
Simple deposit multiplier = 1/CRR.
CRR is under Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934; SLR is under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
SLR is 18% and CRR is 4% (as of recent years).
M3 is broad money; M1 is narrow money.
The MPC was established in 2016 and has 6 members.
A higher currency-deposit ratio lowers the multiplier.
Reserve money = currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with the RBI + other deposits with the RBI.
summary: The answer is (b). The money multiplier rises when people hold less cash and deposit more in banks, because banks then have more deposits to lend and re-lend. A stronger banking habit lowers the currency-deposit ratio, which raises the multiplier.
topic_notes:
Money supply and the multiplier. Reserve money (M0, high-powered money) equals currency in circulation plus bankers' deposits with the RBI plus other deposits with the RBI. The money multiplier is M3 divided by M0, or M1 divided by M0. In the simple deposit-multiplier form it is 1/CRR. In the fuller form it is (1+c)/(c+r), where c is the currency-deposit ratio and r is the reserve-deposit ratio. The multiplier rises when c falls (greater banking habit, digital payments, financial inclusion), when CRR falls, and when excess reserves fall. It falls when the public hoards cash, when CRR or SLR rise, or when banks keep large excess reserves in a crisis.

RBI monetary aggregates: M1 = currency with the public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with the RBI. M2 = M1 + savings deposits with post offices. M3 = M1 + time deposits with banks. M4 = M3 + total post office deposits. M3 is the broad money measure, and M1 is the narrowest.

Tools of monetary policy. The quantitative tools are CRR, SLR, repo and reverse repo, MSF, open market operations, and the LAF. The standing deposit facility (SDF) was introduced in 2022. The qualitative tools are moral suasion and margin requirements. Repo is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks. Marginal Standing Facility is the rate at which banks borrow overnight against SLR securities. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), with 6 members, was created in 2016 and sets the repo rate. The inflation target is 4% with a ±2% band.

Other angles. The credit multiplier, velocity of money, the quantity theory MV=PT, and the effect of demonetisation on the currency-deposit ratio are all possible questions.

question:
In the context of digital technologies for entertainment, consider the following statements :
1. In Augmented Reality (AR), a simulated environment is created and the physical world is completely shut out.
2. In Virtual Reality (VR), images generated from a computer are projected onto real-life objects or surroundings.
3. AR allows individuals to be present in the world and improves the experience using the camera of smart-phone or PC.
4. VR closes the world, and transposes an individual, providing complete immersion experience. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) are immersive technologies used in gaming, films, live events, education and retail. AR keeps the user in the real world and superimposes digital images, sound or data on it. It works through a smartphone or PC camera, tablet or smart glasses. Pokemon Go, Snapchat lenses, IKEA Place and Google Lens are common examples. VR replaces the real environment with a fully computer-generated one. The user wears a head-mounted display such as Oculus Rift or Quest, HTC Vive or PlayStation VR, and the physical world is shut out. Mixed Reality (MR) sits between the two, with digital objects that interact with the real environment (Microsoft HoloLens). Extended Reality (XR) is the umbrella term covering AR, VR and MR. Elimination logic: statement 1 gives VR's feature as AR's, so it is wrong. Statement 2 gives AR's feature as VR's, so it is wrong too. That rules out (a) and (c), both of which contain 1 or 2. Option (d) leaves out statement 3, which is correct. Only (b) remains.
explanations: (a) is wrong. Both statements 1 and 2 are incorrect because they swap the definitions of AR and VR.
(b) is right. Statement 3 correctly describes AR and statement 4 correctly describes VR.
(c) is wrong. It includes statements 1 and 2, which are incorrect, even though statement 3 is correct.
(d) is wrong. Statement 4 is correct, but statement 3 on AR is also correct, so 'only 4' is incomplete.
keyfact: AR = real world plus digital overlay, using a phone or PC camera; VR = real world shut out, with full immersion through a headset.
option_notes: Statements 1 and 2 together would reverse the AR and VR definitions. In fact AR overlays digital content on the real world, while VR replaces the real world with a simulated one. This option is a classic trap that swaps the two technologies. Such swapped-definition options are common in UPSC technology questions. The option is incorrect.

Statements 3 and 4 give the correct pairing. AR enhances the real world through a smartphone or PC camera, and VR immerses the user in a fully virtual environment through a headset. AR examples are Pokemon Go and Snapchat filters. VR examples are Oculus and HTC Vive. This is the official answer.

Statements 1, 2 and 3 mix the swapped definitions with one correct AR statement. Statements 1 and 2 wrongly assign VR traits to AR and AR traits to VR. Only statement 3 is correct. The mixture is meant to tempt students who recognise statement 3 and skim the rest. The option is incorrect.

Statement 4 alone correctly describes VR as closing off the world and giving complete immersion. It ignores that statement 3 on AR is also correct. UPSC often builds partial-correct options like this one, so check every statement. The option is incorrect because it is incomplete.
related: AR overlays digital content on the real world; VR replaces it with a simulated one.
Pokemon Go (2016, Niantic) is the best-known AR game.
Oculus Rift, HTC Vive and PlayStation VR are VR headsets.
Mixed Reality (MR), as in Microsoft HoloLens, lets virtual objects interact with the real environment.
XR (Extended Reality) is the umbrella term for AR, VR and MR.
Facebook was rebranded as Meta in October 2021 to build the metaverse.
Google Cardboard is a low-cost smartphone-based VR viewer.
Apple ARKit and Google ARCore are the main AR development platforms.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Shutting out the physical world and creating a simulated environment describes VR, not AR. AR adds to the real world and never replaces it. AR content is delivered through phone cameras, tablets or smart glasses, and the user still sees their real surroundings. Pokemon Go (2016, Niantic) popularised it. Apple ARKit and Google ARCore are the main developer platforms.

2 — Incorrect: Projecting computer-generated images on real-life objects or surroundings is the defining feature of AR, not VR. VR creates an entirely artificial 3D environment. The user views it through a headset with motion tracking and often hand controllers. Examples include Oculus Rift, HTC Vive and Google Cardboard. Uses include gaming, flight and surgical training, virtual tourism and architecture walkthroughs.

3 — Correct: AR lets the user stay present in the real world while digital layers improve the experience. It uses the camera of a smartphone or PC, plus sensors, GPS and software that recognise surfaces and objects. Examples are Snapchat and Instagram filters, IKEA Place furniture preview, Google Lens and navigation overlays. In entertainment it is used in games, concerts, museum guides and sports broadcasts.

4 — Correct: VR closes off the real world and transposes the user into a simulated one, giving a complete immersion experience. It needs a headset with a display for each eye, head and motion tracking, spatial audio and sometimes haptic gloves. Examples include Oculus Quest (Meta), HTC Vive and PlayStation VR. Immersive gaming, virtual cinemas, simulations and therapy are typical uses. Its current status is growing but niche, driven by the metaverse push.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 3 and 4 are correct. AR overlays computer-generated content on the real world, viewed through a smartphone or PC camera. VR shuts out the real world and immerses the user in a simulated environment. Statements 1 and 2 swap these definitions.
topic_notes: Immersive technologies change how users see and interact with digital content. Virtual Reality (VR) creates a completely computer-generated 3D environment. It needs a head-mounted display (HMD), motion tracking and controllers, and it isolates the user from the real world. Examples are Oculus Rift and Quest (Meta), HTC Vive, PlayStation VR and Google Cardboard. Augmented Reality (AR) overlays digital information such as images, text, sound or 3D models on the live view of the real world. It needs only a smartphone, tablet or smart glasses with a camera and sensors. Examples are Pokemon Go, Snapchat lenses, IKEA Place, Google Lens and Google Glass. Mixed Reality (MR) anchors virtual objects in the real environment and lets them interact with it, as in Microsoft HoloLens and Magic Leap. Extended Reality (XR) covers AR, VR and MR. Key differences are as follows. VR gives full immersion and AR gives partial augmentation. VR requires special hardware and AR works on common devices. VR replaces reality and AR supplements it. Applications go beyond entertainment. They include medical training and surgery simulation, military and flight simulators, education, real estate, retail try-ons, industrial maintenance and tourism. Related ideas are the metaverse (a persistent shared virtual world, popularised by Meta's 2021 rebranding), 360-degree video, haptic technology, digital twins and spatial computing (Apple Vision Pro, 2024). Policy angles include India's AVGC (Animation, Visual Effects, Gaming and Comics) promotion task force and data privacy concerns around immersive devices. UPSC often tests definitions, differences, examples and applications, and swapped-definition statements like these.

question: The word ‘Denisovan’ is sometimes mentioned in media in reference to
options: fossils of a kind of dinosaurs
acave system found in North-East India
a geological period in the history of Indian subcontinent
subject: Environment
detail: Denisovans are an extinct group of archaic humans (genus Homo) identified in 2010 when DNA was sequenced from a finger bone fragment found in Denisova Cave, Altai region, southern Siberia, Russia. The bone dates to roughly 40,000-50,000 years ago, though the cave has older layers. Genetically they are a sister group of Neanderthals; the two lineages split from the line leading to modern humans about 600,000-700,000 years ago. Modern humans interbred with Denisovans: present-day Melanesians, Aboriginal Australians and some South-East Asian populations carry up to about 4-6% Denisovan DNA, and Tibetans carry a Denisovan-derived EPAS1 gene variant that helps in high-altitude adaptation. A jawbone from Xiahe, Baishiya Karst Cave, Tibetan Plateau (China), was identified as Denisovan in 2019 through ancient proteins, and a Denisovan-linked find in Laos and Taiwan has also been reported. Elimination: dinosaurs lived about 230-66 million years ago, long before any human; the name is not linked to any North-East Indian cave (Krem caves are in Meghalaya); and geological periods in India carry names such as Deccan, Gondwana or Siwalik, not Denisovan.
explanations: Incorrect: dinosaurs are Mesozoic reptiles, while Denisovans were hominins who lived in the Pleistocene; no dinosaur fossil is called Denisovan.
Correct: Denisovans are an extinct early human species, known from Denisova Cave fossils and ancient DNA.
Incorrect: Denisova Cave is in Siberia, Russia, not North-East India; North-East Indian caves such as those in Meghalaya (Krem Liat Prah) have different names.
Incorrect: Denisovan is not a geological period; it refers to a hominin group, and Indian geological terms are different.
keyfact: Denisovans: extinct archaic human species, first identified in 2010 from Denisova Cave, Siberia, and a sister group of Neanderthals.
option_notes: Dinosaur fossils: dinosaurs were reptiles that dominated the Mesozoic Era (Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous) and went extinct about 66 million years ago after the Chicxulub impact event. In India, major fossil sites include Jabalpur, Balasinor (Raiholi, Gujarat), Pisdura (Maharashtra) and Ariyalur (Tamil Nadu). Titanosaurus indicus and Rajasaurus narmadensis are well-known Indian dinosaurs. They have no connection with the human lineage.

Early human species: Denisovans are an extinct archaic human group, first identified in 2010 from Denisova Cave in Siberia. They are closely related to Neanderthals, interbred with modern humans, and left DNA in Melanesians, Aboriginal Australians and Tibetans (EPAS1 gene). The Xiahe mandible from Baishiya Karst Cave in Tibet (identified 2019) is the best-known Denisovan fossil outside Siberia. Few physical remains, mostly teeth, bone fragments and a jaw, have been found.

Cave system in North-East India: the region is known for limestone caves in Meghalaya, such as Krem Liat Prah in the Jaintia Hills, India's longest cave, and Krem Puri, the longest sandstone cave in the world. Mawsmai cave is a tourist site. Caves in the region are called krem in Khasi. Denisova Cave is in Russia, not here.

Geological period in Indian history: Indian geological history uses units such as the Archaean, Dharwar, Vindhyan, Gondwana, Deccan Trap (Cretaceous-Eocene volcanism) and Siwalik formations. The Anthropocene and Holocene are recent epochs; the Meghalayan Age (about 4,200 years ago to present) was named in 2018 after a Meghalaya cave stalagmite. Denisovan is not a period.
related: Svante Pääbo won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on ancient genomes, including Denisovans.
Denisova Cave lies in the Altai Mountains of Siberia, Russia.
Tibetans carry a Denisovan-derived EPAS1 gene variant aiding high-altitude adaptation.
Homo naledi was discovered in the Rising Star cave system, South Africa, announced in 2015.
Homo floresiensis, the 'hobbit', was found on Flores island, Indonesia, in 2003.
The Narmada skull from Hathnora in Madhya Pradesh is an archaic human fossil.
The Meghalayan Age (from about 4,200 years ago) was named after a Meghalaya cave stalagmite in 2018.
Neanderthals are named after the Neander Valley in Germany.
summary: The answer is (b): Denisovans are an extinct early human species (archaic hominins) related to Neanderthals. They are known from fossils first found in Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains, Siberia, and from DNA evidence, not from dinosaurs, Indian caves or a geological period.
topic_notes: Human evolution is a recurring prelims theme. Genus Homo emerged in Africa about 2.5-3 million years ago. Key species: Homo habilis (tool user), Homo erectus (first to use fire, spread out of Africa; Java Man and Peking Man), Homo heidelbergensis, Homo neanderthalensis (Europe and West Asia, about 400,000 to 40,000 years ago; Neander Valley, Germany), Homo floresiensis (the 'hobbit' of Flores, Indonesia), Homo naledi (South Africa, 2015, Rising Star cave) and Homo sapiens (about 300,000 years ago, Jebel Irhoud, Morocco). Denisovans were found through palaeogenomics, a field pioneered by Svante Pääbo, who won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for sequencing the Neanderthal genome and discovering the Denisovans. Interbreeding shows that archaic DNA persists in modern populations: Neanderthal DNA in non-Africans (about 1-2%), Denisovan DNA in Oceanians and some Asians. Denisova Cave has also yielded Denet 'Denny', a girl with a Neanderthal mother and Denisovan father (about 90,000 years old, reported 2018). In India, the Narmada skull (Hathnora, Madhya Pradesh) is an archaic human fossil, and Attirampakkam (Tamil Nadu) yielded Middle Palaeolithic tools dated about 385,000 years ago. Related angles: Bhimbetka rock shelters (Palaeolithic to Mesolithic paintings, UNESCO site), Toba eruption (about 74,000 years ago), Out-of-Africa theory, and the Meghalayan Age.

question: With reference to the recent developments in science, which one of the following statements is not correct?
options: Functional chromosomes can be created by joining segments of DNA taken from cells of different species
Pieces of artificial functional DNA can be created in laboratories. 41 BKL~-F-GHP/54A
A piece of DNA taken out from an animal cell can be made to replicate outside a living cell in a laboratory
Cells taken out from plants and animals can be made to undergo cell division in laboratory petri dishes
subject: Environment
detail: The question tests basic biotechnology developments. Artificial DNA synthesis is established: Khorana synthesised a gene in the 1970s, and Craig Venter's team built a synthetic Mycoplasma genome in 2010 (JCVI-syn1.0). PCR, developed by Kary Mullis in 1983 and awarded the Nobel Prize in 1993, copies DNA in a test tube using Taq polymerase, so no living cell is needed. Cell and tissue culture lets plant and animal cells divide in petri dishes. Examples include HeLa cells, plant micropropagation and stem cell lines. Recombinant DNA technology (Cohen and Boyer, 1973) joins DNA from different species, but only as genes inserted into plasmids or vectors. It does not produce a complete functional chromosome of mixed-species origin. The official key treats (a) as not correct, as the question intends a fully functional chromosome assembled from different species' segments. Elimination: (b), (c) and (d) are textbook and clearly true, which leaves (a). Note that artificial yeast chromosomes (Sc2.0 project) and YACs exist, but these are synthetic or vector-based and are not the mixed-species chromosome the question describes.
explanations: Correct choice as the 'not correct' statement per the official key. A functional chromosome made by joining segments from cells of different species was not regarded as an established development, even though recombinant DNA can combine foreign genes in vectors.
Incorrect as the answer, because the statement is true. Artificial functional DNA and genes can be chemically synthesised, as with synthetic genes and the synthetic bacterial genome of 2010.
Incorrect as the answer, because the statement is true. PCR and in vitro replication copy animal DNA outside a living cell using DNA polymerase, primers and nucleotides.
Incorrect as the answer, because the statement is true. Plant and animal cells are routinely grown and divided in petri dishes through cell and tissue culture.
keyfact: Genes from different species can be joined in vectors by recombinant DNA technology, but a mixed-species functional chromosome is the 'not correct' statement; PCR, gene synthesis and cell culture are established.
option_notes: Chromosome engineering from mixed-species DNA: recombinant DNA technology (Cohen and Boyer, 1973) uses restriction enzymes and ligase to join DNA from different species into plasmids. Artificial chromosomes such as YACs and BACs carry cloned inserts. The Sc2.0 project is building a synthetic yeast genome. A complete natural-like chromosome of mixed-species origin was not an established development at the time of the question.

Artificial DNA synthesis: oligonucleotides are made chemically by the phosphoramidite method and assembled into genes. Khorana made the first synthetic gene (tRNA, 1970s) and won the Nobel Prize in 1968. In 2010 Craig Venter's JCVI created Mycoplasma mycoides JCVI-syn1.0, a bacterium run by a synthetic genome. Synthetic biology builds on this.

In vitro DNA replication is done by PCR, invented by Kary Mullis in 1983 (Nobel Prize 1993). It uses Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus, primers, dNTPs and thermal cycles of denaturation, annealing and extension. It is used in diagnostics such as RT-PCR for COVID-19, forensics and cloning.

Cell and tissue culture grows cells outside the organism in sterile media. Examples are HeLa cells (1951, Henrietta Lacks) and plant tissue culture, based on totipotency (Haberlandt, Skoog and Miller). Uses include micropropagation, vaccine production, stem cell research and cultured meat.
related: PCR was developed by Kary Mullis in 1983 and uses heat-stable Taq polymerase.
CRISPR-Cas9 won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for Doudna and Charpentier.
Dolly the sheep (1996) was cloned by somatic cell nuclear transfer.
JCVI-syn1.0 (2010) was the first cell controlled by a chemically synthesised genome.
GEAC under MoEFCC approves the environmental release of GMOs in India.
Bt cotton is the only GM crop commercially cultivated in India.
iPSCs were discovered by Shinya Yamanaka in 2006.
Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences.
summary: The official answer is (a). Statement (a), that functional chromosomes can be created by joining DNA segments from cells of different species, was treated by UPSC as the 'not correct' statement. Options (b), (c) and (d) describe established laboratory techniques: artificial gene synthesis, PCR and cell/tissue culture.
topic_notes: This question covers modern biotechnology. Key areas are recombinant DNA technology, PCR, cell culture, gene editing and synthetic biology. Recombinant DNA: restriction enzymes (molecular scissors, such as EcoRI), DNA ligase, and vectors such as plasmids (pBR322), bacteriophages and YACs. Cohen and Boyer made the first recombinant organism in 1973. PCR: denaturation at about 94°C, annealing at 50-65°C and extension at 72°C. Gene editing: CRISPR-Cas9 (Doudna and Charpentier, Nobel Prize 2020) uses guide RNA to cut DNA at a target site. Other tools are ZFNs and TALENs. Synthetic biology: the 2010 synthetic cell, the Sc2.0 yeast project, and the Human Genome Project-write idea. Cell culture and cloning: Dolly the sheep (1996, somatic cell nuclear transfer, Roslin Institute), stem cells, iPSCs (Yamanaka, 2006, Nobel Prize 2012), and organoids. Applications include GM crops (Bt cotton, the only GM crop commercially approved in India; GM mustard DMH-11 is under Supreme Court scrutiny), gene therapy, and mRNA vaccines. India: the Department of Biotechnology (DBT, 1986), GEAC under the Environment Ministry regulating GMOs, the Genome India Project, and FelUda, a CRISPR-based COVID test. Likely UPSC angles are technique-to-use matching, who discovered what, and the regulatory framework.

question: Consider the following statements : A digital signature is 1. an electronic record that identifies the certifying authority issuing it 2. used to serve as a proof of identity of an individual to access information or server on Internet 3. an electronic method of signing an electronic document and ensuring that the original content is unchanged Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: A digital signature is a mathematical, cryptographic technique used to validate the authenticity and integrity of an electronic message or document. The signer computes a hash (message digest) of the document and encrypts it with their private key. The receiver decrypts the signature with the signer's public key and compares the result with a freshly computed hash. A match proves that the signer is genuine (authentication), that the content is unaltered (integrity), and that the signer cannot easily deny signing (non-repudiation). In India, the Information Technology Act, 2000 gives legal recognition to digital signatures (Section 3) and later to electronic signatures (Section 3A, added in 2008). Certifying Authorities (CAs) are licensed under the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA). The CAs issue Digital Signature Certificates (DSCs), which are the electronic records that identify the certificate holder and the issuing CA, and which bind a public key to an identity. Statement 1 describes this certificate, not the signature. Statement 2 describes identity credentials, such as a certificate used in SSL/TLS or a login. It is not the definition of a signature. Statement 3 matches the standard definition. Eliminating 1 and 2 leaves (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong: statement 1 describes a digital certificate issued by a Certifying Authority, not the digital signature, and statement 3 is also correct, so '1 only' fails.
(b) is wrong: statement 3 is correct, but statement 2 confuses identity-access credentials with the signing function of a digital signature.
(c) is correct: only statement 3 gives the true definition, an electronic way of signing a document that ensures the content stays unchanged.
(d) is wrong: it accepts statements 1 and 2, which describe a digital certificate and authentication credentials, not the signature itself.
keyfact: Digital signature = hash signed with the sender's private key, giving authentication, integrity and non-repudiation; the digital certificate from a Certifying Authority is a separate thing.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would hold if the question asked about a digital certificate. A Digital Signature Certificate is an electronic credential issued by a licensed Certifying Authority that binds a public key to the identity of its holder. It follows the X.509 standard and carries the CA's signature, a serial number and a validity period (usually 1 to 3 years). In India the CCA, created under the IT Act, 2000, licenses CAs and operates the Root CA of India. Certificates are Class 1, 2 or 3 depending on the assurance level.

Option (b), '2 and 3 only', combines the correct statement 3 with statement 2. Statement 2 is about proving identity to access information or a server online. That is authentication, done through passwords, OTPs, tokens, biometrics or SSL/TLS client certificates. The related concept of SSL/TLS lets a website prove its identity to a browser (HTTPS). Statement 2 is therefore not the definition of a digital signature, which signs documents and verifies their integrity.

Option (c), '3 only', is the correct answer. A digital signature is an electronic method of signing a document that ensures the original content has not changed. It uses a private key to sign a hash and a public key to verify it, so it gives authentication, integrity and non-repudiation. Legal basis in India: IT Act, 2000, Section 3 (digital signature) and Section 3A (electronic signature, added in 2008). Section 5 gives legal recognition to electronic signatures, and the CCA regulates the CAs.

Option (d), '1, 2 and 3', treats all three statements as correct. It is wrong because statements 1 and 2 are about digital certificates and authentication, not the signature. UPSC often builds such questions by mixing related concepts: digital signature, digital certificate, encryption and authentication. Students should remember that the signature is created by the signer's private key, while the certificate is issued by a CA to vouch for the signer's public key.
related: IT Act, 2000 gave legal recognition to digital signatures; the 2008 amendment added electronic signatures (Section 3A).
The Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) licenses Certifying Authorities and runs the Root CA of India.
A digital signature uses the signer's private key to sign and the public key to verify.
A digital signature gives authentication, integrity and non-repudiation, but not confidentiality.
Digital certificates follow the X.509 standard and are issued by Certifying Authorities.
Aadhaar eSign allows online signing of documents using Aadhaar-based OTP authentication.
CERT-In is India's nodal agency for cyber security incidents.
Class 3 DSC is used for e-tendering and e-filing.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: An electronic record that identifies the certifying authority which issued it describes a Digital Signature Certificate, not the signature. Under the IT Act, 2000 a DSC is issued by a licensed Certifying Authority. It carries the subscriber's name, public key, serial number, validity period, and the issuing CA's name and digital signature. The certificate is built to X.509 standards. The Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA), set up in 2000 under the Ministry of Electronics and IT, licenses and supervises CAs such as eMudhra, (n)Code Solutions and Capricorn. Certificates come in Class 1, 2 and 3. Class 3 is used for e-tendering and court filing. The CCA's Root CA of India sits at the top of the trust chain.

2 — Incorrect: Serving as proof of identity to access information or a server on the Internet is the function of authentication credentials, such as passwords, tokens, or a client or server digital certificate in SSL/TLS. It is not the defining feature of a digital signature. A digital signature is applied to a document or message. Certificates can enable secure access, and websites use SSL/TLS certificates (HTTPS) to prove the server's identity. Two-factor authentication, biometrics and Aadhaar-based eKYC are related identity proofs. Aadhaar eSign is an online service that lets Aadhaar holders sign documents using OTP-based authentication, and it is related but distinct. The question's wording mixes up identity authentication with signing.

3 — Correct: This is the standard definition. A digital signature is an electronic method of signing an electronic document that also ensures the original content is unchanged (integrity). It uses public-key (asymmetric) cryptography, for example RSA or ECDSA, together with hash functions such as SHA-256. It provides authentication, integrity and non-repudiation, but not confidentiality, because the document is not encrypted unless done separately. Section 3 of the IT Act, 2000 provided for authentication of electronic records by digital signature, and the 2008 amendment added the technology-neutral electronic signature. Under the Second Schedule, eSign methods are notified. The Indian Evidence Act also gives presumptions for secure electronic records.
summary: The official answer is (c): only statement 3 is correct. A digital signature is an electronic method of signing a document that uses asymmetric cryptography and hashing, so it proves the signer's authenticity and shows the content has not been altered. Statements 1 and 2 describe a digital certificate (and, loosely, authentication credentials), not the digital signature itself.
topic_notes: Digital signatures rest on public-key (asymmetric) cryptography. Each user has a key pair: a private key, kept secret, and a public key, shared openly. To sign, the sender hashes the document (SHA-256, for example) and encrypts the hash with the private key. The receiver decrypts it with the public key and compares the hashes. This gives authentication (who signed), integrity (no change) and non-repudiation (the signer cannot deny it). It does not give confidentiality; that needs encryption of the content. Digital certificate: issued by a trusted Certifying Authority, it binds a public key to an identity and follows X.509. Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is the framework of CAs, registration authorities, certificates and revocation lists. Indian legal framework: the Information Technology Act, 2000 gave legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures. The Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) licenses and monitors CAs and runs the Root CA of India (RCAI). The 2008 amendment introduced the technology-neutral 'electronic signature' (Section 3A). Section 10A recognises contracts formed electronically. Related services: eSign, an online Aadhaar-based signing service, and DigiLocker, a government platform for storing digital documents. Class 1, 2 and 3 DSCs differ in assurance level. Class 3 is used for e-tendering, MCA filings and court e-filing. Hashing, encryption, blockchain, and SSL/TLS (HTTPS) are other angles UPSC may test. Related contrasts: digital signature vs electronic signature (the latter is a broader legal term), digital signature vs digitised (scanned) signature, and symmetric vs asymmetric encryption. Other bodies include CERT-In (cyber incidents) and the Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY).

question:
In the context of wearable technology, which of the following tasks is/are accomplished by wearable devices?
1. Location identification of a person
2. Sleep monitoring of a person
3. Assisting the hearing impaired person Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Economy
detail: Wearable technology means electronic devices worn on or close to the body that contain sensors, a processor and wireless connectivity (Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, GPS, NFC). Common examples are smartwatches (Apple Watch, Galaxy Watch), fitness bands (Fitbit, Mi Band), smart rings (Oura), smart glasses, GPS child or elder trackers, ECG patches, and digital hearing aids. Location identification works through built-in GPS/GNSS (including India's NavIC in some devices), Wi-Fi or cellular triangulation, which is why trackers are used for children, elderly people with dementia and athletes. Sleep monitoring uses accelerometers, gyroscopes, heart-rate (PPG) and SpO2 sensors to estimate sleep stages, duration and disturbances. Hearing assistance comes from wearable digital hearing aids, cochlear processors, and smart earbuds with amplification or live-caption functions. Because all three tasks are performed by existing wearables, every statement is correct. Elimination logic: once a student knows that GPS-enabled watches track location, (b) and (c) fall away; knowing that fitness bands track sleep eliminates (a) and (c); the hearing-aid link confirms (d). In such 'which is/are' questions UPSC usually tests how broad modern wearable applications are.
explanations: Wrong: it recognises only location tracking, but sleep monitoring and hearing assistance are also done by wearables.
Wrong: statements 2 and 3 are correct, but it omits statement 1; GPS-enabled wearables identify location.
Wrong: it accepts only hearing assistance and excludes location tracking and sleep monitoring, both common wearable functions.
Correct: all three tasks (location tracking, sleep monitoring, hearing assistance) are performed by wearable devices.
keyfact: Wearables (smartwatches, bands, trackers, hearing aids) can track location via GPS, monitor sleep, and aid hearing, so the answer is 1, 2 and 3.
option_notes: Option (a), location identification only: this is a real wearable function. GPS trackers and smartwatches use GNSS (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, NavIC), Wi-Fi and cell data to give positions. It is used for child and elder safety, geofencing, sports and SOS alerts. As a sole answer it is too narrow because wearables do more.

Option (b), sleep monitoring and hearing assistance: both are true wearable roles. Sleep trackers use accelerometers, heart-rate and SpO2 sensors to estimate sleep stages, and hearing aids or smart earbuds amplify sound for hearing-impaired users. The option wrongly leaves out location tracking, which GPS watches and trackers do.

Option (c), hearing assistance only: wearable hearing aids are digital devices with microphones, processors and receivers, often Bluetooth-enabled, and cochlear implants have wearable external processors. Some smart earbuds now offer hearing-aid modes. The option is incomplete as it ignores location tracking and sleep monitoring.

Option (d), 1, 2 and 3: the official answer. It reflects the broad applications of wearables: navigation and safety (location), health and wellness tracking (sleep, heart rate, SpO2, ECG, steps) and assistive technology (hearing aids, captioning glasses). Wearables also serve payments (NFC), fitness, industrial safety and medicine.
related: Wearables are part of the Internet of Things ecosystem and often use Bluetooth Low Energy to connect to smartphones.
Smartwatches measure heart rate using photoplethysmography (PPG), an optical method.
NavIC is India's regional navigation satellite system, run by ISRO, covering India and about 1,500 km around.
NFC enables contactless payments on wearables over very short ranges, about 4 cm.
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs processing of personal digital data in India, including health and location data from devices.
Google Glass and Microsoft HoloLens are examples of smart or augmented-reality head-worn wearables.
Cochlear implants have an implanted part and an external wearable sound processor.
The ADIP scheme provides assistive devices, including hearing aids, to persons with disabilities in India.
statements: 1 — Correct: Wearables can identify a person's location. GPS-enabled smartwatches, kids' safety bands and elderly-care trackers use GPS/GNSS, Wi-Fi and cell-tower data to report position in real time. Features include geofencing alerts, SOS buttons that share location with emergency contacts, and fall detection. Apple Watch, Garmin, Samsung Galaxy Watch and many Indian-brand smartwatches (boAt, Noise) have such functions. Uses include child safety, dementia patient monitoring, adventure sports, and logistics or workforce tracking. Concerns include privacy, data protection and surveillance, relevant to India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Some devices also use NavIC, India's regional navigation system.

2 — Correct: Wearables monitor sleep. Fitness bands and smartwatches (Fitbit, Mi Band, Apple Watch) and smart rings (Oura) combine accelerometers, gyroscopes, optical heart-rate (PPG) and SpO2 sensors to estimate sleep duration, light, deep and REM stages, restlessness and breathing disturbances. Algorithms then produce sleep scores and tips. They are consumer-grade estimators rather than clinical polysomnography, though some are used in research and for screening sleep apnoea. Sleep tracking is among the most common features of the quantified-self and digital health movement.

3 — Correct: Wearables assist the hearing impaired. Digital hearing aids, behind-the-ear and in-ear devices, are wearable electronics with microphones, DSP chips and Bluetooth streaming to phones. Cochlear implants have an external wearable sound processor. Smart earbuds (for example AirPods Pro hearing-aid feature, approved by the US FDA in 2024) and smart glasses with live captioning and smartwatch vibration alerts for doorbells or alarms also help. In India, the ADIP scheme and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 support access to assistive devices.
summary: The answer is (d): 1, 2 and 3. Wearable devices such as smartwatches, fitness bands, GPS trackers and wearable hearing aids can identify a person's location, monitor sleep and assist people with hearing impairment.
topic_notes: Wearable technology covers electronic devices worn on the body that collect data, process it and communicate wirelessly, often with a smartphone or cloud. Main categories are wrist-worn (smartwatches, fitness bands), head-worn (smart glasses, AR/VR headsets such as HoloLens, Meta Quest), ear-worn (hearables, hearing aids), smart clothing and textiles, smart rings, body-worn medical patches (ECG, continuous glucose monitors) and implantables or ingestibles. Key enabling technologies are MEMS sensors (accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer), photoplethysmography for heart rate, SpO2 sensors, GPS/GNSS, Bluetooth Low Energy, NFC for contactless payment, low-power chips, flexible batteries and AI algorithms. Applications include fitness tracking, remote patient monitoring, fall detection, sleep analysis, safety and SOS alerts, workplace safety, military use, payments, and assistive aid for the disabled. Wearables are part of the Internet of Things (IoT) and the Internet of Medical Things. Issues UPSC may raise include privacy of health and location data, data protection law (DPDP Act 2023), cybersecurity, battery life, accuracy and medical certification, e-waste, and the digital divide. India is among the largest markets for smartwatches and earwear, with domestic brands such as boAt, Noise and Fire-Boltt, and production-linked incentive schemes for electronics manufacturing. Related technologies often asked alongside include AR/VR, IoT, RFID, NFC, Bluetooth and NavIC. Questions have also asked about smart glasses, quantified self, and 3D printing in the same technology section of the paper.

question:
RNA interference (RNAi)’ technology has ~ gained popularity in the last few years. Why?
1. It is used in developing gene silencing therapies.
2. It can be used in developing therapies for the treatment of cancer. ;
3. It can be used to develop hormone replacement therapies.
4. It can be used to produce crop plants that are resistant to viral pathogens. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Science & Tech
detail: RNA interference is a natural cellular process in which double-stranded RNA is cut by the enzyme Dicer into small interfering RNAs (siRNA) of about 21-23 nucleotides, or into microRNAs (miRNA). These are loaded into the RISC complex (RNA-induced silencing complex), where the Argonaute protein uses the guide strand to find complementary messenger RNA and cleave or block it. The result is post-transcriptional gene silencing. Andrew Fire and Craig Mello discovered it in the nematode C. elegans (1998) and won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2006. Applications include therapies that silence disease-causing genes (Patisiran/Onpattro, approved in 2018, treats hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis). They also include cancer research, where oncogenes or survival genes are silenced, and crops resistant to viruses, nematodes and insects, such as virus-resistant papaya and tobacco and RNAi cotton against pests. Hormone replacement therapy supplies a deficient hormone, for example thyroxine, oestrogen or insulin, and this is the opposite of silencing a gene. Statement 3 is therefore wrong. Eliminating 3 removes options (b) and (c). Statement 2 is valid, which removes (d) and leaves (a).
explanations: Correct: statements 1, 2 and 4 are valid applications of RNAi, and statement 3 is not.
Incorrect: it leaves out statement 1 (gene-silencing therapy) and statement 4 (virus-resistant crops), and includes statement 3, which is wrong.
Incorrect: it includes statement 3, which is wrong, and leaves out statements 2 and 4.
Incorrect: it omits statement 2. RNAi is being researched for cancer therapy, so 'only' makes this option wrong.
keyfact: RNAi = dsRNA, then Dicer, then siRNA, then RISC, which degrades target mRNA (gene silencing). It is used in therapies, in cancer research and in virus-resistant crops, but not in hormone replacement.
option_notes: 1, 2 and 4: this is the correct combination. RNAi is used in gene-silencing therapeutics (siRNA drugs such as Onpattro), in cancer research targeting oncogenes, and in crop biotechnology for resistance to viruses, nematodes and insects. All of these rely on sequence-specific degradation of mRNA by the Dicer and RISC machinery. Fire and Mello received the 2006 Nobel Prize for the discovery.

2 and 3: this pairs a true statement (cancer therapy) with a false one (hormone replacement). Hormone replacement uses supplied hormones, such as levothyroxine, oestrogen and insulin, many of them made by recombinant DNA technology. It does not rely on gene silencing, so RNAi is not used for it.

1 and 3: gene silencing therapy is true, but the hormone replacement claim is false. The option also leaves out cancer therapy and virus-resistant crops. Hormone replacement therapy treats deficiency, for example of thyroid hormone, oestrogen or growth hormone, while RNAi reduces the expression of particular genes.

1 and 4 only: both statements are true, but the option wrongly leaves out cancer therapy. siRNAs and miRNA-based approaches targeting oncogenes, drug-resistance genes and angiogenesis factors are in preclinical and clinical development. RNAi is also widely used in cancer biology screens to find genes tumour cells depend on.
related: RNAi was discovered by Andrew Fire and Craig Mello in C. elegans, and they shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Dicer cuts double-stranded RNA into siRNA, and RISC with Argonaute cleaves the target mRNA.
Patisiran (Onpattro, 2018) was the first FDA-approved siRNA drug.
RNAi works post-transcriptionally and does not alter the DNA sequence, unlike CRISPR-Cas9.
miRNAs are endogenous regulators that usually block translation by partial base-pairing.
The 2020 Chemistry Nobel Prize went to Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna for CRISPR-Cas9.
GEAC (Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee) under MoEFCC regulates GM crops in India.
Hormone replacement therapy relies on recombinant hormones, not RNAi.
statements: 1 — Correct: RNAi is the basis of gene-silencing therapies. Therapeutic siRNA or antisense molecules are designed to match a disease-causing mRNA and switch it off. Patisiran (Onpattro) was the first siRNA drug approved by the US FDA, in 2018, for hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis. Givosiran and inclisiran followed. Delivery uses lipid nanoparticles or GalNAc conjugates, which target the liver. Gene silencing happens after transcription, so the DNA itself is not changed.

2 — Correct: RNAi is being developed for cancer therapy. Researchers design siRNAs against oncogenes (such as KRAS or MYC), against genes for drug resistance (MDR1) and against survival or angiogenesis genes (VEGF). Several candidates are in clinical trials, and the main challenges are delivery, stability, off-target effects and immune reactions. RNAi is also used as a laboratory tool for functional genomics screens that identify cancer-dependency genes. miRNAs themselves act as tumour suppressors or oncomiRs.

3 — Incorrect: Hormone replacement therapy gives the body a missing hormone, such as thyroxine in hypothyroidism, oestrogen at menopause or insulin in diabetes. It does not silence a gene, so RNAi has no direct role. Such hormones are made by recombinant DNA technology, for example with E. coli or yeast. RNAi might at most reduce an overactive hormone pathway, which is not replacement.

4 — Correct: RNAi produces crops resistant to viral pathogens. Plants are engineered to express double-stranded RNA matching viral genes, so the plant's own silencing machinery destroys the invading virus. This is the principle behind virus-resistant papaya (ringspot virus, Hawaii), and similar work covers potato, tobacco and cassava. RNAi is also used against root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne incognita in tobacco) and against insect pests such as cotton bollworm, by silencing essential pest genes.
summary: The answer is (a) 1, 2 and 4. RNAi silences specific genes by degrading their mRNA, so it is used in gene-silencing therapies, in experimental cancer therapies and in making virus-resistant crops. It is not a method for hormone replacement therapy.
topic_notes: RNA interference is a conserved eukaryotic mechanism of sequence-specific gene regulation. Key players: double-stranded RNA, Dicer (an RNase III enzyme that cuts it into 21-23 nt fragments), the RISC complex with the Argonaute (slicer) protein, siRNA (exogenous, perfectly complementary, cleaves mRNA) and miRNA (endogenous, partial complementarity, mostly blocks translation). The process was first seen as co-suppression in petunias (1990) and was explained by Fire and Mello in C. elegans (1998). They received the Nobel Prize in 2006. Applications: (1) therapeutics, with Patisiran (2018, first siRNA drug), Givosiran (acute hepatic porphyria), Lumasiran (primary hyperoxaluria) and Inclisiran (LDL cholesterol); (2) agriculture, with virus-resistant crops, nematode-resistant tobacco, pest-resistant cotton and corn (SmartStax PRO uses RNAi against corn rootworm), and decaffeinated coffee or reduced-allergen crops; (3) research, as a tool for loss-of-function studies and genome-wide screens; (4) diagnostics and antiviral approaches. Limitations are off-target effects, delivery, stability and immune activation. Related technologies for comparison: antisense oligonucleotides, CRISPR-Cas9 (which edits DNA, Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020 to Charpentier and Doudna), mRNA vaccines, and gene therapy using viral vectors. India has Bt cotton, which uses Cry genes (not RNAi), and the GM mustard debate. Other angles UPSC may ask: the difference between RNAi and genome editing, the Cartagena Protocol, GEAC regulation of GM crops in India, and the Nobel Prizes in biotechnology.

question: Recently, scientists observed the merger of giant ‘blackholes’ billions of lightyears away from the Earth. What is the significance of this observation?
options: Possibility of inter-galactic space travel through ‘wormhole’ was confirmed
It enabled the scientists to understand ‘singularity’
subject: Science & Tech
detail: When two black holes spiral towards each other and merge, they release enormous energy as gravitational waves, which are ripples in the fabric of spacetime. Albert Einstein predicted them in 1916 in his General Theory of Relativity. LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory), with detectors at Hanford (Washington) and Livingston (Louisiana) in the USA, made the first direct detection on 14 September 2015 (event GW150914), announced in February 2016. The signal came from two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses merging roughly 1.3 billion light-years away. Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne and Barry Barish won the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics. India is planning LIGO-India at Hingoli, Maharashtra, and Indian scientists contributed to the data analysis. Elimination: the Higgs boson is a particle-physics discovery made at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in 2012, unrelated to black hole mergers. Wormholes remain purely theoretical, and nothing about the observation confirms them. A singularity lies inside the black hole and is not directly probed by a merger signal. So only (b) fits.
explanations: (a) Wrong: the Higgs boson was detected at CERN's LHC in 2012 through proton collisions, not through black hole mergers.
(b) Correct: black hole mergers emit gravitational waves, and their detection (LIGO 2015 onwards) is the significance of such observations.
(c) Wrong: wormholes are a theoretical solution of general relativity, and no observation has confirmed them or the possibility of inter-galactic travel.
(d) Wrong: a singularity is a theoretical point of infinite density inside a black hole, hidden by the event horizon. The merger observation does not let scientists directly understand it.
keyfact: Merging black holes emit gravitational waves, first directly detected by LIGO on 14 September 2015.
option_notes: The Higgs boson is the elementary particle associated with the Higgs field, which gives other particles mass. It was proposed in 1964 by Peter Higgs, François Englert and others. It was discovered in July 2012 at CERN's Large Hadron Collider by the ATLAS and CMS experiments. Higgs and Englert received the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physics. It is called the 'God particle' in popular media. It is part of the Standard Model. Satyendra Nath Bose's name is the origin of the term 'boson'.

Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime caused by accelerating massive objects such as merging black holes or neutron stars. Einstein predicted them in 1916. The Hulse-Taylor binary pulsar gave indirect evidence in 1974. LIGO made the first direct detection on 14 September 2015 (GW150914). In 2017 GW170817, a neutron star merger, was also observed with light. Detectors include LIGO (USA), Virgo (Italy), KAGRA (Japan) and the planned LIGO-India at Hingoli, Maharashtra.

A wormhole, or Einstein-Rosen bridge, is a hypothetical tunnel-like structure in spacetime connecting two distant points. It arises as a solution to Einstein's field equations, proposed in 1935 by Einstein and Nathan Rosen. The term was coined by John Wheeler. Traversable wormholes would need exotic matter with negative energy density. No observational evidence exists, and inter-galactic travel through wormholes remains purely speculative science fiction.

A singularity is a point where gravity is thought to be so intense that density becomes infinite and spacetime curvature diverges, as predicted at the centre of a black hole and at the Big Bang. It is hidden behind the event horizon. Roger Penrose proved singularities are generic predictions of general relativity and shared the 2020 Nobel Prize. Understanding singularities needs a quantum theory of gravity, which does not yet exist.
related: Gravitational waves were predicted by Einstein in 1916 in General Relativity.
LIGO's first direct detection, GW150914, was on 14 September 2015.
LIGO-India is planned at Aundha, Hingoli district, Maharashtra.
The 2017 Physics Nobel went to Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne for gravitational waves.
The Higgs boson was discovered at CERN's LHC in 2012.
The first black hole image (M87*) was released by the Event Horizon Telescope in April 2019.
AstroSat, launched in 2015, is India's first multi-wavelength space observatory.
The Chandrasekhar limit is about 1.4 solar masses.
summary: The answer is (b): the merger of giant black holes billions of light-years away was significant because it produced gravitational waves that were detected. These ripples in spacetime, predicted by Einstein, were first detected directly by LIGO in 2015 from a binary black hole merger.
topic_notes: Black holes are regions of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, escapes beyond the event horizon. The Schwarzschild radius defines the horizon size. Types include stellar-mass black holes (formed from collapsing massive stars), intermediate-mass, and supermassive black holes (millions to billions of solar masses at galactic centres, such as Sagittarius A* in the Milky Way). The Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a black hole (M87*) in April 2019, and of Sagittarius A* in 2022. Chandrasekhar limit (about 1.4 solar masses) is the maximum mass of a stable white dwarf; S. Chandrasekhar was an Indian-born Nobel laureate (1983). Stars above the limit can become neutron stars or black holes. Gravitational waves travel at the speed of light and are detected by laser interferometers that measure tiny changes in arm length, smaller than a proton's width. LIGO's first detection GW150914 came from a merger around 1.3 billion light-years away. The Nobel Prize in Physics 2017 went to Weiss, Barish and Thorne. LIGO-India, approved by the Indian government in 2016 with an estimated cost of about Rs 2,600 crore, will be at Aundha, Hingoli district, Maharashtra, in collaboration with the US NSF, and will be the third LIGO detector. Other related topics: Hawking radiation (theoretical black hole evaporation), the Big Bang, dark matter and dark energy, and multi-messenger astronomy. Indian space astronomy includes AstroSat (2015), India's first dedicated multi-wavelength space observatory, which can study black holes and X-ray binaries.

ocr: Which of the following are the reasons for the occurrence of multi-drug resistance in microbial pathogens in India? 1. Genetic predisposition of some people 2. Taking incorrect doses of antibiotics to cure diseases Using antibiotics in livestock farming Multiple chronic diseases in some people . Select the correct answer using the code given below. 1 and 2 (a) 2 and 3 only (b) 1,3and4 _ (c) (d) 2,3 and 4
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an evolutionary response of microbes to selective pressure from antimicrobial drugs. When antibiotics are taken at sub-therapeutic doses, for too short a duration, without prescription, or for viral infections, susceptible bacteria die while resistant mutants survive and multiply. Resistance genes also spread horizontally through plasmids, transposons and conjugation. In India, key drivers are over-the-counter sale of antibiotics, self-medication, quackery, poor sanitation, weak infection control in hospitals, pharmaceutical effluent and heavy use of antibiotics (including colistin, now banned for animal use in 2019) as growth promoters and prophylaxis in poultry, dairy and aquaculture.
