Bangladesh enjoys duty-free, quota-free access to India under SAFTA, except for tobacco and alcohol. Border haats and the Petrapole-Benapole land port are important trade points. A CEPA (Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement) has been discussed between the two countries.

3 — Incorrect: Nepal has not been India's largest trading partner in South Asia over the last five years; Bangladesh has held that position. Nepal is a vital partner with a large trade volume of around USD 7-8 billion, but it remains well behind Bangladesh. India is Nepal's largest trading partner. Nepal is landlocked and depends on Indian ports such as Kolkata/Haldia and Visakhapatnam for third-country trade. The India-Nepal Treaty of Trade (renewed in 2009) provides for duty-free access of Nepal's manufactured goods to India, and the 1950 Peace and Friendship Treaty is the basic framework for the bilateral relationship.
summary: The official answer is (b) 2 only. Textile and textile articles are an important item in India-Bangladesh trade, but India-Sri Lanka trade has not risen consistently every year over the last decade, and Nepal has not been India's largest trading partner in South Asia (Bangladesh has been).
topic_notes: India's trade with South Asia is a small share of its global trade, about 2-3 percent, and intra-regional trade is low compared with other regions. Bangladesh is India's largest trading partner in South Asia, followed by Nepal, Sri Lanka, and then others such as Bhutan, Pakistan and Afghanistan. Trade in the region runs under frameworks including SAFTA (in force since 2006), under which Least Developed Countries get concessions, and bilateral agreements. India-Bhutan trade operates under a free trade regime, and India is Bhutan's largest trade and development partner. The India-Sri Lanka FTA (ILFTA) has been in force since 2000, and India-Nepal trade follows the Treaty of Trade and Transit. India-Pakistan trade has largely collapsed since 2019, after India withdrew MFN status in 2019 following the Pulwama attack. Connectivity projects matter for trade: BBIN Motor Vehicles Agreement, Kaladan Multimodal Project, Agartala-Akhaura rail link, and integrated check posts (ICPs) such as Petrapole. Regional groupings include SAARC, BIMSTEC and BBIN. India also has an FTA with Bhutan, Nepal and Sri Lanka, and a Preferential Trade Agreement with Afghanistan. India provides lines of credit and concessional development assistance to neighbours under its Neighbourhood First policy. Other possible questions: which neighbour imports the most from India, trade routes such as the Nathu La pass, and Indian exports of electricity to Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan.

question:
Under the Kisan Credit Card scheme, short-term credit support is given to farmers for which of the following purposes ? .
1. Working capital for maintenance of farm assets
2. Purchase of combine harvesters, tractors and mini trucks 68.
3. Consumption requirements of farm households 4, Post-harvest expenses B. Construction of family house and setting up of village cold storage facility Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Economy
detail: The Kisan Credit Card was launched in August 1998 on the recommendation of the R.V. Gupta Committee. NABARD framed the model scheme. It gives farmers timely, single-window, flexible credit through commercial banks, RRBs and cooperative banks. In 2004 the scheme was widened to include investment credit. In 2012 the RBI, following the Task Force under T.M. Bhasin, asked banks to issue KCCs as smart cards with ATM use. The scope covers: (i) short-term credit for crop cultivation; (ii) post-harvest expenses; (iii) produce marketing loans; (iv) consumption needs of the farm household; (v) working capital for maintenance of farm assets and allied activities such as dairy, inland fishery and poultry; and (vi) investment credit for agriculture and allied activities. KCC was extended to animal husbandry and fisheries farmers in 2018-19 and then to all farmers in a campaign from 2020. Elimination logic: purchasing tractors, combine harvesters and mini trucks is medium or long-term investment credit. A family house and a village cold storage facility are not short-term working capital for production. So statements 2 and 5 fail, and only 1, 3 and 4 remain, which is option (b).
explanations: (a) Wrong: it includes 2 and 5, which are investment or infrastructure purposes, and it omits 3 and 4, which are valid.

(b) Correct on the scheme's guidelines: 1, 3 and 4 are exactly the short-term purposes (maintenance working capital, consumption needs, post-harvest expenses). The key supplied with this note says (c), but that conflicts with the scheme's guidelines.
(c) Not supported by the scheme's rules: it adds 2 and 5, which are term-loan or infrastructure purposes, and omits 1. This is the option the supplied key marks as correct, so recheck that key.
(d) Wrong: it accepts all five and ignores that tractors, combine harvesters, family houses and cold storage are long-term capital needs.
keyfact: KCC short-term credit = crop cultivation, post-harvest, marketing, household consumption and maintenance working capital, not tractors, houses or cold storage (so 1, 3, 4 = option b, not c).
option_notes: Option (a), 1, 2 and 5: it mixes a valid purpose (maintenance working capital) with two capital purposes. Machinery purchase is covered by agricultural term loans, with possible subsidy under SMAM (Sub-Mission on Agricultural Mechanisation). Cold storage gets support from NHB/MIDH and the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund of 2020. Housing falls under housing finance or PMAY-G, so this is a typical UPSC trap of plausible but non-KCC items.

Option (b), 1, 3 and 4 only: it is the set of purposes that matches the KCC guidelines. KCC was launched in 1998 on the R.V. Gupta Committee's recommendation and NABARD's model scheme. It is issued by commercial banks, RRBs, cooperatives and small finance banks. The Modified Interest Subvention Scheme gives an effective 4% rate on loans up to Rs 3 lakh. Its coverage was extended to fisheries and animal husbandry from 2018-19.

Option (c), 2, 3, 4 and 5 only: it is a mixed combination that wrongly drops statement 1 and adds capital items. Combine harvesters, tractors and mini trucks are bought with term loans. Setting up a village cold storage is rural infrastructure, funded through the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (Rs 1 lakh crore, 2020) or NHB schemes. Family house construction is not an agricultural production credit purpose. It is the option the supplied key marks correct, so verify that key.

Option (d), all five: it is the over-inclusive option. KCC does have an investment-credit window since 2004 for agriculture and allied activities, but it does not cover buying heavy vehicles, building houses or setting up cold storage as short-term credit. UPSC often uses an 'all of the above' option to test whether students know where a scheme's limits lie.
related: KCC launched in 1998 on the R.V. Gupta Committee recommendation; NABARD framed the model scheme.
Interest subvention: effective 4% on KCC crop loans up to Rs 3 lakh with timely repayment.
KCC was extended to animal husbandry and fisheries farmers in 2018-19.
KCC holders get personal accident insurance cover of Rs 50,000 for death or permanent total disability.
NABARD was set up in 1982 on the Shivaraman Committee recommendation.
PM-KISAN pays Rs 6,000 a year in three instalments; launched 2019.
Agriculture Infrastructure Fund: Rs 1 lakh crore (2020) for post-harvest and cold-chain infrastructure.
RBI's priority sector target for agriculture is 18% of ANBC.
statements: 1 — Correct: Working capital for maintaining farm assets and allied activities is an explicit KCC short-term purpose. KCC finances not only crops but also the running costs of farm equipment, dairy, poultry and fisheries. The 2018-19 Budget extended KCC to animal husbandry and fisheries, with a 2% interest subvention and 3% prompt-repayment incentive. The interest subvention scheme (Modified Interest Subvention Scheme) gives loans up to Rs 3 lakh at an effective 4% for timely repayment. NABARD and the RBI issue the guidelines.

2 — Incorrect: Buying combine harvesters, tractors and mini trucks is capital or investment expenditure, financed by term loans such as agricultural machinery loans, not by short-term KCC working capital. KCC does have an investment-credit component (since 2004) for small asset needs, with a limit often around Rs 1 lakh or more depending on the bank, but large vehicles and machinery purchases are treated as separate term loans. The KCC limit is set on the basis of scale of finance, plus allowances for post-harvest, household and maintenance needs.

3 — Correct: Consumption requirements of the farm household are included in the short-term limit. This recognises that farmers' income is seasonal and the household needs liquidity between harvests. The component was part of the R.V. Gupta Committee design and the NABARD model scheme. The card is valid for 3-5 years with annual review. Crop insurance under PMFBY and personal accident insurance (up to Rs 50,000 for death or permanent disability) are linked to the card.

4 — Correct: Post-harvest expenses are an explicit short-term purpose, for example grading, transport, packing and storage for a short period. A related feature is the marketing-loan facility, which lets farmers avoid distress sale. Loans against warehouse receipts (negotiable warehouse receipts, regulated by WDRA, established 2010) give a similar benefit. Crop loans up to Rs 3 lakh are repaid within 12 months of the crop cycle.

5 — Incorrect: Constructing a family house and setting up a village cold storage are not short-term KCC purposes. Cold storage is financed as infrastructure or investment through the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (Rs 1 lakh crore, 2020), NABARD refinance or the MIDH/NHB capital subsidy. Housing is financed by housing loans or schemes such as PMAY-G. These are long-term, non-working-capital purposes.
summary: Under the KCC scheme, short-term credit covers working capital for farm-asset maintenance (1), consumption needs of the farm household (3) and post-harvest expenses (4). That combination is option (b), 1, 3 and 4 only. The key supplied with this note says (c), but (c) includes statements 2 and 5, which are investment or term-loan purposes and not short-term KCC credit, so this note does not support (c). Please recheck the official answer key before memorising the option letter. The facts below are what matter.
topic_notes: The Kisan Credit Card (KCC) was introduced in August 1998 following the R.V. Gupta Committee, with NABARD preparing the model scheme. It provides adequate, timely, single-window credit from the formal banking system for agriculture and allied activities. Implementers include commercial banks, regional rural banks, cooperative banks and small finance banks. Limits are fixed from the scale of finance for the crop, the cropping pattern and the area cultivated, plus allowances for post-harvest, household and maintenance needs, and a term-loan component. The card is generally valid for 3 years (up to 5 in some cases), with annual review. Farmers get personal accident insurance (Rs 50,000 on death or permanent disability, Rs 25,000 for other disability). The Modified Interest Subvention Scheme (MISS) gives a 2% subvention to lenders and an extra 3% prompt-repayment incentive to farmers, so the effective rate is 4% for loans up to Rs 3 lakh. The scheme was extended to animal husbandry and fisheries farmers in 2018-19, with limits of Rs 2 lakh for animal husbandry (without collateral) and Rs 3 lakh for fisheries, and in 2020 the government ran a saturation drive to include all PM-KISAN beneficiaries. Collateral-free loans up to Rs 1.6 lakh are allowed under RBI instructions (raised to Rs 2 lakh in 2024). Related topics are PM-KISAN (Rs 6,000 a year in three instalments, from 2019), PMFBY crop insurance (2016), NABARD (set up 1982 on the Shivaraman Committee recommendation), the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (Rs 1 lakh crore, 2020), the Agriculture Credit Target, and priority sector lending (agriculture at 18% of ANBC). Possible future questions include who issues KCC, the interest subvention rate, the committee behind it and eligible beneficiaries.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. The weightage of food in Consumer Price Index (CPI) is higher than that in Wholesale Price Index (WPI). The WPI does not capture changes in the prices of services, which CPI does. Reserve Bank of India has now adopted WPI as its key measure of inflation and to decide on changing the key policy rates. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Economy
detail: CPI measures the retail prices paid by consumers. Food and beverages carry a weight of about 45.86% in CPI-Combined (base 2012=100), while in WPI (base 2011-12) the food articles weight is only about 15.26% (primary article group about 22.6%), so statement 1 is correct. WPI tracks the price of goods at the wholesale (first bulk transaction) level and has no component for services such as education, health, transport or housing. CPI includes some services, so statement 2 is correct. The RBI Act was amended in 2016 and the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement with the Government formally adopted CPI-Combined as the nominal anchor. The inflation target is 4% with a tolerance band of +/-2% (2% to 6%), reviewed every five years, and the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of six members sets the repo rate. Earlier, the RBI had shifted from WPI to CPI around 2013-14 following the Urjit Patel Committee (2014). So statement 3 is wrong. Elimination: once statement 3 is rejected, options (c) and (d) go, and since statement 1 is correct, (b) goes, leaving (a). Note that the question as OCR'd is garbled: it lists three statements, with the second and third unnumbered in the text.
explanations: Correct: statements 1 and 2 are true and statement 3 is false, which matches this option exactly.
Incorrect: statement 1 is also true (food has a higher weight in CPI than in WPI), so 2 alone is incomplete.
Incorrect: it supports only statement 3 (the question text says 8, an OCR error for 3), and statement 3 is false because the RBI uses CPI, not WPI.
Incorrect: it includes statement 3, which is false because the RBI's policy anchor is CPI-Combined and not WPI.
keyfact: CPI (food weight about 46%, includes services) is the RBI's inflation anchor at 4% +/-2%; WPI (food about 15%) covers goods only.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only: this is the correct answer. It reflects the facts that CPI is food-heavy (about 46%) and covers services, while WPI is goods-only and has a lower food weight. It also rests on the fact that the RBI targets CPI inflation (4% +/-2%) under the flexible inflation targeting framework. The framework was introduced in 2015 by an agreement between the Government and the RBI and given statutory form in 2016 by amending the RBI Act.

2 only: this would be correct if WPI-versus-CPI weights were reversed, but they are not. The claim that WPI excludes services is true. However, the option wrongly rejects statement 1. CPI's food weight (about 45.86%) is much higher than WPI's food articles weight (about 15%). So the option is incomplete.

Option (c) as OCR'd ('8 only') should read '3 only'. It would mean only the claim that the RBI uses WPI is correct. In fact the RBI abandoned WPI as its headline measure in 2013-14 for CPI. WPI is still published monthly by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, with base 2011-12, but is not a policy anchor.

1, 2 and 3: this would hold only if the RBI used WPI as its key inflation measure. It does not. The MPC, set up in 2016 with six members, watches CPI-Combined for the 4% target. Statements 1 and 2 are right, but the false statement 3 rules out this option.
related: CPI-Combined (base 2012) is the RBI's key inflation measure; the target is 4% with a +/-2% band.
The MPC has six members: three from the RBI, including the Governor with a casting vote, and three appointed by the Centre.
The Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommended CPI as the nominal anchor.
WPI is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT (base 2011-12) and excludes services.
CPI is compiled by the NSO (MoSPI); CPI-IW is compiled by the Labour Bureau.
Food and beverages have a weight of about 45.86% in CPI-Combined.
The 2016 amendment to the RBI Act gave the MPC statutory status.
The inflation target was retained at 4% +/-2% for April 2021 to March 2026.
statements: 1 — Correct: Food has a far larger weight in CPI than in WPI. CPI-Combined (base 2012) has food and beverages at about 45.86%, with the CFPI (Consumer Food Price Index) derived from it. WPI (base 2011-12) has food articles at about 15.3%, and the primary articles group at about 22.6%. CPI is compiled by the NSO under MoSPI (CPI-Combined monthly, with rural and urban parts), and CPI-IW comes from the Labour Bureau. CPI is the retail inflation measure used for DA revisions and, since 2016, for the inflation target. Households spend more on food, which is why the weight is high. Food price shocks therefore move CPI more than WPI.

2 — Correct: WPI covers only goods in three groups: primary articles, fuel and power, and manufactured products. It excludes services. It is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, with base year 2011-12 and monthly release. CPI includes services such as housing, education, health, transport and communication. A Services Price Index has been long discussed, and a Producer Price Index (PPI) is being developed to replace WPI. The Abhijit Sen Committee (2003-04) recommended some of these reforms. WPI is used for contracts and escalation clauses and to compute the GDP deflator indirectly.

3 — Incorrect: The RBI has not adopted WPI. Following the Urjit Patel Committee (January 2014), it adopted CPI as the key measure for monetary policy. The RBI Act, 1934 was amended through the Finance Act 2016 to set up the statutory Monetary Policy Committee, with six members (three from the RBI including the Governor, who has a casting vote, and three appointed by the Centre). The target is 4% CPI with a +/-2% band, notified in March 2021 for 2021-26. If inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must explain to the government why.
summary: The answer is (a): statements 1 and 2 are correct and statement 3 is incorrect. CPI gives food a much higher weight than WPI does, and WPI covers only goods, not services. The RBI uses CPI (combined), not WPI, as its key inflation measure for monetary policy.
topic_notes: Inflation indices in India. CPI: four series exist. CPI-IW (Labour Bureau, base 2016) is used for dearness allowance. CPI-AL and CPI-RL (Labour Bureau, base 1986-87) cover agricultural and rural labourers. CPI-Combined (NSO, MoSPI, base 2012) covers rural, urban and combined, and is the RBI's anchor. It has about 299 items, with food and beverages at about 45.86%, housing about 10%, and fuel and light about 6.8%. WPI: compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, with base 2011-12 and about 697 items. Its weights are primary articles about 22.6% (food articles 15.26%), fuel and power about 13.2%, and manufactured products about 64.2%. It has no services and no direct consumer price. WPI is released on the 14th of each month. CPI is released on the 12th. Monetary policy framework: the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommended CPI and a glide path. The Monetary Policy Framework Agreement of February 2015 set a target of 4% +/-2%. The amended RBI Act (Section 45ZA onwards, 2016) set up the MPC. The target was reviewed in March 2021 and retained for 2021-26. Failure is defined as inflation outside the band for three consecutive quarters. Other measures: the GDP deflator is the broadest measure, and core inflation excludes food and fuel. Related concepts include headline inflation, the repo rate, the standing deposit facility, and the marginal standing facility. A Producer Price Index (PPI) is being developed. The Services Price Index is a future prospect. Possible next questions: base year revisions, the role of the MPC, an inflation target comparison, and the difference between CPI-IW and CPI-Combined.

ocr: Consider the following pairs : River Flows into Mekong — Andaman Sea Thames — Irish Sea 3. Volga — Caspian Sea 4. Zambezi — Indian Ocean Which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched ? (a) land 2 only (b) 3only (©) 38and4only (d) 1,2 and 4only 71. 69. Consider the following statements : In the case of all cereals, pulses and di oil-seeds, the procurement at Minimum Support Price (MSP) is unlimited in any State/UT of India. In the case of cereals and pulses, the MSP is fixed in any State/UT at a level to which the market price will never rise. Which of the statements given above is/ar
subject: Economy
detail: Minimum Support Price (MSP) is the price at which the government is ready to buy crops from farmers, and it acts as a floor or safety net. It is announced by the Union Government on the recommendation of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP), which began in 1965 as the Agricultural Prices Commission and was renamed in 1985. MSP covers about 22 mandated crops: 7 cereals, 5 pulses, 7-8 oilseeds and 4 commercial crops (cotton, raw jute, copra, de-husked coconut). Sugarcane has a separate Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP). MSP is not statutory, so there is no legal guarantee. Actual procurement is concentrated in wheat and rice through the FCI and state agencies. Pulses and oilseeds are bought only under limited schemes such as PM-AASHA (2018), with a cap on the share of production bought. Market prices often rise well above MSP, as with wheat in 2022-23 and pulses in some years. Statement 1 fails because procurement is neither unlimited nor covers all crops in every State/UT. Statement 2 fails because MSP is a floor, not a ceiling. Both are wrong, so (d).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect. Procurement is not unlimited, and it does not cover all cereals, pulses and oilseeds in every State/UT.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 is incorrect. MSP is a floor, and market prices can rise above it.
(c) is wrong because neither statement is correct, so 'both' fails.
(d) is correct. Statement 1 overstates procurement, which is limited and mostly wheat and rice. Statement 2 misdescribes MSP as a ceiling, though it is a floor.
keyfact: MSP is a CACP-recommended floor price with selective, capped procurement; it is not a ceiling and not legally guaranteed.
option_notes: Option (a) says only statement 1 is correct. It would be true only if procurement at MSP were open-ended for every crop and State. In practice open-ended buying is mostly for wheat and paddy, and PM-AASHA caps purchases of pulses and oilseeds. It is wrong here.

Option (b) says only statement 2 is correct. It would require MSP to be a ceiling the market never crosses. MSP is a floor and a safety net that the government announces before sowing, so market prices above it are normal. It is wrong here.
Option (c) says both statements are correct. Both rest on misconceptions about MSP, one about unlimited procurement and one about MSP acting as a price ceiling. It is wrong here.
Option (d) says neither statement is correct. This is the official answer. MSP is a CACP-recommended floor price. Procurement is selective and capped, and market prices can exceed MSP.
related: MSP is announced by the Union Government on CACP recommendations, with CCEA approval.
CACP was set up in 1965 as the Agricultural Prices Commission and renamed in 1985.
Sugarcane has a Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP), not an MSP.
PM-AASHA was launched in 2018 with PSS, PDPS and PSF components.
Budget 2018-19 set MSP at 1.5 times the A2+FL cost.
MSP has no statutory backing and is not legally guaranteed.
Wheat and paddy are the crops mainly procured by FCI and State agencies.
The three farm laws of 2020 were repealed in 2021 after farmer protests.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Procurement at MSP is not unlimited for all cereals, pulses and oilseeds in every State/UT. Open-ended procurement is effectively limited to wheat and paddy in some States such as Punjab, Haryana and MP. Pulses and oilseeds are bought under PM-AASHA with a cap, initially 25% of a State's production. The cap was later relaxed for tur, urad and masur. Procurement is done by FCI, NAFED and state agencies. MSP is announced for about 22 crops but is not legally enforceable. Fixing MSP does not oblige the State to buy all produce. The Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) found only about 6% of farmers benefit from MSP procurement.

2 — Incorrect: MSP is a minimum guaranteed floor price, not a price the market can never exceed. Market prices can and often do rise above MSP, in which case farmers sell in the open market. The government buys only when the market price falls below MSP. MSP is a uniform national price and is not fixed State-by-State. CACP considers cost (A2+FL and C2), demand and supply, domestic and international prices, and the terms of trade. Since Budget 2018-19, MSP has been set at least 1.5 times the A2+FL cost. The Agricultural Prices Commission was set up on the Jha Committee's recommendation.
summary: The answer is (d), neither statement is correct. MSP procurement is not unlimited for all cereals, pulses and oilseeds, and MSP is a floor price, not a level the market price can never rise above. (The image also shows a river-pairs question, but the official answer (d) matches this MSP question, so this note covers the MSP question.)
topic_notes: MSP is the government's price-support instrument, announced for Kharif and Rabi seasons on CACP recommendations after consulting State governments and ministries, and approved by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA). The CACP, a statutory-status-less attached office of the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, started in 1965 as the Agricultural Prices Commission and was renamed in 1985. MSP covers about 22 crops: 7 cereals (paddy, wheat, maize, jowar, bajra, ragi, barley), 5 pulses (gram, tur, moong, urad, lentil), 7-8 oilseeds (groundnut, rapeseed-mustard, toria, soybean, sunflower, sesamum, safflower, nigerseed) and commercial crops (cotton, copra, raw jute, de-husked coconut). Sugarcane has the FRP under the Sugarcane Control Order. Cost concepts are A2 (paid-out costs), A2+FL (adding imputed family labour) and C2 (including rental and interest on owned land and capital). Budget 2018-19 promised MSP at 1.5 times A2+FL. Procurement is done by FCI, NAFED, NCCF and State agencies. PM-AASHA (2018) has three parts: Price Support Scheme, Price Deficiency Payment Scheme and Pilot of Private Procurement Stockist. Madhya Pradesh's Bhavantar Bhugtan Yojana is a price-deficiency model. The Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) on FCI restructuring found only about 6% of farmers sell at MSP. MSP has no statutory backing, and demand for a legal guarantee was a central issue in the 2020-21 farmers' protests against the three farm laws, which were repealed in 2021. A committee on MSP was formed in 2022. Related ideas include buffer stocks, the Public Distribution System, the National Food Security Act 2013, the WTO Agreement on Agriculture and Green Box and Amber Box subsidies, and the 'Peace Clause' on food security stockholding.

question: With reference to the Indian economy, consider the following statements : 1, ‘Commercial Paper’ is a_ short-term unsecured promissory note. ‘Certificate of Deposit’ is a long-term instrument issued by the Reserve Bank of India to a corporation. ‘Call Money’ is a short-term finance used for interbank transactions. ‘Zero-Coupon Bonds’ are the. interest 73. bearing short-term bonds issued by the Scheduled Commercial Banks to corporations. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Economy
detail: This question tests money-market instruments. Commercial Paper (CP) is a short-term, unsecured, discounted promissory note issued by highly rated corporates, primary dealers and financial institutions. Its maturity is 7 days to 1 year, and it is regulated by the RBI. Certificate of Deposit (CD) is a negotiable term-deposit instrument issued by scheduled commercial banks and select financial institutions to depositors, with a maturity of 7 days to 1 year for banks. The RBI does not issue CDs to corporations, so statement 2 is wrong. Call Money is overnight money, and notice money runs 2 to 14 days. It is used mainly for interbank lending and borrowing, for example to meet CRR needs, so statement 3 is right. A Zero-Coupon Bond pays no periodic interest. It is issued at a discount and redeemed at face value, so the return is the discount. It is not a bank-to-corporation short-term instrument, so statement 4 is wrong. Eliminating 2 and 4 leaves 1 and 3 only. Option (b), 4 only, would need statement 4 to be true, and it is false on definition. Option (b) is therefore inconsistent with the facts, and the supplied key should be checked.
explanations: (a) is wrong: statement 1 is correct but statement 2 is false, since a CD is a short-term instrument issued by banks to depositors, not a long-term RBI instrument.

(b) is wrong on the facts, although it is the key supplied with this task. Statement 4 is false because zero-coupon bonds pay no interest. Statements 1 and 3 are true, so '4 only' cannot hold. Verify the official key.
(c) is the option that matches the facts: Commercial Paper (1) and Call Money (3) are correctly described, and statements 2 and 4 are wrong.
(d) is wrong: it includes statements 2 and 4, both false, and omits statement 1, which is true.
keyfact: CP and Call Money are valid as described; CDs are issued by banks, not the RBI, and zero-coupon bonds pay no interest. The correct option is (c); verify the supplied key (b).
related: Treasury Bills have maturities of 91, 182 and 364 days and are issued at a discount.
Call money is overnight; notice money is 2 to 14 days.
Commercial Paper maturity is 7 days to 1 year, with a minimum investment of Rs 5 lakh.
CDs are issued by banks; CP is issued by corporates, primary dealers and financial institutions.
The Liquidity Adjustment Facility was introduced in India in 2000.
Zero-coupon bonds are issued at a discount and redeemed at face value, with no interest paid in between.
Masala bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued outside India.
MSF rate is above the repo rate; the reverse repo rate is below it.
statements: 1 — Correct: CP is indeed a short-term unsecured promissory note. Commercial Paper is a money-market instrument issued at a discount to face value by corporates, primary dealers and All-India Financial Institutions. It is unsecured and negotiable. Maturity is 7 days to 1 year. It was introduced in India in 1990 and is governed by RBI directions. Issuers need a minimum credit rating (A3) from an approved agency. Minimum investment is Rs 5 lakh. It is issued in dematerialised form, and it helps corporates meet working-capital needs cheaply.

2 — Incorrect: A CD is not a long-term instrument and the RBI does not issue it to corporations. Certificates of Deposit are negotiable, unsecured usance-based instruments issued by scheduled commercial banks (except RRBs and small finance banks in some cases) and select all-India financial institutions. They are issued against funds deposited by investors. Maturity is 7 days to 1 year for banks, and 1 to 3 years for financial institutions. They were introduced in 1989. They are issued at a discount, in minimum lots of Rs 5 lakh, and are freely transferable after the issue date.

3 — Correct: Call Money is short-term finance used for interbank transactions. Call/notice money is the market where banks and primary dealers borrow and lend for 1 day (call or overnight) or 2 to 14 days (notice money). Banks use it to meet CRR requirements and temporary liquidity gaps. The interest rate is the call rate. It is part of the money market, and the weighted average call rate is a key operating target of monetary policy. The RBI also uses the LAF corridor, with the repo rate and the MSF rate, to guide it.

4 — Incorrect: Zero-coupon bonds do not bear periodic interest and are not specifically issued by banks to corporations. A zero-coupon bond is issued at a deep discount and redeemed at face value on maturity. The investor's return is the difference between issue price and face value. No coupon is paid in between. Issuers include governments, corporations and financial institutions. Maturities are often long, as in US Treasury STRIPS. In India, some institutions such as NABARD and IDBI have issued such bonds. The statement's description as interest-bearing is self-contradictory.
summary: On the facts, statements 1 and 3 are correct and statements 2 and 4 are wrong, which gives option (c), 1 and 3 only. That was the original UPSC 2020 key as I recall it. The key supplied with this task, (b) 4 only, cannot be justified, because Zero-Coupon Bonds carry no periodic interest and are not short-term bank-to-corporation paper. Please verify the key against the official UPSC answer sheet before relying on this note.
topic_notes: The money market handles short-term funds, up to one year. The RBI regulates it. Its main instruments are Treasury Bills (91, 182 and 364 days, issued by the Government of India at a discount), Call/Notice/Term money, Commercial Paper, Certificates of Deposit, Repos and reverse repos, and Collateralised Borrowing and Lending Obligation (CBLO), now replaced by TREPS. Commercial bills are also used. Call money is overnight; notice money is 2 to 14 days; term money is over 14 days. The call rate is a key market rate. CP is unsecured and issued by corporates; CD is issued by banks. Both have a 7-day minimum maturity and are issued at a discount. Treasury bills are the safest instrument and have no credit risk. Cash Management Bills are short-term instruments issued by the government for temporary cash needs. The capital market, by contrast, deals in long-term instruments such as shares, debentures and bonds. Zero-coupon bonds are issued at a discount and redeemed at par. Related ideas include the monetary policy tools: repo rate, reverse repo rate, MSF, bank rate, CRR and SLR. The Liquidity Adjustment Facility was introduced in 2000. UPSC often asks about the difference between money and capital market instruments, who issues each instrument, and their maturities. It also asks about other instruments such as Participatory Notes, ADRs/GDRs, masala bonds and G-Secs.

question:
With reference to the cultural history of India, consider the following pairs :
1. Parivrajaka — Renunciant and Wanderer
2. Shramana — Priest witha high status
3. Upasaka — Lay follower of Buddhism Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched ?
subject: Ancient History
detail: Parivrajaka comes from 'parivraj', to wander. It denotes a wandering renunciant who has left household life and does not stay in one place. Such wanderers were common in the age of the Upanishads and the heterodox sects, and the Buddha and Mahavira were in this tradition. Shramana comes from 'shram', to exert effort. It means an ascetic who seeks liberation through personal effort and austerity, not through Vedic ritual. Shramana movements (Buddhism, Jainism, Ajivika) rejected priestly authority and sacrifice. The high-status priest is the Brahmana, with the purohita or ritual specialist as a related figure. So pair 2 is wrong because it reverses the Shramana-Brahmana contrast. Upasaka (male) and Upasika (female) are lay followers of Buddhism who take the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts but do not take monastic vows. Jain lay followers are called Shravaka and Shravika. Elimination: pair 2 is clearly wrong, which rules out (a), (c) and (d) and leaves (b). The key supplied with the task says (a), which conflicts with these facts.
explanations: Option (a) 1 and 2 only is wrong on the facts, because it treats Shramana as a high-status priest. A Shramana is an ascetic who opposed priestly ritualism. The task says (a) is the official key, but that cannot be reconciled with the meaning of the term.

Option (b) 1 and 3 only fits the facts: Parivrajaka is a wandering renunciant and Upasaka is a Buddhist lay follower, while the Shramana pair is wrong. This matches the facts, and I believe it is the actual UPSC answer.
Option (c) 2 and 3 only is wrong because it includes the incorrect Shramana pair and leaves out the correct Parivrajaka pair.
Option (d) 1, 2 and 3 is wrong because pair 2 is incorrect: a Shramana is an ascetic, not a priest.
keyfact: Shramana = ascetic, not priest (priest = Brahmana); Parivrajaka = wandering renunciant; Upasaka = Buddhist lay follower. On the facts the answer is (b), though the supplied key said (a).
option_notes: Option (a) pairs 1 and 2. Parivrajaka is a wandering ascetic, and Shramana is an ascetic of the non-Vedic traditions (Buddhism, Jainism, Ajivika). A Shramana is not a priest. The priestly class is the Brahmana, whose role was to perform Vedic sacrifices and rituals. In ancient India Brahmanas and Shramanas were two distinct religious currents, and Ashoka's edicts honour both.

Option (b) pairs 1 and 3. Parivrajaka means a wandering renunciant. Upasaka means a Buddhist lay devotee who takes the Three Refuges and Five Precepts. Both pairs are correct. Together they show the distinction between those who renounce household life and those who stay in it while following the faith.

Option (c) pairs 2 and 3. Upasaka is a correct pairing, but Shramana as a high-status priest is not. The Shramana tradition emerged in the 6th century BCE in the Gangetic plains, with figures such as Mahavira, the Buddha and Makkhali Gosala. They emphasised moral conduct, meditation and austerity over sacrifice.

Option (d) pairs 1, 2 and 3. It would be correct only if all three pairs were accurate. Pair 2 fails because a Shramana is an ascetic, so this option is wrong. Related terms to remember are Bhikkhu (Buddhist monk), Sangha (monastic order), Sannyasi, Shravaka (Jain lay follower) and Brahmana (priest).
related: Shramana means an ascetic or striver, and the priestly class is the Brahmana.
Upasaka and Upasika are male and female Buddhist lay followers.
The Buddhist Tipitaka is made up of the Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma Pitakas.
The Jain lay followers are Shravaka and Shravika.
The Brahmanical ashramas are Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha and Sannyasa.
Ajivika leader Makkhali Gosala was a contemporary of Mahavira and the Buddha.
Ashoka's edicts honour both Brahmanas and Shramanas.
Panchasila is the five-precept moral code of Buddhist lay followers.
statements: 1 — Correct: A Parivrajaka is a wandering renunciant. Parivrajaka means a wandering mendicant who has given up home and family life. The term appears in Upanishadic, Buddhist and Jain texts and in the Dharmasutras, where it is a stage of renunciation linked to sannyasa. Wanderers of different sects debated in assemblies and gave rise to heterodox schools. Sariputta and Moggallana were parivrajakas before joining the Buddha. Ashokan edicts mention Brahmanas and Shramanas, and later texts such as the Puranas also use the term.

2 — Incorrect: A Shramana is an ascetic, not a high-status priest. Shramana (Pali 'samana') refers to ascetic seekers of the 6th century BCE who rejected Vedic ritual and priestly dominance. These included Buddhists, Jains, Ajivikas (Makkhali Gosala), and materialists such as Ajita Kesakambali. Ashokan inscriptions often say 'Brahmanas and Shramanas' together as respected groups. The Greek ambassador Megasthenes described 'Sarmanes' and 'Brahmanes' separately. The priest with high status is the Brahmana, and the royal priest is the purohita.

3 — Correct: An Upasaka is a lay follower of Buddhism. Upasaka (male) and Upasika (female) are lay devotees who take refuge in the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha and observe the Five Precepts. They support monks with alms and donations. Ashoka calls himself an upasaka in the Minor Rock Edict. Householders such as Anathapindika and the courtesan Ambapali were prominent lay devotees. Lay followers are distinguished from bhikkhus and bhikkhunis, who are ordained monks and nuns. In Jainism the equivalents are Shravaka and Shravika.
summary: Pairs 1 and 3 are correctly matched, so on the facts the answer is 1 and 3 only, which is option (b). The task states that the official key is (a), but that key would require Shramana to mean a high-status priest, and it does not. Shramana means an ascetic or striver. Please check this against the official UPSC final answer key before relying on the note.
topic_notes: The 6th century BCE saw a wave of religious ferment in the middle Gangetic plains. Brahmanical tradition emphasised Vedic sacrifice, priestly authority and the varna order. The Shramana tradition challenged this with asceticism, ethics, meditation and personal effort toward liberation. Its main streams were Buddhism (Gautama Buddha), Jainism (Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara), Ajivikas (Makkhali Gosala), and materialists (Charvaka/Lokayata, Ajita Kesakambali). Buddhist texts mention 62 heterodox views in the Brahmajala Sutta. The Buddhist community has four parts: Bhikkhu, Bhikkhuni, Upasaka and Upasika. Lay followers take the Three Refuges (Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha) and Five Precepts (Panchasila). Monks follow the Vinaya Pitaka rules and nuns follow additional rules. Jain followers are divided into monks and nuns (Sadhu and Sadhvi) and lay followers (Shravaka and Shravika), with the five Mahavratas for ascetics and the Anuvratas for laity. Brahmanical ashrama stages are Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha and Sannyasa. Parivrajaka is a wandering renunciant and often overlaps with sannyasin. Ashoka's edicts use the phrase 'Shramanas and Brahmanas' to show state respect for both groups. Megasthenes described Sarmanes and Brahmanes. Buddhist councils, the Pali Canon (Tipitaka), and the spread of Buddhism under Ashoka are linked topics. UPSC often asks about terms such as Sangha, Vihara, Chaitya, Stupa, Tirthankara, Jina and Arhat, and about the differences between Theravada and Mahayana.

question:
With reference to Indian elephants, consider the following statements :
1. The leader of an elephant group is a female.
2. The maximum gestation period can be 22 months.
3. Anelephant can normally go on calving till the age of 40 years only.
4. Among the States in India, the highest elephant population is in Kerala. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Asian elephant herds are matriarchal. The herd is led by the oldest, most experienced female, the matriarch, and consists of related females and their young. Adult males leave and live alone or in bachelor groups. Gestation is about 18 to 22 months, the longest of any land mammal, so 22 months is the maximum. A single calf is born, and the calving interval is about 4 to 5 years. Females breed from about 10 to 15 years of age and can continue well past 40, up to roughly 50 or more, so the word 'only' in statement 3 makes it wrong. Under the 2017 census (Synchronous All India Elephant Estimation) India had about 27,312 elephants. Karnataka had the most (about 6,049), then Assam (about 5,719), then Kerala (about 3,054). Statement 4 is therefore wrong. Elimination: statements 1 and 2 are true, which removes (b), (c) and (d), because (b) and (d) include 4 and (c) is only statement 3. This leaves (a). If the key really says (b), it conflicts with the census data.
explanations: (a) Correct on the facts: statement 1 (matriarch leads the herd) and statement 2 (gestation up to about 22 months) are true, while 3 and 4 are false.

(b) Wrong on the facts, although it is the key supplied: it includes statement 4, but Karnataka, not Kerala, has the highest elephant population. It also omits statement 1, which is true. This option does not match the verified data.
(c) Wrong: statement 3 is false because females can calve beyond 40 and the word 'only' makes it incorrect, so '3 only' cannot be right.
(d) Wrong: it includes 3 and 4, both false, and it omits statement 2, which is true.
keyfact: Matriarch leads the herd; gestation is 18 to 22 months; the highest elephant population is in Karnataka, not Kerala, so on the facts the answer is (a) and the supplied key (b) conflicts with the data.
option_notes: Statements 1 and 2 only. This reflects the two true facts: elephant herds are led by a matriarch, and gestation lasts 18 to 22 months. Both are standard facts about the Asian elephant (Elephas maximus). It is a schedule I species under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, is listed as Endangered by the IUCN, and was declared India's National Heritage Animal in 2010. This is the combination consistent with the facts.

Statements 2 and 4 only. Statement 2 is true, but statement 4 is false, since Kerala ranks third after Karnataka and Assam. Kerala has about 3,054 elephants in the 2017 census and has major habitats in Periyar, Wayanad and Silent Valley. The Kerala state animal is the elephant. This combination would be right only if Kerala led the count, which it does not.

Statement 3 only (printed '8' by OCR). It says an elephant can calve only until 40. This is wrong because wild females can reproduce into their 50s. Elephants live 60 to 70 years, with menopause-like decline in fertility only late in life. The option fails because it excludes the true statements 1 and 2.

Statements 1, 3 and 4 only. This mixes the true statement 1 with two false statements, 3 and 4. Karnataka, not Kerala, tops the elephant count, and females calve past 40. It also excludes the true statement 2 on gestation. Such three-statement combinations are used as distractors to test whether you know the state-wise census ranking.
related: Karnataka has the highest elephant population (about 6,049, 2017 census), followed by Assam and Kerala.
Total elephants in India in 2017: about 27,312.
Project Elephant was launched in 1992; the first reserve was Singhbhum (Jharkhand).
Elephant gestation is 18 to 22 months, the longest of any land mammal.
Elephant herds are led by a matriarch; males leave at puberty.
The elephant was declared National Heritage Animal in 2010 on the Standing Committee on National Board for Wildlife's recommendation.
World Elephant Day is 12 August; Gaj Yatra was launched in 2017.
The Asian elephant is Endangered (IUCN) and in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
statements: 1 — Correct: Elephant herds are led by a matriarch, the oldest and most experienced female. Asian and African elephants live in matrilineal family units of related females and their offspring. The matriarch decides where to feed, drink and move, especially in drought, and she stores memory of routes and water sources. Males leave the natal herd at puberty, around 10 to 15 years, and live alone or in loose bachelor groups. Adult males join herds mainly for mating. Matriarch loss can disrupt a herd's survival and its corridor use.

2 — Correct: The gestation period of the Asian elephant is about 18 to 22 months, the longest among land mammals, so 22 months is the maximum. Usually one calf is born, weighing about 100 kg. Twins are rare. Calves are nursed for two years or more, and calving intervals are about 4 to 5 years. Because the reproductive rate is slow, populations recover slowly from poaching or habitat loss. This is one reason the species is listed as Endangered by the IUCN and is in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.

3 — Incorrect: A female elephant is not limited to calving until 40. Females reach sexual maturity at about 10 to 15 years and can breed into their 50s, while wild lifespans reach 60 to 70 years. Fertility declines with age, but 'only till 40' is an absolute claim and is false. The qualifier 'only' is a common UPSC trap. Late-life breeding matters because a long reproductive span partly offsets the very long gestation and the long birth intervals of about 4 to 5 years.

4 — Incorrect: Karnataka has the highest elephant population in India, about 6,049 in the 2017 census. Assam is second with about 5,719 and Kerala third with about 3,054. The 2017 national total was about 27,312, down from about 29,964 in 2012. Elephant numbers are concentrated in the Western Ghats (Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu), the north-east and the central-eastern belt. The next census is conducted at five-year intervals under Project Elephant (launched 1992), and the Gaj Yatra campaign was launched in 2017.
summary: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so the correct answer on the facts is (a) 1 and 2 only. The supplied key says (b), but that would require statement 4 to be true. Karnataka, not Kerala, has India's largest elephant population, so (b) cannot be justified. I believe the official UPSC 2020 key is (a), and the key given with this question should be re-checked.
topic_notes: Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) is India's National Heritage Animal (2010). It is in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, listed as Endangered by the IUCN Red List, and in CITES Appendix I. Project Elephant was launched in 1992 by the MoEFCC to protect elephants, habitats and corridors and to address human-elephant conflict. There are 33 Elephant Reserves, and the first was Singhbhum (Jharkhand). Total elephants in the 2017 census were about 27,312 (29,964 in 2012). The top states are Karnataka, Assam, Kerala, then Tamil Nadu and Odisha. The census method is Synchronous All India Elephant Estimation, with the next due about every five years. Social structure: matriarchal herds of related females, with males leaving at puberty. Males experience musth, a period of raised testosterone and aggression. Gestation is 18 to 22 months, and a single calf is usual. Lifespan is about 60 to 70 years. Threats include habitat fragmentation, human-elephant conflict, train collisions, electrocution, ivory poaching (mostly affecting tusked males) and crop-raiding conflict. Other things UPSC could ask: the Elephant Task Force (Gajah report, 2010), the Right of Passage report on elephant corridors (2005, updated 2017), the 101 identified corridors, the Elephant Reserve of Kaziranga-Karbi Anglong, the Gaj Yatra campaign, and World Elephant Day (12 August). The African elephant is a separate species and is listed as Vulnerable (the savanna elephant is Endangered). Asian elephants have smaller ears, only males have prominent tusks (tushes in females) and the back is convex, whereas African elephants have concave backs and larger ears.

question:
Which of the following Protected Areas are located in Cauvery basin ?
1. Nagarhole National Park
2. Papikonda National Park
3. Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve 4, , Wayanad Wildlife Sanctuary Select the correct answer using the code given below : :
subject: Environment
detail: The Cauvery rises at Talakaveri in the Brahmagiri range of Kodagu, Karnataka, and flows through Karnataka and Tamil Nadu to the Bay of Bengal. Its major tributaries are Hemavati, Lakshmanatirtha, Kabini, Shimsha and Arkavathi (Karnataka), and Bhavani, Noyyal and Amaravati (Tamil Nadu). Nagarhole (Rajiv Gandhi) National Park in Karnataka lies in the Kabini catchment, and the Kabini reservoir separates it from Bandipur. Wayanad Wildlife Sanctuary in Kerala is drained by the Kabini, which flows east into Karnataka. Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve in Erode district, Tamil Nadu, is drained by the Bhavani and Moyar rivers. Papikonda National Park, in the East and West Godavari districts of Andhra Pradesh, is on both sides of the Godavari gorge in the Papi Hills. It belongs to the Godavari basin. Elimination: Papikonda being in the Godavari basin removes (a) and (d). Of the remaining options, (b) leaves out Nagarhole, which is clearly a Kabini-basin park, so (c) is correct.
explanations: (a) 1 and 2 only is wrong. It includes Papikonda, which is in the Godavari basin, and it leaves out Sathyamangalam and Wayanad, which are in the Cauvery basin.
(b) 3 and 4 only is wrong. Both items are correct, but it wrongly leaves out Nagarhole, which lies in the Kabini (Cauvery) basin.
(c) 1, 3 and 4 only is correct. Nagarhole, Sathyamangalam and Wayanad lie in Cauvery tributary catchments (Kabini and Bhavani), and Papikonda does not.
(d) 1, 2, 3 and 4 is wrong because it wrongly adds Papikonda, a Godavari-basin park.
keyfact: Nagarhole, Sathyamangalam and Wayanad are in the Cauvery basin; Papikonda is in the Godavari basin, so the correct answer is (c) 1, 3 and 4 only.
option_notes: Option (a) pairs Nagarhole and Papikonda. Nagarhole is a Karnataka tiger-elephant park in the Kabini catchment, part of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve. Papikonda is an Andhra Pradesh park (notified 2008) in the Papi Hills of the Eastern Ghats, on the Godavari gorge. The two belong to different river basins, so this pairing cannot be right for a question about the Cauvery basin.

Option (b) pairs Sathyamangalam and Wayanad. Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve (Tamil Nadu, 2013) is drained by the Bhavani and Moyar rivers. Wayanad Wildlife Sanctuary (Kerala, 1973) is drained by the Kabini. Both are in the Cauvery basin and are linked through the Nilgiri landscape, a major elephant and tiger habitat. The option is incomplete because it omits Nagarhole.

Option (c) combines Nagarhole, Sathyamangalam and Wayanad. These are Cauvery-basin protected areas in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Kerala. They sit in the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve landscape, which also includes Bandipur, Mudumalai and BRT. The Kabini and Bhavani drain them into the Cauvery. This is the correct answer.

Option (d) adds Papikonda to the other three. Papikonda is the only one outside the Cauvery basin, as it lies in the Godavari basin. It is in Andhra Pradesh and was notified as a national park in 2008. Its forests are threatened by submergence from the Polavaram project, which is why the option fails.
related: The Cauvery rises at Talakaveri in the Brahmagiri hills, Kodagu district, Karnataka.
Kabini and Bhavani are important Cauvery tributaries; the Kabini rises in Wayanad, Kerala.
Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (1986) was India's first biosphere reserve.
Papikonda National Park is on the Godavari in Andhra Pradesh.
Ranganathittu Bird Sanctuary is on the Cauvery near Srirangapatna, Karnataka.
The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal gave its final award in 2007; the Supreme Court revised it in 2018.
Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserve was notified in 2013 and is the largest in Tamil Nadu.
Nagarhole is also called Rajiv Gandhi National Park.
statements: 1 — Correct: Nagarhole lies in the Kabini sub-basin of the Cauvery. Nagarhole, also called Rajiv Gandhi National Park, is in the Kodagu and Mysuru districts of Karnataka. It became a national park in 1983 and a tiger reserve in 1999, and it is part of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve. The Kabini reservoir forms its boundary with Bandipur, and the park is known for tigers, elephants, gaur and dhole.

2 — Incorrect: Papikonda is in the Godavari basin, not the Cauvery. Papikonda National Park lies in the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh, in the East Godavari, West Godavari and Alluri Sitarama Raju districts. The Godavari cuts a gorge through the Papi Hills here. It was notified as a national park in 2008. It is threatened by submergence from the Polavaram project, and it holds tigers, leopards, bison and many bird species.

3 — Correct: Sathyamangalam is drained by the Bhavani, a major Cauvery tributary. The tiger reserve is in Erode district, Tamil Nadu, and was notified in 2013. It is the largest tiger reserve in Tamil Nadu and a key corridor linking the Western Ghats and Eastern Ghats. It connects Bandipur, Mudumalai, BRT and Nilgiri areas, and its fauna includes elephants, tigers and vultures.

4 — Correct: Wayanad Wildlife Sanctuary is in the Kabini (Cauvery) catchment. It lies in Kerala and was established in 1973. It is part of the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve and adjoins Nagarhole, Bandipur and Mudumalai, forming one of the largest elephant habitats in India. The Kabini river, which flows east into Karnataka, drains the area. It has a high density of elephants, along with tigers, gaur and other wildlife.
summary: The correct answer is (c) 1, 3 and 4 only, not (a) as stated in the prompt. Nagarhole, Sathyamangalam and Wayanad all drain into the Cauvery system (Kabini and Bhavani rivers). Papikonda National Park lies on the Godavari in the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh, so statement 2 is wrong. Option (a) would need Papikonda to be in the Cauvery basin, which it is not, so I could not support (a).
topic_notes: The Cauvery is a peninsular river about 800 km long, rising at Talakaveri in Kodagu. It flows through Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, touches Kerala and Puducherry (Karaikal) in its basin, and enters the Bay of Bengal south of Cuddalore. Its basin covers Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala and Puducherry. Left-bank tributaries are Harangi, Hemavati, Shimsha and Arkavathi. Right-bank tributaries are Lakshmanatirtha, Kabini, Bhavani, Noyyal and Amaravati. Famous sites include Shivanasamudra falls and Hogenakkal falls, and the Krishnaraja Sagar and Mettur dams. The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal was set up in 1990 and gave its final award in 2007. The Supreme Court modified the allocation in 2018, and the Cauvery Water Management Authority was constituted in 2018. Protected areas in the basin include Nagarhole, Bandipur (Kabini and Nugu), Mudumalai (Moyar), BRT (Biligiri Rangaswamy Temple) Tiger Reserve, Sathyamangalam, Wayanad, Brahmagiri, Talakaveri, Pushpagiri, Cauvery Wildlife Sanctuary (Karnataka, elephants), Ranganathittu Bird Sanctuary (on the Cauvery near Srirangapatna), and Grizzled Squirrel sanctuary. Related river-basin contrasts: Godavari basin has Papikonda, Kawal and Tadoba-Andhari; Krishna basin has Nagarjunsagar-Srisailam; Tungabhadra has Daroji sloth bear sanctuary. UPSC often asks which park lies in which river basin, which parks fall in a biosphere reserve (Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve was the first, in 1986), and which tiger reserves were notified recently.

ocr: With . reference to India’s biodiversity, 74. Ceylon frogmouth, Coppersmith barbet, Gray-chinned minivet and White-throated redstart are (a) Birds (b) Primates (c) Reptiles (ad) Amphibians
subject: Environment
detail: Ceylon frogmouth (Batrachostomus moniliger), Coppersmith barbet (Psilopogon haemacephalus), Gray-chinned minivet (Pericrocotus solaris) and White-throated redstart (Phoenicurus schisticeps) are all birds (class Aves). The names mislead: 'frogmouth' suggests an amphibian, and 'copper' and 'redstart' suggest nothing in particular, which is the trap UPSC set. The Ceylon frogmouth is a small nocturnal bird of the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, in the nightjar order Caprimulgiformes. The Coppersmith barbet is a common Asian barbet whose call sounds like a hammer on metal. The Gray-chinned minivet is a Himalayan and north-eastern forest bird. The White-throated redstart is a Himalayan chat that moves to lower altitudes in winter. Elimination: primates have hair and live births, and India's primates are macaques, langurs, gibbons and lorises. Reptiles have scales and lay amniotic eggs. Amphibians have moist skin and go through a larval stage. None of the four names belongs to any of those groups. Because the species are verifiably birds, (a) is the factually correct answer. A key of (c) cannot be reconciled with the species named, so it is probably a transcription error in the brief.
explanations: Correct on the facts. All four species are birds (class Aves): a nocturnal frogmouth, a barbet, a minivet and a redstart. This matches their feathers, beaks and egg-laying, and their listing in Indian bird checklists.
Wrong. Primates in India are species like rhesus macaque, lion-tailed macaque, hoolock gibbon, langurs and slender loris. None of the four names is a primate.

This is the option the supplied key marks as correct, but the facts do not support it. None of the four species is a reptile: reptiles are snakes, lizards, turtles, crocodiles and similar animals. The name 'frogmouth' does not make the Ceylon frogmouth an amphibian or a reptile, since it is a bird. Verify the key against the official UPSC answer sheet.
Wrong. Amphibians are frogs, toads, salamanders and caecilians. The word 'frogmouth' is a trap, because the bird is named for its wide, frog-like gape and is not a frog.
keyfact: Ceylon frogmouth, Coppersmith barbet, Gray-chinned minivet and White-throated redstart are all birds, so (a) is the factually correct answer, even though the supplied key says (c).
option_notes: Birds (Aves) are warm-blooded, feathered, egg-laying vertebrates with beaks and forelimbs modified as wings. India has roughly 1,350 or more species, about 12 to 13 percent of the world total. Key bodies and places include the Bombay Natural History Society, founded in 1883, and the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, which gives protection by schedule. The Great Indian Bustard is Critically Endangered. Bharatpur (Keoladeo) is a famous bird sanctuary.

Primates are mammals with grasping hands, forward-facing eyes and large brains. India has about 25 species. These include the rhesus and bonnet macaques, the lion-tailed macaque of the Western Ghats, the Nilgiri langur, the golden langur of Assam, the hoolock gibbon (India's only ape), and the slender and slow lorises. Primates are generally protected under Schedule I or II of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972.

Reptiles are cold-blooded, scaly, amniotic vertebrates, namely snakes, lizards, turtles and tortoises, crocodilians and the tuatara. India has over 600 species. Examples are the gharial, saltwater and mugger crocodiles, the king cobra and Olive Ridley turtles. The Gharial Conservation Project began in 1975. Many reptiles are listed in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972.

Amphibians are cold-blooded vertebrates with moist, permeable skin. They typically have an aquatic larval stage and a mostly terrestrial adult stage. The groups are frogs and toads (Anura), salamanders (Caudata) and caecilians (Gymnophiona). India has about 450 or more species, concentrated in the Western Ghats, which is a biodiversity hotspot. The purple frog (Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis) is a well-known example, as is the Malabar gliding frog. Amphibians are widely seen as indicators of environmental health.
related: Ceylon frogmouth: nocturnal bird of the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka.
Coppersmith barbet: its call imitates a hammer striking metal.
Great Indian Bustard: Critically Endangered, with its main population in Rajasthan.
India has 4 biodiversity hotspots out of 36 globally.
Bombay Natural History Society was founded in 1883.
Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 provides scheduled protection to species.
Purple frog (Nasikabatrachus) is an amphibian endemic to the Western Ghats.
Gharial is a Critically Endangered reptile protected under Schedule I.
summary: All four animals named are birds, so on the facts the correct choice is (a) Birds. The key supplied with this task says (c) Reptiles, but that conflicts with the taxonomy of every species listed. Note that the image shows the question numbered 74, not 68. Check your own source before relying on the key.
topic_notes: This question tests identification of animal groups from common names in India's biodiversity. UPSC often uses names that mislead, such as 'frogmouth' for a bird. The four species are all birds. The Ceylon frogmouth (Batrachostomus moniliger) lives in the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, is nocturnal, and is a relative of nightjars. The Coppersmith barbet (Psilopogon haemacephalus) is a green bird with a crimson forehead and breast, and its metallic 'tuk-tuk' call gives it its name. The Gray-chinned minivet (Pericrocotus solaris) is a colourful forest bird of the Himalayan foothills and north-east India. The White-throated redstart (Phoenicurus schisticeps) is a Himalayan chat that breeds at high altitudes. India is one of 17 megadiverse countries and has 4 of the 36 global biodiversity hotspots: the Himalaya, the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Sundaland (Nicobar). Related institutions are the Bombay Natural History Society (1883), the Zoological Survey of India (1916), the Botanical Survey of India (1890) and the Wildlife Institute of India (Dehradun). The key law is the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, amended in 2022, which governs scheduled species and protected areas. The IUCN Red List categories are Extinct, Extinct in the Wild, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened, Least Concern, Data Deficient and Not Evaluated. UPSC may next ask about threatened birds, such as the Great Indian Bustard, the Forest Owlet and the Bengal Florican, or about Ramsar sites, migratory species under CMS, or the Western Ghats endemics. Sound preparation includes classifying common names by group, noting endemic species and their habitats, and checking IUCN status.

ocr: Which one of the following protected areas is 75. well-known for the conservation of a sub-species of — the Indian swamp deer (Barasingha) that thrives well on hard ground and is exclusively graminivorous ? (a) Kanha National Park 78. (b) Manas National Park (c) . Mudumalai Wildlife Sanctuary (d) Tal Chhapar Wildlife Sanctuary Stee] slag can be the material for which of the 76. following ? 1. Construction of base road 2. Improvement of agricultural soil 3. . Production of cement Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) land2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (ce). land 3 only (d) 1,2and3
subject: Environment
detail: Slag is the molten non-metallic residue that floats on metal during smelting and is then cooled. Blast furnace slag comes from iron-making. Steel slag comes from converting iron to steel in the Basic Oxygen (LD, Linz-Donawitz) furnace or the Electric Arc Furnace. It is rich in calcium, magnesium, silicon, iron oxides and some phosphorus. Hard, dense and abrasion-resistant, it makes good aggregate for road base and sub-base, railway ballast and asphalt. Its lime and silicate content neutralises soil acidity and supplies Ca, Mg, Si and P, so it works as an agricultural liming material and soil conditioner. After processing, it can partly replace clinker or limestone, or serve as a supplementary cementitious material, in cement. Its drawback is free lime and magnesia, which cause volumetric expansion, so it must be weathered or aged before use. Elimination logic: each of the three uses is valid, so any option that leaves one out (a, b, c) is wrong. India is the second-largest steel producer, and slag utilisation supports the circular economy and cuts mining of natural aggregate.
explanations: Wrong: it omits the cement use. Steel slag can also be used in cement production, so '1 and 2 only' is incomplete.
Wrong: it omits the road base use. Steel slag is a well-established road base material, so '2 and 3 only' is incomplete.
Wrong: it omits agricultural soil improvement. Steel slag is a liming and nutrient-supplying soil conditioner, so '1 and 3 only' is incomplete.
Correct: all three uses are valid, namely base road construction, soil improvement and cement production, so 1, 2 and 3 is the right choice.
keyfact: Steel slag is usable for road base, soil conditioning (acidic soils) and cement, so UPSC 2020 answer: 1, 2 and 3.
related: Steel slag is the by-product of steelmaking in BOF/LD and electric arc furnaces.
Granulated blast furnace slag (GGBS) is used to make Portland Slag Cement.
Fly ash is used in Portland Pozzolana Cement, bricks and road embankments.
India's first steel slag road was built at Hazira, Surat, by CSIR-CRRI with industry.
Thomas slag, a phosphate-rich slag, was historically used as a fertiliser.
Red mud is the waste of alumina extraction by the Bayer process.
Phosphogypsum is the by-product of phosphoric acid fertiliser production.
Barasingha (hard-ground swamp deer, Rucervus duvaucelii branderi) is conserved at Kanha National Park.
statements: 1 — Correct: Steel slag is widely used for base and sub-base road construction. Processed steel slag aggregate is hard, dense and has high load-bearing strength and skid resistance. CSIR-Central Road Research Institute (CRRI), the Ministry of Steel and a steel producer built India's first steel slag road at Hazira, Surat, Gujarat (around 2021-22). Slag must be aged or treated to control expansion from free lime. It saves natural aggregate and reduces dumping. It is also used for railway ballast, embankments and asphalt wearing courses.

2 — Correct: Steel slag acts as a soil conditioner and liming material. Its calcium and magnesium silicates and oxides neutralise acidic soils, and it supplies Si, P, Fe and micronutrients. It is used especially for rice and sugarcane, and for acidic soils such as laterites in eastern and southern India. Phosphorus-rich LD slag was historically sold as 'Thomas slag' phosphate fertiliser. Heavy-metal content must be checked and standards followed. Research bodies and the Ministry of Steel promote this use for waste valorisation.

3 — Correct: Steel slag can be used in cement production, either as a raw-mix component for clinker because of its lime and iron content, or ground as a supplementary cementitious material. Granulated blast furnace slag (GGBS) is the classic input for Portland Slag Cement (PSC) under BIS standards. Steel slag is less hydraulically reactive, but ground steel slag can be blended with it. Using slag cuts clinker demand, and with it CO2 emissions and limestone use, helping decarbonise cement.
summary: The answer is (d) 1, 2 and 3. Steel slag, a by-product of steelmaking, is used as road base aggregate, as a soil conditioner for acidic and nutrient-poor soils, and as a raw material or additive in cement. (Note: the image shows Q75 on Barasingha and Q76 on steel slag. The official answer (d) fits the steel slag question, so this note covers that one. The Barasingha question would be answered (a) Kanha.)
topic_notes: Industrial by-products and waste valorisation are recurring UPSC themes. Slag is generated at about 150-200 kg per tonne of steel from the BOF/EAF route and about 300-400 kg per tonne of hot metal from blast furnaces. Types: blast furnace slag (air-cooled or granulated), BOF/LD slag, EAF slag and ladle slag. Main constituents are CaO, SiO2, FeO, MgO, Al2O3 and MnO. Uses: road construction, railway ballast, cement and concrete, soil conditioning, fertiliser (Thomas slag), water treatment, and as a sintering feed. Issues: free CaO and MgO cause expansion and need ageing, and there are heavy-metal leaching concerns. Policy: the Ministry of Steel and NITI Aayog have pushed slag utilisation through a roadmap and steel slag road projects with CSIR-CRRI. Related waste streams: fly ash (thermal power; the fly ash notification mandates its use in bricks, cement and roads), red mud (aluminium; Bayer process), phosphogypsum (fertiliser plants), and mill scale. India is the world's second-largest crude steel producer, with the National Steel Policy 2017 targeting 300 Mt capacity by 2030-31. The Waste Management and circular economy angle: the Environment Protection Act 1986 and Solid Waste Management Rules 2016. Also remember that GGBS is used in Portland Slag Cement and that fly ash is used in Portland Pozzolana Cement (PPC).

ocr: Which of the following are the most likely places to find the musk deer in its natural habitat ? 1. Askot Wildlife Sanctuary 2. Gangotri National Park 3. | Kishanpur Wildlife Sanctuary 4. Manas National Park Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) land 2 only (b) .2.and 3 only (ce) 3and4only (d) land 4only In rural road construction, the use of which of the following is preferred for ensuring environmental sustainability or to: reduce carbon footprint ? 1. Copper slag 2. Cold mix asphalt technology 3. Geotextiles 4, Hot mix asphalt technology 5. Portland cement Select the co
subject: Environment
detail: The Himalayan musk deer (Moschus chrysogaster) is a small, antlerless deer of the high Himalayas. It lives in subalpine forests of birch, rhododendron and conifers at roughly 2,500-4,500 m. It ranges from Kashmir and Himachal through Uttarakhand and Sikkim to Arunachal Pradesh. Males have long canine tusks and a musk pod, which has made them targets of poaching for perfume. The species is listed Endangered on the IUCN Red List, is in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, and is in CITES Appendix II (Himalayan populations moved to Appendix II). Protected areas with musk deer include Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary, Gangotri National Park, Askot Wildlife Sanctuary (Pithoragarh, Uttarakhand, also called the Askot Musk Deer Sanctuary), Great Himalayan National Park and Khangchendzonga. Elimination logic: Kishanpur WLS is a lowland terai sanctuary in Lakhimpur Kheri, known for tigers, swamp deer and the Sharda river. Manas is a low-altitude Assam park known for the golden langur, pygmy hog, wild buffalo and tiger. Removing 3 and 4 leaves 1 and 2, which is option (a). Option (c) cannot be right because it contains only lowland sites.
explanations: (a) 1 and 2 only: Correct on the facts. Askot and Gangotri are Himalayan, high-altitude sites with musk deer. This conflicts with the supplied key.
(b) 2 and 3 only: Wrong because Kishanpur is a lowland terai sanctuary with no musk deer.
(c) 3 and 4 only: This is the supplied key, but both sites are lowland, so it does not match the facts for this question. Please verify the key.
(d) 1 and 4 only: Wrong because Manas, in the Assam plains, has no musk deer.
keyfact: Musk deer live in the high Himalayas (Askot, Gangotri, Kedarnath); lowland Kishanpur and Manas are not habitats, so the factual answer is (a), not (c).
related: Musk deer: no antlers, males have tusk-like canines and a musk pod.
Musk deer is the state animal of Uttarakhand.
The Himalayan musk deer is IUCN Endangered and in Schedule I of the WPA 1972.
Gangotri NP (1989) is in Uttarkashi and holds the Gangotri glacier.
Askot WLS (Pithoragarh) was set up for musk deer conservation.
Hangul or Kashmir stag is found in Dachigam NP.
Manas NP is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1985) in Assam.
Kishanpur WLS is part of Dudhwa Tiger Reserve in Uttar Pradesh.
statements: 1 — Correct: Askot Wildlife Sanctuary is a genuine musk deer habitat. Askot WLS (about 600 sq km) lies in Pithoragarh district, Uttarakhand, on the Nepal and Tibet border. It was set up in 1986 specifically for musk deer conservation and is part of the Askot Conservation Landscape. The altitude range runs from about 600 m to over 6,000 m. Other fauna include snow leopard, Himalayan tahr, serow and monal pheasant. It is part of the Kailash Sacred Landscape and the Askot-Arakot-Mangti area. Its status is a Wildlife Sanctuary and Biosphere Reserve zone (Nanda Devi complex vicinity).

2 — Correct: Gangotri National Park is a typical musk deer habitat. It is in Uttarkashi district, Uttarakhand, covers about 2,390 sq km, and was notified in 1989. The Gangotri glacier, source of the Bhagirathi (Ganga), lies inside it. Altitude runs from about 1,800 m to over 7,000 m. Fauna include snow leopard, Himalayan black bear, bharal (blue sheep), Himalayan tahr and musk deer. Vegetation includes deodar, fir, spruce and birch. It adjoins Govind Pashu Vihar and the Kedarnath sanctuary.

3 — Incorrect: Kishanpur Wildlife Sanctuary is a low-altitude terai habitat, not a musk deer habitat. It is in Lakhimpur Kheri district, Uttar Pradesh, on the Sharda river, and is part of Dudhwa Tiger Reserve (with Dudhwa NP and Katarniaghat). It is known for tiger, swamp deer (barasingha), hog deer, rhino (reintroduced at Dudhwa) and tall grassland. It was established in 1972 and became part of the tiger reserve in 1987-88. Its altitude is only about 150-200 m.

4 — Incorrect: Manas National Park is not a musk deer habitat. It is in Assam, along the Bhutan border, on the Manas river, a tributary of the Brahmaputra. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1985), a Project Tiger reserve, an Elephant Reserve and a Biosphere Reserve. Species include golden langur, pygmy hog, hispid hare, Bengal florican, wild water buffalo and one-horned rhino. It was listed as World Heritage in Danger in 1992 and removed from the list in 2011. Its altitude is low, so it holds subtropical rather than alpine fauna.
summary: The image has two questions (musk deer habitat, and rural road construction), and neither is labelled Q70. The supplied key (c) does not fit either one. For the musk deer question, the factually correct answer is (a) 1 and 2 only, Askot and Gangotri. Kishanpur (Uttar Pradesh terai) and Manas (Assam, eastern Himalayan foothills) are not musk deer habitats. I have not forced (c) to fit. Please check the key against the original paper.
topic_notes: Musk deer species in India: the Himalayan musk deer (Moschus chrysogaster), the Kashmir musk deer (M. cupreus) and the Black musk deer (M. fuscus) are all found in the Himalayas, with a reported total range from Kashmir to Arunachal. Musk deer are not true deer: they have no antlers, no facial glands and no gall bladder. Males have elongated upper canines. The musk pod is a gland in the abdomen of the male, with a secretion used in perfumery and traditional medicine. A single pod yields only about 25-30 g of musk, so poaching is severe. Legal status: IUCN Endangered, Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, CITES Appendix II. The state animal of Uttarakhand is the musk deer. The Kedarnath Musk Deer Breeding Centre at Kanchula Kharak (Chamoli) was set up in 1982 for conservation breeding. Other high-altitude Himalayan fauna include snow leopard (Hemis NP), Kashmir stag or hangul (Dachigam), Himalayan tahr, bharal, Himalayan monal, red panda (Sikkim, Singalila), and the Tibetan antelope or chiru (Ladakh). Lowland sanctuaries are often asked as distractors. Examples: Kaziranga (one-horned rhino), Manas (golden langur, pygmy hog), Dudhwa (swamp deer), Keibul Lamjao (sangai, Manipur), Kishanpur (tiger and swamp deer). The Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve and the Valley of Flowers form a UNESCO site in Uttarakhand. Corbett (1936) was India's first national park and is also in Uttarakhand.

ocr: Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? 82. (a) lonly (b)' 2 and 3 only (c) 3only (d) 1,2and3 * 80. What is the use of biochar in farming ? 1. Biochar can be used as.a part of the growing medium in vertical farming. 2. When biochar is a part of the growing medium, it promotes the growth of nitrogen-fixing microorganisms. 3. When biochar is a part of the growing medium, it enables the growing medium to retain water for longer time. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) land 2 only (b) 2only (c) land 3 only (d) 1,2and3 A)
subject: Environment
detail: Biochar is a stable, carbon-rich charcoal produced by pyrolysis, which is heating biomass such as crop residue, wood or husks with little or no oxygen. When mixed into soil or a growing medium, its porous structure and large surface area do several useful things. It holds water and dissolved nutrients, so the medium stays moist for longer. It also provides a habitat for beneficial microorganisms, including nitrogen-fixing bacteria and mycorrhizal fungi, which promotes their growth. Other benefits are better cation exchange capacity, reduced nutrient leaching, a liming effect on acidic soils, and long-term carbon sequestration, since the carbon stays locked for centuries.
