Related bodies include the NAFSCOB, NUCFDC and the Cooperative Development Fund.

Option (b), the correct answer, combines statements 2 and 3. UCBs can issue equity, preference and special shares under RBI norms. They came under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 through the Banking Laws (Application to Cooperative Societies) Act, 1965, with effect from 1 March 1966. UCBs are primary cooperative banks in urban and semi-urban areas. They serve small borrowers, traders and salaried people, and they follow a dual regulatory system.

Option (c) combines statements 1 and 3, but statement 1 is incorrect, so it is wrong. Statement 3 is true on its own. The 1966 extension of banking law to cooperative banks gave the RBI powers over them, though this was partial. Full powers, such as superseding boards, came much later, with the 2020 amendment.

Option (d) claims all three statements are correct. It fails because statement 1 is false. The RBI and the State Registrar, not local boards set up by State Governments, regulate UCBs. Dual control has been criticised for overlapping jurisdictions, which led to the 2020 amendment and the setting up of the Ministry of Cooperation in July 2021.
related: Cooperative societies: Article 19(1)(c) (right to form), Article 43B (Directive Principle), Part IX-B (Articles 243ZH–243ZT) under the 97th Amendment, 2011.
The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 gave the RBI more power over cooperative banks. It excludes PACS and societies doing long-term agricultural finance.
The Ministry of Cooperation was created on 6 July 2021.
DICGC covers deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, including UCB deposits.
In 2021 the Supreme Court held that Part IX-B provisions on State cooperative societies do not apply, since cooperatives are a State subject.
NUCFDC is the Umbrella Organisation for UCBs, promoted with RBI support.
The Banking Laws (Application to Cooperative Societies) Act, 1965 extended banking law to cooperative banks, effective 1 March 1966.
The RBI's four-tier framework for UCBs (Tier 1 to 4) sets different capital norms by deposit size and area of operation.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: UCBs are regulated by the RBI (banking functions) and by the Registrar of Cooperative Societies (management), not by local boards set up by State Governments. Under the dual control system, the RBI handles licensing, prudential norms, capital adequacy, interest rates and inspections. The State RCS, or the Central RCS for multi-state UCBs, handles registration, elections, audit and liquidation. The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 further strengthened RBI powers over UCBs. In 2020 the RBI also set up a Supervisory Action Framework for UCBs, and in 2019 it set up the Umbrella Organisation (NUCFDC) to support them.

2 — Correct: UCBs can raise capital by issuing equity shares, preference shares and special shares to members and non-members, subject to RBI guidelines. The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 enabled cooperative societies to issue such shares to members or others with RBI's prior approval. RBI's 2022 guidelines on 'Issue and regulation of share capital and securities' allow UCBs to raise equity capital, preference shares and debt instruments such as Tier II bonds. The aim is to improve capital adequacy, with minimum capital requirements tiered by bank category (Tier 1 to Tier 4).

3 — Correct: The Banking Laws (Application to Cooperative Societies) Act, 1965 extended parts of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 to cooperative banks, effective 1 March 1966. This is why the Act is referred to as 'applicable to co-operative societies' (AACS). The change gave the RBI regulatory control over urban cooperative banks' banking activities, such as licensing, reserves and branch opening. Cooperative credit institutions were later covered more widely. The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 extended further provisions, but it excludes primary agricultural credit societies and societies whose main business is long-term agricultural financing.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 2 and 3 are correct, statement 1 is incorrect. Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are regulated by the RBI for banking functions, not by local boards set up by State Governments. They can issue equity and preference shares, and they were brought under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 by an amendment effective 1 March 1966.
topic_notes: Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) are primary cooperative societies that do banking in urban and semi-urban areas. Their roots go back to the 19th-century credit societies, for example in Baroda in 1889, and the Cooperative Credit Societies Act of 1904 and 1912. The cooperative banking structure has a short-term and a long-term credit side. UCBs fall under the urban short-term structure. Rural cooperatives have a three-tier structure of State Cooperative Banks, District Central Cooperative Banks and Primary Agricultural Credit Societies. Regulation is dual. The RBI controls banking functions: licensing, branch opening, capital adequacy, CRR and SLR, exposure limits, and inspection. The State Registrar of Cooperative Societies, or the Central Registrar for multi-state cooperative societies, controls registration, management, audit and winding up. The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 was extended to cooperative banks from 1 March 1966. The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 gave the RBI more powers over UCBs, such as approving the chairman and CEO, and allowed the RBI to prepare schemes of reconstruction or amalgamation without a moratorium. Before this, the Malegam Committee (2011) and the Vishwanathan Committee (2021) examined UCB issues. The RBI introduced a four-tier categorisation of UCBs in 2022 and set up the Umbrella Organisation NUCFDC in 2024. The Ministry of Cooperation was created on 6 July 2021 with Amit Shah as the first minister. The 97th Constitutional Amendment (2011) added the right to form cooperative societies as a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(c), added Article 43B as a Directive Principle, and inserted Part IX-B (Articles 243ZH–243ZT). In 2021 the Supreme Court struck down the part of the amendment on the State cooperative societies' structure, since cooperation is a State subject. Deposit insurance is provided by the DICGC, up to ₹5 lakh per depositor.

question:
Indian Government Bond Yields are influenced by which of the following?
1. Actions of the United States Federal Reserve
2. Actions of the Reserve Bank of India
3. Inflation and short-term interest rates Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Economy
detail: A government bond's yield is the effective return an investor earns, and it moves inversely to the bond's price. Yields reflect expected inflation, the short-term policy rate (the repo rate in India), the term premium, liquidity conditions, fiscal deficit and borrowing size, and global rates. Statement 1: when the US Fed raises rates or tapers asset purchases, US Treasury yields rise, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) may pull money out of Indian debt, the rupee weakens and Indian yields rise (the 2013 taper tantrum is the classic example). Statement 2: the RBI influences yields through the repo rate, CRR and SLR, open market operations (OMO), Operation Twist, G-SAP (2021) and its stance on liquidity. Statement 3: higher inflation erodes real returns, so investors demand higher yields, while short-term rates anchor the front end of the yield curve and feed into longer maturities. Since all three are valid, only (d) is correct. Elimination: (a), (b) and (c) each omit a valid factor, so a student who knows any two of the three can still reach (d).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it leaves out statement 3. Inflation and short-term rates clearly influence bond yields.
(b) is wrong because RBI action matters, but it is not the only influence. Global factors such as the US Fed and domestic inflation also matter.
(c) is wrong because inflation and short-term rates are important, but the Fed and the RBI also affect yields.
(d) is correct because the Fed's actions, the RBI's actions and inflation with short-term rates all influence Indian government bond yields.
keyfact: Indian G-sec yields are driven by global factors (the US Fed), the RBI's policy and liquidity actions, and inflation with short-term rates, so the answer is (d).
option_notes: (a) 1 and 2 only: this combination covers the global factor (the US Fed) and the domestic central bank (the RBI). Both really do influence G-sec yields, through capital flows and through the repo rate, liquidity and OMOs. The option is incomplete because it excludes inflation and short-term rates, which are the fundamental drivers of yields. It is therefore not the answer.

(b) 2 only: this treats the RBI as the sole influence. The RBI does shape yields through the repo rate, CRR, SLR, OMOs, G-SAP and Operation Twist, and it manages government borrowing. Yields are also affected by fiscal deficit, inflation, global rates and FPI flows, so a single-factor view is too narrow.

(c) 3 only: this recognises inflation and short-term rates as drivers. Higher expected inflation raises the required yield, and short-term policy rates anchor the curve. It ignores external influences like the Fed and the RBI's direct market operations, so it is incomplete.

(d) 1, 2 and 3: this is the official answer. Indian G-sec yields reflect global monetary conditions (the Fed), domestic monetary policy and liquidity operations (the RBI), and macro fundamentals (inflation and short-term rates). Other factors include the fiscal deficit, government borrowing, the oil price, the rupee and FPI flows.
related: Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
The 10-year G-sec yield is India's benchmark for long-term interest rates.
RBI's MPC has 6 members and targets CPI inflation of 4% with a band of ±2%.
G-SAP (2021) was the RBI's programme of assured government bond purchases to manage yields.
Operation Twist means buying long-term and selling short-term securities at the same time.
The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) was introduced in 2022 as the floor of the LAF corridor.
Indian G-secs were included in the JP Morgan GBI-EM index from June 2024.
The Retail Direct scheme (2021) lets retail investors buy G-secs directly from the RBI.
statements: 1 — Correct: US Fed actions affect global liquidity, the dollar, and the interest-rate differential, so they move Indian yields. The Federal Reserve is the US central bank, created in 1913, and its policy rate is the federal funds rate, set by the FOMC. Tightening or quantitative tapering raises US Treasury yields and attracts capital back to the US. FPIs then sell Indian bonds, the rupee depreciates and Indian yields rise. The 2013 taper tantrum and the 2022 Fed hikes are the standard examples. Indian bonds' inclusion in the JP Morgan GBI-EM index (June 2024) increases this global linkage.

2 — Correct: The RBI is India's central bank (established 1935, nationalised 1949) and is the debt manager for the Government. It sets the repo rate through the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC, 6 members, statutory since 2016). It also manages liquidity through CRR, SLR, OMO purchases and sales, the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), Operation Twist and G-SAP. OMO purchases raise bond prices and lower yields, while sales do the opposite. The RBI also conducts primary auctions of government securities (G-secs) and sets the inflation-targeting stance (4% target, band 2-6%).

3 — Correct: Inflation and short-term interest rates are core determinants of yields. Under the Fisher relation, nominal yield is approximately the real yield plus expected inflation, so higher inflation pushes yields up. Short-term rates such as the repo rate, T-bill yields and call money rates anchor the short end of the curve, and expectations of their path shape longer yields. India's 10-year benchmark G-sec yield is closely watched. A flat, steep or inverted yield curve signals growth and rate expectations. India's flexible inflation targeting uses CPI (4% ±2%).
summary: The answer is (d): all three factors influence Indian Government bond yields. US Federal Reserve actions drive global capital flows and yield differentials, RBI actions set domestic liquidity and policy rates, and inflation together with short-term interest rates shape the yield curve and investors' return expectations.
topic_notes: A government security (G-sec) is a tradable debt instrument issued by the Central or State Governments. It includes Treasury Bills (under 1 year: 91, 182 and 364 days) and dated securities (5 to 40 years). Yield is the return on the bond and moves inversely to its price. The coupon is the fixed interest rate on face value. The benchmark is the 10-year G-sec yield. The primary market is run through RBI auctions. The secondary market includes NDS-OM, and the Retail Direct scheme (2021) allows retail investors to buy G-secs directly. Determinants of yields: inflation expectations, repo rate and policy stance, liquidity (surplus or deficit), fiscal deficit and gross market borrowing, global yields (US 10-year Treasury), crude oil prices, rupee movement, FPI flows and the demand from banks (SLR requirement, currently 18%). RBI tools: repo and reverse repo, MSF, SDF (introduced 2022), CRR, SLR, OMO, Operation Twist (simultaneous purchase of long-dated and sale of short-dated securities), and G-SAP (Government Securities Acquisition Programme, 2021). The MPC, formed under the RBI Act amendment of 2016, has 6 members and targets CPI inflation of 4% with a ±2% tolerance band. Bond indices: inclusion in JP Morgan's GBI-EM Global index began in June 2024, and in the Bloomberg EM index in 2025. The Fully Accessible Route (FAR) lets non-residents invest in specified G-secs without limits. Corporate bond spreads are measured against G-sec yields. Other angles UPSC could ask: yield curve shapes, the difference between yield and coupon, the effect of rate hikes on bond prices, and sovereign credit ratings.

question:
Consider the following :
1. Foreign currency convertible bonds
2. Foreign institutional investment with certain conditions
3. Global depository receipts
4. Non-resident external deposits Which of the above can be included in Foreign Direct Investments?
subject: Economy
detail: FDI means a non-resident's investment in an Indian company that gives a lasting interest and some control. Under the FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Rules, 2019, and the earlier FDI policy, FDI is investment in equity instruments: equity shares, compulsorily and mandatorily convertible preference shares, compulsorily convertible debentures and share warrants. Portfolio investment (FPI) of up to 10% of a company's paid-up equity is not FDI. When a single foreign investor's holding crosses 10%, the whole holding is reclassified as FDI. This is the 'certain conditions' in statement 2. Convertible instruments such as FCCBs and ADRs/GDRs were treated as FDI under the policy, because they convert into equity and bring in foreign capital for the long term. The DPIIT sets the policy, and the RBI regulates it under FEMA, 1999. NRE, FCNR(B) and NRO deposits are banking liabilities. They are classified under 'NRI deposits' in external commercial and banking capital, not under FDI. Elimination: since 1, 2 and 3 are valid and 4 is not, options (c) and (d) fall. Option (b) falls because it leaves out two valid items. Only (a) remains.
explanations: Correct. FCCBs, conditional foreign institutional investment (holding above 10%) and GDRs can all be included in FDI, while NRE deposits cannot.
Incorrect. GDRs do count as FDI, but FCCBs and conditional institutional investment also qualify, so 'only 3' is incomplete.
Incorrect. Conditional foreign institutional investment counts, but NRE deposits are banking capital and not FDI, and the option leaves out FCCBs and GDRs.
Incorrect. FCCBs count, but NRE deposits do not, and the option omits statements 2 and 3.
keyfact: FCCBs, GDRs and foreign institutional investment above 10% count as FDI; NRE deposits are banking capital and do not.
option_notes: Options 1, 2 and 3: FCCBs, FII investment with conditions and GDRs are all routes by which foreign equity capital enters India. FDI is regulated under FEMA, 1999, with policy set by DPIIT. FPI above 10% in a company is reclassified as FDI. This is the official answer to the question.

Option 3 only: GDRs are negotiable instruments issued abroad against Indian shares held by a domestic custodian bank. They are usually listed in Luxembourg or London. Reliance Industries issued the first Indian GDR in 1992. The Depository Receipts Scheme, 2014 governs them. They are an FDI-type route but not the only one, so this option is incomplete.

Options 2 and 4: Foreign institutional investment (now FPI) is regulated by SEBI, and holdings above 10% in one company are treated as FDI. NRE deposits are rupee accounts of NRIs that are fully repatriable and tax-free in India. They are banking capital and not FDI, which makes this option wrong.

Options 1 and 4: FCCBs are foreign currency bonds convertible into equity or depository receipts, and they are linked to FDI and ECB rules. NRE deposits are NRI bank deposits and not FDI. This option wrongly includes NRE deposits and omits conditional institutional investment and GDRs.
related: FPI holdings above 10% of a company's paid-up equity are reclassified as FDI.
FDI policy is formulated by DPIIT, and the RBI regulates it under FEMA, 1999.
The Foreign Investment Promotion Board was abolished in 2017.
Press Note 3 (2020) needs government approval for FDI from countries bordering India.
GDRs are issued abroad; ADRs are listed in the US.
NRE deposits are rupee accounts; FCNR(B) deposits are in foreign currency.
Participatory Notes are offshore derivatives, regulated by SEBI.
Reliance issued the first Indian GDR in 1992.
statements: 1 — Correct: FCCBs are treated as FDI-type, equity-linked foreign capital because they convert into equity. FCCBs are bonds issued by Indian companies in foreign currency. They carry a fixed interest rate and are convertible into shares or depository receipts. They are raised under the External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) and FDI framework, and the Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds and Ordinary Shares (Through Depository Receipt Mechanism) Scheme, 1993 governed them earlier. Companies use them to raise cheap overseas funds because the coupon is low, since investors expect equity upside. Risks include rupee depreciation, which raises the repayment burden, and dilution of equity on conversion. Under current rules, only compulsorily convertible instruments count as FDI.

2 — Correct: Foreign institutional investment counts as FDI when it meets conditions, mainly when a foreign investor's holding rises above 10% of the paid-up equity capital. FIIs were allowed into Indian markets in 1992 and are now regulated as Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) under SEBI's FPI Regulations, 2014 (replaced in 2019). The aggregate FPI limit is the sectoral cap. Holdings of 10% or less are portfolio investment, while holdings above 10% are FDI. Portfolio flows are 'hot money', since they can leave quickly. FDI is long-term and stable. India's FDI policy is made by DPIIT under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

3 — Correct: GDRs are instruments through which Indian companies issue equity abroad and attract foreign investment, so they are counted as FDI. A GDR is a negotiable instrument issued by an overseas depository bank against shares of an Indian company held by a domestic custodian. It is typically listed in Luxembourg or London. ADRs are the US equivalent, listed on NYSE or NASDAQ. Reliance was the first Indian company to issue a GDR, in 1992. The Depository Receipts Scheme, 2014 now governs them. Holders get dividends but have no direct voting rights unless the deposit agreement says otherwise.

4 — Incorrect: NRE deposits are bank deposits, not FDI, because they do not buy equity or give control in a company. NRE accounts are rupee-denominated, fully repatriable and tax-free in India. They are held by NRIs in Indian banks. FCNR(B) deposits are held in foreign currency. NRO accounts hold income earned in India and are only partly repatriable. In balance of payments data, these deposits fall under banking capital within the capital account, not under FDI or FPI. They form a major source of foreign exchange inflows and have been used by the RBI to stabilise the rupee, as in 2013.
summary: The answer is (a) 1, 2 and 3. Foreign currency convertible bonds (FCCBs), foreign institutional investment that meets certain conditions (such as crossing the 10% equity threshold), and global depository receipts (GDRs) can all count as FDI. Non-resident external (NRE) deposits are bank deposits, a banking capital flow, and are not FDI.
topic_notes: FDI is a cross-border investment in which a non-resident acquires a lasting interest and some control in an enterprise. The IMF benchmark is 10% or more of voting power. In India, FDI is governed by FEMA, 1999. The FEMA (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 apply, and DPIIT issues the Consolidated FDI Policy. The RBI handles the regulation and reporting. Routes: the Automatic Route needs no prior government approval, while the Government Route needs approval through the single-window Foreign Investment Facilitation Portal. Prohibited sectors include lottery, gambling, chit funds, Nidhi companies, real estate business, cigars and tobacco manufacturing, and atomic energy. Indicative caps: defence up to 74% automatic (100% by government route), insurance 74%, and telecom 100% automatic. Single-brand retail is 100% automatic, and multi-brand retail is 51% by government route. Press Note 3 (2020) requires government approval for investments from countries sharing a land border with India. FPI means portfolio investment in listed securities, with each investor below 10%, and it is regulated by SEBI. Other capital flows: ECBs, NRI deposits (NRE, FCNR(B), NRO), ADRs and GDRs, and P-notes. The Participatory Note is an offshore derivative instrument that lets investors take positions without registering as an FPI. The balance of payments has a current account and a capital account. FDI and FPI are in the capital account (financial account in the new IMF format). Top sources of FDI into India have been Mauritius, Singapore, the US, the Netherlands and Japan. Related institutions are the Foreign Investment Promotion Board (abolished in 2017) and Invest India. Likely future angles: sectoral caps, definitions of FDI versus FPI, hot money, ECB versus FDI, and the Press Note 3 restrictions.

question: Consider the following statements : The effect of devaluation of a currency is that it necessarily 1. improves the competitiveness of the domestic exports in the foreign markets 2. increases the foreign value of domestic currency 3. improves the trade balance Which of the above statements is/are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: Devaluation is a deliberate downward adjustment of a currency's official exchange rate by the government or central bank under a fixed or pegged exchange-rate system. Revaluation is the opposite. Depreciation and appreciation are market-driven changes under a floating regime. After devaluation, one unit of foreign currency buys more domestic currency, so domestic goods become cheaper for foreign buyers and imports become costlier for domestic buyers. This improves export competitiveness (statement 1). The external value of the domestic currency falls, so statement 2 is the opposite of the truth. Whether the trade balance improves depends on the Marshall-Lerner condition, which says the sum of the price elasticities of export and import demand must exceed 1. It also depends on the J-curve effect, where the balance first worsens and then improves, on import dependence (for example crude oil in India), and on retaliation by trading partners. Because the word 'necessarily' is used, statement 3 fails. Elimination: statement 2 is wrong, which removes (b) and (d). Statement 3 is not certain, which removes (c). Only (a) remains.
explanations: Correct: statement 1 is true, statement 2 is false and statement 3 is not necessarily true, so only statement 1 holds.
Wrong: statement 2 is false because devaluation lowers the foreign value of the domestic currency.
Wrong: statement 3 is not certain, since the trade balance depends on elasticities and the J-curve, and statement 1 is left out.
Wrong: statement 2 is false and statement 3 is not necessarily true, and statement 1 is left out.
keyfact: Devaluation lowers a currency's external value and makes exports cheaper, but it does not necessarily improve the trade balance (Marshall-Lerner condition, J-curve).
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only, is the official answer. It captures the one certain effect of devaluation: cheaper exports and so greater export competitiveness. The other effects, a fall in the currency's external value and a trade-balance change that depends on elasticities, are not what the statements claim. UPSC often uses 'necessarily' to turn a plausible claim into a wrong one.

Option (b), 1 and 2, is wrong because it treats devaluation as raising the foreign value of the currency. The reverse happens. Appreciation or revaluation raises the external value. Devaluation, a policy cut in the official rate, and depreciation, a market-driven fall, both lower it. Students often confuse these terms.

Option (c), 3 only, is wrong because it assumes devaluation always cures a trade deficit. In practice the outcome depends on the Marshall-Lerner condition and the J-curve. India's heavy dependence on imported oil and electronics weakens the effect, and this option ignores the sure gain in export competitiveness.

Option (d), 2 and 3, is wrong on both counts. Statement 2 reverses the effect on external value, and statement 3 is not certain. It omits the only correct statement. It is the 'fully wrong' distractor in this question.
related: India devalued the rupee in 1949, 1966 and 1991.
Marshall-Lerner condition: the sum of export and import demand elasticities must exceed 1 for devaluation to improve the trade balance.
The J-curve shows the trade balance worsening first and improving later after devaluation.
Revaluation means an official raise in a currency's par value; appreciation is the market-driven version.
India has had a managed floating exchange-rate regime since March 1993.
The Impossible Trinity: a country cannot have a fixed exchange rate, free capital mobility and independent monetary policy together.
India accepted IMF Article VIII (current-account convertibility) in August 1994.
REER is the trade-weighted exchange rate adjusted for inflation differentials.
statements: 1 — Correct: Devaluation makes exports cheaper in foreign currency terms, which improves their price competitiveness abroad. Devaluation is an official, policy-led cut in the par value of a currency under a fixed or pegged regime. India devalued the rupee in 1949 (after sterling), in June 1966 (about 36.5 percent) and in July 1991 (two steps, about 18-19 percent in total). The 1991 move came during the balance-of-payments crisis. The aim is to boost exports, curb imports and ease pressure on the current account.

2 — Incorrect: Devaluation reduces, not increases, the external value of the domestic currency, since more domestic currency is needed to buy one unit of foreign currency. An increase in external value is called appreciation (market-driven) or revaluation (official). Under a floating system, a fall in value is called depreciation. India moved to a market-determined, managed float in 1993. The RBI intervenes only to curb excess volatility, so the term devaluation now applies mainly to pegged regimes such as China before 2005.

3 — Incorrect: A better trade balance is not guaranteed. It requires the Marshall-Lerner condition, that the sum of export and import demand elasticities exceeds 1. The J-curve effect means the deficit may widen first because contracts and volumes adjust slowly. Imported inputs such as oil, gold and electronics become costlier, which can cause imported inflation. Trading partners may retaliate with competitive devaluation, or 'beggar-thy-neighbour' policies, as seen in the 1930s. Hence the word 'necessarily' makes the statement wrong.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 1 is correct. Devaluation lowers the foreign-currency price of a country's exports, so they become more competitive abroad. It does not necessarily increase the currency's foreign value (it reduces it), and it does not necessarily improve the trade balance.
topic_notes: Exchange-rate terms. Devaluation is an official lowering of the par value under a fixed or pegged system. Revaluation is an official raising. Depreciation and appreciation are market-driven changes under a floating system. The nominal exchange rate is the market price of one currency in terms of another. The real effective exchange rate (REER) adjusts the nominal rate for inflation differences and is weighted by trade with partners. A REER that is too high means loss of competitiveness. Effects of devaluation: exports become cheaper, imports costlier, imported inflation rises, external debt burden in domestic currency rises, and the trade balance may improve if the Marshall-Lerner condition holds. The J-curve shows a short-run worsening followed by improvement. Indian history: the rupee was devalued in 1949, in 1966 under Indira Gandhi (from Rs 4.76 to Rs 7.50 per dollar), and in July 1991 (the two-step adjustment by the RBI). The LERMS dual rate came in 1992-93. The rupee became fully market-determined on the trade account in 1993, and current-account convertibility under Article VIII of the IMF came in August 1994. India follows a managed float. The RBI intervenes in the forex market and holds reserves. The IMF classifies regimes such as hard pegs, crawling pegs and free floats. Related ideas: a currency war is competitive devaluation, and the Plaza Accord of 1985 and the Louvre Accord of 1987 were attempts at coordination. China's yuan peg ended in 2005. Possible next angles: the Impossible Trinity (independent monetary policy, free capital flow and fixed exchange rate cannot coexist), the Balance of Payments, the Current Account Deficit, the Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) and the Bretton Woods system.

question: Which one of the following effects of creation of black money in India has been the main cause of worry to the Government of India?
options: Diversion of resources to the purchase of real estate and investment in luxury housing
Investment in unproductive activities and purchase of precious stones, jewellery, gold, etc
Large donations to political parties and growth of regionalism
Loss of revenue to the State Exchequer due to tax evasion
subject: Economy
detail: Black money is income that has escaped taxation, either because it is earned illegally (crime, corruption, smuggling) or because legitimate income is concealed from tax authorities. The parallel economy it creates has many effects: it fuels real estate speculation, inflates the prices of gold and luxury goods, distorts investment toward unproductive assets, funds elections and may even finance illicit activity. However, the effect that most directly and measurably concerns the government is the erosion of the tax base. Lost direct and indirect tax revenue reduces resources for welfare, infrastructure and defence, forces higher borrowing or higher taxes on honest taxpayers, and weakens the effectiveness of fiscal and monetary policy. Government responses reflect this priority: the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015, the SIT headed by a former Supreme Court judge (2014), demonetisation (November 2016), Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act 2016, GST, PAN and AEOI-based information exchange, and Income Declaration Scheme 2016. Elimination: options (a), (b) and (c) describe consequences or channels of black money, but they are secondary, partly arise from the tax-evasion problem itself, and are not the stated principal fiscal concern. Option (d) is the root fiscal damage.
explanations: Incorrect: diversion into real estate and luxury housing is a real effect that inflates property prices, but it is a secondary, sectoral consequence rather than the government's main worry.
Incorrect: unproductive investment in gold, jewellery and precious stones is a known channel for parking black money, but it is not the primary concern compared with revenue loss.
Incorrect: political donations and the growth of regionalism are tenuous and not the principal concern; regionalism is not a standard consequence of black money.
Correct: tax evasion directly reduces government revenue, which constrains public spending, raises the deficit and burdens honest taxpayers. This is the principal fiscal worry.
keyfact: The main government worry about black money is the loss of revenue to the exchequer through tax evasion (answer d).
option_notes: Real estate is a major sink for unaccounted cash, with cash components in property deals and benami holdings. Measures include RERA 2016, the Benami Transactions Amendment Act 2016, stamp duty and circle rate reforms, and a PAN requirement for high-value transactions. It raises prices and makes housing unaffordable, but this is a market distortion, not the principal fiscal concern.

Gold, jewellery and precious stones are classic stores of unaccounted wealth in India, a large importer of gold. Responses include the Gold Monetisation Scheme 2015, Sovereign Gold Bonds (2015), customs duty changes, PAN for purchases above specified limits, and hallmarking. This channel diverts savings from productive use but is not the main government worry.

Political funding is a known source and use of black money in India. Reforms include Electoral Bonds (2018, struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2024), a cap on cash donations (Rs 2,000 from 2017), and Section 29C of the RP Act. Regionalism is not a typical consequence of black money, so this option is weak.

Tax evasion is the non-payment of legally due tax through concealment of income, and it is a legal offence distinct from lawful tax avoidance. It reduces the tax-to-GDP ratio and the revenue of the Consolidated Fund. Key tools include the Income Tax Act 1961, Black Money Act 2015, GST e-invoicing and the CBDT, and it remains the central official concern.
related: Black Money Act 2015 covers undisclosed foreign income and assets, with a 120% tax-plus-penalty on foreign assets.
SIT on black money was constituted in 2014 under Justice M.B. Shah on the Supreme Court's direction.
Demonetisation was announced on 8 November 2016, withdrawing Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 notes.
Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act 2016 took effect on 1 November 2016.
Tax evasion is illegal; tax avoidance uses legal loopholes.
PMLA 2002 is the main law against money laundering; the Enforcement Directorate enforces it.
Electoral Bonds scheme (2018) was held unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in February 2024.
Round-tripping of black money often involves routes such as Mauritius.
summary: The answer is (d). The main worry of the Government of India about black money is the loss of revenue to the State Exchequer through tax evasion. This deprives the government of funds for public expenditure, widens the fiscal deficit and undermines tax compliance and equity.
topic_notes: Black money means income on which tax is due but unpaid, covering both illegal income and legal income that is concealed. Key committees and studies: Wanchoo Committee (1971) on direct taxes; the Direct Taxes Enquiry Committee; the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy (NIPFP), National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) and National Institute of Financial Management (NIFM) studies (2013-14) on the unaccounted income; the SIT on Black Money (2014, chaired by Justice M.B. Shah). Legal framework: the Income Tax Act 1961; the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act 2015 (penalty of 30% tax plus 90% penalty on undisclosed foreign assets, and up to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment); the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act 1988, amended in 2016; the Prevention of Money Laundering Act 2002; the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018. Voluntary disclosure schemes: VDIS 1997, Income Declaration Scheme 2016, and Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Yojana 2016. Administrative measures: demonetisation on 8 November 2016, PAN quoting, GST (from 1 July 2017), e-invoicing, the Annual Information Return, and Tax Information Exchange Agreements, DTAAs and the Automatic Exchange of Information under the OECD Common Reporting Standard, with Swiss banks sharing data with India from 2018. Concerns include the parallel economy, capital flight, hawala, round-tripping through Mauritius and participatory notes, and FATF standards. Likely future angles: differences between tax evasion, avoidance and money laundering, the SIT, the Black Money Act, and demonetisation outcomes.

question: Which one of the following is likely to be the most inflationary in its effects?
options: Borrowing from the public to finance a budget deficit
Borrowing from the banks to finance a budget deficit
Creation of new money to finance a budget deficit
subject: Economy
detail: Inflation arises when aggregate demand grows faster than aggregate supply. A budget deficit can be financed in three ways: borrowing from the public, borrowing from commercial banks, or printing money (monetisation, i.e. the central bank buying government securities or giving ad hoc advances/overdrafts). When the government borrows from the public, it only transfers existing purchasing power from households to the state, so the money supply is unchanged and the inflationary effect is mild, though crowding out of private investment and higher interest rates may result. Borrowing from banks uses existing bank credit and may reduce credit available to the private sector. Because of the money multiplier, it can expand money supply somewhat, but only within the limits of bank reserves and the SLR. Creation of new money raises reserve money (M0) directly, and the money multiplier then expands broad money several times over. This is deficit monetisation, which is why it is called the most inflationary. In India, the 1997 agreement ended automatic monetisation through ad hoc Treasury Bills, and the FRBM Act 2003 barred the RBI from subscribing to primary issues of government securities from 2006. Repayment of public debt withdraws money or leaves it unchanged, so it is least inflationary or even deflationary. Elimination: (a) is contractionary, (b) is neutral to mild, (c) is moderate, and (d) is the highest.
explanations: Wrong: repaying public debt takes money back from the government's balances or leaves money supply unchanged, so it is neutral or contractionary. In some cases it may release funds to lenders, but it is not the most inflationary option.

Wrong: borrowing from the public only transfers existing purchasing power to the government. The money supply does not rise, so the effect is the least inflationary of the three deficit-financing methods, though it may crowd out private investment.
Wrong: borrowing from banks can raise money supply through credit creation, but it is limited by bank reserves, SLR and lending capacity. It is therefore less inflationary than printing money.

Correct: creating new money (monetisation of the deficit) directly raises high-powered money, and the money multiplier expands it further. Demand rises with no matching rise in output, which makes this the most inflationary option.
keyfact: Printing money to finance a deficit (monetisation) raises high-powered money directly, so it is the most inflationary method of financing.
option_notes: Repayment of public debt: the government pays back principal and interest on its past borrowing, from taxes, surpluses or fresh borrowing. When paid out of a fiscal surplus it contracts money in circulation. It reduces the debt-GDP ratio and interest burden. India's central government debt is mostly domestic and held by banks, insurers and the RBI.

Borrowing from the public: the government sells bonds, T-bills, small savings instruments or market loans to households and institutions. Funds move from private savers to the state with no new money created. It can push up interest rates and crowd out private investment, but it is not directly inflationary.

Borrowing from banks: banks buy government securities, partly to meet the statutory liquidity ratio (SLR, currently 18% of NDTL). It may expand credit and the money supply if banks have excess reserves. It can crowd out private credit. The inflationary effect is moderate, between public borrowing and money creation.

Creation of new money: also called deficit monetisation or seigniorage financing. The RBI prints currency or credits the government's account against government securities. It raises reserve money (M0), and the multiplier expands broad money. India used ad hoc Treasury Bills until 1997. Since 2006 the FRBM Act bars RBI from buying in primary auctions, though it may do so in emergencies, as in 2020.
related: Fiscal deficit = total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments.
Ad hoc Treasury Bills were abolished in 1997 and replaced by WMA.
The FRBM Act 2003 barred RBI from buying government securities in primary auctions from 2006.
SLR is the share of NDTL that banks must hold in liquid assets such as government securities.
Reserve money (M0) = currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI.
The N.K. Singh Committee (2017) proposed a 60% general government debt-GDP target.
Crowding out occurs when government borrowing raises interest rates and reduces private investment.
summary: The answer is (d): creation of new money to finance a budget deficit. It directly raises the money supply (high-powered money) without any matching rise in output, so it is the most inflationary way of financing a deficit.
topic_notes: Deficit financing means covering the gap between government expenditure and receipts. The main deficit measures are the revenue deficit (revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts), the fiscal deficit (total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowing, i.e. the total borrowing requirement), and the primary deficit (fiscal deficit minus interest payments). The gross fiscal deficit is financed by market borrowings (dated securities and T-bills), small savings and NSSF, external borrowing, and sometimes RBI support. Monetised deficit is the part financed by the RBI, and it was a major source of reserve money growth before 1997. The 1997 agreement between the Government and RBI abolished ad hoc Treasury Bills. The Ways and Means Advances (WMA) facility remains for temporary mismatches. Under the FRBM Act 2003, effective from 2006, the RBI cannot subscribe to primary issues of central government securities, except in special circumstances. The N.K. Singh FRBM Review Committee (2017) recommended a debt-to-GDP target of 60% (40% for the Centre and 20% for states), with the fiscal deficit as the main anchor. Effects of different financing: borrowing from the public causes crowding out and higher interest rates; borrowing from banks affects credit availability; borrowing from the RBI raises the money supply and inflation; external borrowing exposes the country to exchange-rate risk. Related concepts include the money multiplier, reserve money, the quantity theory of money, cost-push versus demand-pull inflation, and Ricardian equivalence. In 2020-21, the Centre's fiscal deficit rose to about 9.2% of GDP because of Covid, and it was financed through market borrowings, not monetisation. UPSC may also ask about seigniorage, helicopter money and the fiscal-monetary policy mix.

question: The money multiplier in an economy increases with which one of the following?
options: Increase in the Cash Reserve Ratio in the banks
Increase in the Statutory Liquidity Ratio in the banks
Increase in the banking habit of the people
Increase in the population of the country
subject: Economy
detail: The money multiplier links the money supply (M) to high-powered money or reserve money (H): M = m x H. In the simple form, m = (1 + c) / (c + r), where c is the currency-deposit ratio (the public's preference for cash over deposits) and r is the reserve-deposit ratio. The reserve ratio depends on the CRR set by the RBI and on any excess reserves banks keep. The SLR also limits lending capacity, but it is not part of the textbook formula. A higher CRR raises r, so m falls. A higher SLR leaves banks less to lend, so credit creation and the multiplier tend to shrink. A greater banking habit lowers c, since more money stays in the banking system and is re-lent, so m rises. Population by itself does not change c or r, so it has no direct effect. Elimination: (a) and (b) are both contractionary, (d) is irrelevant, so (c) is the only option that raises the multiplier. Remember that the multiplier is inversely related to CRR, SLR, and the cash-holding preference.
explanations: Wrong. A higher CRR means banks must park more of their deposits with the RBI. This raises the reserve ratio and lowers the multiplier.
Wrong. A higher SLR means banks must hold more of their deposits in liquid assets such as government securities. This leaves less for loans and reduces credit creation and the multiplier.
Correct. A greater banking habit means people keep more of their money as bank deposits and less as cash. The currency-deposit ratio falls, banks have more deposits to lend, and the multiplier rises.
Wrong. Population size does not directly change the currency-deposit ratio or the reserve ratio. Total money may grow, but the multiplier does not.
keyfact: Money multiplier = (1+c)/(c+r): it rises when people hold less cash (more banking habit) and falls when CRR or SLR rises.
option_notes: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is the share of a bank's net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) that scheduled banks must keep as cash with the RBI. It is set by the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934 (Section 42). No interest is paid on it. The RBI uses it to manage liquidity and inflation. The CRR was cut to 4% in 2020 and was 4.5% from 2024 after a hike, then lowered again in 2025. The statutory range is now flexible, since the 2006 amendment removed the floor and ceiling.

Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) is the minimum share of NDTL that banks must hold in liquid assets: cash, gold, or approved securities such as G-secs and T-bills. It is under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The RBI sets it, and it is currently 18%. The SLR ensures bank solvency, checks credit expansion, and creates a captive market for government debt. Unlike CRR, banks earn interest on SLR holdings and do not deposit them with the RBI.

Banking habit is the public's tendency to keep savings in bank deposits rather than cash. It is a core part of financial inclusion in India through schemes such as Jan Dhan Yojana (2014), which opened over 50 crore accounts, plus UPI and Aadhaar-linked DBT. More deposits lower the currency-deposit ratio, raise lending capacity, and raise the money multiplier. This is the correct answer.

Population is the number of people in a country. India has the largest population in the world, at about 1.4 billion. A larger population can increase money demand and the economy's size, but it does not directly alter the reserve ratios or cash-holding behaviour that determine the money multiplier. It is therefore a distractor in this question.
related: Money multiplier m = (1 + c)/(c + r); it falls when CRR, SLR, or the cash-deposit ratio rises.
CRR is held with the RBI under Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934, and earns no interest.
SLR is under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and is currently 18%.
M3 (broad money) = M1 + time deposits with banks.
Reserve money (M0) = currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with the RBI + other RBI deposits.
MSF rate is 25 bps above repo; SDF rate is 25 bps below repo.
The MPC has 6 members; the inflation target is 4% with a band of +/- 2%.
The Jan Dhan Yojana was launched in August 2014 to promote financial inclusion.
summary: The answer is (c). The money multiplier rises when people hold less currency and deposit more in banks, because banks can then lend out a larger share of deposits and the money creation chain gets longer. A stronger banking habit lowers the currency-deposit ratio, which raises the multiplier.
topic_notes:
Money supply and the multiplier. Reserve money (H), or high-powered money, equals currency in circulation plus bankers' deposits with the RBI plus other deposits with the RBI. M = m x H. The simple formula is m = (1 + c)/(c + r), where c = currency/deposits and r = reserves/deposits. Deposit multiplier = 1/CRR in the simplest case. A rise in c, CRR, or excess reserves lowers m. A fall in them raises m.

RBI monetary aggregates: M0 is reserve money; M1 is currency with the public plus demand deposits plus other RBI deposits (narrow money); M2 is M1 plus savings deposits with post offices; M3 is M1 plus time deposits with banks (broad money); M4 is M3 plus total post office deposits. M3 is the usual measure of broad money. Since 1998 the RBI has also published liquidity aggregates (L1 to L3) and, from 2020, revised monetary aggregates (M0 to M3).

Tools of monetary policy: quantitative tools are CRR, SLR, repo and reverse repo rates, MSF, the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF, introduced in 2022), OMOs, and the LAF. Qualitative tools are moral suasion and selective credit control. Repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks against securities. MSF rate is 25 bps above repo. The SDF rate is 25 bps below repo. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has six members and sets the repo rate with a CPI inflation target of 4% (+/- 2%), under the 2016 amendment to the RBI Act.

Other angles: the money multiplier is stable only if c and r are stable. In a crisis, banks hoard excess reserves and the multiplier falls, as seen after 2008 in many economies. Demonetisation (2016) increased deposits and temporarily lowered c. Financial inclusion and digital payments push c down over time.

question:
With reference to Indian economy, demand-pull inflation can be caused/ increased by which of the following? 1 Expansionary policies
2. Fiscal stimulus Inflation-indexing wages Higher purchasing power Rising interest rates Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Economy
detail: Demand-pull inflation is described as 'too much money chasing too few goods'. It occurs when aggregate demand (C + I + G + NX) grows faster than the economy's productive capacity, so the price level rises. Typical triggers are expansionary monetary policy (lower repo rate, higher money supply, lower CRR/SLR), expansionary fiscal policy (higher government spending, tax cuts, fiscal stimulus), rising disposable income or purchasing power, credit expansion, higher exports and rising consumer confidence. Cost-push inflation is different: it comes from supply-side increases in input costs such as wages, raw materials, oil prices, taxes or supply disruptions. Inflation-indexed wages (dearness allowance linked to CPI) feed a wage-price spiral and mainly raise costs, so they are usually classed as cost-push, though they can add some demand. Rising interest rates are the standard anti-inflation tool, because they raise borrowing costs, reduce consumption and investment, and so reduce demand-pull pressure. Elimination logic: statements 1, 2 and 4 are clearly demand-side, which fits only option (a). Statement 5 is wrong, which removes every option containing it. The printed options were garbled by OCR, but the official answer (a) is 1, 2 and 4 only.
explanations: Correct: it picks exactly the demand-side factors, expansionary policies, fiscal stimulus and higher purchasing power (1, 2 and 4).
Incorrect: it includes rising interest rates and wage indexation, which are anti-demand or cost-side factors, and it leaves out 1 and 2.
Incorrect: it includes 3 and 5, and wage indexation and rising rates do not cause demand-pull inflation.
Incorrect: it includes all five, but 3 is cost-push and 5 reduces demand, so it cannot be right.
keyfact: Demand-pull inflation comes from excess aggregate demand (expansionary policy, fiscal stimulus, higher purchasing power); rising interest rates reduce it, and wage indexation is cost-push.
option_notes: Option (a), 1, 2 and 4 only: this combination gathers the demand-side drivers, which are expansionary monetary and fiscal policy and rising purchasing power. Demand-pull inflation is also called 'demand-side' or 'excess demand' inflation. It is most visible when an economy nears full employment. Policymakers fight it with higher interest rates, tighter liquidity and fiscal consolidation. The RBI's inflation target is 4% CPI with a ±2% tolerance band.

Option (b), 3, 4 and 5 only: this mixes wage indexation (cost-push or built-in), purchasing power (demand-pull) and rising interest rates (a disinflationary tool). Built-in inflation arises when workers demand higher wages to keep up with prices, producing a wage-price spiral. Rising interest rates are the main brake on inflation, and the repo rate is the RBI's key policy rate.

Option (c), 1, 2, 3 and 5 only: this is the garbled option containing the policy and wage items. It wrongly adds rising interest rates and wage indexation. Cost-push inflation stems from higher input costs such as wages, oil, imported raw materials or taxes. Supply shocks, for example food price spikes from poor monsoons, are another cost-side category. Indirect taxes like GST changes can also push prices.

Option (d), 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5: this claims every factor causes demand-pull inflation, which is incorrect. Demand-pull and cost-push are the two broad types of inflation. Related types are structural inflation, stagflation (high inflation with stagnation and unemployment), reflation, disinflation and deflation. India measures inflation with CPI (base 2012) and WPI (base 2011-12).
related: Demand-pull inflation is 'too much money chasing too few goods'.
Cost-push inflation arises from higher input costs such as wages, oil or raw materials.
The RBI's inflation target is 4% CPI with a ±2% band, under the 2016 flexible inflation targeting framework.
The MPC has six members, three from the RBI and three external, appointed by the Centre.
Raising the repo rate, CRR or SLR is a contractionary tool against inflation.
CPI base year is 2012 and WPI base year is 2011-12.
Stagflation means high inflation together with stagnant growth and high unemployment.
Core inflation excludes food and fuel prices.
statements: 1 — Correct: Expansionary policies raise demand. Expansionary monetary policy means cutting the policy rate, easing liquidity and lowering the CRR, which makes credit cheaper and boosts consumption and investment. Expansionary fiscal policy means higher spending or lower taxes. The RBI adopted accommodative policy in 2020-21 during COVID. Excess demand against limited supply pushes prices up, which is the classic demand-pull case. Under the flexible inflation targeting framework (2016), the RBI targets CPI inflation of 4% with a band of ±2%.

2 — Correct: A fiscal stimulus is extra government spending or tax relief meant to revive demand, as in the Atmanirbhar Bharat packages of 2020. It raises aggregate demand through the multiplier effect. If supply is constrained or the economy is near full capacity, prices rise. Fiscal policy is run by the Union Budget under the FRBM Act 2003, which sets deficit targets. Keynesian economics supports stimulus in a slump, but overuse is inflationary.

3 — Incorrect: Inflation-indexing of wages, for example dearness allowance linked to CPI-IW for central government employees, raises production costs and sets off a wage-price spiral. It is therefore mainly cost-push or built-in inflation, not an original source of demand-pull. Built-in inflation is also called hangover inflation. The Pay Commission and DA revisions happen twice a year, in January and July.

4 — Correct: Higher purchasing power, meaning more disposable income, wages, remittances or credit, directly raises consumer demand. If output does not rise in step, prices go up. This is the demand-side or 'wealth effect' channel. Purchasing power parity (PPP) is a separate concept, and India is the third-largest economy in PPP terms. The Phillips curve links lower unemployment and higher demand with higher inflation in the short run.

5 — Incorrect: Rising interest rates make credit costlier, which reduces consumption and investment and lowers aggregate demand. They are the main tool against demand-pull inflation. The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee (six members, set up in 2016 under the RBI Act amendment) sets the repo rate. The RBI raised the repo rate from 4% to 6.5% between May 2022 and February 2023 to curb inflation.
summary: The answer is (a) 1, 2 and 4 only. Demand-pull inflation arises when aggregate demand outruns supply, and expansionary policies, fiscal stimulus and higher purchasing power all raise aggregate demand. Inflation-indexed wages (a cost-push or wage-price spiral factor) and rising interest rates (which curb demand) do not cause demand-pull inflation.
topic_notes: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. Demand-pull inflation comes from excess aggregate demand, while cost-push inflation comes from rising input costs or supply shocks. Demand-side causes include expansionary monetary policy (lower repo rate, higher money supply), expansionary fiscal policy (spending and tax cuts), rising incomes and remittances, credit growth, export booms, and black money or deficit financing. Supply-side causes include wage hikes, higher commodity and oil prices, supply-chain disruptions, taxes and currency depreciation, which raises import costs. Built-in inflation comes from wage-price spirals and inflation expectations. In India, the RBI Act was amended in 2016 to set up a flexible inflation targeting framework. The target is 4% CPI with a ±2% band, reviewed every five years, and the MPC has six members, three from the RBI and three external. If inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must report to the government. Monetary tools include the repo and reverse repo rates, MSF, CRR, SLR, OMOs and the LAF. Fiscal tools include taxation, subsidies and public spending. Measures: CPI-Combined (base 2012) is the headline measure for targeting, with food having a weight of about 46%. WPI (base 2011-12) is published by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT. The Phillips curve shows a trade-off between inflation and unemployment. Stagflation, seen in the 1970s oil shocks, combines high inflation with low growth. Other angles include core inflation (which excludes food and fuel), headline inflation, the GDP deflator, and the effects of inflation on creditors and debtors, on fixed-income groups and on exports.

question:
With reference to India, consider the following statements :
1. Retail investors through demat account can invest in ‘Treasury Bills’ and ‘Government of India Debt Bonds’ in primary market.
2. The ‘Negotiated Dealing SystemOrder Matching’ is a government securities trading platform of the Reserve Bank of India.
3. The ‘Central Depository Services Ltd.’ is jointly promoted by the Reserve Bank of India and the Bombay Stock Exchange. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: The question tests India's government securities (G-Sec) market and depository infrastructure. G-Secs include Treasury Bills (91, 182 and 364 days; zero-coupon, issued at a discount) and dated securities or bonds. Retail participation was historically limited to the non-competitive bidding window. In November 2021 the RBI launched the Retail Direct Scheme, letting individuals open a Gilt Securities Account with the RBI and buy T-Bills, dated G-Secs, SDLs, Sovereign Gold Bonds and similar instruments in the primary market and trade in the secondary market. Before that, retail investors could bid through demat accounts via stock exchange platforms, which is what the question refers to. NDS-OM (Negotiated Dealing System-Order Matching) is an anonymous, screen-based order-matching system for secondary-market trading in G-Secs, launched in 2005 and owned and operated by the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL) for the RBI. Depositories in India are NSDL (the first, 1996, promoted by IDBI, UTI and NSE) and CDSL (1999, promoted by BSE with banks such as SBI, Bank of India, Bank of Baroda, HDFC Bank and Standard Chartered). The RBI is not a promoter of CDSL, so statement 3 fails. Eliminating 3 removes (c) and (d), leaving (b) as the answer, since statement 1 is correct.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 2 is also correct, so 'statement 1 only' is incomplete.
(b) is right because statement 1 (retail demat access to T-Bills and G-Secs in the primary market) and statement 2 (NDS-OM is the RBI's G-Sec trading platform) are correct, and statement 3 is false.
(c) is wrong because statement 3 is incorrect (CDSL was promoted by BSE with banks, not the RBI), and it also excludes the correct statements 1 and 2.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement 3, which is false, and omits statement 1, which is true.
keyfact: NDS-OM is the RBI's G-Sec secondary trading platform (run by CCIL), and CDSL was promoted by BSE, not the RBI.
option_notes: Option (a), 'statement 1 only', would hold if NDS-OM were not an RBI platform. Statement 1 concerns retail access to primary-market G-Secs: T-Bills (91, 182 and 364 days) and dated securities are issued by the RBI through auctions on behalf of the Centre. Retail investors use the non-competitive bidding window, which allots at the weighted average cut-off price, and RBI Retail Direct (November 2021) opened direct gilt accounts to individuals.

Option (b), 'statements 1 and 2', is the official answer. It combines retail access to the primary G-Sec market through demat or Retail Direct with NDS-OM, the RBI's secondary-market order-matching platform that is operated by CCIL and was launched in 2005. G-Sec trading is anonymous and screen-based, which improves transparency and liquidity. The market is regulated by the RBI under the Government Securities Act, 2006.

Option (c), 'statement 3 only', rests on the false claim that CDSL was jointly promoted by the RBI and BSE. CDSL was in fact promoted by BSE with banks and began in 1999. It is a SEBI-regulated depository under the Depositories Act, 1996, and has been listed since 2017. NSDL, the older depository, was set up in 1996 with IDBI, UTI and NSE as promoters.

Option (d), 'statements 2 and 3', pairs a true statement (NDS-OM) with the false CDSL statement. NDS-OM was launched in 2005 and is operated by CCIL. Its inclusion of statement 3 makes the option wrong. CCIL itself was set up in 2001 and is a central counterparty for G-Secs, forex and money-market trades, promoted by banks, the SBI, the IDBI and others.
related: T-Bills come in 91, 182 and 364 day tenors and are issued at a discount to face value.
RBI Retail Direct was launched on 12 November 2021 for retail investors in G-Secs.
NDS-OM was launched in 2005 and is operated by CCIL for the RBI.
NSDL (1996) was India's first depository, and CDSL (1999) was promoted by BSE.
SEBI regulates depositories under the Depositories Act, 1996.
The Government Securities Act, 2006 governs issuance and holding of G-Secs.
State government bonds are called State Development Loans (SDLs).
Banks hold G-Secs to meet the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR).
statements: 1 — Correct: Retail investors can buy T-Bills and G-Secs in the primary market via demat accounts (non-competitive bids through brokers or exchanges) and, since 2021, through RBI Retail Direct. Treasury Bills are short-term money-market instruments of 91, 182 and 364 days, issued at a discount and redeemed at par, and have no coupon. Dated G-Secs carry fixed or floating coupons and tenors of 5 to 40 years. The non-competitive window lets small investors get allotment at the weighted average auction price. RBI Retail Direct, launched in November 2021, gives free Gilt Account access and removes intermediaries. The Centre borrows through these instruments.

2 — Correct: NDS-OM is an electronic, screen-based, anonymous order-matching platform for secondary-market trading of G-Secs, launched in August 2005. It is owned by the RBI and operated by the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL). Participants include banks, primary dealers, insurers and mutual funds, and it is also open to retail investors through the Retail Direct facility. It is distinct from NDS-Auction (the primary-market bidding platform) and NDS-CALL for call money. Trades settle through CCIL on a T+1 basis, and the platform adds transparency and price discovery to the market.

3 — Incorrect: CDSL (Central Depository Services (India) Ltd) was set up in 1999 and began operations in 1999 as the second depository after NSDL. It was promoted by the Bombay Stock Exchange with banks including Bank of India, Bank of Baroda, HDFC Bank, SBI and Standard Chartered; it was not jointly promoted with the RBI. It is regulated by SEBI under the Depositories Act, 1996. It lists on the stock exchange (2017 IPO). NSDL, the first depository, was promoted by IDBI, UTI and NSE. Depositories hold securities in dematerialised form, and depository participants (DPs) act as their agents.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 1 and 2 are correct and statement 3 is wrong. Retail investors can buy T-Bills and G-Secs in the primary market through demat accounts (RBI Retail Direct), and NDS-OM is the RBI's G-Sec trading platform. CDSL was promoted by BSE with banks, not jointly with the RBI.
topic_notes: Government securities (G-Secs) are tradable debt instruments issued by the Central Government (T-Bills, cash management bills and dated securities) and by state governments (State Development Loans). They are treated as risk-free in credit terms and count toward the banks' Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR). T-Bills are zero-coupon, issued at a discount in 91, 182 and 364 day tenors. Cash Management Bills are short-term instruments of under 91 days issued to meet temporary cash gaps. Dated securities have maturities of 5 to 40 years with half-yearly coupons. The RBI manages public debt and conducts auctions as the government's debt manager. Primary dealers and banks are the major bidders, while retail participation has grown through the non-competitive window and the RBI Retail Direct portal, launched on 12 November 2021. The Government Securities Act, 2006 governs issuance and holding, and securities can be held in SGL accounts, Gilt accounts or demat form. Trading takes place on NDS-OM, with settlement through CCIL, the clearing house. Related instruments include Sovereign Gold Bonds, the Floating Rate Savings Bonds 2020 (Taxable), which replaced the 8% Savings Bonds, and Inflation-Indexed Bonds. The depository system dematerialises securities. NSDL was set up in 1996 and CDSL in 1999, both regulated by SEBI under the Depositories Act, 1996. The RBI also runs open market operations (OMOs), buying and selling G-Secs to manage liquidity. Future questions could cover yields, bond prices, the yield curve, the FPI route (Fully Accessible Route, 2020), the inclusion of Indian G-Secs in global bond indices (JP Morgan, June 2024), and the difference between the money market and the capital market.

question:
With reference to ‘WaterCredit’, consider the following statements :
1. It puts microfinance tools to work in the water and sanitation sector.
2. It is a global initiative launched under the aegis of the World Health Organization and the World Bank.
3. It aims to enable the poor people to meet their water needs without depending on subsidies. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: WaterCredit was pioneered by Water.org (formed in 2009 by merging WaterPartners, founded by Gary White, and H2O Africa, founded by Matt Damon). Its core idea is that the poor can pay for water and toilets if they get access to small, affordable finance rather than charity. Water.org works with local microfinance institutions (MFIs), banks and NGOs, which lend to households for water taps, piped connections, wells, rainwater tanks, water purifiers and toilets. Loans are repaid, and the money is recycled to new borrowers, which makes the model sustainable and reduces dependence on subsidies and grants. Water.org is a non-profit headquartered in the US (Kansas City) and operates in countries including India, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Kenya, Uganda, the Philippines and Peru. Elimination logic: statement 1 describes the model exactly, and statement 3 states its stated purpose. Statement 2 attributes the initiative to WHO and the World Bank, which is a classic UPSC trap of linking a private NGO scheme to big international bodies. With 2 wrong, options (a), (b) and (d) all fall away, leaving (c). The answer can be reached by rejecting statement 2 alone.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement 2, which wrongly credits WHO and the World Bank with launching WaterCredit.
(b) is wrong because it includes the false statement 2 and leaves out the correct statement 1.
(c) is correct because statements 1 and 3 accurately describe WaterCredit as microfinance for water and sanitation that reduces dependence on subsidies, while statement 2 is false.
(d) is wrong because statement 2 is incorrect, so not all three statements can be right.
keyfact: WaterCredit = Water.org's microfinance model (loans, not subsidies) for water and sanitation; it is not a WHO or World Bank initiative.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 and 2 only: this pairs the correct microfinance description with the false claim of WHO/World Bank origin. WHO (est. 1948, Geneva) is the UN health agency and co-runs the JMP on drinking water and sanitation with UNICEF. The World Bank Group (Washington DC) funds development projects including water supply. Neither launched WaterCredit, which belongs to the NGO Water.org.

Option (b), 2 and 3 only: it retains the false statement 2 and drops the correct statement 1. The World Bank was set up in 1944 at Bretton Woods and includes IBRD and IDA. It runs water programmes and the 2030 Water Resources Group but not WaterCredit. Statement 3 is correct, but this combination is wrong.

Option (c), 1 and 3 only: this is the correct answer. WaterCredit is Water.org's microfinance approach to water and sanitation. Water.org was co-founded by Gary White and actor Matt Damon in 2009 through the merger of WaterPartners and H2O Africa. It helps MFIs lend to households for taps, toilets and filters, with repayments recycled, so it reduces reliance on grants and subsidies.

Option (d), 1, 2 and 3: this would be correct only if WaterCredit were a WHO/World Bank initiative, which it is not. UPSC often builds such options by adding one plausible-sounding but false statement about institutional origin. Always verify the parent organisation for named initiatives.
related: WaterCredit is run by Water.org, co-founded by Gary White and Matt Damon.
Water.org was formed in 2009 by merging WaterPartners and H2O Africa.
WHO and UNICEF run the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) on water and sanitation.
SDG 6 is clean water and sanitation for all by 2030.
Jal Jeevan Mission (2019) targets tap water to every rural household.
World Water Day is 22 March; World Toilet Day is 19 November.
NABARD's SHG-Bank Linkage Programme is India's major microfinance model.
Atal Bhujal Yojana focuses on community-led groundwater management.
statements: 1 — Correct: WaterCredit explicitly applies microfinance tools to water and sanitation. Water.org partners with MFIs and banks to give small loans for household water connections, hand pumps, tanks, filters and toilets. Started in the early 2000s by WaterPartners (Gary White) and scaled after the 2009 merger with H2O Africa (Matt Damon). In India it works with MFIs, self-help-group-linked lenders and NBFCs. It has reached tens of millions of people and has mobilised large amounts of capital, showing that the poor are bankable borrowers for WASH needs.

2 — Incorrect: WaterCredit is not a WHO or World Bank initiative. It is run by Water.org, a private, non-profit international NGO. WHO is the UN specialised agency for health, headquartered in Geneva, and works with UNICEF on the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for water supply and sanitation. The World Bank has a Water Global Practice and funds projects, but it did not launch WaterCredit. Do not confuse it with the UN's SDG 6 (clean water and sanitation) or the JMP, which are the actual international monitoring frameworks.

3 — Correct: The aim is to enable poor people to meet water and sanitation needs through affordable credit instead of depending on subsidies or charity. Repayment of loans lets lenders recycle funds, creating a sustainable market-based solution. It supports the idea that the poor can pay if finance is available and that households gain dignity and time savings (particularly women and girls who otherwise spend hours fetching water). Water.org also provides technical assistance to lenders and helps design loan products for WASH.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. WaterCredit is an initiative of the non-profit Water.org, co-founded by Gary White and Matt Damon. It applies microfinance (small affordable loans) to water and sanitation so poor households can meet their needs without relying on subsidies. It is not a WHO/World Bank initiative, so statement 2 is wrong.
topic_notes: WaterCredit is the flagship financial-inclusion approach of Water.org, a global non-profit that aims to provide safe water and sanitation to people in need. Water.org was formed in 2009 by merging WaterPartners International (founded 1990 by Gary White and others) and H2O Africa (founded by Matt Damon). The core idea is that small, affordable loans, rather than grants, allow poor households to install water connections, toilets, rainwater harvesting tanks and filters. Partner MFIs, banks and NBFCs lend the money, borrowers repay, and funds are recycled, building a sustainable market. Water.org works across Asia, Africa and Latin America, with India among the largest country programmes; it focuses on women as borrowers, since women bear most of the burden of water collection. Related global context: SDG 6 aims for clean water and sanitation for all by 2030. The WHO-UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) tracks progress. The UN declared 2018-2028 the International Decade for Action 'Water for Sustainable Development'. World Water Day is 22 March and World Toilet Day is 19 November. Indian schemes UPSC may ask about: Jal Jeevan Mission (2019, functional household tap connections to all rural households by 2024), Swachh Bharat Mission (2014, Urban and Gramin), Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (AMRUT), Namami Gange, and Atal Bhujal Yojana for groundwater management. Other microfinance and financial-inclusion links: NABARD's SHG-Bank Linkage Programme, Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (2014), and the Microfinance Institutions Network. Typical UPSC trap: attributing a private or NGO initiative to the UN, WHO, World Bank or Government of India.

question:
In India, the central bank’s function as the ‘lender of last resort’ usually refers to which of the following?
1. Lending to trade and industry bodies when they fail to borrow from other sources
2. Providing liquidity to the banks having a temporary crisis
3. Lending to governments to finance budgetary deficits Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Economy
detail: The lender of last resort doctrine goes back to Walter Bagehot's Lombard Street (1873). It says that in a panic the central bank should lend freely, against good collateral, at a penal rate, to solvent but illiquid banks. The aim is to prevent bank runs and contagion and to protect financial stability. In India the RBI performs this role under the RBI Act, 1934, through the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF, introduced in 2011, at repo plus 25 bps, drawing on SLR holdings) and the Standing Liquidity Facility. It also uses special liquidity windows during crises, such as the 2008 global financial crisis and the 2020 pandemic. Statement 1 is wrong because the RBI does not lend to trade and industry bodies directly. Credit to industry comes through banks and development finance institutions such as NABARD, SIDBI and EXIM Bank. Statement 3 is wrong because lending to the government is the RBI's role as banker to the government, through Ways and Means Advances (WMA) and overdrafts. It is not LOLR. Since April 1997, and under the FRBM Act 2003 from April 2006, the RBI cannot subscribe to primary issues of government securities, except in special circumstances. Eliminating 1 and 3 leaves option (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement 1. The RBI does not lend directly to trade and industry bodies, so LOLR does not cover this.
(b) is correct because only statement 2 describes LOLR, which is emergency liquidity for banks facing a temporary crisis.
(c) is wrong because it includes statement 3. Financing government deficits is the banker-to-government function, not LOLR.
(d) is wrong because statement 3 alone is incorrect, and it also leaves out the one correct statement, 2.
keyfact: LOLR means emergency liquidity for solvent banks in a temporary crisis (MSF, repo), not lending to industry or financing government deficits.
option_notes: Statements 1 and 2: this combination mixes a correct description of LOLR with a wrong one. Direct lending to trade and industry is not an RBI function. Industry is financed by banks and by development finance institutions such as SIDBI, NABARD and EXIM Bank, and the RBI only influences credit through policy rates and refinance windows. It would also weaken the RBI's focus on price and financial stability.

Statement 2 only: this is the correct reading of LOLR. The central bank gives emergency liquidity to solvent banks that are temporarily short of funds, to prevent panic and systemic contagion. In India this is done through the MSF, repo and special liquidity windows, against eligible collateral such as government securities. The doctrine comes from Bagehot's Lombard Street (1873). Insolvent banks are handled through resolution, merger or moratorium instead.

Statements 2 and 3: this combination pairs the correct statement with the deficit-financing one. Deficit financing is not LOLR. The RBI gives the government Ways and Means Advances for temporary mismatches, but automatic monetisation of the deficit ended in 1997 and the FRBM Act 2003 restricted it further from 2006. Persistent monetisation would be inflationary and would compromise RBI independence.

Statement 3 only: this treats government financing as the LOLR function, which is a common misconception. The RBI acts as the government's banker and debt manager, and WMA and overdraft facilities cover short-term cash gaps. Direct financing of deficits through ad hoc Treasury Bills ended in 1997. The 2020 pandemic saw limited relaxations, such as higher WMA limits, but this is still not LOLR.
related: LOLR doctrine: Walter Bagehot, Lombard Street (1873).
