MSF was introduced on 9 May 2011 at repo plus 25 bps.
SDF was introduced in April 2022 as the floor of the LAF corridor.
The RBI was established on 1 April 1935 and nationalised on 1 January 1949.
WMA is the RBI's short-term facility for the government, and ad hoc Treasury Bills were discontinued in 1997.
The FRBM Act 2003 barred RBI subscription to primary government securities from 2006.
CRR is under Section 42 of the RBI Act, and SLR is under the Banking Regulation Act 1949.
DICGC deposit insurance covers ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The RBI does not lend directly to trade and industry bodies as a last resort. Detail: Industrial and trade credit flows through commercial banks, and refinance is given by institutions such as NABARD (1982), SIDBI (1990) and EXIM Bank (1982). The RBI's Industrial Development Bank of India link was ended in 1964, when IDBI was set up as a subsidiary of the RBI, and IDBI was later separated. The RBI's main tools are repo, reverse repo, CRR, SLR and MSF, all of which work through banks. Direct lending to industry would blur monetary policy with fiscal and developmental roles, which is why banks sit as intermediaries.

2 — Correct: Providing emergency liquidity to banks facing a temporary crisis is the essence of LOLR. Detail: The idea comes from Bagehot (1873): lend freely at a penal rate against good collateral to solvent banks. In India the instruments are the MSF (from 9 May 2011, at repo plus 25 bps, allowing banks to dip into their SLR holdings), repo operations under the LAF, and special liquidity windows. The RBI also supports banks through term repos, and in 2008 and 2020 it opened special liquidity facilities. LOLR assistance is for illiquid banks, not insolvent ones, which are dealt with by the DICGC (insurance up to ₹5 lakh), resolution, or merger.

3 — Incorrect: Lending to the government to finance budgetary deficits is not LOLR. Detail: It belongs to the RBI's role as banker and debt manager to the government, under Sections 17 and 20 of the RBI Act. Ways and Means Advances (WMA) cover temporary mismatches in receipts and payments. The practice of automatic monetisation through ad hoc Treasury Bills ended in 1997. The FRBM Act 2003 barred direct RBI subscription to government securities from 2006, apart from WMA and exceptional circumstances. The Centre's WMA limit is revised periodically.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. The central bank's lender of last resort (LOLR) function means giving emergency liquidity to solvent banks facing a temporary crisis, so that a liquidity shortage does not become a systemic banking failure. It does not mean lending directly to industry or financing government deficits.
topic_notes: The central bank's functions include issuing currency, acting as banker to the government and to banks, managing foreign exchange, regulating and supervising banks, conducting monetary policy, and acting as lender of last resort. The RBI was set up on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934, and was nationalised on 1 January 1949. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), with six members, was statutory from 2016 and targets CPI inflation at 4% with a band of plus or minus 2%. Key policy instruments are the repo rate, reverse repo, MSF (repo plus 25 bps), the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF, introduced in 2022 as the floor of the corridor), CRR (cash reserve ratio, under Section 42 of the RBI Act), SLR (statutory liquidity ratio, under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949), open market operations, and market stabilisation scheme bonds. The LAF corridor is bounded by the MSF rate above and the SDF rate below, with the repo rate in the middle. As banker to banks, the RBI keeps their CRR balances and provides clearing and settlement. The DICGC insures deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank. The RBI regulates NBFCs, payment systems (under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007) and credit information. UPSC may next ask about the difference between LOLR and banker to government, WMA limits, the corridor system, CRR versus SLR, the MPC composition, and the Bagehot rule.

question: R2 Code of Practices’ constitutes a tool available for promoting the adoption of
options: environmentally responsible practices in electronics recycling industry
ecological management of ‘Wetlands of International Importance’ under the Ramsar Convention
sustainable practices in the cultivation of agricultural crops in degraded lands
Environmental Impact Assessment’ in the exploitation of natural resources [ P.T.O
subject: Environment
detail: R2 stands for Responsible Recycling. It is a voluntary certification standard for electronics recyclers and refurbishers, first released in 2008 and developed by Sustainable Electronics Recycling International (SERI) after the US Environmental Protection Agency convened stakeholders. The current version is R2:2013, followed by R2v3 (2020). It covers environmental, worker health and safety, and data security requirements. It requires a hierarchy of reuse, then recycling, then disposal. It also requires proper handling of focus materials such as mercury-containing devices, CRT glass and batteries. It also governs export controls and downstream vendor tracking. Certification is granted by accredited third-party auditors. The standard is relevant to India's e-waste problem and to the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2016 and 2022 (Extended Producer Responsibility). Elimination logic: Ramsar wetlands are managed through the Ramsar Convention's wise-use guidance and Montreux Record, not a code called R2. Degraded-land agriculture relates to UNCCD, land restoration and agroforestry. EIA is governed by India's EIA Notification 2006 under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986. The letter R plus the word 'Practices' points to recycling. So only (a) fits.
explanations: Correct: R2 is the Responsible Recycling Code of Practices for electronics recyclers, promoting environmentally responsible recycling and refurbishing.
Incorrect: Ramsar wetlands are managed through Ramsar wise-use guidelines, Management Plans and the Montreux Record, not R2.
Incorrect: Sustainable cultivation on degraded land is addressed by land restoration, agroforestry and UNCCD frameworks, not R2.
Incorrect: EIA in India rests on the EIA Notification 2006 under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, not on R2.
keyfact: R2 = Responsible Recycling, a voluntary code of practices for electronics recyclers (SERI, USA).
option_notes: Electronics recycling is the processing of discarded electronic goods to recover metals, plastics and glass and to dispose of hazardous parts such as lead, mercury and cadmium safely. Standards include R2 and e-Stewards. India regulates it through the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2016, amended in 2018 and replaced by the 2022 Rules, which use Extended Producer Responsibility and CPCB registration of recyclers. The informal sector handles most of India's e-waste.

Wetlands of International Importance are sites designated under the Ramsar Convention, signed in 1971 at Ramsar, Iran, and in force from 1975. Parties commit to wise use. Sites at risk are listed in the Montreux Record, and Keoladeo and Loktak have been on it. India joined in 1982 and has over 80 Ramsar sites, among the highest counts in Asia. World Wetlands Day is on 2 February. Indian rules include the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017.

Degraded land is land whose productivity has fallen through erosion, salinity, deforestation or desertification. The UNCCD, adopted in 1994, addresses it through Land Degradation Neutrality. India hosted UNCCD COP14 in 2019 at Greater Noida and pledged to restore 26 million hectares by 2030. Tools include agroforestry, watershed management, the Bonn Challenge and the Soil Health Card. ICAR and ICRISAT work on dryland crops.

Environmental Impact Assessment is a process of predicting the environmental effects of a proposed project before approval. In India it follows the EIA Notification 2006 under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, which sets categories A and B, with screening, scoping, public hearing and appraisal. The MoEFCC and State Environment Impact Assessment Authorities appraise projects. A Draft EIA 2020 drew criticism. The concept originated with the US NEPA of 1969.
related: R2 stands for Responsible Recycling, administered by SERI.
e-Stewards is a rival certification from the Basel Action Network.
The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 took effect from 1 April 2023.
Extended Producer Responsibility is the core principle of India's e-waste rules.
The Basel Convention regulates transboundary movement of hazardous waste.
CPCB is the nodal body for registering e-waste recyclers and EPR.
The Montreux Record lists Ramsar sites facing ecological change.
India's EIA regime is the EIA Notification 2006.
summary: The answer is (a). R2 (Responsible Recycling) is a voluntary standard for electronics recyclers, developed in the USA, which promotes environmentally responsible and safe recycling and refurbishing of used electronics.
topic_notes: E-waste is one of the fastest growing waste streams. It includes discarded computers, phones, TVs and appliances, which hold valuable metals such as gold, copper and palladium as well as toxins such as lead, mercury, cadmium, brominated flame retardants and PCBs. India is among the top e-waste generators in the world, after China and the USA, and most of it is processed informally. Legal framework: the Hazardous Wastes Rules 1989 and the E-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules 2011 came first. The E-Waste (Management) Rules 2016 introduced Extended Producer Responsibility, PROs, dismantlers and refurbishers, and deposit refund. The 2018 amendment set EPR targets. The E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022, effective April 2023, introduced EPR certificates, a central portal run by CPCB, and covered more items. International framework: the Basel Convention (1989, in force 1992) controls transboundary movement of hazardous wastes, and the Ban Amendment prohibits exports from OECD to non-OECD countries. Related conventions include Rotterdam (prior informed consent for chemicals and pesticides), Stockholm (POPs), Minamata (mercury) and the Bamako Convention for Africa. Voluntary standards for recyclers are R2 (SERI) and e-Stewards (Basel Action Network). Other themes: urban mining, circular economy, Right to Repair, Mission LiFE, and Battery Waste Management Rules 2022. Related concepts include Producer Responsibility Organisations and the polluter pays principle.

question:
Why is there a concern about copper smelting plants? 15. <Dhey may release lethal quantities of carbon monoxide into environment.
2. The copper slag can cause the leaching of some heavy metals into environment.
3. They may release sulphur dioxide as a pollutant. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Environment
detail: Copper is extracted mainly from sulphide ores such as chalcopyrite (CuFeS2). The ore is concentrated by froth flotation, roasted and smelted in a furnace, and converted in a converter. Sulphur in the ore oxidises to sulphur dioxide (SO2), so smelters are major point sources of SO2. This causes acid rain, respiratory problems and damage to vegetation. Modern plants capture SO2 and convert it into sulphuric acid. The smelting process also generates large amounts of slag, an iron silicate waste containing traces of copper, arsenic, lead, cadmium, zinc and nickel. If dumped carelessly, rain can leach these heavy metals into groundwater and soil. The Sterlite Copper plant at Thoothukudi (Tamil Nadu) drew protests over such pollution concerns, and its closure followed police firing in May 2018. Carbon monoxide is produced in many combustion and metallurgical processes, such as blast-furnace iron making, but it is not the characteristic pollutant of copper smelting. The word 'lethal' in statement 1 is the giveaway of an exaggerated claim. Statements 2 and 3 are correct, so (b) follows.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is not an established concern, and it leaves out statement 3, which is correct.
Correct: statements 2 (slag leaching heavy metals) and 3 (SO2 emissions) are both valid concerns; statement 1 is not.
Wrong: it includes statement 1 and excludes statement 2, which is correct.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, and carbon monoxide in lethal quantities is not characteristic of copper smelting.
keyfact: Copper smelting concerns: SO2 emissions and heavy-metal leaching from slag; lethal CO is not a typical issue.
option_notes: Options 1 and 2 only: this combination pairs the CO claim with slag leaching. It is wrong because it drops SO2, the main smelter pollutant. It is useful to remember that slag leaching of heavy metals is a real concern and is often reused in construction.

Options 2 and 3 only: this is the correct answer. Slag leaching and SO2 emissions are the two main environmental concerns of copper smelting. The Sterlite Copper plant in Thoothukudi was closed in 2018 after protests over pollution, and the Supreme Court later upheld the closure in 2020.

Options 1 and 3 only: this pairs CO with SO2. It is wrong because it rejects the slag leaching concern. SO2 is correct but CO is not a distinctive smelter pollutant; CO comes mainly from incomplete combustion in vehicles, biomass burning and iron-making.

Options 1, 2 and 3: this accepts all three statements. It is wrong because lethal CO release is not a recognised copper smelting concern. UPSC often inserts one exaggerated or unrelated claim in a list of otherwise valid statements.
related: Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) is the chief copper ore.
Sterlite Copper plant at Thoothukudi was ordered shut in May 2018.
Hindustan Copper Ltd mines at Khetri (Rajasthan) and Malanjkhand (MP).
Copper slag can be used in cement, concrete and road construction.
Hazardous and Other Wastes Rules, 2016 regulate hazardous waste in India.
CPCB classifies copper smelting as a Red category industry.
Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin.
SO2 from smelters is converted to sulphuric acid by the contact process.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Copper smelting is not known for releasing lethal quantities of carbon monoxide; its characteristic emissions are SO2 and particulates. CO is a colourless, odourless gas formed by incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels. It binds haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, which reduces oxygen transport in the blood. Major sources are vehicles, biomass burning and iron and steel blast furnaces. India's National Ambient Air Quality Standards (2009) set CO limits of 2 mg/m3 for 8 hours and 4 mg/m3 for 1 hour. Copper plants are mainly regulated for SO2, particulate matter, arsenic and fluoride.

2 — Correct: Copper slag is a vitreous iron-silicate by-product and can leach heavy metals such as lead, arsenic, cadmium, copper and zinc into soil and groundwater if stored badly. Roughly 2 to 3 tonnes of slag are produced per tonne of copper. Slag can be reused as abrasive blasting material, in cement and concrete, in road construction and as railway ballast. Hazardous waste in India is regulated under the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016, and the Basel Convention covers transboundary movement.

3 — Correct: Sulphide ores release sulphur dioxide when roasted and smelted. SO2 is a pungent gas that causes acid rain, respiratory illness and damage to buildings and crops. It is controlled through flue-gas desulphurisation and by converting SO2 to sulphuric acid in the contact process. The NAAQS limits for SO2 are 50 micrograms/m3 (annual) and 80 micrograms/m3 (24-hour). India notified SO2 emission norms for coal power plants in December 2015. Sulphur emissions also arise from coal burning and volcanoes.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 and 3 only. Copper smelting releases sulphur dioxide from sulphide ores, and the slag can leach heavy metals into soil and water. Carbon monoxide in lethal quantities is not a recognised major concern of copper smelters.
topic_notes: Copper (Cu) is a ductile metal that conducts heat and electricity well. Its main ores are chalcopyrite (CuFeS2), malachite, cuprite and chalcocite. Extraction by the pyrometallurgical route involves crushing, froth flotation, roasting, smelting to produce matte (Cu2S and FeS), converting to blister copper (about 98% pure) and electrolytic refining to 99.99% purity. Sulphur dioxide is a by-product and is usually captured to make sulphuric acid. Slag (iron silicate) is produced in large quantities. Environmental concerns include SO2 and acid rain, particulates containing arsenic, lead and cadmium, slag disposal and leaching, and wastewater contamination. In India the major producers are Hindalco (Dahej) and Hindustan Copper Ltd (Khetri in Rajasthan, Malanjkhand in Madhya Pradesh, Ghatsila in Jharkhand). Sterlite's Thoothukudi plant was closed in 2018 after protests and firing. The National Green Tribunal and the Supreme Court dealt with the case, and the Supreme Court dismissed Vedanta's plea in 2020. Legal framework: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981; Water Act, 1974; Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; Hazardous Waste Rules, 2016. Copper smelting is placed in the Red category of industries by the CPCB. Other angles UPSC may ask: effects of SO2 and NOx on acid rain, the Minamata and Itai-itai diseases from heavy metals, red mud from aluminium, fly ash from thermal plants, and e-waste recycling of copper.

ocr: With reference to furnace oil, consider the following statements : 1. It is a product of oil refineries. 2. Some industries use it to generate power. 3. Its use causes sulphur emissions into environment. Which of the statements given above are correct? (a) 1 and 2 only (b) 2 and 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d@) 1,2 and3 11 BXC-U-FTHI/68A
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Furnace oil (FO), also called residual fuel oil or heavy fuel oil, is the heavy, viscous residue left at the bottom of the crude distillation column after petrol, naphtha, kerosene and diesel are drawn off. It is therefore a direct refinery product (statement 1). It is widely used as boiler and furnace fuel in industries such as steel, textiles, cement, ceramics, paper and chemicals. It is also used in some captive and standby power plants and diesel-generator-type units, and in ships as bunker fuel (statement 2). Because it is a residue, it concentrates impurities, notably sulphur (often 2-4% by weight), plus nitrogen compounds, ash and heavy metals. Burning it releases sulphur dioxide (SO2), which causes acid rain and particulate pollution, along with NOx and soot (statement 3). Hence all three statements are correct. Elimination logic: all three are factually sound, so any option that drops one statement fails. Statement 1 is the most basic and statement 3 is well-known environmental science, so both (a) and (b) fail, and (c) fails because of statement 2. IMO 2020 capped sulphur in marine fuel at 0.5% from 1 January 2020, which relates to furnace oil/bunker fuel.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out statement 3, but furnace oil's sulphur content does cause SO2 emissions.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 1, but furnace oil is indeed a refinery product (the residue).
Wrong: it leaves out statement 2, but some industries do use furnace oil for power generation.
Correct: all three statements are accurate, so 1, 2 and 3 together is the right answer.
keyfact: Furnace oil is the sulphur-rich residue of crude refining, burned in industry and some power generation, and a source of SO2 emissions.
related: Furnace oil is the residue left after distillation of crude in the refinery.
Fuel oil/furnace oil has high sulphur and is a major source of SO2.
IMO 2020 reduced the sulphur cap in marine fuel from 3.5% to 0.5%.
BS-VI fuel norms came into force across India on 1 April 2020, with 10 ppm sulphur.
Jamnagar (Reliance) is the world's largest refining complex.
Petcoke is a high-sulphur refinery by-product whose use was restricted in the NCR.
Flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) removes SO2 from power plant emissions.
SO2 and NOx are the main precursors of acid rain.
statements: 1 — Correct: Furnace oil is a product of crude oil refining. It is the residual fraction from atmospheric and vacuum distillation, also called heavy fuel oil, residual fuel oil or bunker fuel. It is dense and viscous, with a boiling range above about 350°C, and often has to be preheated before it can be pumped and burned. Grades include LSHS (low sulphur heavy stock) and FO. Indian refineries such as those of IOCL, BPCL, HPCL and Reliance produce it. Its share has declined as refineries upgrade with cokers and hydrocrackers.

2 — Correct: Industries burn furnace oil in boilers, kilns and furnaces to produce heat and steam, and some use it to generate electricity. It powers captive generators, heavy-fuel-oil engine power plants, and in some places utility stations, particularly in island or remote areas. It is also used as ship bunker fuel. Its use in power has fallen in India because of cost and pollution, and natural gas and coal are preferred. Some states have restricted its use in industrial areas such as the Delhi-NCR region.

3 — Correct: Furnace oil has high sulphur, typically 2-4%, so combustion emits sulphur dioxide (SO2), which causes acid rain, respiratory illness and secondary particulate matter. It also emits NOx, PM and carbon dioxide. Regulations include India's tightening of SO2 limits for industry and the IMO's global marine fuel sulphur cap of 0.5% from 2020, down from 3.5%. Emission-control areas (ECAs) set a 0.1% limit. Scrubbers (flue gas desulphurisation) and low-sulphur fuels are the main mitigation options.
summary: The answer is (d): 1, 2 and 3 are all correct. Furnace oil is a residual fuel left after lighter fractions are distilled in refineries, it is burned in industrial boilers, furnaces and some power generation, and its high sulphur content causes SO2 emissions.
topic_notes: Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation into fractions by boiling point. From lightest to heaviest these are refinery gas/LPG, naphtha, petrol (gasoline), kerosene/ATF, diesel (gas oil), and then residues: furnace oil/fuel oil, lubricating oils, paraffin wax, bitumen/asphalt and petroleum coke. Vacuum distillation of the atmospheric residue yields further gas oils and vacuum residue. Heavy residues are upgraded by secondary processes: cracking (catalytic, thermal and hydrocracking), visbreaking, coking, and the Residue Fluid Catalytic Cracker (RFCC), which convert them into lighter, more valuable products. Furnace oil is used in industrial boilers, furnaces, kilns, ships (bunker fuel) and some power plants. Its drawbacks are high sulphur, ash and heavy metals, so it is a significant source of SO2, NOx and particulates. Related pollution points: SO2 leads to acid rain and secondary PM2.5, and flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) is the standard control. India notified stricter SO2 norms for coal power plants in 2015, with deadlines extended repeatedly. Fuel quality in India moved from BS-IV to BS-VI on 1 April 2020, which cut sulphur in petrol and diesel to 10 ppm. IMO MARPOL Annex VI set the 0.5% global sulphur cap for ships from 1 January 2020. Petcoke, a refinery by-product, is also high in sulphur, and its use was restricted by the Supreme Court and the CPCB in the NCR. Other angles UPSC may ask: LSHS, bitumen, Naphtha as fertilizer and petrochemical feedstock, Nelson complexity index, major Indian refineries (Jamnagar being the largest), and the Petroleum Planning & Analysis Cell.

ocr: What is blue carbon? (a) Carbon captured by oceans and coastal ecosystems (b) Carbon sequestered in forest biomass and agricultural soils (c) Carbon contained in petroleum and natural gas (ad) Carbon present in atmosphere
subject: Environment
detail: Blue carbon is the organic carbon captured by living organisms in coastal and marine ecosystems and stored in their biomass and, above all, in the sediments beneath them. The term was popularised by UNEP, FAO and IUCN around 2009, in the report 'Blue Carbon: The Role of Healthy Oceans in Binding Carbon'. The three key ecosystems are mangroves, tidal salt marshes and seagrass meadows. Kelp forests and other macroalgae are also studied. These habitats cover a small area but bury carbon much faster per unit area than terrestrial forests. Their waterlogged, oxygen-poor sediments slow decomposition, so carbon stays locked up for centuries to millennia. The main store is soil, unlike in forests, where most carbon is in biomass. When these ecosystems are drained, cleared or converted to aquaculture, the stored carbon is released as CO2 and other greenhouse gases, which makes protection and restoration a climate-mitigation tool. Elimination logic: option (b) describes green carbon (terrestrial biomass and soils), option (c) describes fossil carbon, and option (d) is simply atmospheric CO2. Only option (a) matches the 'blue' (ocean and coast) link.
explanations: Correct. Blue carbon is carbon captured by oceans and coastal ecosystems such as mangroves, salt marshes and seagrasses.
Wrong. Carbon in forest biomass and agricultural soils is terrestrial or 'green' carbon, not blue carbon.
Wrong. Carbon in petroleum and natural gas is fossil carbon. Burning it adds CO2 to the atmosphere.
Wrong. Carbon present in the atmosphere is mainly CO2, a greenhouse gas. It is the carbon that blue carbon ecosystems remove, not blue carbon itself.
keyfact: Blue carbon = carbon stored in oceans and coastal ecosystems (mangroves, salt marshes, seagrasses), mainly in sediments.
option_notes: Carbon captured by oceans and coastal ecosystems is blue carbon. The main sinks are mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass meadows, with kelp and algae also studied. The carbon is stored mostly in sediments for centuries or longer. The term was popularised by UNEP, FAO and IUCN around 2009. Degradation of these habitats turns them into emission sources. Blue carbon is now part of coastal restoration and climate-mitigation planning in several countries, including India's mangrove initiatives such as MISHTI.

Carbon sequestered in forest biomass and agricultural soils is terrestrial, or 'green', carbon. Forests store it in trees, roots and litter, and soils store it as soil organic carbon. It is the basis of afforestation, REDD+ and soil-carbon programmes. India's NDC includes a target of an additional 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO2-equivalent carbon sink through forest and tree cover by 2030. Forest carbon is mostly in biomass, whereas blue carbon is mostly in sediments.

Carbon in petroleum and natural gas is fossil carbon. It comes from ancient organic matter buried and transformed over millions of years. Burning it releases CO2 and is the biggest human-caused source of climate change. It is part of the slow carbon cycle. It is not a sink, and it has no connection with the 'blue' ocean-based carbon concept. Carbon capture and storage (CCS) tries to stop it from reaching the atmosphere.

Atmospheric carbon is mainly carbon dioxide, about 0.04 percent of air by volume, or roughly 420 ppm in recent years. It is a major greenhouse gas. It is exchanged with oceans and plants through photosynthesis, respiration and dissolution. It is the carbon pool that sinks such as blue carbon ecosystems draw down, so it is the source pool rather than blue carbon.
related: Blue carbon ecosystems: mangroves, salt marshes, seagrass meadows.
Blue carbon is stored mainly in waterlogged coastal sediments, not in biomass.
Green carbon is carbon in terrestrial forests and soils.
Black carbon is soot from incomplete combustion and a short-lived climate pollutant.
MISHTI, launched in 2023, promotes mangrove plantation along India's coast.
Mangroves fall under CRZ-I in India's Coastal Regulation Zone rules.
The Blue Carbon Initiative is led by Conservation International, IUCN and IOC-UNESCO.
Destroyed blue carbon habitats release stored carbon as CO2 and become emission sources.
summary: The answer is (a). Blue carbon is the carbon captured and stored by oceans and coastal ecosystems, mainly mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass meadows. These habitats absorb CO2 and lock it away for centuries to millennia, mostly in waterlogged sediments.
topic_notes: Carbon is classified by colour. Green carbon is stored in terrestrial vegetation and soils. Blue carbon is stored in coastal and marine ecosystems. Brown carbon is light-absorbing organic aerosol from incomplete combustion. Black carbon is soot, a short-lived climate pollutant that warms the atmosphere and darkens snow and ice. Grey carbon is sometimes used for fossil or industrial carbon. Blue carbon ecosystems are mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass meadows. They occupy under 2 percent of ocean area, yet they account for a large share of carbon burial in ocean sediments. Their carbon accumulates mostly in anoxic sediments, which can hold it for thousands of years. Mangroves protect coasts against cyclones and storm surges, act as fish nurseries and filter pollutants. Seagrasses support dugongs and sea turtles. Main threats are aquaculture such as shrimp farming, reclamation, pollution, port development and sea-level rise. Policy angles: UNEP, FAO and IUCN promoted the concept around 2009, and the Blue Carbon Initiative is led by Conservation International, IUCN and IOC-UNESCO. In India, the Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats and Tangible Incomes (MISHTI) was launched in 2023. The Sundarbans, Bhitarkanika and the Pichavaram mangroves are well known sites. Coastal Regulation Zone rules protect mangroves, which are CRZ-I. The Ramsar Convention covers many coastal wetlands. Blue carbon can be counted under national GHG inventories and carbon markets. Related ideas are the biological pump, ocean acidification, and the Global Mangrove Alliance.

question:
In the nature, which of the following is/are most likely to be found surviving on a surface without soil?
1. Fern
2. Lichen
3. Moss
4. Mushroom Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Geography
detail: The question tests pioneer species and primary ecological succession. On bare rock, the first colonisers are crustose lichens, which are a symbiosis of a fungus (mycobiont) and an alga or cyanobacterium (photobiont). Lichens secrete acids that weather rock and begin forming soil. Mosses (Bryophyta) follow, growing on rock, bark, walls and roofs. They lack true roots and absorb water and nutrients directly through their surfaces, with rhizoids serving only for anchorage. Ferns (Pteridophyta) have true roots, stems and vascular tissue, and normally root in soil or humus, though some epiphytic ferns grow on trees. Mushrooms are fungi, which are heterotrophs, and they need an organic substrate such as soil rich in humus, dead wood or dung. They cannot make their own food on bare surfaces. Elimination: mushroom (4) is wrong, which removes (a) and (d). Fern (1) is wrong, which also removes (d). Option (b) leaves out moss, which is a well-known pioneer. That leaves (c). Remember that lichens are also indicators of air quality, because they are sensitive to sulphur dioxide.
explanations: Wrong: it includes ferns and mushrooms, both of which normally need soil or organic matter, and it leaves out lichen and moss.
Wrong: lichen does survive without soil, but this option leaves out moss, which also grows on bare rock, bark and walls.
Correct: lichens and mosses are pioneer organisms that colonise bare surfaces such as rock without soil, and they start soil formation.
Wrong: ferns and mushrooms depend on soil, humus or decaying organic matter, so they are not the most likely to survive on soilless surfaces.
keyfact: Lichens and mosses are pioneer organisms that grow on bare rock without soil, whereas ferns and mushrooms need soil or organic matter.
option_notes: Ferns and mushrooms together. Ferns are pteridophytes, vascular spore-bearing plants with true roots, stems and fronds, and they prefer moist, shaded soil. Mushrooms are the fruiting bodies of fungi, which are heterotrophic and need organic matter. Both are therefore tied to soil or organic substrates. The combination is wrong here because it excludes lichen and moss, which are the real colonisers of soilless surfaces. Azolla is an aquatic fern used as a biofertiliser because it hosts Anabaena.

Lichen alone. Lichen is a symbiotic association of a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium. It is a pioneer in primary succession on bare rock and secretes acids that weather the rock. Lichens are bioindicators of air pollution, particularly sulphur dioxide. They are slow-growing and found from the poles to the tropics. Litmus is obtained from lichens. This option is incomplete because moss also survives on soilless surfaces such as rocks, bark and walls.

Lichen and moss together, the correct answer. Both are pioneer species in primary succession on bare rock. Lichens are fungus–alga symbioses that break down rock. Mosses are non-vascular bryophytes that absorb water through their surfaces and anchor with rhizoids. Together they trap dust and organic debris and form the first thin soil. Later stages bring in herbs, shrubs and then trees, ending in a climax community. Sphagnum moss forms peat.

Ferns, mosses and mushrooms. Mosses are valid, but ferns and mushrooms are not. Ferns need soil or humus for their roots, apart from a few epiphytes. Mushrooms need organic substrates like humus, dung or dead wood. This option also leaves out lichen, the best-known pioneer organism. Such combinations are designed to tempt students who remember that moss grows on walls. Ferns are called vascular cryptogams, and mushrooms belong to the kingdom Fungi.
related: Lichens are a symbiosis of a fungus (mycobiont) and an alga or cyanobacterium (photobiont).
Lichens are bioindicators of air pollution, especially sulphur dioxide.
Pioneer species on bare rock in primary succession are crustose lichens.
Sphagnum moss forms peat and holds large amounts of water.
Azolla, an aquatic fern, hosts the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium Anabaena.
Bryophytes are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom.
Fungal cell walls are made of chitin and fungi are heterotrophs.
Litmus dye is obtained from lichens.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Ferns are vascular plants with true roots and normally need soil or humus; only a few epiphytic species grow on trees. Ferns are pteridophytes, the first vascular plants, which reproduce by spores and show alternation of generations, with a dominant sporophyte and a small free-living gametophyte called the prothallus. Their leaves are called fronds and are often pinnately compound, with young fronds coiled as fiddleheads. They need moist, shaded habitats because fertilisation requires water. Examples are Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum and Azolla. Azolla is an aquatic fern that hosts the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium Anabaena and is used as a biofertiliser in rice fields.

2 — Correct: Lichens are composite organisms in which a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium live in symbiosis. The alga photosynthesises and the fungus provides anchorage, moisture and minerals. They grow on bare rock, bark, walls and even in Arctic and Antarctic conditions, and they are pioneer species in primary succession. Growth forms are crustose, foliose and fruticose. They are excellent bioindicators of air pollution, especially sulphur dioxide. Lichens are the source of litmus dye and are used in perfumes. Reindeer moss (Cladonia) is an important food for reindeer and caribou in tundra. They are very slow-growing and can live for centuries.

3 — Correct: Mosses are bryophytes, small non-vascular plants that lack true roots, stems and leaves. They absorb water directly through their surfaces and anchor with rhizoids, so they can grow on rocks, walls, bark and roofs. Their dominant stage is the gametophyte, and fertilisation needs water. Sporophytes depend on the gametophyte. Sphagnum moss forms peat, which is used as fuel and as a soil conditioner because it holds water well. Mosses help in soil formation and in preventing soil erosion. They follow lichens in succession, and bryophytes are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom.

4 — Incorrect: A mushroom is the fruiting body of a fungus, mostly Basidiomycetes. Fungi lack chlorophyll and are heterotrophs, either saprotrophs, parasites or symbionts. Mushrooms therefore need an organic substrate such as humus-rich soil, dung, decaying wood or compost, and they cannot live on bare rock. The fungal body is a network of hyphae called mycelium. Examples are Agaricus bisporus (button mushroom), Pleurotus (oyster) and Volvariella (paddy straw). Some are poisonous, for example Amanita, the death cap. Fungal cell walls are made of chitin. Mycorrhiza is a fungus–root association that helps plants absorb phosphorus.
summary: The answer is (c) 2 and 3: lichen and moss are most likely to survive on bare surfaces such as rock, bark or walls without soil. Ferns and mushrooms generally need soil, humus or decaying organic matter as a substrate.
topic_notes: The topic is the ecology and classification of simple plant-like organisms, together with ecological succession. Succession is the orderly, directional change in a community over time. Primary succession starts on a lifeless area with no soil, such as bare rock, a cooled lava flow or a newly exposed sand dune. Secondary succession starts where soil is already present, for example after a fire or flood, and it is faster. Pioneer species on rock are crustose lichens, followed by foliose and fruticose lichens, then mosses, herbs, shrubs and finally trees in the climax community. In hydrarch succession, which begins in water, the sequence runs from phytoplankton to rooted submerged plants, floating plants, reed swamp, sedge meadow, shrubs and forest. Lichens are a mutualistic symbiosis. Their algal partner is the photobiont and the fungal partner is the mycobiont. Because they absorb pollutants directly from the air, they are bioindicators. Lichens are absent or scarce in heavily polluted cities. Bryophytes include mosses, liverworts and hornworts. They are non-vascular, need water for fertilisation and are the amphibians of the plant kingdom. Sphagnum forms peat. Pteridophytes are seedless vascular plants, such as ferns, horsetails and club mosses. Fungi are heterotrophic, have chitinous cell walls and include yeasts, moulds and mushrooms. The nitrogen-fixing Azolla–Anabaena association is another symbiosis UPSC likes to ask about. Related angles are mycorrhiza, Rhizobium in legume root nodules, cyanobacteria such as Nostoc and Anabaena as biofertilisers, and the classification of plants into thallophytes, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms. UPSC may also ask about indicator species, keystone species and ecological niches.

ocr: Which one of the following is used in preparing a natural mosquito repellent? (a) Congress grass (b) Elephant grass (c) Lemongrass (ad) Nut grass
subject: Modern History
detail: Natural mosquito repellents are made from plants whose essential oils contain volatile compounds that mask human odour cues (CO2, lactic acid) or irritate insect olfactory receptors. Lemongrass belongs to the genus Cymbopogon in the family Poaceae. Its oil contains citral, citronellal and geraniol. Closely related species are citronella grass (Cymbopogon nardus and C. winterianus, Java citronella) and palmarosa (C. martinii). Citronella oil is the best-known botanical repellent in candles, coils and lotions. India is a major producer of lemongrass oil, especially Kerala (Odakkali, Pampady), and CSIR-CIMAP, Lucknow has developed improved varieties such as Krishna, Pragati and Suvarna. Elimination logic: Congress grass (Parthenium hysterophorus) is an invasive weed from tropical America that causes allergies and dermatitis; elephant grass (Pennisetum purpureum, Napier grass) is fodder and a biofuel candidate; nut grass (Cyperus rotundus) is a persistent sedge weed whose tubers have a use in Ayurveda. None of these three is known as a mosquito repellent, so (c) is the only choice.
explanations: Wrong: Congress grass (Parthenium) is a harmful invasive weed causing allergies, not a repellent source.
Wrong: Elephant grass (Napier grass) is a fodder and biomass crop, not used for mosquito repellent.
Correct: Lemongrass oil contains citral and citronellal and is widely used in natural mosquito repellents, as is its relative citronella grass.
Wrong: Nut grass (Cyperus rotundus) is a sedge weed, valued in traditional medicine but not a standard mosquito repellent.
keyfact: Lemongrass (Cymbopogon; citral and citronellal) is the grass used in natural mosquito repellents; Congress grass is an invasive weed, elephant grass is fodder, and nut grass is a sedge weed.
option_notes: Congress grass (Parthenium hysterophorus), also called carrot grass or gajar ghas, is an annual herb of the Asteraceae family from tropical America. It entered India in the 1950s, probably with contaminated wheat imports under PL-480 (around 1955 in Pune). It is highly invasive, produces allelopathic chemicals (parthenin), and causes dermatitis, asthma and hay fever. It is controlled biologically with the Mexican beetle Zygogramma bicolorata.

Elephant grass (Pennisetum purpureum), also called Napier grass, is a tall perennial C4 grass from tropical Africa. It is a high-yielding fodder crop in India, and the Napier-bajra hybrid (Pennisetum glaucum x purpureum) is widely grown. It is also being promoted as a biomass and biofuel feedstock, including for compressed biogas and for pellets. It grows up to 3–4 m tall and is propagated by stem cuttings.

Lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus, West Indian; C. flexuosus, East Indian or Cochin grass) is an aromatic perennial grass of the Poaceae family. Its oil is rich in citral and is used in perfumery, flavouring, vitamin A synthesis and insect repellents. Kerala, Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh grow it. CSIR-CIMAP, Lucknow released varieties such as Krishna, Pragati and Praman. It is also used in tea and in Southeast Asian cooking.

Nut grass (Cyperus rotundus), also called purple nutsedge or mustaka/motha, is a perennial sedge (Cyperaceae), not a true grass. It is considered one of the world's worst weeds because it spreads through underground tubers (nutlets) and is hard to eradicate. In Ayurveda the tubers are used for fever, digestive disorders and as a diuretic. Its essential oil is used in perfumery, and it is allelopathic to crops.
related: Citronella grass: Cymbopogon nardus and C. winterianus; its oil is a classic botanical repellent.
CSIR-CIMAP (Lucknow) develops aromatic and medicinal plant varieties, including lemongrass.
Parthenium (Congress grass) is controlled by the beetle Zygogramma bicolorata.
Female Anopheles transmits malaria; Aedes aegypti transmits dengue, chikungunya and Zika.
DEET is the standard synthetic repellent; PMD from lemon eucalyptus is a plant-derived repellent.
Neem's azadirachtin acts as an insect antifeedant and growth regulator.
Wolbachia bacteria in Aedes reduce dengue transmission.
CSIR Aroma Mission promotes cultivation of aromatic crops such as lemongrass and mint.
summary: The correct answer is (c) Lemongrass. Lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus / C. flexuosus) yields an essential oil rich in citronellal, citral and geraniol, which repels mosquitoes and is the plant used in natural repellents.
topic_notes: Natural or botanical mosquito repellents rely on plant essential oils. Key plants: lemongrass and citronella (Cymbopogon spp.; citronellal, citral, geraniol), neem (Azadirachta indica; azadirachtin, also an insect growth regulator), eucalyptus (lemon eucalyptus, Corymbia citriodora; PMD, p-menthane-3,8-diol, recognised by the US CDC), tulsi (Ocimum sanctum; eugenol), lavender, peppermint, catnip (nepetalactone), marigold and garlic. Synthetic comparators: DEET (N,N-diethyl-meta-toluamide), picaridin and IR3535. Mosquito-borne diseases: malaria (Plasmodium, transmitted by female Anopheles), dengue and chikungunya (Aedes aegypti), Japanese encephalitis (Culex), filariasis (Culex), and Zika (Aedes). India's national programme for these is the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP, now under the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control), and the aim is malaria elimination by 2030. Biological control includes Gambusia and Poecilia (larvivorous fish), Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (Bti), and Wolbachia-infected Aedes mosquitoes. The World Mosquito Program and gene-drive and sterile insect techniques are recent frontiers. Aromatic crops: the CSIR Aroma Mission promotes cultivation of lemongrass, mint, palmarosa, citronella, and others for farmers' income. India is a leading producer of mentha oil, and Kannauj is known for attar and perfumery. Congress grass, water hyacinth, Lantana camara and Prosopis juliflora are major invasive species in India, often asked in prelims alongside this type of question. Note that lemongrass is not a repellent for every species equally, and its protection is shorter than DEET's, usually one to two hours unless formulated.

ocr: Consider the following kinds of organisms : 1. Copepods 2. Cyanobacteria 3. Diatoms 4. Foraminifera Which of the above are primary producers in the food chains of oceans? (a) 1 and 2 (b) 2 and 3 (c) 3 and 4 (ad) 1 and 4
subject: Environment
detail: Primary producers are autotrophs that convert inorganic carbon into organic matter, mainly through photosynthesis. In the oceans, nearly all primary production is by phytoplankton: diatoms, dinoflagellates, coccolithophores, and cyanobacteria such as Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus. Phytoplankton are estimated to account for roughly half of global photosynthesis (about 50 Gt C per year) and supply much of the oxygen in the atmosphere. Diatoms are unicellular algae with silica frustules and are dominant in cold, nutrient-rich waters. Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes (blue-green algae) that dominate the nutrient-poor open ocean, and some, like Trichodesmium, also fix nitrogen. Zooplankton, the next trophic level, feed on phytoplankton. Copepods are the most abundant zooplankton, are small crustaceans and are primary consumers. Foraminifera are amoeboid protists with calcareous shells (tests) that feed on plankton and detritus, though some host photosynthetic algal symbionts. They are not classed as primary producers. Elimination: copepods are animals and so cannot be producers, which removes (a) and (d). Foraminifera are heterotrophs, which removes (c). Only (b), 2 and 3, remains.
explanations: Wrong: it includes copepods (1), which are zooplankton consumers, not producers.
Correct: cyanobacteria (2) and diatoms (3) are photosynthetic phytoplankton, and these are the primary producers.
Wrong: it includes foraminifera (4), which are heterotrophic protists, even though diatoms (3) are correct.
Wrong: both copepods (1) and foraminifera (4) are consumers, so neither is a primary producer, and this pair excludes the real producers.
keyfact: In ocean food chains the primary producers are phytoplankton such as diatoms and cyanobacteria. Copepods and foraminifera are consumers.
option_notes: Copepods and cyanobacteria: Copepods are tiny crustaceans and the most abundant zooplankton, acting as grazers that feed fish larvae, fish and baleen whales. Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic bacteria. Together they span two trophic levels, a consumer and a producer, so the pair is incorrect.

Cyanobacteria and diatoms: both are phytoplankton. Cyanobacteria are prokaryotic, oxygen-releasing photosynthesizers dating back about 3.5 billion years, and diatoms are silica-walled eukaryotic algae. Together they make up a large share of marine primary production and support the food web from krill to whales. This is the correct answer.

Diatoms and foraminifera: diatoms are producers, while foraminifera are calcareous-shelled amoeboid protists that are mostly heterotrophic. Their shells form sediments such as globigerina ooze and serve as paleoclimate indicators. Because foraminifera are not producers, the pair is wrong.

Copepods and foraminifera: both are consumers. Copepods are crustacean zooplankton and foraminifera are shelled protists. They are important in the marine food web and sediment record, but neither fixes carbon as a primary producer, so this option is wrong.
related: Phytoplankton produce about half of the world's photosynthetic oxygen.
Diatoms have silica cell walls (frustules) and form diatomite.
Prochlorococcus is the most abundant photosynthetic organism on Earth.
Copepods are the most abundant zooplankton and act as primary consumers.
Foraminiferal shells are used as paleoclimate proxies.
Iron limits productivity in HNLC regions such as the Southern Ocean.
Hydrothermal vent food webs depend on chemosynthetic bacteria.
Only about 10% of energy passes between trophic levels (Lindeman's rule).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Copepods are heterotrophic zooplankton that graze on phytoplankton, so they are primary consumers rather than producers. They are small crustaceans (subclass Copepoda), typically 1-2 mm long, and are among the most numerous multicellular animals on Earth. They link phytoplankton to fish larvae, small fish and whales. Many perform daily vertical migration and help move carbon to the deep ocean as fecal pellets (the biological pump). Calanus is a well-known genus and is vital in North Atlantic food webs.

2 — Correct: Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic prokaryotes (blue-green algae) containing chlorophyll a and phycobilins. They are among the oldest life forms, with fossil stromatolites about 3.5 billion years old, and they caused the Great Oxidation Event about 2.4 billion years ago. Prochlorococcus is the most abundant photosynthetic organism on Earth. Trichodesmium fixes nitrogen and forms blooms in tropical seas. Cyanobacteria also form symbioses, as in Anabaena in Azolla, and are used as biofertiliser in rice fields.

3 — Correct: Diatoms are unicellular, eukaryotic microalgae (class Bacillariophyceae) with cell walls of silica called frustules. They are very productive and are responsible for about 20-25% of global primary production. They are abundant in upwelling and polar waters. Their deposits form diatomaceous earth (diatomite), used in filtration and as an abrasive. They provide food for krill and copepods and also form the basis of the Antarctic food web. They are a major part of the biological carbon pump.

4 — Incorrect: Foraminifera are single-celled amoeboid protists (Rhizaria) with chambered shells (tests) of calcium carbonate. They are mostly heterotrophic, feeding on bacteria, algae and detritus, though some planktonic species host algal symbionts. They are very abundant in marine sediments, and their fossils form limestone and foraminiferal ooze (globigerina ooze). They are widely used as paleoclimate proxies, since the oxygen isotope ratios in their shells indicate past temperatures. The Nummulites in Eocene limestone are an example.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 and 3. Cyanobacteria and diatoms are photosynthetic organisms that fix carbon from sunlight and form the base of ocean food chains. Copepods (zooplankton, mostly grazers) and foraminifera (heterotrophic protists) are consumers.
topic_notes: Primary production is the synthesis of organic compounds from CO2, mainly by photosynthesis and, in a few places, by chemosynthesis. In the oceans, phytoplankton do this work. They are confined to the euphotic (sunlit) zone, usually the upper 100-200 m. Key groups are diatoms, dinoflagellates, coccolithophores (calcareous plates, such as Emiliania huxleyi), cyanobacteria (Prochlorococcus, Synechococcus, Trichodesmium) and green algae. Productivity is highest in upwelling zones (Peru, Benguela, Arabian Sea) and coastal areas, where nutrients such as nitrate, phosphate, silica and iron are abundant. Iron is the limiting nutrient in HNLC (high-nutrient, low-chlorophyll) regions such as the Southern Ocean, which has led to proposals for iron fertilisation. The open ocean gyres are oligotrophic. Chemosynthetic bacteria at hydrothermal vents form the base of food webs in the dark deep sea. The trophic structure runs from phytoplankton to zooplankton (copepods, krill) to small fish to large fish, seals and whales, with roughly 10% energy transfer between levels. The biological pump moves carbon to deep water. Related concepts include algal blooms, eutrophication, red tides (dinoflagellates, toxins), dead zones and ocean acidification, which harms calcifying organisms such as coccolithophores, foraminifera and corals. Plankton classes include phytoplankton, zooplankton, bacterioplankton, nekton (active swimmers) and benthos (bottom dwellers). Sargassum is a floating macroalga forming the Sargasso Sea ecosystem. Mangroves, seagrasses and seaweeds are producers in coastal waters (blue carbon).

ocr: Consider the following animals : 1. Hedgehog 2. Marmot 3. Pangolin To reduce the chance of being captured by predators, which of the above organisms rolls up/roll up and protects/ protect its/their vulnerable parts? (a) 1 and 2 (b) 2 only (c) 3 only (ad) land3 13 BXC-U-FTHI/68A
subject: Environment
detail: This question tests animal defence adaptations, a recurring UPSC theme in biodiversity. Conglobation, or rolling into a ball, is a passive defence in which an animal exposes only a hard or spiny outer surface and hides its vulnerable head, face and belly. The hedgehog (family Erinaceidae, order Eulipotyphla) erects its spines and curls up using a strong orbicularis muscle along its back. Pangolins (order Pholidota, genus Manis) are the only mammals covered in true keratin scales. When threatened they curl into a ball, with the tail wrapped over the face and belly. This makes them hard for lions and leopards to injure, yet it makes them easy for poachers to pick up, so they are the world's most trafficked mammal. Marmots (genus Marmota, family Sciuridae) are large ground squirrels of mountain and grassland areas, including the Himalaya. They hibernate and use burrows and sharp alarm calls as defences, and they have no armour and no rolling behaviour. Elimination logic: marmot is wrong, so options (a) and (b) are removed. Pangolin is definitely right, which leaves (c) or (d). Hedgehog also rolls up, so (d) is correct.
explanations: (a) 1 and 2 is wrong because it includes the marmot, which does not roll up, and it leaves out the pangolin, which does.
(b) 2 only is wrong because the marmot does not roll up, and this option excludes both of the animals that do, the hedgehog and the pangolin.
(c) 3 only is incomplete. The pangolin does roll up, but the hedgehog also rolls up and protects its underparts with spines.
(d) 1 and 3 is correct because the hedgehog and the pangolin both show conglobation, protecting their soft undersides with spines or scales.
keyfact: Hedgehog and pangolin both roll into a ball for defence (conglobation); the marmot escapes into burrows instead.
option_notes: Hedgehog and marmot: this pairing combines a spiny insectivore with a burrowing rodent. The hedgehog (Erinaceidae, Eulipotyphla) is nocturnal and rolls into a ball for defence. The marmot (Marmota, Sciuridae) is a diurnal ground squirrel that hibernates. They belong to different orders, and their defences are different: the hedgehog's is passive and armoured, while the marmot's is escape and alarm calls. The Himalayan marmot is found in Ladakh and the Himalaya.

Marmot only: marmots are heavy-bodied ground squirrels of cold, high-altitude regions in Eurasia and North America. They live in colonies in burrows and hibernate for most of the year. A sentinel marmot whistles to warn the group of predators such as eagles, foxes and wolves. The Himalayan marmot (Marmota himalayana) is found on the Tibetan Plateau and in Ladakh, and the groundhog (woodchuck) is also a marmot. They are not armoured and do not roll into a ball.

Pangolin only: the pangolin is a scaly, toothless, ant-eating mammal of order Pholidota. Eight species exist, four in Asia and four in Africa. India has the Indian pangolin (Manis crassicaudata) and the Chinese pangolin (Manis pentadactyla). It is nocturnal, and it curls into a ball when threatened. It is protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and CITES Appendix I, and illegal trade in its scales is a serious threat.

Hedgehog and pangolin: this is the correct combination. Both are small, nocturnal, insect-eating mammals that have evolved a similar defence, although they are unrelated. The hedgehog uses spines and the pangolin uses keratin scales. When threatened, each curls up so that the exposed surface is hard and sharp, with the face, belly and limbs tucked inside. This is an example of convergent defensive adaptation.
related: Pangolin is the only mammal with true scales made of keratin.
The Indian pangolin (Manis crassicaudata) is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List.
Pangolins are the most trafficked mammals in the world.
Pangolins are in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and in CITES Appendix I.
The hedgehog's spines are modified hairs made of keratin.
The Himalayan marmot (Marmota himalayana) is a hibernating burrowing rodent found in Ladakh and the Himalaya.
The Indian pangolin lives in many habitats, including grasslands, but the Chinese pangolin lives in the Himalayan foothills and northeast India.
World Pangolin Day is observed on the third Saturday of February.
statements: 1 — Correct: The hedgehog rolls into a spiny ball when threatened. It is a small insectivorous mammal with about 5,000-7,000 spines, which are modified hairs made of keratin. Its order is Eulipotyphla and its family is Erinaceidae. Species live in Europe, Asia and Africa, and India has the Indian long-eared hedgehog and the Indian hedgehog (Paraechinus). Hedgehogs are nocturnal, can hibernate or aestivate, and eat insects, worms and snails. The long-eared hedgehog is listed in Schedule II of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.

2 — Incorrect: The marmot does not roll up. It is a large burrowing ground squirrel (genus Marmota, family Sciuridae). It is diurnal and social, and lives in colonies in mountain meadows and steppes. In India the Himalayan marmot (Marmota himalayana) occurs in Ladakh, Himachal and Uttarakhand at high altitude. Marmots hibernate for 6-8 months, and they use warning whistles and burrows to escape predators such as eagles and wolves. The Himalayan marmot is listed as Least Concern.

3 — Correct: The pangolin rolls up into a ball, with overlapping keratin scales on the outside. Order Pholidota. Two species occur in India, the Indian pangolin (Manis crassicaudata) and the Chinese pangolin (Manis pentadactyla). Pangolins are nocturnal and toothless, and they eat ants and termites using a long sticky tongue. They are the most trafficked mammals in the world, and the scales are used in traditional medicine. They are listed in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and in CITES Appendix I. The Indian pangolin is Endangered on the IUCN Red List.
summary: The answer is (d) 1 and 3. The hedgehog and the pangolin both roll into a tight ball when threatened, which protects their soft underparts. The marmot is a burrowing rodent that escapes predators by retreating into burrows and giving alarm whistles, so it does not roll up.
topic_notes: Animal defence mechanisms are a common source of UPSC biodiversity questions. The main types are as follows. Armour and conglobation: pangolins, hedgehogs and armadillos. Of the armadillos, only the three-banded species can roll completely into a ball. Chemical defence: skunks spray, bombardier beetles eject hot fluid, and poison dart frogs carry toxins. Camouflage and mimicry: chameleons, stick insects and leaf insects. Autotomy, or shedding body parts: lizards drop their tails and starfish shed arms. Mobbing and alarm calls: marmots, meerkats and langurs. Burrowing: marmots, rodents and mongooses. Inflation or bluffing: pufferfish, which swell up with water. Thanatosis, or playing dead: opossums. Pangolin facts to know: the four Asian species are the Indian, Chinese, Sunda and Philippine pangolins, and the four African species are the giant, ground, white-bellied and black-bellied pangolins. The Indian pangolin is Endangered, and the Chinese pangolin is Critically Endangered. Pangolins are the most trafficked wild mammals, mainly because of demand for their scales and meat. World Pangolin Day is held on the third Saturday of February. Hedgehog facts: they eat insects, are nocturnal, and may hibernate in cold regions. Hedgehogs show 'anointing', which is spreading frothy saliva on their spines. India's species include the Indian long-eared hedgehog (Hemiechinus collaris) and the Indian hedgehog (Paraechinus micropus). Marmot facts: the Himalayan marmot is found in Ladakh, Spiti and the Tibetan Plateau, and it hibernates. Related UPSC angles include Schedule I species, CITES appendices, the IUCN Red List categories, and the wildlife trade monitoring network TRAFFIC.

ocr: With reference to the ‘New York Declaration on Forests’, which of the following statements are correct? 1. It was first endorsed at the United Nations Climate Summit in 2014. 2. It endorses a global timeline to end the loss of forests. 3. It is a legally binding international declaration. 4. It is endorsed by governments, big companies and_ indigenous communities. 5. India was one of the signatories at its inception. Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1, 2 and 4 (b) 1,3 and 5 (c) 3 and 4 (aq) 2and5
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The New York Declaration on Forests was launched at the UN Climate Summit convened by Ban Ki-moon in New York on 23 September 2014. It is a voluntary, non-legally binding political declaration. Its main goals are to halve natural forest loss by 2020 and end it by 2030, and to restore 350 million hectares of degraded landscapes and forestlands by 2030. It also aims to end deforestation from agricultural commodity supply chains (palm oil, soy, paper and beef) and to support the Paris Agreement and REDD+. The endorsers include national governments, sub-national governments, multinational companies, indigenous peoples' organisations and NGOs. A Progress Assessment is published yearly by the NYDF Assessment Partners. Elimination logic: statement 3 is wrong because the declaration is not legally binding, and this removes (b) and (c). Statement 5 is wrong because India did not endorse it, and this removes (d). That leaves (a), which is the official answer. Remember that India has not endorsed the NYDF, though the Glasgow Leaders' Declaration on Forests and Land Use (2021) is a separate matter.
explanations: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 4 are right: the declaration was endorsed in 2014, it sets a global timeline to end forest loss, and it is backed by governments, companies and indigenous communities.
Incorrect. It includes statement 3, which is false because the declaration is not legally binding, and it also includes statement 5, which is false because India did not sign.
Incorrect. Statement 3 is false because the NYDF is a voluntary political declaration. It also leaves out the correct statements 1 and 2 and the correct statement 4 would be only partly covered.
Incorrect. Statement 5 is false because India did not endorse the NYDF at its inception. Statement 2 is true but this option omits the correct statements 1 and 4.
keyfact: NYDF (2014, New York) is a voluntary, non-binding, multi-stakeholder declaration to end forest loss by 2030, and India is not a signatory.
option_notes: Statements 1, 2 and 4 together describe the NYDF accurately. It was launched at the 2014 UN Climate Summit in New York. Its goals are to halve natural forest loss by 2020, end it by 2030 and restore 350 million hectares. It is a voluntary, multi-stakeholder partnership of governments, companies, indigenous groups and NGOs. The 2020 goals were not met according to assessment reports. It supports REDD+ and the Paris Agreement. India is not an endorser.

Statements 1, 3 and 5 would describe the NYDF as legally binding and as signed by India, and both claims are wrong. The NYDF is non-binding. India has not endorsed it, though India has its own forest goals: the Bonn Challenge pledge of 26 million hectares by 2030, and the NDC carbon-sink target of 2.5-3 billion tonnes CO2e through additional forest and tree cover by 2030.

Statements 3 and 4 would pair a false claim (legally binding) with a true one (multi-stakeholder endorsement). Legally binding global instruments on environment include the UNFCCC (1992), Kyoto Protocol (1997), Paris Agreement (2015, in force 2016), CBD (1992) and UNCCD (1994). A true legally binding forest treaty does not exist. The UN Forum on Forests (UNFF) adopted a non-legally binding instrument on all types of forests in 2007.

Statements 2 and 5 pair a true claim (global timeline to end forest loss) with a false one (India as signatory). The NYDF timeline aims to halve forest loss by 2020 and end it by 2030. India's forest policy rests instead on the National Forest Policy 1988, the Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, the Green India Mission and the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act 2016. India State of Forest Report is published biennially by FSI, Dehradun.
related: NYDF was launched at the UN Climate Summit in New York, September 2014.
NYDF goals: halve natural forest loss by 2020, end it by 2030, restore 350 million ha.
NYDF is voluntary and non-binding, and India has not endorsed it.
Bonn Challenge (2011): 150 million ha by 2020 and 350 million ha by 2030; India pledged 26 million ha.
Glasgow Leaders' Declaration on Forests and Land Use was made at COP26 in 2021, and India did not sign it.
REDD+ is a UNFCCC mechanism that rewards developing countries for reducing deforestation and degradation.
India's NDC aims at an additional carbon sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes CO2e through forests by 2030.
India State of Forest Report is published every two years by the Forest Survey of India, Dehradun.
statements: 1 — Correct: The NYDF was first endorsed at the UN Climate Summit held in New York in September 2014. The summit was convened by UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon ahead of the Paris climate talks (COP21, 2015). Around 30 governments, 20 sub-national governments, 50+ companies, and dozens of indigenous and civil-society groups endorsed it initially. It has since grown to well over 200 endorsers. It is a non-binding political declaration, and it is a key milestone in forest-related climate action and REDD+.

2 — Correct: It endorses a global timeline to end forest loss. The declaration aims to halve the loss of natural forests globally by 2020 and to end it by 2030. It also aims to restore 350 million hectares of degraded land by 2030, later aligned with the Bonn Challenge. Other goals include ending deforestation from agricultural commodity production by 2020, supporting forest-friendly development, and rewarding forest conservation through REDD+ finance. Progress is tracked by the NYDF Assessment Partners in annual reports, and the 2020 goals were largely missed.

3 — Incorrect: The NYDF is voluntary and not legally binding. It is a political declaration, not a treaty, and has no enforcement mechanism or penalties. This contrasts with legally binding instruments such as the Paris Agreement (2015), the UNFCCC (1992), the CBD (1992) and UNCCD (1994). Its force comes from the voluntary commitments of its endorsers and from reputational pressure. Companies and governments report progress through the NYDF platform, and the Climate Focus-led partners publish assessments.

4 — Correct: It is endorsed by a multi-stakeholder coalition of national and sub-national governments, big multinational companies (such as Unilever, Cargill and Nestlé, in supply-chain pledges), indigenous peoples' organisations and civil-society groups. This broad participation is a defining feature, because it joins public and private action against deforestation. Indigenous communities are recognised as important forest guardians, with their rights and role highlighted. Endorsers include countries such as the USA, UK, Germany, Norway, Indonesia (initially), Colombia, Ethiopia and others.

5 — Incorrect: India was not a signatory at its inception and has not endorsed the NYDF. Other large forest-related countries, such as China and Brazil, also did not sign it at the start. India has its own forest and climate commitments: the Paris NDC target of an additional carbon sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent through forest and tree cover by 2030, the Bonn Challenge pledge of 26 million hectares of restoration by 2030, and the Green India Mission (under NAPCC).
summary: The answer is (a) 1, 2 and 4. The New York Declaration on Forests (NYDF) was endorsed at the UN Climate Summit in New York in September 2014. It is a voluntary, non-binding political declaration backed by governments, companies, indigenous groups and civil society, and it sets a global timeline to end forest loss. India was not a signatory at its inception.
topic_notes: The New York Declaration on Forests (NYDF) came out of the UN Climate Summit on 23 September 2014, convened by UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon. It is a voluntary, non-binding political declaration with ten goals. The main goals are to halve natural forest loss by 2020, end it by 2030, restore 350 million hectares of degraded land by 2030, end deforestation driven by agricultural commodities such as palm oil, soy, paper and beef, and reward forest conservation through REDD+ finance. It is supported by a multi-stakeholder platform of governments, sub-national governments, companies, indigenous peoples' organisations and NGOs. Annual Progress Assessments are published by the NYDF Assessment Partners, and these have found that the 2020 goals were missed. Related initiatives include REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and forest Degradation, under the UNFCCC), the Bonn Challenge (2011, launched by Germany and IUCN, with a goal of 150 million hectares by 2020 and 350 million hectares by 2030), the AFR100 and the Glasgow Leaders' Declaration on Forests and Land Use (COP26, 2021), which pledged to halt and reverse forest loss and land degradation by 2030. The UN Forum on Forests (UNFF) was created in 2000 under ECOSOC, and the UN Strategic Plan for Forests 2017-2030 sets Global Forest Goals. India's related commitments include the Bonn Challenge pledge of 26 million hectares by 2030 and the NDC carbon sink target. Its institutions include the Forest Survey of India, which publishes the biennial India State of Forest Report, and the Green India Mission. Other angles UPSC could ask on are the Forest Stewardship Council, the FAO's Global Forest Resources Assessment, the Amazon Fund, the Congo Basin and the Paris Agreement's Article 5 on forests.

question:
Magnetite particles, suspected to cause neurodegenerative problems, are generated as environmental pollutants from which of the following?
1. Brakes of motor vehicles CL i eng Engines of motor vehicles Microwave stoves within homes Power plants Telephone lines Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Magnetite (Fe3O4) is a naturally magnetic iron oxide. Tiny biogenic magnetite exists in the human brain, but a 2016 study (Maher et al., PNAS, Lancaster University, using brains from Mexico City and Manchester) found abundant rounded, combustion-derived magnetite nanoparticles in human brain tissue. These are linked to air pollution and are suspected of generating reactive oxygen species, causing oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, and being associated with Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative disorders. The particles form at high temperatures, when iron-containing material is heated and then condenses, or from friction. Their sources are vehicle brake-pad abrasion, engine exhaust and fuel combustion, and coal-fired power plants, plus open fires and industrial furnaces. The nanoparticles are small enough to enter through the olfactory nerve and bypass the blood-brain barrier. Elimination logic: microwave ovens generate non-ionising electromagnetic radiation and emit no particulate matter. Telephone lines carry electrical signals and also emit no particles. Any option containing 3 or 5 is therefore wrong, which rules out (a), (c) and (d) and leaves (b).
explanations: Wrong: it includes 3 (microwave stoves) and 5 (telephone lines), which emit no particles, and it omits power plants (4), which do.
Correct: brakes, vehicle engines and power plants are the combustion or friction sources of magnetite nanoparticles. Microwaves and telephone lines are not.
Wrong: it leaves out brakes and engines, which are major sources, and includes microwaves and telephone lines, which are not.
Wrong: it includes microwaves and telephone lines, which are not sources of particulate pollution.
keyfact: Pollution magnetite (Fe3O4) nanoparticles come from combustion and friction sources such as brakes, engines and power plants, not from microwaves or telephone lines, and they are linked to Alzheimer's disease.
option_notes: Option (a), 1, 2, 3 and 5 only, combines brakes, engines, microwave stoves and telephone lines. It is a distractor because it drops power plants and adds two non-particulate sources. Brakes and engines are valid sources. Microwave ovens emit non-ionising radiation (about 2.45 GHz) and telephone lines carry signals, so neither releases particulate matter. It would be right only if electromagnetic devices produced iron oxide particles, which they do not.

Option (b), 1, 2 and 4 only, is the correct answer. It covers brake wear, engine exhaust and power plant emissions, which are the friction and combustion sources of magnetite nanoparticles. Magnetite (Fe3O4) is a ferrimagnetic iron oxide. The Maher et al. study (PNAS, 2016) found these pollution-derived particles in human brains and linked them to oxidative stress and neurodegeneration, including Alzheimer's disease.

Option (c), 3, 4 and 5 only, contains power plants (valid) along with microwave stoves and telephone lines (invalid). It omits brakes and engines, which are the most direct urban traffic sources. Microwave ovens use a magnetron to produce non-ionising radiation and telephone lines carry electrical signals. Neither involves combustion or abrasion, so neither can produce magnetite particulates.

Option (d), all five items, is the over-inclusive option. It is wrong because microwave stoves and telephone lines are not particulate sources. UPSC often uses an 'all of the above' option to catch students who assume that anything electrical or magnetic must be a source of magnetite. Magnetite pollution comes from heat and friction acting on iron-containing materials, not from electromagnetic fields.
related: Magnetite is Fe3O4, a ferrimagnetic iron oxide and an important iron ore.
The 2016 Lancaster University study (Maher et al., PNAS) found pollution-derived magnetite in human brains.
Magnetite nanoparticles are linked to oxidative stress and Alzheimer's disease.
Non-exhaust emissions from brakes, tyres and roads remain even for electric vehicles.
Microwave ovens use non-ionising radiation at about 2.45 GHz.
PM2.5 refers to particulate matter of 2.5 micrometres or less in diameter.
The National Clean Air Programme was launched in 2019.
The Commission for Air Quality Management was set up in 2020 for Delhi-NCR.
statements: 1 — Correct: Brake wear releases iron-rich particles, including magnetite, through friction heating. Brake pads and discs contain iron and steel. Braking produces non-exhaust particulate emissions (PM10 and PM2.5) that are a major urban pollutant. Studies of roadside air near busy roads show magnetite-rich nanoparticles. Non-exhaust emissions (brakes, tyres, road wear) will remain significant even as vehicles become electric.

2 — Correct: Vehicle engines release combustion-derived magnetite. Engine wear and high-temperature fuel combustion produce ultrafine iron oxide particles in exhaust, and diesel exhaust is a known source of ultrafine particulate matter. The Maher 2016 study linked traffic pollution to the magnetite found in brains. India's Bharat Stage norms regulate exhaust PM, and diesel exhaust is classified by the IARC as carcinogenic (Group 1).

3 — Incorrect: Microwave ovens heat food using non-ionising microwave radiation at about 2.45 GHz. They produce no combustion or abrasion, so they release no magnetite particles. The magnetron generates the radiation, and the oven is shielded to limit leakage. Do not confuse electromagnetic radiation with particulate pollution. Microwaves are non-ionising and do not make food radioactive.

4 — Correct: Power plants, especially coal-fired thermal plants, burn coal containing iron minerals such as pyrite. At high temperatures the iron is converted into magnetite-rich fly ash spheres and ultrafine particles. Fly ash is a major pollutant in India, and the government mandates its utilisation under notifications from the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. Emission norms for thermal plants were tightened in 2015, including limits on SO2 and NOx.

5 — Incorrect: Telephone lines carry electrical or optical signals through cables. They involve no combustion or friction and release no particulate matter. Any electromagnetic fields they produce are low-frequency and non-particulate. They are not a source of magnetite pollution.
summary: The answer is (b) 1, 2 and 4 only. Airborne magnetite nanoparticles come from combustion and friction sources: vehicle brake wear, vehicle engine exhaust and power plant emissions. Microwave stoves and telephone lines do not generate magnetite particles.
topic_notes:
Magnetite (Fe3O4) is the most strongly magnetic naturally occurring mineral. It is an iron oxide, also called lodestone, and is a major iron ore. In the body, small amounts of biogenic magnetite are produced in the brain, and some organisms use it for magnetoreception, including magnetotactic bacteria, birds and bees. The concern is anthropogenic magnetite: rounded nanoparticles formed by high-temperature combustion and friction, which are chemically and morphologically different from the angular biogenic crystals.

Key study: Maher et al., PNAS, September 2016, from Lancaster University. Brain tissue from people in Mexico City and Manchester contained abundant combustion-derived magnetite nanoparticles. The particles may enter via the olfactory nerve, bypassing the blood-brain barrier. They are suspected of causing reactive oxygen species formation, oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, and are linked to Alzheimer's disease.

Sources: vehicle brake wear, engine exhaust, coal-fired power plants, industrial furnaces, open fires, and indoor stoves and candles.

Related air pollution concepts: PM2.5 (particles of 2.5 micrometres or less) and PM10. Ultrafine particles are below 100 nm. The National Clean Air Programme was launched in 2019 and aims to cut particulate pollution by 20-30% by 2024 against a 2017 baseline. The Air Quality Index (AQI) was launched in 2014 and has six categories. The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was passed in 1981. The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) was set up in 2020 for Delhi-NCR. The Bharat Stage VI norms took effect in April 2020.
