Adenoviruses are among the causes of the common cold (also called acute viral rhinitis or upper respiratory infection), and HIV, a retrovirus, causes AIDS. The common cold is self-limiting, usually lasts 7-10 days, and has no specific cure or vaccine. Rhinoviruses are the most common cause. Treatment is symptomatic, and antibiotics do not work against viruses.
related: Adenoviruses have linear dsDNA genomes and no envelope.
HIV is a retrovirus with two copies of ssRNA and reverse transcriptase.
Covishield uses a chimpanzee adenovirus vector (ChAdOx1).
SARS-CoV-2 is a positive-sense ssRNA coronavirus.
Hepatitis B is a DNA virus that replicates through reverse transcription.
Rhinoviruses are the commonest cause of the common cold.
Smallpox (variola, a dsDNA virus) was declared eradicated in 1980.
Reverse transcriptase was discovered in 1970 by Temin and Baltimore.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Adenoviruses have double-stranded DNA, not single-stranded, and retroviruses have single-stranded RNA, not double-stranded DNA. Adenoviruses were first isolated in 1953 from human adenoid tissue, which gives them their name. They are non-enveloped, icosahedral, about 70-90 nm, with a linear dsDNA genome of roughly 26-45 kb. There are over 50 human serotypes. They cause respiratory illness, conjunctivitis, gastroenteritis and cystitis. Retroviruses (family Retroviridae) include HIV, HTLV-1 and Rous sarcoma virus. They have a diploid ssRNA genome and use reverse transcriptase, discovered by Temin and Baltimore in 1970 (Nobel 1975).

2 — Correct: Adenoviruses are a recognised cause of the common cold and other upper respiratory infections. AIDS is caused by HIV, a retrovirus. The common cold is mostly caused by rhinoviruses, with coronaviruses, adenoviruses, RSV and others also involved. HIV was identified in 1983-84 by Luc Montagnier and Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, and Robert Gallo was credited with related work. It spreads through blood, sexual contact and mother-to-child transmission. HIV targets CD4+ T cells. Diagnosis uses ELISA and Western blot, and treatment is antiretroviral therapy (ART). India's National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) runs the national programme, and World AIDS Day is on 1 December.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. Adenoviruses sometimes cause the common cold and HIV, a retrovirus, causes AIDS. Statement 1 reverses the genome facts: adenoviruses have double-stranded DNA and retroviruses have single-stranded RNA genomes.
topic_notes: Virus classification: the Baltimore system groups viruses into seven classes by genome type and the way mRNA is made. Class I is dsDNA (adenovirus, herpes, pox, papilloma). Class II is ssDNA (parvovirus). Class III is dsRNA (rotavirus, reovirus). Class IV is positive-sense ssRNA (polio, SARS-CoV-2, dengue, hepatitis C, rhinovirus). Class V is negative-sense ssRNA (influenza, measles, rabies, Ebola). Class VI is ssRNA with reverse transcriptase (retroviruses, such as HIV). Class VII is dsDNA with reverse transcriptase (hepatitis B). Retroviruses: HIV has two copies of ssRNA and key enzymes reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease. Its envelope proteins gp120 and gp41 bind CD4 and the co-receptors CCR5 or CXCR4. Antiretroviral drug classes include NRTIs (zidovudine), NNRTIs, protease inhibitors and integrase inhibitors. Related ideas: reverse transcriptase is used in RT-PCR, and the Nobel Prize 1975 went to Baltimore, Temin and Dulbecco. Adenoviral vector vaccines: Covishield (ChAdOx1, a chimpanzee adenovirus), Sputnik V (Ad26 and Ad5) and Johnson & Johnson's Janssen vaccine. mRNA vaccines (Pfizer, Moderna) use no viral vector. Viral diseases and agents: common cold (rhinovirus, coronavirus, adenovirus), influenza (orthomyxovirus), SARS-CoV-2 (coronavirus, +ssRNA), Hepatitis A (picornavirus), HPV (dsDNA), and smallpox (variola, dsDNA, eradicated in 1980). Viroids are infectious RNA without a protein coat, and prions are infectious proteins. UPSC often asks about genome types, vectors in vaccines, gene therapy and diseases caused by particular viruses.

question: Water can dissolve more substances than any other liquid because
options: it is a good conductor of heat
it has high value of specific heat
it is an oxide of hydrogen
subject: Economy
detail: Water (H2O) has a bent geometry with an H-O-H angle of about 104.5 degrees. Oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the O-H bonds are polar covalent and the molecule has a permanent dipole moment (about 1.85 D). When an ionic solid such as NaCl is placed in water, the partially negative oxygen ends attract Na+ and the partially positive hydrogen ends attract Cl-. This ion-dipole attraction overcomes the lattice energy and the ions become hydrated. Water also forms hydrogen bonds with polar molecules such as sugars, alcohols and ammonia, so these dissolve readily. Its high dielectric constant (about 80 at 25 degrees C) reduces the attraction between dissolved ions and keeps them apart. The rule 'like dissolves like' explains why non-polar substances such as oil, fats and wax do not dissolve. Elimination: heat conduction and specific heat are thermal properties and say nothing about dissolving. Being an oxide of hydrogen is only a statement of composition, and many other oxides are not good solvents.
explanations: Correct. The dipolar nature gives ion-dipole and hydrogen-bond interactions that pull solute particles apart and stabilise them in solution, making water the best general solvent.
Wrong. Water is actually a poor conductor of heat compared with metals. Thermal conductivity has no bearing on solvent ability.
Wrong. Water's high specific heat (4.18 J/g/K) is true, but it governs temperature moderation, not dissolution of substances.
Wrong. Being hydrogen oxide only describes its chemical composition. Other oxides, such as H2O2 or many metal oxides, are not universal solvents, so this does not explain the property.
keyfact: Water is the universal solvent because its dipolar (polar) molecules and hydrogen bonding hydrate ions and polar substances.
option_notes: Dipolar nature: unequal sharing of electrons between O and H gives a permanent dipole. This causes hydrogen bonding, high boiling point (100 degrees C), surface tension, cohesion and adhesion, and strong solvent power for ionic and polar compounds. Water is called the universal solvent, though it does not dissolve non-polar substances like oils.

Thermal conductivity of water is low (about 0.6 W/m/K), much lower than metals like copper. Heat moves in water mostly by convection. Good conductors of heat are metals, due to free electrons. Water's thermal behaviour is better known for its high specific heat and high latent heat.

Specific heat is the heat needed to raise 1 g of a substance by 1 degree C. Water's is 4.18 J/g/K (1 cal/g/degree C), among the highest of common liquids. This moderates climate, keeps coastal areas equable, and makes water a good coolant. Land and sea breezes arise from this.

Water is the oxide of hydrogen (H2O), formed by combining two hydrogen atoms with one oxygen atom; hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is another. Water is amphoteric and neutral at pH 7 (25 degrees C). Its composition was established by Cavendish and Lavoisier in the 1780s, showing it is a compound, not an element.
related: Water is densest at 4 degrees C, which is why ice floats.
Water's high specific heat is 4.18 J/g/K, moderating coastal climate.
Heavy water (D2O) is used as a moderator in PHWR nuclear reactors.
Temporary hardness is due to bicarbonates of Ca and Mg and is removed by boiling.
Pure water is a poor electrical conductor; dissolved ions make it conduct.
Capillary action in plants results from cohesion and adhesion of water.
'Like dissolves like': polar solvents dissolve polar solutes, non-polar dissolve non-polar.
Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) is another oxide of hydrogen, used as a bleach and disinfectant.
summary: The answer is (a). Water is a dipolar (polar) molecule, with partial negative charge on oxygen and partial positive charge on hydrogen, so it can surround and stabilise ions and polar molecules, which is why it is called the 'universal solvent'.
topic_notes: Water's properties come from its polarity and hydrogen bonding. Key points: molecular formula H2O; bent shape, bond angle about 104.5 degrees; each molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds. Consequences: (1) Universal solvent due to polarity and high dielectric constant. (2) High specific heat (4.18 J/g/K) and high latent heat of vaporisation (about 2260 J/g) and fusion (about 334 J/g), which moderate climate and body temperature. (3) Cohesion and adhesion, giving high surface tension (about 72 mN/m at 20 degrees C) and capillary action, important for water transport in plants. (4) Anomalous expansion: density is maximum at 4 degrees C, so ice floats and aquatic life survives under frozen lakes. (5) Amphoteric nature and pH 7 when pure. (6) Pure water is a poor conductor of electricity; dissolved ions make it conductive. Hardness of water is due to dissolved calcium and magnesium bicarbonates (temporary) and chlorides and sulphates (permanent); temporary hardness is removed by boiling or Clark's method; permanent hardness by washing soda or ion exchange. Heavy water (D2O) is used as a moderator in nuclear reactors (for example, PHWRs in India). Water pollution indicators include BOD, COD and dissolved oxygen. Related UPSC angles: eutrophication, hydrogen bond examples in DNA, differences between hydrophilic and hydrophobic substances, and the water cycle.

question:
With reference to street-lighting, how do sodium lamps differ from LED lamps?
1. Sodium lamps produce light in 360 degrees but it is not so in the case of LED lamps.
2. As street-lights, sodium lamps have longer life span than LED lamps.
3. The spectrum of visible light from sodium lamps is almost monochromatic while LED lamps offer significant colour advantages in street-lighting. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Street-lighting has moved from high-pressure sodium vapour (HPSV) and low-pressure sodium (LPS) lamps to LEDs. Sodium lamps are gas-discharge lamps. They radiate omnidirectionally, so reflectors and fixtures are needed to push light downward, and much light is wasted as spill and sky glow. LEDs are solid-state semiconductor devices (p-n junction electroluminescence) that emit light in a roughly 120-180 degree cone. This makes them directional and efficient for roads. LPS lamps emit almost purely at about 589 nm (the sodium D-line), so the light is nearly monochromatic and colour rendering is very poor (CRI close to 0). HPSV is broader but still yellowish-orange, with CRI of about 20-25. White LEDs have CRI of 70 or more, and colour temperature can be tuned. Lifespan is the reason statement 2 fails. Sodium lamps last roughly 12,000-24,000 hours, while LEDs last 50,000-100,000 hours. LEDs also use 50% or more less energy, switch on instantly and contain no mercury. India's Street Lighting National Programme (SLNP, by EESL) replaces conventional lamps with LEDs. Elimination: statement 2 is false, so (b) and (d) are out. Statement 3 is true, so (a) is out, leaving (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is also correct, so '3 only' is incomplete.
(b) is wrong because statement 2 is false. LEDs, not sodium lamps, have the longer life span.
(c) is correct because statements 1 and 3 are true and statement 2 is false.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement 2, which is false.
keyfact: Sodium lamps: omnidirectional (360 degrees), near-monochromatic yellow, shorter life; LEDs: directional, good colour rendering, 50,000+ hours.
option_notes: 3 only: Statement 3 is true, but the option leaves out statement 1. It is a trap for students who know the spectrum difference but not the emission geometry. Sodium vapour lamps are gas-discharge lamps, and low-pressure types emit at about 589 nm. Their CRI is very low, so they are suited to uses where colour does not matter, such as roads and security lighting. They have been widely replaced by LEDs.

2 only: This is the false statement. Sodium lamps last roughly 12,000-24,000 hours, while LEDs last 50,000 hours or more. LEDs have lower maintenance and lower lifetime cost. Sodium lamps also need warm-up time, and their output declines with age. Sodium lamps contain sodium metal and sometimes a small amount of mercury, which makes disposal harder.

1 and 3 only: This is the official answer. Sodium lamps are omnidirectional and give a near-monochromatic yellow light. LEDs are directional and offer good colour rendering and tunable colour temperature. LEDs have a longer life and higher efficacy, typically 100-150 lumens per watt. Government schemes such as SLNP and UJALA promote LEDs in India.

1, 2 and 3: This option is wrong because it counts the false lifespan claim. It tests whether students assume that older technology lasts longer. Modern LED street-lights use heat sinks and drivers to reach 50,000-100,000 hours. A common mistake is to confuse the lifespan of a lamp with the lifespan of its driver or power supply, which can fail earlier.
related: Low-pressure sodium lamps emit near-monochromatic light at about 589 nm.
LEDs have a life of about 50,000-100,000 hours, far longer than sodium lamps.
UJALA (2015) is run by EESL under the Ministry of Power.
Street Lighting National Programme (SLNP) was launched in January 2015.
The 2014 Physics Nobel was awarded for the blue LED (Akasaki, Amano, Nakamura).
CRI measures how faithfully a light source shows colours; LPS sodium is near 0.
The Minamata Convention restricts mercury in products such as certain lamps.
BEE's Standards and Labelling programme gives star ratings to appliances.
statements: 1 — Correct: Sodium lamps are omnidirectional, emitting light through 360 degrees, while LEDs are directional and emit in a limited cone. Sodium vapour lamps are gas-discharge lamps in which an electric arc excites sodium vapour. The two main types are low-pressure sodium (LPS), which is very efficient but gives a monochromatic yellow light, and high-pressure sodium (HPS), which gives a broader golden-white light. Both need reflectors or refractors to direct light downward, and much light is wasted as spill and sky glow. LEDs are semiconductor diodes whose light comes from a flat chip, so they naturally emit in a roughly 120-180 degree cone. This reduces the need for reflectors, improves road-surface efficiency and reduces light pollution.

2 — Incorrect: LEDs have the longer life, not sodium lamps. Typical LED street-lights last about 50,000-100,000 hours, against about 12,000-24,000 hours for HPS lamps and roughly 18,000 for LPS. LEDs fade gradually, a measure called lumen depreciation (L70), instead of failing suddenly. They save 50-70% of energy, switch on instantly, can be dimmed and contain no mercury. Sodium lamps need a warm-up of several minutes and their output falls over time. India's Street Lighting National Programme (SLNP), run by EESL under the Ministry of Power, and the UJALA scheme (launched in 2015) promote the shift to LEDs. Lower maintenance and energy cost are the key advantages of LEDs.

3 — Correct: Sodium lamps, especially low-pressure ones, emit nearly monochromatic light at about 589 nm (the sodium D-lines), so the colour rendering index (CRI) is close to zero. Objects appear in shades of yellow and grey, which makes colour identification hard. HPS lamps have a CRI of about 20-25. White LEDs have a CRI of 70-90 and a tunable correlated colour temperature (warm to cool white), and they can also produce coloured light. This improves visibility, recognition of objects and safety. Warm-white or amber LEDs can also reduce effects on wildlife and astronomy. Note that blue-rich LEDs can raise glare and light-pollution concerns.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. Sodium lamps emit light in all directions (360 degrees) while LEDs are directional, and sodium lamps give a near-monochromatic yellow light while LEDs offer a wide choice of colours and better colour rendering. Statement 2 is wrong because LEDs last much longer than sodium lamps.
topic_notes: Street-lighting technologies: incandescent lamps were replaced by mercury vapour, then sodium vapour (LPS and HPS), metal halide, CFL, and now LEDs. Sodium lamps are gas-discharge lamps. Low-pressure sodium gives about 589 nm monochromatic yellow light, with efficacy up to about 180 lm/W but a CRI near 0. High-pressure sodium gives a golden-white light with a CRI of about 20-25 and efficacy of about 80-140 lm/W. LEDs work by electroluminescence in a semiconductor p-n junction. They are directional, instant-on and dimmable, can be controlled by smart systems, and have a long life of 50,000 hours or more. They use no mercury, and white LEDs are made with blue LEDs plus phosphor. The 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura for efficient blue LEDs. In India, UJALA (2015) distributes LED bulbs, tubelights and fans through EESL (Energy Efficiency Services Limited, a joint venture of PSUs under the Ministry of Power). SLNP (Street Lighting National Programme, 2015) replaces conventional street-lights with LEDs. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) runs the Standards and Labelling programme. Light pollution and sky glow are concerns, especially with blue-rich, high colour temperature LEDs. These can disrupt circadian rhythms and harm insects and turtle hatchlings. Related concepts include lumen (light output), lux (illuminance), efficacy (lm/W), CRI and CCT (correlated colour temperature in kelvin). Other angles UPSC can ask: OLED, the Minamata Convention on mercury (CFLs and mercury lamps are being phased out), solar street-lights, and the Montreal Protocol and Kigali Amendment, which concern cooling rather than lighting.

ocr: The term ‘ACE2’ is talked about in the context of (a) genes introduced in the genetically modified plants (b) development of India’s own satellite navigation system (c) radio collars for wildlife tracking (ad) spread of viral diseases 33 BXC-U-FTHI/68A
subject: Science & Tech
detail: ACE2 stands for Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2. It is a membrane-bound enzyme found on the surface of cells in the lungs, heart, kidneys, intestines and blood vessels. Physiologically it helps regulate blood pressure through the renin-angiotensin system, by converting angiotensin II into angiotensin (1-7), which dilates blood vessels. Its link to disease spread came with the COVID-19 pandemic. The spike (S) protein of SARS-CoV-2 binds to the ACE2 receptor through its receptor-binding domain. The host protease TMPRSS2 then primes the spike protein, and the virus fuses with the cell and enters. The earlier SARS-CoV (2002-03) also used ACE2. Because of this, ACE2 is a target for vaccine and drug design, including soluble ACE2 decoys and antibodies that block the spike. Elimination logic: genes in GM plants are usually named as Bt, cry or EPSPS genes, not ACE2. India's own navigation system is NavIC, also called IRNSS. Radio collars are a wildlife telemetry tool, not a biological term. ACE2 is a biological, medical term, so (d) fits.
explanations: Incorrect. Genes in GM plants are things like Cry genes (Bt cotton) or the cp4-EPSPS gene (herbicide tolerance). ACE2 is a human protein receptor and is not introduced into plants.
Incorrect. India's regional navigation system is NavIC (IRNSS), run by ISRO. ACE2 has nothing to do with satellites.
Incorrect. Radio collars are telemetry devices used to track animals such as tigers and elephants. ACE2 is a biological molecule, not a tracking technology.
Correct. ACE2 is the cell-surface receptor that SARS-CoV-2 (and SARS-CoV) uses to enter human cells. It is therefore central to how viral diseases like COVID-19 spread.
keyfact: ACE2 is the human cell receptor that SARS-CoV-2 binds through its spike protein to enter cells, so it is linked to the spread of viral disease.
option_notes: Genes in genetically modified plants are DNA sequences introduced to give new traits. Bt cotton carries Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab from Bacillus thuringiensis for bollworm resistance. Herbicide-tolerant crops use the cp4-EPSPS gene. Bt cotton has been the only GM crop commercially approved in India, since 2002. GM mustard (DMH-11) was under regulatory and judicial scrutiny. GEAC, under the Environment Ministry, is the regulator. Golden Rice carries genes for beta-carotene.

NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation), formerly IRNSS, is India's regional satellite navigation system developed by ISRO. It uses 7 satellites (IRNSS-1A to 1G) and covers India and about 1,500 km beyond its borders. It provides the Standard Positioning Service and a restricted service. It operates in the L5 and S bands. Its first satellite was launched in 2013. Other systems include GPS (USA), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (EU) and BeiDou (China). GAGAN is India's SBAS augmentation system.

Radio collars are devices fitted to animals that transmit signals (VHF or GPS-satellite) so researchers can track their movement, range and behaviour. They are used for tigers, elephants, leopards and snow leopards. In India the Wildlife Institute of India, Dehradun, runs many such studies. Radio collaring was used in tiger reintroduction in Sariska and Panna. It supports human-wildlife conflict management and corridor planning. Tracking also uses camera traps and GPS tags.

Viral diseases are caused by viruses, which are obligate intracellular parasites that spread through droplets, vectors, contact, water or blood. Examples are COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2), dengue, influenza, Ebola, Nipah and HIV. SARS-CoV-2 uses the ACE2 receptor and the TMPRSS2 protease to enter cells. Vaccine types include mRNA, viral-vector and inactivated. India's vaccines were Covaxin (inactivated, Bharat Biotech) and Covishield (viral vector, Oxford-AstraZeneca/Serum Institute). Variants of concern include Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta and Omicron.
related: ACE2 is the host cell receptor for SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV; MERS-CoV uses DPP4.
TMPRSS2 is the host protease that primes the spike protein for cell entry.
SARS-CoV-2 is an enveloped positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus.
INSACOG is India's consortium for genome sequencing of SARS-CoV-2 variants.
ZyCoV-D by Zydus Cadila is the world's first DNA-based COVID vaccine.
Covaxin is an inactivated vaccine developed by Bharat Biotech with ICMR and NIV Pune.
NavIC is India's regional navigation system, with 7 satellites.
Bt cotton is India's only commercially approved GM crop.
summary: The answer is (d). ACE2 (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2) is a receptor protein on human cells that the SARS-CoV-2 virus uses to enter and infect them, so the term comes up in discussions of how viral diseases such as COVID-19 spread.
topic_notes: ACE2 (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2) is a zinc-containing carboxypeptidase on the surface of cells in the lungs (type II alveolar cells), heart, kidney, gut and endothelium. In the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), ACE converts angiotensin I to the vasoconstrictor angiotensin II, while ACE2 converts angiotensin II into angiotensin (1-7), which dilates vessels. ACE2 therefore acts as a counterbalance to ACE. Its role in infection: the S1 subunit of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein binds ACE2 through its receptor-binding domain. The host protease TMPRSS2 (and furin) cleaves the spike, which allows the viral and cell membranes to fuse. SARS-CoV (2003) also used ACE2, whereas MERS-CoV uses DPP4 as its receptor. Research angles: soluble ACE2 as a decoy, monoclonal antibodies against the spike, and concern over ACE inhibitors and ARBs in COVID patients (the evidence showed no harm). Coronaviruses are enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses. COVID-19 was declared a pandemic by WHO on 11 March 2020. Diagnostic tests: RT-PCR (gold standard), rapid antigen test, antibody (serology) test. Vaccine platforms: mRNA (Pfizer, Moderna), viral vector (Covishield, Sputnik V, J&J), inactivated (Covaxin, Sinovac), DNA (ZyCoV-D, the world's first DNA vaccine, from Zydus Cadila) and protein subunit (Covovax, Corbevax). Genome sequencing in India is coordinated by INSACOG. Variant naming by WHO uses Greek letters.

question: Bisphenol A (BPA), a cause of concern, is a structural/key component in the manufacture of which of the following kinds of plastics?
subject: Economy
detail: Bisphenol A (BPA) is an industrial organic compound (two phenol groups joined through a dimethylmethylene bridge), first synthesised in 1891 by Aleksandr Dianin and later used in plastics from the 1950s. Its main use is as a monomer: BPA condensed with phosgene or diphenyl carbonate yields polycarbonate, a hard, transparent, shatter-resistant plastic (recycling code 7 'Other'). It is also the base of epoxy resins used to line food cans, water pipes and in thermal paper receipts. BPA is an endocrine disruptor that mimics oestrogen; unreacted or leached BPA from heated or worn polycarbonate bottles, baby feeding bottles and containers can enter food and drink. Concerns include reproductive, developmental, metabolic and neurobehavioural effects. The EU banned BPA in baby bottles in 2011; India's BIS and FSSAI also restrict it in infant feeding bottles. Elimination: LDPE is made from ethylene, PET from terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol, and PVC from vinyl chloride; none uses BPA as a structural monomer, though additives in some plastics may be controversial. So only polycarbonate fits.
explanations: Incorrect: LDPE is a polymer of ethylene (recycling code 4), used in carry bags and films; BPA is not a monomer in it.
Correct: BPA is the structural monomer of polycarbonate, formed by reaction with phosgene or diphenyl carbonate; leaching from it is the health concern.
Incorrect: PET is made from terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol (code 1); it is BPA-free, though it is often confused with polycarbonate in bottles.
Incorrect: PVC is made by polymerising vinyl chloride (code 3); its concerns relate to phthalate plasticisers, dioxins and vinyl chloride, not BPA as a backbone.
keyfact: BPA is the monomer of polycarbonate (and epoxy resins) and is an oestrogen-mimicking endocrine disruptor.
option_notes: Low-density polyethylene (LDPE) is a branched thermoplastic made by high-pressure polymerisation of ethylene, first produced in 1933 by ICI. It is flexible and tough, with recycling code 4. Uses include carry bags, cling film, squeeze bottles and food wraps. It is considered relatively safe for food contact and is not made with BPA.

Polycarbonate is a tough, transparent, heat-resistant thermoplastic containing carbonate groups, made from BPA and phosgene. It is used in water cooler jugs, reusable bottles, CDs/DVDs, eyewear lenses, helmets and electronic casings. It carries recycling code 7. Its BPA leaching, especially on heating or scratching, led to bans in baby bottles in many jurisdictions.

Polyethylene terephthalate (PET or PETE) is a polyester made from terephthalic acid (or dimethyl terephthalate) and ethylene glycol, recycling code 1. It is used for soft-drink and water bottles, fibres (polyester) and food trays. It is light, strong and recyclable, and does not use BPA. Antimony catalyst residues and acetaldehyde are the usual concerns.

Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) is a thermoplastic made from vinyl chloride monomer, recycling code 3. It is rigid when unplasticised (pipes, window frames) and flexible with plasticisers such as phthalates (cables, flooring, blood bags). Concerns include dioxin release on burning, vinyl chloride carcinogenicity and phthalate toxicity. BPA may occasionally be a stabiliser additive but is not its structural component.
related: BPA is a xenoestrogen, an endocrine-disrupting chemical.
Polycarbonate is recycling code 7 (Other).
BPA is also used in epoxy resin can linings and thermal paper receipts.
PET is code 1, HDPE 2, PVC 3, LDPE 4, PP 5, PS 6.
Phthalates are plasticisers, mainly used to soften PVC.
India banned identified single-use plastic items from 1 July 2022.
EU and Canada banned BPA in baby bottles in 2011 and 2010 respectively.
Bisphenol S and F are common substitutes in 'BPA-free' products.
summary: The answer is (b) Polycarbonate. BPA is the key monomer that is reacted with phosgene (or diphenyl carbonate) to make polycarbonate plastic, and it is also a building block of epoxy resins.
topic_notes: BPA (C15H16O2) is a high-volume industrial chemical, with millions of tonnes produced annually. It serves as a monomer for polycarbonate plastics and epoxy resins, and appears in thermal paper, dental sealants and can linings. It is an endocrine-disrupting chemical (xenoestrogen) that binds oestrogen receptors. Human exposure is mainly dietary, through leaching, which increases with heat, acidic contents and wear. Health concerns include effects on fertility, early puberty, breast and prostate development, obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular risk and neurodevelopment in foetuses and infants. Regulation: Canada declared BPA toxic in 2010 and banned it in baby bottles; the EU banned it in baby bottles in 2011 and later cut the tolerable daily intake sharply (EFSA 2023 reduced it to 0.2 nanograms per kg body weight per day); the US FDA banned it in baby bottles and sippy cups in 2012. In India, the Legal Metrology and FSSAI rules and BIS standards prohibit BPA in polycarbonate infant feeding bottles. 'BPA-free' products often use substitutes like bisphenol S or F, which may have similar effects. Plastic recycling codes: 1 PET, 2 HDPE, 3 PVC, 4 LDPE, 5 PP, 6 PS, 7 Other (including polycarbonate, PLA). Related UPSC themes: microplastics, phthalates, endocrine disruptors, Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 and 2022 amendments including the ban on identified single-use plastics from 1 July 2022, biodegradable plastics such as PLA and PHA, and the Stockholm Convention on POPs.

question: Triclosan’, considered harmful when exposed to high levels for a long time, is most likely present in which of the following?
subject: Environment
detail: Triclosan (and the related triclocarban) is a synthetic, broad-spectrum antimicrobial chemical used since the 1970s in personal-care products (toothpaste such as those aimed at gingivitis, antibacterial soaps, body washes, deodorants, shaving creams, mouthwash), and also in some cosmetics, textiles, kitchenware and toys. Concerns include endocrine (thyroid and reproductive hormone) disruption seen in animal studies, possible contribution to antimicrobial resistance, and aquatic toxicity because it passes through wastewater and bioaccumulates in algae and fish. It can also form dioxins and chloroform on reacting with sunlight or chlorinated water. The US FDA banned it in over-the-counter consumer antiseptic wash products in 2016, and the EU has restricted its use in several product types, including hygiene products such as soaps. Elimination logic: food preservatives are substances such as benzoates, sorbates, nitrites and sulphites, not triclosan. Fruit ripening agents are calcium carbide (which releases acetylene), ethephon and ethylene. Reused plastic containers are linked with chemicals such as BPA and phthalates. Triclosan is a classic toiletry ingredient, so (d) is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: food preservatives are agents like sodium benzoate, sorbic acid, nitrites and sulphites. Triclosan is not a food additive.
Incorrect: fruit ripening uses ethylene, ethephon or illegally calcium carbide (acetylene). Triclosan has no role in ripening.
Incorrect: reused plastic containers are associated with leaching of BPA and phthalates, not triclosan, which is the standard association for this question's distractor.
Correct: triclosan is an antimicrobial in toothpaste, soaps, hand washes, deodorants and other toiletries, with concerns about endocrine disruption and resistance on prolonged high exposure.
keyfact: Triclosan = antibacterial agent in toiletries (toothpaste, soaps, deodorants); endocrine-disruption and antimicrobial-resistance concerns.
option_notes: Food preservatives are substances that prevent spoilage by microbes or oxidation. Examples include class I (salt, sugar, vinegar, natural) and class II (benzoates, sorbates, sulphites, nitrites, nitrates). In India the FSSAI regulates them under the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 and its additive regulations. Excess sulphite can trigger asthma, and nitrites are linked to nitrosamine formation.

Fruit-ripening substances include ethylene gas (permitted, a natural plant hormone) and ethephon, which releases ethylene. Calcium carbide, which produces acetylene and may contain arsenic and phosphorus traces, is banned by FSSAI for ripening. Artificial ripening with it can cause mouth ulcers, gastric problems and neurological effects. Ethylene is permitted in regulated concentrations in ripening chambers.

Reused plastic containers, especially PET bottles and polycarbonate, may leach chemicals like bisphenol A (BPA), phthalates and antimony on heating, scratching or repeated use. BPA is an endocrine disruptor, and India (BIS and FSSAI) regulates BPA in baby feeding bottles. Plastic recycling codes 1-7 indicate resin types, and number 7 often involves polycarbonate.

Toiletries are personal-care items such as soap, toothpaste, shampoo, deodorant, and mouthwash. Triclosan is an antibacterial and antifungal added to many of them. It is regulated by the US FDA (banned in consumer antiseptic washes in 2016) and the EU, and it is a persistent water pollutant that may disrupt thyroid hormones and promote resistant bacteria.
related: Triclosan is an antibacterial and antifungal agent used in toothpaste, soaps and deodorants.
The US FDA banned triclosan in consumer antiseptic wash products in 2016.
Triclosan inhibits the bacterial enzyme enoyl-ACP reductase (FabI).
BPA is an endocrine disruptor in polycarbonate plastics and epoxy resins.
Calcium carbide, used illegally for ripening fruit, is banned by FSSAI.
Microbeads in scrubs are a source of microplastic pollution in water bodies.
Endocrine-disrupting chemicals interfere with hormone systems; examples are BPA, phthalates and some pesticides.
FSSAI, set up under the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006, regulates food additives in India.
summary: The answer is (d) Toiletries. Triclosan is an antibacterial and antifungal agent added to toothpastes, soaps, hand washes, deodorants and similar personal-care products, and long-term exposure to high levels is a health and environmental concern.
topic_notes: Triclosan is a chlorinated aromatic compound (a polychloro phenoxy phenol) with antibacterial and antifungal action. It works by inhibiting the bacterial enzyme enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase (FabI), which is needed for fatty acid synthesis. It was introduced in the 1960s-70s, first in hospital settings as a surgical scrub, and then moved into consumer products. Uses: toothpaste (Colgate Total used triclosan with a copolymer to reduce plaque and gingivitis), antibacterial soaps, hand sanitisers, deodorants, cosmetics, and some plastics, clothes and kitchen items. Health and environmental concerns: studies in animals show lowered thyroid hormone levels and reproductive effects, there are concerns about antibiotic cross-resistance, and it is toxic to algae and aquatic life. It is found in sewage sludge and rivers, and it bioaccumulates. In sunlight it can degrade into dioxins, and with chlorinated tap water it can form chloroform. Regulation: the US FDA 2016 final rule banned triclosan and triclocarban, among other ingredients, in consumer antiseptic washes; the EU progressively restricted its use in cosmetics and food-contact materials; the Stockholm Convention committee has discussed related persistent chemicals. Related UPSC angles include other chemicals of concern in daily life: BPA in plastics, phthalates, parabens in cosmetics, microbeads in scrubs (banned in several countries), PFAS ('forever chemicals'), and endocrine-disrupting chemicals generally. Also remember FSSAI's role in food additives, BIS's role in standards, and the Plastic Waste Management Rules, which restrict single-use plastics.

question: Which one of. the following is a reason why astronomical distances are measured in light-years?
options: Distances among stellar bodies do not change
Gravity of stellar bodies does not change
Light always travels in straight line
Speed of light is always same. [P.7.0
subject: Science & Tech
detail: A light-year is a unit of length, not of time. It equals about 9.46 x 10^12 km (about 9.46 trillion km). It is the distance light covers in one Julian year (365.25 days) in vacuum. The unit is meaningful only because the speed of light in vacuum, c = 299,792,458 m/s, is the same for all observers and in all inertial frames. This is a postulate of Einstein's special relativity (1905), and the metre has been defined through c since 1983. Because c is constant, 'distance = c x time' gives an unambiguous distance. Kilometres give unwieldy numbers: the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.24 light-years away, and the Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across. Elimination: (a) is false because stars and galaxies move, so distances change over time. (b) is false because gravity varies with mass and distance, and it is irrelevant to the choice of unit. (c) is partly true in a uniform medium, but light bends near massive bodies (gravitational lensing) and in different media, and straight-line travel alone does not define a unit of length. Only constant speed makes the unit reliable. Other units: the astronomical unit (AU) is used inside the solar system, and the parsec (about 3.26 light-years) is used in professional astronomy.
explanations: Wrong. Distances among stars and galaxies do change, because of proper motion, orbital motion and cosmic expansion. Even if they were fixed, that would not explain why light-years are chosen as the unit.
Wrong. Gravity depends on mass and distance and varies from body to body. It has no role in defining a light-year.

Wrong. Light travels straight in a uniform medium, but gravity can bend it (gravitational lensing, confirmed in the 1919 eclipse observations) and refraction bends it in other media. Straight-line travel does not by itself justify a unit; constant speed does.

Correct. The speed of light in vacuum is a universal constant, so the distance light travels in a year is a fixed, well-defined length. That is why the light-year serves as a standard unit for astronomical distances.
keyfact: A light-year (about 9.46 x 10^12 km) is a unit of distance, usable because the speed of light in vacuum is constant.
option_notes: Constancy of stellar distances: this is not true. Stars move relative to one another (Barnard's Star has the largest proper motion, about 10.4 arcseconds a year). Galaxies recede because the universe is expanding (Hubble's law, 1929). The Andromeda galaxy, by contrast, is approaching the Milky Way at about 110 km/s. Distances in space are therefore dynamic, not fixed.

Constancy of gravity: gravitational force follows Newton's inverse-square law, F = GMm/r^2. It varies with mass and separation. Einstein's general relativity (1915) describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime. Surface gravity differs between bodies, for example Earth 9.8 m/s^2, Moon about 1.6 m/s^2, Sun about 274 m/s^2. It plays no part in defining distance units.

Straight-line propagation of light: light follows straight paths only in a uniform medium (the rectilinear propagation property). It bends by refraction, diffraction and gravitational lensing. Eddington's 1919 solar-eclipse observations confirmed that starlight is deflected near the Sun. Light-years do not depend on straightness; they depend on a constant speed.

Constant speed of light: in vacuum c = 299,792,458 m/s, about 3 x 10^8 m/s. It is independent of the motion of source and observer (special relativity, 1905). One light-year is about 9.46 x 10^12 km. The speed is lower in media (about 2 x 10^8 m/s in glass). This constancy makes the light-year a dependable unit.
related: 1 light-year is about 9.46 trillion km.
1 parsec is about 3.26 light-years.
1 AU is about 149.6 million km; sunlight takes about 8 min 20 s to reach Earth.
Proxima Centauri (about 4.24 ly) is the nearest known star after the Sun.
Speed of light in vacuum is about 3 x 10^8 m/s, the maximum possible speed.
Andromeda galaxy lies about 2.5 million ly away and is approaching the Milky Way.
The metre has been defined via the speed of light since 1983.
ISRO's AstroSat (2015) is India's first dedicated astronomy satellite.
summary: The answer is (d). A light-year is the distance light travels in one year in vacuum, and it works as a unit of distance because the speed of light in vacuum is a universal constant (about 299,792,458 m/s). That constancy gives a fixed, reliable yardstick for the vast distances in space.
topic_notes: Astronomical distance units: (1) Astronomical Unit (AU) is the mean Earth-Sun distance, about 1.496 x 10^8 km (149.6 million km). It is used within the solar system, and light takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to travel this distance. (2) Light-year (ly) is about 9.46 x 10^12 km. (3) Parsec (pc) is the distance at which 1 AU subtends an angle of 1 arcsecond of parallax. It equals about 3.26 ly or 3.09 x 10^13 km. Kiloparsec, megaparsec and gigaparsec are used for galactic and cosmological scales. Key distances: Moon is about 1.3 light-seconds away. Sun is about 8.3 light-minutes away. Proxima Centauri, the nearest star after the Sun, is about 4.24 ly away. Sirius is about 8.6 ly away. Andromeda galaxy is about 2.5 million ly away. The Milky Way's disc is about 100,000 ly across. The observable universe has a radius of about 46 billion ly. The Sun is about 26,000 ly from the galactic centre. Light-year is a unit of distance, not time. Methods of measuring distance: radar ranging in the solar system; trigonometric parallax for nearby stars (the Gaia mission); standard candles such as Cepheid variables (Henrietta Leavitt) and Type Ia supernovae for far-off galaxies; and redshift with Hubble's law for very distant galaxies. Related physics: speed of light is the maximum speed of information transfer. Looking far into space means looking back in time, because light from distant objects is old. Indian context: ISRO's AstroSat (2015) is India's first dedicated multi-wavelength space observatory, and Aditya-L1 (2023) studies the Sun.

ocr: We adopted parliamentary democracy based on the British model, but how does our model differ from that model? 1. As regards legislation, the British Parliament is supreme or sovereign but in India, the power of the Parliament to legislate is limited. 2. In India, matters related to the constitutionality of the Amendment of an Act of the Parliament are referred to the Constitution Bench by the Supreme Court. Select the correct answer using the code given below. (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 : (ad) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Polity
detail: India borrowed the Westminster model of cabinet government, collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha, and a nominal head of state. It differs in several key ways. Britain has an unwritten, flexible constitution and parliamentary sovereignty: Parliament can make or unmake any law, and courts cannot strike down an Act of Parliament. India has a written Constitution and a federal structure with the Seventh Schedule dividing legislative powers. Part III fundamental rights bind Parliament (Article 13), and courts exercise judicial review (Articles 32, 226, 131-136). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) added the Basic Structure doctrine, which limits even the amending power under Article 368. So statement 1 is correct. Article 145(3) requires a minimum of five judges for substantial questions of constitutional interpretation, and Article 143 references also go to such a bench. Challenges to the validity of constitutional amendments are therefore heard by a Constitution Bench, which makes statement 2 correct. Elimination: since both statements are factually sound, options (a), (b) and (d) fail. India's head of state is an elected President, whereas Britain has a hereditary monarch, which is another difference.
explanations: (a) Wrong: statement 2 is also correct, because Article 145(3) sends such matters to a Constitution Bench, so '1 only' is incomplete.
(b) Wrong: statement 1 is correct, since India's Parliament is not sovereign. '2 only' wrongly rejects it.
(c) Correct: both statements are accurate. Parliament's legislative power is limited in India, and constitutional questions go to a Constitution Bench of at least five judges.
(d) Wrong: it rejects both statements, but both are correct.
keyfact: India has constitutional supremacy, not parliamentary sovereignty, and constitutional questions go to a Constitution Bench of at least five judges under Article 145(3).
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would hold only that Indian parliamentary power is limited. That is true, but it is incomplete. Parliamentary sovereignty in the UK means no body can override Parliament, and India differs because of its written Constitution, federalism and judicial review. The option fails because it ignores the Constitution Bench provision in Article 145(3).

Option (b), '2 only', would hold only that constitutional matters go to a Constitution Bench. Article 145(3) fixes a minimum of five judges for substantial constitutional questions, and larger benches (7, 9, 11 or 13 judges) are used for weightier issues. It is wrong because it denies statement 1, which is correct.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', is the official answer. It reflects two Indian departures from the Westminster model: limited legislative power under a written Constitution with judicial review, and a Constitution Bench of at least five judges under Article 145(3) for constitutional questions, including challenges to amendments. The Basic Structure doctrine ties the two together.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', would mean India matches the British model on both points. That is false: India has a rigid written Constitution, federalism and judicial review, and the UK has parliamentary sovereignty without the power to strike down Acts. Constitution Bench references are also a distinctive Indian feature.
related: Article 145(3): minimum five judges for substantial constitutional questions and Article 143 references.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Parliament can amend the Constitution but not its basic structure; the bench had 13 judges.
Article 13 prohibits laws that take away or abridge fundamental rights.
Parliamentary sovereignty is a feature of the British system, associated with A. V. Dicey.
Article 368 deals with Parliament's power to amend the Constitution and the procedure.
The NJAC and the 99th Amendment were struck down in 2015 by a Constitution Bench.
Article 143 gives the President advisory jurisdiction over the Supreme Court.
Article 124 sets the Supreme Court's establishment; the Supreme Court currently has 34 judges including the CJI.
statements: 1 — Correct: Britain follows parliamentary sovereignty, while India's Parliament is limited by the Constitution, federalism, fundamental rights, judicial review and the basic structure. Facts: A. V. Dicey articulated parliamentary sovereignty. Britain has an uncodified constitution made of statutes, conventions and common law. India's Article 13 voids laws that violate fundamental rights. Article 368 gives the amending power, but Kesavananda Bharati (1973, 13-judge bench, 7:6) held that the basic structure cannot be amended. Minerva Mills (1980) reaffirmed this. Article 245 and the Seventh Schedule's three lists (Union, State, Concurrent) divide legislative competence. Courts can strike down laws as ultra vires, which the UK courts cannot do for Acts of Parliament (though the UK Human Rights Act 1998 allows 'declarations of incompatibility').

2 — Correct: Article 145(3) requires a bench of at least five judges for cases involving a substantial question of law on interpreting the Constitution, or for Article 143 references. This applies to challenges to constitutional amendments, so the Supreme Court refers them to a Constitution Bench. Facts: Article 145(1) lets the Supreme Court make rules with the President's approval. Landmark Constitution Bench cases include Shankari Prasad (1951), Golaknath (1967, 11 judges), Kesavananda Bharati (1973, 13 judges), Minerva Mills (1980) and the NJAC case (2015, the 99th Amendment struck down, 4:1). Article 368 amendments such as the 103rd (EWS quota) were upheld by a five-judge bench in 2022. Britain has no equivalent, since its courts cannot review parliamentary statutes.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. India's Parliament is not sovereign because it is bound by a written Constitution, federal division of powers, fundamental rights and judicial review. The British Parliament is sovereign. Under Article 145(3), any case involving a substantial question of law on interpreting the Constitution must be heard by a Bench of at least five judges, and this covers challenges to constitutional amendments.
topic_notes: India's Constitution adopted the Westminster parliamentary system: a nominal executive (President), real executive in the Council of Ministers headed by the PM, collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)), a bicameral legislature, the rule of law, and single citizenship. Key differences from Britain: (1) India is a republic with an elected head of state; Britain has a hereditary monarchy. (2) India has a written, partly rigid Constitution; Britain's is unwritten. (3) Parliamentary sovereignty exists in Britain, but India has constitutional supremacy, with the judiciary as guardian. (4) India is federal; Britain is unitary. (5) Indian ministers may be drawn from either House, while in Britain the PM and nearly all ministers come from the Commons, and the PM has long been from the Commons. (6) The UK has the doctrine of the legal sovereignty of Parliament, while India has an independent judiciary with power over legislation and the executive. (7) The UK had Law Lords in the House of Lords until the Supreme Court of the UK began functioning in 2009. Important Indian provisions: Article 13 (laws inconsistent with fundamental rights), Article 32 (right to constitutional remedies), Articles 124-147 (Supreme Court), Article 142 (complete justice), Article 143 (advisory jurisdiction), Article 368 (amendment), Articles 226 and 227 (High Courts). Cases: Kesavananda Bharati (basic structure), Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975), Minerva Mills (1980), S. R. Bommai (1994), Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record v UoI (2015, NJAC). The 24th Amendment (1971) and 42nd Amendment (1976) tried to limit judicial review, but the court restricted their effect. UPSC may ask about the origins of various features (Government of India Act 1935, the US, Ireland, Canada, Australia, Weimar Germany), the amending procedure, and the Constitution Bench powers.

ocr: With reference to the Union Government, consider the following statements : 1, (aN Gopalaswamy Iyengar Committee suggested that a minister and a_ secretary be designated solely for pursuing the subject of administrative reform and promoting it. 2. in 1970, the Department of Personnel. was _ constituted on the recommendation of the Administrative Reforms Commission, 1966, and this was placed under the Prime Minister’s charge. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 (ad) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Polity
detail: The question tests the history of administrative reform in India's Union Government. N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar, a minister without portfolio, was asked in 1948-49 to report on the reorganisation of the central machinery of government. His report led to the creation of the Organisation and Methods (O&M) Division in the Cabinet Secretariat in 1954. He also recommended that one Ministry should be responsible for the cadre of the Indian Administrative Service and the Central Secretariat Service, and that the Ministry of Home Affairs should take it up. The Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC) was set up in January 1966 under Morarji Desai, who was succeeded by K. Hanumanthaiya. It submitted 20 reports. It recommended a Department of Personnel, to be headed by the Prime Minister, and the Department was formed in 1970 within the Cabinet Secretariat. Elimination logic: statement 2 matches the ARC outcome precisely, so options (a), (c) and (d) fail. Statement 1 is the trap. The idea of a designated minister and secretary solely for administrative reform is attributed to the Central Secretariat Committee, or to the Ayyangar report only loosely. In the standard text (Laxmikanth), the 'minister and secretary solely for administrative reform' point is not in the Ayyangar proposals. Hence statement 1 is incorrect.
explanations: Wrong: statement 2 is also correct, so 'statement 1 only' wrongly excludes it and wrongly includes the incorrect statement 1.
Right: statement 1 is incorrect and statement 2 is correct, which matches the official answer.
Wrong: statement 1 is not correct, so 'both' fails.
Wrong: statement 2 is correct, so 'neither' fails.
keyfact: The ARC (1966) recommended, and in 1970 the Department of Personnel was created under the PM; the Ayyangar report (1949) led to the O&M Division, not a dedicated reform minister and secretary.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would mean the Ayyangar Committee proposed a dedicated minister and secretary for reform. That is not the case. The Ayyangar report (1949) recommended rational organisation of ministries and an O&M set-up. The idea of a standing reform machinery came much later through the ARC.

Option (b), '2 only', is the official answer. It reflects that the ARC (1966) recommended a Department of Personnel, set up in 1970 in the Cabinet Secretariat under the Prime Minister. Today it is the Department of Personnel and Training under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, handling IAS and central service policy, training (LBSNAA is under it), vigilance and pensions, and public grievances through the DARPG.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', would be right only if statement 1 were also true. It is not. This option is a typical trap, because both statements look plausible: both concern early administrative reform bodies and the PM's role.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', would be right only if statement 2 were also false. But the Department of Personnel was indeed formed in 1970 on the ARC's recommendation, and the Prime Minister is its head, so this option fails.
related: The first ARC was set up in January 1966; Morarji Desai was its first chairman, followed by K. Hanumanthaiya.
The second ARC was set up in 2005 under Veerappa Moily and submitted 15 reports.
The O&M Division was created in 1954 following the Ayyangar report.
The Department of Personnel was created in 1970 under the Cabinet Secretariat.
DoPT is under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions.
The Santhanam Committee on corruption led to the CVC in 1964.
The Indian Institute of Public Administration was established in 1954 on Appleby's recommendation.
Mission Karmayogi (2020) is the National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Gopalaswamy Ayyangar report did not suggest a minister and a secretary designated solely for administrative reform. His recommendations centred on the O&M Division and on a single ministry's responsibility for the services. Facts: N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar was a minister without portfolio and the first Railways Minister in the Union Cabinet after Independence. In 1949 he reported on reorganising the central government machinery. His main recommendations were: the Union government should be organised into ministries on rational lines; the Ministry of Home Affairs should handle personnel and cadre matters; and a staff inspection and O&M unit should be set up. The O&M Division was created in 1954 under the Cabinet Secretariat and later moved. He also chaired the Constituent Assembly's Committee on Kashmir issues and helped draft Article 370.

2 — Correct: The Department of Personnel was created in August 1970 on the ARC's 1966 recommendation and placed under the Prime Minister. Facts: The ARC was set up by a Government of India resolution in January 1966, first under Morarji Desai, who left to become Deputy PM in 1967, and then under K. Hanumanthaiya. It gave 20 reports with 537 recommendations. It recommended a Department of Personnel at the Centre under the Prime Minister's charge, which was set up in the Cabinet Secretariat in 1970. Later it became the Department of Personnel and Administrative Reforms (1977), and then the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) in the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, which the PM holds and a MoS handles day to day.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The Department of Personnel was set up in 1970 on the Administrative Reforms Commission's (1966) recommendation and placed under the Prime Minister's charge. The N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar report (1949) did not suggest a minister and secretary designated solely for administrative reform.
topic_notes: Administrative reform in India has been driven by many committees. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar (1949) reviewed central machinery, and the O&M Division was formed in 1954. A. D. Gorwala (1951) reported on public administration and recommended a neutral, efficient civil service. Paul H. Appleby (1953 and 1956) reviewed Indian public administration and recommended an Indian Institute of Public Administration, which was established in 1954. The Santhanam Committee (1962-64) looked at corruption and led to the Central Vigilance Commission in 1964. The first Administrative Reforms Commission (1966-70) was chaired first by Morarji Desai and then by K. Hanumanthaiya. It made 537 recommendations in 20 reports, covering the Machinery of the Government of India, personnel, Lokpal and Lokayukta, centre-state relations, and other topics. Its recommendations included a Department of Personnel, the Lokpal and Lokayukta institutions, and the use of work study. The second ARC was set up in August 2005 under M. Veerappa Moily (later succeeded by V. Ramachandran) and submitted 15 reports. Its topics include ethics in governance, e-governance, right to information, local governance, crisis management, and organisational structure. The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG) is now the nodal agency for reforms and grievances (CPGRAMS). The Department of Personnel and Training handles personnel policy. Related bodies include the Central Vigilance Commission, the Central Bureau of Investigation, Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration in Mussoorie, UPSC under Article 315, and the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013. Other potential angles are the Sarkaria Commission (1983) and Punchhi Commission (2007) on centre-state relations, the Fifth and Seventh Pay Commissions, and Mission Karmayogi (2020).

question: Right to Privacy’ is protected under which Article. of the Constitution of India?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 21 states that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. Through judicial interpretation (Maneka Gandhi 1978, which made the procedure 'just, fair and reasonable'), it has grown to include many unenumerated rights. Privacy was earlier doubted in M.P. Sharma (1954, 8 judges) and Kharak Singh (1962, 6 judges), which denied a general fundamental right to privacy. Later cases such as Gobind (1975) and R. Rajagopal (1994) recognised it in part. On 24 August 2017 the nine-judge Bench in Puttaswamy, headed by CJI J.S. Khehar, overruled M.P. Sharma and the Kharak Singh majority view. It held privacy to be a fundamental right covering bodily autonomy, informational privacy and decisional autonomy (including choices on marriage, family and sexual orientation). Restrictions must meet a three-fold test: legality (a law), legitimate aim, and proportionality. Elimination: Article 15 prohibits discrimination, Article 19 gives the six freedoms (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession), and Article 29 protects minority cultural interests. None of these is the main home of privacy, though the Court said privacy also draws on them.
explanations: Incorrect: Article 15 bars discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. It is about equality, not privacy.
Incorrect: Article 19 guarantees freedoms such as speech and movement. Privacy touches these, but the Court located its primary source in Article 21, so this is not the best answer.
Correct: Puttaswamy (2017) held that privacy is part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21, and also of Part III as a whole.
Incorrect: Article 29 protects the interests of minorities, including their language, script and culture. It has no connection with privacy.
keyfact: Right to Privacy is part of Article 21 (life and personal liberty), per Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 2017.
option_notes: Article 15 prohibits discrimination by the State on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. Clause (2) covers access to shops, wells and public places. Clauses (3), (4), (5) and (6) permit special provisions for women and children, for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs, for admission to educational institutions, and for the economically weaker sections (103rd Amendment, 2019, with a 10% quota).

Article 19(1) gives citizens six freedoms: speech and expression, peaceable assembly, associations, free movement, residence, and profession or business. Property was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978). Article 19(2) to (6) list reasonable restrictions. These rights are available only to citizens and may be restricted by the State. The Court has read the press freedom and the right to information into 19(1)(a).

Article 21 protects life and personal liberty and is available to citizens and non-citizens alike. Its scope has been widened to include the right to livelihood (Olga Tellis), a clean environment, speedy trial, dignity, health, privacy and the right to die with dignity (passive euthanasia). Article 21A, added by the 86th Amendment (2002), gives the right to education for ages 6 to 14. Article 22 provides safeguards against arrest and detention.

Article 29 protects the interests of minorities: any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve it. Article 29(2) bars denial of admission to State-run or State-aided institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste or language only. Article 30 gives minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions. Both fall under the Cultural and Educational Rights in Part III.
related: Puttaswamy (2017) was decided by a nine-judge Bench headed by CJI J.S. Khehar on 24 August 2017.
The Court overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) on privacy, and also ADM Jabalpur (1976).
Privacy restrictions must pass the tests of legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act was passed in 2023.
The B.N. Srikrishna Committee (2017) drafted the data protection framework.
Article 21 applies to citizens and foreigners; Article 19 applies only to citizens.
Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended during a National Emergency (44th Amendment).
Navtej Singh Johar (2018) read down Section 377 IPC.
summary: The answer is (c) Article 21. In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017), a nine-judge Bench of the Supreme Court unanimously held that the Right to Privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21, and also of the freedoms in Part III.
topic_notes: Right to Privacy is a judicially recognised fundamental right. The path began with M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra (1954), where search and seizure was held not to violate privacy, and Kharak Singh v. State of UP (1962), where night-time domiciliary visits were struck down under Article 21 but privacy was not recognised. Gobind v. State of MP (1975) accepted a limited privacy right subject to compelling public interest. PUCL v. Union of India (1997) set guidelines on telephone tapping, and R. Rajagopal (1994) dealt with the press and a person's life story. In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017), a challenge to the Aadhaar scheme led to a reference to a nine-judge Bench, which unanimously held privacy to be a fundamental right. It overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they denied privacy. Justice Chandrachud's lead opinion overruled ADM Jabalpur (1976). Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul's opinion noted the threat from non-State actors. The Court recommended a data protection law, which led to the B.N. Srikrishna Committee (2017) and then the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. In the Aadhaar judgment (2018), the five-judge Bench upheld Aadhaar's validity with limits: it is not mandatory for bank accounts, mobile connections or school admissions, and Section 57 was struck down. Navtej Singh Johar (2018) decriminalised consensual same-sex relations by reading down Section 377 IPC, drawing on privacy and dignity. Related areas: Information Technology Act 2000, Section 69 interception, Pegasus spyware case (2021 committee), and the right to be forgotten. Remember that Article 21 can be suspended during Emergency only for Articles 20 and 21 not at all, since the 44th Amendment bars suspension of both.

question: Consider the following statements : 1, In India, there is no law restricting the candidates from contesting in one Lok Sabha election from three constituencies. In 1991 Lok Sabha Election, Shri Devi Lal contested from three Lok Sabha constituencies. As per the existing rules, if a candidate contests in one Lok Sabha election from many constituencies, his/her _ party should bear the cost of byeelections to the constituencies vacated by him/her in the event ‘ of him/her winning in all the constituencies. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Contesting more than one seat is governed by Section 33(7) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. Before 1996 there was no cap, and leaders such as Devi Lal (1991) and Atal Bihari Vajpayee (1957, three seats) contested several seats. The Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1996 inserted the limit of two constituencies for the same general election or the same set of bye-elections. Section 70 bars a person from representing more than one Lok Sabha seat at a time. Under the Prohibition of Simultaneous Membership Rules, 1950, if a candidate wins two seats, they must resign one within 14 days of the declaration of results, or both seats fall vacant. The vacated seat then goes to a by-election at public expense. The Election Commission has recommended either banning multiple contests or making the candidate bear the cost, and the Law Commission's 170th and 255th reports discussed the idea. The suggested amounts were Rs 5 lakh for an assembly seat and Rs 10 lakh for a Lok Sabha seat. This has never been legislated, and the proposal was aimed at the candidate, not the party. Elimination: statement 1 is wrong because a limit exists. Statement 3 is wrong because no rule exists. That leaves only statement 2.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false because the law (Section 33(7) of the RP Act) restricts candidates to two constituencies.
Correct: only statement 2 is true, because Devi Lal contested from three seats in 1991, before the 1996 cap.
Wrong: it needs statement 1 and statement 3, and both are incorrect since a two-seat limit exists and no rule makes the party bear costs.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which has no basis in existing rules. By-election costs are borne by public funds.
keyfact: Since 1996 (Section 33(7), RP Act 1951) a candidate can contest at most two constituencies in one election, and no rule makes the party pay for by-elections.
related: Section 33(7) of the RP Act, 1951 limits a candidate to two constituencies, as amended in 1996.
The Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1996 introduced the two-seat limit.
A candidate winning two seats must resign one within 14 days under the 1950 Rules.
Section 70 of the RP Act bars sitting for two seats of the same House.
The Election Commission proposed Rs 5 lakh (assembly) and Rs 10 lakh (Lok Sabha) as the cost on a candidate vacating a seat.
Devi Lal contested Sikar, Rohtak and Ferozepur in 1991.
Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013) struck down the protection of sitting members from immediate disqualification on conviction.
The Lok Sabha security deposit is Rs 25,000 (general) and Rs 12,500 (SC/ST).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Section 33(7) of the RP Act, 1951, as amended in 1996, restricts a candidate to two constituencies. Before 1996 there was no limit, so candidates could contest from many seats. The 1996 amendment followed concern about the cost of repeat polls and the misuse of multiple candidacies. Section 70 separately provides that nobody can sit for two seats of the same House. A candidate who wins two seats must vacate one within 14 days under the 1950 Rules, or both become vacant. The Election Commission has since proposed a total ban, or a cost-sharing rule, through electoral reform proposals. The one-to-two limit applies to Parliament and state legislatures alike.

2 — Correct: Chaudhary Devi Lal, then a prominent Janata Dal and later Samajwadi Janata Party leader and former Deputy Prime Minister, contested the 1991 Lok Sabha polls from Sikar (Rajasthan), Rohtak (Haryana) and Ferozepur (Punjab). Punjab's 1991 election was postponed because of militancy, and the Ferozepur poll was held later. At that time the law placed no restriction on multiple candidacies. He is remembered as a 'Tau' of Haryana politics and was Haryana Chief Minister (1977-79, 1987-89). He was Deputy PM in the V.P. Singh and Chandra Shekhar governments (1989-91). His multiple candidacies were among the cases that built pressure for the 1996 amendment.

3 — Incorrect: No existing rule, statute or Election Commission order requires a party to pay for by-elections caused by a candidate vacating a seat. Costs are borne by the Election Commission and the government from public funds. The Election Commission recommended in 2004 and later that candidates winning two seats should deposit or pay the cost: Rs 5 lakh for assembly seats and Rs 10 lakh for Lok Sabha seats. The Law Commission's 255th Report (2015) discussed this too. The Supreme Court, in a petition seeking a ban on contesting two seats, left the decision to Parliament. The proposals concern the candidate, not the party, and have not been enacted.
summary: The most defensible answer is (b) 2 only. Devi Lal did contest three Lok Sabha seats in 1991 (Sikar, Rohtak and Ferozepur). Since 1996, Section 33(7) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 caps a candidate at two constituencies for the same general election, so statement 1 is false. No existing rule makes the party bear by-election costs, so statement 3 is false.
topic_notes: Contesting from multiple constituencies is regulated by Section 33(7) of the RP Act, 1951. Until 1996 there was no restriction. The Representation of the People (Amendment) Act, 1996 capped it at two seats for the same general election or the same group of bye-elections. Section 70 bars simultaneous membership of two seats in the same House of Parliament or state legislature. The Prohibition of Simultaneous Membership Rules, 1950 require the member to resign one seat within 14 days of the results, failing which both seats fall vacant. If the person is elected to both Parliament and a state legislature, they must resign one within 14 days or lose the seat in Parliament. Article 101 deals with vacation of seats and Article 190 with state legislatures. The Election Commission has repeatedly proposed that either contesting two seats be banned or the candidate pay the cost of the vacated seat's by-election, at Rs 5 lakh for assembly polls and Rs 10 lakh for Lok Sabha polls. The Law Commission's 170th Report (1999) on reform of electoral laws and the 255th Report (2015) discussed this. The Supreme Court, in a petition seeking a ban, left the matter to Parliament. Related topics include disqualification under Article 102 and the Tenth Schedule, Section 8 of the RP Act (disqualification on conviction), and the Lily Thomas judgment (2013) on immediate disqualification. Other angles include the security deposit under Section 34 (Rs 25,000 for general candidates, Rs 12,500 for SC/ST for Lok Sabha), the NOTA option (2013), and the cost of by-elections.
why_dropped: The OCR'd text is garbled, and the question was likely dropped over uncertainty in how the statements and options were worded and checked, though I cannot confirm UPSC's actual reason. The facts themselves point to (b).

ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. ‘Right to the City’ is an agreed human right and the UN-Habitat monitors the commitments made by each country in this regard. 2. ‘Right to the City’ gives every occupant of the city the right to reclaim public spaces and public participation in the city. 3. ‘Right to the City’ means that the State cannot deny any public service or facility to the unauthorized colonies in the city. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 3 only (c) 1 and 2 (@ 2and3
subject: Polity
detail: The 'Right to the City' idea was first articulated by the French sociologist Henri Lefebvre in 'Le Droit à la ville' (1968). It was later developed by David Harvey and others. It argues that urban inhabitants, not only property owners or the formally recognised, have the right to access, use, produce and transform urban space and to take part in decisions about it. The concept appears in Brazil's City Statute (2001), in Ecuador's constitution, and in Mexico City's Charter (2010). It also appears in the World Charter on the Right to the City (2004-05) and in the New Urban Agenda adopted at Habitat III in Quito in 2016, which speaks of 'cities for all'. Importantly, it is a framework or aspiration. It is not a binding, universally agreed human right under any UN treaty, and no UN body monitors country-wise commitments to it. UN-Habitat is the UN programme for sustainable urbanisation, headquartered in Nairobi, and it promotes the concept but does not monitor it as a treaty obligation. Elimination logic: statement 1 is wrong because there is no agreed treaty right and no monitoring. Statements 2 and 3 reflect the inclusive, anti-exclusion spirit of the idea. Dropping 1 leaves only (d).
explanations: (a) 1 only is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect: there is no agreed human right to the city, and UN-Habitat does not monitor country commitments.
(b) 3 only is wrong because it leaves out statement 2, which is also correct, since the concept includes reclaiming public spaces and participation.
(c) 1 and 2 is wrong because it includes the incorrect statement 1, and it omits the correct statement 3.
(d) 2 and 3 is correct because both describe the inclusive, participatory and anti-exclusion core of the concept, while statement 1 wrongly calls it an agreed, monitored human right.
keyfact: 'Right to the City' (Lefebvre, 1968) is an inclusive, participatory concept, not a binding UN-monitored human right: answer (d) 2 and 3.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only would hold if 'Right to the City' were a settled UN human right monitored by UN-Habitat. It is not. The concept comes from Henri Lefebvre (1968) and is promoted through the World Charter on the Right to the City (2005) and the New Urban Agenda (Quito, 2016, Habitat III). These are non-binding. UN-Habitat, based in Nairobi, advises and sets norms on urbanisation, and it tracks SDG 11 indicators. It is not a treaty-monitoring body with country-by-country commitments on this right.

Option (b) 3 only picks out the service-access idea. It is partly right in that the concept implies that residents of unauthorized or informal settlements should not be denied basic services. It is incomplete because it ignores participation and reclaiming of public space. Related Indian points: Delhi's PM-UDAY (2019) gives property rights in unauthorized colonies, Olga Tellis v. BMC (1985) recognised the right to livelihood under Article 21, and the Supreme Court has repeatedly linked shelter to the right to life.

Option (c) 1 and 2 combines a wrong claim with a right one. Statement 2 is accurate, as the concept includes reclaiming public spaces and participation. Statement 1 is false because the concept is not a binding agreed right and UN-Habitat does not monitor commitments. Participatory budgeting, begun in Porto Alegre in 1989, is a well-known practical example of the participation element and is often cited with the concept.

Option (d) 2 and 3 is the official answer. It reflects the concept's two key pillars: the right of all inhabitants to participate in and shape urban life, including reclaiming public spaces, and the right of all residents, whatever the legal status of their settlement, to access services. Key references: Lefebvre (1968), Harvey, Brazil's City Statute (2001), Mexico City Charter (2010), World Charter (2005), New Urban Agenda (2016).
related: Henri Lefebvre coined 'Right to the City' in 1968.
UN-Habitat is headquartered in Nairobi and was created in 1978.
The New Urban Agenda was adopted at Habitat III in Quito in 2016.
SDG 11 covers inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable cities.
The 74th Constitutional Amendment (1992) gave constitutional status to urban local bodies.
Article 243W and the 12th Schedule list functions of municipalities.
PM-UDAY (2019) conferred property rights on residents of unauthorized colonies in Delhi.
Olga Tellis case (1985) linked livelihood and shelter to Article 21.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: 'Right to the City' is not an agreed human right under any binding UN treaty, and UN-Habitat does not monitor country commitments to it. UN-Habitat was created in 1978 (as the UN Centre for Human Settlements) and became a full programme in 2002. It is headquartered in Nairobi and leads the Habitat conferences held every 20 years (Vancouver 1976, Istanbul 1996, Quito 2016). It promotes the New Urban Agenda and SDG 11, and it does not act as a treaty-monitoring body for this concept. The idea originated with Henri Lefebvre in 1968, and it has been advanced through civil society charters and national laws such as Brazil's City Statute of 2001.

2 — Correct: The concept gives all inhabitants the right to use and reclaim public spaces and to take part in city decision-making. Lefebvre described it as a 'cry and a demand' for a renewed urban life, covering the right to appropriate space and to participate. David Harvey later called it a collective right to change ourselves by changing the city. Practical forms include participatory budgeting (Porto Alegre, Brazil, from 1989), street vendors' rights, protection of commons, and inclusive public spaces. The World Charter on the Right to the City (2005) stresses democratic management, social function of the city and equitable use of urban space.

3 — Correct: In the sense of the concept, the State cannot deny public services or facilities, such as water, sanitation and electricity, to residents of unauthorized colonies. The idea rests on inclusion irrespective of legal status of settlement.
