State of Himachal Pradesh (2020) held that the right to property is a human right and a constitutional right, so the state cannot take property without law.
related: 44th Amendment Act, 1978 removed the Right to Property from Fundamental Rights.
Article 300A is in Part XII, Chapter IV.
Article 31 and Article 19(1)(f) were repealed in 1978.
Ninth Schedule was added by the First Amendment, 1951.
I.R. Coelho case (2007) allowed judicial review of Ninth Schedule laws after 24 April 1973.
Remedy for violation of Article 300A lies under Article 226, not Article 32.
Acquisition and requisitioning of property is Entry 42 of the Concurrent List.
The LARR Act, 2013 replaced the Land Acquisition Act, 1894.
summary: The answer is (b): the Right to Property is a legal (statutory/constitutional) right available to any person, not only citizens. The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 removed it from Fundamental Rights and placed it as Article 300A in Part XII.
topic_notes: Right to property has changed greatly in India. Constituent Assembly framed Article 19(1)(f) (acquire, hold, dispose of property) and Article 31 (no deprivation save by authority of law, with compensation for acquisition). Conflicts with land reform led to the First Amendment (1951), which added Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule, to protect land reform laws from judicial review. The Fourth Amendment (1955) made the adequacy of compensation non-justiciable. The Seventeenth Amendment (1964) extended protection to ryotwari lands and added laws to the Ninth Schedule. In Golaknath (1967) the Court held that Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights. The Twenty-fifth Amendment (1971) added Article 31C and replaced 'compensation' with 'amount'. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) upheld the basic structure doctrine. In I.R. Coelho (2007), the Court held that Ninth Schedule laws enacted after 24 April 1973 are open to judicial review if they violate the basic structure. The 44th Amendment (1978) removed property from Part III, and Article 300A was inserted. Article 31A, 31B, and part of 31C remain. Article 31(2) was repealed, but Article 30(1A) ensures compensation for acquisition of minority educational institution property. Land acquisition is now governed by the 2013 LARR Act, which replaced the 1894 Act. Property is in the Concurrent List: Entry 42 (acquisition and requisitioning of property). Other nearby topics: Article 21 and the right to livelihood, and other non-fundamental constitutional rights such as Article 265 (no tax without law), Article 301 (freedom of trade), and Article 326 (adult suffrage).

question: What was the exact constitutional status of India on 26th January, 1950?
options: A Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic
subject: Polity
detail: The Preamble of the original Constitution, adopted on 26 November 1949 and effective from 26 January 1950, declared: 'We, the people of India, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC...'. The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 (passed during the Emergency under Indira Gandhi, often called the 'Mini-Constitution') changed this to 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic' and also changed 'unity of the Nation' to 'unity and integrity of the Nation'. This is the only amendment ever made to the Preamble. The Supreme Court held in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) that the Preamble is part of the Constitution, and in the Berubari Union case (1960) it had earlier held that it is not. Elimination logic: (a) omits 'Sovereign', an essential word present from the start. (c) and (d) include 'Secular' and 'Socialist', which did not exist in 1950. Only (b) matches the original text exactly. Note that secularism and socialism were present in spirit (Articles 25-28, Directive Principles), but not in the Preamble's wording.
explanations: Incorrect: it leaves out 'Sovereign', which was in the original Preamble. The 'exact' status included sovereignty.
Correct: the original Preamble of 1950 described India as a Sovereign Democratic Republic.
Incorrect: 'Secular' was inserted only by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, so it was not part of the 1950 description.
Incorrect: both 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added in 1976, so this describes India after the 42nd Amendment, not in 1950.
keyfact: In 1950 India was a Sovereign Democratic Republic; 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.
option_notes: A Democratic Republic: a state where the head of state is elected, not hereditary, and power rests on popular participation. India's Preamble has always had 'Democratic' and 'Republic', but a description without 'Sovereign' is incomplete. Sovereignty means freedom from external control, which India formally gained on 15 August 1947 and which the Constitution affirmed. Democracy in India covers political, social and economic dimensions, as Dr Ambedkar stressed.

A Sovereign Democratic Republic: the exact wording of the original Preamble. 'Sovereign' means India is independent in internal and external matters. 'Democratic' means government by the will of the people, through universal adult franchise (Article 326). 'Republic' means an elected head of state, the President, under Article 52 and Article 54. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950, which is now Republic Day.

A Sovereign Secular Democratic Republic: this is a mixed form that never officially existed in the Preamble. 'Secular' was added in 1976. Before that, secularism was already in the Constitution through Articles 25-28 (freedom of religion), Article 14-15 (equality) and Article 44 (Uniform Civil Code as a Directive Principle). In S.R. Bommai (1994) the Supreme Court held secularism to be part of the basic structure.

A Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic: the current wording of the Preamble after the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, effective 3 January 1977. The Swaran Singh Committee recommended the amendment. 'Socialist' reflects the aim of reducing inequality, as in Directive Principles (Articles 38, 39). The Supreme Court has said the Preamble's words 'socialist' and 'secular' are part of the basic structure, and recent challenges to their insertion have been rejected.
related: The 42nd Amendment (1976) added 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'integrity' to the Preamble.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution.
Berubari Union case (1960) said the Preamble is not part of the Constitution.
The Preamble is based on Nehru's Objectives Resolution of 13 December 1946.
The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950.
The Preamble has been amended only once, in 1976.
The idea of a Preamble was borrowed from the US Constitution.
Ernest Barker called the Preamble the 'keynote' of the Constitution.
summary: The answer is (b) A Sovereign Democratic Republic. This is how the Preamble described India when the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950. The words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added only later, by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.
topic_notes: The Preamble is the introductory statement of the Constitution and sets out its philosophy and objectives. It is based on the Objectives Resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947. The Preamble was adopted on 26 November 1949 along with some articles (such as citizenship, elections and provisional parliament) that came into effect immediately; the rest took effect on 26 January 1950. The Drafting Committee was chaired by Dr B.R. Ambedkar; Dr Rajendra Prasad was President of the Constituent Assembly. The Constitution took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days. Key Preamble words: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic; Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), Equality (status and opportunity), Fraternity (dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the nation). The source of authority is 'We, the People of India'. The Preamble is not enforceable in court and is neither a source of power nor a limitation on power. Judicial cases: Berubari Union (1960) held that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that it is part and can be amended without altering the basic structure; LIC of India (1995) reaffirmed this. The Preamble has been amended once, by the 42nd Amendment (1976). Ideals borrowed: the idea of the Preamble from the USA; Justice (social, economic and political) from the Russian Revolution; Liberty, Equality, Fraternity from the French Revolution. Ernest Barker called the Preamble the 'keynote' of the Constitution, and K.M. Munshi called it the 'horoscope' of the Constitution.

question: Constitutional government means
options: a representative government of a nation with federal structure
a government whose Head enjoys nominal powers
a government whose Head enjoys real powers
a government limited by the terms of the Constitution
subject: Polity
detail: Constitutionalism means that political authority is derived from, and restrained by, a constitution. A constitutional government therefore acts only within the limits the constitution sets: separation or distribution of powers, fundamental rights, judicial review, and accountability to the people. The concept is separate from the form of the executive or the structure of the state. Britain (an unwritten constitution, nominal monarch), the USA (a presidential system with a real executive Head) and India (a parliamentary federation with a nominal President) are all constitutional governments, though their structures differ. Elimination: (a) mixes in representation and federalism, but unitary states such as the UK and France are also constitutional. (b) describes only the parliamentary system, which is one type of constitutional government. (c) describes the presidential system, which is another type. Both (b) and (c) are partial and arise from the form of the executive, so neither can serve as the general definition. Only (d) states the essential feature, limitation by law. In India, the Supreme Court's Kesavananda Bharati (1973) ruling on the basic structure is the strongest expression of constitutionalism, since even Parliament's amending power is limited.
explanations: Incorrect: federal structure is a feature of how power is divided between levels of government. Unitary states can be constitutional too, so it is not the defining test.
Incorrect: a nominal Head is characteristic of the parliamentary system (UK, India), which is only one kind of constitutional government.

Incorrect: a Head with real powers is characteristic of the presidential system (USA). It is also only one kind of constitutional government, and a real Head does not by itself mean the government is limited.
Correct: constitutional government means government limited by the Constitution, whose powers, procedures and restraints are laid down in it. This is the official answer.
keyfact: Constitutional government = government limited by the Constitution (limited government and rule of law), irrespective of whether the Head's powers are nominal or real.
option_notes: A representative government with a federal structure: a federation divides powers between a central government and units (states or provinces), as in the USA, India, Canada and Australia. Representation means officials are chosen by the people. The two features are common in many democracies but neither defines constitutional government. Unitary states like the UK and France are constitutional without being federal.

A government whose Head has nominal powers: this is the parliamentary system, where the Head of State (monarch or President) is a ceremonial figure and real power rests with the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers. India (Article 74), the UK and Japan follow it. It is a type of constitutional government, not its definition.

A government whose Head has real powers: this is the presidential system, where the President is both Head of State and Head of Government and is not responsible to the legislature. The USA is the model, with strict separation of powers and checks and balances. It is one form of constitutional government, not the definition.

A government limited by the terms of the Constitution: this is the core idea of constitutionalism, in which authority is derived from and restrained by a constitution through rights, separation of powers, judicial review and the rule of law. It applies to written constitutions (USA, India) and unwritten ones (UK, through conventions and statutes). The opposite is arbitrary or absolute rule.
related: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) laid down the basic structure doctrine, restricting Parliament's amending power.
Article 13 declares laws that violate fundamental rights void, ensuring constitutional supremacy.
Article 74 requires the President to act on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the PM.
The UK has an unwritten constitution but is still a constitutional monarchy.
Dicey's rule of law has three elements: supremacy of law, equality before law, and predominance of legal spirit.
Montesquieu propounded the separation of powers in The Spirit of the Laws (1748).
The USA is the model presidential system with checks and balances and judicial review (Marbury v. Madison, 1803).
Minerva Mills (1980) held that limited power to amend the Constitution is itself a basic feature.
summary: The answer is (d): a constitutional government is one whose powers are limited by the terms of the Constitution. It is defined by limited government and the rule of law, not by federalism or by whether the Head holds nominal or real powers.
topic_notes: Constitutionalism is the doctrine that government authority is legitimate only when exercised within established legal limits. Its roots lie in Magna Carta (1215), the English Bill of Rights (1689), Locke's theory of limited government, and Montesquieu's separation of powers in The Spirit of the Laws (1748). The US Constitution (1787) was the first modern written constitution. Essential features include a supreme constitution, separation or distribution of powers, an independent judiciary with judicial review, fundamental rights, periodic free elections, and accountability of the executive. Forms of constitutional government: parliamentary (UK, India) versus presidential (USA); federal (India, USA) versus unitary (UK, France). In India, constitutional supremacy (rather than parliamentary sovereignty) is established through Article 13 (laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are void), Articles 32 and 226 (writ jurisdiction), and Articles 368 and 141. Landmark cases: Golaknath (1967), which held that fundamental rights cannot be amended; Kesavananda Bharati (1973), which established the basic structure doctrine; Minerva Mills (1980), which held that limited amending power is itself a basic feature; and S.R. Bommai (1994), which subjected Article 356 to judicial review. Other angles: constitutional morality (Dr. Ambedkar quoting Grote), the difference between constitutionalism and constitution, the rule of law (Dicey), and conventions in the Indian polity such as the President acting on ministerial advice under Article 74 after the 42nd and 44th Amendments.

question: With reference to India, the terms ‘Halbi, Ho and Kui’ pertain to
subject: Art & Culture
detail: The question tests knowledge of India's tribal linguistic diversity. Halbi is an Indo-Aryan language (close to Marathi, Odia and Chhattisgarhi) spoken in Bastar (Chhattisgarh), and parts of Odisha and Maharashtra; it acts as a link language among tribes of Bastar. Ho is a Munda language of the Austroasiatic family, spoken by the Ho tribe in Kolhan (West Singhbhum) of Jharkhand, and in Odisha and West Bengal; it uses the Warang Chiti script devised by Lako Bodra. Kui (Kandha/Kondh) is a Dravidian language of the Kondh tribe in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. India's languages belong mainly to Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austroasiatic and Tibeto-Burman families. Elimination logic: these names are not dance forms of Northwest India (those would be Ghoomar, Bhangra, Giddha), not musical instruments (such as sitar, sarangi, tumdak), and not cave-painting sites (Bhimbetka, Lakhudiyar). Names ending in tribal community labels such as Ho and Kui strongly indicate a language or tribe, so (d) is the only fit.
explanations: Wrong: dance forms of Northwest India include Bhangra, Giddha, Ghoomar and Kalbelia; none of Halbi, Ho or Kui is a dance.
Wrong: these are not instruments; tribal instruments are things like tumdak, tamak, banam, nagara and madal.
Wrong: pre-historic paintings are associated with sites such as Bhimbetka, Lakhudiyar, Jogimara and Edakkal, not these names.
Correct: Halbi, Ho and Kui are languages spoken by tribal communities in central and eastern India.
keyfact: Halbi (Indo-Aryan), Ho (Munda) and Kui (Dravidian) are tribal languages, so the answer is (d).
option_notes: Northwest Indian dance forms include Bhangra and Giddha (Punjab), Ghoomar and Kalbelia (Rajasthan), Dandiya and Garba (Gujarat), and Chhau is eastern. Bhangra is a harvest dance; Giddha is performed by women; Kalbelia is a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage item (2010) and is performed by the Kalbelia community of Rajasthan.

Musical instruments are classed as tata (string), sushira (wind), avanaddha (membranophone) and ghana (idiophone). Examples are sitar, sarod, veena, shehnai, tabla, mridangam, ghatam. Tribal instruments include tumdak and banam (Santhal), nagara, and algoza (Punjab/Rajasthan). None of the three terms is an instrument.

Indian rock paintings: Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh, a UNESCO site since 2003) is known for Mesolithic and Chalcolithic paintings; others are Lakhudiyar (Uttarakhand), Edakkal (Kerala), Jogimara (Chhattisgarh), and Kupgal (Karnataka). Themes are hunting, animals, and dance in red and white pigments.

Tribal languages are spoken by Scheduled Tribes (about 8.6% of India's population, Census 2011). They fall mainly into Austroasiatic (Munda, e.g. Santali, Ho, Mundari), Dravidian (Gondi, Kui, Oraon/Kurukh) and Tibeto-Burman families. Santali was added to the Eighth Schedule by the 92nd Amendment, 2003.
related: Santali uses the Ol Chiki script, created by Pandit Raghunath Murmu.
Ho uses the Warang Chiti script, created by Lako Bodra.
Halbi is a link language among tribes of Bastar, Chhattisgarh.
Kui is a Dravidian language of the Kondh community in Odisha.
Four languages (Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santali) were added to the Eighth Schedule by the 92nd Amendment (2003).
22 languages are in the Eighth Schedule.
CIIL Mysuru runs SPPEL for endangered languages.
Article 350A: mother-tongue instruction at primary level.
summary: The answer is (d): Halbi, Ho and Kui are tribal languages of India. Halbi is an Indo-Aryan language of Chhattisgarh/Bastar, Ho is a Munda (Austroasiatic) language of Jharkhand/Odisha, and Kui is a Dravidian language of Odisha.
topic_notes: India's linguistic landscape is divided mainly among four families: Indo-Aryan (about 75% of speakers), Dravidian (about 20%), Austroasiatic and Tibeto-Burman. Census 2011 recorded 121 languages with 10,000+ speakers, of which 22 are Scheduled languages in the Eighth Schedule (Article 344 and 351 relate to it). Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santali were added by the 92nd Amendment (2003); Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali by the 71st (1992); Sindhi by the 21st (1967). Classical language status (Tamil 2004, Sanskrit 2005, Telugu and Kannada 2008, Malayalam 2013, Odia 2014; Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali added in 2024). Tribal languages: Halbi (Bastar, Indo-Aryan), Ho (Munda, Warang Chiti script), Kui (Dravidian, Kondh), Gondi (Dravidian, Gondwana region), Santali (Ol Chiki script by Pandit Raghunath Murmu), Mundari, Kurukh/Oraon, Bhili, Khasi (Meghalaya, Austroasiatic), Garo, Mizo. Article 350A provides for instruction in the mother tongue at primary stage; Article 350B created a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities. The National Education Policy 2020 promotes mother-tongue instruction. UNESCO's Atlas lists many Indian tribal languages as endangered; the Central Institute of Indian Languages (Mysuru) works on their preservation, and the Scheme for Protection and Preservation of Endangered Languages (SPPEL) covers languages with fewer than 10,000 speakers.

question:
Consider the following statements in respect of Bharat Ratna and Padma Awards :
1. Bharat Ratna and Padma Awards are titles under the Article 18(1) of the Constitution of India.
2. Padma Awards, which were instituted in the year 1954, were suspended only once.
3. The number of Bharat Ratna Awards is restricted to a maximum of five in a particular year. Which of the above statements are not correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 18 abolishes titles: 18(1) prohibits the State from conferring titles other than military or academic distinctions. In Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996) the Supreme Court held that Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not 'titles' under Article 18(1) and are mere recognition of merit, so they must not be used as prefix or suffix to the recipient's name; misuse can lead to forfeiture. Statement 1 wrongly says they are titles under Article 18(1). The Padma Awards were instituted in 1954 and were discontinued in 1978-77 period (Janata Party government, from July 1977 to January 1980) and again in 1993-1997 (the Bharat Ratna and Padma awards were suspended 1992-1997 owing to PIL challenges in High Courts). Hence suspended twice, so statement 2 is wrong. Bharat Ratna is limited to a maximum of three recipients in a year, so statement 3 is wrong. Since the question asks for statements that are NOT correct and all three are faulty, (d) is correct; (a), (b) and (c) each wrongly treat one statement as correct.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it treats statement 3 as correct, but the Bharat Ratna cap is three per year, not five.
(b) is wrong because it treats statement 1 as correct, but the Supreme Court held these awards are not titles under Article 18(1).
(c) is wrong because it treats statement 2 as correct, but the Padma Awards were suspended twice, in 1977-80 and 1993-97.
(d) is correct because all three statements are factually incorrect, so all are 'not correct'.
keyfact: Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not 'titles' under Article 18(1); Bharat Ratna max is 3 per year; Padma awards were suspended twice (1977-80, 1993-97).
option_notes: Statements 1 and 2 only: this would mean the Article 18(1) claim and the single-suspension claim are wrong while the cap of five is right. The cap of five does not exist; Bharat Ratna is limited to three annually. The option fails because it leaves out statement 3.

Statements 2 and 3 only: this would imply the awards are indeed titles under Article 18(1). The Supreme Court in Balaji Raghavan (1996) ruled otherwise, saying they are honours, not titles, and cannot be used as prefixes or suffixes. Article 18 bans state titles except military and academic distinctions.

Statements 1 and 3 only: this would imply the Padma Awards were suspended only once. In reality suspensions took place in 1977-80 under the Janata government and in 1993-97 owing to court challenges. The Padma Awards were instituted in 1954.

Statements 1, 2 and 3: this is the official answer. The claims about titles under Article 18(1), a single suspension, and a maximum of five Bharat Ratnas in a year are all incorrect. The correct points are: awards are not titles, suspended twice, and a maximum of three Bharat Ratnas per year.
related: Article 18 abolishes titles; clause 1 permits military and academic distinctions.
Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996) held Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles.
Bharat Ratna was instituted on 2 January 1954; maximum three per year.
Padma awards: three categories, Vibhushan, Bhushan and Shri; ceiling 120 per year excluding special categories.
Padma awards were suspended in 1977-80 and 1993-97.
First Bharat Ratna recipients: C. Rajagopalachari, S. Radhakrishnan, C.V. Raman (1954).
Lal Bahadur Shastri (1966) was the first posthumous Bharat Ratna.
Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (1987) was the first non-Indian Bharat Ratna; Nelson Mandela (1990) the second.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Supreme Court (Balaji Raghavan, 1996) held these awards are not 'titles' under Article 18(1). Article 18 abolishes titles: (1) no title other than military or academic distinction by the State, (2) no Indian citizen may accept a foreign title, (3) a foreigner holding office of profit cannot accept a foreign title without President's consent, (4) no person holding office of profit may accept any present, emolument or office from a foreign State without President's consent. The Court's five-judge bench said awards must not be used as prefix or suffix; recipients who do so may forfeit the award. The awards are national honours recognising merit, not hereditary or privileged titles, and fall under Article 18 only in the sense that they were examined against it.

2 — Incorrect: The Padma Awards (Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Shri) were instituted in 1954 and were suspended twice, not once. First suspension came in 1977 with the Janata Party government, ending in 1980. Second suspension came in 1993-1997 after PILs in the Kerala and Madhya Pradesh High Courts challenged the awards as violating Article 18; the Supreme Court bench upheld the awards in 1995. Padma Vibhushan has two classes earlier called Pahela Varg, Dusra Varg, Tisra Varg; renamed in 1955. Announced on the eve of Republic Day and conferred by the President in March or April at Rashtrapati Bhavan.

3 — Incorrect: Bharat Ratna is restricted to a maximum of three recipients in a particular year, not five. Instituted on 2 January 1954, it is the highest civilian award, given for exceptional service in art, literature, science and public service (field scope widened in 2011 to any field of human endeavour). Recommendations are made by the Prime Minister to the President; no formal recommendation is needed. The first recipients (1954) were C. Rajagopalachari, S. Radhakrishnan and C.V. Raman. Non-citizens such as Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan and Nelson Mandela have received it. Posthumous awards began in 1966 with Lal Bahadur Shastri. Padma awards committee has a maximum of 120 awards per year excluding posthumous and NRI/foreigner awards.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are not correct. Bharat Ratna and Padma Awards are not 'titles' under Article 18(1), the Padma Awards were suspended twice (not once), and the Bharat Ratna cap is three per year, not five.
topic_notes: Civilian awards in India are national honours, not titles. Article 18 of the Constitution abolishes titles: the State cannot confer any title except military or academic distinctions; citizens cannot accept foreign titles. The Bharat Ratna (instituted 2 January 1954) is the highest civilian honour; the Padma awards (Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan, Padma Shri) were instituted in 1954, with the three-tier structure formalised in 1955. The Supreme Court in Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India (1996) upheld them as valid, stating they do not amount to titles, and laid down that they must not be used as prefix or suffix. The Bharat Ratna is limited to three per year; Padma awards are limited to 120 per year, excluding NRI, foreigner, OCI and posthumous awards. Padma awards are announced on the eve of Republic Day; a Padma Awards Committee constituted by the Prime Minister each year screens nominations, headed by the Cabinet Secretary, and the committee's recommendations go to the Prime Minister and the President. Nominations are open to the public (self-nomination allowed) through the portal. Suspensions: 1977-80 and 1993-97. Bharat Ratna was not awarded in several years, and the first non-Indian recipients were Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (1987) and Nelson Mandela (1990). Posthumous awards began in 1966 with Lal Bahadur Shastri. Subhas Chandra Bose's 1992 posthumous award was withdrawn after a Supreme Court challenge about his death. Padma awards are not accompanied by cash prizes; recipients get a certificate (sanad) and a medallion. Other awards: Gallantry awards (Param Vir Chakra, Ashoka Chakra), Jnanpith, Dadasaheb Phalke, Sahitya Akademi. Future questions may touch on Article 18 clauses, the Balaji Raghavan case, selection process and recipients.

question: Consider the following statements : Statement 1 : The United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF) and the Arbor Day Foundation have recently recognized Hyderabad as 2020 Tree City of the World. Statement 2 : Hyderabad was selected for the recognition for a year following its commitment to grow and maintain the urban forests. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct and Statement 2 is the correct explanation for Statement 1
Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct but Statement 2 is not the correct explanation for Statement 1
Statement 1 is correct but ; Statement 2 is not correct
Statement 1 is not correct but Statement 2 is correct
subject: Environment
detail: The Tree Cities of the World programme is a joint initiative of the Arbor Day Foundation (USA, founded 1972 in Nebraska) and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN (FAO). It was launched in 2019 to recognise cities that commit to sustainable management of urban trees and forests. A city must meet five standards: (1) establish responsibility, by assigning a staff member or department to care for trees; (2) set the rules, through a legal framework governing urban forests; (3) know what you have, through an updated inventory or assessment of the tree resource; (4) allocate the resources, through a dedicated annual budget; and (5) celebrate achievements, through an annual tree-related event. Recognition lasts for the calendar year and must be renewed. Hyderabad was recognised in 2020, and was the only Indian city in that list, and again in later years. Elimination logic: the UNCDF is the UN's capital investment agency for least developed countries (LDCs), working on local development finance and inclusive finance, so it has nothing to do with urban forestry. This makes Statement 1 wrong. Statement 2 correctly describes the one-year recognition tied to commitment, so only (d) fits.
explanations: Wrong: this treats Statement 1 as correct, but the UNCDF did not give the recognition, so the pairing fails at the first statement.
Wrong: Statement 1 is incorrect because the UNCDF is not the body involved, so 'both correct' cannot hold, whatever the explanation.

Wrong: this accepts Statement 1 as correct and Statement 2 as incorrect. The reverse is true, since the organisations in Statement 1 are wrong and the one-year commitment-based recognition in Statement 2 is right.
Correct: Statement 1 names the wrong organisation (UNCDF instead of FAO), while Statement 2 correctly describes a one-year recognition for committing to urban forests.
keyfact: Tree Cities of the World = Arbor Day Foundation + FAO (not UNCDF); Hyderabad was recognised in 2020, and recognition lasts one year.
option_notes: Option (a) says both statements are correct and Statement 2 explains Statement 1. It is wrong here, but such options are the standard format for assertion-reason questions. The explanation form requires both statements to be true, and Statement 2 must also be the reason for Statement 1. Always check the facts of each statement before judging the causal link.

Option (b) says both statements are correct but Statement 2 does not explain Statement 1. It is wrong here because Statement 1 has the wrong body. In general it applies where both are true facts but unrelated. For this question, remember the Tree Cities of the World programme is run by the Arbor Day Foundation and FAO, not the UNCDF.

Option (c) says Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is not. It is the reverse of the actual position. The UNCDF is a UN fund for least developed countries and does not run tree-city programmes. Statement 2, on one-year recognition for commitment to urban forests, is accurate. This option would be right only if the bodies were correct and the one-year detail wrong.

Option (d) says Statement 1 is incorrect and Statement 2 is correct, and it is the official answer. Hyderabad received the 2020 Tree City of the World recognition from the Arbor Day Foundation and FAO. The recognition is annual and based on meeting five standards for urban forest management, so Statement 2 holds while Statement 1 fails on the named organisation.
related: Tree Cities of the World was launched in 2019 by the Arbor Day Foundation and FAO.
The programme has five standards, including establishing responsibility and allocating resources.
Hyderabad was recognised as a Tree City of the World in 2020 and in later years.
UNCDF was established in 1966 and supports least developed countries.
FAO was founded in 1945 and is headquartered in Rome.
Nagar Van Yojana (2020) aims to develop 200 urban forests across India.
India's Bonn Challenge pledge is to restore 26 million hectares of degraded land by 2030.
The India State of Forest Report is published every two years by the Forest Survey of India.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The recognition came from the Arbor Day Foundation and the FAO, not the UNCDF. The Tree Cities of the World programme began in 2019 as a partnership between the Arbor Day Foundation, a US non-profit founded in 1972 that popularised Arbor Day tree planting, and FAO. It recognises cities worldwide that meet five core standards on urban forest governance. In 2020, 120 cities in 63 countries were recognised, and Hyderabad was among them. The UNCDF, by contrast, is a UN body set up in 1966 that provides investment capital and technical support to LDCs, focusing on microfinance, digital finance and local development.

2 — Correct: Hyderabad was selected for the recognition for a year because it committed to growing and maintaining urban forests, having met the programme's five standards. Tree City status is valid for a single calendar year and has to be renewed through a fresh application. The five standards are: establishing responsibility, setting the rules, knowing what you have, allocating resources and celebrating achievements. Hyderabad's urban greening is driven by Telangana's Haritha Haram programme and the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC), which have increased tree cover and developed urban forest parks. The city later renewed its status in subsequent years.
summary: The official answer is (d): Statement 1 is incorrect and Statement 2 is correct. Hyderabad was recognised as a 2020 Tree City of the World by the Arbor Day Foundation together with the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), not the UNCDF. The recognition is given for one year to cities that commit to growing and maintaining urban forests.
topic_notes:
Tree Cities of the World is a network launched in 2019 by the Arbor Day Foundation and FAO to promote urban forestry. Its aim is to connect cities that share the goal of protecting and expanding urban trees, and to share best practice. The five standards are: establish responsibility, set the rules, know what you have, allocate the resources and celebrate achievements. Recognition is annual, so a city must reapply each year. Hyderabad was recognised in 2020, was the only Indian city in the list that year, and has been recognised again in later years. In 2020 the programme listed 120 cities across 63 countries. Hyderabad's greening is linked to the Telangana Haritha Haram programme, launched in 2015, and to GHMC urban forest blocks.

Related bodies to keep distinct: the UNCDF (founded 1966, headquartered in New York) is the UN's capital investment agency for LDCs. FAO, headquartered in Rome and founded in 1945, leads on food, agriculture and forestry, and produces the State of the World's Forests report. UNEP, headquartered in Nairobi, handles environmental coordination. The Arbor Day Foundation also runs the older Tree City USA programme, begun in 1976.

Other angles UPSC may ask: Arbor Day, Van Mahotsav (first week of July, started in 1950 by K. M. Munshi), the Nagar Van Yojana (urban forests scheme launched in 2020 by MoEFCC to develop 200 urban forests), the National Afforestation Programme, CAMPA, the India State of Forest Report (published biennially by the Forest Survey of India, Dehradun), and the Bonn Challenge, under which India pledged to restore 26 million hectares by 2030. Also revise the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (2021–2030) and the Trillion Trees initiative.

question:
Consider the following statements in respect of the Laureus World Sports Award which was instituted in the year 2000 :
1. American golfer Tiger Woods was the first winner of this award.
2. The award was received mostly by ‘Formula One’ players so far.
3. Roger Federer received this award maximum number of __ times compared to others. Which of the above statements are correct?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Laureus World Sports Awards were instituted in 2000 by the Laureus Sport for Good Foundation, backed by Richemont and Daimler (Mercedes-Benz). The first ceremony was held in Monte Carlo in May 2000, with Nelson Mandela delivering the famous line that sport has the power to change the world. The main categories are Sportsman, Sportswoman, Team, Breakthrough, Comeback, Action Sportsperson, Sportsperson with a Disability, and the Lifetime Achievement award. Winners are chosen by the Laureus World Sports Academy, a group of sporting legends. Tiger Woods won the first Sportsman award in 2000, and Marion Jones won the first Sportswoman award. Federer holds the record of five Sportsman wins (2005-2008, 2018) and also won the Comeback award in 2018 and 2019? Check the 2018 win was Sportsman, while he also won the Comeback of the Year in 2009. The question's blank is the record count, so statement 3 is accepted as correct, as the official key states. Statement 2 fails because tennis, athletics, football, and others have produced many winners. Formula One has produced a few winners such as Schumacher, Hamilton, and Vettel, but not most. Eliminating statement 2 leaves only (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 2, which is false because Formula One drivers do not receive most of the awards.
Wrong: it includes statement 2 as correct, which is false, and it leaves out statement 1, which is true.
Correct: statements 1 and 3 are true, as Woods won the first Sportsman award and Federer holds the record, while statement 2 is false.
Wrong: it counts statement 2 as correct, but the awards are spread across many sports and not mostly Formula One.
keyfact: Laureus Awards began in 2000; Tiger Woods won the first Sportsman award and Federer holds the record with five Sportsman wins.
option_notes: Option (a) pairs statements 1 and 2. The Laureus World Sports Awards were created in 2000 by the Laureus Sport for Good Foundation, founded by Richemont and Daimler. They honour the best individual and team performances of the year and also promote sport as a tool for social change. The first ceremony was in Monte Carlo. The awards are decided by the Laureus World Sports Academy, whose members are retired sports greats. They are often called the Oscars of sport.

Option (b) pairs statements 2 and 3. Formula One is a motorsport championship run by the FIA, started in 1950. Drivers like Schumacher, Hamilton, Vettel, and Verstappen have received Laureus awards, but they are a small share compared to tennis and athletics. Federer, a Swiss tennis player, has 20 Grand Slam singles titles and retired in 2022. His Laureus record is five Sportsman awards.

Option (c) is the correct answer, combining statements 1 and 3. Tiger Woods won the first Sportsman award, and Federer holds the record for the most Sportsman wins. The Laureus Foundation supports sport-for-good programmes for young people through its projects worldwide. Categories include Sportsman, Sportswoman, Team, Breakthrough, Comeback, Action Sportsperson, Sportsperson with a Disability, and Sporting Moment. Statement 2 is wrong because winners come from many sports.

Option (d) includes all three statements. It is wrong because statement 2 claims the awards went mostly to Formula One players. In reality, winners come from tennis, athletics, football, golf, cycling, skiing, rugby, cricket, swimming, and gymnastics. Examples include Usain Bolt, Rafael Nadal, Novak Djokovic, Serena Williams, Simone Biles, Lionel Messi, and Katie Ledecky. Formula One has had only a few winners, such as Schumacher, Hamilton, and Verstappen.
related: Laureus World Sports Awards were instituted in 2000 and first held in Monte Carlo.
Tiger Woods won the first Laureus Sportsman of the Year; Marion Jones the first Sportswoman.
Roger Federer holds the record of five Laureus Sportsman awards.
Laureus winners are chosen by the Laureus World Sports Academy.
The 2011 Laureus Sporting Moment went to Sachin Tendulkar and the Indian team.
Laureus Sport for Good Foundation was backed by Richemont and Daimler.
Nelson Mandela's speech at the first Laureus ceremony said sport has the power to change the world.
statements: 1 — Correct: Tiger Woods won the inaugural Laureus World Sportsman of the Year in 2000. The award was launched in Monte Carlo in 2000 by the Laureus Sport for Good Foundation. Woods was recognised after his dominant 1999-2000 golf season, which included winning several majors. The first Sportswoman winner was American athlete Marion Jones. Mandela spoke at the launch. Woods later received further recognition, including the Comeback of the Year award in 2019 after his Masters win. The award is voted on by the Laureus World Sports Academy.

2 — Incorrect: The awards are spread over many sports, and Formula One does not dominate them. Tennis has had the most winners, with Federer, Nadal, Djokovic, and Serena Williams all honoured repeatedly. Athletics has Usain Bolt, who won the Sportsman award multiple times. Formula One winners include Michael Schumacher, Lewis Hamilton, Sebastian Vettel, and Max Verstappen, but they are a minority. Football, cricket, rugby, cycling, and skiing are also represented. India's Indian cricket team and Sachin Tendulkar won a Laureus Sporting Moment award in 2011.

3 — Correct: Roger Federer holds the record for the most Laureus awards. He won Sportsman of the Year five times in 2005, 2006, 2007, 2008, and 2018, which is more than any other athlete. He also won the Comeback of the Year in 2009 and the Lifetime Achievement award is another honour recognised by Laureus. Novak Djokovic, Usain Bolt, and Lewis Hamilton are among others with multiple wins. Serena Williams and Steffi Graf are among the most decorated women in the awards. The question's blank is the record count.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. Tiger Woods won the first Laureus World Sportsman of the Year award (2000), and Roger Federer has won the Sportsman award a record five times (2005-2008 and 2018, and in total he has won the award more times than anyone else). Statement 2 is wrong because the awards are spread across many sports, not dominated by Formula One.
topic_notes: The Laureus World Sports Awards are often described as the Oscars of the sporting world. They were instituted in 2000 by the Laureus Sport for Good Foundation, which was founded in 1999 by Richemont and Daimler with the backing of Nelson Mandela. The first ceremony was held in Monte Carlo in May 2000. Winners are chosen by the Laureus World Sports Academy, made up of living sporting legends. The foundation also supports community projects that use sport to tackle social issues such as violence, discrimination, and disadvantage. Main categories include Sportsman, Sportswoman, Team, Breakthrough, Comeback, Action Sportsperson, Sportsperson with a Disability, and Sporting Moment. The first Sportsman winner was Tiger Woods and the first Sportswoman winner was Marion Jones. Federer holds the record of five Sportsman awards. Serena Williams has won Sportswoman of the Year multiple times, and Usain Bolt has won Sportsman multiple times. Novak Djokovic, Lewis Hamilton, Lionel Messi, and Rafael Nadal are among later winners. India has featured in the awards: the 2011 Laureus Sporting Moment went to the Indian cricket team and Sachin Tendulkar for being carried on the shoulders of teammates after the World Cup win. UPSC may also ask about other sports honours such as the Khel Ratna, Arjuna Award, Dronacharya Award, Dhyan Chand Award, the Olympic Order, and Ballon d'Or. Keep track of recent Laureus winners and the structure of the awards.

question: Consider the following statements in respect of the 32nd Summer Olympics : 1s The official motto for this Olympics is ‘A New World’. Sport Climbing, Surfing, Skateboarding, Karate and Baseball are included in this Olympics. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The 32nd Summer Olympics were awarded to Tokyo at the IOC Session in Buenos Aires in September 2013. They were postponed by a year because of COVID-19, the first postponement in Olympic history, and were held from 23 July to 8 August 2021 while keeping the name 'Tokyo 2020'. Tokyo was the first Asian city to host the Summer Games twice, after 1964. The Games were largely held without spectators. The official motto was 'United by Emotion'. Separately, the IOC added 'Together' to the Olympic motto 'Faster, Higher, Stronger', making it 'Faster, Higher, Stronger – Together'. Tokyo used the Agenda 2020 reforms, which let a host city propose additional sports. Five sports were added for Tokyo only: baseball/softball, karate, skateboarding, sport climbing and surfing. Karate and baseball/softball were not retained for Paris 2024, while the other three stayed. The elimination logic is that statement 1 gives a wrong motto, so (a) and (c) fall, and statement 2 is correct, so (d) falls. That leaves (b).
explanations: Wrong. Statement 1 is incorrect because the motto was 'United by Emotion', so 'statement 1 only' cannot be right.
Correct. Statement 2 is accurate as the five sports were added at Tokyo 2020, and statement 1 is false.
Wrong. This requires statement 1 to be correct, but the motto 'A New World' is false.
Wrong. Statement 2 is correct, so 'neither' is incorrect.
keyfact: Tokyo 2020 (32nd Olympics, held 2021) had the motto 'United by Emotion' and added five new sports: sport climbing, surfing, skateboarding, karate and baseball/softball.
option_notes: Statement 1 only: this would mean the motto 'A New World' was right. It is not, as the Tokyo motto was 'United by Emotion'. The option is a distractor built from an invented motto. Remember that Tokyo 2020 took place in 2021 after the COVID-19 postponement, and the Games name stayed 'Tokyo 2020' for branding continuity.

Statement 2 only: this is the correct option. The five added sports were proposed by the Tokyo organisers and approved by the IOC in 2016. They brought 18 new events, helped reach younger audiences and were part of Agenda 2020's flexibility for hosts. Tokyo also featured 3x3 basketball, BMX freestyle and mixed team events as new additions, in line with gender equality.

Both 1 and 2: this is wrong because statement 1 is false. The Olympic Games motto is 'Faster, Higher, Stronger – Together', but the Tokyo 2020 slogan was 'United by Emotion'. Candidates must separate the Olympic motto from the host's slogan, as UPSC often tests such distinctions.

Neither 1 nor 2: this is wrong because the sports list in statement 2 is accurate. The sports were indeed all included at Tokyo. Of them, karate and baseball/softball were excluded from Paris 2024, but softball and baseball return at Los Angeles 2028 along with cricket, flag football, lacrosse and squash.
related: Tokyo 2020 was held in 2021 and was the 32nd Summer Olympics.
Tokyo 2020 motto was 'United by Emotion'.
The Olympic motto now reads 'Faster, Higher, Stronger – Together'.
India's best Olympic tally is 7 medals at Tokyo 2020, with Neeraj Chopra's javelin gold.
Karate, surfing and skateboarding debuted at Tokyo; karate and baseball were dropped for Paris 2024.
Paris hosted the 33rd Summer Olympics in 2024.
Los Angeles 2028 will add cricket, squash, lacrosse and flag football.
The IOC is headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The motto of Tokyo 2020 was 'United by Emotion'. 'A New World' is not the motto. The Games' concept stressed diversity and inclusion, and the 'Together' addition was made to the general Olympic motto, not to the Tokyo slogan. Related facts: Tokyo's emblem 'Harmonized Checkered Emblem' used indigo blue. Mascots were Miraitowa (Olympics) and Someity (Paralympics). The motto for the Paralympics was 'United by Emotion' as well. Torch relay began from Fukushima in March 2021, and Tokyo won the bid over Istanbul and Madrid. Medals were made from recycled electronic devices.

2 — Correct: These five sports were included in Tokyo 2020. Sport Climbing, Surfing, Skateboarding, Karate and Baseball (with Softball) were approved by the IOC in 2016 as additional sports proposed by the host city under Agenda 2020. Karate made its Olympic debut, and skateboarding and surfing were also debuts. Baseball/softball returned after being dropped after 2008. Sport climbing, surfing and skateboarding stayed for Paris 2024, with breaking added there. Karate and baseball/softball were dropped for Paris. Baseball and softball, along with flag football, cricket, lacrosse and squash, are in the Los Angeles 2028 programme.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The 32nd Summer Olympics (Tokyo 2020, held in 2021) added Sport Climbing, Surfing, Skateboarding, Karate and Baseball/Softball, but its official motto was 'United by Emotion', not 'A New World'.
topic_notes: Tokyo 2020 was the 32nd Summer Olympics, awarded in 2013 at Buenos Aires, with Tokyo winning over Istanbul and Madrid. It was postponed in March 2020 because of COVID-19 and held from 23 July to 8 August 2021. It was the first Games postponed in peacetime, though earlier Games were cancelled in 1916, 1940 and 1944. It was held mostly without spectators. Japan had earlier hosted the 1964 Summer Games, the 1972 Sapporo Winter Games and 1998 Nagano Winter Games. The motto was 'United by Emotion'. The Olympic motto 'Citius, Altius, Fortius' was amended in 2021 to add 'Communiter' (Together). Mascots were Miraitowa and Someity. India won 7 medals, its best ever: 1 gold (Neeraj Chopra, javelin), 2 silver (Mirabai Chanu, weightlifting; Ravi Dahiya, wrestling) and 4 bronze (PV Sindhu, Lovlina Borgohain, Bajrang Punia and the men's hockey team). Neeraj Chopra's gold was India's first in athletics. The hockey bronze ended a 41-year medal drought. Later Games: Paris 2024 was the 33rd Games, and Los Angeles 2028 will be the 34th, followed by Brisbane 2032 as the 35th. Winter Games: Beijing 2022 (24th), Milan-Cortina 2026 (25th). Paralympics: Tokyo 2020 saw India win 19 medals, including 5 gold. The IOC was founded in 1894 by Pierre de Coubertin, is headquartered at Lausanne, and its president since 2025 is Kirsty Coventry (after Thomas Bach). Agenda 2020 and Olympic Agenda 2020+5 are the IOC's reform roadmaps.

question: Consider the following statements in respect of the ICC World Test Championship : f The finalists were decided by the number of matches they won. New Zealand was ranked ahead of England because it won more matches than England. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The inaugural ICC World Test Championship ran from August 2019 to early 2021, with the final at the Rose Bowl, Southampton, in June 2021, which New Zealand won by 8 wickets against India. Originally the league table was ranked by total points (120 points per series, split across the matches in the series). COVID-19 disrupted many series, so in late 2020 the ICC changed the ranking criterion to Percentage of Points (PCT) = points won / points contested x 100. India (72.2%) and New Zealand (70.0%) took the top two places, while England (61.4%) finished fourth, behind Australia, which had withdrawn from the series with South Africa and so lost out on the percentage. Statement 1 is wrong because the number of wins was not the criterion. Statement 2 is wrong because New Zealand's rank came from its higher PCT. In fact New Zealand won fewer Tests (7) than England (11) in the cycle. Elimination: because both statements rely on 'matches won', the official answer is neither of them.
explanations: (a) is wrong: the finalists were chosen by percentage of points, so statement 1 is false.
(b) is wrong: New Zealand ranked above England on PCT, and it actually won fewer matches than England, so statement 2 is false.
(c) is wrong: both statements are false, so they cannot both be correct.
(d) is right: neither statement holds, because the ranking used percentage of points and not the number of matches won.
keyfact: WTC finalists are decided by Percentage of Points (PCT), not by the number of wins; New Zealand beat India in the 2021 final.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would mean the number of wins decided the finalists. This is untrue. In the 2019-21 cycle the ICC used points, then PCT after pandemic disruption. Win count was never the criterion, although a win does earn the most points. Tied matches earned half and draws one-third of a match's points.

Option (b), '2 only', would mean New Zealand outranked England on the number of wins. This is wrong. New Zealand won 7 Tests and England 11, but New Zealand's PCT was higher (70.0% against 61.4%). England also lost points to over-rate penalties. New Zealand then won the final against India by 8 wickets at the Rose Bowl, Southampton, in June 2021.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', would require both claims to be true. Neither is. The tournament format rewards points share, so winning more matches does not guarantee a higher rank. A team that plays fewer series can rank higher if it wins a larger share of the points available to it.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', is the official answer. It reflects the PCT system, adopted in December 2020 after COVID-19 disruption. The final was decided between India (72.2%) and New Zealand (70.0%). Australia was third and England fourth, on 69.2% and 61.4% respectively.
related: The inaugural WTC final (June 2021) was at the Rose Bowl, Southampton; New Zealand beat India by 8 wickets.
The ranking criterion changed to Percentage of Points (PCT) in December 2020 because of COVID-19 disruption.
The 2021-23 WTC final: Australia beat India at The Oval, London.
The 2023-25 WTC final: South Africa beat Australia at Lord's.
The WTC's first cycle began with the 2019 Ashes (starting 1 August 2019).
Nine teams played in the WTC; each played six series, three at home and three away.
Points for a win, tie and draw in later cycles are 12, 6 and 4 per match.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Finalists were decided by percentage of points (PCT), not the number of matches won. The ICC introduced PCT in December 2020 because the pandemic cancelled or postponed many series, so teams had played different numbers of matches. Points per series were fixed at 120, split evenly among the matches in that series (60 for a two-Test series, 24 for a five-Test series). A win earned full points, a tie half, and a draw one-third. Under PCT, India and New Zealand reached the final in June 2021 at Southampton, and Australia was squeezed out.

2 — Incorrect: New Zealand was ahead of England because of a better PCT (70.0% against 61.4%), not because it won more matches. In fact England won more Tests (11) than New Zealand (7) in the cycle. England also lost points through slow over-rate penalties. New Zealand played fewer Tests (11) than England (21), so its win percentage and points share were higher. This is a classic example of why PCT replaced raw points: it compares teams on points won out of points contested.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. The finalists of the inaugural ICC World Test Championship (2019-21) were decided by percentage of points won (PCT), not by the number of matches won, and New Zealand finished ahead of England on that percentage, not because it won more matches.
topic_notes: The ICC World Test Championship (WTC) is the league competition for Test cricket, with the top two teams of a two-year cycle meeting in a final. The first cycle ran from 1 August 2019 (the Ashes) to 2021. Nine teams took part: Australia, England, India, New Zealand, Pakistan, South Africa, Sri Lanka, West Indies and Bangladesh. Each team played six series, three at home and three away, against different opponents. Zimbabwe, Ireland, Afghanistan did not take part as they lacked the status or the fixtures. In the first cycle, each series carried 120 points regardless of its length. Points were divided by the number of Tests: a two-Test series gave 60 points per match, and a five-Test series gave 24. A win earned the full share, a tie half and a draw one-third. After the pandemic caused cancellations, the ICC ranked teams by percentage of points (PCT). The final was held at the Rose Bowl, Southampton, from 18 to 23 June 2021 with a reserve day. New Zealand beat India by 8 wickets, and Kane Williamson was the captain. In the second cycle (2021-23) Australia and India reached the final at The Oval, London, and Australia won. In the third cycle (2023-25) South Africa beat Australia at Lord's to win the title. Points per match were also standardised in later cycles to 12 for a win, 6 for a tie and 4 for a draw. Over-rate penalties deduct points. The trophy is the ICC Test Championship Mace for the number one team in the rankings, which is distinct from the WTC title.

question:

3. Credit Facility” are related to the provisions of lending by which one of the following ?
options: United Nations Environment Programme Finance Initiative
subject: Economy
detail: Both the RFI and the RCF were created by the IMF in 2011 as part of a reform of its lending toolkit, to give fast, low-conditionality help to members facing urgent balance of payments needs. The RFI is open to all member countries and can be used for varied emergencies such as natural disasters, commodity price shocks, conflict or pandemics. The RCF is the concessional (zero or very low interest) window of the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust (PRGT), meant for low-income countries. Both disburse in a single up-front instalment with no full-fledged programme and no ex-post reviews. Access is limited by quota-based ceilings. During COVID-19 in 2020 many countries, including India's neighbours, drew on these windows. Elimination logic: the Asian Development Bank lends for regional development projects and has its own Asian Development Fund and COVID-19 Active Response and Expenditure Support (CARES). The World Bank finances development projects and policy loans through IBRD and IDA. UNEP FI is a partnership between UNEP and the financial sector for sustainable finance and does not lend at all. Short-term emergency balance of payments support is the IMF's mandate, hence (b).
explanations: Incorrect: the ADB lends for development projects and programmes in Asia-Pacific, and RFI/RCF are not its instruments.
Correct: RFI and RCF are the IMF's emergency financing windows for urgent balance of payments needs, with limited conditionality.
Incorrect: UNEP FI is a UNEP-financial sector partnership promoting sustainable finance. It is not a lender.
Incorrect: the World Bank (IBRD/IDA) gives development loans, grants and policy-based financing, not RFI/RCF, which belong to the IMF.
keyfact: RFI and RCF are the IMF's emergency, low-conditionality lending windows for urgent balance of payments needs (since 2011); RCF is the concessional one for low-income countries.
option_notes: The Asian Development Bank was founded in 1966 and is headquartered in Manila, Philippines. It has 68 members, and Japan and the USA are the largest shareholders. It provides loans, grants, technical assistance and equity for poverty reduction and infrastructure in Asia-Pacific. Presidents have traditionally been Japanese. India is a member and one of the largest borrowers. It is distinct from the IMF.

The International Monetary Fund was created at Bretton Woods in 1944 and began operations in 1945. It is headquartered in Washington DC and has 190 members. It promotes global monetary cooperation, financial stability and balanced trade, and provides lending to countries with balance of payments problems. Its facilities include the Stand-By Arrangement, Extended Fund Facility, Flexible Credit Line, RFI and RCF. It is also the source of SDRs and publishes the World Economic Outlook.

UNEP Finance Initiative was set up in 1992, after the Rio Earth Summit, as a partnership between the United Nations Environment Programme and the global financial sector. It is based in Geneva. It promotes sustainable finance and has launched the Principles for Responsible Banking and the Principles for Sustainable Insurance. It provides guidance and networks, not loans to governments.

The World Bank Group was set up at Bretton Woods in 1944 and is headquartered in Washington DC. It comprises IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID. It provides long-term loans, grants and guarantees for development and poverty reduction. Its reports include Ease of Doing Business (discontinued in 2021), the World Development Report and Human Capital Index. Its president is traditionally an American.
related: RFI and RCF were introduced by the IMF in 2011 and give emergency support with limited conditionality.
The RCF is financed through the IMF's Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust for low-income countries.
The IMF's unit of account, the SDR, has a basket of USD, euro, yuan, yen and pound.
The IMF has 190 member countries and is headquartered in Washington DC.
The Resilience and Sustainability Trust (2022) is the IMF's facility for climate and pandemic resilience.
The IMF's flagship reports are the World Economic Outlook and the Global Financial Stability Report.
The World Bank's IDA gives concessional loans to the poorest countries.
India's IMF quota is about 2.75 percent.
summary: The answer is (b) International Monetary Fund. The Rapid Financing Instrument (RFI) and Rapid Credit Facility (RCF) are IMF emergency lending windows that give quick financial help to member countries with urgent balance of payments needs, with little or no programme-based conditionality.
topic_notes:
The IMF is the global lender of last resort for balance of payments crises. It was established at Bretton Woods in 1944 and became operational in 1945. It has 190 members, and its governance runs through the Board of Governors and the Executive Board. Voting power depends on quota shares, with the USA holding the largest share and an effective veto over 85 percent majority decisions. Quotas determine subscriptions, voting power and access to financing. The IMF's unit of account is the Special Drawing Right (SDR), whose basket comprises the US dollar, euro, Chinese renminbi, Japanese yen and pound sterling. The renminbi was added in 2016.

Lending is of two kinds. Non-concessional loans from the General Resources Account include the Stand-By Arrangement, the Extended Fund Facility, the Flexible Credit Line, the Precautionary and Liquidity Line and the Short-term Liquidity Line, plus the RFI for emergencies. Concessional lending for low-income countries is through the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust: the Extended Credit Facility, the Standby Credit Facility and the RCF. The RFI and RCF were introduced in 2011, replacing the earlier Emergency Assistance windows, and were heavily used during the COVID-19 pandemic. The Catastrophe Containment and Relief Trust gives grant-based debt relief. Newer facilities include the Resilience and Sustainability Trust (2022) for climate and pandemic resilience.

The IMF also does surveillance through Article IV consultations and capacity development. Flagship publications are the World Economic Outlook, Global Financial Stability Report and Fiscal Monitor. Other angles UPSC could ask: the difference between the IMF and the World Bank, SDR composition, quota reforms (India's quota is about 2.75 percent), and the IMF's managing director (Kristalina Georgieva).

ocr: With reference to the Indian economy, consider the following statements : 1. An increase in Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) indicates the appreciation of rupee. 2. An increase in the Real Effective | 4 Exchange Rate (REER) indicates an improvement in trade competitiveness. 3. An increasing trend in domestic inflation relative to inflation in other countries is likely to cause an increasing divergence between NEER and REER. Which of the above statements are correct ? (a) land 2 only (b) 2and8 only (c) land 3 only (d) 1,2and3 With reference to the Indian economy, consider the following st
subject: Economy
detail: NEER is the trade-weighted average of bilateral nominal exchange rates of the rupee against a basket of currencies. It is quoted as an index, so a rise in NEER means the rupee has appreciated against the basket and a fall means depreciation. REER is NEER adjusted for relative price levels, that is, domestic inflation relative to the inflation of trading partners, so it measures the real value of the currency. A rise in REER means domestic goods have become more expensive relative to foreign goods, so exports become less competitive and imports cheaper. A rise in REER therefore signals loss of trade competitiveness, and a fall signals gain. This makes statement 2 wrong, as it states the opposite. REER is approximately NEER multiplied by the ratio of domestic prices to foreign prices. If domestic inflation keeps running above that of partners, the price ratio keeps rising, and REER moves away from NEER. When inflation is equal, the two move together. The RBI publishes 6-currency and 40-currency NEER and REER indices (base year 2015-16 = 100). Elimination logic: once statement 2 is seen to be reversed, options (a), (b) and (d) all fall away, leaving (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement 2, which has the effect of REER reversed; a rising REER signals worse competitiveness.
(b) is wrong because it includes statement 2 and leaves out statement 1, which is correct, since a rising NEER means rupee appreciation.
(c) is right because statements 1 and 3 are correct and statement 2 is incorrect.
(d) is wrong because statement 2 is incorrect, so not all three can be correct.
keyfact: Rising NEER = rupee appreciation; rising REER = rupee real appreciation = loss of competitiveness; higher domestic inflation widens the NEER-REER gap.
related: NEER and REER indices are published by the RBI with base year 2015-16 = 100.
REER rise means loss of export competitiveness; REER fall means gain.
REER = NEER adjusted for the ratio of domestic to foreign prices.
Rupee became current account convertible in August 1994 (IMF Article VIII).
FEMA 1999 replaced FERA 1973 and came into force in June 2000.
India follows a managed floating exchange rate regime.
RBI sells dollars to arrest rapid rupee depreciation.
To fight high inflation, RBI sells government securities (OMO) to absorb liquidity.
statements: 1 — Correct: NEER is an index of the rupee against a weighted basket, so a rise means the rupee has appreciated nominally. NEER is the weighted geometric average of bilateral nominal exchange rates. The RBI releases 6-currency (trade-based) and 40-currency indices, with base year 2015-16 = 100. Weights are based on the share of each partner in India's trade, so the US, China, the Euro area, the UAE and others carry large weights. NEER ignores price differences and shows only nominal movements. An index above 100 shows appreciation relative to the base year, and below 100 shows depreciation.

2 — Incorrect: A rising REER means the rupee is real-terms stronger, which makes exports costlier and imports cheaper, so competitiveness deteriorates. REER is NEER adjusted for the inflation differential between India and its trading partners, using consumer price indices. A REER above 100 suggests the rupee is overvalued compared with the base year, and below 100 suggests undervaluation. The RBI monitors REER to assess external competitiveness. A falling REER, or real depreciation, improves competitiveness. Economists often look to REER rather than NEER when judging whether a currency is overvalued.

3 — Correct: REER equals NEER adjusted by relative prices. If Indian inflation stays higher than that of trading partners, the relative price factor keeps rising, so REER rises faster than NEER, or falls more slowly, and the two diverge. If inflation were the same at home and abroad, REER and NEER would move in step. This is the logic of relative purchasing power parity: a currency with persistently higher inflation should depreciate nominally to keep real competitiveness intact. Without that depreciation, the real exchange rate appreciates and trade competitiveness declines.
summary: The correct answer is (c): statements 1 and 3 are correct, statement 2 is incorrect. A rising NEER means the rupee is appreciating against a trade-weighted basket. A rising REER means the rupee is getting costlier in real terms, so trade competitiveness worsens. Higher domestic inflation relative to trading partners widens the gap between NEER and REER.
topic_notes: Exchange rate indices: NEER is the weighted average of the rupee's nominal exchange rates against a basket of currencies. REER adjusts NEER for relative inflation (consumer prices), giving the real external value of the currency. The RBI compiles 6-currency and 40-currency NEER and REER indices with base year 2015-16 = 100. The 40-currency basket covers around 88-90 percent of India's trade. Interpretation: a rise in NEER means nominal appreciation, and a rise in REER means real appreciation and loss of competitiveness. A fall in NEER means depreciation, and a fall in REER means gain in competitiveness. A REER above 100 is read as overvaluation. Real appreciation can happen even when the nominal rate is steady, if domestic inflation is higher. Exchange rate regime: India follows a managed float, in which the market determines the rate and the RBI intervenes to curb excess volatility, buying or selling dollars, and conducting forward operations and swaps. The rupee became convertible on the current account in 1994 (Article VIII of the IMF), and capital account convertibility is only partial. FEMA 1999 replaced FERA 1973. Related concepts: purchasing power parity, Balassa-Samuelson effect, J-curve, Marshall-Lerner condition, depreciation versus devaluation, and the 1991 crisis, when the rupee was devalued, followed by LERMS in 1992 and unified market-determined rate in 1993. Other angles UPSC may take: forex reserves, the impossible trinity, the Tarapore committees on capital account convertibility, and the use of monetary policy tools (repo, CRR, OMO) to address inflation and the currency.

ocr: If interest rates in the USA or European Union were to fall, that is likely to induce RBI to buy dollars. Which of the statements given above are correct ? (a) land 2 only (b) 2and3 only (©) 1 and 3 only (d) 1,2and3 With reference to the “G20 Common Framework”, consider the following statements : 1. It is an initiative endorsed by the G20 together with the Paris Club. 2. It is an initiative to support Low Income Countries with unsustainable debt. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? : (a) 1only (b) 2only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Economy
detail: The visible statement is about the link between foreign interest rates, capital flows and RBI intervention. When the US Federal Reserve or the ECB cuts rates, returns on dollar and euro assets fall. Global investors then search for yield in emerging markets such as India, which raises FPI debt and equity inflows and increases the supply of dollars in the Indian forex market. This pushes the rupee up (appreciation). A sharp appreciation hurts exporters and competitiveness, so the RBI buys dollars from the market, paying in rupees. This stabilises the exchange rate, adds to foreign exchange reserves and injects rupee liquidity, which the RBI may then sterilise through OMOs or MSS bonds. The reverse also holds: when US rates rise, as in 2013 (taper tantrum) and 2022, capital flows out, the rupee weakens, and the RBI sells dollars. India follows a managed floating exchange rate regime. The RBI intervenes to curb volatility and does not target a fixed level. Elimination logic: the official key makes (b) correct, so statement 3 is correct and statement 1 is wrong, which rules out (a), (c) and (d). The 'all three' option is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect.
explanations: (a) 1 and 2 only is wrong, because it includes statement 1, which the official key treats as incorrect, and it leaves out statement 3, which is correct.
(b) 2 and 3 only is correct as per the official key. Statement 3 follows from capital-flow logic, and statement 2 is also correct, while statement 1 is incorrect.
(c) 1 and 3 only is wrong, because it includes the incorrect statement 1 and omits the correct statement 2.
(d) 1, 2 and 3 is wrong, because statement 1 is incorrect, so not all three can be correct.
keyfact: Lower US/EU rates lead to capital inflows into India, which push up the rupee, so the RBI buys dollars and adds to reserves; the official answer is (b) 2 and 3 only.
related: Lower US/EU interest rates generally cause capital inflows into India and rupee appreciation.
RBI buys dollars to curb rupee appreciation and to build forex reserves.
Rising US rates cause FPI outflows, rupee depreciation and RBI dollar sales.
The 2013 'taper tantrum' was triggered by the Fed's signal to reduce quantitative easing.
India follows a managed floating exchange rate regime.
Forex reserves include foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and the IMF reserve tranche position.
The impossible trinity states that an independent monetary policy, a fixed exchange rate and free capital mobility cannot coexist.
The G20 Common Framework for Debt Treatment was endorsed in 2020 with the Paris Club, to help low-income countries.
statements: 1 — Incorrect (per the official key): its text is cut off in the image, so I cannot comment on its wording. The key says it is wrong, since only the combination '2 and 3 only' is correct. Facts to revise from this topic: India has a managed floating exchange rate. The RBI intervenes in the spot and forward markets only to curb excess volatility. Forex reserves cross-check: they include foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve tranche position in the IMF, and foreign currency assets are the largest part. The reserves peaked at about $642 billion in September 2021. The RBI reports them weekly. Verify the exact wording of statement 1 in the original paper.

2 — Correct (per the official key): its text is cut off in the image, so I cannot comment on its wording. The key says it is correct, since '2 and 3 only' is the right option. Facts to revise from this topic: FPIs are sensitive to the interest rate differential between India and developed economies. Capital inflows raise the rupee's value, and outflows lower it. Exchange rate management is governed by FEMA, 1999, and the RBI is the manager of forex. Verify the exact wording of statement 2 in the original paper.

3 — Correct: if US or EU interest rates fall, capital moves to higher-yielding emerging markets such as India. This is the 'search for yield' or carry trade. The inflows lift the rupee, and the RBI buys dollars to prevent excessive appreciation and to build reserves. Examples: the post-2008 quantitative easing period and the post-COVID easing of 2020-21, when India's reserves rose sharply. Purchases create rupee liquidity, which the RBI may sterilise through OMO sales, MSS bonds or the reverse repo. The opposite case, rising US rates, causes outflows and RBI dollar sales, as in 2013 and 2022.
summary: The official answer is (b) 2 and 3 only. Only statement 3 is fully visible in the image: lower US/EU interest rates push capital towards higher-yielding India, the rupee tends to appreciate, and the RBI buys dollars to smooth the rise and add to reserves. The text of statements 1 and 2 is cut off, so their verdicts below come from the official key (1 incorrect, 2 and 3 correct), not from the wording.
topic_notes: This topic is about how global monetary policy affects India's external sector. Interest rates in advanced economies set the global cost of capital. When the Fed or ECB eases, liquidity increases, risk appetite rises and portfolio capital flows into emerging markets. This leads to rupee appreciation, forex reserve accumulation and surplus rupee liquidity. When the Fed tightens, there are outflows, a weaker rupee, a higher import bill, imported inflation and pressure on the current account deficit. The 2013 taper tantrum is the standard example. Exchange rate regime: India has a market-determined, managed float. The RBI intervenes through spot and forward purchases or sales of dollars, and through swaps. Reserve components: foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve tranche position (RTP) in the IMF. The RBI also sterilises its intervention through OMOs, MSS bonds and LAF operations. Other angles UPSC may ask: the impossible trinity (an independent monetary policy, a fixed exchange rate and free capital flows cannot all be had together), REER and NEER, the difference between FDI and FPI, ECBs, NRI deposits, the Liberalised Remittance Scheme, the balance of payments (current and capital accounts), the Tarapore Committee on capital account convertibility, and the Fully Accessible Route for G-secs. A cut in US rates is generally positive for Indian capital inflows, but a global risk-off episode can still cause outflows. Note also that the image shows a second question on the G20 Common Framework, which is a separate question. That framework is an initiative of the G20 together with the Paris Club to help low-income countries with unsustainable debt, and it is relevant to sovereign debt restructuring.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q4.
ocr: If interest rates in the USA or European Union were to fall, that is likely to induce RBI to buy dollars. Which of the statements given above are correct ? (a) land 2 only (b) 2and3 only (©) 1 and 3 only (d) 1,2and3 With reference to the “G20 Common Framework”, consider the following statements : 1. It is an initiative endorsed by the G20 together with the Paris Club. 2. It is an initiative to support Low Income Countries with unsustainable debt. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? : (a) 1only (b) 2only (c) Both 1 and 2 (d) Neither 1 nor 2
subject: Economy
detail: The G20 Common Framework for Debt Treatments beyond the Debt Service Suspension Initiative (DSSI) was agreed by G20 finance ministers in October-November 2020 under Saudi Arabia's G20 presidency. It was endorsed jointly by the G20 and the Paris Club. The DSSI, launched in May 2020 in response to COVID-19, only paused debt-service payments for the poorest countries and ran until December 2021. It did not reduce debt. The Common Framework goes further by allowing case-by-case restructuring, including maturity extensions and, where needed, reductions in debt. Its main features are as follows. It applies to DSSI-eligible countries (IDA-eligible countries plus least developed countries).
