The debtor must request treatment and have an IMF programme, and a debt sustainability analysis by the IMF and World Bank determines whether the debt is unsustainable. An official creditor committee is formed, and private creditors must give comparable treatment. Its significance is that it brings non-Paris Club creditors such as China, India and Saudi Arabia into a common process. Chad, Zambia, Ethiopia and Ghana have applied. Statement 1 is correct because of the joint G20-Paris Club endorsement, and statement 2 is correct because of the framework's purpose. Both are correct, so (c) is right and (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it says only statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is also correct, since the Framework is meant to help Low Income Countries with unsustainable debt.
(b) is wrong because it says only statement 2 is correct. Statement 1 is also correct, since the G20 and the Paris Club jointly endorsed the Framework.
(c) is correct because both statements are correct. The Framework is a G20-Paris Club endorsed initiative and it targets debt relief for eligible low-income countries.
(d) is wrong because it says neither statement is correct. Both statements match the Framework's origin and purpose.
keyfact: The G20 Common Framework (Nov 2020, endorsed with the Paris Club) provides case-by-case debt restructuring for DSSI-eligible low-income countries with unsustainable debt.
related: The Common Framework was agreed by G20 finance ministers in November 2020 under Saudi Arabia's presidency.
The DSSI ran from May 2020 to December 2021 and only suspended debt service.
The Paris Club was founded in 1956 and is an informal group of official creditors.
Zambia, Chad, Ethiopia and Ghana have sought treatment under the Common Framework.
Comparability of treatment requires private creditors to give relief similar to that of official creditors.
The Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable was launched in 2023 by the IMF, World Bank and the G20 presidency.
India held the G20 presidency from December 2022 to November 2023.
Debt sustainability analyses under the Framework are done by the IMF and the World Bank.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Common Framework was endorsed by the G20 together with the Paris Club in November 2020. The Paris Club is an informal group of official creditor countries, set up in 1956 and based in Paris, that coordinates solutions to payment difficulties of debtor countries. It has about 22 permanent members, mostly advanced economies. India is not a permanent member. The Framework is notable because it brings in large non-Paris Club creditors such as China, India and Saudi Arabia, so that all official bilateral creditors act under the same terms. Its rule of comparability of treatment also expects private creditors to offer similar relief. The G20 leaders formally welcomed it at the Riyadh summit in November 2020.

2 — Correct: The Framework supports Low Income Countries whose debt is unsustainable. It covers countries eligible for the DSSI, which means IDA-eligible countries and least developed countries (73 in total). Debt treatment is decided case by case after an IMF-World Bank debt sustainability analysis. The debtor must have an IMF programme and must request the treatment. It can involve extending maturities, cutting interest, or reducing debt stock. Chad was the first applicant (January 2021), followed by Ethiopia and Zambia, and later Ghana. The process has been criticised for being slow, partly because of coordination problems between China, the Paris Club and private bondholders.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. The G20 Common Framework for Debt Treatments beyond the DSSI was endorsed by the G20 together with the Paris Club in November 2020. Its purpose is to help eligible low-income countries with unsustainable debt.
topic_notes: Background: the COVID-19 shock in 2020 pushed many poor countries towards debt distress. In April-May 2020 the G20 and Paris Club launched the Debt Service Suspension Initiative (DSSI). It temporarily suspended official bilateral debt-service payments from 73 eligible countries (IDA-eligible countries and LDCs), and it ran until 31 December 2021. It was only a deferral and gave no debt reduction. In November 2020 the G20 adopted the Common Framework for Debt Treatments beyond the DSSI, endorsed with the Paris Club, to provide case-by-case restructuring. Key features are: eligibility is the same as for the DSSI; the debtor must request treatment; an IMF programme and a joint IMF-World Bank debt sustainability analysis are required; an official creditor committee is formed, usually co-chaired by two large creditors; comparability of treatment applies to other creditors, including private ones; and debtors must not accumulate new non-concessional debt beyond agreed limits. Applicants include Chad, Zambia, Ethiopia and Ghana. Zambia's creditor committee was co-chaired by China and France, and Zambia reached an agreement in principle with official creditors in 2023. Weaknesses are slow timelines, unclear treatment of private creditors and multilateral lenders, and the exclusion of middle-income countries such as Sri Lanka, which is not eligible. Related institutions: the Paris Club (1956, informal, consensus-based, with principles such as solidarity, conditionality and comparability of treatment); the IMF and World Bank (debt sustainability framework for low-income countries); and the G20, founded in 1999 and elevated to leaders' level in 2008. Possible future angles: the India G20 presidency (2023) and its emphasis on debt vulnerabilities in the Global South, the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable (launched 2023 by the IMF, World Bank and G20 presidency), the HIPC and MDRI initiatives, and the role of China as the largest bilateral creditor.

question:
With reference to the Indian economy, what 7. are the advantages of “Inflation-Indexed Bonds (IIBs)” ?
1. Government can reduce the coupon rates on its borrowing by way of IIBs. 2. _ IIBs provide protection to the investors from uncertainty regarding inflation.
3. The interest received as well as capital gains on IIBs are not taxable. Which of the statements given above are correct ?
subject: Economy
detail: Inflation-Indexed Bonds are government securities whose principal and/or interest payments are adjusted for inflation, giving investors a assured real return. Because investors are shielded from inflation risk, they do not demand an inflation-risk premium, so the government can pay a lower coupon than on conventional bonds; this is advantage 1. Advantage 2 is the very purpose of IIBs: protection of the investor's purchasing power against uncertain inflation. Statement 3 is a trap because no such tax exemption exists. Interest on IIBs is taxed as income under the Income-tax Act, and capital gains are taxed as for other securities; tax-free status applies only to specific instruments, such as certain tax-free bonds, not IIBs. In India, the RBI and government first issued Capital Indexed Bonds in 1997 (WPI-linked, principal indexed), and IIBs linked to WPI in 2013 (for retail and institutions). In 2013 they were followed by IIBs linked to CPI-Combined (CPI-C) for retail investors, called IINSS-C (Inflation Indexed National Savings Securities-Cumulative). Elimination logic: any option with statement 3 (b, c, d) falls once you know the benefit is not tax-free, leaving (a).
explanations: Correct: statements 1 and 2 are true and statement 3 is false, so 1 and 2 only is the official answer.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is false because IIB interest and capital gains are taxable.
Wrong: it pairs statement 1 with the false statement 3 and omits the true statement 2.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is false, so all three cannot be correct.
keyfact: IIBs link principal/interest to inflation (WPI/CPI), protect investors and lower government coupons, but are fully taxable.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only: this is the correct choice. It recognises that IIBs reduce the government's coupon burden and protect investors from inflation, and that they carry no tax exemption. It reflects the standard understanding of inflation-indexed securities issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India, first as Capital Indexed Bonds in 1997 and later as IIBs and IINSS-C in 2013.

2 and 3 only: this is incorrect because statement 3 is false. It would be true only if IIBs enjoyed a tax exemption, but interest and capital gains are taxed as per law. The option correctly includes the inflation-protection feature but wrongly leaves out the lower coupon advantage for the government. Tax-exempt bonds are a different category, such as certain infrastructure bonds approved by the government.

1 and 3 only: this is incorrect because it omits statement 2, the main feature of IIBs, and adds statement 3, which is false. It at least identifies the lower coupon cost to the government. Note that the main purpose of IIBs is inflation protection for investors, with lower coupon costs being a secondary benefit for the issuer.

1, 2 and 3: this is incorrect because statement 3 is false. Option (d) is a typical UPSC trap: two true statements with one plausible but false claim about tax benefits. IIBs offer inflation protection and a lower coupon, but there is no tax exemption on interest or capital gains, so students should verify each statement independently.
related: India's first inflation-linked instrument: Capital Indexed Bonds, 1997.
2013 IIBs were linked to WPI; IINSS-C was linked to CPI (Combined).
US inflation-linked bonds are called TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities), launched 1997.
The RBI manages government borrowing as the debt manager and issues G-secs.
Sovereign Gold Bonds (2015) offer 2.5% interest and tax-exempt capital gains on redemption.
Flexible inflation targeting in India: 4% CPI with a band of +/-2%, under the RBI Act amendment of 2016.
Breakeven inflation equals nominal yield minus real yield on IIBs.
Floating Rate Savings Bonds 2020 (Taxable) replaced the 8% Savings (Taxable) Bonds.
statements: 1 — Correct: Since investors get inflation protection, they accept a lower fixed (real) coupon, so the government's borrowing cost can be lower in nominal terms when inflation expectations are high. IIBs are inflation-linked government securities. In India the first such instrument was Capital Indexed Bonds (1997, WPI-linked, principal indexed, 5-year). Later issues were IIBs (2013, 10-year, WPI-linked, interest on inflation-adjusted principal) and IINSS-C (December 2013, CPI-linked, for retail investors). The real coupon was set low, for example 1.5% for the 2013 IIB, and the inflation-adjusted principal was paid on maturity. Low demand led to poor uptake.

2 — Correct: IIBs protect investors from uncertainty regarding inflation because principal and/or interest is adjusted to a price index such as WPI or CPI, preserving real returns. This is the core feature of inflation-linked bonds worldwide, e.g., TIPS in the USA (1997) and index-linked gilts in the UK (1981). India's 2013 IIB offered a fixed real coupon over an inflation-adjusted principal. IINSS-C paid interest with a floating rate comprising a fixed real rate of 1.5% plus CPI inflation. The RBI is the issuer's agent and the government is the borrower. Retail investors, including trusts and charitable institutions, were eligible for IINSS-C.

3 — Incorrect: There is no blanket tax exemption on IIBs; interest earned is taxable as income and capital gains are taxed under the capital-gains rules, depending on the holding period. Tax-free status belongs to specified instruments, such as certain infrastructure or tax-free bonds approved by the government, and not to IIBs generally. Because the inflation-adjusted principal increment is also treated as income in many jurisdictions, it can create tax inefficiency, one reason for low investor interest. In India, the 2013 IIB and IINSS-C received no special tax benefit, so the assumption of tax-free returns is false. Keep this distinction in mind for statement-based questions.
summary: The answer is (a): statements 1 and 2 are correct and statement 3 is incorrect. IIBs link principal and/or interest to a inflation index (WPI or CPI), so investors are protected from inflation uncertainty and the government can offer lower coupons. Their interest and capital gains are taxable, so statement 3 fails.
topic_notes: Inflation-indexed bonds (IIBs) are debt securities in which principal, interest or both are linked to an inflation index, protecting the real value of the investment. Globally: UK index-linked gilts (1981), US TIPS (1997), and many others. In India: Capital Indexed Bonds were issued in December 1997 (5-year, WPI-linked, principal indexed, interest as a fixed rate on adjusted principal) but were discontinued due to weak demand. In June 2013 the RBI issued 10-year IIBs linked to WPI, with a 1.5% real coupon on inflation-adjusted principal, for institutions and retail. In December 2013 IINSS-C (Inflation Indexed National Savings Securities-Cumulative) were launched, linked to CPI (Combined), for retail investors, with a 10-year tenor and interest compounded and paid at maturity; both products saw poor response, and IINSS-C was discontinued. Benefits: investor protection from inflation, lower coupon for government, an inflation expectation signal (breakeven inflation, the difference between nominal and real yields), and encouragement for household savings to move from gold. Drawbacks: the government bears inflation risk, so costs rise if inflation spikes; tax on accrued principal indexation, which is a negative for investors; limited liquidity and market depth; and index choice problems (WPI vs CPI). Related topics: Sovereign Gold Bonds (2015), whose return is tied to gold prices and whose capital gains on redemption are exempt for individuals; G-secs and T-bills; the RBI's role as debt manager; Floating Rate Bonds (2020, 7.15% linked to NSC rate); the Monetary Policy Committee, with an inflation target of 4% (+/-2%) using CPI; and the difference between nominal and real interest rates (Fisher effect). In recent years, the government has considered reintroducing IIBs, and the RBI has announced the inclusion of such bonds in index-based debates and in global bond index inclusion (JP Morgan, 2024).

question:
With reference to foreign-owned e-commerce firms operating in India, which of the following statements is/are correct ?
1. They can sell their own goods in addition to offering their platforms as market-places.
2. The degree to which they can own big sellers on their platforms is limited. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: India's FDI policy allows 100% FDI under the automatic route in the marketplace model of e-commerce, where the firm is only a technology platform connecting buyers and sellers. FDI is not permitted in inventory-based e-commerce, where the firm owns the stock and sells directly to consumers. Statement 1 is therefore wrong: a foreign-owned marketplace cannot sell its own goods on its platform. Statement 2 is wrong because the policy bars a marketplace entity from owning or controlling inventory, and it bars any entity in which the marketplace entity or its group companies hold equity or control from selling on the platform. Press Note 2 (2018), effective 1 February 2019, also prohibited exclusive sale arrangements, mandated that no single vendor or its group companies account for more than 25% of the sales on the platform, and required fair, non-discriminatory treatment of sellers (no mandated preferential treatment on cashbacks, fees or search). Elimination logic: if you know that inventory-based FDI is banned, statement 1 fails; if you know that sellers cannot be group companies of the platform, statement 2 fails. This leaves (d).
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because marketplace firms with foreign investment cannot sell their own goods, and statement 2 is also incorrect, so '1 only' fails.

Wrong: statement 2 fails because the rule is a prohibition on equity or control of sellers, not a limit on the degree of ownership. It would need statement 1 to be wrong, and it is, but this option still needs statement 2 to be right, which it is not.
Wrong: both statements are incorrect, so 'both' cannot be right.
Correct: statement 1 contradicts the ban on inventory-based FDI, and statement 2 misdescribes the outright bar on equity or control of sellers by the platform or its group.
keyfact: Foreign-owned e-commerce in India is marketplace-only: no own-inventory sales and no equity in or control over sellers on the platform.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only, would be true only if foreign-owned platforms could run an inventory model. That is allowed only for Indian-owned firms. Foreign-owned firms may only act as a marketplace, a technology facilitator, under 100% FDI via the automatic route, as stated in Press Notes 3 (2016) and 2 (2018). Foreign firms may sell their own goods only in B2B e-commerce, which is not retail.

Option (b), 2 only, would be true only if foreign-owned platforms could own sellers up to a limit. In fact, sellers in which the platform or its group companies hold equity or control cannot sell on the platform. The 25% cap applies to the share of sales from a single vendor or its group companies, which is a different rule. This is a common trap.

Option (c), both 1 and 2, would be true only if inventory-based models were open to foreign-owned firms with a partial limit on seller ownership. Neither is correct, so it is wrong. FDI policy keeps a firm wall between marketplace operators and sellers to protect small traders and to prevent price manipulation and preferential treatment.

Option (d), neither 1 nor 2, is the official answer. Foreign-owned marketplace firms cannot sell their own goods and cannot own or control sellers on their platform. Key rules: 100% FDI under the automatic route in the marketplace model, no FDI in the inventory model, no exclusivity, and a 25% cap on sales from a single vendor or its group.
related: FDI in marketplace e-commerce: 100% under the automatic route.
FDI in inventory-based e-commerce is prohibited.
Press Note 2 (2018) took effect on 1 February 2019.
No single vendor or its group can supply more than 25% of a platform's sales.
Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 were notified under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
ONDC was launched by DPIIT as an open e-commerce network.
Multi-brand retail FDI is capped at 51% with government approval.
Single-brand retail allows 100% FDI via the automatic route.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: A foreign-owned marketplace cannot sell its own goods, because inventory-based e-commerce is closed to FDI. Background: FDI in e-commerce was first clarified in the 2016 Press Note 3, which allowed 100% FDI under the automatic route in the marketplace model and barred it in the inventory model. The marketplace is defined as a platform providing an IT network for buyers and sellers. Inventory-based means the firm owns the goods and sells them directly to consumers. FDI is allowed in B2B e-commerce, which is not treated as retail. Indian-owned firms can run inventory models. Foreign investors in Flipkart and Amazon therefore operate only as marketplaces.

2 — Incorrect: The rule is not a limit on the degree of ownership of big sellers. Sellers in which the platform or its group companies have equity or control are barred from selling on the platform altogether. Background: Press Note 2 of 2018, effective 1 February 2019, tightened the rules after complaints from small traders. It also barred the platform from mandating that sellers sell a product exclusively on it, and a seller's sales from any single vendor or its group companies cannot exceed 25% of the platform's sales. Related entities such as insurers or group firms are covered. Concerns about 'preferred sellers' like Cloudtail and Appario led to ED investigations under FEMA and to proposed amendments to the e-commerce rules.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. Under India's FDI policy (Press Note 2 of 2018 and later clarifications), foreign-owned marketplace e-commerce firms cannot sell their own goods, and they are barred from holding equity in, or exercising control over, sellers on their platforms, so the limit is a prohibition, not a degree.
topic_notes: FDI in e-commerce is governed by the Consolidated FDI Policy issued by DPIIT (Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade) under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, and by FEMA, 1999, whose rules are enforced by the Enforcement Directorate. Two models matter. In the marketplace model, the firm provides an IT platform that connects buyers and sellers, and 100% FDI is allowed under the automatic route. In the inventory model, the firm owns the stock and sells to consumers, and FDI is not allowed. B2B e-commerce is treated as wholesale and permits 100% FDI. Timeline: 2016 Press Note 3 formalised the marketplace and inventory distinction; December 2018 Press Note 2 tightened the rules effective 1 February 2019. Its key provisions: a marketplace entity cannot hold inventory of goods or services sold on its platform; entities in which the platform holds equity or control, or whose inventory is controlled by the platform, cannot sell on it; no exclusive sale arrangements with any seller; a vendor and its group companies cannot account for more than 25% of the sales; the platform must maintain a fair and non-discriminatory approach; and must file an annual certificate of compliance with the RBI, with an audit report from a statutory auditor. Related regulation: the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, require grievance officers, display of country of origin, and prohibit unfair trade practices and flash sales that manipulate prices. The Competition Commission of India has investigated Amazon and Flipkart for preferential treatment of sellers. ONDC (Open Network for Digital Commerce), launched in 2022 by DPIIT, is an open protocol network aimed at reducing platform dominance. Other angles: the single-brand retail trading FDI limit of 100% under automatic route, multi-brand retail at 51% with government approval, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

question:
Which of the following activities constitute real sector in the economy ? 1.‘ Farmers harvesting their crops
2. Textile mills converting raw cotton into fabrics
3. A commercial bank lending money to a trading company
4. A corporate body issuing Rupee Denominated Bonds overseas Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Economy
detail: The real sector of an economy is the part that produces physical goods and real services, such as agriculture, mining, manufacturing, construction, and trade and transport services. It contributes directly to GDP as value addition and employment. The financial sector, by contrast, includes banks, NBFCs, insurance companies, stock and bond markets and forex markets. It mobilises savings and channels funds to the real sector, but does not itself make goods. Harvesting crops (primary sector) and converting raw cotton into fabric (secondary sector) are production activities, so both are real sector. A commercial bank lending to a trading company is credit intermediation, a financial transaction. A corporate issuing Rupee Denominated Bonds (Masala Bonds) overseas is raising external debt in the capital market, which is also a financial activity. Elimination: statements 3 and 4 are financial, so any option containing them (b, c, d) is wrong. Only (a) remains. Remember the link: finance supports growth, but real output creates it. Real variables are measured at constant prices, whereas nominal variables are measured at current prices.
explanations: Correct: harvesting and textile manufacturing are production activities (primary and secondary sectors), while the other two are financial transactions.
Wrong: it includes statements 3 and 4, both financial sector activities, and leaves out statement 1, which is a real sector activity.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 2 (manufacturing) and includes statements 3 and 4, which are financial.
Wrong: it includes bank lending and overseas bond issuance, which are financial sector activities and not real sector production.
keyfact: Real sector = production of goods and services (agriculture, manufacturing); lending and bond issuance are financial sector activities.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only: this is the combination of agriculture and manufacturing. Both are production activities producing physical goods, and together the primary and secondary sectors form the core of the real sector. It is the correct answer here. Real sector output is the base of GDP, employment and income generation, and it is measured through GVA, IIP and crop estimates.

2, 3 and 4 only: this mixes manufacturing (real) with bank lending and Masala Bonds (financial). It is wrong because it omits agriculture and includes two financial items. Financial sector activities mobilise and allocate savings, and are regulated by the RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA, not counted as goods production.

1, 3 and 4 only: this includes agriculture (real) but also bank lending and overseas bonds (financial), and leaves out manufacturing. It is wrong. Bank credit and capital raising support real activity, but they are financial flows. Masala Bonds were first issued by IFC in 2014 and are a favoured topic in the external sector.

1, 2, 3 and 4: this treats the whole economy as real sector, which is wrong because it ignores the real-financial distinction. The economy has a real side (goods and services) and a financial side (money, credit, securities, forex). Both interact, but financial activities such as lending and bond issuance do not themselves produce output.
related: Real sector produces goods and services, while the financial sector mobilises and allocates funds.
Masala Bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued overseas, and the investor bears the currency risk.
IFC issued the first Masala Bond in 2014, and HDFC was the first Indian corporate issuer in 2015.
Current GDP series in India uses 2011-12 as the base year.
Real GDP is measured at constant prices, and nominal GDP at current prices.
The RBI regulates banks, SEBI regulates securities markets, IRDAI regulates insurance, and PFRDA regulates pensions.
Primary sector: agriculture, mining. Secondary: manufacturing, construction. Tertiary: services.
Transfer payments and second-hand goods sales are not counted in GDP.
statements: 1 — Correct: Harvesting is primary-sector production of physical output and therefore a real sector activity. Agriculture and allied activities contribute roughly 15-18% of India's GVA but employ about 42-46% of the workforce. Crops are classed as Kharif (sown June-July, harvested Sept-Oct), Rabi (sown Oct-Nov, harvested Mar-Apr) and Zaid. Output is measured through crop production estimates by the Ministry of Agriculture, and MSP is announced by the CCEA on CACP recommendation. Harvested output enters GDP as value added.

2 — Correct: Converting raw cotton into fabric is secondary-sector manufacturing that adds value to a raw material. Textiles are one of India's oldest industries and a major employer and export earner, with the Ministry of Textiles overseeing it. India is among the largest producers of cotton. Schemes include PLI for textiles, PM MITRA Parks (announced 2021) and the Cotton Corporation of India for MSP operations. Manufacturing output is tracked by the Index of Industrial Production (IIP).

3 — Incorrect: Bank lending to a trading company is a financial intermediation activity. Banks accept deposits and lend, with credit creation regulated by the RBI under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, through tools such as the repo rate, CRR and SLR. Credit helps real activity but is not production. Lending is recorded as financial services in GVA, not as the output of goods. Trading itself is a service, but the loan is a financial flow, so it is not a real sector activity.

4 — Incorrect: Rupee Denominated Bonds (Masala Bonds) are rupee-denominated debt instruments issued by Indian entities in overseas markets, so the foreign investor bears the currency risk. IFC first issued them in 2014, and HDFC issued the first Indian corporate one in 2015. They are governed by RBI rules under the External Commercial Borrowings framework. Issuing them is a capital market and external finance activity, so it belongs to the financial sector, not the real sector.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 and 2 only. The real sector covers activities that produce goods and services (agriculture, manufacturing), whereas bank lending and bond issuance are financial sector activities that only move money.
topic_notes: Real sector versus financial sector is a basic macroeconomic distinction. The real sector produces goods and services and includes agriculture and allied activities (primary), mining, manufacturing, electricity and construction (secondary), and trade, transport, hotels, communication and other non-financial services (tertiary). Real variables are output, employment, investment in physical capital, and real GDP at constant prices. The financial sector includes banks, NBFCs, insurance, mutual funds, pension funds, stock exchanges, bond markets and forex markets. Its role is intermediation: converting savings into investment, pricing risk, and providing payment systems. Regulators are the RBI (banking, money market, forex, payments), SEBI (securities), IRDAI (insurance), PFRDA (pension) and IFSCA (International Financial Services Centres). Linkages matter: monetary policy works through the financial sector (repo rate, CRR, SLR, liquidity operations) to affect real investment and demand. Financial crises can spill into the real economy through credit crunches, as in 2008. India's GVA structure is roughly: agriculture 15-18%, industry 25-30%, services about 50-55%. Related concepts include real versus nominal GDP, the GDP deflator, GVA at basic prices, and the base year (2011-12 for current GDP series). External sector items such as ECBs, FDI, FPI, Masala Bonds and NRI deposits are financial or capital account flows. Masala Bonds are issued abroad but denominated in rupees, so the investor bears exchange-rate risk. The RBI also allows Masala Bond issuance for infrastructure and housing under conditions of minimum maturity. Possible next questions: classification of activities as primary, secondary or tertiary, what counts in GDP (transfer payments and second-hand sales are excluded), the difference between money market and capital market, and the roles of different financial regulators.

question: Which one of the following situations best reflects “Indirect Transfers” often talked about in media recently with reference to India?
options: An Indian company investing in a foreign enterprise and paying taxes to the foreign country on the profits arising out of its investment
A foreign company investing in India and paying taxes to the country of its base on the profits arising out of its investment
An Indian company purchases tangible assets in a foreign country and sells such assets after their value increases and transfers the proceeds to India
A foreign company transfers shares and such shares derive their substantial value from assets located in India
subject: Economy
detail: Indirect transfer taxation covers a situation where two foreign entities trade shares of an overseas company (or interest) that in turn derives its value substantially from Indian assets. The Indian asset is not sold directly, but control over it changes hands. The issue arose from Vodafone International Holdings BV v. Union of India (2012): the Supreme Court held that the 2007 Hutchison-Vodafone deal (about USD 11 billion, acquiring CGP Investments, Cayman Islands, which indirectly held Hutchison Essar) was not taxable in India. Parliament responded with the Finance Act 2012, which retrospectively amended Section 9(1)(i) of the Income Tax Act 1961 with Explanation 5, taxing such transfers. This led to the Cairn Energy dispute and international arbitration losses for India. The Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act 2021 removed the retrospective levy for transactions before 28 May 2012 and provided for refund of tax collected, without interest. The test is 'substantial value': Indian assets exceed Rs 10 crore and represent at least 50% of the value of all assets. Options (a), (b) and (c) describe outbound investment, ordinary foreign investment taxed at home, and overseas asset sales, none involving an offshore share transfer deriving value from Indian assets.
explanations: Incorrect: this describes outbound investment where taxes are paid abroad on profits, which is a matter of double taxation relief, not indirect transfer of Indian assets.
Incorrect: this describes foreign direct investment into India with taxes paid in the home country. It does not involve a transfer of shares deriving value from Indian assets.
Incorrect: this describes an Indian company buying and selling tangible assets abroad. The assets are located outside India, so it is not an indirect transfer of Indian assets.
Correct: a foreign company transfers shares that derive substantial value from Indian assets. This is the definition of indirect transfer under Explanation 5 to Section 9(1)(i) of the Income Tax Act.
keyfact: Indirect transfer = offshore transfer of shares deriving substantial value from Indian assets, taxed under Section 9(1)(i) Explanation 5 after the Vodafone case.
option_notes: Outbound foreign direct investment (Overseas Direct Investment) by Indian companies is regulated under FEMA. Profits earned abroad are taxed in the host country, and India's Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements (DTAAs) give credit or exemption so the same income is not taxed twice. India has DTAAs with over 90 countries. This is an ordinary cross-border tax matter and not an indirect transfer.

Inbound FDI is regulated by FEMA, the FDI policy and DPIIT. Foreign investors are taxed in India on income sourced in India, and DTAAs determine whether the home country gives credit. Examples are Mauritius, Singapore and Netherlands route investments, which are often the subject of treaty-shopping and General Anti-Avoidance Rules (GAAR) concerns. GAAR took effect from 1 April 2017.

This describes capital gains on overseas tangible assets owned by an Indian company. Such gains arise abroad and are subject to host-country tax and Indian tax on global income of resident companies, with DTAA relief. It involves no offshore share transfer deriving value from Indian assets, so it is not an indirect transfer.

Indirect transfer of Indian assets means the transfer of shares or interests in a foreign entity whose value is substantially derived from Indian assets. The Finance Act 2012 inserted Explanation 5 in Section 9(1)(i) with retrospective effect from 1962 after the Vodafone ruling. The 2021 amendment made the levy prospective, from 28 May 2012, and the 'substantial' test is Indian assets above Rs 10 crore and at least 50% of global assets.
related: Vodafone case: Supreme Court judgment January 2012 went against the tax department.
Finance Act 2012 inserted Explanation 5 to Section 9(1)(i) of the Income Tax Act 1961.
Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act 2021 ended retrospective indirect transfer tax for pre-28 May 2012 deals.
Cairn Energy won an arbitration award against India in December 2020.
GAAR (General Anti-Avoidance Rules) came into force on 1 April 2017.
Shome Committee 2012 reviewed GAAR and retrospective taxation.
Equalisation Levy of 6% was introduced in 2016 on online advertising services.
Article 265: no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.
summary: The answer is (d). 'Indirect transfer' refers to a foreign company transferring shares or interests whose substantial value is derived from assets located in India. India taxes the resulting gains, even though the transfer takes place offshore between non-residents.
topic_notes: Indirect transfer taxation concerns the source rule of taxation: income is deemed to accrue or arise in India if it arises through the transfer of a capital asset situated in India. The landmark case is Vodafone International Holdings BV v. Union of India (SC, January 2012). Vodafone bought the Cayman company CGP Investments from Hutchison Whampoa in 2007 for about USD 11.1 billion, gaining control of Hutchison Essar. The tax department demanded capital gains tax and the Supreme Court ruled against it. In response, the Finance Act 2012 added Explanation 5 to Section 9(1)(i), clarifying that an asset or capital asset (share or interest in a company registered outside India) is deemed situated in India if it derives its value substantially from assets in India. This retrospective amendment drew criticism as 'tax terrorism' and hurt India's investment image. The Shome Committee (2012) reviewed the issue and recommended prospective application. Cairn Energy (UK) and Vodafone both won arbitration cases against India, with Vodafone's award in 2020 under the India-Netherlands bilateral investment treaty and Cairn's in December 2020 (Permanent Court of Arbitration, The Hague). The Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act 2021 withdrew the retrospective demand for pre-28 May 2012 transfers and allowed refunds without interest, provided litigation was withdrawn. Related concepts include GAAR, Place of Effective Management, Equalisation Levy on digital transactions, the OECD BEPS project, Pillar One and Two global tax reforms, and DTAAs. Future questions may ask about retrospective taxation, Article 265 (no tax without authority of law), and Article 20(1) which bars retrospective criminal laws, not tax laws.

question:
With reference to the expenditure made by an 11. organisation or a company, which of the following statements is/are correct ?
1. Acquiring new technology is capital expenditure.
2. Debt financing is considered capital expenditure, while equity financing is considered revenue expenditure. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Economy
detail: Capital expenditure (capex) is spending to acquire, upgrade or extend the life of long-term assets such as land, machinery, buildings, patents, software and technology. It gives benefits over more than one accounting year and is shown on the balance sheet as an asset, then depreciated or amortised over time. Revenue expenditure covers day-to-day running costs such as salaries, rent, raw materials, electricity, repairs and interest, and is fully charged to the profit and loss account in the year incurred. Statement 1 is correct because new technology (machinery, licences, patents, software) is a long-term asset. Statement 2 confuses the classification of spending with the classification of funding. Debt financing (loans, debentures, bonds) and equity financing (issuing shares, retained earnings) are both ways of raising long-term capital. Neither is an expenditure head. Equity is not revenue expenditure; dividends are an appropriation of profit, while interest on debt is a revenue expense. Elimination: once statement 2 is seen as conceptually flawed, options (b), (c) and (d) fall away, leaving (a).
explanations: Correct: statement 1 is right because technology acquisition creates a long-term asset, and statement 2 is wrong, so only 1 is correct.
Incorrect: statement 2 wrongly treats financing sources as expenditure types, and statement 1 is also correct, so 'only 2' fails.
Incorrect: statement 2 is false, since debt and equity are sources of funds and equity is not revenue expenditure.
Incorrect: statement 1 is correct, since acquiring technology is capital expenditure, so 'neither' fails.
keyfact: Capex builds long-term assets (such as technology); debt and equity are sources of finance, not expenditure types.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: this is the official answer. It recognises that spending on long-term productive assets such as technology is capital expenditure, with benefits over several years, capitalised on the balance sheet and depreciated or amortised. It also rejects the claim that financing methods are expenditure heads.

Option (b), 2 only: this would hold that debt is capital expenditure and equity is revenue expenditure. That is a conceptual error, because financing choices (debt, equity) describe how funds are raised, not how they are spent. Interest on debt is a revenue expense, while equity brings in owner capital and is not an expense at all.

Option (c), 1 and 2: this would need both statements to be correct. Statement 1 is right, but statement 2 mixes up capital receipts or sources of finance with expenditure classification. In government accounts, borrowing is a capital receipt, not capital expenditure, and the same logic applies in company accounts.

Option (d), neither: this would mean even technology acquisition is not capital expenditure. That is wrong, because purchases of technology, patents, licences and machinery with lasting benefit are capitalised. Only minor maintenance, licence renewals of short duration or running costs would be revenue items.
related: Capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities; revenue expenditure does not.
Interest payments are revenue expenditure in the Union Budget.
Grants to states for asset creation are revenue expenditure but count in effective capital expenditure.
Borrowings and disinvestment proceeds are capital receipts.
Fiscal deficit equals total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings.
Primary deficit equals fiscal deficit minus interest payments.
Effective revenue deficit equals revenue deficit minus grants for creation of capital assets.
Depreciation applies to tangible assets and amortisation to intangible assets.
statements: 1 — Correct: Acquiring new technology gives long-term benefit and creates an asset, so it is capital expenditure. Capex includes purchase of plant, machinery, land, buildings, patents, licences, software and R&D that is capitalised. It is recorded on the balance sheet and written off gradually through depreciation (tangible assets) or amortisation (intangible assets). In government budgeting, capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities, for example loans and advances, and infrastructure spending. Capex is a key indicator of investment intent, and the Union Budget has stressed raising effective capital expenditure since 2020-21.

2 — Incorrect: Debt and equity are sources of finance, not categories of expenditure, and neither is revenue expenditure. Debt financing means borrowing through term loans, bonds or debentures, with interest as a revenue expense and principal repayment as a liability movement. Equity financing means raising funds by issuing shares or using retained earnings, which gives owners a claim on profits. Together they form the capital structure, and the debt-equity ratio measures leverage. Dividends are distribution of profit, not an operating expense. Using borrowed funds to buy assets is capital expenditure, but the loan itself is not.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. Acquiring new technology creates a long-term asset or enduring benefit, so it is capital expenditure. Debt and equity are both sources of capital (financing methods), not expenditure categories, so statement 2 is wrong.
topic_notes: Expenditure is classified by the nature and duration of the benefit it gives. Capital expenditure buys or improves fixed assets, gives benefit over several years, is non-recurring in nature, and is capitalised and depreciated. Examples are land, buildings, plant and machinery, vehicles, patents, goodwill purchased, software development and major upgrades. Revenue expenditure maintains earning capacity and operations within the year, and covers wages, rent, utilities, raw materials, advertising, routine repairs, insurance and interest. Deferred revenue expenditure, such as a big advertising campaign, is spent now but spread over several years. Government budget parallels: revenue expenditure covers interest payments, subsidies, salaries, pensions and grants (even grants used to create assets are revenue expenditure). Capital expenditure covers creation of assets, loans and advances by the Centre to states, and repayment of debt. Revenue receipts are tax and non-tax revenue and do not create liabilities. Capital receipts are borrowings, recovery of loans and disinvestment proceeds, and they create liabilities or reduce assets. Key deficit measures: Revenue Deficit is revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. Fiscal Deficit is total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings. Primary Deficit is fiscal deficit minus interest payments. Effective Revenue Deficit is revenue deficit minus grants for creation of capital assets. Corporate finance links: debt versus equity forms the capital structure, and leverage is shown by the debt-equity ratio. Interest is tax-deductible, whereas dividends are not. Working capital relates to short-term finance. Possible future questions include differences between capital and revenue items, the definition of capital receipts, FRBM targets, and the effective capital expenditure concept.

question:
With reference to the Indian economy, consider the following statements :
1. A share of the household financial savings goes towards government borrowings.
2. Dated securities issued at market-related rates in auctions form a large component of internal debt. Which of the above statements is/are correct ?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: India's public debt has two parts: internal debt (borrowed within India) and external debt (borrowed from abroad). Internal debt consists of market borrowings (dated securities or G-secs and Treasury Bills), plus Cash Management Bills, special securities issued to the RBI, compensation and other bonds, and the National Small Savings Fund (NSSF) securities. Dated G-secs are long-term securities with maturities of 5 to 40 years and fixed or floating coupons. The RBI, acting as the government's debt manager, issues them through auctions (yield-based or price-based) at market-determined rates. They account for the bulk of the Centre's outstanding liabilities, so statement 2 is correct. On statement 1, household financial savings go into banks, insurance companies, provident and pension funds and small savings. These institutions are required to invest in G-secs under SLR (banks), IRDAI norms (insurers) and EPFO and pension investment patterns. Small savings are lent to the government through the NSSF. Household savings therefore finance government borrowing, directly or indirectly, and statement 1 is correct. Because both statements hold, (c) is right and (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated. A common trap is to treat internal debt as only small savings or T-bills, which is wrong.
explanations: Wrong: it omits statement 2, which is also correct.
Wrong: it omits statement 1, which is also correct, since household savings are channelled into government borrowing.
Correct: both statements are accurate. Household savings fund government borrowing, and market-rate dated securities form the main part of internal debt.
Wrong: both statements are factually correct, so this option cannot hold.
keyfact: Household savings finance government borrowing, and market-rate dated securities form the largest part of India's internal debt.
option_notes: Option (a) accepts statement 1 only. Statement 1 is true, because household financial savings reach the government through banks, insurers, provident funds and small savings. But the option wrongly rejects statement 2. The household sector is the main net saver in India's economy, and the corporate and government sectors are net borrowers. Household financial savings usually run around 7 to 12% of GDP, with large swings during COVID-19.

Option (b) accepts statement 2 only. Statement 2 is true: dated G-secs, issued by RBI auction at market-related yields, are the largest part of internal debt. The option wrongly rejects statement 1. Dated G-secs have 5 to 40 year maturities and carry fixed or floating coupons. Floating Rate Bonds reset periodically, and Sovereign Green Bonds were first issued in 2023.

Option (c) says both statements are correct, which is the official answer. Household savings are mobilised into G-secs through SLR, insurance and pension norms and the small savings route. Dated securities are the dominant instrument of internal debt, issued by the RBI on the government's behalf under the FRBM framework. Internal debt also includes T-bills, NSSF securities and others.

Option (d) says neither statement is correct, which is false. Both statements are standard facts about public debt. India's Centre and state debts are financed mostly domestically, and external debt is a small share of the Centre's liabilities (about 5%). The Centre's gross fiscal deficit is financed mainly by market borrowings, small savings and external financing.
related: Dated G-secs have maturities of 5 to 40 years and are auctioned by the RBI.
T-bills come in 91, 182 and 364-day tenors and are zero-coupon instruments.
SLR for banks is 18% of NDTL.
The RBI Retail Direct scheme was launched in November 2021.
Article 292 deals with Union borrowing, and Article 293 with state borrowing.
The N.K. Singh Committee recommended a general government debt target of 60% of GDP.
Small savings are deposited in the NSSF, held in the Public Account of India.
Sovereign Green Bonds were first issued by India in 2023.
statements: 1 — Correct: Households' financial savings flow to the government through banks (SLR holdings), insurers, provident and pension funds and small savings schemes. Household financial savings are bank deposits, life insurance, PF/pension funds, small savings, shares and debentures and currency. Banks must hold a share of deposits in G-secs as SLR (currently 18% of NDTL). Insurers have mandatory G-sec investment norms. Post office schemes such as PPF, NSC, Sukanya Samriddhi and Kisan Vikas Patra go to the National Small Savings Fund, which lends to the Centre and states. Household savings are the main source of funds for public borrowing, and a rise in the fiscal deficit can crowd out private investment.

2 — Correct: Dated securities form the largest component of internal debt. Dated G-secs are long-term government bonds with maturities of 5 to 40 years and a half-yearly coupon. The RBI conducts auctions, either uniform-price or multiple-price, and the Centre announces an indicative borrowing calendar. Participants include banks, primary dealers, insurers and mutual funds, and retail investors can bid through the non-competitive window or the RBI Retail Direct platform. Treasury Bills (91, 182 and 364 days) are short-term instruments. State Development Loans (SDLs) are state-level dated securities. Dated securities carry no default risk and count toward SLR.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. Household financial savings (bank deposits, insurance, provident and pension funds, small savings) are channelled into government borrowing, and dated securities auctioned at market-related rates make up the largest part of India's internal debt.
topic_notes: Public debt in India consists of internal and external debt, and the Centre's liabilities appear in the Public Debt Management Cell/Status Paper reports. The Centre's total liabilities are roughly 55-60% of GDP, and the general government debt is around 80-85% of GDP. Internal debt is made up of market borrowings (dated securities and T-bills), Cash Management Bills, special securities, NSSF securities, bonds such as Ways and Means Advances (WMA), and others. The dated securities are issued by the RBI through auctions, and they form roughly 65-70% of total liabilities. The RBI manages debt for the Centre and states under Sections 20 and 21 of the RBI Act, 1934. The Public Debt Management Agency (PDMA) has been proposed but not set up. Fiscal framework: the FRBM Act, 2003 targets a fiscal deficit of 3% of GDP, and the N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended a debt-to-GDP ceiling of 60% for the general government (40% Centre, 20% states). Article 292 allows the Centre to borrow on the Consolidated Fund of India, and Article 293 governs state borrowing. Securities such as T-bills (91, 182, 364 days) are zero-coupon instruments issued at a discount. Cash Management Bills are shorter than 91 days. Liquidity management tools: the repo rate, SLR and open market operations (OMOs). Savings channels: the NSSF (under the Public Account), small savings rates are reset quarterly, and Retail Direct (launched in November 2021) allows individuals to buy G-secs. Future angles are crowding out, the FRBM escape clause, the G-sec yield curve and inclusion in global bond indices (JP Morgan from June 2024).

ocr: Consider the following statements : Pursuant to the report of H.N. Sanyal ¥ Committee, the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 was passed. The Constitution of India empowers the Supreme Court and the High Courts to punish for contempt of themselves. The Constitution of India defines Civil Contempt and Criminal Contempt. In India, the Parliament is vested with the powers to make laws on Contempt of Court. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) 1 and 2 only 1,2 and 4 (b) 3 and 4 only (c) (d) 3 only
subject: Polity
detail: Contempt of court in India has a constitutional basis but a statutory definition. Article 129 declares the Supreme Court a court of record with all powers, including the power to punish for contempt of itself. Article 215 gives the same power to High Courts. Article 142(2) also empowers the Supreme Court to investigate and punish contempt. Article 19(2) lists contempt of court as a ground for reasonable restrictions on free speech. Legislative competence lies with Parliament under Entry 77 of the Union List (constitution, organisation, jurisdiction and powers of the Supreme Court, including contempt of such Court) and Entry 14 of the Concurrent List (contempt of court, excluding the Supreme Court), so both Parliament and state legislatures may legislate on contempt of High Courts and subordinate courts. The H.N. Sanyal Committee, set up in 1961, studied the law, and its recommendations led to the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. Section 2 of that Act defines civil contempt (wilful disobedience of a judgment, order or undertaking) and criminal contempt (scandalising or lowering the authority of the court, prejudicing judicial proceedings, or obstructing the administration of justice). Elimination: statement 3 is wrong because the Constitution does not define them, so any option containing 3 (c and d) is out. Statements 1 and 2 are certainly correct, and statement 4 is also correct, which leaves (b).
explanations: Wrong: it omits statement 4, which is correct, because Parliament has legislative power over contempt of court.
Correct: statements 1, 2 and 4 are right, and statement 3 is wrong because the Constitution does not define the types of contempt.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is incorrect, and leaves out statements 1 and 2, which are correct.
Wrong: statement 3 is incorrect, and the option excludes the correct statements 1, 2 and 4.
keyfact: The Constitution makes superior courts courts of record with contempt power (Arts 129, 215), but civil and criminal contempt are defined only in the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, which followed the H.N. Sanyal Committee.
related: Article 129: the Supreme Court is a court of record with power to punish for its own contempt.
Article 215: High Courts are courts of record with the same power.
Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 follows the H.N. Sanyal Committee (1961).
Section 2(b) defines civil contempt and Section 2(c) defines criminal contempt.
The maximum punishment is six months' simple imprisonment, a fine of Rs 2,000, or both.
The 2006 amendment made truth a defence if it is in public interest and bona fide.
Entry 77 of the Union List and Entry 14 of the Concurrent List cover contempt of court.
Prashant Bhushan was held guilty of criminal contempt in 2020 and fined Re 1.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 followed the recommendations of the H.N. Sanyal Committee. The Committee was set up in 1961 under Additional Solicitor General H.N. Sanyal to examine the law of contempt in the light of the Constitution and the need to balance judicial authority with free speech. It recommended codifying and clarifying the law, and the 1971 Act replaced the Contempt of Courts Act, 1952. It defines civil and criminal contempt and prescribes punishment of up to six months' simple imprisonment, a fine of up to Rs 2,000, or both. It also provides defences such as fair and accurate reporting. The 2006 amendment added truth as a defence if it is in public interest and bona fide.

2 — Correct: Articles 129 (Supreme Court) and 215 (High Courts) make them courts of record, with the inherent power to punish for contempt of themselves. A court of record is one whose proceedings and judgments are kept as permanent evidence and cannot be questioned when produced before any court. This power is constitutional, so the 1971 Act cannot take it away; the Act only regulates procedure and punishment. The Supreme Court held in the Delhi Judicial Service Association case (1991) that it can punish contempt of subordinate courts under Article 129. In Prashant Bhushan (2020), the Court convicted him of criminal contempt and imposed a token fine of Re 1.

3 — Incorrect: The Constitution does not define civil or criminal contempt. It only recognises contempt in Articles 19(2), 129 and 215, and in Article 142(2). The definitions are in Section 2 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971. Civil contempt (Section 2(b)) means wilful disobedience of any judgment, decree, direction, order, writ or other process of a court, or wilful breach of an undertaking given to a court. Criminal contempt (Section 2(c)) means publication or acts that scandalise or lower the authority of a court, prejudice judicial proceedings, or interfere with or obstruct the administration of justice. A common confusion is to think the Constitution defines them.

4 — Correct: Parliament is vested with the power to make laws on contempt of court. Entry 77 of the Union List covers contempt of the Supreme Court, and Entry 14 of the Concurrent List covers contempt of court generally, excluding the Supreme Court. Parliament enacted the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 under these powers. Under Section 15 of the Act, the Supreme Court or a High Court may take cognisance of criminal contempt on its own motion, or on a motion by the Advocate General or by another person with the Advocate General's consent. The Act applies throughout India, subject to the special position of Jammu and Kashmir, which ended with the 2019 reorganisation.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. The Sanyal Committee (1961) report led to the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971; Articles 129 and 215 make the Supreme Court and High Courts courts of record with power to punish for contempt of themselves; and Parliament legislates on contempt through Entry 77 (Union List), Entry 14 (Concurrent List) and the Constitution. The Constitution does not define civil or criminal contempt; the 1971 Act does (Section 2).
topic_notes: Contempt of court is the law that protects the authority and dignity of the judiciary. Constitutional provisions: Article 129 (Supreme Court as a court of record, with power to punish for its own contempt), Article 215 (High Courts), Article 142(2) (Supreme Court's power to investigate and punish contempt), and Article 19(2) (contempt of court as a ground for restricting free speech). Legislative competence: Entry 77 of the Union List, Entry 14 of the Concurrent List. Statute: the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 came after the H.N. Sanyal Committee (1961) and replaced the 1952 Act. Section 2(b) defines civil contempt and Section 2(c) defines criminal contempt. Section 12 provides punishment of up to six months' simple imprisonment, a fine of up to Rs 2,000, or both; an apology may lead to remission of punishment if it is bona fide. Section 13 allows truth as a defence if it is in public interest and bona fide, as inserted by the 2006 amendment. Section 19 provides an appeal from a High Court order punishing contempt. Section 15 governs cognisance of criminal contempt: the court may act on its own motion, or on a motion by the Advocate General or by another person with the Advocate General's consent; for the Supreme Court, the consent of the Attorney General or Solicitor General is required. Case law: Delhi Judicial Service Association v. State of Gujarat (1991) held that the Supreme Court can punish contempt of subordinate courts. In re Arundhati Roy (2002) and Prashant Bhushan (2020) are well-known cases. The Law Commission and other bodies have discussed whether to reform the law, and the Second Administrative Reforms Commission also looked at related questions. Parliament's own powers over contempt are separate, based on privileges under Articles 105 and 194. In the Constitution, the word 'contempt' appears in Articles 19(2), 129 and 215.

question: With reference to India, consider the following statements : 5 Government law officers and legal firms are recognised as advocates, but corporate lawyers and patent attorneys are excluded from recognition as advocates. Bar Councils have the power to lay down the rules relating to legal education and recognition of law colleges. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Advocates Act, 1961 created a unified, all-India legal profession, with the Bar Council of India (BCI) at the apex and State Bar Councils below it. Section 7 lists BCI functions, including laying down standards of professional conduct and etiquette, and promoting legal education and laying down its standards in consultation with universities and State Bar Councils. It also recognises universities whose law degrees qualify holders to enrol as advocates, and it inspects universities. The BCI Rules (Part IV) govern the Centres of Legal Education and the recognition of law colleges, which is why statement 2 is correct. Under Section 24, a person must hold a recognised law degree and be enrolled on a State Bar Council roll to be an advocate. Section 29 recognises only advocates as a class of persons entitled to practise law. Statement 1 is faulty because recognition as an advocate depends on individual enrolment, not on a person's employer or on being a 'legal firm', which is not a person. Firms are not enrolled. Under the Bar Council rules, full-time salaried employees cannot practise as advocates (Rule 49), which affects many corporate in-house lawyers and some government law officers. Patent agents are regulated separately under the Patents Act, 1970. Elimination: statement 1 is muddled and wrong, statement 2 is correct, so (b).
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect, so '1 only' cannot be right. Recognition as an advocate depends on individual enrolment, not on the description given.
Correct: statement 2 is true and statement 1 is false. The Bar Council of India has the statutory power to prescribe legal education standards and recognise law colleges.
Wrong: statement 1 is false, so 'both' cannot be correct.
Wrong: statement 2 is correct, so 'neither' cannot be the answer.
keyfact: The Bar Council of India (Advocates Act, 1961, Sec. 7) sets legal education standards and recognises law colleges and degrees.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would hold that law officers and firms count as advocates while corporate lawyers and patent attorneys do not. This is incorrect. An advocate is a person enrolled on a State Bar Council roll under the Advocates Act, 1961. Section 29 recognises only advocates as persons entitled to practise law. Employment status matters through BCI Rule 49, which restricts salaried employees. Firms are not enrolled as advocates. Patent agents are registered under the Patents Act, 1970, with the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks.

Option (b), '2 only', is the official answer. The Bar Council of India is a statutory body created under the Advocates Act, 1961, with its head office in Delhi. Section 7 lists its functions, including setting standards of legal education, recognising universities and degrees, laying down rules of professional conduct and etiquette, safeguarding advocates' rights, and exercising disciplinary jurisdiction. It has twenty members: eighteen elected by State Bar Councils plus the Attorney General and the Solicitor General as ex-officio members. Its rules, the BCI Rules, set the standards for law colleges.

Option (c), 'both 1 and 2', would require statement 1 to be correct as well. It is not. Statement 1 mischaracterises who is an advocate under the Act. The Advocates Act, 1961 followed the Law Commission's 14th Report (1958) and the All-India Bar Committee (1953). It abolished the old classes of legal practitioners such as vakils and pleaders and created a single class called advocates. It also established the State Bar Councils and the Bar Council of India, and set up the right to practise before all courts.

Option (d), 'neither 1 nor 2', would deny the BCI's role in legal education. That is wrong. The Bar Council of India lays down legal education standards under Section 7(1)(h) and (i), and Section 49(1)(d) gives rule-making power over recognition of degrees. The University Grants Commission and the National Council for Teacher Education have no role in this area. The National Law Universities are created by state statutes but also need BCI approval for their courses. The BCI's Legal Education Committee advises on these matters.
related: Advocates Act, 1961 created the Bar Council of India and State Bar Councils.
The Attorney General of India (Art. 76) and the Solicitor General are ex-officio members of the Bar Council of India.
Article 39A provides free legal aid; NALSA was set up under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
A.K. Balaji (2018): foreign lawyers cannot practise litigation in India.
BCI Rule 49 bars full-time salaried employees from practising as advocates.
Article 165 provides for the Advocate General of a state.
Patent agents are registered under the Patents Act, 1970, not the Advocates Act.
Appeals against Bar Council disciplinary decisions lie to the Supreme Court.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Advocate status comes from individual enrolment under the Advocates Act, 1961, not from being a government law officer or a legal firm. Firms are not enrolled, and salaried in-house lawyers are restricted by BCI Rule 49. Details: Section 24 sets the qualifications for enrolment (citizen of India, 21 years, recognised law degree). Section 29 recognises only advocates as persons entitled to practise law. Rule 49 of the BCI Rules bars a full-time salaried employee from practising while employed, so many corporate lawyers cannot practise as advocates. Patent agents are registered under the Patents Act, 1970 and are a separate class. The Bar Council of India Rules also restrict foreign lawyers. Law firms are regulated indirectly, through the advocates working in them. In Bar Council of India v. A.K. Balaji (2018) the Supreme Court held that foreign lawyers cannot practise litigation in India.

2 — Correct: Section 7 of the Advocates Act, 1961 gives the BCI the power to promote legal education, lay down its standards and recognise universities. Details: The BCI prescribes the minimum infrastructure for law colleges, the curriculum, and the duration of the three-year LLB and five-year integrated law courses. It inspects colleges and grants or withdraws approval. Section 49 gives it rule-making power, including for legal education and recognition of degrees. The BCI has twenty members: the Attorney General of India and the Solicitor General as ex-officio members, and eighteen members elected by State Bar Councils. The Council's term is five years, extended later to six, and a chairman and vice-chairman are elected. The All India Bar Examination was introduced to test the competence of law graduates for practice.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The Advocates Act, 1961 empowers the Bar Council of India to lay down standards of legal education and to recognise law degrees and colleges. Statement 1 is wrong because the Act does not recognise 'government law officers and legal firms' as advocates in the way it describes, and the BCI Rules do not exclude corporate lawyers on that basis.
topic_notes: The legal profession in India is governed mainly by the Advocates Act, 1961, which implemented the recommendations of the Law Commission's 14th Report (1958) on judicial administration and the All-India Bar Committee (1953). It created an integrated Bar by merging the earlier classes of legal practitioners, vakils and pleaders, into one class called advocates. The Act sets up the Bar Council of India at the national level and State Bar Councils in each state. The BCI has twenty members, with the Attorney General and Solicitor General as ex-officio members. Its functions include setting the standards of professional conduct, promoting legal education, recognising universities whose degrees qualify for enrolment, and disciplinary matters through the disciplinary committees, with appeals going to the Supreme Court. State Bar Councils maintain the roll of advocates and conduct disciplinary proceedings. An advocate may enrol with only one State Bar Council at a time but can transfer between them. Under Section 30 an advocate has the right to practise throughout India. Section 35 deals with professional or other misconduct. The Act reserves the right to practise to advocates. The All India Bar Examination, introduced from 2010 and upheld in Bar Council of India v. Bonnie Foi Law College (2023), tests the competence of law graduates. Foreign law firms and lawyers were treated by the Supreme Court in A.K. Balaji (2018) as unable to practise litigation but allowed to give advice on foreign law on a fly-in fly-out basis; the BCI notified rules in 2023 allowing registration of foreign lawyers for non-litigious work. Related: Article 124 and 217 on judges' qualifications, Article 76 on the Attorney General, Article 165 on the Advocate General, the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 under Article 39A, and the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA).

question:
Consider the following statements : 15.
1. A bill amending the Constitution requires a prior recommendation of the President of India.
2. When a Constitution Amendment Bill is presented to the President of India, it is obligatory for the President of India to give his/her assent.
3. A Constitution Amendment Bill must be passed by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha by a special majority and there is no provision for joint sitting. Which of the statements given above are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 368 lays down the procedure for amending the Constitution. A Constitution Amendment Bill can be introduced only in Parliament (not in state legislatures, except the ratification role), by a minister or a private member, in either House. Unlike Money Bills or Financial Bills under Article 117, it does not need the President's prior recommendation, so statement 1 is wrong. The Bill must be passed in each House by a majority of the total membership of that House and by at least two-thirds of members present and voting. The Houses vote separately, and the joint sitting under Article 108 does not apply to Constitution Amendment Bills; a deadlock simply defeats the Bill, so statement 3 is right. For amendments touching federal features (listed in the proviso to Article 368(2)), ratification by half of the state legislatures is also needed. After this, the Bill goes to the President, who 'shall give his assent'. The 24th Amendment Act, 1971 made assent obligatory, reversing the earlier position that left him discretion, so statement 2 is right. Elimination: 1 is false, so (a), (c) and (d) fall, leaving (b).
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because no prior presidential recommendation is required for a Constitution Amendment Bill, so this option fails.
Correct: statements 2 and 3 are right (assent is obligatory since the 24th Amendment, and a special majority in each House applies with no joint sitting), while statement 1 is wrong.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false, and it leaves out statement 2, which is true.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false, so 'all three' cannot be correct.
keyfact: A Constitution Amendment Bill needs no prior recommendation of the President, a special majority in each House separately with no joint sitting, and the President must give assent (24th Amendment, 1971).
option_notes: Option (a), '1 and 2 only', pairs the false claim about a prior presidential recommendation with the true claim about obligatory assent. The topic it points to is the presidential role in amendments. Under Article 368(2) and the 24th Amendment (1971), assent is compulsory. Prior recommendations are required for Money Bills (Article 110 and 117), some Financial Bills, and Bills under Article 3 on states. It is wrong because statement 1 is false and statement 3 is true but left out.

Option (b), '2 and 3 only', is the official answer. It reflects the two key features of Article 368: the President must give assent after the 24th Amendment (1971), and both Houses must pass the Bill separately by a special majority, which is a majority of total membership plus two-thirds of those present and voting. No joint sitting is allowed. Where federal features are affected, half of the state legislatures must also ratify. Ratification by simple majority in the states is enough.

Option (c), '1 and 3 only', combines the false statement on prior recommendation with the true statement on special majority. It is wrong because it rejects the obligatory assent rule. Before the 24th Amendment, there was doubt about whether the President could withhold assent on amendment Bills. Since 1971, Article 368(2) uses the words 'shall give his assent', so the President has no discretion. Ordinary Bills differ because Article 111 allows withholding assent or returning the Bill.

Option (d), '1, 2 and 3', would be correct only if a prior recommendation were needed. It is not, so the option fails. Prior recommendation is required in specific cases: Article 117 (Financial Bills), Article 274 (Bills affecting taxes in which states are interested), Article 3 (new states, boundaries), and Article 304(b). Constitution Amendment Bills are in none of these categories, and they can be introduced by any member of either House after the usual leave.
related: Article 368 was amended by the 24th Amendment Act, 1971 to make presidential assent compulsory.
Joint sittings under Article 108 do not apply to Constitution Amendment Bills or Money Bills.
Special majority under Article 368: majority of total membership plus two-thirds of members present and voting.
Ratification by half of state legislatures is needed for amending federal provisions, by simple majority in each state.
Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Clauses 4 and 5 of Article 368, which barred judicial review of amendments.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that Parliament cannot alter the basic structure of the Constitution.
A Constitution Amendment Bill can be introduced only in Parliament, not in state legislatures.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) is known as the 'mini-Constitution'.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: No prior presidential recommendation is needed to introduce a Constitution Amendment Bill. Prior recommendation is required only for certain Bills, such as Money Bills, certain Financial Bills, and Bills affecting state boundaries (Article 3). Constitution Amendment Bills can be introduced in either House by a minister or private member without it. The only presidential role comes at the end, when the Bill is presented for assent. Article 368 is silent on any prior recommendation requirement, and no state legislature can initiate an amendment. The procedure is set only by Article 368 and Parliament's own rules.

2 — Correct: Article 368(2), as amended by the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971, says the President 'shall give his assent' to the Bill. This was enacted after the Golaknath case (1967) to restore Parliament's amending power and remove any doubt about presidential discretion. The President therefore has no power of withholding assent, returning the Bill for reconsideration, or a pocket veto, unlike with ordinary Bills under Article 111. The 24th Amendment also renamed Article 368 to cover both the power and the procedure of amendment. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) later upheld this change while establishing the basic structure doctrine.

3 — Correct: Under Article 368, a Constitution Amendment Bill must be passed in each House by a majority of the total membership of that House and by at least two-thirds of members present and voting. This is called a special majority. Both Houses have equal powers here, and Article 108's joint sitting applies only to ordinary Bills, not to Constitution Amendment Bills, Money Bills, or Financial Bills (Article 117(1)). A deadlock between the Houses therefore defeats the Bill. The Constitution's proviso requires state ratification by half the legislatures for amending federal provisions, but this adds to the House vote and does not replace it.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 2 and 3 only. Under Article 368, a Constitution Amendment Bill needs no prior recommendation of the President, the President must give assent (24th Amendment, 1971), and it must be passed by a special majority in each House separately with no joint sitting.
topic_notes: Article 368 (Part XX) deals with the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and its procedure. Amendments can be made in three ways: by simple majority of Parliament (e.g., Articles 2, 3, 4, new states, Second Schedule, citizenship, Fifth and Sixth Schedules), by special majority, and by special majority plus ratification by at least half of the states. The Constitution has no provision for a constitutional convention or special body for amendments, unlike the US. Only Parliament can initiate an amendment Bill. The Bill can be introduced in either House by a minister or private member, and the President's prior permission is not needed. Each House must pass it separately, with a majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting. Joint sittings are not available. If the Bill seeks to change federal features, such as the election of the President (Articles 54 and 55), the extent of executive and legislative power of the Union and states, the Supreme Court and High Courts, the representation of states in Parliament, the distribution of legislative powers, or Article 368 itself, it must be ratified by half of the state legislatures by simple majority. The President must then give assent. Key judgments: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) held that Parliament could amend Fundamental Rights; Golaknath (1967) reversed this; the 24th Amendment (1971) restored Parliament's power; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) introduced the basic structure doctrine; Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Clauses 4 and 5 of Article 368, added by the 42nd Amendment, which tried to bar judicial review; and I.R.
