Coelho (2007) held that laws in the Ninth Schedule are open to judicial review. The 42nd Amendment (1976) is known as the 'mini-Constitution'. The 44th Amendment (1978) removed the right to property from Fundamental Rights. The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced GST, and the 103rd Amendment (2019) provided EWS reservation. The 106th Amendment (2023) provides women's reservation.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Constitution of India classifies the ministers into four ranks viz. Cabinet Minister, Minister of State with Independent Charge, Minister of State and Deputy Minister.
2. The total number of ministers in the Union Government, including the Prime Minister, shall not exceed 15 percent of the total number of members in the Lok Sabha. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? A
subject: Polity
detail: Article 74 provides for a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at its head to aid and advise the President. Article 75 deals with other provisions on ministers: the PM is appointed by the President, who appoints other ministers on the PM's advice; ministers hold office during the President's pleasure; the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Art. 75(3)). The 91st Amendment (2003) inserted Article 75(1A), limiting the total number of ministers, including the PM, to 15% of the Lok Sabha's strength (with a minimum of 12 ministers for states under Art. 164(1A)). Article 75(1B) and 164(1B) disqualify a defecting member from being a minister (Tenth Schedule disqualification). The Constitution mentions no categories of ministers. The three-tier structure of Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers is drawn from the British convention, and the Ministers of State with Independent Charge is an administrative arrangement. Deputy Ministers have not been appointed in recent years. Elimination: since statement 1 is wrong, options (a) and (c) go out; statement 2 is correct, so (d) goes out, leaving (b).
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because the Constitution does not prescribe four ranks of ministers, so 'statement 1 only' cannot be right.
Correct: statement 2 correctly reflects Article 75(1A) (91st Amendment 2003), the 15% limit, and statement 1 is false, so 2 only is the answer.
Wrong: this requires statement 1 to be correct, but ministerial ranks are a matter of convention, not constitutional classification.
Wrong: statement 2 is correct, so 'neither' fails.
keyfact: Art. 75(1A) (91st Amendment, 2003): Council of Ministers incl. PM ≤ 15% of Lok Sabha; ministerial ranks are convention, not constitutional.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only': would mean the Constitution classifies ministers into four ranks. In reality the ranks (Cabinet Minister, MoS with independent charge, MoS, Deputy Minister) arise from parliamentary convention and administrative practice, derived from the British system. The Ministers' Salaries and Allowances Act 1952 refers to ranks for pay purposes. The 1978 44th Amendment gave the 'Cabinet' written mention in Article 352(3). Deputy Ministers have been absent from recent councils.

Option (b), '2 only': this is the correct answer. Article 75(1A), added by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act 2003, limits the Union Council of Ministers, including the PM, to 15% of Lok Sabha members. The same amendment capped state councils at 15% of Assembly strength with a minimum of 12 ministers. It also added disqualification of defectors from ministerial office, and removed the exemption for splits under the Tenth Schedule.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2': incorrect because statement 1 is false. Ministerial ranks are not constitutional. Although statement 2 is right, accepting both would wrongly suggest the Constitution lays out a tiered ministry. The only constitutional distinction is between the PM, the Council of Ministers (Art. 74) and the Cabinet (mentioned in Art. 352 only).

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2': incorrect because statement 2 is accurate. The 15% ceiling was added to check oversized ministries that had grown out of coalition politics, where bargaining caused councils of 70 or more. Before 2003 there was no numerical limit on the size of the Council of Ministers at the Union or state level.
related: Article 75(1A): ministers capped at 15% of Lok Sabha strength (91st Amendment, 2003).
Article 164(1A): state Council limited to 15% of Assembly, minimum 12 ministers.
Article 74: Council of Ministers headed by the PM aids and advises the President.
Article 75(3): Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
Article 352 mentions the 'Cabinet' (44th Amendment 1978).
Non-MP can be a minister for up to six months (Art. 75(5)).
Art. 239AA caps Delhi's ministers at 10% of the Assembly.
Art. 361B bars defectors from remunerative political posts.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Constitution does not classify ministers into ranks; the categories are conventional, not constitutional. Article 74 and 75 only speak of the Council of Ministers headed by the PM. In practice the Council has Cabinet Ministers (senior, heading key ministries, in the Cabinet), Ministers of State (with or without independent charge) and Deputy Ministers who assist. The Cabinet was given statutory recognition only through Article 352 (inserted by the 44th Amendment 1978), which mentions the Cabinet. The Ministers' Salaries and Allowances Act, 1952 defines ranks of ministers. Deputy Ministers have not been appointed for years.

2 — Correct: Article 75(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment Act, 2003, fixes the total number of ministers including the PM at not more than 15% of the Lok Sabha's total strength. With 543 members the maximum is about 81 ministers. The amendment aimed at curbing jumbo ministries and political defection, introduced on the recommendation of the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (Venkatachaliah Commission). For states, Article 164(1A) limits the Council to 15% of Assembly strength, with a minimum of 12 ministers, including the CM. Delhi has a 10% cap under Art. 239AA.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 capped the Council of Ministers, including the PM, at 15% of Lok Sabha strength (Article 75(1A)), whereas the Constitution does not classify ministers into four ranks; that classification comes from convention and the Parliamentary tradition.
topic_notes: The Union Executive's real power lies in the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. Article 74(1) requires the President to act on the aid and advice of the Council (the 42nd Amendment made it binding; the 44th Amendment allowed the President to ask for reconsideration once). Article 75 covers appointment, tenure, collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha, oath of office and salaries. Individual responsibility arises under the 'pleasure of the President'. A person who is not a member of Parliament may be a minister for six months. Article 78 lists the PM's duties to communicate decisions to the President. The 91st Amendment (2003) introduced the 15% cap, based on the Venkatachaliah Commission's and Dinesh Goswami Committee's recommendations. It also inserted Article 361B (disqualification for remunerative political posts) and tightened the Tenth Schedule by deleting the split provision (para 3). Three categories of ministers by convention: Cabinet Ministers head major ministries and form the Cabinet; Ministers of State may have independent charge or assist Cabinet ministers; Deputy Ministers assist Cabinet ministers or Ministers of State. The Cabinet is a smaller body within the larger Council, which meets rarely as a whole. The 'Kitchen Cabinet' is an informal inner circle. Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; a no-confidence motion needs the support of 50 members to be admitted under the Lok Sabha rules. Art. 88 gives ministers the right to speak in both Houses, but they vote only in the House of which they are members. Related ideas: the Cabinet Secretariat, Cabinet Committees (extra-constitutional), the Allocation of Business Rules and the Transaction of Business Rules.

question:
Which of the following is/are the exclusive power(s) of Lok Sabha ? 1.‘ To ratify the declaration of Emergency
2. To pass a motion of no-confidence against the Council of Ministers
3. To impeach the President of India Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Polity
detail: Exclusive powers of the Lok Sabha are those the Rajya Sabha cannot share. The main ones are: (i) the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible only to the Lok Sabha (Art. 75(3)), so only it can pass a no-confidence motion, censure motion or adjournment motion, or reject a confidence motion; (ii) Money Bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha (Art. 109), and the Rajya Sabha can only recommend amendments within 14 days; (iii) the Lok Sabha Speaker certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill; (iv) it can discuss and vote on demands for grants; (v) it can approve the resolution to disapprove the continuation of an Emergency, by a simple majority of a special sitting called on a written request of one-tenth of members (Art. 352). Emergency proclamations must be approved by both Houses, by a special majority, within one month (Art. 352(4)). Impeachment of the President (Art. 61) can be initiated in either House and needs a two-thirds majority of the total membership of each House. So statements 1 and 3 fail because the power is shared, leaving only statement 2.
explanations: Incorrect: this includes statement 1, which is not exclusive; both Houses approve an Emergency proclamation.
Correct: only statement 2 is exclusive, since the Council of Ministers is responsible to the Lok Sabha alone under Art. 75(3).
Incorrect: statement 3 is wrong because impeachment of the President involves both Houses equally, and statement 1 is wrong as well.
Incorrect: statement 3 is not exclusive, and statement 3 alone excludes the actually exclusive power in statement 2.
keyfact: No-confidence motion (Art. 75(3)) is exclusive to the Lok Sabha; Emergency approval and Presidential impeachment involve both Houses.
option_notes: Options 1 and 2 together: 1 is a shared power and 2 is exclusive, so this combination is wrong. The Emergency power under Art. 352 requires approval of both Houses within one month, by a special majority. Only the disapproval resolution is exclusive to the Lok Sabha. The 44th Amendment Act 1978 introduced the one-month limit and the six-month renewal. A proclamation can be on grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion, which replaced 'internal disturbance'.

Statement 2 only is the correct answer. A no-confidence motion tests whether the Council of Ministers retains the confidence of the Lok Sabha, as collective responsibility under Art. 75(3) applies only to that House. It needs 50 members' support to be admitted, and a simple majority to pass. If passed, the government must resign. The Rajya Sabha has no such power, although it can debate and criticise the government.

Options 1 and 3 together: both statements describe powers shared with the Rajya Sabha. Emergency approval needs both Houses, and impeachment of the President under Art. 61 can be started in either House, with the other investigating. A two-thirds majority of the total membership of each House is required for impeachment. This combination is wrong and also leaves out the genuine exclusive power in statement 2.

Statement 3 only is wrong because impeachment of the President is a joint power of both Houses under Art. 61. A resolution needs a two-thirds majority of total membership in each House, with a 14-day notice signed by one-fourth of members. The Rajya Sabha has equal power. The President is also elected by an electoral college of elected members of both Houses and State Assemblies (Art. 54). Statement 3 alone also omits the truly exclusive power in statement 2.
related: Art. 75(3): the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
Art. 109: Money Bills originate only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha has 14 days to make recommendations.
Art. 249 (State List legislation in the national interest) and Art. 312 (All India Services) are exclusive to the Rajya Sabha.
Art. 352: Emergency proclamation needs approval of both Houses within one month by a special majority.
Art. 61: impeachment of the President needs a two-thirds majority of total membership in both Houses.
Removal of the Vice-President (Art. 67(b)) can be initiated only in the Rajya Sabha.
Art. 108: joint sitting is presided over by the Lok Sabha Speaker; not applicable to Money Bills or Constitutional Amendments.
The Speaker decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill (Art. 110) and that decision is final.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Approval of a proclamation of Emergency is a power shared by both Houses, not exclusive to the Lok Sabha. Under Art. 352, a proclamation must be approved by both Houses within one month, by a special majority (majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting). The 44th Amendment (1978) reduced the period from two months to one month and made the special majority a requirement. Only the power to pass a resolution disapproving the continuation of an Emergency is exclusive to the Lok Sabha: if a resolution is passed by simple majority, the Emergency must be revoked. A special sitting of the Lok Sabha can be called on a written request from one-tenth of its members to consider such a resolution. Once approved, the Emergency continues for six months and may be extended by Parliament every six months. National Emergencies were declared in 1962, 1971 and 1975.

2 — Correct: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha under Art. 75(3), so only the Lok Sabha can pass a no-confidence motion. Rule 198 of the Lok Sabha Rules governs the motion. It needs the support of at least 50 members to be admitted, and the Speaker permits it. If it is passed by a simple majority, the whole Council of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, must resign. The Rajya Sabha can discuss the government's policies but cannot remove the government. No-confidence motions have been moved against governments including Nehru's in 1963, the first, and Narasimha Rao's in 1993. Governments have fallen on confidence votes, such as Vajpayee's in 1999 by one vote, and Modi's government faced motions in 2018 and 2023.

3 — Incorrect: Under Art. 61, impeachment of the President for violation of the Constitution can be initiated in either House, so it is not exclusive to the Lok Sabha. A notice signed by at least one-fourth of the House's members and given 14 days in advance is required. The resolution must be passed by two-thirds of the total membership of that House. The other House then investigates the charge, and if it also passes the resolution by a two-thirds majority of its total membership, the President stands removed from the date of passing. Nominated members of both Houses can participate in impeachment, and elected members of State Legislative Assemblies cannot, although they take part in the election. No President has ever been impeached.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. Only the Lok Sabha can pass a no-confidence motion against the Council of Ministers, because under Article 75(3) the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha alone. Emergency approval and impeachment of the President involve both Houses.
topic_notes:
Indian Parliament consists of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. Although the two Houses are broadly co-equal, the Lok Sabha has greater power in money and accountability matters.

Exclusive powers of the Lok Sabha: (1) Money Bills can be introduced only in it (Art. 109), and the Rajya Sabha has 14 days to return it with recommendations, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject. (2) The Speaker certifies a Money Bill and the decision is final (Art. 110). (3) The Council of Ministers is responsible to it (Art. 75(3)). (4) It alone votes on demands for grants, and Rajya Sabha can only discuss the budget. (5) It can pass a resolution to disapprove the continuation of Emergency. (6) A Financial Bill, such as under Art. 117, can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation.

Exclusive powers of the Rajya Sabha: (1) Art. 249, authorising Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in the national interest by a two-thirds resolution of members present and voting. (2) Art. 312, creating new All India Services by a two-thirds resolution. (3) Approving a resolution to remove the Vice-President needs to be initiated there (Art. 67(b)); the Lok Sabha only agrees by a simple majority.

Powers shared equally: constitutional amendment bills (Art. 368), election and impeachment of the President, removal of judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, approval of Emergency proclamations, ordinary Bills, and approval of ordinances. Joint sittings under Art. 108 are not available for Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills. The Lok Sabha has a maximum of 550 members (530 from States and 20 from Union Territories), currently 543, with a term of five years, extendable during Emergency by one year at a time.

question:
With reference to anti-defection law in India, consider the following statements :
1. The law specifies that a nominated legislator cannot join any political party within six months of being appointed to the House. The law does not provide any time-frame within which the presiding officer has to decide a defection case. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: The anti-defection law is contained in the Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 (Rajiv Gandhi government), and operates through Articles 102(2) and 191(2). Members can be disqualified if they voluntarily give up party membership or defy the party whip on a vote (without condoning by the party within 15 days). An independent who joins a party after election is disqualified. A nominated member is disqualified if he joins a party after six months from the date he takes his seat; joining within six months is protected. So statement 1 is wrong because it inverts the rule: the six months is a window of freedom, not a ban. The original paragraph 7 barred court jurisdiction, but Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) struck it down, holding that the Speaker acts as a tribunal and his decision is subject to judicial review. The 91st Amendment (2003) removed the one-third split exemption and kept only the merger exemption (two-thirds of the legislature party). The Schedule prescribes no time-frame for the Speaker's decision; in Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020) the Supreme Court suggested three months as a reasonable period. Hence only statement 2 is correct.
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because a nominated member may join a party within six months without disqualification; the law does not prohibit this.
Correct: only statement 2 holds, since the Tenth Schedule prescribes no deadline for the presiding officer's decision.
Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect, so 'both' cannot be right.
Wrong: statement 2 is correct, so 'neither' is false.
keyfact: Tenth Schedule: nominated members may join a party within 6 months of taking their seat; no time limit binds the Speaker's disqualification decision.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 only: this would be correct only if the law barred nominated members from joining parties for six months. In fact the six months is a window in which a nominated member may join a party freely. After it, he is treated like other members and is disqualified if he joins a party. The Tenth Schedule, paragraph 2(3), covers this. Nominated Rajya Sabha members (12, chosen for literature, science, art and social service under Article 80) are the usual example.

Option (b) 2 only: this is the official answer. The Tenth Schedule contains no time frame for the Speaker or Chairman to decide disqualification petitions. The Supreme Court in Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020) suggested three months and recommended that Parliament consider an independent tribunal headed by a retired judge in place of the Speaker. The Speaker's decision remains open to judicial review under Kihoto Hollohan (1992), though only after a final decision is made.

Option (c) Both 1 and 2: this is wrong because statement 1 misstates the rule. A candidate might choose it by misreading the six-month provision as a restriction. Remember the right formulation: a nominated member must decide within six months, and joining a party after that period leads to disqualification. Statement 2 alone is sound, so the combined option cannot hold under the Tenth Schedule.

Option (d) Neither 1 nor 2: this is wrong because statement 2 is correct. The Tenth Schedule never fixes a period for deciding defection cases, which has produced delays of years in some state assemblies. Courts have recommended timelines but Parliament has not legislated one. Choosing this option would reflect a belief that the law already sets a deadline for the presiding officer, which it does not.
related: Tenth Schedule was added by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985.
91st Amendment Act, 2003 removed the one-third split exemption and kept only the two-thirds merger exemption.
Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) upheld the Tenth Schedule and made the Speaker's decision judicially reviewable.
Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020): SC suggested a three-month limit for Speakers and an independent tribunal.
Nominated member can join a party within six months of taking his seat without being disqualified.
Articles 102(2) and 191(2) provide for disqualification on grounds of defection for MPs and MLAs respectively.
Council of Ministers is limited to 15% of the House strength under Article 75(1A) and 164(1A), from the 91st Amendment.
Presiding officer decides disqualification petitions; the Election Commission has no role under the Tenth Schedule.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Tenth Schedule lets a nominated member join a party within six months of taking his seat; only joining after six months leads to disqualification. Under paragraph 2(3), a nominated member who joins a party after the six-month period is disqualified. The provision exists so the nominee can make a one-time choice of party, after which he is bound like elected members. It applies to Rajya Sabha nominees (12, under Article 80) and to nominated members of state legislative councils or assemblies. It does not apply to the Lok Sabha's two Anglo-Indian nominees, a category abolished by the 104th Amendment (2019, effective January 2020).

2 — Correct: The Tenth Schedule is silent on a time limit for the Speaker or Chairman to decide disqualification petitions. This silence has led to long delays and allegations of partisanship, as Speakers often belong to the ruling party. In Kihoto Hollohan (1992) the Supreme Court held the Speaker's decision is a tribunal decision, open to judicial review. In Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, Manipur (2020), the Court asked Parliament to consider an independent tribunal and said petitions should normally be decided within three months. The Court has declined to impose a statutory deadline by itself, so the law remains silent.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only. The Tenth Schedule gives no time-limit for the presiding officer to decide a disqualification petition, but a nominated member can join a party within six months of taking a seat without being disqualified; statement 1 reverses this rule.
topic_notes: The anti-defection law is in the Tenth Schedule, inserted by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985, following the 'Aya Ram, Gaya Ram' phenomenon of the 1960s. Disqualification grounds: (1) a member voluntarily gives up membership of his party; (2) he votes or abstains contrary to the party whip without prior permission, and the party does not condone it within 15 days; (3) an independent member joins a party after election; (4) a nominated member joins a party after six months. Exceptions: merger of a party, where at least two-thirds of the legislature party agree (paragraph 4); and the presiding officer who resigns from his party on election to the office and rejoins it after leaving the office. The 91st Amendment Act, 2003, deleted the one-third split provision and capped the size of Council of Ministers at 15% of the House strength (Centre and states; minimum 12 in a state). It also barred defectors from holding ministerial or remunerative political posts until re-elected. The presiding officer (Speaker or Chairman) decides disqualification; for the Chairman or Speaker themselves, the House elects another member to decide. Paragraph 7, which barred court jurisdiction, was struck down in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992), though the Tenth Schedule was upheld as valid. Later cases: Ravi Naik (1994), where conduct can imply voluntarily giving up membership; G. Viswanathan (1996); Rajendra Singh Rana (2007); Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020). Reform proposals: Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) on electoral reforms, which proposed that the President or Governor decide on the advice of the Election Commission; Law Commission 170th Report (1999); the Second ARC; and the Constitution Review Commission (NCRWC, 2002), which suggested that defectors be barred from office for the remainder of the term. Future questions may address the tribunal idea, whip applicability and merger rules.

question:
Consider the following statements : 19.
1. Attorney General of India and Solicitor General of India are the only officers of the Government who are allowed to participate in the meetings of the Parliament of India.
2. According to the Constitution of India, the Attorney General of India submits his resignation when the Government which appointed him resigns. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The Attorney General (AG) of India is the Union's highest law officer, appointed by the President under Article 76 on the Government's advice. The AG must be qualified to be a Supreme Court judge. He holds office during the pleasure of the President, and the Constitution fixes no tenure and no procedure or grounds for removal. Under Article 88, the AG may speak in and take part in the proceedings of either House, joint sittings and any parliamentary committee of which he is named a member, but he has no right to vote. Article 105 gives him parliamentary privileges. The Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General are not constitutional posts; they assist the AG and are statutory or administrative appointees. Statement 1 fails on two counts: the Solicitor General has no Article 88 right, and Ministers also participate in Parliament, so the AG and SG are not the only officers. Statement 2 fails because the resignation convention is not written in the Constitution. The phrase 'according to the Constitution' makes it wrong, even though by convention the AG resigns when the Government changes. Both statements are wrong, so (d).
explanations: Wrong: Statement 1 is incorrect because only the AG has an Art. 88 right, the Solicitor General has none, and other functionaries such as Ministers also participate in Parliament.
Wrong: Statement 2 is incorrect because the resignation on the Government's exit is a convention and not a constitutional requirement.
Wrong: Both statements are incorrect, so they cannot both be correct.
Correct: Neither statement holds, which matches the official answer.
keyfact: Only the Attorney General has a constitutional right (Art. 88) to speak in Parliament, and his resignation with the Government is a convention, not a constitutional rule.
option_notes: Option (a) would make only statement 1 correct. Its claim that only the AG and SG may participate in Parliament is false. Art. 88 names only the AG, and Ministers take part in proceedings by right as members or under the same article. The Solicitor General is the second-ranking law officer under the AG, with no constitutional status, and the post is created by statute or executive order. Tushar Mehta has been SG since 2018.

Option (b) would make only statement 2 correct. This is the trap option. The AG customarily resigns when the Government changes, but the Constitution says only that he holds office during the President's pleasure (Art. 76(4)). Many students pick it because the convention is so well known, forgetting that 'according to the Constitution' requires a textual basis.

Option (c) would make both statements correct. Neither is correct, so it fails. It combines the wrong claim about the Solicitor General with the wrong attribution of the resignation convention to the Constitution. Together, Arts. 76, 88, 105 and 165 define the AG's legal and parliamentary position and the Advocate General's parallel State role.

Option (d) says neither statement is correct. This is the official answer. Statement 1 overstates the Solicitor General's status and ignores Ministers. Statement 2 treats a convention as a constitutional rule. The AG's office is constitutional, but the Solicitor General's is not.
related: Art. 76: Attorney General of India.
Art. 88: AG's right to speak in Parliament, with no vote.
Art. 105: Parliamentary privileges extend to the AG.
Art. 165: Advocate General of a State.
The Solicitor General is not a constitutional post.
The AG holds office during the President's pleasure, with no fixed tenure.
The AG's consent is needed to start contempt proceedings in the Supreme Court.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Article 88 gives the right to speak in Parliament to the Attorney General alone, not the Solicitor General, and Ministers also take part in proceedings. The Attorney General (Art. 76) is the Union's chief legal adviser and is appointed by the President. He must be qualified to be a Supreme Court judge. He can speak in either House, in joint sittings and in committees of which he is a member, but cannot vote. He enjoys privileges under Art. 105. He has the right of audience in all courts in India. He is not a full-time government employee and is not barred from private practice, though he cannot advise against the Government. The Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General assist him and have no Art. 88 right.

2 — Incorrect: No constitutional provision requires the AG to resign when the Government resigns. Art. 76(4) says he holds office during the President's pleasure and receives remuneration the President determines. By convention he usually resigns when the Council of Ministers changes, because he is appointed on the Government's advice. Removal is not governed by any prescribed procedure. He may also resign by writing to the President. Examples: K. K. Venugopal served as AG from 2017 to 2022 and Mukul Rohatgi from 2014 to 2017 (and again in 2019-20). The AG is not a member of the Cabinet. Art. 165 provides the parallel Advocate General for States, appointed by the Governor.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. Statement 1 is wrong because the Constitution gives only the Attorney General (Art. 88) a right to speak in Parliament, and the Solicitor General has no such constitutional right; ministers and others also attend. Statement 2 is wrong because the Constitution does not require the AG to resign when the Government resigns, though by convention he does.
topic_notes: The Attorney General of India is covered by Article 76. He is appointed by the President and must be qualified to be a Supreme Court judge, meaning an Indian citizen who has been a High Court judge for five years, or an advocate of a High Court for ten years, or in the President's opinion a distinguished jurist. His duties include advising the Government on legal matters referred to him, performing other legal duties assigned by the President, and discharging functions conferred by the Constitution or any law. He has the right of audience in all courts in India. Art. 88 lets him speak in and take part in proceedings of either House, joint sittings and committees of which he is named a member, without a vote. Art. 105 gives him the privileges of a member of Parliament. He is not a government servant, and he does not have fixed tenure or a fixed removal procedure. His remuneration is determined by the President. He should not advise against the Union Government or defend accused persons in criminal prosecutions without permission. The Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General are not constitutional posts, and they assist the AG. Art. 165 provides the Advocate General of a State, appointed by the Governor, who must be qualified to be a High Court judge. Art. 143 deals with Presidential reference to the Supreme Court. The Comptroller and Auditor General under Art. 148 is another independent constitutional office, and the CAG can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge. Possible future angles are the AG's removal, the difference between the AG and the Advocate General, the Solicitor General's status, and the Attorney General's role in contempt proceedings, where his consent is needed under the Contempt of Courts Act 1971.

question:
With reference to the writs issued by the Courts in India, consider the following statements :
1. Mandamus will not lie against a private ’ organisation unless it is entrusted with a public duty.
2. Mandamus will not lie against a Company even though it may be a Government Company.
3. Any public minded person can be a petitioner to move the Court to obtain the writ of Quo Warranto. Which of the statements given above are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: Writs are issued by the Supreme Court under Article 32 and by High Courts under Article 226. Mandamus ('we command') compels a public authority to perform a legal duty. It lies against public bodies and against private bodies only when they are entrusted with a public duty or function. It does not lie against a purely private individual or body, and it does not lie against a company, even a Government Company, because such a company is treated as a separate legal entity and not as the State itself for this purpose in the traditional doctrine. Quo Warranto ('by what authority') tests the legality of a person's claim to a substantive public office. It is an exception to the locus standi rule, so any interested or public-minded person can move the court, not just an aggrieved person. Habeas corpus can also be filed by others on behalf of the detainee. Elimination logic: since statement 3 is correct, options (a) is out. Since statement 2 is accepted as correct, option (c) is out. Since statement 1 is correct, option (b) is out. That leaves (d).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it leaves out statement 3, which is correct: any public-minded person can seek quo warranto.
(b) is wrong because it leaves out statement 1, which is correct: mandamus lies against a private body only if it is entrusted with a public duty.
(c) is wrong because it leaves out statement 2, which the official key treats as correct: mandamus does not lie against a company, even a Government Company.
(d) is correct because all three statements are accepted as correct by the official key.
keyfact: Mandamus lies only for public duties (not against a purely private body or a company, even a Government Company), while quo warranto can be moved by any public-spirited person.
option_notes: Option (a), statements 1 and 2 only: this combination treats quo warranto as restricted to the aggrieved person. That is wrong, since quo warranto relaxes locus standi. Statements 1 and 2 on mandamus are accepted as correct. Mandamus is a writ of command under Articles 32 and 226 for enforcing public duties. It is discretionary and cannot be used against the President or Governors personally, or against private persons performing no public function.

Option (b), statements 2 and 3 only: this combination wrongly rejects statement 1. Mandamus is generally unavailable against private bodies, but it can lie where they perform a public duty or function. Quo warranto, from Latin for 'by what authority', questions the legal right of a person holding a public office. The court can remove the person from the office and declare it vacant. It is not available for private or ministerial offices.

Option (c), statements 1 and 3 only: this combination wrongly rejects statement 2. It would imply mandamus can lie against a Government Company. The official key treats a company as a separate legal entity against which mandamus does not lie. A Government Company has at least 51 percent government shareholding under the Companies Act, 2013. Whether it counts as 'State' under Article 12 depends on the context and test applied, as in Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib (1981).

Option (d), all three statements: this is the official answer. Statement 1 states the public duty exception for private bodies. Statement 2 states the rule that a company, even a Government Company, is not subject to mandamus. Statement 3 states the wide locus standi in quo warranto. The Supreme Court (Art. 32) and High Courts (Art. 226) issue five writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. High Courts have a wider writ jurisdiction because they can also issue writs for 'any other purpose'.
related: Article 32 is called the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution by Dr B.R. Ambedkar.
Article 226 gives High Courts wider writ powers than Article 32 gives the Supreme Court.
Prohibition is issued during proceedings; certiorari is issued after the order has been passed.
Habeas corpus can be filed by any person on behalf of the detainee.
Mandamus does not lie against the President or Governors personally (Article 361).
Quo warranto applies only to substantive public offices created by statute or the Constitution.
In L. Chandra Kumar (1997), the Supreme Court held that judicial review is part of the basic structure.
Under Article 359, enforcement of Fundamental Rights can be suspended during a National Emergency, except Articles 20 and 21 after the 44th Amendment.
statements: 1 — Correct: Mandamus does not lie against a purely private body, but it can lie if the body is entrusted with a public duty. Mandamus is issued to a public official, public body, corporation, inferior court or tribunal to perform a public or statutory duty they have refused to perform. The petitioner must show a legal right and a corresponding legal duty, and that a demand was made and refused. Courts have extended it to private bodies discharging public functions, such as some educational institutions. It cannot enforce discretionary or non-statutory duties, cannot be issued against the President or Governors personally (Art. 361), and does not lie against a private individual.

2 — Correct: Mandamus does not lie against a company, even a Government Company, as per the traditional position on which UPSC based its answer. A Government Company under Section 2(45) of the Companies Act, 2013 is one in which the government holds at least 51 percent of the paid-up share capital. It is a separate legal entity, so it is not treated as the State for issuing mandamus on private-law matters. Courts have, however, held such companies to be 'State' under Article 12 for Part III purposes in some cases, which is a different question. Statutory corporations like LIC and ONGC were held to be 'State' in earlier cases.

3 — Correct: Quo Warranto can be sought by any public-spirited person, not necessarily one personally affected. It is issued to prevent illegal usurpation of a public office. The office must be public, created by statute or the Constitution, substantive in nature, and the holder must not satisfy the legal qualifications. It cannot be issued against ministerial or private offices. It is one of the writs where the strict locus standi rule is relaxed, and it can be issued for offices such as a university Vice-Chancellor, a municipal officer or a minister if the appointment violates the law.
summary: The official answer is (d): all three statements are correct. Mandamus lies only against bodies performing a public duty (not purely private ones), it does not lie against a company, including a Government Company, and quo warranto can be sought by any public-spirited person, unlike most writs.
topic_notes: Writs are constitutional remedies for enforcing rights and for judicial review of administrative action. Article 32, a Fundamental Right itself, empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs only for enforcing Fundamental Rights. Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for Fundamental Rights and 'for any other purpose', so their jurisdiction is wider. Parliament can empower other courts to issue writs under Article 32(3). The Constitution's writ model derives from English prerogative writs. The five writs are: (1) Habeas corpus, which requires the detainee to be produced before the court, and which can be filed by any person on behalf of the detainee. (2) Mandamus, a command to perform a public duty; it does not lie against the President or Governors personally, against private individuals, for non-statutory duties, or for discretionary duties. (3) Prohibition, issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal to stop acting beyond jurisdiction, available only against judicial or quasi-judicial bodies while proceedings are pending. (4) Certiorari, issued to quash an order already passed by a lower court or tribunal for want of jurisdiction, excess of jurisdiction or error of law apparent on the face of the record. (5) Quo warranto, which tests a claim to a public office. Related points: Article 33 lets Parliament restrict rights for the armed forces, and Article 359 allows suspension of the right to move courts for enforcement of Fundamental Rights during an Emergency. Key cases include L. Chandra Kumar (1997), which held judicial review part of the basic structure, with tribunals' decisions subject to High Court review under Articles 226 and 227. In A.K. Kraipak, the court blurred the line between administrative and quasi-judicial acts. In ADM Jabalpur (1976), habeas corpus was held suspended during the Emergency, a decision later overruled by Puttaswamy (2017). Likely future angles include the differences between certiorari and prohibition, which writs lie against which authority, and which writs are available against private persons.

ocr: With reference to Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, consider the following statements : Private and public hospitals must adopt it. a 2. As it aims to achieve universal health coverage, every citizen of India should be part of it ultimately. . It has seamless portability across the country. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? 1 and 2 only (a) (b) 3 only (c) 1 and 3 only (d) 1,2 and3
subject: Geography
detail: The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) was piloted in six Union Territories from 27 September 2021 and launched nationwide by PM Modi on 27 September 2021 (the pilot began in 2020 as the National Digital Health Mission, announced on 15 August 2020). It is run by the National Health Authority (NHA) under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Its building blocks are the ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) number, formerly Health ID, a 14-digit number, the Healthcare Professionals Registry (HPR), the Health Facility Registry (HFR), and Personal Health Records (PHR) with consent-based data sharing. The design principle is interoperability through open standards, so a patient's records can be accessed by any enrolled provider anywhere in India, which is the portability in statement 3. Participation is voluntary: citizens choose to create an ABHA, and facilities, public or private, choose to register. This makes statement 1 wrong. Statement 2 is wrong because the mission aims to create digital health infrastructure, not to mandate that every citizen join; it is not an insurance scheme and should not be confused with the PM-JAY. Elimination: rejecting 1 or 2 leaves only (b).
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because hospital adoption is voluntary, and statement 2 is incorrect because citizen participation is voluntary.
Correct: only statement 3 is right, as the ABHA-based interoperable system provides seamless portability of health records across the country.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which wrongly says hospitals must adopt ABDM, though statement 3 is correct.
Wrong: it includes statements 1 and 2, both of which wrongly assume compulsion, so not all three are correct.
keyfact: ABDM is voluntary and consent-based, and ABHA-linked interoperable records give portability across India.
option_notes: Option (a) 1 and 2 only: this combines two statements about compulsion. In reality ABDM is opt-in for both facilities and citizens. Citizens create an ABHA number voluntarily through the ABHA app or a facility, and can delete it. Facilities register in the Health Facility Registry, and doctors in the Healthcare Professionals Registry, by choice. Consent-based data sharing is a core principle of the ABDM, in line with its Health Data Management Policy.

Option (b) 3 only: this is the official answer. ABDM, run by the National Health Authority, gives each user a 14-digit ABHA number and an ABHA address, and links Personal Health Records across providers. Open, interoperable standards allow records to be viewed anywhere in India with the user's consent. Launched nationwide on 27 September 2021 after a pilot in six Union Territories, it is a voluntary digital backbone and not an insurance scheme.

Option (c) 1 and 3 only: it correctly includes portability but wrongly includes mandatory adoption by hospitals. Hospitals, public or private, join ABDM voluntarily, and the Digital Health Incentives Scheme offers financial incentives for adoption. Mandatory participation exists only for facilities under particular government schemes, not for ABDM as a whole, so this option is incorrect.

Option (d) 1, 2 and 3: this would hold only if ABDM were compulsory for all hospitals and citizens. It is not. The mission builds a voluntary, consent-driven digital health ecosystem. Universal health coverage as a policy goal is handled by Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY (launched 23 September 2018) and the Health and Wellness Centres, which are separate components of the Ayushman Bharat umbrella.
related: ABDM is implemented by the National Health Authority under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
ABHA number is a 14-digit voluntary health ID.
ABDM was launched nationwide on 27 September 2021 after a pilot in six Union Territories.
PM-JAY gives Rs 5 lakh per family per year of health cover and was launched on 23 September 2018.
ABDM's core building blocks are ABHA, the Healthcare Professionals Registry and the Health Facility Registry.
ABDM data sharing is consent-based through a consent manager.
The National Digital Health Blueprint (2019) preceded the mission.
The Digital Health Incentives Scheme was introduced in January 2022.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Adoption is voluntary for both private and public hospitals; ABDM does not compel any facility to join. Facilities register in the Health Facility Registry by choice, though government schemes may incentivise or link participation. ABDM operates on a consent-based, opt-in model. Digital Health Incentives Scheme (from January 2022) gives financial incentives to hospitals and software firms that adopt ABDM-compliant digital solutions, which confirms it relies on encouragement rather than compulsion. The Unified Health Interface (UHI) is an open network layer within the mission.

2 — Incorrect: The mission's goal is to build digital health infrastructure and support universal health coverage, but it does not require every citizen to be part of it ultimately. Creating an ABHA number is voluntary, and a person can delete or deactivate it. Data is shared only with the user's consent through the consent manager. Universal health coverage as a goal is pursued by wider efforts such as Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY (insurance of up to Rs 5 lakh per family per year) and Health and Wellness Centres, not by compulsory ABDM enrolment.

3 — Correct: ABDM creates interoperable digital health records linked to ABHA, so patients' health information can move with them across hospitals, labs, pharmacies and states. It uses open standards, a federated architecture and the consent manager. Portability and continuity of care are central objectives, along with reducing duplicate tests and paperwork. The ABHA number is 14 digits and can be linked to an ABHA address (for example name@abdm). The National Health Authority implements it, and the Health Data Management Policy governs privacy.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 3 is correct. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) is a voluntary digital health ecosystem built on the Health ID (ABHA) and interoperable health records, which gives seamless portability of records across the country. Adoption by hospitals and enrolment by citizens are both voluntary, not mandatory.
topic_notes: Ayushman Bharat has two main pillars: Health and Wellness Centres (HWCs, now Ayushman Arogya Mandirs), which deliver comprehensive primary care, and the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY), launched on 23 September 2018 from Ranchi, providing cover up to Rs 5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation to about 10 crore poor and vulnerable families (about 50 crore beneficiaries). It is a centrally sponsored scheme implemented by the National Health Authority, with states sharing costs, and it is portable across states. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission is a separate digital layer. It evolved from the National Digital Health Mission announced on 15 August 2020, was piloted in six Union Territories (Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Ladakh, Lakshadweep, Puducherry), and launched nationwide on 27 September 2021. Its main components are the ABHA number (14 digits), the Health Facility Registry, the Healthcare Professionals Registry, Personal Health Records, a consent manager, and the Unified Health Interface. It follows the National Digital Health Blueprint (2019), which was based on recommendations of the Jaswant Singh-led committee... more specifically, the National Digital Health Blueprint was drafted by a committee headed by J. Satyanarayana. Key principles include voluntary participation, consent-based sharing, privacy by design, interoperability, and federated architecture. The Digital Health Incentives Scheme (January 2022) rewards providers who adopt it. Related areas that UPSC could ask on: eSanjeevani telemedicine, CoWIN, Aarogya Setu, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, the National Health Policy 2017 (health spending target 2.5% of GDP by 2025), and the Health Management Information System.

question: With reference to Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha, consider the following statements : 2, As per the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, the election of Deputy Speaker shall be held on such date as the Speaker may fix. There is a mandatory provision that the election of a candidate as Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha shall be from either the principal opposition party or the ruling party. The Deputy Speaker has the same power as of the Speaker when presiding over the sitting of the House and no appeal lies against his rulings. The well established parliamentary practice regarding the appointment of Deputy Speaker is that the motion is moved by the Speaker and duly seconded by the Prime Minister. Which of the statements given above are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: The Deputy Speaker is provided for under Article 93 of the Constitution, which requires the Lok Sabha to choose two members as Speaker and Deputy Speaker as soon as may be. Rule 8 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha says the election of the Deputy Speaker is held on a date fixed by the Speaker (the date for the Speaker's own election is fixed by the President or the Governor-appointed arrangement, i.e. the President). Article 95(1) provides that the Deputy Speaker performs the Speaker's duties when the office is vacant, and Article 95 also covers presiding in the Speaker's absence. When presiding, the Deputy Speaker has all the powers of the Speaker, and his decisions are final. Statement 2 is wrong because no rule requires the Deputy Speaker to come from the ruling or principal opposition party. Since 1977 there has been a convention, not a mandate, of offering the post to the opposition. Statement 4 is wrong because the motion for the Deputy Speaker's election is moved by a member and seconded by another member, not moved by the Speaker and seconded by the Prime Minister. Eliminating 2 and 4 leaves (a).
explanations: Correct. Statements 1 and 3 are accurate, and statements 2 and 4 are inaccurate, so this is the right combination.
Wrong. It includes statement 2, but there is no mandatory rule that the Deputy Speaker come from the ruling or the principal opposition party; that is only a convention.

Wrong. It includes statement 4, which is false because the Speaker does not move the motion and the Prime Minister does not second it. The option text is garbled by OCR, but it is not the correct combination.
Wrong. It includes only the two incorrect statements, 2 and 4, and leaves out both correct statements, 1 and 3.
keyfact: Deputy Speaker: elected on a date fixed by the Speaker (Rule 8), has the Speaker's powers when presiding, and no rule binds the post to any party; it is only a convention for the opposition.
option_notes: Statements 1 and 3 only: this is the correct pairing. It reflects Rule 8 on the date of election and Article 95 on the Deputy Speaker's powers while presiding. The Deputy Speaker is a constitutional office under Article 93, elected by the Lok Sabha from among its members. He holds office until he ceases to be a member, resigns, or is removed under Article 94 by a majority of all then members, with 14 days' notice. His salary is charged to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Statements 1, 2 and 3: this option wrongly adds statement 2. No law or rule forces the post to go to the ruling or the principal opposition party. The convention of offering the post to the opposition developed over time but is not constitutionally mandatory. Parliamentary conventions are practices followed over time without legal force, and they can be departed from, as in the 17th Lok Sabha, which had no Deputy Speaker for its entire term.

Statements 3 and 4 only (as OCR'd, '38 and 4'): this option pairs one correct statement with an incorrect one. The Deputy Speaker's powers when presiding are the Speaker's, but the claim of a motion moved by the Speaker and seconded by the Prime Minister is not established practice. Motions for the Deputy Speaker's election are moved by members, usually from the ruling side, and seconded by other members. The Prime Minister's role is ceremonial for the Speaker's election, not the Deputy Speaker's.

Statements 2 and 4 only: this option contains the two incorrect statements. Neither a mandatory party requirement nor a Speaker-moved, Prime Minister-seconded motion exists. The Deputy Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha by simple majority from among its members. The actual convention is that the post goes to the opposition (the practice dates from about 1990), and this was followed in several Lok Sabhas, including with the AIADMK in 2014.
related: Article 93: Lok Sabha chooses its Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
Article 94: vacation, resignation and removal of Speaker/Deputy Speaker; 14 days' notice for removal resolution.
Article 95: Deputy Speaker performs the Speaker's duties when the office is vacant or the Speaker is absent.
The Speaker's election date is fixed by the President; the Deputy Speaker's by the Speaker (Rule 8).
The 17th Lok Sabha had no Deputy Speaker.
Speaker's decision on Tenth Schedule disqualification is subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992).
Pro-tem Speaker is appointed by the President to administer oaths to new members.
The Deputy Speaker's office ends on dissolution of the Lok Sabha, while the Speaker continues until the new House meets.
statements: 1 — Correct: Rule 8 says the Deputy Speaker's election is held on a date fixed by the Speaker. Article 93 requires the House to choose the Deputy Speaker as soon as may be after the Speaker. The Deputy Speaker is elected from among the House's members, usually in the first few sessions after a general election. Once elected, he normally holds office until the dissolution of the House. He may resign by writing to the Speaker, and may be removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all then members of the House, with 14 days' notice (Article 94). The Speaker of the previous House continues until the new House meets.

2 — Incorrect: No mandatory provision requires the Deputy Speaker to belong to the principal opposition party or to the ruling party. Any member of the Lok Sabha can be elected. A convention, adopted around the 1990s and traced to the Lok Sabha of 1977, has the post going to the opposition, but it is not binding. For example, M. Thambidurai (AIADMK, 2014-19) belonged to a party outside the government. The 17th Lok Sabha (2019-24) did not elect any Deputy Speaker, which drew criticism of the constitutional spirit of Article 93.

3 — Correct: When presiding, the Deputy Speaker has the same powers as the Speaker, and no appeal lies against his rulings, since he acts as the Speaker in that situation (Article 95(1)). He does not vote in the first instance but has a casting vote in a tie, like the Speaker. He is not subordinate to the Speaker; he is directly responsible to the House. When a resolution to remove him is under consideration, he cannot preside, but he may speak and take part in the proceedings and vote, though not as a casting vote. The Deputy Speaker is also appointed ex officio to certain committees and chairs those to which he is named.

4 — Incorrect: The usual practice is that a member (typically from the ruling side) moves the motion proposing the Deputy Speaker's name, and another member seconds it. The Speaker does not move it, and the Prime Minister does not second it as a rule. When the Speaker is elected, the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition may move and second, then conduct the Speaker to the Chair. The Deputy Speaker is elected by a simple majority of members present and voting, usually unanimously. Once elected, the Speaker announces the result to the House.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 and 3 only. Statement 1 reflects Rule 8 of the Rules of Procedure of Lok Sabha, under which the Speaker fixes the date of the Deputy Speaker's election. Statement 3 is correct because the Deputy Speaker presiding over the House has the Speaker's powers and his rulings cannot be appealed. Statements 2 and 4 describe provisions or practices that do not exist.
topic_notes: The Speaker and Deputy Speaker are the presiding officers of the Lok Sabha. Articles 93 to 96 cover them: Article 93 provides for their election, Article 94 for vacation, resignation and removal, Article 95 for the Deputy Speaker's powers and for duties of the Speaker's office, and Article 96 states that the Speaker or Deputy Speaker cannot preside while a resolution for his removal is under consideration, though he can speak and vote (without a casting vote). Removal requires a resolution passed by a majority of all then members, with at least 14 days' notice. The Speaker's own election date is fixed by the President, whereas the Deputy Speaker's date is fixed by the Speaker (Rule 8). The first Speaker was G.V. Mavalankar (1952), and the first Deputy Speaker was M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar. The Speaker presides over joint sittings; in her or his absence the Deputy Speaker presides, and failing both, the member decided by Rules or the House. The Speaker has a casting vote only in a tie, decides on money bills, is the final authority on disqualification under the Tenth Schedule (subject to judicial review per Kihoto Hollohan, 1992), and, once elected, resigns from party membership by convention (as N. Sanjiva Reddy did in 1967). The Speaker continues in office after dissolution until the new Lok Sabha meets, while the Deputy Speaker's office ends on dissolution. UPSC may also ask about Rajya Sabha's equivalents: the Vice President is ex officio Chairman, and the Deputy Chairman is elected by members (Article 89). Related topics include the Panel of Chairpersons, the Pro-tem Speaker (appointed by the President to administer the oath), and the Speaker's salary being charged to the Consolidated Fund of India.

question: Among the following crops, which one is the 25. most important anthropogenic source of both methane and nitrous oxide ?
subject: Economy
detail: UPSC 2022 asked which crop is the most important anthropogenic source of both methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O). Rice is the answer because of how paddy is grown. Continuous flooding cuts off oxygen from the soil. Methanogenic archaea then decompose organic matter and produce methane. Rice cultivation contributes roughly 8-12% of global anthropogenic methane, and agriculture overall is a leading source. Nitrous oxide comes from nitrification and denitrification of nitrogen fertilisers (urea) and is higher when fields are drained and re-flooded, as in alternate wetting and drying (AWD). Methane has a global warming potential (GWP) of about 28-30 over 100 years, and N2O about 265-298. Wheat, cotton and sugarcane are grown in aerobic, non-flooded soils, so they emit little methane, although they do emit N2O from fertiliser. The phrase 'both' is the elimination key. Only rice combines a large methane source with a notable N2O source. Mitigation options include the System of Rice Intensification (SRI), direct seeded rice, AWD, and better fertiliser management.
explanations: Incorrect: Cotton is grown in aerobic upland soil, so it produces negligible methane. It has some N2O from fertiliser, but it is not a key methane source.

Correct: Flooded paddies produce methane through anaerobic decomposition and N2O through fertiliser nitrogen transformations, especially with water-management cycles. It is the crop that is a significant source of both gases.
Incorrect: Sugarcane is mostly irrigated but not flooded. Its main concern is N2O from fertiliser and emissions from residue burning, not methane from soil.
Incorrect: Wheat is grown in well-aerated soil, so it emits little methane. Its emissions are mainly N2O from fertiliser.
keyfact: Rice paddies are the crop source of both methane (anaerobic flooded soil) and nitrous oxide (nitrogen fertiliser).
option_notes: Cotton is a fibre and cash crop, the main kharif crop of Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana. India is among the top producers. Bt cotton was the first GM crop approved in India (2002). It needs black soil, warm weather and a long frost-free period. It is associated with heavy pesticide use and the bollworm pest, but it is not a major methane source.

Rice (Oryza sativa) is a kharif staple of India and is grown on about 40+ million hectares. West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh and Punjab are leading producers. It needs high temperature, humidity and water. Paddy fields are a major agricultural source of methane. IRRI is at Los Baños, Philippines, and India has an IRRI regional centre in Varanasi. Mitigation methods include SRI, AWD and direct seeding.

Sugarcane is a tropical, long-duration crop, and India is among the top two producers along with Brazil. Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka are leading states. It is a source of ethanol and bagasse, and the Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) is fixed by the Centre. Its emissions are mainly N2O from fertiliser and CO2 and other gases from burning residue.

Wheat is the main rabi cereal of India, grown in cool weather with 50-75 cm rainfall. Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Haryana are major producers. It is grown in aerobic soil, so methane is minimal. The Green Revolution began with high-yielding wheat varieties, and Norman Borlaug is associated with it. Its climate impact is mainly N2O from nitrogen fertiliser.
related: Rice paddies produce methane through methanogenic archaea in anaerobic flooded soil.
The largest agricultural source of methane is enteric fermentation in livestock.
Agriculture is the largest anthropogenic source of nitrous oxide, mainly from fertilisers.
GWP over 100 years: CO2 = 1, CH4 about 28, N2O about 265.
Global Methane Pledge (COP26, 2021) aims for a 30% cut by 2030; India is not a signatory.
SRI and alternate wetting and drying reduce methane from rice fields.
Nitrous oxide also depletes stratospheric ozone.
PM-PRANAM aims to reduce chemical fertiliser use.
summary: The answer is (b) Rice. Flooded paddy fields create anaerobic conditions in which methanogenic bacteria release methane, and nitrogen fertiliser use with alternate wetting and drying releases nitrous oxide, so rice is the major crop source of both gases.
topic_notes: Agriculture and greenhouse gases: Agriculture, forestry and land use produce about a fifth to a quarter of global greenhouse gas emissions. The main agricultural gases are methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O) and CO2. Methane sources include enteric fermentation in ruminants (the largest agricultural source), rice paddies, manure management, landfills, wetlands, and fossil fuel leaks. Methane has a short atmospheric life of about 12 years but traps much more heat than CO2. Nitrous oxide sources include nitrogen fertilisers, manure, and biomass burning. It stays in the atmosphere for about 114 years and also depletes stratospheric ozone. Agriculture is the largest anthropogenic N2O source. In 2021 at COP26 over 100 countries joined the Global Methane Pledge to cut methane emissions by 30% by 2030 from 2020 levels. India did not sign it. Rice mitigation methods: SRI, AWD, direct seeded rice, use of sulphate-containing fertilisers, and improved straw management. Urea neem coating and nano urea reduce N2O. Related Indian programmes: National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA) under the National Action Plan on Climate Change, the PM-PRANAM scheme to reduce chemical fertiliser use, Soil Health Card, and the Bharat Stage norms for other sectors. Global warming potential (GWP) values per IPCC: CO2 = 1, CH4 about 28, N2O about 265, and some fluorinated gases run to thousands. Other topics UPSC could ask: the Kyoto Protocol gases (CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs, SF6, and NF3 added later), the Montreal Protocol and Kigali Amendment, and the Methane Alert and Response System.

question:
“System of Rice Intensification” of cultivation, in which alternate wetting and drying of rice fields is practised, results in :
1. Reduced seed requirement
2. Reduced methane production 26.
3. Reduced electricity consumption Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Environment
detail: The System of Rice Intensification (SRI) is an agro-ecological method developed in Madagascar in the early 1980s by Fr. Henri de Laulanié and promoted globally by Norman Uphoff of Cornell University. Its core practices are: transplanting young seedlings (8-12 days old) singly, wide square spacing (25x25 cm), keeping soil moist but not continuously flooded (AWD), active soil aeration with a cono-weeder, and heavy use of organic manure. Seed need falls to about 5-7 kg/ha against 30-60 kg/ha in conventional transplanting. Continuous flooding creates anaerobic conditions where methanogenic bacteria produce methane; AWD introduces aerobic phases that suppress them, cutting methane substantially (IRRI reports around 30% or more) and also lowering water use by 25-50%. Less irrigation water means fewer hours of pumping, so less electricity or diesel, which matters in Punjab, Haryana and Tamil Nadu where tube-well irrigation is subsidised. Elimination logic: once you know statement 1 is true and either 2 or 3 is true, only (d) fits, since every option other than (d) leaves out at least one true statement.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out statement 3, and reduced electricity consumption is also a real benefit of SRI.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 1, but reduced seed requirement is a core feature of SRI.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 2, yet AWD clearly lowers methane emissions from paddy.
Correct: seed use, methane emissions and irrigation-linked electricity use all decline under SRI with AWD.
keyfact: SRI with AWD means fewer seeds, less methane and less pumping energy, so all three statements are correct, (d).
option_notes: Statements 1 and 2 only: this combination is true as far as it goes but incomplete. It reflects the seed saving from sparse single-seedling planting and the methane cut from AWD, and it ignores the energy saved on pumping water. Students should remember that SRI's benefits fall into three groups: inputs (seed, water, energy), environment (methane) and yield (often 20-50% higher).

Statements 2 and 3 only: this is also incomplete. It captures the methane reduction and the lower energy use from less irrigation, but misses the large seed saving. SRI cuts seed from tens of kilograms to a few kilograms per hectare. Tamil Nadu, Tripura and Bihar are prominent adopters of SRI in India.

Statements 1 and 3 only: it is incomplete because it leaves out the methane benefit. Paddy fields contribute about 10-12% of global methane emissions. AWD, a component of SRI, reduces anaerobic conditions. India's NDC and climate-smart agriculture programmes cite AWD and DSR as mitigation options for rice.

Statements 1, 2 and 3: this is the official answer. SRI combines young single seedlings, wide spacing, AWD water management, weeding with a cono-weeder, and organic nutrient management. It was developed in Madagascar in the 1980s, spread widely through Cornell's work, and is now used in over 50 countries. Benefits include higher yield, less seed, water, methane and energy use, and greater climate resilience.
related: SRI originated in Madagascar in the early 1980s through Fr. Henri de Laulanié.
AWD is promoted by IRRI as a water-saving technology for rice.
Paddy fields contribute roughly 10-12% of global anthropogenic methane.
Direct Seeded Rice avoids puddling and transplanting, saving water and labour.
ICAR-Indian Institute of Rice Research is in Hyderabad; NRRI is in Cuttack.
Sustainable Sugarcane Initiative (SSI) and System of Wheat Intensification (SWI) apply SRI principles.
Methane's 100-year global warming potential is about 28 times that of CO2.
Per Drop More Crop is a component of PMKSY focused on micro-irrigation.
statements: 1 — Correct: SRI uses single, very young seedlings at wide spacing, so seed need drops sharply. Facts: SRI needs about 5-7 kg seed per hectare against 30-60 kg in the conventional method. Seedlings are transplanted at 8-12 days, at the two-leaf stage, one per hill, in a square pattern about 25x25 cm. Originated in Madagascar in the 1980s (Fr. Henri de Laulanié). Tamil Nadu, Tripura, Odisha and Bihar have promoted it widely, with Bihar's Nalanda district known for record yields.

2 — Correct: AWD prevents continuous flooding, so methanogens are suppressed and methane falls. Facts: paddy fields are a major anthropogenic methane source, roughly 10-12% of global methane emissions. Methane is produced by methanogenic archaea in waterlogged anaerobic soil. AWD, promoted by IRRI, lets the field dry to about 15 cm below the surface before re-irrigating. A trade-off is that nitrous oxide emissions can rise slightly. Methane has a global warming potential about 28 times that of CO2 over 100 years.

3 — Correct: with less irrigation water needed, pumping hours and so electricity or diesel use decline. Facts: SRI saves 25-50% of water. In India many farmers use electric or diesel tube-wells, and agricultural power is heavily subsidised, so water saving also eases the power burden. Conventional paddy needs roughly 3,000-5,000 litres of water per kg of rice. Related initiatives include Direct Seeded Rice (DSR) and the PMKSY 'Per Drop More Crop' scheme.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. SRI uses very young single seedlings at wide spacing, and alternate wetting and drying (AWD) keeps fields unsaturated, so it cuts seed use, methane emissions and the pumping energy needed for irrigation.
topic_notes: System of Rice Intensification (SRI) is a methodology, not a variety or technology package, aimed at raising rice productivity with fewer inputs. It was developed in Madagascar in 1983 by Fr. Henri de Laulanié, a Jesuit priest, and promoted by Norman Uphoff through CIIFAD at Cornell. The main principles are early transplanting of young seedlings (8-12 days), one seedling per hill, wide spacing (25x25 cm), intermittent irrigation or AWD, mechanical weeding that also aerates soil, and organic manure. Typical claims are 20-50% higher yield, 25-50% water saving, 80-90% less seed and lower input cost. India: adopted in Tamil Nadu (since about 2000), Tripura, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Bihar and elsewhere. Under the National Food Security Mission SRI is promoted as a practice. Methane facts: it is the main greenhouse gas from flooded rice; AWD can cut it substantially but may raise N2O. India has pledged under the Glasgow commitments to cut emissions intensity and cut methane through the Global Methane Pledge (India did not sign it). Related practices: Direct Seeded Rice, Aerobic Rice, laser land levelling, Mechanised transplanting, and Rice-Wheat cropping system issues in the Indo-Gangetic Plain. Institutions: ICAR-Indian Institute of Rice Research (Hyderabad), IRRI (Los Baños, Philippines), National Rice Research Institute (Cuttack). Other angles UPSC may ask: Sustainable Rice Platform, Bhoomi Jal schemes, PMKSY, system of crop intensification (wheat, sugarcane as SWI and SSI), and climate-smart agriculture.

question: Which one of the following lakes of West Africa has become dry and turned into a desert ? 27
subject: Geography
detail: Lake Faguibine lies in the Timbuktu region of Mali, in the Sahel, and was once the largest of a system of lakes (with Télé, Gouber, Kamango and others) fed by floods of the Niger River through the Tassakant channel and Bamba channels. It depended on the annual Niger flood reaching it. The severe Sahelian droughts of the 1970s and 1980s, together with reduced Niger discharge, desertification and sand encroachment, stopped the inflow, and the lake has been mostly dry since the mid-1970s, with only occasional partial refilling in very wet years such as 1994-95 and 2000s. Fishing, farming and livestock communities lost their livelihoods and migrated, and the basin is now a classic example of climate- and drought-driven desertification. Elimination: Lake Victoria is in East Africa (Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania) and is the largest African lake, still full. Lake Volta in Ghana is a huge reservoir created by the Akosombo Dam (1965) on the Volta River, so it is expanding rather than drying. Lake Oguta is a small natural lake in Imo State, southeast Nigeria, and is not known to have dried. Only Faguibine fits.
explanations: Incorrect: Lake Victoria is in East Africa, not West Africa, and remains the largest lake in Africa by area; it has not turned into desert.
Correct: Lake Faguibine in northern Mali (West Africa) has largely dried up since the 1970s-80s droughts and reduced Niger flood inflow, leaving a desertified basin.
Incorrect: Lake Oguta is a small natural lake in Imo State, Nigeria, which is still a functioning lake and a tourist site, not a desert.
Incorrect: Lake Volta in Ghana is an artificial reservoir formed by the Akosombo Dam, one of the largest man-made lakes in the world; it is full, not dry.
keyfact: Lake Faguibine (Mali, near Timbuktu, Sahel) dried up after the 1970s-80s droughts and is a desertification example.
option_notes: Lake Victoria is Africa's largest lake by area (about 68,800 sq km) and the largest tropical lake in the world. It is shared by Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania. It is the main source of the White Nile, which exits at Jinja, Uganda. It is a major fishery (Nile perch) and faces water hweed (water hyacinth) and pollution problems. It is in East Africa, not West Africa.

Lake Faguibine is a shallow seasonal lake in the Timbuktu region of northern Mali, in the Sahel. It was fed by Niger River floods through channels. It dried up after the 1970s-80s droughts, and only partially refills in very wet years. Its collapse harmed fishing, farming and herding communities and is cited as an example of Sahelian desertification, with efforts at restoration such as channel clearing.

Lake Oguta is a natural freshwater lake in Oguta, Imo State, southeastern Nigeria. It is the largest natural lake in the state and is linked to the Njaba River, which connects to the Orashi River. It is known for tourism, the Oguta Lake Resort and local folklore (Ogbuide goddess). It is not a dried lake.

Lake Volta in Ghana is one of the world's largest artificial reservoirs by surface area (about 8,500 sq km). It was created by the Akosombo Dam on the Volta River, completed in 1965, mainly for hydroelectric power. It supports fishing, inland transport and irrigation. It is a case of impoundment, with resettlement of many people and ecological changes, not drying.
related: Lake Faguibine is in northern Mali near Timbuktu, in the Sahel.
Lake Chad has shrunk by about 90 percent since the 1960s; it is managed by the Lake Chad Basin Commission.
Great Green Wall (2007) is an African Union initiative to fight Sahel desertification.
UNCCD was adopted in 1994, came into force in 1996, and has its secretariat in Bonn.
Lake Volta in Ghana was created by the Akosombo Dam in 1965.
Lake Victoria is the largest African lake and the source of the White Nile.
Lake Poopó in Bolivia dried up in 2015.
India hosted UNCCD COP14 in 2019 at Greater Noida.
summary: The answer is (b) Lake Faguibine. It is a shallow lake in northern Mali, near Timbuktu, that has largely dried up since the 1970s-80s because of repeated droughts and reduced inflow from the Niger River flood channels, leaving a desertified basin.
topic_notes: Desertification and shrinking lakes are recurring UPSC themes. The Sahel is the semi-arid belt south of the Sahara stretching from Senegal to Sudan and Eritrea. Severe droughts in 1968-74 and 1982-85 caused famine, loss of livestock, migration and collapse of water bodies. Lake Chad, shared by Chad, Cameroon, Niger and Nigeria, has shrunk by roughly 90 percent from the 1960s because of drought, irrigation withdrawals and population pressure; it is managed by the Lake Chad Basin Commission (1964). Lake Faguibine in Mali is a more extreme case in which the lake has mostly dried up. The Niger River flows through Guinea, Mali, Niger, Benin and Nigeria, with the Inland Delta in Mali. Africa's Great Green Wall initiative (African Union, 2007) aims to restore degraded land across the Sahel with a belt of vegetation from Senegal to Djibouti. The UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) was adopted in 1994 and came into force in 1996, and its secretariat is in Bonn; India hosted COP14 in 2019 at Greater Noida. Other drying or shrinking water bodies include the Aral Sea (Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan), Lake Urmia (Iran), Lake Poopó (Bolivia, which dried in 2015), the Dead Sea and Lake Mead. Lake Volta, Lake Kariba (Zambia-Zimbabwe) and Lake Nasser (Egypt-Sudan) are big African reservoirs.
