Vietnam joined ASEAN in 1995 and the WTO in 2007.
Vietnam is a one-party state ruled by the Communist Party of Vietnam.
EVFTA, the EU-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement, came into force in August 2020.
India and Vietnam have a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, upgraded in 2016.
Vietnam is a member of CPTPP and RCEP.
Capital of Vietnam is Hanoi; currency is the dong.
Mekong-Ganga Cooperation includes India, Vietnam, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia.
statements: 1 — Correct: Vietnam has recorded consistently high GDP growth, roughly 6-8% in many recent years, apart from the COVID dip. Facts: Doi Moi (1986) liberalised the economy; it moved from one of the poorest countries to lower-middle-income status; GDP growth was about 8% in 2022; it is a major electronics, textile and agri-export hub, and is part of ASEAN, CPTPP and RCEP.

2 — Incorrect: Vietnam is a one-party socialist republic. Facts: the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) holds the leadership role under Article 4 of the Constitution; the General Secretary is the top leader (Nguyen Phu Trong until 2024, then To Lam); the National Assembly is the legislature; the President is head of state and the Prime Minister head of government; the Party Congress meets every five years.

3 — Correct: Growth is strongly export-led and tied to global supply chains. Facts: exports exceed 80-90% of GDP in trade-to-GDP terms; FDI-driven firms like Samsung dominate exports; the US, China, EU and Japan are key markets; EVFTA (2020), CPTPP (2018) and RCEP (2020) support integration; the 'China plus one' diversification has helped it gain from supply chain shifts.

4 — Correct: Low labour costs and a relatively stable, managed exchange rate drew manufacturers for years. Facts: wages are lower than in China; the State Bank of Vietnam manages the dong through a crawling-peg-like band; there is a young workforce, political stability, and special economic zones and industrial parks with tax incentives; rising wages and infrastructure gaps are emerging constraints.

5 — Incorrect: There is no basis for the claim that Vietnam has the most productive e-service sector in the Indo-Pacific. Facts: its digital economy is growing rapidly (e-commerce, fintech), but Singapore, India, South Korea and Japan are usually ranked higher in digital services; Vietnam's strength is manufacturing exports, not e-services leadership. Beware such superlatives in UPSC statements.
summary: The answer is (c): statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. Vietnam is a fast-growing, export-led economy integrated into global supply chains and long attractive to manufacturers for low labour costs and a stable currency, but it is a one-party socialist state and has no claim to the most productive e-service sector in the Indo-Pacific.
topic_notes: Vietnam's economy was transformed by Doi Moi (renovation), adopted at the Sixth Party Congress in 1986. It shifted from central planning to a socialist-oriented market economy, encouraged private enterprise, agricultural decollectivisation and foreign investment. Vietnam joined ASEAN in 1995, normalised ties with the US in 1995, signed the US bilateral trade agreement in 2000 and joined the WTO in 2007. It is a member of APEC, CPTPP (in force 2018 for Vietnam), RCEP (2020) and has the EU-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA, in force Aug 2020). Exports are dominated by electronics (Samsung alone is a major share), machinery, textiles, footwear, furniture, seafood, coffee and rice. Vietnam is among the top exporters of coffee (Robusta), cashew and pepper. The US is its largest export market, and China its largest source of imports. FDI inflows are driven by South Korea, Japan, Singapore and Taiwan. Politically, the Communist Party of Vietnam rules under Article 4 of the Constitution, with the 'four pillars' of leadership: General Secretary, President, Prime Minister and National Assembly Chair. Currency: dong (VND). Geography: borders China, Laos and Cambodia; the South China Sea is called the East Sea in Vietnam. Disputes with China over the Paracel and Spratly islands are ongoing. India-Vietnam relations: Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (2016), defence cooperation, ONGC Videsh's oil blocks in the South China Sea, a line of credit for defence and BrahMos interest. Vietnam is also part of the Mekong-Ganga Cooperation and the Mekong Delta region. Likely UPSC angles: ASEAN membership, supply chain diversification, the Indo-Pacific, South China Sea disputes, trade pacts and India's bilateral ties.

question: In India, which one of the following is responsible for maintaining price stability by controlling inflation ?
subject: Economy
detail: Price stability through inflation control is the core objective of monetary policy, which in India is run by the Reserve Bank of India. The RBI Act, 1934 was amended by the Finance Act 2016 to provide a statutory Monetary Policy Framework and to set up a six-member Monetary Policy Committee (three RBI members including the Governor, who has a casting vote, and three external members appointed by the Central Government). The inflation target is set by the Government in consultation with the RBI, every five years; since 2016 it is 4% CPI (Combined) with a tolerance band of +/-2% (2% to 6%). If average inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI is deemed to have failed and must report to the Government. Tools include repo rate, reverse repo, CRR, SLR, MSF, OMOs and the standing deposit facility. Elimination: the Department of Consumer Affairs handles consumer protection, essential commodity availability and price monitoring, but not monetary policy. The Expenditure Management Commission (Kelkar-led, 2014) advised on fiscal consolidation and expenditure reform. FSDC is a council for financial stability and inter-regulatory coordination, not inflation targeting. Hence (d).
explanations: Incorrect: The Department of Consumer Affairs (Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution) monitors prices of essential commodities and implements the Essential Commodities Act and consumer protection, but it has no statutory duty or tools to control inflation through monetary policy.

Incorrect: The Expenditure Management Commission was set up in 2014 under Dr Bimal Jalan's predecessor-style fiscal reform effort (headed by Vijay Kelkar) to recommend ways to rationalise government expenditure; it does not manage price stability.

Incorrect: FSDC is an apex inter-regulatory body chaired by the Finance Minister that focuses on financial stability, financial sector development and inter-regulatory coordination; it does not set or implement inflation targets.
Correct: The RBI, via the MPC and the flexible inflation targeting framework (4% +/-2% CPI), is legally responsible for price stability.
keyfact: RBI (through the six-member MPC) targets 4% CPI inflation with a +/-2% band under the RBI Act, 1934 as amended in 2016.
option_notes: The Department of Consumer Affairs is under the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution. It administers the Consumer Protection Act 2019, Legal Metrology, the Essential Commodities Act and the Price Stabilisation Fund, and runs the Price Monitoring Division and the National Consumer Helpline. It can use stock limits and market interventions, but monetary policy is outside its remit.

The Expenditure Management Commission was constituted in 2014 under Dr Bimal Jalan? No: it was chaired by Dr Vijay Kelkar, former Finance Secretary, to suggest reforms for rationalising government expenditure, subsidies and fiscal consolidation, including looking at food, fertiliser and fuel subsidies. It is an advisory fiscal body and has no role in monetary or inflation control.

The Financial Stability and Development Council was set up in 2010 by executive resolution (not statute) as an apex body for financial stability, inter-regulatory coordination and financial literacy and inclusion. It is chaired by the Union Finance Minister, and its members include heads of RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA and the Finance Secretary. It also has a sub-committee headed by the RBI Governor.

The Reserve Bank of India, established on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934, is the central bank, nationalised in 1949. It issues currency, acts as banker to government and banks, regulates the financial system and manages forex under FEMA. Through the six-member MPC it sets the policy repo rate to meet the 4% (+/-2%) CPI inflation target.
related: MPC was established in 2016 under Section 45ZB of the RBI Act, 1934.
India's inflation target is 4% CPI with a tolerance band of +/-2%.
The Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommended CPI-based flexible inflation targeting.
The Governor of RBI has a casting vote in the MPC.
CPI (base 2012) is released by NSO under MoSPI; WPI by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT.
FSDC was set up in 2010 and is chaired by the Finance Minister.
The policy repo rate is the main tool used by the MPC.
Section 45ZN requires RBI to report to Government if the inflation target is missed for three consecutive quarters.
summary: The answer is (d) Reserve Bank of India. The RBI, through its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) under the RBI Act, 1934 (as amended in 2016), is statutorily mandated to maintain price stability while keeping in mind the objective of growth, by targeting CPI inflation.
topic_notes: Monetary policy in India is governed by the RBI Act, 1934, amended in 2016 to create a statutory Monetary Policy Framework. This followed the Urjit Patel Committee (2014), which recommended flexible inflation targeting with CPI as the nominal anchor, and the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement of February 2015 between the Government and RBI. The MPC has six members: the Governor (chair), the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one other RBI officer, and three external members appointed by the Centre for four years, not eligible for reappointment. It meets at least four times a year, quorum is four, decisions are by majority, and the Governor has a casting vote in a tie. The inflation target of 4% with a band of 2-6% was retained in March 2021 for 2021-26. Failure is defined as average inflation above the upper band or below the lower band for three consecutive quarters. Instruments: quantitative (CRR, SLR, repo, reverse repo, MSF, bank rate, OMOs, LAF, SDF) and qualitative (margin requirements, moral suasion, selective credit control). Before 2016, WPI and then CPI-based approaches were used, and the Urjit Patel Committee moved to CPI (Combined). The government complements RBI through fiscal policy, supply side steps, buffer stocks, import duty cuts and export curbs. Other angles: CPI is compiled by the NSO (MoSPI) with base year 2012; WPI is published by the Office of the Economic Adviser (DPIIT); the FRBM Act governs fiscal deficit targets; the FSDC handles systemic risk coordination.

question:
With reference to Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), consider the following statements :
1. They enable the digital representation of physical assets.
2. They are unique cryptographic tokens that exist on a blockchain.
8. They can be traded or exchanged at equivalency and therefore can be used as a medium of commercial transactions. Which of the statements given above are correct ?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: A Non-Fungible Token (NFT) is a unique cryptographic token recorded on a blockchain, most commonly Ethereum using standards such as ERC-721 and ERC-1155. It serves as a verifiable certificate of ownership or authenticity. NFTs can represent digital items (art, music, game assets, collectibles, domain names) and also physical assets (real estate, artwork, luxury goods) through tokenisation, so statement 1 holds. Statement 2 is the textbook definition. 'Non-fungible' means not mutually interchangeable: one NFT differs from another in metadata, token ID and value. Fungible assets such as currency, Bitcoin or gold units are identical and exchangeable at equivalency, which is why they work as a medium of exchange. Statement 3 attributes this fungible property to NFTs, which contradicts their definition. NFTs can be bought and sold at negotiated prices, but they are not traded at equivalency and so are not a medium of exchange. The elimination logic is that statement 3 is wrong, which removes (b), (c) and (d) and leaves (a). In India, the Union Budget 2022-23 introduced a 30% tax on gains from virtual digital assets, which include NFTs.
explanations: Correct: statements 1 and 2 are correct and statement 3 is wrong, which is exactly this combination.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is incorrect, and leaves out statement 1, which is correct.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is incorrect, and leaves out statement 2, which is correct.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is incorrect because NFTs are non-fungible and not exchanged at equivalency.
keyfact: NFTs are unique blockchain tokens that can represent physical or digital assets, but being non-fungible they cannot be exchanged at equivalency like money.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only: This is the correct combination, matching the standard definition of an NFT. NFTs are unique blockchain tokens that can represent digital items or tokenised physical assets. They are not fungible and so do not serve as currency. Remember the pairing 'representation of assets plus uniqueness on blockchain', and 'no equivalency'.

2 and 3 only: This would be correct only if NFTs were exchangeable at equivalency. Statement 2 is right, but statement 3 confuses NFTs with fungible cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin or Ether. Fungibility means each unit is identical and interchangeable, which is the property of money. NFTs lack it, so this option fails.

1 and 3 only: Statement 1 is right but statement 3 is wrong, and the option omits statement 2, the core definition of an NFT. UPSC often builds wrong options by mixing one correct statement with a plausible-sounding but wrong claim. Here the wrong claim is that NFTs work as a medium of exchange.

1, 2 and 3: This would make NFTs interchangeable and usable as money. In reality an NFT's value is individually determined and it cannot be swapped like-for-like. Only statements 1 and 2 hold. Watch for 'all of the above' traps when one statement contradicts a defining feature.
related: NFT = Non-Fungible Token; each token is unique and not interchangeable.
Most NFTs use Ethereum standards ERC-721 and ERC-1155.
Bitcoin and Ether are fungible; NFTs are non-fungible.
India taxes gains on virtual digital assets, including NFTs, at 30% (Section 115BBH), with 1% TDS (Section 194S).
Ethereum moved from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake (The Merge) in September 2022.
Smart contracts are self-executing code on a blockchain, used to mint and transfer NFTs.
RBI's CBDC, the digital rupee, is legal tender, unlike NFTs or private crypto.
Beeple's NFT artwork sold at Christie's in March 2021 for about $69 million.
statements: 1 — Correct: NFTs can digitally represent physical assets through tokenisation. Examples include real estate deeds, artwork, collectibles, tickets and luxury goods, where the token on the blockchain acts as a proof of title or authenticity linked to the real object. The token does not itself change legal ownership unless the law recognises it. Smart contracts can embed rights such as royalties for creators. Digital-native NFTs include art such as Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days', sold at Christie's in March 2021 for about $69 million.

2 — Correct: An NFT is a unique cryptographic token that exists on a blockchain. Each has a distinct token ID and metadata, and its ownership history is publicly verifiable and tamper-resistant. Common standards are ERC-721 (single unique tokens) and ERC-1155 (multi-token standard) on Ethereum, with others on Solana, Polygon and Flow. The term gained mainstream attention in 2021 through CryptoKitties (2017), CryptoPunks and Bored Ape Yacht Club. NFTs are minted via smart contracts and traded on marketplaces such as OpenSea.

3 — Incorrect: NFTs are not traded at equivalency, so they are not a medium of commercial transactions. Fungible assets such as rupees, dollars, Bitcoin and Ether are identical and interchangeable, so one unit equals another. An NFT is unique, so its price is set by negotiation and demand and cannot be swapped one-for-one at a fixed value. They are therefore treated as assets or collectibles and not as money. In India, NFTs are classed as virtual digital assets, with a 30% tax on gains under Section 115BBH and 1% TDS under Section 194S.
summary: The answer is (a): statements 1 and 2 are correct and statement 3 is incorrect. NFTs are unique blockchain-based cryptographic tokens that can represent physical or digital assets. Because each NFT is unique and non-fungible, it cannot be exchanged at equivalency like currency, so it is not a medium of commercial transactions.
topic_notes: NFTs are digital tokens that prove ownership or authenticity of a unique item, recorded on a blockchain. Blockchain is a distributed, tamper-resistant ledger of cryptographically linked blocks, maintained by a network of nodes without a central authority. Key concepts: fungible versus non-fungible (a rupee note or a Bitcoin is interchangeable; a painting or an NFT is unique); smart contracts (self-executing code that mints and transfers tokens and can pay royalties to creators); minting (creating the token on the chain); wallets and gas fees. Standards: ERC-721 and ERC-1155 on Ethereum. Platforms: OpenSea, Rarible, and Indian ones such as WazirX NFT and Bollycoin. Famous cases: CryptoKitties (2017), CryptoPunks, Bored Ape Yacht Club, Beeple's artwork (2021), and Jack Dorsey's first tweet sold as an NFT. Indian context: Budget 2022-23 defined virtual digital assets (VDAs), including NFTs, in the Income Tax Act (Section 2(47A)), with a flat 30% tax on gains (Section 115BBH) and 1% TDS (Section 194S) from 1 July 2022. The RBI has expressed concern about private cryptocurrencies, and India is piloting its central bank digital currency, the digital rupee (e-rupee), launched in pilot form in late 2022. NFTs are not legal tender and are not regulated as securities or currency. Risks: price volatility, copyright infringement, wash trading, money laundering, and environmental costs for proof-of-work chains (Ethereum shifted to proof-of-stake in September 2022). Other angles for UPSC include blockchain applications in land records and supply chains, differences between cryptocurrency, CBDC and NFTs, and the Web3 and metaverse links.

question:
Consider the following pairs : Reservoirs States
1. Ghataprabha — Telangana
2. GandhiSagar — Madhya Pradesh
3. IndiraSagar — Andhra Pradesh
4. Maithon — Chhattisgarh How many pairs given above are not correctly matched ?
subject: Modern History
detail: This is a reservoir-location question, and the key skill is tying each reservoir to its river and state. Ghataprabha is a Krishna tributary rising in the Western Ghats; the Ghataprabha reservoir (Hidkal Dam) is in Belagavi district, Karnataka, not Telangana. Gandhi Sagar is on the Chambal river in Mandsaur district, Madhya Pradesh, and is one of the three Chambal dams along with Rana Pratap Sagar (Rajasthan) and Jawahar Sagar (Rajasthan). Indira Sagar is on the Narmada at Punasa in Khandwa district, Madhya Pradesh, and is the largest reservoir by storage in India's Narmada system, so it is not in Andhra Pradesh. Maithon is on the Barakar river, a Damodar tributary, in Dhanbad district, Jharkhand, and is a DVC project, so it is not in Chhattisgarh. Only pair 2 is correct, which makes three pairs wrong. Elimination logic: if you know any two of the wrong pairs, you can rule out (a) and (b). Knowing that Indira Sagar is on the Narmada, together with Maithon being a DVC dam, gets you to (c) or (d). Gandhi Sagar's location on the Chambal then rules out (d).
explanations: Wrong. Only one pair, pair 2, is correctly matched, so the count of incorrect pairs is three, not one.
Wrong. Two incorrect pairs would require that two of pairs 1, 3 and 4 be correct, but all three are wrong.
Correct. Pairs 1, 3 and 4 are wrongly matched (Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh and Jharkhand are the true states), while pair 2 is right.
Wrong. Gandhi Sagar is in Madhya Pradesh, so at least one pair is correct and not all four are wrong.
keyfact: Gandhi Sagar = Chambal, MP; Indira Sagar = Narmada, MP; Maithon = Barakar (DVC), Jharkhand; Ghataprabha = Karnataka.
option_notes: Only one pair: this would mean three pairs are correct. It is the typical trap for students who recall Indira Sagar or Maithon only vaguely. In this question only Gandhi Sagar is correct, so this option is wrong. In general, 'only one' options reward partial knowledge, so check each pair against its river and state before answering.

Only two pairs: this would mean two pairs are correct. It tempts students who confuse Indira Sagar (Narmada, MP) with Indirasagar Polavaram (Godavari, Andhra Pradesh). Only one pair here is actually correct. Polavaram is a national project under the Polavaram Irrigation Project, and its reservoir is also called Indira Sagar, which is a classic confusion.

Only three pairs: this is the official answer. Pair 1 should be Karnataka, pair 3 should be Madhya Pradesh, and pair 4 should be Jharkhand, so three pairs are incorrect. Only Gandhi Sagar (Chambal, Madhya Pradesh) is correct. Remember that reservoirs are tested by river and state, and that DVC dams sit in Jharkhand and West Bengal.

All four pairs: this would mean every pair is wrong. Gandhi Sagar is on the Chambal in Madhya Pradesh, so this option fails. It is a typical extreme-option trap. UPSC often makes one pair correct to test whether students overgeneralise from doubt, so always verify the one pair you are sure about.
related: Gandhi Sagar Dam is on the Chambal in Madhya Pradesh.
Indira Sagar (Punasa, Khandwa) is on the Narmada in Madhya Pradesh.
Polavaram project on the Godavari in Andhra Pradesh is also called Indirasagar.
Maithon dam is on the Barakar in Jharkhand and belongs to the Damodar Valley Corporation.
Hidkal Dam on the Ghataprabha is in Belagavi, Karnataka.
Tehri Dam on the Bhagirathi in Uttarakhand is India's tallest dam.
Hirakud Dam on the Mahanadi in Odisha is among the world's longest earthen dams.
Nagarjuna Sagar on the Krishna lies on the Telangana and Andhra Pradesh border.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Ghataprabha is in Karnataka, not Telangana. The Ghataprabha is a left-bank tributary of the Krishna that rises in the Western Ghats in Maharashtra and flows through Karnataka. The Hidkal Dam near Gokak in Belagavi district forms the Raja Lakhamagouda reservoir. It serves irrigation and hydropower, and the Gokak Falls lie on the river. It joins the Krishna near the Almatti reservoir area. The Ghataprabha Left Bank and Right Bank Canals irrigate parts of Belagavi and Bagalkot.

2 — Correct: Gandhi Sagar is on the Chambal in Mandsaur and Neemuch district, Madhya Pradesh. Completed in 1960, it was the first of the Chambal Valley Project dams, which is a joint project of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. Its power station serves both states. Downstream are Rana Pratap Sagar at Rawatbhata, Rajasthan, Jawahar Sagar near Kota, and the Kota Barrage. The Gandhi Sagar Wildlife Sanctuary lies nearby, and the Chambal flows into the Yamuna. Cheetahs have been relocated to the Gandhi Sagar sanctuary landscape.

3 — Incorrect: Indira Sagar is in Madhya Pradesh, not Andhra Pradesh. It is at Narmada Sagar/Punasa in Khandwa district and is the main reservoir of the Narmada Valley Development Project. It has one of the largest storage capacities of any Indian reservoir and a 1,000 MW power station. Downstream is Omkareshwar Dam. Andhra Pradesh's counterpart is Indirasagar (Polavaram) on the Godavari, a possible source of confusion. The Narmada flows west into the Arabian Sea, and Sardar Sarovar in Gujarat is the other major dam.

4 — Incorrect: Maithon is in Jharkhand, not Chhattisgarh. It lies in Dhanbad district on the Barakar river near the West Bengal border. Commissioned in 1957 under the Damodar Valley Corporation, which was India's first multipurpose river valley project and was modelled on the Tennessee Valley Authority. It has an underground power station and provides flood control. Other DVC dams are Tilaiya, Konar, Panchet Hill, and Durgapur Barrage. The Damodar was once called the 'Sorrow of Bengal'.
summary: The answer is (c): only three pairs are incorrectly matched. Only Gandhi Sagar–Madhya Pradesh is correct; Ghataprabha is in Karnataka, Indira Sagar is in Madhya Pradesh, and Maithon is in Jharkhand (Jharkhand–West Bengal border, on the Barakar river).
topic_notes:
Reservoirs and river valley projects are a recurring UPSC prelims theme, often asked as pairs of dam, river and state.

Chambal: rises near Mhow (Janapav hills) in Madhya Pradesh and joins the Yamuna. Dams: Gandhi Sagar (MP), Rana Pratap Sagar (Rajasthan), Jawahar Sagar (Rajasthan), Kota Barrage. The Chambal is known for ravines and the National Chambal Gharial Sanctuary.

Narmada: flows west through MP, Maharashtra and Gujarat into the Gulf of Khambhat. Dams: Indira Sagar (largest storage), Omkareshwar, Maheshwar, Bargi, and Sardar Sarovar (Gujarat). It flows in a rift valley, and the Narmada Bachao Andolan is linked to Sardar Sarovar.

Damodar: DVC dams include Maithon and Panchet (Jharkhand/West Bengal), Tilaiya and Konar (Jharkhand). It was India's first multipurpose project (1948 DVC Act).

Krishna basin: Ghataprabha (Hidkal), Malaprabha (Malaprabha dam at Savadatti), Almatti (Karnataka), Nagarjuna Sagar (Telangana and Andhra Pradesh border), Srisailam, Tungabhadra, and Jurala. Koyna in Maharashtra is a major hydropower dam.

Other important dams: Bhakra Nangal (Sutlej, Himachal Pradesh), Hirakud (Mahanadi, Odisha, among the longest earthen dams), Tehri (Bhagirathi, Uttarakhand, tallest in India), Mettur (Cauvery, Tamil Nadu), Idukki (Periyar, Kerala), Rihand/Govind Ballabh Pant Sagar (Uttar Pradesh), Tungabhadra (Karnataka), and Polavaram (Godavari, Andhra Pradesh).

Study tip: group dams by river, then place each river in its state. UPSC often swaps states among similar-sounding names such as Indira Sagar and Indirasagar Polavaram.

question: In India, which one of the following compiles 74, information on industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments and lay-offs in factories employing workers ?
options: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
subject: Economy
detail: The Labour Bureau, headquartered in Shimla with offices in Chandigarh, Chennai, Kolkata, Mumbai, Kanpur and Guwahati, was set up in 1920 and is the Ministry of Labour and Employment's statistical and research arm. Its mandate covers collecting, compiling and publishing labour statistics: Consumer Price Index for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW, base 2016=100), the Consumer Price Index for Agricultural and Rural Labourers, wage rates in occupations, the Annual Survey of Industries-linked labour data, industrial disputes (strikes, lockouts), and data on lay-offs, retrenchments and closures under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (now subsumed in the Industrial Relations Code, 2020). It also runs the Annual Employment-Unemployment Survey and the Quarterly Employment Survey. Elimination: the CSO (under MoSPI) handles national accounts, IIP, and coordination of statistics, not industrial relations data. DPIIT (Ministry of Commerce and Industry) deals with industrial policy, FDI and startups. NTMIS (under the Ministry of Education, earlier AICTE-linked) tracks technical manpower supply and demand. Only the Labour Bureau matches the question.
explanations: Incorrect: The Central Statistics Office (under MoSPI) compiles national accounts, IIP, CPI (since 2011) and the Annual Survey of Industries, but not the industrial disputes, closures, retrenchment and lay-off data.
Incorrect: DPIIT formulates industrial and FDI policy, runs Startup India and manages IPR administration; it is a policy department, not a labour statistics compiler.

Correct: The Labour Bureau, under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, compiles and publishes data on industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments and lay-offs in factories, along with other labour statistics.
Incorrect: NTMIS provides data on supply of and demand for technical manpower and is not concerned with industrial disputes or closures.
keyfact: Labour Bureau (Shimla, est. 1920, Ministry of Labour and Employment) compiles data on industrial disputes, closures, retrenchments and lay-offs, plus CPI-IW.
option_notes: The Central Statistics Office is part of the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI). It coordinates statistical activities, sets standards and compiles National Accounts (GDP, GVA), the Index of Industrial Production, Consumer Price Index (base 2012) and the Annual Survey of Industries. It works with the NSO, which combined the CSO and NSSO in 2019. It is headed by a Director General.

The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) is under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, renamed from DIPP in 2019. It formulates industrial policy, FDI policy, and promotes Startup India, Ease of Doing Business, and the Invest India initiative. It also administers patents, trademarks, designs and GIs and oversees internal trade and the National Single Window System.

The Labour Bureau is an attached office of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, set up in October 1920 and headquartered at Shimla. It compiles labour statistics including CPI-IW (base 2016=100), CPI-AL and CPI-RL, wage rates, industrial relations data, and conducts the Annual Employment-Unemployment Survey and the All India Quarterly Establishment-based Employment Survey (AQEES).

The National Technical Manpower Information System was set up by the Ministry of Education (then HRD) in the 1980s as a nodal system with state-level nodal centres. It maintains data on supply and demand of technical manpower, such as engineers, diploma holders and postgraduates, to aid planning of technical education, and has been linked with AICTE and the National Data Registry.
related: Labour Bureau was established in 1920 and is headquartered in Shimla.
CPI-IW base year is now 2016=100, published by the Labour Bureau.
The Industrial Relations Code, 2020 raised the threshold for layoff and closure permission to 300 workers.
PLFS is conducted by the NSO under MoSPI, not the Labour Bureau.
NSO was formed in 2019 by merging the CSO and the NSSO.
The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 was subsumed into the Industrial Relations Code, 2020.
V.V. Giri National Labour Institute is an autonomous body under the Ministry of Labour and Employment.
DGFASLI handles factory safety and health advice under the Ministry of Labour.
summary: The answer is (c) Labour Bureau. It is an attached office of the Ministry of Labour and Employment, and it compiles and publishes statistics on industrial relations, including disputes (strikes and lockouts), closures, retrenchments and lay-offs in factories, mostly from returns submitted by states and Union Territories.
topic_notes: Labour statistics in India are mainly handled by the Labour Bureau, under the Ministry of Labour and Employment. Established in 1920 and located in Shimla, it publishes the CPI-IW (base 2016=100) monthly, which is used for calculating dearness allowance for central government employees and revising minimum wages in many sectors. It also publishes CPI-AL and CPI-RL, the Pocket Book of Labour Statistics, the Indian Labour Year Book, and the Statistics on Industrial Disputes, Closures, Retrenchments and Lay-offs, as well as reports from the Working Class Family Income and Expenditure Surveys. It runs the Annual Employment-Unemployment Survey and the Quarterly Employment Survey, and operates as the secretariat for the Wage Rate Index. The legal framework for industrial disputes was the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, which dealt with strikes, lockouts, lay-off, retrenchment and closure (Chapter VB covers establishments with 100 or more workers, requiring government permission). In 2020, four Labour Codes were passed: Code on Wages (2019), Industrial Relations Code (2020), Code on Social Security (2020) and Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code (2020). The Industrial Relations Code raised the threshold for government permission for layoffs, retrenchment and closure to 300 workers. Other related bodies: the Directorate General of Factory Advice Service and Labour Institutes (DGFASLI) for factory safety, the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), the ESIC, the Directorate General of Mines Safety, and the V.V. Giri National Labour Institute (NOIDA). Data sources on employment include the PLFS (by NSO), the ASI (by NSO/MoSPI), and EPFO payroll data. Distinguish carefully among these institutions as UPSC likes to test which body does what.

question:
In India, what is the role of the Coal Controller’s Organization (CCO) ?
1. CCO is the major source of Coal Statistics in Government of India.
2. It monitors progress of development of Captive Coal/Lignite blocks. 75.
3. It hears any objection to the Government’s notification relating to acquisition of coal-bearing areas.
4. It ensures that coal mining companies deliver the coal to end users in the prescribed time. Select the correct answer using the code given below : 76
subject: Geography
detail: The Coal Controller's Organisation (CCO) is a subordinate office of the Ministry of Coal, headquartered in Kolkata with zonal offices at Dhanbad, Ranchi, Bilaspur, Nagpur and elsewhere. It traces back to 1916, when the post of Coal Controller was created, and it has been reorganised several times since. Its main functions are: (i) collecting, compiling and publishing coal and lignite statistics, such as production, despatch, stocks, prices, washery data and royalty; (ii) inspecting and monitoring captive and commercial coal blocks, including progress of development, production and compliance with the mine plan; (iii) grading and classifying coal and checking declared grades; (iv) administering the Colliery Control Rules, 2004; (v) acting as the competent authority for hearing objections to acquisition notifications under the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957 (Section 4 notices); and (vi) handling the Coal Mines (Conservation and Development) work, levies and the Stowing Excise Duty. Statement 4 is wrong because supply to consumers is handled by Coal India Limited and its subsidiaries through fuel supply agreements, with the Ministry of Coal and the coal companies overseeing delivery. Elimination: statements 1 and 2 are certain, and statement 3 is a known less obvious function. Options (b), (c) and (d) either drop 3 or include 4, so only (a) fits.
explanations: Correct: statements 1, 2 and 3 describe real CCO functions: coal statistics, monitoring of captive and commercial blocks, and hearing objections under the 1957 Act.
Wrong: it leaves out statements 1 and 2, which are correct, and includes statement 4, which is not a CCO function.
Wrong: statements 1 and 2 are correct, but it omits statement 3, because the CCO does hear objections to acquisition notifications under the 1957 Act.
Wrong: statement 4 about ensuring timely delivery to end users is not a CCO function, and this option also omits statement 3.
keyfact: The Coal Controller's Organisation (Kolkata) gives coal statistics, monitors captive blocks and hears acquisition objections under the 1957 Act, but does not enforce coal delivery.
option_notes: Options 1, 2 and 3 together describe the CCO's actual roles. It is an attached office of the Ministry of Coal, headquartered in Kolkata, and traces back to 1916. It publishes the Coal Directory of India, monitors captive blocks and acts as the competent authority under the Coal Bearing Areas Act, 1957. It also looks after grading and classification of coal, and implements the Colliery Control Rules, 2004.

Options 3 and 4 only: statement 3 is correct, since the 1957 Act gives objection hearing to the competent authority, which is the Coal Controller. Statement 4 is not, because delivery to consumers is managed through coal companies, fuel supply agreements and the Railways. The option fails because it excludes the statistical and monitoring functions, which are the CCO's best-known roles.

Options 1 and 2 only: these are the two best-known CCO functions, namely coal statistics and monitoring of captive and commercial blocks. The option is incomplete because it leaves out the quasi-judicial role of hearing objections to acquisition notices under the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957. This is a popular trap, as students tend to know only the first two roles.

Options 1, 2 and 4: statements 1 and 2 are right, but statement 4 is wrong. Timely supply of coal to power plants and other consumers is a matter for Coal India Limited, SCCL, the Ministry of Coal's linkage policy (SHAKTI, 2017), and railway logistics. The CCO has no power to enforce delivery schedules. The option also drops the correct statement 3.
related: The post of Coal Controller was created in 1916, and the CCO is headquartered in Kolkata.
The CCO publishes the Coal Directory of India each year.
The Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957 allows the Centre to acquire land for coal mining.
The Supreme Court cancelled 204 coal blocks in 2014 (Manohar Lal Sharma case).
Coal India Limited was formed in 1975 and is a Maharatna company.
The SHAKTI policy (2017) governs allocation of coal linkages to power plants.
Commercial coal mining was opened to the private sector in 2020.
The National Coal Gasification Mission targets 100 MT of coal gasification by 2030.
statements: 1 — Correct: The CCO is the main official source of coal and lignite statistics in India. It collects data from mines, washeries, coke ovens and consumers, and publishes the Coal Directory of India each year, along with monthly and quarterly statistics. Coal production, despatch, stocks, grades, prices and imports are reported to it under statutory returns. It is an attached office of the Ministry of Coal, headquartered in Kolkata, and its roots lie in the Coal Controller post created in 1916. Its figures are the reference for policy, planning and parliamentary replies.

2 — Correct: The CCO monitors the development of captive and commercial coal and lignite blocks allotted to companies. It inspects blocks and reviews the status of mine opening permissions, land acquisition, forest and environmental clearances, and progress against milestones. It reports delays to the Ministry of Coal, which can then act through de-allocation or by encashing bank guarantees. After the Supreme Court cancelled 204 coal block allocations in 2014 (Manohar Lal Sharma case), and under the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 and later auction rules, this monitoring role became more significant. Production from captive and commercial blocks has risen sharply since 2020.

3 — Correct: Under the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, the Central Government issues a notification of its intention to acquire coal-bearing land (Section 4). Any person interested in the land may file objections within 30 days with the competent authority, and the Coal Controller acts in that role. After hearing the objections, the authority reports to the Central Government, which decides whether to proceed with a Section 7 declaration of acquisition. The Act lets the Centre acquire land for coal mining, and the acquired land vests in the Government or in a government company. The Act was amended in 1993.

4 — Incorrect: Ensuring that coal is delivered to end users within the prescribed time is not a CCO function. Supply is handled through fuel supply agreements, e-auctions and linkage policies such as SHAKTI (Scheme for Harnessing and Allocating Koyala Transparently in India, 2017), managed by Coal India Limited and its subsidiaries, SCCL and the Ministry of Coal. Railways handle the logistics, and the Central Electricity Authority monitors stocks at power plants. The CCO collects statistics and checks quality, grading and statutory compliance. It is not a delivery regulator, and coal India has no independent regulator, though the Ministry has proposed one.
summary: The answer is (a): statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct, and statement 4 is wrong. The Coal Controller's Organisation (CCO) is the main source of coal statistics, monitors captive and commercial coal and lignite blocks, and is the competent authority that hears objections to acquisition notifications under the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957. It does not police the delivery of coal to end users.
topic_notes: The Coal Controller's Organisation is an attached office of the Ministry of Coal, headquartered in Kolkata, with field offices at Dhanbad, Ranchi, Bilaspur, Nagpur and other places. The post of Coal Controller dates back to 1916, and the organisation has grown into a statutory and statistical body. Its key functions are: collecting and publishing coal and lignite statistics (Coal Directory of India); monitoring captive and commercial coal blocks; grading and quality checks; enforcing the Colliery Control Rules, 2004; collecting levies and excise-related statistics; and acting as the competent authority for hearing objections under Section 4 of the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957. Related background: coal mines were nationalised in two phases (coking coal in 1971-72, non-coking coal in 1973), and Coal India Limited was formed in 1975. It is a Maharatna company. The Supreme Court cancelled 204 coal block allocations in 2014. The Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 introduced auctions, and commercial mining was opened to private firms in 2020 through the Mines and Minerals amendment. Coal is classified as anthracite, bituminous, sub-bituminous and lignite by rank. India's major coalfields are in Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh and Telangana. Lignite is mainly mined at Neyveli (NLC India Limited) in Tamil Nadu, and also in Gujarat and Rajasthan. Other angles UPSC may ask: the Ministry of Coal's Coal Controller as a statutory authority, Singareni Collieries (SCCL, jointly owned by Telangana and the Centre), coal gasification targets, the National Coal Gasification Mission (100 MT by 2030), and the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957.

question: If a particular area is brought under the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution of India, which one of the following statements best reflects the consequence of it ?
options: This would prevent the transfer of land of tribal people to non-tribal people
This would create a local self-governing body in that area
This would convert that area into a Union Territory
The State having such areas would be declared a Special Category State
subject: Polity
detail: The Fifth Schedule, read with Article 244(1), governs the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in all States except Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, which fall under the Sixth Schedule. The President declares Scheduled Areas after consulting the Governor (Para 6), and can also alter or rescind them. The Governor holds the key powers: under Para 5 the Governor may direct that an Act of Parliament or the State Legislature does not apply to a Scheduled Area or applies with modifications. Under Para 5(2), the Governor may make regulations for peace and good government, including (a) prohibiting or restricting transfer of land by or among members of Scheduled Tribes, (b) regulating allotment of land to them, and (c) regulating money-lending to them. Such regulations need Presidential assent. A Tribes Advisory Council (TAC) with up to 20 members, three-fourths from ST MLAs, advises on tribal welfare. Elimination: (b) describes the Sixth Schedule's Autonomous District/Regional Councils. (c) is wrong because UT status needs Article 2/3/4 legislation and not a Schedule. (d) is wrong because Special Category status was a Planning Commission/Gadgil formula concept, not constitutional, and was ended after the 14th Finance Commission.
explanations: Correct: Para 5(2) of the Fifth Schedule empowers the Governor to prohibit or restrict land transfer from tribals to non-tribals in Scheduled Areas.
Incorrect: Creation of autonomous self-governing councils is a feature of the Sixth Schedule (Article 244(2)), not the Fifth. Panchayats in Fifth Schedule areas are governed by PESA 1996.
Incorrect: Scheduled Area status does not alter a region's political status. Union Territories are created by Parliament under Articles 2-4 or Article 239 provisions. The area stays within the State.

Incorrect: Special Category Status was an administrative and financial planning concept based on factors like hilly terrain, low population density and border location. It is not tied to the Fifth Schedule, and several Fifth Schedule States, such as Odisha, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh, were never in that category.
keyfact: Fifth Schedule: the Governor can regulate or bar transfer of tribal land to non-tribals in Scheduled Areas (Para 5(2)); autonomous councils belong to the Sixth Schedule.
option_notes: Land alienation protection: Governor's regulations under Para 5(2) of the Fifth Schedule restrict transfer of tribal land to non-tribals, regulate allotment, and regulate money-lending. Examples include the Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulation 1959/1970 and the Samatha judgment (1997), in which the Supreme Court barred leasing tribal land to private non-tribal parties for mining. Such regulations require the President's assent.

Local self-governing bodies in tribal areas: Sixth Schedule Autonomous District Councils (ADCs) and Regional Councils exist in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. ADCs have up to 30 members, 5-year terms, and legislative, judicial and revenue powers over land, forests and customary law. The Bodoland Territorial Council is an example. For Fifth Schedule areas, PESA 1996 extends Panchayats with special powers to gram sabhas.

Union Territories: Created under Articles 2-4 by Parliament, administered by the President through an Administrator under Article 239. There are 8 UTs. Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh became UTs in 2019, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu merged in 2020. Delhi has a special status under Article 239AA and Puducherry also has a legislature. A Schedule designation does not create a UT.

Special Category Status: Introduced in 1969 on the Gadgil formula recommendation for the Fifth Finance Commission. Criteria included hilly terrain, low population density, tribal share, strategic border location, economic backwardness and non-viable finances. It gave 90:10 central funding. Initially granted to Assam, Nagaland and J&K, and later extended to 11 States. The 14th Finance Commission removed the distinction except for the Northeast and hill States, and the Planning Commission was abolished in 2014.
related: Article 244(1) = Fifth Schedule; Article 244(2) = Sixth Schedule.
Fifth Schedule applies to 10 States, but not to Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura or Mizoram.
Scheduled Areas are declared by the President under Para 6 of the Fifth Schedule.
The Tribes Advisory Council has at most 20 members, three-fourths of them ST MLAs.
PESA Act 1996 extends Panchayats to Fifth Schedule areas.
Article 338A establishes the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (89th Amendment, 2003).
Samatha judgment (1997) restricted transfer of tribal land to private companies for mining.
Autonomous District Councils under the Sixth Schedule have up to 30 members.
summary: The answer is (a). Under the Fifth Schedule, the Governor of a State with Scheduled Areas can make regulations that prohibit or restrict the transfer of land from members of Scheduled Tribes to non-tribals, and can regulate land allotment and money-lending in those areas. Local self-government (Sixth Schedule), UT status and Special Category status are unrelated consequences.
topic_notes: Article 244 provides special administration for tribal regions. Article 244(1) applies the Fifth Schedule to Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in all States other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Article 244(2) applies the Sixth Schedule to those four States. Scheduled Areas are declared by the President (Para 6) after consulting the State Governor. Criteria, not statutory but followed: preponderance of tribal population, compactness and reasonable size, underdeveloped nature, and marked disparity in economic standards. Ten States currently have Fifth Schedule areas: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha and Rajasthan. The Governor submits an annual report to the President on administration of these areas, and the Union executive power extends to giving directions to the State. Tribes Advisory Council: mandatory in Fifth Schedule States (up to 20 members, three-fourths ST MLAs) and may be set up in States with STs but no Scheduled Areas if the President directs. Para 5 gives the Governor power to adapt laws. The Dhebar Commission (1960) and Bhuria Committee (1991) are linked to the Scheduled Areas. PESA 1996 extends Panchayats to Scheduled Areas, with gram sabha powers over resources, minor forest produce and land alienation prevention. The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises forest rights of STs and other forest dwellers. Sixth Schedule bodies: Autonomous District Councils, Regional Councils, and Governor's power to define areas. Other related provisions: Article 275(1) grants-in-aid for tribal welfare, Article 330/332 ST reservation in legislatures, Article 338A National Commission for Scheduled Tribes, Article 342 specification of STs. Landmark case: Samatha v State of Andhra Pradesh (1997). Also Niyamgiri/Vedanta (Orissa Mining Corporation v MoEF, 2013), which upheld gram sabha rights.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. The India Sanitation Coalition is a platform to promote sustainable sanitation and is funded by the Government of India and the World Health Organization.
2. The National Institute of Urban Affairs is an apex body of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs in Government of India and provides innovative solutions to address the challenges of Urban India. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Geography
detail: The question tests whether you can spot wrongly attributed institutional features. The India Sanitation Coalition was set up in 2012 as a multi-stakeholder platform hosted by FICCI. It brings together the private sector, government, civil society, academia and development agencies to promote sustainable sanitation, and it works with the Swachh Bharat Mission. Its funding comes from members, corporate partners and donors, not from the Government of India and the WHO jointly, so Statement 1 fails on its funding claim. The NIUA, in Delhi, began in 1976 as a society registered under the Societies Registration Act. It is a premier national think tank and research and capacity-building institute for urban planning and development. It is autonomous and receives support from MoHUA, but it is not described as an 'apex body of the Ministry'. That label, and the 'innovative solutions' framing, are UPSC's twist, which makes Statement 2 incorrect as framed. NIUA runs the Smart Cities Mission data and knowledge work, the Climate Centre for Cities and the National Urban Learning Platform. Elimination logic: when a statement names unusual funders or inflates an institution's status, treat it with suspicion, and both fail here.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Statement 1 is incorrect because ISC is FICCI-hosted and industry-led, with no joint funding by the Government of India and WHO.
(b) Wrong: Statement 2 is incorrect because NIUA is an autonomous research institute and not an apex body of MoHUA, so it cannot stand alone as correct.
(c) Wrong: Both statements contain inaccuracies, so they cannot both be correct.
(d) Correct: Both statements are inaccurate, as the official answer confirms. ISC is not funded by the Government of India and WHO, and NIUA is not the Ministry's apex body.
keyfact: ISC (2012) is FICCI-hosted and industry-led, not funded by the Government of India and WHO; NIUA (1976) is an autonomous research institute, not MoHUA's apex body, so the answer is (d).
option_notes: Option (a), Statement 1 only: describes the India Sanitation Coalition as funded by the Government of India and WHO. In reality ISC was founded in 2012 and is hosted by FICCI. It is a platform that brings together industry, government, civil society and academia to promote sustainable sanitation, including toilets, faecal sludge management, hygiene and behaviour change. It works alongside Swachh Bharat Mission and uses CSR and partner funding.

Option (b), Statement 2 only: describes NIUA as an apex body of MoHUA. NIUA was founded in 1976 in Delhi and is an autonomous society and think tank for urban research, capacity building and knowledge dissemination. It supports MoHUA programmes such as Smart Cities, AMRUT and the National Urban Learning Platform, and it hosts the Climate Centre for Cities. It is supported by the Ministry but is not its apex body.

Option (c), Both 1 and 2: would hold only if both statements were accurate. This would require ISC to be jointly funded by the Government of India and WHO and NIUA to be the Ministry's apex body. Neither is true. ISC is a FICCI-hosted multi-stakeholder platform, and NIUA is an autonomous research and training institute under a society structure. Such wording shows how UPSC mixes real institutions with wrong attributes.

Option (d), Neither 1 nor 2: the correct answer. It reflects that the statements wrongly describe both institutions. ISC (2012, FICCI-hosted) is industry-led and not funded by the Government of India and WHO. NIUA (1976, Delhi) is an autonomous urban research body supported by MoHUA but not its apex body. This is a typical UPSC pattern of subtle institutional mislabelling.
related: India Sanitation Coalition was set up in 2012 and is hosted by FICCI.
NIUA was established in 1976 and is an autonomous urban research institute in New Delhi.
Swachh Bharat Mission was launched on 2 October 2014; Phase 2 and SBM-U 2.0 run to 2025-26.
74th Constitutional Amendment (1992) added Part IX-A, Articles 243P-243ZG, and the 12th Schedule.
AMRUT 2.0 targets universal water supply and sewerage in cities, launched in 2021.
Indore has been ranked India's cleanest city in Swachh Survekshan for several consecutive years.
CPHEEO is the Ministry's technical wing for urban water supply and sanitation.
ODF++ requires sustainable sanitation, including safe faecal sludge management and treatment.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: ISC is hosted by FICCI and is industry-led. It is not funded by the Government of India and WHO. The India Sanitation Coalition was launched in 2012 as a multi-stakeholder platform. Its aim is to bring together the corporate sector, government, civil society, academia, media and development partners to scale up sustainable sanitation, including toilets, faecal sludge and septage management, waste and hygiene. It is hosted by FICCI, with a secretariat and a governing council from industry. It supports Swachh Bharat Mission (launched 2 October 2014), runs CSR-linked partnerships and promotes behaviour change. It is funded by member contributions, corporate partners and donors, not by a government-WHO arrangement.

2 — Incorrect: NIUA is an autonomous research institute, not an apex body of MoHUA. The National Institute of Urban Affairs, in New Delhi, was established in 1976 and is registered as a society. It is India's national think tank for urban research, policy support, training and knowledge dissemination. It works with MoHUA, state governments and urban local bodies. Its work includes the Smart Cities Mission knowledge platforms, the National Urban Learning Platform (NULP), the Climate Centre for Cities, data and the City Finance work. Its governing body is chaired by the MoHUA Secretary. Although it is supported by the Ministry, it is not called an apex body of the Ministry, which is why UPSC treats the statement as wrong.
summary: The answer is (d), neither statement is correct. The India Sanitation Coalition (ISC) is an FICCI-hosted, industry-led multi-stakeholder platform that is not funded by the Government of India and WHO, and the National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA) is an autonomous research institute, not an 'apex body' of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA).
topic_notes: Urban sanitation and urban governance feature often in UPSC prelims through institutions, missions and platforms. The India Sanitation Coalition (2012, FICCI) is an industry-led platform that works on sanitation, faecal sludge and septage management, and the sanitation economy. It collaborates with the Swachh Bharat Mission - Urban and Gramin, launched on 2 October 2014. SBM-Urban 2.0 was launched in October 2021 for 2021-26, aiming for garbage-free cities, and AMRUT 2.0 aims at water security and universal water supply in cities. The NIUA, established in 1976, is based in Delhi. It is an autonomous think tank that carries out urban research, training and capacity building and manages knowledge hubs, including Smart Cities Mission data and the Climate Centre for Cities. MoHUA is the nodal ministry for urban policy. Its flagship schemes include PMAY-Urban, Smart Cities Mission (2015, 100 cities), AMRUT (2015), Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban, DAY-NULM and HRIDAY. The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act (1992) gave constitutional status to urban local bodies through Part IX-A (Articles 243P to 243ZG) and the 12th Schedule with 18 functions. Related bodies include the Town and Country Planning Organisation (TCPO), the Central Public Health and Environmental Engineering Organisation (CPHEEO) and the Housing and Urban Development Corporation (HUDCO, 1970). Other angles UPSC could ask: ODF, ODF+ and ODF++ categories, Swachh Survekshan rankings (Indore the cleanest for several consecutive years), the Jal Jeevan Mission and the Namami Gange programme. Always verify institutional status, founding year and parent body before accepting a statement.

question: Which one of the following has been constituted under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 ?
subject: Polity
detail: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 was enacted after the Bhopal gas tragedy (1984) and under Article 253 to implement the decisions of the 1972 Stockholm Conference. Section 3(3) empowers the Central Government to constitute authorities to exercise its powers under the Act. Using this, the Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) was constituted by a 1997 notification, following a Supreme Court direction in the M.C. Mehta case, to regulate ground water development, issue NOCs for extraction, and notify over-exploited areas. It functions under the Ministry of Jal Shakti. The Central Water Commission (CWC) is an attached office of the Ministry of Jal Shakti, set up in 1945 as the Central Waterways, Irrigation and Navigation Commission, and has no EPA basis. The Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) is a scientific body set up in 1970 by renaming the Exploratory Tubewells Organisation, and it is the technical body that supports the CGWA. The National Water Development Agency (NWDA) was set up in 1982 as a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, to study inter-basin transfer and river linking. Elimination: any body with 'Authority' tied to environmental regulation is more likely statutory under the EPA, while 'Board', 'Commission' and 'Agency' here are administrative or scientific bodies.
explanations: Incorrect: the Central Water Commission is an attached office of the Ministry of Jal Shakti, set up in 1945 by executive action, not under the EPA.
Incorrect: the Central Ground Water Board is a scientific and technical organisation set up in 1970 and is not constituted under the EPA; it supports the CGWA technically.
Correct: the Central Ground Water Authority was constituted under Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to regulate and control ground water development.
Incorrect: the National Water Development Agency is an autonomous society registered under the Societies Registration Act in 1982, not an EPA body.
keyfact: Central Ground Water Authority = constituted under Section 3(3) of the EPA 1986 (1997); CWC, CGWB and NWDA are not EPA bodies.
option_notes: The Central Water Commission is the apex technical body for water resources in India. It began in 1945 as the Central Waterways, Irrigation and Navigation Commission, on the recommendation of Dr B.R. Ambedkar's initiative as Labour Member. It is headed by a Chairman with the status of ex officio Secretary to the Government, works under the Ministry of Jal Shakti, and handles flood forecasting, dam safety, and river data. It is an attached office with headquarters in New Delhi.

The Central Ground Water Board is the national apex agency for scientific ground water management. It was established in 1970 by renaming the Exploratory Tubewells Organisation, which was set up in 1954, and was merged with the ground water wing of the Geological Survey of India. It is a subordinate office of the Ministry of Jal Shakti. It conducts aquifer mapping, ground water assessment with states, and monitoring through observation wells.

The Central Ground Water Authority was constituted in January 1997 under Section 3(3) of the EPA 1986, following the Supreme Court's directions in the M.C. Mehta v. Union of India case. It regulates ground water extraction, grants NOCs for industries and infrastructure, and notifies areas where ground water is over-exploited. It works under the Ministry of Jal Shakti, and the CGWB provides its technical support.

The National Water Development Agency was set up in July 1982 as an autonomous society under the Societies Registration Act, under the Ministry of Jal Shakti. Its work includes pre-feasibility and feasibility studies for the National Perspective Plan on inter-basin water transfer. It carries out detailed project reports for linking rivers such as the Ken-Betwa link. It has no statutory status and is not an EPA body.
related: The EPA 1986 was enacted under Article 253 after the Bhopal gas tragedy.
The CPCB was set up under the Water Act, 1974, and given powers under the Air Act, 1981.
The NGT was established in 2010 under the NGT Act, and Delhi is its principal bench.
The National Biodiversity Authority is a statutory body in Chennai under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.
The National Tiger Conservation Authority became statutory in 2006 by an amendment to the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
The CGWB was formed in 1970 from the Exploratory Tubewells Organisation.
The Commission for Air Quality Management was set up in 2020 for the NCR and adjoining areas.
Article 48A (DPSP) and Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty) relate to environmental protection.
summary: The answer is (c) Central Ground Water Authority. The CGWA was constituted by the Central Government under Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, to regulate and control development and management of ground water in India. The other bodies were created by executive resolution or as societies, not under the EPA.
topic_notes: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is an umbrella law passed under Article 253 to give effect to the Stockholm Conference (1972) decisions. It came into force on 19 November 1986. Section 3 gives the Centre the power to take all measures to protect and improve the environment, and Section 3(3) lets it constitute authorities. Section 5 gives power to issue directions, including closure of industries. Section 6 allows rules on pollutant standards, and Section 15 sets the penalty of up to 5 years' imprisonment and a fine of up to Rs 1 lakh. Several rules have been made under it, such as the Environment Impact Assessment notification (1994, replaced in 2006), the Coastal Regulation Zone notifications, the Hazardous Waste Rules, the Plastic Waste Management Rules, and the Noise Pollution Rules (2000). Authorities constituted under it include the CGWA and the Environmental Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority for the NCR (EPCA, 1998, later replaced by the Commission for Air Quality Management in 2020 under a separate Act). The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change is the nodal ministry. Related bodies come from other statutes: the Central Pollution Control Board, constituted under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974; the National Green Tribunal, under the NGT Act, 2010; the National Biodiversity Authority, under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002; and the National Tiger Conservation Authority, under the Wildlife (Protection) Act as amended in 2006. UPSC often asks which body is statutory, under which Act, and which ministry controls it.

question:
With reference to the “United Nations Credentials Committee”, consider the following statements :
1. It is a committee set up by the UN Security Council and works under its supervision.
2. ‘It traditionally meets in March, June and September every year.
3. It assesses the credentials of all UN members before submitting a report to the General Assembly for approval. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Credentials Committee is a standing, procedural body of the UN General Assembly, established under Rule 28 of the GA's Rules of Procedure at the start of each regular session. It consists of nine members appointed by the GA on the proposal of the President, usually reflecting the political balance of the Assembly. Rules 27 to 29 govern credentials: each member state's delegation must submit credentials issued by the Head of State, Head of Government or Foreign Minister, and the Committee examines them and reports to the Assembly, which approves the report, often by vote or consensus. It meets typically once a year, late in the year (November or December), after the opening of the GA session in September. The Committee became prominent in disputes over who represents a state, such as Myanmar after the 2021 coup and Afghanistan after the Taliban takeover in 2021, where it deferred decisions. Elimination logic: Statement 1 is wrong because the body is a GA organ, not a Security Council one, which removes options (b) and (d). Statement 2 is wrong on the meeting schedule, which removes (c). Only statement 3 is correct, so the answer is (a).
explanations: Correct: only statement 3 is right, since the Committee examines the credentials of all members and reports to the GA for approval.
Incorrect: it includes statement 1, which wrongly says the Security Council set up the Committee. It is a GA body.
Incorrect: statement 2 is wrong because the Committee meets late in the year, not in March, June and September.
Incorrect: both statements 1 and 2 are wrong, because the Committee is a GA body and does not follow a March, June, September schedule.
keyfact: The UN Credentials Committee is a nine-member General Assembly body that meets once late in the year to examine all members' credentials and report to the GA.
option_notes: 3 only: This is the right combination here. The Credentials Committee verifies the credentials of representatives of all UN member states at each regular GA session and submits a report to the plenary. The Assembly approves it by consensus or vote. This function flows from Rules 27 to 29 of the GA Rules of Procedure. The Committee has nine members, appointed at the start of each session.

1 and 3: This pairs a wrong claim with a right one. The Committee is not a Security Council body, so statement 1 fails. It is an organ of the General Assembly, set up each session under Rule 28. The Security Council has its own separate rules for credentials of its members' representatives, but it does not supervise the GA's Committee.

2 and 3: This pairs a wrong claim with a right one. The Committee does not meet in March, June and September. It generally meets once annually late in the year, such as November or December, after the GA session begins in September. Statement 3 on its assessing and reporting role is accurate.

1 and 2: Both statements are wrong. The Committee is a GA body, not a Security Council one, and it does not meet quarterly in March, June and September. It meets late in the year, typically once, to examine credentials for the current GA session.
related: The Credentials Committee has nine members, appointed by the GA at each regular session.
It acts under Rules 27 to 29 of the GA Rules of Procedure.
Resolution 2758 (1971) gave China's UN seat to the PRC.
In 2021 the Committee deferred decisions on Myanmar and Afghanistan.
Admission of a new UN member needs a Security Council recommendation and a two-thirds GA vote (Article 4).
The Trusteeship Council suspended operations in 1994 after Palau's independence.
Credentials must be issued by the Head of State or Government or the Foreign Minister.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Committee is set up by the General Assembly, not the Security Council, and reports to the GA. Detail: At the beginning of every regular session, the GA appoints a nine-member Credentials Committee under Rule 28 of its Rules of Procedure. Its composition is based on a proposal by the GA President and reflects regional and political balance. Recent members have included major powers such as the US, China and Russia along with other states. The Security Council has no role in supervising it. The Council does not decide credentials for the GA, although its own provisional rules (Rules 13 to 17) deal with representatives' credentials separately. The Committee's report goes to the plenary GA for approval.

2 — Incorrect: The Committee does not traditionally meet in March, June and September. Detail: It meets once a year, usually late in the year (around November or December), after the GA's regular session opens in September. Its work reviews the credentials submitted by member states for that session. The decisions are then adopted by the plenary. Because meetings are tied to the GA session cycle, there is no quarterly schedule. In 2021 the Committee met in December and deferred the decisions on the rival claims for Myanmar and Afghanistan, which kept the incumbent representatives in place for the time being.

3 — Correct: The Committee assesses the credentials of all UN member states' representatives and submits a report to the GA for approval. Detail: Under Rule 27, credentials are issued by the Head of State or Government or the Foreign Minister, and are submitted to the Secretary-General. The Committee examines them and reports to the Assembly, which approves the report, sometimes after a vote. It handles contested representation, such as the 1971 recognition of the PRC in place of Taiwan (Resolution 2758), Cambodia in the 1990s, and the cases of Myanmar and Afghanistan after 2021. Its decisions on credentials do not amount to formal recognition of governments.
summary: The correct answer is (a) 3 only. The UN Credentials Committee is a committee of the General Assembly (not the Security Council), and it assesses the credentials of all UN member representatives and reports to the General Assembly for approval. It traditionally meets in the autumn (around September to December), not in March, June and September.
topic_notes: The UN Credentials Committee is a subsidiary organ of the General Assembly and deals with the question of who legitimately represents a member state. Rules 27 to 29 of the GA Rules of Procedure require credentials from the Head of State or Government or the Foreign Minister. Rule 28 provides for a Credentials Committee of nine members, appointed at the beginning of each session on the proposal of the GA President. The Committee examines credentials, reports to the plenary, and the Assembly approves the report. It usually meets once, late in the year (November or December). Its decisions are procedural, and acceptance of credentials does not amount to recognition of a government. Key cases: Resolution 2758 (1971) gave China's seat to the People's Republic of China, replacing the Republic of China (Taiwan); Cambodia's seat was left vacant in 1979-1981 and contested later; South Africa's apartheid-era delegation was rejected in 1970 and the following years; in 2021 the Committee deferred decisions on Myanmar (the junta versus the representative of the ousted government) and on Afghanistan (Taliban versus the former government), and the incumbent representatives remained. Related UN structure: the six principal organs are the General Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, Trusteeship Council (suspended since 1994), International Court of Justice and the Secretariat. The GA also has Main Committees (First to Sixth) and the General Committee, which are different from the Credentials Committee. Possible future angles: GA Rules of Procedure, the composition of GA committees, the Security Council's separate Rules 13 to 17 on credentials, the process of admission of members (Article 4 of the Charter, Security Council recommendation followed by two-thirds GA vote), and suspension or expulsion (Articles 5 and 6).

question: Which one of the following statements best 79. describes the ‘Polar Code’ ?
options: It is the international code of safety for ships operating in polar waters
It is the agreement of the countries around the North Pole regarding the demarcation of their territories in the polar region
It is a set of norms to be followed by the countries whose scientists undertake research studies in the North Pole and South Pole
It is a trade and security agreement of the member countries of the Arctic Council
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The Polar Code is a mandatory IMO instrument covering the design, construction, equipment, operations, training, search and rescue, and environmental protection aspects of ships in the remote and ice-prone waters around the poles. It was adopted in stages: the safety part (Part I-A) was adopted through amendments to SOLAS (the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974) by the Maritime Safety Committee (MSC) in 2014, and the environmental part (Part II-A) through amendments to MARPOL (the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships, 1973/78) by the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) in 2015. The Code entered into force on 1 January 2017 and applies to ships certified under SOLAS. Key features include the Polar Ship Certificate, categories A, B and C by ice capability, a Polar Water Operational Manual, and limits on discharges of oil, noxious liquids, sewage and garbage. The Code is not about territorial demarcation (option b), which falls under UNCLOS and the continental shelf claims process. It is not a research norm (option c), the area of the Antarctic Treaty System and the SCAR. It is not a trade or security pact (option d), because the Arctic Council is a forum with no military security mandate. Eliminating b, c and d is therefore straightforward.
explanations: Correct: the Polar Code is the IMO's International Code for Ships Operating in Polar Waters, in force since 1 January 2017.
Incorrect: territorial and maritime boundary claims in the Arctic are dealt with under UNCLOS (the CLCS for extended continental shelf claims) and bilateral negotiations, not under the Polar Code.
Incorrect: research conduct in the poles is governed by the Antarctic Treaty System, SCAR guidelines and Arctic Council science agreements, not by the Polar Code.

Incorrect: the Arctic Council is an intergovernmental forum on sustainable development and environmental protection; military security is excluded from its mandate, and it has no trade agreement called the Polar Code.
keyfact: Polar Code = IMO's mandatory International Code for Ships Operating in Polar Waters, in force since 1 January 2017 under SOLAS and MARPOL.
option_notes: The International Code for Ships Operating in Polar Waters was adopted by the IMO (MSC in 2014, MEPC in 2015) and entered into force on 1 January 2017. It is mandatory under SOLAS and MARPOL and covers ship design, equipment, crew training, operations and pollution prevention in Arctic and Antarctic waters. Ships need a Polar Ship Certificate, graded as Category A, B or C by ice capability.

Territorial demarcation in the Arctic is not governed by any single treaty. Coastal states (Russia, Canada, USA, Norway, Denmark via Greenland) make claims under UNCLOS 1982, with extended continental shelf submissions reviewed by the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf (CLCS). Disputes such as the Lomonosov Ridge claims remain unresolved. Antarctica, by contrast, has its claims frozen under the Antarctic Treaty of 1959.

Research norms at the poles come from different instruments. In Antarctica these are the Antarctic Treaty (1959, in force 1961), the Madrid Protocol (1991, in force 1998) and SCAR (Scientific Committee on Antarctic Research). In the Arctic, the 2017 Agreement on Enhancing International Arctic Scientific Cooperation applies. India's research stations are Himadri (Arctic, Svalbard, 2008) and Maitri and Bharati (Antarctica).

The Arctic Council was established by the Ottawa Declaration of 1996. It has eight member states: Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden and the USA. It also has Permanent Participants, who are indigenous peoples' organisations, and observers. India has been an observer since 2013. Its focus is sustainable development and environmental protection, and military security is expressly outside its remit. Its secretariat is in Tromsø, Norway.
related: The Polar Code entered into force on 1 January 2017 and was adopted by the IMO.
It operates through amendments to SOLAS (safety) and MARPOL (pollution).
The Arctic Council was formed by the Ottawa Declaration in 1996, and India has been an observer since 2013.
India's Arctic station Himadri is at Ny-Ålesund, Svalbard, and its Antarctic stations are Maitri and Bharati.
The Antarctic Treaty was signed in 1959 and the Madrid Protocol, which bans mining, in 1991.
The Svalbard Treaty of 1920 gives Norway sovereignty over the archipelago.
India's Arctic Policy was released in March 2022.
The IMO is headquartered in London.
summary: The answer is (a). The Polar Code is the International Code for Ships Operating in Polar Waters, adopted by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) to make ship operations in the Arctic and Antarctic safer and to protect the polar environment.
topic_notes: The Polar Code sits within the IMO's regulatory framework. The IMO is a UN specialised agency headquartered in London, and it administers SOLAS (1974), MARPOL (1973/78), STCW (training standards) and other conventions. The Code has a safety part (Part I) and a pollution-prevention part (Part II), each with a mandatory (A) and a recommendatory (B) section. It applies to the Arctic waters north of roughly 60°N, with some variations, and to Antarctic waters south of 60°S. It only covers ships over 500 gross tonnage certified under SOLAS, so fishing vessels, pleasure yachts and small craft are excluded. Environmental rules prohibit the discharge of oil and noxious liquid substances and restrict sewage and garbage.
