The use and carriage of heavy fuel oil in Antarctic waters has been banned since 2011 under MARPOL, and the IMO has also adopted a ban on heavy fuel oil use in Arctic waters, effective from 2024 with waivers until 2029. Related governance includes the Antarctic Treaty System: the Treaty (1959), CCAMLR (1980) and the Madrid Protocol (1991), which bans mining. India became a consultative party to the Antarctic Treaty in 1983. India's Arctic Policy was released in March 2022, and its Antarctic Act is the Indian Antarctic Act, 2022. The Arctic Council has the Ottawa Declaration (1996) as its founding document. The Svalbard Treaty (1920) gives Norway sovereignty over Svalbard, with equal rights of resource exploitation for the signatories, including India. Likely future angles include other IMO conventions, the Northern Sea Route and the Northwest Passage, and Arctic shipping and climate change.

question:
With reference to the United Nations General Assembly, consider the following statements :
1. The UN General Assembly can grant observer status to the non-member States.
2. Inter-governmental organisations can seek observer status in the UN General Assembly.
3. Permanent Observers in the UN General Assembly can _ maintain missions at the UN headquarters. Which of the statements given above are correct ?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Observer status is not mentioned in the UN Charter. It arose from UN practice, beginning with Switzerland, which was a Permanent Observer before joining in 2002. The General Assembly confers the status by a resolution, usually a simple majority vote or by consensus. Two categories exist: non-member States (currently the Holy See and the State of Palestine, which was upgraded to 'non-member observer State' by UNGA Resolution 67/19 on 29 November 2012) and intergovernmental or other organisations, for example the African Union, the European Union (enhanced rights, 2011), the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, the Commonwealth, the Arab League, ASEAN and the International Committee of the Red Cross. Entities such as the Sovereign Order of Malta also hold it. Observers may attend public meetings, speak and circulate documents, but they cannot vote or sponsor draft resolutions unless the Assembly specifically allows it. Permanent Observers keep permanent observer missions at UN Headquarters, which is why statement 3 is correct. Elimination logic: statements 1 and 2 are basic facts, and statement 3 follows from the term 'Permanent Observer', so options (a), (b) and (c), each of which drops one correct statement, are wrong.
explanations: Wrong: the statements it endorses are right, but it leaves out statement 3, which is also correct because Permanent Observers do maintain missions at UN Headquarters.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 1, yet the General Assembly does grant observer status to non-member States such as the Holy See and Palestine.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 2, yet intergovernmental organisations such as the AU, EU and OIC can seek and obtain observer status.
Correct: all three statements are accurate. The Assembly grants the status to non-member States, intergovernmental organisations can seek it, and Permanent Observers keep missions at UN Headquarters.
keyfact: UNGA grants observer status by resolution to non-member States (Holy See, Palestine) and to organisations; observers keep missions at UN HQ but cannot vote.
option_notes: Option (a), 'statements 1 and 2 only', would be right only if Permanent Observers had no missions. In fact, observers such as the Holy See and Palestine run missions in New York. The option wrongly rejects statement 3.

Option (b), 'statements 2 and 3 only', accepts that organisations can be observers and that observers keep missions, but wrongly denies that the Assembly can grant observer status to non-member States. The Holy See and Palestine are the two such States today.

Option (c), 'statements 1 and 3 only', accepts the status for States and the missions but wrongly denies that intergovernmental organisations can seek it. Many organisations, including the AU, EU, OIC, Commonwealth and ASEAN, hold the status.

Option (d), 'statements 1, 2 and 3', is the official answer. Observer status comes from UN practice, not the Charter. It is granted by General Assembly resolution to non-member States and to organisations. Observers can attend and speak but cannot vote, and Permanent Observers keep missions at UN Headquarters.
related: The Holy See and Palestine are the only non-member observer States in the UNGA.
Palestine was upgraded to non-member observer State by UNGA Resolution 67/19 on 29 November 2012.
Switzerland was a Permanent Observer until it became a UN member in 2002.
Observers can speak but cannot vote in the UNGA.
New members are admitted by the UNGA (two-thirds) on the Security Council's recommendation (Article 4).
The EU gained enhanced observer rights in the UNGA in 2011 (Resolution 65/276).
The UNGA has 193 member States and six Main Committees.
Observer status is a matter of UN practice and is not mentioned in the Charter.
statements: 1 — Correct: The General Assembly grants observer status to non-member States by resolution. Observer status is a matter of UN practice, not the Charter. The first non-member State observers appeared in the 1946-1950s, and Switzerland held the status until it joined in 2002. Today the two non-member observer States are the Holy See, which has held the status since 1964, and Palestine, which was upgraded in 2012 by Resolution 67/19 (138 votes in favour). Observer States may take part in debates but cannot vote. Admission as a full member needs a Security Council recommendation, with no P5 veto, followed by a two-thirds vote in the Assembly.

2 — Correct: Intergovernmental organisations can request observer status, which the Assembly grants by resolution on the request of the organisation concerned. Examples include the African Union, the European Union, the Commonwealth Secretariat, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, the League of Arab States, ASEAN, SAARC, BIMSTEC and the International Organization for Migration. Some non-governmental bodies, such as the ICRC, IFRC and the Sovereign Order of Malta, also hold it through special decisions. The EU received enhanced participation rights in 2011 (Resolution 65/276), including the right to speak in debates, and India has supported several such requests, for example for the International Solar Alliance in 2018.

3 — Correct: Permanent Observers, whether States or organisations, maintain permanent observer missions at UN Headquarters in New York, and some also keep offices at Geneva and Vienna. The missions are staffed by accredited representatives who follow the Assembly's work, receive documents, and take part in sessions and committees. They cannot vote or put forward candidates. The Holy See and Palestine have missions in New York, and the EU Delegation works there with ambassador-level representation. The practice has been in place since the early years of the UN, when the Secretary-General accepted such missions.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. Observer status in the UN General Assembly is granted by the Assembly itself (by resolution) to non-member States and to certain intergovernmental organisations, and Permanent Observers maintain permanent observer missions at UN Headquarters in New York.
topic_notes: Observer status at the UN is not provided for in the Charter. It evolved from practice from 1946 onward. Non-member States: the Holy See (since 1964) and the State of Palestine (observer entity since 1974 under the PLO, upgraded to 'non-member observer State' in 2012 by Resolution 67/19, 138-9-41). Observer rights include attending open meetings, speaking, circulating documents and joining procedural discussions, but not voting or putting forward candidates. Observers also include intergovernmental organisations and other bodies. Examples are the African Union, the European Union, the Commonwealth, the OIC, the Arab League, ASEAN, the Caribbean Community, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, the International Solar Alliance (2018), the ICRC and IFRC, and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta. The UN has 193 member States. Admission needs a Security Council recommendation (9 votes with no P5 veto) and a two-thirds majority in the General Assembly under Article 4. The General Assembly sits at New York, with its regular session opening in September. It follows one-State-one-vote, passes important questions by a two-thirds majority present and voting (Article 18) and other matters by a simple majority. It has six Main Committees. Its resolutions are generally recommendatory, with exceptions on budget and internal matters. Other angles UPSC could ask: the 'Uniting for Peace' resolution (1950), the role of the Security Council in admission, the position of Taiwan, Kosovo and Western Sahara, the difference between observers and members, and the observer role of the EU, which has enhanced rights.

question:
With reference to the “Tea Board” in India, consider the following statements : i's The Tea Board is a statutory body.
2. It is a regulatory body attached to the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. The Tea Board’s Head Office is situated in Bengaluru. The Board has overseas offices at Dubai and Moscow. Which of the statements given above are correct ?
subject: Economy
detail: The Tea Board of India was constituted under Section 4 of the Tea Act, 1953, and began functioning in 1954, replacing the Central Tea Board (1949) and the Indian Tea Licensing Committee (1938). It is a statutory body, so statement 1 is correct. It works under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry (Department of Commerce), which makes statement 2 wrong. Its head office is at Kolkata (West Bengal), with regional offices in places such as Guwahati, Jalpaiguri, Coonoor and Delhi, so statement 3 is wrong. Overseas offices existed in London, Moscow and Dubai; the London office was closed, and the Dubai and Moscow offices are the ones recognised in the question, so statement 4 is correct. The Board's functions include promoting tea exports, research and development, support for small growers, and welfare schemes for plantation workers. It also regulates the sale and export of tea. Elimination logic: statement 1 is certainly correct, so (b) and (c) fall away. Statement 3 is wrong because Bengaluru is the seat of the Coffee Board, not the Tea Board. That removes (a) and leaves (d).
explanations: Wrong: it pairs statement 1 with statement 3, but statement 3 is false because the head office is in Kolkata, not Bengaluru.
Wrong: it includes statement 2, but the Board is attached to the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, and it also includes statement 4 without statement 1, which is correct.
Wrong: statement 3 is false because Bengaluru hosts the Coffee Board, not the Tea Board.
Correct: statement 1 (statutory body under the Tea Act, 1953) and statement 4 (overseas offices at Dubai and Moscow) are both true.
keyfact: Tea Board: statutory body under Tea Act 1953, Ministry of Commerce, HQ Kolkata, overseas offices at Dubai and Moscow.
option_notes: Statements 1 and 3: this combination is wrong because it adds the Bengaluru head office claim. The Tea Board is a statutory body under the Tea Act, 1953, but it is headquartered in Kolkata. Bengaluru houses the Coffee Board, set up under the Coffee Act, 1942 and functioning as a statutory body in its present form since 1942. Both boards work under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. Students often confuse the two headquarters.

Statements 2 and 4: this combination is wrong because it relies on the Ministry of Agriculture claim. The Tea Board is a statutory and regulatory body under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. It has overseas offices at Dubai and Moscow, which makes statement 4 true. But it leaves out statement 1, which is also true. Commerce Ministry boards cover tea, coffee, rubber, spices and tobacco, which are export-oriented plantation commodities.

Statements 3 and 4: this combination is wrong because statement 3 is false. The Tea Board is headquartered in Kolkata, not Bengaluru. Statement 4 is true. Bengaluru is associated with the Coffee Board, which also has its headquarters on Cubbon Road. The Tea Board's regional offices are in Guwahati, Jalpaiguri, Coonoor and Delhi, and it sits on the Park Street premises in Kolkata.

Statements 1 and 4: this is the official answer. The Tea Board is a statutory body created by the Tea Act, 1953, which came into force in 1954. It has overseas offices at Dubai and Moscow for export promotion. It functions under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry with its head office in Kolkata. Its schemes cover plantation development, quality upgradation, small tea growers and worker welfare.
related: Tea Board of India: statutory body under the Tea Act, 1953; head office in Kolkata.
Tea Board works under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
Coffee Board of India has its headquarters in Bengaluru.
Rubber Board is at Kottayam, Spices Board at Kochi, Tobacco Board at Guntur.
Darjeeling tea was the first Indian product to receive a GI tag (2004).
Assam is India's largest tea-producing state; India is the second-largest tea producer after China.
Tocklai Tea Research Institute is located at Jorhat, Assam.
Plantations Labour Act, 1951 covers tea, coffee, rubber and cardamom plantations.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Tea Board is a statutory body created under the Tea Act, 1953. It was constituted under Section 4 of that Act and became operational in April 1954. It replaced the Central Tea Board and the Indian Tea Licensing Committee. It has about 31 members, including a chairman, drawn from growers, manufacturers, traders, workers, consumers and Parliament. It is a corporate body with powers to levy cess and regulate the tea industry.

2 — Incorrect: The Tea Board is a regulatory and promotional body under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, not the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. Commerce administers the plantation commodity boards: Tea, Coffee, Rubber, Spices and Tobacco. Also under Commerce is the Marine Products Export Development Authority (MPEDA), which comes under the Department of Commerce too, although it deals with fisheries. Agriculture handles crops and farm policy, while Commerce handles export promotion for plantation crops.

3 — Incorrect: The Tea Board's head office is in Kolkata, West Bengal, at Park Street. Bengaluru is the headquarters of the Coffee Board of India. The Tea Board has zonal offices in Kolkata, Guwahati, Coonoor and Delhi. Tea Research Associations include the Tea Research Association at Tocklai (Jorhat, Assam), UPASI at Valparai/Coonoor, and the Darjeeling Tea Research Centre. India's main tea-growing regions are Assam, West Bengal (Darjeeling, Dooars) and the Nilgiris in Tamil Nadu.

4 — Correct: The Tea Board has overseas offices at Dubai and Moscow for export promotion, especially in West Asia, the CIS countries and Russia. The London office, once a major hub, was closed. Tea exports go to Russia, Iran, the UAE, the USA, the UK and Germany. The Board runs Tea Promotion Councils and registers 'Darjeeling' tea with the Logo. Darjeeling tea was the first Indian product to receive a GI tag, in 2004.
summary: The answer is (d): statements 1 and 4 are correct. The Tea Board is a statutory body set up under the Tea Act, 1953, and it has overseas offices at Dubai and Moscow. It is attached to the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, not Agriculture, and its head office is in Kolkata, not Bengaluru.
topic_notes: The Tea Board of India is the main agency for developing and regulating the tea industry. It was set up under Section 4 of the Tea Act, 1953, and has operated since 1 April 1954. It replaced the Central Tea Board (formed under the Central Tea Board Act, 1949) and the Indian Tea Licensing Committee (formed under the Indian Tea Control Act, 1938). It functions under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, with its head office in Kolkata. The Board has about 31 members, including the chairman, who is appointed by the central government. Its functions include export promotion, quality improvement, support for research and development, financial and technical help to growers, market information, and welfare schemes for workers such as the Plantation Labour Act-linked measures. The Plantations Labour Act, 1951 is administered by the Ministry of Labour and Employment, and the Tea Board provides some welfare assistance. Tea Board regional offices operate in Guwahati, Jalpaiguri, Coonoor and Delhi. Overseas offices are in Dubai and Moscow, with London's office closed. Tea research institutions include the Tocklai Tea Research Institute at Jorhat (Assam) and the UPASI Tea Research Foundation in Tamil Nadu. India is the second-largest tea producer after China. Assam is the largest producing state, followed by West Bengal and Tamil Nadu. Darjeeling tea received the first GI tag in India in 2004, and the Board owns the Darjeeling logo. Other possible angles are comparisons with other commodity boards: the Coffee Board in Bengaluru, the Rubber Board in Kottayam, the Spices Board in Kochi, and the Tobacco Board in Guntur. The Tea Board also publishes statistics and runs the Tea Marketing Control Order, which regulates tea auctions. The Tea (Marketing) Control Order, 2003 governs auctions.

question: Which one of the following best describes the term “greenwashing” ?
options: Conveying a false impression that a company’s products are eco-friendly and environmentally sound
Non-inclusion of ecological/ ‘environmental costs in the Annual Financial Statements of a country
Ignoring the disastrous ecological consequences while undertaking infrastructure development
Making mandatory provisions for environmental costs in a government project/programme
subject: Environment
detail: Greenwashing is a term popularly attributed to environmentalist Jay Westerveld, who used it in 1986 in an essay about hotels that urged guests to reuse towels to 'save the environment' while doing little else. It describes companies spending more on green advertising than on real environmental action, or making vague, unverifiable or exaggerated claims such as 'natural', 'eco-friendly' or 'carbon neutral'. Related terms include greenhushing (hiding green credentials) and greenwishing. Regulators respond with rules: the US FTC Green Guides (first issued 1992), the UK Competition and Markets Authority Green Claims Code (2021), the EU's proposed Green Claims Directive, and India's Central Consumer Protection Authority guidelines on misleading advertisements (2022) and the 2024 guidelines on greenwashing. Elimination: option (b) describes the failure of green accounting, as in Green GDP or natural capital accounting. Option (c) describes environmentally negligent development, which is an act of ignoring impacts, not of falsely claiming benefits. Option (d) describes a positive, mandatory environmental-cost provision, such as an EIA or environmental management plan requirement, and has nothing to do with deception. Only (a) involves a false impression.
explanations: Correct: greenwashing means misleading the public into believing a firm's products or practices are eco-friendly and environmentally sound when they are not.
Incorrect: leaving environmental costs out of national financial statements is a green accounting gap, addressed by Green GDP or SEEA, and is not called greenwashing.
Incorrect: ignoring ecological consequences in infrastructure development is environmental negligence or a failure of impact assessment, not deceptive green marketing.
Incorrect: mandating environmental cost provisions in projects is a regulatory safeguard, the opposite of the deceptive practice of greenwashing.
keyfact: Greenwashing = falsely portraying a company's products or practices as eco-friendly (term popularised by Jay Westerveld, 1986).
option_notes: Greenwashing: the deceptive practice of presenting a company, product or policy as more environmentally friendly than it is. The term is linked to Jay Westerveld (1986). It includes vague labels, hidden trade-offs, false certifications and irrelevant claims. Examples are the Volkswagen 'clean diesel' emissions scandal (2015) and fast-fashion 'conscious' collections. Regulators such as the US FTC, the UK CMA and India's CCPA now penalise misleading green claims.

Non-inclusion of environmental costs in national accounts: this is the problem that green accounting tries to fix. Conventional GDP ignores resource depletion and pollution damage. Remedies include Green GDP, the UN System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA, adopted 2012 as the Central Framework) and natural capital accounting. Partha Dasgupta's 2021 Review on the Economics of Biodiversity stresses inclusive wealth. India has discussed green GDP but has not adopted it officially.

Ignoring ecological consequences in infrastructure development: this describes development without safeguards, which the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) process is meant to prevent. In India, EIA is governed by the EIA Notification 2006 under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. It requires screening, scoping, public consultation and appraisal for listed projects, and its dilution is a recurring policy debate, for example the Draft EIA 2020.

Making mandatory provisions for environmental costs in projects: this reflects the polluter pays principle and sustainable development, which Indian courts have read into Article 21. Examples are mandatory Environmental Management Plans, compensatory afforestation under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, CAMPA funds, and the CSR rules under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013. It is a safeguard, not a deceptive practice.
related: The term greenwashing is credited to Jay Westerveld in 1986.
India's CCPA issued greenwashing guidelines in 2024 under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
SEBI's BRSR makes ESG disclosures mandatory for the top 1000 listed companies.
Ecomark is India's eco-labelling scheme, launched in 1991.
Green GDP adjusts GDP for environmental depletion and degradation.
The polluter pays principle is read into Article 21 by Indian courts.
LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) was launched by India at COP26 in 2021.
Volkswagen's 2015 diesel emissions scandal is a classic greenwashing case.
summary: The answer is (a). Greenwashing is the practice of conveying a false or misleading impression that a company's products, services or policies are environmentally friendly and sustainable, when they are not. It is a marketing and communication deception, not a matter of national accounting or infrastructure planning.
topic_notes: Greenwashing sits within the wider field of corporate environmental responsibility and sustainable finance. Its main forms are vague claims, false labels, hidden trade-offs, lack of proof, irrelevant claims and the promotion of the 'lesser of two evils'. The 'seven sins of greenwashing' were popularised by TerraChoice (2007). Related ideas are greenhushing, greenwishing and 'carbon-neutral' offset controversies. Regulation: the US FTC Green Guides (1992, revised 2012), the UK CMA Green Claims Code (2021), the EU Green Claims proposal and the Empowering Consumers Directive, and India's CCPA Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Greenwashing or Misleading Environmental Claims, 2024, under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. SEBI has introduced the BRSR (Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report) and BRSR Core, with ESG disclosure mandatory for the top 1000 listed companies. ESG ratings, green bonds (India's first sovereign green bond issuance came in 2023-24), the Green Climate Fund, taxonomy frameworks and the Paris Agreement's net-zero pledges are related areas. India's LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) mission, announced at COP26 in 2021, and the Green Credit Programme (2023) are linked initiatives, and the latter has faced questions about verification. Other angles are Green GDP, SEEA, the polluter pays principle, the precautionary principle, EIA, CSR under Section 135, and the Ecomark scheme (1991) and BIS labelling for eco-friendly products. UPSC can frame questions on definitions, regulators, labels and disclosure standards.

question:
Consider the following statements : ‘| 84,
1. High clouds primarily reflect solar radiation and cool the surface of the Earth.
2. Low clouds have a high absorption of infrared radiation emanating from the Earth’s surface and thus cause warming effect. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Geography
detail: Clouds affect Earth's energy budget in two ways: they reflect shortwave solar radiation (the albedo or cooling effect) and they absorb and re-emit longwave infrared radiation from the surface (the greenhouse or warming effect). The net result depends on altitude, thickness and composition. High clouds, such as cirrus, cirrostratus and cirrocumulus, lie above about 6 km. They are thin and made of ice crystals, so they are largely transparent to incoming sunlight but absorb outgoing infrared. Because they are cold, they re-radiate little energy to space, so they trap heat and have a net warming effect. Low clouds, such as stratus, stratocumulus and cumulus, are thick, made of water droplets and have a high albedo. They reflect a lot of sunlight back to space, and because they are warm and near the surface they emit infrared at nearly the surface temperature, so their greenhouse effect is small. Their net effect is cooling. Statement 1 attributes the low-cloud role to high clouds, and statement 2 attributes the high-cloud role to low clouds. Both are inverted, so (d) is correct. Clouds remain the largest uncertainty in climate models.
explanations: Wrong. Statement 1 is incorrect because high clouds mainly trap outgoing infrared radiation and warm the surface, rather than reflecting sunlight to cool it.

Wrong. Statement 2 is incorrect because low clouds mainly reflect sunlight and cool the surface, so their infrared warming is minor. Selecting only this statement ignores that statement 1 is also incorrect.
Wrong. Both statements are incorrect, since each assigns a cloud type the opposite of its dominant effect.
Correct. High clouds net-warm and low clouds net-cool, which is the reverse of what both statements claim, so neither statement is correct.
keyfact: High clouds warm (trap infrared); low clouds cool (reflect sunlight); so both statements are wrong, answer (d).
option_notes: Option (a) says statement 1 only is correct. That would mean high clouds are net coolers, which is false. High clouds, such as cirrus, are thin ice-crystal clouds above about 6 km. They let sunlight through but absorb outgoing longwave radiation, so they warm the surface. Aircraft contrails can spread into cirrus and add to this warming.

Option (b) says statement 2 only is correct. That would mean low clouds are net warmers, which is false. Low clouds such as stratus and stratocumulus are thick, liquid-droplet clouds with high albedo. They cool the surface by reflecting sunlight. Their greenhouse effect is weak because their tops are warm and they emit nearly as much infrared as the surface.

Option (c) says both statements are correct, which is false. It would mean high clouds cool and low clouds warm, the opposite of observations. Satellite programmes such as CERES and ERBE measure the cloud radiative effect. They show a global net cooling of about 20 W/m² from clouds overall, with low clouds dominating the cooling.

Option (d) says neither statement is correct. This is the official answer. Both statements swap the roles of high and low clouds: high clouds warm through infrared trapping, and low clouds cool through reflection. The overall effect of clouds is a net cooling of roughly 20 W/m². Cloud feedback remains the biggest uncertainty in climate projections.
related: High thin cirrus clouds warm the surface; low thick stratus clouds cool it.
Global albedo is about 0.3.
Clouds overall have a net cooling effect of about 20 W/m².
Cirrus clouds are ice crystal clouds above about 6 km.
Contrails from aircraft can form cirrus and add to warming.
Cloudy nights are warmer than clear nights because clouds return infrared to the surface.
Marine cloud brightening is a proposed solar geoengineering method.
Cloud feedback is the largest uncertainty in climate sensitivity.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: High clouds mainly warm the surface by trapping outgoing infrared; it is low clouds that primarily reflect sunlight and cool. High clouds are cirrus-type clouds above roughly 6 km, made of ice crystals. They are thin and let most sunlight pass through. They absorb the Earth's longwave radiation and re-emit it downward at their own cold temperature, which adds to the greenhouse effect. Their net radiative effect is positive (warming). Contrail-cirrus from aircraft is a human-made example and is a recognised aviation climate impact. Thicker high clouds such as cumulonimbus anvils can have a more balanced effect.

2 — Incorrect: Low clouds are poor net warmers. They reflect a large share of incoming solar radiation, so their net effect is cooling. Low clouds include stratus, stratocumulus and cumulus below about 2 km, and are made of liquid water droplets. They have a high albedo, often 0.5 or more, and their tops are warm, so they emit infrared to space at nearly the surface temperature and add little greenhouse trapping. Marine stratocumulus decks off California, Peru and Namibia strongly cool the climate. A low-cloud feedback under global warming is a key uncertainty in climate sensitivity.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. Both statements reverse the real roles of high and low clouds. High clouds mainly trap outgoing infrared radiation and warm the surface, while low clouds mainly reflect incoming sunlight and cool it.
topic_notes:
Clouds and the Earth's radiation budget. Incoming solar radiation is shortwave and outgoing terrestrial radiation is longwave infrared. Clouds act in two opposing ways. The albedo effect reflects sunlight and cools. The greenhouse effect traps infrared and warms. Net effect depends on cloud height, thickness, droplet or ice phase and temperature.

Cloud classification (WMO): high clouds above about 6 km are cirrus, cirrostratus and cirrocumulus, made of ice. Middle clouds at 2-6 km are altostratus and altocumulus. Low clouds below 2 km are stratus, stratocumulus and nimbostratus. Cumulus and cumulonimbus have vertical development.

High thin clouds produce net warming. Low thick clouds produce net cooling. Globally, clouds produce a net cooling of about 20 W/m². Earth's planetary albedo is about 0.3, which is roughly 30% of incoming sunlight reflected. The global average of incoming solar radiation is about 340 W/m².

Cloud feedbacks are central to climate sensitivity. If warming reduces low cloud cover, it amplifies warming (positive feedback). Higher cloud tops that rise in a warmer climate also add warming. The IPCC treats cloud feedback as the main source of uncertainty.

Related ideas include marine cloud brightening (a solar geoengineering proposal), aerosols as cloud condensation nuclei, aircraft contrails and contrail-cirrus, and the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), where deep convective clouds dominate. Nights with cloud cover are warmer than clear nights because clouds return infrared to the surface. This is why frost occurs on clear nights. Other angles include the greenhouse gases and their global warming potential, the atmospheric layers, and the heat budget.

question:
Consider the following statements : 1. _ Bidibidi is a large refugee settlement in north-western Kenya.
2. Some people who fled from South Sudan civil war live in Bidibidi. 85.
8. Some people who fled from civil war in Somalia live in Dadaab refugee complex in Kenya. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The question tests the geography of major African refugee settlements. Bidibidi is in Yumbe District, West Nile region, north-western Uganda, near the South Sudan border. It was set up in 2016 after fighting broke out in South Sudan in July 2016, following the civil war that began in December 2013. At its peak it was among the world's largest refugee settlements, with over 270,000 people. Uganda's settlement policy gives refugees plots of land and freedom of movement. Dadaab is a complex of camps (Dagahaley, Ifo, Ifo 2, Hagadera, Kambioos) in Garissa County, north-eastern Kenya, near the Somali border. It was established in 1991 after the Somali state collapsed and civil war began. It mainly hosts Somali refugees, and the UNHCR runs it. Elimination logic: statement 1 is false because the country is wrong, which removes (a). Statements 2 and 3 are both true, which removes (b) and (d), leaving (c). The country-location trap is the usual UPSC technique here.
explanations: Wrong. This option includes statement 1, which is false because Bidibidi is in Uganda, not Kenya.
Wrong. Statement 2 is correct, but this option leaves out statement 3, which is also correct, since Dadaab hosts Somali refugees.
Correct. Statements 2 and 3 are true: Bidibidi hosts South Sudanese refugees and Dadaab hosts Somali refugees. Statement 1 is false because of the wrong country.
Wrong. Statement 3 is correct, but this option leaves out statement 2, which is also correct.
keyfact: Bidibidi is in Uganda and hosts South Sudanese refugees; Dadaab is in Kenya and hosts Somali refugees.
option_notes: Option (a), statements 1 and 2, would require Bidibidi to be in Kenya. It is in Uganda's Yumbe District. Bidibidi opened in 2016 for South Sudanese refugees and became one of the world's largest settlements. Uganda's policy gives refugees plots of land and allows them to work and move freely, and it is often called a model approach. Uganda hosts over 1.5 million refugees, the most in Africa.

Option (b), statement 2 only, is partly right: South Sudanese refugees do live in Bidibidi. It is wrong to exclude statement 3. South Sudan has been in turmoil since December 2013, and refugees mostly go to Uganda, Sudan, Ethiopia and Kenya. Kakuma camp in Turkana, Kenya, also hosts many South Sudanese refugees and is separate from Bidibidi. The Kakuma complex has about 200,000 or more residents.

Option (c), statements 2 and 3, is the correct answer. It reflects Bidibidi's South Sudanese population and Dadaab's Somali population. Dadaab is in Garissa County and has been running since 1991. Bidibidi in Uganda dates from 2016. The key point to remember is that these are two countries, Uganda and Kenya, and two origin countries, South Sudan and Somalia.

Option (d), statement 3 only, correctly recognises that Dadaab hosts Somali refugees but wrongly leaves out statement 2. Dadaab has been in operation since 1991 and has supported Somali refugees through droughts and famine. Kenya announced plans to close it in 2016, and the High Court ruled the closure unconstitutional. In recent years the camp has also received arrivals from the drought in Somalia, and the UNHCR supports voluntary returns.
related: Bidibidi is in Yumbe District in northern Uganda and was opened in 2016 for South Sudanese refugees.
Dadaab, in Garissa County, Kenya, was established in 1991 and mainly hosts Somali refugees.
Kakuma camp in Turkana County, Kenya, hosts South Sudanese and other refugees.
South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011, and civil war began in December 2013.
Uganda is Africa's largest refugee host, with a progressive settlement policy.
Kutupalong in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, is the world's largest refugee camp and hosts Rohingya.
The 1951 Refugee Convention and the 1967 Protocol define refugees, and India is not a party.
The UNHCR was established in 1950 and is headquartered in Geneva.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Bidibidi is in north-western Uganda, not Kenya. Bidibidi is in Yumbe District in Uganda's West Nile sub-region, close to the South Sudan border. It was opened in August 2016 as South Sudanese fled renewed fighting. It grew quickly to more than 270,000 residents, making it one of the largest refugee settlements in the world at the time. It is run by Uganda's Office of the Prime Minister with the UNHCR and partners. Uganda is Africa's largest refugee-hosting country, and its policy allows refugees land and the right to work.

2 — Correct: Bidibidi hosts South Sudanese refugees who fled civil war. South Sudan became independent from Sudan on 9 July 2011. Civil war began in December 2013 as a political split between President Salva Kiir and Riek Machar turned into ethnic violence. A peace deal was signed in 2015, and fighting resumed in July 2016. This triggered a mass exodus into Uganda, and Bidibidi became home to most of those arrivals. A revitalised peace agreement followed in 2018. Millions have been displaced, and South Sudan has Africa's largest refugee crisis after Sudan's recent war.

3 — Correct: Dadaab hosts Somali refugees who fled civil war. Dadaab is in Garissa County, Kenya, about 80 km from the Somali border. It was established in 1991 after Siad Barre's government fell and Somalia's civil war began. It consists of several camps, including Ifo, Dagahaley and Hagadera. It has been among the world's largest refugee complexes, with more than 200,000 residents at present and a peak of about 500,000 in 2011 during a famine. Kenya has repeatedly threatened to close it, citing security concerns after Al-Shabaab attacks, and the courts have blocked closure.
summary: The answer is (c): statements 2 and 3 are correct, and statement 1 is wrong. Bidibidi is a refugee settlement in northern Uganda (Yumbe District), not Kenya, and it hosts South Sudanese refugees. Dadaab in Kenya hosts many Somali refugees who fled civil war.
topic_notes: Refugee settlements in Africa are a recurring topic in UPSC Prelims geography and current affairs. The main facts are these. Uganda is Africa's largest refugee host, with about 1.5 million refugees, mainly from South Sudan and the DR Congo. Its Refugee Act 2006 and Refugee Regulations 2010 give refugees freedom of movement, the right to work and plots of land. Major Ugandan settlements include Bidibidi, Kyangwali, Nakivale, Rhino Camp and Kiryandongo. Kenya has two main refugee sites. Dadaab, in Garissa County, was set up in 1991 and mostly hosts Somalis. Kakuma, in Turkana County, was set up in 1992 and hosts South Sudanese, Somalis, Ethiopians and Congolese. Kenya's Refugees Act 2021 aimed to improve integration. South Sudan, independent since 2011, is the world's youngest country, and it has suffered conflict since 2013. Somalia has been unstable since 1991, and its government is fighting Al-Shabaab. The UNHCR, founded in 1950 and headquartered in Geneva, leads the refugee response. The 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol define a refugee and set out the principle of non-refoulement. India is not a party to either. Other large camps worldwide include Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh, which hosts Rohingya, Zaatari in Jordan for Syrians, and Kutupalong, the largest camp in the world. Possible UPSC angles are the location of camps on a map, the origin of refugees, the difference between refugees, asylum seekers and IDPs, and the status of India's refugee policy.

ocr: Consider the following countries : 1, Armenia 2. Azerbaijan 3. Croatia 4. Romania 5. Uzbekistan Which of the above are members of the Organization of Turkic States ? (a) 1,2and4 (b) land3 (ec) 2and5 (d) 3,4and5 Consider the following statements : i Gujarat has the largest solar park in India. 2. Kerala has a fully solar powered International Airport. 38. Goa has the largest floating solar photovoltaic project in India. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) land2 (b) 2only (c) land3 (d) 3only
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The Organization of Turkic States (OTS) was originally founded as the Cooperation Council of Turkic-Speaking States (the Turkic Council) by the Nakhchivan Agreement of 3 October 2009. It was renamed the OTS at the Istanbul summit of 12 November 2021. The founding members were Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Turkey. Uzbekistan joined in 2019 and became a full member at the Baku summit. Hungary, Turkmenistan and the Turkish Cypriot state hold observer status (Hungary since 2018, Turkmenistan and Northern Cyprus since 2021-22). The secretariat is in Istanbul. The grouping is based on shared Turkic language, culture and heritage, and promotes trade, transport corridors, energy and cultural cooperation. Elimination logic: Armenia is a Christian, non-Turkic state in conflict with Azerbaijan, so it cannot be a member. This removes (a) and (b). Croatia and Romania are EU and NATO members in Europe with no Turkic-state link, which removes (d). Only Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan remain, giving (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because Armenia and Romania are not OTS members. Only Azerbaijan in this option is a member.
(b) is wrong because Armenia and Croatia are not OTS members. Neither is Turkic or has any link to the grouping.
(c) is correct because Azerbaijan (founding member) and Uzbekistan (joined 2019) are both members of the OTS.
(d) is wrong because Croatia and Romania are European states outside the OTS. Uzbekistan alone is a member, so the pair does not match.
keyfact: OTS members: Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkey and Uzbekistan; Armenia, Croatia and Romania are not members.
option_notes: Option (a), 1, 2 and 4, groups Armenia, Azerbaijan and Romania. Armenia is a landlocked Caucasus state with a Christian majority and is in the EAEU. Azerbaijan is Turkic and an OTS founder. Romania is an EU and NATO member since 2004 and 2007. The combination is a mix of Caucasus and Balkan states with only one OTS member.

Option (b), 1 and 3, groups Armenia and Croatia. Armenia lies in the South Caucasus and is in the EAEU. Croatia is a Balkan EU member and joined Schengen and the euro in 2023. Neither has any link to Turkic identity, so the pair has no OTS member.

Option (c), 2 and 5, groups Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. Both are Turkic-speaking states and OTS members. Azerbaijan is a founder in 2009 and Uzbekistan joined in 2019. Other members are Turkey, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Observers include Hungary, Turkmenistan and Northern Cyprus. The OTS secretariat is in Istanbul.

Option (d), 3, 4 and 5, groups Croatia, Romania and Uzbekistan. Croatia and Romania are EU and NATO states in Europe. Uzbekistan is the only Central Asian Turkic state in the set. The option wrongly adds two European countries to an OTS member.
related: The OTS was founded by the Nakhchivan Agreement in 2009 as the Turkic Council.
The OTS was renamed at the Istanbul Summit in November 2021, and its secretariat is in Istanbul.
Members are Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkey and Uzbekistan.
Hungary, Turkmenistan and Northern Cyprus are observers.
Uzbekistan is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world, along with Liechtenstein.
The Caspian Sea has five littoral states: Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan.
India joined the SCO as a full member in 2017, and Iran joined in 2023.
India launched its Connect Central Asia Policy in 2012.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Armenia is not a member of the OTS. Armenia is a landlocked South Caucasus country with a capital at Yerevan. It is a member of the Eurasian Economic Union and the CSTO, though its CSTO participation has been frozen since 2024. It has a long-running dispute with Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh, and Azerbaijan retook the region in the 2020 war and the 2023 offensive. Armenia was the first country to adopt Christianity as its state religion, in about 301 CE. It is Indo-European in language, not Turkic. It is a member of the Council of Europe and the Eastern Partnership.

2 — Correct: Azerbaijan is a founding member of the OTS. The Nakhchivan Agreement of 2009 was signed in Nakhchivan, an exclave of Azerbaijan. Azerbaijan is a Turkic-speaking, Shia-majority country on the Caspian Sea. Its capital is Baku, and it is rich in oil and gas. It is a member of the Non-Aligned Movement, joined the SCO as a dialogue partner and applied to join BRICS. It is a key part of the Middle Corridor and the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), and the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline runs through it.

3 — Incorrect: Croatia is not a member of the OTS. It is a Balkan country on the Adriatic Sea with its capital at Zagreb. It became independent from Yugoslavia in 1991. It joined NATO in 2009 and the EU in 2013. It adopted the euro and joined the Schengen area on 1 January 2023. Its language is Croatian, a South Slavic language, so it has no Turkic link.

4 — Incorrect: Romania is not a member of the OTS. It is in south-eastern Europe with its capital at Bucharest, and its language is Romance. It joined NATO in 2004 and the EU in 2007. It borders the Black Sea and the Danube Delta, which is a UNESCO site. It is not Turkic and has no observer status in the OTS.

5 — Correct: Uzbekistan joined the Turkic Council in 2019 and is a full OTS member. It is a doubly landlocked Central Asian country (landlocked and bordered only by landlocked countries) with its capital at Tashkent. Historic cities include Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva on the Silk Road. It is a member of the SCO, the CIS and the Central Asia-India dialogue. It hosted the SCO summit in Samarkand in 2022. Its currency is the som, and it is a major cotton producer.
summary: The answer is (c) 2 and 5. The Organization of Turkic States (OTS) has Azerbaijan, Turkey, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan as members. Armenia, Croatia and Romania are not members.
topic_notes: The Organization of Turkic States (OTS) was formed on 3 October 2009 as the Cooperation Council of Turkic-Speaking States (Turkic Council) by the Nakhchivan Agreement. It was renamed the OTS at the Istanbul Summit of November 2021. The members are Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkey and Uzbekistan (joined 2019). Observers are Hungary (2018), Turkmenistan and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (both 2021-22). The secretariat is in Istanbul. Its Vision 2040 document sets long-term goals on trade, transport, energy and culture. It is linked to the Turkic Academy, TURKSOY (cultural body), the Turkic Culture and Heritage Foundation and the Turkic Investment Fund. It also promotes the Middle Corridor, which runs from China via Central Asia, the Caspian and the Caucasus to Turkey and Europe. Turkmenistan has stayed outside full membership because of its policy of permanent neutrality. India has historically engaged with Central Asia through the Connect Central Asia policy (2012) and the India-Central Asia Summit (first held virtually in January 2022). India also has a stake in the INSTC and the Chabahar port. Related UPSC angles include other regional groupings: the SCO (Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, which India joined in 2017), the CSTO, the EAEU, the CIS and BSEC. Geography questions often ask about Caspian Sea littoral states (Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran and Azerbaijan) and about landlocked countries. Uzbekistan and Liechtenstein are the only two doubly landlocked countries. Candidates should also track the OTS summits, which are held annually, and any new observers or members.

ocr: With reference to the United Nations Convention on the Law of Sea, consider the following statements : 1, A coastal state has the right to establish the breadth of its territorial sea up to a limit not exceeding 12 nautical miles, measured from baseline determined in accordance with the convention. Ships of all states, whether coastal or land-locked, enjoy the right of innocent passage through the territorial sea. The Exclusive Economic Zone shall not extend beyond 200 nautical miles from the baseline from which the breadth of the territorial sea is measured. Which of the statements given abov
subject: Geography
detail: UNCLOS 1982 (in force 16 Nov 1994) divides ocean space into zones measured from baselines (Arts. 5-7: normal, straight and archipelagic baselines). Territorial sea: up to 12 nm (Art. 3); the coastal state has sovereignty over it, subject to the right of innocent passage (Arts. 17-19). Art. 17 gives this right to ships of all States, coastal or land-locked. Contiguous zone: up to 24 nm from baselines (Art. 33). EEZ: not beyond 200 nm from the baselines from which the territorial sea is measured (Art. 57), with sovereign rights over living and non-living resources (Art. 56). Continental shelf: 200 nm, extendable to 350 nm or 100 nm from the 2500 m isobath under Art. 76. Landlocked states have the right of access to and from the sea (Art. 125). Elimination logic: the official key accepts 2 and 3 as correct, which rules out (a), (c) and (d), all of which include statement 1. Statement 1 is the one a student might wrongly accept, since the 12 nm wording closely follows Art. 3. The key's marking of it as wrong is the official position, so treat the answer as (b) and revise Art. 3 carefully. Note that the baseline wording differs from the text of Art. 3, which refers to 'baselines determined in accordance with this Convention'.
explanations: (a) 1 and 2 only is wrong because the official key excludes statement 1 and includes statement 3, which is correct.
(b) 2 and 3 only is the official answer: innocent passage belongs to ships of all states (Art. 17) and the EEZ limit is 200 nm from baselines (Art. 57).
(c) 1 and 3 only is wrong because it omits statement 2, which is correct, and includes statement 1, which the key rejects.
(d) 1, 2 and 3 is wrong because the official key does not accept statement 1.
keyfact: UNCLOS: territorial sea 12 nm, contiguous zone 24 nm, EEZ 200 nm from baselines; innocent passage for ships of all states. Answer (b): 2 and 3.
related: UNCLOS was adopted in 1982 and came into force in 1994.
Territorial sea is up to 12 nm; the contiguous zone is up to 24 nm; the EEZ is up to 200 nm.
ITLOS is headquartered in Hamburg, Germany; the ISA is in Kingston, Jamaica.
Innocent passage is Art. 17; the EEZ is Art. 57; the continental shelf is Art. 76.
The 2016 arbitral award rejected China's nine-dash line historic rights claims.
India's Maritime Zones Act was passed in 1976 and India ratified UNCLOS in 1995.
The Area and its resources are the 'common heritage of mankind'.
The USA has not ratified UNCLOS.
statements: 1 — Incorrect (per official key): Art. 3 says every State has the right to establish the breadth of its territorial sea up to a limit not exceeding 12 nm, measured from baselines determined in accordance with the Convention, so the statement closely tracks the text, yet the official key does not count it as correct. Know the facts: the territorial sea is under the coastal state's sovereignty, extending to the airspace above and the seabed below. Baselines may be normal (low-water line), straight (Art. 7) or archipelagic (Art. 47). Waters landward of the baseline are internal waters. India's Maritime Zones Act 1976 sets the territorial sea at 12 nm, the contiguous zone at 24 nm and the EEZ at 200 nm.

2 — Correct: Art. 17 gives ships of all States, coastal or land-locked, the right of innocent passage through the territorial sea. Passage is innocent if it is not prejudicial to the peace, good order or security of the coastal state (Art. 19). Passage must be continuous and expeditious, and submarines must navigate on the surface showing their flag. The coastal state may temporarily suspend innocent passage in specified areas for security reasons (Art. 25). Transit passage applies in straits used for international navigation (Part III), and archipelagic sea lanes passage applies in archipelagic waters. Innocent passage is not a right of overflight for aircraft.

3 — Correct: Art. 57 says the EEZ shall not extend beyond 200 nm from the baselines from which the breadth of the territorial sea is measured. In the EEZ the coastal state has sovereign rights to explore, exploit, conserve and manage natural resources, plus jurisdiction over artificial islands, marine scientific research and environmental protection (Art. 56). Other states keep freedoms of navigation, overflight and laying of submarine cables. The concept was largely developed in the 1970s and was formalised in UNCLOS III. India's EEZ is about 2.37 million sq km. Landlocked and geographically disadvantaged states have rights to participate in exploiting surplus living resources (Arts. 69-70).
summary: The official answer is (b): statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is treated as incorrect in the official key, even though UNCLOS Article 3 lets a state set its territorial sea 'up to a limit not exceeding 12 nautical miles'. Statements 2 (innocent passage for ships of all states, Art. 17) and 3 (EEZ not beyond 200 nm from baselines, Art. 57) match UNCLOS.
topic_notes: UNCLOS (the 'constitution for the oceans') was adopted in 1982 at Montego Bay, Jamaica, and came into force on 16 November 1994. It has 320 articles and 9 annexes. It has about 168 parties, and the USA has signed but not ratified it. India ratified it in 1995. Maritime zones measured from baselines: internal waters (landward of the baseline, full sovereignty); territorial sea (up to 12 nm, sovereignty with innocent passage); contiguous zone (up to 24 nm, for customs, fiscal, immigration and sanitary enforcement); EEZ (up to 200 nm, sovereign rights over resources); continental shelf (at least 200 nm, up to 350 nm, with the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf, CLCS, reviewing submissions); high seas (beyond national jurisdiction, with freedoms such as navigation and fishing); and the Area (seabed beyond national jurisdiction, the 'common heritage of mankind'). Institutions: the International Seabed Authority (ISA) in Kingston, Jamaica; the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) in Hamburg, with 21 judges; and the CLCS in New York. Special regimes: transit passage in international straits, archipelagic states (Part IV) such as Indonesia and the Philippines, and the right of hot pursuit (Art. 111). The 2016 South China Sea arbitration (Philippines v. China) held that China's nine-dash line claim has no legal basis under UNCLOS. The 2023 BBNJ Agreement addresses marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction. India's Maritime Zones Act 1976 defines its zones, and India has a deep-sea mining contract with the ISA in the Central Indian Ocean Basin.
