ocr: With reference to the United Nations Convention on the Law of Sea, consider the following statements : 1, A coastal state has the right to establish the breadth of its territorial sea up to a limit not exceeding 12 nautical miles, measured from baseline determined in accordance with the convention. Ships of all states, whether coastal or land-locked, enjoy the right of innocent passage through the territorial sea. The Exclusive Economic Zone shall not extend beyond 200 nautical miles from the baseline from which the breadth of the territorial sea is measured. Which of the statements given abov
subject: Geography
detail: The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), also called the Law of the Sea Treaty, was adopted in 1982 at the Third UN Conference (UNCLOS III) and came into force on 16 November 1994. It sets up maritime zones measured from baselines. These are normally the low-water line along the coast (normal baseline) or straight baselines in indented coasts (Art. 7). Internal waters lie landward of the baseline and are under full sovereignty. The territorial sea extends up to 12 nm (Art. 3) and is under sovereignty, subject to innocent passage (Arts. 17-19). The contiguous zone extends up to 24 nm from the baseline (Art. 33). The EEZ extends up to 200 nm (Art. 57), with sovereign rights over resources but freedom of navigation and overflight for others. The continental shelf extends to 200 nm, or up to 350 nm in some cases (Art. 76). The high seas and the Area lie beyond these limits. Elimination logic: statements 1 and 3 are standard textbook limits. Statement 2 is the tricky one, because it might seem that only coastal states have the right. Art. 17 says 'ships of all States, whether coastal or land-locked' enjoy innocent passage. So all three are correct and (d) follows.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it leaves out statement 3, and the EEZ limit of 200 nm from the baseline is correct under Art. 57.
(b) is wrong because it leaves out statement 1, and the 12 nm territorial sea limit is correct under Art. 3.
(c) is wrong because it leaves out statement 2, and Art. 17 gives the right of innocent passage to ships of all states, coastal or land-locked.
(d) is correct because all three statements match UNCLOS: the 12 nm territorial sea (Art. 3), innocent passage for all states (Art. 17), and the 200 nm EEZ limit (Art. 57).
keyfact: UNCLOS 1982: territorial sea 12 nm, contiguous zone 24 nm, EEZ 200 nm from baseline, and innocent passage for ships of all states, coastal or land-locked.
related: UNCLOS came into force on 16 November 1994 and India ratified it in 1995.
The contiguous zone extends up to 24 nm from the baseline (Art. 33).
The ITLOS is headquartered in Hamburg, Germany, and has 21 judges.
The International Seabed Authority is in Kingston, Jamaica, and manages the Area.
The continental shelf may extend up to 350 nm under Art. 76, per the CLCS.
The 2016 South China Sea arbitration rejected China's nine-dash line claims.
Hot pursuit is allowed under Art. 111 and must begin within the maritime zones of the coastal state.
India's EEZ is about 2.37 million sq km.
statements: 1 — Correct: Art. 3 lets every state fix its territorial sea up to 12 nm from baselines determined under the Convention. The territorial sea is the belt of sea adjacent to the coast over which the state has sovereignty, extending to the airspace above and to the seabed and subsoil. Baselines may be normal (low-water line, Art. 5) or straight (Art. 7). India claims 12 nm under the Maritime Zones of India Act, 1976. Before UNCLOS, claims varied from 3 to 200 nm. Sovereignty is limited by the right of innocent passage.

2 — Correct: Art. 17 grants ships of all states, coastal or land-locked, the right of innocent passage through the territorial sea. Passage is innocent if it is not prejudicial to the peace, good order or security of the coastal state (Art. 19). Submarines must navigate on the surface and show their flag. Fishing, weapons practice, spying and pollution make passage non-innocent. Warship passage is contested, and some states require prior notice. Transit passage applies in international straits, and archipelagic sea lanes passage applies in archipelagic waters. Land-locked states also have a right of access to the sea (Part X).

3 — Correct: Art. 57 says the EEZ shall not extend beyond 200 nm from the baselines from which the territorial sea is measured. In the EEZ the coastal state has sovereign rights over living and non-living resources, over energy production from water, currents and winds, and jurisdiction over artificial islands, marine scientific research and environmental protection. Other states keep freedom of navigation, overflight and cable-laying. The EEZ concept was formalised by UNCLOS. India declared its EEZ in 1976 and has about 2.37 million sq km of EEZ.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. UNCLOS 1982 allows a coastal state to claim a territorial sea up to 12 nautical miles from baselines (Art. 3), grants ships of all states, coastal or land-locked, innocent passage (Art. 17), and limits the EEZ to 200 nautical miles from the territorial-sea baselines (Art. 57).
topic_notes: UNCLOS 1982, called the 'constitution for the oceans', was concluded at Montego Bay, Jamaica on 10 December 1982 and entered into force on 16 November 1994. It has 320 articles and 9 annexes. India ratified it in 1995. The US has signed but not ratified. Zones measured from the baseline: internal waters (landward of baseline); territorial sea up to 12 nm (sovereignty, innocent passage); contiguous zone up to 24 nm (customs, fiscal, immigration, sanitary enforcement); EEZ up to 200 nm (sovereign rights over resources); continental shelf (natural prolongation, 200 nm, up to 350 nm or 100 nm beyond the 2500 m isobath, subject to the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf); high seas (freedom for all, Part VII); and the Area (seabed beyond national jurisdiction, the common heritage of mankind, run by the International Seabed Authority in Kingston, Jamaica). The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) is in Hamburg, Germany, with 21 judges. Archipelagic states can draw archipelagic baselines (Part IV), for example Indonesia and the Philippines. The Convention also covers straits used for international navigation (transit passage), hot pursuit (Art. 111), and the rights of land-locked states. Disputes include the South China Sea arbitration of 2016 (Philippines v. China), where the tribunal rejected China's nine-dash line claim. India's Maritime Zones of India Act, 1976 governs its zones. India also settled maritime boundary disputes with Bangladesh (2014, PCA) and with Myanmar and others through agreements.

question: Which one of the following statements best 88. reflects the issue with Senkaku Islands, sometimes mentioned in the news ?
options: It is generally believed that they are artificial islands made by a country around South China Sea
China and Japan engage in maritime disputes over these islands in East China Sea
A permanent American military base has been set up there to help Taiwan to increase its defence capabilities
Though International Court of Justice declared them as no man’s land, some South-East Asian countries claim them
subject: Geography
detail: The Senkaku Islands are a group of five uninhabited islets and three rocks in the East China Sea, northeast of Taiwan and west of Okinawa. Japan administers them as part of Okinawa Prefecture and says it incorporated them in January 1895 after finding them to be terra nullius. China and Taiwan base their claims on historical discovery and usage, and argue that the islands were ceded under the 1895 Treaty of Shimonoseki and should have been returned to China after WWII. The US administered them after WWII and returned them to Japan under the 1971 Okinawa Reversion Agreement, which took effect in 1972. Interest in the islands grew after a 1968 UN survey suggested possible oil and gas reserves. Japan's 2012 purchase of three of the islands from a private owner set off severe tensions. Chinese coast guard vessels and aircraft now regularly enter the surrounding waters and airspace. The US says the islands fall under Article 5 of the US-Japan Security Treaty, though it takes no position on sovereignty. Elimination: (a) is wrong because the islands are natural and the South China Sea is the wrong sea. (c) is wrong because there is no American base there. (d) is wrong because the ICJ has made no such ruling and the claimants are China, Taiwan and Japan, not South-East Asian states.
explanations: Incorrect: the Senkakus are natural uninhabited islets, not artificial islands, and they lie in the East China Sea, not the South China Sea. The artificial island controversy concerns features such as the Spratlys and Paracels.
Correct: Japan administers the islands, and China (which calls them Diaoyu) and Taiwan also claim them. China-Japan tension over them, including coast guard incursions, is the central issue.

Incorrect: no permanent American base exists on the Senkakus. The US has bases elsewhere in Japan, such as Okinawa, and treats the islands as covered by the US-Japan security treaty, but this is unrelated to helping Taiwan's defence.
Incorrect: the ICJ has never declared the islands no man's land. The disputants are Japan, China and Taiwan, not South-East Asian countries.
keyfact: Senkaku (Diaoyu) Islands: uninhabited East China Sea islets administered by Japan and claimed by China and Taiwan.
option_notes: Artificial islands in the South China Sea: China has built artificial islands by reclamation on reefs in the Spratly Islands (Fiery Cross, Subi, Mischief) and has also built up the Paracels. An arbitral tribunal under UNCLOS ruled in July 2016, in the Philippines v. China case, that China's nine-dash line claim has no legal basis. China rejects the ruling. Artificial islands do not generate territorial seas under UNCLOS Article 60 and Article 121.

East China Sea dispute: the Senkaku/Diaoyu islets lie roughly 170 km northeast of Taiwan and about 400 km from the Japanese mainland. Japan controls them, and China and Taiwan claim them. The area has fishing grounds, possible hydrocarbons and key sea lanes. China declared an East China Sea Air Defence Identification Zone in 2013. The US says Article 5 of the security treaty applies to the islands.

Permanent American base: there is no such base on the Senkakus. The US maintains large forces in Japan, including on Okinawa, under the 1960 Treaty of Mutual Cooperation and Security. US policy on Taiwan is governed by the Taiwan Relations Act of 1979 and the One China policy. Two of the islets, Kuba and Taisho, were used by the US as firing ranges during its administration.

ICJ and no man's land: the ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the UN, based in The Hague, and decides only cases brought by consenting states. It has issued no Senkaku ruling. Japan's claim rests on terra nullius incorporation in 1895. Japan says no dispute exists and rejects third-party adjudication. The ICJ did decide the Pedra Branca case (Malaysia v. Singapore, 2008) and the Sipadan-Ligitan case (2002).
related: Senkaku islands are called Diaoyu in China and Diaoyutai in Taiwan.
Japan administers the Senkakus as part of Okinawa Prefecture.
The US returned the islands to Japan under the 1971 Okinawa Reversion Agreement, effective 1972.
The 2016 arbitral tribunal under UNCLOS rejected China's nine-dash line claim in the Philippines v. China case.
China declared an ADIZ over the East China Sea in November 2013.
The Kuril Islands dispute is between Russia and Japan.
Dokdo/Takeshima is disputed between South Korea and Japan.
UNCLOS gives a 12 nautical mile territorial sea and a 200 nautical mile EEZ.
summary: The answer is (b). The Senkaku Islands (called Diaoyu by China and Diaoyutai by Taiwan) are uninhabited islets in the East China Sea that Japan administers and China and Taiwan also claim, which makes them a long-running China-Japan maritime dispute.
topic_notes: The East China Sea and South China Sea disputes are a favourite UPSC theme. The Senkaku/Diaoyu islands lie in the East China Sea and are administered by Japan, while China and Taiwan claim them. Key history: the 1895 Japanese incorporation, the Treaty of Shimonoseki (1895), the San Francisco Peace Treaty (1951), US administration of the islands, and reversion to Japan in 1972. The 1968 ECAFE survey pointed to possible hydrocarbons, after which the Chinese and Taiwanese claims intensified. In 2012 Japan nationalised three islets, buying them from a private owner, which caused anti-Japan protests in China. In 2013 China declared an East China Sea ADIZ. The US says Article 5 of the US-Japan Security Treaty covers the islands, and reaffirmed this under successive presidents. The South China Sea is a separate dispute: China's nine-dash line, the claims of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei, the Spratlys and Paracels, Scarborough Shoal, and the 2016 arbitral award under UNCLOS. Other island disputes to revise: the Kuril Islands or Northern Territories (Russia-Japan), Dokdo/Takeshima (Japan-South Korea) and Spratly claims. Also revise the Quad (India, US, Japan, Australia), the Indo-Pacific concept and UNCLOS 1982 (territorial sea 12 nautical miles, EEZ 200 nautical miles, contiguous zone 24 nautical miles). UPSC often pairs a place name with the right sea, country or dispute, so memorise the location and the parties.

question:
Consider the following pairs : Country Important reason for being in the news recently
1. Chad Setting up of permanent military base by China
2. Guinea Suspension of Constitution and Government by military
3. Lebanon Severe and prolonged economic depression
4. Tunisia Suspension of Parliament by President How many pairs given above are correctly 90. matched ?
subject: Economy
detail: This question tests current affairs from 2021 across Africa and West Asia. Guinea: on 5 September 2021 the special forces under Col. Mamady Doumbouya arrested President Alpha Condé, dissolved the government and suspended the Constitution. Lebanon: the World Bank described its crisis as among the worst depressions globally since the mid-19th century, with the currency collapsing, banks restricting withdrawals and the Beirut port explosion (August 2020) worsening matters. Tunisia: on 25 July 2021 President Kais Saied suspended Parliament, dismissed the PM and assumed executive powers, which critics called a self-coup. Chad: in April 2021 President Idriss Déby was killed fighting rebels (FACT) and his son Mahamat Déby led a military council. There was no news of a Chinese permanent base there. China's only overseas military base is in Djibouti (2017), and reports in 2021 concerned a possible base in Equatorial Guinea, which is probably the source of the trap. Elimination: once you are sure about pairs 2, 3 and 4, the answer must be (c), even if Chad is uncertain.
explanations: (a) is wrong: three, not one, of the pairs are correct (Guinea, Lebanon and Tunisia).
(b) is wrong: two correct pairs would undercount; pair 2 (Guinea), pair 3 (Lebanon) and pair 4 (Tunisia) are all accurate.
(c) is right: pairs 2, 3 and 4 are correct, and pair 1 is incorrect because China has no permanent military base in Chad.
(d) is wrong: pair 1 is false, since China's only declared overseas military base is in Djibouti, not Chad.
keyfact: 2021 headlines: Guinea coup, Lebanon's economic collapse and Tunisia's parliament suspension are true; China's only overseas base is in Djibouti, not Chad.
option_notes: Only one pair: this would mean that just one of the four country-event matches holds. It is incorrect here. It is a typical distractor for students who are unsure of the 2021 African and West Asian events. The correct count includes Guinea's coup, Lebanon's collapse and Tunisia's parliamentary suspension. Remember that UPSC often builds such 'how many pairs' questions from current affairs, so each country's 2021 headline matters.

Only two pairs: this would hold if a student wrongly rejected one of the three true pairs, such as Lebanon (because 'depression' sounds unusual) or Tunisia. In reality all three are well documented. The World Bank called Lebanon's crisis one of the worst since the 1850s, and Tunisia's Saied suspended Parliament on 25 July 2021 under Article 80. This option is therefore not correct.

Only three pairs: this is the official answer. Pairs 2, 3 and 4 are correct: Guinea's September 2021 coup, Lebanon's economic depression and Tunisia's July 2021 suspension of Parliament. Pair 1 fails because China has no permanent military base in Chad. China's only established overseas base is at Doumeira, Djibouti (opened 2017). Reports in 2021 of a possible Chinese Atlantic base concerned Equatorial Guinea.

All four pairs: this would require China to have set up a permanent base in Chad, which did not happen. It is a trap for those who know that China is expanding its military footprint in Africa. China's declared base is in Djibouti, near the Bab-el-Mandeb strait and close to US, French, Japanese and Italian bases. Chad was in the news for the death of Idriss Déby in April 2021.
related: Guinea coup, 5 Sept 2021: Col. Mamady Doumbouya ousted President Alpha Condé.
China's only declared overseas military base is in Djibouti (opened 2017).
Tunisia's President Kais Saied suspended Parliament on 25 July 2021.
Lebanon defaulted on its Eurobonds for the first time in March 2020.
Idriss Déby, long-time Chad president, died in April 2021; his son Mahamat headed the transitional council.
Sudan's military coup took place on 25 October 2021, ousting PM Abdalla Hamdok.
Myanmar's military seized power on 1 February 2021, detaining Aung San Suu Kyi.
The Arab Spring began in Tunisia in December 2010.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: China has not set up a permanent military base in Chad; its only declared overseas base is in Djibouti. Chad is a landlocked Central African state with capital N'Djamena. In 2021 the news was President Idriss Déby's death (April) and the military council led by his son, Mahamat Déby. Chad is a Sahel G5 member and French military partner. The confusion probably arose from reports of a Chinese naval base in Equatorial Guinea (Atlantic coast, Bata), reported by the US in December 2021. Chad's currency is the CFA franc and it is an oil exporter.

2 — Correct: In September 2021 Guinea's army special forces led by Col. Mamady Doumbouya seized power, detained President Alpha Condé, and dissolved the Constitution and government. Condé had won a controversial third term in October 2020 after changing the constitution. Guinea, capital Conakry, is a West African state and a major bauxite producer. ECOWAS and the African Union suspended it. Guinea was a French colony until 1958 under Sékou Touré. Other recent coups: Mali (2020, 2021), Myanmar (Feb 2021), Sudan (Oct 2021).

3 — Correct: Lebanon has faced a severe, prolonged economic depression since 2019. The Lebanese pound lost over 90 percent of its value, banks imposed capital controls, inflation soared and fuel and power shortages followed. The World Bank ranked the crisis among the top three worst globally since the 1850s. The August 2020 Beirut port blast worsened the situation. Lebanon has a confessional power-sharing system (Maronite president, Sunni PM, Shia speaker). Najib Mikati became PM in September 2021. Lebanon has been negotiating an IMF programme and has defaulted on its Eurobonds (March 2020).

4 — Correct: On 25 July 2021 Tunisian President Kais Saied invoked Article 80 of the Constitution to suspend Parliament for 30 days, lift MPs' immunity and dismiss PM Hichem Mechichi, later extending the measures. The opposition, notably the Islamist Ennahda party, called it a coup. Tunisia was the birthplace of the Arab Spring (2010-11) after Mohamed Bouazizi's self-immolation and is seen as the only democratic success of that movement. Saied dissolved Parliament in March 2022 and a new Constitution was adopted by referendum in July 2022, strengthening presidential power.
summary: The answer is (c): only three pairs are correct. Pairs 2, 3 and 4 match real 2021 events (Guinea coup, Lebanon's economic collapse, Tunisia's parliament suspension), while pair 1 is wrong because China has no permanent military base in Chad.
topic_notes:
This question belongs to world current affairs, mainly Africa and West Asia in 2021. Key themes were military coups and democratic backsliding, economic collapse, and great-power competition in Africa.

Coups: Mali (August 2020 and May 2021, Col. Assimi Goïta), Chad (April 2021, military council under Mahamat Déby), Guinea (September 2021, Col. Mamady Doumbouya), Sudan (October 2021, Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan removed PM Hamdok) and Myanmar (1 February 2021, Gen. Min Aung Hlaing). Later came Burkina Faso (January and September 2022) and Niger (2023). The African Union and ECOWAS typically suspend members after coups.

Tunisia: the Arab Spring began there in December 2010 and led to the fall of Ben Ali in January 2011. Saied's actions in 2021 reversed much of the democratic gain. Article 80 allows exceptional measures in case of imminent danger.

Lebanon: the economy has been in free fall since October 2019, with sovereign default in March 2020, the Beirut blast on 4 August 2020, and political deadlock. Its system rests on the 1989 Taif Agreement and confessional power sharing. Hezbollah is a major political and military actor.

China in Africa: the base in Djibouti (2017), Belt and Road investments, FOCAC (Forum on China-Africa Cooperation), and the 2021 reports on Equatorial Guinea. The US has AFRICOM, with a major base at Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti. France's Operation Barkhane in the Sahel was wound down in 2022.

For revision, keep a table of each country, its capital, its leader and the event, because UPSC regularly draws match-the-pair questions from such lists.

question:
Consider the following pairs : Region often mentioned Country in the news
1. Anatolia — Turkey
2. Amhara — Ethiopia
3. Cabo Delgado — Spain
4. Catalonia — Italy How many pairs given above are correctly matched ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This question tests current-affairs geography: regions that were in the news and the countries they belong to. Anatolia (Asia Minor) is the Asian part of Turkey, and it was in the news because of the February 2023-era earthquake zone discussions and the Turkey-related coverage around the paper's time. Amhara is a regional state in northern Ethiopia and was a major theatre of the Tigray conflict that began in November 2020, with Amhara forces and militias involved over disputed areas such as Western Tigray (Welkait). Cabo Delgado is Mozambique's northernmost province, where an Islamist insurgency (Ansar al-Sunna, locally called al-Shabaab, linked to ISIS) has operated since 2017, and it holds large LNG gas projects such as TotalEnergies' Mozambique LNG. Catalonia is an autonomous community of north-eastern Spain with its capital at Barcelona, and it held a disputed independence referendum on 1 October 2017. Elimination logic: once you know that Cabo Delgado is African and Catalonia is Spanish, pairs 3 and 4 fall away, leaving exactly two correct pairs, which is option (b).
explanations: Wrong: more than one pair is correct, since both Anatolia–Turkey and Amhara–Ethiopia are right.
Correct: exactly two pairs, 1 and 2, are matched properly, while Cabo Delgado is in Mozambique and Catalonia is in Spain.
Wrong: pairs 3 and 4 are both incorrect, so three cannot be right.
Wrong: Cabo Delgado–Spain and Catalonia–Italy are mismatched, so not all four are correct.
keyfact: Anatolia = Turkey, Amhara = Ethiopia, Cabo Delgado = Mozambique, Catalonia = Spain.
option_notes: Only one pair: this would hold if just one region matched its country. It is wrong here because two match. The question is about regions in the news: Anatolia (Turkey), Amhara (Ethiopia), Cabo Delgado (Mozambique) and Catalonia (Spain). Students often get only the African regions wrong, so learn each region with its country and the reason it appeared in the news, such as insurgency, civil war or secession movements.

Only two pairs: this is the official answer. Pairs 1 and 2 are correct. Anatolia is the Asian, peninsular part of Turkey, and Amhara is a northern Ethiopian state around Lake Tana, with Bahir Dar as capital. The false pairs swap Cabo Delgado (actually Mozambique) with Spain and Catalonia (actually Spain) with Italy. UPSC typically builds such pairs by deliberately shifting a country.

Only three pairs: this would require one of the two false pairs to be right. Neither is. Cabo Delgado lies in northern Mozambique, which has had an insurgency since 2017 and has major LNG investments. Catalonia lies in Spain and had the 2017 referendum. Italy has regions like Lombardy, Sicily and Sardinia but not Catalonia, though the Sardinian town Alghero has a Catalan-speaking minority.

All four pairs: this would mean every region matched its country. It is wrong because Cabo Delgado is not in Spain and Catalonia is not in Italy. Spain's autonomous communities include Catalonia, Basque Country, Galicia and Andalusia. Mozambique's provinces include Cabo Delgado, Niassa, Nampula and Maputo. Such all-correct options are rarely right in UPSC pair questions on current affairs.
related: Anatolia is also called Asia Minor; Ankara is Turkey's capital.
Lake Tana in Amhara is the source of the Blue Nile.
Tigray War began in November 2020; Pretoria peace deal in November 2022.
Cabo Delgado is in northern Mozambique on the Tanzanian border.
Catalonia's capital is Barcelona; the 2017 referendum was held on 1 October.
Article 155 of the Spanish Constitution allows Madrid to impose direct rule on regions.
Abiy Ahmed won the 2019 Nobel Peace Prize.
Rovuma basin gas fields are off northern Mozambique.
statements: 1 — Correct: Anatolia is the large peninsula forming the Asian part of Turkey. Anatolia, also called Asia Minor, lies between the Black Sea, the Aegean and the Mediterranean. It covers most of Turkey's land area. Ankara, the capital, is in central Anatolia. It was home to the Hittites, Lydians and Phrygians and later to the Byzantine and Ottoman heartlands. The region is seismically active along the North Anatolian and East Anatolian faults. The Anatolian plateau is largely semi-arid, and the region is a key agricultural zone.

2 — Correct: Amhara is a regional state of Ethiopia, home to the Amhara people. Its capital is Bahir Dar, and Lake Tana, the source of the Blue Nile, lies there. Amharic is Ethiopia's federal working language. The region borders Tigray to the north and was heavily involved in the Tigray War (from November 2020), including disputes over Western Tigray and Raya. Lalibela's rock-hewn churches (UNESCO site) and Gondar's castles are in Amhara. Ethiopia's capital is Addis Ababa, and the country is a federal republic with ethnic-based regional states.

3 — Incorrect: Cabo Delgado is in Mozambique, not Spain. It is Mozambique's northernmost province, bordering Tanzania across the Rovuma River, with Pemba as its capital. Since October 2017 an insurgency by Ansar al-Sunna (locally called al-Shabaab, affiliated with ISIS-Mozambique) has caused thousands of deaths and displaced hundreds of thousands, including the 2021 Palma attack. The province has huge offshore natural gas reserves in the Rovuma basin, with the TotalEnergies LNG project suspended after 2021. Rwanda and SADC forces were deployed to help. Mozambique's capital is Maputo.

4 — Incorrect: Catalonia is an autonomous community in Spain, not Italy. Its capital is Barcelona, and its languages are Catalan, Spanish and Aranese. It held an independence referendum on 1 October 2017, which Spain's Constitutional Court had declared illegal, and the Catalan parliament made a unilateral declaration of independence, after which Madrid imposed direct rule under Article 155 of the Spanish Constitution. Leader Carles Puigdemont fled to Belgium. Catalonia is among Spain's wealthiest regions and is a major industrial and tourism centre.
summary: The answer is (b) Only two pairs. Anatolia is in Turkey and Amhara is in Ethiopia, so pairs 1 and 2 are correct. Cabo Delgado is in Mozambique, not Spain, and Catalonia is in Spain, not Italy, so pairs 3 and 4 are wrong.
topic_notes: This question belongs to the 'places in the news' category, which UPSC repeats almost every year in prelims. The method is to link each place to its country, a map position and the reason it was in the news. Key facts: Anatolia is the Asian part of Turkey, lying between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, and is earthquake-prone; Turkey straddles Europe and Asia, with the Bosphorus and Dardanelles as its straits and Ankara as capital. Ethiopia is landlocked, with Addis Ababa as capital and the African Union headquarters there. Its regions include Amhara, Tigray, Oromia, Afar and Somali. The Tigray conflict began in November 2020 between the federal government (PM Abiy Ahmed, Nobel Peace Prize 2019) and the TPLF, and a cessation of hostilities was signed in Pretoria in November 2022. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile is disputed with Egypt and Sudan. Mozambique's Cabo Delgado has an ISIS-linked insurgency, a large LNG potential in the Rovuma basin, and is on the Mozambique Channel. Spain's Catalonia pursued independence in 2017, and Article 155 was used. Other separatist or regional places in the news that UPSC may ask about: Scotland (UK), Quebec (Canada), Flanders (Belgium), Kurdistan (Iraq, Turkey, Syria, Iran), Tigray, Nagorno-Karabakh (Azerbaijan), Donbas and Crimea (Ukraine), Xinjiang (China), Rakhine (Myanmar), Tigray and Ogaden. Also note Sahel countries, Darfur (Sudan), Kivu (DR Congo) and Tigray as African conflict zones. Maps and straits are frequently tested in the same way.

ocr: With reference to Indian laws about wildlife protection, consider the following statements : 1. Wild animals are the sole property of the government. 2. When a wild animal is declared protected, such animal is entitled for equal protection whether it is found in protected areas or outside. 8. Apprehension of a protected wild animal becoming a danger to human life is sufficient ground for its capture or killing. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) land2 (b) 2only (c) land3 (d) 3only Certain species of which one of the following organisms are well known as cultivators of fun
subject: Environment
detail: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (WPA) protects species listed in its Schedules, and the protection travels with the species. Section 9 bans hunting of scheduled animals everywhere, not only in national parks or sanctuaries. Statement 2 is therefore correct. Statement 1 fails because of the word 'sole'. Section 39 makes certain wild animals government property: those hunted illegally, found dead or killed, or kept in captivity in contravention of the Act. It does not make every wild animal the exclusive property of the government, and the Act recognises lawfully held animals and trophies. Statement 3 fails because Section 11(1)(a) lets the Chief Wild Life Warden permit killing or capture of a Schedule I animal only when the animal has actually become dangerous to human life, or is disabled or diseased beyond recovery. The order must be recorded in writing. Capture, tranquilisation or translocation must be tried first, and the killing is allowed only if capture is impossible. Courts have repeatedly held that mere apprehension is not enough. Elimination logic: statement 2 is correct and appears in options (a) and (b), and statement 3 is wrong. That removes (a), (c) and (d), leaving (b).
explanations: (a) 1 and 2 is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect. Wild animals are not the 'sole' property of the government, since Section 39 covers only specified categories.
(b) 2 only is correct. Protection of a declared protected animal applies equally inside and outside protected areas. Statements 1 and 3 are incorrect.
(c) 1 and 3 is wrong because both statements are incorrect. 'Sole property' overstates Section 39, and mere apprehension of danger is not a legal ground for capture or killing.
(d) 3 only is wrong because statement 3 is incorrect. Section 11 needs an actual danger to human life and a written order from the Chief Wild Life Warden. Statement 2 is correct but is omitted here.
keyfact: Under the WPA 1972, protection follows the species, not the location, but killing a dangerous animal is allowed only when it has actually become a danger and capture has failed; mere apprehension does not qualify.
related: WPA 1972 Section 9 prohibits hunting of scheduled animals; Section 11 allows killing only when the animal is actually dangerous or diseased beyond recovery.
Section 39 of WPA makes specified categories of wild animals government property.
The WPA Amendment Act 2022 reduced the Schedules from six to four and came into force on 1 April 2023.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) moved 'protection of wild animals and birds' to the Concurrent List.
Article 48A (DPSP) directs the State to protect the environment, forests and wildlife; Article 51A(g) is the corresponding Fundamental Duty.
Conservation reserves (Section 36A) and community reserves (Section 36C) were added by the 2002 amendment.
The National Tiger Conservation Authority became statutory through the 2006 amendment of the WPA.
The 2022 amendment gave statutory backing to the CITES framework in India.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Section 39 vests specific categories of wild animals in the State, but it does not make all wild animals the 'sole' property of the government. Facts: Section 39 covers animals hunted in contravention of the Act, animals found dead or killed by mistake, and animals kept in captivity illegally. Government property in such animals and in trophies must be reported to the authorities. Lawfully held items, such as animals under a valid licence or certificate of ownership, were recognised. The absolutist word 'sole' is the usual UPSC trap. The Supreme Court has also described wildlife as a national asset held under the public trust doctrine.

2 — Correct: Protection under the WPA depends on the species' scheduled status, not on location. Facts: Section 9 prohibits hunting of any wild animal listed in Schedules I to IV anywhere in India. Protected areas (national parks, sanctuaries, conservation reserves and community reserves) add extra restrictions on entry, habitat alteration and grazing. Schedule I and Schedule II (Part II) species get the highest penalties. The 2022 Amendment, in force from 2023, rationalised the Schedules from six to four. Schedule I now covers species needing the highest protection, with the others covering lower-risk species, specified plants and CITES-listed species.

3 — Incorrect: Apprehension of danger is not sufficient ground. The Act requires that the animal has actually become dangerous to human life. Facts: Section 11(1)(a) lets the Chief Wild Life Warden permit hunting of a Schedule I animal that has become dangerous to human life, or is disabled or diseased beyond recovery. Reasons must be recorded in writing. Killing is allowed only if the animal cannot be captured, tranquilised or translocated. Section 11(1)(b) covers Schedule II to IV animals dangerous to human life or property. Man-animal conflict cases, such as man-eating tigers and leopards, are handled under this section and the NTCA guidelines.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. Under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, protection attaches to the species wherever it is found, inside or outside protected areas. Statements 1 and 3 overstate the law: the government is not the 'sole' owner of all wild animals, and mere apprehension of danger does not justify capturing or killing a protected animal.
topic_notes: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 is India's main wildlife law. It was enacted after the 1960s-70s wildlife decline and applies to the whole country, with Jammu and Kashmir brought under it from 2019. It created the Wildlife Advisory Board, Wildlife Wardens, and the categories of protected areas: national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, conservation reserves and community reserves. The Central Zoo Authority (2002 amendment), the National Tiger Conservation Authority (2006 amendment) and the Tiger Conservation Authority were later additions. Before the 2022 amendment the Schedules were: I and II (Part II) for absolute protection; III and IV for lower protection; V for vermin (such as crows, fruit bats, rats and mice); VI for specified plants such as pitcher plant, Kuth and Ladyslipper orchid. The 2022 Amendment Act, in force from 1 April 2023, cut the Schedules to four: Schedule I (high protection), Schedule II (lower protection), Schedule III (protected plants) and Schedule IV (CITES Appendix-listed species). The vermin schedule was dropped, though Section 62 still allows the Centre to declare vermin. It also gave statutory backing to CITES, added a regime for invasive alien species, allowed voluntary surrender of captive animals, and permitted the Centre to regulate or stop activities in the vicinity of protected areas. Key sections to remember: Section 9 (prohibition of hunting), Section 11 (hunting of dangerous animals), Section 18 (sanctuaries), Section 35 (national parks), Section 36A (conservation reserves), Section 36C (community reserves) and Section 39 (government property in wild animals). Related laws include the Biological Diversity Act 2002, the Forest Rights Act 2006, the Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 and the Environment (Protection) Act 1986. The Constitution links in through Article 48A (State to protect wildlife), Article 51A(g) (citizen duty) and the 42nd Amendment, which moved forests and wildlife protection to the Concurrent List.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q90.
ocr: With reference to Indian laws about wildlife protection, consider the following statements : 1. Wild animals are the sole property of the government. 2. When a wild animal is declared protected, such animal is entitled for equal protection whether it is found in protected areas or outside. 8. Apprehension of a protected wild animal becoming a danger to human life is sufficient ground for its capture or killing. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ? (a) land2 (b) 2only (c) land3 (d) 3only Certain species of which one of the following organisms are well known as cultivators of fun
subject: Environment
detail: Fungus farming (fungiculture) is a classic example of mutualism and of agriculture in non-human animals. Attine ants, found mainly in the Neotropics (Central and South America, with a range reaching the southern USA), cut leaves and carry them to the nest. They do not eat the leaves. They use them as a substrate on which they grow the fungus Leucoagaricus gongylophorus (family Agaricaceae), and the fungus is their main food. The ants weed the garden, secrete antibiotics from metapleural glands and carry actinomycete bacteria (Pseudonocardia) to suppress the parasitic fungus Escovopsis. The queen carries a pellet of the fungus on her mating flight to start a new colony. Termites of subfamily Macrotermitinae (Termitomyces) are the other well-known fungus farmers, and so are ambrosia beetles. Elimination: cockroaches are scavenging omnivores. Crabs are crustaceans, and although some, like fiddler crabs, feed on microbial films, none are known as cultivators. Spiders are predators that trap prey with silk or hunt it. Only ants are textbook fungus cultivators, so (a) is correct.
explanations: Correct. Attine (leafcutter) ants farm the fungus Leucoagaricus on chewed leaf material and feed on it. This is a well-documented mutualism and the standard textbook example.
Wrong. Cockroaches are omnivorous scavengers that eat decaying organic matter and some fungi they find. They do not cultivate or tend fungal gardens.
Wrong. Crabs are crustaceans that scavenge, graze or prey. Some may eat fungi or algae, but none are known as cultivators of fungi.
Wrong. Spiders are arachnid predators that use silk or ambush to catch prey. They have no fungus-farming behaviour.
keyfact: Leafcutter ants (tribe Attini) and Macrotermes termites are the classic fungus-cultivating insects; among the options given, only ants fit.
option_notes: Ants (family Formicidae) are eusocial insects with castes of queen, workers and soldiers. Attine ants (leafcutters, about 250 species) live in the New World and farm fungus on leaf fragments. Ants are also known for weaver ants (Oecophylla), which build nests of leaves, and for army ants. Formic acid is named after ants. Ants form many mutualisms, such as the one with acacia trees and the one with aphids, which they farm for honeydew.

Cockroaches (order Blattodea) are ancient insects dating back to the Carboniferous. They are omnivorous scavengers, mostly nocturnal, with about 4,500 species, of which only about 30 are pests. Periplaneta americana is the American cockroach. They are known for hardiness, carrying pathogens and producing an egg case called an ootheca. Termites, the closest relatives, belong to the same order, and some termites farm fungus, but cockroaches do not.

Crabs are decapod crustaceans with a short tail folded under the body and a hard exoskeleton. They are mostly marine, but some are freshwater or land species. Examples include the fiddler crab, the horseshoe crab (which is not a true crab but a chelicerate) and the coconut crab, the largest land arthropod. They are scavengers, predators or grazers, and they respire through gills. They are not fungus cultivators.

Spiders (order Araneae) are arachnids with eight legs, two body parts (cephalothorax and abdomen) and no antennae. They are predators and use silk for webs, egg sacs and dispersal (ballooning). Venom is used to subdue prey. Spiders are a major insect-pest regulator. They have book lungs or tracheae. They show no fungal farming, although some jumping spiders are known to feed on plant matter.
related: Leafcutter ants farm the fungus Leucoagaricus gongylophorus.
Macrotermitinae termites cultivate Termitomyces fungi.
Escovopsis is a parasitic fungus that attacks ant fungus gardens.
Ambrosia beetles culture fungi in galleries bored into wood.
Lichen is a symbiosis of a fungus with an alga or cyanobacterium.
Mycorrhiza is a fungus-root association that improves phosphorus uptake.
Weaver ants (Oecophylla) are used in biological pest control.
Karl von Frisch decoded the honeybee waggle dance.
summary: The answer is (a) Ant. Leafcutter ants (tribe Attini, genus Atta and Acromyrmex) and their relatives cultivate fungi in underground gardens, feeding them leaf fragments and eating the fungus. Cockroaches, crabs and spiders do not farm fungi.
topic_notes: Fungus farming is a form of animal agriculture that has evolved independently in a few insect groups. Attine ants evolved it about 50-60 million years ago, and it is unusual because it involves obligate mutualism. The fungus gets protection, food and dispersal, while the ants get a nutrient-rich food. Leafcutter ants (Atta, Acromyrmex) are the most advanced farmers and are considered the main herbivores of the Neotropics. Their colonies can hold millions of workers and contain several worker castes. Termites of subfamily Macrotermitinae, found in Africa and Asia (including India), cultivate Termitomyces fungi on combs of faecal material, and the fruiting bodies of the fungus are sometimes eaten by people. Ambrosia beetles (Scolytinae and Platypodinae) bore into wood and culture ambrosia fungi in their galleries. Some marine snails (Littoraria) and damselfish (which farm algae) show comparable gardening. Other important symbiosis examples for UPSC: lichens (fungus plus alga or cyanobacterium), mycorrhiza (fungus plus plant roots, which helps in phosphorus uptake), Rhizobium in legume nodules, coral polyps with zooxanthellae, and cleaner fish. Other insect topics that could come up include honeybee communication (the waggle dance, by Karl von Frisch), pollination mutualisms such as the fig and fig wasp, and weaver ants used in biological pest control in citrus orchards. Remember the difference between mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, the other is unaffected) and parasitism (one benefits, the other is harmed).

question:
Consider the following pairs : 94, Site of Ashoka’s Location in the major rock edicts State of
1. Dhauli — Odisha
2. Erragudi — Andhra Pradesh
3. Jaugada — Madhya Pradesh
4. Kalsi — Karnataka 95. How many pairs given above are correctly matched ?
subject: Ancient History
detail: Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts (14 principal edicts plus 2 separate Kalinga edicts) are found at several sites across the subcontinent. Eastern sites include Dhauli (Khurda, Odisha) and Jaugada (Ganjam, Odisha), where the Separate Kalinga Edicts replace XI-XIII. Southern sites include Erragudi (Yerragudi, Kurnool district, Andhra Pradesh), which has both Major Rock Edicts and Minor Rock Edicts. Northern and western sites include Kalsi (Dehradun, Uttarakhand), Mansehra and Shahbazgarhi (Pakistan), Girnar (Gujarat) and Sopara (Maharashtra). Karnataka has Minor Rock Edicts (Maski, Brahmagiri, Siddapura, Jatinga-Rameshwara), and Maski is notable because it names Ashoka. Madhya Pradesh has Minor Rock Edicts at Rupnath and Gujarra, not Jaugada. Elimination: since pairs 1 and 2 are correct and 3 and 4 are wrong, the count is two. Knowing that Jaugada is a Kalinga site (Odisha) alone eliminates (c) and (d), and knowing Kalsi is in Uttarakhand excludes (c) and (d), leaving (b). Most edicts are in Prakrit written in Brahmi script; the north-west ones use Kharosthi, and Greek and Aramaic appear at Kandahar.
explanations: (a) is wrong because two pairs, not one, are correct: both Dhauli and Erragudi match their states.
(b) is right because pairs 1 and 2 are correct, while Jaugada is in Odisha and Kalsi is in Uttarakhand.
(c) is wrong because it would need one of Jaugada or Kalsi to be correct, but both are misplaced.
(d) is wrong because pairs 3 and 4 are mismatched, so not all four are correct.
keyfact: Dhauli and Jaugada are in Odisha, Erragudi in Andhra Pradesh and Kalsi in Uttarakhand; Karnataka has only Minor Rock Edicts, and Maski names Ashoka.
option_notes: Only one pair: this would hold if just one site were matched correctly. The Ashokan edict sites come in many types: Major Rock Edicts (14), Separate Kalinga Edicts, Minor Rock Edicts, Major Pillar Edicts (7), Minor Pillar Edicts and cave inscriptions. Piyadasi (Devanampiya Piyadasi) is the name used in most edicts. James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837. The question shows that the edict sites are scattered across India, Pakistan, Afghanistan and Nepal, and that most are in Prakrit.

Only two pairs: the correct option. The matched sites show the geographic spread of Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts. The eastern group (Dhauli, Jaugada) was in the Kalinga region. The southern group (Erragudi) marks the Mauryan reach in the Deccan. Other major sites are Girnar (Gujarat), Sopara (Maharashtra), Kalsi (Uttarakhand), Mansehra and Shahbazgarhi (Pakistan). The edicts promote dhamma, welfare, tolerance, and administrative ethics.

Only three pairs: this would require one of Jaugada or Kalsi to be correct. Jaugada is in Ganjam, Odisha, and Kalsi is in Dehradun, Uttarakhand. A common trap is confusing Jaugada with Madhya Pradesh Ashokan sites such as Rupnath (Jabalpur), Gujarra (Datia) and Sanchi, Sarnath and Rampurva (pillars), or Kalsi with Karnataka's Minor Rock Edict sites.

All four pairs: this would mean every site is matched with the right state. It fails because Jaugada (Odisha) and Kalsi (Uttarakhand) are mismatched. Other Ashokan edicts are located in Delhi (Topra and Meerut pillars moved by Firoz Shah Tughlaq), Allahabad (Prayagraj, with the Allahabad pillar also bearing Samudragupta's prashasti), Lauriya-Nandangarh, Lauriya-Araraj and Rampurva in Bihar, and Lumbini and Nigali Sagar in Nepal.
related: Rock Edict XIII describes the Kalinga War and mentions Greek kings including Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Antigonus Gonatas, Magas and Alexander.
Maski (Karnataka) is the first edict to mention the name 'Ashoka' (rather than only Devanampiya Piyadasi).
Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra edicts are in Kharosthi script, which runs right to left.
James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi script in 1837.
The Sarnath lion capital is India's national emblem, and the Ashoka Chakra is on the national flag.
Lumbini pillar edict records that Ashoka visited Buddha's birthplace and reduced the tax there.
The Kandahar bilingual inscription is in Greek and Aramaic.
The Barabar cave inscriptions record Ashoka's gifts to the Ajivikas.
statements: 1 — Correct: Dhauli is in Khurda district near Bhubaneswar, Odisha. It has Major Rock Edicts I-X, XIV and the two Separate Kalinga Edicts. It is traditionally linked to the aftermath of the Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE). A rock-cut elephant sculpture at the top is among the earliest Buddhist sculptures in India, and the Shanti Stupa (a modern Peace Pagoda) stands nearby.

2 — Correct: Erragudi (Yerragudi) is in Kurnool district, Andhra Pradesh. It has a nearly complete set of Major Rock Edicts I-XIV plus Minor Rock Edicts. Its edicts are unusual because they are inscribed in boustrophedon style (alternating line direction). It belongs to the southern group of Ashokan sites, along with Rajula Mandagiri and Gooty, and lay in the Mauryan southern province administered from Suvarnagiri.

3 — Incorrect: Jaugada is on the Rushikulya river in Ganjam district, Odisha, not Madhya Pradesh. Like Dhauli it carries Major Rock Edicts I-X, XIV and the Separate Kalinga Edicts, which address the officials (mahamatras) of Tosali and Samapa and set out a paternal policy: 'all men are my children'. Madhya Pradesh sites such as Rupnath, Gujarra and Sanchi have Minor Rock Edicts and pillars.

4 — Incorrect: Kalsi is in Dehradun district, Uttarakhand, near the Yamuna-Tons confluence, not Karnataka. It has a version of the Major Rock Edicts I-XIV, discovered by Forrest in 1860. Its Edict XIII mentions Greek kings such as Antiochus. Karnataka's Ashokan sites (Maski, Brahmagiri, Siddapura, Jatinga-Rameshwara, Udegolam, Nittur) have Minor Rock Edicts, and Maski contains the name 'Ashoka'.
summary: The answer is (b): only two pairs are correctly matched. Dhauli (Odisha) and Erragudi (Andhra Pradesh) are correct, while Jaugada is in Odisha, not Madhya Pradesh, and Kalsi is in Uttarakhand, not Karnataka.
topic_notes: Ashoka (r. c. 268-232 BCE), the third Mauryan emperor, was the first Indian ruler to inscribe his messages on rocks and pillars. The Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE) led to his conversion to Buddhism and to his policy of dhamma, which was not a religion but an ethical code of tolerance, non-violence, respect for elders, and welfare. Types of inscriptions: (1) Major Rock Edicts, 14 in number, at eight sites: Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra, Kalsi, Girnar, Sopara, Dhauli, Jaugada and Erragudi. (2) Separate Kalinga Edicts at Dhauli and Jaugada. (3) Minor Rock Edicts at Maski, Brahmagiri, Siddapura, Jatinga-Rameshwara, Rupnath, Sahasram, Bairat and Gujarra, among others. (4) Seven Major Pillar Edicts at Delhi-Topra, Delhi-Meerut, Allahabad-Kosam, Lauriya-Araraj, Lauriya-Nandangarh and Rampurva. (5) Minor Pillar Edicts at Sarnath, Sanchi, Kausambi, and the Rummindei (Lumbini) and Nigali Sagar pillars. (6) Cave inscriptions at the Barabar hills, given to the Ajivikas. Scripts: Brahmi mostly; Kharosthi at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra; Greek and Aramaic at Kandahar and in Afghanistan. Language: Prakrit. Edict XIII describes the Kalinga War, with about 100,000 killed and 150,000 deported. Edict XII covers religious tolerance, and Edict II covers medical care for humans and animals. The Maski edict is the first to name Ashoka. The Junagadh (Girnar) inscription of Rudradaman is later and in Sanskrit. James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837. The Ashokan lion capital of Sarnath is India's national emblem, and the Ashoka Chakra is on the national flag.

question:
Consider the following pairs : King . Dynasty
1. Nannuka — Chandela
2. Jayashakti — Paramara
3. NagabhataII — Gurjara-Pratihara
4. Bhoja — Rashtrakuta on How many pairs given above are correctly R matched ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The question tests early medieval north and central Indian dynasties of the Tripartite Struggle and post-Pratihara period. The Chandelas of Jejakabhukti (Bundelkhand) were founded by Nannuka around 831 CE as feudatories of the Gurjara-Pratiharas. Jayashakti (Jejja), whose name gave the region the name Jejakabhukti, was an early Chandela ruler, so linking him to the Paramaras is wrong. Nagabhata II (c. 800-833 CE) was a Gurjara-Pratihara king who defeated Chakrayudha of Kannauj, made Kannauj his capital, and was later defeated by the Rashtrakuta king Govinda III. The name Bhoja belongs to two famous rulers: Bhoja of the Paramaras of Malwa (c. 1010-1055, Dhara, author of Samarangana Sutradhara) and Mihira Bhoja of the Gurjara-Pratiharas (c. 836-885). No famous Rashtrakuta king is named Bhoja. Elimination: once pairs 1 and 3 are known to be right and 2 and 4 wrong, the count is two. Knowing that Nannuka is Chandela alone eliminates (a) only if pair 3 is also recognised, which gives (b).
explanations: Wrong: more than one pair is correct, since both pairs 1 and 3 match.
Correct: exactly two pairs, Nannuka–Chandela and Nagabhata II–Gurjara-Pratihara, are correctly matched.
Wrong: this would need a third correct pair, but Jayashakti was Chandela and Bhoja was not Rashtrakuta.
Wrong: pairs 2 and 4 are incorrect, so not all four match.
keyfact: Nannuka founded the Chandelas, Nagabhata II was a Gurjara-Pratihara, Jayashakti was Chandela, and Bhoja was Paramara or Pratihara, never Rashtrakuta.
option_notes: Only one pair: this would have been right if just one of the pairings held. The question's items cover early medieval dynasties: Chandelas of Jejakabhukti, Paramaras of Malwa, Gurjara-Pratiharas of Kannauj and Rashtrakutas of Manyakheta. Students often confuse kings with the same name, such as the two Bhojas, so check each pair separately. Here two pairs are correct, so this option fails.

Only two pairs: the official answer. Pairs 1 (Nannuka–Chandela) and 3 (Nagabhata II–Gurjara-Pratihara) are right. Nannuka founded Chandela power around 831 CE, and Nagabhata II took Kannauj around 800 CE. Pair 2 is wrong because Jayashakti was Chandela, and pair 4 is wrong because Bhoja was Paramara or Pratihara. Both these kings can be asked in later questions.

Only three pairs: this would need one of the false pairs to be true. Jayashakti is sometimes confused with Paramara kings, but he was an early Chandela ruler after whom Jejakabhukti is said to be named. Bhoja is confused with Rashtrakuta kings because the Rashtrakutas and Pratiharas fought in the Tripartite Struggle, but no major Rashtrakuta was named Bhoja.

All four pairs: this would mean every pairing is correct. That is false because the Paramaras were founded by Upendra (Krishnaraja) and included Munja, Sindhuraja and Bhoja, but Jayashakti was not among them. The Rashtrakutas were founded by Dantidurga around 753 CE, with capital Manyakheta, and did not have a famous Bhoja.
related: Chandela capital: Khajuraho (religious), Mahoba and Kalinjar (fort).
Kandariya Mahadeva temple, Khajuraho, was built by Chandela king Vidyadhara.
Mihira Bhoja took the title Adivaraha; Gwalior Prashasti records his reign.
Rashtrakuta king Amoghavarsha wrote Kavirajamarga, early Kannada poetics.
Paramara Bhoja founded Bhojpur and wrote Samarangana Sutradhara on architecture.
Nagabhata II defeated Chakrayudha and shifted the Pratihara capital to Kannauj.
Kailasa temple at Ellora was commissioned by Rashtrakuta Krishna I.
Prithviraj Chauhan was defeated at Tarain in 1192 by Muhammad of Ghor.
statements: 1 — Correct: Nannuka founded the Chandela dynasty. He was the first Chandela ruler, who established power in Kalinjara-Jejakabhukti region around 831 CE and ruled as a Gurjara-Pratihara feudatory. The Chandelas later became independent under Yashovarman and Dhanga, who built the Lakshmana temple and Vishwanath temple at Khajuraho. Their major forts were Kalinjar and Ajaygarh. Vidyadhara fought Mahmud of Ghazni, and Parmardi (Parmal) lost to Prithviraj Chauhan and Qutbuddin Aibak in 1202-03.

2 — Incorrect: Jayashakti (Jejja or Jejjaka) was a Chandela ruler, not a Paramara. He was the son or successor of Vakpati in the early Chandela line and ruled around 865-885 CE. The Chandela territory Jejakabhukti, later Bundelkhand, is said to be named after him. His brother Vijayashakti followed him. The Paramaras, by contrast, were a Malwa dynasty with capital at Ujjain and later Dhara, with early kings like Upendra, Vakpati Munja, Sindhuraja and Bhoja.

3 — Correct: Nagabhata II belonged to the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty and ruled around 800-833 CE. He defeated Chakrayudha, a protege of the Palas, and took Kannauj, making it the Pratihara capital. He also fought Dharmapala of Bengal. Rashtrakuta king Govinda III defeated him, though the Pratiharas later recovered. His achievements are recorded in the Gwalior inscription of Mihira Bhoja. His grandson was Mihira Bhoja, the greatest Pratihara ruler.

4 — Incorrect: Bhoja is not a Rashtrakuta king. Famous Bhojas were Mihira Bhoja (Gurjara-Pratihara, c. 836-885 CE, Kannauj, Gwalior inscription, Adivaraha coins) and Paramara Bhoja (c. 1010-1055 CE, Dhara, founded Bhojpur and Bhojsagar, patron of learning, wrote works on poetry, architecture and yoga). The great Rashtrakuta rulers included Dantidurga, Krishna I (Kailasa temple at Ellora), Govinda III, Amoghavarsha and Krishna III.
summary: The answer is (b): only two pairs are correct. Nannuka–Chandela (1) and Nagabhata II–Gurjara-Pratihara (3) are correct, while Jayashakti was a Chandela king (not Paramara) and Bhoja is associated with the Paramaras or Gurjara-Pratiharas (not the Rashtrakutas).
topic_notes: Early medieval India (c. 750-1200 CE) saw the rise of Rajput dynasties in the north and central regions. The Tripartite Struggle for control of Kannauj involved the Gurjara-Pratiharas (west and north), the Palas (east) and the Rashtrakutas (Deccan). Gurjara-Pratiharas: Nagabhata I (founder, repelled Arab invaders), Vatsaraja, Nagabhata II, Mihira Bhoja, Mahendrapala (patron of Rajashekhara) and Mahipala. Arab traveller Sulaiman described Bhoja's power. Rashtrakutas: Dantidurga, Krishna I (Kailasa temple), Dhruva, Govinda III, Amoghavarsha (Kavirajamarga), Indra III and Krishna III. Palas: Gopala (founder, elected), Dharmapala (Vikramshila), Devapala. Paramaras of Malwa: Vakpati Munja, Sindhuraja (Navasahasanka-charita by Padmagupta) and Bhoja (Dhara, Bhojshala, Bhojpur, Samarangana Sutradhara, Saraswati Kanthabharana). Chandelas: Nannuka, Jayashakti, Harshadeva, Yashovarman, Dhanga (Khajuraho temples), Ganda, Vidyadhara, Kirtivarman (Prabodhachandrodaya staged), Parmardi. Chauhans: Prithviraj III, Tarain battles in 1191 and 1192. Solankis (Chalukyas of Gujarat): Mularaja, Bhima I (Dilwara temples at Mount Abu, Somnath rebuilt). Kalachuris of Tripuri and Gahadavalas of Kannauj are also important. Common UPSC traps are same-named kings (Bhoja, Mahendravarman), temples with dynasties, and authors with patrons. Remember Khajuraho is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986) of the Chandelas, built roughly 950-1050 CE in Nagara style.

ocr: Which one of the following statements about Sangam literature in ancient South India is correct ? (a) Sangam poems are devoid of any reference to material culture. (b) The social classification of Varna was known to Sangam poets. (c) Sangam poems have no reference to warrior ethic. (d) Sangam literature refers to magical forces as irrational. “Yogavasistha” was translated into Persian by Nizamuddin Panipati during the reign of : (a) Akbar (b) Humayun (c) Shahjahan (d) Aurangzeb
subject: Ancient History
detail: Sangam literature (c. 300 BCE to 300 CE, with the core dated roughly 100 BCE to 250 CE) is the earliest Tamil corpus and includes Ettuttokai (Eight Anthologies), Pattuppattu (Ten Idylls) and the grammar Tolkappiyam. It was composed in assemblies (sangams) patronised by the Pandyas of Madurai, and it describes the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas. The poems are divided into akam (love, interior) and puram (war, kingship, public life). The texts show a society with a developing varna awareness: Tolkappiyam lists four groups (Antanar, Arasar, Vanigar, Vellalar), and Brahmins, who performed sacrifices, appear in the poems along with their patrons. The poems are rich in material culture, including pearl and spice trade with Rome, Yavana traders, ports like Muziris, Korkai and Puhar, iron tools, pottery and textiles. Warrior ethic is central: heroic death, hero stones (nadukal), and the cult of Korravai, goddess of war, are emphasised. Magic, spirit possession (Velan Veriyadal) and omens were treated as real forces, not irrational ones. Elimination: (a) is wrong because of the abundant material references, (c) because the puram poems glorify war, and (d) because magical forces are accepted as real. Only (b) survives.
explanations: Incorrect: Sangam poems are full of references to material culture such as trade, ports, ornaments, food, housing, crafts and Roman wine and gold.

Correct: Sangam poets knew the Varna classification. Tolkappiyam and the poems mention Brahmins (Antanar), rulers (Arasar), merchants (Vanigar) and cultivators (Vellalar), though it was less rigid than in the north.
Incorrect: Warrior ethic is a major theme in the puram poems, which praise bravery, heroic death, hero stones and the war goddess Korravai.
Incorrect: Sangam literature treats magical forces, spirit possession, omens and rituals such as Velan Veriyadal as real and powerful, not irrational.
keyfact: Sangam poets knew the four varnas (Antanar, Arasar, Vanigar, Vellalar), but society was not as rigid as in the north, and the poems are rich in material culture and warrior ethic.
option_notes: Material culture in Sangam texts: the poems describe agriculture (paddy, millet), crafts (weaving, pottery, bead making, iron working), urban centres (Madurai, Uraiyur, Puhar/Kaveripattinam, Korkai) and ports like Muziris, Tondi and Arikamedu. Roman gold flowed in for pepper, pearls, muslin and gems. Archaeological finds such as Roman amphorae and coins, black-and-red ware and megaliths confirm the poems. So the statement that they lack material references is false.

Varna in Sangam society: the four-fold social order is attested in Tolkappiyam (Antanar, Arasar, Vanigar, Vellalar). Brahmins performed Vedic sacrifices and were patronised by kings, as in the Purananuru. However, Tamil society was also organised by tinai (eco-zones) and kin-based groups such as Paratavar, Parayar, Kuravar and Maravar, and the Varna system was not as rigid as in the north.

Warrior ethic: Puram poems praise heroic kings and warriors, cattle raiding (vetci), battle (vanji, tumbai), hero stones (nadukal) for fallen warriors, and the war goddess Korravai. Chiefs like Karikala Chola and Senguttuvan Chera were glorified. Poets such as Kapilar, Avvaiyar and Paranar received gifts from patrons, and the heroic ideal is central to Sangam poetry.

Magic and religion: Sangam texts mention Murugan worship with the frenzied Velan dance (Velan Veriyadal), belief in spirits, omens, the evil eye and rites to propitiate deities such as Murugan, Korravai, Mayon (Vishnu) and Cheyon. These were taken as real forces, not irrational. Murugan is the chief deity of the Kurinji region and is described in Tirumurukarruppatai.
related: Tolkappiyam is the oldest Tamil grammar work, attributed to Tolkappiyar.
Silappadikaram was written by Ilango Adigal and Manimekalai by Sattanar, both post-Sangam epics.
The five Sangam tinais are Kurinji, Mullai, Marutam, Neytal and Palai.
Muziris (Chera) was the major Indo-Roman port on the Malabar coast.
Karikala Chola won the battle of Venni and built the Kallanai (Grand Anicut) on the Kaveri.
Yogavasistha was translated into Persian by Nizamuddin Panipati during Akbar's reign.
Akbar set up the Maktab Khana translation bureau, which translated the Mahabharata (Razmnama) and Ramayana into Persian.
Tirumurukarruppatai (Nakkirar) is a Pattuppattu poem on Murugan.
summary: The correct answer is (b): the social classification of Varna was known to Sangam poets. Sangam texts such as Purananuru and Tolkappiyam mention the four varnas (and groups like Antanar/Brahmins, Arasar, Vanigar, Vellalar), although the strict, rigid Varna hierarchy of the north was not fully in force. The other three options contradict the actual content of Sangam poetry.
topic_notes: Sangam age: the term comes from the sangams (academies) at Madurai said to be patronised by Pandya kings. Tradition speaks of three sangams, though historians accept only the last. The date is roughly 300 BCE to 300 CE. Literature: Ettuttokai (eight anthologies, including Narrinai, Kuruntokai, Aingurunuru, Padirruppattu, Paripadal, Kalittokai, Akananuru, Purananuru), Pattuppattu (ten idylls, including Tirumurukarruppatai and Pattinappalai), and Tolkappiyam, the earliest Tamil grammar by Tolkappiyar. The epics Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal) and Manimekalai (Sattanar) are later, post-Sangam works. Themes are akam (love) and puram (heroism, kingship, charity), and the landscape is divided into five tinais: Kurinji (hills), Mullai (forest), Marutam (agricultural plains), Neytal (coast), Palai (arid). Polity: three kingdoms with emblems, the Chera (bow, Vanji), Chola (tiger, Uraiyur/Puhar) and Pandya (fish, Madurai). Important rulers: Karikala, Senguttuvan (the Red Chera, who brought a stone from the Himalaya for Kannagi), Nedunjeliyan. Economy: Indo-Roman trade through Muziris, Arikamedu and Puhar, with finds of Roman coins, and the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea and Pliny describe the trade. Society: Varna awareness along with tribal groups, and the use of hero stones. Religion: worship of Murugan, Korravai, Mayon, Indra, Varuna, and also Buddhism and Jainism. Position of women: poets such as Avvaiyar and Auvaiyar and the practice of sati are mentioned. UPSC could ask on tinai, authors, epics, ports, trade and rulers.

question: The world’s second tallest statue in sitting pose of Ramanuja was inaugurated by the Prime Minister of India at Hyderabad recently. Which one of the following statements correctly represents the teachings of Ramanuja ?
options: The best means of salvation was devotion
Vedas are eternal, self-existent and wholly authoritative
Logical arguments were essential means for the highest bliss
Salvation was to be obtained through meditation
subject: Polity
detail: Ramanuja (c. 1017-1137 CE), born at Sriperumbudur in Tamil Nadu, was a Vaishnava philosopher and head of the Srirangam temple. He propounded Vishishtadvaita, or qualified non-dualism: Brahman (Vishnu/Narayana) is the one supreme reality, but individual souls (chit) and matter (achit) are real and form his body and attributes. This stands against Shankara's Advaita, which treats the world as maya and upholds jnana (knowledge) as the path to liberation. For Ramanuja, moksha is reached through bhakti, meaning intense, loving devotion, and prapatti (total surrender) to God's grace. His major works are the Sri Bhashya (commentary on the Brahma Sutras), Vedartha Sangraha and Gita Bhashya. He drew on the Alvar saints' devotional tradition. The 216-foot 'Statue of Equality' at Muchintal, Hyderabad, was inaugurated by PM Modi in February 2022. Elimination: (b) is a Mimamsa-type view of the Vedas as eternal and self-existent, not Ramanuja's distinctive teaching. (c) logic as the means to bliss is the Nyaya/Vaisheshika emphasis. (d) meditation as the route is the Yoga/Upanishadic emphasis. Only (a) captures Ramanuja's core teaching.
explanations: Correct: Ramanuja held that bhakti and prapatti to Vishnu are the best way to moksha, with divine grace central.
Incorrect: The eternal, self-existent and wholly authoritative nature of the Vedas is a Mimamsa tenet, not the distinctive teaching of Ramanuja, whose emphasis was on devotion.
Incorrect: Logical argument as the essential means to bliss belongs to Nyaya philosophy; Ramanuja relied on scripture and devotion, not on logic as the way to liberation.
Incorrect: Meditation as the path to salvation is associated with Yoga and some Upanishadic traditions; Ramanuja gave primacy to bhakti, though he did value meditation as upasana leading toward it.
keyfact: Ramanuja: Vishishtadvaita, bhakti and prapatti to Vishnu as the best path to salvation (Sri Bhashya).
option_notes: Bhakti is the path of loving devotion to a personal God. It rose in Tamil Nadu through the Alvars (Vaishnava) and Nayanars (Shaiva) between the 6th and 9th centuries. Ramanuja gave it philosophical grounding in Vishishtadvaita. Later bhakti figures include Madhva, Nimbarka, Vallabha, Ramananda, Kabir, Chaitanya and Tulsidas. Bhakti emphasises grace, surrender, and often social equality across castes.

The Vedas are regarded as apaurusheya (not authored by humans), eternal and self-existent, and are the supreme authority in the Mimamsa school, founded on Jaimini's Mimamsa Sutras. Mimamsa stresses Vedic ritual (karma) and dharma. All the astika (orthodox) schools accept Vedic authority in some form, so this view does not distinguish Ramanuja.

Logic and reasoning (tarka, anumana) as the key to liberation is the Nyaya approach, founded by Gautama (Akshapada) in the Nyaya Sutras. It recognises four pramanas: perception, inference, comparison and testimony. Nyaya holds that right knowledge through logical analysis ends suffering. It is often paired with Vaisheshika, founded by Kanada, which is atomistic.

Meditation and discipline form the core of the Yoga school, systematised by Patanjali in the Yoga Sutras, with the eight-fold ashtanga path (yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, samadhi). The goal is kaivalya through control of mental fluctuations (chitta-vritti-nirodha). Yoga is allied with Samkhya, which is dualistic.
related: Ramanuja's philosophy is Vishishtadvaita (qualified monism).
Shankara propounded Advaita and held that knowledge (jnana) leads to moksha.
Madhva propounded Dvaita (dualism).
The Alvars were Vaishnava saints; their hymns are compiled in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham.
The Statue of Equality at Muchintal, Hyderabad, is 216 feet tall and was inaugurated in February 2022.
Ramanuja's key commentary on the Brahma Sutras is the Sri Bhashya.
Nimbarka propounded Dvaitadvaita; Vallabha propounded Shuddhadvaita.
Ramanuja was born at Sriperumbudur and led the Srirangam temple.
summary: The answer is (a). Ramanuja, the 11th-12th century exponent of Vishishtadvaita, taught that bhakti (loving devotion and self-surrender to Vishnu) is the best means of salvation, rather than knowledge alone or ritual.
topic_notes: Ramanuja (c. 1017-1137 CE) was born at Sriperumbudur near Chennai. He studied under Yadava Prakasha and was the successor of Yamunacharya at Srirangam. He is the main philosopher of the Sri Vaishnava tradition. His Vishishtadvaita holds that Brahman is qualified by souls and matter, which are real and inseparable modes of him. He rejected Shankara's view of maya and identity of soul with Brahman. Salvation means eternal service and communion with Vishnu in Vaikuntha, attained by bhakti and prapatti. He wrote the Sri Bhashya, Vedanta Sara, Vedanta Dipa, Vedartha Sangraha and Gita Bhashya. He is said to have opened temple worship to all castes and is associated with the Melkote (Karnataka) Cheluvanarayana temple. The Chola ruler of his time, Kulottunga I, is said to have persecuted him, so he took refuge among the Hoysalas under Vishnuvardhana. Other Vedanta schools: Advaita (Shankara, 8th century), Dvaita (Madhva, 13th century), Dvaitadvaita (Nimbarka), Shuddhadvaita (Vallabha), Achintya Bhedabheda (Chaitanya). The Statue of Equality at Muchintal (Ramanagar, Hyderabad), made of panchaloha and 216 feet tall, sits on a 54-foot base called Bhadra Vedi. It is part of the 'Sri Ramanujacharya Sahasrabdi' celebrations for his 1000th birth anniversary, built by Chinna Jeeyar Swami's trust. Its sitting pose is the second tallest in the world after the Buddha statue in Thailand. UPSC may also ask about Alvars, Nayanars, the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, Basavanna's Lingayatism and Bhakti saints.

question:
The Prime Minister recently inaugurated the new Circuit House near Somnath Temple at Veraval. Which of the following statements are correct regarding Somnath Temple ?
1. Somnath Temple is one of the Jyotirlinga shrines.
2. A description of Somnath Temple was given by Al-Biruni.

subject: Art & Culture
detail: Somnath, at Prabhas Patan near Veraval in Gir Somnath district, Gujarat, is traditionally counted as the first of the twelve Jyotirlinga shrines of Shiva. Its wealth and fame drew repeated attacks. Mahmud of Ghazni raided it in 1025 CE. Al-Biruni, who accompanied Mahmud's campaigns and wrote Kitab-ul-Hind (Tahqiq-i-Hind) around 1030, described the temple and the lingam, and this account helped spread its fame. Later rebuilding and destruction followed under the Delhi Sultanate, the Gujarat Sultanate and Aurangzeb. Ahilyabai Holkar built a smaller temple nearby in 1783. After Independence, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, with K.M. Munshi, pushed for reconstruction. Patel took the pledge in November 1947 at Junagadh's integration, and Gandhi advised that public contributions fund it. Dr Rajendra Prasad, then President, performed the Pran Pratishtha on 11 May 1951. The temple is built in the Chalukya (Kailash Mahameru Prasad) style. Elimination logic: statement 1 and 2 are certainly true, which rules out (b). Statement 3 names Radhakrishnan, who was Vice-President in 1951 and became President only in 1962, so it is false. That rules out (c) and (d) and leaves (a). The question paper's '8' is an OCR error for '3'.
explanations: Correct: statements 1 and 2 are true and statement 3 is false, so 'a' (1 and 2 only) is right.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is false. It also leaves out statement 1, which is true.
Wrong: it includes statement 3, which is false, and leaves out statement 2, which is true.
Wrong: it includes the false statement 3. Dr Rajendra Prasad, not S. Radhakrishnan, did the Pran Pratishtha.
keyfact: Somnath is the first Jyotirlinga, was described by Al-Biruni, and its present temple was installed in 1951 by Rajendra Prasad, not Radhakrishnan.
option_notes: 1 and 2 only is the correct combination here. It pairs Somnath's status as a Jyotirlinga with Al-Biruni's description of it. The temple is in Prabhas Patan, Gujarat. It was raided in 1025 by Mahmud of Ghazni and rebuilt several times. The current structure dates from 1951 and is managed by the Shree Somnath Trust. The Prime Minister has been the trust's chairman in recent years. The 'Circuit House' news item relates to Veraval tourism infrastructure.

2 and 3 only combines a true statement with the false claim about Radhakrishnan. Radhakrishnan (1888-1975) was a philosopher, India's first Vice-President (1952-62) and second President (1962-67). Teachers' Day on 5 September marks his birthday. He wrote 'Indian Philosophy' and received the Bharat Ratna in 1954. He did not install the Somnath temple.

1 and 3 only (shown as '1 and 8 only' in the OCR) pairs a true statement with the false one about the installation. The installation was done by Dr Rajendra Prasad, President from 1950 to 1962, the only person to serve two full terms. He had earlier been President of the Constituent Assembly, and he received the Bharat Ratna in 1962.

1, 2 and 3 treats all three statements as true. It fails because of the Radhakrishnan claim. UPSC often adds one wrong name to otherwise correct statements, so check each person and date. Prasad was President in 1951 and Radhakrishnan was Vice-President from 1952.

statements: 1 — Correct: Somnath is traditionally listed as the first of the 12 Jyotirlingas. The twelve are Somnath (Gujarat), Mallikarjuna (Srisailam), Mahakaleshwar (Ujjain), Omkareshwar (MP), Kedarnath (Uttarakhand), Bhimashankar (Maharashtra), Kashi Vishwanath (Varanasi), Trimbakeshwar (Nashik), Vaidyanath (Deoghar/Parli), Nageshwar (Dwarka area), Rameshwaram (Tamil Nadu) and Grishneshwar (Maharashtra). Jyotirlinga means a 'radiant sign' of Shiva, and the list appears in the Shiva Purana and in the Dvadasha Jyotirlinga Stotra attributed to Adi Shankaracharya. Somnath stands on the Arabian Sea coast at Prabhas Patan, Veraval.

2 — Correct: Al-Biruni, a Persian scholar from Khwarazm, came to India with Mahmud of Ghazni's army. He wrote Kitab-ul-Hind (Tahqiq-i-Hind) around 1030 CE, covering Indian religion, philosophy, science, astronomy, customs and the caste system. He knew Sanskrit and read Patanjali, the Gita and the Puranas. He describes the Somnath lingam and its worship, and he explains how the temple was destroyed in 1025. Other writers on Somnath include Ibn al-Athir, and Jain chronicles also mention the temple.

3 — Incorrect: The present Somnath temple was designed by architect Prabhashankar Sompura in the Chalukyan style and was inaugurated on 11 May 1951 by Dr Rajendra Prasad, India's first President. Sardar Patel started the reconstruction and K.M. Munshi led the effort. Patel died in December 1950, before the opening. Nehru had reservations about a head of state attending a religious event, but Prasad went ahead. S. Radhakrishnan was Vice-President from 1952 and President from 1962 to 1967, so he had no role here.
summary: The answer is (a): statements 1 and 2 are correct. Somnath is the first of the twelve Jyotirlingas, and Al-Biruni described it in his account of India. Statement 3 is wrong because the present temple's Pran Pratishtha in 1951 was performed by President Dr Rajendra Prasad, not S. Radhakrishnan.
topic_notes: Somnath Temple, at Prabhas Patan in Veraval (Gir Somnath district, Gujarat), is regarded as the first of the 12 Jyotirlingas. Tradition says it was first built in gold by Soma, the moon god, then in silver by Ravana, in wood by Krishna and in stone by Bhimdev. Historically it was attacked many times: Mahmud of Ghazni in 1025, Alauddin Khalji's general Ulugh Khan around 1299, Muzaffar Shah of Gujarat around 1395 and Aurangzeb in 1706. Many chroniclers recorded the 1025 raid, including Al-Biruni, Ibn al-Athir and Persian writers. The Somnath raid was a major event in the history of the Ghaznavids and Indian rulers. In the British period the 'Gates of Somnath' controversy arose, when Lord Ellenborough in 1842 ordered gates to be brought back from Ghazni. Ahilyabai Holkar built a new temple in 1783. After Independence, Patel on 13 November 1947 announced the reconstruction, with K.M. Munshi's support. Gandhi advised that people's donations should fund it. Prabhashankar Sompura designed it in the Chalukya or Solanki style, the Kailash Mahameru Prasad. Dr Rajendra Prasad installed the lingam on 11 May 1951. The Shree Somnath Trust was formed in 1951. Related angles for UPSC include other Jyotirlingas and their states, temple architecture styles (Nagara, Dravida, Vesara), Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind and other foreign travellers (Ibn Battuta, Bernier, Megasthenes, Fa-Hien, Hiuen Tsang), and the integration of Junagadh in 1947.
