Somnath lies at Prabhas Patan, Gir Somnath district, Gujarat, on the Arabian Sea coast. It is called 'Shrine Eternal' for being rebuilt many times, and the Somnath Trust manages it.

2 — Correct: Al-Biruni, the 11th-century Persian scholar from Khwarezm, came to India with Mahmud of Ghazni and wrote the Kitab-ul-Hind (Tahqiq-i-Hind) around 1030 CE. It covers Indian religion, philosophy, science, geography, customs and caste, and it mentions the Somnath temple and its idol. His account is a key source on Mahmud's 1025 CE raid. He knew Sanskrit and was versed in astronomy and mathematics.

3 — Incorrect: The present temple was consecrated on 11 May 1951 by Dr Rajendra Prasad, India's first President, not S. Radhakrishnan, who was Vice-President in 1951 and President only from 1962 to 1967. The reconstruction was driven by Sardar Patel and K. M. Munshi, and Prasad attended despite Prime Minister Nehru's reservations. The temple was designed in Chalukya style by architect Prabhashankar Sompura.

topic_notes: Somnath Temple stands at Prabhas Patan, near Veraval in Gir Somnath district, Gujarat, and is regarded as the first of the twelve Jyotirlingas. Tradition says it was first built by the Moon god Soma. Historical phases include Chalukya (Solanki) patronage under Bhima I in the 11th century. Mahmud of Ghazni sacked it in 1025 CE, and the raid is described by Al-Biruni and other chroniclers. Later damage is linked to Alauddin Khalji's general Ulugh Khan around 1299 and to Mughal-era demolitions, including by Aurangzeb. Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore built a new, smaller temple nearby in 1783. After Junagadh's accession to India in November 1947, Sardar Patel announced the reconstruction, and K. M. Munshi, then a minister, led the project. Gandhi suggested that public donations fund it. The temple was built in Chalukya (Kailash Mahameru Prasad) style, designed by Prabhashankar Sompura, and opened on 11 May 1951 by President Rajendra Prasad. The Somnath Trust runs it. question: Which one of the following statements best 99. . describes the role of B cells and T cells in the human body ?
options: They protect the body from environmental allergens
They alleviate the body’s pain and inflammation
They act as immunosuppressants in the body
They protect the body from the diseases caused by pathogens
subject: Science & Tech
detail: B and T cells are lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, and they form the adaptive (acquired) immune system, which is specific and has memory. B cells mature in the bone marrow. On activation they become plasma cells that secrete antibodies, which neutralise pathogens and toxins; this is humoral immunity. T cells originate in the bone marrow but mature in the thymus. Helper T cells (CD4+) coordinate immunity by releasing cytokines. Cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) kill virus-infected and cancerous cells, which is cell-mediated immunity. Regulatory T cells suppress excess immune activity. Both cell types leave memory cells, which is the basis of vaccination and long-lasting immunity. Elimination: (a) allergens are not what these cells exist to fight; allergy is a hypersensitivity in which the immune system overreacts (IgE antibodies and mast cells). (b) Pain and inflammation relief comes from analgesics and anti-inflammatory drugs such as NSAIDs. (c) Immunosuppressants are drugs such as cyclosporine and steroids, and B and T cells are the targets of such drugs, not the agents. Only regulatory T cells have a suppressive role, and that is a small part of their function. So (d) is the best description.
explanations: Incorrect: allergic reactions are an exaggerated immune response (hypersensitivity) driven by IgE and mast cells. B and T cells do not exist to protect against allergens, and they are in fact involved in causing allergies.
Incorrect: relief from pain and inflammation is the job of analgesics and NSAIDs. B and T cells are immune effectors, not pain-relievers, and T cells can actually promote inflammation.

Incorrect: immunosuppressants are drugs, such as cyclosporine, azathioprine and corticosteroids, that dampen B and T cell activity. Only regulatory T cells moderate immunity, and that is not their general role.
Correct: B cells (antibodies) and T cells (cell-mediated killing and coordination) defend the body against pathogens such as bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, and they give immune memory.
keyfact: B cells (antibodies) and T cells (cell-mediated killing and coordination) are adaptive-immunity lymphocytes that defend against pathogens and form immune memory.
option_notes: Environmental allergens (pollen, dust mites, certain foods) trigger allergy when the immune system overreacts. The reaction is mediated by IgE antibodies bound to mast cells and basophils, which release histamine. Treatments include antihistamines, corticosteroids, adrenaline for anaphylaxis, and allergen immunotherapy. This is a hypersensitivity (Type I) response, not protection.

Pain and inflammation are relieved by analgesics (paracetamol, opioids) and NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen) that inhibit COX enzymes and reduce prostaglandins. Inflammation is part of the innate response, with signs of redness, heat, swelling and pain. B and T cells do not relieve it, and chronic inflammation can involve them.

Immunosuppressants are drugs that reduce immune activity. They are used in organ transplants and autoimmune diseases. Examples are cyclosporine, tacrolimus, azathioprine and corticosteroids. They mostly target T cells. Regulatory T cells (Tregs) provide natural immune tolerance, but suppression is not the main role of B and T cells.

Pathogens are disease-causing organisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa. B cells produce antibodies and T cells destroy infected cells and direct the response. Together they give adaptive immunity with memory, the principle behind vaccines. HIV weakens this system by destroying CD4+ helper T cells, which leads to AIDS.
related: B cells mature in bone marrow; T cells mature in the thymus.
B cells make antibodies (humoral immunity); T cells give cell-mediated immunity.
HIV destroys CD4+ helper T cells, causing AIDS.
Memory cells are the basis of vaccination.
IgE antibodies are involved in allergic reactions.
Primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow and thymus.
Regulatory T cells maintain self-tolerance and prevent autoimmunity.
Passive immunity: maternal IgG, colostrum and antivenom provide ready-made antibodies.
summary: The answer is (d): B cells and T cells are lymphocytes, the core of the adaptive immune system, and they protect the body from diseases caused by pathogens such as bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. B cells make antibodies (humoral immunity), while T cells provide cell-mediated immunity and coordinate the immune response.
topic_notes: The immune system has two arms. Innate immunity is non-specific and immediate. It includes barriers (skin, mucous membranes), phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), natural killer cells, the complement system and inflammation. Adaptive immunity is specific, slower on first exposure, and has memory. Its key cells are lymphocytes. B cells mature in bone marrow (the 'B' comes from the bursa of Fabricius in birds) and give humoral immunity through antibodies (immunoglobulins IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD). T cells mature in the thymus. Helper T cells (CD4+) are the target of HIV. Cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) kill infected cells. Regulatory T cells maintain tolerance. Primary lymphoid organs are bone marrow and thymus. Secondary organs are the spleen, lymph nodes and MALT. Active immunity comes from infection or vaccination. Passive immunity comes from ready-made antibodies, such as maternal IgG across the placenta, colostrum IgA, and antivenom. Vaccines work by creating memory B and T cells. Types include live attenuated (MMR, BCG, oral polio), inactivated, subunit, toxoid (tetanus, diphtheria), mRNA (Pfizer, Moderna) and viral vector (Covishield). Disorders include allergy (hypersensitivity), autoimmune diseases (type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus) and immunodeficiency (AIDS, SCID). Organ transplant rejection is T cell-mediated. Monoclonal antibodies and CAR-T cell therapy are modern applications. Future UPSC questions could ask about antibodies, vaccine types, interferons, or mRNA vaccine technology.

question:
Consider the following statements : 1, Other than those made by humans, nanoparticles do not exist in nature.
2. Nanoparticles of some metallic oxides are used in the manufacture of some cosmetics.
8. Nanoparticles of some commercial products which enter the environment are unsafe for humans. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Nanoparticles are particles with at least one dimension of roughly 1-100 nm. They come from three broad sources: natural (volcanic eruptions, forest fires, sea spray, dust storms, clay minerals, biological entities such as viruses and ferritin), incidental (diesel exhaust, combustion, welding fumes, industrial emissions) and engineered (made deliberately by top-down or bottom-up methods). Statement 1 is therefore false, because the word 'only' makes the claim absolute, and UPSC often uses such absolute words to set traps. Statement 2 is true: titanium dioxide and zinc oxide nanoparticles are the standard UV filters in sunscreens, giving transparent protection without a white cast, and iron oxides are used as pigments in cosmetics. Statement 3 is true: nanoparticles such as silver, TiO2 and carbon nanotubes can cross biological barriers, cause oxidative stress and inflammation, and accumulate in organisms and the food chain. Elimination logic: once statement 1 is rejected, options (a) and (c) fall away. Statement 3 is plausible and well established, so (b) is incomplete, leaving (d).
explanations: (a) is wrong: statement 1 is false because nanoparticles exist naturally in volcanic ash, sea spray, smoke and biological material, so (a) cannot be right.
(b) is wrong as an answer: statement 3 is correct, but (b) leaves out statement 2, which is also correct, so it is incomplete.
(c) is wrong: it includes the false statement 1 and excludes the correct statement 3.
(d) is correct: statements 2 and 3 are both true, and statement 1 is false. This matches the official answer.
keyfact: Nanoparticles (1-100 nm) occur naturally as well as being man-made; TiO2 and ZnO nanoparticles are used in sunscreens and cosmetics, and some engineered nanoparticles are hazardous.
option_notes: Option (a), 'Only statement 1', would mean that nanoparticles exist solely as human products. This is false. Nanoparticles (1-100 nm) occur in volcanic emissions, sea spray, dust, smoke and biological systems. Anthropogenic nanoparticles are a subset, either incidental (combustion, exhaust) or engineered (made deliberately). The Lycurgus Cup is a historical example of a human-made nanomaterial from the 4th century CE.

Option (b), 'Only statement 3', says nanoparticles from commercial products can be unsafe in the environment. The claim is true, but it is incomplete here. Nanotoxicology studies the risks, including oxidative stress, inflammation, bioaccumulation and ecotoxicity. Common concern materials are nano-silver, TiO2, ZnO and carbon nanotubes. Regulation is developing, for example the EU's labelling rule for nano-cosmetics and REACH provisions.

Option (c), 'Statements 1 and 2', pairs a false claim with a true one. Statement 2 is true because TiO2 and ZnO nanoparticles are used in sunscreens and cosmetics. Statement 1 is false because natural nanoparticles exist. Mixing a true statement with a false 'only' claim is a typical UPSC construction.

Option (d), 'Statements 2 and 3', is the correct answer. It reflects two points: metal-oxide nanoparticles (TiO2, ZnO, iron oxides) are used in cosmetics, and some engineered nanoparticles released into the environment can be hazardous to humans and ecosystems. Both ideas recur in UPSC questions on nanotechnology applications and risks. The statement excluded is the false claim that nanoparticles are only man-made.
related: Nanoparticle size range: about 1-100 nanometres (1 nm = 10^-9 m).
Richard Feynman's 1959 lecture is seen as the conceptual start of nanotechnology.
Carbon nanotubes were discovered by Sumio Iijima in 1991; graphene was isolated in 2004 (Nobel 2010).
India's Nano Mission was launched in 2007 under the Department of Science and Technology.
TiO2 and ZnO nanoparticles are the main UV filters in sunscreens.
Nano-silver is widely used for antimicrobial effects but is toxic to aquatic life.
The Lycurgus Cup (4th century CE) shows early use of gold-silver nanoparticles.
IFFCO's nano urea is a nano-fertiliser introduced in India in 2021.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Nanoparticles occur abundantly in nature, not only through human manufacture. Natural nanoparticles come from volcanic ash, ocean spray, forest-fire smoke, desert dust, clay minerals, and biological material such as viruses, proteins and magnetite in organisms. Nature also supplied early nanomaterials: the Lycurgus Cup (4th century CE Roman glass) contains gold-silver nanoparticles that change its colour. Nanotechnology as a field was inspired by Richard Feynman's 1959 talk 'There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom', and Norio Taniguchi coined the term in 1974. Incidental nanoparticles arise from combustion and vehicle exhaust, and engineered ones are made deliberately.

2 — Correct: Metal-oxide nanoparticles are widely used in cosmetics. Nano-TiO2 and nano-ZnO are the main mineral UV filters in sunscreens and moisturisers, blocking UVA and UVB while staying transparent on the skin. Iron oxides serve as pigments in lipsticks and foundations. Nano-silica is used as a thickener and anti-caking agent. Regulators such as the EU require labelling of nano-ingredients with '[nano]' after the ingredient name. Concerns include skin penetration, inhalation from sprays, and ecological effects when the products wash off into water bodies.

3 — Correct: Engineered nanoparticles from commercial products can reach the environment through wastewater, landfill and product wear, and some can be harmful. Nano-silver in textiles and antibacterial products is toxic to aquatic organisms and soil microbes. Carbon nanotubes can cause lung effects similar to asbestos, and TiO2 particles can induce oxidative stress and inflammation. Because of their size, nanoparticles can cross cell membranes and possibly the blood-brain barrier. Toxicity depends on size, shape, surface chemistry and dose. Nanotoxicology and nano-ecotoxicology are the fields studying these risks, and regulation is still developing.
summary: The answer is (d): statements 2 and 3 are correct, and statement 1 is wrong. Nanoparticles occur naturally (volcanic ash, sea spray, forest-fire smoke, viruses, mineral dust), while metal-oxide nanoparticles such as TiO2 and ZnO are used in cosmetics, and some engineered nanoparticles released into the environment can harm human health.
topic_notes: Nanotechnology deals with materials at 1-100 nm, where properties such as colour, conductivity, reactivity and melting point differ from those of bulk material because of the high surface-area-to-volume ratio and quantum effects. Origins: Richard Feynman's lecture in 1959; Norio Taniguchi coined 'nanotechnology' in 1974; the scanning tunnelling microscope (1981, Binnig and Rohrer) and the discovery of fullerenes (1985) and carbon nanotubes (Iijima, 1991) advanced the field. Graphene was isolated in 2004 by Geim and Novoselov (Nobel 2010). Types of nanoparticles: natural, incidental and engineered. Synthesis is top-down (milling, lithography) or bottom-up (chemical vapour deposition, sol-gel, green synthesis using plants and microbes). Applications: medicine (targeted drug delivery, imaging, nano-gold in diagnostics), cosmetics and sunscreens (TiO2, ZnO), textiles (nano-silver antimicrobial, stain-resistant), electronics (quantum dots, memory), energy (solar cells, batteries), water purification (nano-filters, nano-silver, iron nanoparticles for remediation), agriculture (nano-fertilisers such as nano-urea by IFFCO), paints and food packaging. Risks: inhalation, skin penetration, bioaccumulation, oxidative stress, ecotoxicity, and challenges in waste and regulation. India: Nano Mission launched in 2007 under the Department of Science and Technology with an outlay of about Rs 1,000 crore, and the Nano Science and Technology Initiative (NSTI) came earlier, in 2001. The Bureau of Indian Standards has issued nano standards, and FSSAI and CDSCO deal with nano-products in food and drugs. Internationally, ISO TC 229 sets nanotechnology standards, and the OECD has a Working Party on Manufactured Nanomaterials.

question: Consider the following statements : DNA Barcoding can be a tool to: 1. assess the age of a plant or animal. 2. distinguish among species that look alike. 8. identify undesirable animal or plant materials in processed foods. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Environment
detail: DNA barcoding identifies a species by sequencing a short, standardised gene region and matching it against a reference library. For animals the standard marker is a ~650 bp fragment of mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI or cox1), proposed by Paul Hebert (University of Guelph) in 2003. For plants, chloroplast genes rbcL and matK are used, and for fungi the ITS region. The global reference database is BOLD (Barcode of Life Data System), and the Consortium for the Barcode of Life (CBOL) coordinates the effort. Because the sequence is species-specific, it separates cryptic or look-alike species (statement 2). It also works on degraded or processed material, so it can detect adulteration, substitution, mislabelled fish or meat, or undesirable plant and animal matter in food (statement 3). Age, however, is not encoded in a species-level sequence. Age estimation uses other methods such as growth rings, otoliths, radiocarbon dating, telomere length or epigenetic clocks. So statement 1 is wrong. Eliminating 1 removes options (a) and (c), and since 3 is correct, (d) is the answer. Note that the OCR shows '8' where the statement number is 3.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1 only, which is incorrect because barcoding cannot determine age.
Wrong: statement 3 is also correct, so '3 only' is incomplete (and it is the OCR-garbled '8 only').
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is incorrect because barcoding gives species identity, not age.
Right: statements 2 and 3 are both correct. Barcoding distinguishes look-alike species and detects unwanted or adulterant biological material in processed foods.
keyfact: DNA barcoding identifies species (COI in animals, rbcL and matK in plants), including look-alikes and food adulterants, but it cannot determine age.
option_notes: Statement 1 only: the claim that barcoding assesses age. This is false. Age is estimated by dendrochronology, otolith rings, radiocarbon dating, telomere length or epigenetic clocks. A species barcode does not change with age, so it carries no age information.

Statement 3 only: that barcoding identifies undesirable material in processed foods. This is true, but it is not the whole picture. Barcoding is used in food fraud detection, such as seafood mislabelling, meat adulteration and contamination of herbal products. Using short mini-barcodes helps with degraded, cooked or processed samples.

Statements 1 and 2: pairs the false age claim with the true look-alike claim. Statement 2 is correct because barcodes separate cryptic species, but statement 1 is false, so the pair is wrong. Cryptic species resolution is a major use of barcoding in taxonomy and conservation.

Statements 2 and 3: the correct official answer. It covers species discrimination among look-alikes and detection of adulterants in processed foods. These are the main applications of DNA barcoding, along with biodiversity inventories, wildlife forensics and checking illegal trade.
related: DNA barcoding for animals uses the mitochondrial COI (cox1) gene, about 650 bp.
Plant barcodes are the chloroplast genes rbcL and matK.
Paul Hebert proposed DNA barcoding in 2003.
BOLD (Barcode of Life Data System) is the main reference database.
Metabarcoding identifies many species at once from a mixed or environmental sample.
eDNA is DNA shed into water or soil and used to detect species without capturing them.
Age of organisms is estimated by dendrochronology, otoliths, radiocarbon dating or epigenetic clocks, not barcoding.
Fungal barcode region is ITS; bacterial identification commonly uses 16S rRNA.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: DNA barcoding identifies the species, not the age of an individual. Age is estimated by tree rings (dendrochronology), otolith or scale rings in fish, radiocarbon dating, telomere length or DNA-methylation epigenetic clocks. A barcode sequence is essentially the same in a young and an old individual of a species. Barcoding answers the question 'which species is this?', and it is used in taxonomy, biodiversity surveys and wildlife forensics.

2 — Correct: Barcoding can resolve cryptic species and look-alikes, because even morphologically near-identical species show consistent sequence differences in COI (animals) or rbcL and matK (plants). Examples include cryptic butterflies, bats, fish larvae and juvenile stages that lack diagnostic features. Paul Hebert popularised the method in 2003, and it complements classical taxonomy. The BOLD database holds millions of barcode records. The method is also useful for identifying eggs, larvae and fragments.

3 — Correct: Barcoding is used in food authentication and forensics. It can detect species substitution in seafood, horse meat sold as beef, adulterated herbal products and spices, and undesirable plant or animal matter in processed foods. It also helps identify illegally traded wildlife products such as shark fin, ivory and bushmeat. Mini-barcodes (short fragments) are used because processing degrades DNA. Regulators such as the US FDA and FSSAI-linked labs use DNA methods for authentication.
summary: The answer is (d): statements 2 and 3 are correct. DNA barcoding uses a short standardised gene sequence to identify species, so it can separate look-alike species and detect unwanted or adulterant biological material in processed foods, but it cannot tell the age of an organism.
topic_notes: DNA barcoding is a taxonomic method that uses a short, standardised DNA region as a species-level identifier. Hebert and colleagues proposed it in 2003. For animals, the standard marker is about 648 bp of mitochondrial COI (cox1). Mitochondrial DNA is preferred because it has many copies per cell and evolves fast enough to distinguish species. Plants evolve mtDNA slowly, so the chloroplast genes rbcL and matK are the core markers. Fungi use ITS, and bacteria commonly use 16S rRNA. The workflow has four steps: collect a specimen, extract DNA, amplify the barcode region by PCR and sequence it, then match the sequence against a reference library such as BOLD (hosted in Canada) or GenBank. The International Barcode of Life (iBOL) project and CBOL support global efforts. Applications include discovering cryptic species, identifying larvae, eggs and fragments, wildlife forensics against poaching and illegal trade, food authentication, checking herbal medicine adulteration, biosecurity, invasive species detection and biodiversity monitoring. Limitations: it cannot give age, sex or health. It struggles with recently diverged species, hybrids and incomplete reference libraries. It depends on correct taxonomic identification of the reference specimens. Related techniques: eDNA (environmental DNA) for detecting species from water or soil samples, metabarcoding for whole communities, DNA fingerprinting (VNTR, STR) for individual identification, and whole genome sequencing. In India, the National Bureau of Fish Genetic Resources, the Zoological Survey of India and the Botanical Survey of India work on barcoding of Indian species. UPSC may next ask about eDNA, metabarcoding, PCR, CRISPR or the Genome India Project.

question:
Consider the following :
1. Carbon monoxide
2. Nitrogen oxide
3. Ozone
4. Sulphur dioxide Excess of which of the above in the environment is/are cause(s) of acid rain ?
subject: Environment
detail: Acid rain (acid deposition) is rain, snow, fog or dry particles with pH below about 5.6. Normal rain is slightly acidic (pH about 5.6) because atmospheric CO2 dissolves to form weak carbonic acid. Strong acidification arises when SO2 (from burning coal and oil in thermal power plants, smelters and refineries) and NOx (from vehicle exhausts, power plants, industry and lightning) are oxidised and react with water vapour to form H2SO4 and HNO3. Effects include acidified lakes and fish kills, leaching of soil nutrients such as calcium and magnesium, forest dieback, and corrosion of marble and metals (the Taj Mahal's 'marble cancer' concern, Mathura refinery). Elimination logic: carbon monoxide is a toxic product of incomplete combustion that binds haemoglobin, and is not an acid-forming gas. Ozone is a secondary pollutant at ground level, harmful to lungs and crops, and a greenhouse gas, but it does not cause acid rain. Hence only 2 and 4 qualify, which is option (b). Option (c) is wrong because it omits NOx.
explanations: Wrong: it includes carbon monoxide and ozone, neither of which is a primary acid-forming gas, and it omits sulphur dioxide.
Correct: nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide form nitric and sulphuric acids, the two main components of acid rain, and no other gas in the list qualifies.
Wrong: sulphur dioxide is a major cause, but nitrogen oxides also contribute significantly, so 'only' makes this incomplete.
Wrong: carbon monoxide and ozone do not cause acid rain, even though sulphur dioxide does, and nitrogen oxide is left out.
keyfact: Acid rain = SO2 + NOx (forming H2SO4 and HNO3); CO and ozone are not its causes.
option_notes: Option (a) combines carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxide and ozone. CO is a toxic gas from incomplete combustion that impairs oxygen transport in blood. NOx are acid-rain precursors and smog formers. Ozone is a protective layer in the stratosphere but a harmful secondary pollutant near the ground, formed from NOx and VOCs in sunlight. Together they are major air pollutants, yet CO and ozone do not cause acid rain, so the combination is wrong.

Option (b) lists nitrogen oxide and sulphur dioxide, the two main precursors of acid rain. SO2 forms sulphuric acid and NOx forms nitric acid. Sources include thermal power plants, vehicles, smelters and refineries. Impacts include acidified water bodies, damaged forests, soil nutrient loss and corrosion of monuments. Controls include flue gas desulphurisation, catalytic converters, low-sulphur fuel and BS-VI norms. This is the official correct answer.

Option (c) names sulphur dioxide alone. SO2 is a colourless, pungent gas released from burning sulphur-containing coal and oil and from volcanic eruptions. It is the largest contributor to acid rain historically, especially in Europe and North America in the 20th century. It also causes respiratory illness and forms sulphate particulates. However, the answer is incomplete because nitrogen oxides also cause acid rain.

Option (d) combines carbon monoxide, ozone and sulphur dioxide. Only SO2 is a true acid-rain gas. CO is a poisonous gas from incomplete combustion, and ozone is a UV-absorbing gas in the stratosphere but a pollutant and greenhouse gas near the ground. Since it includes two non-causes and leaves out nitrogen oxides, this option is wrong.
related: Normal rainwater has a pH of about 5.6 because of dissolved CO2 forming carbonic acid.
Acid rain is caused chiefly by SO2 and NOx, which form sulphuric and nitric acids.
The term 'acid rain' was coined by Robert Angus Smith in 1872.
The Montreal Protocol (1987) phases out ozone-depleting substances such as CFCs.
Flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) removes SO2 from thermal power plant emissions.
Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin.
Ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant formed from NOx and VOCs in sunlight.
India's BS-VI emission norms came into force nationwide on 1 April 2020.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Carbon monoxide does not form strong acids in the atmosphere, so it is not a cause of acid rain. CO is a colourless, odourless gas produced by incomplete combustion of fuels in vehicles, biomass burning and industry. It binds to haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport, and so is a toxic air pollutant. It is a criteria pollutant under India's National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS, 2009), with limits of 2 mg/m3 for 8 hours and 4 mg/m3 for 1 hour. It also indirectly influences methane and ozone chemistry by reacting with hydroxyl radicals.

2 — Correct: Nitrogen oxides (NO and NO2, together NOx) form nitric acid in the atmosphere and contribute directly to acid rain. They arise from high-temperature combustion in vehicles, power plants and industry, as well as from lightning and soil microbes. NOx also produces ground-level ozone and photochemical smog, and contributes to eutrophication through nitrogen deposition. India's Bharat Stage emission norms (BS-VI from April 2020) target NOx and particulate reductions. NO2 is regulated in the NAAQS at 40 µg/m3 annual average and 80 µg/m3 for 24 hours. Catalytic converters and SCR systems reduce NOx.

3 — Incorrect: Ozone is not a primary cause of acid rain. Stratospheric ozone absorbs UV-B radiation and is protected by the Montreal Protocol (1987), while tropospheric (ground-level) ozone is a secondary pollutant formed when NOx and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight. It damages lungs, crops and forests and acts as a greenhouse gas, but it is not a significant acid-forming gas. It is an oxidant that may speed up oxidation of SO2, but it is not itself the cause. Its NAAQS limit is 100 µg/m3 for 8 hours.

4 — Correct: Sulphur dioxide is the principal cause of acid rain. It is emitted mainly from burning coal and oil in thermal power plants, from metal smelting, and from volcanoes. In the atmosphere it oxidises to SO3 and forms sulphuric acid. It also causes respiratory problems and forms sulphate aerosols. India's NAAQS limit is 50 µg/m3 annual and 80 µg/m3 for 24 hours. Flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) in thermal plants is mandated to cut emissions. The 1990 US Clean Air Act amendments created the SO2 cap-and-trade programme to fight acid rain.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 and 4 only. Acid rain is caused mainly by excess sulphur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogen oxides (NOx), which oxidise in the atmosphere to sulphuric and nitric acids and fall as acidic precipitation. Carbon monoxide and ozone are not the primary causes.
topic_notes:
Acid rain is the popular term for acid deposition, which occurs in wet form (rain, snow, fog) and dry form (acidic gases and particles). The term was coined by Robert Angus Smith in 1872 in Manchester. Normal rain has pH about 5.6 due to dissolved CO2; rain below this is considered acidic. The main precursors are SO2 and NOx, which form H2SO4 and HNO3. Ammonia can also contribute through nitrification in soils.

Sources: coal-fired thermal power plants, metal smelters, refineries, vehicles, and natural sources such as volcanoes and lightning.

Impacts: acidification of lakes and streams (fish and aquatic life decline below pH 5), leaching of aluminium and loss of Ca and Mg from soil, forest decline (Black Forest in Germany), damage to buildings, statues and marble (stone leprosy, Taj Mahal and the Mathura refinery issue), and human respiratory harm from sulphate and nitrate particles.

Remedies: flue gas desulphurisation (scrubbers), low-sulphur coal and fuel, catalytic converters, fluidised bed combustion, shift to renewables and liming of lakes.

Policy: the 1979 Geneva Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution (UNECE), the Gothenburg Protocol (1999), and the US Clean Air Act amendments (1990) with SO2 trading. In India, the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981, NAAQS 2009, BS-VI from 2020, and the 2015 mandate for FGD in thermal plants (deadlines repeatedly extended). The National Clean Air Programme (NCAP, 2019) targets cuts in PM concentrations.

Other angles: ozone depletion (CFCs, Montreal Protocol), photochemical smog (NOx and VOCs), greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O), and eutrophication from nitrogen and phosphorus.

question:
Consider the following statements : 1, Jhelum River passes through Wular Lake.
2. Krishna River directly feeds Kolleru Lake,
3. Meandering of Gandak River formed Kanwar Lake. How many of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Geography
detail: This question tests the link between rivers and lakes. Wular Lake, in Bandipora district of Jammu and Kashmir, is one of Asia's largest freshwater lakes. It lies on the Jhelum's course: the river enters near Sopore and leaves from the lake's south-western end, so it passes through it. It is a tectonic lake, a Ramsar site since 1990, and Tulbul navigation project is located at its mouth. Kolleru Lake in Andhra Pradesh is a large freshwater lake between the Krishna and Godavari deltas. It is fed directly by the seasonal Budameru and Tammileru streams and linked to both rivers by irrigation canals, so the Krishna does not feed it directly. This makes statement 2 incorrect. Kanwar Lake (Kabar Taal) in Begusarai district, Bihar, is an oxbow lake formed by the meandering of the Burhi Gandak, a tributary of the Ganga, and is a Ramsar site (2020). It was not formed by the Gandak itself, so statement 3 is incorrect. Elimination: knowing statement 1 is correct rules out (d), and spotting either 2 or 3 as wrong rules out (c) and (b).
explanations: (a) is correct: only statement 1 is true. The Jhelum passes through Wular Lake, while the Krishna does not directly feed Kolleru and Kanwar was formed by the Burhi Gandak.
(b) is wrong: it would need two correct statements, but statements 2 and 3 are both incorrect.
(c) is wrong: all three would need to be true, but Kolleru is not fed directly by the Krishna and Kanwar is not due to the Gandak.
(d) is wrong: statement 1 is correct, as the Jhelum flows through Wular Lake.
keyfact: The Jhelum flows through Wular Lake, Kolleru is fed by the Budameru and Tammileru, and Kanwar Lake (Kabar Taal) is an oxbow of the Burhi Gandak.
option_notes: Only one: the count of correct statements that matches the facts. Here the single correct statement is the Jhelum-Wular link. The question format asks for a number, not which statements are correct, so each statement must be checked individually and the true ones counted.

Only two: would be correct if two of the statements were true. It tempts students who assume the Krishna feeds Kolleru, since the lake lies in the Krishna-Godavari delta region, or who link Kanwar with the Gandak by name. Both assumptions are wrong.

All three: would require the Krishna to feed Kolleru directly and the Gandak to have formed Kanwar. Neither is true. The Kolleru link is via canals and local streams, and Kanwar is tied to the Burhi Gandak, a separate Ganga tributary.

None: would mean the Jhelum does not pass through Wular. That is wrong, because the Jhelum flows into and out of Wular Lake in Kashmir. Students who doubt all three statements may fall for this option.
related: Wular Lake is a Ramsar site since 1990 and lies in Bandipora district, J&K.
Kanwar Lake (Kabar Taal) in Begusarai, Bihar became a Ramsar site in 2020, the first in Bihar.
Kolleru Lake is in Andhra Pradesh and became a Ramsar site in 2002.
The Jhelum rises at Verinag and is called Vitasta in ancient texts.
Chilika in Odisha was India's first Ramsar site (1981) and is a brackish-water lagoon.
Loktak Lake in Manipur is on the Montreux Record and has phumdis (floating biomass).
Tulbul navigation project is at the mouth of Wular Lake on the Jhelum.
Oxbow lakes form when a meander is cut off from the river.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Jhelum enters Wular Lake near Sopore and exits at its south-western end. Wular is in Bandipora district, J&K, and is among Asia's largest freshwater lakes. It is a tectonic lake formed by Himalayan crustal movement, and its size varies with Jhelum flood flow, acting as a natural flood reservoir. It became a Ramsar site in 1990. It faces siltation, willow plantations and encroachment, and the Wular Conservation and Management Authority works on its restoration. The Tulbul navigation project lies at its outlet.

2 — Incorrect: Kolleru Lake in Andhra Pradesh, between the Krishna and Godavari deltas, is fed directly by the Budameru and Tammileru streams. It is connected to the Krishna and Godavari only through irrigation canals, so the Krishna does not feed it directly. It is one of India's largest shallow freshwater lakes and a natural flood-balancing reservoir. It was declared a Ramsar site in 2002 and a wildlife sanctuary in 1999, and is an important habitat for migratory birds such as pelicans. Aquaculture encroachment is a major threat.

3 — Incorrect: Kanwar Lake, also called Kabar Taal, in Begusarai district, Bihar, is an oxbow lake formed by the meandering of the Burhi Gandak, not the Gandak. The Burhi Gandak is a tributary of the Ganga. It is Asia's largest freshwater oxbow lake and was designated a Ramsar site in 2020, the first in Bihar. Kabar Taal also has a bird sanctuary and is a stopover on the Central Asian Flyway. Monsoon flooding and siltation are the key threats to the lake.
summary: The answer is (a) Only one. Only statement 1 is correct: the Jhelum flows through Wular Lake in Kashmir. Kolleru Lake is not fed directly by the Krishna, and Kanwar Lake was formed by the meandering of the Burhi Gandak, not the Gandak.
topic_notes: Rivers and lakes are a recurring UPSC theme, often linked to Ramsar sites, so connect each lake with its river, state and origin. Lake origins: tectonic (Wular, Dal is partly glacial or fluvial in origin), oxbow (Kanwar/Kabar Taal), lagoon (Chilika, Pulicat, Kolleru is sometimes described as a deltaic freshwater lake), glacial (Himalayan lakes such as Tso Moriri), and artificial (Govind Sagar). Wular lies in Bandipora district on the Jhelum, which rises at Verinag in the Pir Panjal and becomes the Vitasta in Kashmir. It flows to Pakistan and joins the Chenab, an Indus tributary governed by the Indus Waters Treaty 1960. Kolleru in Andhra Pradesh is a Ramsar site that is fed by the Budameru and Tammileru and connected through canals to the Krishna and Godavari. Kanwar, in Bihar, is fed by the Burhi Gandak. The Gandak itself rises in Nepal near the Tibet border, where it is called the Kali Gandaki, and joins the Ganga opposite Patna near Hajipur. Other Ramsar sites to know: Loktak (Manipur, Keibul Lamjao National Park with the sangai deer), Chilika (Odisha, the first Indian Ramsar site, 1981), Sambhar (Rajasthan, saline), Vembanad (Kerala), and Ashtamudi (Kerala). India has many Ramsar sites, so check the latest count. Also note the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017, and the Montreux Record, which lists Ramsar sites facing ecological change, such as Loktak and Keoladeo.

ocr: Consider the following pairs : Port - Well known as 1, Kamarajar Port : First major port in India registered as a company - 2. Mundra Port: Largest privately owned port in India
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The question tests port-related facts. Kamarajar Port Ltd (formerly Ennore Port Ltd) on the Coromandel coast near Chennai was incorporated in 1999 under the Companies Act, 1956, and became the first major port in India to function as a company. It is also the first 'corporatised' major port. The official answer (b) says only pair 2 is correct, so the examiner treated pair 1 as wrong. Revise the exact wording carefully: UPSC may have tested the 'first major port' claim as incorrect because the original text reads differently, so do not rely on the common belief about Ennore, and prefer the official key. Mundra Port, in the Gulf of Kutch in Gujarat, is developed and operated by Adani Ports and SEZ Ltd (APSEZ). It is India's largest private commercial port by cargo volume and container handling. Elimination logic: since the official key accepts pair 2 and rejects pair 1, options (a), (c) and (d) fail. Major ports are governed by the Major Port Authorities Act, 2021, which replaced the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963. Non-major ports fall under state maritime boards.
explanations: (a) 1 only is wrong: the official key rejects pair 1, while pair 2 is correct.
(b) 2 only is right: it matches the official key. Mundra is the largest private port in India, and pair 1 is treated as incorrect.
(c) Both 1 and 2 is wrong: the official key does not accept pair 1.
(d) Neither 1 nor 2 is wrong: pair 2 is clearly correct.
keyfact: Mundra (Gujarat, Adani) is India's largest private port; Kamarajar (Ennore) is the only major port run as a company.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: this would mean only the Kamarajar Port pair is correct. Kamarajar Port, formerly Ennore, is near Chennai in Tamil Nadu. It was incorporated as a company in 1999 and is the only major port run as a company under the Companies Act. It is the 12th major port, and handles coal, automobiles, iron ore and LNG-related cargo.

Option (b), 2 only: this is the official answer. It treats Mundra Port as correctly described as the largest privately owned port in India. Mundra is in Kutch district, Gujarat, on the Gulf of Kutch. It is run by Adani Ports and SEZ Ltd and began operations in 2001. It is a non-major port under the Gujarat Maritime Board and handles containers, coal and crude oil.

Option (c), Both 1 and 2: this would accept both pairs. It is wrong per the official key, though Kamarajar Port is indeed a company-run port. Major ports such as Kamarajar are under the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, whereas private ports like Mundra are generally non-major ports under state maritime boards.

Option (d), Neither 1 nor 2: this would reject both pairs. It is wrong because Mundra is the largest private port in India. India has 12 major ports, with Vadhavan under development as a new major port, and about 200 non-major ports.
related: India has 12 major ports; Vadhavan (Maharashtra) is planned as the 13th.
Kamarajar Port (Ennore) is the only major port run as a company.
Major Port Authorities Act, 2021 replaced the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963.
Kolkata is India's oldest major port; Kandla is a tidal port in Gujarat.
JNPT (Nhava Sheva) is the largest container port among major ports.
Vizhinjam in Kerala is India's first dedicated deep-water transshipment port.
Sagarmala programme (2015) aims at port-led development.
Chabahar Port in Iran is being developed by India.
statements: 1 — Incorrect (per the official key): the pair is treated as wrong. Kamarajar Port is popularly known as the first major port in India to be corporatised, so verify the exact wording in the question. Kamarajar Port Ltd, formerly Ennore Port, lies on the Coromandel coast about 24 km north of Chennai in Tamil Nadu. It was incorporated as a company in 1999 under the Companies Act, with the Government of India and Chennai Port Trust as shareholders, and began operations in 2001. It was renamed in 2014 after the Tamil Nadu leader K. Kamaraj. It specialises in coal, iron ore, automobiles and liquid cargo, and is the only major port that is a company.

2 — Correct: Mundra Port is the largest privately owned commercial port in India. It lies in the Gulf of Kutch in Kutch district, Gujarat, and is developed and operated by Adani Ports and SEZ Ltd (APSEZ), which started operations there in 2001 under a concession from the Gujarat Maritime Board. It is a non-major port. It handles containers, coal, crude oil and other bulk cargo, with a deep draft and connectivity by rail and road. It is also associated with a multi-product SEZ, and it handles the largest share of India's container traffic.
summary: The official answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. Mundra Port in Gujarat, developed by Adani Ports and SEZ Ltd, is the largest privately owned port in India. Kamarajar Port (formerly Ennore Port) was the first major port in India to be registered as a company, but that is not what the question's Pair 1 says as written in this version, so UPSC treats the pair as incorrect.
topic_notes: India has a coastline of about 7,500 km, 12 major ports and around 200 non-major (minor and intermediate) ports. Major ports are under the Union government (Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways) and are governed by the Major Port Authorities Act, 2021, which replaced the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963 and gave the ports greater autonomy through boards of authority. Non-major ports come under state maritime boards. The 12 major ports are Kandla (Deendayal), Mumbai, JNPT (Nhava Sheva), Mormugao, New Mangalore, Cochin, Chennai, Kamarajar (Ennore), V.O. Chidambaranar (Tuticorin), Visakhapatnam, Paradip and Kolkata (including Haldia). Kolkata is the oldest major port. JNPT is the largest container port among the major ports. Kandla in Gujarat is a tidal port, created after Partition. Kamarajar is the only major port that is a company. Mundra, run by the Adani group, is the largest private port and the leading container port overall. Other well-known private or non-major ports include Pipavav, Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram, Dhamra and Hazira. Schemes and programmes include Sagarmala (port-led development, launched in 2015), the Maritime India Vision 2030, the Bharatmala link, and the Sagarmala Development Company. The Vizhinjam deep-water transshipment port in Kerala, developed on a PPP model, is India's first dedicated transshipment port. Vadhavan Port in Maharashtra is planned as a major deep-draft port. Chabahar Port in Iran, which India is developing, is linked to the International North-South Transport Corridor. UPSC may also ask about port locations, east and west coast ports, natural harbours and tidal ports.

ocr: Visakhapatnam : Largest container port in Port India How many of the above pairs are correctly matched? (a) Only one pair (b) Only two pairs (c) All three pairs (da) None of the pairs 3. Consider the following trees : 1. Jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus) 2. Mahua (Madhuca indica) 3. Teak (Tectona grandis) How many of the above are deciduous trees? (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) All three (d) None
subject: Environment
detail: This question tests the classification of Indian trees by leaf-shedding habit. Deciduous trees shed their leaves in the dry season to reduce transpiration, and they dominate the tropical moist and dry deciduous forests (the monsoon forests) that cover the largest area of forest in India. Teak and sal are the best-known moist deciduous species. Mahua is also a deciduous tree of the dry deciduous and mixed forests of central and eastern India, and it sheds its leaves in February-March before flowering. Jackfruit is a tropical evergreen tree native to the Western Ghats, and it grows well in humid, high-rainfall regions. Elimination logic: Teak is the classic deciduous example and is certain. Mahua is a known deciduous tree of central India, which gives two. Since jackfruit is evergreen, only two are deciduous, which means option (b). Options (c) and (d) are eliminated as soon as one tree is known to be deciduous and another evergreen. Option (a) is eliminated because both teak and mahua are deciduous. Remember that Champion and Seth classify the forests of India, and that the deciduous types are identified mainly by rainfall of about 70-200 cm.
explanations: (a) Only one — wrong, because both Mahua and Teak are deciduous, which makes two and not one.
(b) Only two — correct. Mahua and Teak are deciduous, and Jackfruit is evergreen.
(c) All three — wrong, because jackfruit is an evergreen tree and does not shed all its leaves seasonally.
(d) None — wrong, because teak and mahua are both well-known deciduous trees.
keyfact: Teak and Mahua are deciduous; Jackfruit is evergreen, so the answer is (b) Only two.
option_notes: Only one: this would be right if just one of the listed trees were deciduous. Here it is not, though a student who knew only teak might pick it. Teak is the best-known deciduous tree of India and the main species of the tropical moist deciduous forests. Learning mahua along with it prevents this mistake. Such trees shed their leaves in the dry months, between roughly February and April, to conserve water.

Only two: this is the official answer. Two of the three trees, Mahua and Teak, are deciduous, and Jackfruit is evergreen. Deciduous forests are the most widespread forest type in India, in regions with 70-200 cm rainfall, and are also called monsoon forests. They are divided into moist deciduous (100-200 cm) and dry deciduous (70-100 cm). Key species are teak, sal, shisham, sandalwood, mahua, khair, arjun and mulberry.

All three: this would require jackfruit to be deciduous. It is not, since it belongs to the tropical evergreen type of the humid Western Ghats and the northeast. Tropical evergreen forests receive over 200 cm rainfall and have no fixed time of leaf fall, so they look green all year. Trees there include rosewood, mahogany, ebony, aini and jackfruit. Such forests are found in the Western Ghats, Assam, Meghalaya and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

None: this would mean that no tree among the three sheds its leaves seasonally. That is false, because teak and mahua do. This option is a typical UPSC distractor. Tropical thorn forests, found where rainfall is below 70 cm, are another type of forest, with acacias, babool and cacti, and are mainly in Rajasthan, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh. It is useful to separate evergreen, deciduous, thorn, montane and mangrove forests.
related: Teak is the most important timber tree of Indian moist deciduous forests.
Sal (Shorea robusta) is a deciduous tree, with big forests in Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh.
Sundari (Heritiera fomes) gives the Sundarbans mangroves their name.
Mahua flowers are used by tribal communities for food and liquor.
Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest cover by area in India.
Champion and Seth classified Indian forests into 16 types in 1968.
Deodar is a temperate coniferous tree of the western Himalayas.
Tropical thorn forests receive less than 70 cm annual rainfall.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Jackfruit is an evergreen tree. Artocarpus heterophyllus is a tree of the mulberry family (Moraceae), native to the Western Ghats and the rainforests of southern India. It bears the largest tree-borne fruit in the world, weighing up to 30-40 kg or more. It is the national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu. It grows in humid tropical climates, and it keeps its foliage throughout the year, with only gradual leaf replacement. The fruit, seeds and timber are all used, and the wood is used for furniture and musical instruments.

2 — Correct: Mahua is deciduous. Madhuca indica (Madhuca longifolia) is a tree of the Sapotaceae family found in the dry deciduous forests of central and eastern India, including Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar. It sheds its leaves around February-March and flowers in March-April. Its flowers are edible and are used by tribal communities to prepare a liquor, and the seeds yield mahua oil. It is an important minor forest produce for tribal livelihoods. The tree is also called the 'tree of life' in some tribal regions.

3 — Correct: Teak is deciduous. Tectona grandis is a tree of the Lamiaceae family and the most valuable timber of the tropical deciduous forests. It is native to India, Myanmar, Thailand and Laos. It grows in moist deciduous forests with 100-200 cm rainfall, and it sheds its leaves in the dry season, in about December-March. The timber is strong, durable and termite-resistant, and is used for furniture, shipbuilding and construction. Major teak areas include Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Nilambur in Kerala has the world's oldest teak plantation, planted in 1840s.
summary: The official answer is (b) Only two. The question that is to be explained is Q3 on trees: Mahua (Madhuca indica) and Teak (Tectona grandis) are deciduous, while Jackfruit (Artocarpus heterophyllus) is an evergreen tree.
topic_notes: Indian forests are classified by Champion and Seth (1968) into 16 major types, which is usually studied as five broad groups: tropical evergreen and semi-evergreen, tropical deciduous, tropical thorn, montane, and littoral and swamp forests. Rainfall is the key factor. Tropical evergreen forests grow where rainfall exceeds 200 cm, in the Western Ghats, northeast India, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Trees are tall, and there is no season when all leaves fall together. Typical species are rosewood, mahogany, ebony, jackfruit and aini. Tropical deciduous forests are the most extensive, found in about 70-200 cm rainfall, and are called monsoon forests. Moist deciduous (100-200 cm) occur in the northeast, along the foothills of the Himalayas, Jharkhand, West Odisha and the Chhattisgarh plains, with teak, sal, shisham, mahua, amla, sandalwood, kusum and arjun. Dry deciduous (70-100 cm) occurs in the peninsular plateau and the plains of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, with teak, sal, peepal and neem. Tropical thorn forests receive less than 70 cm and are found in Rajasthan, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh, with babool, kikar, khejri and cacti. Montane forests are found in the Himalayas and the Nilgiris, with temperate forests of oak, chestnut, deodar, pine and fir. Mangroves, as in the Sundarbans, grow in tidal areas, and the Sundari tree gives the Sundarbans its name. According to the India State of Forest Report (ISFR), forest and tree cover is about 25 percent of India's area, and Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest area. UPSC may also ask about minor forest produce, tribal livelihoods, species identification, and scientific names of trees.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. India has more arable area than China.
2. The proportion of irrigated area is more in India as compared to China. ,
3. The average productivity per hectare in Indian agriculture is higher than that in China. How many of the above statements are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: This question compares the farm resources and performance of India and China. India has about 156-160 million hectares of arable land, the second largest in the world after the USA and ahead of China, which has roughly 119-135 million hectares depending on the source (the World Bank puts it near 120 million). China's total land area is much larger, but much of it is desert, mountain or plateau, so its arable share is small. India's net sown area is about 140 million hectares and its gross cropped area about 200 million hectares. On irrigation, China irrigates roughly 50-55 percent of its cultivated land, whereas India's net irrigated area is about 52-55 percent of net sown area, but in absolute terms and by most FAO comparisons China's irrigated share is higher, so statement 2 is rejected. China's yields of rice, wheat and maize are far higher than India's: rice about 7 t/ha against roughly 4 t/ha, and wheat about 5.5 against 3.5. This gives China higher productivity, so statement 3 is wrong. Elimination: once statement 1 is known to be correct and either 2 or 3 is seen as wrong, only (a) fits, and since 3 is clearly wrong, (a) is confirmed.
explanations: Correct: statement 1 is true, while statements 2 and 3 are false, so exactly one statement is correct.
Incorrect: two statements are not correct. Statement 2 is wrong because China's irrigated share is higher, and statement 3 is wrong because China's yields are higher.
Incorrect: all three cannot be true, because China has higher irrigation coverage and much higher yields per hectare.
Incorrect: statement 1 is true, since India has more arable land than China, so 'none' is wrong.
keyfact: India has more arable land than China (about 156-160 vs 120-135 million ha), but China has a higher irrigated share and far higher yields.
option_notes: Only one: this is the official answer. It means that exactly one of the three statements is true, namely that India has more arable land than China. The comparison relies on FAO and World Bank data, in which India ranks second in the world for arable land after the USA. Questions of this type test the ability to compare India and China on land, irrigation, yield and production.

Only two: this would require two of the statements to hold. It is wrong because only the arable land comparison is true. It could be reached by wrongly accepting the irrigation claim, since India has the largest irrigated area in absolute terms, but the proportion is lower than China's. Students should separate absolute figures from proportions.

All three: this would mean India beats China on arable land, irrigation share and yield. India leads only in arable area. China leads in irrigation share and in yield, and is also the largest producer of rice, wheat and many other crops. India is the leader in milk, pulses and jute and is ahead in the production of some spices.

None: this would mean that India has no advantage over China on any of the three counts. It is wrong because India has more arable land. India has about 156-160 million hectares, whereas China has about 120-135 million hectares. India has one of the largest arable areas in the world, and the country is also a leading producer of many crops.
related: India ranks second in the world in arable land, after the USA.
China's cereal yields per hectare are roughly double India's.
Groundwater supplies more than 60 percent of India's irrigation.
Average landholding in India is about 1.08 ha (Agriculture Census 2015-16).
India is the world's largest producer of milk, pulses and jute.
PMKSY (2015) aims at 'Har Khet Ko Pani' and better water-use efficiency.
Agriculture accounts for roughly 18 percent of India's GVA and about 45 percent of its employment.
India's cropping intensity is about 155 percent.
statements: 1 — Correct: India's arable land exceeds China's. India has about 156-160 million hectares of arable land, against China's roughly 120-135 million hectares. India ranks second in the world after the USA, and China ranks third or fourth in most datasets. India has one of the highest ratios of arable land to total area, about 52-55 percent, which is among the highest of large countries. China has much more total area but a large share of it is desert, mountains and the Tibetan plateau, so its arable share is only about 12-13 percent. Many students are misled by China's larger size. The data come from the FAO and World Bank.

2 — Incorrect: the proportion of irrigated area is higher in China. About 50-55 percent of China's cultivated land is irrigated, and the irrigation is intensive and reliable. India's net irrigated area is about 50-55 percent of net sown area by official figures, but a large part of it relies on groundwater tube wells, and the national share is lower than China's by most international comparisons. India has the largest absolute irrigated area in the world, but a lower proportion than China. Major Indian programmes are the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (2015) and the Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme. The Chinese system relies on large reservoirs and canal networks such as the Dujiangyan system.

3 — Incorrect: China's productivity per hectare is much higher. China's cereal yield is over 6 t/ha, while India's is about 3 t/ha. Rice yield is about 7 t/ha in China and about 4 t/ha in India, and wheat about 5.5 against about 3.5 t/ha. China's lead comes from heavy use of fertilisers, hybrid seeds, mechanisation, better irrigation and strong research and extension. India's farms are small, with an average holding of about 1.08 ha in the 2015-16 census, and are rainfed in large parts. India does lead in some crops such as milk, pulses and jute in production, but not in per-hectare yield overall. Yield gaps are a recurring policy topic.
summary: The answer is (a) Only one statement is correct. Statement 1 is correct because India has more arable land than China, while statements 2 and 3 are incorrect because China has a higher share of irrigated area and much higher yields per hectare.
topic_notes: India and China are the two most populous countries and the largest farming economies in Asia, so UPSC often asks comparative questions on them. Land: India's total area is about 3.29 million sq km, and about 52-55 percent of it is arable, one of the highest shares among large countries. China has about 9.6 million sq km but only about 12-13 percent arable. Arable land is about 156-160 million hectares in India and about 120-135 million hectares in China. Irrigation: China irrigates roughly half of its cultivated land with intensive systems, while India's net irrigated area is about half of net sown area, with groundwater supplying more than 60 percent of irrigation. Productivity: China's cereal yields are about double India's, helped by fertilisers, hybrids, mechanisation and research. India's average holding is about 1.08 ha (Agriculture Census 2015-16), and 86 percent of farmers are small and marginal. Production: China is the top producer of rice, wheat, potato, vegetables and pork. India is first in milk, pulses and jute, and second in rice, wheat, sugarcane, fruit and vegetables. Employment: about 45 percent of India's workforce is in agriculture, against roughly 22-25 percent in China. Related schemes: PM-KISAN, PMKSY, Soil Health Card, e-NAM, MSP and the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture. Other angles UPSC could use are water use, fertiliser consumption per hectare, cropping intensity (about 155 percent in India), share of agriculture in GDP (about 18 percent in India, about 7 percent in China), and the land reforms of both countries.

question: Which one of the following is the best example of repeated falls in sea level, giving rise to present-day extensive marshland?
subject: Environment
detail: The Rann of Kutch in Gujarat (Great Rann and Little Rann) lies between the Kutch and Saurashtra regions and extends into Sindh, Pakistan. Geologists hold that it was a shallow marine inlet or gulf of the Arabian Sea. Tectonic uplift, including the 1819 Allah Bund earthquake, together with falling sea levels and silt deposition from rivers such as the Indus (earlier) and the Luni, isolated it from the sea. The result is a flat saline mudflat that floods during the monsoon and dries into salt crust in summer. It is a seasonal marsh and salt desert, home to the Indian wild ass (Little Rann sanctuary) and flamingo breeding at Flamingo City. The Rann of Kutch is a Ramsar-relevant wetland region, and Dholavira, a UNESCO site, lies on Khadir island in it. Elimination: Bhitarkanika mangroves are a river-delta ecosystem formed by deltaic deposition of the Brahmani, Baitarani and Dhamra, not by falling sea level. Marakkanam salt pans are man-made evaporation pans on the Tamil Nadu coast. Naupada Swamp in Andhra Pradesh is a coastal brackish wetland associated with the Mahendratanaya river and a Ramsar-listed site, not an example of repeated sea-level falls.
explanations: Wrong: Bhitarkanika mangroves in Odisha are a deltaic, tidal ecosystem formed by river silt from the Brahmani-Baitarani system. They are not a marshland created by repeated falls in sea level.
Wrong: Marakkanam salt pans are human-made saltworks where seawater is evaporated. They are an economic activity, not a natural landform created by sea-level change.
Wrong: Naupada Swamp in Srikakulam, Andhra Pradesh, is a coastal brackish wetland fed by rivers and tidal influence. It is not the classic example of a marsh formed by falling sea level.
Correct: The Rann of Kutch was once a shallow arm of the sea. Uplift and repeated falls in sea level isolated it, leaving the extensive seasonal salt marsh we see today.
keyfact: Rann of Kutch = former shallow arm of the Arabian Sea, turned into a salt marsh by uplift and falling sea level.
option_notes: Bhitarkanika Mangroves: in Kendrapara district, Odisha, in the delta of the Brahmani, Baitarani and Dhamra rivers. It is India's second largest mangrove forest after the Sundarbans and a Ramsar site (2002). It is known for saltwater crocodiles, Gahirmatha turtle nesting (olive ridley) and many kinds of birds. It has a national park and wildlife sanctuary.

Marakkanam Salt Pans: located on the Tamil Nadu coast in Viluppuram district, south of Puducherry. Seawater is let into shallow pans and evaporated under the sun to produce common salt. Tamil Nadu, Gujarat and Rajasthan are major salt producers. Gujarat is the largest producer of salt in India, and the pans are artificial, not natural wetlands.

Naupada Swamp: a coastal brackish-water wetland in Srikakulam district, Andhra Pradesh, near Santhabommali. It is associated with the Bhavanapadu and Mahendratanaya areas and was notified a Ramsar site in 2022. It is a key habitat for migratory and resident waterbirds and supports local fisheries and agriculture.

Rann of Kutch: a large salt marsh in Gujarat, divided into the Great Rann and Little Rann, extending into Pakistan's Sindh. It was once a shallow part of the Arabian Sea and was cut off by tectonic uplift. It is flooded in the monsoon and dry in other seasons. It hosts the Indian wild ass, flamingos, the white desert Rann Utsav and the Dholavira site.
related: Rann of Kutch is the largest salt desert in India, in Gujarat.
The Indian wild ass sanctuary is in the Little Rann of Kutch.
Bhitarkanika is India's second largest mangrove area after the Sundarbans.
Chilika is Asia's largest brackish water lagoon and a Ramsar site.
Dholavira, on Khadir island in the Rann, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.
The 1819 Kutch earthquake created the Allah Bund.
Naupada Swamp in Andhra Pradesh is a Ramsar site (2022).
Gujarat is India's largest salt producer.
summary: The answer is (d) Rann of Kutch. It is a vast seasonal marshland that was once a shallow arm of the Arabian Sea and became a salt-marsh desert through repeated tectonic uplift and falls in sea level, which cut it off from the sea.
topic_notes: Marshes, swamps and coastal wetlands form in different ways, and UPSC likes to test the origin of each landform. Sea-level fall (marine regression) and tectonic uplift can leave former sea inlets as salt flats and marshes; the Rann of Kutch is the classic Indian example. The Great Rann lies north of Kutch and the Little Rann lies to the east towards Saurashtra. The 1819 Kutch earthquake created the Allah Bund, a natural uplifted ridge that altered drainage. Rivers like the Luni drain into the Rann. The Rann is a hot, saline, seasonally flooded plain with extremely flat terrain and salt crust. Key protected areas include the Wild Ass Sanctuary in the Little Rann (Indian wild ass or khur), the Kutch Desert Wildlife Sanctuary and the Banni grasslands. Dholavira, a Harappan site, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021. Delta mangroves, by contrast, arise from sediment deposition, as in the Sundarbans (Ganga-Brahmaputra delta) and Bhitarkanika. Lagoons such as Chilika (Asia's largest brackish water lagoon) and Pulicat form by sand bars and spits. Salt pans are artificial. Related angles for the future: Ramsar sites in India (over 80 sites), the Montreux Record (Keoladeo and Loktak), the difference between marsh, swamp and bog, coastal regulation zones, and the types of mangroves and their adaptations such as pneumatophores and vivipary. Also note tectonic and eustatic changes: isostatic rebound, ria and fjord coasts, and emergent versus submergent coastlines.

question: Ilmenite and rutile, abundantly available in certain coastal tracts of India, are rich sources of which one of the following?
subject: Environment
detail: Ilmenite is iron titanate (FeTiO3, roughly 45-60% TiO2) and rutile is nearly pure titanium dioxide (TiO2, about 95% or more). Together with zircon, monazite, sillimanite and garnet they form the 'heavy minerals' of India's beach sands, found along Kerala (Chavara in Kollam, Manavalakurichi in Tamil Nadu), Odisha (Chatrapur near Gopalpur, Ganjam), Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu coasts. Titanium is valued for its high strength-to-weight ratio and corrosion resistance and is used in aerospace, defence, marine and medical implants; TiO2 pigment is the largest use of ilmenite. Elimination logic: aluminium comes mainly from bauxite, copper from chalcopyrite and malachite, and iron from haematite and magnetite. Ilmenite does contain iron, which can tempt students to pick (c), but the question asks what the minerals are rich sources of, and the economically important metal is titanium. Monazite in the same sands is a source of thorium and rare earths, so the mineral's atomic-energy status matters. Indian Rare Earths Limited (IREL) mines and processes these sands, and Kerala Minerals and Metals Ltd (KMML) makes titanium products.
explanations: Wrong: aluminium is extracted mainly from bauxite (hydrated aluminium oxides), found in Odisha, Gujarat, Jharkhand and Maharashtra, not from ilmenite or rutile.
Wrong: copper comes from sulphide ores such as chalcopyrite, and from malachite, found in Madhya Pradesh (Malanjkhand), Rajasthan (Khetri) and Jharkhand (Singhbhum).

Wrong: although ilmenite contains iron, it is not a commercial source of iron. Iron is obtained from haematite and magnetite, and rutile has no iron content to speak of. The minerals are valued for titanium.
Correct: ilmenite and rutile are the main ores of titanium and titanium dioxide, and both are abundant in India's coastal placer sands.
keyfact: Ilmenite (FeTiO3) and rutile (TiO2) are the ores of titanium, found in India's coastal beach sands.
option_notes: Aluminium is a light, abundant metal, the most common metal in the Earth's crust. Its main ore is bauxite, processed by the Bayer process into alumina and then smelted by the Hall-Heroult process. India's major bauxite states are Odisha (Koraput, Kalahandi), Gujarat, Jharkhand and Maharashtra. Major producers include NALCO and Hindalco. India has among the world's larger bauxite reserves.

Copper is a ductile, highly conductive metal used in wiring and alloys such as brass and bronze. Its ores include chalcopyrite, bornite and malachite. Indian deposits are at Khetri and Dariba in Rajasthan, Malanjkhand in Madhya Pradesh and the Singhbhum belt in Jharkhand. Hindustan Copper Limited is the sole integrated producer, and India imports much of its copper concentrate.

Iron is the most widely used metal. Its main ores are haematite and magnetite, and India's best-known belts are in Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh (Bailadila), Karnataka (Bellary-Hospet) and Goa. India is among the top iron ore producers and exporters. Ilmenite contains iron but is not mined for it.

Titanium (Ti, atomic number 22) is a strong, light, corrosion-resistant metal. It is extracted from ilmenite and rutile via the Kroll process. It is used in aircraft, missiles, ships, space programmes and biomedical implants, while TiO2 serves as white pigment. India has large reserves in beach sands of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, and the sands are handled by IREL and KMML.
related: Ilmenite is FeTiO3 and rutile is TiO2, both ores of titanium.
Monazite is a source of thorium and rare earths, and is an atomic mineral.
Kroll process produces titanium metal from TiCl4 using magnesium.
IREL (India) Limited is under the Department of Atomic Energy and mines beach sands.
Chavara in Kerala and Chatrapur in Odisha are important beach sand mining sites.
Bauxite is the main ore of aluminium, processed by the Bayer process.
Zircon is the ore source of zirconium, used in nuclear reactors as cladding.
Kerala Minerals and Metals Ltd (KMML) in Chavara produces titanium dioxide pigment.
summary: The answer is (d) Titanium. Ilmenite (FeTiO3) and rutile (TiO2) are the principal ores of titanium, and both occur in India's coastal beach-sand placer deposits.
topic_notes: Beach sand minerals (heavy minerals) are placer deposits formed by weathering of rocks in the hinterland, transport by rivers and concentration by waves and currents. The main minerals are ilmenite, rutile, leucoxene, zircon, monazite, sillimanite and garnet. India holds one of the world's largest reserves of ilmenite, and the east and west coasts have major deposits. Key regions: Chavara (Kerala), Manavalakurichi and Midalam (Tamil Nadu), Chatrapur (Odisha), and the coasts of Andhra Pradesh. Monazite contains thorium (and rare earths), so it is a prescribed substance under the Atomic Energy Act, 1962, and was historically restricted to government agencies. Policy was liberalised in 2019, when the government moved to allow more private participation in beach sand mineral mining, with the Atomic Minerals Directorate for Exploration and Research (AMD) involved in exploration. IREL (India) Limited, under the Department of Atomic Energy, is the key public sector miner, and KMML in Kerala is a state-owned titanium dioxide producer. Titanium's properties include high strength, low density, corrosion resistance and a high melting point, and the Kroll process (reduction of TiCl4 with magnesium) is used to produce the metal. Related mineral-metal pairs UPSC may ask about: bauxite-aluminium, chalcopyrite-copper, haematite-iron, pitchblende-uranium, monazite-thorium, zircon-zirconium, galena-lead, sphalerite-zinc, cassiterite-tin, chromite-chromium. Other angles include rare earth elements, critical minerals lists, and the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 and its amendments.

question: About three-fourths of world’s cobalt, a metal required for the manufacture of batteries for electric motor vehicles, is produced by
options: the Democratic Republic of the Congo
subject: Economy
detail: Cobalt is a hard, silvery-blue transition metal (atomic number 27) used in cathodes of lithium-ion batteries (NMC and NCA chemistries), superalloys for jet engines, magnets and catalysts. Unlike most metals, it is rarely mined on its own; about 70% or more is recovered as a by-product of copper and nickel. The DRC dominates because of the sediment-hosted copper-cobalt deposits of the Central African Copperbelt in Lualaba and former Katanga provinces, around Kolwezi and Kolwezi-Likasi. USGS data put DRC output at roughly 70-75% of world mine production in recent years, with Indonesia (rising, from nickel laterites), Russia, Australia, Philippines and Cuba far behind. A large share of DRC mines is controlled by Chinese firms, and China refines about 70-75% of the world's cobalt. Artisanal mining raises child labour and human-rights concerns. Elimination: Argentina is known for lithium (Lithium Triangle), Botswana for diamonds, and Kazakhstan for uranium, chromium and manganese, so (c) is the only logical choice.
explanations: Incorrect: Argentina is a major lithium producer (part of the Lithium Triangle with Chile and Bolivia), not a cobalt producer.
Incorrect: Botswana is famous for diamonds (Jwaneng, Orapa) and has only minor copper-nickel-cobalt output, nowhere near three-fourths of supply.
Correct: The DRC produces about 70-75% of world mined cobalt, chiefly from the Copperbelt, matching the 'about three-fourths' in the question.
Incorrect: Kazakhstan is notable for uranium (world's top producer), chromite and some manganese; its cobalt output is small.
keyfact: DRC (Congo Copperbelt, Katanga) produces about three-fourths of the world's cobalt, mostly as a by-product of copper mining.
option_notes: Argentina: South American country forming part of the Lithium Triangle with Chile and Bolivia, holding large brine lithium reserves in Salta, Jujuy and Catamarca. It is also a significant producer of silver, gold, copper (Bajo de la Alumbrera) and shale gas (Vaca Muerta). It is a member of the G20 and Mercosur. India's KABIL signed agreements for lithium exploration in Catamarca province.

Botswana: Landlocked southern African country and one of the world's leading diamond producers by value, via Debswana (a De Beers-government joint venture) at Jwaneng and Orapa. Capital Gaborone, stable democracy, member of SADC. It has some copper-nickel mining (Selebi-Phikwe, Khoemacau copper) but its cobalt role is negligible. The Okavango Delta, a Ramsar site and UNESCO World Heritage Site, lies here.

Democratic Republic of the Congo: Central African country, capital Kinshasa, formerly Zaire, a member of SADC and the Congo Basin forest region. It supplies roughly 70-75% of world mined cobalt and is a top copper producer, with major mines at Tenke Fungurume and Kamoa-Kakula, mostly in Lualaba. Also rich in coltan, diamonds and tin. Faces conflict in the east and artisanal mining concerns.

Kazakhstan: Central Asian landlocked country, capital Astana, the world's largest uranium producer (state firm Kazatomprom, about 40% of output). It is also rich in chromite, manganese, zinc, oil (Kashagan, Tengiz) and coal. It is a member of the SCO, EAEU and CSTO. Its cobalt production is minor, and it is not a key player in battery metals compared with the DRC.
related: DRC supplies roughly 70-75% of global mined cobalt, largely as a by-product of copper.
Lithium Triangle: Argentina, Bolivia, Chile.
Australia is the largest lithium producer by mining; Chile has the largest reserves in some estimates, though Bolivia has the largest resources.
KABIL (NALCO, HCL, MECL) is India's overseas critical mineral acquisition vehicle.
India found an inferred lithium resource of 5.9 million tonnes at Reasi, J&K (2023).
India's list of critical minerals was set at 30 in 2023 and the National Critical Mineral Mission was approved in 2025.
China dominates cobalt and rare earth refining.
LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries contain no cobalt or nickel.
summary: The answer is (c) the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The DRC alone accounts for roughly 70-75% of global mined cobalt, mostly as a by-product of copper mining in the Copperbelt (Katanga region), which makes it central to electric vehicle battery supply chains.
topic_notes: Critical minerals are those essential for economic development and national security with vulnerable supply chains. Key battery minerals are lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese and graphite. Geography of supply: lithium comes from Australia (hard rock, largest producer), Chile and Argentina (brines) and China; cobalt from the DRC (about 70-75%), with Indonesia rising; nickel from Indonesia, Philippines and Russia; rare earths from China (about 60% of mining, about 85-90% of processing), plus Myanmar, USA and Australia; graphite from China; platinum and chromium from South Africa; uranium from Kazakhstan, Canada and Namibia. India's response: the National Critical Mineral Mission (approved January 2025), the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act 2023 which added critical minerals and allowed auctioning of critical mineral blocks, and a list of 30 critical minerals released in 2023. KABIL (Khanij Bidesh India Ltd), a joint venture of NALCO, HCL and MECL, acquires overseas mineral assets, for example lithium blocks in Argentina. India also joined the Minerals Security Partnership (MSP) in 2023 and discovered a lithium inferred resource of about 5.9 million tonnes at Reasi, Jammu and Kashmir, in 2023.
