Incorrect: the sloth bear raids termite mounds and tree cavities using powerful claws and by sucking up insects through its snout, not with a tool.
keyfact: Orangutans (Asian great apes of Borneo and Sumatra) make stick tools to extract insects and honey from tree holes.
option_notes: Fishing cat (Prionailurus viverrinus): a medium-sized wild cat of wetlands and mangroves in South and Southeast Asia, including the Sundarbans, Chilika and the Terai. It is a strong swimmer that preys mainly on fish. IUCN status: Vulnerable. Protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972. It is the state animal of West Bengal. Chilika Lake has a notable population.

Orangutan (genus Pongo): large arboreal great apes found only in Borneo and Sumatra. Three species: Bornean (Pongo pygmaeus), Sumatran (P. abelii) and Tapanuli (P. tapanuliensis, described in 2017). All are Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List. Threats include palm-oil driven deforestation and hunting. 'Orangutan' means 'person of the forest' in Malay. They are known for intelligence and tool making.

Otter: semi-aquatic carnivorous mammals of the family Mustelidae. India has three species: Eurasian (Lutra lutra), smooth-coated (Lutrogale perspicillata) and small-clawed (Aonyx cinereus). Sea otters (Enhydra lutris) of the North Pacific are well known for using rocks as tools to open shellfish. They are keystone species in kelp forests and indicators of clean river water. Several species are Near Threatened to Vulnerable.

Sloth bear (Melursus ursinus): an insectivorous bear native to the Indian subcontinent (India, Sri Lanka, Nepal). It has shaggy black fur, a white V or Y-shaped chest mark, long curved claws and a protrusible snout adapted to feeding on termites and ants. It carries cubs on its back. IUCN status: Vulnerable. It is in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972.
related: Orangutans are native only to Borneo and Sumatra; all three species are Critically Endangered.
The Tapanuli orangutan (Pongo tapanuliensis) was described as a new species in 2017.
The sloth bear (Melursus ursinus) is Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List and in Schedule I of the WPA 1972.
The fishing cat is the state animal of West Bengal and a Vulnerable species.
Jane Goodall's Gombe chimpanzee studies (from 1960) showed tool making in non-human animals.
New Caledonian crows make hooked tools from twigs and leaves.
Sea otters use rocks to crack open shellfish and are a keystone species of kelp forests.
Orangutans are listed in CITES Appendix I.
summary: The answer is (b) Orangutan. Orangutans are great apes that make and use tools, such as stripping and modifying sticks to extract insects (termites, ants) and honey from tree holes and logs. Fishing cats, otters and sloth bears do not fashion stick tools for this.
topic_notes: Animal tool use is a favourite 'current affairs plus biodiversity' angle. Tool use means employing an external object to achieve a goal; tool making means modifying it first. Great apes (chimpanzees, orangutans, gorillas, bonobos) show the most complex behaviour. Jane Goodall's observations at Gombe (1960) of chimpanzees 'termite fishing' with modified twigs changed the definition of humans as the only tool makers. Orangutans: found in Borneo (Indonesia and Malaysia) and Sumatra; all three species are Critically Endangered; they are the largest tree-dwelling mammals; the Tapanuli orangutan, found in North Sumatra's Batang Toru, is the rarest great ape. Other tool-using animals: New Caledonian crows (hooked twigs), Egyptian vultures (stones to crack ostrich eggs), sea otters (stones), capuchin monkeys (stones as hammers), long-tailed macaques (stone tools), dolphins in Shark Bay, Australia (sponges for foraging), and woodpecker finches of the Galapagos (cactus spines). In India: the sloth bear (Melursus ursinus), the fishing cat, otters and the Indian pangolin are insect or fish specialists and often appear in questions, so remember their habitats, IUCN status and Wild Life Protection Act schedule. Related institutions and conventions: IUCN Red List, CITES (orangutans are in Appendix I), the Convention on Migratory Species and the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972. Tip: for such questions, link each animal to its signature behaviour and conservation status.

question:
Consider the following :
1. Aerosols
2. Foam agents
3. Fire retardants
4. Lubricants In the making of how many of the above are hydrofluorocarbons used?
subject: Environment
detail: HFCs are synthetic fluorinated gases containing hydrogen, fluorine and carbon but no chlorine, so they do not deplete the ozone layer. They were introduced as substitutes for CFCs and HCFCs, which were phased out under the Montreal Protocol (1987). However, HFCs are potent greenhouse gases with high Global Warming Potential, so the Kigali Amendment (2016, in force 1 January 2019) requires their phase-down. Main uses of HFCs: refrigeration and air conditioning (the largest use, e.g., HFC-134a, R-410A), aerosol propellants (e.g., metered-dose inhalers), blowing agents for insulating foams, solvents, and fire suppression/extinguishing agents (HFC-227ea, HFC-125, HFC-23 replacing halons). Lubricants are petroleum-based or synthetic oils/greases and are not made using HFCs, although specific lubricating oils (POE oils) are used inside HFC refrigeration compressors. Elimination logic: knowing that aerosols and foam agents are standard HFC uses eliminates (a); knowing that fire suppressants replace halons eliminates (b); knowing lubricants are not HFC-based eliminates (d), leaving (c).
explanations: Wrong: it says only one, but aerosols, foam agents and fire retardants all use HFCs, so three apply.
Wrong: it says only two, but this undercounts, because fire retardants (suppressants) also use HFCs.
Correct: aerosols, foam agents and fire retardants use HFCs, while lubricants do not, so exactly three apply.
Wrong: lubricants are not made with HFCs, so not all four apply.
keyfact: HFCs are used in aerosols, foam blowing and fire suppression (and refrigeration), but not lubricants; they are ozone-safe yet high-GWP, phased down under the Kigali Amendment.
option_notes: Only one: this would imply a single HFC application. In reality, HFCs have many uses: refrigeration and air-conditioning (the largest), aerosols, foam blowing, solvents and fire suppression. They were introduced as ozone-safe replacements for CFCs and HCFCs after the Montreal Protocol (1987), which is why they are so widespread.

Only two: this would imply that HFCs are limited to two of the listed uses. HFCs are fluorinated gases with no chlorine, with ODP of zero but GWP from hundreds to thousands of times that of CO2. HFC-23 has a GWP of about 12,400 and is a by-product of HCFC-22 manufacture. The Kigali Amendment (2016) targets them.

Only three: this is the correct answer. HFCs are used in aerosols, foam agents and fire retardants (suppressants). The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol (adopted October 2016 in Rwanda, in force 1 January 2019) phases down HFCs. India is in the third group of countries, with a phase-down beginning in 2032, and could avoid up to 0.5°C of warming by 2100 globally.

All four: this would require HFCs in lubricants, which is not the case. Lubricants are made from mineral or synthetic base oils plus additives. HFCs are only the working refrigerant in systems where specialised POE lubricants are used. Remember: HFCs are refrigerants, propellants, blowing agents and extinguishants, but not lubricants.
related: Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol was adopted in 2016 and came into force on 1 January 2019.
India's HFC phase-down starts in 2032 with an 85% reduction by 2047.
HFCs have zero Ozone Depletion Potential but high Global Warming Potential.
HFC-23 is a by-product of HCFC-22 manufacture and has a GWP of about 12,400.
The Montreal Protocol (1987) was adopted under the Vienna Convention (1985).
HFOs such as HFO-1234yf are low-GWP replacements for HFC-134a.
India Cooling Action Plan (2019) aims to cut cooling demand and refrigerant use by 2037-38.
World Ozone Day is observed on 16 September.
statements: 1 — Correct: HFCs are used as aerosol propellants and solvents. Aerosols are fine suspensions or sprays, and HFC-134a and HFC-227ea are used in metered-dose inhalers, cosmetics and household sprays after CFCs were banned. HFCs are ozone-safe but have high GWP, so the Kigali Amendment targets them. Under it, developed countries began the phase-down in 2019, and India begins in 2032 with an 85% reduction by 2047.

2 — Correct: HFCs serve as blowing agents in making polyurethane and polystyrene insulation foams, replacing CFC-11 and HCFC-141b. Foam agents create the cellular structure of the foam, used in refrigerators, buildings and packaging. HFC-245fa and HFC-365mfc are common. Because of their GWP, low-GWP alternatives such as hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs) and hydrocarbons like cyclopentane are replacing them.

3 — Correct: HFCs are used as clean fire-suppression agents replacing ozone-depleting halons (halon-1211, halon-1301). HFC-227ea (FM-200) and HFC-23 are used in data centres, museums and aircraft because they leave no residue and are electrically non-conductive. They are applied in gaseous total-flooding systems. Their use is also being reduced under the Kigali Amendment.

4 — Incorrect: Lubricants are petroleum or synthetic oils and greases and are not made using HFCs. HFCs are refrigerants, propellants, blowing agents and extinguishants. Special polyolester (POE) lubricants are merely used in compressors with HFC refrigerants, but HFCs are not ingredients in making lubricants. So this item is not a use of HFCs.
summary: The answer is (c) Only three. Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) are used in aerosols (propellants), foam agents (blowing agents) and fire retardants/fire suppression (e.g., HFC-227ea, HFC-23), but not as lubricants.
topic_notes: HFCs are man-made gases (hydrogen, fluorine, carbon) developed to replace ozone-depleting substances. The ozone layer is protected by the Vienna Convention (1985) and the Montreal Protocol (1987), which phased out CFCs, halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform and then HCFCs. HFCs do not harm the ozone layer but are strong greenhouse gases, and their use has been growing quickly with demand for air conditioning. The Kigali Amendment (15 October 2016, in force 1 January 2019) commits parties to cut HFC production and consumption by more than 80% over about 30 years. Countries are in three groups: developed countries started in 2019 (85% cut by 2036); most developing countries, including China, freeze in 2024 and cut 80% by 2045; India, Pakistan, Iran, Iraq and Gulf states freeze in 2028 and cut 85% by 2047. Kigali is legally binding, and the Multilateral Fund helps developing countries. Key HFCs include HFC-134a (car air conditioning), HFC-32, R-410A, HFC-23 (by-product of HCFC-22, GWP ~12,400) and HFC-227ea (fire suppression). Replacements include HFOs (e.g., HFO-1234yf), ammonia, CO2 and hydrocarbons such as propane. India has the India Cooling Action Plan (2019) and the Kigali Amendment ratification (cabinet approval in August 2021). HFCs are included among the Kyoto Protocol's greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O, HFCs, PFCs, SF6; NF3 added later). Related terms: ODP (Ozone Depletion Potential) and GWP (Global Warming Potential). Ozone Day is 16 September. UPSC may ask about the gases covered by each treaty, the Montreal Protocol's success, and which substances are ozone-depleting versus greenhouse gases.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement-I : Interest income from the deposits in Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) distributed to their investors is exempted from tax, but the dividend is taxable. Statement-Il : InvITs are recognized as borrowers under the ‘Securitization and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002’. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-Il are correct and Statement-Il is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-Il is correct
subject: Economy
detail: An InvIT is a trust, regulated by SEBI (InvIT Regulations, 2014), that pools money from investors and invests in infrastructure assets such as roads, power transmission and pipelines. It works like a mutual fund and is structured as a sponsor, trustee, investment manager and project manager, usually with Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) holding the assets. Cash flows reach unitholders as interest, dividend, rental income, capital gains or repayment of debt. The pass-through tax treatment (Section 115UA) means the trust is generally not taxed on interest and dividend, and the investor is taxed. Interest that the trust receives from SPVs is exempt in the trust's hands and taxable in unitholders' hands, with TDS (10% for residents, 5% for non-residents). Dividend from SPVs is exempt for investors where the SPV has opted for the new concessional tax regime. So Statement-I reverses the position. Statement-II is correct: the Finance Ministry notified InvITs (and REITs) as 'financial institutions'-type borrowers/recognised entities under SARFAESI, which helps lenders recover dues from InvIT-held assets. Elimination: once Statement-I is seen as reversed, only (d) remains.
explanations: Wrong: Statement-I is incorrect, since interest is taxable and dividend is generally exempt, and so (a) cannot hold.
Wrong: Statement-I is not correct, so the both-correct option fails whatever the reasoning link.
Wrong: Statement-II is in fact correct, and Statement-I is not, so the combination is reversed.
Correct: Statement-I reverses the tax treatment, while Statement-II about the SARFAESI Act is accurate.
keyfact: InvIT interest is taxable in unitholders' hands, dividend is exempt, and InvITs are recognised as borrowers under SARFAESI.
option_notes: Option (a) would mean both are correct with a causal link. It is wrong. It is useful to know InvITs are SEBI-regulated trusts (2014 Regulations), raise funds through units, and must invest mostly in completed, revenue-generating infrastructure SPVs. They need a sponsor, trustee, investment manager and project manager. Listed InvITs include IRB InvIT, India Grid Trust and IndiGrid, and the National Highways Authority of India's own InvIT, which was launched in 2021.

Option (b) says both are correct with no explanatory link. It is wrong, because the tax statement is reversed. InvIT pass-through taxation means interest, dividend, rental and capital gains retain their character on distribution to unitholders. SEBI requires 90% of net distributable cash flows to be distributed to unitholders, at least twice a year (listed ones). Leverage limits apply: aggregate consolidated borrowings may not exceed 70% of asset value, with a credit rating above AAA needed beyond 25%.

Option (c) says Statement-I is correct and Statement-II incorrect, which is the opposite of the truth. Note the SARFAESI Act, 2002 provides for securitisation, asset reconstruction and enforcement of security interest by secured creditors. It was amended in 2016 and 2019. Recognising InvITs and REITs as borrowers under it improved lenders' confidence and the credit access of infrastructure trusts, reducing the cost of funds for projects.

Option (d) is correct. Statement-I is incorrect because interest is taxable and dividend is exempt (under the concessional-regime condition). Statement-II is correct as InvITs are recognised as borrowers under SARFAESI. The related fact is that the Finance Act 2023 also changed the taxation of repayment of debt. Distinguish InvITs from REITs, which hold real estate such as commercial offices, and from Mutual Funds, which have different tax rules.
related: InvITs are regulated by SEBI under the 2014 InvIT Regulations.
The first listed InvIT in India was IRB InvIT Fund (2017).
InvIT interest is taxable in investors' hands, and dividend from concessional-regime SPVs is exempt.
REITs hold income-generating real estate; InvITs hold infrastructure assets.
SARFAESI Act 2002 allows lenders to enforce security without court intervention.
Under SARFAESI a 60-day notice is issued under Section 13(2).
Asset Reconstruction Companies are registered with the RBI.
The National Monetisation Pipeline uses InvITs to monetise public assets.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Interest paid by SPVs to the InvIT is passed through and taxed in investors' hands, while dividend (where the SPV pays tax under the concessional regime) is exempt. The statement reverses this. Further facts: the pass-through status is under Section 115UA of the Income Tax Act. TDS on interest is 10% for resident unitholders and about 5% for non-resident unitholders. Repayment of principal debt is not taxed but reduces the cost of acquisition of units. Capital gains on sale of units are taxed as long- or short-term gains; listed units are held for 12 months for long-term treatment. Rental income applies to REITs rather than InvITs.

2 — Correct: InvITs are recognised as borrowers under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 (Finance Ministry notification, 2021-22 period). This lets lenders enforce security interest against InvIT assets. Further facts: SARFAESI allows banks and financial institutions to take possession of secured assets and auction them without court intervention for NPAs, after a 60-day notice under Section 13(2). It covers assets of 'borrowers' and was enacted in 2002, following the Narasimham Committee recommendations. Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) are registered with the RBI under it. Debt Recovery Tribunals hear appeals under Section 17. The minimum threshold is Rs 1 lakh, and agricultural land is excluded.
summary: The official answer is (d): Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct. Under the Income Tax Act, InvIT distributions are taxed according to their nature: interest income is taxable in investors' hands (with TDS), while dividend from SPVs, which have opted for the concessional regime, is exempt. InvITs are recognised as 'borrowers' under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 (by a 2021-22 notification).
topic_notes: InvITs are collective investment schemes, regulated by SEBI, that allow investors to pool funds and invest in infrastructure assets. The InvIT Regulations were notified in 2014; the first InvIT, IRB InvIT Fund, was listed in 2017. The structure includes the Sponsor, Trustee, Investment Manager and Project Manager. Assets are held directly or through SPVs. Public InvITs must raise at least Rs 500 crore initially, with a minimum public float, and the minimum subscription is Rs 1 lakh. At least 80% of the value of assets must be in completed and revenue-generating assets for the public InvIT, and 10% may go into under-construction assets. Net distributable cash flows must be distributed at least 90% to unitholders. Tax: pass-through under Section 10(23FC) and 10(23FCA); interest income is taxed in unitholders' hands with TDS, dividend is exempt if the SPV opts for the concessional regime (Section 115BAA), and capital gains rules apply on sale of units. Borrowing norms: up to 70% of assets, with higher limits needing credit ratings. SARFAESI: Act of 2002, covers enforcement of security without courts; RBI regulates ARCs; DRTs hear appeals; threshold Rs 1 lakh; excludes agricultural land. REITs, introduced in 2014 for real estate, include Embassy Office Parks (first, 2019). SM REITs were introduced in 2024. Other items UPSC could ask: NHAI InvIT, PowerGrid InvIT, the National Monetisation Pipeline (2021) which uses InvITs, the difference between InvITs and mutual funds, and differences between debt and equity in infrastructure finance.

ocr: Consider the following statements : Statement-I : ‘ In the post-pandemic recent past, many Central Banks worldwide had carried out interest rate hikes. Statement-II : Central Banks generally assume that they have the ability to counteract the rising consumer prices via monetary policy means. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-Il are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I (b) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-Il is not the correct explanation for Statement-I (c) State
subject: Economy
detail: The question tests the link between inflation and monetary policy. After pandemic-era stimulus, supply-chain disruptions and the Russia-Ukraine war (Feb 2022) pushed up food and energy prices, and inflation reached multi-decade highs in the US and Europe. The US Federal Reserve began hiking in March 2022 and took the federal funds rate above 5%. The Bank of England, the ECB and the RBI also tightened; the RBI raised the repo rate from 4% to 6.5% between May 2022 and February 2023. The underlying logic is that a higher policy rate raises borrowing costs, reduces credit and aggregate demand, and so lowers demand-pull inflation. Central banks generally assume they can do this through monetary policy, which is the premise in Statement-II. In India, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has six members and targets CPI inflation of 4% with a band of +/-2%, under the RBI Act 1934 as amended in 2016. Elimination: if Statement-I is true, (d) is out. If Statement-II is true, (c) is out. The choice between (a) and (b) rests on whether Statement-II is the reason for the hikes. It is, so (a) is correct. Caveat: monetary policy cannot fix supply-side shocks directly, but central banks still assume they can counter them.
explanations: Correct. Both statements are true, and Statement-II (the assumption that monetary policy can counter inflation) is the reason central banks hiked rates, as in Statement-I.
Wrong. Both statements are correct, but this option denies that Statement-II explains Statement-I. The assumption about monetary policy's power over prices is exactly what motivated the rate hikes.
Wrong. Statement-II is not incorrect, because central banks do assume they can counter inflation through monetary tools.
Wrong. Statement-I is not incorrect, because rate hikes by many central banks in 2022-23 are well documented.
keyfact: Post-pandemic inflation led central banks to hike rates in 2022-23, on the assumption that monetary policy can counter rising prices; answer (a).
option_notes: Both statements correct and II explains I: the standard 'assertion-reason' pattern in which the second statement is the cause or rationale for the first. Here the central bank belief in monetary control of inflation leads to rate hikes. It is the official answer.

Both correct but II is not the explanation: used when the two statements are true but unrelated causally. For example, 'India's GDP grew' and 'the RBI has six MPC members' would fit this pattern. It is not right here.
Statement-I correct, II incorrect: this would be true if central banks did not believe they could control prices. In reality, inflation targeting rests on that belief, so this option is wrong.
Statement-I incorrect, II correct: this would be true if no major central bank had raised rates. In reality, the Fed, BoE, ECB and RBI all did, so this option is wrong.
related: The RBI repo rate was raised from 4% to 6.5% between May 2022 and Feb 2023.
The MPC has six members: three from the RBI including the Governor, and three external members appointed by the government.
India's inflation target is 4% CPI with a +/-2% tolerance band, in force since 2016.
The Standing Deposit Facility rate is repo minus 0.25%; the MSF rate is repo plus 0.25%.
The US Fed's policy instrument is the federal funds rate, set by the FOMC.
The CPI base year in India is 2012; the WPI base year is 2011-12.
Stagflation means high inflation combined with stagnant growth and high unemployment.
The RBI Act 1934 was amended through the Finance Act 2016 to create the MPC.
statements: 1 — Correct: Many central banks raised interest rates in 2022-23 after the pandemic. The US Fed started in March 2022 and moved from near 0% to above 5%. The Bank of England, the ECB, the Bank of Canada, the RBI and others also tightened. The RBI repo rate went from 4% (kept since May 2020) to 6.5% by Feb 2023 in a series of hikes starting with an off-cycle hike in May 2022. Drivers were post-lockdown demand, supply disruptions and the war-driven commodity shock. Japan was the notable exception, keeping negative rates until 2024.

2 — Correct: Central banks generally assume they can counter rising consumer prices through monetary policy. The tools include the policy rate (repo), CRR, SLR, open market operations and the marginal standing facility. Inflation targeting is the framework: India adopted flexible inflation targeting in 2016, with a 4% target and a +/-2% band set by the government every five years. The MPC has six members, three from the RBI and three external, and the Governor has a casting vote. If inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must report to the government.
summary: The official answer is (a). Both statements are correct: after the COVID-19 pandemic, many central banks (the US Fed, Bank of England, ECB, RBI and others) raised policy rates sharply in 2022-23 to fight inflation. They did so because they assume monetary tools can counter rising consumer prices, so Statement-II explains Statement-I.
topic_notes: Monetary policy and inflation. Monetary policy is the use of interest rates and liquidity to manage inflation, growth and financial stability. Inflation types include demand-pull, cost-push and imported inflation. Tightening raises the policy rate, CRR or SLR, or involves selling securities through OMO, in order to cool demand. Easing does the opposite. India's tools are the repo rate (the rate at which the RBI lends to banks), the reverse repo, the Standing Deposit Facility (introduced April 2022 at repo minus 0.25%), the MSF (repo plus 0.25%), the Bank Rate, CRR and SLR. India's framework: the RBI Act 1934 was amended in 2016 to create the six-member MPC and a statutory flexible inflation targeting regime. The target is 4% CPI with a tolerance band of 2-6%, and the target was retained for 2021-26. The RBI cut the repo rate to 4% in May 2020 during COVID and held it until the May 2022 hike, which began a cycle that took it to 6.5% by Feb 2023. Global context: the US Fed raised rates from 0-0.25% to 5.25-5.50% by July 2023. Supply shocks from the Russia-Ukraine war and supply-chain disruptions limited what rate hikes alone could do. Other angles UPSC could ask: stagflation, the Phillips curve, the difference between monetary and fiscal policy, quantitative easing and tightening, the transmission of policy rates to lending rates through the External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR), and the WPI versus CPI distinction. CPI-Combined is the nominal anchor for the MPC, and the CPI base year is 2012.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement-I : Carbon markets are likely to be one of the most widespread tools in the fight against climate change.
Statement-II : Carbon markets transfer resources from the private sector to the State. , Which one of the following is correct in o are correct and Statement-II is the respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II correct explanation for Statement-I _
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
subject: Environment
detail: A carbon market lets emissions allowances or credits be traded, so that a price is put on carbon. There are two broad types. Compliance markets are created by law, such as the EU Emissions Trading System (2005), China's national ETS (2021) and India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022. Voluntary markets are driven by corporate offsetting. The Kyoto Protocol (1997) created the Clean Development Mechanism, Joint Implementation and Emissions Trading. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement (2015) now governs international cooperation: Article 6.2 covers bilateral trading of ITMOs, and Article 6.4 sets up a UN-supervised mechanism. At COP29 (Baku, 2024) the rules for Article 6 were finalised. Statement-I is correct because more and more countries are adopting carbon pricing. Statement-II is accepted as correct by the official key: where allowances are auctioned or carbon is taxed or levied, private emitters pay money to the State. But the reason carbon markets are widespread is cost-effective emission reduction through a price signal, not revenue transfer to governments. So Statement-II does not explain Statement-I. That rules out (a). Option (c) is ruled out because Statement-II is treated as correct, and (d) because Statement-I is correct.
explanations: Wrong: Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I. Carbon markets spread because they cut emissions cost-effectively, not because they transfer resources to the State.
Correct: both statements are accepted as correct, and Statement-II (revenue flowing to the State) does not explain why carbon markets are widespread. This matches the official key.
Wrong: this option treats Statement-II as incorrect, but the official answer treats it as correct.
Wrong: Statement-I is correct, since carbon markets are expanding globally as a major climate tool.
keyfact: Carbon markets are widespread because they price emissions under the polluter-pays principle; revenue transfer to the State is only a side effect, so the answer is (b).
option_notes: Option (a) says both statements are correct and that Statement-II explains Statement-I. This would need revenue transfer to the State to be the reason carbon markets are widespread. In fact their rationale is the market-based pricing of emissions under the polluter-pays principle, with cap-and-trade as the main design. The revenue is a by-product where allowances are auctioned. So this option is wrong.

Option (b) is the official answer. It says both statements are true but unconnected as cause and effect. Carbon markets include compliance schemes (EU ETS, China ETS, India's CCTS) and voluntary markets. They are tied to Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Their spread comes from cost-effective abatement, while State revenue is a separate feature of auction-based systems.

Option (c) says Statement-I is correct and Statement-II incorrect. It would be right only if carbon markets did not move resources from firms to government at all. But auctions and levies in compliance markets do, which is why UPSC treats Statement-II as correct. Many exchanges are also private to private. The option was therefore not accepted.

Option (d) says Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II correct. This is wrong because carbon pricing is clearly spreading: the EU, UK, China, Korea, Canada, several US states and now India run or are building carbon markets. The World Bank's State and Trends of Carbon Pricing reports document this growth. So Statement-I is correct.
related: Article 6 of the Paris Agreement governs international carbon markets.
The EU ETS (2005) is the world's first and largest international emissions trading scheme.
India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme comes under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022, with the Bureau of Energy Efficiency as administrator.
The CDM under the Kyoto Protocol issued Certified Emission Reductions (CERs).
The EU's CBAM taxes the carbon content of certain imports, with a transitional phase starting in October 2023.
India's PAT scheme trades Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts).
The Green Credit Programme (2023) rewards voluntary pro-environment actions and is distinct from carbon credits.
India's net-zero target is 2070.
statements: 1 — Correct: Carbon pricing and trading are expanding rapidly worldwide, so carbon markets are likely to be among the most widespread climate tools. The World Bank counts over 70 carbon pricing instruments covering roughly a quarter or more of global emissions. Major examples are the EU ETS, the UK ETS, China's ETS (the largest by emissions covered), California's cap-and-trade and Korea's ETS. India launched its Carbon Credit Trading Scheme in 2023, with the Bureau of Energy Efficiency as administrator. Article 6 of the Paris Agreement provides the international framework. Voluntary markets add corporate offsetting through standards such as Verra and Gold Standard.

2 — Correct (per the official key), but not the explanation for Statement-I: Carbon markets can move money from private emitters to the State, through auctioned allowances, fees and compliance purchases. The EU ETS, for instance, raises tens of billions of euros a year for member states, which is revenue for the State. However, this is a side effect, not the reason for their wide adoption. The core logic is the 'polluter pays' principle: a price on carbon encourages least-cost abatement. Many credits are also traded between private parties, so no transfer to the State takes place.
summary: The answer is (b). Statement-I is correct because carbon markets (cap-and-trade, offsets, Article 6 mechanisms) are fast becoming a widespread climate policy tool. Statement-II is accepted as correct by UPSC, since carbon markets can channel resources from private firms to the State, for example through auction revenue and levies, but this is not why they are widely used as a climate tool.
topic_notes:
Carbon markets put a price on greenhouse gas emissions so that reductions occur where they are cheapest. There are two main kinds. Compliance markets are mandated by law, and the main design is cap-and-trade, in which a cap is set and tradable allowances are issued. Voluntary markets let firms and individuals buy credits to offset emissions. Credits come from projects such as afforestation, renewable energy and methane capture.

Key history: the Kyoto Protocol (1997, in force 2005) set up three mechanisms, namely Emissions Trading, the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM, producing Certified Emission Reductions) and Joint Implementation. The EU ETS began in 2005 and is the oldest and biggest international scheme. The Paris Agreement's Article 6 provides for voluntary cooperation: 6.2 covers bilateral trading of Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs), 6.4 creates the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (the successor to CDM), and 6.8 covers non-market approaches.

India: the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022 empowered the Centre to set up a carbon market. The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme was notified in 2023, and the Bureau of Energy Efficiency is the administrator. India's earlier Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme, run under the National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency, traded energy saving certificates (ESCerts). India's NDC aims to cut emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030 and to reach net zero by 2070.

Related issues UPSC may ask: carbon tax versus ETS, carbon leakage, the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM, with a transitional phase from October 2023), additionality and double counting of credits, greenwashing, and the Green Credit Programme (2023) of India's environment ministry, which is separate from carbon credits.

ocr: Which one of the following activities of the Reserve Bank of India is considered to be part of ‘sterilization’? (a) Conducting ‘Open Market Operations’ (b) Oversight of settlement and payment systems (c) Debt and cash management for the Central and State Governments (ad) Regulating the functions of Non- banking Financial Institutions
subject: Economy
detail: Sterilization is a monetary policy operation in which the central bank offsets the impact of foreign exchange intervention on the domestic monetary base. When the RBI buys dollars to stop the rupee from appreciating, it releases rupees into the banking system and raises liquidity and inflationary pressure. To neutralise this, the RBI sells government securities through Open Market Operations, which absorbs the surplus rupees. Other sterilization tools are the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS), introduced in 2004, under which the government issues special securities and the proceeds are held in a separate account with the RBI, and changes in the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR). The reverse is also possible: when the RBI sells dollars and drains rupee liquidity, it can buy securities through OMO purchases to inject liquidity. Elimination logic: payment system oversight (Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007), debt management for Centre and States (the RBI acts as their debt manager and banker under Sections 20 and 21 of the RBI Act, 1934) and regulation of NBFCs (Chapter III-B of the RBI Act) are all RBI functions, but none of them adjusts liquidity to offset forex flows. Hence only (a) fits sterilization.
explanations: Right: OMOs (sale or purchase of government securities) are a core sterilization tool because they absorb or inject rupee liquidity to offset forex market operations.

Wrong: Oversight of payment and settlement systems is a regulatory and developmental function under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. It has no link to managing money supply after forex intervention.
Wrong: Debt and cash management for the Centre and States is the RBI's role as the government's banker and debt manager. It is not meant to neutralise forex-driven liquidity changes.
Wrong: Regulating NBFCs is prudential regulation and supervision under the RBI Act, 1934. It is not a monetary liquidity-neutralising operation.
keyfact: Sterilization = RBI neutralising forex-driven liquidity changes, mainly via OMOs, MSS and CRR.
option_notes: Open Market Operations are the outright purchase or sale of government securities by the RBI in the open market to regulate liquidity. Sales absorb liquidity and purchases inject it. They are a quantitative tool of monetary policy, along with CRR and SLR. Since the introduction of the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) in 2000, OMOs have been used for durable liquidity management. The RBI also uses them for forex-related sterilization and for yield management. Special operations such as Operation Twist, which simultaneously buys long-term and sells short-term securities, were conducted in 2019-20.

The RBI oversees payment and settlement systems under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, through the Board for Regulation and Supervision of Payment and Settlement Systems (BPSS). Examples are RTGS, NEFT, UPI (run by NPCI, which was set up in 2008) and cheque truncation. The RBI authorises operators and sets standards. The aim is a safe, efficient and accessible payment ecosystem. It is a regulatory function, not a monetary policy operation.

Under Sections 20 and 21 of the RBI Act, 1934, the RBI conducts the government's banking business, and under Section 21A it can do so for the States by agreement. It manages the public debt by issuing government securities, auctions T-bills and dated securities, and provides Ways and Means Advances (WMA) and overdraft facilities to meet temporary cash mismatches. The Internal Debt Management Department, which was formerly a part of the RBI, is now handled by the Public Debt Office within the RBI. A separate Public Debt Management Agency has been proposed in the past but not yet established.

NBFCs are regulated by the RBI under Chapter III-B of the RBI Act, 1934. They must register and hold a Certificate of Registration, and the RBI issues prudential norms on capital, asset classification and provisioning. A scale-based regulatory framework has been in place since October 2022, with Upper, Upper, Middle and Base layers. NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits and are not part of the payment and settlement system as bank-like entities. Housing finance companies were moved under RBI regulation in 2019 from the National Housing Bank.
related: OMO sale of securities absorbs liquidity; OMO purchase injects liquidity.
The Market Stabilisation Scheme was introduced in 2004.
The Standing Deposit Facility (2022) is the floor of the LAF corridor; the MSF rate is the ceiling.
The MPC has six members and the inflation target is 4% with a +/-2% tolerance band.
The Payment and Settlement Systems Act was enacted in 2007.
NBFCs are regulated under Chapter III-B of the RBI Act, 1934.
Unsterilized intervention changes the monetary base; sterilized intervention does not.
The RBI was established in 1935 and nationalised in 1949.
summary: The answer is (a). Sterilization is the RBI's action to neutralise the effect of foreign exchange inflows or outflows on domestic money supply, and Open Market Operations (OMOs) are one of its main tools. The other options are regulatory, payment-system or debt-management functions, not liquidity-neutralising operations.
topic_notes:
Sterilization is a central bank's countermeasure to the domestic liquidity effects of forex market intervention. In a country receiving heavy capital inflows, the RBI buys foreign currency to prevent excessive rupee appreciation. This injects rupees, which can fuel inflation. The RBI sterilizes by withdrawing equivalent rupee liquidity.

Main instruments: (1) Open Market Operations, in which the RBI sells G-secs; (2) the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS), launched in April 2004 following an MoU between the government and the RBI, where special T-bills and dated securities are issued and the proceeds are impounded in a separate MSS account, so interest costs are borne by the government; (3) CRR hikes, which lock up bank deposits with the RBI; and (4) LAF operations, such as reverse repo, for short-term absorption.

Related concepts: the Impossible Trinity (a free capital account, fixed exchange rate and independent monetary policy cannot coexist); the monetary base, or reserve money; forex reserves, whose build-up creates net foreign assets on the RBI balance sheet; and unsterilized intervention, which leaves the monetary base to change freely.

Other RBI liquidity tools: Repo, Reverse Repo, Standing Deposit Facility (SDF, introduced April 2022, which is collateral-free and now sets the floor of the LAF corridor), Marginal Standing Facility (MSF, the ceiling), Variable Rate Repo/Reverse Repo auctions, and the Bank Rate. The Monetary Policy Committee (six members, set up in 2016 under the amended RBI Act) sets the repo rate with a 4% inflation target and a band of +/-2%.

UPSC could next ask about the difference between sterilized and unsterilized intervention, the role of MSS, the functions of the RBI as banker, regulator and issuer of currency, or the effect of OMOs on interest rates and yields.

question:
Consider the following markets :
1. Government Bond Market
2. Call Money Market
3. Treasury Bill Market
4. Stock Market How many of the above are included in capital markets?
subject: Economy
detail: Financial markets are split into the money market and the capital market on the basis of the maturity of the instruments. The money market handles short-term funds, up to one year, and provides liquidity. Its segments include call/notice/term money, Treasury Bills (91, 182 and 364 days), commercial paper, certificates of deposit, repos and collateralised borrowing and lending obligations (CBLO, now TREPS). The capital market handles long-term funds, with maturity above one year or no maturity at all, as with equity. It has the equity (stock) market, with primary and secondary segments, and the debt market, which includes corporate bonds and government securities (G-secs, dated securities with maturities from 5 to 40 years). The RBI regulates the money market and G-sec market, while SEBI regulates the stock market and corporate securities. Elimination logic: Treasury Bills are short-term, so statement 3 is out. Call money is overnight to 14 days, so statement 2 is out. Government bonds are long-term, so statement 1 is in. The stock market is in, so statement 4 is in. That gives exactly two items, which is option (b). Students often wrongly lump all government paper together, but T-bills are money market and dated G-secs are capital market.
explanations: Incorrect: Only one would count just one of the two long-term items, but both the government bond market and the stock market are capital market segments.
Correct: The Government Bond Market and the Stock Market are the two capital market items. The Call Money and Treasury Bill markets are short-term money market segments.
Incorrect: Three would require counting either call money or T-bills as capital market, but both have maturities of one year or less.
Incorrect: All four would require treating call money and T-bills as capital market, but they are money market instruments by maturity.
keyfact: Capital market = long-term (above 1 year): stocks and bonds incl. dated G-secs; money market = call money, T-bills, CP, CD (up to 1 year).
option_notes: Only one: this would be right if just one item were a long-term market. Such a count is typical of questions in which only the stock market is treated as the capital market. In fact, long-term government securities also form the debt part of the capital market, so this option undercounts. Remember that the capital market has equity and debt segments, while the money market is for instruments with maturity of one year or less.

Only two: this is the correct option. The capital market consists of long-term instruments, here dated government bonds and equity shares in the stock market. The other two items, call money and T-bills, are money market instruments. The capital market is regulated chiefly by SEBI, while the G-sec market is overseen by the RBI.

Only three: this would wrongly add either call money or Treasury Bills. Both are money market instruments. T-bills are the confusing one because they are government securities, but their maturity is only 91, 182 or 364 days. The money market's total outstanding instruments also include commercial paper, certificates of deposit and repos, all short-term.

All four: this would treat the whole financial market as capital market. The call money market, with overnight to 14-day loans between banks, and T-bills, with maturities up to 364 days, are money market segments. The money market is where the RBI conducts liquidity operations such as repo, reverse repo and the standing deposit facility.
related: Money market: maturity up to one year; capital market: more than one year.
T-bills are issued in 91, 182 and 364 days and are zero-coupon, sold at a discount.
Dated G-secs have maturities of 5 to 40 years in India.
SEBI was established in 1988 and given statutory powers in 1992.
Call money covers overnight lending; notice money covers 2 to 14 days.
The RBI Retail Direct platform opened in November 2021 for retail investors in G-secs.
The NSE began trading in 1994; the BSE was founded in 1875.
The commercial paper market is a money market segment with a maturity of 7 days to 1 year.
statements: 1 — Correct: Government bonds (dated G-secs) are long-term debt, so they belong to the capital market. Dated securities are issued by the RBI on behalf of the Centre and states, with maturities from 5 to 40 years and a fixed or floating coupon. Central government securities are issued through auctions and traded on the NDS-OM platform. State Development Loans are the state equivalent. Retail investors can buy through the RBI Retail Direct portal, launched in November 2021. Holders include banks (which hold them to meet the SLR), insurers and provident funds.

2 — Incorrect: The call money market is a money market segment for overnight to 14-day inter-bank borrowing and lending. Call money is for one day, notice money for 2 to 14 days, and term money for over 14 days up to a year. Participants are mainly scheduled commercial banks and primary dealers, and it is used to manage CRR and liquidity. The interest rate is the call rate, which is the operating target of monetary policy, linked to the repo rate and the weighted average call rate (WACR). The market is regulated by the RBI.

3 — Incorrect: Treasury Bills are zero-coupon short-term government securities issued at a discount and redeemed at par, with maturities of 91, 182 and 364 days. They are issued by the RBI for the Government of India through auctions and are the safest short-term instruments. States do not issue them, but Cash Management Bills are issued for even shorter periods. They are a core money market instrument and fall under the RBI's regulation. Their yields indicate short-term interest rates in the economy.

4 — Correct: The stock market trades equity shares, so it is a capital market segment. It has a primary market (IPOs, FPOs, rights issues) and a secondary market (the BSE, founded in 1875 and Asia's oldest exchange, and the NSE, set up in 1992 and operating electronically from 1994). It is regulated by SEBI, which was set up in 1988 and given statutory status by the SEBI Act, 1992. Equity has no fixed maturity, which makes it a long-term source of funds. Benchmark indices are the Sensex and the Nifty 50.
summary: The answer is (b) Only two. Capital markets deal with long-term funds (maturity above one year): the Government Bond Market (government securities) and the Stock Market. The Call Money Market and Treasury Bill Market are money market segments dealing in short-term funds.
topic_notes: Financial markets are classified into the money market and the capital market. The money market deals with instruments of up to one year, provides liquidity and is mainly dominated by banks, primary dealers, mutual funds and the RBI. Its instruments include call/notice/term money, Treasury Bills (91, 182, 364 days), Cash Management Bills, commercial paper (minimum 7 days up to 1 year), certificates of deposit, repos and TREPS. The RBI is the chief regulator. The capital market deals with long-term funds. The equity segment has the primary market (IPO, FPO, rights, QIP) and the secondary market (BSE, NSE and others). The debt segment has government securities (dated G-secs, SDLs) and corporate bonds and debentures. SEBI regulates it. The central bank manages the G-sec market. Other angles to remember: the call rate is the rate in the call money market, and the operating target of monetary policy is the WACR. Liquidity adjustment facility rates are the repo rate (policy), the standing deposit facility rate (floor) and the MSF rate (ceiling). Mutual funds, FPIs, FDI and depositories (NSDL, CDSL) come under the capital market. The corporate bond market is smaller in India than the G-sec market. Instruments like participatory notes, ADRs and GDRs are routes for foreign capital. Also recall the difference between primary and secondary markets, the Sensex (30 stocks) and the Nifty 50, and SEBI's role in insider trading and investor protection. The Retail Direct scheme allows retail participation in G-secs, and the Indian bond market got a boost from inclusion in global bond indices (JP Morgan GBI-EM from June 2024).

question: Which one of the following best describes the concept of ‘Small Farmer Large Field’? Resettlement of a large number
options: of people, uprooted from their countries due to war, by giving them a large cultivable land which they cultivate collectively and share the produce Many marginal farmers in an area
organize themselves into groups and synchronize and harmonize selected agricultural operations Many marginal farmers in an area

together. make a contract with a corporate body and surrender their land to the corporate body for a fixed term for which the corporate body makes a payment of agreed amount to the farmers A company extends loans, technical
knowledge and material inputs to a number of small farmers in an area so that they produce the agricultural commodity required by the company for its manufacturing process and commercial production
subject: Economy
detail: Small Farmer Large Field is an approach to the problem of fragmented landholdings in India, where over 85 percent of holdings are small and marginal (below 2 hectares). It was promoted by the Food and Agriculture Organization and similar bodies, and was tried in places such as Kerala, Cambodia and parts of Africa. Farmers keep ownership and decision rights over their plots, but they coordinate sowing time, crop choice, input purchase, irrigation, plant protection, harvesting and marketing. This yields economies of scale, better bargaining power, lower costs and easier mechanisation, much like a large farm. It is related to Farmer Producer Organisations, cluster farming and group farming such as Kerala's Kudumbashree collectives. Elimination logic: option (a) describes a collective or cooperative settlement of refugees, which is a resettlement scheme and not a farming-organisation concept. Option (c) describes corporate or lease farming, in which land is surrendered, and this contradicts the idea of small farmers retaining their fields. Option (d) describes contract farming, in which a company supplies inputs and buys the produce. Only (b) matches the idea of coordination without loss of ownership.
explanations: Wrong: this describes a collective farm or refugee resettlement colony with shared produce, not a coordination model among existing small farmers.
Correct: SFLF means many marginal farmers form groups and synchronise and harmonise selected operations, which creates scale while ownership remains with each farmer.
Wrong: this describes corporate or lease farming, in which land is surrendered for a fixed payment. SFLF involves no surrender of land.
Wrong: this describes contract farming or outgrower schemes, in which a company provides inputs and credit and buys the produce for its own processing. It is not SFLF.
keyfact: Small Farmer Large Field = small farmers keep their land but synchronise and harmonise operations in groups to achieve scale.
option_notes: Collective farming and refugee resettlement: land is allotted to displaced people who cultivate it jointly and share the produce. Examples include the kolkhoz in the Soviet Union and the kibbutz in Israel. It involves pooled ownership or tenure and shared output. It is not a standard Indian farm policy model, and Indian land reform generally favoured individual holdings and cooperatives.

Group coordination of farming operations: this is the SFLF concept. Farmers in a contiguous area align crop calendars, share machinery, buy inputs in bulk and market jointly while keeping individual land titles. It tackles fragmentation of holdings and raises productivity and incomes. It is similar to cluster farming and collective action through FPOs, and it is promoted by the FAO.

Corporate or lease farming: farmers hand their land to a company for a fixed term and receive an agreed payment or rent, so the company runs cultivation. Concerns include loss of control, tenancy risk and displacement of farm labour. India's model tenancy laws, such as the NITI Aayog Model Land Leasing Act 2016, regulate such leasing to protect owners' rights.

Contract farming: a company supplies credit, technology and inputs to farmers and buys the specified produce at pre-agreed terms, as with PepsiCo's potato and Amul-style arrangements. Farmers keep their land. The Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement on Price Assurance and Farm Services Act 2020 was passed to regulate it, and the farm laws were repealed in 2021.
related: Over 85 percent of Indian operational holdings are small and marginal (below 2 hectares).
The scheme for 10,000 FPOs was launched in 2020 with NABARD, SFAC and NCDC as implementing agencies.
Model Land Leasing Act 2016 was proposed by NITI Aayog to legalise tenancy and protect owners.
Contract farming law: the 2020 Act on Price Assurance and Farm Services was repealed in 2021.
Kerala's Kudumbashree runs group farming through joint liability groups of women.
Land consolidation merges fragmented plots, as in Punjab and Haryana.
Custom Hiring Centres let small farmers rent machinery under the SMAM scheme.
Agriculture Census 2015-16 gave the average Indian holding as about 1.08 hectares.
summary: The answer is (b). 'Small Farmer Large Field' (SFLF) is a model in which many marginal and small farmers in an area organize into groups and synchronize and harmonize selected agricultural operations, so they gain the benefits of scale without giving up land ownership.
topic_notes: Indian agriculture is dominated by small and marginal farmers. Holdings below 2 hectares make up over 85 percent of the total and operate on roughly 47 percent of the area, according to the Agriculture Census 2015-16, where the average holding was about 1.08 hectares. Fragmentation raises costs, blocks mechanisation, and weakens bargaining power and access to credit and markets. Several models try to solve this. Cooperatives such as Amul pool marketing and processing. Farmer Producer Organisations, promoted through NABARD, SFAC and the 10,000 FPO scheme launched in 2020, aggregate farmers as companies or cooperatives. Contract farming links farmers to buyers under agreements. Corporate or lease farming transfers land use. Collective or group farming is promoted in Kerala through Kudumbashree. Land consolidation, as in Punjab and Haryana, merges scattered plots. SFLF stands apart because it keeps ownership individual but synchronises operations such as the crop calendar, water use, machinery sharing, pest management and sales, giving the benefits of a large farm. Related policy items include Custom Hiring Centres under the Sub-Mission on Agricultural Mechanization, the Model Land Leasing Act 2016, the Agri-Infrastructure Fund, PM-KISAN and the target of doubling farmers' incomes. UPSC may ask about the definitions and differences among contract farming, FPOs, cooperative farming and land leasing, or about the agencies promoting them.

ocr: Consider the following statements : 1. The Government of India provides Minimum Support Price for niger (Guizotia abyssinica) seeds. Niger is cultivated as a Kharif crop. Some tribal people in India use niger seed oil for cooking. ~ How many of the above statements are correct? Only one (a) Only two (b) (c) All three None (a) [ P.T.O.
subject: Economy
detail: Niger (Guizotia abyssinica), also called ramtil or jagni, is a minor oilseed of the Asteraceae (sunflower) family, native to the Ethiopian highlands. In India it is grown on poor, marginal, rainfed and hilly soils, largely by tribal farmers in Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Assam. It is sown in the monsoon (June-August) and harvested in Oct-Dec, so it is a Kharif crop, though it is also grown in some places as a late-season or Rabi/summer crop. Its seed contains about 35-40% oil, which is edible and used for cooking by tribal households, and is also used for lighting, soap and paints; the cake is cattle feed. The seed is also exported as bird feed. The CACP recommends MSP for 22 mandated crops, which include niger seed among the oilseeds (groundnut, soybean, sunflower, sesamum, niger, safflower, rapeseed-mustard, toria, copra). Elimination logic: once a student knows that niger is on the MSP list, or knows its Kharif season and tribal edible use, the remaining statements can be tested and all three are found correct, leaving (c).
explanations: (a) Only one is wrong because none of the three statements is incorrect, so more than one holds.
(b) Only two is wrong because the third statement is also correct; all of MSP, Kharif cultivation and tribal cooking use are factual.
(c) All three is correct: niger gets an MSP, is a Kharif crop and its oil is used for cooking by tribal communities. This matches the official answer.
(d) None is wrong because every statement is accurate, so at least one, in fact all three, are correct.
keyfact: Niger (Guizotia abyssinica, ramtil) is a Kharif tribal oilseed with MSP and edible oil, so all three statements are correct.
option_notes: Only one: this would be the answer if just a single statement were true. It is the typical trap for a student who knows only that niger is a Kharif crop. The question tests whether you know three distinct facets of niger: policy (MSP), agronomy (season) and ethnobotany (tribal cooking). Here it is not correct because all three are true. In UPSC statement-count questions, always verify each statement independently.

Only two: this would apply if one of the three statements were false. A student who doubts MSP for minor oilseeds or the culinary use of niger oil may choose it. It is wrong here because niger is indeed on the MSP list, and tribal groups use the oil for cooking. Always remember that minor millets and minor oilseeds such as niger do get MSP.

All three: the correct option. Niger (Guizotia abyssinica), also called ramtil, is an oilseed of the family Asteraceae from Ethiopia. It is a Kharif crop of tribal rainfed areas, included in MSP announcements, and its oil is edible. Remember it as a minor oilseed that is a livelihood crop of the tribal population in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Madhya Pradesh.

None: this would mean all three statements were false. It is a trap for students unfamiliar with niger. It is wrong because each statement is factually supported. In UPSC, 'none' is used rarely, but occasionally when all statements are flipped, for example by saying Rabi or by saying no MSP exists for the crop.
related: MSP is announced for 22 mandated crops on the recommendation of CACP.
CACP was established in January 1965 and is an attached office of the Ministry of Agriculture.
Niger is also called ramtil, jagni or Ethiopian mustard in some places, a minor oilseed of Asteraceae.
India's top niger producers are Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Maharashtra.
Ethiopia is the origin and the largest producer of niger.
The Technology Mission on Oilseeds was launched in 1986; the Yellow Revolution relates to oilseeds.
NMEO-Oilseeds was approved in 2024 for 2024-25 to 2030-31 to cut edible oil imports.
MSP for sugarcane is called Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP).
statements: 1 — Correct: Niger seed is among the oilseeds for which the Centre announces MSP on CACP advice. Facts: MSP is announced for 22 mandated crops (7 cereals, 5 pulses, 7 oilseeds plus copra... in practice 14 Kharif crops and 6 Rabi crops plus jute, copra and sugarcane FRP). Kharif MSP includes niger seed, groundnut, soybean, sunflower, sesamum. The MSP is recommended by the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP, set up 1965) and approved by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs. It is based on the A2+FL cost with at least 50% margin over it.

2 — Correct: Niger is cultivated in the Kharif season. Facts: it is sown from June to August with the monsoon and harvested from October to December. It tolerates poor, shallow, waterlogged or hilly soils and needs little input, so it suits tribal and rainfed areas. Major producing states are Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Maharashtra and Karnataka. Ethiopia is the centre of origin and the largest producer, and India is the second largest producer. Its yellow flowers appear in Oct-Nov.

3 — Correct: Some tribal communities in India use niger seed oil as a cooking medium. Facts: the seed has about 30-40% oil that is pale yellow, nutty and rich in linoleic acid. In tribal belts of Odisha (Koraput, Kalahandi), Chhattisgarh's Bastar and Jharkhand, it is a traditional cooking oil, and it is also used as a lamp fuel and in cosmetics and paints. The residual cake is cattle feed. Niger seed is also exported as bird feed (thistle seed). It has been promoted under the National Mission on Oilseeds and Oil Palm.
summary: The answer is (c) All three. Niger (Guizotia abyssinica) is a Kharif oilseed grown mainly by tribal farmers in rainfed, marginal lands, its seed oil is used for cooking by some tribal communities, and the Government of India announces an MSP for it every year.
topic_notes: Niger (Guizotia abyssinica) is an annual herb of the family Asteraceae that originates in the Ethiopian highlands. India is the second largest producer after Ethiopia, and the crop is grown on about 1-2 lakh hectares in Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Assam. It is a rainfed, low-input crop suited to hilly, marginal and poor soils; it is sown in June-August and harvested in Oct-Dec. Seeds contain 30-40% oil that is rich in linoleic acid; the oil is used for cooking among tribal groups, for lighting, soap, paints and cosmetics, and the cake is cattle feed. Seeds are exported as bird feed. MSP is announced yearly by the Centre on the recommendation of CACP for 22 mandated crops, covering cereals (paddy, wheat, maize, jowar, bajra, ragi, barley), pulses (gram, tur, moong, urad, lentil), oilseeds (groundnut, rapeseed-mustard, toria, soybean, sunflower, sesamum, safflower, niger), and commercial crops (cotton, jute, copra), while sugarcane has a Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP). CACP was set up in 1965 and is a statutory-like advisory body with no constitutional status. Other angles: the National Mission on Edible Oils (NMEO-Oilseeds, 2024-25 to 2030-31) and NMEO-Oil Palm (2021), India's dependence on imported edible oils (about 55-60% of demand), the Yellow Revolution (oilseeds), the Technology Mission on Oilseeds (1986), India's major oilseeds, and the distinction between Kharif (soybean, groundnut, sesamum, niger) and Rabi (mustard, linseed, safflower) oilseeds. Also note the Millets Year 2023 and the Minor Forest Produce MSP scheme, which can be linked with tribal livelihood.

ocr: Consider the investments in the following assets : 1. Brand recognition 2. Inventory 3. Intellectual property 4. Mailing list of clients How many of the above are considered intangible investments? (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) Only three (ad) All four
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Investments or assets are classed as tangible (physical substance) or intangible (no physical substance, but a source of future economic benefit). Tangible assets include land, buildings, machinery and inventory (raw materials, work-in-progress, finished goods). Intangible assets include patents, copyrights, trademarks, brand value, goodwill, software, databases, customer lists, R&D knowledge and organisational capital. In national accounts (SNA 2008) and in Indian accounting (Ind AS 38), intangibles are identifiable non-monetary assets without physical substance. Economists such as Haskel and Westlake (Capitalism without Capital) argue that modern economies increasingly invest in intangibles. Inventory is also tangible, and stocks of goods are treated as working capital (a current asset) and not as a fixed asset. Elimination logic: inventory is clearly physical, so 'All four' (d) is out. Items 1, 3 and 4 are clearly non-physical, so 'Only one' (a) and 'Only two' (b) are out. Only (c) is left. Remember that the test is physical substance, not whether the item is fixed or current.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Only one would count just one intangible item, but brand recognition, intellectual property and the client mailing list all qualify.
(b) Wrong: Only two undercounts the intangibles, because three of the four items lack physical form.
(c) Right: Items 1, 3 and 4 are intangible, and item 2, inventory, is a tangible physical asset, giving three. This matches the official answer.
(d) Wrong: All four would require inventory to be intangible, but it consists of physical goods.
keyfact: Intangible assets lack physical form (brand, IP, customer lists, goodwill), whereas inventory is a tangible current asset.
option_notes: Only one: this option fits a question where a single asset lacks physical form. Here it would suit a list with one intangible such as a patent among machinery, land and stock. Intangible assets are identifiable non-monetary assets without physical substance, such as patents, copyrights, licences, software and franchises. Under Ind AS 38 they must be identifiable, controlled by the firm and expected to bring future economic benefits. They are amortised over useful life, except that goodwill is tested for impairment.

Only two: this would be correct for a list with two intangibles, such as a patent and a trademark, alongside tangible items. Intangibles can be finite-lived, like patents (20 years in India) and copyrights (generally the author's life plus 60 years), or indefinite-lived, like trademarks, which are renewable every 10 years. Goodwill arises only on acquisition, as the excess of purchase price over the fair value of net identifiable assets. Tangibles and intangibles together make up a firm's total assets.

Only three: this is the correct option here. Three of the four items (brand recognition, intellectual property and the client mailing list) are intangible, while inventory is tangible. Intangible investments include R&D, software, databases, design, branding, training and organisational capital. Countries such as the US and the UK now report intangible investment in national accounts, and in advanced economies it often exceeds tangible investment. The SNA 2008 revision treated R&D as capital formation, and India adopted this in its 2011-12 GDP series revision.

All four: this would hold only if every listed item lacked physical form. Inventory fails this test because it includes physical goods such as raw materials and finished products. Tangible assets are of two kinds: fixed assets (land, buildings, plant, vehicles), held for long-term use, and current assets (inventory, cash, receivables), held for short-term conversion. Inventory is a current asset, and its changes enter GDP as 'change in stocks' under capital formation.
related: Patent term in India is 20 years from the date of filing.
Copyright in India generally lasts for the author's life plus 60 years.
Trademarks in India are registered for 10 years and are renewable indefinitely.
Goodwill arises only on acquisition and is an intangible asset.
Inventory is a current asset, and change in stocks is part of gross capital formation.
SNA 2008 treats R&D as capital formation, and India adopted this in its 2011-12 base-year GDP series.
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act was passed in 2023.
WIPO was established in 1967 and is headquartered in Geneva.
statements: 1 — Correct: Brand recognition is an intangible investment because it has no physical form but creates customer loyalty and pricing power. Brand value is built through advertising, quality and reputation. It is recognised on the balance sheet only when acquired (for example in a takeover), and internally generated brands are generally not capitalised under Ind AS 38 or IAS 38. Interbrand and Kantar publish global brand rankings. Brand equity is closely linked to goodwill and trademarks, which are legally protected under the Trade Marks Act, 1999 in India.

2 — Incorrect: Inventory is a tangible current asset made up of physical goods held for sale or production: raw materials, work-in-progress and finished goods. It is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (Ind AS 2) using methods such as FIFO or weighted average. In GDP accounting, changes in inventories form part of gross capital formation. Inventory is a working-capital item and not a fixed asset, and it is physical, so it is not an intangible investment.

3 — Correct: Intellectual property (IP) covers patents, copyrights, trademarks, designs, geographical indications and trade secrets. It is a classic intangible asset. India's laws include the Patents Act 1970 (amended 2005 for TRIPS compliance), the Copyright Act 1957, the Trade Marks Act 1999, the Designs Act 2000 and the GI Act 1999. The WIPO (Geneva, 1967) administers global IP treaties. India's National IPR Policy was adopted in 2016, and the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks is in Mumbai. TRIPS under the WTO sets minimum standards.

4 — Correct: A mailing list of clients is a customer database, an intangible asset with commercial value for marketing and repeat sales. Customer lists and relationships are recognised as intangibles in business combinations (IFRS 3 and Ind AS 103). Their use is now regulated by data-protection law, in India the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which requires consent for processing personal data. Data and databases are increasingly counted as intangible capital in the knowledge economy.
summary: The answer is (c) Only three. Brand recognition, intellectual property and a mailing list of clients are intangible investments because they have no physical form but give lasting economic value. Inventory is a tangible current asset made up of physical goods.
topic_notes:
Assets are classified by physical form into tangible and intangible, and by use into fixed (non-current) and current. Tangible assets: land, buildings, machinery, vehicles, inventory. Intangible assets: patents, copyrights, trademarks, brand value, goodwill, software, licences, databases, customer lists, R&D know-how and human or organisational capital. Key accounting standards: IAS 38 and Ind AS 38 (Intangible Assets), Ind AS 2 (Inventories), Ind AS 103 (Business Combinations), Ind AS 16 (Property, Plant and Equipment). Internally generated brands, customer lists and goodwill are generally not capitalised, while purchased ones are. Goodwill is not amortised but is tested yearly for impairment under IFRS, though Ind AS also treats it as indefinite-life.

In national accounts, SNA 2008 recognises intellectual property products (R&D, software, databases, entertainment originals) as fixed capital formation. India's 2011-12 base-year GDP revision adopted this. Gross Capital Formation comprises Gross Fixed Capital Formation, change in stocks and valuables. Intangible-heavy firms (technology, pharma, media) rely on IP protection. The Indian IP framework includes the Patents Act 1970, Copyright Act 1957, Trade Marks Act 1999, Designs Act 2000, GI Act 1999, the PPV&FR Act 2001 and the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act 2000. The National IPR Policy was approved in 2016, and the Cell for IPR Promotion and Management (CIPAM) works on awareness. WIPO publishes the Global Innovation Index, where India ranked 40th in 2023. TRIPS is the WTO agreement setting minimum IP standards. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 governs personal data such as customer lists.

Possible next angles: GI-tagged products, patent term (20 years), copyright term (60 years after the author's death), trademark renewal (10 years), the difference between capital and revenue expenditure, and what counts as an 'investment' in the economic sense (capital formation, not financial purchase of shares).

question:
Consider the following :
1. Demographic performance
2. Forest and ecology
3. Governance reforms
4. Stable government
5. Tax and fiscal efforts For the horizontal tax devolution, the Fifteenth Finance Commission used how many of the above as criteria other than population area and income distance?
subject: Economy
detail: Horizontal devolution decides how the states' share of the divisible pool is split among the states. The Fifteenth Finance Commission (chair N.K. Singh, constituted November 2017, with its main report for 2021-26 tabled in February 2021) set the states' share at 41% of the divisible pool, down from 42% because of the creation of the Union Territories of J&K and Ladakh. Its weights were: income distance 45%, population (2011 census) 15%, area 15%, forest and ecology 10%, demographic performance 12.5%, and tax and fiscal efforts 2.5%. These add up to 100. So the criteria other than population, area and income distance are exactly three: demographic performance, forest and ecology, and tax and fiscal efforts. Elimination logic: 'Governance reforms' and 'stable government' sound plausible, but the Commission did not include them in the formula. The 14th Finance Commission used 1971 population, 2011 population, area, forest cover and income distance. Note that the 15th Commission dropped the 1971 population criterion and used 2011 population only. Hence the count is three, and option (b) is correct.
explanations: Wrong: three of the five listed items were used, not just two. Demographic performance, forest and ecology, and tax and fiscal efforts all featured in the formula.
Correct: exactly three, namely demographic performance, forest and ecology, and tax and fiscal efforts, were used beyond population, area and income distance.
Wrong: this would mean that one of governance reforms or stable government was used, but neither was a horizontal devolution criterion.
Wrong: governance reforms and stable government were not formula criteria, so not all five were used.
keyfact: 15th FC horizontal formula: income distance 45%, population 15%, area 15%, demographic performance 12.5%, forest and ecology 10%, tax effort 2.5%; no governance reforms or stable government criterion.
option_notes: Only two: this would be the case if just two extra criteria were used. The 15th Commission actually had six criteria in total: income distance 45%, population 15%, area 15%, forest and ecology 10%, demographic performance 12.5%, tax and fiscal efforts 2.5%. Three of them are the standard ones, and the extra three are the ones the question asks about. So this option undercounts.

Only three: the correct option. The extra criteria were demographic performance (12.5%), forest and ecology (10%) and tax and fiscal efforts (2.5%), which together carry 25% of the weight. The Commission was chaired by N.K. Singh, and its report for 2021-26 gave the states a 41% share of the divisible pool. It used 2011 population rather than 1971 population.

Only four: this would require one of governance reforms or stable government to be a formula criterion. Neither was. The Commission did recommend performance-based grants linked to reforms, such as in power distribution, agriculture and urban local bodies, but these were not part of the tax devolution formula. So this option overcounts.

All five: this would include both governance reforms and stable government. Stable government has never been a devolution criterion at all. Governance reforms are reflected only in incentive-based grants, not in horizontal tax devolution weights. The option is a trap for students who assume that every plausible-sounding factor was used.
related: Article 280 provides for the Finance Commission, constituted every five years.
15th Finance Commission chair: N.K. Singh; 16th Finance Commission chair: Arvind Panagariya.
15th FC gave states 41% of the divisible pool; the 14th FC gave 42%.
Income distance has the highest weight, at 45%, in the 15th FC's horizontal formula.
15th FC used the 2011 census population, whereas the 14th FC used both 1971 and 2011.
Divisible pool excludes cesses, surcharges and the cost of collection.
Article 275 deals with grants-in-aid to states; Article 243I and 243Y deal with Finance Commissions for panchayats and municipalities.
Finance Commission recommendations are advisory and are laid before Parliament with an explanatory memorandum.
statements: 1 — Correct: Demographic performance was a criterion with a 12.5% weight. It rewards states that controlled population growth. It was introduced because the Commission used 2011 population, which would otherwise penalise states that succeeded in family planning. It is measured through the reciprocal of the total fertility rate in 2011 for each state, scaled by the 1971 population.
