The key facts to remember are that Scheduled Areas are declared by Presidential order under Paragraph 6 of the Fifth Schedule, and that the unit of declaration can be a district, block, taluka or cluster of villages. Scheduled Areas exist in 10 states, and the Governor, not the Chief Minister, reports to the President.

Only two: This is the official answer. Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Scheduled Areas are declared by the President after consulting the Governor, and the units range from a district down to a cluster of villages in a block. The annual report is the Governor's duty under Paragraph 3 of the Fifth Schedule and goes to the President. The Chief Minister has no such statutory reporting role to the Home Ministry.

All three: This would require the Chief Minister reporting annually to the Home Ministry, which has no basis in the Fifth Schedule. Paragraph 3 assigns the report to the Governor, addressed to the President. The Union's executive power extends to giving directions to states on Scheduled Areas administration. Related bodies include the Tribes Advisory Council (Paragraph 4) and PESA 1996 for self-governance in Scheduled Areas.

None: This would mean no statement is correct. It is wrong because the President does declare Scheduled Areas by order, and the units of declaration range from district to a cluster of villages in a block. The Fifth Schedule applies to states other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, which come under the Sixth Schedule with Autonomous District Councils.
related: Article 244(1) = Fifth Schedule; Article 244(2) = Sixth Schedule.
Fifth Schedule does not apply to Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
Paragraph 6 of the Fifth Schedule: President declares Scheduled Areas after consulting the Governor.
Governor submits the annual report on Scheduled Areas to the President (Paragraph 3).
Tribes Advisory Council has up to 20 members, about three-fourths being Scheduled Tribe MLAs.
PESA Act 1996 was based on the Bhuria Committee recommendations.
Article 342 deals with the list of Scheduled Tribes; Article 339 with the Commission on Scheduled Areas.
Scheduled Areas are found in 10 states, with Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan among them.
statements: 1 — Correct: Under Paragraph 6(2) of the Fifth Schedule, the President specifies Scheduled Areas by order, after consulting the state Governor. Facts: The first order was the Scheduled Areas Order, 1950 (for Part A and Part B states), followed by the 1977 order for several states. The President can increase or decrease an area, alter boundaries, rescind orders and issue fresh ones. Scheduled Areas currently exist in 10 states: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Himachal Pradesh. A state cannot itself declare a Scheduled Area; the Governor is only consulted. Scheduled Areas are distinct from Scheduled Tribes lists, which are notified under Articles 342.

2 — Correct: As per the UPSC key, the administrative unit forming a Scheduled Area is generally a district at the largest and a cluster of villages in a block at the lowest. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs describes the criteria as preponderance of tribal population, compactness, a viable administrative unit such as a district, block or taluka, and economic backwardness. So Scheduled Areas may be whole districts, blocks, or village clusters. The Dhebar Commission (1960-61) and the Bhuria Committee (1991) examined tribal areas; the Bhuria Committee's recommendations led to PESA, 1996, which extends Panchayat provisions to Scheduled Areas.

3 — Incorrect: Paragraph 3 of the Fifth Schedule requires the Governor, not the Chief Minister, to report annually to the President on the administration of Scheduled Areas, and the report goes to the President, not to the Union Home Ministry. The Union's executive power extends to giving directions to the state about the administration of Scheduled Areas. Paragraph 4 sets up a Tribes Advisory Council of up to 20 members, three-fourths being tribal MLAs, to advise on Scheduled Tribes welfare. Under Paragraph 5, the Governor may direct that a Parliament or state law does not apply to Scheduled Areas or applies with modifications, and may make regulations on land transfer, allotment and money-lending.
summary: The answer is (b) Only two. Statements 1 and 2 are correct as per the UPSC key, while statement 3 is incorrect because the annual report on Scheduled Areas is submitted by the Governor to the President, not by the Chief Minister to the Home Ministry.
topic_notes: Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas are covered by Article 244. Article 244(1) applies the Fifth Schedule to Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in all states except Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Article 244(2) applies the Sixth Schedule to tribal areas in those four states. Fifth Schedule key points: Paragraph 3 requires the Governor's annual report to the President; Paragraph 4 provides the Tribes Advisory Council (maximum 20 members, about three-fourths from Scheduled Tribe MLAs); Paragraph 5 lets the Governor modify or bar application of laws; Paragraph 6 gives the President power to declare Scheduled Areas after consulting the Governor. Ten states have Scheduled Areas: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Himachal Pradesh. Criteria: preponderance of tribal population, compactness and reasonable size, a viable administrative unit, and economic backwardness. Committees: the Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes Commission (Dhebar Commission, 1960), the Bhuria Committee (1991), and the Bhuria Committee led to PESA 1996, which gives Gram Sabhas strong powers over resources, minor forest produce and land alienation in Scheduled Areas. The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises forest rights of Scheduled Tribes. Sixth Schedule: Autonomous District Councils and Regional Councils, with powers of law-making, justice and revenue; there are 10 autonomous districts in the four states (Assam 3, Meghalaya 3, Tripura 1, Mizoram 3). Ladakh was brought under demands for Sixth Schedule status. Article 342 lists Scheduled Tribes by Presidential order, and Article 339 provides for a Commission on Scheduled Areas and the welfare of Scheduled Tribes. Article 275(1) gives grants-in-aid for tribal welfare. The 5th Schedule is also linked to the Samatha judgment (1997) on tribal land transfer. Future questions may test difference between Fifth and Sixth Schedules, PESA, and FRA.

ocr: Consider the following statements : | Statement-I : fl The Supreme Court of India has held in some judgements that the = reservation policies made under Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India would be limited by Article 335 for maintenance of efficiency of administration. Statement-II : Article 335 of the Constitution of India defines the term ‘efficiency of administration’. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I (b) Both Statement-I and Statement
subject: Polity
detail: Article 16(4) lets the State make provision for reservation in appointments or posts in favour of any backward class of citizens not adequately represented in State services. Article 335 says the claims of SCs and STs shall be taken into consideration consistently with the maintenance of efficiency of administration. Courts have repeatedly read the two together. In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) the Court upheld 27% OBC reservation, excluded the creamy layer, fixed the 50% ceiling as a general rule, and barred reservation in promotions. In M. Nagaraj (2006) the Court upheld the 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments. It required the State to show quantifiable data on backwardness and inadequacy of representation, and to show that efficiency is not compromised. The 82nd Amendment (2000) added a proviso to Article 335 permitting relaxation in qualifying marks and evaluation standards for SC/ST promotions. Crucially, the Constitution never defines 'efficiency of administration'. The Court has said it must be judged in context, and that the State decides how to balance it with representation. Elimination: Statement-II is wrong, so options (a), (b) and (d) fall away, leaving (c).
explanations: Wrong. It claims both statements are correct, but Statement-II is incorrect because Article 335 contains no definition of 'efficiency of administration'.
Wrong. Statement-II is not correct, so the question of it explaining Statement-I does not arise, even though Statement-I is correct.
Correct. Statement-I reflects settled case law, and Statement-II is false because Article 335 only requires efficiency to be maintained and does not define it.
Wrong. It reverses the truth values: Statement-I is correct, while Statement-II is incorrect.
keyfact: Article 16(4) reservation is read with Article 335 (efficiency), but Article 335 does not define 'efficiency of administration'.
option_notes: Option (a) says both statements are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I. This form belongs to the assertion-reason style. Here it would imply that Article 335 gives a definition of efficiency which then limits Article 16(4). That is not so. Article 335 is a short provision in Part XVI and sets a general requirement without defining efficiency. The Courts, not the text, give the term its meaning in context. Article 335 was amended by the 82nd Amendment in 2000 to add a proviso on relaxation for SC/ST promotions.

Option (b) says both statements are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I. It is wrong here because Statement-II is false. Both statements concern reservation law. Article 16(4) deals with reservation for backward classes in State services, and Article 335 concerns the claims of SCs and STs consistent with efficiency. Indra Sawhney (1992) is the leading case on Article 16(4), and the nine-judge bench decided it. It set the 50% ceiling and the creamy layer exclusion for OBCs.

Option (c) is the correct answer. It says Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect. The Supreme Court has repeatedly balanced Article 16(4) with Article 335 in cases such as Indra Sawhney, Nagaraj and Jarnail Singh. Article 335 does not define efficiency. The 82nd Amendment (2000) added its proviso permitting relaxation of marks for SC/ST promotion. The Court has said that efficiency must be seen in context, and that the State must justify reservations with data.

Option (d) says Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct. This is the exact reverse of the truth. Statement-I reflects well-established case law. Statement-II wrongly credits Article 335 with defining efficiency. Related provisions include Article 16(1) on equality of opportunity in public employment, Article 16(4A) on promotion reservation for SC/ST, and Article 16(4B) on carry-forward of vacancies. Article 46 is the Directive Principle promoting the educational and economic interests of weaker sections.
related: Article 16(4) enables reservation in State services for backward classes inadequately represented.
Article 335 requires SC/ST claims to be considered consistently with administrative efficiency.
The 82nd Amendment (2000) added a proviso to Article 335 allowing relaxed standards for SC/ST promotion.
Indra Sawhney (1992) set the 50% ceiling and the creamy layer for OBCs.
The 77th Amendment (1995) inserted Article 16(4A) for promotion reservation.
The 81st Amendment (2000) inserted Article 16(4B) on carry-forward vacancies.
The 103rd Amendment (2019) gave 10% EWS reservation under Articles 15(6) and 16(6).
M. Nagaraj (2006) requires quantifiable data to justify promotion reservation.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Supreme Court has in several judgements, such as Indra Sawhney, Nagaraj and Jarnail Singh, held that Article 16(4) reservations must be read with Article 335 and must not undermine administrative efficiency. Article 16(4) is the enabling provision for reservation in public employment for backward classes inadequately represented in State services. Article 16(4A) covers promotions for SC/ST and 16(4B) covers carry-forward of unfilled vacancies. Article 335 requires the claims of SCs and STs to be considered consistently with efficiency. Indra Sawhney (1992) set the 50% cap and the creamy layer exclusion for OBCs. Nagaraj (2006) required quantifiable data on backwardness and inadequate representation. Jarnail Singh (2018) removed the creamy layer requirement for SC/ST promotions on data.

2 — Incorrect: Article 335 does not define 'efficiency of administration'. It only says the claims of SCs and STs to services and posts shall be taken into consideration, consistently with maintaining efficiency, in connection with the affairs of the Union or a State. It sits in Part XVI of the Constitution, which deals with special provisions relating to certain classes. The 82nd Amendment (2000) added a proviso allowing relaxation in qualifying marks or lower evaluation standards for SC/ST promotion. The Court has treated efficiency as a contextual concept. In the 2020 case Mukesh Kumar v. State of Uttarakhand, the Court held that reservation in promotion is not a fundamental right. The Constitution's text gives no definition.
summary: The answer is (c). Statement-I is correct because the Supreme Court has held in several judgements that reservation under Article 16(4) operates subject to Article 335, which requires that the maintenance of efficiency of administration be taken into account. Statement-II is incorrect because Article 335 does not define 'efficiency of administration'.
topic_notes: Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment. Clause (4) lets the State reserve posts for backward classes not adequately represented. Clause (4A), added by the 77th Amendment (1995), covers promotion for SC/ST. Clause (4B), added by the 81st Amendment (2000), allows carry-forward of unfilled vacancies, which are not counted against the 50% ceiling. The 103rd Amendment (2019) added Article 15(6) and 16(6), giving 10% reservation to economically weaker sections among those not covered by existing reservations; the Supreme Court upheld it in Janhit Abhiyan (2022) by a 3:2 majority. Article 335 requires the claims of SCs and STs to be considered consistently with maintaining efficiency of administration. The 82nd Amendment (2000) added a proviso allowing relaxation in qualifying marks and evaluation standards for promotion. Key cases: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951), which led to the First Amendment and Article 15(4); M.R. Balaji (1962), which set the 50% rule; Indra Sawhney (1992), which accepted OBC reservation, the creamy layer and the 50% cap, and rejected promotion reservation; Nagaraj (2006); Jarnail Singh (2018); and Mukesh Kumar (2020), which held that reservation in promotion is not a fundamental right. The Mandal Commission (1979, report 1980) recommended 27% OBC reservation, which was implemented in 1990. The National Commission for Backward Classes got constitutional status through the 102nd Amendment (Article 338B). Next time UPSC could ask about Articles 15, 16, 46, 335, 338, 340 and 342A, the Ninth Schedule, and Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation.

question: In which one of the following regions was Dhanyakataka, which flourished as a prominent Buddhist centre under the Mahasanghikas, located?
subject: Ancient History
detail: Dhanyakataka, also called Dhaññakata or Dharanikota, lay on the lower Krishna river in the Guntur region of ancient Andhra, close to Amaravati. It was the early capital of the Satavahanas in some traditions and a flourishing port and trade centre. After the Second Buddhist Council at Vaishali (c. 383 BCE), the Sangha split into Sthaviravadins and Mahasanghikas. The Mahasanghikas later divided into sub-sects such as the Chaitikas, Purvashailas (Pubbaseliyas) and Aparashailas (Aparaseliyas), which were centred in the Andhra country around Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda and Dhanyakataka. The Amaravati Mahachaitya (stupa) is a famous Andhra school monument built of white marble with sculpted panels. Nagarjunakonda, patronised by the Ikshvakus, was another major site. Elimination: Gandhara (Taxila, Peshawar) is associated with Sarvastivadins and Gandhara art; Kalinga is associated with Ashoka's war and Dhauli/Udayagiri; Magadha is the heartland of Rajagriha, Pataliputra and Bodh Gaya, linked to the early councils and Theravada-Sthavira tradition. So only Andhra fits Dhanyakataka.
explanations: Correct: Dhanyakataka (Dharanikota/Amaravati) lies on the Krishna river in Andhra and was a Mahasanghika centre.
Wrong: Gandhara in the north-west was known for Sarvastivada Buddhism, Kanishka's Fourth Council tradition and Greco-Buddhist art, not Dhanyakataka.
Wrong: Kalinga (Odisha) is known for Ashoka's conquest, Dhauli and Jaugada edicts, and Jain king Kharavela, not Dhanyakataka.
Wrong: Magadha was the political and early Buddhist heartland (Rajagriha, Pataliputra, Bodh Gaya) but Dhanyakataka was not there.
keyfact: Dhanyakataka (Amaravati/Dharanikota, Krishna valley) in Andhra was a Mahasanghika centre.
option_notes: Andhra: the region of the Krishna-Godavari delta and Deccan, ruled by Satavahanas and then Ikshvakus. It has Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Jaggayyapeta and Dharanikota. It was a major centre of Mahasanghika sub-schools (Chaitika, Purvashaila, Aparashaila) and of the Amaravati school of art, noted for white marble sculpture.

Gandhara: ancient region of north-west India and Pakistan (Peshawar, Taxila, Swat), a Mahajanapada. It was a centre of Sarvastivada Buddhism, the Kushana patronage under Kanishka, and Gandhara art that blended Greek and Indian styles, with Buddha images in schist.

Kalinga: ancient eastern region of coastal Odisha and north Andhra. Ashoka conquered it c. 261 BCE, and the war led to his conversion to Dhamma. It has the Dhauli and Jaugada rock edicts. King Kharavela of the Hathigumpha inscription ruled it in the 1st century BCE and favoured Jainism.

Magadha: the most powerful Mahajanapada, with capitals at Rajagriha and later Pataliputra, under the Haryankas, Shishunagas, Nandas and Mauryas. Buddha attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya there, and the First Council (Rajagriha) and Third Council (Pataliputra) were held there.
related: Mahasanghikas split from Sthaviravadins after the Second Buddhist Council at Vaishali.
Chaitika, Purvashaila and Aparashaila were Mahasanghika sub-sects in Andhra.
Amaravati stupa is in Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh, and the Amaravati school used white marble.
Nagarjunakonda was patronised by the Ikshvakus.
Sarvastivada flourished in Mathura, Kashmir and Gandhara.
Third Buddhist Council was held at Pataliputra under Ashoka.
Fourth Buddhist Council was held under Kanishka in Kashmir.
summary: The answer is (a) Andhra. Dhanyakataka (modern Amaravati/Dharanikota area on the Krishna river in Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh) was a major Mahasanghika centre, and the Mahasanghika-derived Chaitika, Purvashaila and Aparashaila schools flourished there.
topic_notes: Buddhist schools: After the Second Council at Vaishali (c. 383 BCE, under Kalasoka), a dispute over Vinaya rules split the Sangha into the orthodox Sthaviravadins (Theravada) and the liberal Mahasanghikas. The Mahasanghikas are regarded as precursors of Mahayana ideas, such as treating the Buddha as supramundane (lokottara). Their sub-sects include Ekavyavaharika, Lokottaravada, Bahusrutiya, Prajnaptivada, Chaitika, Purvashaila and Aparashaila. Southern sects were centred in Andhra, especially Dhanyakataka, Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda. The Sthaviravadins split into Sarvastivada (Mathura, Kashmir, Gandhara), Vatsiputriya, Mahishasaka, Dharmaguptaka and others. Four councils: First at Rajagriha (Ajatashatru, Mahakassapa), Second at Vaishali (Kalashoka), Third at Pataliputra (Ashoka, Moggaliputta Tissa), Fourth in Kashmir/Kundalvana (Kanishka, Vasumitra and Ashvaghosha). Andhra Buddhist sites: Amaravati stupa (Amaravati school of sculpture, Satavahana period), Nagarjunakonda (Ikshvaku, associated with Nagarjuna tradition), Salihundam, Bavikonda, Thotlakonda, Sankaram and Jaggayyapeta. Acharya Nagarjuna, who propounded Madhyamika/Shunyavada, is linked to Andhra. Dignaga and Dharmakirti were also associated with the south. Other art schools: Gandhara (Greco-Buddhist), Mathura (indigenous, red sandstone) and Amaravati (marble, narrative reliefs). Future questions could ask about Buddhist sects, councils, the Mahayana-Hinayana distinction, Buddhist caves and stupas such as Sanchi, Bharhut and Sarnath, and the Satavahana patronage of Buddhism.

question:
With reference to ancient India, consider the following statements :
1. The concept of Stupa is Buddhist in origin.
2. Stupa was generally a repository of relics.
3. Stupa was a votive and commemorative structure in Buddhist tradition. How many of the statements given above are correct? :
subject: Art & Culture
detail: A stupa is a mound-like or hemispherical structure. It began as a burial tumulus, and earthen funerary mounds (called chaityas or 'smashana' mounds in Vedic and later texts) existed before the Buddha. The Mahaparinibbana Sutta says the Buddha's relics were divided among eight claimants, who built stupas over them. Ashoka is said to have redistributed them into 84,000 stupas. Buddhism therefore did not invent the concept but made it central to its worship. Stupas hold relics (sarira) of the Buddha or monks, or objects they used, in a relic chamber (harmika/casket). They also serve as votive structures built to earn merit, and as commemorative ones marking events in the Buddha's life. Examples include Sanchi, Bharhut, Amaravati and Sarnath (Dhamekh). Elimination logic: statement 1 uses the absolute phrase 'Buddhist in origin', which is the trap. Statements 2 and 3 describe the standard function and tradition. So two are correct, which gives (b), and (c) is ruled out. Jainism and Hinduism also had stupa-like structures; Jain stupas are known from Mathura.
explanations: Wrong: 'Only one' would mean only one of the three is correct, but statements 2 and 3 are both correct.
Correct: Statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 1 is wrong because stupas, as burial mounds, existed before Buddhism.
Wrong: Statement 1 is not wholly true, since the stupa concept pre-dates Buddhism, so not all three can be correct.
Wrong: Statements 2 and 3 accurately describe Buddhist stupas, so 'none' cannot be right.
keyfact: The stupa is a pre-Buddhist burial mound form, but Buddhism made it a relic-holding, votive and commemorative monument.
option_notes: Only one: this would be the answer if just one statement held. It does not here, but it is a common trap for students who think only the relic function is valid. Remember that stupas are both relic repositories and commemorative or votive monuments.

Only two: the official answer. Statements 2 and 3 are correct and statement 1 is incorrect. This reflects the nuance that Buddhism adopted an existing funerary mound form and gave it religious and architectural elaboration, as at Sanchi, Bharhut and Amaravati, and Ashoka's 84,000 stupas spread the form.

All three: this would be right only if the stupa were originally Buddhist. Mounds for the dead are older, with Vedic references and megalithic burials, so this option is wrong. Remember that UPSC often tests absolute claims about 'origin'.

None: this would mean no statement is correct. That is wrong because relic enshrining and the votive and commemorative role are both standard features of Buddhist stupas, as in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta and Ashokan tradition.
related: Sanchi Stupa (Madhya Pradesh) was founded by Ashoka and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1989.
The Buddha's relics were divided into eight parts after his death at Kushinagar.
Ashoka is said to have built 84,000 stupas.
The Dhamekh stupa stands at Sarnath, where the Buddha gave his first sermon.
Amaravati stupa in Andhra Pradesh is associated with Satavahana patronage and rich sculpture.
The harmika is the square railing on the top of the dome, and the chhatra is the umbrella on its mast.
Chaityas are prayer halls with a stupa, while viharas are monastic residences.
Jain stupas have been found at Kankali Tila, Mathura.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The stupa was not originally Buddhist; burial mounds pre-date the Buddha and were adopted by Buddhism. Pre-Buddhist India had funerary mounds for chiefs and sages, mentioned in Vedic and later literature (smashana, 'chaitya'). The Buddha is said to have told Ananda that a stupa should be raised for a Chakravartin ruler, which suggests an existing royal practice. Buddhism gave the form religious meaning and spread it across Asia, producing pagodas in East Asia and chortens in Tibet. Jains also built stupas, as at Mathura (Kankali Tila). So 'Buddhist in origin' is wrong, though Buddhism is the tradition most associated with stupas.

2 — Correct: Stupas generally enshrined relics (sarira) of the Buddha, his disciples or revered monks. After the Buddha's death at Kushinagar (c. 483 BCE per the traditional view), his ashes were divided among eight claimants, including the Mallas, Shakyas and Magadha's Ajatashatru, and eight stupas were built. Ashoka is said to have opened them and distributed relics into 84,000 stupas. Relics were placed in caskets in a chamber within the dome (anda). Relic caskets were found at Piprahwa and Bhattiprolu, and Sanchi's Stupa 2 and 3 held relics of Sariputta and Mahamogallana. Some stupas held only objects the person had used, or sacred texts.

3 — Correct: In the Buddhist tradition stupas were commemorative, marking the Buddha's life events and holy places, and votive, built or donated to earn merit. Commemorative stupas mark the four great events at Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar. Votive stupas, often small, were offered by donors, and inscriptions at Bharhut, Sanchi and Amaravati record gifts from kings, merchants, monks and nuns. Features include the anda (dome), harmika, chhatra (umbrella), vedika (railing), torana (gateway) and pradakshina-patha (circumambulation path). Worshippers circle it clockwise, and the Great Stupa at Sanchi is a UNESCO site from 1989.
summary: The answer is (b) Only two: statements 2 and 3 are correct, while statement 1 is incorrect. The stupa as a funerary burial mound predates Buddhism and existed in the Vedic and pre-Buddhist tradition, though Buddhism adopted and popularised it as a relic shrine and commemorative monument.
topic_notes: A stupa (Pali: thupa) is a solid, dome-shaped monument, usually containing relics. Its early form was the burial mound, and Buddhism made it the central object of worship. Eight original stupas were raised over the Buddha's relics. Ashoka (c. 268-232 BCE) is credited with spreading relics into 84,000 stupas, and the Ashokan core of Sanchi (Madhya Pradesh) dates from his time. Later stupas were enlarged under the Shungas, who added stone railings and gateways under the Satavahanas. Parts of a stupa are the anda (hemispherical dome), harmika (square railing on top), yasti (mast), chhatra (umbrella), medhi (drum or base), vedika (railing), torana (gateway) and pradakshina-patha. Major sites are Sanchi, Bharhut (Shunga period, now in Satna district), Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda (Andhra, Satavahana and Ikshvaku), Sarnath (Dhamekh), Piprahwa (Uttar Pradesh, possibly ancient Kapilavastu), Kesaria and Taxila's Dharmarajika. Stupas are classified as saririka (containing bodily relics), paribhogika (objects used by the Buddha), uddesika (commemorative) and votive. Chaitya halls are rock-cut halls of worship with a stupa at the end, such as Karla and Ajanta. Viharas are monasteries. Outside India, stupa forms developed into the pagoda (China and Japan), the chorten (Tibet) and Borobudur (Java) and Sri Lanka's dagoba. Jain stupas appear at Mathura. UPSC could ask next about stupa parts, sites, Buddhist councils and Ashokan edicts.

ocr: With reference to ancient South India, Korkai, Poompuhar and Muchiri were well known as (a) capital cities (b) ports (c) centres of iron-and-steel making (ad) shrines of Jain Tirthankaras [ P.T.O.
subject: Ancient History
detail: The question tests Sangam-age (c. 300 BCE-300 CE) geography and the maritime economy of early Tamilakam. Korkai on the Tamraparni river mouth was the Pandyan port famous for pearl fisheries. Poompuhar (Puhar, Kaveripattinam) was the Chola port at the Kaveri delta, described in Silappadikaram and Pattinappalai, with excavated wharves and warehouses. Muchiri (Muziris, near Kodungallur/Pattanam in Kerala) was the Chera port, a hub of the pepper-for-gold trade with Rome; the Peutinger Table and Periplus of the Erythraean Sea mention it, and the Muziris papyrus records cargo shipments. Elimination logic: the three capitals of the Sangam kingdoms were Madurai (Pandya), Uraiyur (Chola) and Vanji (Chera), so (a) fails. Iron-and-steel centres in the south are associated with Kodumanal, Adichanallur and Telangana's megalithic sites, not these three, so (c) fails. Jain Tirthankara shrines such as Shravanabelagola are in Karnataka, so (d) fails. The coastal, river-mouth locations of all three names point to ports.
explanations: Incorrect: the Sangam capitals were Madurai (Pandya), Uraiyur (Chola) and Vanji/Karur (Chera). Korkai, Poompuhar and Muchiri were primarily ports, though Poompuhar was sometimes a secondary Chola seat.
Correct: all three were major seaports. Korkai was a Pandya pearl port, Poompuhar a Chola emporium and Muchiri a Chera pepper port trading with Rome.
Incorrect: iron-and-steel making is linked to sites such as Kodumanal, Adichanallur, Mayiladumparai and Telangana's megalithic zones, not to these ports.
Incorrect: they were not Jain pilgrimage centres. Jain Tirthankara shrines are associated with places like Shravanabelagola, Madurai hills and Sittanavasal, and the three names are known for trade.
keyfact: Korkai (Pandya), Poompuhar (Chola) and Muchiri/Muziris (Chera) were Sangam-age ports, not capitals.
option_notes: Capital cities: the three Sangam kingdoms had capitals at Madurai (Pandya, with the Tamil Sangams), Uraiyur near Tiruchirappalli (Chola) and Vanji/Karur (Chera). Pandya ports were Korkai and Saliyur, Chola ports Puhar, Chera ports Muziris and Tondi. Kings such as Karikala (Chola), Nedunjeliyan (Pandya) and Senguttuvan (Chera) ruled from these centres. Capitals were political and administrative centres, unlike the ports named here.

Ports: ancient South Indian ports included Korkai (pearls, Pandya), Poompuhar/Kaveripattinam (Chola), Muziris (Chera, pepper), Tondi, Arikamedu (Virapatnam, Roman trading station near Puducherry), Naura, and Nelcynda. Exports were pepper, pearls, ivory, beryl, muslin and spices; imports were gold, wine, amphorae and coral. Roman gold coins found in the south confirm the trade. The Periplus describes these ports in the 1st century CE.

Centres of iron-and-steel making: South India had an Iron Age megalithic culture with sites like Adichanallur (Thoothukudi), Kodumanal (Erode, also beads and gems), Mayiladumparai and Hallur in Karnataka. Wootz steel from Telangana (Konasamudram) and Tamil regions was exported and later known as Damascus steel. Iron ploughshares aided agriculture. These were manufacturing sites and not the ports in the question.

Shrines of Jain Tirthankaras: Jainism reached the south through Bhadrabahu and Chandragupta Maurya traditions, with Shravanabelagola (Karnataka) housing the Gommateshwara/Bahubali statue. Tamil Nadu has Jain caves and Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions at Madurai (Samanamalai, Keezhavalavu) and Sittanavasal paintings. Tirthankaras number 24, with Rishabhanatha first and Mahavira last. These are religious sites and have no link to the three port names.
related: Muziris (Muchiri) was the Chera port, linked with the Roman pepper trade and the Muziris papyrus.
Korkai on the Tamraparni was the Pandya pearl-fishery port.
Poompuhar (Kaveripattinam) was the Chola port described in Silappadikaram and Pattinappalai.
Arikamedu near Puducherry was an Indo-Roman trading station.
Sangam capitals: Madurai (Pandya), Uraiyur (Chola), Vanji (Chera).
Silappadikaram was written by Ilango Adigal; Manimekalai by Sittalai Sattanar.
Kodumanal in Erode was an ancient bead and iron-working centre.
The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century CE) describes ports of the Indian coast.
summary: The answer is (b) ports. Korkai, Poompuhar (Kaveripattinam) and Muchiri (Muziris) were famous coastal trading ports of ancient South India, linked to Indo-Roman and Southeast Asian maritime trade during the Sangam age.
topic_notes: The Sangam age (c. 300 BCE-300 CE) in Tamilakam saw the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas rule alongside chiefs such as the Velirs. Sangam literature includes Tolkappiyam, Ettuthokai, Pattuppattu, and the epics Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal) and Manimekalai (Sittalai Sattanar). Capitals: Madurai (Pandya), Uraiyur (Chola), Vanji (Chera). Emblems: fish (Pandya), tiger (Chola), bow (Chera). Ports: Korkai (pearls), Poompuhar (Chola, also called Kaveripattinam), Muziris/Muchiri (Chera), Tondi, Arikamedu, Saliyur and Nelcynda. Indo-Roman trade flourished after the discovery of monsoon winds, traditionally credited to Hippalus in the 1st century CE. Exports were pepper (called yavanapriya), pearls, ivory, gems, textiles and spices; imports were gold, wine, glassware and coral. Archaeological evidence includes Arikamedu excavations, Pattanam (Kerala) digs, Roman coin hoards and Muziris papyrus. Trade guilds such as Manigramam and Ayyavole later also traded. Society had five tinai landscapes: kurinji, mullai, marutham, neithal and palai. Megalithic burials and iron use mark the earlier phase. The Sangam age declined with the Kalabhra period, followed by Pallavas and Pandyas. UPSC may ask about ports of the east and west coasts, Sangam literature authors, Roman trade evidence and the three Sangams at Madurai.

question: Which one of the following explains the practice of ‘Vattakirutal’ as mentioned in Sangam poems?
options: Learned persons assembling in royal courts to discuss religious and philosophical matters
Young girls keeping watch over agricultural fields and driving away birds and animals
A king defeated in a _ battle committing ritual suicide by starving himself to death
subject: Environment
detail: Vattakirutal literally means 'sitting facing the north' (vatakku = north, iruttal = sitting). In Sangam literature, especially the Purananuru and related puram poems, it describes a king, or sometimes a warrior or chieftain, who suffered defeat, a wound in the back, or public humiliation and chose to starve himself to death in a dedicated spot, in the open, facing north. This was an honour-bound act, akin to the later Jain sallekhana or the Hindu prayopavesa, but it was a martial and heroic code. The best-known case is the Chera king Cheraman Perumcheral Irumporai, who was captured by the Chola king and, humiliated, sat in vatakkiruttal; the Kovur Kizhar and Pisiraanthaiyar poems also describe such acts. Poets sometimes sat with the king in solidarity. Elimination: option (a) refers to the yavana or women bodyguards described in Tamil and Mauryan sources, not this term. Option (b) describes learned assemblies, linked to the Sangams themselves. Option (c) concerns the agricultural practice of 'kuravai' and 'kilikadival' (driving away parrots) in the Kurinji tinai, so it is a different custom.
explanations: Incorrect: Women bodyguards (the 'yavana' and women guards at royal courts) are mentioned in Sangam and Greek sources, but they have nothing to do with the term vattakirutal.
Incorrect: Learned assemblies refer to the Sangams (academies at Madurai) or royal courts with poets, not to vattakirutal, which is a death ritual.
Incorrect: Girls guarding millet fields and scaring away parrots is a theme in Kurinji-tinai poems (kilikadival), not vattakirutal.
Correct: Vattakirutal was the ritual fast unto death by a king, usually after defeat or disgrace, while sitting facing north, as described in the Purananuru.
keyfact: Vattakirutal = Sangam-era ritual fast to death by a defeated or disgraced king, sitting facing north.
option_notes: Women bodyguards: Sangam and early historical texts, including Megasthenes' account of Mauryan courts and Tamil poems, mention armed women attending kings. In Tamil Nadu 'yavanas' also served as palace guards. It reflects royal security arrangements and is a separate topic from the northward fasting custom. It is a plausible distractor but not related to vattakirutal.

Learned assemblies: Royal courts in Tamil country patronised poets (pulavar), bards (panar) and minstrels (viraliyar). The Sangams, held under Pandya patronage at Madurai, were gatherings of poets and scholars. Debates on religion and philosophy are associated more with later periods, including Buddhist and Jain monks, and with Pallava and Chola courts. This option confuses the term with the academies.

Girls guarding fields: In Sangam akam poetry the five tinais (Kurinji, Mullai, Marutham, Neithal, Palai) each have their own landscape and customs. Kurinji (hills) features millet fields guarded by young women who drive away parrots; this is a romantic setting for meetings between lovers. It is a poetic convention, not an act of vattakirutal.

Vattakirutal: A ritual starvation to death by a king facing north, observed in the puram tradition after military defeat, wounds on the back or public disgrace. The Chera king Kokkothai Marban and Cheraman Perumcheral Irumporai are linked with the practice in poems. It shows the high value placed on honour, valour (maram) and heroic death in early Tamilakam, and resembles later Jain sallekhana.
related: Vattakirutal: ritual fasting to death by a defeated king, facing north, in Sangam puram poetry.
Cheraman Perumcheral Irumporai is the Chera king associated with the practice.
Sangam poetry is classified into akam (love) and puram (war, kingship).
Five tinais: Kurinji, Mullai, Marutham, Neithal, Palai.
Karikala Chola won the Battle of Venni and built the Kallanai (Grand Anicut) according to tradition.
Silappadikaram was written by Ilango Adigal; Manimekalai by Sittalai Sattanar.
Hero-stones (nadukal) commemorated warriors who died in battle.
Jain sallekhana is a comparable fast unto death for religious reasons.
summary: The answer is (d). Vattakirutal (also called Vatakkiruttal or Vadakkiruttal) was the Sangam-era practice in which a defeated or dishonoured Tamil king sat facing north and fasted to death, choosing a ritual death over disgrace.
topic_notes: The Sangam age (roughly 3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE) is known from Tamil literature, Greek and Roman accounts and inscriptions. The three ruling dynasties were the Cheras (Vanji, west coast, emblem bow), Cholas (Uraiyur/Puhar, emblem tiger) and Pandyas (Madurai, emblem fish). Sangam literature includes Tolkappiyam (grammar), Ettuthokai (Eight Anthologies), Pattuppattu (Ten Idylls) and the epics Silappadikaram and Manimekalai. Poetry is classified as akam (love, inner life) and puram (war, kingship, public life). The five tinais are Kurinji (hills), Mullai (forest), Marutham (agricultural plains), Neithal (coast) and Palai (arid). Puram poetry also uses themes such as vetchi (cattle raid), vanji (invasion), ulinai (siege), tumbai (battle), vakai (victory) and kanchi (transience); the heroic custom of vattakirutal belongs to this world of honour. Heroic death was commemorated with hero-stones (nadukal). Society had tribal and clan features, with chiefs such as the Velir; the kings were patrons of bards and poets. Trade with Rome was significant, with ports at Muziris, Arikamedu and Puhar, and Roman coins found in many places. Other aspects UPSC may test: the three Sangams in tradition, the Karikala Chola and the Battle of Venni, Senguttuvan Chera and the Pattini cult, the Pandya king Nedunchezhiyan, and the Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions.

question:
Consider the following dynasties :
1. Hoysala
2. Gahadavala
3. Kakatiya
4. Yadava How many of the above dynasties established their kingdoms in early eighth century AD? :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The question tests the chronology of post-Gupta and early medieval dynasties. The early 8th century (c. 700-750 AD) saw the Chalukyas of Badami (Vikramaditya II), the Pallavas of Kanchi (Narasimhavarman II), the Karkota dynasty of Kashmir (Lalitaditya Muktapida), Yashovarman of Kannauj, and the Arab conquest of Sindh (712 AD, Muhammad bin Qasim). The Gurjara-Pratiharas began under Nagabhata I around 730-750, and the Rashtrakutas under Dantidurga around 753. The four dynasties in the question are all later. The Kakatiyas were feudatories of the Western Chalukyas and the Kalyani Chalukyas before becoming independent in the 12th century (Prola II, c. 1162; Prataparudra, Ganapati Deva, Rudramadevi followed). The Hoysalas rose in the 11th-12th centuries under Vishnuvardhana, with capitals at Belur and Halebidu. The Yadavas of Devagiri (Seuna) emerged in the late 12th century under Bhillama V (c. 1187). The Gahadavalas of Kannauj/Varanasi were founded by Chandradeva around 1090 AD, and Jayachandra was defeated by Muhammad Ghori at Chandawar in 1194. Since all four date from the 10th-12th centuries, none was founded in the early 8th century.
explanations: Wrong: saying 'only one' would require one of these dynasties to date from the early 8th century, and none does.
Wrong: no pair among these four was founded in the early 8th century; all arose between the 10th and 12th centuries.
Wrong: even three would be incorrect, since not a single one of the dynasties dates to that period.
Correct: the Hoysala, Gahadavala, Kakatiya and Yadava dynasties all arose from the 10th-12th centuries, so none was established in the early 8th century.
keyfact: Hoysala, Gahadavala, Kakatiya and Yadava dynasties all arose in the 10th-12th centuries, not in the early 8th century, so the answer is None.
option_notes: Only one: This would have been right if, for example, the Karkota dynasty of Kashmir or the Chalukyas of Badami (founded 543 AD) were listed. Early 8th century powers include the Karkotas (c. 625-1003 AD, Lalitaditya Muktapida r. c. 724-760, who built the Martand Sun Temple), the Pallavas under Narasimhavarman II (Rajasimha, who built the Shore Temple and Kailasanatha Temple), and the Chalukyas of Badami under Vikramaditya II. None of the four listed dynasties belongs to this early period, so this option fails.

Only two: Two of the four dynasties would need to have been established in the early 8th century. The Gahadavalas (c. 1090) and Kakatiyas (12th century) belong to the same broad late-early-medieval phase as the Hoysalas and Yadavas. Early 8th century events include the Arab conquest of Sindh in 712 AD, the rise of Yashovarman of Kannauj, and the beginning of the Gurjara-Pratihara power under Nagabhata I. None of these involves the listed dynasties, so this option is incorrect.

Only three: Three of the listed dynasties would need to date to the early 8th century, which is false. The Hoysalas, Kakatiyas and Yadavas were all successor states emerging from the decline of the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani (c. 973-1200), who themselves followed the Rashtrakutas (753-973). Their rise happened in the 11th-12th centuries, and all were eventually overrun by the Delhi Sultanate in the early 14th century, so this option is wrong.

None: This is the official and correct answer. The Hoysalas (11th-12th century, Karnataka), Gahadavalas (c. 1090, Kannauj), Kakatiyas (12th century, Telangana) and Yadavas of Devagiri (c. 1187, Maharashtra) all emerged between the 10th and 12th centuries. The early 8th century belonged to the Badami Chalukyas, Pallavas, Karkotas and the emerging Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas. Hence no listed dynasty was founded in that period.
related: Chalukyas of Badami were founded by Pulakeshin I around 543 AD, with capital at Vatapi.
Rashtrakutas were founded by Dantidurga around 753 AD, with capital at Manyakheta.
Kakatiya Ramappa Temple became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.
Hoysala temples of Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura were inscribed by UNESCO in 2023.
Gahadavala ruler Jayachandra was defeated by Muhammad Ghori at Chandawar in 1194.
Yadava ruler Ramachandra was attacked by Alauddin Khalji in 1296 at Devagiri.
Arab conquest of Sindh by Muhammad bin Qasim occurred in 712 AD.
Lalitaditya Muktapida of the Karkota dynasty built the Martand Sun Temple in Kashmir.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Hoysalas were founded in the 10th-11th centuries and became prominent in the 12th century, not the early 8th. Hoysala rule was centred in southern Karnataka, with Sala traditionally the legendary founder who killed a tiger, which became the dynasty's emblem. Vishnuvardhana (r. 1110-1152) was the great ruler who made them independent of the Western Chalukyas and, under Ramanuja's influence, adopted Vaishnavism. Their capitals were Belur and later Halebidu (Dorasamudra). They are famous for Hoysala architecture in soapstone, seen in the Chennakesava Temple at Belur, the Hoysaleswara Temple at Halebidu and the Keshava Temple at Somanathapura. Veera Ballala III was defeated by Malik Kafur's forces in 1311, and the dynasty ended in the 14th century. The Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura temples were inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 2023.

2 — Incorrect: The Gahadavalas (Gahadvalas) were founded by Chandradeva around 1090 AD, after the decline of the Gurjara-Pratiharas, not in the early 8th century. They ruled from Kannauj and Varanasi over parts of present Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Govindachandra was a powerful ruler, and his minister Lakshmidhara wrote the Kritya-kalpataru. Jayachandra, the last notable ruler, was defeated by Muhammad Ghori at the Battle of Chandawar in 1194 AD. They introduced a tax called Turushkadanda to raise money for defence against Turkish invasions. They were rivals of the Chahamanas (Chauhans) and the Palas. Rajput clans of this period are associated with the Agnikula or Suryavamsha traditions.

3 — Incorrect: The Kakatiyas rose in the Telangana region and became independent in the 12th century, not the early 8th. They began as feudatories of the Rashtrakutas and later the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani. Prola II declared independence around 1162, and Ganapati Deva (r. 1199-1262) expanded the kingdom to the coast. Rudramadevi (r. 1262-1289) was among the few women rulers of medieval India, and Marco Polo praised her rule. Prataparudra was defeated by the Delhi Sultanate (Ulugh Khan, Muhammad bin Tughlaq's general) in 1323. Their capital was Orugallu (Warangal). They are known for the Ramappa (Rudreshwara) Temple in Palampet, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021, the Warangal Fort and the Thousand Pillar Temple, as well as for building large tanks for irrigation.

4 — Incorrect: The Yadavas of Devagiri (Seuna dynasty) rose in the late 12th century, not the early 8th. They were feudatories of the Western Chalukyas and became independent under Bhillama V around 1187 AD, with their capital at Devagiri (later Daulatabad) in Maharashtra. Singhana (r. 1210-1246) expanded the kingdom. Ramachandra was defeated by Alauddin Khalji in 1296 during his raid on Devagiri, and the dynasty was finished off by Malik Kafur in 1307-1312 and later Muhammad bin Tughlaq's conquests. Hemadri (Hemadpant), minister and scholar, wrote the Chaturvarga-chintamani and gave his name to the Hemadpanthi architectural style. The Yadavas patronised Marathi, with poets such as Jnaneshwar, who wrote the Jnaneshwari, flourishing in their court's time.
summary: The answer is (d) None. All four dynasties, the Hoysala, Gahadavala, Kakatiya and Yadava (Seuna), rose to power between the 10th and 12th centuries AD, long after the early 8th century. In the early 8th century the major powers were the Chalukyas of Badami, Pallavas, Pratiharas (emerging) and Rashtrakutas (emerging mid-century).
topic_notes: This question belongs to the early medieval history of India (c. 750-1200 AD), a period of regional kingdoms, feudalism and the Rajput rise. Key chronology: the Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj (8th-9th centuries) among the Gurjara-Pratiharas (north-west and Ganga plain), the Palas (Bengal and Bihar; Gopala c. 750, Dharmapala, Devapala) and the Rashtrakutas (Deccan; Dantidurga c. 753, Amoghavarsha, Krishna I who built the Kailasa temple at Ellora). In the south, the Cholas (Vijayalaya c. 850; Rajaraja I and Rajendra I in the 10th-11th centuries), Pallavas and Pandyas dominated. The Western Chalukyas of Kalyani (973) succeeded the Rashtrakutas; their feudatories, the Hoysalas, Kakatiyas and Yadavas, became independent as the Chalukya power declined in the 12th century. In the north, the Gahadavalas (Kannauj), Chahamanas/Chauhans (Ajmer, Prithviraj III defeated at Tarain in 1192), Paramaras (Malwa, Bhoja), Chandellas (Khajuraho), Solankis/Chalukyas of Gujarat (Mount Abu Dilwara temples) and Senas (Bengal) emerged. Turkish invasions: Mahmud of Ghazni (1000-1027), Muhammad Ghori (First Tarain 1191, Second Tarain 1192, Chandawar 1194), leading to the Delhi Sultanate in 1206. Southern kingdoms fell to Alauddin Khalji's generals (Malik Kafur) in 1296-1311 and then to the Tughlaqs. Architecture: Hoysala (star-shaped plan, soapstone), Kakatiya (Ramappa), Chandella (Khajuraho), Solanki (Modhera Sun Temple), Chola (Dravida). Likely UPSC angles: capitals, founders, temples, UNESCO sites, and the order of dynasties.

question:
With reference to ancient Indian History, , consider the following pairs : Literary work Author
1. ‘Devichandragupta : Bilhana
2. Hammira-Mahakavya : Nayachandra Suri
3. Milinda-panha : Nagarjuna
4. Nitivakyamrita : Somadeva Suri How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
subject: Ancient History
detail: The question tests the authorship of well-known Sanskrit and Pali works. Devichandraguptam is a Sanskrit play by Vishakhadatta, who also wrote Mudrarakshasa. Only fragments survive, and it deals with Ramagupta, Dhruvadevi and Chandragupta II. Bilhana was a Kashmiri poet at the Chalukya court of Vikramaditya VI, and he wrote Vikramankadevacharita and Chaurapanchashika. Hammira-Mahakavya was composed by the Jain scholar Nayachandra Suri in the 15th century. It glorifies the Chauhan ruler Hammira of Ranthambore, who fought Alauddin Khalji. Milinda-panha (Questions of Milinda) is a Pali Buddhist text recording a dialogue between the Indo-Greek king Menander (Milinda) and the monk Nagasena. Nagarjuna was a Mahayana philosopher who founded the Madhyamaka school and wrote the Mulamadhyamakakarika. Nitivakyamrita is a Sanskrit work on polity by the Digambara Jain monk Somadeva Suri, who also wrote Yashastilaka Champu. He lived in the Rashtrakuta period, in the 10th century. Elimination: once you know pairs 2 and 4 are correct and 1 and 3 are wrong, the answer is (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong because two pairs, not one, are correct: pairs 2 and 4.

(b) is correct because Hammira-Mahakavya (Nayachandra Suri) and Nitivakyamrita (Somadeva Suri) are right. Devichandragupta (Vishakhadatta) and Milinda-panha (Nagasena dialogue, no known author) are wrong.
(c) is wrong because it would require pair 1 or pair 3 to be correct, and neither is. Bilhana did not write Devichandragupta, and Nagarjuna did not write Milinda-panha.
(d) is wrong because pairs 1 and 3 are mismatched, so not all four are correct.
keyfact: Devichandragupta = Vishakhadatta; Milinda-panha = Menander and Nagasena; Hammira-Mahakavya = Nayachandra Suri; Nitivakyamrita = Somadeva Suri.
option_notes: Only one: this would mean a single correct pair. It is a distractor here. Many students confuse authors and know only one pair well. Remember that the correct pairs are Nayachandra Suri with Hammira-Mahakavya and Somadeva Suri with Nitivakyamrita, so the count is more than one. Such 'how many' questions need every pair checked individually, since there is no partial credit and a single error changes the answer.

Only two: this is the correct option. The two right pairs are Hammira-Mahakavya by Nayachandra Suri, a Jain poet who wrote on the Chauhan king of Ranthambore, and Nitivakyamrita by Somadeva Suri, a 10th-century Jain writer on polity under the Rashtrakutas. The wrong pairs are Devichandragupta, by Vishakhadatta, and Milinda-panha, a Pali dialogue with Nagasena and not a work of Nagarjuna.

Only three: this would need one of the two wrong pairs to be right. Bilhana is known for Vikramankadevacharita, a biography of the Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI, and for Chaurapanchashika. Nagarjuna was a Madhyamaka Buddhist philosopher, not the author of Milinda-panha. Since both are mismatched, three correct pairs is impossible. It is a trap for students who recognise only some authors' names.

All four: this would need every pair to be correct. It fails because Devichandragupta belongs to Vishakhadatta, the author of Mudrarakshasa, and Milinda-panha records the dialogue of Menander and Nagasena. Choosing it shows overconfidence in familiar-sounding names. UPSC often mixes real authors with the wrong works, so each pair must be checked on its own.
related: Vishakhadatta wrote Mudrarakshasa and Devichandraguptam.
Milinda-panha records the dialogue between Menander and the monk Nagasena.
Kalhana's Rajatarangini (12th century) is a chronicle of Kashmir kings.
Bilhana wrote Vikramankadevacharita on Vikramaditya VI of the Chalukyas of Kalyani.
Somadeva Suri also wrote Yashastilaka Champu (959 CE).
Jayanaka wrote Prithviraja Vijaya on Prithviraj Chauhan.
Kavirajamarga by Amoghavarsha is the earliest available Kannada work on poetics.
Sandhyakar Nandi's Ramacharita is about the Pala king Ramapala.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Devichandragupta (Devichandraguptam) was written by Vishakhadatta, not Bilhana. Vishakhadatta was a Sanskrit dramatist, probably of the Gupta or post-Gupta period, who also wrote Mudrarakshasa, a play on Chanakya and Chandragupta Maurya. Devichandraguptam survives only in fragments, quoted in later works such as the Natyadarpana and by Bhoja. It tells how the Gupta king Ramagupta, besieged by a Shaka ruler, agreed to hand over his queen Dhruvadevi, and how his brother Chandragupta II went disguised as the queen and killed the Shaka. Bilhana was a Kashmiri poet who wrote Vikramankadevacharita on the Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI.

2 — Correct: Hammira-Mahakavya was composed by the Jain scholar Nayachandra Suri, probably in the late 14th or 15th century. It is a Sanskrit epic poem in 14 cantos on the Chauhan (Chahamana) king Hammiradeva of Ranthambore, who sheltered Mongol rebels and resisted Alauddin Khalji. The siege ended in 1301 with Hammira's defeat, and the Rajput women performed jauhar. It is an important source for Chauhan history alongside Prithviraja Vijaya by Jayanaka. Nayachandra was associated with the Tomar court of Gwalior.

3 — Incorrect: Milinda-panha is a non-canonical Pali Buddhist text of uncertain authorship, dated around the 1st century BCE to 1st century CE. It records the dialogue between the Indo-Greek king Menander I (Milinda) of Sakala (Sialkot) and the Buddhist monk Nagasena. The questions concern the soul, rebirth, karma and nirvana. Nagarjuna was a different figure: a Mahayana philosopher of the 2nd century CE, associated with the Satavahana court and Nagarjunakonda, who founded the Madhyamaka (Shunyavada) school.

4 — Correct: Nitivakyamrita was written by Somadeva Suri, a Digambara Jain monk and scholar of the 10th century. He lived under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna III and the Chalukya feudatory Arikesari at Vemulavada. The work is a Sanskrit prose treatise on statecraft, politics and ethics, modelled on Kautilya's Arthashastra. It deals with the state, the king, ministers and diplomacy. Somadeva also wrote Yashastilaka Champu, a Jain prose-and-verse narrative composed in 959 CE, and his works are valued as sources on the social and political life of the period.
summary: The answer is (b): only two pairs are correctly matched. Pair 2 (Hammira-Mahakavya by Nayachandra Suri) and pair 4 (Nitivakyamrita by Somadeva Suri) are correct. Pair 1 is wrong because Devichandragupta was written by Vishakhadatta, not Bilhana, and pair 3 is wrong because the Milinda-panha is a Buddhist text with no known author, not a work of Nagarjuna.
topic_notes: This question belongs to ancient and early medieval Indian literature, where UPSC often asks for author-work matching. Key Sanskrit authors and works to remember: Kalidasa (Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta, Raghuvamsha, Kumarasambhava), Shudraka (Mricchakatika), Vishakhadatta (Mudrarakshasa, Devichandraguptam), Bhasa (Svapnavasavadatta), Banabhatta (Harshacharita, Kadambari), Bilhana (Vikramankadevacharita), Kalhana (Rajatarangini, 12th century, Kashmir), Jayadeva (Gita Govinda), Sandhyakar Nandi (Ramacharita), Jayanaka (Prithviraja Vijaya), Padmagupta (Navasahasankacharita), Hemachandra (Kumarapalacharita, Dvyashraya), Somadeva Suri (Nitivakyamrita, Yashastilaka), Nayachandra Suri (Hammira-Mahakavya), Amoghavarsha (Kavirajamarga, the earliest Kannada work), Pampa (Vikramarjunavijaya), Magha (Shishupalavadha), Bharavi (Kiratarjuniya), Dandin (Dashakumaracharita), Kshemendra and Somadeva Bhatta (Kathasaritsagara). Buddhist and Pali texts include Milinda-panha, Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa, the Jatakas and Buddhacharita by Ashvaghosha. Jain and philosophical works include Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka texts and Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakosha. Sangam literature includes Tolkappiyam, Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal) and Manimekalai (Sattanar). Dharmashastra and polity texts include Arthashastra (Kautilya), Manusmriti and Kamandakiya Nitisara. Astronomy works include Aryabhatiya (Aryabhata, 499 CE) and Brihat Samhita (Varahamihira). Likely angles for the future are historical biographies as sources, plays about the Gupta period, and works linked to specific dynasties and patrons.

question: “Souls are not only the property~ of animal and plant life, but also of rocks, running water and many other natural objects not looked on as living by other religious sects.” The above statement reflects one of the core beliefs of which one of the following religious sects of ancient India?
subject: Environment
detail: Jainism classifies reality into jiva (soul/living) and ajiva (non-living). Jiva is found in beings with one to five senses. Ekendriya (one-sensed) beings include earth-bodied (prithvikaya, e.g. rocks, minerals), water-bodied (apkaya), fire-bodied (tejaskaya), air-bodied (vayukaya) and plant-bodied (vanaspatikaya) beings, all having the sense of touch. This is why Jain ethics demands extreme non-violence (ahimsa), the first of the Five Mahavratas: ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha and brahmacharya (the last added by Mahavira; Parshvanatha taught four). Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara (c. 6th century BCE), consolidated these ideas. The quoted statement, with its phrase 'not looked on as living by other religious sects', points to Jainism's distinctive extension of life to inanimate-seeming objects. Elimination: Buddhism accepts no permanent soul (anatta) and does not ascribe souls to rocks or water. Shaivism and Vaishnavism are theistic devotional traditions centred on Shiva and Vishnu; they do not hold that natural objects each possess souls as a core doctrine. Hence (b).
explanations: Incorrect: Buddhism denies a permanent self (anatta) and does not teach that rocks and water possess souls; its ahimsa is rooted in compassion and intention, not universal animism.
Correct: Jainism holds that jivas exist even in earth, water, fire, air and rocks (one-sensed beings), and the statement describes exactly this belief.
Incorrect: Shaivism is a theistic tradition devoted to Shiva; attributing souls to all natural objects is not its core belief.
Incorrect: Vaishnavism is a devotional tradition centred on Vishnu and his avatars; it does not teach souls in rocks and running water as a core tenet.
keyfact: Jainism attributes jiva (soul) even to rocks, water, fire and air, which is the basis of its strict ahimsa.
option_notes: Buddhism was founded by Siddhartha Gautama (Buddha, c. 563-483 BCE or thereabouts). Core teachings: Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path, Middle Way, anicca (impermanence), dukkha, and anatta (no permanent soul). Its canon is the Tripitaka in Pali (Vinaya, Sutta, Abhidhamma). Councils were held at Rajagriha, Vaishali, Pataliputra and Kashmir/Kundalvana. Schools: Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana. Ashoka patronised it after Kalinga.

Jainism's twenty-four Tirthankaras ended with Mahavira (born Vaishali region, c. 540 BCE, attained kevala jnana at Jrimbhikagrama). Rishabhanatha was the first and Parshvanatha the 23rd. Key ideas: anekantavada, syadvada, triratna (right faith, knowledge, conduct), jiva and ajiva, karma as subtle matter. Schism into Digambara and Svetambara; canon is the Agamas, compiled at Valabhi council (5th century CE). Patrons: Chandragupta Maurya, Kharavela, Ganga, Chalukya and Rashtrakuta rulers.

Shaivism is the tradition worshipping Shiva as the supreme god. Early evidence includes Pashupata sect (founded by Lakulisa), and later Kapalikas, Kashmir Shaivism and Shaiva Siddhanta. In Tamil Nadu, the 63 Nayanars composed the Tirumurai. Chola kings built great Shiva temples such as Brihadeshvara at Thanjavur. Virashaivism (Lingayatism) was founded in the 12th century Karnataka by Basavanna.

Vaishnavism worships Vishnu and his avatars (Rama, Krishna etc.). It grew from the Bhagavata cult of Vasudeva-Krishna, and its key texts include the Bhagavad Gita and Puranas. In Tamil Nadu, the twelve Alvars composed the Nalayira Divya Prabandham. Philosophers include Ramanuja (Vishishtadvaita), Madhva (Dvaita), Nimbarka and Vallabha. Gupta kings patronised it, and the Bhakti movement spread it widely.
related: Jainism has 24 Tirthankaras; Rishabhanatha first, Parshvanatha 23rd, Mahavira 24th.
Mahavira's emblem is the lion; Parshvanatha's is the serpent.
Five Mahavratas: ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha, brahmacharya.
Triratna: samyak darshana, samyak jnana, samyak charitra.
Digambara and Svetambara are the two major Jain sects.
Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela is a major Jain-related source in Odisha.
Gomateshwara (Bahubali) statue at Shravanabelagola was built under the Ganga minister Chavundaraya.
Buddhism rejects a permanent soul (anatta); Jainism affirms jiva in all elements.
summary: The answer is (b) Jainism. Jainism teaches universal animism (jiva): souls exist not only in humans, animals and plants but also in earth bodies, water, fire, air and rocks, which is why ahimsa is central to it.
topic_notes: The question tests the heterodox religious movements of 6th century BCE India and their philosophical distinctions. Jainism: Mahavira (Vardhamana), born to Siddhartha and Trishala, of the Jnatrika clan, left home at 30, attained kevala jnana after 12 years, and died at Pavapuri (c. 468 BCE by tradition). Core principles: five Mahavratas, three jewels (Triratna), anekantavada (many-sidedness of truth), syadvada, and nirgrantha (free from bonds). Jains reject a creator God and believe in karma and rebirth, with moksha through the shedding of karma. Jiva is found in all natural elements, so strict ahimsa is followed, including wearing a mouth cloth (muhapatti) and sweeping the path. Sallekhana is the ritual fast unto death. Digambara (sky-clad) followers of Bhadrabahu migrated south, while Svetambara (white-clad) followers stayed with Sthulabhadra; the first Jain council was at Pataliputra. Prakrit (Ardhamagadhi) was used for the teachings. Art and architecture: Dilwara temples (Mount Abu), Gomateshwara/Bahubali at Shravanabelagola, Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves in Odisha (Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription), and Palitana temples. Compare Buddhism, which stresses the middle path and denies a permanent soul, and Ajivikas (Makkhali Gosala), who stressed fatalism (niyati). Charvaka was materialist. Also remember that Jain literature includes Kalpasutra and Acharanga Sutra.

question: Who among the following rulers of Vijayanagara Empire constructed a large dam across Tungabhadra River and a _ canal-cum-aqueduct several ‘kilometres long from the river to the capital city? ;
subject: Geography
detail: Devaraya I (r. c. 1406-1422) of the Sangama dynasty is credited with major hydraulic works for the capital Vijayanagara (Hampi). Historians cite Nuniz and Persian visitor Abdur Razzaq, along with the inscriptions and the surviving remains. He had a dam built across the Tungabhadra and cut canals to bring water into the city. His Tungabhadra works are often paired with the Turtha canal and the Basavanna canal. Later rulers, especially Krishnadevaraya of the Tuluva dynasty, added tanks (such as the one at Kamalapuram) and more canals, so the empire has a long tradition of irrigation works. NCERT (Themes in Indian History, Part II, Hampi chapter) states that the Kamalapuram tank and the Hiriya canal are associated with the later period, while Devaraya I's works supplied the Royal Centre and the Sacred Centre. Elimination logic: Mallikarjuna (r. 1446-1465) and Virupaksha II (r. 1465-1485) were weak Sangama rulers known for no major hydraulic works, and the Sangama dynasty was already declining under them. Vira Vijaya (Vira Vijaya Bukka, also called Vijaya Raya II, r. c. 1422-1430) is not known for such works. Only Devaraya I fits.
explanations: Correct: Devaraya I is credited with building the dam across the Tungabhadra and the canal-cum-aqueduct that carried water to the capital.
Wrong: Mallikarjuna was a weak Sangama ruler whose reign saw decline and Gajapati attacks, and he is not associated with major irrigation works.
Wrong: Vira Vijaya had a brief reign soon after Devaraya I and is not credited with this hydraulic project.
Wrong: Virupaksha II was a ineffective, dissolute ruler whose reign led to the end of the Sangama dynasty, and he built no such dam.
keyfact: Devaraya I (Sangama dynasty) built the Tungabhadra dam and canal-cum-aqueduct to supply water to Vijayanagara.
option_notes: Devaraya I (r. c. 1406-1422) was a Sangama ruler who strengthened Vijayanagara militarily and administratively. He fought the Bahmani Sultanate and the Reddis of Kondavidu, and employed Muslim archers in his army. Abdur Razzaq's account and the Italian traveller Nicolo Conti's visit belong to this period. He built the Tungabhadra dam and canals to supply Vijayanagara's water.

Mallikarjuna (r. c. 1446-1465), also called Praudha Deva Raya, was the Sangama ruler who succeeded Devaraya II. His reign saw the empire weaken, with Bahmani and Gajapati (Odisha) invasions eroding its territory. He is not known for dams or other irrigation projects. His weakness paved the way for the later usurpation of the throne by Saluva Narasimha.

Vira Vijaya (Vira Vijaya Bukka, also called Vijaya Raya I or II in different lists) was a Sangama ruler who held the throne briefly after Devaraya I, around 1422-1424. His reign is poorly documented, and he is not credited with any known irrigation or architectural initiatives. He is a minor figure in the dynastic list.

Virupaksha II (r. c. 1465-1485) was the last effective Sangama ruler. He was a weak and dissolute king, and he was reportedly killed by his own son. Nobles and provincial governors rebelled, which ended with Saluva Narasimha seizing power around 1485 and founding the Saluva dynasty. He is not linked with any water projects.
related: Vijayanagara was founded in 1336 by Harihara I and Bukka I.
Krishnadevaraya (Tuluva) wrote Amuktamalyada in Telugu.
Battle of Talikota was fought in 1565.
Abdur Razzaq visited Vijayanagara in the reign of Devaraya II.
Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz were Portuguese visitors to Vijayanagara.
Hampi was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.
Nayaka and Amaram systems governed Vijayanagara's military and land grants.
Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu were the four dynasties of Vijayanagara.
summary: The answer is (a) Devaraya I. He built a dam across the Tungabhadra and a long canal-cum-aqueduct to bring water to Vijayanagara, mainly to ease the city's water shortage and to irrigate nearby land.
topic_notes: Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 by Harihara I and Bukka Raya I of the Sangama dynasty, with the capital at Vijayanagara (Hampi) on the Tungabhadra. Dynasties in order: Sangama (1336-1485), Saluva (1485-1505), Tuluva (1505-1570), Aravidu (1570-c.1646). Important Sangama rulers: Harihara I, Bukka I, Harihara II, Devaraya I, Devaraya II (Praudha Deva Raya, the greatest Sangama ruler, who received Abdur Razzaq in 1443). Devaraya I fought the Bahmanis and built the Tungabhadra dam and canals. The Tuluva king Krishnadevaraya (1509-1529) was the empire's greatest ruler. He wrote the Telugu work Amuktamalyada, patronised the Ashtadiggajas, built the Hazara Rama and Vitthala temples, and founded the town of Nagalapuram. Foreign visitors: Nicolo Conti (Italian), Abdur Razzaq (Persian), Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz (Portuguese), Duarte Barbosa. Administration: the empire was divided into rajyas, mandalas, nadus and gramas. The Nayaka system gave military chiefs amaram lands, and the Ayagar system covered village servants. Battle of Talikota (1565) saw Rama Raya defeated by the combined Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar), and the city was sacked. Hampi architecture: the Royal Centre, the Sacred Centre, the Vitthala temple's stone chariot, the Lotus Mahal, the Elephant Stables, and the Mahanavami Dibba. Hampi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986). Water management: tanks, canals and the Kamalapuram tank, and the Hiriya canal. These are the angles UPSC may take up next time.

question: Who among the following rulers of medieval Gujarat surrendered Diu to Portuguese?
subject: Medieval History
detail: Bahadur Shah of the Muzaffarid dynasty ruled Gujarat from 1526 to 1537. He conquered Malwa in 1531 and besieged Chittor in 1535, but came under severe pressure from Humayun, who attacked Gujarat. Seeking naval and military help against the Mughals, he concluded the Treaty of Bassein with the Portuguese governor Nuno da Cunha in December 1534 (ratified 1535). Under it the Portuguese received Bassein (Vasai) and permission to build a fortress at Diu, along with trade concessions. Humayun's invasion (1535-36) briefly overran Gujarat, but Bahadur Shah later recovered his kingdom. Relations with the Portuguese then soured, as he tried to back out of the arrangement. In February 1537, during a meeting on a ship near Diu, a scuffle broke out and he drowned or was killed. Elimination logic: Ahmad Shah (r. 1411-1442) founded Ahmedabad in 1411 and was long before the Portuguese arrival in India in 1498. Mahmud Begarha (r. 1458-1511) fought the Portuguese at the Battle of Chaul (1508) and the Battle of Diu (1509), which he lost, but he did not cede Diu. Muhammad Shah is a vague distractor. Hence (c).
explanations: Incorrect: Ahmad Shah I (1411-1442) founded Ahmedabad and lived about 70 years before the Portuguese reached India, so he could not have surrendered Diu to them.
Incorrect: Mahmud Begarha (1458-1511) was a strong ruler who resisted the Portuguese. He allied with the Mamluks of Egypt and won at Chaul (1508) but lost at Diu (1509). He did not hand over Diu.
Correct: Bahadur Shah, facing Humayun, signed the Treaty of Bassein (1534-35) with the Portuguese, giving them Bassein and the right to build a fort at Diu.
Incorrect: Muhammad Shah is not associated with surrendering Diu; several Gujarat sultans bore this name, but none ceded Diu to the Portuguese.
keyfact: Bahadur Shah of Gujarat ceded Diu to the Portuguese under the Treaty of Bassein (1534-35) and died near Diu in 1537.
option_notes: Ahmad Shah I (r. 1411-1442) was the real founder of the independent Gujarat Sultanate after Zafar Khan (Muzaffar Shah I) declared independence in 1407. He shifted the capital from Patan to Ahmedabad, which he founded in 1411 on the Sabarmati. He fought Rajput chiefs, Malwa and the Deccan Bahmanis, and is remembered for Hindu-Muslim administrative accommodation and early Indo-Islamic architecture.

Mahmud Begarha (r. 1458-1511) was the greatest Gujarat sultan. He earned the name Begarha after capturing two forts (Girnar and Champaner). He founded Mahmudabad and renamed Champaner as Muhammadabad. He patronised the poet Udayaraja. His navy, with Mamluk help, defeated the Portuguese at Chaul in 1508 but lost at Diu in 1509 against Francisco de Almeida.

Bahadur Shah (r. 1526-1537) was the last powerful Gujarat sultan. He took Malwa in 1531, attacked Chittor in 1535 (Rani Karnavati's jauhar), and fought Humayun. He signed the Treaty of Bassein with the Portuguese in 1534-35 and died in 1537 near Diu in a scuffle with them. Gujarat declined afterwards and Akbar annexed it in 1572-73.

Muhammad Shah is a common regnal name among the Gujarat sultans, such as Muhammad Shah II (Qutb-ud-din Ahmad Shah II, 1451-58) and the later Muhammad Shah III (1537-54), who was a child ruler dominated by nobles. None of these is linked to ceding Diu to the Portuguese, and the option is a distractor.
related: Treaty of Bassein (1534-35) between Bahadur Shah and the Portuguese gave them Bassein and a fort at Diu.
Battle of Diu (1509): Francisco de Almeida defeated the Gujarat-Mamluk-Zamorin fleet.
Battle of Chaul (1508): the Gujarat-Mamluk fleet defeated Lourenco de Almeida.
Ahmad Shah I founded Ahmedabad in 1411.
Mahmud Begarha captured Girnar and Champaner, hence 'Begarha'.
Portuguese captured Goa in 1510 under Albuquerque.
Diu was liberated from Portuguese rule in 1961 through Operation Vijay.
Akbar annexed Gujarat in 1572-73.
summary: The answer is (c) Bahadur Shah. Sultan Bahadur Shah of Gujarat (r. 1526-1537), pressed by the Mughal emperor Humayun's attack, signed the Treaty of Bassein with the Portuguese in 1534-35 and allowed them to build a fort at Diu. He was killed in 1537 during a meeting with the Portuguese viceroy off Diu.
topic_notes: The Gujarat Sultanate (1407-1573) was founded by Zafar Khan, a Tank Rajput convert and governor under Firuz Tughluq's successors, who took the title Muzaffar Shah I. Ahmad Shah I founded Ahmedabad (1411). Mahmud Begarha (1458-1511) expanded the state, built a strong navy, and fought the Portuguese: in the Battle of Chaul (1508) the Gujarat-Mamluk fleet defeated Lourenco de Almeida, but in the Battle of Diu (February 1509) Francisco de Almeida defeated the combined fleet of Gujarat, the Mamluks, and the Zamorin of Calicut. This made the Portuguese the dominant naval power in the Arabian Sea. Under Bahadur Shah, Humayun's invasion led to the Treaty of Bassein (1534-35), giving Bassein to the Portuguese and permission to build a fort at Diu (built 1535-36). Bahadur Shah died in 1537 in a clash with the Portuguese. In 1538 an Ottoman fleet under Suleiman Pasha besieged Diu unsuccessfully. The Portuguese held Diu until 1961, when India annexed Goa, Daman and Diu in Operation Vijay. Portuguese milestones: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498; Almeida was viceroy 1505-09; Albuquerque captured Goa from Bijapur in 1510; the cartaz system controlled sea trade; Treaty of Tordesillas (1494). Gujarat's ports, Cambay and Surat, were key trading hubs. Akbar conquered Gujarat in 1572-73, and the last sultan was Muzaffar Shah III.

question: By which one of the following Acts was the Governor General of Bengal ._ designated as the Governor General - of India?
subject: Modern History
detail: The Regulating Act of 1773 created the post of Governor General of Bengal (Warren Hastings was the first) and gave him a supervisory role over Bombay and Madras, and it also set up the Supreme Court at Calcutta in 1774. Pitt's India Act of 1784 created the Board of Control, so the Company's affairs came under dual control: commercial matters with the Directors and political matters with the Crown. The Charter Act of 1793 renewed the Company's charter for 20 years and left the structure largely unchanged. The Charter Act of 1833 centralised the administration: the Governor General of Bengal became the Governor General of India, and the Bombay and Madras Presidencies lost their legislative powers. It ended the Company's trade monopoly (its commercial functions) and made it a purely administrative body. It also added a Law Member (Macaulay was the first) to the Governor General's Council and opened the door to Indians in services, though the provision was not implemented. Elimination logic: the Regulating Act, Pitt's Act and the 1793 Act all kept the Bengal designation, so the only Act that fits is the 1833 one.
explanations: Wrong. The Regulating Act of 1773 created the Governor General of Bengal, not of India.
Wrong. Pitt's India Act of 1784 set up the Board of Control and the dual system, and kept the Bengal designation.
Wrong. The Charter Act of 1793 only extended the Company's charter and its trade rights for 20 years, with minor changes.
Correct. The Charter Act of 1833 made the Governor General of Bengal the Governor General of India. Lord William Bentinck was the first holder.
keyfact: The Charter Act of 1833 made the Governor General of Bengal the Governor General of India, and Bentinck was the first holder of the office.
option_notes: The Regulating Act of 1773, passed by Lord North's government, was the first parliamentary step to control the East India Company. It created the Governor General of Bengal with a four-member council, with Warren Hastings as the first holder. It also made Bombay and Madras subordinate to Bengal in matters of war and peace and established the Supreme Court at Calcutta in 1774, with Elijah Impey as Chief Justice. It also banned private trade by Company servants.

Pitt's India Act of 1784 was passed under Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger. It created a six-member Board of Control to oversee the Company's civil, military and revenue affairs, and the Company's Court of Directors kept commercial matters, which produced a dual system that lasted until 1858. It distinguished the Company's commercial and political functions for the first time. It reduced the Governor General's Council to three members and made the Governor General's control over the other presidencies stronger.

The Charter Act of 1793 renewed the East India Company's charter for 20 years under Lord Cornwallis's period. It continued the Company's trade monopoly and let the Governor General override his council's decisions, a power extended to the governors of Madras and Bombay. It also provided that the salaries of the Board of Control members and staff be paid from Indian revenues. It made no change to the designation of the Governor General of Bengal.

The Charter Act of 1833, passed in Lord William Bentinck's time, was the last major charter Act that renewed the Company's rule. It ended the Company's commercial activities and monopoly, including the China tea trade, and made it an administrative body for the Crown. It made the Governor General of Bengal the Governor General of India and centralised legislative power in the Governor General in Council. It added a fourth ordinary member, the Law Member (Macaulay), and declared that no Indian would be barred from office by religion, birth or descent.
related: Warren Hastings was the first Governor General of Bengal, under the Regulating Act 1773.
Lord William Bentinck was the first Governor General of India (1833–35).
Lord Canning was the first Viceroy of India, under the Government of India Act 1858.
The Charter Act 1813 ended the Company's trade monopoly except for tea and the China trade.
