India's National Green Hydrogen Mission was approved in January 2023 with an outlay of about Rs 19,744 crore, targeting 5 million tonnes per year of green hydrogen production by 2030, about 125 GW of added renewable capacity, and more than Rs 8 lakh crore of investment. The nodal ministry is the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE). The SIGHT programme (Strategic Interventions for Green Hydrogen Transition) gives incentives for electrolyser manufacturing and green hydrogen production. Green Hydrogen Hubs are to be set up, and pilot projects cover steel, mobility and shipping. Key challenges are high cost of production, storage and transport (hydrogen is very light, needing compression to about 350-700 bar or liquefaction at -253 degrees Celsius), embrittlement of metals, safety due to wide flammability, and infrastructure. Applications include fertiliser, refineries, steel via hydrogen-based direct reduction, heavy transport, shipping fuels (green ammonia, methanol), and seasonal energy storage. Hydrogen has the highest energy per unit mass but low energy per unit volume. Related global efforts include the Hydrogen Council and the International Partnership for Hydrogen and Fuel Cells in the Economy (IPHE).

ocr: Consider the following countries : Bulgaria L 2. Czech Republic ‘ Hungary Latvia Lithuania Romania How many of the above-mentioned countries share a land border with Ukraine? (a) Only two Only three (b) (c) Only four (a) Only five
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Ukraine has land borders with seven countries: Belarus to the north, Russia to the east and northeast, Poland, Slovakia and Hungary to the west, Romania and Moldova to the southwest, with the Black Sea and Sea of Azov to the south. Four of these (Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania) are NATO/EU members, which makes the western border the EU's eastern frontier. The question is solved by elimination. Bulgaria lies south of Romania and meets Ukraine only across the Black Sea (a maritime neighbour, not a land neighbour). The Czech Republic is separated from Ukraine by Slovakia and Poland. Latvia and Lithuania are Baltic states; Lithuania borders Belarus, Poland, Latvia and Russia (Kaliningrad), and Latvia borders Estonia, Lithuania, Belarus and Russia, so neither touches Ukraine. Only Hungary (a short border near Zakarpattia) and Romania (the Danube, Prut and Chernivtsi/Odesa region) qualify, giving 'only two'. The trap is assuming Black Sea or Eastern European proximity implies a land border.
explanations: Correct. Only Hungary and Romania from the list share a land border with Ukraine.
Incorrect. Three is too many; no third country in the list borders Ukraine. Bulgaria is only a Black Sea neighbour.
Incorrect. Four would require including two of Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Latvia and Lithuania, none of which has a land border with Ukraine.
Incorrect. Five is far too many; Ukraine's other land neighbours are Belarus, Russia, Poland, Slovakia and Moldova, none of which is listed.
keyfact: Of the list, only Hungary and Romania border Ukraine; Bulgaria is a Black Sea neighbour only, and the Czech Republic and the Baltics are not neighbours.
option_notes: Only two: the correct count here (Hungary and Romania). Ukraine has seven land neighbours in total (Belarus, Russia, Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, Moldova). This question tests the ability to separate land neighbours from nearby Black Sea or Baltic states. Ukraine is the second largest country wholly in Europe after Russia, with an area of about 603,550 sq km and its capital at Kyiv.

Only three: this would be the answer if, for example, Bulgaria were wrongly assumed to border Ukraine. Bulgaria only shares maritime proximity in the Black Sea; its land neighbours are Romania, Serbia, North Macedonia, Greece and Turkey. The Black Sea littoral states are Ukraine, Russia, Georgia, Turkey, Bulgaria and Romania.

Only four: this would require two of the Czech Republic, Latvia, Lithuania or Bulgaria to border Ukraine, which they do not. The Czech Republic, Poland, Slovakia and Hungary form the Visegrad Group, but only Poland, Slovakia and Hungary of those border Ukraine. The Baltic states border Russia and Belarus but not Ukraine.

Only five: this is far from the truth for this list. It would imply that nearly every listed state borders Ukraine. Ukraine's western neighbours are Poland, Slovakia, Hungary and Romania, plus Moldova in the southwest. Belarus lies to the north, and Russia to the east and northeast, which includes the Russian-occupied Crimea across the Kerch Strait.
related: Ukraine has seven land neighbours: Belarus, Russia, Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, Moldova.
Black Sea littoral states: Ukraine, Russia, Georgia, Turkey, Bulgaria, Romania.
The Montreux Convention (1936) governs passage through the Turkish Straits.
The Kerch Strait connects the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov; Crimea was annexed by Russia in 2014.
The Visegrad Group: Poland, Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia.
The Baltic states: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, all NATO and EU members since 2004.
The Danube flows through ten countries and drains into the Black Sea via Romania and Ukraine.
Finland joined NATO in April 2023 and Sweden in March 2024.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Bulgaria does not share a land border with Ukraine; it is across the Black Sea. Bulgaria is in the Balkans, bordered by Romania (north, along the Danube), Serbia, North Macedonia, Greece and Turkey. It joined NATO in 2004 and the EU in 2007, and uses the lev currency (planned euro adoption from 2026). Capital: Sofia. It has a Black Sea coastline with ports such as Varna and Burgas, so it is a maritime neighbour of Ukraine.

2 — Incorrect: The Czech Republic is landlocked in Central Europe and borders Germany, Poland, Slovakia and Austria. Ukraine lies beyond Poland and Slovakia. It emerged from the 1993 'Velvet Divorce' of Czechoslovakia, joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004, and is part of the Visegrad Group (V4) with Poland, Hungary and Slovakia. Capital: Prague. Currency: koruna, not the euro.

3 — Correct: Hungary shares a short border with Ukraine in the Zakarpattia (Transcarpathia) region, around 135 km. Hungary also borders Slovakia, Romania, Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia and Austria. It joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004, is part of the V4, and its capital is Budapest. The Danube and Tisza are its main rivers. Zakarpattia has a notable ethnic Hungarian minority, which is a recurring diplomatic issue.

4 — Incorrect: Latvia is a Baltic state bordering Estonia, Lithuania, Russia and Belarus, plus the Baltic Sea. It has no border with Ukraine. Capital: Riga. It joined NATO and the EU in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2014. The Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) were Soviet republics that regained independence in 1991.

5 — Incorrect: Lithuania borders Latvia, Belarus, Poland and Russia (Kaliningrad oblast). It does not touch Ukraine. Capital: Vilnius. It was the first Soviet republic to declare independence (1990), joined NATO and the EU in 2004, and adopted the euro in 2015. The Suwałki Gap between Poland and Lithuania links the Baltics to the rest of NATO and is strategically important.

6 — Correct: Romania shares the longest border of any EU/NATO state with Ukraine, over 600 km, running along the Prut, the Danube and the Tisza stretches in the north. It also borders Moldova, Bulgaria, Serbia and Hungary, with a Black Sea coast. The Danube Delta (a UNESCO site) lies partly on the Ukrainian border. Capital: Bucharest. It joined NATO in 2004 and the EU in 2007. Snake Island lies in the Black Sea near the border, and Romania has been a key route for grain and refugee flows.
summary: The answer is (a) Only two. Of the six listed countries, only Hungary and Romania share a land border with Ukraine. Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Latvia and Lithuania do not.
topic_notes: Ukraine is in Eastern Europe, and its geography has been central to UPSC questions because of the Russia-Ukraine war since February 2022. Its capital is Kyiv, its main river is the Dnieper, and the Carpathian Mountains lie in the west. It has an area of about 603,550 sq km. Its land neighbours are Belarus (north), Russia (east and northeast), Poland, Slovakia and Hungary (west), Romania and Moldova (southwest and south). Its southern coasts are on the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, connected by the Kerch Strait; Crimea was annexed by Russia in 2014. Key ports are Odesa, Mariupol and Kherson. The Black Sea is linked to the Mediterranean through the Bosphorus and Dardanelles (Turkey), governed by the 1936 Montreux Convention. Black Sea littoral states: Ukraine, Russia, Georgia, Turkey, Bulgaria, Romania. Ukraine's agriculture, grain exports (the 'breadbasket of Europe'), and the Black Sea Grain Initiative (2022, brokered by the UN and Turkey, lapsed in July 2023) are important. The Danube flows through or along ten countries and reaches the Black Sea through the delta in Romania and Ukraine. Moldova and Transnistria, Donbas (Donetsk, Luhansk), Zaporizhzhia and Kherson are other frequent exam names. Related institutions include NATO (Finland joined in 2023, Sweden in 2024), the EU (Ukraine and Moldova were given candidate status in 2022), the Council of Europe and the Budapest Memorandum (1994), under which Ukraine gave up nuclear weapons. The Baltic states, Poland, Finland and the Nordic countries are other regions typically asked about. UPSC could also ask which countries border Russia, Belarus, Poland or the Black Sea, or the rivers and straits around them.

question: With reference to the Earth’s atmosphere, which one of the following statements is correct? The total amount of insolation
options: received at the equator is roughly about 10 times of that received at the poles
Infrared rays constitute roughly two-thirds of insolation. Infrared waves are largely absorbed
by water vapour that _ is concentrated in the lower atmosphere
Infrared waves are a part of visible spectrum of electromagnetic waves of solar radiation. [ P.T.O
subject: Geography
detail: Insolation is incoming solar radiation, mostly short-wave, spanning ultraviolet (about 7-8%), visible light (about 43-50%) and infrared (about 49-50%) wavelengths. Infrared therefore makes up roughly half of insolation, not two-thirds, and it lies just beyond the red end of the visible spectrum (visible light is about 0.4-0.7 micrometre). Water vapour, carbon dioxide and ozone are the key absorbers. Water vapour absorbs strongly in the infrared bands and is concentrated in the lowest layers: about 90% lies below roughly 5-6 km, in the troposphere, and its amount falls rapidly with height and latitude. That is why the lower atmosphere is heated mainly by terrestrial (long-wave) radiation and by absorption, not directly by the Sun. Latitudinal distribution: the equator receives more insolation than the poles, but the ratio is nowhere near 10 times; annual mean insolation at the poles is about 40-50% of that at the equator, so option (a) is exaggerated. Elimination: (a) wrong ratio, (b) wrong share, (d) wrong category, since infrared is invisible. That leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong: the equator gets more insolation than the poles, but the difference is nowhere near tenfold. Annual poles-to-equator insolation is roughly 40-50%, i.e. the equator gets about 2 to 2.5 times as much.
Wrong: infrared radiation accounts for about 49-50% of insolation, roughly half, not two-thirds. Visible light is about 43-44% and ultraviolet about 7-8%.

Correct: water vapour is a strong absorber of infrared radiation, and it is concentrated in the lower atmosphere (the troposphere, mostly below about 5-6 km), so most infrared absorption occurs there.
Wrong: infrared waves lie outside the visible spectrum, beyond the red end, with wavelengths longer than about 0.7 micrometre. They are felt as heat but cannot be seen.
keyfact: Infrared is about half of insolation, invisible, and is largely absorbed by water vapour in the lower atmosphere (troposphere).
option_notes: Latitudinal insolation variation: insolation is highest near the tropics and equatorial belts (clear skies in subtropical deserts can give even higher surface values than the equator) and lowest at the poles. It depends on the angle of the Sun's rays, the length of the day, atmospheric transparency and the Sun-Earth distance. Perihelion (about 3 January) and aphelion (about 4 July) cause small variations of about 7%. The solar constant is about 1361 W per square metre. Annual polar insolation is about half the equatorial value, not a tenth.

Composition of insolation: the Sun emits mostly short-wave radiation. Approximate shares: ultraviolet 7-8%, visible 43-44%, infrared about 49-50%. Only about 51% of insolation reaches the surface (the 'heat budget'): 35 units are reflected back (albedo about 35%), 17 are absorbed by the atmosphere and 48 are absorbed by the surface. The Earth radiates long-wave terrestrial radiation back, balancing the budget at 100 units.

Water vapour is the most variable and most abundant greenhouse gas, making up 0-4% of the atmosphere by volume. It is concentrated in the troposphere, with most below about 5 km, and decreases from the equator to the poles. It absorbs infrared radiation, produces clouds and precipitation, and stores latent heat. It plays a major role in the natural greenhouse effect and the heat budget, and it raises the temperature of the lower atmosphere.

The electromagnetic spectrum, in order of increasing wavelength, runs: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible (violet to red, about 0.4-0.7 micrometre), infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Infrared was discovered by William Herschel in 1800. It is invisible and is felt as heat. The visible spectrum is VIBGYOR. Infrared is divided into near, mid and far infrared. Terrestrial radiation emitted by the Earth is mostly long-wave infrared.
related: Visible light is about 43-44% of insolation; infrared about 49%; UV about 7%.
Planetary albedo of the Earth is about 35% (0.3).
Normal lapse rate is about 6.5°C per km in the troposphere.
Perihelion is about 3 January; aphelion about 4 July.
Ozone layer in the stratosphere (about 20-30 km) absorbs UV-B and UV-C.
Of 100 units of insolation, 48 are absorbed by the Earth's surface and 17 by the atmosphere.
Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas; about 90% sits below 5-6 km.
Terrestrial radiation is long-wave infrared.
summary: The correct answer is (c): infrared (long-wave and near-infrared) radiation is largely absorbed by water vapour, which is concentrated in the lower atmosphere (troposphere). The other options misstate insolation distribution, the share of infrared, or the nature of infrared waves.
topic_notes: Insolation is the incoming solar radiation intercepted by the Earth, mostly short-wave. The Earth intercepts only about two billionths of the Sun's output. The solar constant is about 1.94 calories per square cm per minute, or about 1361 W per square metre. Factors affecting insolation: the angle of incidence of the rays, the duration of the day, the transparency of the atmosphere, the Sun's output, and the Earth-Sun distance (perihelion about 3 January at about 147 million km, aphelion about 4 July at about 152 million km). Heat budget: of 100 units entering, 35 are reflected back to space (6 from the atmosphere, 27 from clouds and 2 from snow and ice), 17 are absorbed by the atmosphere and 48 by the surface. The surface returns 48 as terrestrial radiation: 17 directly to space, 31 absorbed by the atmosphere, with 14 added by the atmosphere through other pathways, and the budget balances. Latitudes between about 40°N and 40°S show a surplus and the poles a deficit, balanced by winds and ocean currents. Heating of the atmosphere occurs by conduction, convection, advection and terrestrial radiation. The main greenhouse gases are water vapour, CO2, methane, nitrous oxide and ozone. Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs UV, and the ozone layer lies at about 20-30 km. Temperature inversion, the lapse rate (about 6.5°C per km) and the albedo of different surfaces are common themes. Fresh snow has an albedo of about 80-90% and forests about 10-15%. The mean planetary albedo is about 0.3.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement-I : The soil in tropical rain forests is rich in nutrients. .
Statement-II : The high temperature and moisture of tropical rain forests cause dead organic matter in the soil to . decompose quickly. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-Il are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-Il is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
subject: Geography
detail: Tropical rain forests (equatorial regions such as the Amazon, Congo basin and Southeast Asia) have hot, humid conditions, with temperatures around 25-30 degrees C and rainfall above 200 cm. These conditions favour intense microbial and fungal activity, so leaf litter and dead matter decompose within weeks. The nutrients released are absorbed almost immediately by shallow, dense root mats, often helped by mycorrhizal fungi, so most nutrients are stored in living biomass rather than in the soil. Heavy rain also leaches soluble nutrients such as calcium, magnesium and potassium downward (leaching), leaving iron and aluminium oxides. This produces acidic, reddish Oxisols (Ferralsols, or laterite-type soils) that are low in humus and fertility. This is why slash-and-burn (shifting) cultivation fails after a few years and why cleared rainforest land degrades fast. In contrast, temperate and boreal forests have slow decomposition and thicker humus layers. Elimination: Statement-II is clearly true, which removes (c). Statement-I is false, which removes (a) and (b). Only (d) remains.
explanations: Wrong. It requires Statement-I to be correct, but rain forest soils are nutrient-poor, so there is no valid explanation to give.
Wrong. It also treats Statement-I as correct, which it is not.
Wrong. It reverses the truth: Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct.
Correct. Rain forest soil is poor in nutrients because of leaching and rapid uptake, while rapid decomposition under heat and moisture is a true statement.
keyfact: Tropical rain forest soils are nutrient-poor because rapid decomposition, fast plant uptake and heavy leaching keep nutrients in biomass, not soil.
option_notes: Option (a) describes a case where both statements are true and the second explains the first. It would apply to something like a fertile soil produced by fast recycling, but in rain forests the same rapid decomposition actually leaves soil depleted, because nutrients are held in biomass and leached. So the causal link does not hold here. Such an option is typical of UPSC assertion-reason questions, where students must check both truth and causation.

Option (b) says both statements are true but unrelated in causation. It is also wrong here because Statement-I is false. Tropical rain forest soils are low in nutrients. Students should remember the distinction between nutrient stock in biomass (very high) and nutrient stock in soil (low) in tropical rain forests.

Option (c) says Statement-I is true and Statement-II is false. That is the reverse of the real situation. Decomposition in tropical rain forests is very fast because of warmth (25-30 degrees C) and constant moisture, so Statement-II is true. Soils are nutrient-poor, so Statement-I is false. Compare with peat bogs and taiga, where cold or waterlogged conditions slow decomposition and organic matter accumulates.

Option (d) is the correct answer. It states that the nutrient-rich claim is wrong while the rapid decomposition claim is right. Tropical rain forest soils (Oxisols, laterites) are leached, acidic, and low in humus, and most nutrients are locked in the vegetation. Rapid decomposition and uptake explain the thin litter layer and the quick loss of fertility when forests are cleared.
related: Laterite soil forms by leaching in hot, humid climates with alternating wet and dry seasons.
Tropical rain forests hold most nutrients in living biomass, not in soil.
Mollisols (chernozem) of temperate grasslands are among the most fertile soils.
Taiga soils (Spodosols/podzols) are acidic with slow decomposition and thick litter.
Shifting cultivation is called jhum in NE India and is linked to rapid fertility loss.
Decomposition is fastest in warm, moist, well-oxygenated conditions.
Mycorrhizal fungi help rain forest trees absorb nutrients from shallow litter layers.
Amazon basin is the world's largest tropical rain forest.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Rain forest soils are typically nutrient-poor, not nutrient-rich. Most nutrients are held in the biomass and the soil is heavily leached. Oxisols and Ultisols dominate the humid tropics. They are deep, weathered, acidic and rich in iron and aluminium oxides but low in humus, nitrogen, phosphorus and base cations. Fertility is maintained only by a rapid nutrient cycle from litterfall to decomposers to roots. Once the forest is cleared, fertility falls within 2-5 years, which explains the failure of agriculture on cleared Amazon land and the practice of shifting cultivation (jhum in NE India, roca in Brazil).

2 — Correct: High temperature and moisture speed up decomposition by bacteria, fungi and termites, so dead organic matter breaks down quickly. The litter layer in rain forests is thin and short-lived, turning over in a few weeks to months, against years in cold boreal forests. Nutrients are quickly recycled into living plants through shallow roots and mycorrhizal associations. Because humus is mineralised so fast, little accumulates in the soil. Decomposition rate depends on temperature, moisture, oxygen and litter quality, and this tropical speed is the reason for the low humus content.
summary: The answer is (d). Statement-I is incorrect because tropical rain forest soils are generally nutrient-poor, while Statement-II is correct because high temperature and moisture cause rapid decomposition of dead organic matter. The rapid decomposition and fast uptake by vegetation leave little humus or nutrients in the soil.
topic_notes: Tropical rain forests lie roughly between 10 degrees N and 10 degrees S of the equator: the Amazon basin, Congo basin, Southeast Asia and parts of the Western Ghats and NE India. Climate: mean temperature 25-30 degrees C with little seasonal variation, rainfall above 200 cm, high humidity. Vegetation: multi-layered canopy (emergent, canopy, understorey, shrub and forest floor), very high biodiversity, broadleaf evergreens. Soils: Oxisols/Ferralsols and Ultisols, acidic, deeply weathered, with laterite formation through leaching of silica (laterisation) and accumulation of iron and aluminium oxides. Nutrient cycling: closed and rapid, with most nutrients in biomass. Roots are shallow, with buttress roots and mycorrhizae. Litter decomposes in weeks. Consequences: shifting cultivation, soil degradation after deforestation, and laterite soils that harden into bricks on exposure (Latin later, brick). Comparison: temperate deciduous forests have moderate decomposition and brown forest soils (Alfisols); taiga/boreal forests have slow decomposition, thick litter and acidic Spodosols (podzols); grasslands (Mollisols, chernozems) are the most fertile with deep humus; deserts have low organic matter. Related angles for UPSC: Amazon deforestation and carbon sink role, Brazil's role, REDD+, India's laterite soils in Kerala, Karnataka, Odisha and Meghalaya, biogeochemical cycles, decomposers and detritus food chain, litter fall, humus formation, and soil horizons (O, A, B, C).

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement-I : The temperature contrast between continents and oceans is greater during summer than in winter.
Statement-II : The specific heat of water is more than that of land surface. Which one of the following is correct in _ respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct 27 XDTG-F-GST/62A
subject: Economy
detail: Specific heat is the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree C. Water has a high specific heat (about 4186 J/kg/K) compared with land (about 800-1000 J/kg/K). Water also mixes vertically and by currents, is transparent so insolation penetrates to depth, and loses heat by evaporation. Land is opaque, heat stays at the surface, and it has low specific heat, so it heats and cools quickly. The contrast between continents and oceans is therefore set by how much more land responds to the season. In summer, land warms a lot but the sea also warms, and the big continental interiors reach high temperatures. In winter, land cools severely (Siberia, Canada) while oceans keep their heat. The contrast is therefore sharper in winter, especially in the Northern Hemisphere with its large landmasses. Isotherm maps for January show strong bending over the continents, evidence of the greater contrast. This is why the Siberian High and Aleutian and Icelandic Lows are best developed in winter. Elimination: Statement-II is a standard fact, so (c) is out. Statement-I fails, so (a) and (b) are out, leaving (d).
explanations: Wrong. Statement-II is correct, but Statement-I is false, so it cannot be the explanation of a false statement.
Wrong. Statement-I is not correct, because the contrast is greater in winter than in summer.
Wrong. This reverses the truth: Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct.
Correct. The land-ocean contrast is greater in winter, so Statement-I is incorrect, while water's higher specific heat than land makes Statement-II correct.
keyfact: Land-ocean temperature contrast is greatest in winter, not summer, because water's high specific heat keeps oceans warm while land cools sharply.
option_notes: Option (a) says both statements are true and II explains I. This is the usual trap choice for assertion-reason items. It would be right only if the contrast were greater in summer. Here the reasoning is valid for seasonal land-sea thermal behaviour in general, but the claimed observation is wrong, because the contrast is greatest in winter.

Option (b) says both statements are true but II is not the explanation. This pattern is used when both are factual yet unrelated. Here Statement-I is factually wrong, so the option fails. Note that specific heat does genuinely cause land-sea differences, so a student might wrongly think it only partly explains them.

Option (c) says Statement-I is correct and Statement-II incorrect. Statement-II, that water's specific heat exceeds that of land, is a basic physical fact, so this fails. Water has about 4-5 times the specific heat of typical soil or rock, which makes it a natural climate moderator, giving maritime climates and a small annual temperature range.

Option (d) says Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct. This is the official answer. The winter contrast is larger because land loses heat quickly and oceans keep it, while in summer both warm and the difference narrows. The statement on specific heat is a sound physical fact.
related: Specific heat of water is about 4.186 J/g/K, among the highest of common substances.
Northern Hemisphere is about 39% land, and the Southern about 19%.
Siberian High forms in winter over Central Asia, causing the cold dry northeast monsoon.
Annual temperature range is greater in continental interiors than on coasts.
Lapse rate: temperature falls about 6.5 degrees C per 1000 m.
In January, isotherms bend equatorward over northern continents and poleward over oceans.
Sea breeze blows by day from sea to land; land breeze blows by night from land to sea.
Thermal equator lies north of the geographic equator, especially in July.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The land-ocean temperature contrast is greater in winter than in summer. Continents, especially in the Northern Hemisphere, cool strongly in winter while oceans retain heat, and January isotherms show the sharpest deflection. In summer, land warms and narrows the gap. Evidence includes the January temperature extremes of Siberia (Verkhoyansk, Oymyakon) against the relatively mild North Atlantic at the same latitude. The Northern Hemisphere has about 39% land against about 19% in the Southern Hemisphere, so seasonal contrasts and isotherm bending are greater in the north. The winter contrast builds the Siberian High and the oceanic lows, which drive the winter monsoon and the northeast trade-wind flow over India.

2 — Correct: Water's specific heat is higher than that of land, so water takes more heat to warm by 1 degree C and releases it more slowly. Water is about 4.2 J/g/K; dry soil and rock are about 0.8-1.0. Together with transparency, mixing by waves and currents, and evaporative cooling, this makes oceans thermally conservative. This explains maritime versus continental climates, a small annual range of temperature at coastal places such as Mumbai against Delhi, land and sea breezes, and the monsoon's pressure-difference mechanism. It does not, however, explain the claim in Statement-I, which is itself false.
summary: The answer is (d): Statement-I is incorrect, Statement-II is correct. Water's specific heat is higher than land's, so oceans heat and cool slowly, but the land-ocean temperature contrast is greater in winter than in summer, not the other way round.
topic_notes: Heating and cooling of land and water is a core topic in climatology. Land heats and cools quickly, while water heats and cools slowly. Reasons: (1) higher specific heat of water; (2) transparency of water, letting insolation penetrate several metres, whereas land is opaque and heats only at the surface; (3) mixing by waves, tides and currents spreads heat through a deep layer; (4) high evaporation from the sea consumes latent heat; (5) land conducts poorly, so heat stays in a thin layer. Consequences: continentality, with a large annual and diurnal range in interiors (Delhi, Verkhoyansk, Kazakhstan) and a small range on coasts (Mumbai, Chennai, Western Europe). Isotherms bend toward the pole over the oceans and toward the equator over land in winter in the Northern Hemisphere, and the opposite in summer. Because the Northern Hemisphere has more land, its isotherms are more irregular than in the Southern Hemisphere, where they run more or less parallel to latitude. Pressure and winds follow: in summer, land is hot and low-pressure, as with the Indian monsoon trough and the Tibetan heating; in winter, land is cold and high-pressure, as with the Siberian High, which gives the northeast monsoon. Sea and land breezes are daily versions of the same process. Other angles: the Coriolis effect, thermal equator (shifts north in July), temperature inversion, lapse rate (6.5 degrees C per km), albedo, and annual and diurnal range of temperature.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. In a seismograph, P waves are recorded earlier than S waves.
2. In P waves, the individual particles vibrate to and fro in the direction of wave propagation whereas in S waves, the particles vibrate up and down at right angles to the direction of wave propagation. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Earthquakes generate body waves (P and S) that travel through the Earth's interior, and surface waves (Love and Rayleigh) that travel along the surface. P (primary) waves are compressional or longitudinal. Particles move to and fro along the direction the wave travels, producing alternating compressions and rarefactions. They travel at roughly 5-8 km/s in the crust, are the fastest, and pass through solids, liquids and gases. S (secondary) waves are shear or transverse. Particles move at right angles to the direction of travel, producing crests and troughs. They are slower (about 3-4.5 km/s in the crust), pass only through solids, and cannot pass through the liquid outer core. Because P waves are faster, the seismograph records them first, then S waves, then the surface waves, which are slowest but most destructive. The gap between P and S arrivals is used to calculate the distance to the epicentre. The absence of S waves beyond about 103° from the epicentre, together with the P-wave shadow zone (103°-142°), revealed the liquid outer core. Elimination logic: statement 1 is a standard fact, so (b) and (d) go. Statement 2 is the textbook wave-motion description, so (a) goes, leaving (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 2 is also correct. It accurately describes the particle motion of both wave types.
(b) is wrong because statement 1 is also correct. P waves are faster and are recorded before S waves.
(c) is correct because both statements are accurate. P waves arrive first and are longitudinal, while S waves are transverse.
(d) is wrong because both statements are correct, so it cannot be right to say neither is.
keyfact: P waves: longitudinal, fastest, travel through solids, liquids and gases, recorded first. S waves: transverse, slower, solids only, recorded second.
option_notes: Option (a) would make only statement 1 correct. That statement concerns arrival order: P waves, the primary waves, are the fastest body waves and are recorded first, followed by S waves and then surface waves. P waves are longitudinal and pass through solids, liquids and gases. They bend (refract) at the core-mantle boundary, which creates a shadow zone between about 103° and 142° from the epicentre.

Option (b) would make only statement 2 correct. It describes wave motion: P waves are longitudinal, and S waves are transverse, moving perpendicular to the direction of travel. S waves are shear waves, slower than P waves, and pass only through solids. They are absent in the liquid outer core, which creates the S-wave shadow zone covering more than 140° of the globe on the side opposite the epicentre.

Option (c), both 1 and 2, is the official answer. Together the statements capture the basic contrast between P and S waves: speed and arrival order on one hand, and particle motion and wave type on the other. Both are core NCERT facts from Class XI Geography, Chapter 3 (Interior of the Earth). They are frequently tested together with shadow zones and the Earth's layered structure.

Option (d), neither, would mean both statements are false. It is wrong because each statement is a standard, accurate fact. Such options are sometimes the answer when UPSC swaps properties, for example by calling P waves transverse, but no swap occurs here. P waves are longitudinal and arrive first, while S waves are transverse and arrive second.
related: P waves are longitudinal and fastest, while S waves are transverse and slower.
S waves cannot pass through liquids, which indicates the outer core is liquid.
The P-wave shadow zone lies between 103° and 142° from the epicentre.
Surface waves (Love and Rayleigh) are slowest but most destructive.
The Mohorovičić discontinuity separates the crust from the mantle; the Gutenberg discontinuity separates the mantle from the core.
The Richter scale is logarithmic, and the Mercalli scale measures intensity from I to XII.
The BIS divides India into seismic zones II to V, with Zone V the most vulnerable.
The National Centre for Seismology under the Ministry of Earth Sciences monitors earthquakes in India.
statements: 1 — Correct: P waves travel faster than S waves, so they arrive first at a seismograph station. Primary waves have a velocity of about 5-8 km/s in the crust and are faster in denser material. They are longitudinal, travel through solids, liquids and gases, and are less damaging than surface waves. S waves follow, and surface waves arrive last. The P-S time lag is used with travel-time curves to find the epicentral distance, and three stations are used to triangulate the epicentre. A seismograph records ground motion as a seismogram, and the Richter scale and moment magnitude scale are derived from such records.

2 — Correct: P waves are longitudinal, so particles oscillate back and forth along the direction of wave travel, like sound waves or a compressed spring. S waves are transverse, so particles move perpendicular to the direction of propagation, up and down or sideways. S waves are shear waves and cannot travel through fluids because liquids have no shear strength. Their disappearance in the outer core proved it is liquid. Their velocity is about 3-4.5 km/s in the crust. They create crests and troughs in the material they pass through. P waves create density differences, with compressions and rarefactions.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. P waves are the fastest seismic body waves, so they reach a seismograph first. They are longitudinal, with particles vibrating parallel to the direction of propagation. S waves are transverse, with particles vibrating perpendicular to it.
topic_notes: Seismic waves are of two kinds. Body waves originate at the focus (hypocentre) and travel through the interior. Surface waves arise when body waves reach the surface and travel along it. The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above the focus. Body waves: P waves (primary, longitudinal, fastest, pass through all media, compress and expand material parallel to travel) and S waves (secondary, transverse, slower, solids only). Surface waves are the slowest but cause the most damage. They include Love waves (horizontal shear) and Rayleigh waves (rolling, elliptical motion). Wave velocity increases with the density and rigidity of the medium, and waves refract when they pass through layers of differing density. Shadow zones: P waves are not recorded between 103° and 142° from the epicentre, because of refraction at the core. S waves are not recorded beyond 103°, because the outer core is liquid. The shadow zone of S waves is larger than that of P waves. Earth's layers: crust, mantle, core. Discontinuities: Mohorovičić (crust-mantle), Gutenberg (mantle-outer core), Lehmann (outer-inner core). Instruments and scales: the seismograph records ground motion. The Richter scale measures magnitude, which is logarithmic, with each whole-number step representing about 32 times more energy. The Mercalli scale measures intensity, from I to XII. Moment magnitude is now preferred. Indian context: the National Centre for Seismology under the Ministry of Earth Sciences monitors earthquakes, and the BIS divides India into seismic zones II-V, with Zone V the most active. Other possible angles are the Himalayan collision as a source of earthquakes, tsunamis, intraplate versus interplate quakes, and the Koyna earthquake of 1967 as an example of reservoir-induced seismicity.

ocr: With reference to coal-based thermal power plants in India, consider the following statements : 1. None of them uses seawater. 2. None of them is set up in water-stressed district. 3. None of them is privately owned. How many of the above statements are correct? (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) All three (da) None ‘Wolbachia method’ is sometimes talked about with reference to which one of the following? (a) Controlling the viral diseases spread by mosquitoes (b) Converting crop residues into packing material (c) Producing biodegradable plastics (a) Producing biochar from thermo- ’ chemical conver
subject: Geography
detail: Q66 uses the 'None of them' construction, which is false if even one counterexample exists. India's coal-fired capacity (about 210 GW, roughly 50% of installed capacity) is spread across central, state and private owners. Central PSUs include NTPC and DVC; state gencos include MAHAGENCO, UPRVUNL and TANGEDCO; private players include Tata Power, Adani Power, JSW, Sterling and CESC. Coastal plants such as Mundra (Tata Power, Gujarat, supercritical, seawater once-through cooling), Adani Mundra, Tuticorin, Vizag (Simhadri), Ennore and Udupi use seawater for cooling, and some use desalination. Meanwhile, many plants sit in water-stressed regions such as Maharashtra's Vidarbha (Nagpur/Chandrapur), Telangana, Rajasthan (Barmer lignite) and Chhattisgarh/Odisha belts, and studies by CSE and WRI show a large share of capacity faces water stress. Elimination: statement 1 fails via Mundra; statement 2 fails via Vidarbha/Marathwada plants; statement 3 fails via Tata, Adani, JSW. So zero are correct, giving (d).
explanations: (a) Only one: Wrong, because none of the three statements holds; each is disproved by existing plants.
(b) Only two: Wrong, since not even two statements are correct. All three 'None of them' claims fail.
(c) All three: Wrong, because coastal seawater-using, water-stressed-district and privately owned plants all exist.
(d) None: Correct. Each statement is an absolute claim and is falsified by counterexamples (Mundra, Vidarbha plants, Tata/Adani plants).
keyfact: Absolute 'None of them' statements fail on a single counterexample: India has seawater-cooled (Mundra), water-stressed-district and privately owned coal plants, so Q66 = (d).
option_notes: Only one: This would mean exactly one of the 'None of them' claims holds. Such a choice requires a universal truth about all Indian coal plants, and none exists because Indian coal capacity is diverse in location, cooling system and ownership. Capacity is about 210 GW, with central, state and private shares, and plants span coastal and inland sites. It is a frequent UPSC technique: absolute words like 'none' or 'all' make statements risky and usually false.

Only two: This would require two universal claims to be true. In reality, Indian coal plants include coastal seawater-cooled units, plants in drought-prone regions and many privately owned units. Such option patterns test whether students check counterexamples. Knowing a few named plants (Mundra, Chandrapur, Sasan UMPP, Simhadri) is enough to eliminate it. Ownership types are central (NTPC, DVC, NLC), state (gencos) and private (Tata, Adani, JSW).

All three: This would mean no plant uses seawater, none is in a water-stressed district and none is private. It is the opposite of reality. India has private coal plants since the Electricity Act 2003 reforms, seawater-cooled coastal plants, and many inland plants in water-scarce areas. Water consumption by thermal power is a major policy issue, with about 70% of India's electricity from coal, and MoEFCC water norms of 2015 apply.

None: The correct answer for this question, meaning no statement is correct. It rests on counterexamples: Mundra (seawater, private), Vidarbha plants (water-stressed, state/central), Tata and Adani plants (private). The question highlights water-energy nexus issues: thermal plants withdraw large volumes of freshwater, and policies push for treated sewage water, dry cooling and seawater use. Coal is about 55% of installed generation capacity historically and above 70% of generation.
related: India's installed electricity capacity is roughly half coal-based; coal supplies about 70% of generation.
Mundra Ultra Mega Power Project (Tata Power, Gujarat) is a coastal supercritical plant using seawater cooling.
MoEFCC 2015 norms set water limits (3.5 m3/MWh) and tightened SO2, NOx and mercury limits for thermal plants.
2016 Ministry of Power policy mandates treated sewage water for thermal plants within 50 km of an STP.
Electricity Act 2003 delicensed thermal generation and enabled private participation.
NTPC is India's largest power generator (central PSU), headquartered in New Delhi.
Flue Gas Desulphurisation (FGD) is used to cut SO2 emissions from coal plants.
Wolbachia method (Q67) is used to control mosquito-borne viral diseases like dengue: answer (a).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Several coastal plants do use seawater, e.g. Mundra (Tata Power) uses seawater for once-through cooling, and others use desalinated seawater. Detail: Seawater cooling is used where plants are located on the coast, such as Mundra and Sikka in Gujarat, Tuticorin and Ennore in Tamil Nadu, Udupi in Karnataka and Vizag in Andhra Pradesh. Once-through cooling withdraws seawater and returns it warmer, while desalination plants supply boiler make-up water. Inland plants rely on rivers, canals and reservoirs. The 2015 MoEFCC norms limited specific water consumption (3.5 m3/MWh for new plants) and required cooling towers, though seawater plants were exempt from some limits. Using seawater reduces freshwater stress but raises concerns about marine thermal pollution and brine discharge.

2 — Incorrect: Many plants are located in water-stressed districts, for example Nagpur, Chandrapur and Parli in Maharashtra, and plants in Telangana and Rajasthan. Detail: Studies by the Centre for Science and Environment and the World Resources Institute found that over 40% of India's thermal capacity is in high water-stress areas. Coal plants consume roughly 3-5 m3 of water per MWh, mostly for cooling. Maharashtra's Vidarbha and Marathwada have seen plants shut or curtailed during droughts (Parli in 2016). Plants are sited near coal fields in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Madhya Pradesh, not where water is plentiful. This has driven policies on mandatory use of treated sewage water within 50 km of sewage treatment plants (2016 Ministry of Power policy).

3 — Incorrect: Many coal plants are privately owned, for example Tata Power's Mundra, Adani Power's Mundra, Tiroda and Godda, JSW Energy, Sterling and CESC. Detail: India's power sector has central, state and private ownership. Private sector share of installed capacity exceeds 40%, notably in coal capacity added after the Electricity Act 2003 opened generation to private investment (delicensed). Ultra Mega Power Projects (UMPPs) were developed through tariff-based competitive bidding under the Ministry of Power, with special purpose vehicles by PFC and REC; Mundra, Sasan, Tilaiya and Krishnapatnam were awarded to private firms such as Tata, Reliance and Adani. NTPC is the largest central generator, and state gencos remain large too.
summary: The answer is (d) None: all three statements are incorrect. Some Indian coal-based thermal plants do use seawater (coastal plants with seawater cooling or desalination), some are located in water-stressed districts, and many are privately owned.
topic_notes: Coal-based thermal power dominates India's electricity, providing about 70-75% of generation from roughly 210 GW (about half of installed capacity). Plants cluster near coal fields in Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh, with coastal plants in Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. Ownership: central PSUs (NTPC, NLC, DVC, NHPC is hydro), state gencos, and private firms (Tata Power, Adani Power, JSW, Torrent, CESC, Sterling). The Electricity Act 2003 delicensed generation and enabled private participation and competitive bidding. Ultra Mega Power Projects (4,000 MW each, supercritical technology) include Mundra (Tata), Sasan (Reliance), Krishnapatnam, Tilaiya and Sipat-like projects. Water: thermal power is a major industrial water user; specific water consumption was about 3-5 m3/MWh. In December 2015 MoEFCC notified norms limiting consumption to 3.5 m3/MWh for plants with cooling towers, 2.5 m3/MWh for new plants after 2017, and zero liquid discharge. Ministry of Power's 2016 policy mandates use of treated sewage water for plants within 50 km of sewage treatment plants. Emissions: the 2015 norms also set limits for particulate matter, SO2 (FGD installation), NOx and mercury; deadlines have been extended repeatedly. Fly ash utilisation is mandated (notification 1999, amended) and the aim is 100% use. Technology: subcritical, supercritical, ultra-supercritical (higher efficiency, lower water and emissions), and the Advanced Ultra Supercritical programme with NTPC and BHEL. Related: coal gasification, carbon capture, Just Transition, India's pledge of net zero by 2070 and 50% non-fossil capacity by 2030 (achieved in installed capacity terms in 2021-22 pledge updates). Also relevant are the Coal India Ltd, Singareni Collieries, captive coal blocks, commercial coal mining auctions (2020), the Shakti policy (2017) for coal linkages, and PAT/UDAY schemes for discoms.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q67.
ocr: With reference to coal-based thermal power plants in India, consider the following statements : 1. None of them uses seawater. 2. None of them is set up in water-stressed district. 3. None of them is privately owned. How many of the above statements are correct? (a) Only one (b) Only two (c) All three (da) None ‘Wolbachia method’ is sometimes talked about with reference to which one of the following? (a) Controlling the viral diseases spread by mosquitoes (b) Converting crop residues into packing material (c) Producing biodegradable plastics (a) Producing biochar from thermo- ’ chemical conver
subject: Geography
detail: Wolbachia is a naturally occurring, maternally inherited bacterium found in an estimated 50-60% of insect species, including some mosquitoes and butterflies. It is not naturally present in Aedes aegypti, the main vector of dengue, Zika, chikungunya and yellow fever. Scientists therefore microinject it into Aedes eggs. There are two broad strategies. Population replacement: Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes are released, and Wolbachia competes with viruses inside the mosquito, so the mosquito transmits fewer viruses. Because the bacterium passes from mother to offspring, it spreads through the local population. Population suppression: Wolbachia-infected males are released. When they mate with uninfected females, the eggs do not hatch (cytoplasmic incompatibility), so the population crashes. The World Mosquito Program (Monash University, Australia) has run trials in Australia (Townsville), Indonesia (Yogyakarta), Brazil and Colombia, with dengue reductions of up to about 70-77% in some trials. In India, pilot work has been done in Madurai and Pune. Elimination logic: options (b), (c) and (d) concern crop residue, bioplastics and biochar, none of which involve a bacterium–insect symbiosis, so only (a) fits.
explanations: Correct. Wolbachia-infected Aedes mosquitoes transmit dengue, Zika, chikungunya and yellow fever viruses less efficiently, or are suppressed in number, which controls the diseases they spread.
Wrong. Converting crop residue into packing material uses fungal mycelium or pulp technology and has nothing to do with Wolbachia.
Wrong. Biodegradable plastics are made from PHA, PLA, starch or cellulose, often using microbial fermentation, but not Wolbachia.
Wrong. Biochar comes from pyrolysis, the thermochemical conversion of biomass in low oxygen. It is a soil amendment and carbon sink, unrelated to Wolbachia.
keyfact: Wolbachia, a maternally inherited bacterium, is put into Aedes mosquitoes to curb dengue, Zika and chikungunya.
option_notes: Mosquito-borne viral diseases include dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, Japanese encephalitis and West Nile. Aedes aegypti spreads dengue, chikungunya, Zika and yellow fever, while Culex spreads Japanese encephalitis. Malaria is not viral. It is caused by Plasmodium and spread by Anopheles. Control methods include vector control, larvicides, sterile insect technique, gene drives, Oxitec's genetically modified mosquitoes and Wolbachia. Vaccines exist for dengue (Dengvaxia, Qdenga) and yellow fever.

Packing material from crop residue is an eco-friendly alternative to thermocol and plastic. Agricultural waste such as straw or husk is bound with fungal mycelium or moulded into pulp. It addresses stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana and plastic pollution. Related ideas include the Plastic Waste Management Rules, the ban on single-use plastic from 1 July 2022, and in-situ and ex-situ crop residue management schemes.

Biodegradable plastics break down through microbial action into water, CO2 and biomass. Examples are PLA (from corn starch or sugarcane), PHA/PHB (produced by bacteria), starch blends and PBAT. Compostable and biodegradable are not the same, as industrial composting may be needed. India's Plastic Waste Management Rules and the single-use plastic ban promote alternatives. Oxo-degradable plastics only fragment into microplastics.

Biochar is charcoal-like carbon-rich material produced by pyrolysis, heating biomass at about 300-700°C with little or no oxygen. It improves soil fertility and water retention, and it sequesters carbon for centuries. Pyrolysis also yields bio-oil and syngas. Gasification and torrefaction are related thermochemical routes. Biochar is promoted for managing crop residue and for climate-smart agriculture.
related: Wolbachia is a maternally inherited bacterium and is not naturally found in Aedes aegypti.
Cytoplasmic incompatibility makes eggs fail when infected males mate with uninfected females.
The World Mosquito Program started at Monash University, Australia.
Aedes aegypti spreads dengue, Zika, chikungunya and yellow fever.
The sterile insect technique releases irradiated sterile males to reduce a pest population.
Gene drive uses CRISPR to spread a trait quickly through a population and has been tested on malaria vectors.
Biochar is made by pyrolysis of biomass in limited oxygen.
Bti (Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis) is a biological mosquito larvicide.
summary: The answer is (a): the Wolbachia method is used to control mosquito-borne viral diseases such as dengue, chikungunya, Zika and yellow fever. Wolbachia is a common intracellular bacterium. When it is introduced into Aedes aegypti, it reduces the mosquito's ability to transmit these viruses, or it suppresses the mosquito population through cytoplasmic incompatibility.
topic_notes: Wolbachia belongs to the alpha-proteobacteria and lives inside the cells of arthropods and some nematodes. It spreads through the egg cytoplasm, so it is inherited only from the mother. It manipulates host reproduction through cytoplasmic incompatibility, male killing, feminisation and parthenogenesis. Aedes aegypti is not naturally infected, so lab microinjection of the strain wMel, wAlbB or wMelPop is needed. The World Mosquito Program, started at Monash University and led by Scott O'Neill, has run Wolbachia releases in Australia, Indonesia, Brazil, Colombia, Vietnam and Fiji. A randomised trial in Yogyakarta showed about a 77% fall in symptomatic dengue and an 86% fall in hospitalisations. In India, the ICMR and the Vector Control Research Centre (VCRC, Puducherry) have studied Wolbachia, and Madurai and Pune have seen pilot work. Other mosquito-control tools UPSC may ask about include the sterile insect technique (irradiated males), Oxitec's genetically modified OX513A mosquitoes, gene drives (CRISPR-based, tested for Anopheles and malaria), Gambusia fish as larvivorous biocontrol, Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (Bti) as a larvicide, and the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP). Dengue vaccines include Dengvaxia (Sanofi) and Qdenga (Takeda). Also note that Aedes bites by day, Anopheles bites at night, and malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a protozoan.

question:
Consider the following activities :
1. Spreading finely ground basalt rock on farmlands extensively
2. Increasing the alkalinity of oceans by adding lime
3. Capturing carbon dioxide released by various industries and pumping it into abandoned subterranean mines in the form of carbonated waters How many of the above activities are often considered and discussed for carbon capture and sequestration?
subject: Environment
detail: Carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) and the wider carbon dioxide removal (CDR) family cover methods that remove CO2 from the atmosphere or from emission sources and store it durably. Statement 1 is enhanced rock weathering: finely ground silicate rock such as basalt reacts with CO2 and water, forming bicarbonates that eventually reach the ocean, and it also improves soil. Statement 2 is ocean alkalinity enhancement: adding lime or other alkaline minerals raises seawater alkalinity, which increases its capacity to absorb CO2 and also counters ocean acidification. Statement 3 is point-source capture with geological storage. CO2 is dissolved in water and injected into basalt or other formations, where it mineralises into carbonate rock, as in Iceland's CarbFix project. Storage in abandoned mines is also proposed. Because UPSC asks whether the activities are 'often considered and discussed', even approaches that are still experimental qualify. Elimination logic: once a student recognises any two of these as geoengineering or CCS options, only (c) remains. The questions are about discussion, not proven large-scale deployment, so option (d) is untenable.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it undercounts, since all three activities are widely discussed as carbon capture and sequestration methods.
(b) Wrong: each of the three is discussed, so limiting it to two is incorrect. Even the experimental ones, rock weathering and ocean alkalinity, count.
(c) Correct: spreading basalt, ocean alkalinity enhancement and capture with carbonated-water storage underground are all CCS or CDR proposals.
(d) Wrong: none of the three is unrelated to carbon sequestration, and all are active areas of research and policy discussion.
keyfact: Enhanced rock weathering, ocean alkalinity enhancement and mineral or dissolved CO2 storage underground are all discussed CCS or CDR methods, so the answer is all three.
option_notes: Only one: this would be right only if exactly one of the listed activities were a recognised CCS or CDR approach. Such 'count' options are common UPSC distractors. In this question it does not apply because all three methods appear in IPCC and scientific CDR literature. CDR methods include afforestation, BECCS, direct air capture, biochar, enhanced weathering and ocean-based methods.

Only two: this would be right if one activity were not a sequestration method. Students may doubt ocean liming because it is marine and unproven, or doubt mine storage because it is unusual. Both still appear in the literature. Ocean alkalinity enhancement is a marine CDR method, and mineral or dissolved CO2 storage is a geological storage route.

All three: this is the official answer. Enhanced rock weathering, ocean alkalinity enhancement and CO2 injection in dissolved form into underground formations are all discussed as CCS or CDR strategies. They differ in maturity. Geological storage is commercially operating, while weathering and ocean alkalinity are at pilot stage. All are linked to net-zero pathways and geoengineering debates.

None: this would mean no listed activity is considered for carbon sequestration. It is wrong because each is treated by scientists and in the IPCC assessment as a way to remove or store CO2. Choosing it reflects confusion between sequestration and unrelated pollution control, or between an unproven method and an irrelevant one.
related: CCUS means carbon capture, utilisation and storage; CCS stores CO2 without utilisation.
BECCS combines biomass energy with carbon capture and storage, which gives net-negative emissions.
CarbFix in Iceland mineralises injected CO2 into basalt rock.
Ocean alkalinity enhancement also counters ocean acidification.
Stratospheric aerosol injection is solar radiation management and does not remove CO2.
India's net-zero target is 2070, announced at COP26 in Glasgow in 2021.
Blue carbon is carbon stored in mangroves, seagrass and salt marshes.
The Sleipner project in Norway has stored CO2 under the North Sea since 1996.
statements: 1 — Correct: Enhanced rock weathering is a recognised CDR method. Basalt is rich in calcium and magnesium silicates that react with CO2 and water to form stable bicarbonates. Facts: it speeds up a natural process that normally takes thousands of years. Grinding increases the surface area. Farmland application may improve soil pH and crop yields. Concerns include mining energy, transport emissions and heavy metals. Field trials are under way in the UK, US and India. It is often grouped with geoengineering.

2 — Correct: Ocean alkalinity enhancement adds alkaline substances such as lime (calcium hydroxide), olivine or magnesium hydroxide to seawater. This shifts carbonate chemistry so the ocean absorbs more atmospheric CO2 and local acidification is reduced. Facts: oceans hold about 50 times more carbon than the atmosphere. The method is a marine CDR approach, still at pilot and modelling stage. Risks include effects on marine ecosystems, the energy needed to make lime and unresolved governance under the London Protocol.

3 — Correct: This is carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) with geological or mineral storage. CO2 from power plants, cement and steel is captured, dissolved in water and injected underground, where it can mineralise. Facts: Iceland's CarbFix project turns CO2 into carbonate rock within about two years in basalt. Other storage sites are depleted oil and gas fields, saline aquifers and unmineable coal seams. Abandoned mines are proposed as storage. India has a National Mission on CCUS under discussion, and NITI Aayog published a CCUS policy framework in 2022.
summary: The answer is (c) All three. Enhanced rock weathering (basalt on farmland), ocean alkalinity enhancement (adding lime or other alkaline minerals) and industrial CO2 capture with mineral or dissolved storage underground are all discussed as carbon capture and sequestration or carbon dioxide removal options.
topic_notes: Carbon capture and sequestration sits within climate mitigation and the wider carbon dioxide removal (CDR) toolkit. CCS captures CO2 from point sources such as power plants, cement, steel and refineries, transports it by pipeline or ship, and stores it in geological formations: depleted oil and gas fields, deep saline aquifers, unmineable coal seams and basalt formations. CCUS adds utilisation, for example enhanced oil recovery, urea, synthetic fuels and building materials. CDR instead removes CO2 already in the air. Main approaches: afforestation and reforestation, soil carbon, biochar, BECCS (bioenergy with carbon capture and storage), direct air capture with storage (DACCS), enhanced rock weathering and ocean alkalinity enhancement, ocean iron fertilisation and blue carbon. Mineralisation, as at Iceland's CarbFix and the Orca and Mammoth direct-air-capture plants, locks CO2 into rock. The Sleipner project in Norway, running since 1996, was among the first commercial storage projects. The IPCC says CDR is needed to reach net zero and limit warming to 1.5°C. Solar radiation management, such as stratospheric aerosol injection, is a different category of geoengineering: it alters the planet's energy balance and does not remove carbon. India's actions: net-zero target for 2070 announced at COP26, the National Green Hydrogen Mission, NITI Aayog's 2022 CCUS report, and pilot CCUS projects at institutions and public-sector companies such as NTPC and ONGC. Risks and criticisms include cost, energy penalties, leakage, moral hazard (delaying emission cuts) and governance gaps for ocean-based work under the London Convention and Protocol. UPSC may ask about the definitions of these terms, differences between CCS and CCUS, BECCS, blue carbon, and geoengineering types.

ocr: ‘Aerial metagenomics’ best refers to which one of the following situations? (a) Collecting DNA samples from air in a habitat at one go (b) Understanding the genetic makeup of avian species of a habitat (c) Using air-borne devices to collect blood samples from moving animals (a) Sending drones to inaccessible areas to collect plant and animal samples from land surfaces and water bodies Microsatellite DNA’ is used in the case of which one of the following? (a) Studying the evolutionary relationships among various species of fauna (b) Stimulating ‘stem cells’ to transform into diverse functional
subject: Environment
detail: Metagenomics is the direct sequencing of the total genetic material in an environmental sample, with no need to isolate or culture individual organisms. Aerial metagenomics applies this to air. Air is filtered or pumped through collectors, the trapped particles (pollen, fungal spores, bacteria, viruses, shed cells, dust, droplets) are extracted for DNA, and the DNA is sequenced and matched against reference databases. This gives a snapshot of biodiversity, pathogens and allergens in a habitat. Its uses include non-invasive biodiversity monitoring, tracking airborne pathogens and antimicrobial-resistance genes, detecting crop diseases, and studying bioaerosols in cities and hospitals. The key ideas to remember are environmental DNA (eDNA), a bulk sample taken all at once, and the absence of any direct handling of organisms. Elimination logic: (b) is about avian genetics, but 'aerial' here refers to air as the sampling medium, not birds. (c) involves blood samples from animals, which is invasive and not metagenomic. (d) describes drone-based sampling of land and water, which is not about airborne DNA. Only (a) matches both 'aerial' (air) and 'metagenomics' (community DNA at once).
explanations: Correct. Aerial metagenomics samples airborne eDNA from a habitat in one collection and sequences the mixed DNA to identify the many organisms present.
Wrong. It is not limited to birds. 'Aerial' refers to the air as the sampling medium, not to avian species, and the technique profiles all organisms whose DNA is in the air.
Wrong. Collecting blood from moving animals is direct, invasive, single-species sampling. Metagenomics is community-level and typically non-invasive.
Wrong. Drones may be used for sampling, but collecting plant and animal samples from land and water is conventional sampling, not DNA from the air.
keyfact: Aerial metagenomics = sequencing airborne environmental DNA collected from the air in one go to identify the organisms in a habitat.
option_notes: Collecting airborne DNA: air is filtered or pumped through collectors to trap bioaerosols such as pollen, spores, microbes and shed cells. The DNA is extracted and sequenced in bulk to identify species. It is a non-invasive eDNA method used for biodiversity surveys, pathogen surveillance, allergen tracking and monitoring antimicrobial-resistance genes. Recent studies in Europe and elsewhere have shown that air can reveal plants, fungi and even vertebrates in an area.

Genetic makeup of avian species: this falls under avian genomics or population genetics. Methods include sequencing feathers, blood or tissue, DNA barcoding and microsatellite analysis. Work such as the Bird 10K (B10K) genome project aims to sequence all bird species. This is species-specific genetics and has nothing to do with sampling air, so it does not define aerial metagenomics.

Using airborne devices to collect blood: this resembles wildlife research using drones or tags to sample animals, for example blowhole exhalate (snot) collection from whales with drones. Blood sampling is direct and invasive, and covers one animal at a time. It is not metagenomics, which sequences mixed DNA from an environmental sample.

Drones to inaccessible areas: drones are increasingly used for remote sensing, wildlife census, mapping and collecting samples from hazardous or remote places such as glaciers, wetlands and cliffs. Collecting plant and animal samples from land and water is conventional field sampling, not airborne eDNA sequencing.
related: Metagenomics sequences total DNA from an environmental sample without culturing organisms.
eDNA is genetic material shed by organisms into water, soil or air.
16S rRNA sequencing is used to identify bacteria and archaea; ITS is used for fungi.
DNA barcoding commonly uses the COI gene for animals.
Microsatellites (STRs) are short repeated DNA sequences used in forensics and population genetics.
GenomeIndia project aims to sequence 10,000 Indian genomes; the data is hosted at IBDC, Faridabad.
Human Genome Project was completed in 2003.
Bioaerosols are airborne particles of biological origin such as pollen, spores and microbes.
summary: The answer is (a): 'Aerial metagenomics' means collecting DNA samples from the air in a habitat at one go. The air carries environmental DNA (eDNA) from pollen, spores, microbes, skin cells and other biological traces. Sequencing it all together (metagenomics) shows which species are present without capturing or observing them.
topic_notes: Metagenomics is the study of the collective genomes of all organisms in an environmental sample, bypassing the need to culture them. Most microbes cannot be cultured in the lab, which is why the approach became so important. The term was coined around 1998 by Jo Handelsman and colleagues. Typical workflow: sample collection, DNA extraction, shotgun sequencing or amplicon sequencing (16S rRNA for bacteria, ITS for fungi, COI for animals), bioinformatic assembly, and taxonomic and functional annotation. Environmental DNA (eDNA) is DNA shed by organisms into soil, water, snow or air. eDNA metabarcoding is used to detect rare, invasive or elusive species, for example fish in rivers or mammals in forests, without capturing them. Aerial eDNA studies, such as those in Copenhagen and in Australia, showed that air samples can reveal plants, fungi, insects and vertebrates. Applications: biodiversity monitoring and conservation, tracking airborne pathogens such as SARS-CoV-2, hospital air surveillance, agriculture (crop pathogen detection), forensic and climate studies, and bioprospecting for enzymes and antibiotics from microbial communities. Related techniques UPSC may ask about: DNA barcoding (a short standard gene region identifies species), DNA fingerprinting (VNTR/STR analysis), microsatellites (short tandem repeats used in population genetics and forensics), CRISPR-Cas9 (gene editing), PCR (amplifying DNA), next-generation sequencing, and the Human Genome Project (completed 2003). Indian context: the Biological Diversity Act 2002, National Biodiversity Authority (Chennai), the Indian Biological Data Centre (IBDC) at Faridabad, the GenomeIndia project (10,000 genomes), and the Earth BioGenome Project aiming to sequence all eukaryotic life.

note: This image may contain more than one question. Answer Q70.
ocr: ‘Aerial metagenomics’ best refers to which one of the following situations? (a) Collecting DNA samples from air in a habitat at one go (b) Understanding the genetic makeup of avian species of a habitat (c) Using air-borne devices to collect blood samples from moving animals (a) Sending drones to inaccessible areas to collect plant and animal samples from land surfaces and water bodies Microsatellite DNA’ is used in the case of which one of the following? (a) Studying the evolutionary relationships among various species of fauna (b) Stimulating ‘stem cells’ to transform into diverse functional
subject: Environment
detail: Microsatellites, also called Simple Sequence Repeats (SSRs) or Short Tandem Repeats (STRs), are tandemly repeated DNA motifs of 1-6 base pairs (for example CACACA) found throughout eukaryotic genomes, mostly in non-coding regions. They are highly polymorphic because of replication slippage, which changes the number of repeats. They are co-dominant, inherited in a Mendelian way, and detected by PCR. These traits make them excellent markers for phylogenetics, population structure, gene flow, kinship, conservation genetics (for example tiger, elephant and snow leopard censuses from scat or hair DNA), wildlife forensics and DNA fingerprinting. Elimination: (b) stem cell differentiation is controlled by growth factors, transcription factors and epigenetic cues, not by microsatellites. (c) Clonal propagation of horticultural plants uses tissue culture, cuttings or grafting. (d) Drug efficacy trials are clinical trials that use statistical designs; pharmacogenomics may use SNPs, but microsatellites are not the tool that defines trials. Only (a) matches the established use of the marker. The official answer is (a).
explanations: Correct. Microsatellite polymorphism lets researchers compare genetic distance, divergence and relatedness among species and populations of fauna, so it is used in evolutionary and phylogenetic studies.
Wrong. Turning stem cells into different tissues relies on induction by growth factors, signalling molecules, transcription factors and epigenetic control. Microsatellite DNA has no role in this.

Wrong. Clonal propagation of horticultural plants is done by tissue culture, cuttings, layering and grafting. Microsatellites can at most check clonal fidelity, but they are not what 'promotes' propagation.

Wrong. Drug efficacy trials are clinical trials with phases and control groups. Microsatellites are not the basis of such assessment, and the option confuses a population trial with a molecular marker.
keyfact: Microsatellite DNA = short tandem repeats (SSRs/STRs), highly polymorphic markers used for phylogeny, population genetics, conservation and DNA fingerprinting; the answer is (a).
option_notes: Studying evolutionary relationships among species is the field of molecular phylogenetics. It uses markers such as mitochondrial DNA (cytochrome b, COI barcodes), rRNA genes, SNPs and microsatellites to build phylogenetic trees. Microsatellites suit recent divergence and population-level questions. Fauna examples include tiger population genetics in India, Asiatic lion genetic diversity and elephant individual identification from dung.

Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can self-renew and differentiate. Types include embryonic (pluripotent), adult or somatic (multipotent) and induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), created by Yamanaka in 2006 using Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc. Differentiation is guided by culture factors and gene regulation. Uses include bone marrow transplants, regenerative medicine and disease modelling. In India, ICMR and DBT issue stem cell research guidelines.

Clonal propagation is vegetative multiplication that produces genetically identical plants. Methods include cuttings, layering, grafting and budding, and micropropagation by tissue culture (explants, callus, totipotency; Murashige and Skoog medium). It is used for banana, orchids, potato, sugarcane and apple rootstocks. It gives disease-free, uniform plants. Molecular markers like SSRs or RAPD can check genetic uniformity afterwards.

Drug efficacy is assessed in clinical trials: Phase I (safety), Phase II (efficacy and dose), Phase III (large-scale confirmation), Phase IV (post-marketing surveillance). In India, the CDSCO under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 regulates trials, and the CTRI registers them. Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled designs are the gold standard. Pharmacogenomics may use genetic markers, but the trial itself is a clinical and statistical exercise.
related: Microsatellites are STRs, repeats of 1-6 bp, and are highly polymorphic markers.
Minisatellites (VNTRs) have 10-60 bp repeats and were used in Jeffreys' DNA fingerprinting (1984).
The CODIS forensic database uses STR loci.
Huntington's disease and fragile X syndrome result from trinucleotide repeat expansions.
PCR was developed by Kary Mullis (1983), and Taq polymerase comes from Thermus aquaticus.
DNA barcoding uses COI for animals and rbcL plus matK for plants.
iPSCs were created by Shinya Yamanaka in 2006.
GenomeIndia project aims to sequence 10,000 Indian genomes.
summary: The answer is (a). Microsatellite DNA consists of short tandem repeats (STRs) that mutate quickly and vary between species and individuals, so it is a standard marker for studying evolutionary and phylogenetic relationships, population genetics and diversity among species of fauna.
topic_notes: Microsatellites (SSRs/STRs) are repeats of 1-6 bp units, such as (CA)n, scattered across genomes. Their high mutation rate (about 10^-3 to 10^-5 per locus per generation) arises from replication slippage, and this produces length polymorphism. They are co-dominant, abundant, reproducible, and typed by PCR with flanking primers and gel or capillary electrophoresis. Minisatellites, also called VNTRs, have 10-60 bp repeat units and were used in Alec Jeffreys' original DNA fingerprinting in 1984-85. Satellite DNA has much longer repeats, is found near centromeres and is used in density-gradient separation. Applications: (1) phylogenetics and population genetics of animals and plants; (2) conservation, where individuals are identified non-invasively from scat, hair or feathers, as in tiger estimation by NCBS and WII; (3) forensics, where the CODIS system uses 20 STR loci, and paternity testing; (4) crop breeding, where marker-assisted selection and QTL mapping are done; (5) genetic disease studies, where trinucleotide repeat expansions cause Huntington's disease, fragile X syndrome and myotonic dystrophy. Other markers: SNPs (single base changes, used in GWAS and the 1000 Genomes Project), RFLP, RAPD, AFLP, mtDNA (maternally inherited), Y-chromosome markers, and DNA barcoding (COI for animals; rbcL and matK for plants). Related biotechnology topics: eDNA, metagenomics (including aerial metagenomics, Q69), CRISPR-Cas9, PCR (Kary Mullis, 1983), the Human Genome Project (completed 2003, with the telomere-to-telomere sequence in 2022), the GenomeIndia project (10,000 genomes, 2020 onwards), and the DNA Technology (Use and Application) Regulation Bill.

question:
Consider the following statements with reference to India : ‘
1. According to the ‘Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (MSMED) Act, 2006’, the ‘medium enterprises’ are those with investments in plant and machinery between 715 crore and 25 crore.
2. All bank loans to the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises qualify * under the priority sector. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: The MSMED Act, 2006 originally classified enterprises by investment in plant and machinery (manufacturing) or equipment (services). Medium manufacturing enterprises had investment above Rs 5 crore and up to Rs 10 crore. The figure of Rs 15-25 crore in statement 1 is wrong. The classification was revised under the Atmanirbhar Bharat package in May 2020, effective 1 July 2020. It now combines investment and turnover: micro is up to Rs 1 crore investment and Rs 5 crore turnover, small is up to Rs 10 crore investment and Rs 50 crore turnover, and medium is up to Rs 50 crore investment and Rs 250 crore turnover. The distinction between manufacturing and services was removed. Under the RBI Priority Sector Lending (PSL) guidelines, all bank loans to micro, small and medium enterprises, both manufacturing and services, qualify for PSL irrespective of the loan size. The earlier loan-size caps applied to services-sector MSMEs but were removed. Elimination logic: statement 1 uses figures that match neither the original Act nor the revised limits, so it is incorrect. Statement 2 is correct, so only (b) fits.
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because the medium-enterprise investment limits are Rs 5-10 crore (original Act) or up to Rs 50 crore (2020 revision), not Rs 15-25 crore.
Right: statement 1 is incorrect and statement 2 is correct, since all bank credit to MSMEs counts as priority sector lending.
Wrong: statement 1 is false, so 'Both' cannot be correct.
Wrong: statement 2 is true, so 'Neither' is incorrect.
