keyfact: MSMED Act 2006 medium enterprise (manufacturing): Rs 5-10 crore investment; since 2020 up to Rs 50 crore investment and Rs 250 crore turnover; all MSME bank loans count as priority sector.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would mean the Rs 15-25 crore definition is right and PSL does not cover all MSME loans. Neither holds. The actual medium enterprise limits are Rs 5-10 crore (2006 Act, manufacturing) and up to Rs 50 crore investment with Rs 250 crore turnover (from 2020). Knowing both sets of figures helps in any definition-based question.

Option (b), '2 only', is the official answer. It reflects RBI's PSL framework, in which all lending to micro, small and medium enterprises qualifies as priority sector without a loan-size cap. PSL targets are 40% of ANBC for commercial banks and 75% for RRBs. Related terms are PSLCs, ANBC, and the sub-targets for agriculture, micro enterprises and weaker sections.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', fails because statement 1 uses incorrect numbers. The MSMED Act, 2006 defined medium manufacturing enterprises as having investment of Rs 5-10 crore in plant and machinery. A candidate who knows only that PSL covers MSMEs and guesses the thresholds would be misled into this option.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', fails because statement 2 is correct. RBI's master directions on priority sector lending include loans to all MSMEs, both manufacturing and services. The loan-size limits once applied to the services sector were removed. Priority sector status is a standing feature of Indian bank regulation, with periodic RBI revisions to targets and categories.
related: Since 1 July 2020, MSME classification uses both investment and turnover criteria.
Medium enterprise today: investment up to Rs 50 crore and turnover up to Rs 250 crore.
Udyam Registration replaced Udyog Aadhaar from 1 July 2020.
PSL target: 40% of ANBC for commercial banks; 75% for RRBs.
PSL agriculture sub-target is 18% of ANBC; micro enterprises 7.5%.
CGTMSE gives collateral-free credit guarantee cover to MSE loans.
SIDBI is the apex financial institution for MSME financing.
Exports turnover is excluded when computing MSME turnover limits.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Under the original Act, medium manufacturing enterprises had investment of Rs 5-10 crore, and under the 2020 revision up to Rs 50 crore, so Rs 15-25 crore matches neither. The MSMED Act, 2006 came into force on 2 October 2006 and replaced the earlier concept of 'small scale industries'. It defined micro, small and medium enterprises separately for manufacturing and services. Manufacturing was judged by investment in plant and machinery, and services by investment in equipment. It also created the National Board for MSMEs. The Ministry of MSME administers it. Since 1 July 2020, a composite criterion of investment plus turnover applies. Exports turnover is excluded from the turnover calculation. Udyam Registration is the online registration route.

2 — Correct: RBI's PSL master directions treat all bank lending to MSMEs (manufacturing and services) as priority sector, with no cap on loan size. Priority sector categories are agriculture, MSME, export credit, education, housing, social infrastructure, renewable energy, and weaker sections. The targets are 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) for domestic commercial banks and small finance banks, and 75% for regional rural banks. Sub-targets include agriculture at 18%, small and marginal farmers at 10%, micro enterprises at 7.5%, and weaker sections at 12%. PSL shortfalls go into funds such as the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) at NABARD. Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSLCs) allow banks to trade their PSL achievement.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. Under the MSMED Act, 2006 as it stood in 2023, a medium enterprise was one with investment in plant and machinery between Rs 5 crore and Rs 10 crore, not Rs 15-25 crore. All bank loans to MSMEs qualify as priority sector lending under RBI norms.
topic_notes: The MSMED Act, 2006 is the legal framework for MSMEs in India. It took effect on 2 October 2006, replacing the older small-scale industry concept under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act framework. The original classification: manufacturing micro up to Rs 25 lakh, small up to Rs 5 crore, medium up to Rs 10 crore, all on plant and machinery investment. For services, equipment-based limits were Rs 10 lakh, Rs 2 crore and Rs 5 crore. In 2020 the Atmanirbhar Bharat package revised this with a composite test. Micro: investment up to Rs 1 crore and turnover up to Rs 5 crore. Small: investment up to Rs 10 crore and turnover up to Rs 50 crore. Medium: investment up to Rs 50 crore and turnover up to Rs 250 crore. The manufacturing/services distinction was dropped. Udyam Registration, launched on 1 July 2020, replaced Udyog Aadhaar. The Ministry of MSME runs schemes such as PMEGP (credit-linked subsidy), the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE), SFURTI (traditional industry clusters), the MSME Champions scheme, and the Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme. SIDBI is the principal financial institution for MSME financing. The TReDS platform facilitates invoice discounting for MSME receivables. The Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) was launched during COVID-19. On priority sector lending: RBI defines the categories, and targets are 40% of ANBC for domestic scheduled commercial banks and foreign banks with 20 or more branches, and 75% for RRBs and small finance banks. Sub-targets cover agriculture, micro enterprises and weaker sections. Shortfalls are deposited in RIDF and similar funds with NABARD, NHB and SIDBI. PSLCs allow banks to buy and sell surplus achievement. Likely future angles: the Udyam portal, definition thresholds, CGTMSE coverage, and the sectoral composition of PSL.

question:
With reference to Central Bank digital currencies, consider the following statements :
1. It is possible to make payments in a digital currency without using US dollar or SWIFT system.
2. A_ digital currency can_ be distributed with a _ condition programmed into it such as a timeframe for spending it. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: A Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) is the legal tender of a country in digital form, issued and backed directly by the central bank. It is a liability of the central bank, unlike cryptocurrencies, which are private and unbacked, and unlike stablecoins, which are backed by private reserves. The RBI defines it as the digital form of legal tender issued by a central bank in the same denomination as fiat currency. India launched the e-rupee (e₹) pilots in November-December 2022: wholesale (e₹-W) on 1 November 2022 and retail (e₹-R) on 1 December 2022. Statement 1 is correct because a domestic CBDC settles in the home currency on the central bank's own ledger. Cross-border CBDC platforms such as mBridge (BIS Innovation Hub with the central banks of China, Hong Kong, Thailand and the UAE) can bypass dollar correspondent banking and SWIFT messaging. Statement 2 is correct because digital money can be programmable. China's e-CNY pilots have used expiring digital vouchers and stimulus coupons that must be spent within a set period. Elimination logic: once either statement is seen to be true, options (a), (b) and (d) fall away, and since both hold, (c) is the answer.
explanations: Wrong: it says only statement 1 is correct, but statement 2 is also true because CBDCs can be programmed with conditions such as expiry.
Wrong: it says only statement 2 is correct, but statement 1 is also true because CBDCs can settle payments without the dollar or SWIFT.
Correct: both statements are true. CBDCs can operate outside dollar and SWIFT rails, and they can be programmed with spending conditions.
Wrong: neither-correct is false because both statements describe real, documented features of CBDCs.
keyfact: CBDC = central bank-issued digital legal tender; it can bypass dollar/SWIFT rails and be programmable (e.g., expiry dates); India's e-rupee pilots began in Nov-Dec 2022.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only: statement 1 on its own is true, since CBDCs can settle payments without the dollar or SWIFT, as in mBridge. Choosing it would ignore programmability. A CBDC is the central bank's digital liability, and legal tender status is conferred by law. India's e-rupee pilots started in late 2022. This option is incomplete.

Option (b), statement 2 only: statement 2 on its own is true, since programmable money allows conditions such as an expiry or a restricted use. Examples include the e-CNY vouchers and e-rupee use cases for targeted subsidies. But statement 1 is also true, so this option is incomplete. Programmability is a design choice, and cash cannot do this.

Option (c), both 1 and 2: this is the official answer. A CBDC is central bank-issued digital legal tender, either retail (for the public) or wholesale (for interbank settlement). Features include direct central bank backing, possible programmability, and the potential for cross-border settlement outside SWIFT. India's pilots launched in 2022 (wholesale on 1 November, retail on 1 December). The RBI says it aims to complement cash, not replace it.

Option (d), neither: this is false, since both statements are accurate. It would apply only if CBDCs were tied to the dollar or SWIFT and could not carry conditions. CBDCs differ from cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, which are decentralised and unbacked, and from private stablecoins. UPSC often tests such distinctions.
related: India's retail e-rupee pilot launched on 1 December 2022; the wholesale pilot started on 1 November 2022.
The Bahamas Sand Dollar (2020) was the first fully launched CBDC.
Nigeria's eNaira launched in October 2021.
China's e-CNY is among the largest CBDC pilots, with programmable vouchers.
Project mBridge is a BIS multi-CBDC cross-border platform with China, Hong Kong, Thailand and the UAE.
SWIFT is a Belgium-based messaging system founded in 1973; it does not hold funds.
CBDC is a central bank liability, whereas cryptocurrency is private and unbacked.
The digital rupee was announced in Union Budget 2022-23.
statements: 1 — Correct: CBDCs can be used for payments without the US dollar or SWIFT, since they are settled directly in the issuing central bank's currency and can be linked bilaterally or through multi-CBDC platforms. Facts: SWIFT (Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication) is a Belgium-based messaging network founded in 1973 that carries payment instructions between banks but does not move money itself. Russian banks were cut off from it in 2022, which spurred interest in alternatives. Project mBridge (BIS Innovation Hub, Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Bank of Thailand, PBoC, and the UAE central bank) tests direct cross-border CBDC settlement. India's CBDC pilot is domestic, and the RBI has also explored cross-border use. Dollar-based correspondent banking is therefore not essential to a CBDC.

2 — Correct: CBDCs can be programmable, meaning rules or conditions can be coded into the digital currency, such as an expiry date, a permitted merchant category, or a purpose restriction. Facts: China's e-CNY pilots distributed digital red packets and vouchers that had to be spent within a fixed period. The RBI's e-rupee pilot has explored programmability for targeted subsidy delivery and for use cases such as the Digital Rupee for government benefits. Programmability differs from cash, which is anonymous and unconditional. It raises concerns about privacy, state control and surveillance. Smart contracts on distributed ledgers or tokens are the usual technical means.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. A CBDC is a digital form of a country's fiat currency issued by its central bank, so it can settle payments without the US dollar or SWIFT, and it is programmable, so conditions such as an expiry or spending window can be built into it.
topic_notes: A Central Bank Digital Currency is a digital form of a country's fiat currency, issued and regulated by the central bank. It is a direct claim on the central bank and counts as legal tender. It differs from cryptocurrencies (decentralised, private, volatile, with no issuer backing) and from stablecoins (privately issued and pegged to assets). Types: retail CBDC (for households and businesses) and wholesale CBDC (for interbank and financial institution settlement). Models: token-based or account-based; direct, indirect or hybrid distribution. India: the RBI announced the digital rupee in the Union Budget 2022-23 (the income tax and RBI Act amendments enabled it). The wholesale pilot began on 1 November 2022 for government securities settlement, and the retail pilot began on 1 December 2022 in four cities (Mumbai, New Delhi, Bengaluru, Bhubaneswar). The RBI's concept note in October 2022 explained the design. The e-rupee can be held in digital wallets, and the pilot offered offline functionality later. Global examples: the Bahamas Sand Dollar (October 2020, the first full launch), Nigeria's eNaira (October 2021), Jamaica's JAM-DEX, and China's e-CNY (pilots from 2020). The BIS Innovation Hub runs Project mBridge and others. Benefits: lower settlement costs, financial inclusion, reduced reliance on cash, and faster cross-border payments. Risks: bank disintermediation, cybersecurity, privacy and surveillance concerns. Related: UPI is a payment system, not a currency, and it moves existing bank money. Payments Systems Act, 2007 is the legal framework for payment systems, and SWIFT is a messaging network.

ocr: In the context of finance, the term ‘beta’ refers to (a) the process of simultaneous buying and selling of an asset from different platforms (b) an investment strategy of a portfolio manager to balance risk versus reward (c) a type of systemic risk that arises where perfect hedging is not possible (ad) a numeric value that measures the fluctuations of a stock to changes in the overall stock market [ P.T.0.
subject: Economy
detail: Beta (β) is a core concept of the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), developed in the 1960s by William Sharpe, John Lintner and Jack Treynor. It is calculated as the covariance of a stock's returns with the market's returns divided by the variance of the market's returns, and is often estimated by regressing stock returns on index returns such as the Nifty 50 or Sensex. The market itself has a beta of 1. A stock with beta greater than 1 is more volatile than the market (aggressive), a beta below 1 means it is less volatile (defensive), a beta of 0 means no correlation with the market, and a negative beta means it moves opposite to the market (gold is sometimes cited). CAPM uses it as: expected return = risk-free rate + beta × (market return − risk-free rate). Beta captures only systematic, non-diversifiable risk, not company-specific risk. Elimination: (a) describes arbitrage; (b) describes a general portfolio balancing or asset allocation strategy; (c) misdescribes beta, because beta measures sensitivity to market movement and has nothing to do with hedging being impossible. Only (d) matches.
explanations: Wrong: simultaneous buying and selling of an asset on different platforms to profit from price differences is arbitrage, not beta.
Wrong: balancing risk and reward is the aim of portfolio management and asset allocation (for example diversification). Beta is a measurement, not a strategy.
Wrong: beta does measure systematic risk exposure, but it is not a type of risk arising where perfect hedging is impossible. It is a numerical sensitivity measure.
Correct: beta is a numeric coefficient measuring the volatility of a stock or portfolio relative to the overall market, so it shows how the stock fluctuates with market changes.
keyfact: Beta = a stock's sensitivity to overall market movements (market beta = 1); it measures systematic risk in CAPM.
option_notes: Arbitrage is the simultaneous purchase and sale of the same or similar asset in different markets or platforms to exploit price differences and earn a nearly risk-free profit. It keeps prices aligned across markets, as with the same stock on NSE and BSE, or in currency and commodity markets. Types include spatial, triangular (currency), statistical and merger arbitrage. Arbitrageurs improve market efficiency and liquidity. The Arbitrage Pricing Theory (Stephen Ross, 1976) is an alternative to CAPM.

This describes portfolio management, which includes asset allocation, diversification and risk-return optimisation. Modern Portfolio Theory (Harry Markowitz, 1952, Nobel 1990) shows that diversification can reduce risk for a given return, giving the efficient frontier. Strategies can be active or passive. Metrics used include standard deviation, the Sharpe ratio, alpha and beta. In India, portfolio managers are regulated by SEBI under the SEBI (Portfolio Managers) Regulations, 2020.

Systematic (market) risk affects the entire market, for example from interest rate changes, inflation, recessions, wars or policy shocks. It cannot be removed by diversification, unlike unsystematic (specific) risk. Hedging with derivatives such as futures and options can reduce exposure to it but rarely eliminates it. Beta is the usual measure of a stock's exposure to systematic risk. The option confuses these ideas and is not a definition of beta.

Beta is a coefficient measuring a security's sensitivity to market movements, calculated as Cov(Ri, Rm)/Var(Rm). Market beta is 1. Beta above 1 means higher volatility than the market, and below 1 means lower volatility. It is central to CAPM, used to estimate the cost of equity. Beta does not capture company-specific risk and depends on the benchmark and time period used. Alpha measures excess return over what beta predicts.
related: Beta of the overall market is 1.
CAPM: expected return = risk-free rate + beta × market risk premium.
Beta measures systematic (non-diversifiable) risk; diversification removes unsystematic risk.
Alpha is the excess return over the benchmark or CAPM-expected return.
India VIX, calculated by NSE, measures expected market volatility.
Harry Markowitz is the father of Modern Portfolio Theory (1952).
Arbitrage is profiting from price differences of the same asset in different markets.
SEBI regulates Portfolio Managers under the 2020 regulations.
summary: The answer is (d). In finance, beta is a numeric value that measures how much a stock's returns fluctuate relative to changes in the overall market, and so it is a measure of systematic (market) risk.
topic_notes: Risk and return measures in finance are a recurring UPSC theme. Systematic risk (market risk) comes from macroeconomic factors and cannot be diversified away. Unsystematic risk is specific to a firm or sector and can be reduced by diversification. Beta measures systematic risk. CAPM, developed by Sharpe, Lintner and Treynor, states: expected return = Rf + β(Rm − Rf), where (Rm − Rf) is the market risk premium. The Security Market Line plots this relationship. Related measures: Alpha is the excess return over the benchmark or CAPM expectation. The Sharpe ratio is excess return per unit of total risk (standard deviation). The Treynor ratio is excess return per unit of beta. Standard deviation measures total volatility. Value at Risk (VaR) estimates the potential loss at a given confidence level. The VIX, India VIX in India, is the 'fear index' that measures expected market volatility from options prices. Interpretation of beta: β = 1 moves with the market, β > 1 is aggressive (for example, many tech and cyclical stocks), 0 < β < 1 is defensive (FMCG, utilities), β = 0 is uncorrelated (cash), and β < 0 is inversely correlated. Index funds and ETFs aim to replicate the market, giving a beta near 1. The term 'smart beta' refers to rules-based strategies that tilt a portfolio toward factors such as value, momentum or low volatility. Regulators and institutions: SEBI regulates Indian securities markets, and the NSE and BSE are the main exchanges. Benchmarks include the Nifty 50 and the Sensex. Other terms UPSC could ask about: arbitrage, hedging, derivatives, bull and bear markets, circuit breakers and short selling.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. The Self-Help Group (SHG) programme was originally initiated by the State Bank of India by providing microcredit to the financially deprived.
2. In an SHG, all members of a group take responsibility for a loan that an individual member takes.
3. The Regional Rural Banks and Scheduled Commercial Banks support SHGs. How many of the above statements are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: Self-Help Groups are voluntary groups of about 10-20 members, usually from similar socio-economic backgrounds and often women. They pool small savings, lend internally and borrow from banks. The key feature is joint liability, which means peer pressure and collective responsibility replace physical collateral. The formal policy origin is NABARD's pilot SHG-Bank Linkage Programme (SBLP), launched in 1992 following NGO experiments such as MYRADA in Karnataka. The RBI permitted banks to lend to SHGs in 1991-92, and SBLP later became the world's largest microfinance programme. Commercial banks, Regional Rural Banks and cooperative banks all take part in it. Later, SGSY (1999) was restructured into the National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY-NRLM, 2011), which promotes SHGs and offers interest subvention. Elimination logic: statement 1 is wrong because it credits SBI with the original initiative, whereas NABARD was the originator. Statements 2 and 3 are standard features of the programme. Since only two are correct, the answer is (b), and options (a), (c) and (d) fail.
explanations: (a) is wrong because two statements, 2 and 3, are correct, not just one.
(b) is right because statements 2 and 3 are correct and statement 1 is incorrect, as NABARD, not SBI, initiated the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme.
(c) is wrong because statement 1 wrongly credits SBI as the originator of the SHG programme.
(d) is wrong because SHGs do rely on joint liability and are supported by RRBs and scheduled commercial banks.
keyfact: SHGs rely on joint liability, are financed by RRBs and commercial banks, and were launched through NABARD's SBLP in 1992, not by SBI.
option_notes: Only one correct: this would hold if just a single statement were valid. Here it fails because both the joint liability and the bank-support statements are true. Remember SHGs are small voluntary groups of 10-20 members who pool savings, lend internally and borrow collectively from banks. Joint liability and peer pressure are the key features, and NABARD's SBLP, started in 1992, is the main framework linking them to the formal banking system.

Only two correct: this is the official answer. Statements 2 and 3 are correct, since SHGs use joint liability and are financed by RRBs and scheduled commercial banks. Statement 1 fails because the programme began under NABARD in 1992, not through SBI. This question shows how UPSC makes one statement false by swapping the institution responsible for a scheme.

All three correct: this would be right only if SBI had originated the SHG programme. It did not. NABARD pioneered the SBLP in 1992 with RBI's backing, drawing on NGO experiments such as MYRADA. SBI, like other commercial banks, joined later as a lender. Be careful with statements that credit a well-known institution with an origin that belongs to another body.

None correct: this would imply that SHGs lack joint liability and bank support, which is false. SHGs operate on collective responsibility for loans, and RRBs, commercial banks and cooperative banks all lend to them under SBLP. Government schemes such as DAY-NRLM further strengthen SHG financing through interest subvention and capacity-building support.
related: NABARD was established in 1982 on the Shivaraman Committee's recommendation.
SHG-Bank Linkage Programme was launched by NABARD in 1992.
MYRADA in Karnataka was an early NGO pioneer of the SHG model.
DAY-NRLM was restructured from SGSY in 2011 and is branded Aajeevika.
RRBs were established in 1975 and governed by the RRB Act 1976.
Joint Liability Groups (JLGs) are a related model of group lending, typically for tenant farmers.
The Malegam Committee (2011) examined the microfinance sector and the NBFC-MFI framework.
Grameen Bank was founded by Muhammad Yunus in Bangladesh.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The SHG programme was initiated through NABARD's SHG-Bank Linkage Programme in 1992, building on NGO efforts, not by SBI. NABARD's pilot began in 1991-92 with RBI's support, linking about 500 SHGs to banks. MYRADA in Karnataka was an early pioneer of the SHG model. Bangladesh's Grameen Bank (Muhammad Yunus) inspired microfinance globally, but the Indian SHG model differs from it. SBLP grew to become the world's largest microfinance programme by the number of groups linked. SBI later became a major lender to SHGs but did not originate the scheme.

2 — Correct: SHGs work on joint liability, so the group collectively stands behind a loan taken by any member. Members save regularly, lend internally at agreed rates and decide loans by group consensus. Repayment discipline comes from peer pressure and social collateral instead of physical security. Banks lend to the group, usually in multiples of its savings, and the group then lends to individuals. This has produced high repayment rates, often above 95 percent. Groups are generally 10-20 members and mostly women. This differs from the Joint Liability Group (JLG) model, which is a related but separate arrangement.

3 — Correct: Regional Rural Banks, scheduled commercial banks and cooperative banks all finance SHGs under the NABARD-led SBLP. RRBs were established in 1975 under the RRB Act 1976 (Narasimham Working Group) to serve rural credit needs. Banks open savings accounts for SHGs and extend credit linked to the group's savings. NABARD offers refinance and promotional support, including grants for capacity-building. Under DAY-NRLM, banks give SHGs interest subvention and collateral-free loans up to specified limits. Ownership of RRBs is shared among the Centre (50 percent), the state (15 percent) and the sponsor bank (35 percent).
summary: The answer is (b): only two statements are correct. Statements 2 and 3 are correct, but statement 1 is wrong because the SHG programme was not initiated by SBI. It grew from NGO/MYRADA experiments, and NABARD launched the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme in 1992.
topic_notes: Self-Help Groups are informal associations, typically of 10-20 members, who pool small savings, lend internally and access bank credit collectively. The model rests on social collateral, joint liability and regular meetings. NGOs such as MYRADA pioneered the approach in the 1980s. NABARD began a pilot SHG-Bank Linkage Programme in 1991-92, and RBI soon allowed banks to lend to SHGs, treating this as normal banking. SBLP is regarded as the world's largest microfinance initiative. Banking linkage models include Model I (bank directly lends to SHGs), Model II (through NGOs as facilitators) and Model III (NGOs as financial intermediaries). Government programmes include SGSY (1999), replaced by NRLM in 2011 and renamed DAY-NRLM (Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana-NRLM), with the Aajeevika brand. It promotes SHG federations at village and cluster levels and offers interest subvention to women SHGs. Urban counterpart: DAY-NULM. MUDRA loans and Stand-Up India also support small borrowers. Related concepts include microfinance institutions (MFIs), NBFC-MFIs regulated by RBI, Joint Liability Groups (JLGs), and the Grameen Bank model of Bangladesh. RRBs were set up in 1975 to provide rural credit, with ownership of Centre 50 percent, state 15 percent and sponsor bank 35 percent. NABARD was established in 1982 on the recommendation of the Shivaraman Committee. UPSC could next ask about the difference between SHGs and JLGs, NABARD's roles, DAY-NRLM features, or the Malegam Committee on MFIs (2011).

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement-I : India’s public sector health care system largely focuses on curative care with limited preventive, promotive and rehabilitative care. Statement-Il : Under India’s decentralized approach to health care delivery, the States are primarily responsible for organizing health services. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-Il are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-Il is not the correct explanation for Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct 31 XDTG-F-GST/62A
subject: Geography
detail: Statement-I reflects a long-standing critique of India's public health system: resources, hospitals and human resources are concentrated on treating illness (district hospitals, medical colleges, tertiary care), while prevention (immunization, sanitation, nutrition), promotion (health education, lifestyle, tobacco and alcohol control) and rehabilitation (physiotherapy, disability care, palliative care) remain under-funded. The Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres (2018) and the National Health Policy 2017 aim to correct this by shifting towards comprehensive primary care. Statement-II is constitutionally correct: 'Public health and sanitation; hospitals and dispensaries' is Entry 6 of the State List (Seventh Schedule), so States organize and deliver health services, while the Centre guides through policy, centrally sponsored schemes (National Health Mission), funding and regulation (medical education, drugs, population control and family planning in the Concurrent List). The causal link fails: the curative bias stems from historical priorities, hospital-centric planning, low public spending (about 1.3-2% of GDP) and insurance schemes covering hospitalization, not from the fact that States run health services. Hence (b); (a) fails on explanation, (c) and (d) deny a correct statement.
explanations: Wrong: Statement-II is true but it does not explain the curative bias in Statement-I, which stems from policy priorities, funding and hospital-centric planning rather than the federal division of responsibility.
Correct: Both statements are factually true, and the State-led delivery structure is not the reason for the curative focus, so Statement-II is not the correct explanation.
Wrong: Statement-II is correct, since health services are organized primarily by States under the State List.
Wrong: Statement-I is correct, as public health care remains largely curative with limited preventive, promotive and rehabilitative emphasis.
keyfact: Health is a State subject (Entry 6, State List) yet the public system stays curative-heavy; the two facts are true but unconnected, so answer (b).
option_notes: Option (a) would require a causal link between decentralization and the curative focus. UPSC uses this format to test whether students can separate two true statements from a genuine explanation. Decentralized delivery exists because health is a State subject (Entry 6, State List), whereas the curative bias reflects spending patterns, hospital-based planning and insurance models. The Centre also shapes priorities through the National Health Mission and centrally sponsored schemes, so States are not fully autonomous in this area.

Option (b) is the official answer: both statements are true, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I. Statement-I describes the functional orientation of the system, namely curative dominance. Statement-II describes the constitutional and administrative structure, with States responsible for organizing services. The two are independent facts. Reforms like Health and Wellness Centres address the first, while cooperative federalism and NHM funding address the second.

Option (c) claims Statement-II is incorrect, which is false. The Constitution places public health, sanitation, hospitals and dispensaries in the State List (Entry 6). States run district hospitals, PHCs and CHCs, and recruit health staff. The Centre supports through funding, norms such as Indian Public Health Standards, regulation of medical education via the National Medical Commission, and drug regulation under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940.

Option (d) claims Statement-I is incorrect, which is false. Evidence for curative orientation includes high out-of-pocket expenditure, hospitalization-focused insurance (PM-JAY), concentration of resources in tertiary hospitals, and weak rehabilitative services such as physiotherapy and palliative care. Preventive efforts like Universal Immunization Programme, Swachh Bharat and Poshan Abhiyaan exist but receive limited share of the budget relative to curative services.
related: Public health and sanitation, hospitals and dispensaries are Entry 6 of the State List.
Population control and family planning is Entry 20A of the Concurrent List.
Ayushman Bharat was launched in 2018 with Health and Wellness Centres and PM-JAY (Rs 5 lakh cover).
National Health Policy 2017 targets public health expenditure of 2.5% of GDP by 2025.
The Bhore Committee (1946) recommended integrating preventive and curative health services.
The National Health Mission (2013) combines NRHM (2005) and the National Urban Health Mission.
Article 47 of the DPSP obliges the State to raise nutrition and public health standards.
Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission was launched nationwide in September 2021.
statements: 1 — Correct: Public health spending and infrastructure are skewed towards curative, hospital-based care. Background: the Bhore Committee (1946) envisioned integrated preventive and curative services with primary health centres as the base. The three-tier structure (sub-centre, PHC, CHC) serves roughly 5,000/30,000/1,20,000 population in plains. The NHP 2017 targets raising public health spending to 2.5% of GDP by 2025 and emphasizes preventive and promotive care. Ayushman Bharat has two pillars: Health and Wellness Centres (comprehensive primary care, launched 14 April 2018 at Bijapur, Chhattisgarh) and PM-JAY (secondary and tertiary hospitalization cover of Rs 5 lakh per family, launched September 2018), which itself is curative in nature.

2 — Correct: Health is primarily a State responsibility. Background: Entry 6 of List II (State List) covers public health, sanitation, hospitals and dispensaries. Entry 29 of List III covers prevention of infectious diseases across states; Entry 20A covers population control and family planning; Entry 26 covers medical profession. The Union provides leadership through the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the National Health Mission (2013, merging NRHM 2005 and NUHM), and Centrally Sponsored Schemes with typical 60:40 funding (90:10 for NE and hill states). Article 47 (DPSP) makes raising nutrition and public health a State duty. Local bodies run services under the 73rd and 74th Amendments (Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules).
summary: The answer is (b). Both statements are correct: India's public health system has historically been curative-heavy, with preventive, promotive and rehabilitative care getting less emphasis, and health is primarily a State subject. However, decentralization does not explain the curative bias, so Statement-II is not the correct explanation of Statement-I.
topic_notes: India's health system is a mixed, federal structure. Constitutionally, health is mainly a State subject: Entry 6 of the State List (public health, sanitation, hospitals, dispensaries). Concurrent List entries include Entry 16 (lunacy and mental deficiency), 18 (adulteration of foodstuffs and drugs), 19 (drugs and poisons), 20A (population control and family planning), 29 (infectious diseases) and 26 (medical profession). Union List covers port quarantine, Entry 81 and institutions of national importance such as AIIMS. Article 47 directs the State to improve public health, and Article 21 has been interpreted to include the right to health. Three-tier delivery: sub-centre, primary health centre, community health centre, then sub-district and district hospitals and medical colleges. Key milestones: Bhore Committee 1946; Alma-Ata Declaration 1978 on primary health care; National Health Policy 1983, 2002 and 2017; NRHM 2005; NHM 2013; Ayushman Bharat 2018. NHP 2017 aims at 2.5% of GDP public health spending by 2025, assurance-based approach, and strengthening primary care with two-thirds of resources. Public spending is about 1.3-2.1% of GDP, and out-of-pocket expenditure is high though falling per National Health Accounts. Other angles: Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (2021), eSanjeevani telemedicine, Integrated Public Health Labs, PM-ABHIM (2021), National Medical Commission Act 2019, the Fifteenth Finance Commission's health sector grants, and the proposal to make health a fundamental right or move it to the Concurrent List. Preventive programs include Mission Indradhanush, Poshan Abhiyaan, Swachh Bharat, NCD screening under NP-NCD, and National Tobacco Control Programme.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement-I : According to the United Nations’ World Water Development Report, 2022’, India extracts more than a quarter of the world’s groundwater withdrawal each year.
Statement-II : India needs to extract more than a quarter of the world’s groundwater each year to satisfy the drinking water and sanitation needs of almost 18% of world’s population living in its territory. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? Both Statement-I and Statement-Il
options: are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I Both Statement-I and Statement-II
are correct and Statement-Il is not the correct explanation for Statement-I Statement-I is correct but
Statement-II is incorrect Statement-I is incorrect but
subject: Economy
detail: The UN World Water Development Report is released by UN-Water, with UNESCO coordinating, usually around World Water Day (22 March). Its 2022 edition was themed 'Groundwater: Making the invisible visible'. It notes that India, along with China, the USA, Iran and Pakistan, is among the largest groundwater users, and that India alone accounts for roughly a quarter of global groundwater withdrawal. So Statement-I is accepted as correct. Statement-II offers a causal explanation, but it is flawed. Most of India's extraction, around 85-90% by various assessments, goes to agriculture (irrigation of rice, wheat and sugarcane, encouraged by free or subsidised power and by assured procurement). Domestic and drinking use is only a small share, with industry also small. India's share of world population is about 17-18%, which is correct, but the population share does not explain the extraction volume. Elimination logic: since the explanation is wrong, (a) and (b), which both need II to be correct, fall. (d) fails because Statement-I is correct. Only (c) remains.
explanations: Wrong: (a) needs both statements correct with II explaining I. Statement-II's reasoning is false because irrigation, not drinking water and sanitation, drives India's extraction.
Wrong: (b) also needs both statements correct. Statement-II is not correct, so this fails.
Correct: Statement-I is accurate, since India extracts over a quarter of global groundwater. Statement-II is incorrect because most extraction is for agriculture.
Wrong: (d) says Statement-I is incorrect, but the UN report supports it. Statement-II is also not correct.
keyfact: India extracts over a quarter of the world's groundwater, but about 90% of it goes to irrigation, not drinking water.
option_notes: Option (a) describes both statements true with II as the correct explanation of I. It would hold if drinking and sanitation needs drove extraction. In reality, irrigation takes about 90% of India's groundwater, with domestic use about 9-10%. UPSC often uses this 'correct explanation' format to test whether the stated cause is true. Always verify the causal link separately from the facts.

Option (b) describes both statements true but II not explaining I. It would suit cases where two accurate facts are unrelated. Here II is itself inaccurate as an explanation, because it attributes extraction to drinking and sanitation. India's population share of about 17-18% is correct, but that alone is not why extraction is so high. Agriculture is the main driver.

Option (c) says Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect. It is the official answer. India is the largest groundwater user in the world (over 25% of global withdrawal), but the main use is irrigation. The UN WWDR 2022 focused on groundwater. India also faces falling water tables in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Delhi, and in parts of Gujarat and Tamil Nadu.

Option (d) says Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct. This reverses the actual position. India's top ranking in groundwater extraction is well documented, and the stated reason for it is wrong. Students should remember the top extractors: India, then China and the USA, with Iran and Pakistan also among the larger users.
related: WWDR is published by UNESCO's WWAP on behalf of UN-Water, and released around World Water Day (22 March).
India is the world's largest groundwater user, followed by China and the USA.
About 87-90% of India's groundwater extraction is used for irrigation.
The CGWB under the Ministry of Jal Shakti assesses dynamic groundwater resources.
Atal Bhujal Yojana was launched in December 2019 and covers 7 states.
Water is Entry 17 of the State List in the Seventh Schedule.
Groundwater categories: Safe, Semi-critical, Critical and Over-exploited.
Jal Jeevan Mission (2019) aims at functional tap water to every rural household.
statements: 1 — Correct: The UN WWDR 2022 and related UN/CGWB data show India as the largest groundwater extractor, with roughly 25% of the global total. The report is published by UN-Water and coordinated by UNESCO's World Water Assessment Programme. The 2022 theme was groundwater, 'the invisible resource'. India extracts about 240-250 billion cubic metres a year, more than China or the USA. CGWB's 2022 assessment puts national extraction at about 60-63% of annual extractable recharge (stage of extraction), with serious over-exploitation in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Delhi. Groundwater supplies about 60% of irrigation and 85% of rural drinking water.

2 — Incorrect: India does hold about 17-18% of world population, but its heavy groundwater use is driven mainly by irrigation (about 87-90% of extraction), not by drinking water and sanitation. Domestic use is about 9-10% and industry only a few percent. Causes of over-extraction include electricity subsidies, free or cheap farm power, water-intensive crops such as paddy and sugarcane, MSP-led procurement and lack of pricing. Policy responses include Atal Bhujal Yojana (2019, World Bank co-funded, Rs 6,000 crore, 7 states), Jal Shakti Abhiyan, Jal Jeevan Mission (2019, tap water to rural homes) and Swachh Bharat Mission for sanitation.
summary: The answer is (c): Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect. India is the world's largest groundwater extractor, with over a quarter of global withdrawal (about 25% by most estimates). Statement-II wrongly claims this is needed for drinking water and sanitation, whereas about 90% of India's groundwater goes to irrigation.
topic_notes: The World Water Development Report (WWDR) is the UN's flagship water report, produced by the UN World Water Assessment Programme (WWAP) under UNESCO on behalf of UN-Water. It is launched annually on World Water Day (22 March). The 2022 edition, 'Groundwater: Making the invisible visible', stressed that groundwater provides about half of the world's domestic water supply, about 25% of irrigation water and a large share of industrial needs. India is the largest user of groundwater globally, followed by China and the USA. Within India, roughly 87-90% of extraction is for irrigation, around 9-10% for domestic use and a small share for industry. The Central Ground Water Board (CGWB, under the Ministry of Jal Shakti) assesses resources with the states. Assessment categories are Safe, Semi-critical, Critical and Over-exploited, based on the stage of extraction (extraction as a percentage of recharge). The national stage of extraction is about 60-63%. Over-exploited regions include Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Delhi and parts of Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. Contamination issues include arsenic in the Ganga plains, fluoride in Rajasthan and nitrate and uranium in Punjab. Key schemes are Atal Bhujal Yojana (2019, community-led management in over-exploited areas of 7 states: Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh), Jal Shakti Abhiyan: Catch the Rain, Jal Jeevan Mission (Har Ghar Jal), the National Aquifer Mapping Programme (NAQUIM) and the Master Plan for Artificial Recharge. Groundwater is a State subject in practice, since water is Entry 17 of the State List, with a Model Groundwater Bill circulated by the Centre. Other angles: the Dublin Principles, UN-Water's SDG 6 (clean water and sanitation) and the UN 2023 Water Conference.

question: Consider the following statements : According to the Constitution of Le India, the Central Government has a duty to protect States from internal disturbances. The Constitution of India exempts the States from providing legal counsel to a person being held for preventive detention. According to the Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2002, confession of the accused before the police cannot be used as evidence. How many of the above statements are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: The question tests three distinct areas: federal duties, detention safeguards and anti-terror law. Article 355 makes it the Union's duty to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance, and to ensure that State governments function in accordance with the Constitution. It is the basis of the Union's power to deploy central forces, and is distinct from Article 356 (President's Rule). Article 22 gives protection against arrest and detention. Clauses (1) and (2) (information of grounds, right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice, production before a magistrate within 24 hours) do not apply to preventive detention under Article 22(3)(b). Article 22(4)-(7) set the safeguards for preventive detention: Advisory Board review for detention beyond three months, and communication of grounds. Courts have held that there is no right to counsel in preventive detention, although the detainee may make a representation. POTA 2002 reversed the ordinary rule of the Evidence Act (Section 25), under which confessions to police are inadmissible, by making confessions to a police officer of SP rank or above admissible (Section 32). Safeguards included producing the accused before a magistrate. Elimination: since 3 is wrong and 1 and 2 are right, only (b) fits.
explanations: Wrong: it would mean only one statement is correct, but two (1 and 2) are correct.
Correct: statements 1 (Article 355) and 2 (Article 22(3)(b)) are correct, and statement 3 is wrong because POTA made confessions to senior police officers admissible.
Wrong: statement 3 is false, since POTA 2002 Section 32 made confessions before the police admissible as evidence.
Wrong: statements 1 and 2 are both correct, so 'none' cannot be right.
keyfact: Article 355 is the Union's duty to protect States from internal disturbance, preventive detainees have no right to counsel under Article 22(3)(b), but POTA 2002 made police confessions admissible.
option_notes: Only one: a count option. It would apply if just one of the three statements held. Here that is not so, as both the Article 355 duty and the Article 22 exemption from counsel for preventive detainees are constitutionally accurate. UPSC's count-type questions reward checking each statement separately and not guessing from the overall flavour of the statements. The popular trap is to treat the detention statement as false because Article 22(1) generally grants the right to a lawyer.

Only two: the correct choice. The two true statements are Article 355 (Union's duty to protect States from external aggression and internal disturbance) and Article 22(3)(b) read with 22(1) (no right to counsel for preventive detainees). The false one concerns POTA 2002, which, unlike ordinary law under the Evidence Act, allowed confessions to a police officer of SP rank or above as evidence. This selection follows the official UPSC 2023 key.

All three: this would require POTA 2002 to bar police confessions as evidence, which is the opposite of the truth. The ordinary law (Sections 25-26 of the Evidence Act, now Sections 23-24 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023) bars such confessions, but POTA and, earlier, TADA (Section 15) made them admissible. That is why these laws were criticised for violating fair-trial rights and were allowed to lapse or be repealed.

None: this would mean Article 355 and Article 22 had both been misread. Article 355 does explicitly create the Union's duty to protect States from internal disturbance, and Article 22(3)(b) does exclude preventive detainees from the Article 22(1) right to counsel. A student who confuses Article 355 with Article 356, or who thinks Article 22 protects all detainees, may wrongly choose this.
related: Article 355: Union's duty to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance.
Article 356: President's Rule on failure of constitutional machinery in a State.
Article 22(3)(b): Article 22(1)-(2) rights do not apply to preventive detention.
Article 22(4): Advisory Board needed for preventive detention beyond three months.
POTA 2002 was repealed in 2004; its provisions were absorbed into the UAPA.
Section 32 of POTA: confession to a police officer of SP rank or above admissible.
S.R. Bommai (1994): President's Rule is subject to judicial review.
In national emergency, Article 359 can suspend enforcement of fundamental rights, but not Articles 20 and 21.
statements: 1 — Correct: Article 355 casts this duty on the Union. Article 355 (in Part XVIII, Emergency Provisions) says the Union shall protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance and ensure that each State's government is carried on according to the Constitution. It is the constitutional basis for deploying central armed police forces or the army in aid of civil authority. The Sarkaria Commission (1988) and the Punchhi Commission (2010) discussed Article 355, and the latter recommended localised use of Article 355 in place of Article 356. In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) the Supreme Court limited the misuse of Article 356 and read it alongside Article 355. Public order is a State subject (Entry 1, List II), but the Union may send forces on request or in a crisis.

2 — Correct: Article 22(3)(b) excludes preventive detention from the Article 22(1) and (2) protections. Article 22(1) gives the right to be informed of grounds and to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice, while Article 22(2) requires production before a magistrate within 24 hours. Neither applies to a person detained under preventive detention law. Article 22(4) bars detention beyond three months unless an Advisory Board of High Court judges or persons qualified to be judges reports sufficient cause. Article 22(5) requires grounds to be communicated and the earliest opportunity to make a representation. The 44th Amendment proposal to shorten the period to two months was never brought into force. Examples of preventive detention laws are the NSA 1980, COFEPOSA and the UAPA (in part). Parliament and State legislatures can both make preventive detention laws (Entry 9 List I, Entry 3 List III).

3 — Incorrect: POTA 2002 permitted such confessions. The Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2002 was enacted after the Parliament attack and a joint sitting of the Houses (March 2002), replacing the POTO. Section 32 made a confession made to a police officer of rank not lower than Superintendent of Police admissible in the trial of the accused, in departure from Sections 25-26 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. It also allowed detention without charge sheet for up to 180 days and a Review Committee. The Act was criticised for misuse. It was repealed in 2004 by the Prevention of Terrorism (Repeal) Act, 2004, and its provisions were folded into the UAPA, 1967 by amendment. PUCL v. Union of India (2003) upheld POTA's validity but required safeguards.
summary: The answer is (b) Only two. Statements 1 and 2 are correct: Article 355 imposes a duty on the Union to protect States against internal disturbance, and Article 22(3)-(4) denies the right to counsel to persons under preventive detention. Statement 3 is incorrect because POTA 2002 made confessions to a police officer admissible as evidence.
topic_notes: The topic joins Union-State relations in emergencies, personal liberty and anti-terror law. Part XVIII covers emergency provisions. Article 352 is national emergency (grounds: war, external aggression, armed rebellion, after the 44th Amendment replaced 'internal disturbance'). Article 355 is a standing duty of the Union, whereas Article 356 is President's Rule on failure of constitutional machinery and Article 360 is financial emergency. Article 355 allows deployment of central forces without proclaiming an emergency. Article 21 protects life and personal liberty, and Article 22 deals with arrest and detention. Punitive detention carries the Article 22(1)-(2) protections: grounds, lawyer, production before a magistrate in 24 hours. These do not apply to enemy aliens or to persons held under preventive detention laws. Preventive detention is based on suspicion of future harm, and can last up to three months without Advisory Board review. A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) upheld the Preventive Detention Act, and Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Article 21 by requiring just, fair and reasonable procedure. D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) laid down guidelines on arrest and custody. Anti-terror laws in sequence: TADA 1985 (lapsed 1995), POTO 2001, POTA 2002 (repealed 2004), and UAPA 1967 (amended 2004, 2008, 2012, 2019). Under UAPA, the 2019 amendment allows individuals to be designated terrorists. The NIA Act 2008 created the National Investigation Agency. The new criminal laws, effective 1 July 2024, are the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam. The Evidence Act also bars confessions to police (Sections 25-26), subject to Section 27 (discovery).

question: Which one of the following countries has been suffering from decades of civil strife and food shortages and was in news in the recent past for its very severe famine?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Somalia, in the Horn of Africa, has had no fully effective central government since President Siad Barre was overthrown in January 1991. Clan-based militias, warlordism and later the Islamist insurgent group Al-Shabaab have disrupted agriculture, aid delivery and trade. Climate shocks add to this: the 2010-12 drought led to a declared famine in 2011 that killed an estimated 258,000 people, about half of them children under five. In 2016-17 a famine was narrowly averted by aid. From 2020 to 2023 the Horn of Africa had five consecutive failed rainy seasons, its worst drought in about 40 years, and in 2022 the IPC warned of a risk of famine in Baidoa and Burhakaba districts. Famine is declared under the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) Phase 5 when at least 20% of households face extreme food gaps, acute malnutrition among children exceeds 30%, and two deaths per 10,000 people occur daily. Elimination: Costa Rica and Ecuador are stable Latin American democracies with no famine. Angola had a civil war from 1975 to 2002 but has not been in the news recently for a severe famine, although southern Angola has had drought-related hunger. Somalia matches both clues.
explanations: Angola: its civil war ended in 2002 and it has had no recent famine declaration of the Somalian kind, though southern provinces have had drought-related hunger. It does not fit the question.
Costa Rica: a stable Central American democracy with no army since 1948 and no civil strife or famine. Wrong.
Ecuador: a South American country with political and security problems such as gang violence, but no decades of civil war and no famine. Wrong.
Somalia: correct. Civil war since 1991, Al-Shabaab insurgency and repeated droughts have caused famines (2011) and a famine warning in 2022.
keyfact: Somalia: civil strife since 1991, Al-Shabaab and repeated droughts led to the 2011 famine and the 2022 famine warning.
option_notes: Angola is a southwest African country whose capital is Luanda. It became independent from Portugal in 1975 and had a civil war between MPLA and UNITA until 2002. It is an oil and diamond exporter and a member of OPEC (it announced its exit in December 2023). It is a Portuguese-speaking country and its currency is the kwanza.

Costa Rica is a Central American country with its capital at San José. It abolished its army in 1948 after a brief civil war, and is known for ecotourism, biodiversity and a high human development ranking. Its currency is the colón. It borders Nicaragua and Panama and has coasts on the Pacific and the Caribbean.

Ecuador is a South American country on the equator, from which it takes its name. Its capital is Quito and it uses the US dollar as currency (since 2000). It includes the Galápagos Islands, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It was a member of OPEC until it left in 2020, and it has faced rising gang violence since 2023.

Somalia is in the Horn of Africa with its capital at Mogadishu. It has the longest mainland coastline in Africa. It became independent in 1960 through the union of British and Italian Somaliland, and Barre's regime fell in 1991. Somaliland declared itself independent in 1991 but is not widely recognised. Piracy off its coast peaked around 2009-11. It joined the East African Community in 2024. It faces Al-Shabaab and recurrent drought.
related: Somalia's capital is Mogadishu; the militant group Al-Shabaab is linked to al-Qaeda.
IPC Phase 5 is the 'Catastrophe/Famine' classification.
Horn of Africa comprises Somalia, Ethiopia, Eritrea and Djibouti.
Somalia's famine of 2011 killed about 258,000 people.
The World Food Programme won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020.
Somalia's government collapsed in 1991 after Siad Barre was ousted.
Somaliland is a self-declared state in northwest Somalia, not widely recognised.
The Gulf of Aden separates Somalia and Yemen.
summary: The answer is (d) Somalia. It has suffered civil war and state collapse since 1991, along with recurrent droughts and insurgency by Al-Shabaab, leading to repeated famines (2011) and a 2022 famine warning.
topic_notes: Famine and hunger hotspots are a recurring current-affairs theme. Famine is formally classified by the IPC (Integrated Food Security Phase Classification), a multi-partner initiative that includes FAO, WFP and others. Phase 5 (Catastrophe/Famine) requires at least 20% of households facing extreme food shortage, 30% acute child malnutrition, and 2 deaths per 10,000 per day. Somalia's famines: 1991-92 (about 300,000 deaths, leading to UNOSOM and the US-led intervention), 2011 (about 260,000 deaths) and the 2022 warning. The Horn of Africa drought of 2020-23 hit Somalia, Ethiopia and Kenya. Other crisis zones: Yemen (civil war since 2014), South Sudan (famine declared in parts of Unity State in 2017), Sudan (conflict since April 2023), Afghanistan, Gaza (IPC famine warnings 2024), Haiti, and the Sahel. Key bodies: the World Food Programme (HQ Rome, Nobel Peace Prize 2020), FAO, and the Global Report on Food Crises. The Global Hunger Index is published by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe, and India ranked 111th of 125 in 2023. In Somalia, the African Union mission (AMISOM, replaced by ATMIS in 2022 and AUSSOM in 2025) fights Al-Shabaab. Indian angles: the National Food Security Act 2013, PMGKAY, and India's food aid shipments to African countries under humanitarian assistance. UPSC may also ask about the Horn of Africa geography, including Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia, and the Gulf of Aden and Bab-el-Mandeb strait.

ocr: Consider the following statements : i Un India, the Biodiversity Management Committees are key to the realization of the objectives of the Nagoya Protocol. 2. The Biodiversity Management Committees have important functions in determining access and benefit sharing, including the power to levy collection fees on the access of biological resources within its jurisdiction. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) 1 only (b) 2 only ‘) Both 1 and 2 (d@) Neither 1 nor 2 33 XDTG-F-GST/62A
subject: Economy
detail: The Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-Sharing (adopted 2010 at COP10, Nagoya, Japan; in force 2014) supplements the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) and aims at fair and equitable sharing of benefits from the use of genetic resources. India ratified it in 2012 and implements it through the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and the Biological Diversity Rules, 2004, and the ABS Regulations, 2014. The Act creates a three-tier structure: the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA, Chennai, est. 2003), State Biodiversity Boards, and Biodiversity Management Committees at the local body level (Section 41). BMCs promote conservation, sustainable use and documentation of biodiversity, and prepare People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs). The NBA/SBBs must consult BMCs on approvals for use of resources in their area, and BMCs may charge collection fees for access to biological resources and levy fees or royalties. The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 retained BMCs' role. Elimination: Statement 1 is correct, as BMCs are the grassroots ABS mechanism. Statement 2 is correct, as the Rules (Rule 22(6)) empower BMCs to levy collection fees. So both are correct, and options (a), (b) and (d) fall.
explanations: Wrong: it ignores that statement 2 is also correct, since BMCs can levy collection fees.
Wrong: it ignores that statement 1 is also correct, since BMCs are key to realising Nagoya's ABS objectives in India.
Correct: both statements accurately describe the BMCs' role in ABS and their power to levy collection fees.
Wrong: both statements are factually correct, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: BMCs (Sec 41, Biological Diversity Act 2002) are India's local ABS bodies for the Nagoya Protocol and can levy collection fees for access to biological resources.
option_notes: Option (a) 'Statement 1 only' would hold if BMCs had no fee-levying power. BMCs are the third tier of India's biodiversity governance under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (Section 41). They are set up by local bodies (panchayats and municipalities), conserve habitats and landraces, and prepare People's Biodiversity Registers. Over 270,000 BMCs have been formed across India. They are consulted by the NBA and State Boards on access applications.

Option (b) 'Statement 2 only' would require statement 1 to be false. The Nagoya Protocol's central idea is Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS). India's ABS mechanism works via the NBA (national), State Biodiversity Boards, and local BMCs. BMCs are therefore the local implementation arm of the protocol's aims. The Protocol also has a compliance regime and recognises traditional knowledge held by indigenous and local communities.

Option (c) 'Both 1 and 2' is the correct answer. It reflects the BMCs' dual role as grassroots implementers of Nagoya Protocol ABS objectives and as bodies with the power to levy collection fees on access to biological resources in their area. The 2002 Act has a three-tier structure: NBA (Chennai), State Biodiversity Boards, and BMCs. The 2023 Amendment decriminalised some offences and eased access for Indian traditional medicine practitioners but kept BMCs.

Option (d) 'Neither 1 nor 2' would suggest BMCs have no ABS role. That is wrong, because BMCs are central to local-level ABS in India. They are consulted on approvals, document knowledge, and can collect fees. The Supreme Court and NGT have also referred to their role in protecting biodiversity. BMCs are funded in part through benefit-sharing flows from the NBA, and the Act's Section 41 and Rule 22 give them concrete functions.
related: Nagoya Protocol: adopted 2010, in force 12 October 2014; India ratified in 2012.
Biological Diversity Act, 2002 has a three-tier structure: NBA, State Biodiversity Boards, BMCs.
NBA is headquartered in Chennai and was established in 2003.
BMCs are created by local bodies under Section 41 of the 2002 Act and prepare People's Biodiversity Registers.
Biodiversity Heritage Sites are notified by State Governments under Section 37; the first was Nallur Tamarind Grove, Karnataka.
Cartagena Protocol concerns biosafety; Nagoya Protocol concerns ABS.
Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) sets the 30x30 target.
Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 eased access for AYUSH practitioners and decriminalised offences.
statements: 1 — Correct: BMCs are the grassroots institutions through which India operationalises ABS, the core of the Nagoya Protocol. The Nagoya Protocol was adopted on 29 October 2010 at CBD COP10 in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, and came into force on 12 October 2014. It is a supplementary agreement to the CBD and gives legal certainty on access to genetic resources and fair sharing of benefits, including traditional knowledge. India ratified it in October 2012 (COP11 was in Hyderabad), and implements it through the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and the ABS Regulations, 2014.

2 — Correct: BMCs advise on and determine ABS at the local level, and Rule 22(6) of the Biological Diversity Rules, 2004 empowers them to levy collection fees for access to biological resources or knowledge within their jurisdiction. BMCs are constituted by local bodies under Section 41 of the 2002 Act, and they document local biodiversity in People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs). The NBA and State Biodiversity Boards consult BMCs on access requests and benefit-sharing decisions. Benefit-sharing money from the NBA is often directed to the BMC or to the benefit claimers in the area.
summary: The answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. Under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) are local-level bodies that give effect to access and benefit sharing (ABS), the central objective of the Nagoya Protocol. They also have the statutory power to levy collection fees on access to biological resources in their area.
topic_notes: The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) was adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and entered into force in 1993. Its three objectives are conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources. The Cartagena Protocol (2000) deals with biosafety and living modified organisms. The Nagoya Protocol (2010) deals with ABS, and the Nagoya-Kuala Lumpur Supplementary Protocol covers liability and redress for biosafety damage. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (COP15, December 2022) set the 30x30 target, to protect 30% of land and oceans by 2030, and a target to restore 30% of degraded ecosystems. India's Biological Diversity Act, 2002 has a three-tier structure: the National Biodiversity Authority (Chennai, 2003, a statutory autonomous body under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change), State Biodiversity Boards, and BMCs at the local level. The NBA regulates access by foreign nationals, NRIs and foreign companies, and restricts transfer of research results and IPR claims on Indian biological resources without approval. Indian citizens must give prior intimation to State Boards for commercial use. BMCs prepare People's Biodiversity Registers recording local knowledge and resources. The Act also provides for Biodiversity Heritage Sites (Section 37), such as Nallur Tamarind Grove in Karnataka (first, 2007). The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 promotes the AYUSH sector, encourages cultivated medicinal plants, decriminalises offences in favour of penalties, and eases access for research and patents. Related topics UPSC might ask include the Nagoya Protocol's definition of utilisation of genetic resources, traditional knowledge, the TKDL, the Access and Benefit Sharing Clearing-House, the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources (ITPGRFA), and the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001.

question:
Consider the following statements in respect of election to the President of India :
1. The members nominated to either House of the Parliament or the Legislative Assemblies of States are also eligible to be included in the Electoral College.
2. Higher the number of elective Assembly seats, higher is the value of vote of each MLA of that State.
3. The value of vote of each MLA of Madhya Pradesh is greater than that of Kerala.
4. The value of vote of each MLA of Puducherry is higher than that of Arunachal Pradesh because the ratio of total population to total number of elective seats in Puducherry is greater as compared to Arunachal Pradesh. How many of the above statements are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: The President is elected by an Electoral College of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States, including Delhi and Puducherry (Article 54, with the 70th Amendment extending this to the UTs of Delhi and Puducherry). Nominated members of Parliament or of an Assembly, and members of Legislative Councils, are not part of it. Article 55 requires uniformity of representation and parity between States and the Union. The value of an MLA's vote is the state's population (1971 Census, frozen until the first Census after 2026 by the 84th Amendment) divided by (number of elected MLAs x 1000), with a fraction above one-half rounded up. The value of an MP's vote is the total value of all MLA votes divided by the number of elected MPs; it was 700 in 2022. Since the number of elective seats is in the denominator, more seats means a lower value per MLA, so statement 2 is wrong. Kerala's value is 152 and Madhya Pradesh's is 131, so statement 3 is wrong. Puducherry's value is 16 and Arunachal Pradesh's is 8. Puducherry has about 15,700 people per seat, against about 7,800 in Arunachal, so statement 4 is right. Hence only one statement is correct.
explanations: Correct: exactly one statement, number 4, is correct, so only one is right.
Wrong: statements 1, 2 and 3 are all incorrect, so 'only two' cannot be right.
Wrong: three correct statements would need at least two of 1, 2 and 3 to hold, but all three fail.
Wrong: statements 1, 2 and 3 are false, so not all four can be correct.
keyfact: Only elected MPs and MLAs vote for the President; the MLA's vote value = 1971 population / (elected seats x 1000), so it falls as seats rise.
option_notes: Only one: this is the correct choice here, with statement 4 as the only true one. In UPSC the 'how many' format tests whether each statement is checked individually. The knowledge needed is the Article 54-55 formula, 1971 population, and state values.

Only two: this would need two true statements. UPSC often uses such options as distractors when students wrongly accept that nominated members vote (statement 1) or that more seats mean higher value (statement 2). Both are traps, since only elected members vote and the value falls as seats rise.

Only three: this would need three true statements. A student who wrongly accepts statements 1, 2 or 3 might choose it. Memorise the real values: Kerala 152, Madhya Pradesh 131, Puducherry 16, Arunachal 8, Sikkim 7 and Uttar Pradesh 208. Madhya Pradesh has the lower value of the two states.

All four: this would mean every statement holds. It fails because nominated members do not vote, and the value is inversely related to elective seats. Madhya Pradesh's value is lower than Kerala's. UPSC uses 'all' options to catch candidates who accept plausible but unchecked statements.
related: Value of an MP's vote in the 2022 presidential election was 700.
Highest MLA vote value: Uttar Pradesh, 208. Lowest: Sikkim, 7.
Article 54: Electoral College of elected members only.
Article 55: manner of election, single transferable vote.
Article 71: Supreme Court decides disputes on the President's election.
The 1971 Census base is frozen until the first Census after 2026 (84th Amendment).
Minimum age for President: 35 years; nominators 50 and seconders 50.
Nominated MPs can vote in the Vice-President's election but not the President's.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Only elected members are in the Electoral College, so nominated members are excluded. Article 54 provides that the college consists of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the Legislative Assemblies of States, including Delhi and Puducherry. The 12 Rajya Sabha members nominated by the President, any nominated Lok Sabha members, and nominated MLAs have no vote. Legislative Council members are also excluded. Nominated members can vote in the Vice-President's election, since that electorate is all members of both Houses of Parliament. The 2022 Electoral College had 4,809 electors: 776 MPs and 4,033 MLAs.

2 — Incorrect: The value of an MLA's vote is inversely related to the number of elective seats. Value = 1971 population / (elected seats x 1000). More seats in the denominator give a lower value per MLA. This is why small-population states with many seats, such as Sikkim (value 7), have the lowest vote values, and Uttar Pradesh (208) has the highest. Fractions above one-half count as one. The formula follows Article 55(2), which aims at uniformity of representation among States and parity between the States and the Union.

3 — Incorrect: Kerala's MLA vote value is 152 and Madhya Pradesh's is 131, so Madhya Pradesh is lower, not greater. The difference arises because Kerala has a higher 1971 population per elective seat (about 152,000, against about 131,000 in Madhya Pradesh). Other values: Uttar Pradesh 208, Tamil Nadu 176, Maharashtra 175, Jharkhand 176, Bihar 173, Delhi 58, Puducherry 16, Arunachal 8, Sikkim 7. Madhya Pradesh has 230 seats and Kerala 140. Population alone does not decide the value; population per seat does.

4 — Correct: Puducherry's MLA vote value is 16 and Arunachal Pradesh's is 8. The reasoning is also right, because a higher population per elective seat gives a higher value. Puducherry's 1971 population of about 4.7 lakh over 30 elected seats gives about 15.7, rounded to 16. Arunachal's population of about 4.68 lakh over 60 seats gives about 7.8, rounded to 8. The two have similar populations but Arunachal has twice the seats. Puducherry and Delhi are the only Union Territories whose legislators vote in the presidential election. J&K's Assembly was also included after it became a UT with a legislature, but it was not part of the 2022 college because the Assembly was not constituted.
summary: The answer is (a): only one statement, statement 4, is correct. Under Articles 54 and 55, nominated members are excluded from the Electoral College. An MLA's vote value falls as the number of elective seats rises, and it rises with the state's 1971 population per elective seat.
topic_notes: Presidential election: Articles 52-62 cover the office and its election. Article 54 defines the Electoral College as the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States (the Explanation in Art 54 includes Delhi and Puducherry as 'States'). Article 55 prescribes the method: uniformity of representation among States, and parity between States as a whole and the Union. It uses the single transferable vote under proportional representation, by secret ballot. The value of an MLA's vote is the state's 1971 population divided by (number of elected MLAs x 1000), rounded up if the fraction exceeds half. The value of an MP's vote is the total value of all MLA votes divided by the number of elected MPs, again rounded as above. In 2022 the MP vote value was 700, and the total value of the college was about 10.86 lakh votes. The winner must obtain a quota: more than 50 percent of valid votes, which is the total valid votes divided by two, plus one. The 1971 Census base was frozen by the 42nd Amendment and extended until after the 2026 Census by the 84th Amendment. Article 58 sets the qualifications: a citizen of India, at least 35 years old, qualified to be an MP, and holding no office of profit. A nominator and a seconder are needed: 50 each, and the security deposit is Rs 15,000. Disputes go to the Supreme Court under Article 71. Under Article 56 the term is 5 years. Nominated members, the Legislative Council and the Vice-President's college are related topics. The Vice-President is elected by all members of both Houses, including nominated members, under Article 66. Other angles: the Rajya Sabha Chairman role, impeachment of the President under Article 61, and the vacancy rules in Article 62 (election within six months).

question: With reference to the Indian History, Alexander Rea, A. H. Longhurst, Robert Sewell, James Burgess and Walter Elliot were associated with
options: establishment of English Press in Colonial India
establishment of Churches in . : Princely States
construction of railways’ in Colonial India
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The question tests knowledge of colonial-era Indian archaeology. The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) was founded in 1861 under Alexander Cunningham, and the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act came in 1904 under Curzon, with John Marshall as Director-General (1902-28). The five names belong to this antiquarian tradition. Alexander Rea (Madras Circle) excavated Adichanallur's urn burials and Buddhist sites such as Amaravati and Bhattiprolu, and wrote on Pallava and Chalukyan architecture. A. H. Longhurst, Superintendent of the Southern Circle, worked at Nagarjunakonda, Hampi and Pallava sites. Robert Sewell wrote 'A Forgotten Empire' (1900) on Vijayanagara and 'Lists of Antiquities' in Madras. James Burgess headed the Archaeological Survey of Western and Southern India, founded the journal Indian Antiquary (1872) and wrote on cave temples. Walter Elliot collected South Indian inscriptions and coins, notably the Amaravati marbles, now in the British Museum. None is linked to railways, the press or church-building. The elimination logic is to recognise even one name, such as Burgess or Sewell, as a historian-archaeologist, and then reject the administrative and commercial options.
explanations: Correct: all five worked on excavating, surveying, documenting or interpreting archaeological sites, monuments and inscriptions in colonial India.
Incorrect: the early English press was associated with figures such as James Augustus Hickey (Bengal Gazette, 1780), not these five.
Incorrect: none of them is known for building churches in princely states; their work was scholarly and archaeological.
Incorrect: railways in colonial India are associated with Dalhousie, the Great Indian Peninsula Railway and engineers such as Rowland Macdonald Stephenson, not these five.
