options: Neither 1 nor 2 On June 21 every year, which of the following latitude(s) experience(s) a sunlight of more than 12 hours ? i Equator 2. — Tropic of Cancer 8. Tropic of Capricorn 4. Arctic Circle
subject: Geography
detail:
The Coriolis force is an apparent (inertial) force caused by the Earth's rotation. It deflects moving objects such as winds and ocean currents to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere (Ferrel's law). Its magnitude is given by F = 2mΩv sinφ, where m is mass, Ω is the Earth's angular velocity, v is the velocity of the moving body and φ is latitude. Statement 1 is correct because the force increases directly with wind speed. Statement 2 is correct because sin 0° = 0 at the equator, so the force is absent there, while sin 90° = 1 at the poles, so it is maximum. The force acts perpendicular to the direction of motion, so it changes direction but not speed. It is the reason cyclones do not form within about 5° of the equator, because there is too little deflection to sustain a low-pressure spiral. It also explains geostrophic winds, which blow parallel to isobars when the pressure-gradient force balances the Coriolis force. Elimination: since both statements follow from the formula, (a), (b) and (d) are ruled out.

Note: the OCR text also contains a stray, unrelated question about June 21 sunlight. It is not answered here because the official answer given applies to the Coriolis question.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 2 is also correct, so '1 only' is incomplete.
(b) is wrong because statement 1 is also correct. The force does increase with wind speed.
(c) is correct because the force is proportional to both wind velocity and the sine of latitude, so it is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles.
(d) is wrong because both statements are factually correct.
keyfact: Coriolis force = 2mΩv sinφ: rises with wind speed, zero at the equator, maximum at the poles.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would be true if only the velocity dependence held. The velocity dependence is real: the Coriolis force F = 2mΩv sinφ grows with speed. This option fails because it ignores the latitude dependence. Winds at higher speed show larger deflection, and the radius of curvature of inertial motion is v/f, where f is the Coriolis parameter.

Option (b), '2 only', captures the latitude dependence: the force is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles. It fails because it omits the velocity dependence. Because of this latitude dependence, cyclones rarely form between about 5°N and 5°S, and geostrophic balance does not hold well near the equator.

Option (c), 'Both 1 and 2', is the official answer. The Coriolis force is an apparent force from Earth's rotation, proportional to velocity and the sine of latitude. It deflects winds right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere. It is central to geostrophic winds, cyclones, ocean gyres and Ekman transport.

Option (d), 'Neither 1 nor 2', is wrong. It would apply only if the Coriolis force were independent of speed and latitude. In reality the force depends on both. It is also not a real force in the Newtonian sense but an effect of the rotating reference frame, though its effects on weather and ocean circulation are very real.
related: Coriolis force is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles.
Winds deflect right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere (Ferrel's law).
Geostrophic wind blows parallel to isobars, with pressure-gradient force balanced by Coriolis force.
Tropical cyclones do not form within about 5° of the equator because Coriolis force is too weak.
Ekman transport moves surface water at roughly 90° to the wind direction.
Friction reduces wind speed near the surface, so winds cross isobars at an angle.
Coriolis force changes direction of motion but does no work and does not change speed.
On June 21 (summer solstice) the Tropic of Cancer gets sunlight of more than 12 hours, the equator exactly 12 hours.
statements: 1 — Correct: Coriolis force is directly proportional to wind velocity. Detail: The formula is F = 2mΩv sinφ. A faster wind is deflected more strongly, while a stationary object feels no Coriolis force. It was described by Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis in 1835. The force is perpendicular to the direction of motion and does no work. In the upper atmosphere, with weak friction, it balances the pressure-gradient force to give geostrophic wind. Near the surface, friction reduces wind speed and so reduces the deflection, which makes surface winds cross isobars at an angle.

2 — Correct: The force varies with the sine of latitude, so it is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles. Detail: At 0° latitude sinφ = 0, and at 90° sinφ = 1. Winds are deflected right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere. This is why tropical cyclones do not form within about 5° of the equator and why the equatorial region has a doldrum-like calm belt. It also governs the direction of cyclonic and anticyclonic circulation in each hemisphere, and Ekman spiral and ocean gyres in the oceans.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. The Coriolis force is proportional to the speed of the moving body (wind) and to the sine of latitude, so it is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles.
topic_notes:
The Coriolis force is an apparent force arising from Earth's west-to-east rotation (about 15° per hour, one rotation in about 24 hours). It acts on any body moving relative to the rotating Earth. Formula: F = 2mΩv sinφ. Key properties: it acts perpendicular to the direction of motion; it deflects to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere; it is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles; it increases with speed; it changes direction but not speed. Discovered mathematically by Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis (1835); Ferrel's law describes the deflection of winds.

Related concepts: Winds are controlled by three forces, the pressure-gradient force, the Coriolis force and friction. Geostrophic wind blows parallel to isobars when the pressure-gradient force is balanced by the Coriolis force, typically at heights above about 1-2 km. Surface winds cross isobars at an angle because friction reduces the Coriolis effect. Cyclones rotate counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. Anticyclones rotate the opposite way. Tropical cyclones are absent near the equator and in the South Atlantic and southeastern Pacific because of weak Coriolis force and cool water, respectively. Ocean currents form gyres, clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counterclockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. Ekman transport moves surface water at about 90° to the wind direction. Global wind belts: trade winds (easterlies), westerlies and polar easterlies are deflected by this force. Other angles UPSC may ask: jet streams, Hadley, Ferrel and Polar cells, ITCZ, the monsoon and the Somali jet, El Niño and Walker circulation.

ocr: Select the correct answer using the code given below : (a) lonly (b) 2only (c) S8and4 (d) 2and4 One of the following regions has the world’s largest tropical peatland, which holds about three years worth of global carbon emissions from fossil fuels; and the possible destruction of which can exert detrimental effect on the global climate. Which one of the following denotes that region ? (a) Amazon Basin (b) Congo Basin (c) Kikori Basin (d) Rio de la Plata Basin 17. With reference to perfluoroalkyl and | 19. polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) that are used in making many consumer products, consid
subject: Environment
detail: The Indian Flying Fox (Pteropus medius, formerly P. giganteus) is one of the largest bats in the world. It is a frugivore and nectarivore that roosts in large colonies on tall trees. It is an important pollinator and seed disperser for mango, banana, guava, silk-cotton and mahua. Only three bat species are true blood feeders, the vampire bats (Desmodus, Diaemus, Diphylla), and all of them are found in Latin America. No Indian bat feeds on blood, so Statement-II is plainly wrong. Under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, Schedule V listed vermin, namely common crow, fruit bats (flying fox), rats and mice. Vermin could be hunted without a licence under certain conditions. The Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 rationalised the schedules from six to four and deleted Schedule V altogether. The Indian Flying Fox is now treated as a Schedule II species (IUCN Least Concern). Elimination: since II is false, (a), (b) and (d) cannot hold. Only (c) is possible, and it is correct only if the older 1972 text is used. A student testing current law finds both statements false, which is not an available option, and this is the likely reason the question was dropped.
explanations: (a) is wrong because Statement-II is false: the Indian Flying Fox is a fruit and nectar eater, not a blood feeder. Hence both statements cannot be correct, and no explanation of one by the other is possible.
(b) is wrong for the same reason: Statement-II is incorrect, so the claim that both statements are correct fails.

(c) is the most defensible choice: Statement-I matches the original Schedule V (vermin) listing in the 1972 Act, and Statement-II is false. It is valid only on the pre-2022 law, which is why the question was flawed.
(d) is wrong because it says Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct. Statement-II is false, since flying foxes do not drink blood, so this reversal cannot hold.
keyfact: Flying foxes eat fruit, not blood; the vermin Schedule V of the WPA 1972 was deleted in 2022.
option_notes: Both statements correct and II explains I: this is a standard assertion-reason format. Here it would require flying foxes to be blood feeders and vermin because of that. In reality they are vermin only because they raid orchards. The Indian Flying Fox (Pteropus medius) is a large frugivorous megabat that roosts communally, can have a wingspan of about 1.2 m and weighs up to roughly 1.6 kg. It is found across the Indian subcontinent and is IUCN Least Concern.

Both statements correct but II does not explain I: this would need both statements to be true. Statement-II fails because no Indian bat feeds on blood. Indian bats are mainly insectivorous (microbats) or frugivorous (megabats like Pteropus). Vampire bats occur only in Central and South America and feed on the blood of livestock, birds and wild mammals. They are associated with rabies transmission to cattle. Bats are the only true flying mammals, in the order Chiroptera.

Statement-I correct but Statement-II incorrect: this is the reading that fits the original 1972 Act, which placed fruit bats in Schedule V as vermin along with common crow, rat and mouse. Vermin could be hunted freely. Schedule V was removed by the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022. It is the likely key, but it is time-sensitive and so the question was open to challenge.

Statement-I incorrect but Statement-II correct: this reverses the facts. Statement-II is false because the Indian Flying Fox is not a blood feeder. Statement-I was true under the original Act, though not under the current Act. Remember that the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 covers wild animals, birds and plants. The 2022 amendment also gave effect to CITES and created a Standing Committee of the State Wildlife Board.
related: The Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 cut the schedules from six to four.
Schedule V (vermin) was deleted in 2022; it had listed common crow, fruit bat, rat and mouse.
Indian Flying Fox (Pteropus medius) is a fruit and nectar eater and is IUCN Least Concern.
Only the three vampire bat species of the Americas feed on blood.
Pteropus bats are the natural reservoir of the Nipah virus.
Section 62 of the WPA 1972 lets the Centre declare animals as vermin.
Bats belong to the order Chiroptera, the only mammals capable of true flight.
CITES-listed species are now covered under Schedule IV of the WPA.
statements: Statement-I — Correct (as per the original 1972 Act, outdated now): Fruit bats were listed in Schedule V as vermin until the 2022 amendment. Facts: Schedule V of the WPA 1972 contained common crow, fruit bat, rat and mouse. Section 62 allowed the Centre to declare wild animals other than those in Schedule I and Part II of Schedule II as vermin for a given area and period. The 2022 Amendment, in force from 1 April 2023, cut the schedules to four: Schedule I, Schedule II, Schedule III (protected plants moved here) and Schedule IV (CITES appendices). Schedule V (vermin) was abolished and fruit bats were not given a separate vermin status.

Statement-II — Incorrect: The Indian Flying Fox does not feed on blood. It eats fruits, flowers, nectar and sometimes leaves. Facts: It is a megabat in the family Pteropodidae and navigates mainly by sight and smell, not by echolocation. It is a key pollinator and seed disperser. Some orchardists regard it as a pest because it damages fruit. The only blood-feeding bats are the three vampire bat species of the Americas. In India the Nipah virus is associated with Pteropus bats as a reservoir, but this does not involve blood feeding. Kerala outbreaks have been traced to fruit contaminated with bat saliva or urine.
summary: The most defensible answer is (c): Statement-I was true under the original Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, where the Indian Flying Fox (Pteropus medius) sat in Schedule V (vermin), and Statement-II is false because the bat is a fruit and nectar eater, not a blood feeder. The question was dropped because the 2022 amendment removed Schedule V, so Statement-I is outdated and no option fits the current law.
topic_notes: The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 is the main law for wildlife protection in India. It created Schedules for graded protection. Before 2022, Schedule I and Part II of Schedule II gave the highest protection and the heaviest penalties. Schedule III and IV covered protected animals with lower penalties. Schedule V listed vermin (common crow, fruit bat, rat, mouse), which could be hunted. Schedule VI listed specified plants whose cultivation and trade were regulated. The Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 reduced the schedules to four: Schedule I (highest protection), Schedule II (lesser protection), Schedule III (protected plants, formerly VI) and Schedule IV (CITES-listed species, specified in Appendices). Vermin Schedule V was deleted. The Act also allows the transfer or transport of captive elephants for religious or other purposes, regulates the possession of live exotic species, and renames some provisions. Key institutions: National Board for Wildlife, State Boards, the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau and the Central Zoo Authority. Chapter on Section 11 allows hunting of animals dangerous to human life in specified situations, and Section 62 allows declaring animals as vermin. Bat facts: India has over 120 bat species. Pteropus medius is the Indian Flying Fox, and its IUCN status is Least Concern. Bats are the reservoir of Nipah virus, which has caused outbreaks in Kerala (2018 onwards) and West Bengal (2001, 2007). Bats also have a role in pollinating durian, agave and banana. Related UPSC angles: CITES appendices, Schedule I species such as tiger, elephant and Great Indian Bustard, and the IUCN Red List categories.
why_dropped: Statement-I relied on Schedule V (vermin), which the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 abolished, so it is outdated, and with Statement-II false no option correctly matches the current law.

question: The organisms “Cicada, Froghopper and Pond 24. skater” are :
subject: Environment
detail: Insects (class Insecta, phylum Arthropoda) have a body divided into head, thorax and abdomen, three pairs of jointed legs on the thorax, one pair of antennae, and usually two pairs of wings. Cicadas (family Cicadidae) and froghoppers or spittlebugs (family Cercopidae and allied families) belong to suborder Auchenorrhyncha of order Hemiptera. Pond skaters or water striders (family Gerridae) belong to suborder Heteroptera of the same order. All Hemiptera have piercing-sucking mouthparts (a rostrum) used to feed on plant sap or on prey. Cicadas are known for loud calls produced by tympanal organs and for nymphs living underground for years; periodic cicadas of North America emerge after 13 or 17 years. Froghopper nymphs hide inside frothy 'spittle'. Pond skaters walk on water using surface tension and hydrophobic leg hairs. Elimination: birds have feathers and a beak, fish have gills and fins, and reptiles are scaly vertebrates. None of the three organisms is a vertebrate, so (a), (b) and (d) fail and (c) is correct.
explanations: Wrong: birds are feathered, warm-blooded vertebrates (class Aves). None of these three organisms has feathers, a beak or a backbone.
Wrong: fish are aquatic gill-breathing vertebrates with fins. A pond skater lives on the water surface but is an arthropod, not a fish.
Correct: all three are insects of order Hemiptera, with six legs and a three-part body (head, thorax, abdomen).
Wrong: reptiles are scaly, cold-blooded vertebrates such as snakes, lizards and turtles. These three are invertebrates.
keyfact: Cicada, froghopper and pond skater are all insects of order Hemiptera (true bugs), with six legs and a three-part body.
option_notes: Birds (class Aves) are warm-blooded, egg-laying vertebrates with feathers, beaks, forelimbs modified into wings and a four-chambered heart. Most can fly, though ostriches and penguins cannot. They have hollow (pneumatic) bones. India's examples include the Great Indian Bustard (critically endangered, state bird of Rajasthan) and the peacock (national bird).

Fish are aquatic, cold-blooded vertebrates that breathe through gills and use fins to swim. They are grouped into Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous, e.g. sharks), Osteichthyes (bony, e.g. rohu) and the jawless Agnatha (e.g. lampreys). Most have a two-chambered heart and scales. Some, like lungfish, can breathe air.

Insects (class Insecta) are the largest animal class, with over a million described species. They have a head, thorax and abdomen, six legs, one pair of antennae, compound eyes and a chitinous exoskeleton. They breathe through tracheae and spiracles and undergo complete or incomplete metamorphosis. Hemiptera (true bugs) includes cicadas, froghoppers, aphids, bed bugs and pond skaters.

Reptiles (class Reptilia) are cold-blooded vertebrates with dry scaly skin, lungs for breathing and mostly leathery-shelled eggs laid on land. Examples are snakes, lizards, crocodiles, turtles and tortoises. Most have a three-chambered heart, while crocodiles have four chambers. Many Indian reptiles, such as the gharial and king cobra, are protected under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
related: Insects have three pairs of legs and a body divided into head, thorax and abdomen.
Cicadas make sound with tymbals; periodic species emerge after 13 or 17 years.
Pond skaters stay afloat on water through surface tension.
Hemiptera has piercing-sucking mouthparts; aphids and bed bugs belong to it.
Coleoptera (beetles) is the largest order of animals.
Honeybee colonies have queen, drones and workers; the waggle dance was decoded by Karl von Frisch.
Anopheles transmits malaria; Aedes transmits dengue, chikungunya and yellow fever.
Silk comes from the cocoon of Bombyx mori, the mulberry silkworm.
summary: The answer is (c) Insects. Cicada, froghopper and pond skater all belong to class Insecta, order Hemiptera (true bugs), and share the insect body plan of three body parts and six legs.
topic_notes: Phylum Arthropoda is the largest animal phylum and includes insects, crustaceans, arachnids and myriapods. Insects (class Insecta) have three body regions, three pairs of legs, and often wings. Their exoskeleton is made of chitin, and they have an open circulatory system and Malpighian tubules for excretion. Metamorphosis may be complete (egg, larva, pupa, adult, as in butterflies, beetles, flies and bees) or incomplete (egg, nymph, adult, as in cockroaches, grasshoppers and Hemiptera). Order Hemiptera has piercing-sucking mouthparts and includes cicadas, froghoppers, leafhoppers, aphids, scale insects, bed bugs, stink bugs, water striders and water boatmen. Other major orders: Lepidoptera (butterflies and moths), Coleoptera (beetles, the largest order), Diptera (flies and mosquitoes, with one pair of wings and halteres), Hymenoptera (ants, bees and wasps), Odonata (dragonflies) and Orthoptera (grasshoppers and crickets). Insects have ecological and economic roles: pollination (bees), silk (Bombyx mori), lac (Kerria lacca), honey, biological control and disease vectors (Anopheles for malaria, Aedes for dengue, sandfly for kala-azar, tsetse fly for sleeping sickness). Pests include the locust (Schistocerca gregaria), the desert locust that swarms in India and Africa. Cicada nymphs feed on xylem sap underground and emerge to moult. Males sing using tymbals. Social insects such as ants, termites and honeybees show caste systems. Pheromones are used for communication. Insect conservation topics include colony collapse disorder in bees and neonicotinoid pesticides, and UPSC often links these to environment questions.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement-I : Many chewing gums found in the market are considered a source of environmental pollution.
Statement-II : Many chewing gums contain plastic as gum base. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements ?
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I 25
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
subject: Environment
detail: Chewing gum has four main components: gum base (the insoluble, chewy part), sweeteners, softeners and flavourings. Traditionally the base was chicle, a natural latex from the sapodilla tree (Manilkara zapota), used by the Maya and Aztecs. Since the mid-20th century most manufacturers have shifted to cheaper synthetic polymers: polyisobutylene (butyl rubber), styrene-butadiene rubber, polyvinyl acetate, polyethylene and similar compounds, which are plastics or synthetic elastomers. These are hydrophobic and do not dissolve or biodegrade quickly; a discarded piece may persist for years, sticks to pavements, is costly to clean, and breaks into microplastics. Animals and birds may ingest it. Hence the plastic gum base is the direct reason the gum is a pollutant, so Statement-II is the correct explanation of Statement-I. Elimination: option (b) fails because the link is causal; (c) and (d) fail because each statement is factually true. Singapore banned the sale and import of chewing gum in 1992 largely over littering, with limited exceptions later (therapeutic/dental gums from 2004).
explanations: Correct: both statements are factually true and the plastic gum base is exactly why gum persists as non-biodegradable pollution, so Statement-II explains Statement-I.
Wrong: although both are correct, Statement-II is not merely an unrelated fact; it is the direct cause of the pollution described in Statement-I.
Wrong: Statement-II is correct, since many gums use synthetic polymer bases that are effectively plastics.
Wrong: Statement-I is correct, since discarded gum is a recognised, persistent litter and microplastic source.
keyfact: Most modern chewing gums use a synthetic plastic-like gum base (e.g. polyvinyl acetate, polyethylene) that does not biodegrade, so gum litter pollutes.
option_notes: Option (a) is the logical relation 'both true and II explains I'. It is the right choice here because synthetic polymer gum base makes gum non-biodegradable, hence a pollutant. In assertion-reason questions, always test for a causal link before settling for the weaker option (b).

Option (b) means both statements are true but the second is not the explanation of the first. It applies when the two facts are independent, for instance if gum were a pollutant due to its packaging rather than its base. Here it fails, as the base itself is the source of persistence in the environment.

Option (c) says Statement-I is true and Statement-II false. That would hold if gum bases were entirely natural, like chicle, which is biodegradable. Chicle is the sap of Manilkara zapota, used historically, but most modern commercial gums use synthetic bases, so this option fails.

Option (d) says Statement-I is false and Statement-II true. It would be right only if gum had plastic yet caused no pollution, which is untrue because discarded gum persists, sticks to surfaces and fragments into microplastics, so Statement-I is correct.
related: Chicle is a natural latex from the sapodilla tree, Manilkara zapota.
Common synthetic gum bases: polyvinyl acetate, polyisobutylene, polyethylene.
Singapore banned chewing gum sales in 1992.
Microplastics are plastic particles smaller than 5 mm.
India banned identified single-use plastic items from 1 July 2022.
Plastic Waste Management Rules were first notified in 2016.
The UNEA in March 2022 agreed to negotiate a global plastics treaty.
Cellulose acetate cigarette filters are the most littered item worldwide.
statements: 1 — Correct: Discarded chewing gum is a widely recognised litter and pollution problem. Gum is non-biodegradable, adheres to surfaces, is expensive to remove, and contributes microplastics to the environment. It can take years to decompose, and is often cited as the second most common litter item after cigarette butts in several countries. Cities spend large sums on removal; Singapore's 1992 ban was motivated by littering and vandalism, with regulated exemptions for nicotine and dental gums.

2 — Correct: Many gums use synthetic polymers such as polyvinyl acetate, polyethylene and polyisobutylene as gum base, which are plastics or synthetic rubbers. Natural chicle from the sapodilla tree was the original base but became costly and scarce, so synthetic bases replaced it after the 1940s-50s. Regulators often list the base as just 'gum base', so the plastic content is not itemised. A few brands now sell biodegradable gums using chicle or other natural resins.
summary: The answer is (a): both statements are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I. Many commercial chewing gums use a synthetic, non-biodegradable gum base such as polyethylene or polyvinyl acetate (essentially plastics/synthetic rubbers), so discarded gum persists as litter and pollutes the environment.
topic_notes: Chewing gum consists of gum base, sweeteners (sugar, or polyols such as xylitol, sorbitol), softeners (glycerin, vegetable oil) and flavours. The gum base is the non-digestible part. Natural bases: chicle (Manilkara zapota, native to Mexico and Central America), jelutong, sorva and similar latexes. Synthetic bases: polyvinyl acetate, polyisobutylene, styrene-butadiene rubber, polyethylene, and also paraffin waxes and elastomers. Because these are petroleum-derived polymers, gum is essentially a form of plastic litter; it is hydrophobic, resists degradation and may last for years. It adds microplastics when worn down by foot traffic and weather, can be ingested by birds and fish, and costs municipalities heavily to scrape off pavements. Singapore banned chewing gum sales in 1992, easing the rule in 2004 for therapeutic gums prescribed or sold by pharmacists. Related UPSC angles: microplastics (plastics below 5 mm), primary versus secondary microplastics, the Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 and amendments (2021 banned identified single-use plastic items from 1 July 2022), Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), the Swachh Bharat Mission, biodegradable versus compostable plastics, the UN Environment Assembly 2022 resolution to develop a legally binding global plastics treaty, and bioplastics such as PLA and PHA. Nicotine gum is a nicotine replacement therapy, another common question angle. Also remember that cigarette filters (cellulose acetate) are the most littered item globally.

question:
Consider the following pairs : real Animal found in its ibe natural habitat |1. [Brazil |Indri
2. Indonesia Elk
8. Madagascar [Bonobo How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched ?
subject: Environment
detail: This question tests the geographic distribution of animals that are easily confused. The Indri (Indri indri) is the largest living lemur, and lemurs are endemic to Madagascar, which has been isolated for about 88 million years. The Elk (Cervus canadensis, called wapiti in North America) is a large deer of North America and East Asia; in Europe 'elk' refers to the moose (Alces alces). Neither lives in tropical Indonesia, whose famous fauna includes the orangutan, Komodo dragon, Sumatran tiger and Javan rhino. The Bonobo (Pan paniscus) is a great ape found only south of the Congo River in the DR Congo's rainforests. Brazil's native primates are New World monkeys (howler, spider, golden lion tamarin), and no lemurs or apes occur there. Elimination logic: once one pair is shown wrong, options (c) is out; since all three are wrong, (d) is correct. Tip: link each animal to its country by endemism, as UPSC regularly frames 'animal-habitat' pairs.
explanations: (a) Only one: Wrong, because none of the three pairs is correct; even the pair that might look plausible fails on geography.
(b) Only two: Wrong, since Indri, Elk and Bonobo are each placed in the wrong country, so not even two match.
(c) All three: Wrong, as the Indri is Madagascan, the Elk is a northern-hemisphere deer and the Bonobo is Congolese.
(d) None: Correct, because Indri belongs to Madagascar, Elk to North America and Eurasia, and Bonobo to the DR Congo, so no pair matches.
keyfact: Indri = Madagascar lemur, Elk = North America/Eurasia deer, Bonobo = DR Congo ape; none matched with Brazil, Indonesia, Madagascar respectively, so the answer is (d) None.
option_notes: Only one: This would mean exactly one pair was right. In geography-based matching questions, such options test whether you can spot a single correct pair among plausible-sounding ones. Here it is not valid. The correct matches would be Indri with Madagascar, Elk with North America or Eurasia, and Bonobo with the DR Congo. Because none of the given pairs matches these, this option is wrong, though it is the type of option that suits a question where one pair has been intentionally corrected.

Only two: This would mean two of three pairs were correct. UPSC uses it to catch students who are sure of two animals but unsure of the third. Here it fails, as all three are mismatched. Useful related facts: the Indri and other lemurs are endemic to Madagascar, and the bonobo and the chimpanzee are both Pan species, separated by the Congo River, with bonobos only to its south.

All three: This would require every pair to match. It would be true only if Brazil held the Indri, Indonesia the Elk and Madagascar the Bonobo, none of which is true. In an exam, a correct 'all three' answer usually needs solid knowledge of every item. Here, knowing even one item such as the Indri being Madagascan would eliminate it. Such options reward careful elimination and linking species to their endemic regions.

None: This is the official and correct answer. It states that no pair is correctly matched. The Indri is a lemur of Madagascar, the Elk is a large deer of North America and northern Asia, and the Bonobo is an ape of the Congo basin. UPSC often uses 'None' when all items are deliberately swapped between regions. A student who knows each animal's true range can answer with confidence even without knowing the other options.
related: Madagascar is home to nearly all lemur species, and the Indri is the largest living lemur.
The bonobo is found only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, south of the Congo River.
Orangutans live only in Sumatra and Borneo.
The golden lion tamarin is endemic to Brazil's Atlantic Forest.
Elk or wapiti (Cervus canadensis) is a deer of North America and East Asia; the European 'elk' is the moose.
The Komodo dragon is native to Indonesian islands including Komodo and Rinca.
Indri is Critically Endangered and bonobo is Endangered on the IUCN Red List.
The aye-aye is a nocturnal lemur endemic to Madagascar.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Indri is native to Madagascar, not Brazil. The Indri (Indri indri), also called babakoto, is the largest living lemur, about 60-70 cm long with a very short tail. It lives in the eastern rainforests of Madagascar, feeds mainly on leaves, and is known for its loud, whale-like song that carries for kilometres. It is Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List because of deforestation and slash-and-burn farming, and it does not survive well in captivity. Brazil has no lemurs; its primates are New World monkeys such as the golden lion tamarin and howler monkeys.

2 — Incorrect: The Elk does not occur naturally in Indonesia. The Elk or wapiti (Cervus canadensis) is one of the largest deer species, found in North America and eastern Asia, with large antlers on males. It is assessed as Least Concern by the IUCN. In Europe the word 'elk' refers to the moose (Alces alces). Indonesia's native deer include the Javan rusa and the Bawean deer, and its famous mammals include the orangutan, Sumatran rhino and Komodo dragon among reptiles.

3 — Incorrect: The Bonobo is not found in Madagascar. The Bonobo (Pan paniscus), formerly the pygmy chimpanzee, is a great ape that lives only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, south of the Congo River. It is closely related to humans, shares about 98.7% of our DNA, and lives in female-dominated, relatively peaceful societies. It is listed as Endangered by the IUCN because of poaching, habitat loss and the bushmeat trade. Madagascar's famous fauna are lemurs, fossas and chameleons, and it has no apes.
summary: The answer is (d) None. Each pair is wrongly matched: the Indri is a lemur native to Madagascar (not Brazil), the Elk is found in North America, Europe and northern Asia (not Indonesia), and the Bonobo is found only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (not Madagascar).
topic_notes:
This question belongs to species-habitat geography under Environment and Biodiversity. UPSC regularly asks which animal lives where, often mixing animals from different continents.

Madagascar: it is a biodiversity hotspot, with about 90% of its wildlife endemic. Lemurs (ring-tailed lemur, aye-aye, indri, sifaka), fossa, tenrecs and most chameleon species live there. The island separated from India about 88 million years ago.

Congo basin: it holds the bonobo (DR Congo only), the okapi (DR Congo), the mountain gorilla (Virunga, Bwindi), and forest elephants. Chimpanzees and gorillas live across equatorial Africa, whereas bonobos are found only south of the Congo River.

Asia: orangutans live only in Borneo and Sumatra (Indonesia and Malaysia). The Komodo dragon is found on Komodo, Rinca, Flores and Gili Motang. The Sumatran rhino, Javan rhino and Sumatran tiger are also Indonesian.

South America: Brazil has the golden lion tamarin, jaguar, giant otter, Amazon river dolphin and the maned wolf. New World monkeys have prehensile tails in many species and flat noses.

North America and Eurasia: the elk or wapiti, moose, caribou (reindeer) and bison.

IUCN categories: Extinct, Extinct in the Wild, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened, Least Concern, Data Deficient, Not Evaluated. Indri is Critically Endangered, bonobo is Endangered, and elk is Least Concern.

Study approach: build a table of animal, country, habitat and IUCN status. UPSC has asked similar questions on the Indian elephant, hornbills, migratory birds and Ramsar sites. Pay special attention to endemic species and their conservation programmes.

question: Consider the following statements regarding World Toilet Organization : It is one of the agencies of the United & Nations. World Toilet Summit, World Toilet Day and World Toilet College are the initiatives of this organization, to inspire action to tackle the global sanitation crisis. The main focus of its function is to grant funds to the least developed countries and developing countries to achieve the end of open defecation. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The World Toilet Organization was founded in 2001 by Jack Sim in Singapore as a global non-profit that works on the sanitation crisis. It is not part of the UN system, so statement 1 fails. It runs the World Toilet Summit (first held in Singapore in 2001), the World Toilet College (training in toilet design, sanitation management and business) and it campaigned for World Toilet Day on 19 November. The UN General Assembly officially designated 19 November as World Toilet Day in 2013 (Resolution A/RES/67/291, with Singapore leading the push), and UN-Water coordinates the observance. The WTO's work is advocacy, networking, training and awareness, not funding. Statement 3 therefore fails, because it describes a donor or financing agency such as the World Bank or a development fund. Elimination logic: once statement 1 is rejected (the WTO is not a UN agency), options (c) and (b, which is an OCR error for '3 only') cannot hold. Statement 3 is also false, which rules out (d). Only (a) is left. Related: SDG 6 targets clean water and sanitation for all, and India's Swachh Bharat Mission targeted an end to open defecation.
explanations: Correct: statement 2 alone is accurate, since the Summit, College and World Toilet Day are the WTO's initiatives and it is not a UN agency or a funder.
Incorrect: this is an OCR-garbled option for '3 only', and statement 3 is false because the WTO does not grant funds.
Incorrect: statement 1 is false because the WTO is an independent Singapore-based NGO, not a UN agency.
Incorrect: statement 3 is false because the WTO's main role is advocacy, not grant-making, so it cannot be combined with 2.
keyfact: The World Toilet Organization is a Singapore-based NGO (2001, Jack Sim), not a UN agency, and it advocates rather than funds.
option_notes: 2 only: this is the correct choice. It reflects that the WTO is a non-profit NGO founded in 2001 by Jack Sim in Singapore. It runs the World Toilet Summit and the World Toilet College and campaigns for World Toilet Day on 19 November. The UN designated that day in 2013 after Singapore's initiative.

3 only (OCR-garbled as '8 only'): this would mean the WTO's main function is to grant funds to LDCs and developing countries to end open defecation. That is false. Funding comes from the World Bank, bilateral donors, foundations and national governments, while the WTO focuses on advocacy, training and awareness.

1 and 2 (OCR 'land2'): this would make the WTO a UN agency. It is not one. UN-linked sanitation actors include UN-Water (a coordination mechanism), UNICEF and WHO, which together run the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for water supply, sanitation and hygiene.

2 and 3: this wrongly adds the funding role. The WTO is a small advocacy NGO and not a financing institution. Real sanitation financing bodies include the World Bank, regional development banks, the Gates Foundation, and in India the Swachh Bharat Mission (Grameen and Urban) funds.
related: World Toilet Organization was founded in 2001 in Singapore by Jack Sim.
World Toilet Day is observed on 19 November; the UN designated it in 2013.
SDG 6 aims at clean water and sanitation for all by 2030.
Swachh Bharat Mission was launched on 2 October 2014.
Rural India was declared ODF on 2 October 2019.
UN-Water coordinates UN work on water and sanitation and World Toilet Day.
WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme monitors WASH progress.
Sulabh International was founded by Bindeshwar Pathak in 1970.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The WTO is an NGO, not a UN agency. It was founded in 2001 by Jack Sim, is headquartered in Singapore, and is a non-profit global body. UN bodies working on sanitation include UNICEF, WHO and UN-Water (a coordination mechanism). Jack Sim is called 'Mr Toilet' and also founded the Restroom Association of Singapore (2001) and the BoP Hub. The WTO has no UN agency status.

2 — Correct: The World Toilet Summit began in 2001 in Singapore and is held annually in different cities. The World Toilet College, set up in 2005, offers training in sanitation. World Toilet Day, observed on 19 November, was started by the WTO in 2001 and adopted by the UN in 2013. These initiatives aim to raise awareness and spur action on the sanitation crisis. The UN's 2013 resolution was backed by Singapore and 122 countries.

3 — Incorrect: The WTO does not mainly grant funds. It is a network and advocacy body that does awareness campaigns, capacity-building, training and policy engagement. Funding for sanitation comes from the World Bank, the Gates Foundation, bilateral donors and national schemes such as India's Swachh Bharat Mission (launched 2 October 2014). SDG 6 (clean water and sanitation) targets an end to open defecation by 2030, and WHO/UNICEF's JMP monitors progress.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement 2 is correct. The World Toilet Organization (WTO) is a Singapore-based non-profit NGO, not a UN agency, and it works through advocacy, not by granting funds. Its initiatives are the World Toilet Summit, World Toilet College and the push for World Toilet Day.
topic_notes: Sanitation is a recurring UPSC theme across international bodies, SDGs and Indian schemes. The World Toilet Organization (2001, Singapore, Jack Sim) is a non-profit that runs the World Toilet Summit, World Toilet College and World Toilet Day advocacy. World Toilet Day falls on 19 November; the UN made it official in 2013 and UN-Water coordinates it each year with a theme. SDG 6 covers clean water and sanitation, and Target 6.2 calls for an end to open defecation and access to adequate sanitation and hygiene by 2030. The WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) tracks progress on drinking water, sanitation and hygiene. India's Swachh Bharat Mission was launched on 2 October 2014. Rural India was declared open-defecation-free on 2 October 2019, and SBM-Urban 2.0 and SBM-Grameen Phase II continue the work with a focus on solid and liquid waste management and ODF Plus status. Related Indian initiatives include Jal Jeevan Mission (tap water to rural households, 2019), AMRUT, and Namami Gange. Other global days to know: World Water Day (22 March), Global Handwashing Day (15 October), World Environment Day (5 June). The Sulabh International movement, founded by Bindeshwar Pathak in 1970, pioneered the two-pit pour-flush toilet. The Right to sanitation was recognised by the UN General Assembly in 2010 (water and sanitation as a human right), and in 2015 it was separated as a distinct right. UPSC often tests whether a body is a UN agency, an NGO or a treaty body, so check the legal status carefully.

ocr: Consider the following statements : Lions do not have a particular breeding Ae season. Unlike most other big cats, cheetahs do not roar. Unlike male lions, male leopards do not proclaim their territory by scent marking. Which of the statements given above are correct ? (a) land 2 only (b) 2and3 only (c) land3 only 1,2 and 3 (d)
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This question tests basic big-cat biology, which UPSC often draws from wildlife and conservation themes. The genus Panthera (lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar, snow leopard) can roar because of a specialised larynx and an incompletely ossified hyoid apparatus. The cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) belongs to a separate genus. Its hyoid is fully ossified, so it cannot roar. It purrs continuously, chirps and yelps. Lions are the only truly social big cats and live in prides. They are not seasonal breeders, so mating and births can occur in any month, and a pride often synchronises births after a takeover. Territory marking by scent is universal among big cats. Males spray urine, rub their faces and scrape the ground, and leopards also leave claw marks on trees. Elimination logic: statement 3 is false, so options (b), (c) and (d) are eliminated. Only (a) remains, which needs statements 1 and 2 to be true. Remember that India's cheetah was declared extinct in 1952 and that African cheetahs were reintroduced at Kuno National Park from September 2022.
explanations: Correct. Statements 1 and 2 are true and statement 3 is false, so 'only 1 and 2' is the exact combination.
Wrong. It includes statement 3, which is false because male leopards do scent-mark their territory.
Wrong. It includes statement 3, which is false, and leaves out statement 2, which is true.
Wrong. It includes the false statement 3, so not all three statements can be correct.
keyfact: Lions breed year-round, cheetahs purr rather than roar, and all male big cats, including leopards, scent-mark their territory.
option_notes: Statements 1 and 2 only. Together they describe lions as non-seasonal breeders and cheetahs as unable to roar. Both are accurate. Lions (Panthera leo) are social cats of Africa, with an Asiatic relict population in Gir. Cheetahs are in genus Acinonyx and purr rather than roar.

Statements 2 and 3 only. This combination fails because statement 3 is false. Male leopards scent-mark through urine spraying, scrapes and claw marks. Leopards are solitary, adaptable and found across Africa and Asia. They are listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List and in Schedule I of India's Wildlife (Protection) Act.

Statements 1 and 3 only. This combination fails because statement 3 is false and statement 2 is true. Leopards and lions both mark territory with scent, so the contrast in statement 3 does not exist. The leopard is the most widespread big cat and the one most often involved in human-wildlife conflict in India.

All three statements. This fails because statement 3 is false. It would require male leopards not to scent-mark, whereas in reality they spray urine and scratch trees to advertise their territory. Statements 1 and 2 alone are correct.
related: Roaring big cats belong to genus Panthera; the cheetah (Acinonyx) cannot roar and purrs.
Asiatic lions survive only in Gir, Gujarat (674 in the 2020 census).
India's cheetah was declared extinct in 1952; Kuno National Park received African cheetahs in 2022.
The International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA) was launched in 2023 in Mysuru.
Project Tiger was launched in 1973; India had 3,682 tigers in 2022.
The snow leopard is Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List and is the state animal of Ladakh.
The lion is the only social big cat and lives in prides.
The NTCA became a statutory body in 2006 under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
statements: 1 — Correct: Lions have no fixed breeding season and can mate and give birth in any month. Lions (Panthera leo) live in prides of related females, their cubs and a coalition of males. Females are polyestrous. Gestation lasts about 110 days and litters are typically 1 to 4 cubs. Females in a pride often synchronise births, and a takeover by new males can trigger oestrus after infanticide. The Asiatic lion (P. l. persica) survives only in Gir, Gujarat. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List and is in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972. The 2020 census estimated 674 lions.

2 — Correct: Cheetahs cannot roar. They purr, chirp, yelp and growl. The cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) is the fastest land animal, reaching about 100 to 110 km/h in short bursts. Its semi-retractable claws and its tear-like black facial 'tear lines' are distinctive. It is classed as Vulnerable by the IUCN. The Asiatic cheetah survives only in Iran. India's cheetahs were declared extinct in 1952. Under Project Cheetah, Namibian cheetahs arrived at Kuno National Park, Madhya Pradesh, on 17 September 2022, and South African cheetahs followed in 2023. The cheetah is listed in CITES Appendix I and in the Wildlife (Protection) Act Schedule I.

3 — Incorrect: Male leopards do scent-mark their territory, as lions do. Leopards (Panthera pardus) are solitary and mainly nocturnal. Both sexes mark with urine spray, claw scratches on trees, faecal deposits and rubbing, and they also use loud 'sawing' calls. Males hold larger territories that overlap those of several females. The leopard is Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List and is in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act. India's leopard population was estimated at about 13,874 in the 2022 report, and Madhya Pradesh has the most. It is the most widespread big cat, found across Africa and Asia.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 and 2 only. Lions breed throughout the year with no fixed season, and cheetahs cannot roar because they purr instead. Statement 3 is wrong because male leopards also mark territory by scent (urine spraying, scrapes and scratch marks).
topic_notes: Big cats are a frequent UPSC theme, often tied to conservation news. The 'roaring cats' belong to genus Panthera: lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar and snow leopard. Roaring is made possible by an elastic ligament in the larynx and a partly ligamentous hyoid. The cheetah (Acinonyx), puma and lynx cannot roar and instead purr. The lion is the only social cat, living in prides. The tiger is solitary and the largest cat. The leopard is solitary, adaptable and widespread. Indian conservation facts: Project Tiger started in 1973. India had 3,682 tigers in the 2022 census, about 75 percent of the world's wild tigers. Project Lion was announced in 2020 for the Gir landscape. Gir National Park in Gujarat is the only home of the Asiatic lion, whose population was 674 in 2020. Project Cheetah was launched in 2022, and Kuno National Park hosts the introduced African cheetahs. The snow leopard lives in the high Himalayas and is the state animal of Ladakh. The clouded leopard lives in the north-east. The IUCN statuses to remember are: tiger Endangered, Asiatic lion Endangered, snow leopard Vulnerable, leopard Vulnerable, cheetah Vulnerable. The International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA) was launched by India in April 2023 at Mysuru. Other things to revise are the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 schedules, CITES appendices, and the National Tiger Conservation Authority, which became a statutory body in 2006. Marking behaviour, breeding habits, vocalisations and social structure are the common biology angles.

question: Which one of the following is the correct 28. description of “100 Million Farmers” ?
options: It is a platform for accelerating the transition towards food and water systems that are net-zero (carbon), nature-positive and that aims to increase farmer resilience
It is an international alliance and a network of individuals and farming organisations interested in supporting and strengthening the development of the organic animal husbandry. 29
It is a digital platform fully integrated with service providers and built on blockchain that lets buyers, sellers and third parties trade fertilizers quickly and securely

It is a platform with the mission of encouraging the farmers to form Farmer Product Organisations or Agribusiness Consortiums, thus facilitating the access to global open markets to sell their products
subject: Economy
detail: The '100 Million Farmers' initiative is a multi-stakeholder, action-oriented platform hosted by the World Economic Forum. It was announced around COP26 (Glasgow, 2021) under the WEF's food-systems work, and it is associated with the WEF's Food Innovation Hubs and 'First Movers Coalition' style coalitions. Its aim is to bring together agribusinesses, food companies, financial institutions, governments, NGOs and farmer groups so that 100 million farmers adopt regenerative, climate-resilient and nature-positive practices. The goal is to move food and water systems towards net-zero emissions and nature-positive outcomes while raising farmer incomes and resilience. Elimination logic: option (b) describes an organic animal husbandry network, which is a niche, livestock-specific body, whereas the title refers to farmers in general and to climate and nature goals. Option (c) describes a blockchain-based fertilizer trading platform, which is a commercial digital marketplace and not a global coalition. Option (d) describes the FPO/agribusiness-consortium promotion model, closer to India's FPO scheme or SFAC. Only (a) uses the climate language (net-zero, nature-positive, resilience) that matches the WEF's framing. Treat the platform's details as WEF-linked and global, not Indian.
explanations: Correct: it matches the WEF-hosted platform that aims to accelerate net-zero, nature-positive food and water systems and to raise farmer resilience.
Wrong: this describes an organic animal husbandry alliance or network. The 100 Million Farmers platform is not livestock-specific and not limited to organic farming.
Wrong: this describes a blockchain-based fertilizer trading platform. 100 Million Farmers is a coalition for sustainability and resilience, not a trading marketplace.
Wrong: this describes promotion of FPOs or agribusiness consortiums for market access, as in India's FPO scheme. It is not the goal of this WEF platform.
keyfact: 100 Million Farmers = a WEF platform for net-zero, nature-positive food and water systems that builds farmer resilience.
option_notes: Correct option. 100 Million Farmers is a WEF-hosted global platform linked to the food-systems agenda. It brings together companies, financiers, governments and farmer groups to help farmers adopt regenerative, climate-smart practices. The goals are net-zero emissions, nature-positive outcomes and greater resilience and incomes for farmers. It was announced around COP26 in 2021 and ties into the WEF's wider food and water systems work.

This describes a network for organic animal husbandry, in the style of organic livestock alliances such as the international organic movement's sector networks (IFOAM-type bodies). Such groups promote organic standards for animals, feed, welfare and certification. They are focused on livestock and on organic methods, which is far narrower than the 100 Million Farmers platform. It is a plausible-sounding distractor, but it is not the correct description.

This describes a blockchain-based digital fertilizer trading platform, a private B2B e-commerce concept in which buyers, sellers and third parties transact securely. Blockchain gives traceability and tamper-proof records. Government counterparts in India include the DBT in fertilizers and the e-NAM market for agricultural produce. It has no link to the WEF's climate and nature-based farmer coalition.

This describes the FPO or agribusiness-consortium route. In India, the Central Sector Scheme for the formation and promotion of 10,000 FPOs was launched in 2020 with NABARD, NCDC and SFAC as implementing agencies. FPOs give small farmers collective bargaining power, better inputs and market access. This is a market-linkage idea and not the sustainability-focused 100 Million Farmers platform.
related: 100 Million Farmers is a World Economic Forum platform for net-zero, nature-positive food and water systems.
WEF was founded in 1971 by Klaus Schwab and is headquartered in Geneva.
Nature-positive means halting and reversing biodiversity loss by 2030.
The FPO scheme for 10,000 FPOs began in 2020, with NABARD, NCDC and SFAC as implementing agencies.
e-NAM is India's online pan-India electronic trading portal for agricultural commodities.
Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana promotes cluster-based organic farming.
Regenerative agriculture focuses on soil health, cover crops, reduced tillage and carbon sequestration.
COP28 (Dubai, 2023) included a declaration on sustainable agriculture, resilient food systems and climate action.
summary: The answer is (a). '100 Million Farmers' is a World Economic Forum (WEF) initiative, launched as a platform to speed up the shift to food and water systems that are net-zero, nature-positive and that build farmer resilience and livelihoods. It is not an organic livestock network, a blockchain fertilizer exchange or an FPO-promotion scheme.
topic_notes: 100 Million Farmers belongs to the World Economic Forum's food-systems and climate work. The WEF is an international NGO based in Geneva, founded in 1971 by Klaus Schwab, and is best known for its annual meeting at Davos. Its food-related platforms include the Food Innovation Hubs, the Global Alliance for Food Security and the Uplink innovation platform. The 100 Million Farmers initiative follows a pattern UPSC likes to test: a named international initiative with an exact stated purpose. The platform is built around the idea that farmers must be supported financially and technically to adopt regenerative agriculture, reduce emissions, protect biodiversity and manage water better. Several themes sit alongside it. Nature-positive means halting and reversing nature loss by 2030. Net-zero means balancing emissions with removals. Regenerative agriculture covers cover crops, reduced tillage, agroforestry and better soil carbon. Related international bodies include the FAO, IFAD, CGIAR and the Global Alliance for Climate-Smart Agriculture. Indian parallels are the FPO scheme, e-NAM, PM-KISAN, the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture, Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana for organic farming and the Soil Health Card scheme. UPSC often sets this style of question on indexes, reports and global initiatives, so students should note the host body, the launch year and the main purpose of each. Likely future angles are the full form and mandate of such initiatives, the difference between organic and regenerative farming, and the climate-smart agriculture commitments made at COP28.

question:
Consider the following : as Battery storage 30. 2 Biomass generators
3. Fuel cells 4 Rooftop solar photovoltaic units How many of the above are considered “Distributed Energy Resources” ?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) are decentralised, modular, smaller-scale units that generate, store or manage electricity close to where it is used, typically at the distribution level (or behind the meter), instead of in large centralised plants feeding the high-voltage transmission grid. The category covers distributed generation (rooftop solar PV, small wind, biomass or biogas gensets, micro-hydro, small CHP or cogeneration, diesel gensets), distributed storage (batteries, EV batteries in vehicle-to-grid use, thermal storage), fuel cells, and demand-side resources such as demand response and controllable loads or EVs. In India, DERs are promoted through schemes such as PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (rooftop solar, launched Feb 2024), PM-KUSUM (decentralised solar for farmers), net-metering rules and the Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Rules 2020. Benefits include lower transmission losses, resilience, faster deployment and better access in remote areas. Challenges include grid balancing, bidirectional power flow, voltage control and the need for smart grids, aggregators and virtual power plants. Elimination logic: every listed item is small-scale and can be sited near the load, so none can be dropped, which leaves 'All four'.
explanations: Incorrect: this undercounts. Not just one but all four items qualify as DERs.
Incorrect: this undercounts. Excluding any two of the items has no basis, because each is small-scale and located near the load.
Incorrect: one qualifying item would be left out, yet none can be excluded. Biomass gensets, fuel cells, batteries and rooftop PV are all DERs.
Correct: battery storage, biomass generators, fuel cells and rooftop solar PV are all decentralised generation or storage assets connected near the point of consumption, so all four are DERs.
keyfact: DERs are small decentralised generation or storage units near the load (rooftop solar, batteries, biomass gensets, fuel cells, etc.), so all four listed items qualify.
option_notes: Only one: this would imply that just a single item is a DER. In fact the DER umbrella is broad: it includes distributed generation, storage, controllable loads and EVs. Only large centralised plants such as ultra-mega thermal, large hydro or utility-scale solar parks are conventionally treated as non-DER because they feed the transmission grid at high voltage.

Only two: this would imply that only a pair of the items is a DER. The usual groupings are generation (rooftop PV, small wind, biomass), storage (batteries) and flexible demand. Fuel cells and biomass are often missed by students who think of DER as only solar and batteries, which is the trap in this question. DERs typically connect at distribution voltage, often below 33 kV.

Only three: this would mean one of the four is not a DER. A student might wrongly exclude fuel cells because they are seen as emerging technology, or biomass because it is seen as conventional combustion. Both are recognised DERs when small-scale and sited locally. Hydrogen fuel cells are modular, from kW to MW scale, and used in microgrids and as backup.

All four: this is the official answer. DERs are decentralised energy units, near the load, that can operate independently or with the grid. The category includes solar PV, wind, biomass, fuel cells, microturbines, CHP, batteries, EVs and demand response. Aggregated DERs can function as Virtual Power Plants. They improve resilience and reduce transmission and distribution losses, but they require smart grid management.
related: PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana was launched in February 2024 and targets 1 crore households with rooftop solar.
PM-KUSUM supports solar pumps, solarisation of agricultural feeders and small grid-connected solar plants.
A Virtual Power Plant aggregates DERs and operates them like a single power plant.
A microgrid is a localised grid that can disconnect from the main grid and operate autonomously (islanding).
Net metering lets prosumers export surplus rooftop power to the grid and offset their bills.
The National Green Hydrogen Mission aims for 5 MMT of green hydrogen per year by 2030.
The International Solar Alliance has its headquarters in Gurugram and was launched with France in 2015.
India's target is 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030, and net zero by 2070.
statements: 1 — Correct: Battery storage is a distributed energy resource, as the storage form of DER. Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), whether at homes, buildings, substations or feeders, store energy and discharge it locally. They support peak shaving, frequency regulation, renewable smoothing and backup. India approved Viability Gap Funding for 4,000 MWh of BESS in 2023 and has a National Framework for Promoting Energy Storage. Lithium-ion is the dominant chemistry. EV batteries can also act as DER through V2G.

2 — Correct: Biomass generators are a distributed generation source. Small biomass or biogas gensets burn agricultural residue, wood pellets or gasified biomass to produce power at village, industry or cooperative-sugar-mill scale. Biomass is a renewable, dispatchable (non-intermittent) source. India's biomass power capacity is around 10 GW including bagasse cogeneration. The MNRE runs a Biomass Programme. Co-firing of biomass pellets in thermal plants is also being pushed to reduce stubble burning.

3 — Correct: Fuel cells are DERs. They convert chemical energy of a fuel, usually hydrogen, directly into electricity through an electrochemical reaction, with water and heat as by-products and high efficiency. They are modular and used for backup power, microgrids, buildings, telecom towers and combined heat and power. Types include PEM, SOFC, MCFC and PAFC. They link to India's National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023, outlay about Rs 19,744 crore), which aims for 5 MMT of green hydrogen per year by 2030.

4 — Correct: Rooftop solar PV units are the classic DER. Installed on consumer premises, they generate power on site and can export the surplus to the grid through net or gross metering. Under PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (Feb 2024, outlay Rs 75,021 crore) the target is 1 crore households with up to 300 units of free electricity per month. Rooftop solar is also covered by the Phase II rooftop programme. India's solar capacity has crossed roughly 90 GW, with rooftop solar being a growing share.
summary: The answer is (d) All four. Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) are small-scale generation or storage units located near the point of consumption, usually connected to the distribution grid. Battery storage, biomass generators, fuel cells and rooftop solar PV all fit this definition.
topic_notes: Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) are small, modular energy units connected to the distribution network or located behind the consumer's meter. Categories: (1) distributed generation: rooftop and small solar PV, small wind, biomass or biogas, micro-hydro, CHP, diesel gensets; (2) storage: batteries, thermal storage, pumped micro-storage, EVs with V2G; (3) fuel cells; (4) demand-side resources: demand response, smart appliances, controllable loads. Related concepts: microgrids (a localised grid that can island from the main grid), Virtual Power Plants (aggregation of DERs managed as one plant), prosumers (consumers who also produce), net metering and gross metering, smart grids, and Distributed Energy Resource Management Systems (DERMS). Benefits: lower T&D losses, greater resilience, rural electrification, faster and cheaper deployment, and lower emissions. Challenges: intermittency, bidirectional flows, voltage and frequency regulation, protection coordination, discom revenue loss and cybersecurity. Indian context: PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (Feb 2024; 1 crore households; Rs 75,021 crore), PM-KUSUM (solar pumps, feeder solarisation, and small solar plants of up to 2 MW), Electricity (Rights of Consumers) Amendment Rules 2021–2022 (net metering up to 500 kW or the sanctioned load), the Green Energy Open Access Rules 2022, the National Green Hydrogen Mission, and the BESS VGF scheme. India's target is 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070. International: IEA, IRENA and the International Solar Alliance (HQ Gurugram) promote distributed renewables.

question: Which one of the following shows a unique relationship with an insect that has coevolved with it and that is the only insect that can pollinate this tree ?
subject: Environment
detail: Figs show one of the best-known cases of obligate mutualism and coevolution. The fig 'fruit' is a syconium, an enclosed inflorescence with a tiny opening called the ostiole. A female fig wasp (Agaonidae, e.g., Blastophaga psenes for the edible fig Ficus carica) enters through the ostiole, losing her wings in the process. She pollinates the female flowers and lays eggs in some of the ovaries, forming galls. Wasp larvae develop, wingless males hatch first and mate with females, and the females then collect pollen and fly out to find another receptive syconium. Most Ficus species have their own host-specific wasp, so the plant depends on the wasp for pollination and the wasp depends on the plant for breeding. Figs are keystone species in tropical forests because they fruit asynchronously and feed many birds and mammals. Elimination: Mahua (Madhuca longifolia) is pollinated by bats, bees and other animals, and its flowers are eaten by many mammals. Sandalwood (Santalum album) is a root hemiparasite pollinated by many generalist insects, and its seeds are dispersed by birds. Silk cotton (Bombax ceiba) is pollinated mainly by birds, which feed on its nectar, and by squirrels. None of these has an exclusive insect partner.
explanations: Correct: Fig trees (Ficus) are pollinated only by their specific coevolved fig wasps, which complete their life cycle within the syconium. This is an obligate mutualism.
Incorrect: Mahua (Madhuca longifolia) has fleshy, nectar-rich flowers visited by bats, bees, birds and mammals. It has no single exclusive insect pollinator.
Incorrect: Sandalwood (Santalum album) is pollinated by a variety of generalist insects such as bees, flies and wasps. It has no exclusive insect partner.
Incorrect: Silk cotton (Bombax ceiba) is mainly bird-pollinated (myna, crows, bulbuls) and also visited by squirrels. It is not insect-exclusive.
keyfact: Fig and its specific fig wasp (Agaonidae) form an obligate coevolved pollination mutualism, with the wasp breeding inside the syconium.
option_notes: Fig (Ficus spp.) is a genus of over 750 species in the family Moraceae. The 'fruit' is a syconium, an inverted inflorescence. Pollination is by fig wasps (Agaonidae), usually one wasp species per fig species. Figs are keystone species in tropical forests. Ficus benghalensis (banyan) is India's national tree, and Ficus religiosa (peepal) is sacred. Some species are monoecious, others dioecious. Figs show coevolution and cospeciation with their wasps.

Mahua (Madhuca longifolia, family Sapotaceae) is a tree of central and eastern India and an important source of tribal livelihood. Its flowers are eaten and fermented to make liquor, and its seeds yield oil. It is a Non-Timber Forest Produce (NTFP). Its flowers open at night and attract bats, bees and mammals such as deer and bears. A 2004 national policy decision on its collection and sale has been discussed in tribal-rights debates.

Sandalwood (Santalum album, family Santalaceae) is a hemiparasite that draws water and nutrients from the roots of host plants. It is valued for its fragrant heartwood and oil, and Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are the main producing states. Mysore sandalwood has a GI tag. The tree is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. Its seeds are dispersed by birds. Marayoor in Kerala has a natural sandal forest.

Silk cotton or red silk-cotton (Bombax ceiba, family Malvaceae) is a tall deciduous tree with spiny trunks and large red flowers appearing in leafless branches in spring. Its capsules yield kapok-like fibre used to stuff pillows and for insulation. Its nectar-rich flowers are visited by birds, squirrels and insects. Seeds are dispersed by wind. It is also called semal.
related: Fig wasp family: Agaonidae, which pollinates Ficus and is host-specific.
Fig 'fruit' is a syconium, an enclosed inflorescence with an ostiole.
Yucca and yucca moth (Tegeticula) form another obligate pollination mutualism.
Darwin predicted the hawk moth pollinator of the Madagascar star orchid, Angraecum sesquipedale.
Mycorrhiza is a mutualism between fungi and plant roots.
Sandalwood is a root hemiparasite, and its Mysore variety has a GI tag.
Ficus benghalensis (banyan) is India's national tree.
Keystone species have a disproportionate ecological impact relative to their abundance; figs are an example.
summary: The answer is (a) Fig. Each fig species (Ficus) has an obligate, coevolved mutualism with a specific fig wasp (family Agaonidae), which is the only insect able to pollinate it, while the wasp breeds inside the fig's syconium.
topic_notes: Coevolution and mutualism are frequent UPSC themes. Mutualism is an interaction in which both species benefit; obligate mutualism means neither can survive without the other. Classic examples: fig and fig wasp (Ficus-Agaonidae); yucca and yucca moth (Tegeticula) in North America; the Madagascar orchid Angraecum sesquipedale and the hawk moth Xanthopan praedicta, which Darwin predicted; mycorrhiza (fungus and plant roots); lichens (alga/cyanobacterium and fungus); root nodules (Rhizobium and legumes); coral polyps and zooxanthellae; cleaner fish and larger fish; oxpeckers and large herbivores; ants and Acacia (Vachellia) trees. Other interactions: commensalism (epiphytes on trees, cattle egret and cattle), amensalism (Penicillium and bacteria), parasitism (Cuscuta, Rafflesia, mistletoe), competition and predation. Pollination types: entomophily (insects), ornithophily (birds), chiropterophily (bats), anemophily (wind), hydrophily (water), malacophily (snails). In figs, the stages are the female phase, the interfloral phase and the male phase. Some fig species are dioecious, as in the edible fig, with male caprifigs and female figs, which gives rise to caprification. Figs are keystone species because many animals depend on them when other fruits are scarce. The parasitic wasp species within figs, called non-pollinating fig wasps, are exploiters of the mutualism. Conservation relevance: loss of a pollinator can cause extinction of the dependent plant.

question:
Consider the following : a: Butterflies 2.-.- Bish
3. Frogs How many of the above have poisonous species among them ?
subject: Environment
detail: The question tests the difference between poisonous and venomous animals and whether students know that toxicity occurs in unexpected groups. A poisonous organism delivers its toxin passively, when it is eaten, touched or absorbed. A venomous organism injects its toxin through a bite or sting. Butterflies such as the monarch (Danaus plexippus) and the Indian Plain Tiger and Common Crow feed on toxic host plants like milkweed (Asclepias) as caterpillars. They store cardenolides, which make them distasteful or poisonous to predators. The Crimson Rose and Common Rose swallowtails store aristolochic acids. Fish such as the pufferfish (fugu) carry tetrodotoxin, a deadly neurotoxin concentrated in the liver and ovaries, and reef fish can cause ciguatera poisoning. Frogs of the family Dendrobatidae, the poison dart frogs of Central and South America, secrete batrachotoxin and other alkaloids through the skin. Because each of the three groups has poisonous members, none can be ruled out. This eliminates (a), (b) and (d), and only (c) is consistent. The usual trap is assuming that only frogs or fish can be poisonous.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Only one group having poisonous species would ignore the monarch butterfly, the pufferfish and the poison dart frog, each of which is poisonous.
(b) Wrong: Only two groups would leave out one of the three, but butterflies, fish and frogs all include poisonous species.
(c) Correct: Butterflies (monarch), fish (pufferfish with tetrodotoxin) and frogs (poison dart frogs with batrachotoxin) all have poisonous species, so all three qualify.
(d) Wrong: None is impossible, because well-documented poisonous species exist in every one of the three groups.
keyfact: Poisonous species occur in butterflies (monarch), fish (pufferfish) and frogs (poison dart frog), so the UPSC 2024 answer is all three.
option_notes: Option (a), Only one: this would be true if just one of the groups had poisonous species. The usual mistake is to think only frogs, such as poison dart frogs, are poisonous. Other animals also use toxins for defence. Poisonous means harmful when eaten or touched, while venomous means injecting toxin by bite or sting. Snakes, scorpions and stonefish are venomous. Many examples, such as pufferfish and monarch butterflies, are poisonous.

Option (b), Only two: this would suit a case where one group, perhaps butterflies, was wrongly thought harmless. Students often forget that butterflies can be chemically defended. Toxicity in butterflies comes from sequestering plant compounds in the caterpillar stage. Monarchs hold cardenolides, and rose swallowtails hold aristolochic acids. Fish and frogs are better known for toxins, but butterflies also qualify, so this count is too low.

Option (c), All three: this is the official answer. Butterflies such as the monarch and Plain Tiger, fish such as the pufferfish, and frogs such as the poison dart frog all contain poisonous species. The toxins are cardenolides, tetrodotoxin and batrachotoxin respectively. Remember that not every species in these groups is toxic, and the question asks only whether poisonous species exist among them.

Option (d), None: this would mean that no butterfly, fish or frog is poisonous, which is false. Poison is widespread in nature as a defence against predators. It appears in plants, insects, fish, amphibians, reptiles and birds. The pitohui of New Guinea is a poisonous bird that carries batrachotoxin. Because poisonous species exist in all three listed groups, this option fails.
related: Poisonous animals harm when eaten or touched; venomous animals inject toxin by bite or sting.
Pufferfish toxin is tetrodotoxin, which blocks sodium channels in nerves.
Poison dart frogs (Dendrobatidae) secrete batrachotoxin and get alkaloids from their diet.
Monarch butterflies store cardenolides from milkweed, so they are unpalatable to predators.
Batesian mimicry is a harmless species copying a harmful one; Müllerian mimicry is harmful species resembling each other.
The slow loris is the only venomous primate, and the male platypus has a venomous spur.
The hooded pitohui of New Guinea is a poisonous bird carrying batrachotoxin.
Aposematism means bright warning colours that signal toxicity to predators.
statements:
1 — Correct: Some butterflies are poisonous because their caterpillars store plant toxins. The monarch, for example, stores cardenolides from milkweed. Butterflies of this kind are unpalatable to birds and other predators. This protects them and is a classic case of chemical defence. Bright warning (aposematic) colours advertise the toxicity.
The monarch (Danaus plexippus) is famous for its long migration across North America. Its caterpillars feed on milkweed, so adults retain cardenolide glycosides. In India the Plain Tiger, Striped Tiger and Common Crow (Euploea core) are distasteful. The Common Rose and Crimson Rose (Pachliopta) store aristolochic acids. Batesian mimics like the Common Mime copy these toxic species, while Müllerian mimicry occurs among several toxic species that look alike.

2 — Correct: Several fish are poisonous to eat, most famously the pufferfish, which carries tetrodotoxin. This neurotoxin blocks sodium channels in nerves and has no known antidote. Other fish cause ciguatera or scombroid poisoning when eaten.
Pufferfish (Tetraodontidae) are prepared as fugu in Japan only by licensed chefs, because the liver, ovaries and skin are lethal. Tetrodotoxin is produced largely by symbiotic bacteria. Ciguatera comes from toxins of dinoflagellates that accumulate in reef fish such as barracuda and grouper. Stonefish and lionfish are venomous rather than poisonous because they inject toxins through spines. Students should keep the poisonous and venomous distinction clear.

3 — Correct: Some frogs have poisonous skin secretions. The best known are the poison dart frogs (family Dendrobatidae) of Central and South America. The golden poison frog (Phyllobates terribilis) carries enough batrachotoxin to kill several humans.
The frogs gain many of their alkaloids from the ants, mites and other arthropods they eat, so captive frogs fed other food become non-toxic. Indigenous Emberá people tipped blowgun darts with these secretions. Bright colours warn predators (aposematism). Toads such as the cane toad (Rhinella marina) secrete bufotoxin from parotoid glands, and this is another poisonous amphibian. Amphibians are widely threatened, notably by chytrid fungus.
summary: The answer is (c): all three groups have poisonous species. Some butterflies, some fish and some frogs carry toxins that make them harmful or deadly to eat or handle. Examples are the monarch butterfly, the pufferfish and the poison dart frog.
topic_notes: The topic is chemical defence in animals, covering poisonous and venomous species, warning colouration and mimicry. A poisonous animal is harmful when eaten, touched or absorbed, and a venomous animal injects toxin using fangs, stings or spines. Poisonous examples are the pufferfish (tetrodotoxin), poison dart frogs (batrachotoxin), monarch butterflies (cardenolides) and cane toads (bufotoxin).
