Originally it had no explicit statement of the power; the 24th Amendment Act, 1971 (following Golak Nath, 1967) rewrote Article 368 to say that Parliament may, in exercise of its constituent power, amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of the Constitution, in accordance with the procedure laid down. It also made the President's assent obligatory and excluded Article 13 from applying to constitutional amendments. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) upheld Parliament's wide power but held that the Basic Structure cannot be amended. The 42nd Amendment (1976) tried to remove all limits, but Minerva Mills (1980) struck down those clauses. Three methods of amendment exist: simple majority (outside Article 368), special majority, and special majority plus ratification by half of the states. Since the Article explicitly lists all three modes, none can be eliminated, so every combination other than 1, 2 and 3 is wrong.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out repeal, which Article 368 expressly includes.
Wrong: it leaves out addition, which Article 368 expressly includes.
Wrong: it leaves out variation, which Article 368 expressly includes.
Correct: Article 368(1) states that Parliament may amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of the Constitution.
keyfact: Article 368 lets Parliament amend by addition, variation or repeal, but not the Basic Structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).
option_notes: 1 and 2 only: this is an incomplete set of the modes of amendment. The Article lists three modes (addition, variation, repeal). It is a typical distractor that omits the most drastic mode, repeal, though repeal of provisions has been used often, such as removal of Article 31.

2 and 3 only: this omits addition. Additions are common in Indian constitutional history, such as new Parts (IXA on municipalities, XIVA on tribunals), new Schedules (Ninth in 1951, Tenth in 1985, Eleventh and Twelfth in 1992-93), and new Articles such as 21A and 338B.

1 and 3 only: this omits variation, the modification of existing text. Variation underlies many amendments such as the change in Article 368 itself, alterations in the number of Lok Sabha seats, and changes in representation, which are matters needing special majority and sometimes state ratification.

1, 2 and 3: this is the official answer. Article 368(1), as substituted by the 24th Amendment Act 1971, empowers Parliament in exercise of its constituent power to amend by addition, variation or repeal. Amendments must respect the Basic Structure doctrine and follow the prescribed procedure.
related: Article 368 is in Part XX of the Constitution.
24th Amendment Act 1971 made Article 368 explicitly confer the power of addition, variation or repeal.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Parliament cannot alter the Basic Structure; decided by a 7:6 majority of a 13-judge bench.
Minerva Mills (1980) struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 inserted by the 42nd Amendment.
Special majority: majority of total membership plus two-thirds of members present and voting.
Ratification by half of the state legislatures is required for federal provisions.
A constitutional amendment bill can be introduced in either House, and needs no prior permission of the President.
Waman Rao (1981): Ninth Schedule laws after 24 April 1973 are open to judicial review.
statements: 1 — Correct: Addition is expressly mentioned in Article 368(1). Parliament can add new articles, schedules or parts, as in the 9th Schedule (1st Amendment, 1951), Part IXA, and Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002). Added provisions are valid unless they violate the Basic Structure doctrine laid down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

2 — Correct: Variation is expressly mentioned in Article 368(1). It covers modifying existing provisions, for example changing the retirement age of judges, raising the number of Supreme Court judges, or changing the Union territory and state boundaries' effect on schedules. The 24th Amendment (1971) inserted this wording, and Article 368(1) now carries it explicitly.

3 — Correct: Repeal is expressly mentioned in Article 368(1). It means removal of provisions entirely. Examples are the deletion of Article 31 on the right to property as a fundamental right by the 44th Amendment (1978), and the omission of Article 370's special status effect in 2019 (done through Article 370(3) presidential order, not Article 368). Repeal is limited by the Basic Structure doctrine.
summary: The answer is (d): 1, 2 and 3. Article 368 empowers Parliament to amend the Constitution by way of addition, variation or repeal of any provision, in accordance with the procedure laid down in that Article.
topic_notes: Part XX, Article 368 deals with amendment of the Constitution. The Constitution is partly rigid and partly flexible. There are three types of amendment. First, by simple majority of Parliament, outside Article 368: admission or establishment of new states, alteration of state areas and boundaries (Articles 2, 3, 4), the Second Schedule, citizenship, Fifth and Sixth Schedules, the Legislative Council (Article 169), official language, and quorum in Parliament. Second, by special majority, meaning a majority of the total membership of each House and two-thirds of members present and voting: Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, and everything not in the first or third categories. Third, by special majority plus ratification by at least half of the state legislatures: election of the President, extent of executive and legislative power of the Union and states, the Supreme Court and High Courts, the Seventh Schedule lists, representation of states in Parliament, the Article 368 itself, and the GST related provisions (101st Amendment, 2016). There is no joint sitting in case of a deadlock, and no provision for a Constituent Assembly. The President must give assent and cannot withhold it after the 24th Amendment. Key cases: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) held that Fundamental Rights could be amended; Golak Nath (1967) reversed this; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) laid down the Basic Structure doctrine; Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975); Minerva Mills (1980); Waman Rao (1981) fixed 24 April 1973 as the cut-off date for the Ninth Schedule; I.R. Coelho (2007) held that Ninth Schedule laws are open to judicial review. The 42nd Amendment (1976) is called the Mini-Constitution. The 44th Amendment (1978) removed the right to property from the fundamental rights (Article 300A now). The 101st brought GST, the 103rd brought EWS reservation, and the 106th (2023) gave women's reservation.

question: Which of the following statements are correct in respect of a Money Bill in the Parliament ? Article 109 mentions special procedure a in respect of Money Bills. A Money Bill shall not be introduced in the Council of States. The Rajya Sabha can either approve the Bill or suggest changes but cannot reject it. Amendments to a Money Bill suggested by the Rajya Sabha have to be accepted by the Lok Sabha. Select the answer using the code given below : 1 and 2 only
subject: Polity
detail: Money Bills are defined in Article 110 and are the Lok Sabha's special preserve. Under Article 109, a Money Bill cannot be introduced in the Rajya Sabha. After the Lok Sabha passes it, it is sent to the Rajya Sabha with the Speaker's certificate that it is a Money Bill. The Rajya Sabha must return it within 14 days with or without recommendations. It has no power to reject or amend the Bill. The Lok Sabha may accept or reject any of the recommendations. If it accepts one, the Bill is deemed passed in the modified form. If it rejects them all, the Bill is deemed passed in its original form. If the Rajya Sabha does not return the Bill within 14 days, it is deemed passed by both Houses. The Speaker's decision on whether a Bill is a Money Bill is final (Article 110(3)). The President cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration, though he can withhold assent. A Money Bill needs the President's recommendation for introduction. Statements 1 to 3 therefore match the Constitution. Statement 4 fails because the word 'have to' makes acceptance compulsory. So 1, 2 and 3 is correct, and any option containing 4 is eliminated.
explanations: Wrong. It omits statement 3, which is correct. The Rajya Sabha may only return a Money Bill with recommendations and cannot reject it.
Wrong. It omits statement 1, which is also correct. Article 109 is the provision for the special procedure on Money Bills.
Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 3 are all consistent with Articles 109 and 110. Statement 4 is excluded because the Lok Sabha need not accept the Rajya Sabha's recommendations.
Wrong. It includes statement 4, which is false, and leaves out statement 2, which is true.
keyfact: Money Bill: introduced only in the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha has 14 days to make recommendations only, and the Lok Sabha may accept or reject them.
related: Article 110 defines a Money Bill; Article 109 gives its special procedure.
The Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill within 14 days.
The Speaker's certification that a Bill is a Money Bill is final under Article 110(3).
Article 117 deals with special provisions for Financial Bills.
Article 114 is the Appropriation Bill; Article 112 is the Annual Financial Statement (Budget).
The Aadhaar Act 2016 was passed as a Money Bill and upheld in 2018 by a 4:1 majority.
The President cannot return a Money Bill for reconsideration, though he can withhold assent.
A joint sitting under Article 108 does not apply to Money Bills.
statements: 1 — Correct: Article 109 is titled 'Special procedure in respect of Money Bills'. It sets out the Rajya Sabha's limited role. Article 109 governs the passage of Money Bills. Article 110 defines them, covering taxation, borrowing, the Consolidated Fund and similar matters. Article 117 lays down the special provisions for Financial Bills. Money Bills are introduced only in the Lok Sabha, on the President's recommendation. The Speaker certifies a Bill as a Money Bill, and that decision is final. Examples include the Finance Bill and the Appropriation Bill. The Aadhaar Act 2016 was passed as a Money Bill and was upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018 by a 4:1 majority.

2 — Correct: Article 109(1) says a Money Bill shall not be introduced in the Council of States. It is introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and only on the President's recommendation, and only by a Minister. This reflects the Lok Sabha's financial primacy, because it is directly elected and accountable for taxation. A Financial Bill under Article 117(1) is similar but is not a Money Bill. Ordinary Bills can start in either House, but Money Bills and Financial Bills under Article 117(1) can start only in the Lok Sabha.

3 — Correct: Under Article 109(2) and (3), the Rajya Sabha receives the Bill after the Lok Sabha passes it. It must return it within 14 days with or without recommendations. It cannot reject or amend the Bill. If it does not return the Bill in 14 days, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses. In effect the Rajya Sabha can only delay the Bill, and only for a maximum of 14 days. This is why the Rajya Sabha is said to have only an advisory role in financial matters. There is no joint sitting provision for Money Bills under Article 108, since a deadlock cannot arise.

4 — Incorrect: Article 109(3) and (4) say the Lok Sabha may accept or reject any or all of the Rajya Sabha's recommendations. If it accepts a recommendation, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses with that amendment. If it rejects them, the Bill is deemed passed in the form originally passed by the Lok Sabha, without the Rajya Sabha's changes. So acceptance is not mandatory. Recommendations are advisory, and in practice the Lok Sabha often rejects them. This is the key difference from ordinary Bills, where both Houses have equal powers apart from joint sittings.
summary: The answer is (c): statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct, and statement 4 is wrong. Article 109 lays down the special procedure for Money Bills. Such a Bill can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations, and the Lok Sabha is free to accept or reject them.
topic_notes: Money Bills belong to Article 110 and Article 109. Article 110(1) defines a Money Bill as one that contains only matters such as imposition, abolition or regulation of any tax, regulation of government borrowing, custody of the Consolidated Fund or the Contingency Fund, appropriation of money from the Consolidated Fund, expenditure charged on it, receipt or audit of public money, and any matter incidental to these. A Bill is not a Money Bill merely because it deals with fines, fees for licences or services, or local taxes. The Speaker of the Lok Sabha decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill (Article 110(3)), and this decision is final and cannot be questioned in any court or in either House. Procedure: it is introduced only in the Lok Sabha, on the President's recommendation. After the Lok Sabha passes it, it goes to the Rajya Sabha, which has 14 days to return it. The Rajya Sabha can make recommendations but cannot reject or amend it. The Lok Sabha may accept or reject the recommendations. If the Rajya Sabha does not return it within 14 days, it is deemed passed. The President may give or withhold assent but cannot return it for reconsideration. A joint sitting under Article 108 does not apply. Related terms: Financial Bill (Article 117) has three categories. Category I contains Article 110 matters plus other matters and can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, but the Rajya Sabha has full powers over it. Category II involves expenditure from the Consolidated Fund and can start in either House. An Appropriation Bill (Article 114) authorises withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund. A Finance Bill implements the Budget's tax proposals. The Constitution (Article 112) requires an Annual Financial Statement, the Budget. The Aadhaar case (K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 2018) upheld the Money Bill route for the Aadhaar Act by a 4:1 majority, with Justice Chandrachud dissenting. The Rojer Mathew case (2019) referred the question of Money Bill certification to a larger bench, which remains pending.

question:
Which of the following matched in terms of equivalent rank in the three services of Indian Defence forces ? Army Airforce Navy 1.|Brigadier Air Commander Commodore
2. Major Air Vice Vice Admiral General Marshal 72.
3. Major Squadron Lieutenant Leader Commander
4. Lieutenant Group Captain Colonel Captain Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Tri-service rank equivalence is fixed by the officer-rank tables. The ladder runs: Lieutenant / Flying Officer / Sub-Lieutenant (Army/IAF/Navy); Captain / Flight Lieutenant / Lieutenant; Major / Squadron Leader / Lieutenant Commander; Lieutenant Colonel / Wing Commander / Commander; Colonel / Group Captain / Captain; Brigadier / Air Commodore / Commodore; Major General / Air Vice Marshal / Rear Admiral; Lieutenant General / Air Marshal / Vice Admiral; General / Air Chief Marshal / Admiral. Field Marshal / Marshal of the IAF / Admiral of the Fleet are five-star ranks, ceremonial and rarely conferred. Elimination logic: item 1 fails because 'Air Commander' is not an IAF rank (the equivalent of Brigadier is Air Commodore). Item 2 fails because Vice Admiral corresponds to Lieutenant General, not to Major General or Air Vice Marshal (Rear Admiral). Item 4 fails because Lieutenant Colonel corresponds to Wing Commander and Commander, not to Group Captain and Captain. Only item 3 is a correct triple. Options (a), (b) and (c) each include a wrong item, so only (d) survives.
explanations: (a) 1 and 4 is wrong: both items contain mismatches, since 'Air Commander' is not an IAF rank and Lieutenant Colonel is not equal to Group Captain or Captain.
(b) 1 and 3 is wrong: item 3 is correct but item 1 is not, as 'Air Commander' is not a valid rank (the correct rank is Air Commodore).
(c) 2, 3 and 4 is wrong: items 2 and 4 are mismatches (Vice Admiral is not equal to Major General, and Lieutenant Colonel is not equal to Group Captain or Captain).
(d) 3 only is correct: Major, Squadron Leader and Lieutenant Commander are the only valid equivalent triple.
keyfact: Major = Squadron Leader = Lieutenant Commander; Lt Col = Wing Commander = Commander; Colonel = Group Captain = Captain; Brigadier = Air Commodore = Commodore.
option_notes: Items 1 and 4. It would pair the Brigadier row with the Lieutenant Colonel/Colonel row. Both rows are defective, so the combination is wrong. The correct pairs are Brigadier = Air Commodore = Commodore (one-star) and Colonel = Group Captain = Captain. Lieutenant Colonel = Wing Commander = Commander. One-star ranks are the first general-officer or flag-officer level in Indian practice.

Items 1 and 3. It combines a flawed row (Air Commander is not a rank) with the correct Major row. The valid IAF rank is Air Commodore, introduced on the RAF model after independence. Item 3 is right, but item 1 prevents this option from being fully correct. Remember the one-star triple: Brigadier, Air Commodore, Commodore.

Items 2, 3 and 4. It adds two wrong rows to the correct one. Vice Admiral is a three-star rank equal to Lieutenant General and Air Marshal. A Major is far junior to any general officer. Lieutenant Colonel corresponds to Wing Commander and Commander. Selecting this would mean mixing up the two-star and three-star ladders.

Item 3 only. Major, Squadron Leader and Lieutenant Commander. This is the official answer. Each is the fourth officer rank from the bottom (after Second Lieutenant/Lieutenant/Captain in the Army). Officers reach these ranks after roughly 6 to 13 years of service. These ranks are above Captain/Flight Lieutenant/Lieutenant and below Lieutenant Colonel/Wing Commander/Commander.
related: Brigadier = Air Commodore = Commodore (one-star).
Major General = Air Vice Marshal = Rear Admiral (two-star).
Lieutenant General = Air Marshal = Vice Admiral (three-star).
Lieutenant Colonel = Wing Commander = Commander.
Colonel = Group Captain = Captain (Navy).
Chief of Defence Staff post created 2019; first CDS General Bipin Rawat.
Field Marshals of India: Sam Manekshaw (1973) and K. M. Cariappa (1986); Marshal of the IAF: Arjan Singh (2002).
The President is Supreme Commander of the armed forces (Article 53).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: 'Air Commander' is not an IAF rank. The IAF equivalent of Brigadier is Air Commodore, and the Navy equivalent is Commodore. Facts: Brigadier is a one-star rank, senior to Colonel and junior to Major General. Air Commodore is the IAF's first air officer rank. Commodore is a Navy one-star rank, often held as a temporary or appointment rank. In the Army, Brigadiers command brigades. Air Commodores command large air bases or serve as senior staff, and Commodores command naval bases, flotillas or dockyards. The three ranks sit above Colonel/Group Captain/Captain and below the two-star ranks.

2 — Incorrect: Vice Admiral is a three-star rank equal to Lieutenant General and Air Marshal. It does not match Major General or Air Vice Marshal, whose Navy equivalent is Rear Admiral. A plain Major is far lower, equal to Squadron Leader and Lieutenant Commander. Facts: Major General commands a division, and Air Vice Marshal is a two-star IAF officer, often an Air Officer Commanding. Rear Admiral is a two-star naval officer, such as a Flag Officer commanding a fleet or a Command Chief of Staff. Vice Admirals head Naval Commands, for example Western or Eastern Naval Command.

3 — Correct: Major, Squadron Leader and Lieutenant Commander are equivalent mid-level officer ranks. Facts: all three sit above Captain/Flight Lieutenant/Lieutenant and below Lieutenant Colonel/Wing Commander/Commander. A Major commands a company or sub-unit, wears a crown insignia, and is typically in service for about 6 to 13 years. A Squadron Leader commands a flight or small squadron. A Lieutenant Commander has two and a half stripes and commands smaller ships or serves as a department head. These ranks are reached by time-scale promotion after around 6 years of commissioned service.

4 — Incorrect: Lieutenant Colonel equals Wing Commander and Commander, whereas Colonel equals Group Captain and Captain (Navy). The row mixes these levels. Facts: Lieutenant Colonel commands a battalion or regiment. Colonel is a senior rank, often a selection-grade post, and below Brigadier. Group Captain commands an air station or large wing. Naval Captain commands a major warship such as a destroyer, frigate or aircraft carrier. Note that Navy 'Captain' differs from Army 'Captain', which is equivalent to Flight Lieutenant and Lieutenant (Navy).
summary: The answer is (d), 3 only. Major (Army), Squadron Leader (IAF) and Lieutenant Commander (Navy) are equivalent ranks. The other rows each mismatch at least one service. Note: the OCR'd text is garbled, so the reasoning for items 1, 2 and 4 follows the standard rank tables and the official answer.
topic_notes: Indian armed forces use parallel rank structures with fixed equivalence. Commissioned officers: Lieutenant/Flying Officer/Sub-Lieutenant; Captain/Flight Lieutenant/Lieutenant; Major/Squadron Leader/Lieutenant Commander; Lieutenant Colonel/Wing Commander/Commander; Colonel/Group Captain/Captain; Brigadier/Air Commodore/Commodore (one-star); Major General/Air Vice Marshal/Rear Admiral (two-star); Lieutenant General/Air Marshal/Vice Admiral (three-star); General/Air Chief Marshal/Admiral (four-star, Service Chiefs). Five-star: Field Marshal (Army; only Sam Manekshaw 1973 and K. M. Cariappa 1986), Marshal of the Air Force (Arjan Singh, 2002), while no Indian officer has held Admiral of the Fleet. Chiefs of Staff are Army Chief (COAS), Chief of Naval Staff, and Chief of Air Staff; the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) post was created in December 2019, with General Bipin Rawat as first CDS (Jan 2020), and he is a four-star officer who heads the Department of Military Affairs. Army commands: Northern, Western, Eastern, Southern, South Western, Central and ARTRAC. Navy commands: Western (Mumbai), Eastern (Visakhapatnam), Southern (Kochi). IAF commands: Western, Eastern, Central, Southern, South Western, Training, and Maintenance. The Supreme Commander of the armed forces is the President (Article 53). Warrant of precedence ranks service chiefs just below Cabinet ministers. Other related areas UPSC may ask: JCOs (Naib Subedar, Subedar, Subedar Major), NCOs (Naik, Havildar), Navy and IAF equivalents, Territorial Army, Agnipath scheme (2022), theatre commands, gallantry awards (Param Vir Chakra, Ashoka Chakra, Maha Vir Chakra).

question:
The North Eastern Council (NEC) was established by the North Eastern Council Act, 1971. Subsequent to the amendment of NEC 78. Act in 2002, the Council comprises which of the following members ?
1. Governor of the Constituent State 2, Chief Minister of the Constituent State
3. Three Members to be nominated by the President of India
4. The Home Minister of India Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Polity
detail: The North Eastern Council was set up under the North Eastern Council Act, 1971, as an advisory body for the economic and social planning of the north-eastern states. It was initially made up of the Governors and Chief Ministers of Assam, Meghalaya, Manipur, Nagaland, Tripura, Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram, with its headquarters at Shillong. The 2002 amendment (the North Eastern Council (Amendment) Act, 2002) added Sikkim as a member in 2002, and the Council was restructured as a regional planning body. Its members are the Governors and Chief Ministers of the constituent states and three members nominated by the President. The Union Minister of DoNER is the ex-officio Chairman, and the Council is advised by a Secretariat and a Plan Review mechanism. The Home Minister's earlier role as chairman was replaced by this arrangement, so statement 4 is wrong. Elimination logic: statements 1, 2 and 3 are all correct, and 4 is incorrect. Option (a) is the only option that excludes statement 4 while keeping 1, 2 and 3. Options (b) and (c) wrongly include 4 and drop 2 or 1, and (d) includes 4.
explanations: Correct: statements 1, 2 and 3 are accurate and statement 4 is not, and this option lists exactly those three.
Incorrect: it includes the Home Minister (statement 4), who is not a member, and it omits the Chief Ministers, who are members.
Incorrect: it leaves out the Chief Ministers, who are members, and includes the Home Minister, who is not.
Incorrect: it includes statement 4, but the Home Minister is not a member of the NEC after the amendment.
keyfact: NEC members: Governors and Chief Ministers of the eight states plus three Presidential nominees; the DoNER Minister chairs it, not the Home Minister.
option_notes: Governors, Chief Ministers and three Presidential nominees together form the NEC's membership after the 2002 amendment. The Union Minister of DoNER is the Chairman. The NEC is a statutory advisory and planning body for the eight north-eastern states, headquartered at Shillong, and is distinct from constitutional bodies such as the Finance Commission.

This combination keeps the Governors and the Presidential nominees but adds the Home Minister and drops the Chief Ministers. It does not match the Act. The Home Minister's role in the north-east relates to internal security, and the Ministry of Home Affairs oversees law and order and insurgency issues, not NEC membership.

The Chief Ministers and the Home Minister alone do not form the Council. The Home Minister once chaired the Council before the restructuring, but this is no longer the case. The Council includes Governors and nominees as well. The Chief Ministers are important for state-level planning inputs.

This includes all four statements. The Home Minister is not a member of the amended Council, so it is wrong. The NEC's chair is the DoNER Minister, and the Council's mandate is regional planning, which is why the DoNER Ministry, not the Home Ministry, is its nodal ministry.
related: The NEC was established by the North Eastern Council Act, 1971; its headquarters are in Shillong.
Sikkim was added to the NEC in 2002, bringing the member states to eight.
The Union Minister of DoNER is the ex-officio Chairman of the NEC.
The Ministry of DoNER became a full ministry in 2004.
NEDFi was set up in 1995 to finance industrial and commercial ventures in the north-east.
Sixth Schedule is under Articles 244(2) and 275(1).
Article 371A gives Nagaland special provisions; Article 371C covers Manipur.
Zonal Councils were set up under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, and the Inter-State Council is under Article 263.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Governor of each constituent state is a member of the NEC. The NEC is a statutory body under the 1971 Act and covers eight states: Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura. Governors were members from the start, and the 2002 amendment retained them. The Council's headquarters are in Shillong, Meghalaya. It acts as the nodal agency for the region's economic and social development and advises on common interests such as security and inter-state transport.

2 — Correct: The Chief Minister of each constituent state is a member of the NEC. The Chief Ministers represent the state governments in regional planning, and their presence ensures that state priorities feed into the Council's plans. Sikkim was added to the Council in 2002, which brought the member states to eight. The NEC prepares a regional plan and recommends the priority of projects. It has the power to discuss matters of common interest and to recommend the Central and State governments' use of resources.

3 — Correct: Three members are nominated by the President of India. This was introduced by the 2002 amendment and is part of the restructured Council. The nominees are chosen from persons with experience in the region's affairs and relevant expertise. The change made the NEC more of a regional planning body than only an advisory one. The Council is assisted by a Secretariat headed by a Secretary and uses the funds allocated by the Ministry of DoNER.

4 — Incorrect: The Union Home Minister is not a member of the NEC under the amended Act. Earlier, the Union Home Minister chaired the Council. After the 2002 amendment, the Union Minister of the Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER), created in 2004 as a ministry, became the ex-officio Chairman. The Ministry of DoNER came into being in 2001 as a department and became a full ministry in 2004. The Home Ministry still handles security issues in the region.
summary: The answer is (a): after the 2002 amendment the NEC consists of the Governors and Chief Ministers of the constituent states plus three members nominated by the President. The Union Home Minister is not a member of the Council; the Minister of DoNER serves as its ex-officio Chairman.
topic_notes: The North Eastern Council was created by the North Eastern Council Act, 1971, to give the north-eastern states a forum for coordinated development. It started with Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Tripura, and later included Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram, and Sikkim was added in 2002. Its headquarters are at Shillong. The 2002 amendment restructured the Council into a regional planning body, with the Governors and Chief Ministers of the member states and three Presidential nominees as members, and the Union Minister of DoNER as its Chairman. The Ministry of DoNER was set up as a department in 2001 and became a full ministry in 2004. It acts as the nodal ministry for the region's development and funds projects through schemes like the Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR), which was later replaced by the North East Special Infrastructure Development Scheme (NESIDS) and PM-DevINE (announced in the 2022-23 Budget). The NEC also supports bodies like the North Eastern Development Finance Corporation (NEDFi), set up in 1995, and the North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation (NERAMAC). Other related topics UPSC may ask are: the Sixth Schedule (Articles 244(2) and 275(1)) for tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; Article 371A for Nagaland and Article 371C for Manipur; the Look East/Act East policy; and the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project. Remember that the NEC is advisory, not a constitutional body, and that it differs from bodies like the Inter-State Council (Article 263) or the Zonal Councils created by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

question: How many Delimitation Commissions have been constituted by the Government of India till December 2023 ?
subject: Polity
detail: Delimitation means redrawing the boundaries of Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly constituencies to reflect population changes. Article 82 requires Parliament to enact a Delimitation Act after every Census. Article 170 provides the same for State Assemblies. Four Delimitation Commissions have been constituted: under the Delimitation Commission Act, 1952; the Act of 1962; the Delimitation Act, 1972; and the Delimitation Act, 2002. No commission was set up after the 1981 and 1991 Censuses. The 42nd Amendment (1976) froze the number of seats, based on the 1971 Census, until 2000. The 84th Amendment (2001) extended the freeze to the first Census after 2026. The 87th Amendment (2003) allowed readjustment on the 2001 Census, but it changed only boundaries and reservations, not seat numbers. The Commission's orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court. Elimination logic: one, two or three commissions are too few, because the 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002 commissions are all well documented. Hence (d).
explanations: Incorrect: One commission would cover only the first (1952) exercise. Three more were set up later.
Incorrect: Two would cover only 1952 and 1962. The 1972 and 2002 commissions also exist.
Incorrect: Three would omit the 2002 commission, which worked on the 2001 Census. The 1952, 1962 and 1972 commissions alone make three.
Correct: Four commissions were constituted, in 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002, matching the official answer.
keyfact: Four Delimitation Commissions so far: 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002.
option_notes: One: Only the first Delimitation Commission (1952) was constituted under the Delimitation Commission Act, 1952. It drew the constituencies for the 1951-52 general elections and the subsequent elections. It was chaired by Justice Mehr Chand Mahajan's successor-era appointees, so this is a point to verify.
Two: The first two commissions were those of 1952 and 1962. The 1962 commission used the 1961 Census to readjust Lok Sabha and Assembly seats. Two is too few, since two more commissions followed.

Three: The commissions of 1952, 1962 and 1972 make three. The 1972 commission used the 1971 Census and fixed the Lok Sabha strength at 543. Its work ended with the freeze imposed by the 42nd Amendment. Three is incomplete because of the 2002 commission.

Four: The commissions of 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002 make four. The 2002 commission was chaired by Justice Kuldip Singh. It used the 2001 Census to redraw boundaries and revise SC/ST reservations without changing the number of seats. Its orders took effect from 2008.
related: Article 82 provides for readjustment of Lok Sabha seats after every Census.
Article 170 covers delimitation of State Legislative Assembly constituencies.
Delimitation Commission orders have the force of law and cannot be challenged in court.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) froze seat allocation on the basis of the 1971 Census.
The 84th Amendment (2001) extended the freeze until the first Census after 2026.
The 2002 Commission was headed by Justice Kuldip Singh.
The J&K Delimitation Commission was headed by Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai.
The Women's Reservation Act, 2023 is the 106th Constitutional Amendment.
summary: The answer is (d) Four. Parliament has set up four Delimitation Commissions under Delimitation Commission Acts, in 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002. The 1972 commission was the last one before the 2002 exercise, and the 2002 commission is the most recent.
topic_notes: Delimitation is the redrawing of territorial constituencies. Article 82 covers readjustment of Lok Sabha seats after each Census. Article 170 covers State Assembly seats. Articles 81 and 330/332 deal with composition and reservation of seats for SC/ST. The Delimitation Commission is a high-powered, independent body. It is headed by a retired Supreme Court judge, with the Chief Election Commissioner or an Election Commissioner and the State Election Commissioners as ex-officio members. Its orders are final and have the force of law, and no court can question them (Article 329). Commissions: 1952 (Act of 1952), 1962 (Act of 1962), 1972 (Act of 1972) and 2002 (Act of 2002, chaired by Justice Kuldip Singh). The 42nd Amendment (1976) froze seat allocation among States based on the 1971 Census until 2001. The 84th Amendment (2001) extended the freeze until the first Census after 2026. The 87th Amendment (2003) changed the basis for readjustment from the 1991 Census to the 2001 Census. The 2002 exercise fixed boundaries and reserved seats but did not change the number of seats. The Lok Sabha has 543 elected seats. Delimitation in Jammu and Kashmir was carried out by a commission headed by Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai, constituted in 2020 under the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019. Delimitation in Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur and Nagaland was deferred in 2020 and was later taken up. The Women's Reservation Act, 2023 (106th Amendment) ties reservation to the next delimitation after the first Census following its commencement. A likely future question is the North-South debate over seat redistribution.

question:
The Constitution (715* Amendment) Act, 1992 amends the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution to include which of the following languages ?
1. Konkani
2. Manipuri
3. Nepali
4. Maithili Select the correct answer using the code given below :
subject: Polity
detail: The Eighth Schedule (Articles 344(1) and 351) lists the languages recognised by the Constitution. It had 14 languages at commencement in 1950. Sindhi was added by the 21st Amendment in 1967. The 71st Amendment of 1992, which came into force on 31 August 1992, added Konkani, Manipuri (Meitei) and Nepali, raising the total to 18. The 92nd Amendment of 2003 added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali, making 22. A student should remember the sequence 14, 15, 18, 22. The elimination logic is that Maithili belongs to the 2003 group, so any option containing statement 4 is wrong. That removes (b), (c) and (d). Only (a), with Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali, remains. Note that the question's option (c) contains an OCR error and should read 1, 3 and 4, but it is wrong either way because it includes Maithili. Inclusion in the Eighth Schedule does not make a language an official language of the Union. It gives entitlement to representation on the Official Language Commission and to the Sahitya Akademi's recognition, and it allows use in UPSC examinations. The classical language status is a separate matter.
explanations: Correct. Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali were all added by the 71st Amendment of 1992, and this matches the official answer.
Wrong. It includes Maithili, which was added in 2003 by the 92nd Amendment, and it leaves out Nepali.
Wrong. It includes Maithili (2003) and omits Manipuri or Nepali, so it cannot be the 1992 set. The printed code seems to have an OCR error.
Wrong. It includes Maithili (2003) and omits Konkani, which was added in 1992.
keyfact: 71st Amendment (1992) added Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali, making 18; Maithili came with Bodo, Dogri and Santhali in 2003 (92nd Amendment), making 22.
option_notes: Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali were the three languages added by the 71st Amendment, 1992, which took the Eighth Schedule from 15 to 18 languages. Konkani is the language of Goa. Manipuri (Meitei) is the language of Manipur. Nepali is the language of Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills. The amendment came into force on 31 August 1992. It was the first expansion of the Schedule since Sindhi in 1967. Each language gained the recognition and representation that Eighth Schedule listing carries.

The combination of Konkani, Manipuri and Maithili is not a real amendment grouping. Konkani and Manipuri were added in 1992 and Maithili in 2003. Maithili was added with Bodo, Dogri and Santhali by the 92nd Amendment, which came into force on 7 January 2004. Maithili is spoken in Bihar and Jharkhand. Its demand for inclusion was long standing and was finally accepted in 2003 during the NDA government.

This combination, with Maithili in it, does not match any amendment. The printed code seems to be 1, 3 and 4, meaning Konkani, Nepali and Maithili. The languages come from two different amendments, 1992 and 2003. Konkani and Nepali are 1992 additions, and Maithili came with the 92nd Amendment. Knowing which amendment added which language is the key to such mixed combinations.

Manipuri, Nepali and Maithili come from two different amendments. Manipuri and Nepali were added in 1992 and Maithili in 2003. This option wrongly omits Konkani, which was added in 1992. The Eighth Schedule now has 22 languages, including Sanskrit, Sindhi, Urdu and Kashmiri. The 92nd Amendment also added Bodo, Dogri and Santhali, whose communities had long campaigned for recognition. Bodo is spoken in Assam, Dogri in Jammu and Santhali in Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal.
related: The Eighth Schedule originally had 14 languages and now has 22.
Sindhi was added by the 21st Amendment, 1967.
The 92nd Amendment, 2003 added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali.
The 96th Amendment, 2011 changed Oriya to Odia.
Article 343 makes Hindi in Devanagari script the official language of the Union.
Article 351 is the Union's directive to promote the spread of Hindi.
Article 350A provides for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage.
Tamil was the first language to be declared a classical language, in 2004.
statements: 1 — Correct: Konkani was added by the 71st Amendment, 1992. Konkani is an Indo-Aryan language spoken mainly in Goa, coastal Karnataka, Maharashtra and Kerala. It is the official language of Goa, under the Goa Official Language Act, 1987, which was passed after the Konkani agitation. Goa became a state on 30 May 1987. Konkani can be written in Devanagari, Roman, Kannada and Malayalam scripts, and Devanagari is the official script in Goa. It was recognised by the Sahitya Akademi in 1975.

2 — Correct: Manipuri (Meitei or Meiteilon) was added by the 71st Amendment, 1992. It is a Tibeto-Burman language and the official language of Manipur. It is traditionally written in the Meitei Mayek script, which was revived in the 20th century, and in the Bengali script. Manipur became a full state in 1972. Meitei is the lingua franca of the state. It is one of the few Tibeto-Burman languages in the Eighth Schedule, along with Bodo. The Sahitya Akademi recognised it in 1972.

3 — Correct: Nepali was added by the 71st Amendment, 1992. It is an Indo-Aryan language written in Devanagari and spoken in Sikkim, Darjeeling and Kalimpong in West Bengal, Assam and elsewhere. It is an official language of Sikkim. The Akhil Bharatiya Nepali Bhasha Samiti led the demand for inclusion for decades. The language is also an official language of Nepal. The Sahitya Akademi recognised it in 1975. Its inclusion is celebrated as Nepali Language Recognition Day on 20 August.

4 — Incorrect: Maithili was added by the 92nd Amendment Act, 2003, not the 71st. The 92nd Amendment brought in Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali, and it came into force on 7 January 2004. Maithili is an Indo-Aryan language spoken mainly in Bihar (Mithila region) and in eastern Nepal. It is associated with the poet Vidyapati. It is written in Tirhuta, Mithilakshar and Devanagari scripts. The Sahitya Akademi recognised it in 1965.
summary: The answer is (a): the Constitution (71st Amendment) Act, 1992 added Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali to the Eighth Schedule. Maithili was not part of it; it was added later by the 92nd Amendment Act, 2003, along with Bodo, Dogri and Santhali.
topic_notes: The Eighth Schedule relates to Articles 344(1) and 351. Article 344(1) provides for a Commission to advise on the official language, and Article 351 provides for the development of Hindi. The Schedule originally listed 14 languages: Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Kashmiri, Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Tamil, Telugu and Urdu. Sindhi was added by the 21st Amendment, 1967. Konkani, Manipuri and Nepali were added by the 71st Amendment, 1992, which brought the total to 18. Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali were added by the 92nd Amendment, 2003, which brought it to 22. Odia replaced the spelling Oriya by the 96th Amendment, 2011. Hindi in Devanagari is the official language of the Union under Article 343. English may continue to be used for official purposes under the Official Languages Act, 1963. Article 345 lets states adopt their own official languages. Article 347 deals with a language spoken by a substantial proportion of a state's population. Article 350A provides for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage. Article 350B provides for a Special Officer for linguistic minorities. Classical language status is separate from the Eighth Schedule. It has been given to Tamil (2004), Sanskrit (2005), Telugu and Kannada (2008), Malayalam (2013), Odia (2014), and Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali (2024). The Sitakant Mahapatra committee examined the demands for inclusion of more languages. The Pahwa Committee (2003) earlier set criteria for inclusion. Demands are pending for languages such as Bhojpuri, Rajasthani and Tulu.

question:
Consider the following pairs : Party Its Leader 1. |Bharatiya Jana Dr. Shyama Prasad Sangh Mukherjee
2. Socialist Party C. Rajagopalachari
3. Congress for Jagjivan Ram Democracy 4. |Swatantra Party Acharya Narendra Dev How many of the above are correctly matched ?
subject: Modern History
detail: The question tests knowledge of the founders and leaders of post-Independence Indian parties. The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was founded on 21 October 1951 by Dr. Syama Prasad Mukherjee, with support from the RSS, and it later merged into the Janata Party in 1977. The Congress for Democracy (CFD) was formed in 1977 by Jagjivan Ram, along with H. N. Bahuguna and Nandini Satpathy, after they left the Congress over the Emergency. It then merged with the Janata Party. The Socialist Party was founded by Acharya Narendra Dev, Jayaprakash Narayan and Ram Manohar Lohia, who came out of the Congress Socialist Party in 1948. Its leader in this context is Acharya Narendra Dev, not C. Rajagopalachari. The Swatantra Party was founded in August 1959 by C. Rajagopalachari, with Minoo Masani and N. G. Ranga, and it opposed the Nehruvian economic model and state controls. Pairs 2 and 4 swap the leaders, so exactly two pairs are correct. Elimination: once pairs 1 and 3 are confirmed and either 2 or 4 is seen to be wrong, only (b) fits.
explanations: (a) Wrong: two pairs, not one, are correctly matched, since pairs 1 and 3 are both correct.
(b) Correct: pairs 1 and 3 are correct, and pairs 2 and 4 have swapped leaders (Narendra Dev for the Socialist Party, Rajagopalachari for Swatantra).
(c) Wrong: three correct would need pair 2 or 4 to be right, but both are mismatched.
(d) Wrong: all four correct is impossible because the Socialist Party and Swatantra leaders are swapped.
keyfact: Jana Sangh – Syama Prasad Mukherjee; CFD – Jagjivan Ram; Socialist Party – Acharya Narendra Dev; Swatantra – C. Rajagopalachari.
option_notes: Only one: this would mean a single correct pair. It is not the case here, since two pairs match. Such options test partial knowledge, and a student who knows only the Jana Sangh–Mukherjee pair might pick it. The Jana Sangh was founded in 1951 and later became part of the Janata Party and then the BJP.

Only two: this is the official answer. Pairs 1 (Jana Sangh–Mukherjee) and 3 (CFD–Jagjivan Ram) are correct. Pairs 2 and 4 are swapped: the Socialist Party's leader was Acharya Narendra Dev and Swatantra's was C. Rajagopalachari. The pairing shows how UPSC creates traps by swapping the leaders of similar-sounding opposition parties.

Only three: this would need one of the two swapped pairs to be correct. A student who confuses the founders of the Socialist and Swatantra parties might choose it. The Socialist Party dates from 1948 and Swatantra from 1959, and they stood on very different ideologies, socialism against free-market liberalism.

All four: this would need every pair to be right. It is wrong because the Socialist Party (1948) was led by Acharya Narendra Dev and the Swatantra Party (1959) by C. Rajagopalachari, with the two names swapped in the question. This is the typical trap for students who only half-remember the founders.
related: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was founded on 21 October 1951 by Syama Prasad Mukherjee.
The Swatantra Party was founded in 1959 by C. Rajagopalachari, with Minoo Masani and N. G. Ranga.
Jagjivan Ram founded the Congress for Democracy in 1977 and was Deputy PM in 1979 (Charan Singh's tenure was separate; he served under Desai in 1977).
The Janata Party was formed in January 1977 and won the March 1977 elections.
The Bharatiya Janata Party was founded in April 1980, with Vajpayee as its first president.
The Praja Socialist Party was formed in 1952 by the merger of the Socialist Party and the KMPP.
The 44th Amendment (1978) restored many safeguards weakened by the 42nd Amendment.
The Shah Commission (1977) probed Emergency excesses.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was founded by Dr. Shyama Prasad Mukherjee. It was established on 21 October 1951 in Delhi, after Mukherjee left Nehru's cabinet over the Nehru–Liaquat Pact. It was ideologically close to the RSS, stood for cultural nationalism and a Uniform Civil Code, and used the lamp (diya) as its symbol. Leaders after Mukherjee included Deendayal Upadhyaya, Atal Bihari Vajpayee and L. K. Advani. It merged into the Janata Party in 1977, and its successor, the BJP, was formed in 1980.

2 — Incorrect: The Socialist Party is not associated with C. Rajagopalachari. It was led by Acharya Narendra Dev, and Jayaprakash Narayan and Ram Manohar Lohia were among its other leaders. It was formed in 1948 when the Congress Socialist Party left the Congress. It merged with the Kisan Mazdoor Praja Party in 1952 to form the Praja Socialist Party, and the Samyukta Socialist Party was a later split. Rajagopalachari founded the Swatantra Party, and he was also the last Governor-General of India and the first Indian to hold that post.

3 — Correct: The Congress for Democracy was formed by Jagjivan Ram in 1977, just before the March 1977 Lok Sabha elections. He had been a senior Congress minister, and he broke away with H. N. Bahuguna and Nandini Satpathy in protest at the Emergency (1975–77). The CFD allied with the Janata coalition and later merged into the Janata Party, which defeated Indira Gandhi's Congress. Jagjivan Ram became Deputy Prime Minister in 1977 in the Morarji Desai government.

4 — Incorrect: The Swatantra Party was led by C. Rajagopalachari, not Acharya Narendra Dev. It was founded in August 1959 after the Congress Nagpur Resolution on land ceilings and cooperative farming. Leaders included Minoo Masani, N. G. Ranga and K. M. Munshi. It supported free enterprise, opposed the licence-permit raj and favoured a strong private sector. It did well in the 1967 elections, becoming the largest opposition group in some states, and it declined and dissolved in the 1970s.
summary: The answer is (b) Only two. Pair 1 (Bharatiya Jana Sangh – Dr. Shyama Prasad Mukherjee) and pair 3 (Congress for Democracy – Jagjivan Ram) are correct, while pairs 2 and 4 have the leaders swapped.
topic_notes: Opposition parties after Independence. Early opposition was fragmented, and the Congress dominated until 1967 (the 'Congress system' described by Rajni Kothari). The Socialist Party (1948) came from the Congress Socialist Party; Acharya Narendra Dev, J. P. Narayan and Lohia were its leaders. It merged with the KMPP in 1952 to form the Praja Socialist Party, and the Samyukta Socialist Party followed after a split. The Communist Party of India was founded in 1925 and split in 1964, giving rise to the CPI(M). The Bharatiya Jana Sangh (1951, Mukherjee) stood for cultural nationalism; Deendayal Upadhyaya propounded 'Integral Humanism'. The Swatantra Party (1959, Rajagopalachari, Masani) opposed planning and state controls. The Republican Party of India grew out of Ambedkar's plan for a party after the Scheduled Castes Federation. The 1967 elections saw the Congress lose many states and the rise of non-Congress coalitions (Samyukta Vidhayak Dal). The Congress split in 1969 into Congress (O) and Congress (R). The Emergency ran from 25 June 1975 to March 1977. The Janata Party was formed in 1977 by merging Congress (O), Jana Sangh, the Bharatiya Lok Dal and the Socialist Party, with the CFD joining. Morarji Desai became PM in 1977. Janata fell in 1979 and the BJP was formed in 1980. Other possible questions: Jayaprakash Narayan's 'Total Revolution', the Shah Commission, the 42nd and 44th Amendments, and the Anti-Defection Law (the 52nd Amendment, 1985, which added the Tenth Schedule).

question:
Which of the following statements are correct 77. about the Constitution of India ? aL, Powers of the Municipalities are given in Part IX A of the Constitution.
2. Emergency provisions are given in Part XVIII of the Constitution.
3. Provisions related to the amendment of the Constitution are given in Part XX of the Constitution. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Polity
detail: This question tests the Part-wise layout of the Constitution, a staple of UPSC prelims. Part IXA was inserted by the 74th Amendment Act, 1992 (in force 1 June 1993) and contains Articles 243P to 243ZG on Municipalities, with the 12th Schedule listing 18 functions. Part XVIII covers Emergency Provisions in Articles 352 to 360: national emergency (352), President's Rule in a state (356), and financial emergency (360). Part XX has only one article, Article 368, which gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution and lays out the procedure. Since all three statements match the actual Parts, the answer is (d). The elimination logic is simple: if a student knows any two statements are correct, only (d) can survive, because every other option leaves out one of the correct statements. Related items to learn: Part IX covers Panchayats (Arts. 243-243O, 73rd Amendment, 11th Schedule), Part IXB covers Cooperative Societies (97th Amendment, 2011), Part XIX is Miscellaneous, and Part XXI is Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out statements 2 and 3, which are also correct; Part XVIII is Emergency Provisions and Part XX is Amendment.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 1, which is correct because Part IXA covers Municipalities.
Wrong: it leaves out statement 2, which is correct because Emergency provisions are in Part XVIII (Arts. 352-360).
Correct: all three statements match the Parts of the Constitution: IXA (Municipalities), XVIII (Emergency) and XX (Amendment).
keyfact: Part IXA = Municipalities (Arts. 243P-243ZG); Part XVIII = Emergency (Arts. 352-360); Part XX = Amendment (Art. 368).
option_notes: Option (a), 1 and 2 only, would be right if Part XX did not cover amendment. Both of its statements are true: Part IXA covers Municipalities (74th Amendment, Arts. 243P-243ZG) and Part XVIII covers Emergency (Arts. 352-360). It is incomplete only because it excludes statement 3, since Part XX with Article 368 is the amendment Part.

Option (b), 2 and 3 only, includes the true statements on Emergency (Part XVIII) and Amendment (Part XX, Art. 368). It wrongly excludes the Municipalities statement. Part IXA was inserted in 1992 and effective from 1 June 1993. Part IX, by contrast, deals with Panchayats under the 73rd Amendment (Arts. 243-243O). Students sometimes confuse the two Parts.

Option (c), 1 and 3 only, includes the true statements on Municipalities (Part IXA) and Amendment (Part XX). It wrongly excludes Emergency provisions. Part XVIII has Articles 352-360, including national emergency (352), state emergency or President's Rule (356) and financial emergency (360). Emergencies were borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany, and the 44th Amendment (1978) tightened them.

Option (d), 1, 2 and 3, is the official answer. It combines Part IXA (Municipalities), Part XVIII (Emergency Provisions) and Part XX (Amendment, Art. 368). Together these show the structure of the Constitution: 25 Parts in the current text, 22 Parts originally, with additions such as IVA, IXA, IXB and XIVA, and Part VII repealed.
related: Part IX (Panchayats) was inserted by the 73rd Amendment Act, 1992; the 11th Schedule has 29 subjects.
Part IXA (Municipalities) came from the 74th Amendment Act; the 12th Schedule has 18 subjects.
Part IXB (Co-operative Societies) was added by the 97th Amendment, 2011.
Part XIVA (Tribunals) was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
Part IVA (Fundamental Duties, Art. 51A) was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
Article 368 is the only Article in Part XX.
Article 352 (National Emergency) uses 'armed rebellion', replacing 'internal disturbance' (44th Amendment, 1978).
Part VII of the Constitution was repealed by the 7th Amendment, 1956.
statements: 1 — Correct: Part IXA of the Constitution deals with Municipalities, and it gives their powers, authority and responsibilities. Part IXA was added by the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, which came into force on 1 June 1993. It covers Articles 243P to 243ZG. It provides for three types of urban bodies: Nagar Panchayat for transitional areas, Municipal Council for smaller urban areas and Municipal Corporation for larger urban areas. It also provides for ward committees, reservation of seats for SC/ST and women (not less than one-third), a five-year term, a State Election Commission, a State Finance Commission and the District and Metropolitan Planning Committees. The 12th Schedule lists 18 functional items.

2 — Correct: Emergency provisions are in Part XVIII, Articles 352 to 360. Article 352 covers national emergency on grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion (the term 'armed rebellion' replaced 'internal disturbance' by the 44th Amendment, 1978). Article 356 covers failure of constitutional machinery in a state (President's Rule), and Article 360 covers financial emergency. National emergency has been declared three times: 1962, 1971 and 1975. Article 355 imposes a duty on the Union to protect states. Article 359 allows suspension of the right to move courts for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, and Article 358 automatically suspends Article 19 during a war or external aggression emergency. The idea was borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany.

3 — Correct: Part XX contains only Article 368, titled 'Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor'. Amendments can be made by simple majority (for example, new states under Arts. 2-4), by special majority, or by special majority plus ratification by at least half of the states (federal features such as the representation of states in Parliament, the Seventh Schedule and Article 368 itself). The 24th Amendment (1971) made it obligatory for the President to give assent to a Constitution Amendment Bill and affirmed Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) laid down the Basic Structure doctrine. The 42nd Amendment (1976) tried to remove limits on amendment powers, and Minerva Mills (1980) struck those provisions down.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. Part IXA (Arts. 243P-243ZG) deals with Municipalities, Part XVIII (Arts. 352-360) with Emergency Provisions, and Part XX (Art. 368) with Amendment of the Constitution.
topic_notes: The Constitution of India originally had 22 Parts, 395 Articles and 8 Schedules. It now has 25 Parts (after counting IVA, IXA, IXB, XIVA), about 470 Articles and 12 Schedules. Part VII (States in Part B of the First Schedule) was repealed by the 7th Amendment in 1956. Key Parts to remember: Part I Union and its Territory (Arts. 1-4); Part II Citizenship (5-11); Part III Fundamental Rights (12-35); Part IV Directive Principles (36-51); Part IVA Fundamental Duties (51A, added by 42nd Amendment in 1976); Part V Union (52-151); Part VI States (152-237); Part VIII Union Territories (239-242); Part IX Panchayats (243-243O); Part IXA Municipalities (243P-243ZG); Part IXB Co-operative Societies (243ZH-243ZT); Part X Scheduled and Tribal Areas (244-244A); Part XI Centre-State Relations (245-263); Part XII Finance, Property, Contracts (264-300A); Part XIII Trade and Commerce (301-307); Part XIV Services (308-323); Part XIVA Tribunals (323A-323B); Part XV Elections (324-329A); Part XVI Special Provisions for certain classes (330-342); Part XVII Official Language (343-351); Part XVIII Emergency (352-360); Part XIX Miscellaneous (361-367); Part XX Amendment (368); Part XXI Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions (369-392); Part XXII Short title, commencement, authoritative text in Hindi and repeals (393-395). Possible future angles: Schedule-to-Part links (11th Schedule for Panchayats, 12th Schedule for Municipalities), the borrowed features (Emergency from Weimar, Amendment procedure from South Africa), constitutional amendments that added Parts, and the Articles that fall under each Part.

question: Which one of the following statements is correct as per the Constitution of India ?
options: Inter-State trade and commerce is a State subject under the State List
Inter-State migration is a State subject under the State List
Inter-State quarantine is a Union subject under the Union List
Corporation tax is a State subject under the State List
subject: Polity
detail: The Seventh Schedule (Article 246) divides legislative powers into the Union List (List I, originally 97 entries, now 98 in practice), the State List (List II, 61 entries, now 59 in practice) and the Concurrent List (List III, 52 entries). Entry 81 of List I reads 'Inter-State migration; inter-State quarantine', so both migration and quarantine across State boundaries belong to Parliament. This makes (c) correct and (b) wrong, because migration is not a State subject. Inter-State trade and commerce is Entry 42 of List I, so (a) is wrong. Article 301 guarantees freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse throughout India, and Articles 302-305 allow restrictions in the public interest. Taxes on income other than agricultural income are Entry 82, and corporation tax is Entry 85 of List I, so (d) is wrong. The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced GST and Article 279A, the GST Council. It did not make corporation tax a State subject. Elimination logic: any matter that crosses State boundaries, such as trade, migration, quarantine or corporation tax, is generally Union territory. Purely local matters such as public order, police, public health, land and agriculture belong to States.
explanations: Incorrect. Inter-State trade and commerce is Entry 42 of the Union List, not the State List. Entry 26 of the State List covers only trade and commerce within the State, subject to Entry 33 of List III.
Incorrect. Inter-State migration falls under Entry 81 of the Union List, so Parliament legislates on it. It is not in the State List.
Correct. Entry 81 of the Union List covers 'Inter-State migration; inter-State quarantine', so inter-State quarantine is a Union subject.
Incorrect. Taxes on corporations (corporation tax) are Entry 85 of the Union List. States cannot levy them, though the Union shares the proceeds under Article 270.
keyfact: Union List Entry 81 is 'Inter-State migration; inter-State quarantine', so both are Union subjects.
option_notes: Inter-State trade and commerce is Entry 42 of the Union List. Article 301 declares trade, commerce and intercourse free throughout India. Article 302 lets Parliament impose restrictions in the public interest, and Article 303 limits discrimination between States. Article 304 allows States to impose reasonable restrictions and non-discriminatory taxes, with the President's sanction required for some bills. Article 307 provides for an authority to carry out Articles 301-304. Intra-State trade is Entry 26 of the State List.

Inter-State migration is in Entry 81 of the Union List, together with inter-State quarantine. Entry 17 of the Union List deals with emigration and passports, visas and immigration. Article 19(1)(d) and (e) give citizens the right to move and reside freely, subject to reasonable restrictions. The Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act, 1979 was later subsumed into the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. Parliament, not States, legislates on this subject.

Entry 81 of the Union List covers inter-State quarantine. Quarantine in ports and seas is under Entry 28 of the Union List (marine hospitals). Public health and sanitation, hospitals and dispensaries are State List Entry 6. Prevention of the spread of infectious diseases across States is Concurrent List Entry 29. The Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 and the Disaster Management Act, 2005 were used during COVID-19.

Corporation tax is Entry 85 of the Union List, and taxes on income other than agricultural income are Entry 82. Agricultural income tax is State List Entry 46. Corporation tax proceeds are part of the shareable pool of Union taxes under Article 270, distributed under Finance Commission recommendations. Entry 85 is a Union entry. The Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019 cut the base corporate rate to 22 percent.
related: Entry 81 of the Union List is 'Inter-State migration; inter-State quarantine'.
Entry 42 of the Union List is inter-State trade and commerce.
Entry 85 of the Union List is corporation tax.
Entry 46 of the State List is taxes on agricultural income.
Article 248 and Entry 97 give residuary powers to Parliament.
The 42nd Amendment moved education and forests to the Concurrent List.
Article 249 allows Parliament to legislate on a State subject through a two-thirds Rajya Sabha resolution.
The 101st Amendment introduced GST and Article 279A.
summary: The correct answer is (c). Inter-State quarantine is a Union subject: Entry 81 of the Union List (List I, Seventh Schedule) covers 'Inter-State migration; inter-State quarantine'. The other options wrongly place Union subjects in the State List.
topic_notes: The Seventh Schedule distributes legislative subjects between the Union and States under Article 246. List I (Union) has 98 entries now and covers defence, foreign affairs, banking, railways, currency, atomic energy, inter-State trade and commerce, and corporation tax. List II (State) has 59 entries now and covers public order, police, public health, agriculture, land, local government and intra-State trade. List III (Concurrent) has 52 entries and covers criminal law, marriage, education, forests, economic planning and population control. The 42nd Amendment (1976) moved education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice to the Concurrent List. Residuary powers rest with Parliament under Article 248 and Entry 97 of List I. In case of conflict on a Concurrent subject, the Union law prevails under Article 254, unless a State law has received Presidential assent. Parliament can legislate on State List subjects in specific cases: Article 249 (Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds in the national interest), Article 250 (during Emergency), Article 252 (consent of two or more States) and Article 253 (international agreements). Article 258 lets the Union entrust functions to States. Article 301-307 provide for freedom of trade within the country. Article 279A set up the GST Council after the 101st Amendment (2016). Article 280 establishes the Finance Commission, and Article 270 governs the shareable Union taxes. Likely UPSC angles include which entry belongs to which list, residuary powers, the transfer of subjects between lists and Parliament's power to legislate on State subjects.

question: Under which of the following Articles of the Constitution of India, has the Supreme Court of India placed the Right to Privacy ?
subject: Polity
detail: The Right to Privacy is not expressly mentioned in the Constitution. It has been read in by the judiciary. Earlier, M.P. Sharma (1954, eight judges) and Kharak Singh (1962, six judges) had held that privacy was not a fundamental right. Later cases such as Gobind v. State of M.P. (1975), R. Rajagopal (1994) and PUCL v. Union of India (1997, telephone tapping) gradually recognised privacy under Article 21. The nine-judge bench in Puttaswamy (2017), which arose from the challenge to Aadhaar, overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh to the extent they denied privacy. It held that privacy is protected under Article 21 and also draws on Articles 19 and 14. The lead opinion was by Justice D.Y. Chandrachud, and Justice Chelameswar, Justice Bobde and others wrote concurring opinions. Privacy includes bodily integrity, informational privacy, decisional autonomy and sexual orientation. Restrictions must satisfy a three-part test: legality (a law), legitimate aim, and proportionality. Elimination logic: Articles 15 and 16 deal with non-discrimination and equality of opportunity, so they are unrelated. Article 19 gives freedoms such as speech and movement, and privacy is linked to it only as a supporting basis. The Court's primary placement is Article 21, so (d) is correct.
explanations: Incorrect: Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. It is not the source of privacy.
Incorrect: Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment. It has no bearing on privacy.

Incorrect: Article 19 guarantees the freedoms of speech, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession. Puttaswamy mentions these freedoms as interlinked with privacy, but the Court's primary location of the right is not Article 19.
Correct: Puttaswamy (2017) placed privacy within the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21, as part of the guarantees of Part III.
keyfact: Right to Privacy is part of Article 21 (life and personal liberty), per Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 24 Aug 2017, by a nine-judge bench.
option_notes: Article 15 prohibits discrimination by the State on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. It permits special provisions for women, children, socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs, and (103rd Amendment, 2019) economically weaker sections. Clause (2) bars discrimination in access to shops, restaurants, wells and public places.

Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment. Clause (4) allows reservation for backward classes inadequately represented in services, and Article 16(4A) allows reservation in promotions for SCs and STs. Indra Sawhney (1992) upheld 27% OBC reservation, introduced the creamy layer concept and set the 50% ceiling.

Article 19(1) originally gave seven freedoms: speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession and property. The right to property was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978). Article 19(2)-(6) allow reasonable restrictions. Article 19 is available only to citizens. Privacy is linked to it only as a supporting basis, not as its source.

Article 21 states that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except by procedure established by law. Maneka Gandhi (1978) made the procedure required to be fair, just and reasonable. It has been expanded to include dignity, livelihood, clean environment, speedy trial, and privacy (Puttaswamy 2017). Article 21A (right to education) was added by the 86th Amendment (2002).
related: Puttaswamy (2017) was decided by a nine-judge bench and was unanimous.
M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) were overruled to the extent that they denied privacy as a right.
Maneka Gandhi (1978) expanded Article 21 and required 'procedure established by law' to be fair, just and reasonable.
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is India's data protection law.
Navtej Singh Johar (2018) decriminalised consensual same-sex relations between adults.
Article 21A (right to education, ages 6-14) was inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002.
Article 21 is available to both citizens and non-citizens, while Article 19 is available only to citizens.
PUCL (1997) laid down safeguards on telephone tapping, rooted in privacy.
summary: The answer is (d) Article 21. In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (24 August 2017), a nine-judge Constitution Bench unanimously held that the Right to Privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21, and of the freedoms in Part III as a whole.
topic_notes: Right to Privacy: it is not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution, and the Supreme Court recognised it as a fundamental right in Puttaswamy I (2017). The case began when Justice K.S. Puttaswamy, a retired Karnataka High Court judge, challenged Aadhaar. A five-judge bench referred the question of privacy to a nine-judge bench. The bench ruled unanimously on 24 August 2017. It overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) in part. Privacy was held to be an intrinsic part of life and liberty under Article 21 and of the freedoms in Part III. Its facets include bodily autonomy, informational privacy and decisional autonomy. Any restriction must satisfy legality, legitimate aim and proportionality. Puttaswamy II (2018) upheld Aadhaar's validity with limits: Section 57 was struck down, and Aadhaar cannot be made mandatory for bank accounts, mobile connections or school admission. Related developments: Navtej Singh Johar (2018) decriminalised consensual same-sex acts under Section 377 IPC, relying on privacy and dignity. Joseph Shine (2018) struck down adultery as a crime. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is India's data protection law, and it provides for a Data Protection Board. The Justice B.N. Srikrishna Committee (2017) drafted an earlier data protection bill. Other rights read into Article 21 include the right to health, a clean environment, shelter, legal aid, a speedy trial and the right to die with dignity (passive euthanasia, Common Cause 2018). Article 20 protects against self-incrimination, which is also related to privacy and personal autonomy.
