question: The longest border between any two countries 81. in the world is between :
options: Canada and the United States of America
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Canada-US boundary measures roughly 8,891 km (about 5,525 miles). Of this, around 2,477 km is the Alaska-Canada border and the rest is the southern border. It is often called the longest undefended border, although it is well monitored. It is defined by treaties such as the Treaty of Paris (1783), the Jay Treaty (1794), the Webster-Ashburton Treaty (1842), the Oregon Treaty (1846) and the Alaska boundary settlement (1903). The International Boundary Commission maintains it. It follows rivers, the Great Lakes, the 49th parallel and the 141st meridian. Next in length is Kazakhstan-Russia at about 7,500 km, which is the longest continuous border between two countries in Eurasia and the second longest in the world. Chile-Argentina is about 6,691 km, the third longest and the longest in South America. China-India is only about 3,488 km by India's reckoning, and the line is disputed. Elimination: you only need to recall that Canada-USA is the world's longest, and knowing the Kazakhstan-Russia border is second also helps. The India-China border is far shorter, so option (c) can be dropped at once.
explanations: Correct: Canada-USA is about 8,891 km including Alaska, the longest in the world.
Incorrect: Chile-Argentina is about 6,691 km, the longest in South America but only third in the world.
Incorrect: China-India is about 3,488 km (India's figure), much shorter, and parts are disputed.
Incorrect: Kazakhstan-Russia is about 7,500 km, the second longest in the world, so it is not the longest.
keyfact: The longest international land border is Canada-USA, about 8,891 km including Alaska.
option_notes: Canada-USA: about 8,891 km, the longest international land border. It includes the 49th parallel, the Great Lakes and the Alaska-Yukon 141st meridian line. It was fixed by treaties from 1783 to 1908 and is managed by the International Boundary Commission. It is known as the longest undefended border, and crossings such as Ambassador Bridge and Peace Bridge are among the busiest.

Chile-Argentina: about 6,691 km along the Andes, the third longest border in the world. It is the longest in South America. The line follows Andean peaks and watersheds, with disputes settled by arbitration (1902 British award, Beagle Channel 1984 Treaty of Peace and Friendship). It runs from the Atacama region to Tierra del Fuego and the Strait of Magellan.

China-India: about 3,488 km by India's reckoning, divided into Western (Ladakh), Middle (Himachal, Uttarakhand) and Eastern (Arunachal, Sikkim) sectors. The boundary is not fully delimited and is disputed. The Line of Actual Control (LAC) is the de facto line. The McMahon Line (1914) is the Eastern sector boundary, and India fought a war with China in 1962.

Kazakhstan-Russia: about 7,500 km, the second longest land border in the world and the longest continuous land border. It is also the longest border in Asia. It runs across the steppe, was formerly an internal Soviet boundary, and was formally delimited by a 2005 treaty that came into force in 2006. Both countries are members of the CSTO, the EAEU and the SCO.
related: Canada-USA border is about 8,891 km, the longest in the world.
Kazakhstan-Russia is the second longest border, about 7,500 km.
India's longest land border is with Bangladesh, about 4,096 km.
The Durand Line (1893) separates Afghanistan and Pakistan.
The Radcliffe Line (1947) divides India and Pakistan.
The McMahon Line (1914) is the eastern India-China boundary.
China has the most neighbours, 14 countries.
Uzbekistan and Liechtenstein are doubly landlocked.
summary: The answer is (a) Canada and the United States of America. Their border, including the Alaska-Canada segment, runs about 8,891 km, which makes it the longest international land border between any two countries in the world.
topic_notes: World borders are a frequent theme in UPSC geography. The longest land border is Canada-USA at about 8,891 km, which includes the Alaska segment. Next come Kazakhstan-Russia (about 7,500 km) and Chile-Argentina (about 6,691 km). Others include China-Mongolia (about 4,677 km), USA-Mexico (about 3,145 km) and Russia-China (about 4,200 km in total across the eastern and western sections). The country with the most land neighbours is China, with 14, followed by Russia with 14 by some counts. India shares about 15,106 km of land border with seven countries and the longest is with Bangladesh at about 4,096 km, followed by China, Pakistan (about 3,323 km), Nepal (about 1,751 km), Myanmar (about 1,643 km), Bhutan (about 699 km) and Afghanistan (about 106 km, in the part of Ladakh that India claims). Famous boundary lines include the Radcliffe Line (India-Pakistan, 1947), the Durand Line (Afghanistan-Pakistan, 1893), the McMahon Line (India-China, 1914), the 38th parallel (North and South Korea), the 49th parallel (Canada-USA) and the 17th parallel (former North and South Vietnam). The Line of Control (LoC) is about 740 km. Countries with the most coastline: Canada is first, followed by Indonesia and Norway. Landlocked countries number about 44 to 45, including two doubly landlocked ones: Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan.

question:
Which of the following statements about the Ethics Committee in the Lok Sabha are correct ?
1. Initially it was-an ad-hoc Committee. 82.
2. Only a Member of the Lok Sabha can make a complaint relating to unethical conduct of a member of the Lok Sabha.
3. This Committee cannot take up any matter which is sub-judice. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Polity
detail: The Ethics Committee of the Lok Sabha oversees the moral and ethical conduct of members and examines cases of misconduct referred to it by the Speaker. The Committee of Privileges and the Ethics Committee are separate bodies. The idea of an ethics panel came from the Presiding Officers' Conference in 1996. The Rajya Sabha constituted its Ethics Committee on 4 March 1997. In the Lok Sabha, the Speaker constituted an ad-hoc Ethics Committee on 16 March 2000, and it became a permanent part of the committee system in 2015 (16th Lok Sabha). Under the rules, any person can complain about a Member's unethical conduct, but a complaint from a person other than a Member must be forwarded by a Member along with an affidavit, and the complainant must satisfy the Committee about the evidence. A Member who files the complaint need not give an affidavit. The Committee does not entertain matters that are sub-judice, and it can recommend sanctions such as censure, reprimand or suspension for a specified period. Elimination: statement 2 is incorrect because of the word 'only', so options (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated, leaving (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 2, which is incorrect because complaints are not restricted to Members of Lok Sabha.
Wrong: it includes statement 2 and leaves out statement 1, which is correct because the Committee was initially ad-hoc.
Correct: statements 1 and 3 hold, since the Committee began as an ad-hoc body and does not take up sub-judice matters.
Wrong: statement 2 is incorrect, so not all three statements are correct.
keyfact: Lok Sabha Ethics Committee: ad-hoc in 2000, permanent from 2015; takes no sub-judice matters; outside complaints must be routed through a Member with an affidavit.
option_notes: Option (a) pairs statements 1 and 2. The Ethics Committee of Lok Sabha was ad-hoc at first, in 2000, and permanent from 2015. The claim that only a Member can complain is false, because any person may complain through a Member with an affidavit. The Committee has up to 15 Members nominated by the Speaker. It deals with ethical conduct, not constitutional privileges.

Option (b) pairs statements 2 and 3. The sub-judice bar is accurate, but the limit on who may complain is not. Complaints come from Members directly, or from others through a Member with an affidavit. The Committee can recommend censure, reprimand or suspension of a Member, and the House decides on acting on the recommendation.

Option (c) is the correct answer, covering statements 1 and 3. The Lok Sabha Ethics Committee was set up as ad-hoc on 16 March 2000 and made a permanent committee in 2015. It does not take up sub-judice matters. It works on complaints referred by the Speaker and oversees Members' moral conduct.

Option (d) claims all three statements are correct. It fails because of statement 2: complainants are not limited to Lok Sabha Members. Outsiders can file through a Member with an affidavit. The Rajya Sabha has its own Ethics Committee, formed in 1997, which is a separate body.
related: Rajya Sabha Ethics Committee was constituted on 4 March 1997.
Lok Sabha Ethics Committee was ad-hoc in 2000 and permanent from 2015.
Lok Sabha Ethics Committee has up to 15 members nominated by the Speaker.
Article 105 deals with powers and privileges of Parliament and its members.
Lok Sabha Privileges Committee has 15 members; Rajya Sabha's has 10.
Estimates Committee has 30 members, all from Lok Sabha.
Public Accounts Committee has 22 members, 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha.
Mahua Moitra was expelled from Lok Sabha in December 2023 following an Ethics Committee report.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Committee started as an ad-hoc body in 2000 and was made permanent later. The Rajya Sabha's Ethics Committee was set up in March 1997 after the 1996 Presiding Officers' Conference proposed such a body. The Lok Sabha's Speaker, G.M.C. Balayogi, constituted the ad-hoc Ethics Committee on 16 March 2000. It was institutionalised as a standing committee in 2015 during the 16th Lok Sabha. Its members are nominated by the Speaker, usually for a one-year term, and it has up to 15 members.

2 — Incorrect: Complaints are not limited to Lok Sabha Members. Any person can complain against a Member, but if the complaint comes from outside Parliament it must be routed through a Member of Lok Sabha and accompanied by an affidavit. Members can complain directly, without an affidavit. The Committee examines complaints referred by the Speaker and can also take up cases on its own motion. It can recommend sanctions such as admonition, reprimand, censure or suspension for a period. The 2023 'cash for query' complaint against Mahua Moitra was referred to it.

3 — Correct: The Committee does not take up matters that are sub-judice, meaning pending before a court. The Committee also does not examine matters that are already before the Privileges Committee, or that fall under its jurisdiction. The Committee examines only complaints with prima facie evidence, and a complaint cannot be based merely on media reports. It examines a complaint in the first instance and then makes a recommendation to the Speaker. The Speaker may then place the report before the House for consideration.
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only. The Ethics Committee of Lok Sabha began as an ad-hoc committee and became permanent later, and it does not take up sub-judice matters. Statement 2 is wrong because complaints can be made by any person, not only by a Member of Lok Sabha.
topic_notes: Parliamentary Ethics Committees: The 1996 Presiding Officers' Conference proposed ethics panels for Parliament. The Rajya Sabha's Committee on Ethics was formed on 4 March 1997 by Chairman K.R. Narayanan, and it became a permanent committee in 1997-98. The Lok Sabha's Ethics Committee was constituted as ad-hoc on 16 March 2000 and became permanent in 2015. The Lok Sabha committee has up to 15 members nominated by the Speaker. It examines complaints of unethical conduct against Members referred to it by the Speaker, and it recommends sanctions. The House can accept sanctions such as censure, reprimand or suspension. The Committee does not entertain sub-judice matters. The Code of Conduct for Members of Rajya Sabha was adopted in 2005. The Committee of Privileges is another body; it examines breaches of parliamentary privileges, including contempt of the House. The Lok Sabha's Committee of Privileges has 15 members and the Rajya Sabha's has 10. Other Lok Sabha committees include the Committee on Absence of Members, Rules Committee, Business Advisory Committee, and Committee on Petitions. Financial Committees: Public Accounts Committee (22 members, 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha), Estimates Committee (30 members, all from Lok Sabha), and Committee on Public Undertakings (22 members). In December 2023, Mahua Moitra was expelled from Lok Sabha after the Ethics Committee report in the cash for query case. Articles 105 and 194 deal with the powers and privileges of members of Parliament and State legislatures.

question:
Consider the following statements regarding ‘Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam’ :
1. Provisions will come into effect from the 188 Lok Sabha.
2. This will be in force for 15 years after becoming an Act.
8. There are provisions for the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes Women within the quota reserved for the Scheduled Castes. Which of the statements given above are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023, called the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, was introduced as the 128th Amendment Bill and passed in September 2023. Lok Sabha passed it on 20 September 2023 and Rajya Sabha on 21 September 2023. The President gave assent on 28 September 2023. It inserts Articles 330A (Lok Sabha), 332A (State Legislative Assemblies) and 334A. Article 239AA is also amended for the Delhi Assembly. One-third of all seats, including seats reserved for SCs and STs, are reserved for women. The reservation is to come into effect only after delimitation is undertaken based on the first census taken after the commencement of the Act. It continues for 15 years, and may be extended by Parliament. Rotation of reserved seats takes place after each delimitation. It does not apply to the Rajya Sabha or Legislative Councils. Elimination logic: statement 1 is wrong because the 2024 general election (18th Lok Sabha) is held without the reservation, so any option containing 1 is out: (a), (b) and (d). That leaves (c), with statements 2 and 3 both correct.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect: the Act does not take effect from the 18th Lok Sabha, since implementation awaits census and delimitation.
(b) is wrong because it includes statement 1, which is false, and leaves out statement 3, which is true.
(c) is correct because statement 2 (15-year duration) and statement 3 (SC women sub-quota within the SC quota) are both accurate, while statement 1 is not.
(d) is wrong because it includes statement 1, which is false, and omits statement 2, which is true.
keyfact: 106th Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023): one-third women's seats in Lok Sabha and Assemblies, 15 years, SC/ST sub-quota, effective only after census and delimitation.
option_notes: Option (a), statements 1, 2 and 3 together, would be correct only if the quota applied from the 18th Lok Sabha. It does not. The Act is linked to census and delimitation, so the 2024 elections were held without it. The Act is the 106th Constitutional Amendment (introduced as the 128th Amendment Bill), passed in September 2023.

Option (b), statements 1 and 2 only, wrongly accepts the immediate-effect claim. The 15-year term in it is correct. The Act inserts Articles 330A, 332A and 334A and is not effective until delimitation follows the first census after commencement. It would cover the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly, not the Rajya Sabha or Legislative Councils.

Option (c), statements 2 and 3 only, is the official answer. The quota lasts 15 years, with extension possible by Parliament. One-third of SC and ST seats are reserved for SC and ST women. It applies to the Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly. It starts only after delimitation based on the first census after commencement.

Option (d), statements 1 and 3 only, wrongly accepts the immediate-effect claim and rejects the 15-year term. The SC/ST women sub-quota is a genuine feature. Implementation, however, depends on a fresh census and a delimitation exercise. Seats reserved for women are to be rotated after each delimitation. No separate quota for OBC women exists in the Act.
related: Women's reservation: first introduced as the 81st Amendment Bill, 1996, under the Deve Gowda government.
The Rajya Sabha passed the Women's Reservation Bill in 2010, but it lapsed with the 15th Lok Sabha.
Articles 243D and 243T provide at least one-third reservation for women in Panchayats and municipalities.
Article 82 provides for readjustment after each census; Article 81 fixes the Lok Sabha seat structure.
The 84th Amendment (2001) froze the seat allocation until the first census after 2026.
The 104th Amendment (2019) ended the Anglo-Indian nomination and extended SC/ST reservation to 2030.
The Delimitation Commission's orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in a court.
The Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Councils are not covered by the 106th Amendment.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The provisions do not apply from the 18th Lok Sabha (2024). They come into force only after the first census following the Act's commencement and the subsequent delimitation exercise. The 18th Lok Sabha was constituted in 2024 without this reservation. Practically, implementation is likely only after the next census and delimitation, so the 2029 election at the earliest. The Act's commencement date is notified by the Central Government. The census due in 2021 was delayed because of COVID-19. Delimitation is carried out by a Delimitation Commission under a Delimitation Act. Seat rotation follows each delimitation.

2 — Correct: The reservation lasts 15 years from commencement, under the new Article 334A. Parliament may extend the period by law. The Act reserves one-third of seats for women in the Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly. Reservation is for direct elections only. It does not cover the Rajya Sabha or State Legislative Councils. Seats reserved for women are rotated after each delimitation exercise. Earlier reservations for SCs and STs under Article 334 were likewise time-bound and have been repeatedly extended, most recently by the 104th Amendment to 2030.

3 — Correct: One-third of the seats reserved for SCs and STs are reserved for women belonging to those categories. This is achieved through Articles 330A and 332A, which provide that one-third of the seats reserved for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies shall be reserved for women. There is no separate reservation for OBC women. The one-third women's quota also applies to the total number of seats, including those filled by direct election. Women reserved seats may be allotted in different constituencies by rotation. The Act applies to direct elections only.
summary: The correct answer is (c): statements 2 and 3 are correct, statement 1 is incorrect. The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023) reserves one-third of Lok Sabha and State Assembly seats for women for 15 years, including a sub-quota within SC/ST seats, but it takes effect only after the next census and delimitation, not from the 18th Lok Sabha.
topic_notes: The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam is the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023. It was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 19 September 2023 as the Constitution (128th Amendment) Bill, 2023. Lok Sabha passed it on 20 September 2023 and Rajya Sabha on 21 September 2023, with near-unanimous support. The President gave assent on 28 September 2023. It provides one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly. Within the seats reserved for SCs and STs, one-third are reserved for women of those groups. New Articles 330A (Lok Sabha), 332A (State Assemblies) and 334A (commencement, duration and rotation) were inserted. Article 239AA is amended for Delhi. The reservation takes effect after delimitation based on the first census taken after the Act commences. It lasts 15 years and may be extended. Seats are rotated after each delimitation. The Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils are not covered. There is no OBC sub-quota. Related background: the first women's reservation bill was the 81st Amendment Bill of 1996 under the H. D. Deve Gowda government. Rajya Sabha passed a bill in 2010 but it lapsed in the Lok Sabha. Panchayati Raj institutions under Article 243D and municipalities under Article 243T already reserve not less than one-third of seats for women. Several states have raised this to 50 percent. Women make up roughly 14 percent of the Lok Sabha, about 78 of 543 members in 2024 versus 82 in 2019. Likely future questions: the delimitation commission, Article 82 and Article 170, the freeze on seat allocation until the first census after 2026, and the 84th and 87th Amendments.

question:
Which of the following statements about ‘Exercise Mitra Shakti-2023’ are correct ? dis This was a joint military exercise between India and Bangladesh.
2. It commenced in Aundh (Pune).
3. Joint response during counter-terrorism operations was a goal of this operation. 4, Indian Air Force was a part of this exercise. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Mitra Shakti is a biennial/annual joint military exercise between the Indian Army and the Sri Lanka Army. The 9th edition (2023) was held at the Foreign Training Node, Aundh, Pune, from 16 to 29 November 2023. The 2018 edition was held at Pune and the 2019 edition at Sri Lanka's Ampara; later editions followed in Sri Lanka and India. Its objective was to enhance interoperability and joint response in counter-terrorism and counter-insurgency operations in a sub-conventional environment under a United Nations mandate (Chapter VII of the UN Charter). The 2023 edition was notable because the Indian Air Force took part for the first time, alongside the Army (the Sri Lankan side also included air force personnel). Elimination logic: statement 1 is wrong because the partner is Sri Lanka, not Bangladesh. Every option containing 1, namely (a), (b) and (c), is therefore eliminated. Only (d), 2, 3 and 4, remains. A student who knows that the partner is Sri Lanka can answer without verifying the other statements. Do not confuse it with India-Bangladesh exercises such as Sampriti, or with other bilateral exercises like Maitree (Thailand) and Nomadic Elephant (Mongolia).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement 1; the exercise was with Sri Lanka, not Bangladesh.
(b) is wrong because it includes statement 1 (Bangladesh), which is false; it also omits statement 3, which is true.
(c) is wrong because it includes statement 1 and omits statement 2, which is true because the exercise began at Aundh, Pune.
(d) is correct: statements 2 (Aundh, Pune), 3 (counter-terrorism goal) and 4 (IAF participation) are all true, and the false statement 1 is excluded.
keyfact: Mitra Shakti = India-Sri Lanka army exercise; the 2023 edition (Aundh, Pune) was counter-terrorism focused and had the IAF join for the first time.
option_notes: Option (a), statements 1, 2 and 3, would be right only if the partner were Bangladesh and the IAF were absent. It wrongly pairs the Bangladesh claim with the true venue and objective. India-Bangladesh army ties are shown through Exercise Sampriti, first held in 2010. Navy ties are shown through Bongosagar and CORPAT, and the air forces have limited bilateral drills. Bangladesh is a key neighbour in the Bay of Bengal region and a BIMSTEC member.

Option (b), statements 1, 2 and 4, wrongly accepts Bangladesh as the partner. It is a trap built from two true statements and one false one. Remember that Mitra Shakti is with Sri Lanka. India and Bangladesh also share a Joint Consultative Commission and a land boundary of about 4,096 km, the longest India has with any neighbour. Exercise Sampriti is the army exercise between the two.

Option (c), statements 1, 3 and 4, wrongly accepts Bangladesh and omits the Pune venue. The Sri Lankan partnership has a long history: the Indian Peace Keeping Force operated there in 1987-90. Defence cooperation includes training Sri Lankan officers at Indian institutions such as the National Defence College and the Defence Services Staff College at Wellington. India also hosts Sri Lankan navy ships under SLINEX.

Option (d), statements 2, 3 and 4, is the official answer. Mitra Shakti-2023 was the ninth edition, held 16 to 29 November 2023 at Aundh, Pune, between India and Sri Lanka. It focused on counter-terrorism and interoperability under UN Chapter VII, with the IAF participating for the first time. It forms part of India's regular military diplomacy with its Indian Ocean neighbour and its Neighbourhood First policy.
related: Mitra Shakti is the India-Sri Lanka army exercise; its 2023 edition was the ninth, held at Aundh, Pune.
Sampriti is the India-Bangladesh army exercise, while Bongosagar is the naval one.
SLINEX is the India-Sri Lanka naval exercise.
Maitree is the India-Thailand army exercise and Nomadic Elephant the India-Mongolia one.
Surya Kiran is the India-Nepal army exercise; Ekuverin is India-Maldives.
Malabar is the naval exercise among India, USA, Japan and Australia (Quad members).
Dharma Guardian is the India-Japan army exercise; Yudh Abhyas is India-USA.
Garuda is the India-France air force exercise, and Shakti is the India-France army exercise.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: the exercise was with Sri Lanka, not Bangladesh. Mitra Shakti is the India-Sri Lanka army exercise, started in 2013 as a counter-insurgency and counter-terrorism drill. Editions alternate between India and Sri Lanka. The India-Bangladesh army exercise is Sampriti, and the India-Bangladesh naval exercise is Bongosagar. The Sri Lankan contingent in 2023 was drawn from the Gajaba Regiment and other units, and the Indian contingent included the Rajputana Rifles. India-Sri Lanka also hold the naval exercise SLINEX and the Sri Lanka-India Defence Dialogue.

2 — Correct: the 2023 edition began at the Foreign Training Node, Aundh Military Station, Pune, Maharashtra, on 16 November 2023 and ran until 29 November. Aundh also hosts other bilateral army exercises. Pune is the home of the Southern Command and hosts many joint exercises, such as Ajeya Warrior and Dharma Guardian in some years. The 2019 edition was held at Ampara, Sri Lanka, and the 2021 edition at Rajasthan's Mahajan field firing range. The 2023 edition was the ninth.

3 — Correct: the exercise aims to enhance interoperability and joint response in counter-terrorism operations in a semi-urban and sub-conventional environment. Training includes tactical drills, heliborne operations, room intervention and clearing of built-up areas. It is conducted under a United Nations mandate (Chapter VII). It reflects India's 'Neighbourhood First' policy and SAGAR/MAHASAGAR vision for the Indian Ocean region, and it strengthens defence ties with the island nation.

4 — Correct: the Indian Air Force participated in the 2023 edition for the first time, which was a distinguishing feature. The Indian Army contingent comprised about 120 personnel, mostly from the Rajputana Rifles, and the Sri Lankan side had a similar number. IAF involvement enabled joint air-ground operations such as heliborne insertion and air support in counter-terror drills. This marks a move towards tri-service jointness, in line with India's theatre command reforms under the Chief of Defence Staff.
summary: The answer is (d): statements 2, 3 and 4 are correct. Exercise Mitra Shakti-2023 was a joint exercise between India and Sri Lanka, not Bangladesh, so statement 1 is wrong. It began at Aundh Military Station, Pune, focused on counter-terrorism, and included the Indian Air Force.
topic_notes: Mitra Shakti is the India-Sri Lanka joint army exercise, begun in 2013 as a counter-insurgency and counter-terrorism drill and held alternately in India and Sri Lanka. The 2023 edition (9th) was held at Aundh, Pune, on 16-29 November 2023 and, notably, included the Indian Air Force. It operates under a UN mandate (Chapter VII) and emphasizes interoperability and joint response in a sub-conventional, semi-urban environment. India-Sri Lanka ties also include the Colombo Security Conclave (India, Sri Lanka, Maldives, Mauritius, Bangladesh as a member), the 1987 Indo-Lanka Accord, Katchatheevu, the Adam's Bridge and Sethusamudram issues, and the Trincomalee energy hub.

question: A Writ of Prohibition is an order issued by the 85. Supreme Court or High Courts to :
options: a government officer prohibiting him from taking a particular action
the Parliament/Legislative Assembly to pass a law on Prohibition
the lower court prohibiting continuation of proceedings in a case
the Government prohibiting it from following an unconstitutional policy. 86
subject: Polity
detail: Prohibition literally means 'to forbid'. It is a preventive, judicial writ: it is issued while proceedings are still pending before an inferior court or quasi-judicial tribunal, commanding it to stop continuing them. Grounds are: (i) excess of jurisdiction or absence of jurisdiction, (ii) violation of principles of natural justice, (iii) the body acting under an unconstitutional law, or (iv) infringement of fundamental rights. It is available only against judicial and quasi-judicial authorities, not against administrative authorities, legislative bodies or private individuals. The Supreme Court issues writs under Article 32 (for fundamental rights only), while High Courts issue them under Article 226 (for fundamental rights and 'any other purpose', so a wider scope). Elimination: (a) is wrong because administrative officers are not covered; the writ against them would be mandamus or certiorari-type remedies. (b) is wrong because courts cannot direct a legislature to pass or not pass a law. (d) is wrong because the government acting in an executive capacity is not a judicial body. Only (c) correctly names a lower court as the target. Prohibition is issued before the decision is made; certiorari is issued after the decision to quash it.
explanations: Wrong: prohibition does not lie against administrative officers or executive action; it is directed at judicial or quasi-judicial bodies.
Wrong: courts cannot direct a legislature to pass or not pass any law, and prohibition has nothing to do with the subject of 'Prohibition' (liquor).
Correct: the writ is issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal to stop proceedings that exceed its jurisdiction or violate natural justice.
Wrong: the government acting in executive or policy capacity is not a judicial body; unconstitutional policies are challenged through other writs or judicial review, not prohibition.
keyfact: Prohibition = higher court tells a lower court/tribunal to stop proceedings (preventive); Certiorari = quashes the order after it is passed (curative).
option_notes: Administrative officers are typically controlled through mandamus (a command to perform a public duty) and, in some cases, quo warranto (to test the legality of a claim to public office). Prohibition does not apply to purely administrative action. Mandamus cannot be issued against the President or Governors, private individuals, or to enforce departmental instructions lacking statutory force.

Legislatures enjoy parliamentary privilege and separation of powers. Courts can strike down a law through judicial review (Art. 13, 32, 226, 246) but cannot compel or forbid legislation. Prohibition, as a subject, is a State subject (intoxicating liquors, Entry 8, State List), and Art. 47 (a Directive Principle) directs the State to work toward prohibition of intoxicating drinks.

Writ of Prohibition: issued by a higher court to a lower court or tribunal to prevent it from exceeding its jurisdiction or usurping one it lacks. It is issued only while proceedings are pending, so it is preventive. It is available only against judicial and quasi-judicial authorities, and is often called a 'stay order' in effect.

The government is not a target of prohibition in its executive role. Unconstitutional policies or laws are challenged through judicial review, using writs such as mandamus or certiorari, or declarations of invalidity under Art. 13. Prohibition and certiorari are both restricted to judicial or quasi-judicial functions.
related: Art. 32 (SC writs) is itself a Fundamental Right; Art. 226 (HC writs) is not.
Prohibition is preventive (during proceedings); Certiorari is curative (after the order).
Mandamus cannot be issued against the President or Governors.
Habeas Corpus can be issued against both public authorities and private persons.
Quo Warranto applies only to substantive public offices created by statute or the Constitution.
L. Chandra Kumar (1997): judicial review by SC and HCs is part of the basic structure.
Art. 139 allows Parliament to give the SC power to issue writs for purposes other than fundamental rights.
Art. 359 allows suspension of enforcement of Fundamental Rights during Emergency, except Arts 20 and 21.
summary: The answer is (c). A Writ of Prohibition is issued by a higher court (Supreme Court under Art. 32, High Courts under Art. 226) to a lower court or tribunal, directing it to stop proceedings in a case that is beyond its jurisdiction or in violation of natural justice.
topic_notes: Writs are prerogative remedies borrowed from English law. Art. 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for enforcing Fundamental Rights, and Art. 32 itself is a Fundamental Right (Dr Ambedkar called it the 'soul and heart' of the Constitution). Art. 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs for fundamental rights and for any other purpose, which gives them wider jurisdiction. Parliament may empower other courts to issue writs under Art. 32(3). Five writs: 1) Habeas Corpus ('to have the body'): protects personal liberty against unlawful detention; can be issued against public authorities and private individuals. 2) Mandamus ('we command'): orders a public official to perform a legal duty; not against the President, Governors, private individuals, or a non-statutory body. 3) Prohibition: preventive, issued to inferior courts or tribunals while proceedings are pending. 4) Certiorari ('to be certified'): curative, issued to quash an order already passed by an inferior court; expanded in scope after 1991 to include administrative authorities affecting rights. 5) Quo Warranto ('by what authority'): tests the legality of a claim to a substantive public office; cannot be used for ministerial or private offices. Prohibition and certiorari are issued against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies. Habeas corpus and mandamus have wider reach. Quo warranto may be sought by any interested person, not just the aggrieved one. Writ jurisdiction is part of the basic structure (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997, on judicial review by High Courts and SC). Art. 359 permits suspension of enforcement of Fundamental Rights during a National Emergency (except Arts 20 and 21 after the 44th Amendment). Related: Art. 139 allows Parliament to confer further writ powers on the SC.

question:
Consider the following statements :
1. It is the Governor of the State who recognizes and declares any community of that State as a Scheduled Tribe. 87.
2. A community declared as a Scheduled Tribe in a State need not be so in another State. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 342(1) empowers the President, after consulting the Governor of the State concerned, to specify by public notification the tribes or tribal communities, or parts of or groups within them, to be Scheduled Tribes in relation to that State or Union Territory. Article 342(2) provides that only Parliament, by law, can include or exclude any community from the list; a later notification cannot vary it. The Governor therefore only gets consulted and has no power to recognise or declare an ST. Statement 1 is wrong on this ground. The lists are State/UT-specific, so the same community may be an ST in one State and be unlisted or even listed as SC or OBC in another. Examples include the Gonds and Santhals, who have different status across States. Article 366(25) defines Scheduled Tribes as those communities deemed so under Article 342. The Governor does have a role under the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas, Tribes Advisory Council) and the Sixth Schedule, but not in declaring STs. Elimination: since statement 1 is wrong, (a), (c) and (d) fall away if statement 2 is right, leaving (b). Compare with Article 341 for SCs, which follows the same pattern.
explanations: Wrong: it holds that only statement 1 is correct, but the Governor does not declare STs. The President does, under Article 342.
Correct: statement 1 is false because the President specifies STs, and statement 2 is true because lists are State-specific.
Wrong: this would need statement 1 to be right, but the Governor only gets consulted.
Wrong: statement 2 is true, since ST status is State-specific, so 'neither' cannot hold.
keyfact: STs are notified by the President under Article 342 (Governor only consulted), only Parliament can change the list, and ST status is State-specific.
option_notes: Option (a) says only statement 1 is correct. It matches a common confusion in which the Governor is assumed to notify STs. In fact the Governor's constitutional role is consultative under Article 342(1). The Governor's real tribal powers lie in the Fifth Schedule, covering Scheduled Areas in States such as Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Himachal Pradesh. Governors can make regulations on land transfer, money-lending and allotment of land in these areas.

Option (b) says only statement 2 is correct, and it is the official answer. It reflects Article 342 and the State-specific nature of ST lists. The President notifies the lists after consulting the Governor and Parliament amends them. Inclusion or exclusion is done through Acts such as the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order (Amendment) Acts. The Registrar General of India and the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A) are involved in the process.

Option (c) says both statements are correct. It fails because statement 1 wrongly gives the Governor the power of declaration. Article 342 gives that to the President. The modification procedure is also special: the Ministry of Tribal Affairs proposes, the State Government recommends, the Registrar General of India and National Commission for Scheduled Tribes concur, then Cabinet approves and a Bill is introduced in Parliament.

Option (d) says neither statement is correct. It fails because statement 2 is true: ST status is area-specific. For example, a community may be listed in one State and absent in another, so reservation benefits do not carry over on migration. Similar logic applies to SCs under Article 341, while OBC lists exist at both Central and State levels.
related: Article 342: President notifies STs; Parliament alone can alter the list.
Article 341: the same procedure for Scheduled Castes.
Article 338A: National Commission for Scheduled Tribes, created by the 89th Amendment, 2003.
Fifth Schedule: Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in States other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
Sixth Schedule: Autonomous District Councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
PESA Act 1996 extends Panchayat provisions to Scheduled Areas.
Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises individual and community forest rights.
There are 75 PVTGs in India, identified from among STs.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The President, not the Governor, specifies STs under Article 342(1), after consulting the Governor. Parliament alone can amend the list by law under Article 342(2). The Governor's role is consultative. The Governor does have separate powers over Scheduled Areas administration under the Fifth Schedule, such as directing that laws of Parliament or the State legislature do not apply or apply with modification, and making regulations for peace and good governance of Scheduled Areas after consulting the Tribes Advisory Council. Article 244 deals with administration of Scheduled and Tribal Areas.

2 — Correct: The ST lists are specified separately for each State and UT. A community notified in one State need not be notified in another, because tribal status depends on the local social, economic and educational conditions and the region's history. The Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order 1950 and its State-wise orders, plus later amendment Acts, hold these lists. Migrants from one State to another do not carry ST status automatically, which matters for reservation benefits and certificates. Criteria traditionally cited are primitive traits, distinctive culture, geographical isolation, shyness of contact and backwardness (Lokur Committee, 1965).
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. Under Article 342, Scheduled Tribes are specified by the President by public notification (after consulting the Governor for a State), not by the Governor, and the list is State-specific, so a community may be an ST in one State but not in another.
topic_notes: Scheduled Tribes are defined in Article 366(25) as those communities deemed to be STs under Article 342. Article 342(1): the President, after consulting the Governor (for a State), specifies tribes by public notification. Article 342(2): only Parliament, by law, may include or exclude communities. The Constitution does not define the criteria. The Lokur Committee (1965) criteria are primitive traits, distinctive culture, geographical isolation, shyness of contact and backwardness. The first ST list came through the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950. Article 338A created the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes through the 89th Amendment (2003), separating it from the joint SC/ST Commission. Article 330 and 332 give reserved seats in Lok Sabha and Assemblies. Article 335 covers service claims. Article 244 and the Fifth Schedule govern Scheduled Areas, where the Governor has regulatory powers and a Tribes Advisory Council is set up. The Sixth Schedule covers tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram through Autonomous District Councils. Article 244A allows autonomous States within Assam. PESA 1996 extends Panchayats to Scheduled Areas. The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises forest rights. PVTGs are identified from among STs (Dhebar Commission 1960-61 gave the 'Primitive Tribal Groups' category), and there are 75 PVTGs. Tribal affairs sit with the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, created in 1999. Likely angles include the Article 341 comparison for SCs, the Article 342A power over socially and educationally backward classes (102nd and 105th Amendments), the Sixth Schedule vs Fifth Schedule, and PESA.

question:
Consider the following statements : 91.
Statement-I : Sumed pipeline is a strategic route for Persian Gulf oil and natural gas shipments to Europe.
Statement-II : Sumed pipeline connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean Sea. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements ?
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-IT is correct
subject: Geography
detail: The Sumed pipeline (Arab Petroleum Pipelines Company, headquartered in Egypt) is a roughly 320 km twin-pipeline system. It carries crude oil from Ain Sukhna on the Gulf of Suez (Red Sea) to Sidi Kerir near Alexandria on the Mediterranean. It was built after the 1967 war and the Suez Canal closure, and it began operating in 1977. It is an alternative to the Suez Canal for tankers too large to transit the canal fully laden, because the oil is offloaded at Ain Sukhna, piped across Egypt and reloaded at Sidi Kerir. Gulf producers such as Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE and Iraq use it to ship crude to Europe. It is therefore a strategic bypass, which makes it a key alternative if the Suez Canal or the Bab-el-Mandeb is disrupted. Elimination logic: Statement-II is clearly true because the pipeline connects the Red Sea and the Mediterranean. Statement-I is true because it is a strategic route for Gulf oil going to Europe. The Red Sea-Mediterranean link is exactly what makes it a strategic bypass, so Statement-II explains Statement-I. This eliminates (b), (c) and (d). One caveat is that Sumed carries mainly crude oil, though the question treats it as an oil and gas route, and the official answer accepts Statement-I as correct.
explanations: Correct. Both statements are true, and Statement-II (the Red Sea-Mediterranean link) is the reason Sumed works as a strategic route for Gulf oil going to Europe.
Wrong. Both statements are correct, but Statement-II does explain Statement-I, because the geographic link is what makes the route strategic.
Wrong. Statement-II is correct, since Sumed does connect the Red Sea with the Mediterranean.
Wrong. Statement-I is also correct, since Sumed is a strategic route for Gulf oil to Europe.
keyfact: Sumed pipeline: Ain Sukhna (Red Sea) to Sidi Kerir (Mediterranean), Egypt, operating since 1977, a Suez Canal bypass for Gulf oil going to Europe.
option_notes: Option (a) is the official answer. It says both statements are true and Statement-II is the explanation. In assertion-reason questions, check that each statement is true and then ask whether the second gives the cause or mechanism of the first. Here the pipeline's Red Sea-Mediterranean link is the mechanism that makes it a bypass of the Suez Canal.

Option (b) says both statements are true but unrelated as explanation. It would be right if Statement-II were just an independent fact. UPSC often uses this form when the second statement is true but gives no cause. Here the geography is the cause, so (b) is wrong.

Option (c) says Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect. It would apply if Sumed did not link two seas. The pipeline does connect the Gulf of Suez (Red Sea) with the Mediterranean, so (c) is wrong.

Option (d) says Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct. It would apply if Sumed were not a strategic route for Gulf oil. It is a recognised alternative to the Suez Canal for Gulf crude going to Europe, so (d) is wrong.
related: Sumed pipeline runs from Ain Sukhna (Red Sea) to Sidi Kerir (Mediterranean) in Egypt.
Suez Canal opened in 1869 and was nationalised by Egypt in 1956.
Bab-el-Mandeb separates Yemen from Djibouti and Eritrea and links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman.
Saudi East-West pipeline carries oil to Yanbu on the Red Sea.
Habshan-Fujairah pipeline in the UAE bypasses Hormuz.
Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline carries Iraqi oil to Turkey's Mediterranean coast.
IMEC was announced at the G20 Delhi summit in 2023.
statements: 1 — Correct: Sumed is a strategic bypass for Persian Gulf crude oil going to Europe and the Mediterranean. Facts: it is owned by the Arab Petroleum Pipelines Company, a joint venture of Egypt's EGPC, Saudi Aramco, Kuwait, the UAE and others. Capacity is about 2.5 million barrels per day. It was commissioned in 1977 and has two parallel 42-inch lines. It handles tankers too big for the Suez Canal, and it gains importance when Red Sea or Suez shipping is disrupted, as in the 2021 Ever Given blockage and the Houthi attacks of 2023-24.

2 — Correct: Sumed connects the Red Sea, via the Gulf of Suez at Ain Sukhna, with the Mediterranean at Sidi Kerir, west of Alexandria. Facts: the route is about 320 km long and runs parallel to but independent of the Suez Canal. Ain Sukhna has the storage and loading terminals, and Sidi Kerir is the Mediterranean terminal. The pipeline was conceived after the 1956 and 1967 Suez crises. It lets supertankers (VLCCs) offload, pipe their cargo across Egypt and reload, which saves transit costs and avoids the longer route around the Cape of Good Hope.
summary: The answer is (a). The Sumed (Suez-Mediterranean) pipeline runs from Ain Sukhna on the Red Sea (Gulf of Suez) to Sidi Kerir on the Mediterranean, and it is the reason Persian Gulf oil can reach Europe without passing through the Suez Canal. Statement-II gives the geographic fact that explains the strategic role described in Statement-I.
topic_notes:
Sumed (Suez-Mediterranean Pipeline) is an Egyptian-based pipeline system run by the Arab Petroleum Pipelines Company, established in 1974 with Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE and Qatar as shareholders. It runs about 320 km from Ain Sukhna on the Gulf of Suez to Sidi Kerir near Alexandria, and it began operating in 1977. It has two 42-inch parallel lines with a capacity of about 2.5 million barrels per day. It lets large tankers bypass the Suez Canal, which has draft and size limits for fully laden very large crude carriers.

Related chokepoints are important for UPSC. The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, and about a fifth of global oil passes through it. Bab-el-Mandeb links the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, between Yemen and Djibouti/Eritrea. The Suez Canal, opened in 1869 and nationalised by Nasser in 1956, links the Red Sea and the Mediterranean. The Cape of Good Hope is the alternative route around Africa.

Other bypass pipelines: Saudi Arabia's East-West (Petroline) pipeline runs to Yanbu on the Red Sea. The UAE's Habshan-Fujairah pipeline reaches the Gulf of Oman outside Hormuz. The Iraq-Turkey (Kirkuk-Ceyhan) pipeline reaches the Mediterranean.

Current relevance: the 2021 Ever Given grounding and the Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping since late 2023 have raised the importance of alternatives such as Sumed and have forced ships to reroute around the Cape. India's concerns include oil and freight costs and its trade with Europe, and links such as the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC, announced at the G20 in 2023) and the International North-South Transport Corridor.

question:
Consider the following statements : 92.
1. The Red Sea receives very little precipitation in any form.
2. No water enters the Red Sea from rivers. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Geography
detail: The Red Sea is a narrow, elongated inlet of the Indian Ocean between Africa (Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea, Djibouti) and Asia (Saudi Arabia, Yemen). It lies in the subtropical high-pressure desert belt, with annual rainfall of only a few centimetres, mostly under 100-200 mm. Evaporation is very high, over 2 m per year, which far exceeds precipitation and river input. This makes it one of the saltiest and warmest open seas, with salinity around 36-41 parts per thousand. Because no perennial river drains into it, the water deficit is made up by inflow of Indian Ocean water through the Bab-el-Mandeb strait from the Gulf of Aden. Only seasonal wadis (dry stream beds) carry water during rare flash floods, and these do not count as rivers. The Nile flows to the Mediterranean, not the Red Sea. The Red Sea connects to the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal (opened 1869). Elimination logic: statement 1 is clearly true, and statement 2 is true in the standard sense of 'no permanent river', so (a), (b) and (d) fail. UPSC accepts (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 2 is also correct, so 'statement 1 only' is incomplete.
(b) is wrong because statement 1 is correct too, and the sea does get very little rain.
(c) is right because the sea has very little rainfall and no perennial river inflow, so both statements hold.
(d) is wrong because both statements are correct.
keyfact: The Red Sea has almost no rain and no perennial river inflow, so evaporation makes it very salty and it is topped up via Bab-el-Mandeb.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only: The Red Sea's low rainfall is a well-known fact. It lies in the Saharan-Arabian desert belt, between about 30°N and 13°N. Rain is rare and irregular, and humidity is moderate to high near the coast. Because this statement is true, it is one of the two correct statements, but the answer must also include statement 2.

Option (b), statement 2 only: This would mean the 'no river' claim is true but the low-precipitation claim is false. That is not so. The Red Sea has no perennial rivers, only seasonal wadis such as Wadi Hamdh and Wadi Gasus. Lack of river flow is one reason for its high salinity. Because the sea is also low in precipitation, this option is incomplete.

Option (c), both 1 and 2: This is the official answer. The Red Sea (Erythraean Sea in ancient times) is a semi-enclosed inlet of the Indian Ocean. It is the world's northernmost tropical sea and has high temperature, high salinity, and high evaporation. Its water budget depends on exchange via Bab-el-Mandeb and on evaporation. It has some of the world's northernmost coral reefs.

Option (d), neither: This would mean the Red Sea has substantial rainfall and river inflow. The opposite is true, since the Red Sea is a classic example of a sea in an arid region. Other seas with heavy river input, such as the Black Sea and Baltic Sea, have lower salinity. This is why the Red Sea is far saltier than the average ocean's roughly 35 parts per thousand.
related: Red Sea is among the saltiest open seas, at about 36-41 ppt.
Bab-el-Mandeb connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
The Suez Canal opened in 1869 and links the Red Sea with the Mediterranean.
The Red Sea is a young rift ocean between the African and Arabian plates.
The Dead Sea has salinity of about 340 ppt and lies in the Jordan rift valley.
The Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba are the northern arms of the Red Sea.
The Red Sea has no perennial river inflow, only seasonal wadis.
Houthi attacks since late 2023 disrupted Red Sea shipping.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Red Sea lies in an arid zone with minimal rainfall, and evaporation greatly exceeds precipitation. Detail: The sea is about 2,250 km long and up to about 355 km wide. Its maximum depth is about 3,000 m, and the average is about 490 m. It is a young ocean basin formed by rifting of the Arabian and African plates, and it is part of the Great Rift system with a spreading axis. Annual rainfall is typically below 100-200 mm. Evaporation of 2 m or more per year makes it very saline. Coral reefs are extensive, and Ras Mohammed and the Egyptian coast are major diving sites.

2 — Correct: No perennial river empties into the Red Sea, and only occasional seasonal wadis carry flash-flood water. Detail: Water balance is maintained by inflow from the Gulf of Aden through the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, about 29 km wide at its narrowest and guarded by Perim Island. Surface water flows in and dense saline water flows out at depth. The northern end splits into the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba. The Suez Canal links it to the Mediterranean. Hot brine pools such as Atlantis II Deep hold metal-rich sediments. The Red Sea is a major global shipping route, and the Houthi attacks of 2023-24 disrupted traffic there.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. The Red Sea lies in a hot, hyper-arid belt with very low rainfall and very high evaporation, and no perennial river flows into it.
topic_notes: The Red Sea is a rift-formed marine basin between Africa and Arabia. It stretches roughly 2,250 km north to south, from the Sinai Peninsula and the Gulfs of Suez and Aqaba down to the Bab-el-Mandeb strait. It opens to the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea. Its surface water is among the warmest and saltiest of any sea, at about 36-41 ppt salinity and 21-30°C surface temperature. The climate is hot and arid, with rainfall of only a few centimetres. Evaporation of over 2 m a year exceeds the water supplied by rain and rivers, so the sea relies on inflow from the Gulf of Aden. There is surface inflow from the south and deep outflow of saline water. Coastal states include Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea, Djibouti, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Israel and Jordan. The Suez Canal (1869, Ferdinand de Lesseps) links it to the Mediterranean, shortening the Europe-Asia route and carrying roughly 12% of global trade. Strategic points include Bab-el-Mandeb, the Hanish Islands, Perim, and the Tiran Strait. Nearby bodies are the Persian Gulf, the Gulf of Aden, and the Gulf of Oman. Other UPSC angles are the Dead Sea (about 34% salinity, in the Jordan rift), the Black Sea (anoxic deep water), the Caspian Sea (largest lake), the Mediterranean (evaporation and inflow from the Atlantic), and the Baltic Sea (low salinity, many rivers). Also remember the Houthi crisis, Operation Prosperity Guardian, and the diversion of shipping around the Cape of Good Hope. India's concerns include trade and energy routes and its naval deployments in the Gulf of Aden against piracy.

question: According to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), which one of the following is the largest source of sulphur dioxide emissions ?
subject: Environment
detail: Sulphur dioxide is a colourless gas with a pungent smell, belonging to the group of sulphur oxides (SOx). The US EPA states that the largest source of SO2 in the atmosphere is the burning of fossil fuels by power plants and other industrial facilities. Coal contains sulphur as pyrite and organic sulphur, and combustion converts it to SO2. Smaller sources include industrial processes such as extraction of metal from ore (smelting of copper, lead, zinc), natural sources such as volcanoes, and mobile sources such as locomotives, ships and heavy equipment burning high-sulphur fuel. SO2 causes respiratory problems, forms acid rain with nitrogen oxides, and contributes to fine particulate (PM2.5) formation through secondary sulphate aerosols. It is a NAAQS criteria pollutant in the US and in India's NAAQS (CPCB, 2009; 24-hour standard 80 µg/m3 for residential areas). Elimination logic: options (a), (b) and (c) are real but secondary sources by volume, so the word 'largest' points to (d). Control tools include flue gas desulphurisation (FGD), low-sulphur coal and Bharat Stage VI fuel norms.
explanations: Wrong: locomotives burning fossil fuels, especially diesel, are a small, mobile source of SO2, far smaller than power generation, and fuel sulphur is now much reduced.
Wrong: ships burning high-sulphur bunker fuel are a significant source, especially near ports and coasts, but they are not the largest source overall according to the EPA.
Wrong: smelting and extraction of metals from ores does release SO2 from sulphide ores, but it is a smaller industrial source than power plants.
Correct: the EPA identifies fossil fuel combustion at power plants and other industrial facilities as the largest source of SO2 emissions.
keyfact: Per the US EPA, fossil-fuel burning in power plants is the largest source of SO2 emissions, so answer (d).
option_notes: Locomotives: diesel locomotives burn diesel, which formerly carried high sulphur. Indian Railways has moved heavily towards electrification, with a target of 100 percent broad-gauge electrification, reducing direct emissions. Non-road diesel engines are regulated by sulphur limits in fuel. Their SO2 share is small compared with stationary combustion, though they emit NOx and particulates.

Ships: marine bunker fuel historically contained up to 3.5 percent sulphur. The IMO's MARPOL Annex VI cap of 0.50 percent sulphur in fuel took effect on 1 January 2020 (IMO 2020), with a 0.10 percent limit inside Emission Control Areas. Scrubbers are an alternative. Shipping is a major regional source near coasts, but not the largest overall.

Extraction of metals from ores: smelting sulphide ores of copper, zinc, lead and nickel releases SO2 when sulphur is oxidised during roasting. Smelters often capture SO2 to produce sulphuric acid. Historic examples include the Sudbury smelters in Canada and Norilsk in Russia, a major hotspot. It is an important industrial source but smaller than power generation.

Power plants: coal-fired thermal plants burn coal containing sulphur, emitting SO2, NOx, PM and mercury. In India, the MoEFCC notified emission norms for thermal plants in December 2015, requiring FGD installation, with repeated deadline extensions. India is among the world's largest anthropogenic SO2 emitters, with coal power a dominant source.
related: SO2 plus NOx leads to acid rain; the pH of normal rain is about 5.6.
IMO 2020 limits marine fuel sulphur to 0.50 percent, from 3.5 percent.
India's thermal power plant emission norms were notified in December 2015, requiring FGD.
BS-VI fuel with 10 ppm sulphur was adopted nationwide from 1 April 2020.
NCAP was launched in 2019 and is aimed at reducing particulate pollution in non-attainment cities.
Flue gas desulphurisation using limestone yields gypsum as a by-product.
Stone cancer is damage to marble monuments caused by acid rain.
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was enacted in 1981.
summary: The answer is (d) Power plants using fossil fuels. According to the US EPA, the burning of fossil fuels, mainly coal and to a lesser extent oil, by power plants and other industrial facilities is the largest single source of sulphur dioxide (SO2) emissions, because fuels contain sulphur that oxidises to SO2 on combustion.
topic_notes: Sulphur dioxide (SO2) is a major air pollutant and a precursor of acid rain and secondary particulate matter. Sources: anthropogenic, mainly burning of coal and oil in power plants, industry and shipping, plus metal smelting, and natural, mainly volcanoes. Health effects include irritation of the eyes and respiratory tract, asthma aggravation and bronchitis. Environmental effects include acid deposition damaging forests, soils, lakes, buildings and monuments (Taj Mahal marble 'stone cancer'), and a cooling effect through sulphate aerosols. Control: flue gas desulphurisation (wet limestone scrubbers producing gypsum), use of low-sulphur coal, coal washing, fluidised bed combustion, cleaner fuels such as BS-VI (10 ppm sulphur) in India from April 2020, and the IMO 2020 sulphur cap. India: NAAQS by CPCB include SO2, NO2, PM10, PM2.5, ozone, lead, CO, ammonia, benzene, benzo(a)pyrene, arsenic and nickel. The National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) was launched in 2019, targeting 20-30 percent reduction in PM concentrations by 2024, later revised to 40 percent by 2025-26. The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, is the main law. SAFAR and the AQI, launched in 2014, report SO2 among its pollutants. Satellite data (NASA OMI) shows India has among the highest SO2 hotspots, such as Singrauli and Korba. Other angles: Gothenburg Protocol, the Montreal Protocol (ozone, not SO2), the US Acid Rain Program under the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, and the Kyoto Protocol (GHGs).

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement-I : There is instability and worsening security situation in the Sahel region.
Statement-II : There have been military takeovers/coups d’état in several countries of the Sahel region in the recent past. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements ?
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Sahel is the semi-arid belt south of the Sahara, running from Senegal and Mauritania in the west through Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, Nigeria's north and Chad to Sudan and Eritrea in the east. It faces jihadist insurgencies (JNIM, linked to al-Qaeda; Islamic State Sahel Province; Boko Haram and ISWAP around Lake Chad), ethnic violence, climate stress, poverty and weak state presence. Military juntas took power in Mali (Aug 2020, May 2021), Chad (April 2021), Guinea (Sept 2021, though Guinea is West African and not strictly Sahelian), Sudan (Oct 2021), Burkina Faso (Jan and Sept 2022) and Niger (July 2023). Soldiers justified coups by citing governments' failure to defeat insurgents. The coups then caused the withdrawal of French forces (Operation Barkhane ended 2022), the exit of the UN mission MINUSMA (2023), suspension from ECOWAS and the African Union, and growing Russian (Wagner/Africa Corps) presence, which further weakened counter-terror cooperation. The G5 Sahel collapsed after Mali's exit in 2022. In Sept 2023 Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), and in Jan 2024 they announced their exit from ECOWAS. Elimination logic: both statements are factually true, and the causal link makes (b) wrong, since (b) denies that Statement-II explains Statement-I. (c) and (d) fail because each calls a true statement false.
explanations: Correct: both statements are true, and the coups, which stemmed from and then worsened governance and security failures, explain the instability and deteriorating security.

Wrong: both statements are true, but this option says Statement-II does not explain Statement-I. The coups are a direct driver of the loss of foreign troops, sanctions and fragmented regional security.
Wrong: Statement-II is correct, since coups have occurred in Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad.
Wrong: Statement-I is correct, since the Sahel is currently the global epicentre of terrorism and instability.
keyfact: Coups in Mali, Chad, Burkina Faso and Niger since 2020 both stemmed from and deepened the Sahel's insecurity, so Statement-II explains Statement-I.
option_notes: Both statements correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I. This is the standard assertion-reason format for the case where the second statement gives the cause or reason for the first. Here the coups, driven by governance and security failures, further weakened counter-insurgency, ended Western military presence and fragmented regional cooperation. This is the official UPSC 2024 answer.

Both correct but with no explanatory link. This would apply if the two were true yet independent, for example if the instability stemmed only from climate change and the coups were unrelated. In the Sahel the coups are causally tied to the crisis, so this option is wrong.

Statement-I correct, Statement-II incorrect. This would apply if there had been no recent coups. In fact Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad have all had military takeovers since 2020, so the option fails.

Statement-I incorrect, Statement-II correct. This would apply if the Sahel were stable despite coups. In reality the region has seen escalating jihadist violence, mass displacement and the highest global terrorism toll, so Statement-I is true and the option fails.
related: The Sahel lies between the Sahara to the north and the Sudanian savanna to the south.
The G5 Sahel was formed in 2014 and Mali withdrew in 2022.
Operation Barkhane was the French counter-terror operation in the Sahel (2014-2022).
Niger's coup of July 2023 deposed President Mohamed Bazoum.
The Alliance of Sahel States (AES) was formed in Sept 2023 by Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger.
The Great Green Wall is an African Union initiative to combat desertification across the Sahel.
MINUSMA, the UN peacekeeping mission in Mali, ended in 2023.
ECOWAS is the West African regional bloc, headquartered in Abuja.
statements: Statement-I — Correct: Security in the Sahel has deteriorated sharply. The region has seen jihadist insurgency, banditry, ethnic massacres, displacement of millions, food insecurity and the highest global terrorism deaths (the Global Terrorism Index ranks the central Sahel as the world's terrorism epicentre). The crisis began after the 2012 Tuareg rebellion in northern Mali and the 2011 collapse of Libya, which flooded the region with arms. Key actors include JNIM, ISGS/ISSP and Boko Haram, and operations such as Serval (2013) and Barkhane (2014-22) failed to stabilise the region. Climate change, desertification and the shrinking of Lake Chad worsen the crisis.

Statement-II — Correct and explanatory: Since 2020 the Sahel has been called part of Africa's 'coup belt'. Mali (2020, 2021), Chad (2021), Burkina Faso (two coups in 2022), Niger (July 2023, ousting President Mohamed Bazoum) and Sudan (2021) all saw military takeovers. Juntas cited failure against insurgents, but military rule has led to the expulsion of Western troops, sanctions, a Russian security pivot, the break-up of the G5 Sahel and the AES exit from ECOWAS. These changes have weakened regional counter-terrorism and so deepened insecurity, which is why Statement-II explains Statement-I.
summary: The answer is (a). Both statements are correct, and the recent coups (Mali 2020 and 2021, Chad 2021, Guinea 2021, Burkina Faso 2022 twice, Niger 2023) are a major cause and reinforcer of the Sahel's instability and worsening security situation, so Statement-II explains Statement-I.
topic_notes: The Sahel is the transition belt between the Sahara and the Sudanian savanna, stretching about 5,400 km across Africa. The core states are Mauritania, Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad, with Senegal, Nigeria, Sudan and others often included. The crisis has several layers. The Tuareg rebellion and the Libya fallout of 2011-12 led to jihadist takeover of northern Mali in 2012. France intervened with Operation Serval (2013), followed by Barkhane (2014-22). The G5 Sahel (2014: Mauritania, Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, Chad) created a joint force, but Mali left in 2022 and the group effectively dissolved. MINUSMA (UN mission in Mali, 2013) was ended in 2023 at the junta's request. Coups: Mali (Aug 2020, May 2021, Col. Assimi Goita), Chad (2021, Mahamat Deby), Burkina Faso (Jan 2022 Damiba, Sept 2022 Ibrahim Traore), Niger (July 2023, Gen. Tchiani), plus Guinea (2021) and Gabon (2023) outside the Sahel. The AES (Alliance of Sahel States) was founded in Sept 2023 under the Liptako-Gourma Charter, and the three states announced exit from ECOWAS in Jan 2024. Other angles include Lake Chad Basin, the Multinational Joint Task Force against Boko Haram, the Great Green Wall initiative (African Union, 2007) to restore degraded land, the Sudan civil war (RSF vs army since April 2023), uranium in Niger (Orano, Arlit), gold in Mali and Burkina Faso, Russia's Wagner Group presence, the US drone base at Agadez, and India's interests, including Operation Raahat-type evacuations, trade and energy in Africa, and the India-Africa Forum Summit.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement-I : India does not import apples from the United States of America.
Statement-II : In India, the law prohibits the import of Genetically Modified food without the approval of the competent authority. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements ?
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I : ;
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does noé¢ explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
subject: Economy
detail: India is one of the largest importers of fresh apples from the USA among other sources, with Washington State apples a prominent import. In 2018 India raised import duty on US apples by 20 percentage points (to 70%) as retaliation against US withdrawal of GSP benefits and steel and aluminium tariffs. At the G20 summit in September 2023 India and the USA settled six pending WTO disputes, and India removed the retaliatory duties on US apples, almonds and walnuts, so apples continue to be imported. Hence Statement-I is false. On GM food, the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 (Section 22) deals with genetically modified foods, and the FSS (Import) Regulations 2017 require FSSAI approval for importing GM food. Separately, under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 and the 1989 Rules, the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) in the MoEFCC must approve the import, use and release of GM organisms. A 2021 FSSAI order made a non-GM/GM-free certificate mandatory for 24 listed crops. So Statement-II is true. Elimination: since Statement-I is false, options (a) and (b) fall away, as does (c), leaving (d).
explanations: Wrong: it needs Statement-I to be correct, but India does import US apples.
Wrong: Statement-I is incorrect, so both cannot be correct.
Wrong: Statement-I is incorrect, and Statement-II is correct, which is the reverse of what this option claims.
Right: Statement-I is false because India imports apples from the USA; Statement-II is true as GM food import needs approval from FSSAI and GEAC.
keyfact: India imports US apples (Statement-I false), while GM food import needs FSSAI/GEAC approval (Statement-II true), so the answer is (d).
option_notes: Option (a) would make both statements correct with a causal link. It is wrong here because the premise is false. For context, the 'explains' logic would apply if India banned US apples because they are GM, which is not true. The only commercially grown GM apples in the US are the Arctic apple (non-browning) varieties, which are a very small share of output. India's apple imports are mostly conventional fruit from the USA, Turkey, Italy, Chile and New Zealand.

Option (b) says both statements are correct but unrelated. It is wrong because India does import US apples. The USA exports Washington apples to India in large volumes. Apple import duty in India is 50% (basic customs duty), and import price conditions have been applied to some imports. The 2023 settlement removed the extra 20% retaliatory duty.

Option (c) says Statement-I is correct and Statement-II incorrect. It is the opposite of the facts. India's legal framework (FSS Act 2006, FSS Import Regulations 2017, EP Act 1986 and the GEAC regime) prohibits unapproved GM food imports, so Statement-II holds. Import of GM food needs FSSAI approval, plus GEAC clearance, so Statement-II cannot be called incorrect.

Option (d) is the official answer: Statement-I incorrect, Statement-II correct. India imports apples from the USA, and importing GM food without approval from the competent authority is illegal. Competent authorities are FSSAI for food safety clearance and GEAC under MoEFCC for GMOs. The Arctic apple is a GM variety, but the generic apple imports are not GM.
related: GEAC functions under MoEFCC and approves environmental release of GMOs.
Bt cotton, approved in 2002, is the only GM crop commercially cultivated in India.
Section 22 of the FSS Act 2006 regulates GM food.
India is a party to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000).
In 2022 India exempted SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome-edited plants from GM rules.
In 2023 India withdrew retaliatory duties on US apples, almonds and walnuts.
Bt brinjal was placed under a moratorium in 2010.
GM mustard DMH-11 was cleared by GEAC in October 2022 and is under Supreme Court review.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: India does import apples from the USA. Washington apples have been imported for years, though India's total apple imports also come from Turkey, Italy, Chile, New Zealand and others. In 2019 India imposed a 50% retaliatory duty on US apples, on top of the existing 50% customs duty. The 2018 tariff move was a response to US removal of India from GSP and imposition of steel and aluminium tariffs. In September 2023, during PM Modi's US visit, India withdrew these retaliatory duties on apples, chickpeas, lentils, walnuts and almonds, settling six WTO disputes. The duty on US apples is now back to the standard 50% rate, and imports continue.

2 — Correct: Indian law prohibits import of GM food without approval. The Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 and the FSS (Import) Regulations 2017 require FSSAI approval for GM food imports. GEAC under MoEFCC regulates GMOs under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 and Rules 1989. Bt cotton is the only GM crop approved for commercial cultivation, in 2002. GM mustard (DMH-11) was cleared for environmental release by GEAC in October 2022, but the matter is under Supreme Court scrutiny. FSSAI has also required non-GM certificates for 24 crops in imports since 2021.
summary: The answer is (d). Statement-I is incorrect because India does import apples from the USA (Washington apples are a well-known import, and India withdrew the retaliatory tariff on them in 2023). Statement-II is correct because the FSSAI Act and the Environment Protection Act framework require approval for importing GM food.
topic_notes: GM food regulation in India has two pillars. Environmental pillar: Environment (Protection) Act 1986 and the 1989 Rules for manufacture, use, import, export and storage of hazardous microorganisms and genetically engineered organisms. The apex body is the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) under MoEFCC, which approves environmental release and commercial use. The Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation (RCGM) under DBT oversees research. Food safety pillar: the FSS Act 2006 (Section 22) bars manufacture, sale, import or use of GM foods, ingredients and additives except as per regulations; FSSAI is the regulator. The FSS (Import) Regulations 2017 require approval for GM food imports. A 2021 FSSAI order requires a non-GM-origin certificate and GM-free test for 24 crops including apple, soybean, maize and rice. The only GM crop commercially cultivated is Bt cotton, approved in 2002. Bt brinjal was put under a moratorium in 2010 by the environment minister. GM mustard (DMH-11) was approved by GEAC in 2022 and is under litigation in the Supreme Court, which gave a split verdict in July 2024. India is a party to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000), under the Convention on Biological Diversity, which governs transboundary movement of living modified organisms. India–US trade: the 2018 US withdrawal of GSP for India led to Indian retaliatory duties on 28 US products, removed in 2023. Related angles include Golden Rice, the Arctic apple, herbicide-tolerant Bt cotton (HTBt) being unapproved, and gene-edited crops being exempted from GM rules in 2022 (SDN-1 and SDN-2).

question:
With reference to the Speaker of the 95. Lok Sabha, consider the following statements : While any resolution for the removal of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha is under consideration
1. He/She shall not preside.
2. He/She shall not have the right to speak. 83. He/She shall not be entitled to vote on the resolution in the first instance. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 94 provides for the Speaker to vacate office, resign, or be removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the House (an effective majority), after at least 14 days' notice. Article 96 protects the Speaker's position while such a resolution is pending. Article 96(1) says the Speaker shall not preside at any sitting while the resolution is under consideration, even if present. The Deputy Speaker, or another person under the Rules, presides instead. Article 96(2) says the Speaker has the right to speak in, and otherwise take part in, the proceedings of the House while the resolution is under consideration. He or she can vote on it only as a member in the first instance, and not in the case of an equality of votes. This differs from the normal rule in Article 100, under which the presiding Speaker has only a casting vote in a tie. Elimination logic: Statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 contradicts Article 96(2).
