Statement 3 is wrong because the Speaker does vote in the first instance. So only 1 survives, which gives (a).
explanations: Correct: statement 1 is right because Article 96(1) bars the Speaker from presiding. Statements 2 and 3 are wrong, so only 1 is correct.
Wrong: statement 2 is incorrect because the Speaker has the right to speak under Article 96(2), so 1 and 2 cannot both be correct.
Wrong: neither 2 nor 3 is correct. The Speaker can speak, and can vote in the first instance, though not in a tie.
Wrong: statements 2 and 3 are incorrect, so 1, 2 and 3 cannot all be correct.
keyfact: Article 96: while a removal resolution is pending, the Speaker cannot preside but can speak, and can vote only in the first instance, not in a tie.
option_notes: 1 only: this is the correct option. It reflects Article 96, under which the Speaker cannot preside during consideration of a removal resolution but keeps the right to speak and to vote in the first instance. It captures the idea that the Speaker must not sit in judgment on his or her own removal while still being allowed to defend himself or herself.

1 and 2 only: this is wrong because it wrongly takes away the Speaker's right to speak. Article 96(2) specifically gives that right, along with the right to take part in proceedings. The Speaker is also entitled to be present. Only the presiding role and the casting vote are denied.

2 and 3 only: this is wrong. It excludes statement 1, which is correct, and includes two incorrect statements. The Speaker can speak, can vote in the first instance as a member, and cannot vote only in a tie. It wrongly suggests the Speaker keeps the chair.

1, 2 and 3: this is wrong because it makes the Speaker totally disabled, as if he or she were not a member at all. In fact the Speaker retains membership rights, including speaking and voting in the first instance, while giving up the chair.
related: Article 94: the Speaker is removed by a resolution of all the then members of the Lok Sabha, with 14 days' notice.
Article 96: the Speaker or Deputy Speaker cannot preside while a resolution for his or her own removal is under consideration.
Article 100: the presiding Speaker has only a casting vote in a tie.
Article 93: the Lok Sabha chooses its Speaker and Deputy Speaker as soon as may be.
Article 108: the Speaker presides over a joint sitting of the two Houses.
Article 110: the Speaker certifies Money Bills and his or her decision is final.
Tenth Schedule: the Speaker decides disqualification on grounds of defection, subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992).
No Lok Sabha Speaker has ever been removed; motions against Mavalankar (1954), Hukam Singh (1966) and Balram Jakhar (1987) failed.
statements: 1 — Correct: Article 96(1) bars the Speaker from presiding at any sitting while a resolution for removal is under consideration, even if present in the House. The Deputy Speaker or another authorised member presides. This keeps the Speaker from judging his or her own cause. The same rule applies to the Deputy Speaker under Article 96 when his or her removal is being considered. Removal needs 14 days' notice and a majority of all the then members of the House (an effective majority). The Speaker also vacates office on ceasing to be an MP, except that after dissolution he or she continues until the new House meets.

2 — Incorrect: Article 96(2) gives the Speaker the right to speak in, and otherwise take part in, the proceedings of the House while the resolution is pending. The right to defend oneself is therefore preserved. This is an exception to the usual position of a presiding officer, who rarely speaks on matters before the House. The Speaker is also entitled to be present. The Lok Sabha Rules of Procedure on the removal motion give effect to these provisions. No Speaker has ever been removed. Resolutions were moved against G.V. Mavalankar (1954), Hukam Singh (1966) and Balram Jakhar (1987), and all failed.

3 — Incorrect: Under Article 96(2), the Speaker may vote on the resolution, or on any proceedings during it, but only in the first instance, as an ordinary member. He or she cannot vote in the case of an equality of votes, so no casting vote is available. This differs from Article 100(1), which gives the presiding Speaker a casting vote in a tie in normal business. The Speaker is therefore treated as an ordinary member on the resolution, and the Constitution denies the casting vote because the Speaker is not presiding and has a personal interest.
summary: The answer is (a) 1 only. Under Article 96, the Speaker cannot preside while a resolution for his or her removal is under consideration. The Speaker may still speak and take part in the proceedings, and may vote in the first instance as an ordinary member, though not in a tie.
topic_notes: The Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha from among its members, and the date of election is fixed by the President. The Speaker presides over the House, decides questions of order, and interprets the Rules of Procedure. He or she also decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill (Article 110), presides over joint sittings (Article 108), and decides disqualification petitions under the Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law). The Speaker is the final authority on such questions, subject to judicial review (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992). The Speaker's salary is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. Article 93 provides for the election of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker. Article 94 covers vacation, resignation and removal. Removal needs 14 days' notice and a majority of all the then members of the House. Article 95 covers the Deputy Speaker performing the duties of the Speaker when the office is vacant. Article 96 deals with the Speaker or Deputy Speaker not presiding while a removal resolution is under consideration. Article 97 deals with salaries. Article 100 gives the presiding Speaker a casting vote in a tie. Under Article 94, the Speaker continues in office after dissolution until immediately before the first meeting of the new House. Under Article 93, the House is to choose a Speaker as soon as possible. The Speaker's resignation is addressed to the Deputy Speaker. The first Speaker was G.V. Mavalankar (1952-56), and the first Deputy Speaker was M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar. The Speaker is traditionally expected to be impartial and to resign from party membership, which in the UK tradition is expected after election. The Speaker also presides over the Business Advisory Committee and Rules Committee, and appoints chairpersons of committees. In the Rajya Sabha, the Chairman (Vice-President) can be removed by a resolution under Article 67(b), and the Deputy Chairman under Article 90.

question:
With reference to the Indian Parliament, consider the following statements :
1. A bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on its dissolution.
2. A bill passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha.
3. A bill in regard to which the President of India notified his/her intention to summon the Houses to a joint sitting lapses on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: The lapse of bills follows from Article 107 and the Lok Sabha's life under Article 83(2). The rules are: (i) a bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on dissolution; (ii) a bill passed by the Lok Sabha but pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on dissolution; (iii) a bill originating in the Rajya Sabha and passed by it but pending in the Lok Sabha lapses; (iv) a bill pending in the Rajya Sabha that has not been passed by the Lok Sabha does not lapse, because the Rajya Sabha is a permanent House; (v) a bill passed by both Houses and awaiting the President's assent does not lapse; (vi) a bill returned by the President to the Houses for reconsideration does not lapse; (vii) Article 108(5) provides that a joint sitting may still be held after the Lok Sabha is dissolved, so a bill for which the President has notified a joint sitting does not lapse. Elimination logic: statement 1 is plainly correct, so (c) and (d) are out. Statement 3 is wrong because of Article 108(5), so (b) is the answer rather than (a) or (c).
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 is correct, but statement 2 is also correct, so '1 only' is incomplete.
Correct: statements 1 and 2 are correct, and statement 3 is wrong because of Article 108(5).
Wrong: this option accepts statement 3, which is incorrect, and rejects statement 1, which is correct.
Wrong: statement 3 is incorrect, and this option excludes the correct statements 1 and 2.
keyfact: Bills pending in the Lok Sabha, or passed by it and pending in the Rajya Sabha, lapse on dissolution; Rajya Sabha-only pending bills and bills with a notified joint sitting (Article 108(5)) do not.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would be right if only bills pending in the Lok Sabha lapsed. Under Article 107(5), a bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on dissolution. A bill passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha also lapses, so (a) leaves out a correct statement. Bills pending only in the Rajya Sabha, and not passed by the Lok Sabha, do not lapse. A bill awaiting the President's assent after passing both Houses also survives.

Option (b), '1 and 2', is the official answer. Bills pending in the Lok Sabha, and bills passed by the Lok Sabha but pending in the Rajya Sabha, both lapse when the Lok Sabha is dissolved. Bills that do not lapse include those pending only in the Rajya Sabha, those passed by both Houses and awaiting assent, those returned by the President, and those for which a joint sitting has been notified.

Option (c), '2 and 3', pairs a correct statement with an incorrect one. A bill passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha does lapse. A bill for which a joint sitting has been notified does not lapse, because Article 108(5) allows the joint sitting to proceed even after dissolution. The option also wrongly drops statement 1. Joint sittings are presided over by the Speaker, and the Deputy Speaker presides in the Speaker's absence.

Option (d), 'Only 3', rests on the false idea that a bill with a notified joint sitting lapses, and it denies the basic rules in statements 1 and 2. Article 108(5) preserves the joint sitting even after the Lok Sabha is dissolved. Joint sittings have taken place only three times, in 1961, 1978 and 2002. The 2002 sitting dealt with the Prevention of Terrorism Bill (POTA).
related: Article 107(5): a bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on its dissolution.
Article 108: joint sitting of Parliament for ordinary bills, presided over by the Speaker.
Article 108(5): a joint sitting may be held even after the Lok Sabha is dissolved.
Joint sittings so far: Dowry Prohibition Bill 1961, Banking Service Commission Repeal Bill 1978, POTA Bill 2002.
Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills cannot go to a joint sitting.
A bill pending only in the Rajya Sabha does not lapse on dissolution of the Lok Sabha.
Prorogation does not end pending bills, while dissolution of the Lok Sabha does lapse some of them.
Article 83(2): the Lok Sabha's term is five years, extendable one year at a time during a National Emergency.
statements: 1 — Correct: a bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses when the House is dissolved. Under Article 107(5), a bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on dissolution. This covers both government and private members' bills. Lapsed bills can be reintroduced in the new House, but they must go through the stages afresh. The Lok Sabha has a five-year term under Article 83(2), and the President can dissolve it earlier under Article 85(2)(b). The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House and is not subject to dissolution. Bills pending before the Lok Sabha are the most common casualties of dissolution, and lapsing is why many bills are rushed through in the final session.

2 — Correct: a bill passed by the Lok Sabha but pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses when the Lok Sabha is dissolved. Article 107(5) says a bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on dissolution. Practice and the Constitution's scheme extend this to bills passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha, because the Lok Sabha's passage is tied to that House's life. The Lok Sabha would have to pass such a bill afresh. This is different from a bill originating in the Rajya Sabha and still pending there, which does not lapse. Examples include the Citizenship Amendment Bill 2016, which lapsed in 2019, and the Triple Talaq Bill, which was reintroduced after lapsing.

3 — Incorrect: a bill for which the President has notified a joint sitting does not lapse on dissolution. Article 108(5) says the joint sitting may still be held and the bill passed even after the Lok Sabha is dissolved. Article 108 provides for a joint sitting when the Houses disagree on an ordinary bill, such as after a six-month delay or rejection. The Speaker presides, and the bill is decided by a majority of the total members present and voting. Money Bills and Constitution Amendment Bills are excluded from joint sittings. Joint sittings have happened only three times: the Dowry Prohibition Bill 1961, the Banking Service Commission Repeal Bill 1978, and the POTA Bill 2002.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 1 and 2 are correct, statement 3 is incorrect. A bill pending in the Lok Sabha, or passed by it and pending in the Rajya Sabha, lapses when the Lok Sabha is dissolved. A bill on which the President has notified a joint sitting does not lapse, as Article 108(5) expressly protects it.
topic_notes: Lapse of bills in Parliament is governed by Article 107 for pending bills and Article 108 for joint sittings. The key principle is that the Lok Sabha is a dissolvable House, while the Rajya Sabha is permanent, with one-third of its members retiring every two years. The Lok Sabha's term is five years under Article 83(2). It can be extended during a National Emergency, one year at a time, up to a maximum of six months after the Emergency ends. Dissolution can be by the President under Article 85(2)(b). Bills that lapse: any bill pending in the Lok Sabha, whether introduced there or passed by the Rajya Sabha and transmitted to it; and a bill passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha. Bills that do not lapse: bills pending only in the Rajya Sabha and not passed by the Lok Sabha; bills passed by both Houses and awaiting the President's assent; bills returned by the President for reconsideration and pending in the Houses; and bills for which the President has notified a joint sitting. A lapsed bill can be reintroduced, but it must go through all stages again. Joint sitting under Article 108 applies only to ordinary bills and financial bills that are not Money Bills. It does not apply to Money Bills or Constitution Amendment Bills. It is called by the President after one House rejects a bill or the Houses disagree, or after six months pass without the other House acting. The Speaker presides, and the decision is by a majority of members present and voting. Other related ideas include the prorogation of Houses, which does not affect pending bills. Ordinances under Article 123 must be laid before Parliament and lapse six weeks after it reassembles unless approved earlier.

question:
With reference to the Parliament of India, consider the following statements :
1. Prorogation of a House by the President of India does not require the advice of the Council of Ministers.
2. Prorogation of a House is generally done after the House is adjourned sine die but there is no bar to the President of India prorogating the House which is in session.
3. Dissolution of the Lok Sabha is done by the President of India who, save in exceptional circumstances, does so on the advice of the Council of Ministers. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Polity
detail: Under Article 85, the President summons the Houses, prorogues them and dissolves the Lok Sabha. Like most presidential powers, these are exercised on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister (Article 74, as amended by the 42nd and 44th Amendments, which makes the advice binding). Statement 1 is therefore wrong. Adjournment sine die is ordered by the Presiding Officer (Speaker or Chairman) and ends a sitting without fixing a date to reassemble. Prorogation, ordered by the President, ends a session. It usually comes shortly after adjournment sine die, but the Constitution does not bar the President from prorogating a House that is still sitting, so statement 2 is correct. Dissolution under Article 85(2)(b) applies only to the Lok Sabha, because the Rajya Sabha is a permanent House. The President dissolves it on the Council's advice, but may act on his own discretion in exceptional situations, for example when a Prime Minister who has lost majority advises dissolution, or when no stable government can be formed. Statement 3 is therefore correct. Elimination: since statement 1 is wrong, options (a) and (b) fall away. The option marked (d) is an OCR corruption of '3 only', which ignores the correct statement 2, so (c) remains.
explanations: Wrong: it includes only statement 1, which is incorrect because prorogation requires the Council's advice, and it omits the two correct statements.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is incorrect, and it omits statement 3, which is correct.

Correct: statement 2 is correct because prorogation usually follows adjournment sine die but a sitting House can also be prorogued, and statement 3 is correct because the President dissolves the Lok Sabha normally on the Council's advice.
Wrong: this option corresponds to statement 3 only, as the OCR garbled it, and it leaves out statement 2, which is also correct.
keyfact: Prorogation and dissolution are done by the President on the Council of Ministers' advice; prorogation ends a session, dissolution applies only to the Lok Sabha.
option_notes: Option (a), statement 1 only: this would hold that the President prorogues independently of the Council. It is wrong because Article 74 binds the President to ministerial advice in nearly all matters. Prorogation is the formal end of a session, notified by the President, and it follows the Council's recommendation. Discretionary presidential powers are very limited, such as appointing a Prime Minister when no party has a majority, or returning a bill once for reconsideration.

Option (b), statements 1 and 2: this pairs the incorrect statement 1 with the correct statement 2. Statement 2 reflects the practice that adjournment sine die by the Presiding Officer is followed by prorogation by the President. The power to prorogue under Article 85 can in principle be used even when the House is in session. Adjournment, prorogation and dissolution are the three ways of ending a sitting, session or House.

Option (c), statements 2 and 3: this is the official answer. Prorogation can follow adjournment sine die or be done in session, and the Lok Sabha is dissolved by the President, usually on ministerial advice. Dissolution ends the life of the Lok Sabha, so a general election follows, and bills pending in the Lok Sabha lapse. Prorogation ends only a session and does not end the House.

Option (d), '8 only' in the OCR, which stands for '3 only': it accepts the dissolution statement but wrongly rejects statement 2. Statement 2 is correct because the Constitution places no bar on prorogation during a session, so this option is incomplete. Dissolution applies only to the Lok Sabha and also covers State Legislative Assemblies under Article 174.
related: Article 85: President summons, prorogues and dissolves the Lok Sabha.
Article 83(2): the Lok Sabha's normal term is five years, extendable by one year at a time during an Emergency.
The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House and is not subject to dissolution.
Not more than six months may elapse between two sessions of Parliament (Article 85(1)).
Adjournment sine die is declared by the Presiding Officer, while prorogation is by the President.
Article 74: the Council of Ministers aids and advises the President, and the advice is binding.
Bills pending in the Lok Sabha lapse on its dissolution.
Joint sitting of Parliament under Article 108 is presided over by the Speaker.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The President prorogues on the advice of the Council of Ministers, so the advice is required. Prorogation ends a session and is notified by the President under Article 85(2)(a). It is different from adjournment, which ends only a sitting and is ordered by the Presiding Officer. After prorogation, pending motions and notices generally lapse, though bills pending in the Lok Sabha do not lapse merely because of prorogation. The Council of Ministers decides when to summon and prorogue, and the Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs recommends session dates. Article 74(1) makes the President bound by ministerial advice. The President may prorogue both Houses or one House separately. Under Article 85(1), no more than six months may pass between two sessions.

2 — Correct: Adjournment sine die is declared by the Presiding Officer at the end of the last sitting, and the President prorogues soon afterwards. The Constitution does not bar the President from proroguing a House while it is still in session, and this has been done in practice. Prorogation ends the session, whereas adjournment ends only a sitting. Types of adjournment include adjournment to a fixed time and adjournment sine die. Prorogation does not affect pending bills, but it lapses pending notices and motions, and the President may also summon the House before the next scheduled session. Ordinances can be promulgated under Article 123 only when Parliament is not in session, and the position of ordinances after prorogation is a recurring exam point.

3 — Correct: Under Article 85(2)(b) the President can dissolve the Lok Sabha, which has a five-year term under Article 83(2) from its first sitting. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House and cannot be dissolved. Dissolution is normally on the advice of the Council of Ministers. The President may use discretion in exceptional circumstances, such as when the Council has lost its majority or when a caretaker situation arises. On dissolution, pending bills in the Lok Sabha lapse, while bills pending in the Rajya Sabha but not passed by the Lok Sabha do not lapse. Dissolution is distinct from the term expiring by itself. During a Proclamation of Emergency the Lok Sabha's term can be extended by one year at a time (Article 83(2)).
summary: The answer is (c): statements 2 and 3 are correct, and statement 1 is incorrect. Prorogation is done by the President on the advice of the Council of Ministers, so it is not independent of that advice. It generally follows adjournment sine die, but the President can also prorogue a House that is still in session. The Lok Sabha is dissolved by the President, normally on the Council's advice.
topic_notes:
Sessions of Parliament are governed by Articles 85 and 87. The President summons each House so that no more than six months pass between its last sitting in one session and the first sitting in the next, so Parliament meets at least twice a year. In practice there are three sessions: Budget (Feb to May), Monsoon (July to Sept) and Winter (Nov to Dec). Summoning is done by the President on the Council's advice, and the Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs fixes the dates.

Terms to distinguish: a sitting is a single meeting of the House, and a session is the period from first summoning until prorogation. Adjournment suspends a sitting for hours, days or weeks and is ordered by the Presiding Officer, while adjournment sine die ends a sitting with no date fixed for reassembly. Prorogation is ordered by the President and ends a session. Dissolution applies only to the Lok Sabha and ends its life.

Effects: on dissolution, bills pending in the Lok Sabha lapse, but bills passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha also lapse, while bills pending in the Rajya Sabha but not passed by the Lok Sabha do not lapse. On prorogation, pending bills remain alive, but notices and motions typically lapse. Under Article 85(1) the President may summon a prorogued House again before its next session if needed.

The Lok Sabha's normal term is five years (Article 83(2)), extendable by one year at a time during a national Emergency. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House, with a third of its members retiring every two years. Article 74 makes the Council's advice binding after the 42nd and 44th Amendments, though the President can ask for reconsideration once. Other related topics include the joint sitting under Article 108, the quorum of one-tenth of the House, and the Speaker's role and powers.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement-I : The European Parliament approved The Net-Zero Industry Act recently.
Statement-II : The European Union intends to achieve carbon neutrality by 2040 and therefore aims to develop all of its own clean technology by that time. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements ?
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct
subject: Economy
detail: The Net-Zero Industry Act is a regulation proposed by the European Commission in March 2023 as part of the Green Deal Industrial Plan, alongside the Critical Raw Materials Act. The European Parliament approved it in April 2024, and the Council adopted it in May 2024. It aims to scale up EU manufacturing of clean technologies such as solar PV, onshore and offshore wind, batteries and storage, heat pumps, electrolysers, CCS and grid technologies. Its benchmark is that the EU should manufacture at least 40% of its annual deployment needs in these technologies by 2030. It also aims to capture about 15% of global production of these technologies by value. It does this by speeding up permitting, designating strategic projects, and introducing resilience and sustainability criteria in public procurement and auctions. Statement-II fails on two counts. The legally binding EU target under the European Climate Law (2021) is climate neutrality by 2050, with a 55% cut in emissions by 2030 versus 1990 levels. A 90% cut by 2040 has been proposed as an interim target, but 2040 is not the neutrality date. The EU also does not aim for full self-sufficiency in clean tech, only a 40% benchmark. So (c) is right, and (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated because each accepts Statement-II as correct.
explanations: Wrong. This option accepts Statement-II as correct, but the EU's neutrality target is 2050 and it is not aiming for full clean-tech self-reliance.
Wrong. This option also treats Statement-II as correct. Statement-II is factually wrong, so the question of whether it explains Statement-I does not arise.

Correct. The Parliament did approve the NZIA in April 2024. Statement-II is wrong on the 2040 date, which should be 2050, and on the claim of developing all clean technology domestically, since the benchmark is 40% by 2030.
Wrong. It reverses the truth: Statement-I is correct and Statement-II is incorrect.
keyfact: EU climate neutrality target = 2050 (not 2040); the NZIA, approved in April 2024, sets a 40% domestic manufacturing benchmark for clean tech by 2030.
option_notes: Option (a) is the 'both correct and II explains I' format. It would apply only if the 2040 neutrality and full-self-reliance claims were true, and they are not. The real driver of the NZIA is the EU's 2050 neutrality goal, together with competitiveness concerns, energy security and the need to counter the US Inflation Reduction Act (2022) and Chinese dominance of clean-tech supply chains. The EU Green Deal (2019) is the umbrella policy, and the European Climate Law (2021) makes the 2050 target legally binding.

Option (b) is the 'both correct but II does not explain I' format. UPSC uses it where both statements are factually true but unrelated causally. Here Statement-II is factually incorrect, so this option fails. The NZIA itself is a regulation directly applicable in all member states. It identifies eight core net-zero technologies, and a wider list of technologies is also covered under 'strategic' status. It has a 2030 benchmark and a streamlined permit regime.

Option (c) is the official answer. Statement-I is correct: the Parliament approved the NZIA in April 2024, with the Council following in May 2024. Statement-II is incorrect because the EU target is climate neutrality by 2050, and the Act sets a 40% domestic manufacturing benchmark by 2030 rather than complete self-sufficiency. The EU has also proposed a 90% net emissions cut by 2040 as an interim milestone. The Act is complemented by the Critical Raw Materials Act of 2024.

Option (d) says Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct, which is the reverse of the facts. The Parliament's April 2024 vote on the NZIA is well documented. The 2040 neutrality date in Statement-II is wrong because the EU's date is 2050. Note that the 2040 figure appears in the Commission's proposed interim 90% emissions reduction target, which is probably the source of the confusion in the statement.
related: The EU's legally binding climate neutrality target is 2050 under the European Climate Law, 2021.
The NZIA sets a 40% benchmark of domestic manufacturing for strategic net-zero technologies by 2030.
The NZIA was proposed in March 2023, approved by the Parliament in April 2024 and adopted by the Council in May 2024.
The Critical Raw Materials Act sets 2030 targets of 10% extraction, 40% processing, 25% recycling, and at most 65% dependence on one third country.
CBAM, the EU carbon border tax, began its transitional phase on 1 October 2023.
Fit for 55 aims at a 55% net emissions cut by 2030 versus 1990 levels.
India's net-zero target is 2070, announced at COP26 in Glasgow in 2021.
The US Inflation Reduction Act (2022) was a key trigger for the EU's Green Deal Industrial Plan.
statements: 1 — Correct: The European Parliament approved the Net-Zero Industry Act in April 2024, and the Council adopted it in May 2024. The Act was proposed by the Commission in March 2023 under the Green Deal Industrial Plan. It sets a benchmark of 40% domestic manufacturing capacity for strategic net-zero technologies by 2030, covering solar, wind, batteries, heat pumps, electrolysers, CCUS and grid technologies. It also seeks about 15% of global production of these technologies. It streamlines permitting, with shorter timelines for strategic projects, and adds non-price criteria in public procurement and auctions. It is a response to the US Inflation Reduction Act and to dependence on Chinese supply chains. It works together with the Critical Raw Materials Act, which sets 2030 targets for extraction, processing and recycling.

2 — Incorrect: The EU's legally binding target under the European Climate Law (2021) is climate neutrality by 2050, not 2040. The interim target is a net 55% emissions cut by 2030 (Fit for 55), and the Commission has recommended a 90% cut by 2040 as an intermediate step. The EU does not aim to develop all of its clean technology itself. The NZIA only sets a 40% benchmark of domestic manufacturing for deployment needs by 2030, and it accepts imports and trade partners. The European Green Deal, launched in 2019 under Ursula von der Leyen, is the overarching framework for these goals.
summary: The answer is (c). Statement-I is correct: the European Parliament approved the Net-Zero Industry Act (NZIA) in April 2024. Statement-II is incorrect: the EU targets climate neutrality by 2050, not 2040, and it does not aim to develop all of its own clean technology.
topic_notes: The Net-Zero Industry Act (NZIA) is the EU's main industrial law for the green transition. The Commission proposed it on 16 March 2023 as part of the Green Deal Industrial Plan. The Parliament approved it in April 2024 and the Council adopted it in May 2024. Its main benchmark is that EU manufacturing capacity for strategic net-zero technologies should meet at least 40% of annual EU deployment needs by 2030. It also aims for the EU to reach about 15% of global production of these technologies. The covered technologies include solar PV and thermal, onshore and offshore wind, batteries and storage, heat pumps and geothermal, electrolysers and fuel cells, sustainable biogas and biomethane, carbon capture and storage, and grid technologies. Key tools include faster permitting (shorter timelines for strategic projects), net-zero strategic projects, regulatory sandboxes, and sustainability and resilience criteria in public procurement and auctions. It also provides for skills academies. Related policies: the European Green Deal (December 2019) aims at climate neutrality by 2050. The European Climate Law (2021) makes the 2050 target and the 55% cut by 2030 legally binding. The Fit for 55 package implements these, and the Commission has recommended a 90% cut by 2040. The Critical Raw Materials Act (2024) sets 2030 benchmarks of 10% extraction, 40% processing, 25% recycling, and no more than 65% dependence on a single third country. The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) began its transitional phase in October 2023 and covers cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen. The EU Emissions Trading System is the other major tool. The US Inflation Reduction Act (2022) and China's clean-tech dominance are the competitive background to the NZIA. Possible next questions concern the EU's institutions (Commission, Council, Parliament), the Paris Agreement and NDCs, COP28 outcomes, and India's own net-zero target of 2070.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement-I : Recently, Venezuela has achieved a rapid recovery from its economic crisis and succeeded in preventing its people from fleeing/emigrating to other countries.
Statement-II : Venezuela has the world’s largest oil reserves. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements ?
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct 100
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Venezuela's crisis began around 2013-14 after oil prices crashed. The economy was heavily dependent on oil, which gave it about 95% of export earnings. Mismanagement, price controls, expropriations, falling output at PDVSA, corruption and US sanctions (tightened from 2017 and 2019) deepened the collapse. GDP shrank by roughly three-quarters between 2013 and 2021 or so, and hyperinflation ran into the millions of percent. The result was one of the largest displacement crises in the world. The UNHCR and IOM Regional Platform count over 7.7 million Venezuelan refugees and migrants, mostly in Colombia, Peru, Brazil, Chile and Ecuador. Some stabilisation came after 2021 through dollarisation and a partial easing of controls, but the recovery is fragile, inflation stays high and emigration continues. So the claim of a rapid recovery that stopped emigration is false. Venezuela's proven reserves are about 300 billion barrels, mostly heavy crude in the Orinoco Belt, which exceeds Saudi Arabia's, so Statement-II is correct. Elimination: once Statement-I is seen to be false, options (a), (b) and (c) fall away and only (d) remains. The lesson is that large reserves do not guarantee prosperity, an idea known as the resource curse or Dutch disease.
explanations: Wrong. Statement-I is false, because Venezuela has neither recovered rapidly nor stopped emigration, so Statement-II cannot be explaining it.
Wrong. This option calls Statement-I correct, but it is not. Millions have continued to flee and the recovery is partial and fragile.
Wrong. It reverses the truth of the two statements. Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct.
Correct. Statement-I is incorrect because of the mass emigration and weak recovery. Statement-II is correct because Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves.
keyfact: Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves but suffered economic collapse and over 7 million emigrants, so it is a resource-curse example.
option_notes: Option (a) would require both statements to be true with a causal link. Such an option shows a typical UPSC assertion-reason pattern. Here the link fails because Statement-I is false. Venezuela's oil wealth did not produce recovery, since a dependence on oil, mismanagement, a fall in PDVSA output and sanctions led to the collapse. This is the resource curse in practice.

Option (b) says both statements are true but unrelated. It fails because Statement-I is false. The Venezuelan crisis is the standard example of a petro-state collapse. Inflation peaked at over 60,000% in 2018 by some estimates, and the bolívar was redenominated several times. The 2018-19 period saw the largest migration outflows.

Option (c) says Statement-I is correct and Statement-II incorrect. This is the opposite of the truth. Statement-II is factually right, since OPEC data and the US EIA put Venezuela first in proven reserves, at about 17-20% of the global total. Venezuelan heavy crude needs upgrading, which limits the benefit of this.

Option (d), the correct answer, says Statement-I is incorrect and Statement-II is correct. It matches the facts. Venezuela is a Bolivarian republic led by Maduro (since 2013, after Hugo Chávez, who ruled 1999-2013). It is a paradox that the largest reserves coexist with an economic and humanitarian crisis, along with sanctions, shortages and mass migration.
related: Venezuela has the world's largest proven crude oil reserves, about 300 billion barrels.
The Orinoco Belt is the main heavy crude region of Venezuela.
Venezuela was a founding member of OPEC in 1960 at Baghdad.
PDVSA is Venezuela's state oil company.
More than 7 million Venezuelans have left the country since about 2014.
Colombia hosts the largest number of Venezuelan migrants.
Nicolás Maduro succeeded Hugo Chávez as president in 2013.
ONGC Videsh has a stake in Venezuela's San Cristóbal oil project.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Venezuela has not recovered rapidly, and emigration has not been stopped. Its output collapsed from 2013, inflation reached hyperinflation levels, and more than 7 million people have left, the largest displacement in Latin American history. Partial stabilisation after 2021 came through informal dollarisation and relaxed controls, but poverty, weak public services, sanctions and political disputes persist. Nicolás Maduro, who has been president since 2013, contested the 2024 election result, and that prompted further departures. Colombia hosts the most migrants, about 2.8 million, and it granted them a Temporary Protection Status of 10 years. Peru, Brazil, Ecuador and Chile also host large numbers.

2 — Correct: Venezuela has the world's largest proven crude oil reserves, about 300 billion barrels, ahead of Saudi Arabia, Iran and Canada. Most of it is extra-heavy crude in the Orinoco Belt, which is costly to extract and refine and needs diluents. Venezuela was a founding member of OPEC in 1960 (Baghdad Conference), together with Iran, Iraq, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. Oil was nationalised in 1976 and PDVSA was created. Production fell from about 3 million barrels a day in the late 1990s to under 1 million barrels a day in recent years, so large reserves have not meant high output.
summary: The answer is (d). Statement-I is incorrect because Venezuela has not recovered rapidly from its crisis and more than 7 million people have fled the country. Statement-II is correct because Venezuela holds the world's largest proven crude oil reserves.
topic_notes: Venezuela is in northern South America, with its capital at Caracas. It borders Colombia, Brazil and Guyana, and has a Caribbean coastline. Hugo Chávez started the Bolivarian Revolution in 1999, with social programmes (misiones) funded by oil revenue. After he died in 2013, Nicolás Maduro took over. The oil price fall of 2014, falling production, price controls, forex controls, expropriations and corruption led to shortages of food and medicine and hyperinflation. US sanctions on PDVSA (2019) and on the government cut off oil exports to the US. In 2019, Juan Guaidó, the National Assembly leader, declared himself interim president, and many countries recognised him. The Maduro government remained in control. The 2024 presidential election was disputed and the opposition and many countries rejected the declared Maduro victory. Over 7 million citizens have left, which makes this one of the world's largest external displacement crises, comparable to Syria. The Orinoco Belt holds the heavy oil. Venezuela is a founding OPEC member. Other angles for UPSC: the resource curse and Dutch disease, OPEC and OPEC+ membership (Venezuela is in OPEC), other oil-rich countries with reserves in order (Saudi Arabia, Iran, Canada, Iraq, UAE), India's relations with Venezuela (ONGC Videsh has a stake in the San Cristóbal project and Reliance bought Venezuelan crude), the Lima Group, Mercosur (Venezuela suspended), and sanctions as a foreign policy tool. Also revise countries with economic crises, such as Sri Lanka in 2022, Lebanon, Argentina and Zimbabwe.

question:
With reference to the Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme, consider the following statements : a To implement the scheme, the Central Government provides 100% funding.
2. Under the Scheme, Cadastral Maps are digitised.
3. An initiative has been undertaken to transliterate the Records of Rights from local language to any of the languages recognized by the Constitution of India. Which of the statements given above are correct ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme (DILRMP) was launched on 21 August 2008 by merging two earlier schemes: the Computerisation of Land Records (CLR) and the Strengthening of Revenue Administration and Updating of Land Records (SRA&ULR). It is run by the Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development. It was renamed DILRMP in 2016 and converted to a Central Sector Scheme with 100% central funding from 1 April 2016. Before that it was a centrally sponsored scheme with cost sharing. The programme has been extended to 2025-26. Its main components are computerisation of the Record of Rights (RoR), digitisation and computerisation of cadastral maps, survey and re-survey, computerisation of registration and integration of the registration and land record systems, and modern record rooms at tehsil level. Other initiatives include a Unique Land Parcel Identification Number (ULPIN, 'Bhu-Aadhaar'), a 14-digit alphanumeric ID. The National Generic Document Registration System (NGDRS) is also part of the programme. Transliteration of RoR into the Eighth Schedule languages is under way through Bhashini-supported tools. Elimination logic: statements 1, 2 and 3 are all accurate, so any option leaving out one of them is wrong. Option (c) 'and 8' is an OCR error for 'and 3'.
explanations: Wrong: statements 1 and 2 are correct, but this option leaves out statement 3, which is also correct.
Wrong: statements 2 and 3 are correct, but this option leaves out statement 1, which is also correct because funding is 100% central.
Wrong: this option is garbled by OCR ('1 and 8 only') and in any case leaves out statement 2, which is correct.
Correct: all three statements are accurate. The scheme is 100% centrally funded, it digitises cadastral maps, and it has an RoR transliteration initiative covering the Eighth Schedule languages.
keyfact: DILRMP (2008; Central Sector Scheme with 100% Union funding since 2016) digitises RoR and cadastral maps, transliterates RoR into Eighth Schedule languages, and introduces ULPIN.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 and 2 only', pairs the funding statement with cadastral map digitisation. Both are true, but it omits transliteration. Cadastral maps are the spatial record of land parcels. They are digitised under DILRMP and made available through Bhu-Naksha. The 100% funding pattern has applied since 2016, when DILRMP became a Central Sector Scheme. Its predecessors CLR and SRA&ULR were merged in 2008 and were centrally sponsored, with cost sharing.

Option (b), '2 and 3 only', pairs map digitisation with RoR transliteration. Both are true, but it omits the 100% central funding. Transliteration into Eighth Schedule languages (22 listed) is supported by language technology such as Bhashini. The Record of Rights (RoR) is the textual document that shows ownership, cultivation and other details of a land holding, and it is often called Khatauni, Jamabandi, Pahani or 7/12 extract depending on the state.

Option (c), '1 and 8 only', is an OCR corruption of '1 and 3 only', and there is no statement 8. Read as '1 and 3', it would combine the 100% central funding with RoR transliteration and leave out cadastral map digitisation. DILRMP is run by the Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development, and has been extended to 2025-26, with ULPIN and NGDRS as major components.

Option (d), '1, 2 and 3', is the official answer. It reflects DILRMP as a Central Sector Scheme with 100% Union funding, digitised cadastral maps, and the transliteration of RoR into scheduled languages. DILRMP aims to move from presumptive to conclusive land titling. It was launched on 21 August 2008 and has been extended to 2025-26. Its goals include a single integrated land information system, ULPIN, and linkage of registration with land records.
related: DILRMP launched on 21 August 2008 by merging CLR and SRA&ULR.
Since 1 April 2016, DILRMP has been a Central Sector Scheme (100% central funding).
DILRMP is under the Department of Land Resources, Ministry of Rural Development.
ULPIN (Bhu-Aadhaar) is a 14-digit alphanumeric ID for each land parcel.
NGDRS is the National Generic Document Registration System for property registration.
SVAMITVA scheme (2020, Ministry of Panchayati Raj) uses drones to map rural abadi land.
The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution lists 22 languages.
India follows presumptive titling; DILRMP aims at conclusive titling.
statements: 1 — Correct: DILRMP has been a Central Sector Scheme with 100% central funding since 1 April 2016. Earlier it was centrally sponsored, with the states sharing costs. Facts: The programme began on 21 August 2008 by merging CLR and SRA&ULR. The Department of Land Resources (Ministry of Rural Development) administers it. It was renamed Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme in 2016 to align with Digital India. It has been extended to 2025-26. Under a central sector scheme, the Centre bears the whole cost, with states implementing it. Land is a State subject (Entry 18, List II), so states carry out the work of record-keeping.

2 — Correct: Digitisation of cadastral maps is a core DILRMP component. Facts: Cadastral maps show the boundaries of land parcels, such as village maps and field plot maps, and they are the spatial record, while the RoR is the textual record. Under DILRMP these maps are digitised, and the digital maps are linked with the textual RoR. Other components are survey and re-survey with modern technology (ETS, GPS, drones, as in SVAMITVA), computerised registration, and the ULPIN or Bhu-Aadhaar, a 14-digit ID for each parcel. The goal is conclusive titling in place of the present presumptive titling. Bhu-Naksha is the portal for maps.

3 — Correct: An initiative exists to transliterate RoR from the local language into any of the 22 Eighth Schedule languages. Facts: The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution lists 22 languages. Transliteration helps people who do not know the local language, and it supports citizens and investors who move between states. The work uses AI and language tools, with Bhashini, the National Language Translation Mission, supporting it. Other DILRMP features include linking RoR with courts through the Land Records–Court case integration, linking Aadhaar to land records, and a National Generic Document Registration System (NGDRS) for registration.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. DILRMP is a Central Sector Scheme funded 100% by the Centre, it digitises cadastral (village) maps, and it includes transliteration of Records of Rights (RoR) from the local language into any of the Eighth Schedule languages.
topic_notes: DILRMP was launched in 2008 by merging CLR and SRA&ULR. The Department of Land Resources under the Ministry of Rural Development administers it. Since 1 April 2016 it has been a Central Sector Scheme with 100% central funding, and it has been extended to 2025-26. Land and land records are State subjects (Entry 18 of List II, Seventh Schedule, and Entry 45 for land revenue), so states implement the work. Main components: computerisation of the Record of Rights (RoR); digitisation of cadastral maps and their linkage with RoR; survey and re-survey using ETS, GPS, drones and aerial imagery; computerisation of registration through NGDRS, which is also called the 'One Nation One Registration Software'; modern record rooms at tehsil level; integration of land records with court data, with the Registrar's office and with Aadhaar seeding; and ULPIN (Bhu-Aadhaar), a 14-digit ID for each parcel. Transliteration of RoR into the 22 Eighth Schedule languages uses AI tools. The long-term goal is conclusive titling, with the state guaranteeing ownership, and the present system is presumptive titling, in which registration only records a transaction and does not guarantee the title. Related schemes: SVAMITVA (Panchayati Raj, drone mapping of abadi areas, launched 2020); Bhu-Naksha; the Bhoomi project of Karnataka (an early model); and the Torrens system, which is a title registration model. The Land Titling Bill and the model Land Titling Act have been proposed by NITI Aayog. Future questions may ask about the ministry, the funding pattern, ULPIN, SVAMITVA, or the difference between presumptive and conclusive titling.

question: With reference to the ‘Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan’, consider the following statements : 3 This scheme guarantees a minimum package of antenatal care services to women in their second and third trimesters of pregnancy and six months post-delivery health care service in any government health facility. Under this scheme, private sector health care providers of certain specialities can volunteer to provide services at nearby government health facilities. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA) was launched by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare in 2016. Its aim is to provide assured, comprehensive and quality antenatal care, free of cost, to all pregnant women on the 9th of every month. It is delivered at designated government health facilities such as CHCs, PHCs, district hospitals and urban health facilities. The minimum package covers antenatal check-ups, examination, investigations and counselling, and it targets the second and third trimesters. Obstetricians, gynaecologists and physicians examine women in these trimesters. High-risk pregnancies are identified and tracked, and the programme also uses colour-coded stickers for risk categories. A key feature is the voluntary participation of private-sector specialists, who can offer their services at government facilities on PMSMA day. The programme includes a drive to engage the private sector through the Indian Medical Association (IMA) and FOGSI. Statement 1 is wrong because the scheme does not guarantee six months of post-delivery care; its focus is antenatal care. Statement 2 is correct, so (b) is the answer. By elimination, (a), (c) and (d) all fail on one of these two points.
explanations: (a) is wrong because statement 1 is incorrect: PMSMA covers antenatal care only, with no six-month post-delivery guarantee, and statement 2 is correct.
(b) is right because only statement 2 is correct: private specialists can volunteer at government facilities under PMSMA.
(c) is wrong because statement 1 is not correct, so both statements cannot be right.
(d) is wrong because statement 2 is correct, so it is not true that neither statement is correct.
keyfact: PMSMA (2016) gives free antenatal care to women in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters on the 9th of every month, and private specialists can volunteer at government facilities.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 only: it would be correct only if PMSMA guaranteed six months of post-delivery care. In fact PMSMA is an antenatal programme focused on the 2nd and 3rd trimesters, with free check-ups on the 9th of every month. Postnatal care falls under other schemes: JSSK gives free delivery and care for mother and sick newborn up to 1 year, and ASHAs make home visits for postnatal care (HBNC and HBYC). Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) promotes institutional delivery through cash incentives. So option (a) is wrong.

Option (b), 2 only: this is the correct answer. PMSMA, launched in 2016 by the Union Health Ministry, offers a fixed package of antenatal care to women in their 2nd and 3rd trimesters on the 9th of every month at government facilities. It invites private-sector specialists to volunteer, with support from IMA and FOGSI. High-risk pregnancies are identified and followed up, using colour-coded stickers, and the scheme aims to cut maternal and neonatal mortality.

Option (c), both 1 and 2: this would hold only if both statements were correct. Statement 2 is accurate, because private specialists can volunteer at government facilities. Statement 1 is inaccurate, because PMSMA does not guarantee six months of postnatal care. Postnatal services come from separate programmes such as JSSK, HBNC and the Postpartum Programme. Options that combine one wrong statement with a right one are common UPSC traps, so check each statement separately.

Option (d), neither 1 nor 2: this would mean both statements are false. That is not the case, because statement 2 correctly describes the voluntary involvement of private practitioners under PMSMA. The scheme actively seeks volunteer obstetricians, gynaecologists, radiologists and physicians for the 9th-of-the-month clinics at government facilities, in partnership with IMA and FOGSI. The Health Ministry also encourages recognition and publicity for volunteers, so option (d) is wrong.
related: PMSMA was launched in 2016 and gives free antenatal care on the 9th of every month.
PMSMA targets women in their 2nd and 3rd trimesters of pregnancy.
Private-sector specialists can volunteer under PMSMA with support from IMA and FOGSI.
JSSK (2011) gives free delivery, drugs and diagnostics to pregnant women and sick newborns.
PMMVY (2017) gives Rs 5,000 in instalments for the first living child.
JSY (2005) is a conditional cash transfer scheme to promote institutional delivery.
LaQshya focuses on improving quality of care in labour rooms and maternity operation theatres.
PMSMA uses colour-coded stickers to flag high-risk pregnancies.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: PMSMA guarantees antenatal care in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters, but it does not guarantee six months of post-delivery care. PMSMA was launched in 2016 by the Union Health Ministry under the National Health Mission. Its assured package covers check-ups, laboratory tests such as haemoglobin, urine and blood group, ultrasound where possible, and counselling on nutrition and birth preparedness. Services are given on the 9th of every month, free of cost, at government facilities. Its goal is to reduce maternal and infant mortality by detecting and following up high-risk pregnancies. Postnatal care is handled by other programmes, such as JSSK and home-based newborn and postnatal visits by ASHAs, not by PMSMA.

2 — Correct: PMSMA invites private-sector specialists (obstetricians, gynaecologists, physicians, radiologists) to volunteer their services at government facilities on the 9th of each month. The aim is to widen the pool of specialists available at public facilities. The scheme works through partnerships with the Indian Medical Association (IMA) and the Federation of Obstetric and Gynaecological Societies of India (FOGSI). A volunteer-based approach (the 'Adopt a Facility' idea) lets women in remote areas get specialist care. PMSMA also includes the high-risk pregnancy (HRP) tracking through colour-coded stickers: green for low-risk, red for high-risk pregnancies. Extended PMSMA (ePMSMA) was later introduced to ensure quality care for high-risk pregnancies.
summary: The answer is (b): only statement 2 is correct. PMSMA gives a fixed package of antenatal care to pregnant women in their second and third trimesters, not six months of post-delivery care, and it does let private-sector specialists volunteer at government facilities.
topic_notes: PMSMA (Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan) was launched in 2016 by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, under the National Health Mission. It guarantees a fixed package of antenatal care, free of cost, to pregnant women in their second and third trimesters. Services are provided on the 9th of every month at government facilities, with check-ups by obstetricians, gynaecologists and physicians. Private-sector doctors can volunteer, with support from IMA and FOGSI. Key features: identification and tracking of high-risk pregnancies (HRP), colour-coded stickers (green for low risk, red for high risk), and counselling on nutrition, danger signs and birth preparedness. The extended version, ePMSMA, gives high-risk pregnancies additional follow-up and care. Related maternal and child health programmes: Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY, 2005), a conditional cash transfer for institutional delivery; Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK, 2011), which entitles pregnant women and sick newborns to free delivery, drugs, diagnostics, diet and transport; Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY, 2017), which gives Rs 5,000 for the first living child in instalments, under the Ministry of Women and Child Development; LaQshya, for quality of care in labour rooms and maternity operation theatres; MAA (Mothers' Absolute Affection), for breastfeeding promotion; Mission Indradhanush, for immunisation; and POSHAN Abhiyaan, for nutrition. Indicators to remember: maternal mortality ratio (MMR), infant mortality rate (IMR) and neonatal mortality rate. UPSC often tests the distinction between antenatal, intranatal and postnatal schemes, and between the ministries that run them.

question: With reference to the Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maan-dhan (PM-SYM) Yojana, consider the following statements : The entry age group for enrolment in tL: the scheme is 21 to 40 years. Age specific contribution shall be made by the beneficiary. Each subscriber under the scheme shall receive a minimum pension of = 3, 000 per month after attaining the age of 60 years. Family pension is applicable to the spouse and unmarried daughters. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: PM-SYM was launched in 2019 (operational from 15 March 2019) by the Ministry of Labour and Employment as a voluntary, contributory pension scheme for unorganised sector workers. Eligibility: entry age 18-40 years, monthly income of ₹15,000 or less, and not covered by NPS, ESIC or EPFO and not an income-tax payer. The subscriber makes an age-specific monthly contribution, from about ₹55 at age 18 to ₹200 at age 40, and the Central Government contributes an equal matching amount. The subscriber gets an assured minimum pension of ₹3,000 per month after turning 60. If the subscriber dies, the spouse is entitled to 50% of the pension as family pension. Family pension applies only to the spouse, not to children or daughters. The scheme is run by the Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC) as pension fund manager, with enrolment through Common Service Centres (CSCs). Elimination logic: statement 1 fails on the age band (18-40), which removes options (a) and (d). Statement 4 fails because family pension covers the spouse only, which also removes (a) and (d). Statement 2 is correct, which removes (c) because statement 3 is also correct. That leaves (b).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statements 1 and 4, which are incorrect. The entry age is 18-40, and family pension covers only the spouse.
Right: statement 2 (age-specific contribution) and statement 3 (₹3,000 minimum pension after 60) are correct, and statements 1 and 4 are wrong.
Wrong: statement 3 is also correct, so 'only 2' is incomplete.
Wrong: it includes statements 1 and 4, which are incorrect, and omits the correct statement 3.
keyfact: PM-SYM: age 18-40, income up to ₹15,000, age-linked contribution matched by the Centre, ₹3,000 pension after 60, 50% family pension to spouse only.
option_notes: Statements 1, 3 and 4: this combination mixes one correct statement with two incorrect ones. PM-SYM's age band is 18-40, not 21-40, and family pension is for the spouse only, at 50% of the pension. The assured pension of ₹3,000 per month at 60 is correct. The scheme was launched in 2019 for unorganised workers earning up to ₹15,000 per month. It is administered by the Ministry of Labour and Employment, with LIC as pension fund manager and CSCs for enrolment. The government matches the subscriber's contribution.

Statements 2 and 3 only: this is the correct option. It reflects the age-specific contributions (₹55 to ₹200 per month) with matching government contribution, and the ₹3,000 per month assured pension after age 60. PM-SYM covers unorganised workers aged 18-40 with income up to ₹15,000 per month, who are not in NPS, ESIC or EPFO and not income-tax payers. The spouse gets 50% as family pension. LIC manages the fund, and enrolment is through CSCs.

Statement 2 only: this option is incomplete. The age-specific contribution is correct, but it omits the assured ₹3,000 minimum pension at 60, which is also correct. Contribution rates: about ₹55 at age 18, ₹100 at 29 and ₹200 at 40, matched by the Centre. The scheme is voluntary and contributory. The related PM-KMY for farmers has the same pension and contribution structure. The related PM-LVMD (Laghu Vyapari Maan-dhan) covers small traders and the self-employed.

Statements 1, 2 and 4: this combination includes two incorrect statements. The entry age is 18-40, not 21-40. Family pension goes to the spouse only (50% of the pension, ₹1,500), not to unmarried daughters. It leaves out statement 3, the ₹3,000 pension, which is correct. PM-SYM is for unorganised workers such as street vendors, rickshaw pullers, domestic workers and construction workers. Subscribers must hold an Aadhaar card and a savings or Jan Dhan bank account.
related: PM-SYM: entry age 18-40, income up to ₹15,000 per month, pension ₹3,000 after 60.
Family pension under PM-SYM: only the spouse, 50% of the pension.
PM-KMY (2019): ₹3,000 pension for small and marginal farmers aged 18-40.
Atal Pension Yojana (2015): PFRDA-run, pension ₹1,000-5,000 per month, ages 18-40.
LIC is the pension fund manager for PM-SYM, and CSCs handle enrolment.
PM-LVMD: pension scheme for traders and the self-employed with turnover up to ₹1.5 crore.
e-Shram portal (2021): national database of unorganised workers.
PFRDA regulates NPS and is a statutory body under the PFRDA Act 2013.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: the entry age is 18 to 40 years, not 21 to 40. PM-SYM targets unorganised workers such as rickshaw pullers, street vendors, mid-day meal workers, head loaders, brick kiln workers, cobblers, rag pickers, domestic workers, washermen, home-based workers, agricultural labourers and similar workers. Eligibility also requires monthly income of ₹15,000 or less, and the worker must not be an NPS, ESIC or EPFO member or an income-tax payer. Enrolment is done at Common Service Centres using an Aadhaar card and a savings bank or Jan Dhan account. The scheme is voluntary and contributory.

2 — Correct: the contribution depends on the age of entry. It ranges from about ₹55 per month at age 18 to ₹100 at age 29 and ₹200 at age 40, payable until age 60. The Central Government pays an equal matching contribution into the subscriber's pension account. Contributions are auto-debited from the savings bank account. LIC manages the fund as pension fund manager, and the Ministry of Labour and Employment is the nodal ministry. The scheme was announced in the Interim Budget 2019-20.

3 — Correct: each subscriber receives an assured minimum pension of ₹3,000 per month after reaching age 60. The scheme is a defined-benefit pension scheme in this sense, with the government matching contributions. If a subscriber leaves early, there are exit provisions. Within 10 years of joining, the subscriber gets back only their own contribution with savings bank interest. After 10 years but before 60, the subscriber gets their own contribution plus accumulated interest at the actual fund earning rate or the savings bank rate, whichever is higher. The pension is payable through LIC.

4 — Incorrect: family pension applies only to the spouse, not to unmarried daughters. If the subscriber dies after age 60, the spouse receives 50% of the pension, i.e. ₹1,500 per month, as family pension. If the subscriber dies before 60, the spouse may continue the scheme by paying the remaining contributions or may exit. Children are not covered. The family pension is available only to the spouse. A related scheme is PM-KMY (Kisan Maandhan Yojana) for small and marginal farmers, which also offers ₹3,000 pension and is aimed at farmers aged 18-40.
summary: The answer is (b): statements 2 and 3 are correct. PM-SYM is a contributory pension scheme for unorganised workers, with age-specific contributions and an assured minimum pension of ₹3,000 per month after age 60. The entry age is 18-40 years (not 21-40), and family pension goes only to the spouse (not to unmarried daughters).
topic_notes: PM-SYM (Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maan-dhan) was announced in the Interim Budget 2019-20 and launched in 2019. It provides old-age protection to unorganised workers, who make up about 90% of India's workforce. Key features: voluntary and contributory; entry age 18-40; monthly income of ₹15,000 or less; not covered by NPS, EPFO or ESIC; not an income-tax payer. The subscriber pays ₹55-200 per month depending on entry age, and the Centre matches it. The assured pension is ₹3,000 per month after 60. If the subscriber dies, the spouse gets 50% of the pension as family pension. Exit provisions apply for early exit. The scheme is run by the Ministry of Labour and Employment, with LIC as pension fund manager and CSCs for enrolment. Related schemes: PM-KMY (Kisan Maandhan Yojana, 2019) offers ₹3,000 pension to small and marginal farmers aged 18-40, with contributions of ₹55-200. PM-LVMD (Laghu Vyapari Maan-dhan) covers traders, shopkeepers and the self-employed aged 18-40 with turnover up to ₹1.5 crore. Atal Pension Yojana (2015) is run by PFRDA for unorganised workers aged 18-40, with pensions of ₹1,000-5,000 per month. NPS is regulated by PFRDA (statutory under the PFRDA Act 2013). The e-Shram portal (2021) is the national database of unorganised workers. The Code on Social Security 2020 covers gig and platform workers. Other angles UPSC may ask: the EPFO schemes (EPF, EPS, EDLI), National Social Assistance Programme (IGNOAPS for the elderly), and Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY.

question:
With reference to investments, consider the following :
I. Bonds Il. Hedge Funds Ill. Stocks
IV. Venture Capital How many of the above are treated as Alternative Investment Funds?
subject: Economy
detail: Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are privately pooled investment vehicles, set up in India as trusts, companies, LLPs or bodies corporate, that collect money from Indian or foreign investors and invest it under a defined policy for their investors' benefit. They are regulated by SEBI under the SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012. There are three categories. Category I covers funds with positive spillover effects on the economy: venture capital funds, SME funds, social venture funds, infrastructure funds and angel funds. Category II covers private equity funds and debt funds, which do not use leverage beyond day-to-day operational needs. Category III covers funds that use complex or diversified trading strategies and may use leverage: hedge funds and PIPE funds. The minimum investment is Rs 1 crore (Rs 25 lakh for angel funds). Bonds (debt instruments) and stocks (equity shares) are traditional asset classes traded in the conventional market; they are things AIFs may invest in, not AIFs themselves. Elimination logic: Hedge Funds and Venture Capital are clearly AIFs, so options (a) and (c) are out. Bonds and Stocks are not AIFs, which rules out (d). That leaves (b).
explanations: (a) Only one is wrong because two items, Hedge Funds and Venture Capital, are AIFs.
(b) Only two is correct: Hedge Funds (Category III) and Venture Capital (Category I) are AIFs, while Bonds and Stocks are not.
(c) Only three is wrong because it would require either Bonds or Stocks to be an AIF, and neither is.
(d) All the four is wrong because Bonds and Stocks are plain securities, not privately pooled fund vehicles.
keyfact: AIF = privately pooled fund regulated by SEBI (2012): Cat I venture capital, Cat II private equity/debt, Cat III hedge funds; bonds and stocks are not AIFs.
option_notes: Only one: this would be right only if exactly one of the four items qualified as an AIF. Here two qualify. A common mistake is to remember only 'venture capital' or only 'hedge funds' as AIFs. Both appear in SEBI's classification, in Category I and Category III respectively.

Only two: this matches SEBI's AIF framework of 2012. Category I includes venture capital, SME, social venture, infrastructure and angel funds. Category II includes private equity and debt funds. Category III includes hedge funds and PIPE funds. AIFs are privately pooled vehicles with a Rs 1 crore minimum investment, which is why bonds and stocks are excluded.

Only three: this would mean one of bonds or stocks counts as an AIF. That is a trap for students who think any 'investment' is an AIF. AIFs are fund structures, whereas bonds and stocks are the instruments in which funds invest. Mutual funds are also outside the AIF category, as they fall under the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996.

All the four: this over-generalises 'alternative' to every investment. Bonds and stocks are mainstream, traditional asset classes. AIFs are 'alternative' because they sit outside conventional mutual funds and direct holdings. Typical alternatives include private equity, venture capital, hedge funds, real estate funds and commodity-linked funds.
related: AIFs are regulated by SEBI under the AIF Regulations, 2012.
Category I AIFs include venture capital, angel, SME, social venture and infrastructure funds.
Category II AIFs include private equity and debt funds, which cannot use leverage beyond day-to-day operations.
Category III AIFs include hedge funds and use complex strategies and leverage.
Minimum AIF investment is Rs 1 crore; angel funds Rs 25 lakh.
Category I and II AIFs are closed-ended with a minimum three-year tenure.
SEBI replaced the VCF Regulations, 1996 with the AIF Regulations, 2012.
SIDBI manages the Fund of Funds for Startups, which invests in SEBI-registered AIFs.
statements: I. Bonds — Incorrect: bonds are conventional debt securities, not a fund category. Bonds are fixed-income instruments through which an issuer (government, PSU or company) borrows money and pays periodic interest, then repays the principal at maturity. Examples are G-secs, corporate bonds, tax-free bonds and sovereign gold bonds. They are regulated by RBI (G-secs) and SEBI (corporate bonds). AIFs, especially Category II debt funds, may invest in bonds, but the bond itself is an asset class, not an AIF.

II. Hedge Funds — Correct: hedge funds fall under Category III AIFs. They pool money from high-net-worth investors and use complex strategies such as leverage, short selling, derivatives and arbitrage to generate returns. The term originated with Alfred W. Jones in 1949. In India they are regulated by SEBI under the AIF Regulations, 2012, which place Category III funds in the open-ended or closed-ended structure, with a minimum investment of Rs 1 crore. Category III funds may trade in listed and unlisted derivatives.

III. Stocks — Incorrect: stocks (equity shares) are units of ownership in a company, traded on exchanges such as BSE and NSE. They are a conventional asset class regulated by SEBI under the SCRA, 1956 and the SEBI Act, 1992. An AIF may invest in stocks, but stocks are not themselves AIFs. Mutual funds and individual investors hold stocks directly, with no AIF pooling structure needed.

IV. Venture Capital — Correct: venture capital funds are Category I AIFs. They invest in start-ups and early-stage, high-growth enterprises, typically in exchange for equity. Before 2012, they were governed by the SEBI (Venture Capital Funds) Regulations, 1996, which were replaced by the AIF Regulations, 2012. Category I also includes SME funds, social venture funds, infrastructure funds and angel funds. The Government's Fund of Funds for Startups, run through SIDBI, invests in SEBI-registered AIFs.
summary: The answer is (b) Only two. Under SEBI's AIF Regulations, 2012, Hedge Funds (Category III) and Venture Capital Funds (Category I) are Alternative Investment Funds, whereas Bonds and Stocks are conventional securities, not AIFs.
topic_notes:
Alternative Investment Funds are defined in Regulation 2(1)(b) of the SEBI (AIF) Regulations, 2012, which came into force on 21 May 2012. An AIF is a privately pooled investment vehicle, set up as a trust, company, LLP or body corporate, that is not covered by other SEBI fund regulations such as those for mutual funds or collective investment schemes. It collects funds from sophisticated investors, Indian or foreign, for investing according to a defined policy.

Categories:
- Category I: funds that invest in start-ups, early-stage ventures, social ventures, SMEs, infrastructure or other sectors the government or regulators consider socially or economically desirable. Includes venture capital funds, angel funds, SME funds, social venture funds and infrastructure funds. They may receive incentives from the government or regulators.
- Category II: private equity funds and debt funds, plus funds not in Category I or III. They do not undertake leverage except to meet day-to-day operational needs.
- Category III: hedge funds and similar funds using complex trading strategies, including leverage and listed or unlisted derivatives.

Key features:
- Minimum investment is Rs 1 crore per investor, and Rs 25 lakh for employees or directors of the AIF or its manager.
- Angel funds have a lower minimum of Rs 25 lakh.
- Category I and II funds must be closed-ended with a minimum tenure of three years. Category III may be open-ended.
- The minimum corpus is Rs 20 crore, and Rs 10 crore for angel funds.
- The sponsor or manager must contribute 2.5% of the corpus or Rs 5 crore, whichever is lower, for Category I and II funds.
- Foreign investment is allowed.
- Accredited investors are a recent concept in the framework.

Other angles: SIDBI's Fund of Funds for Startups invests via AIFs. The India Aspiration Fund is a SIDBI-backed fund-of-funds for venture capital. GIFT City hosts AIFs regulated by IFSCA. Specialised Investment Funds (SIF), a new mutual fund product, were introduced in 2025. Mutual funds differ from AIFs in having a lower entry threshold and retail participation.

question:
Which of the following are the sources of income for the Reserve Bank of India?
I. Buying and selling Government bonds
II. Buying and selling foreign currency
III. Pension fund management
IV. Lending to private companies
V. Printing and distributing currency notes Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Economy
detail: The RBI's income comes chiefly from (1) interest on its holdings of government securities, plus gains on their purchase and sale through open market operations; (2) earnings on foreign currency assets and gains from forex transactions, including interest on deposits and securities held abroad; (3) interest on LAF/repo lending to commercial banks; and (4) fees and commissions for managing government debt and for services to the Centre and states. Expenditure includes the cost of printing notes (via BRBNMPL and SPMCIL presses), agency charges and staff costs. Surplus is transferred to the Central Government under Section 47 of the RBI Act, 1934, following the Bimal Jalan Committee (2018-19) and its Economic Capital Framework, which set the Contingent Risk Buffer at 5.5-6.5% of the balance sheet. Elimination: pension fund management is done by PFRDA and the NPS Trust, not the RBI, so III is wrong, which rules out (c). The RBI lends to banks, not to private companies, so IV is wrong, which rules out (b). Note printing is a cost, not income, so V is wrong, which rules out (d). That leaves (a).
explanations: Correct: Government securities operations and forex operations are both genuine RBI income sources, and the other three items are not.
Wrong: It includes IV (lending to private companies), which the RBI does not do, and the question's own printed option is garbled.
Wrong: It includes III (pension fund management, PFRDA's domain), IV (no lending to private firms) and V (note printing is a cost).
Wrong: It includes V, since note printing is an expense for the RBI, not income, even though I and II are right.
keyfact: RBI income = interest and gains on G-secs plus forex operations (and LAF/fees); note printing is a cost, and pensions belong to PFRDA.
option_notes: Statements I and II: government bond operations and forex operations. These are the RBI's major income streams, along with interest from LAF lending to banks and fees for managing government debt. The surplus is transferred to the Centre under Section 47 of the RBI Act, 1934. In recent years the transfer has been large, for example about Rs 2.1 lakh crore for FY2023-24, a record at the time, and about Rs 2.69 lakh crore for FY2024-25.

Option (b) as OCR'd was garbled, but it denotes a set including IV, lending to private companies. The RBI is the banker to banks and the government, not a lender to companies. Its credit tools are the repo rate, the MSF (repo plus 25 bps), the standing deposit facility (SDF, introduced in 2022 as the floor of the corridor) and WMA to governments. Private firms borrow from banks, NBFCs or markets.

Option (c) combines I, III, IV and V. Pension fund management belongs to PFRDA and fund managers, lending to private firms is not RBI business, and note printing is a cost. The RBI Act's Section 22 gives it sole authority over note issue, while the Issue Department backs notes with assets such as gold, forex and rupee securities under the Minimum Reserve System (1957, Rs 200 crore of which Rs 115 crore is gold).

Option (d) combines I, II and V. It is a trap because printing and distributing notes looks like an income activity. In reality printing is a cost borne by the RBI, which pays the presses.
