Currency distribution through currency chests, which are held at designated bank branches, is also a service function. The RBI's indirect benefit is seigniorage, since notes are interest-free liabilities.
related: The RBI surplus transfer to the Centre is made under Section 47 of the RBI Act, 1934.
The Bimal Jalan Committee (2018-19) set the Contingent Risk Buffer at 5.5-6.5% of the RBI balance sheet.
PFRDA, not the RBI, regulates the NPS and Atal Pension Yojana.
The RBI is the sole issuer of notes (Section 22), while the Finance Ministry issues one-rupee notes and coins.
The MPC was made statutory in 2016 and has 6 members, 3 of them external, with the RBI Governor as ex officio chair.
The SDF (2022) sets the floor of the LAF corridor, and the MSF rate is the ceiling.
The RBI's accounting year was changed from July-June to April-March from 2020-21.
BRBNMPL, an RBI subsidiary, runs note presses at Mysuru and Salboni.
statements: I — Correct: The RBI earns interest and trading gains from government securities. Open market operations (OMOs) buy and sell G-secs to manage liquidity, and the RBI's holdings of G-secs yield coupon income. This is a major income component. G-secs are issued by the Centre (T-bills, dated securities) and by states (SDLs), and the RBI manages the public debt as the government's debt manager. OMOs, the LAF and the MSF are the tools of liquidity management. The Retail Direct scheme (2021) lets retail investors open gilt accounts with the RBI.

II — Correct: Buying and selling foreign currency, along with investing forex reserves, brings in income through interest on foreign securities and deposits and through valuation and trading gains. The RBI intervenes in the forex market to smooth rupee volatility. India's forex reserves have been roughly 600-700 billion dollars in recent years. Reserves consist of foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve tranche position at the IMF. Valuation changes go to the Currency and Gold Revaluation Account (CGRA), not to income directly.

III — Incorrect: Pension fund management is not an RBI income source. The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA, statutory since 2013) regulates the NPS, and licensed pension fund managers such as SBI, LIC and UTI run the funds. The NPS Trust holds the assets. The RBI only acts as banker to the government and regulates banks and NBFCs. The Atal Pension Yojana is administered by PFRDA.

IV — Incorrect: The RBI does not lend to private companies. It lends to scheduled commercial banks through repo, MSF and the standing deposit facility, and acts as lender of last resort. It can also lend to the Centre through Ways and Means Advances (WMA). Since the 1997 agreement ended automatic monetisation of deficits through ad hoc treasury bills, direct commercial lending is not part of its role. Banks, not the RBI, lend to private firms.

V — Incorrect: Printing and distributing notes is an expenditure for the RBI, not an income source. Notes are printed at the presses of BRBNMPL (Mysuru and Salboni) and SPMCIL (Nashik and Dewas), and the RBI bears the printing cost. Currency is an RBI liability under Section 22 of the RBI Act, which gives it the sole right to issue notes (except one-rupee notes and coins, which the Finance Ministry issues). Seigniorage benefits arise indirectly because currency is a non-interest-bearing liability held against interest-earning assets.
summary: The answer is (a): statements I and II only. The RBI earns income mainly from buying and selling government securities (interest and trading gains) and from foreign exchange operations (its forex reserves and transactions). Pension fund management, lending to private companies and note printing are not income sources in the sense the question intends.
topic_notes: The RBI was established on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934, and was nationalised on 1 January 1949. Its headquarters moved from Calcutta to Mumbai in 1937. Its income comes mainly from interest on G-secs, earnings on foreign currency assets and gold-related operations, LAF/repo interest, and fees for services such as debt management. Its expenses cover printing costs, agency commissions to banks for government business, staff costs and provisions. The surplus after contributions to funds goes to the Central Government under Section 47. The Bimal Jalan Committee (2018-19) reviewed the Economic Capital Framework. It recommended a Contingent Risk Buffer of 5.5-6.5% of the balance sheet and transferring all realised profit, and the RBI's accounting year was aligned to April-March from 2020-21. The RBI keeps the Contingency Fund, the Asset Development Fund, the Currency and Gold Revaluation Account (CGRA) and the Investment Revaluation Account. Functions include monetary policy through the MPC (six members, formed in 2016 under the amended RBI Act), currency issuer, banker to the government, banker's bank, forex manager under FEMA 1999, and regulator of banks, NBFCs and payment systems. Tools include CRR, SLR, repo, reverse repo, MSF, SDF, OMOs and the Market Stabilisation Scheme. The CRR is the share of NDTL banks keep with the RBI in cash, and the SLR is the share they keep in liquid assets with themselves. Related institutions are SEBI (securities), IRDAI (insurance), PFRDA (pensions) and IFSCA (GIFT City). The Governor is appointed by the Centre, and Sanjay Malhotra took over in December 2024. UPSC could next ask about the Central Board, the dividend/surplus transfer, the CRR/SLR definitions, the MPC's composition, or RBI's role in debt management.

question: With reference to the Government of India, consider the following information : Organization| Some of its It works functions under Directorate of |Enforcement Enforcement jof the Security Division-I, Ministry of Home Affairs II. |Directorate of Enforces the Department Revenue of Revenue, Intelligence the Customs Ministry of Act, 1962 Finance III.|Directorate Carrying out Department General of big data of Revenue, Systems analytics to {Ministry of and Data assist tax Finance Management |officers for better policy and nabbing tax evaders In how many of the above rows is the information correctly matched?
subject: Economy
detail: The question tests which ministry and department each enforcement or tax-administration body sits under, and what it does. The Directorate of Enforcement (ED) is a multi-disciplinary agency under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance. It enforces the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, and the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018. It does not work under the Ministry of Home Affairs, so Row I fails. The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) is the apex anti-smuggling intelligence and investigation agency, under the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC), Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance. It enforces the Customs Act, 1962, and also laws such as the NDPS Act, the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act and the Wildlife Protection Act in relevant respects, so Row II is correct. The Directorate General of Systems and Data Management (DGSDM) is the CBIC's data analytics and IT wing, and it is not a stand-alone body directly described as in the question's Row III; the official key treats Row III as incorrect. With exactly one correct row, the answer is (a). Elimination: since Row I is clearly wrong, (c) is ruled out, and since Row II is clearly right, (d) is ruled out.
explanations: Correct: only Row II is correctly matched, since the DRI works under the Department of Revenue and enforces the Customs Act, 1962.
Incorrect: two correct rows would require Row I or Row III to be right, but the ED is under the Finance Ministry and Row III does not match the official position.
Incorrect: Row I is clearly wrong because the ED is not under the Ministry of Home Affairs, so all three cannot be correct.
Incorrect: Row II is correct, so the answer cannot be none.
keyfact: ED, DRI, FIU-IND and CBIC all sit under the Finance Ministry's Department of Revenue, not the Home Ministry; the DRI enforces the Customs Act, 1962.
option_notes: Only one: this is the official answer. Exactly one row, the DRI row, is correctly matched. The DRI is the anti-smuggling intelligence body in CBIC under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance, and it enforces the Customs Act, 1962 along with other laws.

Only two: this would require one of Rows I or III to be correct as well. The ED belongs to the Finance Ministry's Department of Revenue, not the Home Ministry, and Row III is treated as incorrect in the official key. The ED enforces PMLA and FEMA and was founded in 1956.

All the three: this would need the ED to be under the Ministry of Home Affairs, which it is not. The Home Ministry controls bodies such as the CBI's parent-level policing links, the IB, NIA and CAPFs, but not the ED. The Finance Ministry controls the ED, DRI, CBIC and CBDT.

None: this is wrong because the DRI row is accurate. The DRI, founded in 1957, is a premier intelligence agency against smuggling and customs duty evasion, working under the CBIC in the Department of Revenue.
related: The ED enforces PMLA 2002, FEMA 1999 and the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018.
The DRI was set up in 1957 and is under CBIC, Department of Revenue.
FIU-IND was set up in 2004 and reports to the Economic Intelligence Council.
The CBI is under the Department of Personnel and Training, not the Home Ministry.
The SFIO is under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.
The CBDT and CBIC are the two boards under the Department of Revenue.
The NCB is under the Ministry of Home Affairs and enforces the NDPS Act 1985.
The Intelligence Bureau works under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Directorate of Enforcement is under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance, not the Ministry of Home Affairs (Internal Security Division-I). The ED was set up in 1956 as an 'Enforcement Unit' in the Department of Economic Affairs. It has its headquarters in New Delhi and is headed by a Director of Enforcement. It enforces PMLA 2002, FEMA 1999 and the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018. Its investigations into money laundering and foreign-exchange violations are often in the news, but its administrative control is with the Finance Ministry.

2 — Correct: The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence is under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance (CBIC). It was established in 1957 and is headed by an Additional Director General or Director General. It is the apex anti-smuggling intelligence agency, handling gold, narcotics, wildlife, arms, counterfeit currency and commercial fraud. It enforces the Customs Act 1962 and has powers under related laws. It is also the nodal agency in India for the Regional Intelligence Liaison Office network of the World Customs Organization.

3 — Incorrect: The big-data analytics function for tax administration is performed by the Directorate General of Systems and Data Management (DGSDM) of the CBIC, with its centre of work in data analytics and IT systems for customs, GST and central excise. It provides tax officers with analytics for risk assessment and for catching evasion. The official key treats the row as not correctly matched, so students should remember it as a CBIC wing, with the related Directorate General of Analytics and Risk Management (DGARM) also in CBIC.
summary: The answer is (a) Only one. Only Row II is correctly matched: the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence works under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance, and enforces the Customs Act, 1962 (among other laws). Row I is wrong because the Directorate of Enforcement is under the Department of Revenue, not the Ministry of Home Affairs. Row III is wrong because the big-data analytics body (Directorate General of Systems and Data Management) works under the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC), while the line in the question assigns it to the Department of Revenue in a way that does not match the official organisation; the official answer treats it as incorrect.
topic_notes: The question is about the Finance Ministry's Department of Revenue and its enforcement and intelligence agencies. The Department of Revenue has two apex boards: the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT), which administers income tax, and the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC), which administers customs, GST and central excise. Key agencies: the Directorate of Enforcement (ED), established 1956, enforces PMLA 2002, FEMA 1999 and FEOA 2018. The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI), 1957, fights smuggling and enforces the Customs Act 1962. The Financial Intelligence Unit-India (FIU-IND), set up in 2004, receives and analyses suspicious transaction reports and reports to the Economic Intelligence Council. The Directorate General of GST Intelligence (DGGI) investigates GST evasion. The Directorate General of Systems and Data Management and the Directorate General of Analytics and Risk Management are CBIC data bodies. The Central Economic Intelligence Bureau coordinates economic intelligence among agencies. The Ministry of Home Affairs by contrast controls the Intelligence Bureau, NIA, NCB, CAPFs, and the Border Management and Internal Security divisions. The CBI is under the Department of Personnel and Training (Ministry of Personnel), and the SFIO is under the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. UPSC often asks which agency sits under which ministry and which Act each enforces, so memorise these links carefully.

question:
Consider the following statements :
I. The Reserve Bank of India mandates all the listed companies in India to submit a Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR). Il. In India, a company submitting a BRSR makes disclosures in the report that are largely non-financial in nature. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) is the ESG (Environmental, Social and Governance) disclosure framework for Indian listed entities. It was introduced by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) under Regulation 34(2)(f) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015. It replaced the earlier Business Responsibility Report (BRR), which followed the 2011 National Voluntary Guidelines (NVGs) and the 2019 National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct (NGRBC). BRSR became voluntary in FY 2021-22 and mandatory from FY 2022-23 for the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation. It is built around nine principles of the NGRBC, with Essential and Leadership indicators. SEBI later added BRSR Core, a subset of key performance indicators with reasonable assurance, and ESG disclosures for the value chain. Statement I is wrong on two counts: the regulator is SEBI, not the RBI, and the mandate covers only the top 1,000 companies, not all listed ones. Statement II is right because the report covers emissions, energy, water, waste, employee well-being, diversity, human rights, community engagement and governance, which are mostly non-financial and complement the financial statements. Hence (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong: Statement I is false because the regulator is SEBI, not the RBI, and BRSR is not mandated for all listed companies. Statement II is true, so 'I only' fails.
(b) is correct: Statement II is true because BRSR is largely non-financial ESG disclosure, and Statement I is false (SEBI, top 1,000 companies).
(c) is wrong: Statement I fails on both the regulator and the coverage, so both statements cannot be correct.
(d) is wrong: Statement II is correct, as BRSR content is mainly ESG and non-financial, so 'neither' is incorrect.
keyfact: BRSR = SEBI-mandated, top 1,000 listed companies, ESG and largely non-financial, based on the nine NGRBC principles; not an RBI requirement.
option_notes: Option (a) 'I only' would hold if the RBI mandated BRSR for all listed companies. In reality BRSR comes from SEBI under the LODR Regulations, 2015, and covers the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation. The RBI is the central bank, established in 1935 and nationalised in 1949, and handles monetary policy, banking supervision and currency issue. It issues climate-risk and sustainable-finance guidance for regulated entities, but it does not mandate BRSR.

Option (b) 'II only' is the official answer. It reflects that BRSR is a SEBI-mandated ESG report whose content is largely non-financial. It covers environmental metrics, social indicators such as employee welfare and diversity, and governance disclosures under the nine NGRBC principles. It is mandatory from FY 2022-23 for the top 1,000 listed companies, and it replaced the earlier Business Responsibility Report introduced in 2012 for the top 100 companies.

Option (c) 'Both I and II' is wrong because Statement I misattributes the mandate to the RBI and overstates coverage. A common trap in UPSC is swapping the regulator: SEBI regulates capital markets and listed-company disclosures, the RBI regulates banks and monetary policy, IRDAI regulates insurance, and the MCA administers the Companies Act, 2013 (which governs CSR under Section 135).

Option (d) 'Neither I nor II' is wrong because Statement II is accurate. BRSR is essentially a sustainability and ESG report, not a financial statement. Financial reporting is covered separately by annual financial statements under the Companies Act, 2013 and Ind AS. BRSR sits within the annual report alongside them, and its non-financial data can be assured through BRSR Core assurance.
related: BRSR was introduced by SEBI and is mandatory for the top 1,000 listed companies from FY 2022-23.
BRSR replaced the Business Responsibility Report (BRR), which started in 2012 for the top 100 companies.
BRSR is based on the nine principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct (NGRBC), 2019.
BRSR Core is a subset of KPIs with reasonable assurance, introduced by SEBI in 2023.
CSR is governed by Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Schedule VII, at 2% of average net profit.
SEBI regulates ESG Rating Providers (ERPs) under a 2023 framework.
India's first Sovereign Green Bonds were issued in January 2023.
SEBI's LODR Regulations, 2015 govern disclosures by listed entities.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: BRSR is mandated by SEBI, not the RBI, and only for the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation. SEBI is the statutory securities market regulator, set up in 1988 and given statutory status by the SEBI Act, 1992. It frames the LODR Regulations, 2015, which govern disclosures by listed entities. The BRSR requirement was notified in May 2021 under Regulation 34(2)(f), voluntary for FY 2021-22 and mandatory from FY 2022-23. The RBI regulates banks, monetary policy and payment systems, and does not prescribe BRSR. Smaller listed companies may report voluntarily. Later SEBI circulars (2023) introduced BRSR Core with assurance requirements and phased value-chain disclosures for the top 250 companies.

2 — Correct: BRSR disclosures are largely non-financial, covering ESG performance rather than accounts. The report has three sections: A (General Disclosures), B (Management and Process Disclosures) and C (Principle-wise Performance Disclosures). Section C is organised around the nine NGRBC principles: ethics and transparency, sustainable products, employee well-being, stakeholder engagement, human rights, environment, policy advocacy, inclusive growth and consumer responsibility. Each principle has Essential indicators (mandatory) and Leadership indicators (voluntary). Data include GHG emissions, energy intensity, water use, waste, gender diversity, safety incidents and CSR. BRSR Core has nine ESG attribute KPIs with reasonable assurance. Some turnover and CSR figures are financial, but the report is largely non-financial. It is aligned with global frameworks such as GRI and TCFD.
summary: The answer is (b): only Statement II is correct. BRSR disclosures are largely non-financial (ESG-related), but BRSR is mandated by SEBI, not the RBI, and it applies to the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation, not all listed companies.
topic_notes: BRSR is India's mandatory ESG disclosure format for listed companies. The evolution runs as follows: the 2009 Corporate Social Responsibility Voluntary Guidelines, the 2011 National Voluntary Guidelines (NVGs) on Social, Environmental and Economic Responsibilities of Business, the 2012 SEBI requirement of a Business Responsibility Report (BRR) for the top 100 listed companies (extended to the top 500 in 2015 and the top 1,000 in 2019), the 2019 National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct (NGRBC) issued by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and the 2021 BRSR notification, mandatory from FY 2022-23. A committee under the chairmanship of Mr. Gagan? is not needed to remember; focus on the structure. BRSR has Sections A (general), B (management and process) and C (principle-wise performance). The nine principles of NGRBC are the base. BRSR Core, introduced in 2023, has nine ESG attributes with reasonable assurance, and value-chain disclosures are phased in, starting with the top 250 listed entities. Related frameworks are the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI), TCFD, the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) under the IFRS Foundation, and the EU's CSRD. Other angles: CSR under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 (2% of average net profit over three years for companies with net worth of Rs 500 crore or more, turnover of Rs 1,000 crore or more, or net profit of Rs 5 crore or more), green bonds, SEBI's ESG rating providers regulations (2023), India's Sovereign Green Bonds (2023), and the RBI's climate-risk disclosure draft. Know which regulator handles what: SEBI for the capital markets, the RBI for banks, the MCA for companies law.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I : In India, income from allied agricultural activities like poultry farming and wool rearing in rural areas is exempted from any tax.
Statement II : In India, rural agricultural land is not considered a capital asset under the provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II does not explain Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct
Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct
subject: Economy
detail: The Income-tax Act, 1961 exempts 'agricultural income' under Section 10(1), and Section 2(1A) defines it. It covers rent or revenue from land used for agricultural purposes, income from agricultural operations on the land, and income from farm buildings on or near the land, subject to conditions. The core test is that the income must derive from land through basic operations (tilling, sowing, planting) and subsequent operations that make the produce marketable. Poultry farming, dairy, wool rearing, fish farming and similar activities are not land-based in this sense, so their income is taxable as business income, though it may attract special treatment or deductions. Under Section 2(14), 'capital asset' excludes rural agricultural land, meaning land outside specified municipal limits and outside prescribed distance bands from them (2 km, 6 km or 8 km depending on population). Its sale therefore gives no capital gains. Urban agricultural land is a capital asset. Elimination: Statement I fails, which rules out (a), (b) and (c), leaving (d). Statement II is a true statement, but it does not explain Statement I anyway.
explanations: Wrong: it treats Statement I as correct, but poultry and wool income is not agricultural income, and it is taxable.
Wrong: it also treats Statement I as correct. Statement II is true, but Statement I fails, so this option cannot hold.
Wrong: it says Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect, which is the reverse of the actual position.

Correct: Statement I is false, since allied activities are not exempt as agricultural income, and Statement II is true, since rural agricultural land is excluded from 'capital asset' under Section 2(14).
keyfact: Only land-based agricultural income is exempt under the Income-tax Act; poultry and wool income is taxable, and rural agricultural land is not a capital asset.
option_notes: Option (a) claims both statements are correct and that II explains I. It is wrong because Statement I is false. The two statements concern different matters: Section 10(1) exempts agricultural income from income tax, while Section 2(14) concerns capital gains on transfer of land. Neither explains the other.

Option (b) claims both statements are correct but unconnected. It is wrong on Statement I. It would be correct only if allied activities such as poultry and wool rearing were treated as agricultural income, and they are not. Agricultural income exemption is tied to land-based operations under Section 2(1A).

Option (c) claims Statement I is correct and II is incorrect. This inverts the true position. Statement II is a settled provision of Section 2(14)(iii), while Statement I overstates the exemption available to rural allied activities.

Option (d) is the official answer. Allied activities like poultry, dairy and wool rearing are taxable as business income. Rural agricultural land is not a capital asset, so no capital gains arise on its sale. Urban agricultural land stays within the capital gains net.
related: Entry 82 of the Union List covers taxes on income other than agricultural income.
Section 10(1) exempts agricultural income from tax in India.
Section 2(1A) of the Income-tax Act defines agricultural income.
Section 2(14) excludes rural agricultural land from 'capital asset'.
Partial integration applies when agricultural income exceeds Rs 5,000 along with taxable non-agricultural income.
Tea income is treated as 60 percent agricultural and 40 percent business.
Section 54B gives capital gains relief on reinvestment in agricultural land.
Section 80P gives deductions to cooperative societies, including dairy and agricultural ones.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Income from poultry farming, wool rearing and other allied activities is not agricultural income under Section 2(1A), so it is not exempt merely because it is rural. Section 10(1) exempts only agricultural income, defined as income from land used for agriculture, with basic and subsequent operations performed on the land. Activities such as poultry, dairy, bee-keeping, sericulture without land-based cultivation, and fish farming are treated as business income and taxed, though some may qualify for deductions or special regimes. Courts have repeatedly held that agriculture requires an effort on the land, not simply the rearing of animals. Nursery income from plants grown on land is treated as agricultural, and the Act deems it so.

2 — Correct: Under Section 2(14)(iii), rural agricultural land in India is excluded from 'capital asset', so its transfer produces no capital gains tax. Land counts as rural if it is outside the limits of a municipality or cantonment board with a population of 10,000 or more, and outside specified aerial distances from the limits. The distances are 2 km for populations of 10,000 to 1 lakh, 6 km for 1 lakh to 10 lakh, and 8 km for above 10 lakh. Agricultural land inside these limits is an urban capital asset and is taxed on transfer. Section 54B offers relief when the proceeds from urban agricultural land are reinvested in other agricultural land.
summary: The answer is (d). Statement I is incorrect because income from poultry farming, wool rearing and similar allied activities is not 'agricultural income' under Section 2(1A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, so it is taxable. Statement II is correct because rural agricultural land is excluded from 'capital asset' under Section 2(14), so its transfer attracts no capital gains tax.
topic_notes: Agricultural income and tax in India: Agricultural income is exempt from central income tax under Section 10(1) because Entry 82 of the Union List empowers Parliament to tax income 'other than agricultural income'. Agricultural income falls outside the Union's taxing power, and the States could tax it in principle under their own powers, but in practice they largely do not. Section 2(1A) defines it in three parts: rent or revenue from land used for agriculture, income from agricultural operations, and income from farm buildings on or near the land, subject to conditions. The land must be in India. Partial integration: where a person has both non-agricultural income above the basic exemption limit and agricultural income above Rs 5,000, the agricultural income is added in a notional way to compute tax on the non-agricultural income, which prevents avoiding higher slabs. This applies to individuals, HUFs, AOPs and BOIs, and it is not available under the new tax regime. Mixed-income cases: tea growing is treated as 60 percent agricultural and 40 percent business, coffee grown, cured and sold is 75 percent agricultural, and rubber is 65 percent agricultural. Income from sale of nursery plants raised on land is agricultural. Income from poultry, dairy, fisheries, bee-keeping and wool is business income. Capital gains: urban agricultural land is a capital asset. Section 54B gives relief on reinvestment in agricultural land within 2 years. Section 10(37) exempts compensation on compulsory acquisition of urban agricultural land in specified circumstances. Related: the Kelkar Committee and others have argued for taxing large farm incomes, but this remains politically sensitive. Dairy and FPO income may attract specific benefits, for example Section 80P for cooperatives.

question:
Consider the following statements :
I. India has joined the Minerals Security Partnership as a member.
II. India is a resource-rich country in all the 30 critical minerals that it has identified. Ill. The Parliament in 2023 has amended the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 empowering the Central Government to exclusively auction mining lease and composite license for certain critical minerals. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Geography
detail: The question tests India's critical minerals policy. The Minerals Security Partnership is a US-led initiative launched in June 2022 to build secure and diversified supply chains for critical minerals. India joined it in 2023 as a member. India's expert committee under the Ministry of Mines identified 30 critical minerals in 2023. These include lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, rare earth elements, niobium, and others. India has limited or no reserves of several of these, such as lithium, cobalt and nickel in commercial quantities. It imports most of its requirement of these minerals, so Statement II is wrong, and the phrase 'all 30' is the trap. The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2023 amended the 1957 Act. It added a list of 24 critical and strategic minerals in Part D of the First Schedule and empowered the Central Government to auction mining leases and composite licences for them. It also removed atomic status from six minerals, including lithium and beryllium, and allowed exploration licences. Elimination: since II is incorrect, options (a), (b) and (d) fall. Only (c) remains.
explanations: Wrong: it includes Statement II, which is false, because India lacks resources in many of the 30 critical minerals.
Wrong: it excludes Statement I, which is true (India joined the MSP), and it includes the false Statement II.
Correct: Statements I and III are true (India's MSP membership and the 2023 MMDR amendment), while II is false.
Wrong: it includes Statement II, which wrongly claims India is resource-rich in all 30 critical minerals.
keyfact: India joined the MSP in 2023 and the MMDR Amendment Act 2023 lets the Centre auction critical mineral blocks, but India is not resource-rich in all 30 critical minerals.
option_notes: I and II only: this combination is a distractor. It pairs the true MSP statement with the false claim of resource richness in all 30 minerals. Remember that India has a significant import dependence for lithium, cobalt, nickel and some rare earth elements. The MSP, launched in 2022, is a US-led group of about a dozen partners, and India joined in 2023.

II and III only: this combination is wrong because it relies on Statement II. India's critical mineral list of 30 was released in 2023 by the Ministry of Mines. The list was drawn up after considering the needs of clean energy, defence and electronics. Having a mineral on the list does not mean India has large reserves of it. Many of them are imported.

I and III only: this is the correct answer. India joined the Minerals Security Partnership in 2023, and the MMDR Amendment Act, 2023 empowered the Centre to conduct auctions of critical mineral blocks. Together these show a policy push for supply security through diplomacy and domestic reform. Also note the National Critical Mineral Mission, approved in January 2025.

I, II and III: this is wrong because Statement II is false. India has no commercially significant reserves of several critical minerals, such as cobalt and lithium. Only a small lithium inferred resource was found at Reasi in J&K, and it is of poor grade. The answer therefore cannot be all three.
related: India joined the Minerals Security Partnership in 2023; the MSP was launched in June 2022 by the US.
The expert committee of the Ministry of Mines identified 30 critical minerals in 2023.
The MMDR Amendment Act, 2023 inserted Part D into the First Schedule for critical and strategic minerals.
KABIL was set up in 2019 by NALCO, HCL and MECL for overseas mineral assets.
The National Critical Mineral Mission was approved in January 2025.
Lithium inferred resources were reported at Reasi, Jammu and Kashmir, in 2023.
The MMDR Act, 1957 regulates mining in India other than for mineral oil and gas.
The Lithium Triangle comprises Argentina, Bolivia and Chile.
statements: 1 — Correct: India became a member of the MSP in 2023. The MSP was launched in June 2022 by the US with partners to catalyse public and private investment in critical mineral supply chains. It aims at responsible, diversified and secure sourcing of minerals needed for clean energy and technology. Founding partners include Australia, Canada, Finland, France, Germany, Japan, South Korea, Sweden, the UK, the US and the EU. India joined in 2023. India's membership supports its National Critical Mineral Mission and overseas asset acquisition through KABIL.

2 — Incorrect: India is not resource-rich in all 30 identified critical minerals. The Ministry of Mines committee identified 30 critical minerals in 2023, including antimony, beryllium, cobalt, copper, graphite, lithium, nickel, niobium, PGEs, REEs, tin, titanium, tungsten, vanadium and zirconium. India has deposits of some, such as titanium, graphite and REEs in beach sands, but lacks adequate reserves of lithium, cobalt and nickel. It imports a large share of its needs, especially from China. Hence KABIL, the NCMM (2025) and recycling incentives.

3 — Correct: The MMDR Amendment Act, 2023 empowered the Central Government to auction mining leases and composite licences for critical minerals specified in Part D of the First Schedule. This was to speed up exploitation and attract investment. The Act also removed six minerals, including lithium, beryllium, niobium, titanium, tantalum and zirconium, from the atomic minerals list, and it allowed exploration licences for deep-seated critical minerals. The Centre auctions the blocks, and states then handle the grant of leases.
summary: The answer is (c): Statements I and III are correct, and Statement II is incorrect. India joined the Minerals Security Partnership (MSP) in 2023 and Parliament amended the MMDR Act in 2023 to let the Centre auction critical mineral blocks. India is not resource-rich in all 30 critical minerals and depends heavily on imports for many of them.
topic_notes: Critical minerals are minerals essential for economic development, clean energy and national security whose supply is at risk of disruption. In 2023 the Ministry of Mines expert committee identified 30 critical minerals for India. They include antimony, beryllium, bismuth, cobalt, copper, gallium, germanium, graphite, hafnium, indium, lithium, molybdenum, niobium, nickel, PGEs, phosphorus, potash, REEs, rhenium, silicon, strontium, tantalum, tellurium, tin, titanium, tungsten, vanadium, zirconium, selenium and cadmium. The MMDR Amendment Act, 2023 placed 24 critical and strategic minerals in Part D of the First Schedule and empowered the Centre to auction their blocks. It also allowed exploration licences, removed six minerals from the atomic list, and allowed the Centre to notify the list of critical minerals. Khanij Bidesh India Ltd (KABIL), a joint venture of NALCO, HCL and MECL, was created in 2019 to acquire overseas mineral assets, and it has lithium projects in Argentina. India is also a member of the Minerals Security Partnership (joined 2023) and of Mineral Security Partnership Finance Network. The National Critical Mineral Mission was approved in January 2025 with an outlay of about Rs 16,300 crore and PSU investment, aiming at exploration, recycling, processing and stockpiling. Other angles include the Quad critical minerals initiative, the India-Australia critical minerals partnership, the Lithium Triangle (Argentina, Bolivia, Chile), China's dominance in rare earth processing, the Geological Survey of India's role in exploration, and the Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Act, 2002 for seabed mining.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I : As regards returns from an investment in a company, generally, bondholders are considered to be relatively at lower risk than stockholders.
Statement II : Bondholders are lenders to a company whereas stockholders are its owners. Statement III : For repayment purpose, bondholders’ are prioritized over stockholders by a company. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement II and Statement III are correct and both of them explain Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement I explains Statement II
Only one of the Statements II and III is correct and that explains Statement I
Neither Statement II nor Statement III is correct
subject: Economy
detail: A company raises capital through debt (bonds, debentures) or equity (shares). A bondholder lends money and is a creditor. The company must pay fixed interest (coupon) and return the principal on maturity, whether or not it makes a profit. A stockholder (equity shareholder) is a part-owner. Dividends are paid only out of profits and at the board's discretion, and the shareholder has a residual claim on assets. In liquidation the order of payment runs roughly: secured creditors and workmen's dues, then unsecured creditors including bondholders, then preference shareholders, and last equity shareholders. Under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (section 53), this priority is called the waterfall mechanism. Because of the fixed returns and the priority in repayment, bonds carry lower risk and, usually, lower expected returns. Equity carries higher risk but offers unlimited upside, voting rights and capital gains. Elimination: Statement II is factually right, which rules out (c) and (d). Statement III is also right, so (c) fails and (b) is incomplete, because (b) ignores the priority of repayment as an explanation. Statement II alone does not explain risk fully, but II and III together do. So (a) is correct.
explanations: Correct. Statement II (lenders vs owners) and Statement III (priority in repayment) are both true, and together they explain why bondholders bear lower risk, as Statement I says.
Incorrect. Statements I and II are true, but Statement I (lower risk) does not explain Statement II. The causation is the other way round, and this option also leaves out Statement III.
Incorrect. Both Statements II and III are correct, not only one of them.
Incorrect. Both Statement II and Statement III are correct, so this denial is false.
keyfact: Bondholders are creditors with fixed claims paid first; stockholders are owners with residual claims paid last, so equity is riskier than debt.
option_notes: Option (a) says that Statements II and III are correct and both explain Statement I. This is the official answer. The explanation has two parts: the bondholder's creditor status gives a contractual, fixed claim, and the priority in repayment gives protection in default or liquidation. The risk of equity is higher but so is the potential return. This is the basic risk-return tradeoff in corporate finance.

Option (b) says that Statements I and II are correct and Statement I explains Statement II. It reverses the logic, because lower risk is the result of the lender status and does not cause it. Lender and owner are legal categories: debt versus equity. It also ignores Statement III. UPSC often builds such options to test the direction of explanation in assertion-reason questions.

Option (c) says that only one of Statements II and III is correct and that it explains Statement I. This is false because both statements are factually true. Such options test whether students can verify each statement separately. Preference shareholders rank between creditors and equity holders, since they get a fixed dividend and priority over equity.

Option (d) says that neither Statement II nor Statement III is correct. This is wrong, since the creditor-owner distinction and the repayment priority are standard facts. Under the IBC, 2016, a 'financial creditor' such as a bondholder or debenture holder sits on the Committee of Creditors, while equity shareholders do not.
related: IBC 2016 section 53 sets the liquidation waterfall; equity shareholders rank last.
Bond prices and market interest rates (yields) move in opposite directions.
Masala bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued by Indian entities in overseas markets.
SEBI regulates corporate bonds and debentures of listed companies in India.
Preference shareholders get a fixed dividend and are paid before equity holders.
AT1 (perpetual) bonds carry higher risk, and the Yes Bank 2020 write-off hit AT1 holders.
Government securities (G-secs) are treated as having practically no credit risk.
Convertible debentures can be converted into equity shares after a stated period.
statements: 1 — Correct: Bondholders face lower risk than stockholders because their income is contractual and they rank higher in repayment. A bond is a debt instrument with a fixed coupon, a face value and a maturity date. Risks still exist, such as default, interest-rate risk and inflation risk, and credit rating agencies like CRISIL, ICRA and CARE grade them. Equity returns are variable and depend on profits and market prices, so equity is generally riskier but offers higher long-term expected returns.

2 — Correct: Bondholders are lenders (creditors) and stockholders are owners. A bondholder has a debt claim and no voting rights or ownership in the company. A stockholder owns a proportionate share, votes at general meetings, elects directors, and receives dividends from profits. Ownership gives the shareholder a residual claim on assets and profits after all debts are paid. Liability is limited to the unpaid amount on the shares, under the Companies Act, 2013.

3 — Correct: Bondholders are prioritized over stockholders for repayment. Interest on debt is paid before dividends, and in liquidation creditors are paid before shareholders. Under section 53 of the IBC, 2016, the order is: insolvency costs, secured creditors and workmen's dues, employee dues, financial unsecured creditors, government dues, other debts, preference shareholders, and finally equity shareholders. Equity holders are residual claimants, so they absorb losses first. This priority explains why bonds are considered safer.
summary: The answer is (a). Statements II and III are both correct, and together they explain why Statement I holds. Bondholders are lenders with a prior claim on the company's money, so their returns are less risky than those of stockholders, who are owners and are paid last.
topic_notes: Companies raise long-term finance through equity (ordinary shares), preference shares and debt (bonds, debentures, loans). Equity holders are owners with voting rights and a residual claim; their dividends are discretionary and their returns are variable. Bonds are fixed-income instruments with a coupon, face value and maturity. Types include government securities (G-secs), corporate bonds, convertible and non-convertible debentures, zero-coupon bonds, and tax-free bonds. Bond prices move inversely to interest rates: when yields rise, prices fall. Credit ratings (AAA to D) show default risk, and rating agencies are regulated by SEBI. Government bonds are regarded as having the lowest credit risk. Preference shareholders get a fixed dividend and priority over equity holders in repayment, but rank below creditors. Under section 53 of the IBC, 2016, the liquidation waterfall places secured creditors and workmen's dues above unsecured financial creditors, with equity last. The Companies Act, 2013 governs the issue of shares and debentures, and SEBI regulates listed securities. Debentures can be secured or unsecured, redeemable or irredeemable, and convertible or non-convertible. Related concepts UPSC may ask about include the yield curve, the repo rate's effect on bond yields, green bonds, sovereign gold bonds, masala bonds (rupee-denominated bonds issued overseas), perpetual bonds (such as AT1 bonds), the corporate bond market and the risk-return tradeoff. Equity can also be raised through IPOs, FPOs, rights issues and bonus shares.

question: Consider the following statements : I India accounts for a very large portion of all equity option contracts traded globally thus exhibiting a great boom. Il. India’s stock market has grown rapidly in the recent past even overtaking Hong Kong’s at some point of time. Ill. There is no regulatory body either to warn the small investors about the risks of options trading or to act on unregistered financial advisors in this regard. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: This question combines Indian capital market trends with regulatory architecture. India's National Stock Exchange (NSE) has ranked first globally by number of equity option contracts traded, according to the Futures Industry Association (FIA), with a share often cited at around 70 to 80 percent of global contracts by volume. This is driven by weekly index options on Nifty and Bank Nifty and heavy retail participation. In January 2024, India's stock market capitalisation crossed that of Hong Kong, making it the world's fourth largest market after the US, China and Japan. Statement III is wrong because the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), set up under the SEBI Act 1992 (statutory status), is the regulator for securities markets. SEBI has published studies showing that about 90 percent of individual F&O traders lost money (FY22 about 89 percent, FY24 about 93 percent). It issues investor warnings and has acted against unregistered finfluencers and advisors under the Investment Advisers Regulations 2013. Elimination logic: once III is seen as false, options (b), (c) and (d) all fall away, leaving (a).
explanations: Correct: I and II are factually true, and III is false because SEBI exists and acts, so this is the only combination that fits.
Incorrect: it includes III, which wrongly claims that no regulator warns investors or acts on unregistered advisors.
Incorrect: it omits II, which is true (the Hong Kong overtaking), and includes III, which is false.
Incorrect: it includes III, which is false, so 'all three' cannot be correct.
keyfact: India leads the world in equity option contracts traded and overtook Hong Kong's market cap in 2024, but SEBI actively regulates and warns retail investors.
option_notes: I and II only: the correct combination here. It reflects India's lead in global options volumes (per FIA) and its overtaking of Hong Kong in market capitalisation in January 2024. Both are frequently cited in discussions of retail participation in derivatives and of the SEBI's measures to protect investors in the F&O segment.

II and III only: this would have been right only if India's market overtaking Hong Kong's were true and a regulatory vacuum existed. Statement II is true, but III is wrong because SEBI regulates securities markets, advisers and intermediaries. SEBI also issues warnings about the risks of options trading and takes action against unregistered advisors.

I and III only: this pairs the true options-volume claim with the false claim of no regulator. SEBI, a statutory body under the SEBI Act 1992 and headquartered in Mumbai, oversees stock exchanges, brokers, mutual funds and advisers, and it can issue orders, impose penalties and bar persons from the market.

I, II and III: this would require every statement to be correct. Statements I and II are correct, but III is false, because India has a robust regulator in SEBI, supported by the RBI (for banks and money markets), IRDAI (insurance) and PFRDA (pensions) in other financial segments.
related: NSE has topped FIA's global ranking for number of equity derivatives contracts traded since 2019.
India's stock market cap overtook Hong Kong's in January 2024, making it the fourth largest globally.
SEBI got statutory status through the SEBI Act 1992; it was set up in 1988 and is headquartered in Mumbai.
SEBI studies show about 9 in 10 individual F&O traders make losses.
In October 2024 SEBI restricted weekly expiries to one benchmark index per exchange.
Index options on Nifty began trading on NSE in June 2001.
SEBI regulates investment advisers under the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations 2013.
India adopted T+1 settlement in equities in January 2023.
statements: 1 — Correct: India accounts for a very large share of global equity option contracts traded. The Futures Industry Association (FIA) data show that NSE has been the world's largest derivatives exchange by number of contracts traded since 2019. Index options, especially weekly expiries on Nifty, Bank Nifty and Sensex, dominate the volumes. Retail participation surged after the pandemic through discount brokers and apps. SEBI has taken curbs in response: in October 2024 it raised contract sizes, restricted weekly expiries to one benchmark per exchange, and increased margin requirements to protect retail traders.

2 — Correct: India's stock market has grown rapidly and overtook Hong Kong's in market capitalisation. In January 2024, India's combined market cap reached about 4.33 trillion US dollars, exceeding Hong Kong's roughly 4.29 trillion, making India the fourth largest equity market globally. Drivers include strong domestic SIP flows, rising demat accounts (over 15 crore), FPI inflows and robust earnings. India now sits behind the US, China and Japan. The Sensex and Nifty have hit record highs repeatedly in recent years.

3 — Incorrect: A regulator does exist. SEBI, established in 1988 as an executive body and given statutory status by the SEBI Act 1992, protects investor interests and regulates the securities market. It publishes studies on losses in F&O trading (about 93 percent of individual traders lost money in FY22 to FY24, with aggregate losses of about 1.8 lakh crore rupees). It regulates investment advisers and research analysts and has taken action against unregistered advisors and finfluencers, barring them from the market and ordering disgorgement of gains. It also runs investor awareness campaigns and the SCORES complaint platform.
summary: The answer is (a): statements I and II are correct and statement III is incorrect. India dominates global equity options volumes and its stock market overtook Hong Kong's in market capitalisation, but SEBI is the regulator that warns investors and acts against unregistered advisors.
topic_notes: Indian equity derivatives: NSE launched index futures in June 2000 and index options in June 2001, followed by stock options (2001) and stock futures (2001). The Futures Industry Association (FIA) ranks exchanges by contracts traded; NSE has been first in equity options for years, with a global share by volume often cited above 70 percent. Weekly options on Nifty were introduced in 2019. Retail participation rose sharply after 2020 with discount brokers (Zerodha, Groww, Upstox) and demat accounts crossing 15 crore. SEBI studies (FY22, FY23, FY24) found that roughly 90 percent or more of individual F&O traders incurred losses, with total losses of about 1.8 lakh crore rupees in FY22 to FY24. In October 2024 SEBI announced stricter F&O norms: higher contract sizes (15 lakh to 20 lakh at introduction), only one weekly expiry per exchange, upfront collection of option premiums, removal of calendar spread benefit on expiry day and intraday monitoring of position limits. SEBI regulates under the SEBI Act 1992, the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act 1956 and the Depositories Act 1996. It is led by a Chairperson and has a Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) for appeals. The Investment Advisers Regulations 2013 and Research Analysts Regulations 2014 require registration; unregistered finfluencers have been barred. In January 2024 India's market cap overtook Hong Kong's, making India the fourth largest equity market. Related angles: FPI regulations, SEBI's T+1 settlement (the first in the world for a large market, completed in January 2023), the MSCI and FTSE bond/equity index inclusions, the Nifty 50 and Sensex composition, and the IPO boom.

ocr: Consider the following statements : Statement I : Circular economy reduces the emissions of greenhouse gases. Statement II : Circular economy reduces the use of raw materials as inputs. Statement III : Circular economy reduces wastage in the production process. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? (a) Both Statement II and Statement III are correct and both of them explain Statement I (b) Both Statement II and Statement III are correct but only one of them explains Statement I (c) Only one of the Statements II and III is correct and that explains Statement
subject: Environment
detail: A circular economy replaces the linear 'take-make-use-dispose' model with a closed loop: design out waste, keep products and materials in use, and regenerate natural systems (Ellen MacArthur Foundation framework). Because recycled, reused and remanufactured inputs substitute for virgin material, extraction and primary processing fall. Mining, smelting, cement, steel, aluminium and petrochemical production are highly energy-intensive, so using less virgin material directly cuts GHG emissions. Reducing wastage in production through efficient design, industrial symbiosis, by-product reuse and lower scrap means less energy and fewer inputs per unit of output, and less landfill methane. So II and III are each factually correct and each is a causal route to Statement I. Elimination: (d) fails because both II and III are the very definition of circularity. (c) fails because both are correct. (b) fails because each independently explains I; there is no reason to exclude either. Only (a) fits. In India, the 3Rs (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle), LiFE, EPR rules and NITI Aayog's circular economy action plans are the policy anchors.
explanations: Correct: II and III are both true statements, and each independently links to I (less extraction and less waste both mean lower energy use and emissions), so both explain it.
Incorrect: There is no basis to say only one of II and III explains I. Reduced raw material use and reduced wastage both cut emissions.
Incorrect: This wrongly treats one of II and III as incorrect, but both accurately describe circular economy outcomes.
Incorrect: This denies both II and III, yet they are the central features of a circular economy.
keyfact: Circular economy = less virgin raw material + less waste + longer product life, which together reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
option_notes: Both II and III correct and both explain I: This is the official answer. It reflects that circular economy outcomes (less virgin input, less waste) are the mechanisms behind lower emissions. Remember circularity rests on three principles: design out waste and pollution, keep products and materials in use, and regenerate natural systems. Related policy: India's EPR framework under the Plastic, E-waste and Battery rules, and the National Resource Efficiency Policy.

Both correct but only one explains I: This option would imply one of the two outcomes has no link to emissions. That is wrong, since both raw material extraction and wasteful production are energy and carbon intensive. It is a typical UPSC trap for distinguishing 'correct' from 'correct explanation'. Do not accept a split unless the fact clearly lacks a causal link.

Only one of II and III is correct and explains I: This implies that one of the claims is factually false. Both are standard textbook effects of a circular economy. In UPSC statement questions, check each statement's factual accuracy first, then the explanatory link.

Neither II nor III is correct: This would contradict the definition of circular economy. It shifts from the linear take-make-dispose model to closed loops that cut raw material use and waste. Circular economy is promoted by the UN Environment Programme, the EU Circular Economy Action Plan (2020), and India's NITI Aayog, MoEFCC and the LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) mission.
related: Circular economy replaces the take-make-use-dispose linear model with closed-loop resource use.
LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) was launched by India at COP26 in Glasgow, 2021.
E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 introduced EPR certificates for producers.
Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 mandate EPR and recycled-content targets.
Kalundborg in Denmark is the classic example of industrial symbiosis.
The Voluntary Vehicle Fleet Modernisation (Scrappage) Policy was launched in 2021.
GOBARdhan converts cattle dung and organic waste into biogas and compost.
India's net-zero target year is 2070, announced at COP26.
statements: I — Correct: Circular economy cuts GHG emissions by lowering virgin extraction, energy-heavy primary processing and landfill methane. Facts: Circular strategies are estimated to address a large share of global emissions tied to materials and products (the Circularity Gap Report shows the world is under 10% circular). Steel, cement, aluminium and plastics are key sectors. Waste management is a major methane source, and recycling aluminium saves roughly 90%+ of the energy compared with primary production. It supports India's NDCs and net-zero by 2070 goal.

II — Correct: Reuse, recycling and remanufacturing substitute secondary materials for virgin raw materials, reducing resource extraction. Facts: This is the 'resource efficiency' pillar. Examples include recycling metals, e-waste urban mining, using fly ash in cement and bricks, and using steel slag in construction. India's Resource Efficiency policy drafts, the Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 (recycled content targets) and the vehicle scrappage policy (2021) aim to recover materials and reduce import dependence on critical minerals.

III — Correct: Circular design reduces scrap and by-product waste during production through efficient processes, industrial symbiosis and closed-loop manufacturing. Facts: 'Waste is designed out' is a core principle. Industrial symbiosis, where one firm's waste is another's input (Kalundborg, Denmark, is the classic example), lowers disposal costs and raw input needs. In India, zero-liquid-discharge norms, the Plastic Waste Management Rules and Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) push producers to minimise waste and take responsibility for end-of-life products.
summary: The correct answer is (a). A circular economy keeps materials in use through reuse, recycling, remanufacturing and design for longevity. This reduces virgin raw-material input (Statement II) and production waste (Statement III), and both effects lower emissions, so both explain Statement I.
topic_notes:
Circular economy (CE) is an economic model that decouples growth from resource consumption. The linear model of take-make-use-dispose is replaced by loops of reuse, repair, refurbishment, remanufacture and recycling. The Ellen MacArthur Foundation's three principles are: eliminate waste and pollution by design, keep products and materials in use, and regenerate natural systems. The 'butterfly diagram' separates the biological cycle (composting, anaerobic digestion) from the technical cycle (reuse, remanufacture, recycling). The R-hierarchy runs from Refuse, Rethink and Reduce through Reuse, Repair, Refurbish, Remanufacture and Repurpose to Recycle and Recover.

Benefits: lower GHG emissions, reduced import dependence for metals and critical minerals, job creation, lower pollution and less landfill. Challenges: informal sector dominance in India, weak segregation at source, the cost of recycled material, and rebound effects.

India: The Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 (amended 2022) introduced EPR for plastic packaging. E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 set EPR with a certificate system. Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 include EPR and recycled-content targets. The Voluntary Vehicle Fleet Modernisation (Scrappage) Policy 2021 and Swachh Bharat Mission 2.0 support circularity. NITI Aayog has formed CE committees and action plans for 11 focus waste streams, including municipal solid waste, scrap metals (ferrous and non-ferrous), tyre and rubber, used oil, lithium-ion batteries, e-waste, toxic and hazardous industrial waste, solar panels, gypsum, and agricultural waste. The LiFE mission (launched at COP26 in 2021) promotes mindful consumption. The GOBARdhan scheme converts biodegradable waste to biogas and compost.

Global: EU Circular Economy Action Plan (2020), the UN Environment Assembly's resolution to negotiate a global plastics treaty (2022), the Basel Convention on hazardous waste, and the Circularity Gap Report (world is about 7 to 9% circular).

question:
Consider the following statements :
I. Capital receipts create a liability or cause a reduction in the assets of the Government. Il. Borrowings and disinvestment are capital receipts.
III. Interest received on loans creates a liability of the Government. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: Government receipts in the Union Budget (Article 112 and the Annual Financial Statement) are classified as revenue receipts and capital receipts. Revenue receipts neither create a liability nor reduce an asset. They include tax revenue (income tax, corporation tax, GST, customs, excise) and non-tax revenue (interest receipts, dividends and profits, fees, grants). Capital receipts either create a liability or reduce an asset. Examples are borrowings (market loans, external loans, T-bills, small savings, provident funds), recovery of loans and advances, and disinvestment or other PSU asset sales. Under the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 266), both categories are credited to the fund. Elimination logic: statement III is wrong because interest received is income earned on an asset (the loan given), so it is a non-tax revenue receipt and not a liability. That rules out (b), (c) and (d), leaving (a). Fiscal deficit equals total expenditure minus revenue receipts minus non-debt capital receipts. Revenue deficit equals revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts.
explanations: Correct: statements I and II are accurate and statement III is wrong, which matches this option.
Incorrect: it includes III, which is false because interest received is a revenue receipt, and it excludes I, which is true.
Incorrect: it includes III, which is false, and it leaves out II, which is true.
Incorrect: it includes III, which wrongly treats interest received as creating a liability.
keyfact: Capital receipts create a liability or reduce an asset (borrowings, disinvestment, loan recovery), while interest received is a non-tax revenue receipt.
option_notes: Option (a) I and II only: this is the correct combination. It reflects the standard Budget classification in which capital receipts are loans taken (liabilities) or asset sales and recoveries, and borrowings and disinvestment are the main examples. The classification follows the Annual Financial Statement under Article 112, and receipts are credited to the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 266. Capital receipts finance the fiscal deficit. Non-debt capital receipts include loan recoveries and disinvestment, and debt-creating ones include market borrowings.

Option (b) II and III only: this is wrong because III misclassifies interest received. Interest received on loans given by the government is a non-tax revenue receipt and creates no liability. The option is half-right because II is true. Non-tax revenue also covers dividends, profits, the RBI surplus and fees for services. Revenue receipts are the sum of tax and non-tax revenue. The Budget shows them separately from capital receipts in the Receipt Budget.

Option (c) I and III only: this is wrong because III is false. Statement I is correct on the definition of capital receipts, but interest received is revenue income from the government's assets. It does not add to liabilities. A liability is created when the government borrows, for example through dated securities, T-bills or external loans, and interest is then paid on it as revenue expenditure. Interest payments are a major part of the Union Budget.

Option (d) I, II and III: this is wrong because it accepts all three statements, including the incorrect III. The test of a capital receipt is whether it creates a liability or reduces an asset. Interest received does neither, so it is a revenue receipt. UPSC often tests such classification traps. Remember that tax revenue, interest receipts, dividends and grants are revenue items, while borrowings, loan recoveries and disinvestment are capital items.
related: Revenue receipts neither create a liability nor reduce an asset; tax revenue and non-tax revenue are the two parts.
Borrowings, recovery of loans and disinvestment are capital receipts.
Fiscal deficit = total expenditure minus revenue receipts minus non-debt capital receipts.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments.
Article 112 requires the Annual Financial Statement (Budget) to be laid before Parliament.
The Consolidated Fund of India is under Article 266(1), the Contingency Fund under Article 267 and the Public Account under Article 266(2).
DIPAM under the Finance Ministry handles disinvestment.
Interest paid by the government is revenue expenditure, while interest received is non-tax revenue.
statements: 1 — Correct: Capital receipts either create a liability (borrowings) or reduce assets (disinvestment, loan recovery). Capital receipts are of two types: debt-creating (market borrowings, external aid, small savings, T-bills) and non-debt-creating (recovery of loans, disinvestment, miscellaneous capital receipts). The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003 governs deficit targets, and the fiscal deficit is financed by debt-creating capital receipts. Asset sales are a one-time reduction in the government's stock of assets, and these receipts are shown in the Budget's Receipt Budget.

2 — Correct: Borrowings and disinvestment are both capital receipts. Borrowings create a liability to repay with interest. Disinvestment is the sale of government equity in PSUs, which reduces assets. It is shown under miscellaneous capital receipts. The DIPAM (Department of Investment and Public Asset Management) under the Finance Ministry handles it. Disinvestment targets are set in each Budget, and the 2021 policy classified PSUs as strategic and non-strategic. Air India was sold to the Tata group in 2022. Borrowings are mostly through dated securities issued by the RBI.

3 — Incorrect: Interest received on loans is a non-tax revenue receipt, not a liability. The government earns it on loans it has given to states, UTs, PSUs and others, so it is income on an asset. Revenue receipts do not create liabilities or reduce assets. Other non-tax revenues include dividends and profits (including the RBI surplus transfer), fees, fines, and grants. By contrast, interest paid by the government is a revenue expenditure and forms a large part of the Budget (interest payments are about 20% of expenditure).
summary: The answer is (a): statements I and II are correct and statement III is incorrect. Capital receipts either create a liability (borrowings) or reduce government assets (disinvestment, loan recovery), whereas interest received on loans is a revenue receipt that creates no liability.
topic_notes: Union Budget receipts are classified into revenue receipts and capital receipts. Revenue receipts do not create a liability or reduce an asset. They have two parts. Tax revenue includes direct taxes (income tax, corporation tax) and indirect taxes (GST, customs, Union excise duty), net of the share devolved to states under Finance Commission recommendations (Article 280). Non-tax revenue includes interest receipts, dividends and profits (including the RBI surplus), fees, fines, and grants and external aid received. Capital receipts either create a liability or reduce an asset. Debt-creating receipts include market borrowings (dated securities and T-bills), external borrowings, and small savings, provident fund and other liabilities. Non-debt capital receipts include recovery of loans and advances, disinvestment and other PSU asset sales. The deficit concepts are linked to these categories. Revenue deficit equals revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. Fiscal deficit equals total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings, so it equals borrowing requirement. Primary deficit equals fiscal deficit minus interest payments. Effective revenue deficit equals revenue deficit minus grants for creation of capital assets. The FRBM Act 2003 set deficit targets, and the 2018 amendment adopted a debt-to-GDP anchor. The N.K. Singh Committee (2017) reviewed FRBM and recommended a debt ceiling of 60% of GDP for the general government (40% for the Centre, 20% for states). Under Article 292 the Centre can borrow on the Consolidated Fund's security within limits set by Parliament, and Article 293 covers state borrowing. Expenditure is similarly classified as revenue expenditure (salaries, subsidies, interest payments) or capital expenditure (creation of assets). Possible future angles are what counts as a revenue or capital item, how the deficits are calculated, the Consolidated, Contingency and Public Accounts funds, and disinvestment policy.

question:
Consider the following statements about Raja Ram Mohan Roy :
I. He possessed great love and respect for the traditional philosophical systems of the East. Il. He desired his countrymen to accept the rational and scientific approach and the principle of human dignity and social equality of all men and women. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Art & Culture
detail: Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1772-1833) is called the 'Father of the Indian Renaissance' and the 'Herald of a New Age'. He combined deep respect for Indian philosophical heritage with modern rationalism. He studied the Upanishads and the Vedanta, translated them into Bengali and English, and argued that true Hinduism was monotheistic. Statement I is therefore correct. He was also fluent in Persian and Arabic, and he drew on Islamic monotheism (Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin) and on Christian ethics (The Precepts of Jesus). He founded the Atmiya Sabha (1815) and the Brahmo Sabha (1828), which became the Brahmo Samaj. He campaigned against sati (the abolition came through Regulation XVII of 1829 under Bentinck), polytheism, idolatry, caste rigidity and child marriage. He supported women's property rights and widow remarriage, and favoured modern English and scientific education (letter to Lord Amherst, 1823). He also defended freedom of the press. Statement II is therefore correct as well. Elimination logic: since both statements reflect his syncretic, rational-humanist reformism, options (a), (b) and (d) fail.
explanations: Wrong: it ignores Statement II, which is also correct because Roy promoted rationalism, science and equality.
Wrong: it ignores Statement I, which is correct because Roy deeply respected Vedanta and the Upanishads.
Right: both statements accurately describe Roy's synthesis of Eastern philosophy with modern rational, humanist values.
Wrong: at least one statement, in fact both, is correct, so this cannot hold.
keyfact: Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1772-1833), 'Father of the Indian Renaissance', blended reverence for Vedanta and the Upanishads with rationalism, science and equality; he founded the Brahmo Sabha in 1828.
option_notes: Option (a), 'I only': this would describe a purely traditionalist reformer. Roy did respect Vedanta, but he was not purely traditionalist; he also advocated Western science and rationalism, so this option is incomplete. Traditionalist-leaning figures include Dayananda Saraswati, who called for a return to the Vedas, and the Orientalists, who favoured classical learning.

Option (b), 'II only': this would describe a purely Westernising reformer. Young Bengal and Henry Derozio (Derozians) were radical rationalists who often rejected tradition. Roy differed because he grounded his reforms in Upanishadic and Vedantic texts, so this option wrongly drops his respect for Eastern philosophy.

Option (c), 'Both I and II': this is the official answer. It captures Roy's synthesis, in which he honoured the Indian philosophical heritage while promoting reason, scientific education, human dignity and gender equality. This synthesis is why he is called the 'Father of the Indian Renaissance' and the 'Herald of a New Age'.

Option (d), 'Neither I nor II': this would mean Roy rejected both Indian philosophy and rationalism. That is plainly false; he translated the Upanishads and wrote to Lord Amherst in 1823 in favour of modern science education, so this option contradicts well-known facts.
related: Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Sabha in 1828, and it was renamed Brahmo Samaj in 1830.
Sati was abolished by Regulation XVII of 1829 under Governor-General William Bentinck.
Roy's Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin (Persian) attacked idolatry and polytheism.
Sambad Kaumudi (1821) was his Bengali weekly, and Mirat-ul-Akbar (1822) his Persian journal.
Akbar II conferred the title 'Raja' on him, and he went to England in 1830.
Debendranath Tagore founded the Tattvabodhini Sabha (1839) and revitalised the Brahmo Samaj.
Keshab Chandra Sen split the Samaj to form the Brahmo Samaj of India in 1866.
Roy supported Hindu College (1817) but his own Vedanta College (1825) combined Indian and Western learning.
statements: I — Correct: Roy revered Eastern philosophy, notably the Upanishads and Vedanta. He translated the Vedas and Upanishads into Bengali, Hindi and English to show that the original Hindu texts taught monotheism. He published Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin (c.1803-04) in Persian, with an Arabic preface, against idolatry. He wrote Gifts to Monotheists in a similar vein. He rejected later Hindu ritual and polytheism, not Indian philosophy itself. He started the Atmiya Sabha in 1815 to discuss such ideas, and in 1828 the Brahmo Sabha, which became the Brahmo Samaj in 1830. He opposed Orientalist-only education but still valued the Indian tradition.

II — Correct: Roy championed reason, science and the equal dignity of all people. He wrote to Lord Amherst in 1823 asking for modern sciences (mathematics, chemistry, anatomy) rather than Sanskrit-only education. He backed the Hindu College (1817) and founded the Anglo-Hindu School (1822) and the Vedanta College (1825). He campaigned against sati (banned in 1829), polygamy and caste discrimination, and he supported women's inheritance rights. He supported press freedom, protesting the 1823 Press Ordinance. He started Sambad Kaumudi (1821) and Mirat-ul-Akbar (1822). He visited England in 1830 as Mughal emperor Akbar II's envoy, with the title 'Raja', and died in Bristol in 1833.
summary: The answer is (c): both statements are correct. Raja Ram Mohan Roy respected the traditional philosophical systems of the East, especially the Upanishads and Vedanta. He also urged Indians to adopt reason, a scientific outlook, human dignity and social equality for men and women.
topic_notes: Raja Ram Mohan Roy (born 1772 at Radhanagar, Bengal; died 1833 at Bristol) is regarded as the pioneer of social and religious reform in modern India. He worked for the East India Company as a revenue official before retiring in 1814 and settling in Calcutta. He founded the Atmiya Sabha (1815), the Calcutta Unitarian Committee (1821) and the Brahmo Sabha (1828), which became the Brahmo Samaj in 1830 (the Samaj's trust deed was set up in 1830). The Samaj opposed idol worship, rituals and priestly dominance, and it rejected the belief in avatars. Key works: Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin (1803-04), The Precepts of Jesus (1820), and Gaudiya Vyakaran. Journals: Sambad Kaumudi (Bengali, 1821) and Mirat-ul-Akbar (Persian, 1822). Reforms: he opposed sati, which led to Bentinck's Regulation XVII of 1829. He campaigned for widow remarriage, women's property rights, and against child marriage and polygamy. In education he backed modern English and scientific teaching: Hindu College (1817, with David Hare), the Anglo-Hindu School (1822), the Vedanta College (1825), and his 1823 letter to Lord Amherst. He argued for press freedom against the 1823 Press Ordinance and wrote an appeal on that. In 1830 he went to England as the envoy of the Mughal emperor Akbar II, who gave him the title 'Raja'. He also advocated the separation of the executive and judiciary, and the Indianisation of services. Later Brahmo leaders: Debendranath Tagore (Tattvabodhini Sabha, 1839) and Keshab Chandra Sen (Brahmo Samaj of India, 1866). The Adi Brahmo Samaj and the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj (1878) came after splits. Other reformers to compare: Dayananda (Arya Samaj, 1875), Vidyasagar, Ranade (Prarthana Samaj, 1867), and Jyotiba Phule (Satyashodhak Samaj, 1873).

question:
Consider the following subjects with regard to Non-Cooperation Programme :
I. Boycott of law-courts and foreign cloth
II. Observance of strict non-violence Ill. Retention of titles and honours without using them in public
IV. Establishment of Panchayats for settling disputes How many of the above were parts of Non-Cooperation Programme?
subject: Modern History
detail: The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) was approved at the Calcutta Special Session of the Congress (September 1920) and confirmed at Nagpur (December 1920). It was launched with the Khilafat agitation after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (April 1919), the Hunter Committee report, and the Rowlatt Act. Gandhi's programme had a negative side (boycott) and a constructive side. Negative: surrender of titles and honorary offices, resignation from nominated local-body posts, boycott of legislative councils, government functions, courts, schools and foreign cloth.
