keyfact: Article 6 of the Paris Agreement: 6.2 bilateral ITMO trading, 6.4 UN-supervised crediting mechanism (PACM), 6.8 non-market approaches.
option_notes: Option (a) says both statements are correct and both explain Statement I. This matches Article 6's structure: markets under 6.2 and 6.4, and non-market approaches under 6.8. It was finalised in the Paris rulebook through COP26 (Glasgow) and COP29 (Baku). It is the official answer.

Option (b) says both statements are correct but only one explains Statement I. It is wrong because market and non-market elements together make up Article 6. Both elements drive the global debate on carbon pricing, finance and cooperation, so neither can be treated as irrelevant to Statement I.

Option (c) says only one of Statements II and III is correct. It is wrong because Article 6 includes both carbon markets (6.2, 6.4) and non-market approaches (6.8). A student who knows only the market side might wrongly pick this option.

Option (d) says neither statement is correct. It is wrong because Article 6 expressly covers both markets and non-markets. It would be true only if Article 6 dealt with something unrelated, such as adaptation finance alone, and it does not.
related: Article 6.2 allows bilateral trading of ITMOs with corresponding adjustments.
Article 6.4 creates the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism, the successor to the Kyoto CDM.
Article 6.8 provides a framework for non-market approaches.
The Paris Agreement was adopted at COP21 (2015) and entered into force on 4 November 2016.
India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme was notified in 2023 under the Energy Conservation Act.
COP29 in Baku (2024) agreed the Article 6 rules and a USD 300 billion per year climate finance goal.
India's net-zero target is 2070, announced at COP26 in Glasgow.
The Loss and Damage Fund was agreed at COP27 and operationalised at COP28.
statements: 1 — Correct: Article 6 is a central topic in global climate and sustainable development discussions because it governs how countries cooperate to meet their targets. It was the last major piece of the Paris rulebook to be settled, after years of disagreement at COP25 (Madrid), COP26 (Glasgow, 2021) and COP29 (Baku, 2024). It attracts attention for carbon pricing, climate finance flows, and environmental integrity concerns such as double counting and the quality of credits. Developing countries, including India, follow it closely for investment and technology opportunities.

2 — Correct: Articles 6.2 and 6.4 form the carbon market part of the Paris Agreement. Article 6.2 lets countries trade ITMOs bilaterally, with corresponding adjustments so that a reduction is not counted by both the seller and the buyer. Article 6.4 creates the Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism, overseen by a Supervisory Body, as the successor to the Kyoto Protocol's CDM. It aims for a net decrease in global emissions, and the transition of old CDM projects was a negotiated issue. The mechanism is open to public and private participation.

3 — Correct: Article 6.8 recognises non-market approaches (NMA) to help countries implement their NDCs without carbon trading. These include finance, technology transfer, capacity building, mitigation, adaptation and sustainable development cooperation. A 'Framework for Non-Market Approaches' was established under it, together with a work programme. The approach is driven by developing-country demands, especially from groups such as the Like-Minded Developing Countries, which prefer cooperation to market offsets. Article 6.8 stresses that these approaches should be coordinated and transparent.
summary: The answer is (a). Article 6 of the Paris Agreement covers both market-based cooperation (Articles 6.2 and 6.4, i.e. carbon markets) and non-market approaches (Article 6.8). Both Statement II and Statement III are therefore correct, and together they explain why Article 6 is so prominent in climate and sustainable development discussions.
topic_notes: The Paris Agreement was adopted at COP21 in December 2015 and entered into force on 4 November 2016. Its goal is to hold the global temperature rise well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. Countries submit Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) every five years, and the Global Stocktake reviews collective progress. The first Global Stocktake concluded at COP28 in Dubai (2023). Article 6 enables voluntary cooperation to raise ambition. Article 6.2 covers decentralised bilateral trading of ITMOs with corresponding adjustments. Article 6.4 creates the centralised Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (PACM), supervised by a UN body and replacing the Kyoto Protocol's CDM. Article 6.8 sets out non-market approaches. Key concerns include double counting, additionality, environmental integrity, and a share of proceeds for adaptation (5% of credits under 6.4, plus a contribution to the Adaptation Fund). Carbon markets differ in kind: compliance markets such as the EU Emissions Trading System, and voluntary markets. India launched its Carbon Credit Trading Scheme in 2023 under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022, and the Bureau of Energy Efficiency oversees its implementation. Other related angles are the Kyoto Protocol (1997) mechanisms (CDM, Joint Implementation, Emissions Trading), the Loss and Damage Fund (agreed at COP27, operationalised at COP28), the New Collective Quantified Goal on climate finance (USD 300 billion per year by 2035 agreed at COP29), and India's NDC targets (net zero by 2070, 50% non-fossil electric capacity by 2030, and a reduction in emission intensity of GDP of 45% from 2005 levels by 2030).

question: Which one of the following launched the Nature Solutions Finance Hub for Asia and the Pacific’?
options: The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD)
subject: Economy
detail: The Nature Solutions Finance Hub for Asia and the Pacific was launched by the ADB during COP28 at Dubai in December 2023. It is a platform to help developing member countries design, prepare and finance bankable nature-based projects, such as mangrove and forest restoration, sustainable agriculture, coastal and marine ecosystem protection and watershed management. It aims to crowd in private capital, blended finance and carbon or biodiversity credits, and to offer technical assistance and project preparation support. ADB's reported target was to mobilise about US$3 billion in this area, and the hub supports its Climate Change Action Plan and its goal of 100 percent commitments aligned with the Paris Agreement. ADB is headquartered in Manila, was founded in 1966, and has 68 members. Elimination logic: AIIB (Beijing, 2016) focuses on infrastructure and has no Asia-Pacific nature hub. NDB (Shanghai, BRICS, 2015) funds sustainable infrastructure in emerging economies. IBRD is a global World Bank arm and would not use an Asia-Pacific regional label. The regional wording 'Asia and the Pacific' is ADB's own usage.
explanations: Correct: ADB launched the Nature Solutions Finance Hub for Asia and the Pacific at COP28 in Dubai in December 2023.
Wrong: AIIB is an infrastructure-focused multilateral lender, and it did not launch this hub.
Wrong: NDB is the BRICS bank, global in its focus on emerging economies, and has no such regional hub.
Wrong: IBRD is the World Bank's global lending arm, not a regional Asia-Pacific body, and did not launch this hub.
keyfact: The Nature Solutions Finance Hub for Asia and the Pacific was launched by the ADB at COP28, Dubai, in December 2023.
option_notes: The Asian Development Bank is a regional development bank established in 1966 and headquartered in Manila, Philippines. It has 68 members, of which 49 are from Asia and the Pacific. Japan and the US are its largest shareholders, and its presidents have traditionally been Japanese. It lends to developing member countries, gives grants and technical assistance, and runs climate and nature finance initiatives. India is a member and a major borrower.

The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank is a multilateral development bank proposed by China, with its Articles of Agreement in force from December 2015 and operations starting in January 2016. It is headquartered in Beijing, and its first president was Jin Liqun. It finances sustainable infrastructure, connectivity and energy projects. It has over 100 approved members, and India is the second-largest shareholder after China.

The New Development Bank was set up by the BRICS countries (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa), agreed at the 2014 Fortaleza summit and established in 2015. It is headquartered in Shanghai, with a regional office in Johannesburg. Its first president was K.V. Kamath. It funds sustainable infrastructure in emerging economies, and new members include Bangladesh, UAE, Egypt and Algeria.

The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development is the original World Bank institution, created at Bretton Woods in 1944 and headquartered in Washington, DC. It lends to middle-income and creditworthy low-income governments. It is part of the World Bank Group, along with IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID. It has 189 members and does not use regional hubs of this name.
related: ADB was founded in 1966 and is headquartered in Manila.
AIIB is headquartered in Beijing and began operations in 2016.
NDB is the BRICS bank, headquartered in Shanghai.
COP28 was held in Dubai, UAE, in December 2023.
The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework has a 30 by 30 target.
The Loss and Damage Fund was operationalised at COP28.
IBRD was created at Bretton Woods in 1944 and is part of the World Bank Group.
India's Green Credit Programme was launched in 2023.
summary: The answer is (a) the Asian Development Bank (ADB). ADB launched the Nature Solutions Finance Hub for Asia and the Pacific at COP28 in Dubai (December 2023) to mobilise public and private finance for nature-based solutions and biodiversity in the region.
topic_notes: Nature-based solutions (NbS) are actions that protect, sustainably manage and restore natural or modified ecosystems while addressing societal challenges such as climate change, food security and disaster risk. The UN Environment Assembly adopted an NbS definition in 2022. Development banks are increasingly tying finance to nature. ADB's Nature Solutions Finance Hub, launched at COP28 (Dubai, 30 Nov to 12 Dec 2023), supports project preparation, blended finance and private investment, linked to ADB's Healthy Oceans and Sustainable Blue Economy action plan (2019) and its Strategy 2030. ADB also runs the Asia Pacific Climate Finance Fund and the Ocean Finance Framework. Related global frameworks: the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (December 2022, COP15), with its 30 by 30 target and a goal of US$200 billion per year for biodiversity; the Global Environment Facility and its Global Biodiversity Framework Fund; the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD); and the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure. India-specific angles include the Green Credit Programme (2023), Mission LiFE, the Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats and Tangible Incomes (MISHTI), the Compensatory Afforestation Fund, the National Mission for a Green India, and India's updated NDCs. UPSC often asks which institution launched or hosts what, so remember headquarters, founding years and membership of ADB, AIIB, NDB, IBRD and IMF, and the COP28 outcomes such as the Loss and Damage Fund and the Global Stocktake.

question:
With reference to ‘Direct Air Capture’, an emerging technology, which of the following statements is/are correct?
I. It can be used as a way of carbon sequestration. Il. It can be a valuable approach for plastic production and in food processing. Ill. In aviation, it can be a source of carbon for combining with hydrogen to create synthetic low-carbon fuel. Select the correct answer using the code given below
options: None of the above statements is correct
subject: Environment
detail: Direct Air Capture (DAC) is a Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) technology that uses chemical processes (liquid solvent systems or solid sorbent filters) to extract CO2 from ambient air, where its concentration is only about 420 ppm. The CO2 is then released as a concentrated stream by applying heat, and can be handled in two ways. First, it can be stored permanently in deep geological formations or mineralised in basalt, which is DAC with storage (DACCS) and counts as carbon sequestration; this makes statement I correct. Second, it can be used (DACCU) as a feedstock: in chemicals and polymers (including plastics), in carbonated beverages and food processing, in greenhouse horticulture and in concrete curing; this makes statement II correct. In aviation, captured CO2 combined with green hydrogen (from electrolysis using renewable power) gives synthetic e-fuels or power-to-liquid sustainable aviation fuel via Fischer-Tropsch or methanol routes; this makes statement III correct. Since all three are valid, (c) is right, and (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated. Key facts: DAC is energy-intensive and costly, and it differs from point-source capture at power plants or factories. Examples: Climeworks' Orca and Mammoth plants in Iceland, and 1PointFive's Stratos plant in Texas.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out statement III, which is also correct, since DAC CO2 plus hydrogen gives synthetic aviation fuel.
Wrong: statement III is correct, but I and II are also correct, so it is incomplete.
Correct: all three statements are accurate: sequestration, use in plastics and food processing, and synthetic fuel with hydrogen for aviation.
Wrong: the statements are accurate, so 'none correct' cannot hold.
keyfact: Direct Air Capture pulls CO2 from ambient air for storage (sequestration) or use (plastics, food, drinks, e-fuels with hydrogen), so all three statements are correct.
option_notes: Options I and II only: this would mean DAC supports sequestration and industrial uses but not fuels. It is wrong here because CO2 from DAC is also used for e-fuels. It still reflects the two real pathways, storage (DACCS) and utilisation (DACCU) in products like plastics, chemicals, beverages and greenhouses. Sequestration gives long-term removal, while most utilisation holds carbon only temporarily. The distinction matters in climate policy and carbon accounting, and the IPCC counts only durable storage as true removal.

Option III only: this would mean DAC's only role is making aviation fuel. It is wrong because storage and industrial use are also valid. The fuel pathway itself is real: CO2 plus green hydrogen gives e-fuel or power-to-liquid SAF via Fischer-Tropsch or methanol synthesis. Aviation is hard to electrify, so SAF matters for decarbonisation. ICAO's CORSIA and the EU's ReFuelEU Aviation mandate push SAF uptake. Cost and power demand are the limits.

Options I, II and III: this is the official answer. It reflects that DAC is a flexible platform technology. Captured CO2 can be stored geologically (DACCS), used in products (plastics, food, drinks, building materials) or turned into synthetic fuels with hydrogen. DAC is distinct from point-source capture because it works on dilute atmospheric CO2 (about 420 ppm), needs much energy, and can deliver negative emissions if powered by clean energy and paired with permanent storage.

None of the above: this would mean none of the three uses applies to DAC. It is wrong because all three are established applications. Such an option is typically a distractor in UPSC questions on emerging technology. The core idea to remember is that DAC is a CDR technology with two main routes, storage and utilisation, and each route has real projects and policy backing, though high cost and energy needs limit scale-up.
related: DAC is a Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) method, not an emission-avoidance one.
DACCS means DAC with geological storage; DACCU means DAC with utilisation.
Climeworks' Orca (2021) and Mammoth (2024) plants are in Iceland and use basalt mineralisation with Carbfix.
Atmospheric CO2 is about 420 ppm, so DAC is more energy-intensive than point-source capture.
E-fuel is made from captured CO2 plus green hydrogen via Fischer-Tropsch or methanol synthesis.
India's net-zero target is 2070; the National Green Hydrogen Mission was approved in 2023.
India's SAF blending targets are 1% in 2027 and 2% in 2028 for international flights.
BECCS combines bioenergy with carbon capture and storage to give negative emissions.
statements: I — Correct: DAC with geological storage or mineralisation is a recognised carbon sequestration and CDR method. DAC extracts CO2 from air with solvents or sorbents, concentrates it, and injects it deep underground into saline aquifers or basalt, where it mineralises. Climeworks' Orca (2021) and Mammoth (2024) plants in Iceland work with Carbfix. The IPCC treats DACCS as a CDR option needed for net-zero. It is costly, often $400-1000 per tonne, and energy-intensive. The US 45Q tax credit supports it, and the US DOE funds DAC hubs.

II — Correct: Captured CO2 is a feedstock for plastics and food processing. In carbon capture and utilisation (CCU), CO2 is turned into polymers such as polycarbonates and polyurethane, and into chemicals like methanol and urea. In food and drink it is used for carbonation, packaging gas and dry ice, and in greenhouses to boost plant growth. Using DAC CO2 rather than fossil CO2 lowers lifecycle emissions. However, utilisation usually gives short-lived storage unlike geological sequestration. Companies such as Climeworks supply CO2 to beverage firms and greenhouses.

III — Correct: In aviation, DAC CO2 is combined with green hydrogen to make synthetic fuel. Green hydrogen from renewable-powered electrolysis is reacted with captured CO2 to make syngas, then liquid hydrocarbons via Fischer-Tropsch, or methanol, giving e-kerosene or power-to-liquid sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). Because the CO2 came from air, the fuel can be close to carbon-neutral over its lifecycle. It can be blended with jet fuel in existing engines. ICAO's CORSIA and the EU's ReFuelEU Aviation mandate promote SAF. Costs and renewable power needs are major hurdles.
summary: The answer is (c): all three statements are correct. Direct Air Capture (DAC) pulls CO2 straight from ambient air, and the captured CO2 can be stored underground (sequestration) or used as a feedstock for products such as plastics, food and drink carbonation, and synthetic fuels.
topic_notes: Direct Air Capture (DAC) removes CO2 directly from the atmosphere. Two main designs exist. Liquid solvent systems use potassium hydroxide and high-temperature calcination, as in Carbon Engineering (1PointFive) plants. Solid sorbent systems use amine-based filters regenerated at about 80-100°C, as in Climeworks plants. Atmospheric CO2 is only about 420 ppm, so capture needs far more energy than capture from flue gas (about 4-15% CO2). DAC is a Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) technique, distinct from emission-reduction measures. Related terms: CCS (capture and storage), CCUS (capture, utilisation and storage), BECCS (bioenergy with CCS), DACCS and DACCU. Uses of captured CO2 include e-fuels and SAF, methanol, polymers and plastics, carbonated drinks, greenhouse enrichment, concrete mineralisation and enhanced oil recovery. Key projects: Climeworks Orca (Iceland, 2021, about 4,000 t/yr) and Mammoth (2024, about 36,000 t/yr nameplate), and Stratos in Texas (1PointFive, planned about 500,000 t/yr). Policy: the US 45Q tax credit gives up to $180 per tonne for DAC with storage, and the US DOE runs DAC hubs and a 'Carbon Negative Shot' target of under $100 per tonne. IPCC reports say CDR is needed to reach net-zero. India's context: net-zero by 2070, a National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023) and the IIT Bombay and NITI Aayog work on CCUS. Limits include cost (currently $400-1000 per tonne), energy demand, water use, and the risk of delaying emission cuts ('moral hazard'). Related UPSC angles: blue vs green hydrogen, SAF blending targets in India (1% in 2027 for international flights, 2% in 2028), CORSIA, the Article 6 carbon markets, and biochar and enhanced rock weathering as other CDR methods.

ocr: Regarding Peacock tarantula (Gooty tarantula), consider the following statements : I. It is an omnivorous crustacean. Il. Its natural habitat in India is only limited to some forest areas. Ill. In its natural habitat, it is an arboreal species. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? (a) I only (b) 1 and Ill (c) I only (d) 1 and Il [ P.T.O.
subject: Environment
detail: The Peacock tarantula, also called the Gooty tarantula or metallic tarantula (Poecilotheria metallica), is a strikingly blue-coloured tarantula endemic to India. It was first described by Pocock in 1899 from a specimen at Gooty, Anantapur district, Andhra Pradesh. It is an arachnid in the class Arachnida, phylum Arthropoda, so it is not a crustacean. Crustaceans such as crabs, prawns and lobsters belong to a different class. It is a carnivorous ambush predator that feeds on insects and small vertebrates, so it is not omnivorous. It is arboreal and lives in holes and crevices of old, tall trees. Its known range is extremely restricted, to the Nandyal-Cuddapah region of the Eastern Ghats in Andhra Pradesh, within reserve forest areas such as the Nandyal reserve forest. The IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered, and it is also in Schedule IV of the Wildlife (Protection) Act. Elimination logic: statement I is false, which removes (a) and (b). Of the remaining options, III is true, which removes (c) and leaves (d).
explanations: (a) I only — Wrong, because statement I is false (it is a carnivorous arachnid, not an omnivorous crustacean) and statements II and III are true.
(b) I and III — Wrong, because it includes the false statement I, and it leaves out the true statement II.
(c) II only — Wrong, because although II is true, III is also true (the spider is arboreal), so this option is incomplete.
(d) II and III — Correct, because its natural range is limited to some forest areas in Andhra Pradesh and it lives in trees.
keyfact: Gooty (Peacock) tarantula, Poecilotheria metallica: a carnivorous, arboreal arachnid, Critically Endangered, found only in a small area of Andhra Pradesh's Eastern Ghats.
option_notes: Statement I alone: this describes the tarantula as an omnivorous crustacean. It is wrong. Tarantulas are carnivorous arachnids of the order Araneae, family Theraphosidae. Crustaceans (crabs, shrimps, lobsters, barnacles) are a separate group of arthropods that are mostly aquatic and have two pairs of antennae. Arachnids (spiders, scorpions, mites, ticks) have no antennae and have eight legs.

Statements I and III: combines the false crustacean claim with the true arboreal claim. The Gooty tarantula is arboreal, which is typical of the genus Poecilotheria, whose members live in tree hollows in India and Sri Lanka. Because it also includes the false statement I, this combination is incorrect. Other Indian Poecilotheria species include P. regalis (Indian ornamental), P. rufilata and P. formosa.

Statement II alone: this says its Indian habitat is limited to some forest areas. This is true, since the species is found only in a small area of the Eastern Ghats in Andhra Pradesh (Nandyal and Cuddapah region). However, this option is incomplete because statement III is also true. The species is Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List and protected under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.

Statements II and III: the official correct answer. The Gooty tarantula, Poecilotheria metallica, lives only in a restricted patch of Eastern Ghats forest in Andhra Pradesh and is arboreal, living in tree hollows. It is carnivorous, which is why statement I is false. It is Critically Endangered, and it is notable for its metallic blue colouring. It is threatened by habitat loss and by the illegal pet trade.
related: Gooty tarantula scientific name: Poecilotheria metallica.
It is endemic to the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh and listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN.
Tarantulas are arachnids (class Arachnida), not insects or crustaceans.
Poecilotheria species are arboreal tarantulas found only in India and Sri Lanka.
The species was described by Pocock in 1899 and rediscovered in 2001.
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 protects scheduled species, and the Gooty tarantula is in Schedule IV.
Eastern Ghats are discontinuous hill ranges along the east coast, with Mahendragiri as one of the highest peaks.
Crustaceans include crabs, prawns and lobsters, and have two pairs of antennae.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Gooty tarantula is an arachnid, not a crustacean, and it is carnivorous rather than omnivorous. Tarantulas belong to phylum Arthropoda, class Arachnida, order Araneae, family Theraphosidae. They have eight legs, two body segments (cephalothorax and abdomen) and fangs that inject venom. They prey on insects, small lizards, frogs and occasionally small birds or rodents. Crustaceans (class Crustacea) have two pairs of antennae and mostly live in water. Examples are crabs, prawns and woodlice.

2 — Correct: Its natural habitat in India is very limited. It is found only in some forest areas of the Eastern Ghats in Andhra Pradesh, in the Nandyal and Cuddapah region near Gooty. It was thought extinct after the original 1899 specimen, and was rediscovered in 2001. The habitat is fragmented, degraded reserve forest of around 100 sq km. Threats include deforestation, tree felling and collection for the pet trade. The IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered, and the Andhra Pradesh forest department has proposed protecting its habitat.

3 — Correct: In its natural habitat it is arboreal, meaning tree-dwelling. It lives in cavities and hollows of mature, tall trees, often in the old trunks of trees such as tamarind and other large trees. The genus Poecilotheria is made up of arboreal Old World tarantulas from India and Sri Lanka. They are fast and agile, with a leg span up to about 15-20 cm. Females live longer than males, and the spiders are known for their blue and metallic colouring, with intricate fractal-like patterns on the abdomen.
summary: The correct answer is (d) II and III. The Gooty tarantula (Poecilotheria metallica) is an arboreal spider found only in a small patch of degraded forest in the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh. Statement I is wrong because it is an arachnid (a carnivorous spider), not a crustacean.
topic_notes: The Peacock or Gooty tarantula (Poecilotheria metallica) is one of the most striking spiders in the world, with a vivid blue body and intricate patterns on its abdomen. It was described by R. I. Pocock in 1899 from a specimen found in a railway yard at Gooty in Andhra Pradesh. It was then not seen for over a century, and was rediscovered in 2001 in the Eastern Ghats. It is endemic to India and its known range is a few hundred square kilometres of reserve forest in Nandyal, Kurnool and Cuddapah districts. The species is arboreal, living in hollows of old, large trees, and is a carnivorous ambush predator that eats insects and small vertebrates. Tarantulas belong to Arachnida, so they have eight legs, no antennae, a cephalothorax and an abdomen. They are not crustaceans or insects. Conservation: the IUCN lists it as Critically Endangered. It is in Schedule IV of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and is listed in CITES Appendix II as part of the tarantula family. The main threats are deforestation, firewood collection, tree felling for agriculture and the international pet trade. Related angles for UPSC include the Eastern Ghats (their geology, biodiversity and extent across Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Tamil Nadu), other spiders and arachnids of India, the difference between arboreal and terrestrial species, and the IUCN categories (Extinct, Extinct in the Wild, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened, Least Concern, Data Deficient, Not Evaluated). Questions may also ask about CITES, Wildlife Protection Act schedules, endemic species of India and recently rediscovered species.

question:
Consider the following statements :
I. Carbon dioxide (CO) emissions in India are less than 0°5 t CO)/ capita. Il. In terms of CO, emissions from fuel combustion, India ranks second in Asia-Pacific region. Ill. Electricity and heat producers are the largest sources of CO, emissions in India. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Environment
detail: The question rests on IEA-type data on CO2 emissions from fuel combustion. India's per capita CO2 emissions are roughly 1.8-2.0 t CO2 per person, well below the world average of about 4.5 t and far below the US (around 14 t) and China (around 8 t). They are nowhere near 0.5 t, so statement I is false. In absolute terms India is the third-largest emitter globally after China and the USA. Within the Asia-Pacific region it ranks second after China, so statement II is true. By sector, electricity and heat generation, which is heavily coal-based, accounts for about half or more of India's fuel-combustion CO2, followed by industry and transport. Statement III is therefore true. Elimination: once statement I is rejected, options (a) and (d) fall away, since both include I. Option (b) accepts only II and so ignores III, which is true. That leaves (c). A useful tip is to check numerical claims first, because UPSC often plants an implausible figure in them.
explanations: Wrong: option (a) includes statement I, which is false because India's per capita CO2 is about 1.9-2 t, not under 0.5 t.
Wrong: option (b) leaves out statement III, which is also true, since the power and heat sector is India's largest emitter.
Correct: statements II and III are both true. India is second in Asia-Pacific after China, and electricity and heat generation is the largest source.
Wrong: option (d) accepts statement I, which is false, so the combination cannot be right.
keyfact: India: 3rd largest CO2 emitter globally, 2nd in Asia-Pacific after China, about 2 t per capita, and power and heat is the largest sector.
option_notes: Option (a), I and III only: it pairs a false per capita claim with a true sector claim. India's per capita CO2 is about 2 t against a world average of about 4.5 t. The power sector's dominance comes from coal, which supplies about 70% of India's electricity. India's coal reserves are the fifth largest in the world, and coal-fired capacity is still being added. The false half makes the option wrong.

Option (b), II only: it recognises India's rank in Asia-Pacific but misses the sector fact. India is second in the region after China and third globally. Its absolute emissions are rising with economic growth, but its per capita and historical shares remain low. It is incomplete because statement III is also true.

Option (c), II and III only: this is the official answer. India is the second-largest Asia-Pacific emitter from fuel combustion, and electricity and heat producers are its largest source. These facts come from IEA-style data. India's Nationally Determined Contributions include cutting emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030, and net zero by 2070.

Option (d), I and II only (OCR-garbled, but evidently including statement I): any option with statement I fails. India's per capita CO2 is about 2 t. Per capita emissions are often used to compare countries fairly, and developed countries' figures are several times India's. India invokes equity and CBDR, principles under the UNFCCC, to argue for differentiated climate responsibilities.
related: India is the third-largest CO2 emitter globally after China and the USA.
India's net zero target year is 2070, announced at COP26 in Glasgow.
Panchamrit includes a target of 500 GW non-fossil electricity capacity by 2030.
About 70% of India's electricity is generated from coal.
The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme was notified in 2023 under the Energy Conservation Act.
The International Solar Alliance was launched by India and France in 2015 at COP21.
The Paris Agreement aims to keep warming well below 2°C, with efforts towards 1.5°C.
India's per capita CO2 emissions (about 2 t) are below the world average (about 4.5 t).
statements: I — Incorrect: India's per capita CO2 emissions are about 1.9-2 t, not below 0.5 t. Per capita emissions are total national CO2 divided by population. India's population is very large, so its per capita figure stays low compared with developed nations, but it is not that low. The world average is about 4.5 t. India uses per capita equity as a key argument in climate negotiations, in line with Common But Differentiated Responsibilities (CBDR). The US is around 14-15 t and China around 8 t. India's target is net zero by 2070.

II — Correct: Among Asia-Pacific countries, China is first and India second in CO2 emissions from fuel combustion. Fuel combustion emissions come mainly from coal, oil and gas used for power, industry, transport and buildings. Globally India is third after China and the USA. India's share of global emissions is about 7-8%. Its cumulative historical emissions remain far lower than those of the USA and EU. Japan is usually third in Asia-Pacific. The IEA and the Global Carbon Project publish these rankings.

III — Correct: Electricity and heat producers are the largest source of India's CO2 emissions, at roughly 50% or more of the total. This is because about 70% of India's electricity comes from coal-fired plants. The next largest sectors are industry (steel, cement), then transport (mostly road). Decarbonising the power sector is therefore central to India's plans, including 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030, 50% non-fossil electricity capacity by 2030, and the National Solar Mission.
summary: The answer is (c): statements II and III are correct, and statement I is incorrect. India's per capita CO2 emissions are about 1.9-2 t, far above 0.5 t. India is the second-largest CO2 emitter in Asia-Pacific after China, and electricity and heat producers are its largest emitting sector.
topic_notes: Topic: India's CO2 emissions profile and climate commitments. India's total CO2 emissions are about 2.8-2.9 billion tonnes a year, third after China and the USA, with a share of about 7-8% of the global total. Per capita emissions are about 1.9-2 t, well below the world average of about 4.5 t. By sector, power and heat generation is the largest, at about 50% or more, followed by industry (steel, cement), transport and residential use. Coal is the dominant fuel for power. Key data sources are the IEA, the Global Carbon Project, EDGAR and Our World in Data. India's climate commitments: at COP26 Glasgow (2021) it announced the Panchamrit: 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030, 50% of energy requirements from renewables by 2030, a 1 billion tonne cut in projected emissions by 2030, a 45% cut in emissions intensity of GDP by 2030 relative to 2005, and net zero by 2070. The updated NDC (2022) set a 45% emissions intensity reduction, 50% non-fossil installed electric capacity by 2030, and a 2.5-3 billion tonne CO2 equivalent additional carbon sink. Related institutions and schemes: UNFCCC, the Paris Agreement (2015), the Kyoto Protocol, the National Action Plan on Climate Change (2008) with its eight missions, the International Solar Alliance (2015), the Perform Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme, the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (2023), the Green Hydrogen Mission and the National Clean Energy Fund. Possible next questions: the largest emitters, per capita rankings, differences between GHGs and CO2 equivalents, CBDR, the Emissions Gap Report (UNEP) and Global Stocktake outcomes.

ocr: Consider the following pairs : Plant Description I. Cassava : Woody shrub Il. Ginger : Herb with pseudostem Ill. Malabar spinach : Herbaceous climber IV. Mint : Annual shrub V. Papaya : Woody shrub How many of the above pairs are correctly matched? Only two (a) Only three (b) Only four (c) All the five (a)
subject: Environment
detail: This question tests basic plant morphology and growth habit, which UPSC often draws from crop and vegetable botany. Growth habit categories are herb (soft, non-woody stem), shrub (woody, multi-stemmed, low), tree (woody, single trunk) and climber (needs support). Cassava (Manihot esculenta, Euphorbiaceae) is a perennial woody shrub grown for starchy tuberous roots. Ginger (Zingiber officinale) is a rhizomatous herb whose aerial 'stem' is a pseudostem formed by tightly rolled leaf sheaths. Malabar spinach (Basella alba, Basellaceae) is a fleshy, twining herbaceous climber. Mint (Mentha) is an aromatic perennial herb that spreads by runners, so calling it an 'annual shrub' is wrong on both counts. Papaya (Carica papaya) is a fast-growing, soft-wooded, usually unbranched plant, often described as a giant herb or tree-like herb; it has a hollow, non-woody trunk. Elimination logic: once pairs I, II and III are confirmed and IV and V are rejected, exactly three are correct. Pair IV is the easiest to reject, and pair V is the subtle trap.
explanations: (a) Only two is wrong because three pairs (I, II, III) are correct, not two.
(b) Only three is correct: cassava, ginger and Malabar spinach are matched correctly, while mint and papaya are not.
(c) Only four is wrong because both mint (perennial herb) and papaya (soft-wooded tree-like herb) are mismatched, so four cannot be correct.
(d) All the five is wrong because pairs IV and V are incorrect.
keyfact: Cassava = woody shrub, ginger = herb with pseudostem, Malabar spinach = herbaceous climber; mint is a perennial herb and papaya a soft-wooded tree-like herb, so the answer is 'only three'.
option_notes: Only two: this would be the case if just two pairs matched. Students often wrongly reject cassava or Malabar spinach. Cassava is a woody shrub and Malabar spinach a twining herbaceous climber, so this undercounts. It is a typical distractor in matching questions, where the count is the real test. Knowing the growth habit of common crops (herb, shrub, tree, climber) helps avoid such errors in UPSC botany questions.

Only three: this is the official answer. Pairs I (cassava, woody shrub), II (ginger, herb with pseudostem) and III (Malabar spinach, herbaceous climber) are correct. Pairs IV and V fail on growth habit. Such questions test precise classification of plants by habit: herb, shrub, tree, climber, creeper. Remember that pseudostems occur in ginger, banana and canna, and that papaya is a large herb-like soft-wooded plant.

Only four: this would need one of mint or papaya to be correct. Mint is a perennial herb, and papaya is a soft-wooded tree-like herb with a hollow trunk, not a woody shrub. Students who treat papaya as a woody plant, or consider mint a shrub, are drawn here. Mint is in Lamiaceae and papaya in Caricaceae, and both are commercially important in India.

All the five: this option would be right only if the descriptions were all accurate. Mint is not annual or shrubby, and papaya is not a true woody shrub. UPSC often includes 'all' as a trap for students who accept familiar-sounding descriptions. Careful checking of each pair against botanical definitions of habit and life cycle (annual, biennial, perennial) prevents this mistake.
related: Pseudostem is formed by overlapping leaf sheaths in banana, ginger and canna.
Ginger and turmeric are rhizomes, modified underground stems of Zingiberaceae.
Cassava is propagated by stem cuttings and contains cyanogenic glycosides that need processing.
Potato is a stem tuber; sweet potato is a root tuber.
Papaya yields papain, a proteolytic enzyme; papaya is trioecious/polygamous.
Mint (Mentha) belongs to Lamiaceae, which have square stems and opposite leaves.
Basella alba (Malabar spinach) is a twining vine in family Basellaceae.
India is the largest producer of ginger, turmeric and mint oil (menthol mint).
statements: I — Correct: Cassava is a woody shrub. Manihot esculenta is native to South America (Brazil/Paraguay region) and belongs to Euphorbiaceae. It is a perennial shrub 1-3 m tall, grown for starch-rich tuberous roots (tapioca, sago-like products). Kerala and Tamil Nadu are the main producing states in India. It is drought tolerant and a staple in tropical Africa. Raw roots contain cyanogenic glycosides (linamarin) and need processing. It was introduced to India by the Portuguese.

II — Correct: Ginger is a herb with a pseudostem. Zingiber officinale (Zingiberaceae) is a perennial rhizomatous herb, with the pseudostem made of overlapping leaf sheaths. It is propagated by rhizome bits (seed rhizomes). India is the largest producer; Kerala, Assam, Karnataka and Meghalaya are major states. The pungent compounds are gingerols and shogaols. Related Zingiberaceae members are turmeric, cardamom and Curcuma species. Ginger thrives in warm, humid climates with well-drained loamy soils.

III — Correct: Malabar spinach is a herbaceous climber. Basella alba (Basellaceae) is a fast-growing, fleshy, twining vine with thick, glossy leaves eaten as a leafy vegetable in India (called poi or pui sag). It is perennial in the tropics, often grown as an annual elsewhere, and a good source of vitamins A and C, iron and calcium. Red-stemmed Basella rubra is a variety. It grows well in hot, humid conditions and needs trellis support.

IV — Incorrect: Mint is a perennial aromatic herb, not an annual shrub. Mentha species (Lamiaceae) such as Mentha arvensis (Japanese mint/menthol mint), M. piperita (peppermint) and M. spicata (spearmint) spread by stolons and runners. India, especially Uttar Pradesh (Barabanki, Chandausi, Bareilly), is a leading producer of mint oil and menthol. Key constituents are menthol and menthone. Lamiaceae plants have square stems and opposite leaves.

V — Incorrect: Papaya is not a woody shrub. Carica papaya (Caricaceae) is native to tropical America (southern Mexico and Central America). It is a fast-growing, soft-wooded, usually unbranched tree-like herb with a hollow trunk and palmately lobed leaves at the top. It has male, female and hermaphrodite plants (trioecious/polygamous). It is the source of papain, a proteolytic enzyme used in meat tenderising and medicine. India is among the top producers; papaya ringspot virus is a major disease.
summary: The answer is (b) Only three. Cassava (woody shrub), ginger (herb with pseudostem) and Malabar spinach (herbaceous climber) are correctly matched. Mint is a perennial herb, not an annual shrub, and papaya is a large soft-wooded herbaceous tree-like plant, not a woody shrub.
topic_notes: Plant growth habit and life cycle are core to UPSC agriculture-botany questions. Herbs have soft, green, non-woody stems; shrubs are woody, branched from the base and shorter than trees; trees have a single woody trunk; climbers and creepers need support or spread along the ground. Life cycles: annuals complete life in one season (wheat, mustard, marigold), biennials in two years (carrot, onion, cabbage), perennials live many years (mango, mint, ginger, cassava). Pseudostems are formed by leaf sheaths in banana, ginger and canna. Cassava (tapioca) is a root crop in Euphorbiaceae, rich in starch but poor in protein, and contains cyanogenic glycosides. Ginger and turmeric are rhizomes (modified underground stems) of Zingiberaceae. Malabar spinach (Basella) is a vine grown as a leafy vegetable. Mint is grown for essential oil, and India is a top producer of menthol mint. Papaya gives papain and is a nutritious fruit rich in vitamin A and C. Other related angles: classification of vegetables by edible part (root, tuber, bulb, leaf, fruit), modified stems (rhizome, tuber, corm, bulb, runner, stolon), modified roots (tap root in carrot, tuberous in sweet potato), vegetative propagation (cuttings in cassava, rhizome in ginger and turmeric, runners in mint), and plant families such as Solanaceae (potato, tomato, brinjal), Fabaceae, Poaceae and Cucurbitaceae. Spices such as cardamom, pepper, clove and cinnamon, and their origin and producing states, are also frequent.

question: With reference to the planet Earth, consider the following statements : Rain forests produce more oxygen than that produced by oceans. Marine phytoplankton and photosynthetic bacteria produce about 50% of world’s oxygen. Well-oxygenated surface water Ill. contains several folds higher oxygen than that in atmospheric air. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? I and II
options: None of the above statements is
subject: Geography
detail: Oxygen on Earth comes mainly from photosynthesis. Oceanic phytoplankton (diatoms, dinoflagellates, coccolithophores) and photosynthetic bacteria such as Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus (cyanobacteria) contribute about 50% of global oxygen production, and some estimates put it at 50-80%. The Amazon is often called the 'lungs of the Earth', but this is a popular myth. Tropical forests do produce a great deal of oxygen, but they consume almost as much through respiration and decomposition, so their net contribution is very small. Statement I is therefore wrong. Statement III fails on basic physics. Dry air is about 21% oxygen, or roughly 210 ml per litre. Well-oxygenated surface water holds only about 5-10 ml per litre, because oxygen dissolves poorly and less so as temperature and salinity rise. Water therefore holds much less oxygen than air, not several-fold more. Eliminating I and III leaves only II. Linked ideas include the Great Oxidation Event about 2.4 billion years ago, caused by cyanobacteria, oxygen minimum zones, and ocean deoxygenation under climate change.
explanations: Wrong. It includes statement I, which is false, because the oceans produce about half of the world's oxygen and rain forests do not exceed this.
Correct. Only statement II is true. Phytoplankton and photosynthetic bacteria produce about 50% of the world's oxygen, while I and III are false.
Wrong. It includes I and III, both of which are false, and it omits the true statement II.
Wrong. Statement II is correct, so it is not true that none of the statements is correct.
keyfact: Oceanic phytoplankton and photosynthetic bacteria give about 50% of Earth's oxygen, rain forests are roughly oxygen-neutral, and air holds far more oxygen than water.
related: Dry air is about 78% N2, 21% O2, 0.93% argon and about 0.04% CO2.
Prochlorococcus is the most abundant photosynthetic organism on Earth.
The Great Oxidation Event occurred about 2.4 billion years ago and was caused by cyanobacteria.
Cold water holds more dissolved oxygen than warm water.
Oxygen minimum zones in the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal are expanding.
BOD measures the oxygen needed by microbes to decompose organic matter in water.
Hypoxia is generally defined as dissolved oxygen below about 2 mg/L.
The Amazon is called the 'lungs of the Earth' but is roughly oxygen-neutral in net terms.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Rain forests do not produce more oxygen than the oceans. Oceans contribute about half of global production, and forests' net contribution is small because respiration and decay use up most of what they make. Facts: the Amazon basin covers about 5.5 million sq km, mostly in Brazil. Its gross photosynthesis is huge, but net oxygen export is close to zero. The 'lungs of the Earth' label is a misleading popular phrase. Forests matter more as carbon stores, as regulators of rainfall and as biodiversity reservoirs. Over geological time, burial of organic carbon is what allowed oxygen to accumulate in the atmosphere.

2 — Correct: Marine phytoplankton and photosynthetic bacteria produce about 50% of the world's oxygen. Facts: phytoplankton are microscopic drifting autotrophs living in the sunlit (euphotic) zone. Prochlorococcus is the smallest and most abundant photosynthetic organism and alone is credited with about 5% of global oxygen. Cyanobacteria, once called blue-green algae, caused the Great Oxidation Event about 2.4 billion years ago. Phytoplankton form the base of marine food webs and drive the biological carbon pump. Their growth depends on light, nitrogen, phosphorus and iron. Warming and stratification threaten their productivity.

3 — Incorrect: Well-oxygenated surface water does not contain several-fold more oxygen than air. Air has about 210 ml O2 per litre, while water at saturation holds only about 5-10 ml per litre. Facts: dissolved oxygen (DO) falls as temperature and salinity rise, so cold polar waters hold more than warm tropical waters. DO is measured in mg/L or ml/L. Oxygen enters water by diffusion from air, wave mixing and photosynthesis. Oxygen minimum zones occur at mid-depths, for example in the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. Hypoxia is generally defined as DO below about 2 mg/L, and it causes dead zones and fish kills.
summary: The answer is (b), II only. Marine phytoplankton, cyanobacteria and other photosynthetic microbes produce roughly half of the oxygen generated each year. Rain forests do not out-produce the oceans, and air holds far more oxygen per unit volume than even well-oxygenated water.
topic_notes: Oxygen budget. Atmospheric oxygen is about 20.95% by volume, nitrogen about 78% and argon about 0.93%. Oxygen is produced mainly by oxygenic photosynthesis (6CO2 + 6H2O gives C6H12O6 + 6O2). It is consumed by respiration, decomposition, combustion and weathering of rocks. Roughly half of annual production is marine, from phytoplankton and cyanobacteria, and the rest is terrestrial, from forests, grasslands and crops. Mature forests are close to oxygen-neutral, because respiration and decay balance photosynthesis. Early Earth had almost no free oxygen. Cyanobacteria released it, and the Great Oxidation Event of about 2.4 billion years ago produced banded iron formations and the first ozone shield. Stromatolites are fossil cyanobacterial mats. Dissolved oxygen in water depends on temperature, salinity, pressure, turbulence and photosynthesis. Cold water holds more oxygen. Oxygen minimum zones lie at about 200-1000 m depth. They are growing because of warming, stratification and nutrient runoff that causes eutrophication and algal blooms. Hypoxic coastal dead zones include those in the Gulf of Mexico and the Baltic Sea. Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) measures organic pollution in water, and low BOD indicates clean water. Phytoplankton also drive the biological carbon pump and form the base of marine food chains. Iron fertilisation is a proposed geoengineering method. Other angles UPSC may ask about are the Amazon as a carbon sink, ocean acidification, coral bleaching, the ozone layer (the ozone shield protects against UV-B) and the Montreal Protocol.

question:
Consider the following types of vehicles :
I. Full battery electric vehicles Il. Hydrogen fuel cell vehicles Ill. Fuel cell-electric hybrid vehicles How many of the above are considered as alternative powertrain vehicles?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: An alternative powertrain (alternative propulsion) vehicle is one that is driven wholly or partly by an energy source and drive system other than a conventional internal combustion engine (ICE) running on petrol or diesel. The category covers battery electric vehicles (BEVs), hybrids (HEV, PHEV), fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs, which run on hydrogen), and ICE vehicles on alternative fuels such as CNG, LPG, ethanol or biofuel blends. BEVs store electricity in a battery and drive an electric motor, with zero tailpipe emissions. Hydrogen fuel cell vehicles combine hydrogen with oxygen in a fuel cell to generate electricity, and water vapour is the only tailpipe emission. Fuel cell-electric hybrids pair a fuel cell with a battery or supercapacitor buffer, which handles peak loads and recovers braking energy. Each type departs from the pure ICE drivetrain, so each qualifies. Elimination logic: once you know that BEVs and FCEVs are the standard examples of alternative powertrains, options (a), (b) and (d) cannot hold, and (c) follows. In India, the FAME-II scheme, the PM E-DRIVE scheme (2024) and the National Green Hydrogen Mission support such technologies.
explanations: (a) is wrong: it would count only one type, but all three are alternative powertrains.
(b) is wrong: it would exclude one of the three, but none of them uses a conventional ICE drivetrain alone, so none can be left out.
(c) is right: BEVs, hydrogen FCEVs and fuel cell-electric hybrids are all alternative powertrain vehicles.
(d) is wrong: it would mean none qualify, which contradicts the basic definition of alternative powertrains.
keyfact: BEVs, hydrogen fuel cell vehicles and fuel cell-electric hybrids are all alternative powertrain vehicles, i.e. they do not rely solely on a conventional petrol or diesel ICE.
option_notes: Only one: this option would admit just a single type. Alternative powertrains actually form a broad family: BEV, HEV, PHEV, FCEV, and ICE vehicles on CNG, LPG, ethanol or methanol. In India, ethanol blending (E20 reached in 2025) and CNG are widely used alternatives. Counting just one type is a common trap in 'how many' questions.

Only two: this option would leave out one of the listed types. Students may wrongly treat fuel cell hybrids as just a variant of fuel cell vehicles, or doubt whether hydrogen counts. Both are valid alternatives. The classification depends on whether the primary propulsion departs from a conventional ICE running on fossil fuel. BEV, FCEV and hybrid fuel cell systems all do.

All the three: this is the correct, official answer. Alternative powertrain vehicles are those using non-conventional propulsion: full electric, hydrogen fuel cell, fuel cell hybrids, plug-in hybrids and strong hybrids. Government policy such as FAME-II and PM E-DRIVE promotes electrification, and the Green Hydrogen Mission promotes hydrogen mobility.

None: this option is wrong because conventional powertrains means petrol or diesel ICE vehicles, and none of the three listed types fits that description. BS-VI norms apply to ICE vehicles, whereas BEVs and FCEVs are classed as zero tailpipe emission vehicles. Such vehicles are central to India's net-zero 2070 target and its transport decarbonisation.
related: FAME-II ran from April 2019 with an outlay of Rs 10,000 crore and was extended to March 2024.
PM E-DRIVE was launched in 2024 to promote e-2W, e-3W, e-buses and charging infrastructure.
The National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023) targets 5 MMT of green hydrogen production a year by 2030.
Fuel cell vehicles emit only water vapour from the tailpipe.
The PLI ACC Battery scheme targets 50 GWh of advanced chemistry cell manufacturing capacity.
The Toyota Mirai and Hyundai Nexo are well-known hydrogen fuel cell cars.
A plug-in hybrid (PHEV) has a larger battery that can be charged from an external source, unlike a regular hybrid.
India has set a target of net zero emissions by 2070.
statements: I — Correct: Full battery electric vehicles run only on stored electricity and an electric motor, with no ICE, so they are alternative powertrain vehicles. A BEV uses a lithium-ion battery pack (LFP or NMC chemistry), an inverter and a motor, and charges from the grid. It has zero tailpipe emissions, and regenerative braking recovers energy. Examples in India include the Tata Nexon EV, Tata Tiago EV and MG Windsor. Support comes from FAME-II, PM E-DRIVE, a reduced 5% GST on EVs, and PLI schemes for auto and Advanced Chemistry Cell batteries. India's national aim is 30% EV sales share by 2030.

II — Correct: Hydrogen fuel cell vehicles generate electricity on board from hydrogen in a fuel cell (usually a PEM fuel cell), and that electricity drives a motor. The only emission is water. Examples are the Toyota Mirai and Hyundai Nexo. Hydrogen is stored in high-pressure tanks, typically at 700 bar. India's National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023) targets 5 MMT of green hydrogen a year by 2030. Pilot hydrogen buses and trucks are running, for example with NTPC, Tata Motors and Ashok Leyland. Challenges are fuelling infrastructure, cost and the efficiency losses in producing hydrogen.

III — Correct: A fuel cell-electric hybrid combines a fuel cell stack with a battery or supercapacitor. The fuel cell supplies steady power, and the battery covers peak demand and stores energy from regenerative braking. This improves efficiency and fuel cell life. Most modern FCEVs are in effect such hybrids. It differs from a conventional hybrid (HEV) such as the Toyota Prius, which pairs an ICE with an electric motor. Both count as alternative powertrains, since the electric drive is either the main or a supplementary source of propulsion.
summary: The answer is (c) All the three. Battery electric vehicles, hydrogen fuel cell vehicles and fuel cell-electric hybrid vehicles all use powertrains other than a conventional petrol or diesel internal combustion engine, so all are alternative powertrain vehicles.
topic_notes: Powertrain means the set of components that generate power and deliver it to the wheels: engine or motor, transmission, drive shafts and differential. A conventional powertrain is an ICE on petrol or diesel. Alternative powertrains include: (1) BEV, with a battery and motor and zero tailpipe emissions; (2) HEV, a self-charging hybrid such as the Toyota Hybrid; (3) PHEV, a hybrid with a larger battery that can be plugged in; (4) FCEV, which runs on hydrogen through a fuel cell; and (5) alternative-fuel ICE vehicles running on CNG, LPG, ethanol, biodiesel or methanol. Indian policy: the National Electric Mobility Mission Plan 2020; FAME India (Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Hybrid and Electric Vehicles), with FAME-II running from 2019 with an outlay of Rs 10,000 crore; PM E-DRIVE (2024) with about Rs 10,900 crore, covering e-2W, e-3W, e-buses, e-trucks and charging infrastructure; the PLI scheme for Automobiles and Auto Components (Rs 25,938 crore) and the PLI ACC Battery scheme (Rs 18,100 crore, 50 GWh); the SPMEPCI scheme for EV manufacturing, with a reduced customs duty for investment of at least $500 million; the National Green Hydrogen Mission (Rs 19,744 crore); and the Scheme for Faster Adoption of E-buses. GST on EVs is 5%. Battery chemistries to know are Li-ion (NMC, LFP), sodium-ion and solid-state. Other points: the Bharat Charge standards, the battery swapping policy, the Battery Waste Management Rules 2022, and the global EV30@30 campaign. In terms of well-to-wheel emissions, green hydrogen from electrolysis powered by renewables is the cleanest, while grey hydrogen comes from natural gas.

question:
With reference to Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), consider the following statements :
I. All types of UAVs can do vertical landing. Il. All types of UAVs can do automated hovering. Ill. All types of UAVs can use battery only as a source of power supply. How many of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: UAVs (drones) are classified by airframe: fixed-wing, rotary-wing (multirotor or helicopter), hybrid VTOL (vertical take-off and landing) and flapping-wing. Capability depends on the design. Rotary-wing drones can take off and land vertically and hover, because lift comes from rotors. Fixed-wing drones need forward airspeed to stay aloft. They usually take off by runway, catapult or hand launch, and they land by belly landing, parachute, net recovery or a runway. They cannot hover. Only hybrid VTOL designs combine both abilities. Power sources also differ: lithium-polymer or lithium-ion batteries on small drones, petrol or diesel engines on larger MALE/HALE drones (for example the Predator/MQ-9 Reaper uses a turboprop engine), hydrogen fuel cells, solar cells (high-altitude pseudo-satellites) and hybrid systems. India's Drone Rules 2021 classify drones by weight: nano (up to 250 g), micro (250 g to 2 kg), small (2 to 25 kg), medium (25 to 150 kg) and large (over 150 kg). Elimination logic: statements with 'all' or 'only' are risky in UPSC. A single counter-example, a fixed-wing or fuel-powered drone, falsifies each statement, so the answer is none.
explanations: (a) Only one — wrong, because none of the three statements is correct. Each one fails because of the word 'all'.
(b) Only two — wrong, because no pair of statements is correct either. Fixed-wing drones cannot hover or land vertically, and many drones do not run on battery alone.
(c) All three — wrong, because it would require every UAV type to land vertically, hover and run on batteries. Fixed-wing and fuel-powered drones are counter-examples.
(d) None — correct, because each statement is falsified by at least one UAV type. This matches the official answer.
keyfact: UAV capabilities depend on design: only rotary or VTOL types hover and land vertically, and power may be battery, fuel, solar or hybrid, so 'all UAVs' claims are false.
option_notes: Only one: this would be true if exactly one statement held universally. Here none does. The choice is a typical UPSC distractor for 'how many' questions, tempting students who recall that multirotors can hover or that small drones use batteries. Always test 'all' claims against the most extreme counter-example, such as a fixed-wing or fuel-powered military UAV. 'How many' questions give no partial credit.

Only two: this would need two statements to be universally true. A student might assume vertical landing and hovering go together because both belong to rotary-wing drones. They do not apply to fixed-wing or hybrid types in all phases. Multirotor features are not shared across all UAV types, so this is wrong. UAV classes are fixed-wing, multirotor, single-rotor helicopter, hybrid VTOL and flapping-wing.

All three: this would mean every UAV lands vertically, hovers and runs on batteries only. That ignores fixed-wing drones such as Rustom-II and MQ-9B SkyGuardian, which are fuel-driven and runway-based. India's Drone Rules 2021 cover all categories (nano to large), and the Drone Shakti and PLI schemes support the sector. It is a trap for students who think only of small quadcopters.

None: the correct and official answer. UAV capabilities depend on design. Fixed-wing drones need forward motion, land conventionally and cannot hover. Power sources include batteries, fuel engines, solar and hydrogen fuel cells. Remember the classification by airframe, weight (Drone Rules 2021) and role (MALE, HALE, tactical, micro). The word 'all' in a statement usually signals a false claim.
related: Drone Rules 2021 classify drones by weight: nano, micro, small, medium and large.
Digital Sky Platform shows green, yellow and red airspace zones for drones.
DGCA is India's civil aviation regulator and handles drone certification.
Namo Drone Didi scheme (2023) provides drones to women self-help groups for agriculture.
India signed a deal for 31 MQ-9B drones with the US in 2024.
Fixed-wing drones cannot hover, while multirotors can.
MALE means Medium Altitude Long Endurance and HALE means High Altitude Long Endurance.
PLI scheme for drones and drone components was approved in 2021.
statements: I — Incorrect: Only VTOL-capable drones (multirotors, helicopters, hybrid VTOL) land vertically; fixed-wing drones do not. Fixed-wing UAVs such as the Rustom-II, MQ-9B or Heron land on runways, or by parachute or net recovery. They rely on forward motion for lift. Vertical landing needs rotors or tilt-rotor or tail-sitter designs. Hybrid VTOL drones add rotors to a fixed-wing body so they can launch and land without a runway. Fixed-wing designs offer greater endurance and range, and multirotors offer manoeuvrability but shorter endurance. So the claim 'all types' fails.

II — Incorrect: Hovering means holding a fixed position in the air, which needs rotors that produce lift without forward speed. Multirotors and helicopter-type drones can hover, often with GPS and sensor-aided stabilisation (automated position hold). Fixed-wing drones must keep moving forward or they stall, so they cannot hover and can only loiter in circles. Hybrid VTOL drones can hover only in the vertical flight phase. Hovering is useful for photography, inspection, surveying and spraying, which is why multirotors dominate these uses.

III — Incorrect: Battery power is common, especially in small drones (lithium-polymer or lithium-ion), but it is not the only source. Larger military UAVs use internal combustion or turboprop engines (the MQ-9 Reaper uses a Honeywell TPE331 turboprop). Other options are hydrogen fuel cells, solar panels (for example Airbus Zephyr, a high-altitude pseudo-satellite), and hybrid gas-electric systems. Battery limits on endurance and payload push long-endurance drones toward fuel or solar power. India's Drone Rules 2021 do not restrict the power source.
summary: The answer is (d) None. Each statement uses the word 'all types of UAVs', and UAVs vary widely, so none of the three claims holds universally. Fixed-wing UAVs land conventionally and cannot hover, and many UAVs use fuel engines, hybrid systems or solar power instead of batteries alone.
topic_notes: UAVs (drones) are aircraft operated without a pilot on board, controlled remotely or autonomously. Classification by airframe: fixed-wing (long endurance, efficient, needs runway or launcher), rotary-wing (multirotor or helicopter; VTOL and hover), hybrid VTOL (combines both) and flapping-wing (bio-inspired). Classification by altitude and endurance: MALE (Medium Altitude Long Endurance, for example Heron, MQ-9B) and HALE (High Altitude Long Endurance, for example Global Hawk). Power sources: Li-Po batteries, internal combustion engines, turboprops, hydrogen fuel cells, solar and hybrid. Indian regulation: Drone Rules 2021 replaced the UAS Rules 2021 (March 2021). They were liberalised on 25 Aug 2021 and abolished many approvals, and the Digital Sky Platform handles registration and airspace maps (green, yellow, red zones). Weight categories: nano (up to 250 g), micro (250 g to 2 kg), small (2 to 25 kg), medium (25 to 150 kg) and large (over 150 kg). Schemes: PLI scheme for drones and components (2021, ₹120 crore), a ban on import of foreign drones (Feb 2022), Kisan Drones for agriculture, and Namo Drone Didi (2023) giving drones to women self-help groups. DGCA is the regulator; the Ministry of Civil Aviation oversees policy. Defence: India has the Rustom, Archer-NG, Heron, Nagastra loitering munitions, and has contracted 31 MQ-9B drones from the US (2024). Possible angles: counter-drone systems, swarm drones, the use of drones in conflicts such as Ukraine, and drone use in agriculture, disaster management and health delivery.

question:
In the context of electric vehicle batteries, consider the following elements :
I. Cobalt Il. Graphite
I. Lithium
IV. Nickel How many of the above usually make up battery cathodes?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: An EV lithium-ion cell has a cathode (positive electrode), an anode (negative electrode), an electrolyte and a separator. During discharge, lithium ions move from anode to cathode through the electrolyte. The cathode is a lithium metal oxide or phosphate. Common chemistries are NMC (lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide), NCA (lithium nickel cobalt aluminium oxide), LCO (lithium cobalt oxide), LFP (lithium iron phosphate) and LMO (lithium manganese oxide). Nickel gives high energy density, cobalt gives structural stability and longer life, and lithium is the charge-carrying ion in every chemistry. The anode is usually graphite (natural or synthetic), with silicon or lithium titanate as emerging or alternative options. Elimination logic: lithium is in every cathode, so (a) is out. Cobalt and nickel are both used in NMC and NCA, so (b) is out. Graphite is the anode, so it cannot be counted among the cathode elements, which rules out (d) and leaves (c). Note that LFP cathodes contain no nickel or cobalt, which is why the word 'usually' appears in the question.
explanations: (a) Wrong: Only one would be correct only if a single element were cathode material, but lithium, nickel and cobalt all are.
(b) Wrong: Two would leave out one of cobalt, nickel or lithium, yet all three occur in common cathodes such as NMC and NCA.
(c) Correct: Cobalt, lithium and nickel usually make up the cathode, while graphite forms the anode. That makes three.
(d) Wrong: Graphite is the anode material, so not all four are cathode components.
keyfact: In EV Li-ion batteries, lithium, nickel and cobalt (with manganese or aluminium) form the cathode, while graphite forms the anode.
option_notes: Only one: this would match a battery with a cathode of a single active metal. In practice the cathode is a lithium metal oxide or phosphate, which is a compound of lithium with at least one transition metal. Examples: LiFePO4 (LFP) has lithium and iron, and LiCoO2 has lithium and cobalt. A single-element cathode is not the usual EV design.

Only two: this would fit simpler chemistries such as LCO (lithium and cobalt) or LFP (lithium and iron). It does not fit NMC and NCA, the dominant EV cathodes, which combine lithium with nickel and cobalt, plus manganese or aluminium. LFP is growing quickly in India and China because it is cheaper and safer and contains no cobalt or nickel.

Only three: cobalt, lithium and nickel together describe NMC and NCA cathodes. NMC ratios such as 111, 523, 622 and 811 show nickel:manganese:cobalt. Higher nickel gives more energy but less thermal stability. Cobalt supports stability and cycle life. This is the official answer, because graphite is excluded as an anode.

All four: this is the trap that treats every battery material as a cathode material. Graphite is the standard anode, hosting lithium ions during charging. The cathode, anode, electrolyte (lithium salts such as LiPF6 in organic solvents) and separator are the four main parts of a cell. Knowing which part each material belongs to is the key skill tested.
related: Graphite is the usual anode material in Li-ion batteries.
LFP cathodes contain lithium, iron and phosphate, with no cobalt or nickel.
DR Congo produces roughly 70% of the world's cobalt.
Lithium Triangle: Argentina, Bolivia and Chile.
Indonesia is the world's largest nickel producer.
India's National Critical Mineral Mission was approved in January 2025.
KABIL is the joint venture of NALCO, HCL and MECL for overseas mineral assets.
Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 introduced Extended Producer Responsibility.
statements: I — Correct: Cobalt is a usual cathode component. Cobalt stabilises the layered oxide structure in LCO, NMC and NCA cathodes. About 70% of world cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of Congo, and ethical sourcing and child-labour concerns are well documented. Cobalt is a by-product of copper and nickel mining. Producers are reducing cobalt content through high-nickel cathodes (NMC 811) and cobalt-free LFP. India has listed cobalt as a critical mineral.

II — Incorrect: Graphite is the usual anode material, not a cathode material. It stores lithium ions between its carbon layers when charging (intercalation). Both natural and synthetic graphite are used. China dominates graphite mining and anode processing. Graphite is on India's critical minerals list. The US and EU also classify it as critical. Silicon-graphite composite anodes are an emerging trend.

III — Correct: Lithium is in every Li-ion cathode, for example LiCoO2, LiFePO4 and NMC. Lithium ions shuttle between the electrodes. Major sources are the 'Lithium Triangle' (Argentina, Bolivia, Chile) and Australia's hard-rock spodumene. China leads in refining. India's first lithium inferences were at Reasi (Jammu and Kashmir) and Mandya (Karnataka). KABIL (Khanij Bidesh India Ltd) is acquiring overseas lithium assets.

IV — Correct: Nickel is a usual cathode component. High-nickel cathodes such as NMC 811 and NCA give high energy density and longer range. Indonesia is the largest nickel producer, followed by the Philippines and Russia. Class 1 (battery-grade) nickel is needed. Nickel is also used in stainless steel. It is on India's critical minerals list. Nickel-metal hydride batteries are an older, different technology.
summary: The answer is (c) Only three. Cobalt, lithium and nickel are the metals that usually make up the cathode of an EV lithium-ion battery (as in NMC, NCA and LCO chemistries). Graphite is the standard anode material, not the cathode.
topic_notes:
Lithium-ion batteries power most EVs. A cell has a cathode (positive), anode (negative), electrolyte and separator. On discharge, lithium ions move from anode to cathode and electrons flow through the external circuit. On charge the process reverses.

Cathode chemistries: NMC (nickel-manganese-cobalt) is widely used in cars. NCA (nickel-cobalt-aluminium) is used by Tesla in some models. LFP (lithium iron phosphate) is cheaper, safer and longer-lived but has lower energy density, and is rising in share. LCO is common in consumer electronics. LMO is also used in some applications.

Anode: graphite dominates. Silicon is an emerging additive, and lithium titanate (LTO) offers fast charging. Current collectors are aluminium for the cathode and copper for the anode.

Next-generation technologies: solid-state batteries, sodium-ion batteries (no lithium, cobalt or nickel), lithium-sulphur, and metal-air batteries.

Critical minerals: lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, rare earths and others. India's 2023 critical minerals list has 30 minerals. The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act 2023 allowed auctions of critical minerals blocks. The National Critical Mineral Mission was approved in January 2025. KABIL secures overseas assets, for example in Argentina's Catamarca. India is a member of the Minerals Security Partnership.

Schemes: FAME-II, PM E-DRIVE (2024), the PLI scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) batteries with 50 GWh capacity, and the PLI scheme for the automobile sector.

Supply concentration: China dominates refining of lithium, cobalt and graphite. DR Congo produces most cobalt. Indonesia leads nickel. Australia and Chile lead lithium production. Battery recycling rules in India are under the Battery Waste Management Rules 2022, which set Extended Producer Responsibility.

ocr: Consider the following : Cigarette butts I. Eyeglass lenses Il. Car tyres Ill. How many of them contain plastic? Only one (a) Only two (b) All the three (c) (a) None
subject: Environment
detail: The question tests awareness of hidden plastics in everyday items, a theme linked to microplastic pollution, the Plastic Waste Management Rules and the global plastics treaty negotiations. Plastics are synthetic or semi-synthetic polymers. Cigarette filters are made of cellulose acetate, a semi-synthetic thermoplastic derived from cellulose; they are non-biodegradable in practical terms, are among the most littered items worldwide, and shed microfibres. Eyeglass lenses are mostly organic polymer lenses: CR-39 (allyl diglycol carbonate), polycarbonate, Trivex and high-index plastics, which replaced heavier glass lenses. Car tyres are made from natural rubber plus synthetic rubbers such as styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR) and butadiene rubber, with carbon black and additives; tyre wear is one of the largest sources of primary microplastics in oceans and rivers. Elimination logic: once a student recognises that any one item contains plastic, (d) None is ruled out. Knowing that cigarette filters are plastic-based and tyres contain synthetic polymers rules out (a) and (b), leaving (c). The key lesson is that plastic is not only packaging; it is present in textiles, filters, lenses, tyres, cosmetics and paints.
explanations: (a) Only one is wrong because all three items contain plastic or plastic-type polymers, not just one.
(b) Only two is wrong because the third item also contains polymer plastics: cigarette filters, lenses and tyres all qualify.
(c) All the three is correct: cigarette butts (cellulose acetate), eyeglass lenses (CR-39 or polycarbonate) and car tyres (synthetic rubber and polymers) all contain plastic.
(d) None is wrong because every item listed contains plastic or a plastic-like polymer.
keyfact: Cigarette filters (cellulose acetate), spectacle lenses (CR-39 or polycarbonate) and tyres (synthetic rubber) all contain plastic polymers.
option_notes: Only one: this option would apply if just a single item contained plastic. It is a distractor for students who think of plastic only as bottles and bags. In reality, plastics are embedded in many everyday goods, including filters, optical lenses and automotive parts. Hidden plastics in such items contribute to microplastic pollution that UPSC often links to environment questions.

Only two: this is a distractor for students who identify two items, usually lenses and tyres or lenses and filters, but miss the third. Cellulose acetate in filters is the item most often missed because it looks like cotton. Tyres are often overlooked as plastic because they are called rubber, but they contain synthetic polymers.

All the three: this is the official answer. Cigarette filters (cellulose acetate), spectacle lenses (CR-39, polycarbonate) and tyres (synthetic rubber such as SBR and polybutadiene) all contain polymers classed as plastics or plastic-like materials. They are significant sources of microplastics and persistent pollution, and they matter in discussions of the plastics treaty and extended producer responsibility.

None: this would be correct only if none of the items had polymer content. It is a distractor for the view that plastic means only packaging. Glass lenses and natural rubber do exist, but most modern lenses are plastic and tyres are blended with synthetic polymers, so this option fails.
related: Cellulose acetate is the semi-synthetic polymer used in cigarette filters.
Microplastics are plastic particles smaller than 5 mm.
Tyre wear is one of the largest sources of primary microplastics.
CR-39 and polycarbonate are common plastic spectacle lens materials.
India banned identified single-use plastic items from 1 July 2022 under the Plastic Waste Management Rules.
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) makes producers, importers and brand owners responsible for plastic waste.
UNEA-5.2 (2022) launched negotiations for a legally binding global plastics treaty.
World Environment Day 2018, themed 'Beat Plastic Pollution', was hosted by India.
statements: I — Correct: Cigarette filters are made of cellulose acetate, a plastic-type polymer. Cellulose acetate is a semi-synthetic thermoplastic made by acetylating cellulose from wood pulp or cotton. It was first developed in the late 1800s and commercialised in the 20th century for films, fibres and, from the 1950s, cigarette filters. Filters degrade very slowly, break into microfibres, and leach nicotine, heavy metals and other toxins. Cigarette butts are among the most common items found in beach clean-ups worldwide. Some countries and regions are considering bans or extended producer responsibility for filters.

II — Correct: Most modern eyeglass lenses are made of plastic polymers. The common materials are CR-39 (allyl diglycol carbonate, introduced in the 1940s), polycarbonate (impact-resistant, used in safety and children's glasses), Trivex and high-index plastics. They are lighter and safer than traditional glass, and they can be coated for UV protection and scratch resistance. Glass lenses are still used but are now a minority. Polycarbonate lenses are also used in sports eyewear and visors because of their high impact resistance.

III — Correct: Car tyres contain synthetic rubber polymers and are a major microplastic source. Tyres are made of natural rubber blended with synthetic rubbers such as styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR) and polybutadiene, plus carbon black, silica, steel or textile cords (often nylon or polyester) and chemical additives.
