Tyre-wear particles released during driving are among the largest sources of primary microplastics, and they carry additives such as 6PPD, which can form toxic 6PPD-quinone. Tyre dust reaches soil, rivers and oceans through road runoff.
summary: The answer is (c) All the three. Cigarette butts contain cellulose acetate (a plastic-like bioplastic polymer), most modern eyeglass lenses are made of plastics such as CR-39 or polycarbonate, and car tyres contain synthetic rubber (a polymer) and are a significant source of microplastics.
topic_notes: Plastics are polymers of repeating monomer units. Thermoplastics (polyethylene, PET, PVC, polypropylene, polystyrene) soften on heating and can be remoulded, while thermosets (Bakelite, epoxy) cannot. Semi-synthetic plastics such as cellulose acetate are made by modifying natural polymers. Microplastics are plastic particles under 5 mm, and nanoplastics are under 1 micrometre. Primary microplastics are released directly, for example from tyre wear, textile fibres and microbeads in cosmetics. Secondary microplastics come from the breakdown of larger plastic items. Hidden sources include synthetic clothing (polyester, nylon, acrylic), tea bags that are heat-sealed with polypropylene, chewing gum bases, paints, wet wipes, glitter and cigarette filters. Microplastics have been found in oceans, Himalayan snow, drinking water, human blood and placenta, and they carry adsorbed toxic chemicals. Indian policy: Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016, with amendments in 2018, 2021 and 2022, ban identified single-use plastic items from 1 July 2022, increased the minimum thickness of carry bags (75 to 120 microns), and introduced Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) guidelines for producers, importers and brand owners (PIBOs). India championed the UNEA-5.2 resolution of 2022 to negotiate a legally binding global plastics treaty through an Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC). Other angles: biodegradable plastics such as PLA and PHA, bioplastics, the 'Beat Plastic Pollution' theme of World Environment Day 2018 hosted by India, recycling codes 1-7, and alternatives such as jute and bamboo.

ocr: Consider the following substances : Ethanol I Nitroglycerine Il. Ill. Urea Coal gasification technology can be used in the production of how many of them? Only one (a) Only two (b) All the three (c) (d) None
subject: Geography
detail: Coal gasification converts coal, by partial oxidation with steam and oxygen or air at high temperature and pressure, into synthesis gas (syngas), a mixture mainly of carbon monoxide and hydrogen with some CO2 and methane. Syngas is a building block of the chemical industry. Hydrogen from it is combined with nitrogen in the Haber-Bosch process to make ammonia, and ammonia reacts with CO2 (also available from the gasifier and the water-gas shift reaction) to give urea. This is why coal-based fertiliser plants, such as the Talcher Fertilizers project in Odisha, use gasification. Syngas can also be turned into methanol, ethanol, DME, synthetic natural gas and Fischer-Tropsch fuels; ethanol can be made by catalytic conversion of syngas or by microbial fermentation of syngas. Nitroglycerine (glyceryl trinitrate) is an explosive made by nitrating glycerol, a by-product of fats and oils or of biodiesel, with a nitric and sulphuric acid mixture. Its feedstock is not coal syngas. So I (ethanol) and III (urea) fit, II does not, and the answer is 'only two'. Elimination: since urea is clearly a coal-gasification product, (d) None is out. Since nitroglycerine is made from glycerol, (c) All three is out. Since ethanol is also possible, (a) is out.
explanations: (a) Wrong: more than one of the listed substances can come from coal gasification. Both ethanol and urea can, so 'only one' undercounts.

(b) Right: ethanol and urea can be produced from syngas obtained by coal gasification, while nitroglycerine is made from glycerol and nitrating acids. This matches the official answer, so exactly two.
(c) Wrong: nitroglycerine is made by nitrating glycerol with nitric and sulphuric acid, not by a coal gasification route, so not all three qualify.
(d) Wrong: coal gasification is a proven route to urea (via ammonia) and can also be used for ethanol, so 'none' is incorrect.
keyfact: Coal gasification gives syngas, which yields ammonia and urea and can yield ethanol, but nitroglycerine comes from glycerol, so the answer is only two.
option_notes: Only one: this is a count option and not a substance. It would be correct only if exactly one of ethanol, nitroglycerine or urea were a coal-gasification product. Remember that syngas-based chemicals include ammonia, urea, methanol, DME, ethanol and synthetic fuels, so more than one item here qualifies. Such 'how many' questions need each item checked separately, and guessing from one familiar example is risky.

Only two: this is the correct count. Ethanol and urea can be derived from coal syngas, while nitroglycerine cannot. India's National Coal Gasification Mission targets 100 million tonnes of coal gasified by 2030, supporting products like methanol, ammonia, urea, DME and synthetic natural gas, and cutting imports of natural gas, methanol and ammonia.

All three: this would be true only if nitroglycerine also came from coal gasification. It does not. Nitroglycerine is a nitrate ester made from glycerol and mixed acid. Some nitric acid is made from ammonia, which can come from syngas, but that is a remote upstream link. The question refers to production of the substance by the technology, so this is not accepted. It is a trap for students who over-generalise about syngas.

None: this would mean coal gasification gives none of the substances. This is wrong because syngas is a major route to ammonia and urea, and it is used in coal-to-chemicals plants worldwide, such as in China and South Africa (Sasol uses coal gasification for fuels and chemicals). India is developing similar plants, for example the Talcher coal-to-urea project.
related: Syngas is a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen.
National Coal Gasification Mission target: 100 million tonnes of coal gasified by 2030.
Urea was first synthesised in 1828 by Friedrich Wöhler.
Haber-Bosch process makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
Nitroglycerine is made by nitrating glycerol with nitric and sulphuric acids; Nobel made dynamite from it in 1867.
Underground coal gasification (UCG) converts coal to gas in situ in the seam.
IGCC means integrated gasification combined cycle for power generation.
India's ethanol blending target of 20% (E20) was met around 2025.
statements: 1 — Correct: Ethanol can be produced from coal-derived syngas. Ethanol (C2H5OH) is a two-carbon alcohol. It is made mainly by fermenting sugars from sugarcane juice, molasses or grains, and it is blended with petrol under India's Ethanol Blending Programme (E20 reached around 2025). It can also be made from syngas, either through catalytic conversion or through fermentation by acetogenic bacteria. Coal gasification is therefore a possible but not the common route. Ethanol is also used as a solvent and in making chemicals, and the government has promoted second-generation (2G) ethanol from agricultural residues.

2 — Incorrect: Nitroglycerine is made by nitrating glycerol, not from coal syngas. Nitroglycerine (glyceryl trinitrate) was first made by Ascanio Sobrero in 1847. Alfred Nobel stabilised it as dynamite in 1867 by absorbing it in kieselguhr. It is a shock-sensitive liquid explosive and is also used medicinally as a vasodilator for angina. It is made by adding glycerol to a cold mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids. Glycerol comes from fats, oils or biodiesel, and coal gasification is not a step in the route.

3 — Correct: Urea can be produced from coal gasification. Urea (CO(NH2)2) is the most widely used nitrogenous fertiliser in India, with about 46% nitrogen. It was first synthesised by Friedrich Wöhler in 1828, an event that weakened vitalism. Industrially, ammonia is reacted with CO2 to give ammonium carbamate, which is then dehydrated to urea. Syngas from coal supplies hydrogen for the ammonia and also CO2. India has promoted coal-gasification-based urea, as at the Talcher plant, to cut dependence on imported LNG and urea. Urea is also neem-coated to reduce diversion and loss.
summary: The answer is (b) Only two. Coal gasification produces syngas (CO + H2), which is a feedstock for ethanol (via fermentation of syngas or catalytic conversion) and for urea (syngas gives hydrogen, which is combined with nitrogen to make ammonia, and the ammonia is reacted with CO2 to make urea). Nitroglycerine is made by nitrating glycerol (glycerin) with nitric and sulphuric acids, and coal gasification is not part of that route.
topic_notes: Coal gasification is the conversion of coal into syngas (CO + H2, with CO2, CH4 and H2O) by reacting it with a controlled amount of oxygen or air and steam at 700-1500 °C and high pressure. Main gasifier types are fixed (moving) bed, fluidised bed and entrained flow, and underground coal gasification (UCG) is done in situ in deep or unmineable seams. The key reactions are partial oxidation, the water-gas reaction (C + H2O gives CO + H2) and the water-gas shift (CO + H2O gives CO2 + H2). Syngas uses: hydrogen, ammonia and urea, methanol and its derivatives (formaldehyde, acetic acid), DME as an LPG substitute, Fischer-Tropsch diesel and petrol, synthetic natural gas, and electricity via IGCC (integrated gasification combined cycle). Indian policy: the Ministry of Coal launched the National Coal Gasification Mission in 2021 with a target of 100 million tonnes of coal gasified by 2030, with financial incentives approved in 2024 for pilot projects. Coal India has pursued gasification for ammonium nitrate and methanol, BHEL has developed a fluidised-bed gasifier, and the Talcher Fertilizers project in Odisha is a coal-gasification-based urea plant. India's high-ash coal makes gasification technically challenging. Benefits include reduced imports of LNG, urea, methanol and ammonia, and cleaner use of coal, since pollutants can be removed from syngas, though CO2 emissions remain, so carbon capture is often paired with it. Related: coal liquefaction (direct and indirect), coal bed methane (CBM), shale gas, and hydrogen colours (grey hydrogen from natural gas, black or brown from coal, green from electrolysis with renewables). Other angles UPSC may ask: ethanol blending (E20), second-generation ethanol, the Haber-Bosch process, urea pricing and neem coating, and how explosives are made.

question: What is the common characteristic of the chemical substances generally known as CL-20, HMX and LLM-105, which are sometimes talked about in media? These are alternatives to hydro
options: fluorocarbon refrigerants These are explosives in military
weapons These are high-energy fuels for
cruise missiles These are fuels for rocket
subject: Science & Tech
detail: CL-20, HMX and LLM-105 belong to the class of 'energetic materials': nitramine and nitro-heterocyclic compounds that release large amounts of energy on detonation. The OCR'd question text is garbled. The stem seems to say these are alternatives to hydro-based refrigerants, and each option begins with a fragment of the next. Reading the options as 'explosives in military weapons', the official key (b) fits. HMX (octogen) is a widely used military high explosive, found in plastic-bonded explosives, shaped charges and warhead fills, and as an ingredient in solid rocket propellants. CL-20 (hexanitrohexaazaisowurtzitane) is a newer, denser and more powerful nitramine, about 14-20% more energetic than HMX, and is used in advanced munitions and propellants. LLM-105 (2,6-diamino-3,5-dinitropyrazine-1-oxide), developed at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, is a insensitive high explosive with performance near HMX but much safer handling. Elimination: refrigerants (a) are fluorocarbons or hydrofluorocarbons such as HFC-134a and have no link to nitramines. Cruise-missile fuel (c) is liquid hydrocarbon fuel such as JP-10. Rocket propulsion fuel (d) would involve things like hydrazine, kerosene or LOX/LH2. The shared feature is explosive use, so (b) is correct.
explanations: Wrong. Fluorocarbon refrigerants are CFCs, HCFCs and HFCs. CL-20, HMX and LLM-105 are nitrogen-rich, nitro-group explosives with no cooling role.
Correct. All three are high-energy explosive compounds used in military weapons, such as warheads, munitions and detonating charges.
Wrong. Cruise missiles run on hydrocarbon jet fuels such as JP-10. These three compounds are explosives, not fuels, though they may be in the warhead.

Wrong. Rocket propulsion uses propellants like hydrazine, kerosene, LH2 and ammonium perchlorate composites. HMX and CL-20 can be additives in solid propellants, but their defining character is as explosives, not as fuels.
keyfact: CL-20, HMX and LLM-105 are high-energy nitro/nitramine explosives used in military weapons, not refrigerants or fuels.
option_notes: Fluorocarbon refrigerants are halogenated carbon compounds. CFCs such as CFC-12 were phased out under the Montreal Protocol (1987) because they deplete ozone. HCFCs are transitional. HFCs such as HFC-134a do not harm ozone but are strong greenhouse gases, and the Kigali Amendment (2016) phases them down. India is to begin its phase-down in 2028. They are unrelated to explosives.

Military explosives are high-energy materials that detonate to produce a shock wave and gas. Common ones are TNT, RDX, HMX, PETN, CL-20 and LLM-105. They fill bombs, missile warheads, shells and mines. Modern work focuses on 'insensitive munitions', meaning high power with low accidental-detonation risk. This is the correct category for the three compounds in the question.

Cruise missiles are low-flying, air-breathing guided missiles. They use turbofan or turbojet engines on hydrocarbon fuels such as JP-10, and ramjets in some cases, as in BrahMos. India's examples are BrahMos (supersonic) and Nirbhay (subsonic). Their warheads hold explosives, but their fuels are not these compounds.

Rocket propulsion uses liquid propellants (kerosene/LOX, LH2/LOX, UDMH/N2O4, hydrazine) or solid propellants (ammonium perchlorate, aluminium powder and a HTPB binder). Cryogenic engines use LH2 and LOX. HMX or CL-20 appear only as energetic additives in some solid propellants, so they are not 'fuels' as such.
related: CL-20 is a polycyclic nitramine and one of the most powerful non-nuclear conventional explosives.
HMX is also called octogen, and its full name is cyclotetramethylene-tetranitramine.
RDX is also called cyclonite, and its full name is cyclotrimethylenetrinitramine.
HEMRL Pune is a DRDO lab working on high-energy materials.
The Kigali Amendment (2016) to the Montreal Protocol phases down HFCs.
BrahMos is a supersonic cruise missile developed by India and Russia.
Insensitive munitions are designed to resist accidental detonation.
LLM-105 was developed at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.
summary: The answer is (b): CL-20, HMX and LLM-105 are high-energy explosive compounds used in military weapons (warheads, munitions, detonators and propellant formulations). They are energetic materials, not refrigerants or primarily rocket or cruise-missile fuels.
topic_notes: Energetic materials are substances that store chemical energy and release it rapidly. They fall into explosives (primary, secondary, tertiary), propellants and pyrotechnics. Primary explosives such as lead azide and mercury fulminate are sensitive and used in detonators. Secondary explosives such as TNT, RDX, HMX, PETN, CL-20 and LLM-105 are more stable and form the main charge. TNT has a detonation velocity of about 6,900 m/s. RDX (cyclonite) reaches about 8,750 m/s. HMX (octogen) is denser and has a higher melting point, with velocity about 9,100 m/s. CL-20, first synthesised in the 1980s at China Lake in the US, has the highest performance among them but is costly and sensitive. LLM-105, from Lawrence Livermore, is an insensitive high explosive with about 80-85% of the power of HMX. Plastic-bonded explosives (PBX) combine these with polymer binders. The common theme in recent news is insensitive munitions and the Indian push for indigenous production, through DRDO's High Energy Materials Research Laboratory (HEMRL), Pune, and the Explosives Research and Development Laboratory. India has reported indigenous work on CL-20 and HMX. UPSC may ask about the differences between explosives, propellants and fuels, the Montreal Protocol and Kigali Amendment, hypersonic or cruise missiles, or the Chemical Weapons Convention. Remember that nitramine explosives are not chemical weapons, since they work by blast and not by toxicity.

ocr: Consider the following statements : I. It is expected that Majorana 1 chip will enable quantum computing. Il. Majorana 1 chip has _ been introduced by Amazon Web Services (AWS). Ill. Deep learning is a subset of machine learning. Which of the statements given above are correct? (a) 1 and II only (b) 1 and III only (c) 1 and III only (a) 1, Il and Ill
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Majorana 1 was unveiled by Microsoft in February 2025 as the first quantum processing unit built on a 'topological core' architecture. It uses a new class of material called a topoconductor, made from indium arsenide and aluminium, to create and control Majorana zero modes (quasi-particles) that encode topological qubits. These qubits are expected to be more stable and less error-prone, and Microsoft says the design can scale to a million qubits on a single chip, which would make useful, fault-tolerant quantum computing possible. The claim is 'expected', which is why Statement I is correct. AWS has its own quantum chip, Ocelot (February 2025), which uses cat qubits for error correction. Google has Willow (December 2024). So Statement II confuses the company. On Statement III, the hierarchy is AI ⊃ machine learning ⊃ deep learning. Deep learning uses multi-layered artificial neural networks. Elimination logic: Statement II is wrong, so options (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated, leaving (c).
explanations: Wrong. It includes Statement II, which wrongly credits AWS with Majorana 1; the chip is Microsoft's. It also leaves out the correct Statement III.
Wrong. It includes Statement II, which is incorrect, and leaves out Statement I, which is correct.
Correct. Statements I and III are correct, and Statement II is incorrect because Majorana 1 is Microsoft's chip.
Wrong. It includes Statement II, which is factually incorrect because AWS's chip is Ocelot.
keyfact: Majorana 1 = Microsoft's topological quantum chip; AWS = Ocelot; Google = Willow; deep learning ⊂ machine learning.
related: Majorana 1 is Microsoft's topological quantum chip (Feb 2025).
AWS's quantum chip is Ocelot, which uses cat qubits.
Google's quantum chip is Willow (Dec 2024, 105 qubits).
National Quantum Mission: approved April 2023, outlay about ₹6,003 crore, 2023-31.
NQM has four T-Hubs: computing, communication, sensing and metrology, materials and devices.
AI ⊃ Machine Learning ⊃ Deep Learning ⊃ Generative AI.
2025 was declared the International Year of Quantum Science and Technology by the UN.
IndiaAI Mission was approved in March 2024 with an outlay of ₹10,372 crore.
statements: 1 — Correct: Majorana 1 is expected to enable scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computing. Microsoft announced it in February 2025 as the first quantum chip based on topological qubits. It uses a topoconductor (indium arsenide with aluminium) to host Majorana zero modes. The qubits are intended to be stable, with built-in error resistance. Microsoft claims it can scale to one million qubits on a palm-sized chip. It was developed partly with DARPA's US2QC programme support. The technology is still at an early stage and parts of the claim are debated by scientists.

2 — Incorrect: Majorana 1 was introduced by Microsoft, not Amazon Web Services. AWS's quantum chip is Ocelot, announced in February 2025, which uses cat qubits to reduce the cost of quantum error correction. Google's chip is Willow (December 2024, 105 qubits), and IBM has the Condor and Heron processors. The name Majorana comes from the Italian physicist Ettore Majorana, who predicted in 1937 particles that are their own antiparticles.

3 — Correct: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which is itself a subset of artificial intelligence. Deep learning uses multi-layered artificial neural networks (deep neural networks) to learn representations from large data. It powers image recognition, speech recognition, natural language processing and generative AI models such as large language models. Key architectures include CNNs, RNNs and Transformers. Pioneers include Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio, who received the 2018 Turing Award. Hinton also shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics.
summary: The answer is (c) I and III only. Majorana 1 is a quantum processor chip introduced by Microsoft (not Amazon Web Services) in February 2025, and it is expected to enable scalable quantum computing. Deep learning is indeed a subset of machine learning.
topic_notes: Quantum computing uses qubits, which exploit superposition (being in multiple states at once), entanglement (correlated states) and interference. Qubits are fragile and suffer decoherence and errors, so error correction is the central engineering challenge. Different hardware approaches include superconducting qubits (Google, IBM), trapped ions (IonQ, Quantinuum), photonic qubits, neutral atoms, cat qubits (AWS Ocelot) and topological qubits (Microsoft Majorana 1). Microsoft's topological approach uses Majorana zero modes in a topoconductor, aiming for hardware-level protection against noise. Key recent chips: Google Willow (Dec 2024) with 105 qubits, which showed error reduction as qubits scale; AWS Ocelot (Feb 2025); Microsoft Majorana 1 (Feb 2025). India's National Quantum Mission (NQM) was approved in April 2023 with an outlay of about ₹6,003 crore for 2023-31. It is run under the Department of Science and Technology and aims to build intermediate-scale quantum computers of 50-1000 physical qubits. It has four thematic hubs (T-Hubs): quantum computing, quantum communication, quantum sensing and metrology, and quantum materials and devices. Related concepts include quantum supremacy (advantage), quantum key distribution, post-quantum cryptography and the NIST standards. The AI hierarchy is: AI contains machine learning, which contains deep learning, which contains generative AI. Types of machine learning are supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. Likely future angles: the IndiaAI Mission (₹10,372 crore, approved March 2024), large language models, and the Transformer architecture. Other angles are quantum communication in India (ISRO's free-space QKD demonstrations; DRDO-IIT Delhi), the 2025 International Year of Quantum Science and Technology (declared by the UN), and the physics Nobel for 2025 (macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits).

ocr: With reference to monoclonal antibodies, often mentioned in news, consider the following statements : I. They are man-made proteins. Il. They stimulate immunological function due to their ability to bind to specific antigens. Ill. They are used in treating viral infections like that of Nipah virus. Which of the statements given above are correct? (a) 1 and II only (b) 1 and III only (c) 1 and III only (da) 1, II and Ill
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Monoclonal antibodies are identical immunoglobulin (protein) molecules produced by a single clone of B-cells or hybridoma cells, so every molecule recognises the same epitope on one antigen. The technique was developed by Georges Köhler and César Milstein in 1975 (hybridoma technology), and they shared the 1984 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Early mAbs were murine (-omab), later ones chimeric (-ximab), humanised (-zumab) and fully human (-umab). Their binding to specific antigens can neutralise pathogens, tag cells for destruction by immune cells, block receptors or checkpoints (for example PD-1 inhibitors), and thereby modulate or stimulate immune function. Uses include cancer (trastuzumab, rituximab), autoimmune disease (adalimumab), COVID-19 (casirivimab-imdevimab) and Ebola (Inmazeb, Ebanga). For Nipah, the human mAb m102.4 was developed in the USA and sent to Kerala/India for compassionate use. Elimination logic: statement I is a basic definitional fact, and II and III are widely reported. Once you know any two of them are correct, only (d) can survive, because each of (a), (b) and (c) drops one statement.
explanations: Wrong: it leaves out statement III, which is correct because mAbs such as m102.4 are used against Nipah virus.
Wrong: it leaves out statement I, but mAbs are indeed man-made proteins.
Wrong: it leaves out statement II, but mAbs do stimulate immune function through specific antigen binding.
Correct: statements I, II and III are all accurate, so this is the official answer.
keyfact: mAbs are lab-made, single-clone antibody proteins that bind one specific antigen; they are used against cancers and viruses, including Nipah (m102.4).
option_notes: Option (a), 'I and II only', would mean mAbs are made-made and immune-stimulating but not used for viral infections. It is wrong. mAbs are in fact used against RSV, Ebola, COVID-19 and, on a compassionate basis, Nipah. They are lab-made proteins whose specificity lets them work as passive immunotherapy. UPSC often tests such partial combinations, so check each statement independently.

Option (b), 'II and III only', would mean that mAbs are not man-made proteins. That is wrong, because they are artificially produced by hybridoma or recombinant technology. Natural polyclonal antibodies come from many B-cell clones, whereas mAbs come from one clone. Their protein nature means they are usually given by injection or infusion rather than orally, since digestion would break them down.

Option (c), 'I and III only', would deny that mAbs stimulate immunological function by binding specific antigens. That is wrong. Binding specific antigens is the very basis of their immune action, whether by neutralisation, opsonisation, complement activation or checkpoint blockade. In cancer immunotherapy, mAbs such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab release T-cells to attack tumours.

Option (d), 'I, II and III', is the official answer. It reflects that mAbs are lab-made protein reagents or drugs, act through antigen-specific binding to modulate immunity, and have antiviral use, including for Nipah (m102.4). The related Nobel Prizes are 1984 (Köhler and Milstein) and 2018 (Allison and Honjo, checkpoint therapy).
related: Köhler and Milstein developed hybridoma technology in 1975 and won the 1984 Nobel Prize.
The first therapeutic mAb approved was muromonab-CD3 in 1986.
Nipah mAb m102.4 targets the viral G glycoprotein.
Nipah is carried by Pteropus fruit bats and is a Henipavirus.
Kerala reported Nipah outbreaks first in 2018, in Kozhikode.
Pembrolizumab and nivolumab are PD-1 checkpoint-inhibitor mAbs.
Trastuzumab targets HER2 in breast cancer.
The 2018 Chemistry Nobel recognised phage display, used to make human antibodies.
statements: 1 — Correct: mAbs are man-made (laboratory-produced) immunoglobulin proteins. They are made by hybridoma technology or recombinant DNA methods, in which a single B-cell clone is immortalised by fusion with myeloma cells. Every antibody is identical and targets one epitope. The technique was introduced by Köhler and Milstein in 1975, and the first therapeutic mAb, muromonab-CD3, was approved in 1986 to prevent transplant rejection. Modern mAbs are humanised or fully human, which lowers immunogenicity, and are produced in mammalian cell cultures such as CHO cells.

2 — Correct: a mAb binds specifically to its target antigen, and this action can enhance immune function. It can opsonise pathogens, activate complement, trigger antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, or block inhibitory checkpoints such as PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4 so that T-cells attack tumours. Checkpoint-inhibitor research won the 2018 Nobel Prize for James Allison and Tasuku Honjo. Specificity is the key feature of mAbs and the reason they are called targeted or 'magic bullet' therapy. The same principle underlies passive immunisation.

3 — Correct: mAbs are used against viral infections. For Nipah virus, the human mAb m102.4 targets the viral G glycoprotein and was supplied to India for compassionate use during Kerala outbreaks. Nipah is a zoonotic paramyxovirus carried by fruit bats (Pteropus), first identified in Malaysia in 1998-99, and Kerala has had outbreaks since 2018. Other antiviral mAbs include palivizumab (RSV), nirsevimab (RSV), Inmazeb and Ebanga (Ebola), and casirivimab-imdevimab (COVID-19). No licensed Nipah vaccine or drug exists yet.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are laboratory-made proteins that bind to one specific antigen, which directs or boosts the immune response. They are also used against viral infections, including Nipah virus, where the mAb m102.4 has been used on a compassionate-use basis.
topic_notes: Monoclonal antibodies are antibodies, which are Y-shaped immunoglobulin proteins, made by identical immune cells that are clones of a single parent B-cell. Because they come from one clone, they recognise a single epitope. Hybridoma technology (Köhler and Milstein, 1975) fuses antibody-producing B-cells with immortal myeloma cells, producing hybridomas that grow indefinitely and secrete one antibody type. Later advances include phage display (Nobel 2018 in Chemistry for George Smith and Gregory Winter), which allows fully human mAbs, and recombinant production in CHO cells. Naming: -omab (mouse), -ximab (chimeric), -zumab (humanised), -umab (human). Applications: cancer (trastuzumab for HER2 breast cancer, rituximab for CD20 lymphoma, pembrolizumab and nivolumab as PD-1 inhibitors), autoimmune diseases (adalimumab and infliximab against TNF-alpha), asthma, migraine (CGRP mAbs), osteoporosis (denosumab) and infections (palivizumab for RSV; Ebola mAbs; COVID-19 mAbs; Nipah m102.4). Diagnostics use include pregnancy test kits, ELISA, immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry. Related terms: passive immunity (ready-made antibodies given, short-lived, versus active immunity from vaccines), antibody-drug conjugates (trastuzumab emtansine), and bispecific antibodies. Nipah virus: a Henipavirus in the Paramyxoviridae family, spread by Pteropus fruit bats, via contaminated date-palm sap or pigs, and by human contact; fatality is high (40-75%); outbreaks occurred in Malaysia, Singapore, Bangladesh, and in India in West Bengal (2001, 2007) and Kerala (2018 onwards). ICMR has been working on a Nipah mAb and vaccines. Limitations: high cost, injection-only delivery, immunogenicity, and viral escape mutations, as seen with COVID-19 variants.

question:
Consider the following statements :
I. No virus can survive in ocean waters. Il. No virus can infect bacteria. Ill. No virus can change the cellular transcriptional activity in host cells. How many of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites. They are acellular, with a nucleic acid genome (DNA or RNA) inside a protein capsid, and some have a lipid envelope. They replicate only inside living host cells, using the host's machinery. Statement I is wrong because the oceans are the largest viral reservoir on Earth: roughly 10^7 viruses per mL of seawater, about 10^30 in total. Most are bacteriophages and viruses of phytoplankton. They drive nutrient cycling through the 'viral shunt', lysing 20-40% of marine bacteria daily, and they influence carbon cycling and climate. Statement II is wrong because bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria. Examples are T4, lambda and M13. Phage therapy is based on them. Statement III is wrong because viruses routinely alter host transcription. HIV's Tat protein boosts transcription, retroviruses integrate proviral DNA, influenza 'cap-snatches' host mRNA, and oncogenic viruses such as HPV (E6/E7) and EBV change host gene expression. Elimination logic: each statement uses the absolute word 'No', so a single counterexample falsifies it. Since all three fail, the answer is (d).
explanations: (a) Only one is wrong, because no statement is correct; each is contradicted by established virology.
(b) Only two is wrong, because even two correct statements are not possible here; all three absolute claims fail.
(c) All three is wrong, because the statements say 'No virus', which is false in each case: marine viruses, phages and transcription-altering viruses all exist.
(d) None is correct, because viruses are abundant in oceans, infect bacteria as phages, and modify host transcription.
keyfact: Viruses abound in oceans, phages infect bacteria, and many viruses reprogram host transcription, so none of the three 'No virus' claims is correct.
option_notes: Only one: this would mean exactly one of the statements is true. Here it is not the case. As a question format, the 'how many' type tests whether you can check each statement independently, and the 'one' option is a common distractor.

Only two: this would mean two statements are true. In this question none is true. 'How many correct' questions in UPSC often hinge on absolute words such as 'No', 'only' and 'all', which are usually wrong in biology.

All three: this would mean viruses cannot survive in the ocean, cannot infect bacteria and cannot alter host transcription. All of these are contradicted by evidence. It is the opposite of the real situation.

None: no statement is correct. This is the official answer. Viruses are the most abundant biological entities in the oceans, bacteriophages infect bacteria, and many viruses reprogram host gene expression and transcription.
related: Bacteriophages were discovered by Twort (1915) and d'Herelle (1917).
Marine viruses number about 10^30 and drive the 'viral shunt'.
Tobacco mosaic virus was the first virus discovered (Ivanovsky 1892).
Retroviruses such as HIV use reverse transcriptase to make DNA from RNA.
HPV E6 and E7 proteins inactivate p53 and Rb, leading to cervical cancer.
Viroids are naked circular RNA infecting plants (Diener, 1971).
CRISPR-Cas is a bacterial adaptive defence against phages.
Transduction is gene transfer between bacteria via phages.
statements: I — Incorrect: Viruses are abundant in the oceans and survive there in large numbers. Marine viruses number about 10^30 and are the most abundant biological entities in the sea. Most infect bacteria (phages), cyanobacteria and algae. Viral lysis releases dissolved organic matter in the 'viral shunt', which recycles nutrients and affects carbon export. Cyanophages infect Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus. Viral lysis can end algal blooms, for example Emiliania huxleyi blooms through EhV. Marine viromes have been surveyed by projects such as Tara Oceans, which found thousands of previously unknown viral populations.

II — Incorrect: Viruses that infect bacteria exist and are called bacteriophages (phages). They were discovered by Frederick Twort (1915) and Félix d'Herelle (1917), who coined the term. Phages attach to bacterial receptors and inject their genome. They then follow a lytic cycle, which kills the cell, or a lysogenic cycle, in which the prophage integrates into the host genome. Phages enable transduction, a form of horizontal gene transfer. They carry toxin genes, as in cholera and diphtheria. Phage therapy is being revived against antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Phage display and CRISPR research also use them.

III — Incorrect: Viruses commonly alter host-cell transcription. They hijack host RNA polymerase and transcription factors and shut off host gene expression. HIV Tat enhances viral transcription. Influenza virus uses cap-snatching from host pre-mRNA. Herpesviruses and poxviruses carry their own transcription machinery or modulators. HPV E6 and E7 inactivate p53 and Rb, which changes cell-cycle gene expression and can lead to cervical cancer. Retroviruses integrate as proviruses under host transcription control. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA, which is the basis of the central dogma exception noted by Temin and Baltimore.
summary: The answer is (d) None. All three statements are false: viruses are abundant in ocean waters, bacteriophages infect bacteria, and many viruses reprogram host-cell transcription.
topic_notes: Viruses are non-cellular, obligate intracellular parasites, typically 20-300 nm in size. They are classified by genome type (Baltimore classification, seven groups), host range (animal, plant, bacterial, archaeal, fungal) and morphology. Outside a host they are inert virions. Replication stages are attachment, entry, uncoating, synthesis, assembly and release. Bacteriophages follow lytic or lysogenic cycles, and transduction, either generalised or specialised, moves genes between bacteria. Marine virology: about 10^30 viruses in the oceans, the viral shunt, regulation of algal blooms, and control of bacterial populations. Viruses influence host transcription by shutting off host mRNA synthesis, using host RNA polymerase II, cap-snatching (influenza), integrating proviruses (retroviruses) and encoding oncoproteins (HPV E6/E7, SV40 large T antigen). Related ideas include viroids (naked RNA that infect plants, discovered by T.O. Diener, 1971), prions (infectious proteins), and giant viruses such as Mimivirus and Pandoravirus. Other angles UPSC may test: vaccines (live attenuated, inactivated, mRNA, viral vector), reverse transcriptase and the central dogma, CRISPR-Cas as a bacterial defence against phages, oncolytic viruses, zoonotic spillover (Nipah, SARS-CoV-2, H5N1), antivirals (acyclovir, remdesivir), the role of interferons, and the distinction between DNA and RNA viruses. Also remember that antibiotics do not work against viruses, and that the first virus discovered was tobacco mosaic virus (Ivanovsky 1892, Beijerinck 1898), with Stanley crystallising it in 1935.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I : Activated carbon is a good and an attractive tool to remove pollutants from effluent streams and to remediate contaminants from various industries.
Statement II : Activated carbon exhibits a large surface area and a strong potential for adsorbing heavy metals. Statement III : Activated carbon can be easily synthesized from environmental wastes with high carbon content. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement II and Statement III are correct and both of them explain Statement I
Both Statement II and Statement Il are correct but only one of them explains Statement I
Only one of the Statements II and Ill is correct and that explains Statement I
Neither Statement II nor Statement Ill is correct [ P.T.O
subject: Environment
detail: Activated carbon is carbon processed (by carbonisation followed by physical activation with steam or CO2, or chemical activation with agents such as H3PO4, KOH or ZnCl2) to develop an extensive network of micropores and mesopores. Its surface area typically ranges from about 500 to 1500 m2/g, sometimes more. This gives huge adsorption capacity, because adsorption is a surface phenomenon in which molecules stick to the solid surface. It removes organic pollutants, dyes, phenols, pesticides, odours, chlorine and heavy metals such as lead, mercury, cadmium, chromium and arsenic from water, air and industrial effluents. The feedstock can be coconut shells, rice husk, sawdust, bagasse, fruit stones, agricultural residues, tyres or coal, so production is cheap and also converts waste into a useful product. Statement II explains the effectiveness (a technical reason) and Statement III explains the attractiveness (an economic and environmental reason). Elimination: since both II and III are factually correct and both support I, options (b), (c) and (d) fail, because each denies either the correctness or the explanatory link of at least one statement.
explanations: Correct: Statement II (large surface area, strong heavy metal adsorption) and Statement III (easy, cheap synthesis from carbon-rich waste) are both true, and together they explain why activated carbon is a good and attractive remediation tool.
Wrong: this says only one of the two explains Statement I, but both do. Effectiveness comes from II and attractiveness (low cost, sustainability) from III.
Wrong: this says only one of II and III is correct, but both are factually correct.
Wrong: this says neither II nor III is correct, which is false because both are established facts about activated carbon.
keyfact: Activated carbon works because of its huge porous surface area (adsorption of heavy metals and organics), and it is attractive because it can be cheaply made from carbon-rich waste.
option_notes: Both II and III correct and both explain I: this is the right option here. It recognises that adsorption capacity (technical reason) and low-cost waste-based production (economic reason) jointly make activated carbon attractive for pollution control. Activated carbon is used in water treatment, air purification, solvent recovery and medicine, and is made from coconut shell, wood, coal and agricultural waste.

Both II and III correct but only one explains I: this is a plausible-looking distractor. UPSC uses such options to test whether you can judge the explanatory link. Here the link holds for both, because performance depends on surface area and wide adoption depends on cheap feedstock, so the 'only one explains' claim fails.

Only one of II and III is correct and it explains I: this would apply if one statement were factually false. Both statements are true, so it fails. In such 'statement-explanation' questions, first check each statement's factual accuracy, then check the explanatory relationship.

Neither II nor III is correct: this would mean activated carbon lacked high surface area and could not be made from waste, which is plainly wrong. Activated carbon surface area often exceeds 500 m2/g, and waste-derived carbons from rice husk and coconut shell are common in research and industry.
related: Adsorption is a surface phenomenon, while absorption occurs throughout the bulk of a material.
Activated carbon surface area can exceed 1000 m2/g.
Biochar is produced by pyrolysis of biomass and is used for soil amendment and carbon sequestration.
Common activating agents: steam, CO2, H3PO4, KOH and ZnCl2.
Coconut shell is a major raw material for activated carbon in India.
Heavy metals commonly removed: Pb, Hg, Cd, Cr and As.
The BET method measures specific surface area using nitrogen adsorption.
CPCB is the body that sets effluent standards in India.
statements: 1 — Correct: Activated carbon is widely used in effluent treatment and remediation. It is a form of carbon with a highly porous structure, used since ancient times (Egyptians used charcoal for medicine and Indians for water filtration). Modern industrial use began in the early 1900s. It is used in water purification, gas masks, air filters, sugar decolourisation, gold recovery, and medical treatment of poisoning. It is available as powdered (PAC), granular (GAC) and extruded forms. Spent carbon can be regenerated thermally.

2 — Correct: Activated carbon has a very large specific surface area and a porous structure with surface functional groups (carboxyl, hydroxyl) that bind heavy metal ions. Adsorption is a surface phenomenon, different from absorption. Pore sizes are classified by IUPAC as micropores (<2 nm), mesopores (2 to 50 nm) and macropores (>50 nm). It adsorbs metals like Pb, Cd, Hg, Cr(VI) and As, and the process depends on pH, contact time and temperature. Surface area is often measured by the BET method using nitrogen adsorption.

3 — Correct: Activated carbon can be made from low-cost, carbon-rich wastes such as coconut shell, rice husk, wood waste, bagasse, nut shells, fruit peels, sewage sludge and waste tyres. Preparation involves pyrolysis (carbonisation) at about 400 to 800 degrees C in limited oxygen, then activation by steam or CO2 at higher temperatures, or by chemicals such as KOH or H3PO4. This lowers cost, reduces waste disposal problems and supports a circular economy and waste-to-wealth goals. India is a major producer from coconut shells.
summary: The answer is (a). Activated carbon has a very large surface area and a strong capacity to adsorb heavy metals (Statement II), and it can be made cheaply from carbon-rich wastes (Statement III). Together these explain why it is a good and attractive tool for cleaning effluents and remediating industrial contaminants (Statement I).
topic_notes: Activated carbon (activated charcoal) is a highly porous carbonaceous adsorbent. Production has two steps: carbonisation (pyrolysis of the raw material in an oxygen-poor atmosphere) and activation (physical, using steam or CO2 at about 800 to 1000 degrees C; or chemical, using H3PO4, ZnCl2 or KOH at lower temperatures). Typical raw materials are coal, coconut shell, wood, peat, rice husk, bagasse, fruit stones and agricultural residues. Surface area is usually 500 to 1500 m2/g, and it is measured by the BET method. Adsorption works by physical forces (van der Waals) and sometimes chemical bonding (chemisorption). Forms are powdered (PAC), granular (GAC) and pelletised. Uses include drinking water purification (removal of taste, odour, chlorine, organics), industrial effluent treatment (dyes, phenols, heavy metals), air and gas purification, gas masks, solvent recovery, decolourising sugar, gold extraction (carbon-in-pulp), food and beverage processing, and emergency treatment of oral poisoning. Limitations: it is less effective for some small polar compounds, it saturates and needs regeneration (thermal, chemical) or disposal, and its performance depends on pH, temperature and contact time. Related concepts: adsorption versus absorption, biochar (made from biomass pyrolysis, used for soil improvement and carbon sequestration), bioremediation, phytoremediation, nanomaterials such as graphene and carbon nanotubes, ion exchange, reverse osmosis, and zeolites. Policy angles: waste-to-wealth, circular economy, Swachh Bharat, Namami Gange, effluent standards under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986, and the role of CPCB. UPSC often asks assertion-reason style questions on environmental technologies, so know both the mechanism and the use.

question:
With reference to the Indian polity, consider the following statements :
I. An Ordinance can amend any Central Act. Il. An Ordinance can abridge a Fundamental Right. Ill. An Ordinance can come into effect from a back date. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Article 123 empowers the President to promulgate Ordinances when Parliament is not in session and immediate action is necessary. Under Article 123(2), an Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament, but only on subjects within Parliament's legislative competence. It can therefore amend or repeal any Central Act, and it can even amend a tax law. It can also be retrospective, as Parliament's own laws can be. The limits are these. First, it cannot amend the Constitution, since that needs the Article 368 procedure. Second, it cannot violate Part III. Article 13(3)(a) defines 'law' to include an Ordinance, and Article 13(2) bars the State from making any law that takes away or abridges Fundamental Rights. Third, it must be laid before Parliament and lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles, or earlier if both Houses disapprove it. The Ordinance route also cannot be used when Parliament is in session. Judicial cases include RC Cooper (1970), which held the satisfaction of the President to be justiciable, DC Wadhwa (1987), which condemned repeated re-promulgation, and Krishna Kumar Singh (2017). Elimination logic: II is wrong, so (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated, leaving (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes II, but an Ordinance cannot abridge a Fundamental Right because Article 13(2) bars it.
Wrong: it includes II, which is incorrect, and it leaves out I, which is correct.
Correct: I and III hold. An Ordinance can amend Central Acts and can be retrospective, while II fails because of Article 13.
Wrong: it counts II as correct, but Fundamental Rights bind Ordinances through Article 13(3)(a).
keyfact: An Ordinance equals an Act in force and can amend Central Acts and be retrospective, but it is 'law' under Article 13 and cannot abridge Fundamental Rights.
option_notes: Option (a), I and II only, combines the correct statement I with the wrong statement II. It is a trap for students who think the President's legislative power is absolute. Ordinance power is limited by Part III, by the Parliament-only subject limit, and by the bar on amending the Constitution. The Ordinance must also be placed before Parliament, and it lapses after six weeks from reassembly. The President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

Option (b), II and III only, wrongly accepts that an Ordinance can abridge Fundamental Rights. Fundamental Rights in Part III (Articles 12-35) bind every organ of the State, and Article 13(2) voids any law that violates them. Statement III is correct, but the combination fails because of II and because it excludes I. Remember that Ordinances are executive-issued legislation and are subject to judicial review, as in RC Cooper and Krishna Kumar Singh.

Option (c), I and III only, is the official answer. It reflects that an Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament under Article 123(2). Such Ordinances can amend any Central Act and can have retrospective effect, but they are bound by Article 13 and cannot amend the Constitution. The same pattern applies to Governors' Ordinances under Article 213, which are limited to State subjects and sometimes require the President's instructions.

Option (d), I, II and III, is wrong because it accepts all three statements, including the false claim that an Ordinance can abridge Fundamental Rights. The mistake is to treat an Ordinance as being above the Constitution. An Ordinance is subordinate to the Constitution, and its validity can be challenged in court, including on grounds of mala fides or fraud on the Constitution (Krishna Kumar Singh, 2017).
related: Article 123: the President's power to promulgate Ordinances when Parliament is not in session.
Article 213: the Governor's Ordinance-making power.
Ordinance must be laid before Parliament; it lapses six weeks after reassembly.
Article 13(3)(a): 'law' includes an Ordinance.
DC Wadhwa (1987): re-promulgation of Ordinances is a fraud on the Constitution.
An Ordinance cannot amend the Constitution (Article 368).
44th Amendment (1978) removed the bar on judicial review of the President's satisfaction.
Krishna Kumar Singh (2017): the Ordinance's effect after lapse and the duty to lay it before the Legislature.
statements: I — Correct: An Ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament and can amend or repeal any Central Act, subject to the limits of Parliament's competence. Article 123 allows the President to promulgate Ordinances only when Parliament is not in session, and only when the President is satisfied that immediate action is needed. The Ordinance must be laid before Parliament, and it ceases to operate six weeks after Parliament reassembles, or sooner if both Houses pass disapproving resolutions. It can cover only subjects on which Parliament can legislate, and it may also amend taxation laws. Governors have a similar power for State subjects under Article 213.

II — Incorrect: An Ordinance is 'law' under Article 13(3)(a), so Article 13(2) applies to it and it cannot take away or abridge Fundamental Rights. A court can strike it down if it violates Part III. Article 13 also covers laws in force, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs and usages. Under Article 13(2), a law that contravenes Part III is void to the extent of the contravention. The same restriction applies to Parliament itself. Under Article 368, a constitutional amendment is not 'law' for Article 13 purposes (Shankari Prasad, Golak Nath, Kesavananda Bharati). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) limited this by establishing the basic structure doctrine.

III — Correct: Parliament can make laws with retrospective effect, and an Ordinance has the same force, so it can also operate from a back date. Retrospectivity is generally allowed except for criminal laws that create new offences, which Article 20(1) bars. Taxation Ordinances have been made retrospective, for example validating earlier levies. Courts examine the legislative competence behind such Ordinances and whether they violate rights. Article 123 does not prohibit retrospective operation. Ordinances usually come into effect on the date of promulgation unless they state a different date, and the Ordinance's own text may specify an earlier date, subject to constitutional limits.
summary: The answer is (c): statements I and III are correct, and statement II is incorrect. An Ordinance under Article 123 has the same force as an Act of Parliament, so it can amend Central Acts and can be made retrospective. It cannot abridge Fundamental Rights, because it is 'law' under Article 13(3)(a) and is therefore bound by Article 13(2).
topic_notes: Ordinance-making power: Article 123 covers the President and Article 213 covers the Governor. Conditions: Parliament, or the State Legislature, must not be in session, meaning at least one House is not sitting, and the President or Governor must be satisfied that circumstances require immediate action. The Ordinance has the same force as an Act, but only on matters within legislative competence. It must be laid before Parliament when it reassembles and ceases to operate at the expiry of six weeks from reassembly, or earlier if both Houses pass resolutions disapproving it. It can be withdrawn at any time by the President. There is no fixed maximum duration. Its maximum life is six months plus six weeks if Parliament is not summoned for the full gap. The Ordinance is not a constitutional amendment. It is a form of legislation made by the Executive on the advice of the Council of Ministers. Key cases: RC Cooper (1970), where the satisfaction of the President can be challenged on the ground of mala fides; DC Wadhwa v State of Bihar (1987), where re-promulgation of Ordinances without placing them before the Legislature was held to be a fraud on the Constitution; Krishna Kumar Singh v State of Bihar (2017), where the Ordinance's laying before the Legislature was held mandatory, and where the Court held that an Ordinance's effect continues unless it is struck down. Comparisons: Governors cannot promulgate Ordinances in certain cases without the President's instructions, such as when a Bill on the same subject would need the President's prior sanction or reservation. The 38th Amendment tried to make the President's satisfaction final, but this was later removed by the 44th Amendment. Other angles include the Ordinance route versus money bills, the limits on Ordinance for constitutional amendments, and the Ordinance versus delegated legislation.

question:
Consider the following pairs : State Description
I. Arunachal : The capital is named after Pradesh a fort, and the State has two National Parks Il. Nagaland : The State came into existence on the basis of a Constitutional Amendment Act Il. Tripura : Initially a Part ‘C’ State, it became a centrally administered territory with the reorganization of States in 1956 and later attained the status of a full-fledged State How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
subject: Polity
detail: The question tests the political and administrative history of three North-eastern States. Pair I: Itanagar, the capital of Arunachal Pradesh, takes its name from the Ita Fort, a brick fort of the 14th-15th century. Arunachal has two National Parks, Namdapha (Changlang, a Project Tiger reserve) and Mouling (Upper Siang). Pair II: Nagaland was made the 16th State by the State of Nagaland Act, 1962, which was enacted under the 13th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962. It inserted Article 371A and amended Article 3 and the First Schedule. The State was formally inaugurated on 1 December 1963. Pair III: Tripura, a princely state, merged with India in 1949 and became a Part C State in 1950. The States Reorganisation Act and the 7th Amendment (1956) turned it into a Union Territory. The North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971 made it a full State on 21 January 1972, along with Manipur and Meghalaya. Because every pair is factually correct, the options 'Only one', 'Only two' and 'None' are all eliminated.
explanations: Incorrect: this option implies that two of the pairs are wrong, but all three are correct.
Incorrect: this option implies that one pair is wrong, but all three descriptions are factually accurate.
Correct: Itanagar is named after Ita Fort and Arunachal has two National Parks; Nagaland was created via the 13th Amendment; Tripura moved from Part C State to UT (1956) to State (1972).
Incorrect: none would hold only if every pair were wrong, but each pair is accurate.
keyfact: Nagaland: 13th Amendment 1962 (Art 371A); Tripura: Part C, UT 1956, State 1972; Itanagar is named after Ita Fort.
option_notes: Only one: this would mean that exactly one pair is right. It is a common trap in 'how many pairs' questions, which are built to test whether you verify every item. Here it does not apply, because all three pairs are right. The question concerns Arunachal (State since 1987), Nagaland (State since 1963) and Tripura (State since 1972).

Only two: this would mean that exactly one pair is wrong. Likely doubts were the number of Arunachal's National Parks (two: Namdapha and Mouling) or whether Nagaland's creation relied on a Constitutional Amendment (the 13th, 1962). Both check out, as does Tripura's Part C to UT to State path. So this option is wrong.

All the three: the official answer. It requires knowing the origin of Itanagar's name (Ita Fort), the number of Arunachal's National Parks (2), Nagaland's statehood through the 13th Amendment and State of Nagaland Act 1962 (Article 371A), and Tripura's Part C status, UT status in 1956 and statehood in 1972.

None: this would mean every pair is wrongly matched. It is the least likely outcome in a UPSC question that combines three facts, and it is false here, because each description is accurate. UPSC does use 'None' at times, so check each item rather than guessing by pattern.
related: Nagaland became the 16th State on 1 December 1963.
Article 371A protects Naga customary law and land ownership.
Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram became States on 20 February 1987.
Sikkim became the 22nd State in 1975 via the 36th Amendment.
Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura attained statehood on 21 January 1972.
Namdapha National Park has four big cat species.
The 7th Amendment 1956 abolished Part A, B, C and D States.
Itanagar was named after Ita Fort.
statements: I — Correct: Itanagar is named after Ita Fort, and Arunachal has two National Parks, Namdapha and Mouling. Itanagar became the capital in 1974 (formerly Arunachal was NEFA). Ita Fort is a brick fort in the Papum Pare district, dated to the 14th-15th century and linked to the Jitari dynasty. Namdapha National Park lies in Changlang district and is the largest protected area in the Eastern Himalaya biodiversity hotspot. It is the only park in the world with four big cats (tiger, leopard, snow leopard, clouded leopard). Mouling National Park is in the Siang valley, and the Siang is part of the Brahmaputra system. Arunachal became a UT in 1972 and a State on 20 February 1987 (55th Amendment).

II — Correct: Nagaland was created by the State of Nagaland Act, 1962, following the 13th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962. That amendment added Article 371A, which gives special protection to Naga customary law, religious and social practices, and land ownership. The Naga Hills district of Assam merged with the Tuensang Frontier Division to form the Naga Hills-Tuensang Area. The 16-Point Agreement of 1960 between the Centre and the Naga People's Convention paved the way for statehood. The State was inaugurated on 1 December 1963, and Kohima is its capital. It became the 16th State of the Indian Union.

III — Correct: Tripura was a princely state that acceded to India in 1949 and became a Part C State in 1950. The Fazl Ali Commission (SRC) recommended the abolition of Part C status. Through the 7th Amendment Act, 1956, Tripura became a Union Territory with effect from 1 November 1956, administered by the President through an Administrator. It got a Territorial Council in 1957 and a Legislative Assembly in 1963. The North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971 gave Tripura, Manipur and Meghalaya full statehood on 21 January 1972. Agartala is its capital.
summary: The answer is (c): all three pairs are correctly matched. Itanagar is named after Ita Fort, and Arunachal has two National Parks (Namdapha and Mouling). Nagaland was created by the 13th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962. Tripura was a Part C State, became a Union Territory in 1956, and became a full State in 1972.
topic_notes: Reorganisation of North-East India. Assam was split step by step. Nagaland became a State in 1963 (13th Amendment, Article 371A). Meghalaya became an autonomous State within Assam in 1970 (22nd Amendment) and a full State in 1972. The North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971 made Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura States on 21 January 1972, and Arunachal (NEFA) and Mizoram UTs. Mizoram became a State on 20 February 1987 (53rd Amendment), the same day as Arunachal (55th Amendment). Sikkim joined India as the 22nd State in 1975 through the 36th Amendment, with Article 371F. The 1956 reorganisation under the States Reorganisation Act and the 7th Amendment abolished the Part A/B/C/D categories and created 14 States and 6 UTs. Tripura and Manipur were Part C States, then UTs. Special provisions: Article 371A (Nagaland), 371B (Assam), 371C (Manipur), 371F (Sikkim), 371G (Mizoram), 371H (Arunachal). The Sixth Schedule covers tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Key parks: Namdapha (Arunachal), Kaziranga and Manas (Assam), Dibru-Saikhowa, Keibul Lamjao (Manipur, floating park), Balphakram (Meghalaya), Intanki (Nagaland), Khangchendzonga (Sikkim). Capitals: Itanagar, Kohima, Agartala, Imphal, Shillong, Aizawl, Gangtok, Dispur. Likely UPSC angles: dates of statehood, the amendments involved, the Article 371 provisions, the Sixth Schedule, and the Fazl Ali Commission.

question:
With reference to India, consider the following :
I. The Inter-State Council
II. The National Security Council Ill. Zonal Councils How many of the above’ were established as per the provisions of the Constitution of India?
subject: Polity
detail: The question tests the difference between constitutional bodies, statutory bodies and extra-constitutional/executive bodies. Article 263 empowers the President to establish an Inter-State Council if it appears that the public interest would be served by one. The Council investigates and discusses subjects of common interest between the Centre and States and between States, and makes recommendations. The President set up the Inter-State Council by a Presidential Order in 1990, following the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation. The National Security Council was set up in 1998 by an executive resolution of the Government of India under the Vajpayee government. It has no constitutional or statutory basis. It consists of the Prime Minister, the Home, Defence, External Affairs and Finance Ministers, and the Deputy Chairman of NITI Aayog, with the National Security Adviser as secretary. Zonal Councils were created under Part III of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, not by the Constitution, so they are statutory. There are five of them, and they are advisory bodies. Eliminating (c) and (b) is easy once you know that the NSC and the Zonal Councils fall outside the Constitution. Option (d) is eliminated because Article 263 clearly covers the Inter-State Council.
explanations: Correct. Only the Inter-State Council has a constitutional basis, in Article 263. The NSC is executive and the Zonal Councils are statutory.
Wrong. It would require two bodies to be constitutional, but the Zonal Councils are statutory under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, and the NSC is an executive creation.
Wrong. The NSC and the Zonal Councils do not derive from constitutional provisions, so not all three qualify.
Wrong. The Inter-State Council was established under Article 263, so at least one qualifies.
keyfact: Inter-State Council: constitutional (Art. 263); Zonal Councils: statutory (1956 Act); NSC: executive (1998).
option_notes: Only one: this is the correct answer. The only constitutional body in the list is the Inter-State Council under Article 263, set up in 1990. Constitutional bodies include the Finance Commission (Art. 280), the UPSC (Art. 315) and the Election Commission (Art. 324). Article 263 is permissive, so the Council exists only when the President chooses to establish it.

Only two: this would mean that one of the NSC or the Zonal Councils is constitutional, and neither is. The Zonal Councils are statutory under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. The NSC dates from 1998 and is purely executive. Statutory bodies, such as the NHRC and NITI Aayog's predecessor bodies, differ from constitutional ones in origin and in how easily they can be changed.

All the three: this is wrong because the NSC (1998, executive) and the Zonal Councils (1956 Act, statutory) are not constitutional. Note that extra-constitutional bodies such as NITI Aayog (2015, by Cabinet resolution) and the former Planning Commission (1950) share the NSC's executive origin.

None: this is wrong because Article 263 provides for the Inter-State Council. Another example of a constitutional but non-statutory body is the Finance Commission. Article 263 is in Part XI, Chapter II (Administrative Relations), and the Council was created in 1990.
related: Article 263 provides for the Inter-State Council; it was set up in 1990.
The Zonal Councils (5) were created under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956; the Union Home Minister chairs them.
The North Eastern Council was created by the NEC Act, 1971, and is separate from the Zonal Councils.
The NSC was created in 1998 by executive decision; the NSA acts as its secretary.
The GST Council is constitutional (Art. 279A, 101st Amendment).
NITI Aayog (2015) is an executive body, neither constitutional nor statutory.
The Finance Commission (Art. 280) is constitutional and is appointed every five years.
The NHRC is a statutory body created under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
statements: I — Correct: It is provided for by Article 263 of the Constitution, which empowers the President to establish it. The Inter-State Council was set up by a Presidential Order on 28 May 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation. It is a recommendatory body for Centre-State and inter-State coordination. The Prime Minister is the Chairman. Its members are the Chief Ministers of all States, the Chief Ministers of Union Territories with legislatures, the Administrators of other Union Territories, and six Union Cabinet Ministers nominated by the PM. It is not a permanent constitutional body, because the Constitution only authorises its creation when the President finds it to be in the public interest. The Punchhi Commission (2007-10) also examined it. The Council is supposed to meet at least three times a year.

II — Incorrect: The National Security Council was created in November 1998 by an executive decision of the Government of India, not by a constitutional provision or a statute. It advises the PM on national security and strategic matters. Its structure has three tiers: the Strategic Policy Group, the National Security Advisory Board and the Joint Intelligence Committee. The National Security Adviser is the PM's principal adviser on security. Brajesh Mishra was the first NSA. The NSC Secretariat sits within the Cabinet Secretariat. The NSAB was reorganised in 2024, but the NSC remains an executive body.

III — Incorrect: Zonal Councils are statutory bodies, not constitutional ones. They were established under Part III (Sections 15-22) of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. There are five: Northern, Central, Eastern, Western and Southern. The Union Home Minister is the Chairman of each. The Chief Ministers act as Vice-Chairman by rotation, each for one year. Each Council also includes two other Ministers from each state, and the Administrators of the Union Territories in the zone. The idea came from Jawaharlal Nehru in 1956. The North Eastern Council was created separately by the North Eastern Council Act, 1971. Zonal Councils are advisory bodies that discuss economic and social planning, border disputes and linguistic minorities.
summary: The answer is (a) Only one. Of the three bodies, only the Inter-State Council is established under a constitutional provision (Article 263). The National Security Council was created by an executive decision in 1998, and Zonal Councils were created by a statute, the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
topic_notes: Indian institutions fall into four categories. Constitutional bodies are mentioned directly in the Constitution, such as the Election Commission (Art. 324), UPSC (Art. 315), Finance Commission (Art. 280), CAG (Art. 148), Attorney General (Art. 76) and the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (Art. 350B). Statutory bodies are created by Acts of Parliament, such as the NHRC (1993 Act), CVC, CBI (DSPE Act 1946), SEBI, TRAI and the Zonal Councils. Executive or extra-constitutional bodies are created by Cabinet resolutions or government orders, such as NITI Aayog (2015), the NSC (1998) and the National Development Council (1952). Inter-State Council: Art. 263 gives a three-part role of inquiring into disputes, investigating subjects of common interest, and recommending policy coordination. It was set up in 1990, has a standing committee, and has an Inter-State Council Secretariat. Related constitutional provisions are Art. 262 (inter-State water disputes), Art. 261 (public acts and records) and Art. 307 (an authority for inter-State trade and commerce). The Sarkaria Commission (1983) recommended a permanent Inter-State Council. The Punchhi Commission (2010) examined Centre-State relations. The National Development Council is neither constitutional nor statutory and is headed by the PM. The GST Council was created under Art. 279A through the 101st Amendment (2016), so it is a constitutional body. The Zonal Councils and the NEC give regional coordination. Future questions may ask which bodies are constitutional or statutory, who chairs each, or their composition.

question:
Consider the following statements :
I. The Constitution of India explicitly mentions that in certain spheres the Governor of a State acts in his/her own discretion. Il. The President of India can, of his/her own, reserve a bill passed by a State Legislature for his/her consideration without it being forwarded by the Governor of the State concerned. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: The Governor is normally a constitutional head who acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister (Article 163(1)). The same Article, however, excludes matters in which the Constitution requires the Governor to act in his discretion. Express discretion appears in the Sixth Schedule, para 9(2), where the Governor decides the share of royalties from mineral exploration payable to autonomous district councils in Assam. Similar provisions cover Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Article 371A(1)(b) gives the Nagaland Governor a special responsibility for law and order, and Article 371(2) and Article 371H have comparable provisions. The Governor's report under Article 356 is also treated as discretionary. Article 200 lets the Governor assent to a bill, withhold assent, return it, or reserve it for the President. Article 201 then governs the President's action on a reserved bill. The Constitution gives the President no power to call up or reserve a State bill on his own initiative, and the bill must reach him through the Governor. Statement II is therefore wrong, so only I is correct. Eliminating (b), (c) and (d) follows directly. The Supreme Court's 2025 Tamil Nadu Governor judgment also dealt with Articles 200 and 201 and set timelines for decisions.
explanations: Correct. Statement I is true, with express discretion in the Sixth Schedule and Articles 371A and 371H, and Statement II is false because only the Governor can reserve a State bill.
Incorrect. It would make II alone correct, but the President cannot reserve a State bill on his own without the Governor forwarding it.
Incorrect. It requires II to be correct, but Article 200 gives the power of reservation only to the Governor.
Incorrect. It would make I false, but the Constitution does explicitly provide for gubernatorial discretion, for example in Sixth Schedule para 9(2).
keyfact: Only the Governor can reserve a State bill for the President (Article 200), and the Constitution expressly gives him discretion in places such as Sixth Schedule para 9(2) and Article 371A.
option_notes: Option (a) says only Statement I is correct. This is the official answer. It reflects that the Governor has express constitutional discretion in specified areas, such as the Sixth Schedule para 9(2), Article 371A and Article 163(1). It also reflects that State bills go to the President only on the Governor's reservation under Article 200, and the President cannot reserve a bill himself. The Governor is the nominal executive head of the State and is appointed by the President under Article 155. He holds office during the President's pleasure and normally for five years.

Option (b) says only Statement II is correct. This is wrong. It would require the President to have a suo motu power to reserve State bills, and the Constitution has no such provision. The President's role begins only after the Governor reserves a bill (Article 201). The President does hold other powers over State legislation, such as the instructions-based prior sanction requirements under Article 304(b) and the Article 31A and 31C assent conditions, but these are different from suo motu reservation.

Option (c) says both statements are correct. This is wrong because Statement II is false. It is a tempting choice, since the President is seen as superior to the Governor and may seem able to intervene directly. But the constitutional route for State bills runs through the Governor. In an emergency under Article 356, Parliament exercises the State legislature's powers, which is a separate situation.

Option (d) says neither statement is correct. This is wrong because Statement I is true. Some students think the Governor never has discretion because Article 163 stresses ministerial aid and advice. But the text itself says 'except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise his functions in his discretion'. The Sixth Schedule para 9(2) and Article 371A(1)(b) are the standard examples. The Sarkaria Commission and Punchhi Commission also examined the Governor's discretion.
related: Article 163: Council of Ministers aids and advises the Governor, except where he acts in his discretion.
Article 200: the Governor may assent, withhold assent, return a non-money bill, or reserve it for the President.
Article 201: the President decides on bills reserved by the Governor.
Article 213: the Governor can promulgate ordinances when the legislature is not in session.
Sixth Schedule para 9(2): the Governor's discretion on royalty shares for district councils.
Article 371A(1)(b): the Nagaland Governor has a special responsibility for law and order.
Article 155 and 156: the Governor is appointed by the President and holds office during his pleasure.
Article 161: the Governor's power to grant pardons, reprieves and similar relief.
statements: 1 — Correct: The Constitution explicitly mentions the Governor acting in his own discretion in certain spheres. Examples are Sixth Schedule para 9(2) on royalty shares for autonomous district councils (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram) and Article 371A and Article 371H on special responsibilities. Article 163(1) states the general rule of acting on ministerial advice, except where the Constitution requires discretion. Article 163(2) makes the Governor's own decision on whether a matter is discretionary final and not open to question in court. Situational discretion, such as inviting a leader when no party has a clear majority, or recommending President's Rule under Article 356, is also recognised by convention, though it is not explicit in the text.

2 — Incorrect: Under Article 200 the Governor may reserve a bill for the President's consideration, and Article 201 then governs the President's action: assent, withholding assent, or directing the Governor to return a non-money bill to the House. The President has no power to reserve or call up a State bill on his own initiative. A State bill reaches him only through the Governor. Reservation is mandatory where the bill would endanger the position of the High Court (Article 200 proviso). Article 254(2) covers bills on Concurrent List subjects that conflict with Union law, which need Presidential assent to prevail. Article 31A, 31C and 288(2) also involve reservation. The Supreme Court in 2025 (State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor) discussed time limits for Article 200 and 201 decisions.
summary: The answer is (a): Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect. The Constitution explicitly provides for gubernatorial discretion in certain spheres, such as the Sixth Schedule (para 9(2)) and Article 163(1). The President cannot reserve a State bill on his own, because under Article 200 only the Governor can reserve a bill for the President's consideration.
topic_notes: The Governor is the constitutional head of a State (Articles 153 to 167). He is appointed by the President (Article 155), holds office during the President's pleasure (Article 156), and normally serves a five-year term. The qualifications are citizenship of India and a minimum age of 35. The Governor acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers under Article 163(1), except where the Constitution requires discretion. Article 163(2) says the Governor's decision on whether a matter is discretionary is final. Express discretion examples: Sixth Schedule para 9(2) on royalty shares for district councils; Article 371A(1)(b) on Nagaland law and order; Article 371H on Arunachal Pradesh; and the Governor's special responsibilities under Article 371 for Maharashtra and Gujarat and under Article 371J for Karnataka. Situational discretion includes choosing the Chief Minister in a hung House, dismissing a ministry that has lost its majority, and reporting under Article 356. Legislative powers: Article 200 allows assent, withholding assent, returning a non-money bill, or reservation for the President. Article 201 governs the President's action on reserved bills. Article 213 gives the Governor power to issue ordinances when the legislature is not in session, and the ordinance must be laid before the legislature and lapses six weeks after it reassembles.
