Article 161 gives the Governor the power to grant pardons, reprieves and similar relief. Key cases: Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974), Nabam Rebia (2016), S.R. Bommai (1994) and the 2025 Tamil Nadu Governor case on timelines. Commissions: Sarkaria (1983), Punchhi (2010) and the Rajamannar Committee. Related topics UPSC may ask next include Article 356, Article 365, the Governor's role in universities as Chancellor, and the Governor's discretion over Assembly dissolution.

question: Consider the following pairs : Stated under Provision in the Constitution of India The Directive Separation of Judiciary Principles from the Executive in of the State the public services of Policy the State The FundaValuing and preserving Il. mental Duties of the rich heritage of our composite culture : The FundaProhibition of employIll. mental Rights ment of children below the age of 14 years in factories above pairs are How many of the correctly matched?
subject: Polity
detail: The question tests which part of the Constitution houses a provision: Part III (Fundamental Rights, Articles 12-35), Part IV (Directive Principles, Articles 36-51) or Part IVA (Fundamental Duties, Article 51A). Article 50, in Part IV, directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in public services. Article 51A(f) makes it a duty of every citizen to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture. Article 24, in the Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24), prohibits employment of children below 14 in factories, mines or other hazardous work. Article 21A (education, ages 6-14) was added by the 86th Amendment in 2002. The 86th Amendment also added the duty in Article 51A(k) for parents to provide education opportunities. The Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976 on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation. Elimination logic: if all three pairs match the Parts and Articles, the answer is (d). The supplied key (c) holds only if the original paper had at least one mismatched pair that the OCR text does not show. Always verify the original wording against the official key. In UPSC pair questions, the trap is usually a swapped category, such as a DPSP item placed under Fundamental Rights.
explanations: (a) Only two: this would apply only if exactly one pair were mismatched. As OCR'd, no pair appears mismatched.
(b) Only one: this would apply only if exactly two pairs were mismatched. As OCR'd, none appears so.
(c) None: this is the supplied official key. It implies that all three pairs are mismatched in the original paper. The OCR text as given does not show this, so verify it against the original paper.
(d) All the three: this is what the OCR'd pairs support on the facts of Articles 50, 51A(f) and 24. It conflicts with the supplied key, so verify before relying on it.
keyfact: Article 50 (DPSP), Article 51A(f) (Duty), Article 24 (Right): the supplied key says (c) None, but these pairs look correct as OCR'd, so verify the original.
option_notes: Only two: the answer would be this if exactly one of the three pairs were wrongly placed, such as a DPSP item listed as a Fundamental Right. UPSC often builds pair questions on that kind of single swap, for example Article 40 (village panchayats), Article 44 (UCC) or Article 45 (early childhood care), which are all DPSPs.

Only one: the answer would be this if two pairs were mismatched. Pair questions of this type test knowledge of Parts III, IV and IVA. The usual confusions are Article 21A (a Fundamental Right) versus Article 45 (a DPSP), and Article 24 versus Article 39(e)-(f).

None: the answer would be this if every pair were mismatched. It is the supplied official key. UPSC sometimes sets 'none correct' when each pair has a swapped category or a changed detail. Check the original statement wording carefully.
All the three: the answer would be this if every pair were correct. As OCR'd, Article 50 (DPSP), Article 51A(f) (Fundamental Duty) and Article 24 (Fundamental Right) all match their categories.
related: Article 50: separation of judiciary from executive (DPSP).
Article 51A(f): preserve the rich heritage of the composite culture.
Article 24: no child below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous work.
Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 (Swaran Singh Committee).
Article 21A: free and compulsory education for ages 6-14 (86th Amendment, 2002).
Article 45 (DPSP) now covers early childhood care and education below 6.
Article 37: DPSPs are not enforceable by courts.
Child Labour Amendment Act 2016 bans work below 14 and hazardous work below 18.
statements: 1 — Correct (as OCR'd): Article 50 in Part IV is a DPSP. It directs the State to take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State. It is a liberal-intellectual principle. It aims to secure judicial independence at the level of subordinate courts and magistrates. The CrPC of 1973 largely implemented it by separating judicial and executive magistrates. DPSPs are non-justiciable under Article 37 but are fundamental in governance.

2 — Correct (as OCR'd): Article 51A(f) in Part IVA lists the duty to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture. Fundamental Duties were inserted by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation, with 10 duties. The 86th Amendment in 2002 added the eleventh duty, in clause (k). They are non-justiciable, and the idea came from the USSR Constitution. The Verma Committee (1999) suggested ways to implement them.

3 — Correct (as OCR'd): Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 in factories, mines or any other hazardous employment. It sits under the Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24), together with the ban on trafficking and forced labour. It is enforceable against private parties as well as the State. Related laws are the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 and its 2016 amendment, which bans work below 14 and hazardous work below 18. The M.C. Mehta case (1996) is a key judgment.
summary: The key supplied for this task gives (c) None. However, the pairs as OCR'd read: Article 50 (DPSP, separation of judiciary from executive), Article 51A(f) (Fundamental Duty, composite culture) and Article 24 (Fundamental Right, no child labour below 14 in factories). Each of these is correct as written, which would give (d). The OCR text may have lost a mismatch in the original, so check the original paper and the official answer key before relying on this note.
topic_notes: Part III (Articles 12-35) contains the Fundamental Rights. They are justiciable, and Article 32 allows direct approach to the Supreme Court. The Right against Exploitation covers Article 23 (ban on trafficking and forced labour) and Article 24 (no employment of children below 14 in hazardous work). Article 21A, added by the 86th Amendment in 2002, makes education free and compulsory for ages 6-14, and the RTE Act came into force in 2010. Part IV (Articles 36-51) contains the DPSPs, which are non-justiciable (Article 37) and drawn from the Irish Constitution. They are grouped as socialistic (Articles 38, 39, 41-43, 43A, 47), Gandhian (Articles 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48) and liberal-intellectual (Articles 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51). Article 50 is the separation of the judiciary from the executive. Article 51 covers international peace. Part IVA, Article 51A, contains the Fundamental Duties, added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. They were 10 at first, and clause (k) was added in 2002. They apply only to citizens and are non-justiciable. Duty (f) concerns the composite culture, (g) the environment, (h) scientific temper, and (a) respect for the Constitution and the National Flag and Anthem. Cases to remember are Minerva Mills (1980, balance between Parts III and IV), Kesavananda Bharati (1973, basic structure), and M.C. Mehta (1996, child labour). The Child Labour Amendment Act 2016 bans employment below 14 and hazardous work for 14-18. Likely UPSC angles: which Part or Article a provision sits in, which amendment added it, and whether it is justiciable.

question: Consider the following statements : With reference to the Constitution of India, if an area in a State is declared as Scheduled Area under the Fifth Schedule I. the State Government loses its executive power in such areas and a local body assumes total administration Il. the Union Government can take over the total administration of such areas under certain circumstances on the recommendations of the Governor Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: The Fifth Schedule (Article 244(1)) governs the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in States other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, which come under the Sixth Schedule. The President declares Scheduled Areas by order, after consulting the State Governor, and can alter or rescind them. The executive power of the State extends to Scheduled Areas, so the State does not lose it. The Governor must submit an annual report (or whenever required by the President) on the administration of Scheduled Areas. The Union's executive power extends to giving directions to the State on administering them (Para 3). The Governor may direct that any Act of Parliament or the State Legislature does not apply to a Scheduled Area, or applies with modifications (Para 5). The Governor may also make regulations on land transfer by tribals, allotment of land and money-lending (Para 5(2)). A Tribes Advisory Council (TAC) with up to 20 members, three-fourths of them ST MLAs, advises on tribal welfare. Statement I is wrong because there is no total takeover by a local body; the Sixth Schedule's autonomous district councils are a different arrangement and still do not displace the State executive entirely. Statement II is wrong because the Union has no power of total administrative takeover under the Fifth Schedule on the Governor's recommendation; the nearest idea is Article 356, which is a different provision and is based on the Governor's report of constitutional breakdown. So both statements fail.
explanations: Wrong: Statement I is incorrect, since the State executive power continues in Scheduled Areas and no local body assumes total administration.
Wrong: Statement II is incorrect, since the Fifth Schedule gives the Union only the power to give directions, not to take over total administration.
Wrong: neither statement is correct, so 'both' fails.
Correct: both statements are incorrect, as the State retains executive power with the Governor having special powers and the Union limited to directions.
keyfact: In Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas the State executive continues, with the Governor's special powers and a Tribes Advisory Council; the Union only gives directions and has no takeover power.
option_notes: Option (a) endorses statement I alone. It describes a local body taking total administration, which does not happen in Fifth Schedule areas. It resembles the Sixth Schedule's autonomous district and regional councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram (Article 244(2)), which have legislative, judicial and executive powers over specified subjects, but even these are within the State's framework. The Governor administers the Fifth Schedule areas with the Tribes Advisory Council.

Option (b) endorses statement II alone. It confuses the Fifth Schedule with emergency provisions. The Union's role in Scheduled Areas is limited to executive directions under Para 3 and the Article 339 commissions. A takeover of State administration comes only through Article 356 (President's Rule), which operates on the whole State and does not depend on Scheduled Area status. The Governor's report is relevant under Article 356 but not for Scheduled Areas specifically.

Option (c) says both are correct. Neither is. Fifth Schedule areas remain under State executive power with a special role for the Governor. The Governor can direct that laws do not apply or apply with modifications, and can regulate tribal land transfer. The Tribes Advisory Council is mandatory in States with Scheduled Areas and may be established in States with Scheduled Tribes but no Scheduled Areas, if the President directs.

Option (d) is correct. The Fifth Schedule keeps State administration intact, with the Governor having special responsibility for tribal protection, a Tribes Advisory Council, annual reports to the President, and Union directions on the administration. It differs sharply from the Sixth Schedule, which creates autonomous councils. Neither schedule provides for a Union takeover on the Governor's recommendation.
related: Fifth Schedule: Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes outside Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
Sixth Schedule covers tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram under Article 244(2).
The President declares Scheduled Areas after consulting the Governor.
Tribes Advisory Council has up to 20 members, three-fourths from ST MLAs.
PESA Act 1996 extends Panchayat provisions to Fifth Schedule areas.
Governor can make regulations on tribal land transfer and money-lending.
Article 339 allows commissions on Scheduled Areas; the Dhebar Commission was formed in 1960.
Article 275(1) gives grants-in-aid to States for tribal welfare.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The State executive power continues in Scheduled Areas; no local body assumes total administration. The Governor gets special responsibilities, and the Union can only issue directions. Fifth Schedule areas are Scheduled Areas declared by the President under Para 6 after consulting the Governor. Present States with Scheduled Areas include Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Himachal Pradesh. The Tribes Advisory Council advises on welfare. The Governor can make regulations on land transfer and money-lending and can adapt laws. The PESA Act 1996 extended Panchayat provisions to these areas with special powers for Gram Sabhas. Total local administration resembles Sixth Schedule autonomous councils, which still operate within the State.

2 — Incorrect: There is no Fifth Schedule provision for the Union to take over total administration on the Governor's recommendation. Under Para 3, the Governor reports annually to the President on the administration of Scheduled Areas, and the Union's executive power extends to giving directions to the State on administering them. Article 339(1) allows the President to appoint a commission to report on Scheduled Areas' administration and tribal welfare. The first Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes Commission was the Dhebar Commission (1960-61), and the Bhuria Committee (1991) led to PESA. Takeover of State government is possible only through Article 356, upon the Governor's report or otherwise, and applies to the whole State, not specifically to Scheduled Areas. This confusion is the trap in the statement.
summary: The answer is (d): neither statement is correct. Declaring an area a Scheduled Area under the Fifth Schedule does not strip the State of its executive power, and does not hand total administration to a local body or to the Union on the Governor's recommendation. The State's executive power continues, with special protective powers given to the Governor and the Union's executive power limited to giving directions.
topic_notes: Article 244 sets up two regimes for tribal areas. Article 244(1) applies the Fifth Schedule to Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in all States except Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Article 244(2) applies the Sixth Schedule to those four States. The President declares Scheduled Areas under Para 6 after consulting the Governor, and can rescind or alter them. Criteria used are preponderance of tribal population, compactness and reasonable size of area, a viable administrative unit, and economic backwardness. Under Para 5 the Governor may direct that a central or State law shall not apply to a Scheduled Area or applies with modifications. Para 5(2) allows regulations for peace and good government: prohibiting or restricting land transfer by or among tribals, regulating allotment of land, and regulating money-lending to tribals. Such regulations need Presidential assent and may repeal or amend laws. Para 4 provides the Tribes Advisory Council of up to 20 members, three-fourths from ST MLAs. Para 3 requires the Governor's annual report and gives the Union power to direct the State. Article 339 provides for commissions on Scheduled Areas, such as the Dhebar Commission (1960). Related laws: PESA 1996 extends Panchayat provisions to Fifth Schedule areas and empowers Gram Sabhas; the Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises forest rights of tribals; the Samatha judgment (1997) restricted transfer of tribal land to non-tribals for mining. Article 275(1) grants Union funds to States for tribal welfare. Article 244A allows an autonomous State within Assam. Sixth Schedule bodies include district councils with legislative powers over land, forests and village administration. Ladakh demands Sixth Schedule status. Possible future questions include comparing both Schedules, Governor's discretionary powers, PESA features, and the list of Fifth Schedule States.

question:
With reference to India, consider the following pairs : Organization Union Ministry
I. The National : Ministry of Automotive Board Commerce and Industry II: The Coir Board : Ministry of Heavy Industries Ill. The National : Ministry of Micro, Centre for Trade Small and Medium Information Enterprises How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
subject: Economy
detail: This question tests whether a student knows the parent ministry of well-known boards and bodies. The pattern UPSC uses is to swap the ministries between the organizations. The National Automotive Board (NAB) is an apex body under the Ministry of Heavy Industries, associated with the automotive sector and schemes such as FAME. The Coir Board was set up under the Coir Industry Act, 1953 and is a statutory body under the Ministry of MSME. Its headquarters is in Kochi, Kerala. The National Centre for Trade Information (NCTI) is run by India Trade Promotion Organisation (ITPO) and the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, and it provides trade information. Since each pair assigns the wrong ministry, no pair is correct, so the answer is (d). The elimination logic is that confirming even one pair as wrong rules out 'All three'. Confirming two as wrong leaves only 'Only one' or 'None', and confirming the third as wrong gives (d). The Coir Board is the easiest to anchor, because coir is a traditional MSME-sector industry. Remember the commodity boards: Coffee, Tea, Rubber, Spices and Tobacco are under Commerce, while Coir is under MSME.
explanations: Wrong: (a) says one pair is correct, but all three have the ministry swapped or wrongly assigned.
Wrong: (b) says two pairs are correct, but every pair is mismatched.
Wrong: (c) says all three are correct, but none of the ministries is right.
Correct: (d) None. The NAB is under Heavy Industries, the Coir Board under MSME and the NCTI under Commerce and Industry, so no pair matches.
keyfact: NAB = Heavy Industries; Coir Board = MSME; NCTI = Commerce and Industry, so all three pairs were wrong and the answer is (d) None.
option_notes: Only one: this would hold if exactly one pair were correct. It is wrong here, but the pairs still reward recall of the correct ministries: NAB (Heavy Industries), Coir Board (MSME) and NCTI (Commerce). Questions of this type often ask how many pairs match, so students should know each body's parent ministry and its statutory or non-statutory status.

Only two: this would hold if two pairs were correct. It is wrong in this question because all three ministries are misassigned. The pairs mix up Commerce, Heavy Industries and MSME, which are three ministries that regularly appear together in questions on boards, commodity bodies and industrial promotion.

All the three: this would hold only if every ministry were matched correctly. UPSC sometimes sets this as the right answer, but here the pairings are deliberately scrambled. Verifying the parent ministry of each body is the key skill tested, and the Coir Board and NAB are the most common traps.

None: this is the correct option because each pair is mismatched. The right pairings are National Automotive Board with Heavy Industries, Coir Board with MSME, and National Centre for Trade Information with Commerce and Industry. This type of question rewards precise institutional knowledge over general familiarity.
related: Coir Board: statutory body under the Coir Industry Act 1953, HQ Kochi, under MSME.
Tea Board, Coffee Board, Rubber Board and Spices Board are all under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
The National Automotive Board works with the Ministry of Heavy Industries.
The Central Silk Board is under the Ministry of Textiles.
KVIC is a statutory body under the Ministry of MSME, set up under the KVIC Act 1956.
ITPO, which runs Bharat Mandapam, is under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
FAME India and PM E-DRIVE are schemes of the Ministry of Heavy Industries.
The Coir Board's headquarters is at Kochi, Kerala.
statements: I — Incorrect: The National Automotive Board is under the Ministry of Heavy Industries, not Commerce and Industry. The NAB was set up as an apex body for the automotive sector, working with the Department of Heavy Industry. It has been involved in implementing schemes that promote vehicle manufacturing and electric mobility, such as FAME India. Heavy Industries also oversees automotive-related public sector enterprises and policies, so students should link automotive policy and the Automotive Mission Plan to this ministry. Related schemes include the PLI for automobiles and auto components and the PM E-DRIVE scheme.

II — Incorrect: The Coir Board is under the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, not Heavy Industries. It is a statutory body established under the Coir Industry Act, 1953, to promote the coir industry's development, research, marketing and export. Its headquarters is in Kochi, Kerala, and it is active in coir-producing states such as Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Odisha. It supports coir exports, quality standards, welfare of coir workers and skill training. Coir is a natural fibre from coconut husk. Coir Udyami Yojana is among its schemes.

III — Incorrect: The National Centre for Trade Information is under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, not MSME. NCTI is a trade information service, operated by ITPO under the Commerce Ministry. It collects and disseminates trade-related data, including information on export and import opportunities, to Indian businesses, especially exporters. It is associated with the Department of Commerce, which also oversees the Directorate General of Foreign Trade, ITPO and the commodity boards. ITPO runs Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi and organises the India International Trade Fair.
summary: The answer is (d) None. All three pairs are mismatched: the National Automotive Board comes under the Ministry of Heavy Industries, the Coir Board under the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME), and the National Centre for Trade Information under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
topic_notes: This question belongs to the area of ministries and the statutory or other bodies attached to them. UPSC regularly asks about boards, councils and commissions together with their parent ministries. The Ministry of Commerce and Industry has two departments, Commerce and DPIIT. It oversees the commodity boards (Tea Board, Coffee Board, Rubber Board, Spices Board, Tobacco Board), the Marine Products Export Development Authority (MPEDA), the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA), ITPO, the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) and the Export Inspection Council. The Ministry of MSME covers the Coir Board, the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), the National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC) and the Development Commissioner (MSME). It also administers the PMEGP scheme and the MSME Champions scheme. Note that the Ministry of Textiles oversees the Central Silk Board, the Jute Commissioner and the Textiles Committee. The Ministry of Heavy Industries covers automotive policy, capital goods, heavy electrical equipment, and schemes such as FAME, PM E-DRIVE and the PLI scheme for automobiles and advanced chemistry cell batteries. Related bodies include the Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI) and the International Centre for Automotive Technology (ICAT). Strategy for such questions: group bodies by the sector they serve, then associate each sector with one ministry. Typical traps are swapping Heavy Industries with Commerce, or MSME with Textiles or Agriculture. Also remember the statutory basis, such as the Coir Industry Act 1953, the Tea Act 1953, the Rubber Act 1947, the Coffee Act 1942 and the Spices Board Act 1986.

ocr: Consider the following subjects under the Constitution of India : I. List LUnion List, in the Seventh Schedule Il. Extent of the executive power of a State Ill. Conditions of the Governor’s office For a constitutional amendment with respect to which of the above, ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States is required before presenting the bill to the President of India for assent? (a) 1 and II only (b) 1 and III only (c) 1 and III only (a) 1, Il and Il
subject: Polity
detail: Article 368 gives Parliament its constituent power. Most provisions can be amended by a special majority: a majority of the total membership of each House and at least two-thirds of members present and voting. The proviso to Article 368(2) lists federal provisions that also need ratification by the legislatures of not less than one-half of the States before the Bill goes to the President for assent. These are: (a) election of the President (Articles 54, 55); (b) extent of the executive power of the Union and the States (Articles 73, 162); (c) Supreme Court and High Courts, including Union Territory High Courts (Chapter IV of Part V and Chapter V of Part VI, plus Article 241); (d) distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States (Part XI Chapter I); (e) any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule; (f) representation of States in Parliament; (g) Article 368 itself. Elimination logic: Statement I (Seventh Schedule Lists) and Statement II (extent of State executive power, Article 162) are both in the proviso. Statement III, the Governor's conditions of office (Article 158), is not, so it needs only a special majority. That rules out (b), (c) and (d), leaving (a). The Governor's appointment, term and conditions are federal in flavour but are not entrenched.
explanations: Correct. I (Seventh Schedule Lists) and II (extent of State executive power, Article 162) are both in the Article 368(2) proviso and need ratification by at least half of the States.
Wrong. It includes III, the Governor's conditions of office, which is not in the proviso, and it leaves out I, which is.
Wrong. It includes III, which does not need State ratification, and it leaves out II, which does.
Wrong. It includes III, which needs only a special majority in Parliament, so the three items together are not all entrenched.
keyfact: Seventh Schedule Lists and State executive power (Article 162) need half of the States to ratify; the Governor's conditions of office (Article 158) do not.
option_notes: I and II only: This is the correct combination. The Seventh Schedule Lists (Union, State, Concurrent) distribute legislative powers between the Centre and the States under Article 246. Article 162 sets the extent of a State's executive power, which is co-extensive with its legislative power. Both are federal features, so Parliament cannot change them alone. The proviso to Article 368(2) requires ratification by at least half of the State legislatures, by simple majority in each, before the Bill goes to the President.

II and III only: This pairs State executive power (Article 162, entrenched) with the Governor's conditions of office (Article 158, not entrenched). Article 158 deals with the Governor not being a legislator, not holding an office of profit, having an official residence, and receiving emoluments and allowances set by Parliament and the Second Schedule. The Governor is the State's nominal head, appointed by the President under Article155 and holding office during the President's pleasure (Article 156).

I and III only: This pairs the Seventh Schedule Lists (entrenched) with the Governor's conditions of office (not entrenched). The Seventh Schedule's three Lists have been revised by the 42nd Amendment (1976), the 88th Amendment (2003, service tax, entry 92C) and the 101st Amendment (2016, GST, which changed entries 54 and 92 and added Article 246A). The 101st Amendment was ratified by more than half of the States, which shows how this proviso works in practice.

I, II and III: This claims all three need State ratification. It is wrong because the Governor's conditions of office (Article 158) fall outside the proviso. Parliament can amend them by a special majority under Article 368(2), without State ratification. The Governor's role as Union representative and State head is a constitutional design, but its terms are not among the entrenched federal provisions.
related: Article 368 deals with Parliament's power to amend the Constitution and its procedure.
Article 368(2) proviso lists the provisions needing ratification by at least half of the States.
The 24th Amendment (1971) made Presidential assent compulsory for amendment Bills.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic structure doctrine.
Minerva Mills (1980) struck down the 42nd Amendment's clauses 4 and 5 of Article 368.
The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced GST and Article 246A, and was ratified by the States.
Articles 2, 3 (new States) and Fifth and Sixth Schedules can be amended by simple majority.
Article 158 gives the Governor's conditions of office, including no other office of profit.
statements: I — Correct: Any amendment to any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule requires ratification by at least half of the States. The Seventh Schedule, under Article 246, has the Union List (originally 97 entries, now 98 after the 88th Amendment added entry 92C and the 42nd Amendment moved some entries), the State List (originally 66, now 59) and the Concurrent List (originally 47, now 52). The 42nd Amendment (1976) transferred five subjects to the Concurrent List: education, forests, protection of wild animals and birds, weights and measures, and administration of justice. Residuary powers rest with the Union under Article248. Legislative power is distributed under Articles 245-255.

II — Correct: The extent of the executive power of a State (Article 162) is in the proviso, as is the Union's executive power (Article 73). Article 162 says a State's executive power extends to matters on which its legislature can make laws, subject to Article 162's proviso on Concurrent List matters, where Union law prevails. The Governor exercises this power under Article 154, directly or through subordinate officers. Article 163 provides a Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister to aid and advise the Governor, except where the Constitution requires discretion. Articles 256-257 require States to comply with Union laws and directions.

III — Incorrect: Conditions of the Governor's office (Article 158) are not in the proviso to Article 368(2). Under Article 158, the Governor must not be a member of Parliament or a State legislature, holds no other office of profit, and is entitled to emoluments and allowances fixed by Parliament. The Governor is appointed by the President under Article 155 and holds office during the President's pleasure (Article 156), normally for five years. The qualifications are in Article 157: citizen of India and aged at least 35. The Second Schedule covers emoluments. The 7th Amendment (1956) allowed one Governor for two or more States.
summary: The answer is (a) I and II only. Under Article 368(2) proviso, amendments touching the Seventh Schedule lists and the extent of a State's executive power need ratification by at least half of the State legislatures. The conditions of the Governor's office (Article 158) are not in that proviso, so a simple Article 368 special majority in Parliament is enough.
topic_notes: Constitutional amendment procedure is in Part XX, Article 368. There are three methods of amendment. (1) Simple majority, outside Article 368: admission or formation of new States (Articles 2, 3), Fifth and Sixth Schedules, Citizenship, Official Language, Rajya Sabha composition, Union Territories, and quorum. (2) Special majority under Article 368: most provisions, including Fundamental Rights, DPSPs and everything not in the other categories. This needs a majority of the total membership of each House plus two-thirds of members present and voting. (3) Special majority plus ratification by at least half of the State legislatures, covering the entrenched federal provisions: election of the President (Articles 54, 55), extent of Union and State executive power (Articles 73, 162), Supreme Court and High Courts, Union Territory High Courts, distribution of legislative powers (Part XI Chapter I), the Seventh Schedule Lists, representation of States in Parliament (Fourth Schedule), and Article 368 itself. No time limit is set for States to ratify. Key facts: a Bill can be introduced in either House, with no prior President permission. There is no joint sitting for a deadlock. The President must give assent under the 24th Amendment (1971), which made it obligatory. The 24th also confirmed that Parliament can amend any part, including Fundamental Rights. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) laid down the basic structure doctrine. Minerva Mills (1980) struck down clauses 4 and 5 of Article 368 added by the 42nd Amendment. Golaknath (1967) was overruled. Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) held that Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights. The 101st Amendment (GST, 2016) needed ratification. The 106th Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023) is another recent one. UPSC often asks which provisions need special majority only, which need ratification, and which need a simple majority. The 61st Amendment lowered the voting age to 18, and the 42nd is called the Mini-Constitution.

question:
With reference to the Indian polity, consider the following statements :
I. The Governor of a State is not answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of his/her office. Il. No criminal proceedings shall be instituted or continued against the Governor during his/her term of office. Ill. Members of a State Legislature are not liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said within the House. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Immunity in the Indian Constitution comes in two forms: personal immunity for constitutional heads and privilege for legislators. Article 361 covers the President and Governors (and Rajpramukhs). Clause (1) says they are not answerable to any court for exercising and performing the powers and duties of office, or for acts done in that exercise. Clause (2) bars criminal proceedings, institution or continuation, against them during the term of office. Clause (3) bars arrest or imprisonment during the term. Clause (4) allows civil proceedings only after two months' written notice. Article 361 does not stop the Government from being sued, and the Supreme Court in the Rameshwar Prasad case (2006) held that the immunity does not bar judicial review of the motives for Governor's actions, such as dissolving an Assembly. Article 194(2) gives State legislators immunity from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given in the Legislature or its committees. Article 105(2) is the Parliament equivalent. The same article also protects a person from liability for publishing a report, paper, votes or proceedings under the authority of the House. Since all three statements restate these provisions, elimination leaves only (d).
explanations: Wrong: it omits Statement III, which is correct under Article 194(2).
Wrong: it omits Statement I, which is correct under Article 361(1).
Wrong: it omits Statement II, which is correct under Article 361(2).
Correct: all three statements match Articles 361(1), 361(2) and 194(2).
keyfact: Article 361: Governor and President are immune from court answerability for official acts and from criminal proceedings during their term; Article 194(2) protects what legislators say in the House.
option_notes: I and II only would cover the Governor's immunity under Article 361 alone. Article 361 gives the President and Governors immunity from court answerability for official acts and from criminal proceedings and arrest during the term. Civil proceedings need two months' notice. It is incomplete here because legislative privilege under Article 194(2) is also correct.

II and III only would combine the Governor's criminal immunity with legislator privilege. Criminal immunity comes from Article 361(2) and applies only during the term. Legislators' speech immunity comes from Article 194(2) for State Legislatures and Article 105(2) for Parliament. It is incomplete because Statement I is also correct.

I and III only would pair the Governor's non-answerability for official acts with legislative speech privilege. The first is under Article 361(1), and the second under Article 194(2). It is incomplete because the bar on criminal proceedings in Article 361(2) is also correct.

I, II and III is the correct option. It combines the Governor's immunity under Article 361(1) and (2) with the freedom of speech privilege of State legislators under Article 194(2). Together they show the constitutional separation of personal immunity and legislative privilege, both subject to judicial interpretation.
related: Article 361 protects the President and Governors; clause (4) requires two months' notice for civil suits.
Article 105 covers Parliament privileges; Article 194 covers State Legislature privileges.
Sita Soren (2024) overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998) on bribery and legislative privilege.
Article 155: Governor appointed by the President; Article 156: holds office at the President's pleasure.
Article 122 and Article 212 bar courts from questioning legislative proceedings on grounds of procedural irregularity.
Rameshwar Prasad (2006): Governor's actions can be judicially reviewed despite Article 361.
Article 361A protects true media reports of legislative proceedings.
Article 164 and Article 163: Governor acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, except for discretionary functions.
statements: I — Correct: Article 361(1) protects the Governor from answerability to any court for exercising and performing the powers and duties of office. Article 361 covers the President, Governors and Rajpramukhs. The protection is for official acts and is not absolute, because the Supreme Court has held that the motives behind such acts can be judicially reviewed (Rameshwar Prasad, 2006; S.R. Bommai, 1994 on Article 356). Immunity attaches to the person, so the Union or State government can still be made answerable. A Governor is appointed under Article 155 and holds office at the pleasure of the President under Article156.

II — Correct: Article 361(2) says no criminal proceedings whatsoever shall be instituted or continued against the President or a Governor in any court during the term of office. Article 361(3) bars arrest or imprisonment in any court process. Civil proceedings are allowed after two months' written notice (Article 361(4)). In 2024, the Supreme Court examined the scope of this immunity in the West Bengal Governor matter, and held that investigation may continue even though prosecution is barred, with evidence preserved. The immunity is temporary and ends when the term ends.

III — Correct: Article 194(2) provides that no member of a State Legislature is liable to any court proceedings for anything said or any vote given in the Legislature or any committee. Article 105(2) gives the same protection to MPs. This is a privilege, along with freedom of speech in the House under Article 194(1). It is subject to the Constitution and the rules of procedure, and the House can itself punish misconduct. In P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998) the Supreme Court extended it to bribery for votes, but in Sita Soren (2024) a seven-judge bench overruled that position and held bribery is not protected.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. Article 361 gives the Governor immunity from answerability to courts and from criminal proceedings during the term of office, and Article 194(2) protects legislators from court proceedings for what they say in the House.
topic_notes: Immunities and privileges in the Constitution fall into several groups. First, personal immunity of the President and Governors under Article 361. It gives protection from answerability to courts for official acts, from criminal proceedings during the term, and from arrest or imprisonment. Civil suits for personal acts need two months' notice. Article 361A protects the publication of true reports of the proceedings of Parliament and State Legislatures, and Article 361B bars remunerative political posts for disqualified members. Second, legislative privileges. Article 105 covers Parliament and Article 194 covers State Legislatures. They include freedom of speech in the House, immunity for votes and committee proceedings, protection for publication under the House's authority, and the power to regulate internal proceedings. Parliament has not codified privileges, so they rest on the Constitution, rules of procedure and conventions, and members cannot be arrested in civil cases during sessions, 40 days before and after. Courts cannot question the validity of proceedings on the ground of procedural irregularity (Articles 122 and 212). Third, judicial immunity. Judges are protected by the Judges (Protection) Act 1985, and their conduct cannot be discussed in Parliament except on a motion for removal (Article 121). Key cases: Rameshwar Prasad (2006), which dealt with the Bihar Assembly dissolution and held the Governor's actions are open to judicial review; P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998); Sita Soren (2024), which held that bribery is not protected by privilege; Raja Ram Pal (2007) on expulsion of members; and Keshav Singh (1965) on conflict between the Legislature and the courts. Governors are appointed under Article 155 and removable by the President, and their term is five years, although they hold office at the President's pleasure under Article 156.

question:
Suppose the revenue expenditure is 80, 000 crores and the revenue receipts of the Government are 60, 000 crores. The Government budget also shows borrowings of = 10, 000 crores and interest payments of ©€6, 000 crores. Which of the following statements are correct?
I. Revenue deficit is € 20, 000 crores. Il. Fiscal deficit is € 10, 000 crores. Ill. Primary deficit is € 4, 000 crores. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Economy
detail: Budget deficits measure the gap between government spending and income. Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts, so 80,000 − 60,000 = 20,000 crore. It shows that the government is not even meeting its day-to-day consumption spending from its current income. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − total receipts excluding borrowings, and is equal to the net borrowing requirement. The question states that borrowings are 10,000 crore, so the fiscal deficit is 10,000 crore. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments = 10,000 − 6,000 = 4,000 crore. It shows the borrowing needed for current spending other than interest on past debt. All three statements therefore hold. The code 'I, II and III' is option (d); the OCR renders it as '1, I and I'. Elimination: (a), (b) and (c) each leave out one of the three correct statements, so none of them can be right. A student who computes each deficit and finds all three correct can choose (d) directly. Note that the figures are internally unusual, since revenue deficit exceeds fiscal deficit, which implies a capital surplus. Even so, the question defines fiscal deficit through borrowings.
explanations: Wrong: it omits statement III, which is also correct because primary deficit = 10,000 − 6,000 = 4,000 crore.
Wrong: it omits statement I, and the revenue deficit of 20,000 crore is correct.
Wrong: it omits statement II. Fiscal deficit equals the borrowings of 10,000 crore, which is correct.
Correct: all three statements, revenue deficit 20,000, fiscal deficit 10,000 and primary deficit 4,000 crore, are correct.
keyfact: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments; fiscal deficit = borrowing requirement; revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts.
option_notes: Option (a), statements I and II only, would leave out the primary deficit. Revenue deficit and fiscal deficit are two of the three main deficit indicators. Revenue deficit shows the shortfall in revenue account, while fiscal deficit shows total borrowing. Primary deficit, the third indicator, removes interest from the fiscal deficit. Budget documents also report effective revenue deficit. Together these indicators are used to judge fiscal health. This option is wrong because it ignores the primary deficit.

Option (b), statements II and III only, would leave out the revenue deficit. The fiscal deficit shows the total borrowing need and the primary deficit removes interest payments from it. Both are tracked as percentages of GDP in the Union Budget. Revenue deficit is the third key measure, defined as revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. This option is wrong because the revenue deficit is also correct.

Option (c), statements I and III only, would leave out the fiscal deficit. The revenue deficit shows the shortfall on revenue account, and the primary deficit is fiscal deficit minus interest. Primary deficit cannot be calculated without a fiscal deficit figure. Fiscal deficit is the headline indicator under the FRBM framework, and it is the most widely cited measure. This option is wrong because the fiscal deficit is correct too.

Option (d), statements I, II and III, includes all three deficit measures. Revenue deficit is 20,000 crore, fiscal deficit is 10,000 crore, and primary deficit is 4,000 crore. Each follows from the standard definitions used in the Union Budget and the FRBM Act. UPSC regularly tests such computations. This is the official answer and it is correct.
related: Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts.
Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − total receipts excluding borrowings.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments.
FRBM Act was enacted in 2003, and the N.K. Singh Committee reported in 2017.
The 2025-26 Budget estimate for the Centre's fiscal deficit is 4.4 percent of GDP.
Article 112 provides for the Annual Financial Statement; Article 292 deals with Union borrowing.
Effective revenue deficit excludes grants used for creating capital assets.
Fiscal deficit is financed through net borrowing, so it equals the borrowing requirement.
statements: 1 — Correct: Revenue deficit = 80,000 − 60,000 = 20,000 crore. The revenue deficit is the excess of revenue expenditure over revenue receipts. The term was formalised in Indian budgeting in the 1990s and is a key indicator under the FRBM Act, 2003. Revenue receipts include tax and non-tax revenue; revenue expenditure creates no assets, for example salaries, subsidies, interest and pensions. A high revenue deficit means government savings are negative and capital receipts are being used to fund consumption. The FRBM Act originally targeted its elimination, and the 2018 amendments dropped it as a statutory target. The Centre has since shifted to a fiscal deficit glide path. Effective revenue deficit excludes grants for capital asset creation.

2 — Correct: Fiscal deficit equals total borrowings, which is given as 10,000 crore. Fiscal deficit is total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings, so it is the amount the government must borrow. Finance sources include market borrowing, treasury bills, external loans and, formerly, RBI monetisation. It is expressed as a percentage of GDP. FRBM targeted 3 percent of GDP; the Centre had 5.9 percent in 2022-23 and 5.6 percent in 2023-24. It was brought to 4.8 percent in 2024-25 (RE) and the Budget estimate for 2025-26 is 4.4 percent. From 2026-27 the government will target a debt-to-GDP ratio instead. The N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended a debt-to-GDP anchor.

3 — Correct: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments = 10,000 − 6,000 = 4,000 crore. Primary deficit shows the government's borrowing requirement apart from interest on past borrowings, so it reflects the current year's fiscal imbalance. If the primary deficit is zero, borrowing is used only to pay interest. A fall in the primary deficit signals fiscal consolidation. Primary balance = fiscal balance + interest payments. Interest payments take around 35-40 percent of the Centre's revenue receipts. Gross primary deficit is a related concept, and a primary surplus means that interest payments exceed the fiscal deficit.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. Revenue deficit = 80,000 − 60,000 = 20,000 crore; fiscal deficit equals total borrowings = 10,000 crore; primary deficit = 10,000 − 6,000 = 4,000 crore.
topic_notes: Budgetary deficits are central to the Indian public finance topic. Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts. Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts), which is also the net borrowing requirement. Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments. Effective revenue deficit = revenue deficit − grants for creation of capital assets. Budget deficit, the older concept, was total expenditure minus total receipts and was abolished after 1997. Monetised deficit, which referred to RBI's net credit to the government, was dropped when the ways and means advances system replaced ad hoc treasury bills in 1997. Fiscal legislation: the FRBM Act of 2003 targeted a 3 percent fiscal deficit and eliminating the revenue deficit. The N.K. Singh Committee in 2017 recommended debt-to-GDP of 40 percent for the Centre and 20 percent for the states, giving a combined 60 percent, and a fiscal council. Escape clauses allow deviations in a national calamity, war or a severe economic slowdown. Deficits were suspended during COVID, when the fiscal deficit rose to 9.2 percent in 2020-21. Financing: market borrowings by dated securities, treasury bills, small savings through the National Small Savings Fund, external assistance and, in some cases, RBI support. Related ideas: crowding out, the twin deficit with the current account, and the debt trap. Fiscal consolidation is judged through the primary deficit trend. Article 112 mandates the annual financial statement, Article 266 the consolidated fund, and Article 292 borrowing by the Union. Article 293 covers borrowing by states.

question: India is one of the founding members of the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), a multimodal transportation corridor, which will connect
options: India to Central Asia to Europe via Iran
India to Central Asia via China
India to South-East Asia through Bangladesh and Myanmar
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The International North-South Transport Corridor was launched by India, Iran and Russia on 12 September 2000 in St Petersburg. The agreement entered into force in May 2002. It is a 7,200 km multimodal network of ship, rail and road routes. Cargo moves from Mumbai or Jawaharlal Nehru Port by sea to Iranian ports (Bandar Abbas, Chabahar), then by rail or road across Iran to the Caspian ports (Bandar Anzali, Amirabad). From there it goes by ship, or by road and rail through Azerbaijan, to Russia (Astrakhan, Moscow, St Petersburg) and onward to northern Europe. It also has an eastern leg via Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to Central Asia. Its aim is to cut transit time from about 40 days to about 20-25 days and cost by 30 percent, compared with the Suez route. Members now number 13 or more, including Azerbaijan, Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Oman, Tajikistan, Turkey, Ukraine, Bulgaria (observer) and Syria. Elimination: (b) is wrong because China is not on the route. (c) describes the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway, a different project. (d) is incomplete because Azerbaijan is only a transit link and the route's key node is Iran, so (a) is the best answer.
explanations: Correct: the INSTC links India with Central Asia, Russia and Europe, with Iran as the central transit country through Chabahar and Bandar Abbas.
Wrong: the route bypasses China. China's connectivity initiative is the Belt and Road Initiative, which India has not joined.
Wrong: connecting India to South-East Asia via Bangladesh and Myanmar describes the Trilateral Highway and BCIM-type links, not the INSTC.
Wrong: Azerbaijan is only a transit link on the western route. The option ignores Iran, the essential hub, so it is incomplete and misleading.
keyfact: INSTC (2000; India-Iran-Russia) is a 7,200 km multimodal route linking India to Central Asia, Russia and Europe via Iran, using Chabahar and Bandar Abbas.
option_notes: India to Central Asia to Europe via Iran: this is the INSTC. It began in 2000 as an India-Iran-Russia agreement and covers about 7,200 km. It has three routes: western (via Azerbaijan), central (across the Caspian) and eastern (via Central Asia). Iran's Chabahar port, which India is developing, is a key node. The Rasht-Astara rail link is the missing piece.

India to Central Asia via China: this is not the INSTC. It would run through Xinjiang and resembles Belt and Road routes such as the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor. India opposes CPEC because it passes through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, and India stayed out of BRI. India's Central Asia access is mainly via Iran and Afghanistan, and the India-Central Asia Summit and Connect Central Asia policy support this.

India to South-East Asia through Bangladesh and Myanmar: this refers to eastern connectivity projects. These include the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway, the Kaladan Multimodal Transit Transport Project (Kolkata-Sittwe-Paletwa-Mizoram), and the BCIM Economic Corridor. They fall under India's Act East Policy and are separate from the INSTC.

India to Europe through Azerbaijan: Azerbaijan is a member and a transit country on the INSTC's western route, linking Iran with Russia via Astara and Baku, but it is not the whole corridor. The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), announced at the G20 in 2023, is a different route via the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Israel and Greece.
related: INSTC was launched on 12 September 2000 by India, Iran and Russia.
INSTC covers about 7,200 km using ship, rail and road.
Chabahar port in Iran is being developed by India Ports Global Limited.
The Rasht-Astara rail link in Iran is the main missing section of the INSTC.
IMEC was announced at the G20 in New Delhi in 2023 and links India, the Gulf, Israel and Europe.
The Kaladan project links Kolkata to Mizoram via Sittwe in Myanmar.
The Ashgabat Agreement is a multimodal transit pact of which India is a member.
India has not joined China's Belt and Road Initiative.
summary: The answer is (a). The INSTC is a multimodal (ship, rail, road) route that links India with Central Asia, Russia and Europe through Iran, using Chabahar and Bandar Abbas ports and the Caspian Sea region. It was set up to cut transit time and cost compared with the Suez Canal route.
topic_notes: The INSTC is a 7,200 km multimodal trade route proposed to link the Indian Ocean and Persian Gulf with the Caspian Sea, Russia and northern Europe via Iran. The founding agreement was signed on 12 September 2000 in St Petersburg by India, Iran and Russia, and it came into force on 16 May 2002. Membership later grew to over a dozen states, including Azerbaijan, Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkey, Ukraine, Oman and Syria, with Bulgaria as an observer. Routes: western (Iran-Azerbaijan-Russia by rail), central (across the Caspian by ship) and eastern (Iran-Turkmenistan-Kazakhstan-Central Asia). Key nodes are Mumbai/JNPT, Bandar Abbas, Chabahar, Bandar Anzali, Astrakhan and the Rasht-Astara rail gap, which is still unbuilt. The expected benefits are about 30 percent lower cost and 40 percent shorter transit time than the Suez route. India's Chabahar port (Shahid Beheshti terminal) is developed by India Ports Global Limited under a 10-year contract signed in May 2024. India has also taken part in the Ashgabat Agreement on transit with Central Asia and Iran, and in the Eurasian Economic Union free trade discussions. Compare this with other connectivity projects: IMEC (India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, 2023), BRI/CPEC (China), the Trilateral Highway and Kaladan project (India-Myanmar-Thailand), BBIN Motor Vehicles Agreement, the Chennai-Vladivostok Maritime Corridor, the Suez Canal and the Northern Sea Route. UPSC often asks which countries are on each route, which ports are involved, and which states are members.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I : Of the two major ethanol producers in the world, i.e., Brazil and the United States of America, the former produces more ethanol than the latter.
Statement II : Unlike in the United States of America where corn is the principal feedstock for ethanol production, sugarcane is the principal feedstock for ethanol production in Brazil. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement Il explains Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II does not explain Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct
Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct
subject: Economy
detail: The United States is the world's largest ethanol producer, making about 15-16 billion gallons a year (around 58 billion litres), almost all from corn (maize) through dry-mill and wet-mill processes. Brazil is second, producing about 7-8 billion gallons a year, mainly from sugarcane juice and molasses. Corn ethanol has been supported by the Renewable Fuel Standard (2005, expanded in 2007) and by blending mandates such as E10 and E15. Brazil began the Proálcool programme in 1975 after the oil shock, and it now mandates blending of about 27% (E27-E30) with anhydrous ethanol. It also has a large flex-fuel vehicle fleet. Together the two countries produce over 80% of the world's ethanol. India is third or fourth and has reached E20 (20% blending) in 2025. For elimination, Statement II is a well-known, correct fact, so options (a) and (b) fail if Statement I is wrong. Option (c) claims II is wrong, which is false. Because the US out-produces Brazil, Statement I is false, which leaves only (d). The trap is that Brazil is famous for ethanol and is often assumed to lead in volume.
explanations: Wrong. Statement I is incorrect because the US out-produces Brazil, so this option fails regardless of whether Statement II explains it.
Wrong. It also treats Statement I as correct, but Brazil does not produce more ethanol than the US.
Wrong. It reverses the truth: Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct.
Correct. The US is the larger producer, so Statement I is false. The feedstock contrast in Statement II (corn in the US, sugarcane in Brazil) is accurate.
keyfact: The US, not Brazil, is the world's largest ethanol producer (corn-based); Brazil is second (sugarcane-based).
option_notes: Both statements correct, with II explaining I. This would require Brazil to lead in volume and its sugarcane feedstock to be the reason. In reality the US leads, and the US-Brazil pair accounts for over 80% of world ethanol. Brazil's sugarcane ethanol is more efficient per hectare, but volume is driven by the scale of US corn production and its mandates.

Both statements correct, but II does not explain I. This is a common UPSC pattern. It fails here because Statement I is factually wrong: the US, not Brazil, is the largest producer, with about 15-16 billion gallons a year against Brazil's 7-8 billion.

Statement I correct and II incorrect. This reverses the facts. Corn is indeed the main US feedstock and sugarcane the main Brazilian feedstock. Brazil also uses some corn ethanol now, mainly in Mato Grosso, but sugarcane remains dominant, at roughly 80% or more of output.

Statement I incorrect and II correct, which is the official answer. The US is the top ethanol producer, with about 55-58% of the global share, while Brazil is second with about 25-27%. The feedstock contrast is accurate: US corn against Brazilian sugarcane. The two countries are the biggest producers, and India is next.
related: Brazil's Proálcool programme was launched in 1975.
India's National Policy on Biofuels 2018 targeted E20, later advanced to 2025.
The Global Biofuels Alliance was launched at the G20 Summit in New Delhi in 2023.
PM JI-VAN Yojana supports 2G ethanol plants using agricultural residue.
The US Renewable Fuel Standard dates from 2005 and was expanded in 2007.
Second-generation ethanol uses lignocellulosic biomass such as straw and bagasse.
Distillers' dried grains (DDGS) are a by-product of corn ethanol and are used as cattle feed.
Anhydrous ethanol, which is over 99% pure, is the type used for blending with petrol.
statements: I — Incorrect: The US produces more ethanol than Brazil, not the reverse. The US makes roughly 55-58% of global ethanol, against about 25-27% for Brazil. US output is around 15-16 billion gallons a year, mostly from corn grown in the Midwest (Iowa, Nebraska, Illinois). Brazil's output is about 7-8 billion gallons a year and is concentrated in São Paulo state. Brazil is the world's second-largest producer and the largest exporter of sugar. Brazil's per-capita ethanol use and its share of ethanol in transport fuel are higher than in the US, which may explain the common misconception. The US Renewable Fuel Standard drives its volumes.

II — Correct: Corn is the main feedstock in the US, which uses about 35-40% of its corn crop for ethanol, and the by-product is distillers' grains used as animal feed. In Brazil sugarcane is the main feedstock, and mills can switch between sugar and ethanol depending on prices. Sugarcane ethanol has a better energy balance and lower lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions than corn ethanol. Brazil's Proálcool programme began in 1975, and flex-fuel cars arrived in 2003. Brazil is now also expanding corn ethanol in Mato Grosso. India uses sugarcane juice, B-heavy molasses, damaged grains and FCI rice, and under the National Policy on Biofuels 2018 it advanced its E20 target to 2025.
summary: The answer is (d). Statement I is incorrect because the United States produces more ethanol than Brazil (roughly 55-58% of world output for the US against about 25-27% for Brazil). Statement II is correct: US ethanol is mainly corn-based, while Brazil's is mainly sugarcane-based.
topic_notes: Ethanol is a biofuel made by fermenting sugars or starch, and it is blended with petrol to reduce crude imports and emissions. Global production is about 100 billion litres a year. The US leads with around 55-58%, Brazil is second with about 25-27%, and then come the EU, China and India. The US uses corn, driven by the Renewable Fuel Standard, and blends E10 and E15. Brazil uses sugarcane, has mandated blends of about E27-E30, has flex-fuel vehicles and began Proálcool in 1975. India's Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) programme started in 2003. The National Policy on Biofuels 2018 set an E20 target for 2030, and this was advanced to 2025-26. India reached about 10% blending in 2022 and E20 in 2025. Feedstocks in India include sugarcane juice, B-heavy and C-heavy molasses, damaged food grains, maize and surplus FCI rice. Related schemes and bodies: the PM JI-VAN Yojana (second-generation 2G ethanol from agricultural residue), the SATAT scheme for compressed biogas, the Global Biofuels Alliance (launched at the G20 in 2023, Delhi), Oil Marketing Companies as the buyers, and the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas as the nodal ministry. Generations of biofuel: first generation uses food crops, second uses lignocellulosic waste, third uses algae, and fourth uses genetically engineered organisms. Related concerns include the food versus fuel debate, water use by sugarcane and maize, and indirect land-use change.

question:
The World Bank warned that India could become one of the first places where wet-bulb temperatures routinely exceed 35°C. Which of the following statements best reflect(s) the implication of the above-said report?
I. Peninsular India will most likely suffer from flooding, tropical cyclones and droughts. Il. The survival of animals including humans will be affected as shedding of their body heat through perspiration becomes difficult. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Economy
detail: Wet-bulb temperature (WBT) is the lowest temperature air can reach through evaporative cooling. It combines heat and humidity. A WBT of about 35°C is widely treated as the upper limit of human survivability. At that point, even a healthy person resting in shade cannot lose metabolic heat by sweating, because the air is too saturated for sweat to evaporate. Core body temperature then rises and can cause heat stroke, organ failure and death within hours. This applies to other mammals and birds too, so Statement II is correct. The World Bank report, 'Climate Investment Opportunities in India's Cooling Sector' (2022), warned that India could be among the first places to experience such WBTs. Statement I links the same warming to hydrometeorological extremes. A warmer ocean and atmosphere hold more moisture, so extreme rainfall and floods, intense cyclones in the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal, and erratic monsoon patterns that cause droughts all become more likely in peninsular India, which has a long coastline and is monsoon-dependent. Neither statement contradicts the report's implications, so (c) holds. Eliminate (a), (b) and (d) by recognising that both statements are plausible consequences of a hotter, more humid India.
explanations: (a) is wrong because Statement II is also a correct implication, so 'I only' is incomplete.
(b) is wrong because Statement I is also valid, since warming and humidity are tied to floods, cyclones and droughts in peninsular India.
(c) is correct because both statements reflect the implications: heat stress on survival through failed perspiration cooling, and intensified extreme weather in the peninsula.
(d) is wrong because both statements are valid implications.
keyfact: At 35°C wet-bulb temperature, sweat cannot evaporate, so the human body cannot shed heat, and India is flagged by the World Bank as an early hotspot.
option_notes: Option (a), 'I only', would accept only the extreme-weather statement. Peninsular India, with its long coast and monsoon dependence, is exposed to cyclones from the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea, floods and droughts. The IMD classifies cyclones by wind speed, and the Bay of Bengal sees more cyclones than the Arabian Sea, though Arabian Sea cyclones have been increasing. This is only part of the answer here.

Option (b), 'II only', would accept only the physiological statement. Wet-bulb temperature of 35°C is the limit of human adaptability, because sweat cannot evaporate and the body cannot dump heat. Hyperthermia leads to heat stroke and death within about six hours of exposure even for fit people in shade. This is the core implication but not the whole answer.

Option (c), 'Both I and II', is the official answer. It combines the direct physiological threat of wet-bulb temperatures above 35°C with the broader climate-linked hazards of floods, cyclones and droughts in peninsular India. The World Bank's 2022 cooling report said India could see lethal heat waves and a large demand for cooling, with about 160-200 million people potentially exposed to lethal heat waves annually.

Option (d), 'Neither I nor II', would reject both implications. This is wrong because the physiological limit of heat shedding is well established, and climate science links warming with more extreme weather events. UPSC often uses such an option as a distractor in questions based on reports and warnings.
related: Human survivability limit is about 35°C wet-bulb temperature.
India Cooling Action Plan was launched in 2019.
Kigali Amendment phases down HFCs; India's phase-down starts in 2028.
Ahmedabad Heat Action Plan (2013) was South Asia's first.
IMD declares a heat wave at 40°C or more in plains with a departure of 4.5°C or more.
NDMA issued heat wave guidelines in 2019.
World Bank cooling report on India was released in 2022.
Wet-bulb temperature combines heat and humidity.
statements: 1 — Correct: Warming and higher humidity are associated with more extreme floods, intense tropical cyclones and drought-flood swings in peninsular India. Peninsular India has a long coast on the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal. Sea surface warming raises cyclone intensity and moisture supply. The IMD and the IPCC AR6 report an increase in extreme rainfall events in central India and rapidly intensifying cyclones in the north Indian Ocean. Monsoon variability brings flash droughts and floods in the same season. Coastal states such as Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Gujarat are vulnerable. India has run cyclone warning systems and the NDMA's disaster management plans, and the Heat Action Plan model began in Ahmedabad in 2013.

2 — Correct: At a wet-bulb temperature near 35°C, sweat cannot evaporate, so the body cannot cool and survival is threatened. Humans maintain a core temperature of about 37°C by shedding heat through sweating and evaporation. When ambient humidity is very high, evaporation stops. The 35°C WBT threshold is the theoretical limit, and recent studies suggest harm may begin at lower levels, around 30-31°C for vulnerable people. Outdoor workers, the elderly, children and those without cooling are most at risk. Livestock and wildlife are also affected. India's heat action plans and the NDMA guidelines address heat waves, and the World Bank report stressed the need for sustainable cooling.
summary: The official answer is (c): both statements reflect the implications of the warning. A wet-bulb temperature above 35°C means the body cannot shed heat through sweating, which threatens survival (Statement II). The same warming and humidity trend is linked with more extreme events in peninsular India, such as floods, cyclones and droughts (Statement I).
topic_notes: Wet-bulb temperature is measured by a thermometer covered with a wet cloth and exposed to airflow. It reflects both temperature and humidity, unlike the dry-bulb temperature in ordinary weather reports. The theoretical human survivability limit is 35°C WBT, and harm begins at lower values for vulnerable groups. Heat index and WBGT (wet bulb globe temperature) are related measures used in occupational safety. The World Bank's report, 'Climate Investment Opportunities in India's Cooling Sector' (2022), projected cooling demand growth, an investment opportunity of about US$1.6 trillion by 2040, and the creation of about 3 million jobs. It linked cooling to the India Cooling Action Plan (ICAP), launched in 2019, which targets a 20-25% reduction in cooling demand by 2037-38 and a 25-30% reduction in refrigerant demand. Related topics include the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol, which phases down HFCs and which India has committed to phasing down from 2028 to 2047, the IMD's heat wave definition (maximum temperature at least 40°C in the plains and at least 4.5°C above normal, or 45°C and above in absolute terms), and state heat action plans, with Ahmedabad's 2013 plan the first in South Asia. NDMA guidelines on heat waves came out in 2019. Other angles include urban heat islands, the Lancet Countdown on health and climate, the IPCC AR6 projection of rising humid heat, and the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C. Regions at risk of high wet-bulb temperatures include the Indo-Gangetic Plain, the Persian Gulf and the Sahel.

question: A country’s fiscal deficit stands at €50, 000 crores. It is receiving 10, 000 crores through non-debt creating capital receipts. The country’s interest liabilities are £1, 500 crores. What is the gross primary deficit?
subject: Economy
detail: Fiscal deficit (GFD) = Total expenditure − (Revenue receipts + Non-debt creating capital receipts), where non-debt capital receipts are recovery of loans, miscellaneous capital receipts such as disinvestment proceeds. It therefore equals the government's net borrowing requirement. Because non-debt receipts are already netted out in arriving at the fiscal deficit figure given in the question, they must not be subtracted again. Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Interest payments. It shows the borrowing needed for current non-interest spending, i.e. the fiscal gap excluding the burden of past debt. Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts. Effective revenue deficit = Revenue deficit − grants for creation of capital assets. Elimination: option (b) 51,500 wrongly adds interest to the deficit. Option (c) 58,500 wrongly adds the 10,000 of non-debt receipts and subtracts interest, which double counts. Option (d) is wrong because the correct value is among the options. Terms such as 'gross primary deficit' are used loosely here as the gross fiscal deficit minus interest. The currency symbol is garbled by OCR; the figures are in rupees.
explanations: Correct: 50,000 − 1,500 = 48,500 crores. Primary deficit is fiscal deficit minus interest payments, and non-debt receipts are already reflected in the fiscal deficit.
Incorrect: 51,500 results from adding interest to the fiscal deficit, which is the wrong direction. Interest is subtracted to get the primary deficit.
Incorrect: 58,500 arises from adding 10,000 of non-debt receipts to 48,500. Those receipts are already netted out in the fiscal deficit, so adding them double counts.
Incorrect: A valid answer, 48,500 crores, is given in option (a), so 'None of the above' cannot be right.
keyfact: Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Interest payments, so 50,000 − 1,500 = ₹48,500 crores, and non-debt receipts are already netted out of the fiscal deficit.
option_notes: ₹48,500 crores is the primary deficit: fiscal deficit of 50,000 less interest of 1,500. A primary deficit shows how much the government borrows to finance non-interest spending. If it is zero, borrowing is used only to pay interest. India's primary deficit has fallen sharply since the pandemic peak of 2020-21, reflecting fiscal consolidation under the FRBM framework.

₹51,500 crores would be the figure if interest were added to the fiscal deficit (50,000 + 1,500). This is a conceptual error, because interest payments are already included in total expenditure and so in the fiscal deficit. Subtracting them isolates the primary balance. No standard fiscal indicator is computed by adding interest to the fiscal deficit.

₹58,500 crores would come from wrongly adding 10,000 of non-debt receipts to 48,500. Non-debt creating capital receipts include recovery of loans and disinvestment proceeds and do not create future repayment liabilities. They are deducted while computing the fiscal deficit, so they should not be treated again. Borrowing and other liabilities are the debt-creating receipts.

'None of the above' is the standard fallback option in UPSC numerical questions. It is correct only if the computed value is missing from the options. Here the computed value, 48,500 crores, appears as option (a), so this option is incorrect. Always compute first, then check the options.
related: Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Interest payments.
Fiscal deficit = Total expenditure − (Revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts).
Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts.
Effective revenue deficit = Revenue deficit − grants for creation of capital assets.
Disinvestment proceeds and recovery of loans are non-debt capital receipts.
FRBM Act was enacted in 2003, and the N.K. Singh Committee reviewed it in 2017.
Article 112 provides for the Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget).
Ad hoc Treasury Bills were discontinued in 1997, ending automatic monetisation.
summary: The answer is (a) ₹48,500 crores. Gross primary deficit = Gross fiscal deficit − Interest payments = 50,000 − 1,500 = ₹48,500 crores. The non-debt creating capital receipts of ₹10,000 crores are already accounted for in the fiscal deficit and are a distractor.
topic_notes: Fiscal deficit is the central indicator in India's Union Budget. Fiscal deficit = Total expenditure − Total receipts excluding borrowings, that is, revenue receipts plus non-debt capital receipts (recovery of loans, disinvestment). It equals the net borrowing requirement of the government. Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Interest payments. Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts. Effective revenue deficit = Revenue deficit − grants for creation of capital assets, introduced in the 2011-12 Budget. Budget deficit (old concept) = Total expenditure − Total receipts; it was discontinued after 1997 when ad hoc Treasury Bills were phased out. Monetised deficit was also an older concept. The FRBM Act 2003 set targets for deficit reduction. The N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended debt-to-GDP of 60% (40% Centre, 20% states) and a fiscal deficit of 3% of GDP. Escape clauses in the FRBM Act allow deviation for national security, calamities and similar shocks. The pandemic raised the fiscal deficit to about 9.2% of GDP in 2020-21. The Union Budget 2025-26 targets about 4.4% of GDP, and the government has adopted a debt-to-GDP glide path from 2026-27 onward. A positive primary deficit means borrowing exceeds interest burden. A primary surplus means the government borrows less than its interest bill. Deficit financing sources include market borrowings, external borrowing, small savings and Treasury Bills. Article 112 requires the annual financial statement, Article 266 deals with the Consolidated Fund of India, and Article 267 with the Contingency Fund. UPSC often tests formulas and the classification of receipts such as recovery of loans as capital receipts.

question:
Which of the following statements with regard to recommendations of the 15th Finance Commission of India are correct?
I. It has recommended grants of 4, 800 crores from the year 2022-23 to the year 2025-26 for incentivizing States to enhance educational outcomes. Il. 45% of the net proceeds of Union taxes are to be shared with States. Ill. ©45, 000 crores are to be kept as performance-based incentive for all States for carrying out agricultural reforms.
IV. It reintroduced tax effort criteria to reward fiscal performance. Select the correct answer using the code given below
subject: Economy
detail: The 15th Finance Commission was constituted in November 2017 under N.K. Singh under Article 280. Its main report for 2021-26 was tabled in February 2021.
