It recommended a 41% share for states in the divisible pool of Union taxes. This was down from the 14th FC's 42%, with the 1% adjustment made for the newly created UTs of J&K and Ladakh. The 14th FC's 42% was a big jump over the 10% earlier. The 15th FC changed the criteria: it gave 45% weight to income distance, 15% to population (1971 census), 15% to demography performance, 15% to forest and ecology, and 12.5% to area, and it brought back tax effort with a 2.5% weight. It recommended performance-based incentives, including grants for education outcomes (Rs 4,800 crore, 2022-23 to 2025-26) and Rs 45,000 crore for agricultural reforms. Elimination: the option must exclude II, since 45% is wrong. That leaves (c) as the only option without II. Remember that 45% is the weight for income distance, which is where the number is confused.
explanations: Wrong: option (a) includes statement II, which is incorrect because the states' share is 41%, not 45%, and it omits IV, which is correct.
Wrong: option (b) includes II, which is incorrect, and omits III, which is correct.
Correct: I, III and IV are right, and the incorrect statement II is excluded.
Wrong: option (d) includes II, which is incorrect, and omits I, which is correct.
keyfact: The 15th FC gave states 41% of the divisible pool (not 45%); 45% is the income-distance weight, and tax effort (2.5%) was reintroduced.
option_notes: Option (a) combines I, II and III. It would be correct only if the 45% devolution share were true. In fact 45% is the weight for income distance, and the actual devolution is 41%. The 14th FC gave 42%, which was a big rise from earlier commissions. The mistake in this option is treating the weight as the share.

Option (b) combines I, II and IV. It drops the agricultural reforms incentive of Rs 45,000 crore, which the commission did recommend. It also wrongly includes the 45% claim. Students should recall the main performance-based grants: education, agriculture, power, and others for the 2021-26 period.

Option (c) combines I, III and IV, and is the official answer. It correctly includes the education grant of Rs 4,800 crore, the agricultural reform incentive of Rs 45,000 crore, and the reintroduction of tax effort. It leaves out the incorrect 45% devolution claim. The 15th FC's award period is 2021-26 and its chair was N.K. Singh.

Option (d) combines II, III and IV. It misses the education incentive and contains the incorrect 45% claim. The key to avoiding it is to remember the 41% states' share. The 15th FC's report was tabled in Parliament on 1 February 2021 together with the Union Budget.
related: 15th FC chairman: N.K. Singh; award period 2021-26
States' share in the divisible pool under the 15th FC: 41%
14th FC (Y.V. Reddy) recommended 42%
16th FC chaired by Arvind Panagariya; covers 2026-31
Article 280 provides for the Finance Commission; Article 275 covers grants-in-aid
Income distance has the highest weight, 45%, in the 15th FC's criteria
Tax effort weight in the 15th FC: 2.5%
First Finance Commission (1951) was chaired by K.C. Neogy
statements: I — Correct: the FC recommended Rs 4,800 crore for 2022-23 to 2025-26 to incentivise states to improve educational outcomes. The grant sits within the performance-based incentives meant to improve social-sector delivery. The FC also proposed grants for health, with a large part going to local bodies, and recommended a nodal agency framework for statistics and for school education. These performance incentives reward states that show measurable improvement against indicators, and they sit alongside the 15th FC's focus on outcome-linked transfers rather than unconditional devolution. The grant period matches the final four years of the award period (2021-26).

II — Incorrect: the states' share is 41%, not 45%. The 14th FC had given 42%. The 15th FC's interim report for 2020-21 kept 42%, but this was cut to 41% for 2021-26 because J&K ceased to be a state and the Centre needed to fund its UT responsibilities. The 45% figure is the weight given to income distance among the devolution criteria. The vertical devolution share is a core Finance Commission topic and is often asked about. Total transfers, including grants, come to around 1/3 or more of the Union's resources.

III — Correct: the FC recommended Rs 45,000 crore as performance-based incentives for states to carry out agricultural reforms. The incentives cover areas such as improving farm-sector productivity, agricultural exports, pulses and oilseeds, and similar reforms. These were part of its larger idea of grants tied to reforms. Related incentives included those for power sector reforms, for urban and local bodies, and for Make in India-type targets. The commission also recommended grants for the agricultural sector alongside rural local bodies, health, and disaster management, as part of the 2021-26 award.

IV — Correct: the 15th FC reintroduced tax effort as a criterion, with a 2.5% weight. It rewards states with higher tax collection relative to their capacity, measured by the ratio of per capita own tax revenue to per capita state GDP. The 14th FC had dropped it. Other criteria include demographic performance at 12.5% and forest and ecology at 10%, in the final weights. The income distance criterion carries the highest weight at 45%. Tax effort is meant to encourage fiscal discipline and revenue mobilisation.
summary: The official answer is (c): statements I, III and IV are correct. Statement II is wrong because the 15th Finance Commission kept the states' share of the divisible pool at 41% (after the creation of the UT of J&K and Ladakh), not 45%.
topic_notes: The Finance Commission is a constitutional body under Article 280, constituted every five years by the President. It recommends the distribution of net tax proceeds between the Union and the states (vertical devolution) and among the states (horizontal devolution), grants-in-aid under Article 275, and measures to supplement state funds for panchayats and municipalities. The 15th FC was chaired by N.K. Singh, constituted in November 2017, with an interim report for 2020-21 and a final report for 2021-26. Its vertical devolution is 41%. Its horizontal criteria are income distance 45%, population (2011 census) 15%, area 15%, forest and ecology 10%, demographic performance 12.5%, and tax effort 2.5%. It used the 2011 population census, unlike the 1971 census earlier, which drew complaints from southern states. It recommended revenue deficit grants to a number of states, and sector-specific and performance-based grants for health, education, agriculture, and local bodies. It proposed a fiscal roadmap with a debt-to-GDP target of around 56.6% by 2025-26 for the general government and a fiscal deficit glide path. It also recommended funds for disaster risk management (NDRF/SDRF), defence and internal security funding mechanisms, and incentives for states to adopt measures such as power sector reform. The 16th Finance Commission, chaired by Arvind Panagariya, was constituted in December 2023 and covers 2026-31. Earlier FCs: the 14th (Y.V. Reddy) gave 42%, and the 13th (Vijay Kelkar) gave 32%. The first FC was chaired by K.C. Neogy in 1951.

question:
Consider the following statements in respect of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) :
I. It provides loans and guarantees to middle income countries.
II. It works single-handedly to help developing countries to reduce poverty.
III. It was established to help Europe rebuild after the World War
II. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: The IBRD was conceived at the Bretton Woods Conference (July 1944) and began operating in 1945-46, with its first loan in 1947 to France for reconstruction. Its original purpose was to finance rebuilding of war-torn Europe; it later shifted to development lending to the developing world. It is the oldest and original institution of the World Bank Group, headquartered in Washington, D.C. It raises most of its funds by issuing bonds on international capital markets (AAA-rated) rather than relying on grants, and it lends at near-market rates to governments of middle-income and creditworthy low-income countries. Its products include loans, guarantees, risk-management tools (derivatives) and advisory services. The World Bank Group has five institutions: IBRD, IDA (poorest countries, concessional), IFC (private sector), MIGA (investment guarantees) and ICSID (investment disputes). The IBRD plus IDA together constitute the 'World Bank'. Elimination logic: statement II uses the absolute phrase 'single-handedly', which is a classic UPSC trap. The IBRD works with IDA and the other group institutions, the IMF, UN agencies and governments. Since II is wrong, options (a), (b) and (d) are eliminated, leaving (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes II, which is false: the IBRD does not work single-handedly in poverty reduction, and it also leaves out the correct statement III.
(b) is wrong because it includes II (false) and omits I, which is correct since the IBRD gives loans and guarantees to middle-income countries.
(c) is right because I (loans and guarantees to middle-income countries) and III (set up to rebuild postwar Europe) are both accurate, while II is false.
(d) is wrong because it accepts II, but the IBRD works with IDA, IFC, MIGA and other partners rather than alone.
keyfact: IBRD: created at Bretton Woods 1944 to rebuild postwar Europe, now lends and guarantees to middle-income countries as part of (not alone in) the World Bank Group.
option_notes: Option (a) pairs I and II. It would describe the IBRD as a lender that also acts alone against poverty. The IBRD is the World Bank's non-concessional arm, in the same group as IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID, so no single institution works alone. IDA provides concessional loans and grants to the poorest countries, with replenishment every three years. IFC, founded 1956, supports the private sector. MIGA, founded 1988, offers political-risk guarantees. ICSID, founded 1966, settles investment disputes.

Option (b) pairs II and III. III is true: the IBRD came out of Bretton Woods (1944) and funded postwar reconstruction, with its first loan to France in 1947. II is false. The Bretton Woods twins are the IBRD (World Bank) and the IMF, which handles monetary cooperation and balance-of-payments support, while the World Bank handles long-term development finance. The ITO planned at the same time failed and led to GATT in 1947, later replaced by the WTO in 1995.

Option (c) pairs I and III and is the official correct answer. The IBRD lends to middle-income and creditworthy low-income governments, offers guarantees and advisory services, and funds itself via AAA-rated bonds. It was founded at Bretton Woods in 1944 for European reconstruction, began operations in 1946, and shifted to development lending afterwards. Capital subscriptions from members determine voting power, with the US holding the largest share. The World Bank president is traditionally American; Ajay Banga has held the post since June 2023.

Option (d) combines all three statements. It is wrong only because II is false. Remember the typical UPSC trap of absolute words like 'single-handedly', 'only' or 'always'. The World Bank Group works through five institutions and with partners such as the IMF, UN bodies and regional banks. Its goals are to end extreme poverty and boost shared prosperity. Bank flagship reports include the World Development Report, Doing Business (discontinued 2021) and Ease of Doing Business rankings, which have been replaced by the B-READY project.
related: Bretton Woods Conference: July 1944, 44 nations, created the IMF and IBRD.
The IBRD's first loan (1947) went to France for postwar reconstruction.
IDA (1960) gives concessional loans and grants to the poorest countries.
IFC (1956) focuses on private sector investment; MIGA (1988) offers political risk guarantees.
ICSID (1966) handles investment dispute settlement.
The World Bank was a mediator in the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) between India and Pakistan.
Ajay Banga became World Bank president in June 2023.
The World Bank's 'Doing Business' report was discontinued in 2021 after data irregularities.
statements: I — Correct: The IBRD provides loans, guarantees and advisory services to middle-income and creditworthy low-income countries. It is the World Bank's non-concessional lending arm, funded mainly by bond issuance on capital markets, with a AAA credit rating. Lending is to sovereign governments or with sovereign guarantee, for development projects and policy-based programmes. Loans have long maturities, often 15-20 years or more, and priced on a benchmark rate plus spread. Poorest countries use IDA's concessional credits and grants, and some countries 'blend' IBRD and IDA. Graduation from IBRD happens at higher income levels.

II — Incorrect: The IBRD does not work single-handedly. It is one of five World Bank Group institutions: IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA and ICSID. The IBRD and IDA together form the 'World Bank'. The group's twin goals, adopted in 2013, are ending extreme poverty (to below 3 percent by 2030) and boosting shared prosperity. It works in partnership with the IMF, UN agencies, regional development banks (ADB, AfDB, AIIB, NDB), governments, NGOs and the private sector, and co-finances projects. 'Single-handedly' makes the statement wrong.

III — Correct: The IBRD was established in 1944 at the Bretton Woods Conference (New Hampshire, USA), attended by 44 allied nations, and began operating in June 1946. Its first loan, about $250 million, went to France in 1947 for postwar reconstruction. Its original name reflects 'Reconstruction' of Europe and Japan. Once the Marshall Plan took over European recovery, the focus moved to developing countries. India was a founding member. The Bank's first president was Eugene Meyer. The IBRD has about 189 member countries, with headquarters in Washington, D.C.
summary: The answer is (c): statements I and III are correct. The IBRD lends to and guarantees for middle-income and creditworthy low-income countries, and it was created at Bretton Woods in 1944 initially to finance post-WWII European reconstruction. Statement II is wrong because the IBRD does not work single-handedly; it works with IDA, IFC, MIGA, ICSID and other partners.
topic_notes: The World Bank Group (WBG) is a set of five institutions headquartered in Washington, D.C. The IBRD (1944/1946) lends to middle-income and creditworthy low-income countries. The IDA (1960) offers zero or low-interest credits and grants to the poorest nations and is replenished every three years by donors. The IFC (1956) invests in the private sector in developing countries. MIGA (1988) provides political risk insurance and guarantees. ICSID (1966) arbitrates investment disputes. The IBRD and IDA are collectively called the World Bank. Origins lie in the Bretton Woods Conference of July 1944, attended by 44 nations, which also created the IMF. The IMF has 190 members, and the IBRD has about 189. India is a founding member of both. Voting power in the IBRD reflects capital subscriptions, and the US has the largest share, which gives it effective veto over major decisions that need an 85 percent majority. The president has traditionally been an American, while the IMF's managing director is traditionally European. The WBG's goals since 2013 are ending extreme poverty (below 3 percent by 2030) and promoting shared prosperity for the bottom 40 percent. Key publications include the World Development Report, Global Economic Prospects, International Debt Statistics and the Human Capital Index. The Bank also hosts the Global Environment Facility as trustee. Related angles for UPSC include India as a borrower (IBRD and IDA, India having graduated from IDA), the Bank's role in the Indus Waters Treaty 1960 as mediator, the New Development Bank (BRICS, 2015, Shanghai), the AIIB (2016, Beijing), the ADB (1966, Manila), and the IMF's SDR basket and quota system.

question:
Consider the following statements in respect of RTGS and NEFT :
I. In RTGS, the settlement time is instantaneous while in case of NEFT, it takes some time to settle payments. Il. In RTGS, the customer is charged for inward transactions while that is not the case for NEFT. Ill. Operating hours for RTGS are restricted on certain days while this is not true for NEFT. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
subject: Economy
detail: RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement) and NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer) are RBI-operated retail and large-value electronic fund transfer systems. RTGS settles each transaction individually and continuously, so funds move instantly and finally. It is meant for large-value payments, with a minimum of Rs 2 lakh and no upper limit. NEFT works on Deferred Net Settlement (DNS) in batches, historically hourly and then half-hourly, with no minimum and no maximum limit set by RBI. So Statement I is correct. On charges, RBI prohibits charging customers for inward (receiving) transactions in both RTGS and NEFT; only the sender may be charged, within RBI ceilings. So Statement II is wrong. On hours, NEFT became available 24x7x365 from 16 December 2019, and RTGS from 14 December 2020, so neither is restricted on specific days. So Statement III is wrong. Elimination: II is false, which removes (b); III is false, which removes (c) and (d). That leaves (a).
explanations: Correct. Only Statement I is true: RTGS is real-time gross settlement and NEFT is batch-based deferred net settlement. II and III are false.
Wrong. Statement II is false because customers are not charged for inward transactions in either RTGS or NEFT.
Wrong. Statement III is false because RTGS has run 24x7 since December 2020, so its hours are not restricted on particular days.
Wrong. Statement III is false, so III alone cannot be the answer, and Statement I is in fact true.
keyfact: RTGS = real-time gross settlement (minimum Rs 2 lakh); NEFT = batch-based deferred net settlement; both are 24x7 and free for inward receipts.
option_notes: Option (a), Statement I only. RTGS settles payments individually in real time and finally. NEFT settles in half-hourly batches under deferred net settlement. RTGS has a Rs 2 lakh minimum; NEFT has no minimum. Both systems are run by RBI under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. This is the official answer.

Option (b), I and II. Statement I is right, but II is wrong because RBI bars charging customers for inward transactions in both systems. Remitters can be charged for outward transfers, within RBI ceilings. This pairing fails on the charge rule.

Option (c), I and III. Statement I is right, but III is wrong because both systems operate 24x7x365. NEFT began round-the-clock operation on 16 December 2019, and RTGS did so on 14 December 2020. The claim of restricted RTGS days is outdated.

Option (d), III only. This is wrong because III is false and I is true. The option reflects the old pre-2019 and pre-2020 regime of limited hours and working days only. It ignores the 24x7 move for both systems and the settlement difference.
related: RTGS minimum amount is Rs 2 lakh with no upper limit.
NEFT is available 24x7x365 since 16 December 2019.
RTGS became 24x7 on 14 December 2020.
NEFT uses deferred net settlement in half-hourly batches.
Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 empowers RBI to regulate payment systems.
NPCI, set up in 2008, runs UPI, IMPS and RuPay.
Inward RTGS and NEFT transactions cannot be charged to the customer.
Digital rupee retail pilot began on 1 December 2022.
statements: 1 — Correct: RTGS settles transaction by transaction in real time, while NEFT settles in batches. RTGS is gross settlement: each payment is processed and settled individually, so it is final and irrevocable once done. It is used for large-value payments, with a minimum of Rs 2 lakh and no cap. NEFT uses deferred net settlement in half-hourly batches, so credit takes some time. Both are run by RBI, and the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 governs them. Beneficiary banks must credit the customer promptly, typically within two hours of batch settlement for NEFT.

2 — Incorrect: Neither RTGS nor NEFT allows customers to be charged for inward transactions. RBI has directed that receiving funds is free of charge for the beneficiary. Only outward transactions can be charged, and RBI caps the charges (for example, RTGS charges are capped at Rs 25 to 30 plus GST for higher slabs, and NEFT charges are lower, in the Rs 2 to 25 range by slab). RBI had waived charges on online RTGS and NEFT transfers by savings account holders in 2019 after the Bimal Jalan committee recommendation. Banks may levy limited charges for branch-based transfers.

3 — Incorrect: Both systems are available around the clock. NEFT has operated 24x7x365 since 16 December 2019, including holidays. RTGS became 24x7x365 from 14 December 2020, making India among the few countries with round-the-clock RTGS. Earlier, RTGS ran on bank working days from about 7 am to 6 pm, and NEFT ran from 8 am to 7 pm with Sunday and holiday exceptions. Hence the claim that RTGS hours are restricted on certain days, while NEFT's are not, is false. Only the system's brief technical maintenance windows are exceptions.
summary: The answer is (a): only Statement I is correct. RTGS settles payments individually in real time (gross settlement), whereas NEFT settles in deferred half-hourly batches. Statements II and III are wrong because inward transactions are not charged for either system, and it is NEFT and RTGS that both operate 24x7x365 now.
topic_notes: RBI operates the key electronic payment rails: RTGS, NEFT, and the National Electronic Clearing Service (NECS), and it oversees retail systems run by NPCI. Legal basis is the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. RTGS began in March 2004 and is for large-value payments, with a Rs 2 lakh minimum and no cap, and it settles in central bank money in real time. NEFT began in November 2005 and uses deferred net settlement, with half-hourly batches since 2019, with no minimum or maximum limit set by RBI, though banks may set their own limits. NEFT has been 24x7 since 16 December 2019, and RTGS since 14 December 2020. Charges: RBI waived charges on online transfers by savings account holders from July 2019 and bars charging for inward transactions. A Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) is required for large-value transactions of Rs 50 crore and above. NPCI, set up in 2008, runs IMPS (24x7, instant, introduced 2010), UPI (2016), RuPay, NACH, Aadhaar-enabled Payment System, and Bharat BillPay. UPI is real-time, with a typical per-transaction limit of Rs 1 lakh, higher for specific categories. RBI's Payments Vision 2025 aims at wider digital payments. Other angles: Digital Rupee (e-rupee, CBDC pilots began in December 2022 for retail), Payments Infrastructure Development Fund, Payment Systems Operators, Cross-border UPI linkages, and the Payments Regulatory Board. The settlement distinction between gross and net settlement is a frequent UPSC angle.

question:
Consider the following countries :
I. United Arab Emirates Il, France Ill. Germany
IV. Singapore
V. Bangladesh How many countries amongst the above are there other than India where international merchant payments are accepted under UPI?
subject: Economy
detail: UPI (Unified Payments Interface), launched by NPCI in 2016, is now being extended abroad through NPCI International Payments Limited (NIPL), the international arm of NPCI set up in 2020. Cross-border acceptance takes two forms: (i) merchant payments, where an Indian traveller scans a QR code at a foreign shop, and (ii) person-to-person remittances or linkages with foreign fast-payment systems. The countries where UPI is accepted at merchants include Bhutan, Nepal, Singapore, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, the UAE and France, where Eiffel Tower ticket payments were launched in 2024. Singapore's link with PayNow (Feb 2023) is a P2P linkage, and QR-based merchant acceptance was also enabled there. In the UAE, NIPL works with Mashreq Bank's Network International. Germany and Bangladesh are not on the list of countries where UPI merchant payments are accepted. Elimination logic: UAE, France and Singapore are established, which makes 'only three' correct. Germany and Bangladesh must be excluded, which rules out (c) and (d). Since three are confirmed, (a) is too low.
explanations: (a) Only two is wrong. Three of the listed countries (UAE, France, Singapore) accept UPI merchant payments, not two.
(b) Only three is correct. UAE, France and Singapore are the countries in the list where UPI merchant payments are accepted. Germany and Bangladesh are not.
(c) Only four is wrong. It would require counting either Germany or Bangladesh, and neither has UPI merchant acceptance.
(d) All the five is wrong. Germany and Bangladesh do not accept UPI at merchants.
keyfact: UPI merchant payments abroad: UAE, France and Singapore (plus Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Mauritius), but not Germany or Bangladesh.
option_notes: Only two: this would be correct for a list with just two acceptance countries. In reality UPI merchant payments run in more countries, including Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, Singapore, the UAE and France. The number of countries keeps growing as NIPL signs new tie-ups, so students must track the current list.

Only three: the right answer here. The UAE, France and Singapore are the three listed countries that accept UPI. NIPL, the international arm of NPCI created in 2020, drives these deals. UPI's global reach is part of India's push to internationalise its digital payments and to promote the rupee in cross-border transactions.

Only four: this would require one of Germany or Bangladesh to accept UPI. Germany is in Europe, where only France has been launched, and Bangladesh has no UPI link. It is a distractor to catch students who assume neighbouring or large European economies are included.

All the five: this would mean UPI is accepted in Germany and Bangladesh as well. It is not. UPI's footprint is concentrated in Asia, West Asia, Africa (Mauritius) and, since 2024, France in Europe. Linkages are bilateral and are negotiated individually by NIPL and the RBI.
related: UPI was launched in 2016 by NPCI.
NIPL (NPCI International Payments Ltd) was set up in 2020 as NPCI's international arm.
Bhutan was the first country to adopt UPI QR code acceptance (2021).
UPI–PayNow link with Singapore went live in February 2023.
France was the first European country to accept UPI (Eiffel Tower, 2024).
Sri Lanka and Mauritius launched UPI services in February 2024.
UPI 123PAY enables UPI payments on feature phones.
NPCI was set up in 2008 under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 framework.
statements: I — Correct: UPI is accepted at merchants in the UAE. NIPL tied up with Network International (Mashreq) in 2024 to accept UPI at its point-of-sale terminals in the UAE. Earlier, in 2023, the RBI and the Central Bank of the UAE agreed to link UPI with the UAE's Aani instant payment platform. The UAE has a large Indian diaspora and is a major remittance corridor and tourist destination for Indians.

II — Correct: France accepts UPI. In February 2024 NIPL and Lyra, a French payments firm, launched UPI at the Eiffel Tower, the first European country to accept UPI. Indian tourists can pay for tickets by scanning a QR code. The launch came during the Indian PM's visit to France, and the plan is to extend acceptance to other French merchants.

III — Incorrect: Germany is not a country where UPI merchant payments are accepted. Although there have been discussions on promoting Indian digital payments in Europe, no operational UPI merchant acceptance had been launched there at the time of the paper. France is the European country where it is live. Germany uses SEPA-based payments and cards such as Girocard.

IV — Correct: Singapore accepts UPI. The UPI–PayNow linkage was launched in February 2023 by the RBI and the Monetary Authority of Singapore, enabling real-time P2P remittances between the two countries. Merchant QR acceptance has also been enabled through NIPL's tie-ups in Singapore. Singapore was among the first countries to connect with UPI in a cross-border payment linkage.

V — Incorrect: Bangladesh does not have UPI merchant payments. UPI works in neighbouring Bhutan (RuPay and UPI, 2021 onwards) and Nepal (2024 merchant payments), as well as Sri Lanka, but Bangladesh has no such arrangement. Bangladesh runs its own system, Bangladesh National Payment Switch (BNPS), and has no operational link with UPI.
summary: The official answer is (b) Only three. Of the listed countries, UPI merchant payments are accepted in the UAE, France and Singapore, but not in Germany or Bangladesh. NIPL (NPCI International Payments Ltd) has signed these tie-ups, so exactly three of the five qualify.
topic_notes: UPI is a real-time instant payment system developed by NPCI, an umbrella body for retail payments in India that was set up in 2008 with RBI and Indian Banks' Association support. UPI was launched in April 2016 and is the world's largest real-time payment system by volume, accounting for a very large share of India's digital transactions and nearly half of global real-time payments. Its mobile-first features include virtual payment addresses (VPAs), QR codes, one-click authentication and interoperability across banks. NPCI International Payments Limited (NIPL) was formed in 2020 to take UPI and RuPay abroad. UPI overseas works in several ways. In Bhutan, UPI was launched in 2021 and Bhutan was the first country to adopt the UPI QR code standard. In Nepal, a link between NPCI and Nepal's Gateway Payment Services was established. In Singapore, UPI is linked with PayNow for P2P payments (2023). In Sri Lanka and Mauritius, UPI was launched in February 2024, and Mauritius also adopted RuPay cards. In the UAE, UPI is linked to Aani, and Network International accepts UPI at merchants. France was the first European country to accept UPI, starting at the Eiffel Tower. Other related efforts include RuPay, BHIM, UPI Lite, UPI 123PAY for feature phones, and the Unified Payments Interface's 'UPI One World' wallet for foreign visitors in India. The G20 under India's presidency promoted interlinking fast payment systems. Future questions may be asked on NPCI's role, NIPL, RuPay, BHIM, cross-border remittance tie-ups and the RBI's payment system regulation under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.

question:
Consider the following statements about PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana’ :
I. It targets installation of one crore solar rooftop panels in the residential sector. Il. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy aims to impart training on installation, operation, maintenance and repairs of solar rooftop systems at grassroot levels. Ill. It aims to create more than three lakhs skilled manpower through fresh skilling, and upskilling, under scheme component of capacity building. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana was announced by the Prime Minister on 13 February 2024 and approved by the Union Cabinet on 29 February 2024, with an outlay of about Rs 75,021 crore, running up to FY 2026-27. It is implemented by the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE), with DISCOMs and State implementing agencies and a national portal (pmsuryaghar.gov.in) for applications. The target is rooftop solar installation in one crore residential households. Central Financial Assistance (CFA) is about Rs 30,000 per kW for the first 2 kW and Rs 18,000 for the additional 1 kW, capped at 3 kW, so the maximum subsidy is about Rs 78,000. Households can get up to roughly 300 units of free electricity per month. The scheme also has components for model solar villages, incentives for DISCOMs, and capacity building, which covers training of installers, technicians, and others and is intended to create more than 3 lakh skilled workers. It also promotes local manufacturing and entrepreneurship. Elimination logic: since statements I and II and III all match official scheme features, only the option with all three can be right. Any option that omits one statement is wrong.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it leaves out statement III, which is also correct: the scheme aims to create over three lakh skilled workers.
(b) is wrong because it leaves out statement II, and MNRE does plan grassroots training in installation, operation, maintenance and repair.
(c) is wrong because it leaves out statement I, and the one crore household target is the central goal of the scheme.
(d) is correct because all three statements accurately describe the scheme's target, its training plan, and its manpower creation goal.
keyfact: PM Surya Ghar (Feb 2024): one crore households, up to Rs 78,000 subsidy for 3 kW, 300 free units a month, and 3 lakh+ skilled workers via capacity building.
option_notes: Options I and II only: this is a combination that would be right if capacity building had no numerical manpower target. The scheme does have one, namely more than 3 lakh skilled people, so the combination is incomplete. Statements I and II cover the one crore household target and the grassroots training role of MNRE. The scheme was approved in Feb 2024 with an outlay of Rs 75,021 crore.

Options I and III only: this combination ignores the training and upskilling element at grassroots level, which is part of the capacity-building component. The scheme does target one crore households and over 3 lakh skilled workers, but the MNRE's grassroots training of installers and technicians is also stated, so this option is incomplete. The scheme runs until FY 2026-27.

Options II and III only: this combination omits the headline target of one crore residential rooftop solar installations. That target is the core of the scheme and is why it is called 'Muft Bijli' (free electricity), with subsidy up to Rs 78,000 for 3 kW systems. Omitting it makes the option wrong, even though the training and manpower statements are correct.

Options I, II and III: this is the correct combination. The scheme targets one crore households, provides grassroots training through MNRE, and aims for over 3 lakh skilled workers via fresh skilling and upskilling. It was announced on 13 Feb 2024 and approved by the Cabinet on 29 Feb 2024, with an outlay of Rs 75,021 crore, and is implemented by MNRE.
related: PM Surya Ghar was launched on 13 February 2024 and approved by the Cabinet on 29 February 2024.
Outlay is Rs 75,021 crore, up to FY 2026-27.
CFA: Rs 30,000/kW for first 2 kW, Rs 18,000 for 3rd kW, capped at 3 kW.
Households can get about 300 units of free electricity per month.
Nodal ministry is MNRE; the national portal is pmsuryaghar.gov.in.
PM-KUSUM supports solar pumps and grid-connected solar for farmers.
The International Solar Alliance has its HQ in Gurugram, and was co-launched by India and France in 2015.
India's targets are 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070.
statements: I — Correct: The scheme targets one crore households with rooftop solar. It was launched on 13 Feb 2024 with an outlay of Rs 75,021 crore, up to FY 2026-27. Subsidy is Rs 30,000 per kW for the first 2 kW and Rs 18,000 for the third kW, capped at 3 kW. Households get up to about 300 free units a month, and surplus power can be sold to DISCOMs. Applications go through the national portal, with the MNRE as the nodal ministry and DISCOMs as local implementers. Loans are available at concessional rates.

II — Correct: MNRE's capacity-building component aims to train people at grassroots level in installation, operation, maintenance and repair of rooftop solar systems. Training is delivered through institutions such as ITIs, the Suryamitra skill programme (run via the National Institute of Solar Energy), and DISCOM or state agencies. The aim is to ensure quality installation and after-sales service, and to create local jobs and entrepreneurs, supporting the rooftop solar value chain nationwide.

III — Correct: Under the capacity building component, the scheme aims for more than 3 lakh skilled workers through fresh skilling and upskilling. This covers solar technicians, installers, fitters, electricians, plumbers, and others. It is part of the scheme's wider employment potential, estimated at around 17 lakh direct jobs across manufacturing, installation, and O&M. The training programmes link with the Skill India framework and the Suryamitra initiative, and they also support the vendor ecosystem and the local manufacturing of solar modules and inverters.
summary: The answer is (d): all three statements are correct. PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana targets rooftop solar in one crore households, includes grassroots training by MNRE, and aims to build a skilled workforce of over three lakh people through capacity building.
topic_notes: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana is India's flagship residential rooftop solar scheme, announced on 13 February 2024 and approved by the Union Cabinet on 29 February 2024. Its outlay is about Rs 75,021 crore up to FY 2026-27. The target is one crore households. Subsidy (CFA) is Rs 30,000 per kW for up to 2 kW and Rs 18,000 for the third kW, capped at 3 kW, so the maximum is Rs 78,000. Households can get up to about 300 units of free electricity monthly. The scheme is implemented by MNRE through DISCOMs and state agencies, with a national online portal for registration, vendor selection, and subsidy transfer directly to bank accounts. Collateral-free low-interest loans are available (about 7% for up to 3 kW). Other components include model solar villages (one in each district, with incentives of Rs 1 crore per district), incentives for urban local bodies and panchayats, DISCOM incentives for exceeding capacity targets, and capacity building, with a target of over 3 lakh skilled workers. Employment is estimated at around 17 lakh direct jobs. Estimated benefits include savings on electricity bills, extra income from selling surplus power, and emission reduction of about 720 million tonnes of CO2 over 25 years. Related topics: the earlier Rooftop Solar Programme Phase II (4 GW target 40 GW by 2022 revised), PM-KUSUM for agriculture, the International Solar Alliance (HQ Gurugram, launched 2015 with France), National Solar Mission (2010), and India's goal of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070. UPSC could also ask about subsidy amounts, implementing agencies, or components.

question: “Sedition has become my religion” was the famous statement given by Gandhiji at the time of the Champaran Satyagraha
options: publicly violating Salt Law at Dandi
Conference in London the launch of the Quit India
subject: Modern History
detail: The OCR has merged the stem with the options. Read in order, they are (a) Champaran Satyagraha, (b) publicly violating the Salt Law at Dandi, (c) attending the Second Round Table Conference in London, and (d) the launch of the Quit India Movement. The statement is linked to Gandhi's 1930 Civil Disobedience campaign. In March-April 1930 he marched from Sabarmati to Dandi (12 March to 6 April, about 240 miles) and broke the Salt Law, openly inviting arrest under laws he regarded as unjust. Section 124A IPC (sedition) had already been used against him in 1922, when he was tried for articles in Young India. Under it, 'disaffection' towards the government was a crime, and Gandhi treated that disaffection as a moral duty. Elimination: Champaran (1917) was a local, constructive agitation for indigo cultivators, and Gandhi was then still cooperating with the government. The Second Round Table Conference (Sept-Dec 1931) was a negotiation after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, so it was a cooperative moment. Quit India (August 1942) is remembered for 'Do or Die'. This leaves Dandi as the best fit with the official answer.
explanations: Incorrect for this question. Champaran (1917) was Gandhi's first satyagraha in India. It was a limited agitation against the tinkathia system and was resolved through the Champaran Agrarian Act 1918. It was not framed as defiance of sedition law.
Correct. The remark belongs to Gandhi's 1930 Civil Disobedience campaign around the Dandi March and the breaking of the Salt Law, when he defied the colonial legal order openly and invited arrest.

Incorrect. The Second Round Table Conference (1931) followed the Gandhi-Irwin Pact, when Gandhi was negotiating constitutionally as the Congress's sole representative. This is not a context of declaring sedition a religion.
Incorrect. Quit India (8 August 1942, Gandhi's 'Do or Die' speech at Gowalia Tank, Bombay) is associated with a different slogan and call. It is not tied to this quote.
keyfact: Gandhi's 'Sedition has become my religion' is linked to the 1930 Civil Disobedience/Dandi Salt Law defiance (answer b).
option_notes: Champaran Satyagraha (1917, Bihar): Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, at the request of Rajkumar Shukla. It was against the tinkathia system, under which peasants had to grow indigo on 3/20 of their land. The Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918 ended the system. Rajendra Prasad, J.B. Kripalani and Mahadev Desai were associates. It was here that he was first called 'Mahatma' (by some accounts, by Tagore).

Dandi March and breach of the Salt Law (12 March to 6 April 1930): Gandhi marched from Sabarmati Ashram with 78 followers to Dandi, Gujarat, and picked up salt, launching the Civil Disobedience Movement. It protested the Salt Tax and the 1882 Salt Act. Gandhi had sent the 'Eleven Demands' to Viceroy Irwin. The movement spread to Vedaranyam (Rajagopalachari), Dharasana (Sarojini Naidu) and the North-West Frontier (Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan).

Second Round Table Conference (7 Sept to 1 Dec 1931, London): Gandhi attended as the sole Congress representative after the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931). He claimed the Congress represented all of India and opposed separate electorates for minorities and the Depressed Classes. The conference failed over communal representation, and civil disobedience resumed in January 1932. The Communal Award followed in August 1932.

Quit India Movement (launched 8 August 1942, Bombay): the Congress passed the resolution at Gowalia Tank (August Kranti Maidan) after the failure of the Cripps Mission. Gandhi gave the 'Do or Die' call. Leaders were arrested on 9 August, and Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the flag. Parallel governments arose in Ballia, Tamluk and Satara. The movement was crushed by 1944.
related: Dandi March: 12 March to 6 April 1930, from Sabarmati to Dandi, with 78 marchers.
Gandhi was tried for sedition in 1922 (Section 124A IPC) for Young India articles and sentenced to six years.
Kedar Nath Singh v State of Bihar (1962) upheld Section 124A but limited it to incitement to violence.
The Supreme Court put Section 124A in abeyance in May 2022 (S.G. Vombatkere case).
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 replaced the IPC; Section 152 deals with acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity.
The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931) led to Gandhi's attendance at the Second Round Table Conference.
Champaran Satyagraha (1917) was Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, against indigo planters.
The Quit India call 'Do or Die' was given on 8 August 1942 at Gowalia Tank, Bombay.
summary: The answer is (b): Gandhi's remark 'Sedition has become my religion' belongs to the Civil Disobedience phase of 1930, when he publicly broke the Salt Law at Dandi. By then, defying the colonial state's laws, including the sedition provisions, was an openly declared duty.
topic_notes: Gandhi's phases of mass struggle should be read together. In 1917-18 he led the local satyagrahas at Champaran, Kheda and the Ahmedabad mill strike. The Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919) and Jallianwala Bagh (13 April 1919) came next. The Non-Cooperation and Khilafat Movement ran from 1920 to 1922 and was withdrawn after Chauri Chaura (February 1922). In 1922 Gandhi was tried for sedition under Section 124A IPC for his Young India articles and was sentenced to six years. In court he called sedition a 'prince among the political sections of the IPC' meant to suppress liberty, and he invited the maximum penalty. The Lahore Congress of December 1929 declared Purna Swaraj, and 26 January 1930 was observed as Independence Day. The Civil Disobedience Movement began with the Dandi March (12 March to 6 April 1930). The Gandhi-Irwin Pact followed on 5 March 1931. Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in 1931. The Poona Pact (24 September 1932) settled reserved seats for the Depressed Classes after Gandhi's fast against separate electorates in the Communal Award. The Individual Satyagraha ran in 1940-41, the Cripps Mission came in 1942, and Quit India began on 8 August 1942. In independent India, Section 124A was put in abeyance by the Supreme Court in S.G. Vombatkere v Union of India (May 2022). The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 replaced the IPC and has no section titled sedition, but Section 152 penalises acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India. Kedar Nath Singh (1962) confined sedition to acts involving incitement to violence or public disorder. UPSC often tests sequence, venue, slogans and associated persons in these events.

question: Subsequent to which one of the following events, Gandhiji, who consistently opposed untouchability and appealed for its eradication from all spheres, decided to include the upliftment of ‘Harijans’ in his political and social programme?
options: Arrest of Congress leadership at the time of the Quit India Movement
Promulgation of the Government of India Act, 1935
subject: Modern History
detail: Gandhi opposed untouchability from his South Africa days and in the Congress constructive programme from 1920. But the Communal Award of 16 August 1932, announced by Ramsay MacDonald, gave separate electorates to the Depressed Classes. Gandhi saw this as a threat to Hindu unity and began a fast unto death on 20 September 1932 in Yeravada Jail. Talks among Madan Mohan Malaviya, B.R. Ambedkar, Rajendra Prasad and others produced the Poona Pact on 24 September 1932. It gave up separate electorates, kept joint electorates with reserved seats (148 in provincial legislatures, up from 71 in the Award, and 18% of central seats), and provided for education grants and public service representation. Gandhi then took up Harijan work as a mission. The All India Anti-Untouchability League was set up in September 1932 and renamed Harijan Sevak Sangh in December 1932, with G.D. Birla as president. He launched the weekly Harijan on 11 February 1933 and made the Harijan tour from November 1933 to July 1934. Elimination logic: the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931) dealt with civil disobedience, prisoners and salt. The Quit India arrests (1942) came much later. The 1935 Act came after the Harijan campaign had started, and it only provided for Scheduled Castes.
explanations: Correct: the Poona Pact of September 1932 ended Gandhi's fast over separate electorates, and he then made Harijan upliftment a major part of his political and social programme, setting up the Harijan Sevak Sangh and the journal Harijan.

Incorrect: the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931 was about suspending civil disobedience, releasing prisoners and participation in the Round Table Conference. It was unconnected with the start of the Harijan campaign.
Incorrect: the Quit India arrests of August 1942 came about ten years after the Harijan campaign began in 1932-33. Gandhi was by then already deeply involved in Harijan work.

Incorrect: the Government of India Act 1935 came after the Poona Pact and the Harijan campaign. It introduced the term Scheduled Castes in a Schedule and continued reserved seats, but it did not trigger Gandhi's Harijan work.
keyfact: Poona Pact (24 Sept 1932) ended Gandhi's fast; he then launched Harijan work (Harijan Sevak Sangh, weekly Harijan).
option_notes: The Poona Pact was signed on 24 September 1932 at Yeravada Jail, Poona, between Ambedkar, representing the Depressed Classes, and Hindu leaders including Malaviya, with Gandhi's assent. It replaced separate electorates with reserved seats in joint electorates, giving 148 seats in provincial legislatures, 18% of central seats, a primary election panel system, and education and public service provisions. The British government accepted it as an amendment to the Communal Award.

The Gandhi-Irwin Pact, or Delhi Pact, was signed on 5 March 1931 between Gandhi and Viceroy Lord Irwin. Congress suspended civil disobedience and agreed to attend the Second Round Table Conference. The government released non-violent political prisoners, allowed salt making for personal use in coastal areas, and permitted peaceful picketing. Radicals such as Bhagat Singh's supporters criticised it because the executions were not commuted. The Karachi session (March 1931) endorsed it.

The Quit India Movement began on 8 August 1942 with the 'Do or Die' call at Gowalia Tank, Bombay. The next morning (9 August) the entire top Congress leadership was arrested, including Gandhi, who was held at the Aga Khan Palace, and the Congress was banned. Leaders like Aruna Asaf Ali, Jayaprakash Narayan and Ram Manohar Lohia led an underground resistance. Parallel governments emerged at Ballia, Tamluk and Satara.

The Government of India Act 1935 provided for an All-India Federation (never implemented), provincial autonomy, abolition of dyarchy in the provinces and introduction of dyarchy at the Centre. It created the Federal Court (1937), the Reserve Bank, and separated Burma and Aden. It expanded the electorate to about 10% of the population and continued separate electorates. Elections held under it in 1937 gave the Congress ministries in 8 of 11 provinces.
related: Communal Award: announced 16 August 1932 by Ramsay MacDonald.
Poona Pact signed 24 September 1932; Ambedkar and Malaviya were key signatories.
Harijan Sevak Sangh was founded in 1932, with G.D. Birla as first president.
Gandhi started the weekly 'Harijan' on 11 February 1933.
Article 17 of the Constitution abolishes untouchability.
Vaikom Satyagraha (1924-25) was for temple road access in Travancore.
Ambedkar led the Mahad Satyagraha in 1927 for access to the Chavdar tank.
Temple Entry Proclamation of Travancore was issued in 1936.
summary: The answer is (a) The Poona Pact. After the Communal Award (August 1932) gave separate electorates to the Depressed Classes, Gandhi fasted in Yeravada Jail. The Poona Pact (24 September 1932) settled the matter, and Gandhi then made Harijan upliftment a core part of his programme, founding the All India Anti-Untouchability League (later Harijan Sevak Sangh) and the weekly Harijan.
topic_notes: Gandhi's engagement with untouchability: he campaigned against it in South Africa and made its removal a pillar of the Congress constructive programme from the 1920s, along with Hindu-Muslim unity and khadi. He called Dalits 'Harijans' (children of God), a term many Dalit leaders, including Ambedkar, disliked. The Vaikom Satyagraha (1924-25) in Travancore was a major temple-entry agitation that Gandhi supported but advised to remain non-violent. The Communal Award (16 August 1932) extended separate electorates to the Depressed Classes. Gandhi fasted from 20 September 1932, and the Poona Pact followed on 24 September. The Harijan Sevak Sangh was founded in 1932, and the weekly Harijan (English), along with Harijan Bandhu (Gujarati) and Harijan Sevak (Hindi), began in 1933. Gandhi toured India for Harijan funds from November 1933 to July 1934. Ambedkar's counterpoints: the Mahad Satyagraha (1927) for water rights, the Kalaram Temple entry at Nasik (1930), the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924), the Independent Labour Party (1936), the Scheduled Castes Federation (1942), and conversion to Buddhism (1956). Constitutional follow-up: Article 17 abolished untouchability, the Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955 was renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976, and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989 is also relevant. Other angles UPSC may test: the Round Table Conferences, the Temple Entry Proclamation of Travancore (1936), Jotiba Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj, Periyar's Self-Respect Movement, and M.C. Rajah's role in the Rajah-Moonje Pact.

question:
Consider the following fruits :
I. Papaya Il. Pineapple Ill. Guava How many of the above were introduced in India by the Portuguese in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Columbian Exchange moved crops between the Americas and the Old World after 1492. The Portuguese, who held Goa from 1510, Cochin, Daman, Diu and Bassein, carried many American plants to India. Papaya, pineapple and guava are native to tropical America (Central and South America, the Caribbean). Pineapple is usually dated to the mid-16th century, and Goa and the Konkan coast became early centres of its cultivation. Papaya and guava spread from the western coast across the subcontinent. Other Portuguese-linked introductions include cashew, potato, tomato, maize, chilli, tobacco, groundnut, custard apple, sweet potato, cassava and the Alphonso mango (a grafted variety developed from Indian mangoes, named after Afonso de Albuquerque). Elimination logic: all three fruits are American in origin, so none could be native to India or have come from pre-Columbian trade. Anyone who knows that even one of them came via the Portuguese should reject (d). Anyone who recognises that all three belong to the same American-origin group should choose (c) over (a) or (b). A common trap is to treat guava as indigenous because it is so widespread in India.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it counts only one fruit, when papaya, pineapple and guava were all introduced by the Portuguese.
(b) is wrong because it leaves out one of the three, but all three came through the Portuguese.
(c) is correct: all three are American fruits that reached India via the Portuguese in the 16th–17th centuries, which matches the official answer.
(d) is wrong because it claims none were introduced by the Portuguese, yet all three were.
keyfact: Papaya, pineapple and guava are New World fruits brought to India by the Portuguese in the 16th–17th centuries.
option_notes: Only one: this would be right if just one of the three fruits were a Portuguese introduction. It is not, so the option is a distractor. Students are tempted by it because guava looks indigenous, or because pineapple is associated with the North-East and papaya with the tropics generally. Tropical America is the shared origin of all three, and the Portuguese were the main carriers to India.

Only two: this option would hold if one fruit were native to India or arrived by another route, such as the Arab or Central Asian trade that brought many Old World fruits. That is not the case here. Native or older Indian fruits include mango, jackfruit, jamun, banana (an old introduction from Southeast Asia) and citrus. None of the three fruits listed belongs to that group.

All the three: this is the official answer. Papaya, pineapple and guava are all New World fruits spread by the Portuguese from Goa and other coastal settlements after 1498. They belong to the Columbian Exchange, which also brought chilli, potato, tomato, maize, cashew, tobacco and custard apple to India. Portuguese influence on Indian agriculture was strongest on the western coast.

None: this would apply only if all three fruits were native or arrived before the Portuguese. It is the opposite of the facts, since all three are American in origin and absent from India before 1498. The option may attract students who think these common fruits are ancient Indian crops. Fruits with ancient Indian roots include mango, jamun, jackfruit, banana and wood apple.
related: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498.
Portuguese captured Goa in 1510 under Afonso de Albuquerque.
Goa was liberated from Portuguese rule in 1961.
Cashew, potato, tomato, chilli and maize are other American crops brought to India.
Garcia de Orta wrote Colloquies on the Simples and Drugs of India (1563).
The first printing press in India was set up in Goa in 1556.
Papaya contains papain; pineapple contains bromelain.
Alphonso mango is named after Afonso de Albuquerque.
statements: I — Correct: Papaya is native to tropical America and was brought to India by the Portuguese in the 16th century. Papaya (Carica papaya) comes from southern Mexico and Central America. The Spanish took it to the Philippines and the Portuguese to Goa and Malabar. It then spread across India, which is now one of the world's largest producers. It is rich in the enzyme papain, used as a meat tenderiser and in medicine. It is also a short-lived, fast-growing herbaceous tree.

II — Correct: Pineapple is native to South America (Brazil and Paraguay) and was introduced by the Portuguese in the 16th century. Pineapple (Ananas comosus) was carried to Europe and then to Asia and Africa. In India it became established in Goa, Kerala and the Konkan coast, and it is now grown widely in the North-East, with Assam, Tripura, Meghalaya and West Bengal as key producers. It is a bromeliad and contains the enzyme bromelain. Mizoram and Tripura's Queen variety are notable.

III — Correct: Guava is native to tropical America (Mexico to northern South America) and was introduced by the Portuguese in the 16th–17th centuries. Guava (Psidium guajava) spread quickly through India and became naturalised. Allahabad (Prayagraj) is famous for its guavas, and Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar are major producers. It is rich in vitamin C, more so than citrus fruits, and is hardy, which makes it a popular fruit across the country.
summary: The answer is (c) All the three. Papaya, pineapple and guava are all New World fruits that reached India through the Portuguese, who arrived after Vasco da Gama's landing at Calicut in 1498 and based themselves at Goa, in the 16th and 17th centuries.
topic_notes: The topic is the Columbian Exchange and the Portuguese impact on India. Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498. Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa in 1510, and it remained Portuguese until 1961. The Portuguese set up a chain of trading posts including Cochin, Daman, Diu, Bassein and Hooghly, and Goa became the centre for introducing and spreading new crops. Cashew (from Brazil) was introduced to Goa in the 16th century, partly to prevent soil erosion. Chilli replaced black pepper as the main pungent spice in many dishes. Potato, tomato, maize, sweet potato, cassava, groundnut, custard apple, papaya, pineapple, guava, sapota, tobacco and the green pepper (capsicum) also came from the Americas. Garcia de Orta's work on Indian medicinal plants (Colloquies, 1563) was published in Goa. The Portuguese also introduced the printing press to India (Goa, 1556), Gothic architecture and the grafting of mangoes. Many Indian crops, however, are native or came from elsewhere: rice, mango, banana, jackfruit, brinjal, cucumber, sugarcane, and citrus from Southeast Asia and the Himalayan foothills. Wheat and barley came from West Asia. UPSC often tests origin by region, so keep three groups in mind: native Indian, Old World introductions (Central Asian, Arab, Southeast Asian) and New World introductions (Portuguese, Spanish, British). The British later introduced tea cultivation on a commercial scale (Assam), coffee estates and cinchona, and the Portuguese also gave Konkani cuisine its vindaloo and similar dishes.

question:
Consider the following countries :
I. United Kingdom Il. Denmark Ill. New Zealand
IV. Australia Vv. Brazil How many of the above countries have more than four time zones?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The question tests whether you know that a country's time zones include those of its overseas territories, not just its mainland. France has the most time zones in the world (12-13 with Antarctica), followed by the US and the UK (about 9). The UK has the Pitcairn Islands (UTC-8), the Falklands (-3), South Georgia (-2), Bermuda and the Caribbean territories (-4), the British Isles (0/+1), Ascension, St Helena and Tristan da Cunha (0), and the British Indian Ocean Territory (+6), so well over four. Denmark spans the Faroes (UTC+0), mainland Denmark (+1) and Greenland (roughly -4 to 0), which gives about five. New Zealand covers the Cook Islands (-10), Niue (-11), NZ mainland (+12), the Chatham Islands (+12:45) and Tokelau (+13). Australia has three mainland zones (AWST +8, ACST +9:30, AEST +10), plus Lord Howe (+10:30), Norfolk Island (+11), Christmas Island (+7) and the Cocos Islands (+6:30). Brazil has exactly four (Fernando de Noronha -2, Brasília -3, Amazon -4, Acre -5), and four is not 'more than four'. So four countries qualify, which is option (b). Elimination: if you know Brazil has four, (a) is out. If you know that Denmark, via Greenland, and New Zealand, via its Pacific dependencies, have many zones, (c) and (d) are out.
explanations: (a) is wrong because Brazil has exactly four time zones, not more than four, so not all five countries qualify.
(b) is correct. The UK, Denmark, New Zealand and Australia each have five or more zones once their territories are counted, and Brazil has only four.
(c) is wrong because it undercounts. Four countries, not three, exceed four zones. Denmark (through Greenland and the Faroes) and New Zealand (through Pacific dependencies) are often wrongly dropped.
(d) is wrong because it undercounts badly. Only a student who ignores overseas territories would conclude that two countries qualify.
keyfact: The UK, Denmark, New Zealand and Australia each have more than four time zones counting their territories, while Brazil has exactly four.
option_notes: (a) All five: this would require Brazil to have five or more zones, but it has four (UTC-2 to -5). The world's countries with the most zones are France (12-13), the US (11 with territories), Russia (11) and the UK (9). Brazil's zone count is a common trap because of its size, since it is the fifth largest country, but its east-west extent is limited.

(b) Only four: the UK, Denmark, New Zealand and Australia each have more than four zones. This is the official answer. These are all countries with far-flung overseas territories or dependencies. Counting rules matter: UPSC and most sources include overseas territories, so mainland-only counting gives a wrong answer. Four-zone countries include Brazil, and Canada, which has six, is a related case.

(c) Only three: this would apply if you excluded Denmark or New Zealand, for example by counting only the mainland or main territory. Mainland Denmark has one zone and mainland New Zealand has one (plus the Chatham Islands). A count of three does not match any standard list, which makes it a plausible distractor but a factually wrong one.

(d) Only two: this would apply if only the UK and Australia were counted. Australia has three mainland zones, and both countries are known for many zones. Denmark and New Zealand are the less obvious ones, and the question is built to test them. Counting overseas dependencies shows that two is too low.
related: France has the most time zones in the world (about 12-13), followed by the US and the UK.
India uses a single time zone, IST (UTC+5:30), based on the 82°30'E meridian near Mirzapur.
China spans five geographical zones but officially uses only Beijing Time (UTC+8).
Brazil has four time zones, from UTC-2 (Fernando de Noronha) to UTC-5 (Acre).
Greenland is the largest island in the world and an autonomous territory of Denmark.
Kiritimati (Kiribati) is at UTC+14, the earliest time zone in the world.
Nepal uses UTC+5:45 and the Chatham Islands (NZ) UTC+12:45, both quarter-hour offsets.
Russia has 11 time zones on its mainland, the most for any country by this measure.
statements: I — United Kingdom — Correct: with its overseas territories it has about 9 time zones, from UTC-8 to UTC+6. The UK itself uses GMT (UTC+0) in winter and BST (+1) in summer. Pitcairn Islands are at -8, the Falklands at -3, South Georgia at -2, Bermuda, Anguilla, Montserrat and the BVI at -4, the Cayman Islands at -5, Ascension, St Helena and Tristan da Cunha at 0, and the British Indian Ocean Territory (Diego Garcia) at +6. The Greenwich Meridian passes through the UK, and GMT is its historical reference time.

II — Denmark — Correct: the Kingdom of Denmark includes mainland Denmark (UTC+1, CET), the Faroe Islands (UTC+0, WET) and Greenland, which spans roughly UTC-4 to UTC+0. Greenland is the world's largest island and a self-governing territory of the Danish Realm. Most of it uses -3 (West Greenland time), Danmarkshavn is at 0, Ittoqqortoormiit is at -1, and Thule/Pituffik is at -4. Together this gives about five zones, so more than four.

III — New Zealand — Correct: it has about five zones. Niue is at UTC-11 and the Cook Islands at -10, both in free association with NZ. Mainland NZ is at +12 (NZST) with daylight saving at +13, the Chatham Islands at +12:45 and Tokelau at +13. NZ is among the first countries to see each new day. The Ross Dependency in Antarctica also uses NZ time. NZ is a Commonwealth member and part of the Five Eyes.

IV — Australia — Correct: it has more than four zones when its external territories are counted. The mainland has AWST (+8), ACST (+9:30) and AEST (+10), with daylight saving in some states. Lord Howe Island is at +10:30, Norfolk Island at +11, Christmas Island at +7, and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands at +6:30. Eucla in Western Australia unofficially uses +8:45. The Australian Antarctic Territory has bases on other times, which adds further zones. Queensland does not observe daylight saving.

V — Brazil — Incorrect: it has exactly four zones, the largest of which is Brasília Time (UTC-3) covering the capital, the southeast and the coast. Fernando de Noronha and the Atlantic islands (including Trindade and Martim Vaz) are at -2, the Amazon Time zone (Amazonas, Mato Grosso, Rondônia, Roraima) is at -4, and Acre and southwestern Amazonas are at -5. Brazil abolished daylight saving in 2019. Four is not more than four, so it is excluded.
summary: The answer is (b): only four countries have more than four time zones. The UK, Denmark, New Zealand and Australia do, once their overseas territories and dependencies are counted. Brazil has exactly four (UTC-2, -3, -4, -5), so it does not qualify.
topic_notes: Time zones: the Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours, so each hour corresponds to 15° of longitude, giving 24 standard zones. The Prime Meridian (0°) passes through Greenwich, and GMT/UTC is the reference. The International Date Line (about 180°) is a zigzag line in the Pacific. India uses a single zone, IST (UTC+5:30), based on 82°30'E longitude passing near Mirzapur (Prayagraj/Naini), and is 5h30m ahead of GMT. Countries with the most time zones: France about 12-13 (with overseas territories and Antarctica), the US 11 (including territories), Russia 11 on the mainland, and the UK 9. China spans five geographical zones but officially uses only one (Beijing Time, UTC+8). Mainland zone counts: Russia 11, Canada 6 (Newfoundland at -3:30), the US mainland 4 (Eastern, Central, Mountain, Pacific), Australia 3, Brazil 4 (including islands), Indonesia 3. Daylight saving time moves clocks forward by an hour in summer to use daylight better, and India does not use it. Nepal is at UTC+5:45, and Chatham Islands at +12:45, Lord Howe at +10:30 and Newfoundland at -3:30 are odd offsets. UPSC could next ask which countries use half-hour or quarter-hour offsets, which country has the most zones, why China has one zone, the longitude of the IST meridian, and the Date Line and its deviations (Kiribati, Samoa). Samoa skipped 30 Dec 2011 by moving to the west of the Date Line. Kiribati straddles the line, and Kiritimati (Christmas Island, UTC+14) is the earliest time zone in the world.
