question: Who among the following was the founder of the ‘Self-Respect Movement’?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Self-Respect Movement was launched by E. V. Ramasamy 'Periyar' (1879-1973) in 1925 in the Madras Presidency, after he left the Indian National Congress. He resigned in 1925, disillusioned by the Congress's reluctance to support reservation for non-Brahmins, and by the Cheranmadevi gurukulam controversy, in which Brahmin and non-Brahmin students were given separate dining. His journal Kudi Arasu (1925) became the movement's main voice, followed by Revolt (English) and Pagutharivu. The movement stressed rationalism, atheism, rejection of priestly authority, abolition of caste and untouchability, women's rights, widow remarriage, birth control, and Self-Respect (suyamariyadai) marriages without Brahmin priests. Periyar had earlier led the Vaikom Satyagraha (1924-25) in Kerala, earning the title 'Vaikom Hero'. He later headed the Justice Party (1938), which he transformed into Dravidar Kazhagam (1944). Elimination: Ambedkar led the Mahad Satyagraha, Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha and the Depressed Classes movement, not this one. Bhaskarrao Jadhav and Dinkarrao Javalkar were Maharashtra's Satyashodhak/non-Brahmin movement leaders, which descended from Jyotiba Phule, so they are linked to a different movement.
explanations: Correct: Periyar E. V. Ramasamy founded the Self-Respect Movement in 1925 in Tamil Nadu.

Wrong: Ambedkar led Dalit movements such as the Mahad Satyagraha (1927), the Kalaram Temple entry movement (1930), the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924) and the Independent Labour Party. He did not found the Self-Respect Movement.
Wrong: Bhaskarrao Jadhav was a Maharashtra non-Brahmin leader associated with the Satyashodhak Samaj and the Non-Brahmin Party, not with the Self-Respect Movement.
Wrong: Dinkarrao Javalkar was a Maharashtra Satyashodhak leader who was prominent in the non-Brahmin movement, and was not associated with the Self-Respect Movement.
keyfact: Self-Respect Movement = Periyar E. V. Ramasamy, 1925, Tamil Nadu; journal Kudi Arasu.
option_notes: Periyar E. V. Ramasamy Naicker (1879-1973), born in Erode, was a social reformer and rationalist. He led the Vaikom Satyagraha, left Congress in 1925, founded the Self-Respect Movement, led the Justice Party from 1938, and founded Dravidar Kazhagam in 1944. He published Kudi Arasu and Viduthalai. He is called 'Father of the Dravidian Movement'. He opposed Hindi imposition and promoted women's rights and inter-caste marriage.

Dr. B. R. Ambedkar (1891-1956) was the chief architect of the Constitution and chair of the Drafting Committee. He founded the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924), led the Mahad Satyagraha (1927), the Kalaram temple entry (1930), the Independent Labour Party (1936), the Scheduled Castes Federation (1942) and the People's Education Society (1945). He signed the Poona Pact (1932) and embraced Buddhism in 1956. He edited Mooknayak and Bahishkrit Bharat.

Bhaskarrao Jadhav (1867-1953) was a Maratha non-Brahmin leader in Maharashtra and a member of the Satyashodhak movement. He was associated with the Non-Brahmin Party and the Bombay Legislative Council, and served as a minister in the Bombay Presidency. He worked closely with Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur and promoted education and political representation for non-Brahmins.

Dinkarrao Javalkar (1898-1975) was a Satyashodhak leader and writer in Maharashtra who belonged to the non-Brahmin movement. He was active in the Satyashodhak Samaj tradition begun by Jyotiba Phule in 1873, and wrote works criticising Brahminical dominance. He was an associate of Keshavrao Jedhe and a follower of Phule's ideas, and is frequently associated with the 'Jedhe-Javalkar' non-Brahmin political group.
related: Self-Respect Movement was founded in 1925 by Periyar.
Periyar's journal Kudi Arasu was launched in 1925.
Periyar led the Vaikom Satyagraha (1924-25) in Travancore.
Justice Party was founded in 1916 by T. M. Nair and P. Theagaraya Chetty.
Dravidar Kazhagam was formed in 1944 at Salem.
C. N. Annadurai founded the DMK in 1949.
Satyashodhak Samaj was founded by Jyotiba Phule in 1873.
SNDP Yogam was founded by Sree Narayana Guru in 1903.
summary: The answer is (a) Periyar E. V. Ramaswamy Naicker. He founded the Self-Respect Movement in Tamil Nadu in 1925 to fight Brahminical dominance, caste hierarchy and religious orthodoxy, and to promote rationalism, equality and dignity for non-Brahmins and women.
topic_notes: The Self-Respect Movement began in 1925 as a Tamil-speaking region's radical anti-caste and rationalist movement. Periyar broke with the Congress over the Cheranmadevi gurukulam issue and the party's reluctance to endorse communal reservation for non-Brahmins. Key aspects included: rejection of Brahmin priests in marriages; legalisation of Self-Respect marriages by the Madras state in 1967 under C. N. Annadurai through an amendment to the Hindu Marriage Act; support for women's equality, widow remarriage, contraceptive use, and opposition to the devadasi system; criticism of Hindu scriptures and the Manusmriti; and opposition to compulsory Hindi in schools (1937-38) under C. Rajagopalachari's government. Conferences included the Chengalpattu Self-Respect Conference (1929), which endorsed gender equality and the abolition of caste suffixes. In 1944 the Justice Party was renamed Dravidar Kazhagam at the Salem conference. In 1949 C. N. Annadurai split to form the DMK. Related non-Brahmin movements: Justice Party (South Indian Liberal Federation, 1916, by T. M. Nair, P. Theagaraya Chetty and C. Natesa Mudaliar), the Satyashodhak Samaj (Phule, 1873), the Nadar and Ezhava movements (Sree Narayana Guru, SNDP 1903; 'One caste, one religion, one god'), Mahar movements in Maharashtra, Vokkaliga and Lingayat movements in Mysore, and the Adi-Dravida and Adi-Andhra organisations. Shahu Maharaj introduced 50% reservation for backward classes in Kolhapur in 1902. UPSC often asks to match leaders to movements and journals.

question: Consider the following pairs : Country Resource-rich in Va Botswana : Diamond Il. Chile : Lithium Ill. Indonesia : Nickel In how many of the above rows is the given information correctly matched?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The question tests basic world resource geography, which UPSC increasingly links to critical minerals and the energy transition. Botswana's economy has long depended on diamonds, mined mainly at Jwaneng and Orapa and marketed through the Debswana partnership with De Beers. Chile holds the largest lithium reserves in the world (USGS estimates about 9-11 million tonnes), concentrated in the Salar de Atacama brines, and ranks among the top two producers alongside Australia. Indonesia has the largest nickel reserves (around 40-50 percent of the world total) and is the largest producer. It banned raw nickel ore exports in 2020 to promote domestic smelting and battery supply chains, and WTO disputes followed. Elimination logic: once you are confident of any two pairs, options (a) and (b) fail. Since no pair is wrong, (d) also fails. Only (c) remains. When a question has three well-known pairs, check for traps such as swapped countries, but none appear here. Note that the 'Lithium Triangle' is Chile, Argentina and Bolivia.
explanations: Incorrect: this assumes only one pair is right, but all three pairs are factually correct.
Incorrect: this assumes one pair is wrong. Botswana-diamond, Chile-lithium and Indonesia-nickel are all valid.
Correct: all three pairs are accurate, matching the official answer.
Incorrect: it would require every pair to be wrong, which is clearly false for these well-known associations.
keyfact: Botswana = diamonds, Chile = lithium (largest reserves), Indonesia = nickel (largest producer and reserves).
option_notes: Only one: would mean two pairs were wrong. It is a typical distractor in match-the-pairs questions where the aspirant is sure of just one pair. Here it fails because all three pairs reflect widely documented facts about world mineral production and reserves, as reported by USGS and the Kimberley Process.

Only two: would mean one pair was wrong. UPSC often plants one swapped pair, such as pairing Chile with cobalt or Indonesia with bauxite. Here no swap exists. Chile is known for lithium and copper, the DR Congo for cobalt, and Guinea and Australia for bauxite.

All the three: the correct option. It reflects Botswana's diamond dependence, Chile's lithium dominance and Indonesia's nickel leadership. All three resources are linked to the global economy: diamonds to gems and jewellery, lithium and nickel to the energy transition and EV battery supply chains.

None: would mean all three pairs were wrong. It is an extreme option and rarely correct when the pairs are standard knowledge. All three associations appear regularly in news on critical minerals and trade policy.
related: Chile has the world's largest lithium reserves; Australia is the largest lithium producer.
Indonesia banned raw nickel ore exports in 2020.
Botswana's Debswana is a 50:50 venture of the government and De Beers.
DR Congo supplies over 70 percent of the world's cobalt.
KABIL is India's joint venture for acquiring overseas critical mineral assets.
India's National Critical Mineral Mission was approved in January 2025.
The Kimberley Process Certification Scheme began in 2003 to stop conflict diamonds.
The Lithium Triangle consists of Chile, Argentina and Bolivia.
statements: I — Correct: Botswana is a major diamond producer. Diamonds make up most of its exports. Debswana, a 50:50 venture between the government and De Beers, runs the mines at Jwaneng, Orapa, Letlhakane and Damtshaa. The Lucara-run Karowe mine has yielded very large stones, including the 1,758-carat Sewelô found in 2019. Botswana is usually among the top two or three producers by value and the largest in Africa by value. The Kimberley Process certifies rough diamonds to curb conflict diamonds. The Okavango Delta is a Ramsar site and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Botswana, but it is unrelated to diamonds.

II — Correct: Chile has the world's largest lithium reserves and is the second-largest producer after Australia. Lithium is extracted from brines in the Salar de Atacama, mainly by SQM and Albemarle. It is part of the South American 'Lithium Triangle' with Argentina and Bolivia. Chile is also the world's top copper producer. Its 2023 National Lithium Strategy gave the state a bigger role through a Codelco partnership. Lithium is vital for EV and storage batteries. India's KABIL, a joint venture of NALCO, HCL and MECL, seeks overseas lithium assets in Argentina, Chile and Australia. India's first lithium inferred resource was found at Reasi, J&K, in 2023.

III — Correct: Indonesia is the world's largest nickel producer and holds the largest reserves, with major mining at Sulawesi and Halmahera (Weda Bay). Nickel is used in stainless steel and in EV battery cathodes (NMC). Indonesia banned raw nickel ore exports in January 2020 to force downstream processing, and the EU challenged this at the WTO. Chinese investment dominates its smelters, for example at Morowali. Other major nickel producers are the Philippines, Russia, New Caledonia, Canada and Australia. Indonesia also leads in tin exports and is a major coal and palm oil exporter.
summary: The answer is (c) All the three. Botswana is a leading diamond producer, Chile holds the world's largest lithium reserves, and Indonesia is the world's largest nickel producer and reserve holder, so all three pairs are correctly matched.
topic_notes: Critical minerals are a growing UPSC theme. Lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths are central to batteries, renewables and electronics. Key producers and reserve holders: lithium comes from Chile (largest reserves), Australia (largest producer, hard-rock spodumene), Argentina, Bolivia and China. Cobalt is dominated by the DR Congo, with over 70 percent of output. Nickel comes from Indonesia, the Philippines and Russia. Rare earths come mainly from China, which dominates processing. Platinum comes from South Africa. Diamonds come from Russia (ALROSA), Botswana, Canada, Angola and the DR Congo. Copper comes from Chile and Peru. Uranium comes from Kazakhstan, Canada and Namibia. Related institutions and schemes: India's National Critical Mineral Mission was approved in January 2025. KABIL (Khanij Bidesh India Ltd) acquires overseas assets. The Minerals Security Partnership is a US-led group that India joined in 2023. The MMDR Amendment Act 2023 added lithium, beryllium, niobium and others to the list of critical minerals, and India's 2023 critical minerals list names 30 minerals. Other angles: Kimberley Process (2003) for conflict diamonds, the Lithium Triangle, export bans by Indonesia, and the Reasi lithium find in J&K. Also remember that India imports most of its lithium, cobalt and nickel. Expect future questions that pair countries with minerals, or ask which minerals are classified as critical.

question: Consider the following pairs : Region Country i Mallorca 2 Italy Il. Normandy: Spain Il. Sardinia r France In how many of the above rows is the given information correctly matched?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This question tests basic European political geography, which UPSC often asks through current-affairs hooks such as tourism, wars, or climate events. Mallorca (Majorca) is the largest of Spain's Balearic Islands in the western Mediterranean, with Palma as its capital. Normandy is a historic region of northern France on the English Channel. It is known for the Norman Conquest of England in 1066 under William the Conqueror and for the D-Day landings of 6 June 1944, at Omaha, Utah, Gold, Juno and Sword beaches. Sardinia is the second-largest Mediterranean island after Sicily and is an autonomous region of Italy, with Cagliari as its capital. The question assigns each region to a wrong country: Mallorca to Italy, Normandy to Spain, and Sardinia to France. Elimination logic: once you know that even one pair is wrong, options (b) and (c) fall away if you are sure of two pairs. Here all three are wrong, so (d) is the only option that fits. Note that Corsica, not Sardinia, is the French Mediterranean island, just north of Sardinia, separated by the Strait of Bonifacio. This is a common trap.
explanations: (a) Only one is wrong because no pair is correct. Mallorca is Spanish, Normandy is French and Sardinia is Italian, so none of the three matches.
(b) Only two is wrong because not even two pairs are correctly matched. All three pairs assign the region to the wrong country.
(c) All the three is wrong. Every pair swaps the country: Mallorca-Italy, Normandy-Spain and Sardinia-France are all incorrect.
(d) None is correct. Mallorca is in Spain, Normandy in France and Sardinia in Italy, so no row is correctly matched.
keyfact: Mallorca is Spanish, Normandy is French and Sardinia is Italian, so none of the three pairs in the paper is correct.
option_notes: Only one: this would require exactly one correct pair. It is a typical distractor in matching questions. Here it would only work if, for example, Sardinia had been paired with Italy, but the paper pairs it with France.

Only two: this would require two correct pairs. In UPSC 'how many pairs' questions the answer is often a middle value, so students who are unsure tend to guess it. It is wrong here because every pair is mismatched.

All the three: this would require every pair to be correct. It would hold if Mallorca-Spain, Normandy-France and Sardinia-Italy had been given. The paper swapped the countries to make all three wrong.

None: this means zero correct pairs. It is the official answer. Mallorca belongs to Spain, Normandy to France and Sardinia to Italy, while the paper pairs them with Italy, Spain and France respectively.
related: Corsica is French, and Sardinia is Italian; the Strait of Bonifacio separates them.
The Balearic Islands (Mallorca, Menorca, Ibiza, Formentera) are an autonomous community of Spain.
Sicily is the largest Mediterranean island and is part of Italy.
D-Day, 6 June 1944, took place on the Normandy coast in France.
Catalonia, with Barcelona as its capital, is an autonomous community of Spain with a separatist movement.
The Aland Islands are an autonomous demilitarised region of Finland.
Greenland is an autonomous territory of Denmark.
Cyprus is the third-largest Mediterranean island and has been divided since 1974.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Mallorca is in Spain, not Italy. Mallorca is the largest island of the Balearic archipelago, an autonomous community of Spain in the western Mediterranean. The other main islands are Menorca, Ibiza and Formentera. The capital is Palma de Mallorca. The island is a major tourist destination, and its Serra de Tramuntana is a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape. Catalan and Spanish are the official languages. Overtourism protests have occurred there in recent years.

2 — Incorrect: Normandy is in France, not Spain. It is a region in northwestern France bordering the English Channel, with Rouen as its capital. Its name comes from the Norse (Viking) settlers, the 'Northmen', who were granted land under the 911 Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte. Key sites include Mont-Saint-Michel, the Bayeux Tapestry and the D-Day beaches of 1944. Its products include Camembert cheese, cider and Calvados.

3 — Incorrect: Sardinia is in Italy, not France. It is the second-largest island in the Mediterranean after Sicily and an autonomous region of Italy with special statute. Its capital is Cagliari. It lies south of Corsica (France), across the Strait of Bonifacio. It is known for the Nuragic civilisation, whose stone towers (nuraghi) date to the Bronze Age, and for its Sardinian language. Its economy depends on tourism, pastoralism and mining.
summary: The answer is (d) None. All three pairs are mismatched: Mallorca belongs to Spain (not Italy), Normandy belongs to France (not Spain), and Sardinia belongs to Italy (not France).
topic_notes: This question belongs to world political geography, with a focus on Mediterranean and European regions. UPSC often pairs places with countries, often through news hooks. Mediterranean islands: the largest is Sicily (Italy), followed by Sardinia (Italy), Cyprus (a separate country, divided), Corsica (France), Crete (Greece), Mallorca (Spain) and Malta (a country). The Balearic Islands (Spain) are Mallorca, Menorca, Ibiza and Formentera. Spain also holds the Canary Islands in the Atlantic, off Africa, and the North African enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla. France's regions include Normandy, Brittany, Provence, Alsace and Corsica, which is a territorial collectivity. Normandy is historically significant for the 1066 Norman Conquest and for D-Day, 6 June 1944, the Allied Operation Overlord. Italy's autonomous regions with special status are Sardinia, Sicily, Aosta Valley, Trentino-South Tyrol and Friuli-Venezia Giulia. Important straits: Bonifacio (between Corsica and Sardinia), Messina (between Sicily and mainland Italy), Gibraltar (between Spain and Morocco) and the Strait of Sicily (between Sicily and Tunisia). Study technique: use an outline map and link each region to its country with a historical or current-affairs hook. Related UPSC themes include Catalonia (Spain's separatist movement), Crimea, Donbas, Nagorno-Karabakh, Svalbard, the Aland Islands (Finland) and Greenland (Denmark).

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I : Some rare earth elements are used in the manufacture of flat television screens and computer monitors.
Statement II : Some rare earth elements have phosphorescent properties. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II does not explain Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct
Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Rare earth elements (REEs) are the 17 elements made up of the 15 lanthanides plus scandium and yttrium. They are not especially rare in the crust, but they are dispersed and hard to separate. Many of them have unusual electronic structures (partly filled 4f orbitals) that give sharp luminescent emission. Europium gives red (and blue) light, terbium gives green, and yttrium compounds (Y2O3, YVO4) act as host lattices. These phosphors are used in CRT and plasma displays, LCD and LED backlights, and fluorescent lamps. They are therefore used in flat TV screens and computer monitors, which makes Statement I correct. Statement II is also correct, because phosphorescence/luminescence is a real property of some REEs. In strict physics, fluorescence is immediate emission and phosphorescence is delayed, but UPSC uses the term loosely for phosphors. The causal link holds: the luminescent property is the reason these elements are used in displays. Elimination: (b) fails because II is the reason for I. (c) and (d) fail because both statements are true.
explanations: Correct. Both statements are true, and the luminescent (phosphor) property in II is why REEs are used in display screens in I.
Wrong. Both statements are correct, but II does explain I, because phosphors are what make screens produce coloured light.
Wrong. Statement II is also correct, since some REEs are luminescent/phosphorescent.
Wrong. Statement I is correct, since REEs are used in flat-panel displays and monitors.
keyfact: Rare earths such as europium, terbium and yttrium are phosphors, and their luminescence is why they are used in flat screens and monitors.
option_notes: Both statements correct, with II explaining I. This is the standard assertion-reason format in UPSC. The explanation must be a real causal link, not just a shared topic. Here the luminescent property of europium, terbium and yttrium compounds is the causal reason for their use in displays. This is the official answer.

Both statements correct, but II does not explain I. This option is chosen when the two facts are true yet unrelated, for example if one said REEs are used in magnets and also have luminescence. It is wrong here because the link is direct.
Statement I correct and II incorrect. This would apply if REEs were used in screens but had no luminescent property. Not true, because REE phosphors are central to display technology.
Statement I incorrect and II correct. This would apply if REEs were luminescent but not used in displays. Not true, since europium and terbium are widely used in display and lighting phosphors.
related: There are 17 rare earth elements: 15 lanthanides plus scandium and yttrium.
Europium gives red phosphors and terbium gives green phosphors in displays.
Monazite is the main Indian source of REEs and thorium, found in Kerala, Odisha and Tamil Nadu beach sands.
IREL (Indian Rare Earths Ltd) is under the Department of Atomic Energy.
Neodymium is used in strong permanent magnets for EVs and wind turbines.
China dominates global REE refining.
The National Critical Mineral Mission was approved by India in January 2025.
Gadolinium is used as an MRI contrast agent.
statements: 1 — Correct: Rare earths such as europium, terbium and yttrium are used as phosphors in display screens. Phosphors are materials that emit visible light when struck by electrons, UV light or other radiation. Europium gives red, terbium gives green, and europium or cerium-doped materials give blue. They are used in CRTs, plasma panels, LCD/LED backlighting and energy-saving fluorescent lamps. Neodymium is used in magnets in speakers and hard drives. China dominates REE mining and processing, with about 60% of mining and about 85-90% of refining. India has large monazite reserves in the coastal sands of Kerala, Odisha and Tamil Nadu. IREL (Indian Rare Earths Ltd) handles these under the Department of Atomic Energy.

2 — Correct: Some REEs have phosphorescent/luminescent properties, and this explains their use in displays. Their 4f electrons are shielded by outer shells, so they emit narrow, stable, colour-pure spectral lines. Europium-doped yttrium oxide (Y2O3:Eu) is the classic red phosphor. Erbium is used in fibre-optic amplifiers, and lanthanide-doped materials are used in lasers (Nd:YAG) and in glow-in-the-dark products. Strictly, phosphorescence is delayed emission after excitation, while fluorescence is immediate. Many display phosphors are technically fluorescent, but UPSC accepts the general luminescence sense. Statement II is the scientific reason behind Statement I.
summary: The answer is (a). Both statements are correct, and Statement II explains Statement I. Some rare earth elements (europium, terbium, yttrium, cerium) are phosphors, and they emit light when excited. That property is why they are used in flat screens and monitors.
topic_notes: Rare earth elements (REEs) are 17 metals: the 15 lanthanides (atomic numbers 57-71, lanthanum to lutetium) plus scandium and yttrium. They split into light REEs (La to Eu) and heavy REEs (Gd to Lu, plus Y). Despite the name, they are fairly abundant, but they rarely occur in concentrated, economically mineable deposits. The main ores are monazite, bastnäsite and xenotime. Uses: neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium and terbium in permanent magnets (EV motors, wind turbines, hard drives); europium, terbium and yttrium in phosphors for displays and lighting; cerium in catalytic converters and glass polishing; lanthanum in camera lenses and battery electrodes; erbium in fibre optics; gadolinium in MRI contrast agents; samarium in SmCo magnets. China controls most of the world's mining and especially refining, and has used export restrictions as a strategic tool. Other producers include the USA (Mountain Pass), Australia (Lynas), Myanmar and Vietnam. India holds large reserves, mostly monazite beach sands, which also contain thorium. IREL, under the Department of Atomic Energy, is the main producer, and monazite is regulated as a prescribed substance. In January 2025 India approved the National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM), and in 2023 the Mines and Minerals Act was amended to open some critical minerals for private auction. India is also a member of the Minerals Security Partnership, and the Quad has critical minerals initiatives. Related questions could cover critical minerals lists, lithium, cobalt, graphite, and the strategic and thorium-based nuclear programme.

question:
Consider the following statements :
I. Indian Railways have prepared a National Rail Plan (NRP) to create $ tacks ready’ railway system by 028. Il. ‘Kavach’ is an Automatic Train Protection system developed in collaboration with Germany. Ill. ‘Kavach’ system consists of RFID tags fitted on track in station section. Which of the statements given above are not correct?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The question asks which statements are NOT correct, so the logic is inverted. The National Rail Plan (draft released December 2020) is a long-term vision for a 'future ready' railway system by 2030. It aims to build capacity ahead of demand up to 2050, raise the freight modal share to about 45%, and cut logistics costs. The statement as printed gives a different target year, so it is wrong. Kavach is India's indigenous Automatic Train Protection (ATP) system, designed by RDSO (Research Designs and Standards Organisation, Lucknow) with Indian firms such as Medha, HBL and Kernex. It is not a German collaboration, so II is wrong. Kavach has three main parts: RFID tags on the track (at stations and at intervals along the line), an on-board loco unit, and trackside radio communication towers. III is therefore correct. Since I and II are wrong and III is right, only (a) fits. Option (d) fails because III is correct. The other two options include III as 'not correct', so they fail too. Note that the OCR garbled the numerals and option labels; the stated official answer (a) corresponds to I and II.
explanations: Correct: statements I and II are not correct. The NRP target year differs from the 2030 target, and Kavach is indigenous, not a German collaboration. Statement III is correct, so it is not part of the answer.
Wrong: this option as printed is the pairing with II and III (or a pairing that includes III). Statement III on RFID tags is correct, so III cannot be in the 'not correct' set.
Wrong: this option as printed includes III, which is correct. It also omits statement II, which is incorrect, so it fails.
Wrong: not all three statements are incorrect. Statement III about RFID tags on the track is accurate, so 'I, II and III' cannot be the answer.
keyfact: Kavach is India's indigenous Automatic Train Protection system (RDSO plus Indian firms, SIL-4) using RFID tags on the track, not a German collaboration; the National Rail Plan looks to 2030.
option_notes: Option (a) is I and II only. This is the official answer. It reflects that the NRP's goal is a future-ready railway by 2030, with the statement's year being wrong, and that Kavach is indigenous. The NRP is a Ministry of Railways long-term strategy released in draft in December 2020, while Kavach is the indigenous ATP from RDSO. It is the only option that excludes the correct statement III.

Option (b), as printed in the OCR, is the pairing involving II and III. It is wrong because statement III, about RFID tags, is correct. Kavach's architecture includes RFID tags on the track and at stations, an on-board loco unit with an RFID reader, and radio towers. Version 4.0 added 4G LTE communication and better location accuracy, and was approved by RDSO in 2024.

Option (c) is I and III only. It is wrong because statement III is correct and statement II is incorrect, so II needs to be in the answer. Kavach's RFID tags are laid on the track at stations and at regular intervals. Statement II is wrong because Kavach was developed by RDSO with Indian firms, not with Germany.

Option (d) is I, II and III. It is wrong because III is correct. Kavach does use RFID tags on the track in station sections. The system is certified at SIL-4. It is rolled out on high-density routes first, and the Budget targets to cover thousands of route kilometres under the 'Aatmanirbhar Bharat' programme. The NRP is linked to PM Gati Shakti.
related: The NRP vision is a future-ready railway by 2030, with demand projections to 2050.
NRP aims to raise rail freight modal share to about 45%.
Kavach was developed by RDSO (Lucknow) with Indian industry and is SIL-4 certified.
Kavach components are RFID tags on the track, an on-board loco unit and radio towers.
Kavach 4.0 was approved by RDSO in July 2024.
Indian Railways targets net-zero carbon emissions by 2030.
The Mumbai–Ahmedabad bullet train is 508 km long, with Japanese Shinkansen technology.
DFCCIL builds the Eastern and Western Dedicated Freight Corridors.
statements: I — Incorrect: The NRP envisions a future-ready railway system by 2030, and the target year in the statement does not match this. The National Rail Plan was released in draft in December 2020 by the Ministry of Railways. It looks ahead to 2030 and 2050. Its goals include raising the railways' freight modal share from about 27% to about 45%, creating capacity ahead of demand, cutting transit times, and boosting multimodal logistics. It plans Dedicated Freight Corridors and high-density network upgrades. It also identifies new dedicated freight corridors, high-speed corridors, and ways to increase average freight train speed. It is linked to the PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan. Remember 2030 for the NRP horizon and 2050 for the demand projection.

II — Incorrect: Kavach is indigenous, developed by RDSO with Indian industry partners, not in collaboration with Germany. Kavach is the 'Train Collision Avoidance System' (TCAS), developed from 2012 and trialled from 2016. It was adopted as the National ATP system in 2020. It is certified at Safety Integrity Level 4 (SIL-4), the highest level. Indian firms such as Medha Servo Drives, HBL Power and Kernex Microsystems are among its manufacturers. Version 4.0 was approved in 2024. It works by automatically applying brakes if the loco pilot fails to act, preventing signal passing at danger (SPAD) and enforcing speed limits. It is a key Aatmanirbhar Bharat safety initiative and is being rolled out on the Delhi–Mumbai and Delhi–Howrah routes.

III — Correct: Kavach uses RFID tags laid on the track. Its architecture includes passive RFID tags on the track at stations, signals and along the line (at fixed intervals) that give train location and track details. It also has an on-board Kavach unit with an RFID reader in the locomotive, and radio communication infrastructure (towers, now 4G LTE in version 4.0) linking the loco to the station Kavach. The system lets the train know its position, speed and signal aspect. It works in all weather, including fog. It can trigger automatic braking, give SOS messages and display signals in the cab. It is a low-cost alternative to the European ETCS Level 2, at a fraction of the cost per km.
summary: The answer is (a): statements I and II are not correct, and statement III is correct. The National Rail Plan targets a future-ready railway by 2030, and the date in the statement as given does not match that. Kavach is an indigenous Automatic Train Protection system developed by RDSO with Indian industry, not in collaboration with Germany. Its RFID tags on the track in station sections are accurately described.
topic_notes:
National Rail Plan (NRP): prepared by the Ministry of Railways, draft released December 2020. It is a vision for a 'future ready' railway system by 2030 and a long-term capacity plan to 2050. Its aims are to raise the freight modal share to about 45%, reduce logistics cost, and create capacity ahead of demand through high-density network upgrades and Dedicated Freight Corridors (DFCs). It is aligned with PM Gati Shakti (launched October 2021), the National Master Plan for multimodal connectivity.

Kavach: India's indigenous Automatic Train Protection (ATP) system, also called the Train Collision Avoidance System (TCAS). It was developed by RDSO (Lucknow) with Indian industry. Trials began in 2016 and it was adopted as the National ATP system in 2020. It is certified at SIL-4. Components are RFID tags on the track, a loco unit, station Kavach and communication towers. Functions include automatic braking, preventing signal passing at danger (SPAD), speed control, SOS messages, and display of signals in the cab. Kavach 4.0 was approved in July 2024. Deployment started on the South Central Railway (Lingampalli–Vikarabad–Wadi). It is a cheaper alternative to the European ETCS Level 2.

Other railway topics UPSC could ask: Dedicated Freight Corridors (Eastern, DFCCIL; Western); Vande Bharat Express (Train 18, built by ICF Chennai); Mumbai–Ahmedabad High Speed Rail (508 km, Japan-assisted with Shinkansen technology); Amrit Bharat Station Scheme; Mission Raftaar; Indian Railways' target of net-zero carbon emissions by 2030; the Railway Safety Commissioner; and the zones (18) and Railway Board.

question:
Consider the following space missions :
I. Axiom-4 Il. SpaDeX Ill. Gaganyaan How many of the space missions given above encourage and support microgravity research?
subject: Science & Tech
detail: Microgravity research studies how physical, biological and material processes behave when gravity's effect is almost absent, as in low Earth orbit. Axiom-4 was a private crewed mission to the International Space Station launched in June 2025 by Axiom Space on a SpaceX Dragon. Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla flew as the first Indian on the ISS, and ISRO-linked experiments covered muscle loss, microalgae, crop seeds (such as methi and moong), and others, so it clearly supports microgravity research. Gaganyaan is ISRO's human spaceflight programme, planned to place a crew of 3 in a roughly 400 km orbit for up to 3 days. Its crewed and uncrewed flights are meant to enable microgravity experiments, and ISRO has invited scientific proposals for these. SpaDeX (Space Docking Experiment) launched on PSLV-C60 on 30 December 2024 with two small satellites, SDX01 (Chaser) and SDX02 (Target). It demonstrated rendezvous, docking and undocking, with successful docking on 16 January 2025, making India the 4th country to do so. Its purpose is technology for Bharatiya Antariksh Station, Chandrayaan-4 and similar missions. Because its principal aim is docking, not microgravity science, the official answer counts only two missions. The elimination logic: since Axiom-4 certainly qualifies, (d) is out; since SpaDeX is primarily a docking demonstrator, (c) is out; since Gaganyaan qualifies too, (a) is out.
explanations: (a) Wrong: it undercounts, because both Axiom-4 and Gaganyaan support microgravity research.
(b) Correct: Axiom-4 and Gaganyaan support microgravity research, while SpaDeX is a docking technology demonstration.
(c) Wrong: SpaDeX's main goal is rendezvous and docking technology, not microgravity science.
(d) Wrong: Axiom-4 clearly carried microgravity experiments on the ISS, so not none.
keyfact: Axiom-4 (ISS) and Gaganyaan support microgravity research; SpaDeX is mainly a docking technology demonstrator, so the answer is two.
option_notes: Only one: this would fit if just Axiom-4 counted. Axiom-4 was a June 2025 private mission to the ISS by Axiom Space, with a Dragon capsule carrying four astronauts, including India's Shubhanshu Shukla. It was the fourth Axiom private mission to the ISS and carried about 60 experiments from many countries, including 7 Indian studies. It is not the right answer here because Gaganyaan also counts.

Only two: the official answer. The two are Axiom-4, a mission with ISS microgravity experiments, and Gaganyaan, India's crewed orbital flight programme, which provides a microgravity platform. SpaDeX is excluded because it is a docking technology demonstrator. Remember the pattern: crewed missions mean microgravity science, while docking demos mean enabling technology for stations and sample-return missions.

All the three: this would hold if SpaDeX counted as a microgravity mission. SpaDeX (Space Docking Experiment) was launched on PSLV-C60 on 30 December 2024 with Chaser and Target satellites. It achieved docking on 16 January 2025 and undocking later, giving India docking capability, the fourth country to do so. Its aim is technology for space stations and Chandrayaan-4, so UPSC treats it as not primarily microgravity research.

None: this is wrong because crewed missions such as Axiom-4 and Gaganyaan involve microgravity experiments. Microgravity is the near weightless condition in orbit, where free fall cancels the sensation of gravity. It enables research on fluid physics, crystal growth, cell biology, human physiology, and materials without convection or sedimentation. India's facilities for this include the planned Bharatiya Antariksh Station and PSLV POEM platforms.
related: Axiom-4 launched in June 2025 with Shubhanshu Shukla as the first Indian on the ISS.
SpaDeX was launched on PSLV-C60 on 30 December 2024; docking succeeded on 16 January 2025.
India became the fourth country to achieve space docking, after the USA, Russia and China.
Gaganyaan plans a crew of 3 at 400 km for up to 3 days, with splashdown in the sea.
Bharatiya Antariksh Station is targeted for 2035, with its first module around 2028.
Rakesh Sharma was the first Indian in space in 1984 aboard Soyuz T-11.
The POEM (PSLV Orbital Experimental Module) reuses the PS4 stage as an orbital research platform.
The Human Space Flight Centre of ISRO is in Bengaluru.
statements: I — Correct: Axiom-4 carried microgravity experiments. It was a commercial crewed mission to the ISS, flown by Axiom Space on a SpaceX Crew Dragon in June 2025, with Shubhanshu Shukla as pilot and crew from India, Poland and Hungary. India's experiments, selected by ISRO and DBT, covered muscle regeneration, microalgae, sprouting of seeds, cyanobacteria and tardigrades. It was the first Indian presence on the ISS and gave experience for Gaganyaan. It was a research and training mission in microgravity.

II — Incorrect: SpaDeX is mainly a docking demonstration, not a microgravity research mission. Launched on PSLV-C60 on 30 December 2024, it placed two roughly 220 kg satellites, SDX01 Chaser and SDX02 Target, in a 470 km orbit. Docking was achieved on 16 January 2025, making India the fourth country after the USA, Russia and China to do so. It prepares for Bharatiya Antariksh Station, Chandrayaan-4 sample return and satellite servicing. The POEM-4 stage carried small payloads, but research was not the main objective.

III — Correct: Gaganyaan is ISRO's human spaceflight programme. It aims to take a crew of three to about 400 km low Earth orbit for up to three days and return them to the sea, using the HLVM3 launcher and the Orbital Module. Uncrewed test flights (G1, etc.) precede the crewed flight, and the Vyommitra humanoid will fly on one. Four astronaut-designates were named in 2024, including Shubhanshu Shukla. The missions give a platform for microgravity experiments in biology, materials and medicine, and lead on to the Bharatiya Antariksh Station, planned by 2035.
summary: The answer is (b) Only two. Axiom-4 (with Indian astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla on the ISS) carried microgravity experiments, and Gaganyaan is designed to provide a microgravity research platform. SpaDeX is a docking technology demonstration and is not mainly a microgravity research mission, although its POEM-4 platform did carry some experiments.
topic_notes: Microgravity is the condition of apparent weightlessness in orbit, where objects and people are in continuous free fall. Gravity is still about 90 percent of its surface value at ISS altitude. Research areas include human physiology (bone and muscle loss, fluid shift), cell and plant biology, protein crystal growth, fluid physics, combustion and new materials. Key platforms are the ISS (since 1998, with the USA, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada), China's Tiangong station, drop towers, parabolic flights and sounding rockets. India's programme: Gaganyaan is the crewed mission, with HLVM3, the Orbital Module (crew module plus service module), a planned 3-day flight at 400 km, and the first uncrewed test (G1) with Vyommitra. Four astronaut-designates were announced in February 2024: Prasanth Balakrishnan Nair, Ajit Krishnan, Angad Prathap and Shubhanshu Shukla. The Bharatiya Antariksh Station is planned for 2035 and the first module by 2028. SpaDeX (December 2024, PSLV-C60) tests docking, and POEM-4 carried over 20 payloads, including experiments by startups and institutions such as a cowpea seed sprouting experiment by VSSC. Axiom-4 (June 2025) was a private astronaut mission with Shubhanshu Shukla; he became the first Indian on the ISS and the second Indian in space after Rakesh Sharma in 1984. Other angles: India's ISRO-NASA collaboration (NISAR), Chandrayaan-4 sample return, Aditya-L1 for solar studies, Mangalyaan and Shukrayaan. Facility questions could ask about ISRO centres: Human Space Flight Centre in Bengaluru, VSSC in Thiruvananthapuram, and the Gaganyaan launch from Sriharikota.

question: Artificial way of causing rainfall to reduce air pollution makes use of silver iodide and potassium iodide
subject: Environment
detail: Artificial rainfall is produced by cloud seeding, a weather-modification technique. Aircraft, rockets or ground generators release tiny particles into clouds that already hold moisture. Silver iodide (AgI) has a crystal structure close to that of ice, so it acts as an ice-forming nucleus in supercooled clouds. Droplets freeze on it, grow heavy and fall as snow or rain. Potassium iodide (KI), along with sodium chloride and dry ice (solid CO2), is also used. Hygroscopic salts promote condensation in warm clouds. Seeding works only if suitable clouds exist; it cannot create rain in a clear sky. Rain can scrub particulate matter (PM2.5, PM10) from the air, but the effect is temporary. Delhi's IIT Kanpur conducted trials of cloud seeding for pollution control in 2025. India's earlier effort was Tamil Nadu's 1983 experiment. Elimination logic: silver nitrate and potassium nitrate are not the standard nucleating agents, and a pure chloride or potassium alone does not fit. In the garbled options, the pairing of silver and iodide compounds is the one that matches the real method, which supports the official key (a).
explanations: Correct. Per the official key, the silver and iodide-based compounds (AgI, KI) are the cloud-seeding agents that induce precipitation.
Incorrect. Potassium nitrate is a fertiliser and an ingredient of gunpowder, not a standard cloud-seeding agent.
Incorrect. Elemental potassium is highly reactive and is never used for seeding; silver nitrate is not the nucleating compound.
Incorrect. Chloride alone is not a specific agent. Only certain salts such as sodium chloride are used, and the option does not name the silver and iodide compounds.
keyfact: Cloud seeding uses silver iodide and potassium iodide (also NaCl and dry ice) as nuclei to trigger rain from existing clouds.
option_notes: Silver nitrate (AgNO3) is the soluble silver salt used to make silver iodide, in photography and as an antiseptic. Potassium iodide (KI) is a salt used in cloud seeding and in iodised salt, and as a thyroid protectant in nuclear emergencies. Silver iodide (AgI) is made from these two, and it is the main seeding compound because its crystals resemble ice.

Silver iodide (AgI) is the classic ice-nucleating agent discovered by Bernard Vonnegut in 1946 at General Electric. Potassium nitrate (KNO3), or saltpetre, is used in fertilisers, fireworks and gunpowder, and is not a seeding agent.

Silver nitrate is a caustic salt used in lab analysis and medicine. Potassium is an alkali metal that reacts violently with water and is stored under oil. Neither is used for seeding. Seeding relies on AgI, KI, NaCl, and dry ice.

Chloride is an anion, not a compound by itself. Sodium chloride and calcium chloride are hygroscopic salts used to seed warm clouds through flares. Chloride ions are also found in sea spray, which is a natural source of cloud condensation nuclei.
related: Cloud seeding agents: silver iodide, potassium iodide, sodium chloride, dry ice.

Vincent Schaefer used dry ice for the first seeding experiment in 1946.
CAIPEEX is the MoES programme studying cloud-aerosol interaction, run by IITM Pune.
IIT Kanpur conducted cloud-seeding trials over Delhi in 2025 for pollution control.
NCAP launched in 2019 aims to cut PM concentration by 20-30% by 2024 against 2017 levels.
CAQM (Commission for Air Quality Management) was set up in 2021 for the Delhi-NCR region.
Cloud seeding cannot create clouds; it only enhances precipitation from existing ones.
summary: The answer is (a): cloud seeding, the artificial rain method, uses silver iodide and potassium iodide as seeding agents. (The OCR'd question appears garbled, but the official key (a) is treated as correct.) These salts act as ice or condensation nuclei, so cloud droplets grow, fall as rain and wash out pollutants.
topic_notes: Cloud seeding is a weather-modification technique that increases precipitation, suppresses hail or clears fog. It was pioneered by Vincent Schaefer (1946, dry ice) and Bernard Vonnegut (silver iodide). Types: static seeding (introducing ice nuclei such as AgI), dynamic seeding (boosting updrafts through released latent heat), and hygroscopic seeding (salts in warm clouds). Delivery is by aircraft flares, ground generators or rockets. Preconditions: clouds with enough moisture, and ideally supercooled liquid water, with the right temperature. It cannot make rain from a clear sky. India's experience includes Tamil Nadu (1983-84), Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra, and the Cloud Aerosol Interaction and Precipitation Enhancement Experiment (CAIPEEX) of the Ministry of Earth Sciences, run through IITM Pune. IIT Kanpur ran trials over Delhi in 2025 to test seeding for pollution control, because rain washes out PM2.5 and PM10. Concerns include limited and temporary effect, cost, uncertain efficacy, ecological and toxicity effects of silver, and disputes over moving moisture across regions. Other countries: China's large weather modification programme (used before the 2008 Olympics), UAE (rain enhancement), USA. Related topics: smog towers, GRAP in Delhi, Air Quality Index, NCAP (2019), and CAQM. Other angles UPSC can ask: the role of aerosols, cloud condensation nuclei, the Bergeron process, and the difference between artificial rain and natural monsoon rainfall.

question: Consider the following statements with regard to pardoning power of the President of India : The exercise of this power by the Ls President can be subjected to limited judicial review. The President can exercise this power without the advice of the Central Government. Which of the statements given above is/are correct? I only
subject: Polity
detail: Article 72 empowers the President to grant pardons, reprieves, respites and remissions, and to suspend, remit or commute sentences. It covers punishment by court martial, offences under Union law, and all death sentences. It is not a personal discretion. Article 74(1), as amended by the 42nd and 44th Amendments, makes the advice of the Council of Ministers binding, though the President may send it back for reconsideration once. In Maru Ram v. Union of India (1980) the Supreme Court held that the power is exercised on government advice. Kehar Singh v. Union of India (1989) held that the President may re-examine the evidence and that the order is reviewable only on narrow grounds. Epuru Sudhakar v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2006) listed those grounds: mala fides, irrelevant considerations, non-application of mind, arbitrariness and discrimination. Shatrughan Chauhan (2014) accepted unexplained delay as a ground for commuting a death sentence. Elimination: statement II contradicts Article 74, so any option containing it (b and c) is out. Statement I is supported by case law, so option (d) is out, leaving (a).
explanations: Correct. Statement I is right because limited judicial review of pardon orders is permitted. Statement II is wrong because the President acts on Council of Ministers' advice under Article 74.
Wrong. Statement II alone is incorrect, since the President cannot exercise the pardoning power independently of the Central Government's advice.
Wrong. Statement II is incorrect, so 'both' cannot be right.
Wrong. Statement I is correct because the Supreme Court has allowed limited review of pardon orders. So 'neither' is false.
keyfact: Under Article 72 read with Article 74, the President pardons on Council of Ministers' advice, and courts can review only on limited grounds.
option_notes: Option (a), statement I only, is the official answer. It reflects the position that the pardoning power under Article 72 is a constitutional power with limited judicial review. The Court checks mala fides, arbitrariness, irrelevant considerations and non-application of mind, as laid down in Kehar Singh and Epuru Sudhakar. It is not a matter of personal discretion, and the President acts on ministerial advice.

Option (b), statement II only, is wrong. It claims the President can pardon without the Central Government's advice. Article 74(1) makes the Council of Ministers' advice binding, with one right of reconsideration after the 44th Amendment (1978). Maru Ram (1980) confirmed that the power is exercised on government advice, so there is no independent presidential discretion.

Option (c), both statements, is wrong. Statement I is correct, but statement II is not, because the President cannot act without the Council of Ministers' advice. The Council can be asked to reconsider its advice only once, after which its advice binds. The President has genuine discretion only in a few situations, such as appointing a PM when no party has a majority.

Option (d), neither statement, is wrong. Statement I is correct: courts can review pardon orders on limited grounds such as mala fides, arbitrariness or irrelevant considerations, even though they cannot reassess the merits. This was established in Maru Ram, Kehar Singh, Epuru Sudhakar and Shatrughan Chauhan.
related: Article 72 gives the President pardoning power; Article 161 gives the Governor similar power.
Only the President can pardon a death sentence or a court-martial sentence; the Governor cannot.
Article 74(1) makes the Council of Ministers' advice binding; the 44th Amendment allows one reconsideration.
Kehar Singh (1989) allowed limited judicial review and held that the President may re-examine evidence.
Maru Ram (1980) held that the pardoning power is exercised on government advice, not arbitrarily.
Epuru Sudhakar (2006) allowed review for mala fides, arbitrariness and irrelevant considerations.
Shatrughan Chauhan (2014) held that unexplained delay in deciding mercy petitions can justify commuting a death sentence.
Commutation substitutes a lighter punishment; remission reduces its duration; respite is a lesser sentence for special reasons; reprieve is a temporary stay.
statements: 1 — Correct: Judicial review of pardon orders is allowed, but only within narrow limits. The Court does not re-assess the merits of the decision. It examines only whether the decision was made lawfully. Kehar Singh (1989) held that the President may scrutinise the evidence afresh, and that the Court cannot sit in appeal over the decision. Maru Ram (1980) held that the power must not be exercised arbitrarily. Epuru Sudhakar (2006) allowed review on grounds such as mala fides, irrelevant or ignored considerations, and arbitrariness or discrimination. Swaran Singh (1998) quashed a Governor's remission for non-consideration of relevant material. Shatrughan Chauhan (2014) accepted unexplained delay as a ground for commutation. The President need not give reasons for the order, and there is no right to an oral hearing.

2 — Incorrect: Article 74(1) says there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President, who shall act in accordance with that advice. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made this advice binding. The 44th Amendment (1978) allowed the President to send the advice back for reconsideration once, after which the President must act on it. Maru Ram (1980) and Kehar Singh (1989) held that the pardoning power is exercised on the advice of the Central Government, specifically the Council of Ministers, in practice through the Ministry of Home Affairs. Although the Constitution calls it the President's power, it is a formal constitutional power rather than a personal discretion. The same principle applies to the Governor under Article 161, who acts on the State Council of Ministers' advice.
summary: The answer is (a): only statement I is correct. The President's pardoning power under Article 72 is open to limited judicial review, but under Article 74(1) the President must act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, so statement II is wrong.
topic_notes: Article 72 gives the President power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites and remissions of punishment, and to suspend, remit or commute sentences. It applies to: (a) punishment by court martial, (b) offences against Union law, and (c) all death sentences. Article 161 gives the Governor a similar power, but it does not extend to court-martial sentences or to pardoning a death sentence. A Governor can suspend, remit or commute a death sentence. The terms differ. Pardon removes both sentence and conviction. Commutation substitutes a lighter punishment. Remission reduces the duration without changing the nature of the sentence. Respite means a lesser sentence because of special facts such as pregnancy or a convict's physical condition. Reprieve is a temporary stay of execution, for example to allow time to seek a pardon. Key cases: Kehar Singh (1989), where the President may re-examine evidence and the petitioner has no right to an oral hearing. Maru Ram (1980), which held that the power is exercised on advice and not arbitrarily, and addressed the relationship with CrPC remission powers (Sections 432-433A). Epuru Sudhakar (2006) set out the grounds for review. Shatrughan Chauhan (2014) held that inordinate delay in deciding mercy petitions is a ground for commutation, and Devender Pal Singh Bhullar (2013) is related. Mercy petitions: the President's decision is made on the Home Ministry's advice. Related: Article 74 (Council of Ministers), Article 77, Articles 52-53, and the Supreme Court's own powers under Article 142. Also revise the Governor's powers under Articles 161 and 163, and the Commutation of death penalty in the Rajiv Gandhi assassination case (Perarivalan, 2022, using Article 142).

question:
Consider the following statements :
I. On the dissolution of the House of the People, the Speaker shall not vacate his/her _ office until immediately before the first meeting of the House of the People after the dissolution.
II. According to the provisions of the Constitution of India, a Member of the House of the People on being elected as Speaker shall resign from his/her political party immediately. Ill. The Speaker of the House of the People may be removed from his/her office by a resolution of the House of the People passed by a majority of all the then Members of the House, provided that no resolution shall be moved unless at least fourteen days’ notice has been given of the intention to move the resolution. Which of the statements given above are correct?
subject: Polity
detail: Articles 93 to 96 deal with the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha. Article 94 says the Speaker vacates office if they cease to be a member of the House, resign by writing to the Deputy Speaker, or are removed by a resolution of the House passed by a majority of all the then members. Such a resolution needs at least 14 days' prior notice. Under the proviso to Article 94, whenever the House is dissolved, the Speaker does not vacate office until immediately before the first meeting of the House after dissolution. This ensures continuity, which is why the Speaker, unlike ordinary members, stays in office during dissolution. Article 96 bars the Speaker from presiding while a resolution for their removal is under consideration, but allows them to speak and take part in the proceedings and to vote in the first instance, though not to cast a casting vote. Article 95 gives the Deputy Speaker the Speaker's duties when the office is vacant. The Constitution does not require the Speaker to quit their party. The convention of political impartiality is a British tradition that India has only partly followed. Members such as Neelam Sanjiva Reddy did resign from their party in 1967, but this was a personal choice. The Tenth Schedule, paragraph 5, exempts a Speaker who voluntarily gives up party membership from disqualification. So I and III are correct, which gives (c).
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement II, which is not a constitutional requirement, and leaves out III, which is correct.
(b) is wrong because it includes II, which is incorrect, and leaves out I, which is correct under the proviso to Article 94.
(c) is correct because I follows the proviso to Article 94 and III follows Article 94(c) with its 14-day notice. II has no constitutional basis.
(d) is wrong because II is incorrect: nothing in the Constitution requires the Speaker to resign from their party.
keyfact: Article 94: the Speaker stays in office after dissolution until just before the new House meets, and can be removed only by an effective majority with 14 days' notice, with no constitutional duty to resign from the party.
option_notes: Option (a), I and II only, is wrong. It pairs the true continuity rule on dissolution with the false claim of mandatory party resignation. The Tenth Schedule paragraph 5 only protects a Speaker who voluntarily resigns from the party, so it is not a requirement. Remember that the Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha from among its members, and that the Speaker's office is not tied to party resignation.

Option (b), II and III only, is wrong. It accepts the false claim of mandatory resignation from the party and rejects the correct statement I. The 14-day notice for removal of the Speaker under Article 94 is a point students often confuse with the Vice-President's removal, which also requires 14 days' notice under Article 67(b).

Option (c), I and III only, is the official answer. It combines the continuity of the Speaker's office after dissolution with the removal rule requiring an effective majority and 14 days' notice. Both come from Article 94. Statement II is a trap built on the British convention of a non-partisan Speaker, which India has not codified.

Option (d), I, II and III, is wrong because it adds the incorrect statement II. UPSC often adds one plausible but false statement to otherwise correct ones. The Constitution only protects the Speaker from anti-defection disqualification if they voluntarily give up party membership, under paragraph 5 of the Tenth Schedule.
related: Article 94 governs vacation, resignation and removal of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
Removal of the Speaker needs a majority of all the then members, with 14 days' notice.
Article 96: the Speaker does not preside during their own removal resolution but may speak and vote only in the first instance.
Tenth Schedule paragraph 5 protects a Speaker who voluntarily gives up party membership.
The Speaker decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill under Article 110.
G. V. Mavalankar was the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha (1952).
Meira Kumar was the first woman Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
The Speaker presides over joint sittings of Parliament under Article 108.
statements: I — Correct: The proviso to Article 94 lets the Speaker continue in office after dissolution until immediately before the first sitting of the new House. This keeps the office from falling vacant between Lok Sabha terms. The Speaker is the presiding officer and is elected by the House from among its members soon after the first sitting. The Speaker's role during dissolution is mostly administrative, and the new House then elects its Speaker. The same continuity applies to a Speaker during the House's term. The Speaker of the 17th Lok Sabha, Om Birla, was re-elected in 2024 for the 18th.

II — Incorrect: No constitutional provision requires the Speaker to resign from their political party on election. Paragraph 5 of the Tenth Schedule, added in 1985, protects a Speaker who voluntarily gives up party membership on taking office, and who rejoins the party after leaving office, from disqualification. This exemption was meant to promote impartiality. Neelam Sanjiva Reddy resigned from the Congress in 1967 when elected Speaker. Most Speakers have retained party affiliation. Recommendations for a non-partisan Speaker, as in the UK convention, have been made by committees of presiding officers but not made law.

III — Correct: Article 94(c) provides that the Speaker may be removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the House, which is an effective majority, not a majority of those present and voting. The proviso requires at least 14 days' notice of the intention to move the resolution. Article 96 bars the Speaker from presiding during the resolution's consideration, though they may speak and vote in the first instance, not casting vote on a tie. The same procedure applies to the Deputy Speaker. No Speaker has ever been removed by this method.
summary: The answer is (c): statements I and III are correct and statement II is incorrect. Article 94 provides that the Speaker continues in office after dissolution until immediately before the first meeting of the new House, and that the Speaker can be removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members, with 14 days' notice. The Constitution has no provision requiring the Speaker to resign from their party on election.
topic_notes: The Speaker is the presiding officer of the Lok Sabha. Articles 93 to 97 deal with the Speaker and Deputy Speaker. Article 93 requires the House to choose them as soon as may be. The President fixes the date for the Speaker's election, while the Speaker fixes the date for the Deputy Speaker's election. Article 94 covers vacation, resignation and removal. Resignation is addressed to the Deputy Speaker, and the Speaker's resignation to the Deputy Speaker is the usual route. Removal requires a resolution by a majority of all the then members, meaning an effective majority, with 14 days' notice. Article 95 lets the Deputy Speaker or another person perform the Speaker's duties when the office is vacant. Article 96 prevents the Speaker or Deputy Speaker from presiding while their own removal is under consideration, but allows them to speak and vote only in the first instance. Article 97 deals with salaries and allowances, which are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. The Speaker has a casting vote in case of a tie. The Speaker decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill (Article 110), presides over joint sittings (Article 108), and decides disqualification under the Tenth Schedule, which the Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan (1992) held is subject to judicial review. The first Speaker was G. V. Mavalankar (1952). M. A. Ayyangar, Hukam Singh and others followed. G. M. C. Balayogi was the first Speaker to die in office. Meira Kumar was the first woman Speaker. Sumitra Mahajan was the second. The Deputy Speaker is customarily from the opposition by convention, but the 17th Lok Sabha had no Deputy Speaker. The Speaker pro tem administers oath to new members before the Speaker's election. Rajya Sabha has the Vice-President as ex-officio Chairman and a Deputy Chairman, who is elected from members.

question:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I : In India, State Governments have no power for making rules for grant of concessions in respect of extraction of minor minerals even though such minerals are located in their territories.
Statement II : In India, the Central Government has the power to notify minor minerals under the relevant law. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? Both Statement I and Statement II
options: are correct and Statement II explains Statement I Both Statement I and Statement II
are correct but Statement II does not explain Statement I Statement I is correct but
Statement II is not correct Statement I is not correct but
subject: Geography
detail: The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act) is enacted under Entry 54 of the Union List (regulation of mines and mineral development to the extent Parliament declares it expedient in public interest), read with Entry 23 of the State List (regulation of mines subject to Union List provisions). Minerals are split into major minerals, regulated mainly by the Centre (e.g. coal, iron ore, bauxite, lignite, atomic minerals), and minor minerals. Section 3(e) defines minor minerals as building stones, gravel, ordinary clay, ordinary sand (other than sand used for prescribed purposes), and any other mineral the Central Government declares to be minor by notification in the Official Gazette. Section 15 gives State Governments the power to make rules for grant of quarry leases, mining leases and other mineral concessions for minor minerals, so Statement I, which denies this power, is false. Statement II is true because the Centre alone notifies a mineral as minor. Elimination: since Statement I is false, options (a), (b) and (c) fail, leaving (d).
explanations: Wrong: Statement I is false because Section 15 of the MMDR Act gives States rule-making power for minor mineral concessions, so both cannot be correct.
Wrong: this also requires Statement I to be correct, but it is incorrect.
Wrong: this treats Statement I as correct and Statement II as incorrect, which is the reverse of the true position.
Correct: Statement I is incorrect since States do make concession rules under Section 15, and Statement II is correct since the Centre notifies minor minerals under Section 3(e).
keyfact: Centre notifies minor minerals (MMDR Act Section 3(e)); States make concession rules for them (Section 15).
option_notes: Option (a) says both statements are true and II explains I. This would be the right pattern only if States lacked power because the Centre controlled notification. In reality the Centre's notification power only determines which minerals are minor, and the Constitution and MMDR Act then hand concession-granting for those minerals to the States. Such a causal link does not exist, so (a) is wrong.

Option (b) says both are true but II does not explain I. It needs Statement I to be true, which it is not. Statement II is true, but the claim that States cannot make concession rules fails because Section 15 of the MMDR Act authorises exactly that. Hence (b) is incorrect.

Option (c) says Statement I is correct and Statement II is not. It reverses the facts: Statement II is accurate because Section 3(e) lets the Centre notify minor minerals, while Statement I is inaccurate because of State power under Section 15. So (c) is incorrect.

Option (d) says Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct, matching the law. States frame rules and grant leases and permits for minor minerals under Section 15, and the Centre notifies what counts as a minor mineral under Section 3(e). This split, with Entry 54 of the Union List and Entry 23 of the State List, defines Centre-State mineral jurisdiction.
related: Section 3(e) of the MMDR Act, 1957 defines minor minerals; the Centre notifies additions.
Section 15 of the MMDR Act empowers States to make rules for minor mineral concessions.
Entry 54 of the Union List and Entry 23 of the State List cover mines and minerals.
District Mineral Foundation is provided under Section 9B of the MMDR Act (2015 amendment).
The National Mineral Exploration Trust is under Section 9C of the MMDR Act.
In 2024 the Supreme Court held that royalty on minerals is not a tax and States can tax mineral rights.
The Indian Bureau of Mines functions under the Ministry of Mines in Nagpur.
PMKKKY uses DMF funds for welfare in mining-affected areas.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Section 15 of the MMDR Act, 1957 expressly empowers State Governments to make rules for grant of concessions for minor minerals in their territories. Section 15 covers quarry leases, mining leases, permits and licences, along with royalty, dead rent, security deposit, period of lease and related conditions. States also run their own minor mineral concession rules, for instance on sand mining, brick earth and road metal. The 2015 amendment added Section 15(3), under which States may make rules for preventing illegal mining, transport and storage of minerals. Section 15A lets States make rules for the conservation and development of minor minerals. Central powers over minor minerals are limited mostly to notification and general oversight, so the claim that States have no power is wrong.

2 — Correct: Section 3(e) of the MMDR Act, 1957 defines minor minerals as building stones, gravel, ordinary clay, ordinary sand used for filling or building, and 'any other mineral which the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare to be a minor mineral'. The Centre has used this power to notify items such as boulders, shale, limestone used in kilns for lime burning, murrum, brick earth, fuller's earth, bentonite, dolomite and quartz in particular uses. A mineral can be notified as minor in India only by the Centre, not by a State. The Centre has also added or removed minerals from the list over time, for example by notifying certain minerals as minor in 2015 and 2017, so Statement II is correct.
summary: The answer is (d): Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct. Under Section 15 of the MMDR Act, 1957, State Governments make rules for grant of concessions (quarry leases, permits, licences) for minor minerals in their territories, while Section 3(e) empowers the Central Government to notify minerals as 'minor minerals'.
topic_notes: Legal framework: The MMDR Act, 1957 governs mining regulation. Constitutional basis is Entry 54 of the Union List and Entry 23 of the State List; Entry 50 of the State List covers taxes on mineral rights, subject to limits set by Parliament. The Supreme Court in Mineral Area Development Authority v. SAIL (2024, nine-judge bench) held that States have the power to tax mineral rights and that royalty is not a tax. Major minerals: coal, lignite, iron ore, manganese, bauxite, copper, gold and others, with grants regulated by the Centre and States using auction, while the Centre has influence over rules and approvals. Minor minerals: building stones, gravel, ordinary clay, ordinary sand, and others notified by the Centre; concessions are by State rules. Key amendments: the 2015 amendment introduced mandatory auctions for major mineral concessions, created District Mineral Foundations (Section 9B) and the National Mineral Exploration Trust (Section 9C), and set up Special Courts. The 2021 amendment removed the distinction between captive and merchant mines to some extent, allowing captive mine owners to sell up to 50% of annual production after meeting end-use needs, and let the Centre reserve minerals for auctions where State auctions fail. The 2023 amendment allowed private-sector exploration licences for 29 critical and deep-seated minerals and listed 6 atomic minerals for removal from the atomic category, to be dealt with by auction. DMF: funded by a share of royalty to benefit mining-affected areas; Pradhan Mantri Khanij Kshetra Kalyan Yojana (PMKKKY) uses DMF funds. Related bodies: Ministry of Mines, Geological Survey of India, Indian Bureau of Mines (regulates mineral conservation and Mining Plans), National Mineral Development Corporation. Sand mining is governed by State rules and Sustainable Sand Mining Management Guidelines 2016 and Enforcement and Monitoring Guidelines 2020. Environmental clearance for minor minerals is assessed by State Environment Impact Assessment Authorities, with District Environment Impact Assessment Authorities for small areas.

question: Which organization has enacted the Nature Restoration Law (NRL) to tackle climate change and biodiversity loss? The European Union
options: Cooperation and Development The Food and Agriculture
subject: Economy
detail: The Nature Restoration Law (Regulation (EU) 2024/1991) is the first continent-wide, comprehensive law of its kind. It is a key part of the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030 and the European Green Deal. The European Commission proposed it in June 2022, the European Parliament voted in February 2024, and the Council of the EU gave final approval in June 2024. It entered into force in August 2024. The law aims to restore at least 20% of the EU's land and sea areas by 2030 and all ecosystems in need of restoration by 2050. It covers forests, wetlands, grasslands, rivers, marine ecosystems, agricultural land, urban green spaces and pollinator populations. Member states must prepare National Restoration Plans, and as an EU regulation the law is binding on them. Elimination: the World Bank is a development lender and does not legislate. The OECD is a policy-research forum whose instruments are non-binding or recommendatory. The FAO is a UN specialised agency that sets standards and provides technical support, but it does not enact binding laws on member states. Only the EU can pass binding regulations of this kind.
explanations: Correct. The EU (Parliament and Council) enacted the Nature Restoration Law in 2024 as a binding regulation.

Incorrect. The World Bank finances development projects and cannot enact binding environmental legislation on states. The option as OCR'd is also muddled, since the text 'The European Union' sits next to option (a).
Incorrect. The OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) produces policy analysis and non-binding guidelines, not binding law.
Incorrect. The FAO, a UN specialised agency headquartered in Rome, provides standards, data and technical assistance but has no law-making power over members.
keyfact: The Nature Restoration Law (2024) is an EU regulation that aims to restore 20% of EU land and sea by 2030.
option_notes: The European Union is a political and economic union of 27 member states. It evolved from the EEC through the Maastricht Treaty (1993) and the Lisbon Treaty (2009). Its institutions include the European Commission, the European Parliament, the Council of the EU and the European Council. It makes binding regulations, directives and decisions, and it enacted the Nature Restoration Law in 2024 as part of the Green Deal.

The World Bank was created at the Bretton Woods Conference in 1944 and is headquartered in Washington, D.C. It comprises the IBRD and the IDA, with the IBRD set up first. It gives loans and grants for development and poverty reduction, and it publishes reports such as Doing Business (discontinued) and the Ease of Doing Business index. It does not legislate for member countries.

The OECD was established in 1961 and is headquartered in Paris. It has about 38 member countries, and India is not a member, though it is a key partner. It conducts research and publishes PISA, the Economic Outlook and tax standards such as the BEPS and Pillar Two framework. Its instruments are mostly non-binding recommendations and peer review.

The FAO is a UN specialised agency founded in 1945 and headquartered in Rome. It leads international efforts to defeat hunger and publishes The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World (SOFI) and the Global Forest Resources Assessment. It administers the Codex Alimentarius with WHO and the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources, and World Food Day is on 16 October.
related: The Nature Restoration Law is Regulation (EU) 2024/1991, in force from August 2024.
EU targets: restore 20% of land and sea by 2030, all needing restoration by 2050.
Kunming-Montreal GBF (2022) sets the 30x30 target.
UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration is 2021-2030.
Bonn Challenge: 350 million hectares by 2030, and India pledged 26 million hectares.
The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) has a transitional phase starting in October 2023.
The European Climate Law targets climate neutrality by 2050.
India is not an OECD member.
summary: The Nature Restoration Law was enacted by the European Union, so the correct answer is (a) as per the official key. It is an EU regulation adopted in 2024 that sets legally binding targets to restore degraded ecosystems, addressing both biodiversity loss and climate change.
topic_notes: The Nature Restoration Law is a core component of the EU Green Deal and the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030. It was proposed in 2022 and adopted in 2024 after fierce debate, with farmer protests and opposition from some member states. Targets: restore at least 20% of EU land and sea by 2030, and all ecosystems needing restoration by 2050. It requires reversal of the decline in pollinators, no net loss of urban green space, restoration of drained peatlands, reconnection of 25,000 km of rivers into free-flowing rivers, and improvement of forest biodiversity indicators. Member states submit National Restoration Plans, and the European Environment Agency and the Commission monitor progress.
