statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Olympiad has no individual final, and Gukesh's youngest-champion feat came against Ding Liren at the 2024 World Championship, not against Nepomniachtchi. The 45th Olympiad was in Budapest (10-23 September 2024). India won double gold, with the Open team scoring 21/22 points and the Women's team also winning. Gukesh won individual gold on board 1. He became the 18th World Champion on 12 December 2024 in Singapore, aged 18 years and 8 months, breaking Garry Kasparov's record, who won the title at 22 in 1985. Ding Liren was the 17th champion, having won in 2023 against Nepomniachtchi in Astana.

2 — Correct: Abhimanyu Mishra, a US player of Indian descent born in 2009, became the youngest Grandmaster in June 2021 at 12 years, 4 months, 25 days. He broke Sergey Karjakin's record, which had stood for almost 19 years since 2002. He achieved the final GM norm at the Vezerkepzo GM Mix tournament in Budapest, Hungary. Gukesh had earlier been the third-youngest GM at 12 years, 7 months, 17 days in 2019. Other notable young GMs include Praggnanandhaa (12 years, 10 months) and Leonid Ivanovich. The GM title is awarded by FIDE after three norms and a rating of 2500.
summary: The answer is (b): only Statement II is correct. Abhimanyu Mishra, an American of Indian origin, became the youngest Grandmaster in history in June 2021 at age 12 years, 4 months, 25 days. Statement I mixes up events: Gukesh's famous win was at the 2024 World Championship, not an Olympiad final.
topic_notes: Chess has featured heavily in recent current affairs. The Chess Olympiad is a biennial team event organised by FIDE (Fédération Internationale des Échecs, founded 1924, headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland). The 44th Olympiad was held in Chennai (Mamallapuram) in 2022, the first time in India, and the 45th in Budapest in 2024. India won its first-ever Olympiad gold medals (Open and Women's) in 2024. The Open team included Gukesh, Arjun Erigaisi, Praggnanandhaa, Vidit Gujrathi and Pentala Harikrishna. The Women's team included Harika Dronavalli, Divya Deshmukh, Vantika Agrawal, Vaishali and Tania Sachdev. The World Championship is a one-on-one match of 14 classical games. Viswanathan Anand was the first Indian GM (1988) and won the world title in 2000 and 2007-2013. Magnus Carlsen held the title from 2013 to 2023 and then declined to defend it. Ding Liren won in 2023 and Gukesh took the title in 2024. Gukesh also won the 2024 Candidates in Toronto at age 17, becoming the youngest challenger. Koneru Humpy won the 2024 Women's World Rapid Championship, and Divya Deshmukh won the 2024 World Junior Girls title. In 2025 Divya Deshmukh won the Women's World Cup, defeating Koneru Humpy in the final. Other angles: the FIDE rating system (Elo), the GM title requirements, the Chess Olympiad trophy names (Hamilton-Russell Cup for Open, Vera Menchik Cup for Women), and India's number of Grandmasters, which crossed 85.

question: Which one of the following Carnatic music 4, ragas is similar to Raga Bilawal in Hindustani music ?
subject: Art & Culture
detail: Hindustani music classifies ragas into ten thaats under the Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande system, and Bilawal is the thaat taken as the basic 'shuddha' (natural) scale. It uses Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni, all shuddha, and corresponds to the Western major (Ionian) scale. Carnatic music uses the 72 melakarta scheme attributed to Venkatamakhin and later systematised in the Katapayadi form. The 29th melakarta, Dheera Shankarabharanam (Sankarabharanam), has Shadja, Chatushruti Rishabha, Antara Gandhara, Shuddha Madhyama, Panchama, Chatushruti Dhaivata and Kakali Nishada. This matches the Bilawal notes exactly. Elimination: Nat Bhairavi is the Carnatic name linked to Hindustani Asavari/Natabhairavi (Aeolian, the natural minor), with flat Ga, Dha and Ni. Kamavardhini (Pantuvarali, 51st melakarta) has Ri1, Ga3, Ma2, so it matches Hindustani Poorvi. Hanumatodi (8th melakarta) has Ri1, Ga2, Da1, Ni2 and corresponds to Bhairavi thaat. So only (d) is the major scale.
explanations: Incorrect: Nat Bhairavi corresponds to the natural minor scale (Hindustani Asavari thaat), with komal Ga, Dha and Ni, not Bilawal.
Incorrect: Kamavardhini (Pantuvarali) has Ri1 and Ma2 (tivra Ma), so it matches Hindustani Poorvi thaat, not Bilawal.
Incorrect: Hanumatodi (Todi) has komal Re, Ga, Dha and Ni, so it corresponds to Hindustani Bhairavi thaat, not Bilawal.
Correct: Dheera Shankarabharanam, the 29th melakarta, has all the notes of Bilawal (S R2 G3 M1 P D2 N3), matching the Western major scale.
keyfact: Hindustani Bilawal = Carnatic Dheera Shankarabharanam (29th melakarta), the major scale.
option_notes: Nat Bhairavi is a Carnatic raga (Janya of the 20th melakarta Natabhairavi) whose scale resembles the Hindustani Asavari thaat and the Western natural minor. It has Sa, Ri2, Ga2, Ma1, Pa, Da1, Ni2. It is a popular raga in the Carnatic repertoire and used in light and film music, with a serious, devotional mood.

Kamavardhini is the 51st melakarta, better known as Pantuvarali. Its notes are S R1 G3 M2 P D1 N3, using a tivra Madhyama. Its Hindustani counterpart is Poorvi thaat. It is an evening raga with a deep, serious mood, and a janya of the Rudra chakra group, with Muthuswami Dikshitar composing in it.

Hanumatodi is the 8th melakarta (Todi in Hindustani usage, though the Hindustani Todi thaat differs). Its notes are S R1 G2 M1 P D1 N2. It corresponds to Bhairavi thaat and is a major, elaborate raga in the Carnatic system. It has a pathos-laden character and is performed as a main piece in concerts.

Dheera Shankarabharanam is the 29th melakarta, commonly called Sankarabharanam. Its notes are S R2 G3 M1 P D2 N3, equal to the Western major scale and Hindustani Bilawal. It is one of the most important Carnatic ragas, a favourite of Tyagaraja and others. It is a sampoorna raga that is also the parent of many janya ragas.
related: Bilawal is the 'shuddha' thaat of Bhatkhande's ten-thaat system.
Dheera Shankarabharanam is the 29th melakarta.
Carnatic has 72 melakartas in 12 chakras of 6 each.
Mayamalavagowla (15th melakarta) corresponds to Hindustani Bhairav.
Mechakalyani (65th) corresponds to Hindustani Kalyan (Yaman).
Harikambhoji (28th) corresponds to Hindustani Khamaj.
Natabhairavi (20th) corresponds to Hindustani Asavari.
Purandara Dasa is called the Pitamaha of Carnatic music.
summary: The answer is (d) Dheera Shankarabharanam, so the unofficial key is correct. Raga Bilawal is the Hindustani 'Shuddha' scale (Bilawal thaat) with all natural notes, and its Carnatic equivalent is the 29th melakarta, Dheera Shankarabharanam, which has the same notes (S R2 G3 M1 P D2 N3 S).
topic_notes: Indian classical music has two traditions, Hindustani (north) and Carnatic (south), sharing swaras but differing in classification and treatment. Hindustani ragas are grouped into ten thaats by V.N. Bhatkhande: Bilawal, Khamaj, Kafi, Asavari, Bhairavi, Bhairav, Kalyan, Marwa, Poorvi and Todi. Carnatic music uses the 72 melakarta (parent) ragas, arranged into 12 chakras of six ragas each, with the Katapayadi sutra giving the number from the name. Janya ragas derive from melakartas. The first 36 melakartas use Shuddha Madhyama (Ma1) and the last 36 use Prati Madhyama (Ma2). Key equivalents: Bilawal is Dheera Shankarabharanam (29), Kalyan is Mechakalyani (65), Khamaj is Harikambhoji (28), Kafi is Kharaharapriya (22) (approx., Kafi is also linked to Anandabhairavi), Asavari is Natabhairavi (20), Bhairavi is Hanumatodi (8), Bhairav is Mayamalavagowla (15), Poorvi is Kamavardhini or Pantuvarali (51), Marwa is Gamanashrama (53), and Todi is Subhapantuvarali (45). Carnatic music has the kriti as the major form, with the trinity Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar and Syama Sastri. Purandara Dasa is called the Pitamaha of Carnatic music. Hindustani has dhrupad, khayal, thumri and tappa forms. Tansen of Akbar's court and Amir Khusrau are notable figures. Other angles to know are the 22 shrutis, the saptak, vadi and samvadi, and rasas.

question: The artificially fixed rupee-sterling exchange rate prescribed by the Hilton-Young Commission (1926) was adopted by the British Government for which one of the following reasons ?
options: Aiding the flow of remittances from India and maintaining India’s creditworthiness
Encouraging export of cotton produce from India 5
Preventing depreciation of the Rupee in terms of gold
subject: Economy
detail: The Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance (1926), chaired by Edward Hilton-Young, reported in 1926 and its recommendations led to the Currency Act of 1927. It recommended a gold bullion standard, with no gold coins in circulation, and a rupee-sterling ratio of 1s 6d (18d), against the market rate of about 1s 4d. It also recommended setting up a central bank, which later became the RBI in 1935. The 1s 6d rate overvalued the rupee. An overvalued rupee made imports from Britain cheaper, hurt Indian exports (especially cotton and jute), and reduced the rupee burden of the Home Charges (interest, pensions, and administrative costs paid to Britain). It thereby favoured British interests and the flow of remittances to Britain. Indian nationalists, led by industrialists such as Purshottamdas Thakurdas and by the Indian National Congress, opposed 1s 6d and demanded 1s 4d. Elimination: (b) is wrong because the overvalued rupee actually hurt exporters and favoured importers only incidentally, and it was not the aim. (c) is wrong because an overvalued rupee discourages exports. (d) is a stated aim of currency stability, but it does not explain the specific choice of the 18d ratio. (a) fits the colonial economic motive best.
explanations: Most likely correct. An overvalued rupee (1s 6d) reduced the rupee cost of sterling obligations such as Home Charges, helped remittances to Britain, and preserved the creditworthiness of the Indian government in London.

Weak. Importers did benefit incidentally from the high rupee, but this was a side effect and not the stated reason. The question asks for the British Government's reason, and the Home Charges and remittance motive was the central one.
Wrong. A high rupee made Indian cotton costlier abroad and discouraged exports. The ratio hurt Indian exporters.

Plausible but weaker. The gold bullion standard aimed at stability, but the 18d ratio was higher than the market rate and was not set to prevent depreciation. The ratio served British remittance and trade interests.
keyfact: The Hilton-Young Commission (1926) fixed the rupee at 1s 6d, an overvaluation that favoured British remittances and trade at the cost of Indian exporters.
option_notes: Home Charges were the payments India made annually to Britain for interest on debt, pensions, and stores. Remittances were also made by British officials and traders. A higher rupee value made these obligations cheaper in rupee terms. India's creditworthiness in London mattered for borrowing and for confidence in the sterling-linked system.

Importers gain from an overvalued currency because foreign goods become cheaper in domestic terms. In the 1920s this mainly helped British manufactures such as Lancashire textiles, which were sold in India. Indian industrial interests such as the Bombay mill owners criticised the policy.

Cotton was a major Indian export, along with jute, tea, and wheat. A high rupee raised the foreign price of Indian goods and so reduced competitiveness. The Indian business community, including the Indian Merchants' Chamber, argued for 1s 4d to protect exporters.

The gold bullion standard of 1927 made the rupee convertible into gold bars of about 400 oz, with no gold coins in circulation. The aim was to link the rupee to gold for stability. In 1931, after Britain left the gold standard, the rupee was tied to sterling.
related: Hilton-Young Commission (1926) recommended 1s 6d per rupee and a gold bullion standard.
The Currency Act 1927 fixed the ratio at 18d.
The RBI was set up under the RBI Act 1934 and began operating on 1 April 1935.
Fowler Committee (1898) recommended 1s 4d and a gold standard.
Ambedkar wrote 'The Problem of the Rupee: Its Origin and Its Solution'.
Home Charges were India's payments to Britain for debt interest, pensions, and stores.
Britain left the gold standard in September 1931.
summary: The unofficial answer (a) is most likely correct. The Hilton-Young Commission recommended a gold bullion standard and a ratio of 1s 6d per rupee (18d), which overvalued the rupee. This helped the British government and British interests by making Home Charges and remittances to Britain cheaper in rupee terms, and by supporting British exports to India. (d) is the main distractor, since the commission's stated aim was stability linked to gold, but the colonial motive behind the 1s 6d rate is better captured by (a).
topic_notes: Indian currency history before independence is a recurring UPSC theme. After the 1893 Herschell Committee closed the mints to free silver coinage, the Fowler Committee (1898) recommended a gold standard with the rupee fixed at 1s 4d. The Gold Exchange Standard was adopted in 1899 to 1900 and was developed further by the Chamberlain Commission (1913) and by the writings of J. M. Keynes, who explained it in 'Indian Currency and Finance' (1913). The Babington Smith Committee (1919) recommended 2s per rupee, which failed in practice. The Hilton-Young Commission (1926) recommended 1s 6d, a gold bullion standard, and a central bank. The Currency Act of 1927 set the 18d ratio. The Reserve Bank of India Act of 1934 created the RBI, which began operating on 1 April 1935. Its first Governor was Osborne Smith. Dr B. R. Ambedkar's book 'The Problem of the Rupee' (1923) was presented to the commission and influenced its thinking. Other key points are the Home Charges, the drain theory of Dadabhai Naoroji, and Britain leaving the gold standard in 1931. After that, the rupee stayed linked to sterling at 1s 6d until independence, and in 1946 the Bretton Woods system came into place and India became a founding member of the IMF.

question:
Consider the following statements : 1s Pali texts contain the first definite references to coins, e.g., kahapana, nikkha, kamsa, and kakanika.
II. The literary evidence from Pali texts is corroborated by archaeological evidence of punch-marked coins from many sites, most of them made of silver. The above statements have been associated 6with which of the following ?
1. Emergence of urban life
2. Transition to money economy: Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: Pali texts such as the Vinaya Pitaka, Sutta Pitaka and Jatakas mention coin denominations like kahapana (karshapana), nikkha, kamsa and kakanika. Archaeology backs this up with punch-marked coins (PMC, also called Aahat or Purana), mostly silver, found at many sites. They were issued in the Mahajanapada period, roughly 6th-5th century BCE onward, and are the earliest coinage of India. Typical features are a silver bent bar or round shape and a weight standard of about 32 ratti (karshapana, c. 3.3-3.4 g). Symbols such as the sun, six-armed wheel, hill, tree, fish and animals were punched on them, often by different punches. Coinage meant standardised exchange, taxation in cash, and wage payment. It emerged with towns such as Rajagriha, Shravasti, Kaushambi, Vaishali, Ujjain and Varanasi, along with trade guilds (shrenis), merchants (setthis and gahapatis), and craft specialisation. So coins are evidence both for a money economy and for urban life. Because the statements concern coinage, option (b) alone is incomplete: coinage and the growth of cities and trade are linked in the second urbanisation, so (c) is correct. Option (a) wrongly leaves out the money-economy link, which is the most direct one. Option (d) is clearly wrong.
explanations: (a) is wrong: it leaves out the money economy, which coinage evidence supports most directly.
(b) is wrong: the money economy is clearly linked, but the statements are also associated with urbanisation, so 'only' is incorrect.
(c) is correct: coins named in texts and punch-marked silver coins mark both the transition to a money economy and the growth of towns, trade and guilds in the second urbanisation.
(d) is wrong: the statements are clearly associated with both themes.
keyfact: Pali kahapana and silver punch-marked coins point to both a money economy and the second urbanisation (c. 6th century BCE), so the answer is (c).
option_notes: Emergence of urban life: the second urbanisation (c. 6th century BCE) in the Gangetic plains, with the sixteen Mahajanapadas, fortified towns, iron use, rice agriculture, trade routes and guilds. Cities included Rajagriha, Shravasti, Kaushambi, Champa, Varanasi and Ujjain. Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) is its archaeological marker. The first urbanisation was the Harappan one, which declined around 1900 BCE.

Transition to money economy: the shift from barter and cattle or grain exchange to metallic currency. Punch-marked coins (6th century BCE onward) were the first Indian coins, in silver and copper, issued without inscriptions. Later came Indo-Greek coins with legends and portraits, Kushan gold coins, and Gupta dinaras. Coinage enabled taxation in cash, wage payment, and growth of trade and moneylending.

Both 1 and 2: the coin names in Pali texts and the archaeological punch-marked coins both indicate an urban, trade-oriented, monetised society. Mahajanapada-era towns, merchant guilds (shrenis), the setthi class and long-distance trade like the Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha depended on standardised currency. This is the combined answer.

Neither 1 nor 2: this would apply only if the statements were about unrelated themes, such as the rural economy, Vedic pastoralism or megalithic burials. Coinage is a core urban and monetary indicator, so it does not fit.
related: Kahapana = Pali form of karshapana, the standard silver PMC.
Punch-marked coins are the earliest Indian coinage, 6th century BCE onward, without legends.
Indo-Greeks introduced die-struck coins with portraits and legends.
Kushans issued the first large gold coinage in India; Guptas issued dinaras.
Northern Black Polished Ware marks the second urbanisation.
Arthashastra mentions the pana and mint officer Lakshanadhyaksha.
Satavahanas issued lead coins.
Sixteen Mahajanapadas are listed in the Anguttara Nikaya.
statements: I — Correct: Pali texts do mention coin names like kahapana, nikkha, kamsa and kakanika, which are the first definite literary references to coinage. Kahapana is the Pali form of karshapana, the standard silver punch-marked coin of about 32 ratti. Nikkha (nishka) was a gold ornament or unit of value, kamsa a bronze or metal vessel-like unit, and kakanika (kakini) a small copper denomination. The Pali Canon was compiled around the 5th century BCE onward, and the Jatakas frequently refer to payments in kahapanas.

II — Correct: Punch-marked coins have been found at many sites across the subcontinent, including Taxila, Mathura, Kaushambi, Patna, Ujjain, Eran and Amaravati. Hoards such as Bhir Mound (Taxila) and Chandravalli are known. They were mostly silver, with some copper, and are linked to the Mahajanapadas and later the Mauryas. They were issued by traders, guilds and states, and carry symbols stamped with separate punches. Archaeology thus corroborates the Pali literary record.
summary: The statements are associated with both the emergence of urban life and the transition to a money economy, so the answer is (c) Both 1 and 2. The unofficial answer (a) looks wrong: coins named in Pali texts and punch-marked silver coins show a monetised economy, which was tied to the second urbanisation of the Mahajanapada period (c. 6th-4th century BCE).
topic_notes: Indian coinage began with punch-marked coins (PMC) of the Mahajanapada period, roughly 6th-5th century BCE. Early texts call them karshapana or pana (Pali kahapana) or purana. Silver PMCs weighed about 32 ratti (about 3.3-3.5 g), and copper PMCs also existed. Early PMCs were issued by janapadas such as Kosala, Kashi, Avanti, Gandhara and Magadha. Magadhan PMCs later became the Mauryan standard, with Arthashastra mentions of the pana, with silver rupyarupa, copper tamrarupa, and officer Lakshanadhyaksha (mint) and Rupadarshaka (examiner). Coins were punched with separate symbols, with no legends. Indo-Greek rulers (Demetrius, Menander) introduced die-struck coins with portraits and legends. The Kushans (Kanishka, Vima Kadphises) issued gold coins. The Satavahanas issued lead coins and the Guptas issued gold dinaras, with gold coins declining after the Guptas, which some historians (R. S. Sharma) link to urban decline and 'feudalism'. Coin hoards and finds give evidence on trade, political history and chronology. Numismatics is therefore a key source. Related are the Roman gold coin finds in South India (Arikamedu), showing Indo-Roman trade, and the earliest inscriptions of Ashoka. Pali sources: Tipitaka (Vinaya, Sutta, Abhidhamma), Jatakas, and Digha Nikaya describing towns and trade. UPSC can ask about the second urbanisation, NBPW, the sixteen Mahajanapadas (Anguttara Nikaya list), guilds and the Mauryan economy.

question:
Which of the following temples has/have a Nagara-style shikhara ? ali Malegitti Shivalaya, Badami 2: Huchimalligudi Temple, Aihole
3. Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh 4. _Virupaksha Temple, Pattadakal Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Art & Culture
detail: Early Chalukya architecture at Badami, Aihole and Pattadakal experimented with both northern (Nagara) and southern (Dravida) forms, so the question tests which temple carries which superstructure. Nagara temples have a curvilinear (rekha-prasada) shikhara rising over the sanctum, usually on a plinth with no enclosing wall. Dravida temples have a pyramidal, stepped vimana of storeys topped by a domed stupika or shikhara. Malegitti Shivalaya (7th c., Badami) is an early Dravida temple with a stepped, pyramidal roof. Virupaksha (c. 740 CE, built by Queen Lokamahadevi, Vikramaditya II) is a mature Dravida temple modelled on the Kanchi Kailasanatha. Huchimalligudi (Aihole, 7th c.) has a Nagara-type curvilinear tower. Dashavatara at Deogarh (c. 500-525 CE, Gupta, UP, Vishnu) was among the first north Indian temples with a surviving shikhara. Elimination: Statements 1 and 4 are Dravida, so only 2 and 3 are correct, which is option (b). Options (a) and (d) each include a Dravida temple, and (c) omits 2.
explanations: Wrong: includes statement 1, Malegitti Shivalaya, which is Dravida in style.
Correct: Huchimalligudi (2) and Dashavatara Deogarh (3) both have Nagara shikharas.
Wrong: '3 only' ignores Huchimalligudi, which also has a Nagara shikhara. The unofficial key appears to be mistaken.
Wrong: includes statement 4, Virupaksha, which is Dravida in style, even though 3 is correct.
keyfact: Huchimalligudi (Aihole) and Dashavatara (Deogarh) are Nagara; Malegitti and Virupaksha are Dravida, so the answer is (b).
option_notes: Options 1 and 2: this pairing wrongly includes the Dravida Malegitti Shivalaya. Malegitti is an early 7th-century Chalukyan temple in Badami, on a rock outcrop, with a pyramidal tower. Huchimalligudi, though, is Nagara. Early Chalukya temples show mixed experiments, so the pair is a trap.

Options 2 and 3: this is the correct pairing. Huchimalligudi (Aihole, 7th c.) has a curvilinear shikhara. Dashavatara (Deogarh, Gupta, c. 500-525 CE) is a Vishnu temple with a Nagara tower, a pancharatha plan and famous sculpture panels. Together they show Nagara features in both central and south India.

Option 3 only: it names Dashavatara correctly but omits Huchimalligudi. Dashavatara is a Gupta temple at Deogarh on the Betwa, with Vishnu panels, a high plinth and a ruined tower. The option is incomplete and therefore wrong.

Options 3 and 4: this pairing wrongly includes Virupaksha. Virupaksha at Pattadakal (c. 740 CE) is Dravida, built by Lokamahadevi. It is a UNESCO site and a model for Ellora's Kailasa. Dashavatara is Nagara, but 4 is not.
related: Nagara temples have a curvilinear shikhara; Dravida temples have a pyramidal vimana.
Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh: Gupta, Vishnu, in Lalitpur, UP.
Virupaksha Temple, Pattadakal: built by Queen Lokamahadevi c. 740 CE.
Pattadakal became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.
Aihole's Meguti Jain temple has Ravikirti's inscription (634 CE).
Kandariya Mahadeva (Khajuraho) is a Chandela Nagara temple.
Vesara is the hybrid style of the Deccan.
Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur is a Chola Dravida temple (c. 1010 CE).
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Malegitti Shivalaya has a Dravida (southern) pyramidal vimana, not a Nagara shikhara. It is an early Chalukyan Shiva temple on a hillock at Badami, built in the 7th century. It is among the oldest surviving structural temples in Karnataka, with a square sanctum, a pillared porch and a stepped tower. It is dedicated to Shiva and sits near the Badami Bhutanatha group.

2 — Correct: Huchimalligudi has a Nagara-style curvilinear shikhara. It is a 7th-century Chalukyan temple at Aihole, Bagalkot district, Karnataka. It is notable for its Nagara tower and an ardhamandapa/porch with a sanctum. Aihole, known as the 'cradle of Indian temple architecture', has over 100 temples at the Durga, Ladkhan and Huchimalli sites. Its experiments mix Nagara and Dravida elements.

3 — Correct: Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh (Lalitpur, UP) is a Gupta temple of about the early 6th century (c. 500-525 CE). It is a Vishnu temple on a raised plinth, with a pancharatha plan and a high shikhara, now partly ruined. It has fine panels of Sheshashayi Vishnu, Nara-Narayana and Gajendra Moksha. It is an early example of Nagara style and a Gupta panchayatana-type temple.

4 — Incorrect: Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal is a Dravida temple with a multi-storeyed pyramidal vimana. It was built c. 740 CE by Queen Lokamahadevi, wife of Vikramaditya II, to commemorate his victory over the Pallavas. Its architect was Gundan Anivaritacharin. It has a pillared mandapa, a Nandi pavilion and a gateway. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site (1987), and inspired the Kailasa temple at Ellora.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 and 3, so the unofficial key (c) looks wrong, and in any case '3 only' does not fit because Huchimalligudi also has a Nagara shikhara. Dashavatara at Deogarh (Gupta) is an early Nagara temple. Huchimalligudi at Aihole has a curvilinear Nagara tower. Malegitti Shivalaya (Badami) and Virupaksha (Pattadakal) are Dravida.
topic_notes: Indian temple architecture is classified into Nagara (north), Dravida (south) and Vesara (hybrid, Deccan). Nagara temples have a curvilinear shikhara (rekha-prasada), a square plan with projecting ratha offshoots (pancharatha, saptaratha), an amalaka and kalasha at the top, and typically no boundary wall or large gateway. Dravida temples have a pyramidal vimana of storeys, a kalasha and stupika on top, an enclosing prakara wall, large gopurams and a water tank. Vesara blends both and is seen in Chalukya (Badami, Aihole, Pattadakal) and later Hoysala temples. Gupta temples include Dashavatara (Deogarh), Bhitargaon (brick) and Parvati temple (Nachna Kuthara). Aihole has Durga temple (apsidal), Lad Khan, Huchimalligudi and Meguti (Jain, 634 CE, with Ravikirti's inscription). Pattadakal (UNESCO 1987) has Nagara temples such as Papanatha and Kashi Vishwanatha, and Dravida ones such as Virupaksha, Sangameshvara and Mallikarjuna. Badami has cave temples (Caves 1-4) and the Bhutanatha group. Later Nagara examples include Khajuraho (Kandariya Mahadeva, Chandela, c. 1030), Lingaraja (Bhubaneswar), Jagannath (Puri), Konark Sun Temple (Odisha style) and Modhera Sun Temple (Solanki). South examples include Pallava Shore Temple and Kailasanatha at Kanchipuram, Brihadisvara at Thanjavur (Chola, 1010 CE) and Gangaikonda Cholapuram. Hoysala temples at Belur, Halebidu and Somnathpur have a stellate plan.

ocr: Among the four main forms of existence of life recognized in Jainism, which one of the following is not included ? (a) Deva (gods) (b) Yaksha (demi-gods) (c) Manushya (humans) (d) Tiryancha (animals and plants) The Hallisalasya painting in the Bagh Caves represents : (a) A joyous folk dance (b) Buddha in a meditative pose (c) The depiction of Shiva and Parvati on Kailasha (d) Samudramanthan (Churning of the Ocean) uf Consider the following statements relating to the use of the place-value system in India : 1. The earliest epigraphic use of the place-value system in India is found in the Mankan
subject: Art & Culture
detail: The question asks which pieces of evidence support two claims about the Rigvedic period. Claim I is that well irrigation let agriculture expand beyond flood plains. Claim II is that draught animals were used to draw water from wells. The Rigveda mentions khanitra (water dug up), avata (well or reservoir), kulya (channel), ashma-chakra (stone wheel or pulley) and ahava (a trough or pail that was filled and emptied). Together these show water-lifting devices on wells. Rigvedic society was pastoral-agricultural, and cattle were central to it. Oxen yoked to ploughs (langala, sira) and carts (anas) are well attested, and ox-drawn ploughing goes back to the Harappan period, for example the furrows at Kalibangan. Elimination: statement 2 (parashu/kulisha axe, datra/sreni sickle) shows only cutting and harvesting tools, so it supports neither well irrigation nor draught power. Any option that includes 2 is out, which removes (a) and (b). That leaves (c) and (d). Statement 1 clearly supports Claim I, so (d), which excludes 1, is out. The answer is (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 2, the axe and sickle, which says nothing about wells or draught power, and it leaves out statement 3.
Wrong: statement 2 is not evidence for either claim, so 'all three' is incorrect.
Correct: statement 1 (ashma chakra and ahava) supports well irrigation, and statement 3 (ox-drawn ploughing and carts) supports draught-animal power. Statement 2 is irrelevant.
Wrong: statement 3 alone omits statement 1, which is the most direct evidence of wells and water-lifting devices.
keyfact: Ashma-chakra and ahava (well-lifting devices) plus ox-drawn ploughing and carts support Rigvedic well irrigation and draught power; axe and sickle do not, so the answer is (c).
related: Ashma-chakra and ahava are the Rigvedic terms for the stone wheel and pail used to lift well water.
Langala or sira means plough, and sita means furrow, in the Rigveda.
Yava (barley) is the main cereal of the Rigveda.
Kalibangan has the earliest known ploughed field, a Harappan site.
Parashu means axe, and datra or sreni means sickle.
The Rigveda's Sarasvati is the most celebrated river, and the Sindhu is the most frequently mentioned.
Rigvedic political bodies were the sabha, samiti and vidatha.
Later Vedic texts show a bigger role for agriculture and the use of iron.
statements: 1 — Correct: Ashma chakra (stone wheel) and ahava (strapped pails) are water-lifting devices, which supports Claim I (well irrigation). A strapped-bucket and wheel system also implies hauling power, which suits Claim II. The Rigveda (for example 10.101.7 and 10.102.11) refers to wells, wheels and buckets. Irrigation by wells and channels (kulya) is attested, and ahava is a trough or pail. These references show that Rigvedic people lifted groundwater and so could farm land beyond the flood plains of the Sapta Sindhu, the Punjab and Haryana region.

2 — Incorrect: Parashu or kulisha (axe) and datra or sreni (sickle) show tools for felling trees, clearing land and reaping. They do not show irrigation or the use of animal power at wells. The Rigveda mentions the parashu as a tool and as a weapon, and the sickle for harvesting barley (yava), the main Rigvedic cereal. These items show cultivation and clearing in general. They are not evidence for lifting water from wells or for yoked animals.

3 — Correct: The use of oxen, even before the Rigveda, to plough and pull carts supports Claim II, because it shows that people could harness draught animals and could therefore use them to draw water. The Harappan ploughed field at Kalibangan, terracotta bull and plough models, and bullock carts at Harappan sites show animal traction well before the Rigvedic period. The Rigveda has many references to oxen (ukshan), the plough (langala) and carts (anas).
summary: The answer is (c) 1 and 3 only, so the unofficial key looks correct. Information 1 (ashma chakra and ahava) directly shows well-irrigation using a wheel and strapped pails. Information 3 (oxen used for ploughing and pulling carts) supports the use of draught-animal power. Information 2 (axe and sickle) says nothing about wells or animal power.
topic_notes: The Rigvedic (early Vedic) period is dated roughly 1500-1000 BCE. Its people lived mainly in the Sapta Sindhu region, the Punjab and Haryana plains. The economy was pastoral first and agriculture became more important over time. Cattle were the main wealth, and terms such as gavishti (search for cows) and gomat reflect this. Common cereals were yava (barley) and dhanya. The plough was called langala or sira, and furrows were sita. Water sources and structures included kupa and avata (wells), kulya (channels) and khanitra (dug water). The ashma-chakra and ahava belong to well-based lifting systems. Tools mentioned include the parashu (axe), the datra or sreni (sickle) and the sup (winnowing basket). Rigvedic society was tribal, with kinship units of kula, grama, vis and jana. Political bodies were the sabha, samiti, vidatha and gana. The chief was the rajan, helped by the purohita and senani. Taxes were bali, a voluntary offering. Later Vedic texts show a growing role for agriculture, iron (shyama or krishna ayas), a wider variety of crops such as rice (vrihi) and wheat (godhuma), and the idea of private landholding. Related Harappan evidence includes the ploughed field at Kalibangan, bullock carts and canal remains at Dholavira. Typical UPSC angles on this topic are Rigvedic terms and their meanings, comparisons of Rigvedic and later Vedic society, rivers (Sindhu, Sarasvati, Drishadvati), and archaeological links such as the PGW and OCP cultures.

ocr: Consider the following assertion : 14. In the Pleistocene period either the Yamuna once flowed into the Indus, or the Sutlej flowed into the Yamuna and one major tributary of either had shifted from the Ganga to the Indus or vice versa. Which of the following is/are the basis of the above assertion ? 1. The Nadi-Sukta of the Rigveda 2. The explorations of the Sutlej and the Yamuna by Robert Bruce Foote 3. The presence of the same species of dolphins in both the Indus and the Ganga river systems Select the answer using the code given below : (a) lonly (b) 2only (c) land2 (dd) 8
subject: Ancient History
detail: The assertion is a geomorphological hypothesis: during the Pleistocene (about 2.58 million to 11,700 years ago), the Yamuna may once have drained westward into the Indus system, or the Sutlej may have flowed into the Yamuna, and a major tributary may have shifted between the Ganga and Indus basins. The Ghaggar-Hakra palaeochannel debate and the Sutlej-Yamuna river capture ideas belong to this field. The basis for such a claim must be scientific evidence about the Pleistocene, such as geology, sediment provenance or biogeography. Statement 3 is the best fit: the South Asian river dolphin (Platanista gangetica) occurs in both the Ganga-Brahmaputra and Indus systems (the Indus subspecies is P. g. minor). Freshwater dolphins cannot cross land or the sea, so the same species in both systems suggests past connectivity of the drainage. The Nadi-Sukta (Rigveda 10.75) is a hymn listing rivers from the Ganga/Yamuna westward to the Indus and its tributaries, and it describes the Vedic geography of roughly 1500-1000 BCE, which is Holocene, not Pleistocene. R. B. Foote (1830s-1912) was a geologist who pioneered Indian prehistory and surveyed Tamil Nadu and Gujarat, but he did not explore the Sutlej and Yamuna to establish Pleistocene river shifts. So only statement 3 holds, and (d) is correct.
explanations: Wrong: statement 1 alone is a Vedic-era literary description (Holocene) and does not establish a Pleistocene drainage shift, and statement 3 is also a basis.
Wrong: Foote's work was on prehistoric archaeology and geology of peninsular India, not on proving Pleistocene Sutlej-Yamuna changes, and statement 3 is also a basis.
Wrong: both statements 1 and 2 fail for the Pleistocene claim, and this pair omits statement 3, which is the valid basis.
Correct: only statement 3, the shared dolphin species in the Indus and Ganga systems, gives natural-history evidence for a past connection between the drainage systems.
keyfact: The same river dolphin species in the Indus and Ganga systems (Platanista gangetica) is biogeographic evidence of past drainage connection, so only statement 3 is correct: (d).
option_notes: Statement 1 alone: the Nadi-Sukta (Rigveda 10.75) is a hymn praising rivers in a west-to-east listing from the Indus to the Ganga. It is a key source for Vedic geography and for the Sarasvati identification debate. It is composed in the late Rigvedic period, around 1500-1000 BCE. It is a literary source and so is not a scientific basis for Pleistocene events.

Statement 2 alone: R. B. Foote (1834-1912) was a British geologist of the Geological Survey of India. He is called the father of Indian prehistory because of the 1863 Pallavaram Palaeolithic find. He documented Stone Age sites across south and western India and the Billa Surgam caves. His collection is in the Chennai Government Museum. He was not known for work establishing Sutlej-Yamuna drainage history.

Statements 1 and 2 only: this combination pairs a Vedic literary source with a prehistory and geology survey. Neither one provides evidence about Pleistocene drainage shifts, so the combination is invalid. Remember that the Pleistocene is the older epoch (2.58 million to 11,700 years ago), while Vedic texts belong to the Holocene.

Statement 3 only: the South Asian river dolphin (Platanista gangetica) is found in both the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna and the Indus systems. The Indus subspecies is P. g. minor (bhulan). It is the National Aquatic Animal of India, is Endangered on the IUCN Red List, is in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, and is the focus of Project Dolphin.
related: Ganges river dolphin is India's National Aquatic Animal (2009).
Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary in Bihar is the only dolphin sanctuary in India.
Project Dolphin was announced on 15 August 2020 by the Government of India.
The Indus river dolphin (bhulan) survives in the Beas in Punjab.
Nadi-Sukta is Rigveda 10.75 and lists the Vedic rivers.
Pleistocene is about 2.58 million to 11,700 years ago, followed by the Holocene.
R. B. Foote found the Pallavaram hand axe in 1863.
The Ghaggar-Hakra palaeochannel is often linked with the Vedic Sarasvati.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Nadi-Sukta describes rivers in the time of the Rigveda, which is Holocene (c. 1500-1000 BCE), not Pleistocene. It is a literary source and cannot establish a Pleistocene drainage shift. Facts: it is Rigveda Book 10, hymn 75, in the Mandala 10 group of later hymns. It lists rivers in a geographical order from east to west: Ganga, Yamuna, Sarasvati, Sutudri (Sutlej), Parushni (Ravi), Asikni (Chenab), Marudvridha, Vitasta (Jhelum), Arjikiya and then the Sushoma and others. The Indus is praised as the foremost river, and the hymn is the most important Vedic source for river geography. It is often cited in the Sarasvati debate, but it does not date any drainage change.

2 — Incorrect: Robert Bruce Foote is known as the father of Indian prehistory, not for exploring the Sutlej and Yamuna to prove Pleistocene river shifts. Facts: he was a British geologist with the Geological Survey of India and in 1863 discovered a Palaeolithic hand axe at Pallavaram near Madras. He did extensive survey work in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra and Gujarat and also studied caves such as the Billa Surgam caves in Kurnool. His collection of Indian prehistoric artefacts went to the Madras Government Museum. His work concerned stone-age cultures and geology, not river-capture questions in the Indus-Ganga region.

3 — Correct: The South Asian river dolphin occurs in both the Indus and the Ganga-Brahmaputra systems, which is biogeographic evidence of past connectivity. Facts: Platanista gangetica (Ganges river dolphin) is called susu and is the National Aquatic Animal of India (declared 2009). The Indus river dolphin is P. g. minor (bhulan), found in Pakistan's Indus and a small population in the Beas in Punjab, India. They are functionally blind and use echolocation. They are listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List and are in Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972. Project Dolphin was announced in 2020, and Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary in Bihar is the only dolphin sanctuary in India.
summary: The unofficial key (d) looks correct: only statement 3 is a valid basis. The assertion is about Pleistocene river capture and drainage shifts between the Indus and Ganga systems, which is supported by the biogeographic evidence of the same dolphin species (Platanista gangetica) in both systems. The Nadi-Sukta is a Vedic-period text and Foote's work was on prehistoric archaeology and geology, so neither supports a Pleistocene drainage-change claim directly.
topic_notes: The topic is the evolution of the Indus-Ganga drainage and the Pleistocene history of the Himalayan rivers. Rivers of the north Indian plains have changed course through tectonics, climate shifts and river capture. The Sutlej and Yamuna are often discussed in this context. Geologists suggest the Sutlej once flowed partly into the Ghaggar-Hakra channel and the Yamuna may have flowed westward into the same system, and that later tectonic uplift and capture turned them to the Indus and the Ganga respectively. The Ghaggar-Hakra system is linked by some scholars to the Vedic Sarasvati, and the Indus Valley (Harappan) settlements along the dry channel in Haryana, Rajasthan and Cholistan, such as Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi and Ganweriwala, are discussed in this context. Evidence used by geologists includes palaeochannels, sediment provenance, satellite imagery and optically stimulated luminescence dating. Biogeography uses species distribution, and the river dolphin is a classic example. Key facts: the Ganges river dolphin was declared National Aquatic Animal in 2009 (Prime Minister's National River Ganga Basin Authority meeting), and the Vikramshila sanctuary (Bhagalpur, Bihar) was notified in 1991. Project Dolphin was announced on 15 August 2020 and is led by MoEFCC. The International Whaling Commission and the CMS (Appendix I) also list river dolphins. The Indus dolphin is found in the Beas (Punjab), where a population was confirmed in 2007. Other possible angles are the Pleistocene and Holocene boundary at 11,700 years ago, the Siwalik formation and the Himalayan foreland basin, the Ganga's tributary changes such as the Kosi shifting over 100 km, and the Vedic river names (Ganga as Jahnavi, Sutlej as Shutudri, Beas as Vipasa, Ravi as Parushni, Chenab as Asikni, Jhelum as Vitasta).

question: What does an empty seat represent in early Buddhist iconography ?
subject: Ancient History
detail: Early Buddhist art, roughly 3rd century BCE to 1st century CE, was aniconic. Depicting the Buddha as a person was avoided, probably out of reverence, and his presence was shown through symbols. The common symbols were the Bodhi tree with an empty seat or vajrasana (enlightenment and meditation), the Dharmachakra or wheel (First Sermon at Sarnath), the stupa (Mahaparinirvana at Kushinagar), a riderless horse with an umbrella (the Great Departure, Mahabhinishkramana), the lotus (birth), and footprints (buddhapada). The empty throne is a seat of meditation and awakening, so it stands for the Buddha seated in dhyana under the Bodhi tree. Elimination: (b) the First Sermon is shown by the wheel, often with deer; (c) Mahaparinibbana is shown by the stupa; (d) Mahabhinishkramana is shown by the horse Kanthaka with no rider, with Chandaka holding an umbrella over the empty space. That leaves (a). Anthropomorphic images of the Buddha began around the 1st century CE in Gandhara and Mathura, under Kushana patronage.
explanations: Correct. The empty seat or throne, usually under the Bodhi tree, signifies the Buddha's presence in meditation and enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, as in the Bharhut and Sanchi reliefs.
Incorrect. The First Sermon at Sarnath (Dhammachakkappavattana) is symbolised by the Dharmachakra, the wheel, often flanked by deer, not by an empty seat.
Incorrect. Mahaparinibbana, the death of the Buddha at Kushinagar, is symbolised by the stupa, not by an empty seat.
Incorrect. Mahabhinishkramana, the Great Renunciation, is shown by a riderless horse (Kanthaka) with an umbrella held over the empty space, not by an empty seat.
keyfact: Early aniconic Buddhist art: empty seat/Bodhi tree = meditation and enlightenment; wheel = First Sermon; stupa = Mahaparinirvana; riderless horse = Great Renunciation.
option_notes: Meditation of the Buddha: the Buddha meditated under the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya (Bihar) and attained enlightenment (nirvana) at about age 35, after Sujata's offering and Mara's temptation. In aniconic art this is shown by the empty vajrasana, the diamond throne, beside the Bodhi tree. The Mahabodhi temple at Bodh Gaya is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2002).

First Sermon: the Buddha's first teaching to the five ascetics at Isipatana (Sarnath, near Varanasi) is called Dhammachakkappavattana, 'turning the wheel of dharma'. It set out the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. Its symbol is the Dharmachakra, often with deer, as on the Ashokan Sarnath pillar capital. It is commemorated on Asalha Puja (Dhamma Chakra Day).

Mahaparinibbana: the Buddha's final passing away at Kushinagar (Kushinara, Uttar Pradesh), at about age 80, in the Malla territory, around 483 or 400 BCE depending on the chronology. The Mahaparinibbana Sutta of the Digha Nikaya records it. Its symbol is the stupa, and the relics were divided among eight claimants and enshrined in stupas.

Mahabhinishkramana: the Great Renunciation, when Prince Siddhartha left Kapilavastu at 29, leaving his wife Yashodhara and son Rahula, on his horse Kanthaka with the charioteer Channa (Chandaka). Aniconic reliefs show a riderless horse with an umbrella above. It is one of the four great sights/events, together with birth, enlightenment and death, that mark his life.
related: Aniconic phase of Buddhist art lasted until about the 1st century CE.
Dharmachakra symbolises the First Sermon at Sarnath.
Stupa symbolises Mahaparinirvana.
Riderless horse Kanthaka symbolises the Great Departure.
Lotus symbolises the Buddha's birth.
Gandhara and Mathura schools produced the first human images of the Buddha.
Bhumisparsha mudra represents enlightenment at Bodh Gaya.
Bharhut stupa is Shunga-period, with Jataka reliefs and labelling inscriptions.
summary: The answer is (a). In early aniconic Buddhist art (Bharhut, Sanchi, Amaravati), the Buddha was not shown in human form. An empty seat or throne, often the vajrasana under the Bodhi tree, stood for his presence in meditation and enlightenment. The unofficial key (a) is correct, though 'enlightenment' is the more precise label, and (a) is the closest option.
topic_notes: Aniconism in early Buddhist art: before the Kushana period, the Buddha was not shown in human form in Hinayana-phase art. Symbols stood in for him. The key events and their symbols are: birth at Lumbini (lotus or Maya's dream of a white elephant); renunciation (horse Kanthaka, riderless); enlightenment (Bodhi tree, empty throne or vajrasana); First Sermon (Dharmachakra, deer); Mahaparinirvana (stupa); and general veneration (footprints or buddhapada, and the triratna symbol). The main sites are the Bharhut stupa (Shunga period, 2nd century BCE, with Jataka scenes and labelling inscriptions), the Sanchi stupas (Mauryan core under Ashoka, with toranas added in the Satavahana period, 1st century BCE to 1st century CE), the Amaravati and Nagarjunakonda stupas (Andhra, Satavahana and Ikshvaku), and Bodh Gaya railings. The turn to human images of the Buddha came around the 1st to 2nd centuries CE, in two schools: Gandhara (Greco-Roman influence, grey schist, wavy hair, drapery) and Mathura (indigenous, red sandstone, a Yaksha-like form). The Gupta period (Sarnath school) produced the classical Buddha image. Related ideas: the Mahayana phase brought Bodhisattva worship and image-making; the four main pilgrimage sites are Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar; and the mudras are Dhyana (meditation), Bhumisparsha (earth-touching, enlightenment), Dharmachakra (preaching) and Abhaya (fearlessness). Other angles UPSC may ask: Ashokan pillars and edicts, the rock-cut chaityas and viharas at Karle, Ajanta and Bhaja, the Buddhist councils, and the Jataka scenes.

question:
Which of the following pairs of ancient and modern names of rivers is/are correctly matched ?
1. ‘Vitasta z Chenab
2. Asikni : Jhelum
3. Parushni i Ravi
4. Yavyavati B Beas Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Geography
detail: The Rig Veda's Nadistuti Sukta (X.75) and the Dasarajna battle hymn (VII.18) name the rivers of the Sapta Sindhu region. The standard ancient-to-modern equivalents are: Sutudri = Sutlej; Vipasa = Beas; Parushni (Iravati) = Ravi; Asikni = Chenab (Greek Acesines); Vitasta = Jhelum (Greek Hydaspes); Sindhu = Indus; Saraswati = the Ghaggar-Hakra (traditional identification). Greek names are often tested alongside: Hyphasis = Beas, Hydraotes = Ravi, Acesines = Chenab, Hydaspes = Jhelum, Zaradros = Sutlej. Yavyavati is a minor Rigvedic river that is generally not identified with the Beas; some scholars link it to a tributary of the Indus or the Gomal. Elimination: Vitasta is the Jhelum, so pair 1 is wrong. Asikni is the Chenab, so pair 2 is wrong. Pair 3 is correct. Beas is Vipasa, so pair 4 is wrong. Only pair 3 survives, which matches the option 'only 3'. The OCR of the options is corrupted, so the student should match the option that says 3 only.
explanations: Wrong: pairs 1 and 2 are both incorrectly matched, since Vitasta is the Jhelum and Asikni is the Chenab.
Wrong: pair 3 is correct but pair 4 is not, because the Beas was Vipasa and not Yavyavati.
Right if read as '3 only': Parushni = Ravi is the sole correct pair. The OCR text '30 only' is garbled and most likely means 3 only.
Wrong: pair 4 is incorrect, since Yavyavati is not the Beas, and it also leaves out the correct pair 3.
keyfact: Vitasta = Jhelum, Asikni = Chenab, Parushni = Ravi, Vipasa = Beas, Sutudri = Sutlej.
option_notes: Pairs 1 and 2 are the Vitasta and Asikni pairings. Vitasta is the Jhelum (Hydaspes), which rises at Verinag and flows through Srinagar and Wular Lake. Asikni is the Chenab (Acesines), formed by the Chandra and Bhaga at Tandi. Both are western rivers under the Indus Waters Treaty and are allotted to Pakistan. As matched in the question, both pairs are swapped or wrong.

Pairs 3 and 4 are the Parushni and Yavyavati pairings. Parushni is the Ravi, but Yavyavati is not the Beas; the Beas is Vipasa (Greek Hyphasis). The Beas rises near Rohtang and joins the Sutlej at Harike. Yavyavati is a minor Rigvedic river. The combination fails because of pair 4.

This option reads as '3 only' (the OCR shows '30 only'). The Parushni, or Iravati, is the Ravi (Greek Hydraotes). It rises in Himachal Pradesh near Rohtang, flows past Chamba and the Punjab border, and joins the Chenab in Pakistan. It is an eastern river under the Indus Waters Treaty, and Ranjit Sagar Dam is on it.

This option says only pair 4 is correct. Yavyavati is a little-known Rigvedic river that is not the Beas. The Beas is Vipasa, also called Arjikiya in some Vedic texts. It flows through Himachal Pradesh and Punjab, passes Manali and Kullu, and has the Pong and Pandoh dams. The Beas-Sutlej link is also connected to the Indus Waters Treaty.
related: Vitasta = Jhelum = Hydaspes; Alexander defeated Porus there in 326 BCE.
Asikni = Chenab = Acesines; formed by Chandra and Bhaga at Tandi.
Parushni (Iravati) = Ravi = Hydraotes; site of the Dasarajna battle.
Vipasa = Beas = Hyphasis; Alexander's army turned back here.
Sutudri = Sutlej = Zaradros; it flows from Rakshastal near Mansarovar.
Indus Waters Treaty 1960: India gets Ravi, Beas and Sutlej; Pakistan gets Indus, Jhelum and Chenab.
Rigveda's Nadistuti Sukta is in Mandala X, hymn 75.
The Beas is the only Punjab river wholly within India.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Vitasta is the Jhelum, not the Chenab. The Vitasta is the Jhelum of Kashmir, called Hydaspes by the Greeks and Behat in Kashmiri. It rises at Verinag in the Pir Panjal range, flows through Srinagar and Wular Lake, and joins the Chenab near Trimmu in Pakistan. The Indus Waters Treaty (1960) assigns it to Pakistan as a western river. Alexander fought Porus on its banks in 326 BCE, the Battle of the Hydaspes.

2 — Incorrect: Asikni is the Chenab, not the Jhelum. The Rigvedic Asikni, meaning dark-coloured, is the Chenab, which the Greeks called Acesines. It is formed by the union of Chandra and Bhaga at Tandi in Lahaul, Himachal Pradesh, and is also called Chandrabhaga. It flows through Jammu and Kashmir into Pakistan, where it joins the Sutlej to form the Panjnad. Projects on it include Salal, Baglihar and Dulhasti.

3 — Correct: Parushni is the Ravi. Parushni, also called Iravati, is the Ravi, the Greek Hydraotes. It rises near Rohtang in the Kullu Himalaya of Himachal Pradesh, flows past Chamba, and then runs along the India-Pakistan border near Gurdaspur. It meets the Chenab in Pakistan. It is one of the three eastern rivers allotted to India by the Indus Waters Treaty, and Ranjit Sagar (Thein) Dam is on it. The Dasarajna battle was fought on its banks.

4 — Incorrect: Yavyavati is not the Beas; the Beas is the Vipasa. Vipasa, the Greek Hyphasis, rises near Beas Kund by the Rohtang Pass and joins the Sutlej at Harike in Punjab. It marks the eastern limit of Alexander's advance, where his army refused to go further. The Beas is the only major Indus-system river entirely within India. Yavyavati is a minor Rigvedic stream with uncertain identification.
summary: The unofficial key (c) is wrong as far as I can tell; the correct answer appears to be (c) only if it means 'Parushni–Ravi' alone, but the OCR'd option '30 only' is garbled. Reading the OCR as '3 only', that is correct: only pair 3 (Parushni = Ravi) is correctly matched. Vitasta is the Jhelum, Asikni is the Chenab, and Vipasa (not Yavyavati) is the Beas, so pairs 1, 2 and 4 are wrong.
topic_notes: The Rigveda describes a land of seven rivers (Sapta Sindhu), and the Nadistuti Sukta (X.75) lists the major ones in geographic order from east to west. The Indus system's five Punjab tributaries are the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, which together form the Panjnad. Ancient Sanskrit names and their modern equivalents: Sutudri/Shutudri = Sutlej; Vipasa = Beas; Parushni/Iravati = Ravi; Asikni = Chenab; Vitasta = Jhelum; Sindhu = Indus; Kubha = Kabul; Gomati = Gomal; Krumu = Kurram; Suvastu = Swat; Saraswati = Ghaggar-Hakra by common identification. Greek names are also tested: Hydaspes = Jhelum, Acesines = Chenab, Hydraotes = Ravi, Hyphasis = Beas, Zaradros = Sutlej, Indos = Indus. The Dasarajna (Battle of Ten Kings) took place on the Parushni, where Sudas defeated a confederation of ten tribes. The Indus Waters Treaty (1960), brokered by the World Bank, gave India the eastern rivers Ravi, Beas and Sutlej and Pakistan the western rivers Indus, Jhelum and Chenab, with limited use for India on the western rivers. Rivers linked to Gangetic history include Ganga (Jahnavi, Bhagirathi), Yamuna (Kalindi), Gandak (Sadanira), Kosi (Kausiki), Son (Hiranyabahu) and Sarayu. In the south, Godavari is Gautami and Krishna is Krishnaveni. Peninsular names such as Pennar (Pinakini) and Kaveri (Ponni) are also useful. UPSC often pairs ancient names with Greek names or battle sites, so learn all three for each river.

question:
Which of the following statements on the Amaravati Stupa and its relief sculpture is/are correct ? iG It was located in the lower Krishna valley.
2. In India, it was next only to the Sanchi Stupa in size.
3. The Amaravati school of sculpture made a lasting impact on the later South Indian sculpture, and its products were carried to Sri Lanka and South-east Asia. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Art & Culture
detail: Amaravati (ancient Dhanyakataka, Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh) lies on the Krishna river's lower valley. The Mahachaitya began in the Mauryan period (c. 3rd century BCE) and was enlarged and decorated under the Satavahanas and later the Ikshvakus, up to about the 3rd century CE. Its casing slabs, drum slabs, railings and ayaka platforms were carved in a pale greenish-white Palnad limestone. The style is known for slender, dynamic, tribhanga figures and crowded narrative panels such as Jataka scenes. Early panels show the Buddha aniconically (stupa, footprints, empty throne, Bodhi tree, wheel), and later panels show him in human form. The style travelled by sea and monastic networks to Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam, and it influenced Pallava and Chola sculpture. Colin Mackenzie surveyed the site in 1797. Many sculptures went to the Madras Museum, the British Museum ('Elliot Marbles') and the Amaravati Site Museum. Elimination logic: statement 1 is certainly correct and statement 3 is a standard art-history point, so (b) or (d) remains. Statement 2 fails because the stupa's diameter of about 50 m exceeded Sanchi's 36.6 m, so the ranking claim is unsound. That leaves (b).
explanations: (a) 1 only: Wrong, because statement 3 is also correct, so this option is incomplete.
(b) 1 and 3 only: Correct. The location in the lower Krishna valley and the wide artistic influence are both accurate, and statement 2 is rejected.
(c) 2 and 3 only: Wrong, because statement 2 is not accepted and statement 1 is correct but omitted.
(d) 1, 2 and 3: Wrong, because statement 2 wrongly ranks Amaravati as second to Sanchi in size; Amaravati's base diameter was larger than Sanchi's.
keyfact: Amaravati (Guntur, lower Krishna) was South India's largest stupa, larger than Sanchi's, and its art influenced Sri Lanka and South-east Asia.
related: Amaravati was ancient Dhanyakataka, a Satavahana-era Buddhist centre in Guntur district.
Amaravati sculpture is carved in Palnad limestone (greenish-white).
The three major early schools of Buddhist art are Gandhara, Mathura and Amaravati.
Nagarjunakonda was the Ikshvaku capital Vijayapuri, now an island museum in Nagarjuna Sagar.
Colin Mackenzie surveyed Amaravati in 1797.
Sanchi Stupa 1 is in Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh, and a UNESCO site since 1989.
Early Buddhist art showed the Buddha aniconically through the wheel, footprints, Bodhi tree and stupa.
The Amaravati Buddha style travelled to Sri Lanka and South-east Asia.
statements: 1 — Correct: Amaravati stands on the right bank of the Krishna in Guntur district, in the lower Krishna valley (Krishna–Guntur region). Amaravati was ancient Dhanyakataka (Dhaanyakatakam), a major Buddhist centre and a Satavahana and later Ikshvaku-era centre. The Mahachaitya began around the 3rd century BCE (Ashokan/Mauryan phase) and was expanded until about the 3rd century CE. Nagarjunakonda, also in the lower Krishna valley, is a nearby Buddhist site. Colin Mackenzie surveyed the ruins in 1797. Later excavations were by Walter Elliot, Robert Sewell, James Burgess and Alexander Rea. The Kalachakra initiation was held here in 2006.

2 — Incorrect: The claim that it was 'next only to Sanchi' in size is unsupported. The Amaravati Mahastupa had a base diameter of roughly 50 m and a height of about 27–30 m, so it is usually called the largest stupa in South India. By comparison, Sanchi Stupa 1 has a diameter of about 36.6 m and a height of about 16.5 m, built of brick and stone in a Mauryan core later enlarged under the Shungas. Sanchi is in Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh, and is a UNESCO site (1989). Its torana gateways of the Satavahana period carry famous narrative carvings. Sanchi is therefore not a size benchmark that places Amaravati second.

3 — Correct: The Amaravati school (Andhra school) is one of the three major early Buddhist art schools, along with Gandhara and Mathura. Its slender, graceful, flowing figures, strong narrative panels and use of white limestone shaped later Pallava, Chola and Andhra art. Through maritime trade and monastic exchange, Amaravati-style Buddha images and motifs reached Sri Lanka (Anuradhapura), Thailand, Myanmar, Indonesia, Vietnam and Java. Examples include bronze Buddhas found at Dong Duong in Vietnam and in Sulawesi. Its dated influence runs from the 2nd century BCE to the 3rd century CE and later.
summary: The correct answer is (b), 1 and 3 only, so the unofficial key is right. Amaravati lay in the lower Krishna valley (Guntur, Andhra Pradesh), and its sculptural school strongly influenced later South Indian art, Sri Lanka and South-east Asia. Statement 2 is wrong because the Amaravati Mahastupa is generally described as the largest stupa of South India and, in its base diameter, larger than Sanchi's Great Stupa, so 'next only to Sanchi' is incorrect.
topic_notes: Buddhist art in India developed in several regional schools. Sanchi, Bharhut and Bodh Gaya reflect the early aniconic phase (Shunga and Satavahana periods). Gandhara (Indo-Greek influence, grey schist, Kushana) and Mathura (indigenous, red sandstone, Kushana) produced the first Buddha images, around the 1st–2nd centuries CE. The Andhra school, which includes Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Jaggayyapeta and Goli, used Palnad limestone. Amaravati is known for lively narratives, the tribhanga pose, railings, drum slabs and ayaka platforms. The Amaravati Mahachaitya was probably founded under Ashoka and later enriched under the Satavahanas (Vasishthiputra Pulumavi and others) and the Ikshvakus. Nagarjunakonda in the Krishna valley (Ikshvaku capital Vijayapuri) was submerged under the Nagarjuna Sagar reservoir. Its monuments were relocated to an island museum. Amaravati sculptures are held at the Government Museum in Chennai, the British Museum (Elliot Marbles) and the Amaravati Archaeological Museum. Maritime trade (Roman and South-east Asian) helped spread the style to Sri Lanka and South-east Asia, for example Buddha images in Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam. Other stupa details to remember: Sanchi (UNESCO 1989, Ashoka, Shunga enlargement, Satavahana toranas), Bharhut (Madhya Pradesh, Shunga, now in the Kolkata Indian Museum), Sarnath (Dhamek Stupa, Gupta era), Piprahwa (Buddha relics), Kesaria (Bihar, very large). The tribhanga posture and the Buddhist symbols (wheel, footprints, empty throne, stupa, Bodhi tree) are common prelims angles.

question:
Which of the following pairs of the king and his dynasty in early historical Tamilakam is/are not correctly matched ?
1. Senguttuvan : Chera
2. Udiyanjeral : Chola
3. Nedunjeliyan : Pandya Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Ancient History
detail: Early historical Tamilakam (c. 300 BCE to 300 CE) was ruled by the Three Crowned Kings: the Cheras (Vanji, in the west and Kerala; symbol bow and arrow), the Cholas (Uraiyur and Puhar; symbol tiger) and the Pandyas (Madurai and Korkai; symbol fish). Our main sources are Sangam literature (Ettuthogai, Pattuppattu, Silappadikaram, Manimekalai), the Asokan inscriptions (Rock Edict II and XIII mention Cholas, Pandyas, Keralaputra and Satiyaputa), Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions and Greek and Roman accounts. The question asks which pairs are NOT correctly matched. Senguttuvan, the 'Red Chera', is linked with the Pattini (Kannagi) cult and the Silappadikaram, so pair 1 is correct. Nedunjeliyan, who won at Talaiyalanganam and is associated with the Kovalan episode in the Silappadikaram, was a Pandya, so pair 3 is correct. Udiyanjeral is the Chera king who fed both armies at Kurukshetra according to tradition, so pair 2 is incorrect. Only pair 2 is wrong, hence (b).
explanations: Wrong. This would mean pairs 1 and 2 are incorrectly matched, but pair 1 (Senguttuvan - Chera) is correct.
Correct. Only pair 2 is wrongly matched, because Udiyanjeral was a Chera and not a Chola.
Wrong. This implies pairs 1 and 3 are not correctly matched, but both are correct.
Wrong. This implies pair 3 alone is incorrect, but Nedunjeliyan was a Pandya, so the pair is correct.
keyfact: Udiyanjeral was a Chera, not a Chola, so only pair 2 is mismatched and the answer is (b).
option_notes: Pairs 1 and 2: Senguttuvan-Chera is correct, while Udiyanjeral-Chola is wrong. Pair 1 is correct because Senguttuvan was the Chera king who established the Pattini (Kannagi) cult, the best-known Chera ruler of the Silappadikaram. So this option is wrong as it wrongly includes pair 1. The Cheras held the Malabar coast, with Vanji/Karur as capital and Muziris and Tondi as ports.

Pair 2 only: Udiyanjeral is the Chera king (Udiyan Cheralatan) and not a Chola, so the pair is mismatched and this option is right. The Cholas of the Sangam age, such as Karikala, who won the battle of Venni and built the Kallanai (Grand Anicut) on the Kaveri, ruled from Uraiyur and Puhar (Kaveripattinam), with the tiger as emblem.

Pairs 1 and 3 (the printed 'lands' is an OCR garble of 'l and 3'): both pairs are correctly matched, so neither is mismatched. Senguttuvan was a Chera and Nedunjeliyan a Pandya. The Pandyas ruled the south from Madurai, had Korkai as a pearl-fishery port, and sent embassies to Augustus' Rome, as recorded by Strabo.

Pair 3 only (the printed '8 only' is an OCR garble of '3 only'): Nedunjeliyan is correctly a Pandya, so it is not a mismatch. The Pandyas are known for the Sangam academies at Madurai, for foreign trade in pearls and spices, and for the Pandya king Nedunjeliyan of the Silappadikaram. Pandya rulers also appear in Ashoka's inscriptions.
related: Silappadikaram was composed by Ilango Adigal; its hero Kovalan and heroine Kannagi.
Manimekalai was composed by Sattanar and is a Buddhist epic.
Karikala Chola won the battle of Venni and built the Kallanai on the Kaveri.
The Chera emblem was the bow, the Chola emblem the tiger and the Pandya emblem the fish.
Ashokan Rock Edict II and XIII mention Chola, Pandya, Satiyaputra and Keralaputra.
Muziris (Chera), Korkai (Pandya) and Puhar (Chola) were major ports.
Udiyan Cheralatan is said to have fed the armies at Kurukshetra.
Arikamedu, near Pondicherry, was an Indo-Roman trading station.
statements: 1 — Correct: Senguttuvan (Cheran Senguttuvan) was a Chera king of the Sangam age. He was the son of Imayavaramban Nedunjeralathan and is the hero of the Silappadikaram, where Ilango Adigal is traditionally called his brother. He is said to have led an expedition to the Himalayas to bring a stone for Kannagi's image and to have established the Pattini cult. His capital was Vanji (Karur) and his port was Muziris. He is also credited with a victory over northern kings. The Pugalur inscriptions mention Chera rulers.

2 — Incorrect: Udiyanjeral (Udiyan Cheralatan, 'Perunjoru Udiyan Cheralatan') was a Chera king, not a Chola. He is praised in the Purananuru for feeding the armies of both the Pandavas and the Kauravas at Kurukshetra, which is why he is called 'Perunjorru'. He is among the early Chera rulers, belonging to the Udiyan line, and was a patron of poets such as Mudinagarayar. The Cholas include Karikala, Killivalavan and Kocengannan.

3 — Correct: Nedunjeliyan was a Pandya king, and the Sangam texts mention at least two rulers of that name. Aariyap Padai Kadantha Nedunjeliyan defeated an Aryan army. Talaiyalanganattu Cheruvenra Nedunjeliyan won the battle of Talaiyalanganam against the Cheras and Cholas, and the Mathuraikkanji by Mangudi Maruthanar is on him. Nedunjeliyan is also the Pandya in the Silappadikaram who wrongly executed Kovalan. The Pandya capital was Madurai, the port was Korkai and the emblem was the fish.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 only, so the unofficial key is correct. Senguttuvan was a Chera king and Nedunjeliyan was a Pandya king, but Udiyanjeral (Udiyan Cheralatan, Perunjoru Udiyan Cheralatan) was a Chera, not a Chola, so pair 2 is wrongly matched.
topic_notes: Early historical Tamilakam covers roughly 300 BCE to 300 CE, the region south of Venkatam hills (Tirupati) up to Kanyakumari. The Sangam literature comprises Tolkappiyam (grammar), Ettuthogai (eight anthologies), Pattuppattu (ten idylls) and the Pathinenkilkanakku, with the epics Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal) and Manimekalai (Sattanar). The three ruling dynasties were the Cheras (Vanji; Kerala; bow), Cholas (Uraiyur, Puhar; Kaveri delta; tiger) and Pandyas (Madurai, Korkai; fish). Important Chera kings: Udiyanjeral, Nedunjeral Adan, Senguttuvan and Perumcheral Irumporai. Chola: Karikala (Venni; Kallanai), Killivalavan, Kocengannan and Perunarkilli (Rajasuya). Pandya: Nedunjeliyan, Mudukudumi Peruvaluthi and Nedunjeliyan the Aryan-defeater. The Sangam period had a chieftain system with minor chiefs (Velirs) such as Pari, Ori, Adiyaman and Kari, and the Velirs were patrons of poets. The poets included Kapilar, Avvaiyar and Paranar. Trade with Rome was important: Muziris, Arikamedu, Puhar and Korkai were ports, with Roman gold coins and amphorae found at Arikamedu and Pattanam. Exports were pepper, pearls, ivory, textiles and semi-precious stones. The Sangam landscape was divided into five tinais (Kurinji, Mullai, Marutam, Neytal and Palai). Society was organised in the clans of Paraiyar, Panar and Kuravar. The Sangam period is followed by the Kalabhra interregnum. Asoka's Rock Edicts II and XIII name Cholas, Pandyas, Satiyaputras and Keralaputras as independent neighbours, and the Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela mentions a confederacy of Tamil states.

question:
Which of the following factors contributed to 18. the formation of the Forward Bloc by Subhas Chandra Bose in 1939 ? i Bose failed to win the confidence of Mahatma Gandhi.
2. The Congress Left was disunited and failed to support Bose.
3. The Communists did not support Bose in his endeavours.
4. The supporters of M.N. Roy and socialist leaders like Jayaprakash Narayan preferred Congress unity to supporting Bose. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Modern History
detail: Bose was elected Congress President at Haripura (1938) and stood again at Tripuri (1939) against Gandhi's wishes. He defeated Gandhi's candidate Pattabhi Sitaramayya by 1580 to 1377 votes. Gandhi called Pattabhi's defeat 'my defeat'. Twelve Working Committee members, including Patel, Rajendra Prasad and Nehru's colleagues, resigned or withdrew cooperation. At Tripuri the Govind Ballabh Pant resolution asked Bose to form his Working Committee in accordance with Gandhi's wishes. Bose could not win Gandhi's confidence, and he could not rely on the Left. The Congress Left was divided. The Congress Socialist Party under JP, Narendra Dev and others stayed neutral or abstained. M.N. Roy's followers and the socialists preferred keeping the Congress united and avoided a split with the Gandhian majority. Bose resigned in April 1939 and formed the Forward Bloc within the Congress on 3 May 1939 to rally Left and anti-compromise forces. He was expelled from the Congress in August 1939 for three years. For elimination, statements 1, 2 and 4 are the core factors. Statement 3 is the doubtful one: the Communists were themselves divided and took a mixed stance, so options (a) and (c) are the ones to drop. Option (d) omits the Gandhi factor, which is the central cause.
explanations: (a) is wrong because it includes statement 3 but leaves out statement 4. Statement 4 is clearly among the recognised factors, and statement 3 is the doubtful one.
(b) is right because statements 1, 2 and 4 all describe recognised causes: Bose's rift with Gandhi, the disunited Left, and the Roy-ites and socialists choosing Congress unity.
(c) is wrong because it drops statement 2, the disunity of the Congress Left, which is a central cause, and it adds the doubtful statement 3.
(d) is wrong because 'only' excludes statement 1, and Bose's failure to win Gandhi's confidence was the main trigger for his resignation and the new party.
keyfact: After defeating Gandhi's candidate at Tripuri (1939), Bose lost the Gandhians' trust and the divided Left's support, resigned, and founded the Forward Bloc on 3 May 1939.
option_notes: Option (a) combines statements 1, 2 and 3. The Gandhi rift and the disunited Left were real causes. The statement on the Communists is the problem, because their stance was mixed and not plain non-support. Bose's own allies included some Left elements, and the Left's weakness stemmed more from the socialists' neutrality and the Roy-ites' choice. This option is wrong because it leaves out the socialists' preference for unity.

Option (b) combines statements 1, 2 and 4. It gives the standard account: Gandhi and the Congress Old Guard turned against Bose after Tripuri, the Left was divided, and Roy's followers and the Congress Socialists such as JP preferred unity. The Forward Bloc was launched on 3 May 1939 at Calcutta, with Bose as president and S.S. Caveeshar as vice-president. It aimed to unite all radical, anti-imperialist forces.

Option (c) combines statements 1, 3 and 4. It omits the disunity of the Congress Left, which was a main reason Bose lacked a solid backing. Statement 3 on the Communists is also doubtful. The Communist stance was not uniformly hostile, so this option is wrong. The Communists were still working inside the Congress Socialist Party in 1939, and many of them later turned against Bose over his wartime stand.

Option (d) says only 2 and 4. It correctly names the divided Left and the preference of the Roy-ites and socialists for unity. It wrongly leaves out the Bose-Gandhi rift, which was the immediate trigger: the Pant resolution, the Working Committee resignations and Bose's own resignation in April 1939 all came from it. This is a typical 'only' trap.
related: Bose defeated Pattabhi Sitaramayya at Tripuri in 1939, by 1580 to 1377 votes.
The Forward Bloc was founded on 3 May 1939 at Calcutta.
The Pant resolution at Tripuri asked Bose to form his Working Committee as Gandhi wished.
After Bose resigned, Rajendra Prasad became Congress President in 1939.
The Congress Socialist Party was formed in 1934 under JP, Narendra Dev and Masani.
M.N. Roy founded the Radical Democratic Party in 1940.
Bose launched the Azad Hind government at Singapore on 21 October 1943.
The Anti-Compromise Conference met at Ramgarh in March 1940.
statements: 1 — Correct: Bose's open conflict with Gandhi and the Gandhians, and his failure to win their trust, left him unable to run the Congress. Bose won the 1939 presidential election against Gandhi's nominee Pattabhi Sitaramayya. Gandhi called the defeat his own. Patel and 11 other Working Committee members resigned, and Bose faced a deadlock over forming the Committee. The Pant resolution at Tripuri (March 1939) demanded that he nominate the Committee according to Gandhi's wishes. Bose's request for Gandhi's guidance produced no settlement, and he resigned in April 1939.

2 — Correct: The Congress Left was fragmented among the Congress Socialists, Communists, Roy-ites and Bose's own followers, and it never acted as one bloc behind him. The Congress Socialist Party was formed in 1934 under JP, Acharya Narendra Dev and Minoo Masani. Its leaders were ambivalent at Tripuri and many abstained. Bose's talk of a united Left front therefore had little organised backing. He then formed the Forward Bloc to build that base himself.

3 — Doubtful/Incorrect as framed: The Communists were not simply opposed to Bose. Many Communists, working within the Congress Socialist Party, were close to the Left and had a mixed, unclear stance. The CPI was then divided over how to treat the Congress leadership, and some of its members supported the compromise. Treating 'Communists did not support Bose' as a clean cause is the weakest claim. The CPI was founded in 1920 (Tashkent) or 1925 (Kanpur), and was banned in 1934. It adopted the Popular Front line from 1935.

4 — Correct: M.N. Roy's followers (the League of Radical Congressmen) and socialists such as Jayaprakash Narayan put Congress unity ahead of a showdown with Gandhi. They feared a split would weaken the national movement. They therefore stayed neutral or backed the compromise, and Bose lost a possible base. M.N. Roy (Narendra Nath Bhattacharya) was a founder of the Mexican and Indian communist parties, and he later founded the Radical Democratic Party in 1940.
summary: The answer is (b) 1, 2 and 4, so the unofficial key looks right. Bose's clash with Gandhi after Tripuri (1939) left him isolated in the Congress. The Left was split, and the Roy-ites and Congress Socialists such as JP put Congress unity ahead of backing him. He resigned the presidency and founded the Forward Bloc on 3 May 1939. Statement 3 is the weakest link, because the Communists were not clearly hostile to him.
topic_notes: Subhas Chandra Bose became Congress President at Haripura (February 1938), where he set up the National Planning Committee under Nehru. He stood again in January 1939 against Pattabhi Sitaramayya, who had Gandhi's backing, and won by 1580 votes to 1377. Maulana Azad had withdrawn from the contest. Bose wanted to give the British a six-month ultimatum to concede independence and to use the European war situation. Gandhi and the Old Guard opposed this. At the Tripuri session (March 1939, Madhya Pradesh) Bose was ill. The Pant resolution reaffirmed faith in Gandhian leadership and told Bose to form a Working Committee as Gandhi wished. Rajendra Prasad took over as president after Bose resigned in April 1939. Bose founded the Forward Bloc on 3 May 1939, and the Congress barred him from office for three years in August 1939. He organised the Left Consolidation Committee and the Anti-Compromise Conference at Ramgarh (March 1940), alongside the Congress session. He was arrested in July 1940 for the Holwell Monument agitation and escaped from house arrest in January 1941, reaching Germany and then Japan. In 1943 he took over the Indian National Army from Rash Behari Bose and formed the Provisional Government of Free India (Azad Hind) at Singapore, on 21 October 1943. He led the INA's 'Delhi Chalo' campaign. Other angles: the Congress Socialist Party (1934, Patna/Bombay), the Communist Party of India, M.N. Roy's Radical Democratic Party (1940), the Left Consolidation Committee, Gandhi's individual satyagraha (1940) and the August Offer (1940).

question:
Consider the following statements regarding the British policy in Awadh immediately after 19, its annexation in 1856 : iL, The talugdars were dispossessed of their estates but allowed to retain their arms and forts.
2. A Summary Revenue Settlement was made in 1856 assuming that the taluqdars were outsiders.
3. The British believed in taking revenue directly from the peasants by removing the taluqdars. a0 Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Modern History
detail: Awadh was annexed by Lord Dalhousie in 1856 on grounds of alleged misgovernance, after Wajid Ali Shah was deposed and sent to Calcutta.
