They give mass, redundancy and the ability to overwhelm air defences cheaply. Uses include military strikes, ISR, electronic warfare decoys, agriculture, disaster relief, light shows and mapping. India's examples: the Army's swarm demonstration in January 2021, with 75 drones, by the startup NewSpace Research; the Army and the Indian Air Force have tested swarm and loitering munition concepts; and Operation Sindoor in May 2025 saw large-scale drone use and counter-drone action by both sides. Counter-UAS (C-UAS) tools: radar and RF detection, electro-optical and acoustic sensors; soft kill (RF and GNSS jamming, GPS spoofing, cyber takeover); hard kill (guns, missiles, lasers or directed-energy weapons, high-power microwaves, nets, interceptor drones). India's DRDO has developed the Anti-Drone System, which was used at Independence Day events, and the Bhargavastra micro-missile system for swarm defence has been reported. Regulation: the Drone Rules 2021 (replacing the 2021 draft UAS rules), a PLI scheme for drones and components (2021), Digital Sky platform, and the traffic-light airspace map (green, yellow, red). The Drone Shakti scheme supports startups. Other angles: GNSS systems (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou, NavIC), jamming versus spoofing, 6G and Terahertz, loitering munitions (Harop, Nagastra-1), and the Armenia-Azerbaijan and Russia-Ukraine drone wars.

question:
Which of the following statements with regard to GenomeIndia Project is/are correct ?
1. It is a part of the Human Genome Project.
2. The project is funded by _ the Department of Biotechnology (DBT), Government of India.
3. Its primary aim is to build a catalogue of genetic diversity of the Indian population. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Science & Tech
detail: GenomeIndia is a national genomics initiative launched by DBT, coordinated by the Centre for Brain Research (CBR), IISc Bengaluru, with about 20 partner institutions. It aims to sequence 10,000 genomes initially, drawn from over 99 distinct population groups across India, to build a reference genome database for the Indian population. In January 2025 the PM released the first phase data of 10,000 genomes, which is stored at the Indian Biological Data Centre (IBDC), Faridabad, under the Indian Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy framework. The aim is to understand population-specific variants, support precision medicine and diagnosis of genetic and rare diseases, and reduce reliance on Western reference datasets. The Human Genome Project (HGP) was a separate international effort, run from 1990 to 2003 and led by the US and UK with other countries, and India did not take part. Elimination logic: statement 1 is false, which removes (a), (c) and (d). Statements 2 and 3 are both true, leaving (b).
explanations: Wrong: it includes only statement 1, which is false because GenomeIndia is not part of the Human Genome Project, and it leaves out the true statements 2 and 3.
Correct: statements 2 (DBT funding) and 3 (cataloguing Indian genetic diversity) are true, and statement 1 is false.
Wrong: it accepts statement 1, which is false, and rejects statement 3, which is true.
Wrong: it includes the false statement 1, so 'all three' cannot hold.
keyfact: GenomeIndia is a DBT-funded national project to catalogue the genetic diversity of Indians, not a part of the Human Genome Project.
option_notes: Statement 1 alone. It would hold only if GenomeIndia were a sub-project of the Human Genome Project, which it is not. The HGP (1990-2003) was an international effort to map all human genes and sequence the roughly 3 billion base pairs. It was funded mainly by the US NIH and DOE and by the UK Wellcome Trust, and its data was released publicly under the Bermuda Principles. India was not a partner.

Statements 2 and 3 only. GenomeIndia is a DBT-funded programme. It is led by the Centre for Brain Research, IISc, and builds a genetic variation catalogue of the Indian population. The first 10,000 genomes were announced in January 2025, and the data is hosted at the IBDC, Faridabad. It supports precision medicine and the diagnosis of rare diseases.

Statements 1 and 2 only. This pairs the DBT funding fact, which is true, with the wrong claim of HGP linkage. DBT is under the Ministry of Science and Technology, was set up in 1986, and is headquartered in New Delhi. It runs BRIC, the Indian Biological Data Centre and the BioE3 policy. It also funded INSACOG for genome surveillance of SARS-CoV-2.

All three statements. This option fails because statement 1 is false. Genome projects related to the HGP include ENCODE, the 1000 Genomes Project, HapMap and the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium. Other national projects include UK Biobank, Genome of Europe, Genome Asia 100K, and Saudi and Emirati genome programmes. GenomeIndia is India's counterpart of these.
related: GenomeIndia phase 1 data of 10,000 genomes was released in January 2025.
The Centre for Brain Research at IISc Bengaluru coordinates GenomeIndia.
GenomeIndia data is hosted at the Indian Biological Data Centre, Faridabad.
The Human Genome Project ran from 1990 to 2003.
INSACOG was launched in December 2020 to track SARS-CoV-2 variants.
The CSIR IndiGen programme sequenced 1,008 Indian genomes.
The Department of Biotechnology was set up in 1986 under the Ministry of Science and Technology.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: GenomeIndia is an independent Indian initiative, not a component of the Human Genome Project. The HGP was an international public consortium that began in 1990 and declared the sequence essentially complete in April 2003. It was coordinated by the US NIH and the Department of Energy, with major contributions from the UK (Wellcome Trust Sanger), Japan, France, Germany and China. India was not a formal member. It produced the first reference human genome of about 3 billion base pairs, and the Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) consortium completed the gaps in 2022.

2 — Correct: The project is funded and driven by the Department of Biotechnology under the Ministry of Science and Technology. DBT approved it in 2020 as a mission-mode project. It is coordinated by the Centre for Brain Research at IISc Bengaluru, with partners including IITs, CSIR labs, NIBMG Kalyani and other universities and research institutes. DBT also supports related efforts such as the Indian Biological Data Centre at Faridabad, the Biotech-KISAN scheme, the BioE3 policy and the Indian SARS-CoV-2 Genomics Consortium (INSACOG).

3 — Correct: The primary aim is to create a catalogue of genetic variation across Indian populations, and eventually a reference genome. Samples were collected from about 99 groups across the country, with 10,000 genomes sequenced in phase 1 using whole genome sequencing and genotyping arrays. India has thousands of endogamous groups, so it harbours unique variants. The catalogue helps in precision medicine, polygenic risk scores and understanding genetic disorders such as thalassemia and sickle cell disease. Data access is through the IBDC under controlled-access rules.
summary: The answer is (b) 2 and 3 only, so the unofficial expected answer is correct. GenomeIndia is an Indian national project funded by the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) to catalogue the genetic diversity of the Indian population. It is not a part of the international Human Genome Project, so statement 1 is wrong.
topic_notes: Genomics is a recurring UPSC theme. The Human Genome Project ran from 1990 to 2003, sequenced about 3 billion base pairs, and identified roughly 20,000-25,000 genes. The Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) consortium published a gapless human genome in 2022. India's major genomic efforts include GenomeIndia (DBT), which has 10,000 genomes in phase 1. Its ambition is to scale to a larger number later, and it covers 99 populations. Data is stored at the Indian Biological Data Centre (IBDC) at Faridabad, and the project is coordinated by the Centre for Brain Research at IISc. The Indian SARS-CoV-2 Genomics Consortium (INSACOG), launched in December 2020, tracks coronavirus variants through a network of sequencing labs. The Genome Sequencing for Public Health Challenge and the Phenome India project at CSIR add to this. CSIR's IGIB ran the 'Indigen' programme, which sequenced 1,008 Indian genomes. The Human Pangenome aims to capture diversity beyond a single reference. Related applications include precision or personalised medicine, pharmacogenomics, CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing (Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020 to Doudna and Charpentier), gene therapy for sickle cell disease and the Casgevy approval, and India's own gene therapy trials for haemophilia. Also note the National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission (2023), the DNA Technology (Use and Application) Regulation Bill, and the Biological Diversity Act 2002. UPSC could ask about institutions such as DBT, ICMR, CSIR and NIBMG, and about terms like SNP, whole genome versus exome sequencing, and reference genome.

ocr: Which of the following statements with regard 51. to the National Quantum Mission (NQM) is/are correct ? 5 It aims at developing intermediate-scale quantum computers with 50-1000 physical qubits. Its implementation includes setting up of four Thematic Hubs (T-Hubs) in academic and national R&D institutes across India. Select the answer using the code given below : (a) lonly (b) 2 only (c) Both 1 and 2 Neither 1 nor 2 (d)
subject: Science & Tech
detail: The National Quantum Mission (NQM) was approved by the Union Cabinet on 19 April 2023 for 2023-24 to 2030-31, with an outlay of about Rs 6,003.65 crore. It is under the Department of Science and Technology (DST), and the Principal Scientific Adviser's office guides it. Its aim is to seed, nurture and scale up scientific and industrial R&D in quantum technology (QT) and make India a leading nation in the field. Its targets are intermediate-scale quantum computers with 50-1000 physical qubits within 8 years on superconducting and photonic platforms, satellite-based secure quantum communication over 2,000 km within India, inter-city quantum key distribution over 2,000 km, and multi-node quantum networks with quantum memories. Sensing and metrology and quantum materials and devices are also covered. Four Thematic Hubs (T-Hubs) are set up in top academic and national R&D institutes, covering quantum computing, quantum communication, quantum sensing and metrology, and quantum materials and devices. Since both statements match the Mission's design, option (c) is correct, and (a), (b) and (d) fail because each denies at least one true statement.
explanations: (a) 1 only is wrong because statement 2 is also correct: the Mission does include four T-Hubs.
(b) 2 only is wrong because statement 1 is also correct: the 50-1000 physical qubit target is part of the Mission.
(c) Both 1 and 2 is correct, as the qubit target and the four T-Hubs are both features of NQM.
(d) Neither 1 nor 2 is wrong because both statements match the Mission's official design.
keyfact: NQM (approved April 2023, Rs 6,003.65 crore, to 2030-31): 50-1000 physical qubit computers and four T-Hubs, so both statements are correct and the answer is (c).
option_notes: (a) 1 only would be right if the Mission had no T-Hub structure. But NQM does include four hubs, so this is incomplete. The qubit target of 50-1000 physical qubits is correct, as are the satellite communication and sensing goals.
(b) 2 only would be right if the qubit target in statement 1 were misquoted. In fact the official target is 50-1000 physical qubits in 8 years, so this option wrongly excludes a true statement.

(c) Both 1 and 2 is the correct choice. NQM was approved in April 2023 with an outlay of about Rs 6,003.65 crore for 2023-24 to 2030-31. It is run by DST, aims at intermediate-scale quantum computers of 50-1000 physical qubits, and builds four T-Hubs at IISc, IIT Madras, IIT Bombay and IIT Delhi.

(d) Neither 1 nor 2 would be right only if both statements were wrong. Both match official descriptions, so this option is wrong. Students should note that UPSC often tests whether a statement's numbers match the official document.
related: NQM was approved by the Union Cabinet in April 2023 with Rs 6,003.65 crore for 2023-24 to 2030-31.
NQM is implemented by the Department of Science and Technology.
Four T-Hubs cover computing, communication, sensing and metrology, and materials and devices.
NQM targets satellite-based quantum communication over 2,000 km.
A qubit can exist in superposition of 0 and 1, unlike a classical bit.
Quantum key distribution offers theoretically secure key exchange based on quantum mechanics.
Entanglement links qubits so that their states are correlated regardless of distance.
Logical qubits are error-corrected combinations of many physical qubits.
statements: 1 — Correct: NQM targets intermediate-scale quantum computers with 50-1000 physical qubits over 8 years. The Mission's computing goals use superconducting and photonic technologies, with neutral atoms and trapped ions also in the mix. Physical qubits are the actual hardware qubits and are error-prone, unlike logical qubits, which are error-corrected combinations of many physical qubits. The Mission's staged target is 20-50 qubits in 3 years, 50-100 in 5 years and 50-1000 in 8 years. The Mission is run by DST, and the National Quantum Mission has a Mission Director and governance bodies. It places India among the few countries with a dedicated national quantum programme, such as the USA, China, the EU, the UK and Japan.

2 — Correct: NQM sets up four Thematic Hubs in leading academic and national R&D institutes. The hubs cover quantum computing (IISc Bengaluru), quantum communication (IIT Madras with C-DOT), quantum sensing and metrology (IIT Bombay), and quantum materials and devices (IIT Delhi). They work as a hub-and-spoke network linking institutions across India, and they train a skilled workforce, create IP, and support start-ups and industry. The hubs are meant to concentrate expertise while spreading research around the country. NQM also has the broader aim of building a quantum ecosystem, including fabrication facilities, testbeds and international collaboration.
summary: The correct answer is (d) Neither 1 nor 2, so the unofficial key (c) looks wrong. The National Quantum Mission (2023-24 to 2030-31, Rs 6,003.65 crore) targets intermediate-scale quantum computers with 50-1000 physical qubits, which makes statement 1 correct. It sets up four T-Hubs, so statement 2 is also correct, and (c) is the right answer. Correction: on re-verification, (c) is right and the unofficial key stands.
topic_notes: The National Quantum Mission was approved by the Union Cabinet on 19 April 2023 with an outlay of Rs 6,003.65 crore for 2023-24 to 2030-31. It is implemented by the Department of Science and Technology under the Ministry of Science and Technology. Its goal is to build a quantum ecosystem in India and make the country a leader in quantum technologies. Key deliverables include intermediate-scale quantum computers of 50-1000 physical qubits, satellite-based secure quantum communication between ground stations over 2,000 km within India, long-distance communication with other countries, inter-city quantum key distribution over 2,000 km, multi-node quantum networks with quantum memories, magnetometers and atomic clocks with high precision for sensing, and design and synthesis of quantum materials such as superconductors, semiconductor structures and topological materials. Four T-Hubs are being set up: computing, communication, sensing and metrology, and materials and devices. Concepts to know: qubit, superposition, entanglement, quantum supremacy, quantum key distribution, post-quantum cryptography, logical versus physical qubits, and decoherence. India's other efforts include QpiAI's quantum computer, the DRDO-IIT Delhi quantum communication demonstration, and ISRO's work on free-space quantum communication. Other nations with national quantum strategies include the USA (National Quantum Initiative Act 2018), China, the EU (Quantum Flagship), the UK and Japan. UPSC could ask next about qubit definitions, quantum key distribution, the ministry in charge, the hubs' host institutions, and applications in drug discovery, cryptography and sensing.

ocr: Which of the following statements with regard to India’s Deep Ocean Mission is/are correct ? It was launched by the Ministry of i Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Government of India. Matsya-6000 has been designed to carry 3 people for deep sea exploration. Samudrayaan is a project under this mission. Select the answer using the code given below : (a) lonly (b) 2and 3 only (c) land 2 only (dd) 1,2and3 Mr. X, a senior officer, was overseeing a critical vaccination programme during a pandemic. He found that a private service provider responsible for vaccine distribution was compromising on quality
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Deep Ocean Mission was approved by the Union Cabinet in June 2021 with a budget of about Rs 4,077 crore over five years. It is implemented by the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) and supports the 'Blue Economy' vision. The nodal technical institute is the National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), Chennai. The mission has six components: (1) technologies for deep-sea mining and a manned submersible, (2) ocean climate change advisory services, (3) technological innovations for exploration and conservation of deep-sea biodiversity, (4) deep-ocean survey and exploration, (5) energy and freshwater from the ocean, including offshore OTEC, and (6) an advanced marine station for ocean biology. The manned submersible is Matsya-6000, which is designed to carry 3 people to a depth of 6,000 m. The project is called Samudrayaan. The vehicle has a titanium alloy personnel sphere, about 2.1 m in diameter, and can operate for about 12 hours, with emergency endurance of 96 hours. Elimination logic: statement 1 is wrong because the ministry is MoES. That removes (a), (c) and (d), leaving (b).
explanations: (a) Wrong: it accepts only statement 1, which is false because the mission was launched by MoES, and it rejects the correct statements 2 and 3.
(b) Correct: statements 2 and 3 are true, since Matsya-6000 carries 3 people and Samudrayaan is the project under the mission. Statement 1 is false.
(c) Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false, and omits statement 3, which is true.
(d) Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is false, so 'all three' cannot be correct.
keyfact: Deep Ocean Mission = Ministry of Earth Sciences (not Ports/Shipping); Samudrayaan's Matsya-6000 carries 3 people to 6,000 m.
option_notes: Option (a), '1 only', would be true if the ministry were Ports, Shipping and Waterways. That ministry is the one that runs Sagarmala, launched in 2015 for port-led development, and it oversees major ports and inland waterways. It does not run the Deep Ocean Mission, which sits with MoES, the ministry that handles ocean science and technology, weather and polar research.

Option (b), '2 and 3 only', is the correct combination. It says that Matsya-6000 is a 3-person submersible designed to reach 6,000 m, and that Samudrayaan is the project under which it is being built. Both are developed by NIOT, Chennai, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences. The Deep Ocean Mission has an outlay of about Rs 4,077 crore for five years.

Option (c), '1 and 2 only', would need statement 1 to be true, but it is false because DOM is a MoES mission. It would also exclude Samudrayaan, which is the manned-submersible project under DOM. Note that Matsya-6000 itself is the vehicle and Samudrayaan is the project name for the manned deep-ocean mission.

Option (d), '1, 2 and 3', would be correct only if all three statements were true. Statement 1 is false because the Ministry of Earth Sciences, not the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, launched the mission. UPSC often puts a wrong ministry name into an otherwise true set of statements, so always verify the nodal ministry.
related: The Deep Ocean Mission is implemented by the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
Matsya-6000 is a manned submersible for 3 people, designed for 6,000 m depth.
NIOT, Chennai is the nodal institute for the Deep Ocean Mission technologies.
Samudrayaan is the manned deep-sea project under DOM.
Sagarmala is run by the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways.
The International Seabed Authority is based in Kingston, Jamaica, and was set up under UNCLOS.
India holds ISA exploration rights for polymetallic nodules in the Central Indian Ocean Basin.
DOM was approved by the Union Cabinet in June 2021 with an outlay of about Rs 4,077 crore.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The Deep Ocean Mission was launched by the Ministry of Earth Sciences, not the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. The Cabinet approved it in June 2021 with an outlay of about Rs 4,077 crore over 5 years. It is one of the main pillars of India's Blue Economy policy. The Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways runs Sagarmala, which is a port-led development programme. MoES also handles INCOIS, NCPOR, NIOT and the Indian Antarctic programme.

2 — Correct: Matsya-6000 is a manned submersible designed to carry 3 people to a depth of 6,000 m in the ocean. It is developed by NIOT, Chennai. Its personnel sphere is made of titanium alloy and is about 2.1 m in diameter. It is designed for about 12 hours of normal operation and 96 hours of emergency endurance. Its purpose is to explore polymetallic nodules, gas hydrates, hydrothermal sulphides and cobalt crusts. The sea trials were planned in the Bay of Bengal off Chennai. India would join the US, Russia, France, Japan and China in having crewed deep-sea vehicles.

3 — Correct: Samudrayaan is the project under the Deep Ocean Mission to send humans into the deep sea in the Matsya-6000 submersible. It was launched in 2021 by MoES, and NIOT is responsible for it. The target depth is 6,000 m, with the aim of studying deep-sea resources and biodiversity. Other related efforts include the Polymetallic Nodules programme in the Central Indian Ocean Basin, where India holds exploration rights from the International Seabed Authority, and the unmanned vehicle ROSUB 6000.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 2 and 3 only, so the unofficial expected answer is right. The Deep Ocean Mission (DOM) was launched by the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES), not the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, so statement 1 fails. Matsya-6000 is a manned submersible designed for 3 people, and Samudrayaan is the project under which it is being built.
topic_notes: The Deep Ocean Mission (DOM) was approved by the Union Cabinet in June 2021 with an estimated cost of Rs 4,077 crore over five years, in phases. It is implemented by the Ministry of Earth Sciences. It supports the Blue Economy, which is one of the 'New India 2030' priorities. NIOT, Chennai is the nodal institute for technology development. The six components are: deep-sea mining and a manned submersible; ocean climate change advisory services; deep-sea biodiversity exploration and conservation; deep-ocean survey and exploration; offshore energy and freshwater (including OTEC); and an advanced marine station for ocean biology. Matsya-6000 is a crewed submersible for 3 people, rated to 6,000 m depth, with a titanium personnel sphere of about 2.1 m diameter. Samudrayaan is the project name. India holds exploration contracts with the International Seabed Authority (ISA), based in Kingston, Jamaica, for polymetallic nodules in the Central Indian Ocean Basin (about 75,000 sq km) and for polymetallic sulphides on the Southwest Indian Ridge. ISA was set up under UNCLOS (1982). Related MoES bodies include INCOIS (Hyderabad), NCPOR (Goa), NCCR (Chennai), IITM (Pune) and the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services. Other angles UPSC may ask: polymetallic nodules (manganese, nickel, cobalt, copper), gas hydrates, hydrothermal vents, OTEC, the Sagarmala programme, the Blue Economy policy, and the Exclusive Economic Zone (200 nautical miles) under UNCLOS. Past UPSC questions have asked about ISA and the Central Indian Ocean Basin.

question: Which one among the following principles of public administration was most strongly demonstrated by Mr. X’s actions ?
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This is a case-based question on the principles of public administration, mostly drawn from Henri Fayol's 14 principles and later administrative thought. The method is to match X's behaviour to the principle it shows. Accountability means being answerable for the use of power and resources and for results, and it is enforceable through consequences. Examples are owning a failure, submitting to audit or inquiry, giving reasons, or facing sanction. Delegation means passing authority and tasks to subordinates while the superior stays ultimately responsible. Esprit de corps is Fayol's 14th principle, 'union is strength': team morale, harmony and cohesion. Equity is Fayol's 13th principle, kindliness plus justice in treating subordinates, and in modern thought it means fairness and social equity in service delivery. Elimination: look for the key verb in the passage. 'Assigned' or 'entrusted' points to delegation. 'Motivated the team' or 'fostered unity' points to esprit de corps. 'Treated all fairly' or 'gave extra support to the disadvantaged' points to equity. 'Took responsibility', 'explained', 'was answerable' or 'faced inquiry' points to accountability. Without the passage, this mapping is the reliable way to decide.
explanations: Esprit de corps is right only if the passage shows X building team unity, morale or cohesion. I could not check this because the passage is missing.
Equity is right only if X treated people with fairness and kindliness, or favoured disadvantaged groups. I could not check this because the passage is missing.

Accountability is the unofficial answer. It is right if X took responsibility, answered for outcomes or submitted to oversight. I cannot confirm it without the passage, and I have no basis to call it wrong.
Delegation is right only if X passed authority or tasks to subordinates. I could not check this because the passage is missing.
keyfact: Match the verb in the passage: assigned = delegation, took responsibility = accountability, fair treatment = equity, team unity = esprit de corps; the unofficial answer (c) is unverified because the passage is missing.
option_notes: Esprit de corps is Fayol's 14th principle (from his 1916 work on industrial and general administration). It means 'union is strength': harmony and unity among staff. Fayol warned against divide and rule and against over-reliance on written communication, and urged face-to-face contact to build team spirit. It supports morale, cooperation and cohesion in an organisation.

Equity is Fayol's 13th principle: a combination of kindliness and justice in how managers treat subordinates, so that staff are loyal and devoted. In New Public Administration (Minnowbrook Conference, 1968; H. George Frederickson), social equity became a central value, alongside relevance, values and change. It also underpins fairness in public service delivery.

Accountability is the obligation of officials to answer for their actions and results to a higher authority or to the public. It has two parts: answerability (explaining) and enforceability (consequences). In India its tools include Parliamentary committees, the CAG, the RTI Act 2005, the Lokpal and Lokayukta, and social audits. Article 75(3) makes the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

Delegation is the passing of authority and the right to act from a superior to a subordinate. Responsibility stays with the delegator. It relates to Fayol's principles of authority and responsibility, centralisation and scalar chain. It supports decentralisation, speeds up decisions and develops juniors. Effective delegation needs clear goals, matching authority and monitoring.
related: Fayol's 14th principle is esprit de corps; the 13th is equity.
Accountability = answerability plus enforceability.
POSDCORB was given by Gulick and Urwick in 1937.
The Minnowbrook Conference (1968) launched New Public Administration with its focus on social equity.
Article 75(3): collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha.
RTI Act, 2005 strengthens transparency and accountability.
The Second ARC was chaired first by Veerappa Moily, then by M. Veerappa Moily's successor V. Ramachandran.
Delegation passes authority but not ultimate responsibility.
summary: The question stem refers to 'Mr. X's actions', but the case passage did not come through in the text I received, so I cannot verify the unofficial answer (c) Accountability. I also cannot say it is wrong. If X answered for outcomes, accepted responsibility, or reported to a higher authority, (c) fits. If the passage describes handing tasks to juniors, team spirit or fair treatment, another option would be correct.
topic_notes: Principles of public administration come from classical theorists. Henri Fayol's 14 principles are: division of work, authority and responsibility, discipline, unity of command, unity of direction, subordination of individual interest to the general interest, remuneration, centralisation, scalar chain, order, equity, stability of tenure, initiative, and esprit de corps. Luther Gulick and Lyndall Urwick gave POSDCORB: Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Co-ordinating, Reporting, Budgeting. Max Weber described bureaucracy by hierarchy, rules, impersonality, specialisation and merit-based careers. Woodrow Wilson's 1887 essay began the separate study of administration. Frederick Taylor stressed scientific management. Mary Parker Follett and Elton Mayo's Hawthorne studies brought in human relations. Chester Barnard wrote on cooperation and authority. Herbert Simon introduced bounded rationality. Frederickson and the Minnowbrook Conference (1968) gave New Public Administration, with an emphasis on social equity. The 1990s New Public Management stressed efficiency, markets and results. Good governance values include transparency, accountability, responsiveness, rule of law and participation. Related concepts often asked include delegation versus decentralisation, line and staff agencies, span of control, unity of command, hierarchy and coordination. Indian references include the Second ARC (2005–09), which emphasised ethics in governance, the Citizens' Charter, and RTI. For case questions, identify the central action in the passage and map it to the closest principle.

ocr: Ina multi-ethnic district where both economic 53 competition and _ historical grievances : frequently led to community tensions, a flashpoint has arisen with a Government decision to allocate land for a waste management facility near a tribal hamlet, sparking protests by the tribal community, which claimed that the land was sacred and critical to their cultural identity. At the same time, urban residents and local industries supported the project, citing severe solid waste challenges and health concerns due to lack of a proper disposal site. The conflict has escalated with road blockades, soci
subject: Environment
detail: This is an ethics and case-study question on conflict resolution, built on the principles of participatory governance, procedural justice and sustainable development. A good resolution process builds trust first, then uses evidence, then reaches a negotiated solution. Recognising the sacredness of the land is the first step because it shows respect and legitimacy. Next, a multi-stakeholder platform brings tribal leaders, experts, municipal bodies and civil society together. An independent ESIA then supplies neutral, transparent evidence and can compare alternative sites. Legal anchors a student should know: Fifth Schedule (Scheduled Areas), PESA Act 1996 (Gram Sabha consultation before land acquisition and for minor forest produce), Forest Rights Act 2006 (Gram Sabha consent and recognition of cultural and community rights), the LARR Act 2013 (Social Impact Assessment, consent), and the Environment Impact Assessment Notification 2006 (public hearing). The Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 (replaced in 2026 by the 2026 rules) require sites that follow environmental norms. The elimination logic is simple: any statement that dismisses a minority's sentiments or says 'proceed without delay' is an absolutist, majoritarian stance and fails the test of mediation. Dropping statement 2 leaves 1, 3 and 4, which is option (a).
explanations: Correct. Statements 1, 3 and 4 all contribute to resolving the conflict through acknowledgement, dialogue and evidence, and statement 2 does not.
Incorrect. It includes statement 2, which promotes unilateral action and disregards tribal concerns, so it would deepen the conflict.
Incorrect. It includes statement 2 and leaves out statement 1, which is the essential first step of acknowledging cultural concerns.
Incorrect. It includes statement 2, which is a majoritarian and non-consultative stance that contradicts mediation.
keyfact: In conflict resolution, acknowledge concerns, create inclusive dialogue and use transparent evidence (ESIA); never override a community's rights unilaterally.
option_notes: Option (a), 1, 3 and 4 only, is the set of the three conflict-resolution statements: acknowledging cultural concerns, setting up multi-stakeholder dialogue, and carrying out an independent, transparent ESIA. It reflects the participatory, rights-based approach recommended in governance and ethics. It is the correct answer to this question, and it excludes the unilateral approach in statement 2.

Option (b), 2, 3 and 4 only, combines statement 2 (proceed immediately because urban health concerns outweigh a small group's sentiments) with the dialogue and ESIA statements. It is internally inconsistent: it asks for dialogue while ignoring the sentiments of one party. It is wrong because statement 2 is a majoritarian, utilitarian shortcut that breaches tribal rights under PESA, FRA and the Fifth Schedule.

Option (c), 1 and 2 only, pairs the correct first step of acknowledgement with the incorrect decision to proceed regardless. It is wrong because it excludes the dialogue platform and the ESIA, which are practical mechanisms for a sustainable outcome, and because statement 2 contradicts statement 1. Acknowledging concerns while pushing ahead without delay would be tokenism.

Option (d), 1, 2, 3 and 4, accepts every statement. It is wrong because statement 2 weakens mediation: it dismisses minority concerns as 'sentiments of a small group' and prioritises speed over consensus. UPSC often uses an 'all of the above' option to test whether students can spot a single flawed statement.
related: PESA Act 1996 makes the Gram Sabha central in Scheduled Areas.
Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises community and cultural rights over forest land.
Niyamgiri (2013): Supreme Court let Gram Sabhas decide on religious and cultural rights over the hills.
LARR Act 2013 requires a Social Impact Assessment for land acquisition.
EIA Notification 2006 under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 mandates public hearings for listed projects.
Mediation Act 2023 provides a legal framework for mediation in India.
National Green Tribunal was established in 2010 to handle environmental disputes.
Article 29 protects the distinct culture of minorities.
statements: 1 — Correct: Acknowledging the community's cultural concerns first builds trust and legitimacy, and mediation requires parties to feel heard before technical options are discussed. Background: sacred groves and sites are protected as cultural and community rights under the Forest Rights Act 2006, which recognises community rights over sacred and customary areas. Gram Sabhas have the power to protect cultural identity and heritage. Article 29 protects the distinct culture of any section of citizens, and Article 342 provides for the notification of Scheduled Tribes. Empathy and active listening are core values in Ethics (GS-IV) for dealing with conflict.

2 — Incorrect: It treats the tribal community's concerns as less important and proceeds unilaterally, which would escalate the conflict and violate principles of justice, inclusiveness and tribal rights. Background: the idea that majority interests override minority interests is a utilitarian-majoritarian approach that constitutional morality rejects. PESA 1996 requires Gram Sabha consultation before land acquisition in Scheduled Areas, and the LARR Act 2013 requires consent and Social Impact Assessment in many cases. The Supreme Court in Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997) restricted transfer of tribal land to non-tribals, and in Orissa Mining Corporation v. MoEF (Niyamgiri, 2013) upheld the Gram Sabhas' role on religious and cultural rights.

3 — Correct: A multi-stakeholder dialogue platform is a classic mediation and deliberative tool that builds mutual understanding and de-escalates tension. Background: participatory governance and stakeholder consultation are central to public administration. Examples include public hearings under the EIA Notification 2006, Gram Sabhas under PESA, and local ward committees under the 74th Amendment (Article 243S). Inclusion of tribal leaders, experts and municipal representatives reflects the principles of procedural fairness, transparency and collective problem solving that the Second ARC also stressed for citizen-centric administration.

4 — Correct: An independent Environmental and Social Impact Assessment, with findings shared openly, provides neutral evidence, tests alternative sites and reduces mistrust. Background: ESIA combines environmental impact analysis with social effects such as displacement, livelihoods and cultural loss. In India, the EIA Notification 2006 under the Environment (Protection) Act 1986 requires prior environmental clearance and public consultation for listed projects, and the LARR Act 2013 mandates a Social Impact Assessment. Transparency and evidence-based decision-making are core to good governance and the Right to Information Act 2005.
summary: The answer is (a) 1, 3 and 4 only, so the unofficial key is correct. Statements 1, 3 and 4 are standard conflict-resolution and mediation steps: acknowledge cultural concerns, create a multi-stakeholder dialogue, and run a transparent independent ESIA. Statement 2 is a majoritarian, unilateral approach that would escalate the conflict and conflicts with tribal rights and constitutional ethics.
topic_notes:
This question belongs to the area of ethics, public administration and conflict resolution in development projects. The core tension is between public interest (urban waste management, health) and community rights (tribal cultural identity, sacred land). Good practice follows a sequence: acknowledge, consult, assess with evidence, negotiate, and implement transparently with safeguards and monitoring.

Key legal and institutional framework: the Fifth Schedule (Article 244(1)) governs administration of Scheduled Areas, with the Governor's power to regulate land transfer and the Tribes Advisory Council. The Sixth Schedule covers tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. The PESA Act 1996 empowers Gram Sabhas in Scheduled Areas and requires consultation before land acquisition. The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises individual and community forest rights, including cultural and religious ones, and gives Gram Sabhas a role in consent for diversion of forest land. The LARR Act 2013 requires a Social Impact Assessment and consent in certain cases. The EIA Notification 2006 sets out screening, scoping, public hearing and appraisal. The Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 set out waste-site, segregation and processing requirements, and the National Green Tribunal (2010) hears environmental disputes.

Ethics concepts: utilitarianism versus rights-based approaches, justice and fairness, empathy, transparency, accountability, constitutional morality and the principle of 'do no harm'. Mediation methods include negotiation, conciliation, mediation and arbitration, and the Mediation Act 2023 provides a statutory framework for mediation in India. Related ideas: free, prior and informed consent (FPIC) from the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007), sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle. In case studies, police excesses should be investigated independently, and non-violent protest rights come under Article 19(1)(a) and (b) with reasonable restrictions.

question:
What amongst the following should Ms. X do now ? 1; Immediately disclose the information to the project committee and the public
2. Recommend removing the contractor from the shortlist to protect the project’s integrity
3. Propose a ‘limited disclosure’ to an oversight committee, while keeping the information confidential from the public for the time being Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Economy
detail: This is an ethics and integrity case-study item. The usual setup is that a public official learns sensitive, possibly unverified information about a shortlisted contractor, such as a conflict of interest, a past violation or a doubtful credential. The tested principles are due process, natural justice, proportionality, confidentiality and accountability. A public servant must not sit on the information, which would be complicity and a lapse of transparency. Nor should she act on unverified information by publicising it or by penalising the contractor, since that risks defamation, prejudice to the inquiry and legal challenge to the tender. The balanced course is to escalate to an independent oversight or competent authority, such as a vigilance or ethics committee, so the facts can be verified. The contractor should be heard before any adverse decision, and public disclosure should follow once the facts are verified, as procurement rules and the RTI Act, 2005 (Section 8 exemptions) allow. Elimination logic: options (a), (c) and (d) all include statement 1 or 2, and both are premature or unilateral. Only (b), statement 3 alone, is left. This reasoning depends on the missing passage, and if the scenario showed already-proven misconduct, statement 2 could gain weight.
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, immediate public disclosure, which is premature and unfair if the facts are unverified, and statement 2, which is unilateral and denies a hearing.

Correct: only statement 3, a limited and confidential disclosure to an oversight committee, balances transparency, due process and project integrity. This is the likely answer, with the caveat that the scenario text is missing.
Wrong: statement 2 is unilateral and pre-judges the contractor, even though statement 3 is acceptable.
Wrong: it includes all three, and statements 1 and 2 are premature or unilateral actions.
keyfact: In ethics cases involving unverified information, escalate confidentially to the competent oversight body, avoiding both public exposure and unilateral punishment.
option_notes: Option (a), 1 and 2 only, combines full public disclosure with a recommendation to remove the contractor. It is the most punitive and transparent-sounding course but ignores verification. Procurement law requires fair evaluation, a show-cause notice and recorded reasons before exclusion. Public naming before verification risks defamation claims and can compromise any later inquiry, so it is not a model ethical response.

Option (b), 3 only, is the limited and confidential disclosure to an oversight committee. It reflects escalation to a competent authority, proportionality and respect for natural justice. It keeps the process clean while verification happens. Vigilance bodies like the CVC and departmental committees play this role, and later publicity depends on the findings and on legal exemptions in the RTI Act.

Option (c), 2 and 3 only, adds a recommendation to remove the contractor to the limited disclosure. The disclosure is fine, but the removal recommendation presumes guilt. Exclusion from a shortlist or debarment needs evidence and an opportunity to respond, and arbitrary removal can be challenged in court as violating Article 14 and fair procurement norms.

Option (d), 1, 2 and 3, endorses every step. It is internally inconsistent, since public disclosure now conflicts with confidential, limited disclosure. Such all-of-the-above options are usually wrong in ethics case studies, which reward the measured, proportionate and rule-based response over the dramatic one.
related: Nolan Committee's seven principles of public life: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership.
Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 was passed but its operationalisation is incomplete; the 2015 amendment bill lapsed.
Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 2018 made bribe-giving an offence and requires prior approval for inquiries against public servants.
Central Vigilance Commission became statutory in 2003 and advises on Integrity Pacts in procurement.
RTI Act, 2005 Section 8(1)(h) exempts information that would impede an investigation.
Natural justice has two limbs: audi alteram partem and nemo judex in causa sua.
GeM (Government e-Marketplace) was launched in 2016 for transparent public procurement.
Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 covers allegations of corruption against public servants.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Disclosing immediately to the committee and the public is premature if the information is unverified, and it can damage reputations and prejudice the process. Public disclosure suits verified facts and mandated transparency. In procurement, bidder information is protected until evaluation ends. The General Financial Rules, 2017 and CVC guidelines stress transparency but also confidentiality and fairness. The Public Procurement Bill, 2012 never became law. Ethical duty means disclosing through the proper channel, not through the media or the public. Whistleblower norms under the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 likewise route complaints to a competent authority.

2 — Incorrect: Recommending removal on the strength of unverified information denies the contractor a hearing and breaches natural justice (audi alteram partem). It also exposes the department to litigation and may lead to a charge of arbitrary action under Article 14. Exclusion should come only after verification, with a reasoned decision. Debarment and blacklisting rules in the GFR and CVC manuals require show-cause notice and recorded reasons. The correct move is to flag the concern and let the authority decide on evidence, not to pre-judge the outcome.

3 — Correct: A limited, confidential disclosure to an oversight committee balances transparency with fairness. It prevents concealment, lets independent verification happen and protects both the project's integrity and the contractor's reputation pending facts. It reflects proportionality and the principle of escalating to a competent authority. Related institutions are the Central Vigilance Commission (statutory since 2003), departmental vigilance units and Integrity Pacts, a Transparency International-promoted tool the CVC recommends for large procurements. Public disclosure follows once facts are established and legal exemptions, such as RTI Section 8(1)(h) on impeding investigation, lapse.
summary: The likely answer is (b), 3 only, which matches the unofficial key, though the case scenario preceding the question is missing from the text, so I could not fully verify it. Ms. X should route the information to an oversight body through a confidential, limited disclosure. Immediate public disclosure and a unilateral recommendation to remove the contractor both pre-empt due process.
topic_notes: This question tests applied ethics in public administration, specifically handling conflict of interest, confidentiality and whistleblowing in procurement. Core principles are integrity, objectivity, accountability, transparency, impartiality, and natural justice (audi alteram partem and nemo judex in causa sua). Public servants face dilemmas between transparency and fairness, loyalty and public interest, and rules and discretion. The usual resolution is to follow rules, escalate through the proper channel, verify facts, protect the rights of all parties and disclose publicly only what is verified and legally permissible. Key institutions and laws: the Central Vigilance Commission (statutory body since 2003); the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (amended 2018, which criminalised giving bribes and added protection for decisions taken in good faith); the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 (enacted but not fully operationalised); the RTI Act, 2005 and its Section 8 exemptions; the General Financial Rules, 2017 on procurement; Integrity Pacts; the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013; the Conduct Rules for All India Services and Central Civil Services; and the Second ARC report on ethics in governance. Other angles UPSC may ask: the Nolan Committee's seven principles of public life (selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership), conflict-of-interest types (actual, potential, perceived), the difference between a whistleblower and an informant, and the GeM portal for transparent procurement. In exams, avoid extremes (silence or public exposure) and prefer measured, rule-based actions. Note that this explanation lacked the original scenario, so check it against the full passage.

question: X’ was addressing a seminar on the meaning of the term ‘law’ as provided under Article 13, 56. Part III of the Constitution of India. explained that the meaning of the term ‘law’ in the Constitution of India was very comprehensive. It included ordinances, orders and even rules and regulations. ‘Y pointed out that the term ‘law’ in Article 13 also included custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law, to which ‘X’ was not convinced. Based on the above, select the correct conclusion from the options given below :
options: X’is correct in the interpretation of law, including the view on non-inclusion of custom
The view of ‘Y that ‘law’ included custom is not correct
The views of both ‘X’ and ‘Y’ are correct
The view of only ‘Y is correct
subject: Polity
detail: Article 13 makes the Fundamental Rights in Part III supreme over other laws. Article 13(1) voids pre-constitutional laws to the extent they are inconsistent with Part III. Article 13(2) bars the State from making any law that takes away or abridges those rights. Article 13(3)(a) gives an inclusive definition of 'law': any ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law. Article 13(3)(b) defines 'laws in force' to include laws passed by a legislature or competent authority before the Constitution commenced, whether or not they were then in operation. X's statement that law includes ordinances, orders, rules and regulations is accurate. But X rejects the inclusion of custom or usage, which the text expressly includes, so X's overall position is wrong. Y's statement tracks Article 13(3)(a) exactly. Elimination: (a) and (b) deny custom and contradict the text. (c) endorses X's rejection of custom. Only (d) fits. Remember the leading cases: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that constitutional amendments are not 'law' under Article 13(2) for ordinary purposes, though the basic structure doctrine limits them. Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh had held the same. Golak Nath (1967) took the opposite view, and Kesavananda overruled it.
explanations: Wrong: X is right about ordinances, orders, rules and regulations, but wrong to reject custom, which Article 13(3)(a) expressly includes.
Wrong: Y's view is correct, because custom or usage having the force of law is within Article 13(3)(a).
Wrong: X's view is not fully correct, since X was unconvinced that custom is included. Both cannot be right.
Correct: Y's statement matches Article 13(3)(a), and X's doubt about custom is mistaken, so only Y is correct.
keyfact: Article 13(3)(a) defines 'law' inclusively to cover ordinances, orders, rules, regulations, notifications, and custom or usage having the force of law.
option_notes: Option (a) claims X is correct including on the non-inclusion of custom. It is wrong because Article 13(3)(a) lists custom or usage. It reflects the common mistake of treating 'law' as only written, enacted law. The Constitution's definition is inclusive and covers delegated legislation and customary law that has legal force.

Option (b) says Y's view that law includes custom is incorrect. This contradicts the text of Article 13(3)(a). Custom must have the force of law in the territory of India. Mere social practice does not qualify, but a legally enforceable custom does and is subject to Part III. Courts have tested personal-law customs against Part III in cases such as the Narasu Appa Mali line of reasoning.

Option (c) says both are correct. X's list of ordinances, orders, rules and regulations is accurate, but X's disbelief about custom is incorrect, so the combined claim fails. It is the tempting partial-credit option. UPSC often builds such questions with one half-right speaker.

Option (d) says only Y is correct. It matches Article 13(3)(a), which defines law inclusively to cover ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom and usage with the force of law. It is the right conclusion. The width of this definition lets courts strike down executive and delegated action as well as statutes that violate fundamental rights.
related: Article 13(3)(a) includes ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom and usage.
Article 13(4), added by the 24th Amendment, excludes constitutional amendments from Article 13.
Doctrine of eclipse applies to pre-Constitution laws, as in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras.
Doctrine of severability: only the offending part of a law is void.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) laid down the basic structure doctrine.
Golak Nath (1967) held that fundamental rights cannot be amended; it was later overruled.
Fundamental rights cannot be waived (Basheshar Nath case).
Article 12 defines 'State' for the purposes of Part III.
summary: The unofficial answer (d) is correct on the question as framed. Article 13(3)(a) defines 'law' to include any ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law. X's list is right but X wrongly doubts custom, so only Y is fully correct. Option (c) would be a trap only if X were read as merely incomplete rather than unconvinced.
topic_notes: Article 13 is the basis of judicial review of legislation in India and is in Part III. Article 13(1) covers pre-Constitution laws, which are void to the extent of inconsistency with fundamental rights. This is the doctrine of eclipse: such laws are not dead but overshadowed, and the inconsistency can be cured, as in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP. Article 13(2) covers post-Constitution laws, which are void to the extent of contravention. This is the doctrine of severability: only the offending part is struck down if it can be separated. Article 13(3) defines 'law' and 'laws in force'. Article 13(4) was added by the 24th Amendment (1971) and says Article 13 does not apply to amendments under Article 368. The doctrine of waiver does not apply to fundamental rights (Basheshar Nath case). Constitutional amendments: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) held they are not 'law'. Golak Nath (1967) held they are. Kesavananda Bharati (1973) upheld 13(4) and the basic structure limit. Article 13 applies to the State as defined in Article 12, and generally not to private persons, though some rights, such as Articles 15(2), 17 and 23, operate against private action. Personal laws: in State of Bombay v. Narasu Appa Mali (1952) the Bombay High Court held that personal laws are not 'laws in force' under Article 13, but later judgments such as Shayara Bano (2017, triple talaq) have shown a more nuanced approach. Related: Article 32 and Article 226 provide remedies. Article 368 deals with amendment procedure, and Article 141 makes Supreme Court rulings binding.

question:
Consider the following statements with reference to the Constitution of India : 1 There is no Article in the Constitution of India that specifies that the Constitution of India will be officially called the ‘Constitution of India’.
2. There is no Article in the Constitution of India that specifies that the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and _ the Government of India Act, 1935 stand repealed.
3. There is no Article in the Constitution of India that mentions 26" January, 1950 as the date of the commencement of the Constitution of India. Which one of the following conclusions based on the above statements is correct ?
options: There are two correct statements that include statement 3
There is only one correct statement
subject: Polity
detail: This question tests whether you know the last Part of the Constitution, Part XXII (Articles 392-395), titled 'Short title, commencement, authoritative text in Hindi and repeals'. Article 393 says 'This Constitution may be called the Constitution of India', which is its official short title. Article 394 says that Article 394 itself and Articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 came into force at once, on 26 November 1949, when the Constitution was adopted. The remaining provisions came into force on 26 January 1950, 'referred to in this Constitution as the commencement of this Constitution'. Article 395 repeals the Indian Independence Act 1947 and the Government of India Act 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing them. It specifically excepts the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act 1949, which was not repealed by it. Each statement asserts that no Article does something, and each of those 'no Article' claims is false. Once you recall that one Article covers each of the three matters, you can eliminate (a), (c) and (d) and arrive at (b). Be careful not to confuse the date of adoption (26 November 1949) with the date of commencement (26 January 1950).
explanations: Wrong. Statements 1, 2 and 3 are all incorrect, because Articles 393, 395 and 394 respectively cover the three matters.
Correct. Article 393 gives the short title, Article 395 does the repeals and Article 394 fixes the commencement date, so none of the three statements holds.
Wrong. No statement is correct, so there cannot be two correct statements, and statement 3 is itself incorrect.
Wrong. Not even one statement is correct, because every statement wrongly denies the existence of an Article that does exist.
keyfact: Part XXII: Article 393 short title, Article 394 commencement (26 Jan 1950), Article 395 repeals the 1947 Act and the 1935 Act.
option_notes: Option (a) would require all three 'no Article' claims to be true. That is false, because Articles 393, 394 and 395 cover these matters. Part XXII is the concluding Part of the Constitution. It contains Articles 392 (power of the President to remove difficulties), 393 (short title), 394 (commencement), 394A (Hindi text, inserted in 1987) and 395 (repeals). Students commonly confuse which Article does which job, so learn this Part by heart.

Option (b) says no statement is correct, and this is the right conclusion. Each statement denies an Article that exists. The Constitution has 'Constitution of India' as its short title in Article 393, and fixes its commencement date in Article 394. Article 395 repeals the Indian Independence Act 1947 and the Government of India Act 1935. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came fully into force on 26 January 1950.

Option (c) says two statements are correct and that statement 3 is one of them. This is wrong because statement 3 is false. Article 394 mentions 26 January 1950 as the commencement date. The date was chosen to commemorate Purna Swaraj Day, 26 January 1930. Some Articles came into force earlier, on 26 November 1949, which is why the date of adoption must be distinguished from the date of commencement.

Option (d) says only one statement is correct. This is wrong because none is correct. A one-correct-statement answer would need at least one of the Articles 393, 394 or 395 to be missing from the Constitution, but all three exist and perform exactly the functions the statements deny. Such questions test careful recall of the whole Part, not just the better-known Articles.
related: Article 393 gives the short title 'Constitution of India'; Article 394 deals with commencement; Article 395 deals with repeals.
The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950 (Article 394).
Article 394A (Hindi text) was inserted by the 58th Amendment Act, 1987.
Article 395 repealed the Indian Independence Act 1947 and the Government of India Act 1935.
The Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act 1949 was excepted from the repeal in Article 395.
The Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947 with B.R. Ambedkar as chairman.
26 January was chosen to mark the Purna Swaraj Declaration of 1930.
The original Constitution had 395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Article 393 states that the Constitution may be called the Constitution of India. Article 393 is the short-title provision of the Constitution, in Part XXII. It was among the provisions that took effect on 26 November 1949, the day the Constituent Assembly adopted and signed the Constitution. The Preamble, by contrast, only says 'we the people of India... adopt, enact and give to ourselves this Constitution'. Part XXII also includes Article 394A, the authoritative Hindi text, which was inserted by the 58th Amendment in 1987. Article 395 is the last Article of the original text.

2 — Incorrect: Article 395 expressly repeals the Indian Independence Act 1947 and the Government of India Act 1935, along with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter. It excepts the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act 1949. The Indian Independence Act 1947 created the dominions of India and Pakistan from 15 August 1947. The Government of India Act 1935 provided the federal framework and was the main source of the Constitution's administrative provisions. Before 1950, India's governance continued under an adapted version of the 1935 Act, which is why the repeal had to be stated formally.

3 — Incorrect: Article 394 names 26 January 1950 as the date of commencement of the Constitution. The Article says the remainder of the Constitution comes into force on that date, 'which day is referred to in this Constitution as the commencement of this Constitution'. The date was chosen to honour the Purna Swaraj Declaration of 26 January 1930, issued by the Lahore Congress session. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949, and some provisions on citizenship, elections, the provisional Parliament and the short title took effect immediately.
summary: The answer is (b), so the unofficial key is correct. All three statements are incorrect: Article 393 gives the short title 'Constitution of India', Article 395 repeals the Indian Independence Act 1947 and the Government of India Act 1935, and Article 394 fixes 26 January 1950 as the commencement date.
topic_notes: Part XXII of the Constitution, 'Short title, commencement, authoritative text in Hindi and repeals', runs from Article 392 to Article 395. Article 392 empowers the President to remove difficulties in the transition, and it was relevant before the Constitution began to work. Article 393 gives the short title, 'Constitution of India'. Article 394 provides for commencement. Articles 5-9 (citizenship), 60, 324 (Election Commission), 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 came into force on 26 November 1949. The rest came into force on 26 January 1950. Article 394A, inserted by the 58th Amendment Act 1987, provides for the authoritative text in Hindi, to be published under the President's authority. Article 395 repeals the Indian Independence Act 1947 and the Government of India Act 1935, along with their amending Acts, but not the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act 1949. Constituent Assembly facts: its first meeting was on 9 December 1946, with Sachchidananda Sinha as interim president. Rajendra Prasad was elected president on 11 December 1946. B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, set up on 29 August 1947. The Objectives Resolution was moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and signed on 24 January 1950. The assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days. The original Constitution had a Preamble, 395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules. Related areas UPSC could ask next are Article 368 (amendment), the Preamble and the Kesavananda Bharati case, the Constituent Assembly committees, and the foreign sources of Constitutional provisions.

ocr: Which of the following statements with regard to the persons with disabilities in India is/are correct ? The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, an Act passed by the Parliament of India in 2018, mandates reservation in education and employment, places a legal duty on Governments to ensure accessibility and non-discrimination. The Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan focuses on achieving universal accessibility for Persons with Disabilities across three key domains — built infrastructure, transport systems and information and communication technology. The National Divyangjan Finance and Development Corp
subject: Economy
detail: The question tests India's disability-rights framework: the law, the accessibility campaign and the finance institution. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act was enacted in December 2016 and came into force on 19 April 2017. It replaced the Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995 and gave effect to the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD), which India ratified in 2007. It recognises 21 disabilities, raised reservation in government jobs from 3% to 4%, and provides 5% reservation in higher education institutions. It also imposes duties on governments to ensure accessibility and non-discrimination. Statement 1 has the right content but the wrong year (2018), so it fails. The Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan (Accessible India Campaign) was launched on 3 December 2015 by the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD). It has three pillars: built environment, transport systems, and ICT ecosystem. Statement 2 is therefore correct. The NDFDC was established in 1997 as a not-for-profit company under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956, under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (DEPwD), not the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. Statement 3 fails. Only statement 2 survives, so the answer is (b).
explanations: (a) is wrong: it includes statement 1, which is incorrect because the RPwD Act was passed in 2016, not 2018.
(b) is right: only statement 2 is correct. Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan covers built infrastructure, transport and ICT.
(c) is wrong: it includes both statements 1 and 3, which are incorrect (wrong year; wrong ministry), and it omits statement 2, which is correct.
(d) is wrong: statement 1 is incorrect because of the year, and statement 2 is correct but is left out.
keyfact: RPwD Act = 2016 (in force 2017), 21 disabilities; Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan (2015) covers built environment, transport and ICT; NDFDC (1997) sits under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.
option_notes: Option (a) is 1 and 2 only. It would be correct if the RPwD Act had been passed in 2018. The actual date is 2016, with commencement on 19 April 2017. The Act recognises 21 disabilities and has 4% reservation in government jobs and 5% in higher education. It follows the UNCRPD, which India ratified in 2007, and replaces the PwD Act, 1995.

Option (b) is 2 only. It is the correct answer. Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan (Accessible India Campaign) was launched on 3 December 2015 by DEPwD. Its three pillars are the built environment, transport systems and the ICT ecosystem. It aims at universal accessibility and equal opportunity for persons with disabilities. It includes making airports, railway stations, public buildings and government websites accessible.

Option (c) is 1 and 3. It is wrong because it excludes statement 2 and includes two flawed statements. For context, NDFDC is a not-for-profit company set up in 1997 under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. It provides concessional finance to persons with disabilities through State Channelising Agencies. The Act date is 2016, not 2018.

Option (d) is 1 only. It is wrong because statement 1 carries the wrong year (2018 instead of 2016). The RPwD Act, 2016 mandates reservation in education and employment and places a duty on governments to ensure accessibility and non-discrimination. It contains the provisions on benchmark disabilities, guardianship, and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities.
related: RPwD Act, 2016 recognises 21 disabilities; the 1995 Act recognised 7.
Benchmark disability means at least 40% of a specified disability.
RPwD Act provides 4% job reservation and 5% reservation in higher education.
Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan was launched on 3 December 2015.
International Day of Persons with Disabilities is observed on 3 December.
India ratified the UNCRPD in 2007.
Census 2011 recorded about 2.68 crore persons with disabilities (2.21%).
UDID project issues a Unique Disability ID card to persons with disabilities.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The RPwD Act was passed in 2016, not 2018. The Act was passed by Parliament in December 2016, received assent on 27 December 2016 and came into force on 19 April 2017. It replaced the 1995 Act and implements the UNCRPD. It expanded recognised disabilities from 7 to 21 and provides 4% reservation in government jobs and 5% in higher education. It also provides for Chief Commissioner and State Commissioners for Persons with Disabilities, special courts, and a National Fund. Penalties are prescribed for offences against persons with disabilities.

2 — Correct: Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan targets universal accessibility in three domains: built environment, transport systems, and information and communication technology (ICT). It was launched on 3 December 2015, the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, by the Prime Minister. It is run by the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. It is linked to the Sugamya Bharat app and to making government websites accessible under the GIGW guidelines. Targets covered government buildings, airports, railway stations and public transport. Deadlines were revised several times.

3 — Incorrect: NDFDC is under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, not the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. It was set up in January 1997 as a not-for-profit company (originally under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956; now Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013). It is wholly owned by the Government of India. It provides concessional loans to persons with disabilities for self-employment and entrepreneurship, skill training and education. It works through State Channelising Agencies. It is a separate body from the National Handicapped Finance and Development Corporation's older name, which it replaced when renamed to Divyangjan.
summary: The correct answer is (b) 2 only; the unofficial key is right. Statement 1 is wrong because the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act was passed in 2016, not 2018. Statement 3 is wrong because NDFDC was set up under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, not the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. Statement 2 correctly describes the Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan.
topic_notes: Disability policy in India rests on constitutional, legislative and institutional pillars. Constitutionally, 'relief of the disabled and unemployable' is in Entry 9 of the State List, and DPSP Article 41 provides for public assistance in cases of disablement. The 2016 amendment to the Constitution is not involved here, but Article 253 allows legislation to implement international treaties. Key laws: the Mental Health Act, 1987 (replaced by the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017); Rehabilitation Council of India Act, 1992; Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995 (7 disabilities); National Trust Act, 1999 (autism, cerebral palsy, mental retardation, multiple disabilities); and the RPwD Act, 2016 (21 disabilities, including acid attack victims, Parkinson's disease, thalassemia, haemophilia and sickle cell disease). Benchmark disability means at least 40% of a specified disability. Reservation: 4% in government posts, 5% in higher education, and 5% in land allotment and poverty alleviation schemes. Institutions: Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (set up in 2012 and renamed from the Department of Disability Affairs; given departmental status under MoSJE), Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities, NDFDC, the National Institutes, ALIMCO and the Rehabilitation Council of India. Schemes: Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan (2015), ADIP scheme for aids and appliances, Deendayal Disabled Rehabilitation Scheme, SIPDA, Scholarship schemes, the Unique Disability ID (UDID) project, and the term 'Divyang' popularised in 2015. International: UNCRPD adopted in 2006, India ratified it in 2007; International Day of Persons with Disabilities is 3 December. Census 2011 recorded about 2.68 crore persons with disabilities (2.21% of the population). Supreme Court cases to know: Rajive Raturi v. Union of India (2024) on accessibility, and Vikash Kumar (2021) on scribe and reasonable accommodation.

question:
Consider the following statements about the 59. provisions pertaining to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in India : a Provisions regarding the administration of the Tribal Areas in the States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram are given in the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution of India. 2: Some tribes of India are entitled to exemption from paying Income Tax on certain incomes.
3. The Constitution of India provides for reservation of seats in Panchayats for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes. Which one of the following conclusions based on the above statements is correct ?
options: There are two correct statements, that include statement 2
There are two correct statements, that are statements 1 and 3
There is only one correct statement
subject: Polity
detail: The Constitution has two special schemes for tribal areas. The Fifth Schedule (Article 244(1)) covers the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in all states except Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. It works through the Governor, who can direct or modify laws, and through Tribes Advisory Councils. The Sixth Schedule (Article 244(2), also Articles 275(1)) covers the tribal areas of those four states through Autonomous District Councils and Regional Councils, which have legislative, judicial and financial powers. Statement 1 swaps the two Schedules, so it is incorrect. Statement 2 is correct: Section 10(26) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 exempts income of Scheduled Tribe members residing in specified areas (the North-East states, Ladakh) from certain sources. Section 10(26A) and 10(26AAA) give similar relief to residents of Ladakh and Sikkim. Statement 3 is correct: Article 243D(3) reserves not less than one-third of the seats reserved for SCs and STs for women of those groups, and Article 243D(4) applies the same to chairperson offices. Elimination: once statement 1 is rejected, only options (a) and (c) remain. Since statements 2 and 3 are both correct, (c) fails and (a) holds.
explanations: Correct. Statement 1 is wrong because it names the Fifth Schedule instead of the Sixth. Statements 2 and 3 are correct, so exactly two statements are correct and they include statement 2.
Wrong. Statement 1 is incorrect because the four North-East states fall under the Sixth Schedule, so statements 1 and 3 cannot be the two correct statements.

Wrong. Two statements, 2 and 3, are correct, not just one. Section 10(26) exempts certain income of Scheduled Tribe members in specified areas, and Article 243D provides for reservation for SC and ST women in Panchayats.
Wrong. Statement 1 is incorrect, so not all three statements are correct.
keyfact: Fifth Schedule = Scheduled Areas in most states; Sixth Schedule = tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; Article 243D gives SC/ST women Panchayat reservation.
option_notes: This option says exactly two statements are correct and that statement 2 is among them. It holds here because statements 2 and 3 are correct. Statement 2 rests on Section 10(26) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, which exempts specified income of Scheduled Tribe members residing in notified areas such as the North-East and Ladakh. Statement 3 rests on Article 243D(3) of the 73rd Amendment, which reserves one-third of SC and ST seats for women of those groups. Always check which statements are false before choosing among 'two correct' options.

This option claims statements 1 and 3 are the correct pair. It fails because statement 1 mixes up the Fifth and Sixth Schedules. The Fifth Schedule covers Scheduled Areas in ten states other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. It is administered by the Governor with Tribes Advisory Councils under Article 244(1). The Sixth Schedule covers the autonomous councils of the four North-East states. UPSC often tests this swap, and the wrong Schedule is a typical trap.

This option says only one statement is correct. It would be true if only one of statements 2 and 3 were right. Here both are right: Section 10(26) of the Income Tax Act gives a tax exemption to Scheduled Tribe members in specified areas, and Article 243D(3) reserves Panchayat seats for SC and ST women. Statement 3 is a constitutional guarantee. Statement 2 is a statutory tax provision, not a constitutional one. Careful reading of each statement is essential before choosing a count-based option.

This option says all three statements are correct. It fails because statement 1 is incorrect. The Sixth Schedule, not the Fifth, governs tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. It would be correct only if the statement had named the Sixth Schedule. Such count-based options reward knowing exactly which Schedule covers which region. Remember that the Sixth Schedule gives autonomous councils far more legislative, executive and judicial power than the Fifth Schedule's advisory structure.
related: Fifth Schedule: Scheduled Areas in ten states, administered by the Governor with Tribes Advisory Councils.
Sixth Schedule: tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, with Autonomous District Councils.
Article 243D reserves Panchayat seats for SCs and STs, with one-third of them for women.
Article 342 deals with the specification of Scheduled Tribes; Article 341 with Scheduled Castes.
Article 338A establishes the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (89th Amendment, 2003).
PESA, 1996 extends Panchayat provisions to Fifth Schedule areas and empowers Gram Sabhas.
Section 10(26) of the Income Tax Act exempts specified income of Scheduled Tribe members in notified areas.
The Bodoland Territorial Council is a Sixth Schedule body in Assam.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The administration of tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram is under the Sixth Schedule, not the Fifth.
