India's work there includes the Greater Malé Connectivity Project, a USD 500 million line of credit and defence training. Mangdechhu belongs to Bhutan, a Himalayan kingdom with which India has the 2007 Friendship Treaty and major hydropower cooperation.

Code (b) 3-2-4-1 is the correct match. A-3 Bhutan (Mangdechhu, 720 MW, inaugurated 2019). B-2 Afghanistan (Stor Palace, Kabul, restored with the Aga Khan Trust for Culture). C-4 Sri Lanka (Dickoya hospital for plantation communities). D-1 Maldives (ISLES, an MNDF training institute). All four are examples of India's development partnerships under neighbourhood-first policy.

Code (c) 3-4-2-1 gets A and D right but swaps B and C. It would place Stor Palace in Sri Lanka and the Dickoya hospital in Afghanistan. Sri Lanka has Indian-backed projects like housing in the Northern and Eastern provinces, the 1990 ambulance service and the Jaffna Cultural Centre. Afghanistan has the Parliament, Salma Dam and Zaranj-Delaram road.

Code (d) 1-2-4-3 gets B and C right but swaps A and D. It would place Mangdechhu in the Maldives and the security institute in Bhutan. Bhutan's Indian-assisted projects include Chukha, Tala, Kurichhu, Punatsangchhu I and II and Mangdechhu. In the Maldives, India has provided defence training, a coast guard harbour and the Hanimaadhoo airport.
related: Mangdechhu (720 MW) in Bhutan was inaugurated by PM Modi in 2019.
The Afghan Parliament building in Kabul was built by India and inaugurated in 2015.
The Salma Dam in Herat is called the Afghan-India Friendship Dam.
Greater Malé Connectivity Project is India's largest infrastructure project in the Maldives.
Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project links Kolkata to Sittwe and Paletwa in Myanmar.
The Development Partnership Administration (DPA) under the MEA was set up in 2012.
ITEC is India's flagship technical cooperation programme, launched in 1964.
Tala (1020 MW) is the largest hydropower project in Bhutan built with India's help.
statements: A — Correct: Mangdechhu Hydroelectric Project matches 3 (Bhutan). It is a 720 MW run-of-the-river project on the Mangdechhu river in Trongsa district, developed by Mangdechhu Hydroelectric Project Authority with Indian grant and loan support. It was inaugurated in August 2019 by PM Modi with Bhutan's PM Lotay Tshering. It is among India-Bhutan cooperation projects like Chukha, Tala, Kurichhu and Punatsangchhu. Power is exported to India under agreements and it strengthens the energy partnership.

B — Correct: Restoration of Stor Palace matches 2 (Afghanistan). Stor Palace in Kabul is a historic building that houses the Afghan Ministry of Foreign Affairs. India helped restore it, working with the Aga Khan Trust for Culture. It was opened in 2016 as a symbol of cultural cooperation. India's other Afghan projects include the Parliament building (2015), Salma Dam in Herat (2016), Zaranj-Delaram highway and Shahtoot Dam.

C — Correct: District Hospital at Dickoya matches 4 (Sri Lanka). Dickoya (Dikoya) is in Nuwara Eliya district, in the hill country of Sri Lanka, home to many plantation Tamils of Indian origin. India funded the Dickoya District Hospital as a grant project and PM Modi opened it in 2023 during his Sri Lanka engagement. India also supports housing, the 1990 Suwa Seriya ambulance service and other projects in Sri Lanka.

D — Correct: Institute of Security and Law Enforcement Studies matches 1 (Maldives). Known as ISLES, it is a Maldives National Defence Force training institute built with Indian assistance in the Maldives. It underscores India-Maldives defence cooperation. Other India-linked work includes the Greater Malé Connectivity Project, the Hanimaadhoo airport, Exercise Ekuverin and Ekatha, and the Maldives coast guard harbour (Uthuru Thila Falhu).
summary: The correct answer is (b): A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1. Mangdechhu is in Bhutan, Stor Palace is in Kabul (Afghanistan), the Dickoya district hospital is in Sri Lanka, and the Institute of Security and Law Enforcement Studies is in the Maldives. The unofficial answer (b) is verified as correct.
topic_notes: India's development partnership is delivered through grants, lines of credit (concessional loans via EXIM Bank) and capacity building, coordinated by the MEA's Development Partnership Administration (DPA), set up in 2012. India's partnership spans Asia and Africa, with major focus on neighbours. In Bhutan, hydropower is central: Chukha (336 MW), Kurichhu (60 MW), Tala (1020 MW), Mangdechhu (720 MW), and Punatsangchhu I and II. India is Bhutan's largest trade and development partner, and the 2007 Friendship Treaty replaced the 1949 treaty. In Afghanistan, India has built the Parliament (2015), Salma Dam (2016), Zaranj-Delaram Highway (2009), Stor Palace (restored), and supports Chabahar via Iran for access. In Sri Lanka, there are housing projects (50,000 houses), the 1990 Suwa Seriya ambulance service, the Dickoya hospital, Jaffna Cultural Centre and Palaly airport and Kankesanthurai harbour development. In the Maldives, India has built the Greater Malé Connectivity Project (GMCP), the National College for Policing and Law Enforcement, and the Hanimaadhoo airport. In Nepal, India has the Motihari-Amlekhgunj petroleum pipeline, Integrated Check Posts and the Arun-3 project. In Bangladesh, the Maitree Super Thermal Power Project (Rampal) and the Akhaura-Agartala rail link. Myanmar has the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport project and the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway. In the Indian Ocean, India works with Mauritius and Seychelles on infrastructure and on maritime security. Other schemes to know: SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region), Neighbourhood First, ITEC (Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation) and Act East. Expect questions that match projects to countries, as this one does.

question:
Which of the following items of defence 70. hardware is/are manufactured in India ?
1. Su-30 MKI Fighter Jets 2.‘ T-90 MK-III Tanks
8. Akula Class Submarine Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Economy
detail: The question tests defence hardware that is produced in India, including licensed production. Su-30 MKI: designed by Russia's Sukhoi and licence-built by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) at Nashik since the early 2000s under a 2000 licence agreement; India has contracted well over 200 aircraft, with an additional 12 ordered in 2024. T-90 tanks: India first imported T-90S from Russia (2001), then began licence production at the Heavy Vehicles Factory (HVF), Avadi (Tamil Nadu), named 'Bhishma'; the T-90 MK-III is the modernised variant with thermal imaging sights and the Kalina fire control system, produced under licence with Russian components. Akula-class: a Russian Project 971 nuclear-powered attack submarine. India leased INS Chakra (Chakra II) from Russia in 2012 for 10 years, and a new lease (Chakra III) has been agreed. It was built in Russia and not manufactured in India. Elimination: once you know Akula is leased, options (b) and (c)/(d) combos containing 3 fall away; knowing both Su-30 and T-90 are made in India settles (a).
explanations: Correct: both the Su-30 MKI (HAL, Nashik) and the T-90 tanks (HVF Avadi) are made in India under licence, and the Akula submarine is excluded.
Wrong: it includes the Akula-class submarine, which is leased from Russia and was built there, not manufactured in India.
Wrong: it omits the T-90 tanks, which are manufactured in India at Avadi, so it is incomplete.
Wrong: it omits the Su-30 MKI, which HAL produces in Nashik, so it is incomplete.
keyfact: Su-30 MKI (HAL Nashik) and T-90 (HVF Avadi) are licence-made in India; the Akula submarine is only leased from Russia.
option_notes: Su-30 MKI and T-90 tanks: both are Russian-origin platforms licence-produced in India by HAL (Nashik) and the Ordnance Factory Board successor HVF Avadi (now under Armoured Vehicles Nigam Limited, AVNL). They illustrate India's licensed-production model of defence manufacturing, with a gradually rising indigenous content. Licence production is not indigenous design, which is why Tejas and Arjun are described differently.

Su-30 MKI and Akula submarine: this combination is wrong because the Akula is a Russian-built vessel leased by India. It is not a product of Indian shipyards. Indian-built naval platforms include the Arihant-class SSBN, the Kalvari-class (Scorpene) submarines at MDL and the INS Vikrant aircraft carrier built by Cochin Shipyard, commissioned in 2022.

Su-30 MKI only: this reflects only partial knowledge. The Su-30 MKI is made in India, but this option wrongly excludes the T-90 tank. The T-90 is produced at HVF Avadi in Tamil Nadu, which started producing it in the 2000s and delivers hundreds of units, including the T-90 'Bhishma' variant.

T-90 MK-III only: this option wrongly excludes the Su-30 MKI. The T-90 MK-III is a modernised version of the Russian T-90 main battle tank with a thermal imager and a Kalina fire control system, and it is made at HVF Avadi. The Su-30 MKI is produced at HAL's Nashik division, so both belong in the correct answer.
related: HAL Nashik produces Su-30 MKI under licence from Russia.
T-90 'Bhishma' tanks are produced at HVF Avadi, Tamil Nadu.
INS Chakra is an Akula-class SSN leased from Russia.
Kalvari-class (Scorpene) submarines are built by MDL, Mumbai, with France's Naval Group.
INS Vikrant, India's first indigenous aircraft carrier, was built by Cochin Shipyard and commissioned in 2022.
Defence FDI limit: 74% automatic route, up to 100% via government route.
The Ordnance Factory Board was corporatised into seven DPSUs in 2021.
Defence Industrial Corridors are in Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
statements: 1 — Correct: Su-30 MKI is manufactured in India by HAL at Nashik under licence. The Su-30 MKI is a twin-engine, two-seat, long-range multirole air superiority fighter, developed by Sukhoi for India, and uses thrust-vectoring AL-31FP engines (some engine production at HAL Koraput). The licence production deal was signed in 2000. India's IAF operates about 260 of them, the backbone of its fighter fleet. Upgrade programmes ('Super Sukhoi') add AESA radar and indigenous systems. HAL Nashik also performs overhaul work.

2 — Correct: T-90 tanks are manufactured in India at HVF Avadi, Chennai, under licence from Russia. The T-90S 'Bhishma' is a 3rd-generation main battle tank with a 125 mm smoothbore gun that can fire missiles. The first import was in 2001 after Pakistan's Al-Khalid tanks emerged, and licence production followed from 2003. The MK-III version has a thermal sight, upgraded engine of 1000 hp and a Kalina fire control system. India operates over 1,000 T-90s, alongside the indigenous Arjun and T-72 Ajeya.

3 — Incorrect: The Akula-class submarine is a Russian-built nuclear-powered attack submarine (Project 971 Shchuka-B). India leased INS Chakra from Russia, first from 1988 to 1991 (a K-43 Charlie class) and then the Akula-class Chakra II from 2012 to 2022. It is not made in India. India's own nuclear submarines are the Arihant-class SSBNs built at Visakhapatnam under the Advanced Technology Vessel project; India's conventional Scorpene submarines (Kalvari class) are built by MDL, Mumbai.
summary: The unofficial answer (a) '1 and 2' looks correct. Su-30 MKI fighters are built by HAL at Nashik under licence from Russia, and T-90 tanks (T-90S 'Bhishma') are assembled/manufactured at HVF Avadi. The Akula-class submarine (Chakra) is leased from Russia, not made in India, so statement 3 is wrong.
topic_notes: India's defence manufacturing has three layers: indigenous design (Tejas LCA, Arjun MBT, Pinaka, BrahMos jointly with Russia, Akash, INS Vikrant, Arihant), licence production (Su-30 MKI, T-90, Scorpene/Kalvari, MiG-21/27 earlier), and direct import or lease (Rafale, S-400, Akula SSN). Key public bodies: HAL (Bengaluru; Navratna, produces aircraft and helicopters including Dhruv, LCH Prachand, Tejas), BEL, BDL, MDL, GRSE, GSL, Cochin Shipyard, and since 2021 seven DPSUs formed out of the Ordnance Factory Board (AVNL, MIL, YIL, AWEIL, IOL, TCL, GIL). Policy: Make in India (2014), Defence Acquisition Procedure 2020 with the 'Buy (Indian-IDDM)' category, positive indigenisation lists (five lists of platforms, with import bans), Defence Industrial Corridors in Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence), FDI in defence allowed up to 74% under automatic route and 100% by government route, and the Strategic Partnership model. India set a defence export target of ₹50,000 crore by 2029 and a manufacturing target of ₹3 lakh crore. Related: Project 75I for six conventional submarines with Germany's TKMS and MDL, Project 75 Alpha for nuclear attack submarines, and the Indo-Russian lease of the Akula. Other angles: AMCA fifth-generation fighter programme, GE F414 engine deal with HAL, and Tejas Mk1A deliveries.

question:
Consider the following statements about platforms for multilateral co-operation :
1. The ‘Colombo Process’ is a regional consultative process in which member states take binding decisions by consensus. a1;
2. The ‘Abu Dhabi Dialogue’ is a voluntary non-binding consultative process among Asian countries of labour origin and destination to facilitate regional cooperation on contractual labour mobility.
3. The ‘Global Forum for Migration and Development’, created upon the proposal of a former UN Secretary General, is a voluntary forum whose decisions are non-binding in nature. Which of the statements given above is/are correct ?
subject: Economy
detail: Regional Consultative Processes (RCPs) on migration are informal, state-led, non-binding dialogue platforms. They let governments share information, build trust and develop common positions without creating treaty obligations. The Colombo Process (2003, Colombo, Sri Lanka) brings together Asian countries of origin of overseas contract workers. Its Secretariat is at IOM. Its recommendations are voluntary, which makes statement 1 wrong, because 'binding decisions' contradicts the RCP model. The Abu Dhabi Dialogue (2008) widened this to Asian countries of origin and destination, including Gulf states. It is a voluntary, non-binding forum on temporary contractual labour mobility, so statement 2 is correct. The Global Forum on Migration and Development (GFMD) was proposed by UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan in 2006 at the UN High-Level Dialogue on International Migration and Development. The first meeting was held in Brussels in 2007. It is voluntary, informal, state-led and non-binding, and it is outside the formal UN system. Statement 3 is therefore correct. Elimination: once statement 1 is seen to be incorrect, options (a) and (b) are ruled out. Statement 3 being correct rules out (d), which leaves (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes statement 1, which is incorrect because the Colombo Process takes no binding decisions.
Wrong: it includes statement 1, which wrongly describes the Colombo Process as binding, even though statement 3 is correct.
Right: statements 2 and 3 correctly describe the Abu Dhabi Dialogue and the GFMD, and statement 1 is incorrect.
Wrong: statement 3 is also correct, so 2 alone is incomplete.
keyfact: RCPs and the GFMD (Kofi Annan's idea, 2007) are voluntary and non-binding; the Colombo Process (2003) and Abu Dhabi Dialogue (2008) take no binding decisions.
option_notes: Option (a), 1, 2 and 3: this would require all three statements to be correct. That fails because the Colombo Process is a non-binding RCP and takes no binding decisions. The three platforms (Colombo Process, Abu Dhabi Dialogue, GFMD) are all voluntary, state-led and non-binding. They sit alongside the binding-treaty route, such as the 1990 ICRMW, which is a UN convention on migrant workers' rights and has not been ratified by major destination countries.

Option (b), 1 and 3 only: this treats the Colombo Process as binding and wrongly excludes the Abu Dhabi Dialogue. The Colombo Process (2003) is a non-binding forum of Asian origin countries. The Abu Dhabi Dialogue (2008) is its extension to include destination countries in Asia. India is a member of both. The Colombo Process secretariat is supported by IOM.

Option (c), 2 and 3 only: this is the correct answer. The Abu Dhabi Dialogue (2008) is a voluntary, non-binding forum of Asian origin and destination countries on temporary contractual labour. The GFMD, which grew from Kofi Annan's 2006 proposal and first met in Brussels in 2007, is voluntary and non-binding. Both aim to build dialogue and share good practices without creating legal obligations on states.

Option (d), 2 only: this correctly identifies the Abu Dhabi Dialogue but wrongly excludes the GFMD. The GFMD is a non-binding, voluntary, government-led forum. It was created after Kofi Annan's proposal, with the first meeting in 2007 in Brussels. It meets annually under a rotating chair, and civil society participates through separate Civil Society Days.
related: Colombo Process: launched 2003; Asian labour-origin countries; IOM provides Secretariat.
Abu Dhabi Dialogue: launched 2008; links Colombo Process members with Asian destination countries.
GFMD: first held in Brussels in 2007 after Kofi Annan's proposal; non-binding.
Global Compact for Migration was adopted in Marrakech in December 2018 and is non-binding.
1990 ICRMW came into force in 2003; India has not ratified it.
Bali Process (2002) deals with people smuggling and trafficking in persons.
IOM became a UN related organisation in 2016.
India's Emigration Act 1983 is being replaced by a proposed Overseas Mobility Bill.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: the Colombo Process is a non-binding consultative forum, not a body that takes binding decisions. It was launched in 2003 as the Ministerial Consultations on Overseas Employment and Contractual Labour for Countries of Origin in Asia. Its members include India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Nepal, the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, China, Afghanistan and others. Its priority areas are skills and qualification recognition, fair recruitment, pre-departure orientation, remittances and labour market analysis. It is chaired on a rotating basis and its Secretariat is supported by IOM. It issues recommendations and declarations only.

2 — Correct: the Abu Dhabi Dialogue was launched in 2008 as a forum for Colombo Process member states and Asian destination countries. It is a voluntary, non-binding consultative process on temporary contractual labour mobility. Members include Gulf Cooperation Council states, plus Malaysia, Singapore, Yemen and Colombo Process origin countries. It focuses on fair recruitment, skills, labour-market information and welfare of migrant workers. The UAE has hosted and chaired meetings, and IOM acts as Secretariat. It produces partnership frameworks and pilot projects, not treaties.

3 — Correct: the GFMD arose from the 2006 UN High-Level Dialogue on International Migration and Development, following a proposal by then UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan. The first Forum was held in Brussels in 2007, with Belgium as chair. It is a voluntary, informal, non-binding, government-led process outside the UN system, and civil society takes part through the Civil Society Days. It rotates its chairmanship every year. Its outcomes feed into later global frameworks such as the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration (2018).
summary: The answer is (c): statements 2 and 3 are correct and statement 1 is incorrect. The Colombo Process is a non-binding regional consultative process, so it does not take 'binding decisions by consensus'. The unofficial key (c) is correct.
topic_notes: Migration governance has no single binding global regime. It relies on soft-law dialogues, RCPs and a few treaties. Regional Consultative Processes (RCPs) are informal, non-binding, state-led forums. Examples include the Colombo Process (2003, Asian origin countries), the Abu Dhabi Dialogue (2008, Asian origin and destination), the Bali Process (2002, people smuggling, trafficking and related transnational crime, co-chaired by Indonesia and Australia), the Budapest Process, the Puebla Process and the Rabat Process. IOM often acts as Secretariat. The Global Forum on Migration and Development (GFMD), proposed by Kofi Annan in 2006 and first held in Brussels in 2007, is a voluntary, informal and non-binding state-led process. Binding instruments include the 1990 International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families (in force 2003), ILO Conventions 97 and 143 on migrant workers, and the 1951 Refugee Convention. The Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration (GCM) was adopted in Marrakech in December 2018. It is a non-binding, state-led framework with 23 objectives, and India supported it. IOM became a related organisation of the UN in 2016. The International Migration Review Forum (IMRF) reviews GCM progress every four years, starting in 2022. India's migration framework includes the Emigration Act 1983, the e-Migrate portal, the Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (9 January), the Pravasi Bharatiya Bima Yojana, the Madad portal and the MADAD/ECNR regime. India is also negotiating labour mobility agreements with Gulf and European countries. India is the world's largest remittance recipient, receiving over USD 100 billion a year (World Bank).

ocr: Consider the following UN organisations/ agencies : 1. World Food Programme 2. United Nations Children’s Fund 3. | United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees 4, International Labour Organisation How many of the above has/have been awarded the Nobel Prize twice ? (a). (b) 2 ( 3 (dd) 4 Match ListI with List II and select the answer using the code given below the Lists : List I List IT (UN Peacekeeping (Period of Operation) Operation) A. UNMIL 1. 2007-2010 B. MINURCAT 2. 2002 — 2005 C. MINUSTAH 8. 2003 —- 2018 D. UNMISET 4. 2004-2017 Code: A Bs CoD (a) 3 1 2 (b) 3 1 4 2 (c) 2 al 4 3 (d) 2 4 if
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Nobel Peace Prize has gone to several UN agencies, but very few organisations have won it more than once. The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, is one: it won in 1954 for work with European refugees and again in 1981 for assistance to refugees worldwide. The only other multiple winner usually cited is the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which won in 1917, 1944 and 1963, and the Red Cross movement shared the 1963 prize with the League of Red Cross Societies (now the IFRC). The other three bodies in the question won once each. UNICEF won in 1965 for its work for children. The ILO won in 1969, its 50th anniversary year, for improving labour conditions and promoting justice among peoples. The World Food Programme won in 2020 for fighting hunger and preventing hunger from being used as a weapon of war. Elimination logic: once you know that only UNHCR is a double winner, the count is 1. If you remember UNICEF (1965), ILO (1969) and WFP (2020) as single wins, options (b), (c) and (d) fall away.
explanations: Correct. Only UNHCR (1954 and 1981) has won twice, so the count is 1.
Wrong. This would require a second double winner among the WFP, UNICEF and ILO. All three have won only once (2020, 1965 and 1969).
Wrong. Three double winners would mean the WFP, UNICEF or ILO also won twice, which is not true.
Wrong. No more than one of these four organisations has won twice, so the count cannot be 4.
keyfact: UNHCR is the only UN agency to win the Nobel Peace Prize twice (1954 and 1981); UNICEF (1965), ILO (1969) and WFP (2020) won once each.
option_notes: Count of 1: this is the correct number. The one double winner is UNHCR (1954 and 1981). Other repeat winners outside this list include the ICRC, which has won three times (1917, 1944 and 1963). Individuals who won two Nobel Prizes in different fields include Marie Curie, Linus Pauling and Frederick Sanger, but only Pauling won a Peace Prize as one of them.

Count of 2: this would need a second double winner among the four. Students often confuse the ILO or UNICEF with UNHCR because all three are UN bodies with Peace Prizes. ILO won in 1969 and UNICEF in 1965, so each won only once. The UN itself and Kofi Annan shared the Peace Prize in 2001.

Count of 3: this would mean three of the four won twice. In fact only UNHCR did. Note that the 1988 prize went to UN Peacekeeping Forces, and the 2020 prize to the WFP. These are single wins. Total UN-system Peace Prizes include UNHCR (twice), UNICEF, ILO, WFP, the IAEA (2005), the IPCC (2007) and OPCW (2013).

Count of 4: this would mean all four organisations had won twice, which is false. Three of them (WFP, UNICEF, ILO) have each won once. A common trap is to assume that any prominent UN agency with a Nobel has won repeatedly. Only UNHCR and the ICRC (three times) are multiple winners among humanitarian organisations.
related: UNHCR won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1954 and 1981.
The ICRC has won the Nobel Peace Prize three times: 1917, 1944 and 1963.
UNICEF won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1965; the ILO won it in 1969.
The WFP won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020.
India is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol.
The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo; the other Nobel Prizes are awarded in Stockholm.
The IPCC (with Al Gore) won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2007.
UN Peacekeeping Forces won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: The WFP has won the Nobel Peace Prize only once, in 2020. It is the UN's food-assistance agency, set up in 1961 on a pilot basis and made permanent in 1965. It is headquartered in Rome and is funded entirely by voluntary contributions. It is the world's largest humanitarian organisation fighting hunger. The Nobel citation credited it for combating hunger, improving peace conditions in conflict areas, and preventing hunger from being used as a weapon of war. Its executive head is the Executive Director.

2 — Incorrect: UNICEF won the Nobel Peace Prize once, in 1965. It was created in 1946 by the UN General Assembly as the International Children's Emergency Fund to help children after World War II. It became a permanent UN body in 1953 and its name was shortened to United Nations Children's Fund, keeping the acronym. It is headquartered in New York and works on child health, nutrition, education, water and protection. It is funded by voluntary contributions.

3 — Correct: UNHCR won the Nobel Peace Prize twice, in 1954 and 1981. It was established by the UN General Assembly on 14 December 1950 and began work in 1951. It is headquartered in Geneva. Its legal basis is the 1951 Refugee Convention and the 1967 Protocol. India is not a party to either. The principle of non-refoulement is central to its mandate. The agency's first High Commissioner was Gerrit Jan van Heuven Goedhart. It was preceded by the Nansen International Office for Refugees, which won in 1938.

4 — Incorrect: The ILO won the Nobel Peace Prize once, in 1969, for its 50th anniversary. It was founded in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles and became a UN specialised agency in 1946. It is headquartered in Geneva. Its tripartite structure brings together governments, employers and workers. It sets international labour standards through Conventions and Recommendations. India is a founding member of the ILO.
summary: The answer is (a): only 1 of the 4 bodies, the UNHCR, has won the Nobel Peace Prize twice (1954 and 1981). The WFP (2020), UNICEF (1965) and ILO (1969) have each won once. The unofficial answer (a) is correct. The image also shows a second question, a UN peacekeeping matching item, which I have not explained here.
topic_notes: The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded by the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo, unlike the other Nobel Prizes, which are awarded in Stockholm. It has been awarded since 1901 under Alfred Nobel's will. Prize announcements are in October and the ceremony is on 10 December. Many UN-linked bodies have won. The UN itself and Kofi Annan shared the 2001 prize. UNHCR won in 1954 and 1981. UNICEF won in 1965. The ILO won in 1969. UN Peacekeeping Forces won in 1988. The IAEA and Mohamed ElBaradei won in 2005. The IPCC and Al Gore shared the 2007 prize. The OPCW won in 2013. The WFP won in 2020. Dag Hammarskjold received a posthumous prize in 1961. The ICRC is the most decorated organisation, with prizes in 1917, 1944 and 1963. Other repeat patterns to know include Linus Pauling, who won Chemistry (1954) and Peace (1962). Related UN facts: UNHCR is headquartered in Geneva, UNICEF in New York, the WFP in Rome and the ILO in Geneva. The 1951 Refugee Convention defines a refugee and sets out non-refoulement, and India is not a signatory. UN peacekeeping is run by the Department of Peace Operations, and India is among the largest troop contributors. Possible future angles: Indian Nobel Peace laureates (Mother Teresa 1979 and Kailash Satyarthi 2014), laureates from the 2020s, organisations versus individuals, and which Nobel Prizes are awarded in Oslo versus Stockholm.

United Nations Children’s Fund 3. | United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees 4, International Labour Organisation How many of the above has/have been awarded the Nobel Prize twice ? (a). (b) 2 ( 3 (dd) 4 Match ListI with List II and select the answer using the code given below the Lists : List I List IT (UN Peacekeeping (Period of Operation) Operation) A. UNMIL 1. 2007-2010 B. MINURCAT 2. 2002 — 2005 C. MINUSTAH 8. 2003 —- 2018 D. UNMISET 4. 2004-2017 Code: A Bs CoD (a) 3 1 2 (b) 3 1 4 2 (c) 2 al 4 3 (d) 2 4 if
subject: Current Affairs
detail: This question tests the dates and locations of closed UN peacekeeping missions. Anchor each acronym to its country. UNMIL is the UN Mission in Liberia, set up by Security Council Resolution 1509 in September 2003 after the second Liberian civil war. It ended in March 2018, so it matches 2003-2018. MINURCAT is the UN Mission in the Central African Republic and Chad, set up by Resolution 1778 in 2007 to protect Darfur refugees and displaced people. It was terminated at the end of 2010, so it matches 2007-2010. MINUSTAH is the UN Stabilisation Mission in Haiti, set up by Resolution 1542 in June 2004 after President Aristide's exit. It closed in October 2017, so it matches 2004-2017. UNMISET is the UN Mission of Support in East Timor, which succeeded UNTAET in May 2002 and ended in May 2005, so it matches 2002-2005. For elimination, you only need two certain anchors. UNMIL as 2003-2018 is the longest mission and gives A=3. That removes (c) and (d). MINURCAT as the short 2007-2010 mission gives B=1, which removes (a) and leaves (b). India has contributed troops and police to UNMIL (including the first all-women formed police unit), MINUSTAH and others.
explanations: (a) is wrong. It gives B=4 and C=1, which swaps MINURCAT (2007-2010) and MINUSTAH (2004-2017). Only A and D are right.
(b) is correct. A-3 (UNMIL 2003-2018), B-1 (MINURCAT 2007-2010), C-4 (MINUSTAH 2004-2017) and D-2 (UNMISET 2002-2005) are all right.
(c) is wrong. It gives A=2 and D=3. UNMIL did not run 2002-2005, and UNMISET did not run 2003-2018.
(d) is wrong. All four pairings are incorrect. UNMIL is not 2002-2005, MINURCAT is not 2004-2017, MINUSTAH is not 2007-2010 and UNMISET is not 2003-2018.
keyfact: UNMIL (Liberia) 2003-18; MINURCAT (Chad/CAR) 2007-10; MINUSTAH (Haiti) 2004-17; UNMISET (East Timor) 2002-05, so the code is 3-1-4-2, option (b).
option_notes: Code 3-4-1-2 gets UNMIL (2003-2018) and UNMISET (2002-2005) right. It wrongly gives MINURCAT 2004-2017, which is Haiti's MINUSTAH period, and MINUSTAH 2007-2010, which is MINURCAT's period. It is a plausible distractor because it swaps one pair of dates. Remember that Haiti's mission started in 2004 and Chad/CAR's in 2007.

Code 3-1-4-2 is the correct set. UNMIL in Liberia ran 2003-2018. MINURCAT in Chad and CAR ran 2007-2010. MINUSTAH in Haiti ran 2004-2017. UNMISET in East Timor ran 2002-2005. Each mission was created by a Security Council resolution under Chapter VII or a similar mandate. The long missions (UNMIL, MINUSTAH) are the easiest to place.

Code 2-1-4-3 gets MINURCAT and MINUSTAH right. It wrongly gives UNMIL the dates 2002-2005 and UNMISET the dates 2003-2018. UNMISET was a short transitional support mission after East Timor's independence, and UNMIL was a long mission, so the two are easy to separate by duration.

Code 2-4-1-3 gets none of the four pairings right. It shifts every date to a wrong mission. It is useful only as a reminder of the true dates: UNMIL 2003-2018, MINURCAT 2007-2010, MINUSTAH 2004-2017 and UNMISET 2002-2005.
related: The first UN peacekeeping mission was UNTSO (1948). UNMOGIP (1949) in India-Pakistan is one of the oldest.
UN Peacekeeping Forces received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988.
UNHCR won the Nobel Peace Prize twice, in 1954 and 1981. The ICRC won three times.
The WFP won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020, and UNICEF won in 1965.
MINUSTAH (Haiti, 2004-2017) was succeeded by MINUJUSTH.
India deployed the first all-women UN Formed Police Unit, in Liberia (UNMIL), in 2007.
UNAMID (Darfur) was a joint UN-African Union mission, 2007-2020.
The Security Council authorises UN peacekeeping missions.
statements: A (UNMIL) — Correct match with 3 (2003-2018): UNMIL was the UN Mission in Liberia. The Security Council created it by Resolution 1509 (19 September 2003) to support the ceasefire and peace agreement after the second Liberian civil war. Its tasks covered disarmament, security-sector reform, elections and human rights. It supervised the 2005 elections, which brought Ellen Johnson Sirleaf to power as Africa's first elected woman head of state. India sent an all-women Formed Police Unit to it. It closed in March 2018.

B (MINURCAT) — Correct match with 1 (2007-2010): MINURCAT was the UN Mission in the Central African Republic and Chad. Resolution 1778 (September 2007) created it to protect civilians, especially refugees from Darfur and internally displaced people in eastern Chad and north-eastern CAR. It also trained the Chadian police (DIS) and supported the rule of law. It worked alongside the EU force EUFOR Tchad/RCA. Chad asked for its withdrawal, and it ended in December 2010.

C (MINUSTAH) — Correct match with 4 (2004-2017): MINUSTAH was the UN Stabilisation Mission in Haiti. Resolution 1542 (30 April 2004) created it after the political crisis and the departure of President Aristide. It was led for years by Brazilian military commanders. It was criticised for the 2010 cholera outbreak linked to Nepalese peacekeepers and for abuse allegations. It closed in October 2017 and was succeeded by the smaller MINUJUSTH, which ended in 2019.

D (UNMISET) — Correct match with 2 (2002-2005): UNMISET was the UN Mission of Support in East Timor. It followed UNTAET after Timor-Leste became independent on 20 May 2002. Resolution 1410 (May 2002) created it to help build an administration, law and order and external security. It was replaced by the political mission UNOTIL, and then by UNMIT in 2006 after the unrest.
summary: The answer is (b), so the unofficial key is correct: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2. UNMIL (Liberia) ran 2003-2018, MINURCAT (Chad/CAR) 2007-2010, MINUSTAH (Haiti) 2004-2017 and UNMISET (East Timor) 2002-2005. The image shows two questions and does not show the numbers. I took the matching-list question as Q71 because it is the one for which (b) is the correct answer. If the Nobel question was meant, the correct answer is (a) 1, because only UNHCR has won twice (1954 and 1981).
topic_notes: UN peacekeeping was started in 1948 with UNTSO, the first mission, in the Middle East. It is authorised by the Security Council, and the Department of Peace Operations manages it. The three basic principles are consent of the parties, impartiality, and non-use of force except in self-defence and defence of the mandate. Peacekeepers wear blue helmets. The 1988 Nobel Peace Prize went to UN Peacekeeping Forces. Funding comes from a separate peacekeeping budget assessed on member states, with the largest shares from the USA and China. India is among the largest historical troop contributors, with over 280,000 personnel in more than 50 missions. It has also provided force commanders. Indian women led the first all-female formed police unit, in Liberia (2007). Current missions include UNIFIL (Lebanon), MONUSCO (DR Congo), UNMISS (South Sudan), UNFICYP (Cyprus), UNDOF (Golan), MINURSO (Western Sahara), UNMOGIP (India-Pakistan), UNISFA (Abyei), MINUSCA (CAR) and UNTSO. Closed missions to remember: UNAMIR (Rwanda), UNPROFOR (Yugoslavia), UNOSOM (Somalia), UNTAC (Cambodia), UNTAET and UNMISET (East Timor), UNMIL (Liberia), MINUSTAH (Haiti), UNOCI (Côte d'Ivoire), UNAMSIL (Sierra Leone), MINURCAT, UNAMID (Darfur, with the African Union, 2007-2020) and MINUSMA (Mali, 2013-2023). Related UN Nobel facts: UNHCR won in 1954 and 1981, the ICRC three times (1917, 1944, 1963), UNICEF in 1965, the ILO in 1969, the WFP in 2020 and the IAEA in 2005. The UN itself and Kofi Annan shared the 2001 prize.

ocr: Match List I with List II and select the | 74 answer using the code given below the Lists : List II List I (Location) (BIMSTEC Centre /Establishment) 1. NOIDA BIMSTEC Cultural Industries Observatory 2. Bengaluru BIMSTEC Energy Centre 3. Colombo BIMSTEC Centre for Weather and Climate BIMSTEC Technology 4. Thimphu Transfer Facility Code: AB OB (a) (b) -(c) 75. (d)
subject: Current Affairs
detail: BIMSTEC (Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation) was founded in 1997 through the Bangkok Declaration. It has seven members: Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand. Its secretariat is in Dhaka, and the 6th Summit (Bangkok, April 2025) adopted the Bangkok Vision 2030. Member states host specialised centres, each tied to a sector. India hosts the Energy Centre in Bengaluru and the Centre for Weather and Climate in Noida, at NCMRWF. Sri Lanka hosts the Technology Transfer Facility in Colombo. Bhutan hosts the Cultural Industries Observatory in Thimphu. Elimination works well. Colombo is the obvious home of the Technology Transfer Facility, so D=3. That rules out (a) and (b) only if you also know D, and in fact (a) and (b) both give D=4. Options (c) and (d) both have D=3. Between them, the Energy Centre is in Bengaluru (B=2), which removes (d), where B=1. Only (c) then remains: A=4, B=2, C=1, D=3.
explanations: (c) is correct: A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3 matches the true locations of all four centres.
(a) is wrong: it gives A=3 (Colombo) and C=1 with B=2 correctly, but D=4 (Thimphu) is wrong, and A=3 is also wrong.
(b) is wrong: it gives B=1 (Noida) and C=2 (Bengaluru), which swaps the Energy Centre and the Weather and Climate Centre, and it also has A=3 and D=4 wrong.
(d) is wrong: A=4 and D=3 are right, but B=1 and C=2 swap the two Indian centres, Bengaluru (Energy) and Noida (Weather and Climate).
keyfact: BIMSTEC centres: Cultural Industries Observatory - Thimphu; Energy Centre - Bengaluru; Weather and Climate - Noida; Technology Transfer Facility - Colombo.
option_notes: Option (a) A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4: it would place the Cultural Industries Observatory in Colombo and the Technology Transfer Facility in Thimphu, which is the reverse of reality. Only B and C are right. Remember that Colombo hosts the Technology Transfer Facility and Thimphu hosts the Cultural Industries Observatory. Sri Lanka's other BIMSTEC link is that it chaired the grouping from 2018 to 2022.

Option (b) A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4: this is wrong on every item. It mislocates the cultural and technology centres and also swaps the two Indian centres. The Energy Centre is in Bengaluru and the Weather and Climate Centre is in Noida at NCMRWF. It is useful as a trap showing how UPSC mixes up host cities.

Option (c) A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3: this is the correct code. Thimphu hosts the Cultural Industries Observatory, Bengaluru the Energy Centre, Noida the Centre for Weather and Climate, and Colombo the Technology Transfer Facility. The Secretariat is in Dhaka. India hosts two centres, Bhutan and Sri Lanka one each. Learn this as a set because UPSC may ask the reverse mapping.

Option (d) A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3: it gets the Thimphu and Colombo centres right but swaps Bengaluru and Noida. The Energy Centre is in Bengaluru, and the Weather and Climate Centre is in Noida. Both are in India, so the swap is a typical trap. Remember that Noida is linked with NCMRWF under the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
related: BIMSTEC was founded in 1997 through the Bangkok Declaration.
The BIMSTEC Secretariat is in Dhaka, Bangladesh.
BIMSTEC has seven members: Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand.
The BIMSTEC Charter was adopted in 2022, giving the group a legal personality.
The 6th BIMSTEC Summit was held in Bangkok in April 2025 and adopted the Bangkok Vision 2030.
The BIMSTEC Centre for Weather and Climate is at NCMRWF, Noida.
Of the seven members, only Bhutan and Nepal are landlocked, and neither touches the Bay of Bengal.
The Bay of Bengal is the group's geographic link, connecting South Asia and Southeast Asia.
statements: A — BIMSTEC Cultural Industries Observatory matches 4 (Thimphu): Correct. The observatory is hosted by Bhutan and meant to map, promote and gather data on creative and cultural industries such as crafts, performing arts and heritage across member states. It was agreed in the BIMSTEC cultural cooperation framework, and Bhutan's Ministry of Home and Cultural Affairs is the lead agency. It supports cultural exchange and the creative economy.

B — BIMSTEC Energy Centre matches 2 (Bengaluru): Correct. India hosts the centre in Bengaluru, and it is meant to coordinate regional energy cooperation, including renewables, efficiency, grid interconnection and policy. The BIMSTEC Grid Interconnection MoU was signed in 2018. The centre supports the broader energy-security agenda of the grouping.

C — BIMSTEC Centre for Weather and Climate matches 1 (Noida): Correct. The BCWC is hosted at the National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF), under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, in Noida. It provides weather and climate forecasting, early warning and capacity building for member states, which is important for cyclones in the Bay of Bengal. It was inaugurated in 2021 after India offered to host it.

D — BIMSTEC Technology Transfer Facility matches 3 (Colombo): Correct. Sri Lanka hosts the facility in Colombo, and it was set up through an MoU signed in 2008. It promotes technology transfer, innovation and technology cooperation among member states. It is a longstanding example of Sri Lanka's role as a BIMSTEC host, and it is often confused with Indian-hosted centres.
summary: The correct answer is (c): A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3. The BIMSTEC Cultural Industries Observatory is in Thimphu, the Energy Centre in Bengaluru, the Centre for Weather and Climate in Noida and the Technology Transfer Facility in Colombo. The unofficial answer (c) is correct.
topic_notes: BIMSTEC was formed on 6 June 1997 through the Bangkok Declaration, initially as BIST-EC with Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka and Thailand. Myanmar joined in December 1997 and was followed by Nepal and Bhutan in 2004, after which it was renamed BIMSTEC. Its Secretariat is in Dhaka, Bangladesh. The grouping has seven members and links South Asia with Southeast Asia, so it bridges SAARC and ASEAN. It is also seen as an alternative to SAARC, which has been stalled. Sectoral cooperation was originally divided among member-state leads, and in 2021 it was reorganised into seven pillars, with India leading security, including counter-terrorism. The 4th Summit (Kathmandu, 2018) and the 5th Summit (virtual, Colombo, 2022) adopted the BIMSTEC Charter (2022), which gave the group a legal personality. The 6th Summit (Bangkok, April 2025) adopted the Bangkok Vision 2030 and a Maritime Transport Cooperation Agreement. Other points include the Coastal Shipping Agreement, the Master Plan for Transport Connectivity, the Convention on Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters and the Grid Interconnection MoU. India hosts the National Disaster Management Authority-linked disaster management exercises, and the BIMSTEC Disaster Management Exercise was held in 2017. In 2024, India also announced the BIMSTEC Chamber of Commerce and Industry and a BIMSTEC Cultural Industries Observatory initiative. Possible future questions include the founding year, the member list, the Secretariat location, the Charter, the sectors and the host cities of the specialised centres, as well as its relevance to India's Act East and Neighbourhood First policies.

question: Which one of the following pairs is not correctly matched ? (Headquarters) (Indian Army Corps) Dimapur
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The Indian Army has 14 corps, each a large formation led by a Lieutenant General and usually made up of two or more divisions. Corps are tied to a Command and to a geographic area of responsibility. The northern and eastern corps are often asked about because of the China and Pakistan borders. 3 Corps (Spear Corps) is at Rangapahar, Dimapur, Nagaland, under Eastern Command. 4 Corps (Gajraj Corps) is at Misamari near Tezpur, Assam, and covers Arunachal Pradesh and the Assam sector. 14 Corps (Fire and Fury Corps) is at Leh, Ladakh, under Northern Command, and covers Siachen, Kargil and eastern Ladakh. 15 Corps (Chinar Corps) is at Srinagar and handles the Kashmir Valley. 33 Corps (Trishakti Corps) is at Sukna, Siliguri, under Eastern Command, and guards Sikkim and north Bengal near the Siliguri Corridor. Elimination: three pairs match the standard locations. The Srinagar–33 Corps pairing fails because Srinagar belongs to 15 Corps, and a candidate who knows that can mark (d) without recalling every corps.
explanations: Correct pairing: 3 Corps is headquartered at Dimapur, so this is not the answer.
Correct pairing: 4 Corps is headquartered at Tezpur (Misamari), so this is not the answer.
Correct pairing: 14 Corps is headquartered at Leh, so this is not the answer.
Incorrect pairing: Srinagar is headquarters of 15 Corps, while 33 Corps is at Sukna, Siliguri. This is the pair not correctly matched, so (d) is the answer.
keyfact: 33 Corps (Trishakti) is at Sukna, Siliguri; Srinagar is the headquarters of 15 Corps (Chinar).
option_notes: 3 Corps, the Spear Corps, is headquartered at Rangapahar, Dimapur, Nagaland. It was raised in 1941 in Burma and now serves under Eastern Command. Its role is mainly counter-insurgency and border security in Nagaland, Manipur and neighbouring areas. Dimapur is a major military and commercial centre in the northeast. The corps is among the Army's oldest formations and has historic links with the Burma campaign in the Second World War.

4 Corps, the Gajraj Corps, has its headquarters at Misamari near Tezpur in Assam, under Eastern Command. It guards the Arunachal Pradesh and Assam frontier with China, including Tawang. It was reraised after the 1962 war and was originally created in 1940. Tezpur is also a major Air Force base, and the corps coordinates with the Air Force and the Assam Rifles in the region.

14 Corps, the Fire and Fury Corps, is headquartered at Leh, Ladakh, under Northern Command. It was raised in 1999 after the Kargil War. Its area covers the Siachen Glacier, Kargil, Drass and the Line of Actual Control in eastern Ladakh. It is regularly in the news for Corps Commander-level talks with China since 2020 after the Galwan clash. Operating at extreme altitude is its defining feature.

33 Corps, the Trishakti Corps, is headquartered at Sukna near Siliguri, West Bengal, under Eastern Command. It is responsible for Sikkim and north Bengal and guards the Siliguri Corridor, the narrow strip linking the northeast with the rest of India. It was raised in 1962 and has been central to the Doklam and Nathu La region security. Srinagar, by contrast, hosts 15 Corps (Chinar Corps).
related: 15 Corps (Chinar Corps) has its headquarters at Srinagar under Northern Command.
17 Corps, the mountain strike corps, is at Panagarh, West Bengal.
Eastern Command is headquartered at Fort William, Kolkata.
The Siliguri Corridor, or 'Chicken's Neck', is guarded by 33 Corps.
14 Corps was raised in 1999 and is based at Leh.
16 Corps (White Knight) is at Nagrota, Jammu.
Northern Command is headquartered at Udhampur.
statements: (a) Dimapur – 3 Corps — Correct: 3 Corps has its headquarters at Rangapahar, Dimapur. It is the Spear Corps, raised in 1941 in Burma and now under Eastern Command. It looks after Nagaland, Manipur and parts of the northeast, including counter-insurgency duties. Dimapur is Nagaland's commercial hub and its only railway and airport gateway. The corps has a long history in the 1942 Burma campaign and is among the Army's oldest formations.

(b) Tezpur – 4 Corps — Correct: 4 Corps is the Gajraj Corps, with its headquarters at Misamari near Tezpur, Assam. It is under Eastern Command and is responsible for Arunachal Pradesh and the Assam sector facing China. It was originally raised in 1940 and was a key formation in the 1962 war, when it was reconstituted. It was relocated to Tezpur after the 1962 conflict. Its area includes Tawang and the Kameng sector.

(c) Leh – 14 Corps — Correct: 14 Corps is the Fire and Fury Corps, headquartered at Leh, Ladakh, under Northern Command. It was raised in 1999 after the Kargil conflict. Its area includes the Siachen Glacier, Kargil and eastern Ladakh facing China. It held the 2020 Galwan standoff talks, called Corps Commander-level talks, with the PLA. It is a high-altitude mountain formation and has the world's highest battlefield under its charge.

(d) Srinagar – 33 Corps — Incorrect: 33 Corps (Trishakti Corps) is based at Sukna, near Siliguri in West Bengal, under Eastern Command. Srinagar hosts 15 Corps (Chinar Corps) at Badami Bagh Cantonment, under Northern Command. 33 Corps covers Sikkim and north Bengal, including the Siliguri Corridor, the 'Chicken's Neck'. It was raised in 1962 and was involved in the Doklam standoff of 2017. 15 Corps leads counter-terrorism operations in Kashmir.
summary: The answer is (d), so the unofficial key is correct. Reassembled, the pairs are: Dimapur–3 Corps, Tezpur–4 Corps, Leh–14 Corps, Srinagar–33 Corps. 33 Corps (Trishakti) is headquartered at Sukna near Siliguri, West Bengal. Srinagar is the headquarters of 15 Corps (Chinar Corps).
topic_notes: The Indian Army is organised into seven operational commands: Northern (Udhampur), Western (Chandimandir), South Western (Jaipur), Southern (Pune), Central (Lucknow), Eastern (Kolkata) and Army Training Command (Shimla). Under them are 14 corps, each with two or more divisions plus supporting brigades. Northern Command has 14 Corps (Leh, Fire and Fury), 15 Corps (Srinagar, Chinar) and 16 Corps (Nagrota, White Knight). Eastern Command has 3 Corps (Dimapur, Spear), 4 Corps (Tezpur, Gajraj), 33 Corps (Sukna, Trishakti) and 17 Corps (Panagarh, the mountain strike corps, Brahmastra). Western Command has 1 Corps (Mathura, Strike One) and 11 Corps (Jalandhar, Vajra). South Western Command has 10 Corps (Bathinda, Dagger/Sapta Shakti). Southern Command has 21 Corps (Bhopal, Sudarshan Chakra) and 12 Corps (Jodhpur, Konark). Central Command has 9 Corps (Strike Corps, Pathankot area, Sapta Shakti Command). Army Training Command is in Shimla. The Chief of Army Staff heads the Army, and the Chief of Defence Staff has headed the Department of Military Affairs since 2019. Theatre command reorganisation is under discussion. Likely angles for the exam include corps nicknames, headquarters locations, high-altitude areas such as Siachen, the Siliguri Corridor, Doklam, and the commands that control each corps.

question:
Which of the following statements with respect to the Revamped Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan (RGSA) is/are correct ? ib The period of its implementation is 15t April, 2021 to 315* March, 2026. Zz The key objective of the Revamped RGSA is to develop the governance capabilities of the Panchayati Raj Institutions to deliver on _ the Sustainable Development Goals.
3. The share of the Central funding for the Revamped RGSA is 100% for all States and Union Territories. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Polity
detail: The Revamped Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan was approved by the Union Cabinet on 13 April 2022. It is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme of the Ministry of Panchayati Raj, and it continues and restructures the earlier RGSA of 2018-22. It runs for four years, from 2022-23 to 2025-26, with a total outlay of about Rs 5,911 crore. Of this, the Central share is about Rs 3,700 crore and the State share about Rs 2,211 crore. The key objective is to develop the governance capabilities of PRIs so they can deliver the Sustainable Development Goals, mainly through Localisation of SDGs (LSDGs) and Panchayat Development Plans themed on the nine Local SDG themes. The funding pattern is differentiated. It is 60:40 (Centre:State) for general States, 90:10 for North-Eastern and hill States, and 100% Central for Union Territories. Pure Central-sector components are also 100% funded by the Centre. Elimination logic: statement 1 fails on the start date (2021 instead of 2022), and statement 3 fails because of the word 'all' and the 100% claim. That leaves only statement 2, which is option (b).
explanations: Option (a) is wrong because statement 1 gives a wrong period (it begins in April 2021, whereas the scheme starts in 2022-23), so '1 and 2' cannot be correct.
Option (b) is correct because only statement 2 is accurate. It states the scheme's real objective of building PRI governance capacity to deliver the SDGs.
Option (c) is wrong because statements 1 and 3 are both factually incorrect, on the start date and on the funding share.
Option (d) is wrong because statement 3 is incorrect. The Central share varies (60:40, 90:10, and 100% only for UTs), so it is not 100% for all.
keyfact: The Revamped RGSA runs from 2022-23 to 2025-26 with a Rs 5,911 crore outlay and a shared funding pattern, and it aims to strengthen PRIs to deliver the SDGs.
option_notes: Option (a), statements 1 and 2: statement 2 is right but statement 1 has the wrong dates. The Revamped RGSA covers FY 2022-23 to 2025-26. Cabinet approval came on 13 April 2022, and the total outlay is Rs 5,911 crore. It follows the earlier RGSA of 2018-22. Many UPSC options pair one true and one false statement, so check each date carefully.

Option (b), statement 2 only: this is the correct option. The Revamped RGSA is a Ministry of Panchayati Raj scheme meant to strengthen PRIs, including in non-Part IX areas. It supports capacity building, Localisation of SDGs, the e-Gram Swaraj portal, and thematic Gram Panchayat Development Plans. It also supports Panchayat Bhawans and Gram Sabha strengthening. Its funding is shared between Centre and States.

Option (c), statements 1 and 3: both statements are wrong. The period is not April 2021 to March 2026, and Central funding is not 100% for all States. The real pattern is 60:40 for general States, 90:10 for North-Eastern and hill States, and 100% for UTs. It also leaves out the correct statement 2, which is why it fails.

Option (d), statements 2 and 3: statement 2 is right, but statement 3 is wrong because only UTs and certain Central-sector components get 100% Central funding. States contribute their share, 40% for general States and 10% for NE and hill States. Absolute words such as 'all' and '100%' are red flags in UPSC statements.
related: The 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 added Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule, which has 29 subjects, and came into force on 24 April 1993.
National Panchayati Raj Day is observed on 24 April every year.
The Revamped RGSA was approved by the Union Cabinet on 13 April 2022 with an outlay of Rs 5,911 crore.
Funding pattern: 60:40 for general States, 90:10 for NE and hill States, and 100% for UTs.
Article 243I provides for the State Finance Commission and Article 243K for the State Election Commission.
The SVAMITVA scheme (2020) gives property cards to rural households using drone mapping.
The e-Gram Swaraj portal supports panchayat planning, accounting and reporting.
Localisation of SDGs in panchayats is organised around nine themes.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: the Revamped RGSA covers 2022-23 to 2025-26 (1 April 2022 to 31 March 2026), not from 1 April 2021. The Cabinet approved it on 13 April 2022. It is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme of the Ministry of Panchayati Raj. It replaced the RGSA launched in 2018 for 2018-22. Its outlay is Rs 5,911 crore, of which the Central share is Rs 3,700 crore and the State share Rs 2,211 crore. Remember that approval came in 2022 and that the scheme is aligned with the 15th Finance Commission cycle ending March 2026. Scheme continuation beyond March 2026 would need fresh appraisal and approval.

2 — Correct: the stated aim is to develop the governance capabilities of PRIs to deliver the SDGs. Panchayats are expected to prepare Gram Panchayat Development Plans (GPDPs) around nine Local SDG themes, such as poverty-free, healthy, child-friendly, water-sufficient, clean and green, self-sufficient infrastructure, socially just, good governance, and women-friendly villages. The scheme stresses capacity building, e-governance through the e-Gram Swaraj portal, Mission Antyodaya convergence, and strengthening Gram Sabhas. It also covers non-Part IX areas, which are the Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas and others where Part IX of the Constitution does not apply.

3 — Incorrect: Central funding is not 100% for all States and UTs. The share is 60:40 for general States and 90:10 for North-Eastern and Himalayan States. Only Union Territories get 100% Central funding, along with some Central-sector components. The scheme combines Central-sector and Centrally Sponsored elements. Funds support training, infrastructure such as Panchayat Bhawans, Panchayat Learning Centres, and technical and administrative support. The word 'all' is the usual UPSC trap in statements like this.
summary: The answer is (b), 2 only, so the unofficial key is correct. The Revamped RGSA aims to build the governance capacity of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) to deliver the SDGs. Statement 1 is wrong because the scheme runs from 2022-23 to 2025-26, not from April 2021. Statement 3 is wrong because Central funding is shared with States and is not 100% everywhere.
topic_notes: Panchayati Raj in India rests on the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, which came into force on 24 April 1993. It added Part IX (Articles 243 to 243O) and the Eleventh Schedule, which lists 29 subjects. The Ministry of Panchayati Raj was created in 2004, and National Panchayati Raj Day is observed on 24 April. The RGSA was launched in 2018 for 2018-22 as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme. It was revamped and approved by the Cabinet on 13 April 2022 for 2022-23 to 2025-26. The outlay is Rs 5,911 crore, with Rs 3,700 crore from the Centre and Rs 2,211 crore from the States. The scheme focuses on capacity building and training of elected representatives and functionaries, on Localisation of SDGs through nine themes, and on e-governance. It supports basic infrastructure such as Panchayat Bhawans, with priority to Gram Panchayats lacking buildings. It also covers non-Part IX areas, which are Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas and others where Part IX does not apply. Funding is 60:40 for general States, 90:10 for NE and hill States, and 100% for UTs. Related initiatives include the e-Gram Swaraj portal and the SVAMITVA scheme (April 2020) for property cards using drones. Other related items are the Gram Manchitra spatial planning application, the Panchayat Advancement Index, and Mission Antyodaya. Finance Commission grants are an important source of money for panchayats: the 15th Finance Commission covers 2021-26 and gives tied and untied grants to rural local bodies. The State Finance Commission is provided for by Article 243I, and the State Election Commission by Article 243K. Future questions may ask about these constitutional provisions, scheme features, funding ratios or related portals.

question:
Which of the following countries are members of the European Union ? 1. _ Belarus
2. Poland 3: Germany
4. Switzerland Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Current Affairs
detail: The European Union is a political and economic union of 27 member states after the United Kingdom left on 31 January 2020 (Brexit). Its roots lie in the European Coal and Steel Community (1951, Treaty of Paris) and the European Economic Community (1957, Treaty of Rome). The six founders were France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. The Maastricht Treaty (signed 1992, in force 1993) created the EU and the path to the euro, and the Lisbon Treaty (2009) is the current constitutional framework. The big eastern enlargement came on 1 May 2004, when ten countries including Poland joined. Croatia was the latest entrant, in 2013. Switzerland stays outside the EU and relies on bilateral agreements and EFTA membership, and it rejected EEA membership in a 1992 referendum. Belarus is a post-Soviet state in the Eurasian Economic Union and the Union State with Russia, and has no EU membership. Elimination: Poland and Germany are certain, so any option containing Belarus or Switzerland (a, b, d) is eliminated, leaving (c).
explanations: Wrong: it includes Belarus and Switzerland, neither of which is an EU member.
Wrong: Belarus and Switzerland are both outside the EU, and this option leaves out Germany and Poland.
Correct: Poland (since 2004) and Germany (founding member, 1957) are both EU members.
Wrong: Switzerland is not an EU member, and this option omits Germany, a founding member.
keyfact: Germany (founding member, 1957) and Poland (2004) are in the EU; Switzerland (EFTA) and Belarus are not.
option_notes: Belarus, Poland and Switzerland together: Poland is an EU member, but Belarus and Switzerland are not. Belarus is in the Eurasian Economic Union and has a Union State with Russia. Switzerland is in EFTA and works with the EU through bilateral treaties. Because it mixes members with non-members, this combination is wrong.

Belarus and Switzerland only: neither is an EU member. Belarus is a former Soviet republic (independent since 1991) with Minsk as capital. Switzerland is a neutral federal state with Bern as capital, in EFTA and Schengen but not in the EU or the customs union. This combination contains no members.

Poland and Germany: both are EU members. Germany is a founding member of 1957 and Poland joined in 2004. Both are in NATO and in Schengen. Germany uses the euro, while Poland keeps the zloty. This is the correct combination.

Poland and Switzerland only: Poland is a member, but Switzerland is not. Switzerland is an EFTA state with bilateral accords, Schengen membership since 2008, and a policy of armed neutrality. It also leaves out Germany, so the combination is wrong.
related: The EU had 27 members after Brexit took effect on 31 January 2020.
Croatia (2013) is the most recent country to join the EU.
Treaty of Rome 1957 created the EEC; Maastricht (1992) created the EU.
Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein are in EFTA but not in the EU.
Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein are in the EEA but not in the EU.
The ECB is in Frankfurt, and the Court of Justice of the EU is in Luxembourg.
Poland uses the zloty and has not adopted the euro.
Turkey has been an EU candidate since 1999.
statements: 1 — Incorrect: Belarus is not an EU member. Belarus is a landlocked Eastern European country with its capital at Minsk. It was part of the USSR until independence in 1991. It has been led by Alexander Lukashenko since 1994. It belongs to the CIS, the Eurasian Economic Union and the CSTO, and has a Union State arrangement with Russia. It joined the EU's Eastern Partnership in 2009, but its participation was suspended in 2021. The EU has imposed sanctions over the 2020 election crackdown and support for Russia's war in Ukraine.

2 — Correct: Poland joined the EU on 1 May 2004 in the largest single enlargement, together with the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Cyprus and Malta. Its capital is Warsaw. Poland uses the zloty (PLN), not the euro. It is a member of NATO (since 1999) and the Schengen Area (since 2007). It is the largest of the 2004 entrants by population, and Solidarity's movement in the 1980s was central to ending communist rule.

3 — Correct: Germany is a founding member of the European Communities. It signed the Treaty of Rome in 1957 as West Germany, and reunification came in 1990. Its capital is Berlin. It uses the euro and is in the Schengen Area. It is the EU's largest economy and most populous member state, and the European Central Bank is headquartered in Frankfurt. It is also a member of NATO and the G7.

4 — Incorrect: Switzerland is not an EU member. It is a landlocked Alpine federal republic with its capital at Bern. It is a member of EFTA, has about 120 bilateral agreements with the EU, and joined the Schengen Area in 2008. It uses the Swiss franc, joined the UN only in 2002, and follows armed neutrality. Voters rejected EEA membership in 1992, and the EU application submitted in 1992 was later frozen and then withdrawn in 2016.
summary: The answer is (c) 2 and 3, so the unofficial expected answer is correct. Poland (joined 2004) and Germany (founding member, 1957 Treaty of Rome) are EU members, while Belarus and Switzerland are not.
topic_notes: The EU has 27 members. The UK left on 31 January 2020. The founding six of 1957 were France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. Later enlargements: 1973 (UK, Ireland, Denmark), 1981 (Greece), 1986 (Spain, Portugal), 1995 (Austria, Finland, Sweden), 2004 (ten states), 2007 (Bulgaria, Romania) and 2013 (Croatia). Key treaties are Paris 1951, Rome 1957, Maastricht 1992/93, Amsterdam 1997, Nice 2001 and Lisbon 2009. Main institutions: the European Commission (Brussels), the European Parliament (Strasbourg and Brussels), the Council of the EU, the European Council, the Court of Justice (Luxembourg) and the ECB (Frankfurt). The Eurozone has 21 members after Bulgaria's planned entry in 2026, and earlier it had 20 after Croatia joined in 2023. Denmark has an opt-out from the euro, and Sweden and Poland remain outside it. Schengen is separate from the EU: Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein are in Schengen but not in the EU, while Ireland is in the EU but outside Schengen. EFTA members are Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland. The Copenhagen criteria (1993) set the conditions for joining. Candidate countries include Turkey, Ukraine, Moldova, Albania, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The EU won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2012. India and the EU are negotiating a free trade agreement, and the EU is one of India's largest trading partners.

question: Match List I with List II and select the 77, answer using the code given below the Lists : List IT List I (Description) (INTERPOL Notice) To seek information on A. Silver Notice 1. unidentified bodies To collect additional B. Blue Notice 2. information about a person’s identity, location, or activities in relation to a criminal investigation To provide warning C. Black Notice 3. about a __ person’s criminal activities, where the person is considered to be a possible threat to public safety To identify and trace D. Green Notice 4. criminal assets Code:
subject: Current Affairs
detail: INTERPOL issues colour-coded notices so that police in its 196 member countries can share alerts and requests for cooperation. The Red Notice asks for the location and provisional arrest of a wanted person pending extradition; it is not an international arrest warrant. The Blue Notice collects additional information about a person's identity, location or activities in relation to a crime. The Green Notice warns about a person's criminal activities where the person is considered a possible public safety threat. The Yellow Notice helps locate missing persons, often minors. The Black Notice seeks information on unidentified bodies. The Orange Notice warns of an imminent threat. The Purple Notice describes modus operandi. The Silver Notice is the newest. It was launched as a pilot in January 2025 and helps trace and identify criminal assets. The UN Security Council Special Notice covers sanctioned individuals and entities. Elimination logic: Silver must be 4 (assets), which removes (a) and (b). Between (c) and (d), Blue must be 2 (information about identity or activities), which leaves (c). Black is 1 (unidentified bodies) and Green is 3 (warning about a threatening person).
explanations: Incorrect: it pairs Silver with 3, but Silver is for tracing criminal assets, not warning about a person's threat.
Incorrect: it also pairs Silver with 3, which is wrong, even though Blue-2 and Black-1 are right.
Correct: Silver-4 (assets), Blue-2 (additional information on identity, location or activities), Black-1 (unidentified bodies). Green-3 is implied by elimination.
Incorrect: Silver-4 is right, but Blue is not for unidentified bodies and Black is not for additional information on a person.
keyfact: Silver = assets, Blue = extra information, Black = unidentified bodies, Green = warning about a threatening person.
option_notes: Option (a) starts with Silver-3, which is wrong. The warning described in 3 belongs to the Green Notice, which alerts police about a person's criminal activities when that person is a possible public safety threat, such as a repeat offender. Green Notices are issued to share intelligence and are not requests for arrest.

Option (b) also begins with Silver-3, which is wrong. It does match Blue with 2 and Black with 1. The Blue Notice collects extra information on identity, location or activities in a criminal investigation. The Black Notice concerns unidentified bodies and helps identify the dead across borders.

Option (c) pairs Silver with tracing criminal assets, Blue with collecting additional information and Black with unidentified bodies. The Silver Notice was launched in a pilot phase in January 2025, with dozens of countries taking part, and India was among them. It supports asset recovery and seizure. This is the matching option.

Option (d) pairs Silver correctly with 4 but gets Blue and Black wrong. It uses Blue-1 and Black-2, which swaps their meanings. Blue is for gathering information on a person, and Black is for unidentified bodies.
related: Red Notice is not an international arrest warrant.
Yellow Notice is used to locate missing persons, often minors.
Orange Notice warns of an imminent threat to public safety.
Purple Notice shares details of modus operandi, objects or concealment methods.
INTERPOL was founded in 1923 and has its headquarters in Lyon, France.
India's INTERPOL National Central Bureau is the CBI.
Bharatpol portal was launched by the CBI in January 2025.
Silver Notice was started as a pilot in January 2025.
summary: The correct answer is (c) only if the code is read as A-4, B-2, C-1 and D-3. Silver Notice traces criminal assets, Blue Notice collects extra information on identity, location or activities, Black Notice seeks information on unidentified bodies, and Green Notice warns about a person's criminal activities. The OCR'd code lists only three digits for four items, so the question is garbled, but option (c) 4-2-1 matches the first three correct pairings.
topic_notes: INTERPOL is the International Criminal Police Organization. It was founded in 1923 as the International Criminal Police Commission and took the name INTERPOL in 1956. Its headquarters are in Lyon, France, and it has a General Secretariat and National Central Bureaus in member countries. India's NCB is the CBI. INTERPOL has no powers of arrest and cannot compel any country to act. Notices are requests or alerts that member countries apply under their own laws. Diffusions are less formal requests. The Commission for the Control of INTERPOL's Files (CCF) reviews complaints, and Article 3 of its constitution bars activity of a political, military, religious or racial character. The 2025 General Assembly was held in Marrakech. India hosted the 2022 General Assembly in New Delhi. Notice colours: Red for wanted persons to be arrested, Yellow for missing persons, Blue for additional information, Black for unidentified bodies, Green for warnings, Orange for imminent threats, Purple for modus operandi, Silver for assets, and the INTERPOL-UN Security Council Special Notice for sanctioned parties. Related systems are I-24/7, the secure communications network, and the stolen and lost travel documents database. Bharatpol is the CBI portal for cooperation with INTERPOL, launched in January 2025.

question:
Which of the following statements in relation to NIRANTAR (National Institute for Research and Application of Natural Resources to Transform, Adapt and Build Resilience), a platform of institutions under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, is/are correct ?
1. Ecosystem Survey and Analysis is a vertical under this platform, the lead institute of which is Botanical Survey of India, Kolkata.
2. Research and Management of Ecosystem Service is a vertical under this platform, the lead institute of which is Central Zoo Authority, New Delhi.
3. Capacity Development Support is a vertical under this platform, the lead institute of which is Indian Institute of Forest Management, Bhopal. Select the answer using the code given below :
subject: Environment
detail: NIRANTAR is a platform that brings together research, survey and training institutions under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC). It is meant to give science-based support for managing natural resources, adapting to climate change and building ecological resilience. It works through thematic verticals, each led by a specialist institute. The verticals include ecosystem survey and analysis, research and management of ecosystem services, and capacity development support. Survey and documentation work fits MoEFCC's survey organisations such as the Botanical Survey of India (BSI, Kolkata, est. 1890) and the Zoological Survey of India (ZSI, Kolkata, est. 1916). Training and capacity building fits the Indian Institute of Forest Management (IIFM), Bhopal. Research on ecosystem services would logically sit with a research body such as ICFRE or a similar institute. The elimination logic is that the Central Zoo Authority (CZA, set up under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, in 1992) only regulates and recognises zoos and coordinates conservation breeding, so it is an implausible lead for a research vertical. That makes statement 2 wrong and removes options (a) and (c). Statement 3 is plausible, which removes (c) and leaves (b) over (d). Treat the exact vertical names as the examiner's wording, and revise them from the MoEFCC or PIB notification.
explanations: Wrong: statement 2 is incorrect because the Central Zoo Authority is a regulator, not a research lead, so not all three statements can be true.
Correct: statements 1 and 3 fit the institutes' mandates (BSI for survey and analysis, IIFM for capacity building), and statement 2 fails.
Wrong: this would make only statement 2 correct, but that is the one statement with an implausible lead institute.
Wrong: statement 1 is also correct, because BSI Kolkata leads the survey and analysis vertical, so statement 3 alone is incomplete.
keyfact: NIRANTAR networks MoEFCC institutes into verticals, with BSI Kolkata leading survey and analysis and IIFM Bhopal leading capacity development; CZA is a zoo regulator and not a research lead.
option_notes: Option (a) claims all three statements are correct. It fails on statement 2 because CZA is a zoo regulator. The Central Zoo Authority was created in 1992 under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, with its office in New Delhi. It recognises zoos, prescribes standards, and oversees conservation breeding programmes and the exchange of animals. It is not a research institute.

Option (b) says statements 1 and 3 only are correct, which is the likely answer. BSI Kolkata (est. 1890) is the apex body for plant survey and taxonomy. IIFM Bhopal (est. 1982) is the MoEFCC institute for forest management education and training. Together they cover the survey and capacity development verticals of NIRANTAR.

Option (c) says statement 2 only is correct, which is wrong. It would rest on CZA leading ecosystem-services research. CZA's remit covers regulation of zoos, standards for animal housing and welfare, and ex-situ conservation of endangered species. The ecosystem-services domain is more naturally suited to research bodies such as ICFRE (Dehradun) or other MoEFCC research institutes.

Option (d) says statement 3 only is correct, which is incomplete. IIFM Bhopal leading capacity development is plausible, but statement 1 is also correct because BSI Kolkata leads ecosystem survey and analysis. BSI is the national authority on plant diversity, runs herbaria such as the Central National Herbarium at Howrah, and documents the flora of India.
related: BSI was founded in 1890 and is headquartered in Kolkata.
ZSI was founded in 1916 and is headquartered in Kolkata.
IIFM is an autonomous MoEFCC institute at Bhopal.
CZA is a statutory body under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, based in New Delhi.
ICFRE is headquartered in Dehradun and is an autonomous body under MoEFCC.
Forest Survey of India publishes the India State of Forest Report every two years.
NBA, Chennai, was set up under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.
Ecosystem services are classified as provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural.
statements: 1 — Correct: a survey and analysis vertical led by the Botanical Survey of India, Kolkata, fits the BSI's mandate of floristic survey and documentation. BSI is the apex taxonomic body under MoEFCC. It was founded in 1890, is headquartered in Kolkata, and has regional centres across India. It surveys and documents plant resources, maintains herbaria and botanical gardens, and publishes Floras and Red Data information. Its sister organisation, the Zoological Survey of India, was founded in 1916, is also headquartered in Kolkata, and documents fauna.

2 — Incorrect: the Central Zoo Authority is a regulator, not a research institute that leads ecosystem-services work. CZA is a statutory body under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, established in 1992 and based in New Delhi. It is chaired by the Union Environment Minister. It sets standards for zoos, recognises or derecognises them, and coordinates species conservation breeding and animal exchange. Its work concerns ex-situ conservation, so it is not a natural lead for ecosystem-service valuation or management research.

3 — Correct: Capacity Development Support led by IIFM Bhopal matches the institute's role. The Indian Institute of Forest Management was set up in 1982 and is an autonomous institute under MoEFCC. It is based in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, and offers postgraduate programmes in forestry management and sustainability. It also runs management development programmes, training for forest officers and policy research. Training and capacity building for environment and forest managers is therefore its natural role within the platform.
summary: Answer (b) 1 and 3 only appears correct. Statement 2 is almost certainly wrong because the Central Zoo Authority is a statutory regulator of zoos, not a research institute that could lead an ecosystem-services vertical.
